The *Śāradātilaka*, composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra,
together with the commentary *Padārthādarśa* composed by the venerable Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
Now begins the first chapter:
He whose body is eternal bliss, by whom— through the fifty phonemes flowing forth incessantly in sequence—
this entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is pervaded in the form of both word and meaning.
May that splendor—the abode of the moon, the sovereign of speech, which the virtuous have called the inner consciousness of the Word-Brahman—protect you perpetually. || 1 ||
*Padārthādarśaḥ*:

To Śrīkaṇṭha, who experiences the rising of intense joy through his devotion to his own *tāṇḍava* dance, and in whom an emotion has repeatedly arisen due to his fondness for wonder and curiosity as she gazes upon him—

May the playful, languid glance from the corners of Bhavānī’s eyes—which resembles the graceful movement of waves upon the gently swaying Ocean of Milk—bestow prosperity and auspiciousness upon you all. || 1 ||
Served by sages headed by Sanaka and others, accessible through yoga, imperishable,
the primordial source, the heart of saṃsāra, and the essence of the inquiry into the core of the Vedas—
May the great splendor of Śiva bestow joy upon my mind. || 2 ||
May the speech of Bhārati, permeated with devotion, lead to your welfare—she from whom memory blossoms forth and whose play of words is exceedingly rare. || 3 ||
In the *Śāradātilaka Tantra*, this commentary, the *Padārthādarśa*, is composed by Rāghava according to the instructions of his gurus. || 4 ||
Whatever has been stated here, having come down through tradition and being in accordance with both calculation and scripture, you virtuous ones ought to examine it. || 5 ||
If a slanderer should be a corrupter, that corruption does not constitute a fault;
for it is a morbid transformation that brings about harm, whereas one's true nature is indeed difficult to abandon.
Now, the Lord has taught all the Śrutis for the sake of heaven and liberation to living beings bound by the fetters of worldly existence.
Furthermore, it is well known that other works, such as the Smṛti-śāstras, possess authority because they are rooted in those [Śrutis] and because they expound their meaning.
But how can this Āgama-smṛti be rooted in them?

Furthermore, when it is argued that by those very same [means] being specifically investigated, either heaven or even liberation will be attained, so what is the use of this [inquiry]? To this we reply:
"He thought, 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and likewise, "Seek to know that from which these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter at their passing."
Having begun thus: "From bliss indeed, verily, these beings are born; by bliss, once born, they live; into bliss they enter at their departure," and so forth, [the text] concludes with:
"All this is what this Self is.
Now—
The opening and the conclusion, repetition, novelty, fruit,
explanatory praise, and logical justification are the marks for determining the intended meaning [of a text].

Because it has been stated thus, the meaning established by the scriptural passages through both the introduction (*upakrama*) and the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) is as follows: the Supreme Brahman alone—which is of the nature of supreme bliss, eternally pure and enlightened by its very essence, and endowed with the aid of beginningless, indeterminable ignorance (*anirvācyā-avidyā*) consisting of its own sport (*līlā*)—creates the entire universe as a transformation (*vivarta*) of its own self.
Now, one might ask: "Granted that Brahman is the creator of the universe, for what purpose is beginningless ignorance accepted? If this is asked, the answer is no.
Without that [power], it is logically impossible for Him, who is unattached, to be a cause.
Thus, both Śruti and Āgama also express this meaning:
"Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion (māyā)."

"For Śiva, devoid of Śakti, is not able to do anything. Thus, when the world had come into being, living beings— bound by the fetters of their own karma, ignorant of the Self, and fallen into the stream of birth and death— were unable to cross the ocean of saṃsāra.

Beholding them in such a state, out of supreme compassion and assuming certain specific adjuncts (*upādhi*), he taught all the *Śrutis*. Among those *Śrutis*, there are three sections (*kāṇḍa*) distinguished by action (*karman*), meditation (*upāsanā*), and Brahman.
Of these, the section on action (*karmakāṇḍa*) has been thoroughly expounded by Jaimini and others.
This section on worship (*upāsanākāṇḍa*) was [expounded] by Nārada and others, while the section on Brahman (*brahmakāṇḍa*) was [expounded] by the venerable Vyāsa and others.
Its basis in the Śruti is twofold: that which is based on Śruti directly perceived, and that which is based on Śruti not directly perceived.
Indeed, the Śruti itself is directly perceived in the form of the *Pūrvottaratāpanīya* of Rāma, the *Pūrvottaratāpanīya* of Nṛsiṃha, the *Saura-aṣṭākṣara*, and the *Śaiva-pañcākṣara*.
In that regard, everyone is qualified for the *karmakāṇḍa* (the section on ritual action),

because even for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), there exists the possibility of qualification for performing rituals until the attainment of knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), both for the sake of purifying one's own mind and for the avoidance of transgression (*pratyavāya*).
The same applies to the *upāsanākāṇḍa* (the section on meditative worship).
For from the worship of the Lord with attributes (*sākāropāsanā*), there arises the manifold fruit of heaven and so forth, as well as liberation (*mukti*) by gradual stages;
whereas from the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), heaven and the like are attained only through great expense and exertion.

Furthermore, even liberation from the knowledge-section (*brahmakāṇḍa*) occurs only after many such births have passed, when it has been accomplished through practice characterized by earnestness, continuity, and long duration.
"Having attained perfection through many births, one then goes to the supreme goal"—from this statement [it follows].
Therefore, it is established that this very section on worship (*upāsanākāṇḍa*), consisting of the scriptures of the *Āgama*, is the most important.

In that regard, Śrī Lakṣmaṇācārya, the disciple of the venerable feet of the teacher Utpalācārya, [composed a work] concerning each of the numerous individual mantra-ordinances found within the extensive *pūrvatantaras*.

Now, observing that this [tantra] is difficult to fathom due to the incapacity of people of the present day— who are of shallow intellect, short-lived, and yet desire the entire ritual procedure for mantras within a single work— the most compassionate author, wishing to compose the *Śāradātilaka Tantra*, desired its completion without obstacles and its widespread propagation; and thus, at the commencement of his intended undertaking, in accordance with the unanimous consensus of all the learned, he [performed the preliminary rites].

Thinking that auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) should be performed by those desiring the completion of this work, the author—composing at the outset an auspicious invocation characterized by the remembrance of the Supreme Deity, as enjoined by the Vedic revelation inferred from the practice of the virtuous (*sadācāra*) for the sake of instructing his disciples—says: "May His glory [protect] you eternally.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "May that glory protect you incessantly."

Although that great [homage] is established by this much alone through the recollection of the Supreme Deity, since there is still a requirement for some action on the part of this verse, the Deity’s presence is indicated by the prescription of the act of protection (*avana*), which consists in the bestowing of the desired fruit by way of the pacification of obstacles.
In that regard, while a general connection with ritual action might be expected, [the author], desiring the unimpeded recitation of the work being composed, directs compassion toward his disciples.
The phrase "sūcayato va" is an indication of the object [of the action].
"Vo" means "you," that is, the disciples;
for it is these alone who are worthy of address here, and because the word "yuṣmad" (you) primarily functions as a term of address.
For it was solely out of compassion for his disciples that the teacher, having mastered all that is to be known, engaged in composing this work.

He stated "constantly" (*aniśam*) because, once their protection has been secured for a certain period, the propagation of the book would otherwise fail to occur due to the impossibility of uninterrupted study among his own disciples and the disciples of those disciples.

Thus, once their long-term residence [in the forest] is established, the intention is that the propagation of the text will occur through the unimpeded mastery of recitation by their own disciples and even the disciples of those disciples.
In response to the inquiry "What is that festival?", he says: "The embodiment of eternal bliss."
This eternal bliss is his very body; by this, the nature of Paraśiva as non-different from Śakti is stated.

Now, one might object: since it is said, "In the subtle Śiva, without Śakti, neither name nor abode exists," how can he—who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), unattached (asaṅga), and formless (nirākāra)—be the agent of the act of protecting? To this, he says: "The Lord of Speech" (vācām adhīśam).
By this, the form consisting of Sadāśiva, endowed with power (*śakti*), is described as the teacher through speech.

Now, one might object that the status of being a teacher through speech also belongs to the one endowed with the adjunct (*upādhi*) of the four-faced Brahmā; therefore, to exclude that, he says: "the abode of the moon.
This means the abode or place of the moon (*śaśāṅka*), that is to say, the one who has the digit of the moon as his crest-ornament (*candrakalāvataṃsa*).

Since the creation of sound is primary here, it indicates that its essential nature consists of mantra. Because *ya* and *da* are *abhyāsa* (repetition), they become *viṣṇu*; by that [term] is meant *saṅkarṣaṇa*. Together with that, *au*, and *niśā* which is the letter *ha*, there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with elision of the final member (*uttarapadalopa*), resulting in *hau*.
Thus, *hau* is established.
By the verse beginning with "śaśāṅka," the *bindu* is described.

In that context, augmenting the sovereignty over speech (*vāgaiśvarya*) and indicating the creation of sound and meaning (*śabdārtha*) which is about to be explained, he declares its pervasiveness: by which this world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving—that is, the mobile and the immobile—composed of sound and meaning, has been pervaded in succession.
"By which"—by those fifty phonemes (*arṇa*) that flow continuously, meaning they manifest without interruption or ceaselessly.

Here, in this compound, the elision of *va* is to be stated for the word *varṇa*, so that like the word *svarṇa*, the word *arṇa* denotes "color" or "phoneme" through the elision of *va*. Some, however, say that the portion beginning with *nitya* and ending with *arṇaiḥ* constitutes a single compound word.
In this context, although there are fifty-one phonemes (*varṇa*), the number fifty is stated by means of *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) based on the relationship of proximity.
This is because, just as the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvaya-anupapatti*) is accepted as a basis for *lakṣaṇā*, so too is the impossibility of intended meaning (*tātparya-anupapatti*).
Alternatively, since it is said that "the letter *ma* is the *puruṣa*," and because he is their own essential nature (*svarūpa*), the expression "fifty" is used.

Alternatively, because the letter *kṣa* consists of the conjunction of *ka* and *ṣa*, its instruction is achieved through the very instruction of those two; thus, the mention of "fifty" is not redundant.

Or else, since the *visarga* is purely *śakti* (power), lacks the nature of the five elements (*pañcabhūta*), and is the cause of the production of all phonemes, it is excluded when that statement was made.
As it has been said:
"Or it is indeed *amāya* (without deceit) or infinite.

This statement is made either because even in the external [world], only that many [letters] are employed, or else because the fifty letters reside within the six cakras from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *ājñā*. Thus, the expression "fifty" is used.
The distinction between these two explanations should be understood as being based on the difference between the external and the internal.
Furthermore, it should be understood that because the internal is primary, the scripture everywhere employs the primary [explanation].
By this, the internal placement of the *mātṛkās* (*antarmātṛkānyāsa*) is also indicated.
And this will become clear in the final chapter (25) during the discussion on Kuṇḍalinī.
For this very reason, it is also indicated that everything elaborated from the second chapter up to the twenty-fourth is a modification of Mātṛkā.
Now, one might object: since it will be stated later that "Sadāśiva is all-pervasive" (Śā. 1.15), and since He is all-pervasive by His own nature, how [could there be pervasion] and by whom?
If it is argued that [the cause] depends on a cause, that is true;
however, its pervasiveness over all things is due to itself alone.
But here, in this scripture, the statement regarding its causality as "the fifty letters flowing without interruption" is intended to highlight the primacy of the creation of sound.

Furthermore, although it was previously stated that [the Lord] is qualified by some power (*śakti*) or limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), the expression "the sovereign of speech" (*vācām adhīśam*) was used; here, too, there is the statement regarding the pervasiveness of the phonemes (*varṇa*) over the form of the meaning (*artharūpa*).
In that regard, because the form of the meaning pervades only after having pervaded the nature of the word (*śabdasvarūpa*), the term "successively" (*kramāt*) is employed.
Their pervasion of sound-forms is indeed possible;
however, their pervasion of object-forms is to be understood from the rule that every object whatsoever is necessarily manifested by speech.
As it was said by the venerable Bhartṛhari:
"There is no cognition in the world that is without the accompaniment of words;
all this knowledge is perceived as permeated by speech. (Vākyapadīya)
Alternatively, this was stated by relying on the view of those for whom there is no difference between word and meaning.
As he himself said:
"The division of the single Self alone exists as word and meaning, which abide inseparably."
Thus [it is said]. (Vā.
For this very reason, in the science of mantras, there is an identity between the mantra and its deity.

Therefore, the extraction of the mantra of Sadāśiva was presented first. Alternatively, because he is permeated by Śakti, it should be understood that his pervasion of the form of sound occurs through his aspect as Śakti, while his pervasion of the form of meaning occurs through his aspect as Śiva.
As it is stated in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
"The beloved of Śaṅkara supports the entire collection of sounds,
while the one whose crest-jewel is the charming moon supports the entire nature of objects."

In this view, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) should be understood as indicating a secondary characteristic (*upalak�ṣaṇa*), for they [the Vedas] have arisen from that [Brahman]. Strengthening precisely the primacy of the creation of sound, he says: "The consciousness inherent within those who have performed meritorious deeds is what they call the Śabdabrahman."
The meaning is that those who have performed meritorious deeds are the knowers of reality (*tattvajña*).
This is because it will be stated later: "It is my conviction that the consciousness of all beings is the *Śabdabrahman*" (Śā.

1.13). Since that [Brahman] is all-pervading, and since a portion of it alone constitutes the consciousness of every living creature, it is indeed possible for the pure Brahman to be the *Śabdabrahman*.
Furthermore, since the emergence of Śabdabrahman occurs from the *bindu*, it is also possible that the emergence of Sadāśiva likewise occurs from that very same *bindu*.

In this regard, the distinction is merely that the term "Śabdabrahman" is used for the creation of sound, whereas "Sadāśiva" is used for the creation of meaning. From the supreme *bindu* as it undergoes differentiation, the unmanifested sound (*rāva*) came into being.
"Those proficient in all the scriptures call him Śabdabrahman. (Śā.
1.11, 12) Then, from Śambhu, who is of the nature of the Bindu, the binder of time, and whose essence is Kalā, there was born Sadāśiva, the witness of the world and the all-pervading one. (Śā. 1.15)
This is because it will be stated [later] in this way.
Alternatively, the connection should be made by way of the relationship between cause and effect:

since those of meritorious deeds have declared that the consciousness inherent within [the body] is the Śabdabrahman, therefore the world is pervaded by it through the fifty letters flowing without interruption.

For it will be stated [later]: "Having reached that form of Kuṇḍalinī situated within the bodies of living beings, she manifests in the form of phonemes through the distinctions of prose, verse, and so forth" (Śā. 1.14).
Others, however, interpret it differently:
that which is the nature of Paramaśiva, which the virtuous Vedāntins have called by the word *brahman*.
The meaning is this: we call it *Paramaśiva*, while they call it *brahman*; thus, there is only a difference in terminology.
In reality, we indeed accept that His essential nature consists of eternal bliss and so forth, just as they do.
As for what kind of "Lord of Speech" He is: His status as the Lord of Speech is well-known from such Vedic scriptures as, "The Vedas are His very breath.
Since He is the Lord of Speech, it should be applied there as far as possible that the world is pervaded by Him through the fifty letters flowing forth incessantly.

Since the Veda consists of phonemes (*varṇa*), or because in this scripture both the creation of sound and the creation of meaning arise from Kuṇḍalinī alone—and since she is declared to be the Supreme Deity in the statement, "Kuṇḍalī is the Supreme Deity" (Śā.
1.57)—it is appropriate to remember her alone; thus, by the word *mahaḥ*, Kuṇḍalinī, whose nature is light, is expressed.

For it is said: "The all-pervasive [Śakti] consists of that which is intoxicated by the splendor of the sun, moon, and fire. Of what nature is she? She is whose body is eternal bliss (*nityānandavapuḥ*).
This very [nature] he will describe as the form of Kuṇḍalī in the final chapter, beginning with: "Consisting of eternal bliss, with showers of falling supreme nectar" (Śā. 25.69).

By that *kuṇḍalī*, which—because it generates sound through the forms of *parā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*—is of the nature of sound (by metaphorically attributing the cause to the effect); and because it is the object [of cognition] through its essential nature as meaning (by metaphorically attributing the cause to the effect), it is both "moving" (*cara*) due to a predominance of the earth element and "not moving" (*acara*). Thus, the world (*jagat*)—that is, the perishable body—is pervaded by such [a power].
Or rather, [she is she] by whom the entire universe—the world consisting of moving and non-moving things, whose nature is both word and meaning—is pervaded.
This is because it will be stated later: "She is all-pervading, possessing universal form, and unconditioned by space, time, and so forth" (Śā.
1.53). By what means? By the fifty phonemes that flow without interruption: "Multiplied by fifty gates, the garland of fifty phonemes gives birth [to the universe]" (Śā. 1.111).
This is because it will be stated [later]:

"The virtuous ones (*sukṛtinaḥ*), meaning those of meritorious nature who know reality (*tattvajña*), call her that which consists of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahmamayī*)," for it will be stated [in Śāradātilaka 1.108]: "She gives birth to Kuṇḍalinī, the all-pervasive one who consists of the Word-Brahman."
Consciousness (*caitanya*) has the nature of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).
This very point he will state later: "And therefore, she is of the nature of consciousness" (*Śā. 1.51*).
"Internal" means situated within the *suṣumnā* [nerve].
This is because of the statement: "She who has entered the cavity within the column at the *mūlādhāra*.
She resides in the abode of the moon (*śaśāṅkasadana*) because she is situated in the lunar orb upon reaching the *sahasrāra*.
She is the sovereign of speech (*vācām adhīśam*) because she is the source of all sounds and the originator of all mantras.
Thus, he himself will say: "Awakened as the soul of the universe, she gives birth to the world consisting of mantra" (Śā.

1.57). Alternatively, the meaning is that she is the sovereign of speech, having the form of the goddess of speech (Vāgdevatā), according to the statement: "She who is called Śakti and Kuṇḍalinī is known by the name Āī."

Alternatively, since Sarasvatī is the presiding deity (devatā) relevant to the commencement of this work, by recollecting her alone, the manifestation of the work will come to pass. Furthermore, because it is the mantras of Sarasvatī that are to be expounded first in this treatise,
the recollection of the deity Sarasvatī is indeed appropriate.
May that splendor—the essence of Sarasvatī, the sovereign of speech—protect you.
Now, by the phrase "the sovereign of speech," it is stated that the *vāgbhava* [syllable] alone constitutes the mantra of Sarasvatī.
Reciting this, the best of men on earth [attains] that which is called the *vāgbhava*.
He attains perfection in speech that is like the essence of nectar.
Because of this statement, what kind of abode of the moon is that? By this, meditation on [Śiva] as having the digit of the moon as his crest-ornament is expressed.
As they say: "Whose crest-jewel is radiant with the held fragment of the moon..."
"May the Mistress of Speech instantly grant you prosperity.
Furthermore, of what nature is she? It means: "Ānanda," that which constantly and at all times causes bliss; [the Lord] whose body is such [a source of bliss].
The meaning is that it generates delight through the manifestation of eloquent sayings as sweet as the essence of nectar for the practitioners.
And likewise, the Teachers [state] in the *Sarasvatī-stava*: "In her who is clothed in silken garments, adorned with pearl ornaments, and who is the abode of joy..."
Furthermore, what kind of consciousness is contained within? By this, the subtle, synonymous with the "other" (*parā*), is described.
As they say:
"They call the non-departing subtle speech the very light of one's own nature (*svarūpa-jyotis*)."
Thus it is said.
Also elsewhere: "The subtle Kuṇḍalinī in the center is considered the supreme, consisting of pure light."
By which [Speech], through its fifty letters flowing without interruption, the entire world—consisting of both the moving and the non-moving, and characterized by both word and meaning—is pervaded.
Here, by the phrase "by the fifty letters," *paśyantī* in the form of phonemes (*varṇa*) is expressed;
by the phrase "characterized by word and meaning," *madhyamā* in the form of words (*pada*) is expressed.
That greatness of Sarasvatī which the virtuous have called *śabdabrahman*—
here, by the term *śabdabrahman*, the Vedas are meant;
thus, the meaning is "consisting of the Vedas."
This has been stated by the venerable author of the Vārttika in the section on the planets (Grahādhikaraṇa):
"That which is called the Veda-śāstra, known as the Veda, is termed Śabdabrahman."
By this, *vaikharī* in the form of speech is described.
As they say:
"Sound (*dhvani*), phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and sentences (*vākya*)—this is the fourfold basis."

"We worship her, the Mistress of Speech, who [manifests] through the divisions of the subtle and so forth. Also elsewhere: "That fourth [state], consisting of the sciences beginning with the Vedas, which triumphs having embraced the three worlds by its eager delight in the play of the letters from 'A' to 'Kṣa'—[that is she]."
Thus [it is said]. Others, however, maintain that the extraction of the Bhairavī-mantra was performed by the author of this work here. It is as follows:
May that splendor of Tripura protect you. Of what nature is it? It is *agalat*, meaning imperishable.

Furthermore, of what nature is it? It has the form of eternal bliss (*nityānandavapuḥ*). "Eternal" refers to the Puruṣa; by him, the letter *ha* [is formed]. Because she consists of bliss, or because she generates bliss, the Power (*śakti*) is Bliss (*ānanda*).

Therefore, he [is called] *vapuḥ* because his body (*śarīra*) is such; by this, it is stated that these two possess *sattva* even within the three seed-syllables (*bīja*). *Antaḥ* means the middle; that is to say, the middle seed-syllable.

What is that [seed-syllable], and by what sequence? *Ka*, *ra*, and *ma*—these are the *karamas*. It "eats" (takes) them by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇayā*). Thus, there is the letter *ka*, and below it the letter *la*.
Here, the letter *la* is grasped by the letter *ra* according to the technical rules of grammar (*vyākaraṇaparibhāṣā*).
And it has been said: "By that [reason], even the letter *la* is intended to be included.
Also, in the *Saṃhitā*: "For this very reason, O Great Goddess, there is an equivalence between *ra* and *la*."
Below that is the letter *ma*, which is the Puruṣa; by him [is formed] *ha*. Again, of what nature is it? It is that wherein *ra* (the letter *r*) has entered—that is, joined—at the end (*anta*).
Again, of what nature is it? It is pervaded (*vyāpta*); *viḥ* signifies the number four, the fourth vowel (*ī*), and by that it is obtained (*āpta*) or grasped.
In this context, the convention (saṅketa) intended by the author Vāraruca is meant;
it will become clear in the second chapter.
"When preceded by the negative particle (nañ), it should be understood as 'void' (śūnya)"—this is the convention of Vāraruca.
It is empty of that [sound] because it has the form of a *bindu*; thus, the *bindu* is extracted.
By this, the central seed-syllable consisting of six peaks (*ṣaṭkūṭa*) is extracted.

For this very reason, it will be stated later: "The mantra of Tripurā consists of six peaks. Having thus explained the middle seed-syllable, [the author now speaks] regarding the letter *ha* and *sa* in the first seed-syllable...

Since it has already been stated previously, the letter *e* should also be applied in this manner. Of what kind is the first abode of the moon? By this, [the letter] *i* is situated at the *bindu*. Thus, the first seed-syllable is extracted.

What is the nature of the final [syllable] here in terms of sound and meaning? Here, by the word *śabda* (sound), the objects beginning with sound (*śabdādi*) are understood; the word *artha* (meaning) signifies the sense-objects (*viṣaya*). Thus, the objects beginning with sound are ten in number, and by that number ten, the vowel *au* is indicated; that which has that as its form is so described. Furthermore, according to the rule "the movement of numbers is from left to right" (*aṅkānāṃ vāmato gatiḥ*), and by the convention of Vararuci, the letter *ta* represents the number six.
According to the statement, "The numbers are [indicated] by the final letters of the *piṇḍa*," the letter *ya*, which ends with the letter *nya*, has the number one.
Thus, there are sixteen; by that, the *visarga* [is indicated].
In this way, the third seed-syllable is extracted.
As it is stated in the *Siddheśvarīmata*:
"The three *haṃsa*s joined with the dental *sa* are differentiated by the vowels of the eight, the four oceans, and the ten;
the last one has the *visarga*, the other two have the *bindu*, and the middle one is joined with Viriñci, Indra, Hara, and Agni."
This is its meaning: *vasu* is the number eight;
*abdhi* is the number four;
*paṅkti* is the number ten.
And likewise, Amara states: "The word *paṅkti* refers to the meter of ten syllables as well as a series of the number ten.
The *haṃsas* are three *ha*-letters;
of what kind? They are joined with the dental *sa*.

Likewise, in sequence, [the vowels] are joined with the eighth (*e*), the fourth (*ī*), and the tenth (*au*)—excluding the neuter vowels—by means of the sounds *vasu* (8), *abdhī* (4), and *paṅkti* (10). This is because it has been stated: "The quartet beginning with the vowel *ṛ* is neuter; that which is in the middle of the vowels is a quartet of neuters" (Śāradātilaka 2.6).
Thus, by excluding the neuter vowels, one should understand that among the vowels accompanied by the *bindu* and *visarga*, the eighth is *ekāra* and the tenth is *aukāra*.
He states the distinction: the third [syllable] is joined with the *visarga*; the other two, the first and second, possess nasal vowels (*anusvāra*).
Furthermore, the middle one is joined with Viriñci and the others—Viriñci being *ka*, Indra being *la*, Hara being *ha*, and Agni being the letter *ra*—joined with these.
This is the six-peaked (*ṣaṭkūṭa*) middle seed-syllable.

This Bhairavī consists of three seeds. Furthermore, because [the letters] *e* and *ca* are mentioned independently, because of the inclusion of the word *āpta* meaning "pervaded," and because of the employment of the word *rūpa* meaning "form" in the phrase "having the form of sound and meaning," it is indicated that these three vowels alone constitute the conscious mantra (*cetanīmantra*) of this [Bhairavī].
As they say:

"The eighth [letter] of Śiva alone is the first seed-syllable; the other is the eighth seed-syllable of Bhaga. The supreme [syllable] ending with the head (Ś) is declared to be the Trivarga, the secret science accessible only from the mouth of the Guru. Thus it is said.
Śiva is the syllable *ukāra*; its eighth is *ekāra*.
Bhaga is *ekāra*; its eighth preceding it is the fourth vowel (*ikāra*).
The head is the bindu; that which has this at its end is the syllable *aukāra* (śiro'nta).
He explains the nature of the previously mentioned seed-syllables (*bīja*) in sequence as *vāgbhava*, *kāmarāja*, and *śākta*.

By the phrase "the sovereign of speech" (*vācām adhīśam*), the status of the first [seed-syllable] as *vāgbhava* is stated. Because the world—consisting of the moving and the unmoving—is produced through sexual union and arises from desire (*kāma*), the middle seed-syllable is called *kāmarāja*.
By the statement, "The wise call that which is the final seed Śabdabrahman," the nature of the final [seed] as being of the power of Śakti (śākta) is expressed;
for it will be stated later: "The Goddess, the mother of the three abodes, has the nature of Śabdabrahman" (Śāradātilaka 1.56).
As it is said in the Siddheśvarīmata:
"The first seed-syllable is Vāgbhava, the second is Kāmarāja, and the third is Śaktibīja; these bestow the fruits of the four aims of life.
Furthermore, according to the statement, "The designation of Brahman is remembered as threefold: Om, Tat, and Sat," Brahman is of the nature of sound.
"Śabdabrahman" refers to the *praṇava* (the syllable Om).

It is called the "seed of desire" because the world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, arises from it; and because [sexual] creation originates from desire, it is produced by speech, which is the letter *na*.
In the *Bṛhattattvanyāsa*, because the *śabdatattva* (the principle of sound) is placed together with the letter *na*,
*ma* is [the first] and *dhīḥ* is of the nature of power (*śakti*).

The Lord (īśaḥ) is the Sovereign (prabhuḥ); by this, the creative emission (visarga) is indicated, according to the statement: "The emission called the power of Māyā is the Sovereign who consists of all beings.
Thus is the word *namaḥ*.
Thus, the *hlādinī* mantra of this [deity] has been declared.
As they say:
"The lotus [syllable], with its middle and final vowels elided, joined with *Īśa* (the letter *i*) and provided with the *bindu* and *nāda*."
"This is declared to be the Heart of the Goddess, shining upon the earth between the *nigama* [the mantra *namaḥ*] and the end [the mantra *namaḥ*].
Thus [it is said]. He states a general qualification for the three seed-syllables with the word "constantly" (*aniśam*):
"wherein there is no night"—that is, the letter *ha*, which does not exist at the beginning; this is the ellipsis.
In the *Keśavādinyāsa*, the night is the letter *ha*, which is the *śakti*.
Therefore, it is stated that in the absence of *ha* at the beginning, the letter *sa* occupies the initial position.
Thus, *sa* comes first, followed by *ha*.

Alternatively, since the initial seed-syllable *bindu* is also extracted by this very word *nir*, [the term] *aniśam* means "constantly devoid of the letter *ha*. In *śaśāṅkasadanam*, *śaśāṅka* refers to the letter *sa*, and it is that whose *sadana*—meaning its place—is [there].
By this, the letter *sa* is substituted for the position of the letter *ha*; thus, the letter *ha* follows below it by implication.
And it has been said:

"If the Bhairavīya [Vidyā] preceded by Akula becomes preceded by Kula when taught by the teachers, that very Vidyā bestows swift results on earth; it is called a Vidyā that must be kept strictly secret from the ranks of the bound souls (paśus). Thus it is said.
By this, its status as both *mantra* and *vidyā* is stated. As it says in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"That which begins with Śakti is called *vidyā*, while that which begins with Śiva is called *mantra*."
"Indeed, initiation, consecration, and worship bestow enjoyment and liberation upon living beings.
Thus [it is said]. He states another general and specific qualification of the three seed-syllables (*bīja*): "characterized by the fifty phonemes"—this is the meaning.
By this, the recitation (*japa*) of every mantra through the interposition of the *mātṛkā* is taught.
As they say:
"One should recite this king of mantras, which is the cause of the delusion of the entire world,
interspersed with the *mātṛkās*, both in direct and reverse order."

Alternatively, by this qualification, the internal Mātṛkā-nyāsa is also indicated, such as *haha saiṃ sahasaiṃ* and so forth; *hasakalahrīṃ sahakalahrīṃ* and so forth; and *ahasauḥ āhasauḥ* and so forth.
As they say:

"The knower of mantras should sequentially place the letters of the six cakras upon their petals, and likewise, according to the sequence of the two cakras, the goddesses and the extracted [seed-syllables]. Thus it is said. Furthermore, in another [text], in the context of describing the *mūlādhāra*:
Upon the four lotus petals, one should place the goddesses Nirṛti, Jaleśa, Agni, and Vāyu, either alone or with the nasal bindu,
well-known for their unassailable power.
Thus it is said.

Alternatively, by using the word "fifty" (pañcāśat) through the secondary function of indication (lakṣaṇā) based on a relationship of proximity, fifty-one is understood; by this, it is indicated that the extraction of the *Dīpinī* for all three seed-syllables (*bīja*) is intended.
Among those, the *Dīpinī* of the first seed-syllable consists of seventeen letters, formed by separating the consonants and vowels.
The second seed-illuminator consists of twenty-five syllables, just as before;
the third seed-illuminator consists of nine syllables, likewise as before.
Thus, it consists of fifty-one phonemes in total.
In that regard, since the letter *kṣa* exists in both the second and third [syllables], only one consonant is taken for it,
because it is taught separately in the *Mātṛkā*.
If this were composed of two consonants, then like the letter *kṣa*, it too would not be taught separately.
There are indeed two *bindus* belonging to those two [vowels], yet they are not counted separately;

for such a form constitutes the fifteen vowels themselves. Furthermore, since the *bindu* in the *praṇava* is also included within the *praṇava*, it is not counted separately; thus, everything is beyond reproach.
And this extraction of the *dīpinī* has been indicated here by the author of the treatise;
however, I shall clarify it in the *Bhairavī-paṭala* (chapter 12).
Alternatively, it may be intended that the extraction of the *bālā-mantra* is what was meant by the author of the treatise.
For he alone is the fundamental source even for Bhairavī and the others;
as they say, omitting the word "Bālā": "This origin of the Vidyā-mūla has been declared by me; it should be known by teachers who desire spiritual accomplishment."
Thus:
"The lord of speech" refers to Vāgbhava;
"the interior," "the middle," and "that which stands in the center" [refer to the same].
In sequence: *ka* and *ra*, and *mā* is Lakṣmī; by that, the vowel *ī* [is formed].
By *reṇa*, as before, there is the inclusion of *la*.
*Niḥ* signifies the *bindu*.
Thus, the middle seed-syllable consists of the moon, which is the letter *sa*; *sat* is the syllable *oṃ*.
The letters *a* and *na* constitute the two voids (*śūnya*), by which the visarga is formed.
This is because it is said: "The void (*śūnya*) should be known as *ne* and *ña*, likewise when a solitary vowel is uttered."

If it is asked how the word *sat* includes the syllable *oṃ*, it is replied as follows: First, because both are denotative of Brahman—as stated in the passage, "The designation of Brahman is traditionally held to be threefold: *oṃ*, *tat*, and *sat*"—and because of the statement, "*Sat* is declared to be *oṃ*," the word *sat* possesses the capacity to denote [Brahman]. Here, however, it is intended solely in its unmodified (non-sandhi) form.
And that [o-kāra] indicates the subsequent [au-kāra] through the relation of proximity (*sāmīpya-sambandha*).
Alternatively, as stated by the Teacher: "By its connection with u-kāra, it likewise becomes the syllable au-kāra," it is o-kāra itself that indicates its own product, au-kāra.

Alternatively, the suffix *ac* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), as in "that which has the form of a rabbit (*śaśa*) is here. Thus, *śaśa* means the moon; by that [moon], he [is Śiva]. Or, *śaśan* means one whose nature is to move; *śaśa* is the *haṃsa*; by that [haṃsa] as well, he [is Śiva].
By the word *aṅka*, according to the logic of the "lump" (*piṇḍanyāya*), the letter *a* is meant.
For example, in the phrase "sa vāmadṛk pavanaguṇānvitaḥ karaḥ," the word *kara* refers to the phoneme *ka*.
Similarly, in the phrase "harahayaṣaṣṭhavat vanam," the word *vana* refers to the phoneme *va*,
and by the word *sat*, it is indeed the diphthong *o* that is meant.
The vowel *au* occurs at the junction with its predecessor;
from the two *an* syllables, the *visarga* arises.
Now, since the *praṇava* possesses the bindu, the author will mention only the *visarga* in the final seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Bālā.
If it is argued that there is a contradiction here because both the *bindu* and the *visarga* have been extracted [from the mantra], we say no;

for among the various forms of the *bālā* mantra, in some instances the *bindu* is extracted, in some the *visarga*, and in others both the *bindu* and the *visarga* are extracted. It was for the purpose of indicating this variety that such an extraction has been performed here.
As it is said in the Sanatkumāra:
"The third [syllable] of the eighth [group], joined with the fourteenth—
this indeed is declared to be the *daṇḍakuṇḍala*, the *sārasvata* [mantra]."
But elsewhere it is said: "The entire *daṇḍi* [family], joined with the end of the *danta* [group], is the family known as *Sammohana*.
The rest is as before; this is the summary.
And these two explanations have been composed by me, constrained by the words of my guru; therefore, they should be forgiven by the lords of teachers. || 1 ||
Adorned with the crescent moon, his face radiant with an inner smile,
and beautified by eyes resembling the interior of a blue lotus— he who is the cause of the prosperity of the three worlds, the one whose head bears the new moon.
May the inner apartments [of the Lord] bestow auspiciousness upon you with devotion. || 2 ||

He praises that creative agency of Śiva which is conditioned by [Māyā] with the verse beginning "Antar" (Within). The construction is: "May the inner apartment of the one whose crest is the new moon bestow auspiciousness upon you with reverence.
Here too, by the phrase "may it bestow auspiciousness upon you," his compassion for the disciples is indicated.
Although, in reality, according to the Śaiva philosophy:
"Without Śiva there is no Śakti, and Śiva is not devoid of Śakti;
in truth, there is no difference between the two, just as there is none between the moon and its moonlight."
Although there is indeed the identity of Śakti and Śiva, nevertheless, because creation is impossible without a second, her form assumed for sport—the nature of a woman—is described.
By this, sexual creation is indicated.
He states her status as the cause of the universe: "she is the cause of the glory of the three worlds."

Pervasiveness (*vibhava*) consists in being the self of all that is moving and unmoving. Of what nature is it? It is "shining with an inner smile" (*antah-smitollasitam*); for this imagined world shines forth as a cause for laughter.
Or, the laughter arises from a longing for the Lord.
By this, her power to agitate the Lord (Īśvara) is indicated.

Furthermore, according to the Smṛti text, "Where there is harmony between husband and wife, the three aims of life (trivarga) flourish there," it is indicated that the creation of the manifold world proceeds from the harmony of the couple.
Furthermore, of what nature is he who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament (*avataṃsa*)?
Here, by the word *avataṃsa*, a head-ornament or crown-jewel is meant.
Thus, it is stated in the *Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana*:
"In the masculine, *uttaṃsa* and *avataṃsa* both mean an ear-ornament as well as a crest.
Furthermore, of what nature is she?
She is radiant with eyes that resemble the interior of a blue lotus (*indīvara*).
By this, his beauty surpassing all else is described.
Alternatively, by the phrase "of the one whose crest is the new moon," the mantra of Bhuvaneśī is indicated;
its extraction [is performed] by means of the qualifiers.
Śiva is the cause of the manifestation of the three worlds; therefore, he is represented by the letter *ha*.
The fire within his smile is the light that shines from within; thus, it is "the fire with an internal smile," which is the letter *ra*. It is "resplendent with" that [fire], meaning joined with it.
The phrase "adorned with a digit of the moon" refers to the *bindu*.
She whose eyes are like the interior of a blue lotus (indīvara) is Lakṣmī; thus, there is a long *ī* [forming *indīvarodare*].

Alternatively, her eye which is the "uterine brother" (sahodara)—meaning a friend—of the interior of the blue lotus is in the form of the moon, and that is on the left; thus, there is a long *ī* [forming *indīvarodarasahodaranetram*]. Being joined with that, it is "endowed with beauty.
Thus, when combined, it is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Bhuvaneśī. (2)
I bear upon my head the gurus, who are the sole cause for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra and whose very nature is Śiva—
the dust of whose lotus feet [is the means of purification].
They bring about the glory of bathing at sacred fords.
For that high-souled one who possesses supreme devotion to the Divine, and who regards the teacher as he does the Divine, these truths thus explained indeed shine forth.

From such scriptural authority, since devotion to the Guru is understood to be an internal means for the attainment of knowledge—just like devotion to the Supreme Deity—he states the salutation to the Guru immediately after the remembrance of the Supreme Deity with the words "saṃsāra... (the cycle of existence).
The grammatical connection is: "I place upon my head the Gurus, whose very nature is Śiva."
The meaning is that they have the nature of Śiva and the form of Śiva.
By this, it is stated that the meditation on the Guru should be performed by regarding him as having the form of each respective deity.
As it has been said:
"One should not perceive the Guru as a mortal; for if one perceives him so, then never shall there be success through mantras or the worship of deities.
Thus it is said elsewhere: "Therefore, having understood this, one should regard the Guru as a deity and not otherwise."
"One should offer sacrifice through prostrations at the three times and through the yoga of meditation. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, elsewhere: "Having placed the eye on the forehead, the digit of the moon, and also the two arms within [the self], I shall speak; the Guru is honored among mortals. Thus it is said.
By the phrase "placed upon the head," it is stated that the meditation on the Guru should be performed upon the crown of the head.
As it has been said: "In the morning, one should remember the Guru—two-eyed and two-armed, with a serene countenance and peaceful disposition—upon a white lotus on the head, preceded by his name."
Elsewhere it is also said: "He who constantly remembers the lotus feet of the venerable Guru situated upon his own head with sattvic dispositions shall, before long, become a *khecarī*.
The plural number in the word "gurus" (*gurūn*) is for the sake of honor, or it may refer to the Guru, the Paramaguru, the Parāparaguru, and the Parameṣṭhiguru.
And thus is the lineage of the author’s gurus:
"Śrīkaṇṭha, Vasumān, Śrī Somānanda, and Utpalācārya.
His disciples [state]: "I bow to Lakṣmaṇa, Abhinavagupta, and the venerable Kṣemarāja."
Of what kind [are they]? They are the sole cause for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra.
It has also been stated that without this instruction from the Guru, crossing the saṃsāra is impossible.
And so says the Śruti:
"A person who has a teacher knows," and "He should approach a guru alone.
And from the scripture: "Salutation to that illustrious Guru by whom the eye was opened for one blinded by the darkness of ignorance with the ointment-stick of knowledge. Thus.
He describes the greatness of bowing to the guru with the words "rajāṃsi" (dust).
By this, it is stated that one should perform salutation to the guru preceded by grasping his feet. || 3 ||
I shall proclaim the essence of the tantras, the auspicious *Śāradātilaka*, which is the primary cause for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (4)
In this tantra, the creation of words and meanings, together with the sages, meters, and deities,
as well as the ritual procedures for the mechanical diagrams (yantras) and mantras, are set forth.
A listener proceeds to listen to that which has an accomplished purpose and an established connection;
therefore, at the beginning of a treatise, the connection must be stated along with its purpose.

Having spoken thus, in order to conform to the intellect of his disciples, he reveals the greatness of the work and demonstrates the subject matter (*viṣaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), relationship (*sambandha*), and qualified student (*adhikārin*)— which serve as the motives for the listener’s engagement— by means of the two verses beginning with "The essence" (*sāram*).
By the phrase "the essence of the tantras, the most excellent, and in the form of a compendium," its worthiness to be adopted and its extreme conciseness are stated.
In this context, "of the tantras" refers to those of the Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Śākta, Gāṇapatya, and Saura traditions; it is "essence" because it is for this reason that they are "auspicious.
Even in the brevity of its words, its auspiciousness consists precisely in its capacity to convey all desired meanings.
He will state this later in the passage beginning with "dharma, artha, kāma," and so forth.
The designation of its means [of realization] is "Śāradātilaka. That which perishes is *śāra*, meaning the gross fruit of karma; that which bestows this is *śāradā*.
Alternatively, being established as the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) through its various causes, it tears or shatters [ignorance]; thus, *śāradā* is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).

Alternatively, *śara* is independence (*svātantrya*); its state is *śāra*, which is independence. That which gives this is [the Goddess], who bestows supreme sovereignty by dispelling the beginningless ignorance and the limited individuality (*jīvabhāva*) of the soul.
As it was stated by Gautama in the *Tantravyākaraṇa*:
"Śara" means independent; "hṛdaya" means throbbing; "parameśitā" means the Supreme Sovereign.
The words "śāra," "citi," and so forth are synonyms that denote their own respective meanings. Thus it is said.
Her *tilaka* (forehead mark) is her ornament.
By this, his preeminence is shown.
Even there, he does not take the form of another ornament, but rather that of a *tilaka* (forehead mark).
The intention is that just as a *tilaka* situated on the face is the very first thing seen from all sides, so too is he.
The first cause is the primary cause.
How its primacy is established has already been explained by us previously in the context of discussing the structural coherence of the treatise.
Its subject matter concerns the creation of words, meanings, and so forth.
The fruit is the fourfold aim of human life (*caturvarga*).
The relationship between these two is that of the subject matter and its exposition (*pratipādya-pratipādakabhāva*).
And the qualified person (*adhikārī*) is one who seeks that [fruit].
The relationship between this treatise and [its subject] is that of the expounder and the expounded;
the relationship between the subject matter of the treatise and its fruit is that of the means and the end to be achieved.
Other such relationships should also be inferred accordingly.
The word "saha" (with) is connected with the three [preceding terms]:

with the sages (*munibhiḥ*), who by the power of austerity and yoga were the first knowers of the mantra and the first worshippers. As it was said by Gautama: "Having learned the mantra from the mouth of Maheśvara, the guru [attained it] through austerity."

"The pure-souled one accomplishes [the goal], and he is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi) from the outset. Likewise, elsewhere: "That mantra by which it was seen by a certain seer and by whom success was indeed attained—that mantra is said to belong to that seer; its state as such is the 'seer-attribute' (ārṣaka)."
The etymology of the word *chandas* has been stated elsewhere:
"It is designated as *chandas* because it covers (*chādanāt*), like two garments over a form;
in ancient times, it was indeed covered by the gods who were afraid of death."
"By the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Rudras, those very *chandas* [were established].

Likewise, elsewhere it is said: "In ancient times, the gods, fearing death, recollected the *chandas* here for the sake of concealing themselves; they were then concealed by them, and thus became immortal."
"Because it covers, it is designated as *chandas*; everything is enveloped by *chandases*.
This refers to the well-known [metres] such as *gāyatrī* and others. The deity is that which is indicated by each respective mantra.
As they say:
"Whatever deity is specified for whichever mantra, that mantra shall take on the form of that deity; such is the divinity of the deity. Thus it is said.
The phrase "by the deities" is also an indication of the application (viniyoga).
Its nature has been stated elsewhere:
"In a former aeon, the mantras arose solely for the purpose of ritual action."

"By this, this must be performed; that is called *viniyoga* (application). Also elsewhere: "The application (*viniyoga*) of a perfected mantra, which consists of its employment for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa according to the path of the scriptures, has been declared by the wise."
The fault arising from the absence of that knowledge is stated elsewhere:
"The mantra of one who does not know its application becomes weak.
Knowledge of the *chandas*, *ṛṣi*, and *devatā* is indispensable for the efficacy of the mantra.

This has been stated in the *Ārṣeyabrāhmaṇa* of the Chandogas: "Whoever, indeed, performs a sacrifice or teaches with a mantra whose seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), deity (*daivata*), and explanatory formula (*brāhmaṇa*) are unknown, either strikes against a wooden post, falls into a pit, perishes, or becomes worse off."
The meters of one who does not know these become exhausted;
but he who knows them in every mantra reaches a full lifespan, becomes superior, and his meters do not become exhausted.
Therefore, one should know these in every mantra. He becomes established in the station of the ṛṣis, he becomes established in the station of Brahman, and he is glorified in the heavenly world.
"One who remembers [the Veda] is not born again.

Kātyāyana also says: "He who studies, recites, mutters, offers oblations, sacrifices, or officiates at a sacrifice without knowing these [phonemes], his power as a knower of Brahman (*brahmavīrya*) becomes exhausted.
But he who studies after having fully understood these, and he who knows them according to their true meaning—his power becomes most excellent."

"Having recited [the mantra], having offered oblations, and having sacrificed, one obtains the fruit"—thus it is stated in the Āgama as well, beginning with: "And he who knows in accordance with reality the ṛṣi, the meter, and the deity... and so forth.
Yājñavalkya also says: "The seer, the meter, the deity, and likewise the application—these must be known with effort, especially by a Brahmin."
"But for one who performs sacrifice, study, recitation, fire-oblation, or anything else whatsoever without knowing [the rules], the fruit thereof shall be meager.
Thus [ends the citation]. Regarding the word "vidhi" (rule):
[The sequence consists of] placement (nyāsa), recitation (japa), worship (pūjā), fire-offering (homa), libation (tarpaṇa), consecration (abhiṣeka), the falling of [the deity], and so forth.
The word "and" (ca) serves to conjoin the primary and secondary elements of the creation of sound and the rest.
Although the term "of mantras and yantras" is used as a single compound, they are to be connected with the sages and others as appropriate.
In that regard, in the case of the *municchandasī* [meter], the mantra alone is used for the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
The deities and other such factors apply to both.

However, the pouring of the residue (*sampātapāta*) is connected to the yantra, as well as to those things indicated by it—namely, the effigy, the water-pot, the stone, the image, the finger-ring, the oil, the clarified butter, and so forth.
These have been described as the gross forms for the worshiper of the deity.
Their subtle forms are as follows,
as they say:
One's own self alone is declared to be the deity, delightful and possessing a universal form;
the ritual placement (nyāsa), however, is the conceptualization of one's own body as being the very nature of the deity.
Japa is the cultivation of the form of absorption in that [mantra]; it is the correct praise.
Worship, however, is the state of non-negligence regarding absorption in that [mantra], even when there is restlessness.
The dissolution of all conceptual constructions within the Self is considered to be the state of the human being;
the contemplation of their mutual union is known as *tarpaṇa* (satiating).
Consecration (abhiṣeka) is indeed knowledge (vidyā), which is the Great Self itself as its own substratum;
the ritual applications (prayoga) consist of the conditions (upādhi), while the cause is the self-reflection of one's own nature (svātmavimarśana).
"Devotion to them during the twilights, avoiding [the world] at its beginning, middle, and end, and the firm setting within the Self of the sufferings of delusion, ignorance, and so forth. (4–5)
The eternal Śiva is to be known as both devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and possessed of qualities (saguṇa).
He who is devoid of qualities is distinct from Prakṛti; he who is possessed of qualities is remembered as the manifest (sakala). || 6 ||
He states the introductory context for speaking of creation with the words "nirguṇa" (devoid of qualities).
Śiva is to be known as both eternal (*sanātana*), which means permanent, and as both devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and possessed of qualities (*saguṇa*).
He describes the nature of the former [the one devoid of qualities] with the word "nir".

"Other than primordial nature" means devoid of connection with it; for here, by the use of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), primordial nature is primarily intended as the object of reference. Therefore, the meaning is "subtle."
For this very reason, because there is no referent for another word, this is not a fifth [case-ending]. If it were so, it would result in a mere restatement (anuvāda).
As it has been stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Śiva is to be known as eternal, omnipresent, subtle, ever-blissful, free from disease, devoid of transformation, the witness, and the ancient one. Thus [it is said].
Also in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "He is actionless, devoid of qualities, peaceful, bliss, unborn, and undecaying."
Unaging, immortal, unmanifest, unknowable, immovable, and eternal.
"The Supreme Brahman, whose nature is knowledge, is self-cognizable and resides in the heart;
it is remembered as truth, beyond the intellect, eternal, stainless, and partless.
Thus [the first form has been described]. He states the nature of the second [form] with the word "sa" (He).
He possesses qualities (*saguṇaḥ*), is manifest (*sakalaḥ*), and is joined with *kalā* and *prakṛti*.
In the Sāṃkhya system, *prakṛti*—also known by its synonym *pradhāna*—is the state of equilibrium among the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
For this very reason, he is described as "possessing qualities."
In the Vedānta system, however, it is *avidyā*;
in the Śiva-tantra, it is *śakti*.
And it has been said in the Nārāyaṇīya and the Prayogasāra:
"Having become that power, the Lord of All is distinct from the forms of Brahmā and the others;
he is the creator, the enjoyer, and the destroyer—the Sakala, who consists of the entire universe. (6)
From the Supreme Lord, who is the all-pervading manifestation of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss, there arose Śakti;
from that, Nāda; and from Nāda, the emergence of Bindu. || 7 ||
He states the creation with the word "Being" (sat).

To dispel the doubt as to how that [Being], being insentient due to its being variegated by ignorance (avidyā), can be the agent of creation, he says, "from the glory of Being-Consciousness-Bliss" (saccidānandavibhavāt).
By this, the meaning is that even when conditioned by ignorance, there is no loss of its essential nature (svarūpa).
The construction of the sentence is: "From the Sakala [state], Śakti arose.
If it is asked, "How could Śakti arise from that which is already accompanied by Śakti?", the answer is: True;

however, that which exists in a subtle state during the Great Dissolution (mahāpralaya) through the superimposition of consciousness (*caitanya*) as an eternal form—of that [Śakti, the arising is spoken].

In accordance with the predominance of the specific qualities (guṇas), the state of being "swollen" (ucchūnāvasthā) during the accomplishment of the effects of the manifest world to be created—whether characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)—is itself figuratively designated as "origination.
It should be understood that this statement by the author of the text is made by relying on the Sāṃkhya doctrine of the origination of the existent (sadutpatti).
As it is said in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Therefore, she has emerged as eternal, omnipresent, and the source of the universe.
Also, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*: "By the will of Śiva, the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) attained oneness with the Śiva-principle."

"Then, at the beginning of creation, [the power] vibrates forth like oil from sesame seeds. Also, in the *Pañcarātra*: "Having thus perceived at the beginning of creation that [power] whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, which is the form of the substratum for the manifestation of the entire aggregate of principles (*tattva*)."
"The Supreme Person makes that eternal Prakṛti manifest.
Of that very [Prakṛti], Nāda and Bindu are the forms of the states conducive to creation.
As it is said in the *Prayogasāra*:
When that Śakti, awakened by means of the Nāda, is oriented toward the state free from affliction and turned toward Śiva, she is then remembered as having the form of the Puruṣa.
Therefore, that [power] alone is capable of creation.
Thus say the Teachers: "That designation 'tattva' [arises] then from the proximity of the light of pure consciousness."
"Desiring to act, she becomes condensed and in some place attains the state of a drop.
Also elsewhere: "The supreme power (*parā śakti*), characterized by inseparable concomitance, is manifested;
it is the undivided power of pure consciousness (*paracicchakti*), all-pervading, of the nature of consciousness, and omnipresent."
"Endowed with the desire for manifestation (*vivarta*) as the totality of all principles (*tattva*),
she attains the state of *bindu*, which is characterized by the predominance of action (*kriyā*).
For this very reason, among the Śiva-principles (*śivatattva*) to be described hereafter, only the five pure ones are taken up.

In this regard, although the state of *nāda* was not mentioned at the outset by other authors of treatises, nevertheless, this statement was made by the author of this work to indicate that *tāra* consists of seven aspects.
Indeed, the state of *nāda* was already indicated by the teachers while introducing the topic of time (*kāla*).
As they say: "In the self of Sound (Rava), and likewise in the principle of Time (Kālatattva).
And in the *Bhuvaneśīstuti*, the Teachers also state: "Salutations to You, who are designated as a principle through the nature of Sound. || 7 ||
Consisting directly of the supreme power (para-śakti), it is further divided into three ways;
its divisions are declared to be the point (bindu), the sound (nāda), and the seed-syllable (bīja). || 8 ||
The *bindu* is of the nature of Śiva and the *bīja* is Śakti;
their mutual conjunction is declared as *nāda* by those learned in all the Āgamas. || 9 ||
He states that the *bindu* has a threefold nature by way of its forms as *icchā-śakti* (will-power), *sattva*, and so forth, saying "para" (supreme).
It consists directly of the supreme power (*para-śakti*); therefore, it is subsequently described as being of the very nature of those [three] states.
Alternatively, "para" refers to Śiva; "tanmaya" means consisting of that [Śiva] and consisting of power (*śakti*), and thus it is of a dual nature.
Because it will be stated later that "the *bindu* has the nature of Śiva," this [Śiva] is divided into three ways.
These two, *nāda* and *bindu*, should be understood as distinct from the previously mentioned *nāda* and *bindu*, being of the nature of their effects.
Thus it has been said: "That bindu becomes threefold. (8)
He describes the nature of the succession of the three divisions beginning with the *bindu* with the words "the *bindu*," etc.

Having stated the two substrata (*dharmin*), he intends to state their relationship; thus there is a reversal of order, as this conforms to the sequence of the arising of power (*śakti*), whereas in the previous [section] the order was otherwise.
Inherence (*samavāya*) is the relationship characterized by the nature of the agitated and the agitator, which is the cause of emanation.
Regarding the stated point, he provides the authoritative proof: "by those learned in all the scriptures" (*sarvāgamaviśāradaiḥ*). || 9 ||
From the *bindu* arose Raudrī, from the *nāda* Jyeṣṭhā, and from the *bīja* Vāmā was born; from these [three] were produced Rudra, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu (Rama-adhipa). || 10 ||
Regarding "Raudrī": from that [source], namely the *bindu*, Raudrī arises; since she consists of Śiva (*śivamayatva*), her name is thus etymologically appropriate (*anvarthatā*).
Regarding Jyeṣṭhā from the *nāda*: because it is uttered in the middle, its etymological appropriateness should be understood as being by virtue of that very nature.
The connection is that Vāmā was born from the seed (*bīja*);
it possesses its literal meaning because it consists of power (*śakti*).
As it is said in the *Prayogasāra*:
The Bindu there is of the nature of Śiva, and the Bīja is remembered as being of the nature of Śakti. From the union of these two arises Nāda; from these [three] the three Śaktis are born.
Raudrī was born from the Bindu; Jyeṣṭhā was born from the Nāda;
Vāmā arose as Śakti from the Bīja; from these three, the three gods came into being. Thus [ends verse 10].
Consisting of perception, desire, and action, and having the nature of fire, the sun, and the moon, from the supreme Bindu being differentiated, there arose the unmanifest sound (rāva). || 11 ||
Regarding the term *saṃjñāne*:

in *saṃjñāna* (consciousness), there are the powers of will (*icchā*) and action (*kriyā*), whose essence is that [consciousness]. Therefore, Rudra, Brahmā, and Īśvara are, respectively, the embodiments of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), the power of will (*icchāśakti*), and the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
In some places, the reading *jñānecchā* (knowledge and will) occurs, but that is indeed non-traditional.

These— Rudra, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu (the Lord of Ramā)— who possess the nature of fire, moon, and sun, and who are included within the creation of sound, should be understood as specific states of Śakti alone, taking the forms of *nirodhikā*, the half-moon (*ardhendu*), and the point (*bindu*).
Their essence consists of will, action, and knowledge, because they have arisen from Śakti.
And he will say: "He consists of will, knowledge, and action.
Also in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*: "Because they desire by their own will to know or to perform actions..."
For immediately thereafter follows the capacity for the knowledge and vision of that effect.

"For that purpose, the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is indeed that which is the state of intense exertion; that is declared to be the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and from that, the entire supreme universe [arises].
Since those [powers] will be explained further on, it follows that from that [power of action] Rudra arises, from him Viṣṇu, and from him Brahmā.
Otherwise, there would also be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows;
for the author of the text will later state, "the Sun, Moon, and Fire [are represented] by the three syllables of the *praṇava*.
In that context, the components of the *praṇava*—the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*—are identical with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, respectively.
This is because it will be stated later that [the syllable] is produced from Brahmā by means of the letter *a*, and so forth;
and in another scripture: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara are established within their respective maṇḍalas."
Therefore, in that context, the letter *A* is Brahmā in the form of the sun, while here Viṣṇu is in the form of the sun;
thus, the sequence to be described hereafter should be understood in accordance with the creation of objects (*arthasṛṣṭi*).
And the author of the text will state:
"She who, in the form of the Moon, creates the world consisting of word and meaning; who, again, in the form of the Sun, sustains it by her own power;
and who, as the nature of Fire, withdraws all that at the end of the age—I never forget that Śāradā in my mind.
Thus [it is said]. Also in the *Gorakṣasaṃhitā*:
Will, action, and likewise knowledge— Gaurī, Brāhmī, and Vaiṣṇavī—
the triple power (śakti) that resides therein is the supreme light, Om.
The teachers also state this: "That which [arises] from the first three divisions ending with 'tapaṇa'";
thus, with the words "from that which is being divided," he describes the origin of the Śabdabrahman.

By the phrase "from the supreme *bindu*," it is meant that from that first *bindu*, which consists of the state of *śakti*, there arose the unmanifest self—the undivided, mere *nāda* devoid of specific qualities such as phonemes (*varṇa*) and the like. || 11 ||
Those proficient in all the scriptures call it Śabdabrahman;
others have declared that "Śabdabrahman" refers to the meaning of words, while still others have sung that it is the word itself. || 12 ||
For the establishment of those two does not occur for them, because both are insentient;
it is my conviction that the consciousness of all beings is the Śabdabrahman.
He states its essential nature with the words "In sound," etc.
Those who are "proficient in all scriptures" are those who know the meaning of all the Vedas.
This has been stated by the Teachers:
"That sound, when perfected through hearing, is called Śabdabrahman.
Thus, it is the mere first manifestation of Supreme Śiva intent on creation; it is the undivided, unmanifest, all-pervading sound consisting of Nāda and Bindu, which is of the nature of Brahman.

The meaning is "the Word-Brahman" (śabdabrahman). And it has been said: "For the Prakṛti, who consists primarily of the power of action and whose form is the moon, the supreme Śabdabrahman became the cause of both word and meaning."

Now, he begins to refute the view of the proponents of the internal sphoṭa—which consists of both the universal (jāti) and the individual (vyakti)—as well as the view of the external sphoṭa, with the words "śabda... and so forth.
Certain teachers declare that the word-meaning, which is the internal sphoṭa, is the Śabdabrahman.
For instance:

"The *sphoṭa* is indeed partless, indivisible, eternal, of the nature of consciousness, and internal, consisting of both word and meaning. Other grammarians, however, assert that the *śabdabrahman* is the *vākyasphoṭa*— the word characterized as a sentence— which reveals an undivided single meaning, being manifested by the utterance of preceding phonemes and awakened by the apprehension of the final word aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of each respective word.
As it has been said:
"The sphoṭa, which is manifested by sentences, is one, eternal, partless, and manifold in form—whether it be the individual-sphoṭa (vyakti-sphoṭa) or the class-sphoṭa (jāti-sphoṭa). || 12 ||
Refuting both of those views, he states his own position with the words "not so" (*na hi*).
In the opinion of those disputants, the establishment of those two— the word and the word-meaning— does not constitute the establishment of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*),
because both of them are insentient (*jaḍa*).
If either the word or its meaning is called *śabdabrahman*, then it is not tenable for it to be denotable by the term "Brahman.
This is because the referent of the term "Brahman" consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*),
whereas those two [the word and its meaning] are insentient (*jaḍa*).
This has been stated by Bhartṛhari: "Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the essence of speech, the imperishable syllable;
it manifests in the form of objects, from which the process of the world proceeds."
Elsewhere also: "The wise know that the 'Word-Brahman' (śabdabrahman) is the object understood through words;
because it does not itself cognize its own meaning, such a sound is not so described."
"But being woven everywhere, when the mine of the elements has arisen,
it manifests within the bodies of living beings, expanded for their sake.
Thus, this [statement] forms a single syntactical unit with the phrase "those who are experts in all the scriptures."
For it will be stated that the resonance (*rava*) of that very [Bindu] manifests within all bodies;
as it is said in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Then that Inner Self, the Goddess whose nature is Sound (*nāda*), sounds forth by herself."
"Just as it has attained the state of color through the differentiation of its configuration, so too, being impelled by the wind, it will emerge from the mass [of air] into manifestation.

Some, however, having construed the phrase "the Word-Brahman" (*śabdabrahma*) to mean that the meaning of a word is the word itself, maintain the position that they are experts in all scriptures; this is one view.
Others say that the second [position] is "the drop" (*bindu*), and they state the refutation of those two.
That is not so;
for the reason "because of insentience" (*jaḍatvāt*) is not possible in the first position, and it would result in a contradiction with the Master’s doctrine.
Therefore, the position that "they are experts in all the scriptures" is precisely the one favored by the author of the treatise. || 13 ||
Having reached that form of Kuṇḍalinī situated within the bodies of living beings, it manifests as the nature of phonemes through the distinctions of prose, verse, and so forth. || 14 ||
Having thus described that supreme creation of sound in general, he concludes with the words "having attained that.

The connection is as follows: that consciousness, which exists within the bodies of living beings in the form of Kuṇḍalinī—that is, the essential nature of Kuṇḍalinī—manifests itself in the form of phonemes through the distinctions of prose, verse, and so forth.
Having done what? The ellipsis is "having reached the instruments such as the throat.
Therefore, it should be understood that the creation to be described hereafter proceeds from Kuṇḍalinī. || 14 ||
Then, from Śambhu, who is of the nature of the Bindu and the bond of time, and who is of the nature of Kalā, there was born Sadāśiva, the witness of the world, the all-pervading one. || 15 ||
From Sadāśiva arises Īśa; from him is born Rudra;
from him Viṣṇu, and from him Brahmā—such is their origin. || 16 ||

Having thus described that supreme *parā* creation of sound—which was mentioned first in order to highlight its preeminence—the author now begins to discuss the creation of meaning (*arthasṛṣṭi*) with the word "atha" (*now*). This is because it is impossible to describe *paśyantī* and the other levels of speech apart from their function as the creation of the body (*śarīrasṛṣṭi*). [The term] "kalā-māyā-tadātmanaḥ" means "from that whose nature consists of *kalā* and *māyā*," because [the subsequent creations] have arisen from that source.
The *bindu* is also merely another state (*avasthāntara*) of that very [Self].
The phrase "of its own nature" (*tadātmanaḥ*) is used in both cases through the metaphorical attribution of the cause to the effect.
As it has been said:
"Always non-different from oneself, endowed with qualities such as omniscience.
Alternatively, the *kalās*—namely Nivṛtti and the others—are the producers, in reverse order, of Sadāśiva and the other presiding deities; [the Goddess] is of their very nature.
Regarding the term "of Kālabandhu":
the meaning is that [He arises] from the Self in the form of Nāda, aided by Time (kāla) in the form of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), throughout beginningless and endless time.

From Śambhu, who is Paramaśiva, [He arises as] the performer of the fivefold functions of emanation, maintenance, withdrawal, suppression, and grace; for this very reason, He is the seed-form of the creation of the universe.
Sadāśiva has become the witness of the world.
Furthermore, because he is the bond of time—and for this very reason the self of time—the connection is established through the relationship of cause and effect.
As stated by the Teacher: "But that [power] is always known perfectly by me alone in the form of Time."
By these two qualifiers, the continued existence of both primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and time (*kāla*) even during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) is stated.
Therefore, the relative permanence belongs to these two;
absolute permanence belongs to the person (*puruṣa*) alone.

The reasoning should be understood as follows: because the destruction of all things has the person (*puruṣa*) as its ultimate limit, otherwise there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and so forth.
Furthermore, by the word "kinsman" (*bandhu*) in the phrase "the kinsman of time" (*kālabandhu*), it is indicated that time is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*).
As they say:

"This [universe], beginning with the creation and ending with the dissolution, is the manifestation of the power of darkness (*tamaḥ-śakti*). Time is the instrumental cause for the birth and destruction of all entities. Thus it is said.
Elsewhere also: "O twice-born one, the Blessed Lord Time is without beginning, and its end does not exist."
"Therefore, these [powers of] restraint over creation, maintenance, and dissolution are uninterrupted.
By the phrase "of the binder of time" (*kālabandhoḥ*), another [dimension of] time, beginning from a *lava* and ending with the cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), is also indicated;
for by that very [term], the higher time (*parakāla*) has been expressed.
And it is said:
"The time required to pierce each petal of a cluster of lotus leaves with a fine needle— that time is designated as a *lava*."
This has been analyzed by the Teachers through this textual composition beginning with, "Thirty lavas shall constitute a truṭi," and ending with, "Your lifespan is my breath, impelled by time alone."
We have not stated this, however, for fear of making the book too voluminous.
Others, on the other hand, explain it thus: by the pratyāhāra "kaśca laśca," the consonants are grasped from *kālabandhu*, which means "having time as its self";
and by the term "aśca," the vowels are also grasped.
Regarding the phrase "of that self" (*tadātmanaḥ*):
others, however, explain it differently—as *ka*, *la*, *ātma*, and the long vowel *ī*.
This is because it is stated [in the grammatical tradition] that it is the fourth among the four *ātman*s.
By the word *kāla* (time), the sun is meant; therefore, *maḥ*.
Alternatively, by the word *kāla*, Mahākāla is intended, as the letter *m* is taken as a form of Rudra, just as in the case of *Bhīma* [being] *Bhīmasena*.
Therefore, there is the letter *ma*.
Thus, having been combined, the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*) is extracted. From that, it is said: "therefore."

Because he is the root of the universe, one should meditate upon that Śambhu as Kāma, revolving within the womb, possessing the luster of a throbbing, crimson bandhūka flower, and rising to the peak of ten million moons in his belly; for by such statements, he is described as being in the body at the *mūlādhāra* in the form of the three-fold light, and as being of the nature of *bindu* because he is of the nature of *śakti*.
As it has been said:

"The entire universe—consisting of the elements, the senses, and the internal organs, and taking the form of the sun, moon, and fire—is composed of phonemes; all this is gradually [dissolved] into the lotus-eyed Pradhāna, which is of the nature of the seed."

"Having led her into the male [seed-syllable] which is the nature of the *bindu*, and from there into the sun-natured [syllable], then into the principle of *kāla* (time), and having led that indeed into the power (*śakti*) which is the conscious self (*cidātman*), one should lead her into the solitary, peaceful abode.

Others, however, maintain that from the letter *ha* of Śambhu comes the *kalā*; the *ardhendu* is the *ātman* (the letter *ī*); the *bindu* is the *bindu* itself; and *kāla* is fire (*agni*), because it causes the destruction of all at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*).
Thus, the seed-syllable of Māyā has been extracted.
