Therefore, it has been stated that its status as the fundamental seed of this world is indeed well-known.
Furthermore, this interpretation is approved by the venerable teacher.
As it has been said by the Teachers:
"O Lord, be gracious, O Sovereign of the Universe! Who are we, and by whom have we been brought forth?
What is our root, and what is our activity? You ought to tell us all this."
Thus questioned, the Supreme Light spoke in measured words.
In his commentary on this verse, Padmapādācārya explained: "The Lord of All has stated the material cause and so forth in brief," as expressed by the words "thus questioned.

That which is measured or known preeminently is *pramitā*, namely *prakṛti* (primordial nature); that which measures or knows is *pramitaḥ*, namely *puruṣa* (the spirit), for he measures [or perceives].

"Paricchinatti" means that time is measured; the syllable that expresses those measured [units of time] is non-different from them, and thus it is "pramitākṣara. The meaning is that the supreme speech (parā vāk), which is the true reality, is the letter *ha*.
Its capacity to denote *prakṛti* and the rest should be understood through its form as the seed (*bīja*), the drop (*bindu*), and the sound (*nāda*).
By this [statement], the meaning is that he spoke the subsequent [verse].
Perceiving that [the audience] might not understand what was stated in brief, he explains that very point:
"You are born from the Imperishable (akṣara), the causes of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
This is according to the etymology "that which does not perish (na kṣarati) or which pervades (aśnute)," as stated in passages such as, "From the Imperishable, the universe here comes into being."
Regarding the phrase "of them":
their emergence in the creation of sound has already been stated;
such is their emergence in the creation of objects.
This is the detailed meaning. || 15-16 ||
From that unmanifest, primordial, and transformed Supreme Reality, it is said that the principle of Mahat arose, consisting of the qualities and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). || 17 ||

Thus, having established the creation of objects (*arthasṛṣṭi*), he begins to describe the creation of principles (*tattvasṛṣṭi*) starting from the root: "From the root"—that is, from the supreme reality which is the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the source of all creation, and which exists in the form of the *bindu*;
or alternatively, from the modified *śabdabrahman* when it is oriented toward creation—the principle called *mahat*, the entity known as the Great One, came into being.

In the Śaiva system, that which is designated as the *buddhitattva* (the principle of intellect) is of what nature? It consists of the qualities (*guṇas*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and its essential form is that of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*).
Its nature as the fourfold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is due to the metaphorical attribution of the cause to the effect, since these [four] are its effects.
Thus it is for the followers of the Śaiva Siddhānta. As it was said by Īśānaśiva:
"That very [power], manifested as Śakti, is Nature (prakṛti) characterized by that which is to be known."
"The principle of intellect (buddhitattva) becomes manifest, resting upon the quality of sattva;
that very intellect is called the principle named Mahat in the Sāṃkhya. Thus it is said.
Also in the Vāmakeśvara:
"From the unmanifest form of the Śabdabrahman, the cause of all things,

the manifest principle of intellect (buddhitattva), characterized by the quality of sattva, was produced. In the Sāṃkhya system, however, *prakṛti*— also known by the synonym *pradhāna*— is that which consists of the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and is denoted by the term "unmanifest" (*avyakta*).
That supreme reality (paravastu) is the root of all things.
From it, when modified by a deficiency or excess of qualities (guṇa), Mahat is produced.
What is it like?
The Self whose nature consists of the qualities and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
The "qualities" (*guṇāḥ*) are the subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*) of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell;
it is the causal form of these as well as of the fourfold internal organ.
By way of metaphorical designation, it possesses the nature of both;
likewise, the sequence of its creation is also from primordial matter (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat), and from the Great One comes the I-principle (ahaṅkāra). || 17 ||
From that [intellect], the threefold ego (ahaṅkāra) arose according to the distinction of its creative functions. From the ego known as vaikārika, the ten vaikārika deities were born. || 18 ||

From the principle of fire (taijasa), the sense organs arose through the sequential application of the subtle elements (tanmātra): namely, those of direction, wind, sun, rain-god, the two Aśvins, fire, Indra, Upendra, and Mitra. || 19 ||
Thus it was said: "From that Mahat, the threefold Ahaṃkāra arose through the distinction of creation—
namely, Vaikārika, Taijasa, and Bhūtādi."
As it has been said:
"The unmanifest itself becomes manifest, characterized by the name 'Mahat';
from that arises the principle of *ahaṅkāra*, which is differentiated by the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* and the rest."
That *ahaṅkāra* is threefold, distinguished separately by the divisions of *sattva* and the others:
the *vaikārika* is named *sāttvika*, the *taijasa* is remembered as *rājasa*, and the *bhūtādi* is *tāmasa*; these too produced separate principles (*tattvas*), and so forth.
By stating the respective effects in this manner with the words "from the vaikārika," and so forth, he reveals its threefold nature.
It is called *vaikārika* because it has arisen from the Supreme Lord when He is transformed through the state of equilibrium with *śakti*.
Because they have arisen from that [state], the gods likewise possess that same nature.
In the Sāṃkhya system as well, there is the same [fault], because the production of the Pradhāna—which is modified by the predominance of the Guṇas—is of that nature. || 18 ||
He states those very [deities] with the words "Direction," and so forth.
Regarding "Aśvī": although these two are the Aśvinī-kumāras, they are spoken of as one because of their constant association and simultaneous birth. Upendra is one form of Viṣṇu.
Mitra is the third sun;
as it is said: "Mitra is the third light.
Ka is one form of Brahman.
Candra is also to be known [as such].
These are to be understood as the presiding deities of the sense organs (indriya-adhiṣṭhātṛ-deva). As they say:
"The eleven beginning with the sense of direction (dig) and so forth, which are known as the vaikārika [tanmātras],
are proclaimed to be the presiding deities of the sense organs. Thus,
[it is said] "from the taijasa [ego]."
From the *taijasa* ego arise the organs—the organs of action, the organs of knowledge, and the mind.
As it has been said:
"And that other principle which is the mind (*manas*), characterized by conceptualization and doubt..."
"It is produced from the *taijasa* [element] alone.
Also elsewhere: "Therein, the mind arises from the *taijasa*, and the senses become modified (*vaikārita*)."
"From *bhūtādi* [the tanmātras arise], for their creation proceeds from this.
Here, "senses" (*akṣāṇi*) refers to the deities presiding over the senses.
According to the Sāṃkhya system, the sense organs (*indriyāṇi*) emerge from the *vaikārika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*), conjoined with the *taijasa* ego.
In this way, from the *bhūtādi* [tamas-ahaṃkāra] as well, when accompanied by the *taijasa* [rajas-ahaṃkāra], the production of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) occurs.
As it has been said:
"The group of eleven, characterized by *sattva*, proceeds from the *vaikārika* (or *sāttvika*) *ahaṃkāra*."
From the *bhūtādi* [ego] arises the subtle element (*tanmātra*), which is *tāmasa*; from the *taijasa* [ego] arise both. Thus [ends verse 19].
From the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), which consists of the subtle elements and so forth, the five gross elements were born:
from sound, first the ether (viyat); from touch, air (vāyu); and from form, fire (hutāśana). || 20 ||
From taste arises water, from smell arises earth; such is their origin.
Space is clear, wind is black, fire is red, and water is white.
The wise know that yellow is the earth, and that the five elements each have their own support.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are recorded as the qualities of the elements.
Regarding the word "bhūta":

the connection is that the five elements (pañcabhūtāni) were born from the *ahaṃkāra*—beginning with the *bhūtādi* [type]—through the sequential application of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). What is its own meaning? [It refers to the state of being an element.]
In that regard, first, the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) which serve as the causes of space and the other elements are produced:
the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form, the subtle element of taste, and the subtle element of smell.
From these, the five gross elements—space, air, fire, water, and earth—in their respective forms, arise.
And it has been said: "Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—
these subtle elements (tanmātras) themselves became the objects [of the senses] from the *bhūtādi* in due order."
From that, space arose, having the nature of the subtle element of sound;
from that, air, whose essence is touch; and from that, fire, whose essence is form.
"Water consists of the essence of taste; from that [comes] earth, which consists of the essence of smell.
From those [elements] come the gross elements, five in number, and from them also Virāj.
In this regard, he describes the manner of the origin of the elements with the words "from sound," etc.

From the subtle element of sound (śabda-tanmātra) arises ether (ākāśa); from the subtle element of touch (sparśa-tanmātra), air (vāyu); from the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra), fire (agni); from the subtle element of taste (rasa-tanmātra), water (jala); and from the subtle element of smell (gandha-tanmātra), earth (pṛthivī).
Some maintain that these [gross elements] have as their cause those [subtle elements] accompanied by each preceding one, due to the force of the word "preceding" (pūrva).
As it has been said:
From sound, space; from touch, by that [sound], wind; from those two and form, fire; from these three and taste, water; from these four and smell, earth.
Thus.
He teaches the colors of the five elements, beginning with "transparent.
"Transparent" means white.
Here, the description of the color of certain formless substances is for the purpose of meditation (upāsanā), in accordance with the requirements of one's own scripture.
Their essential natures have been described elsewhere:
"Space is characterized by vacuity; wind is intent on movement; fire possesses the quality of ripening;
water is possessed of taste; and earth is solid."
Thus; the meaning is that these [means] are known by means of those [objects].
"Based on each one individually" means:
The meaning is that they are supported by their respective causes.
As it has been said: "The entire visible world is produced by the fourfold great elements, which have mutually entered into one another and pervade space."
Elsewhere it is also said: "In space there is air; there fire, and in that [fire] water is situated; upon that [water] rests the earth.
The Naiyāyikas maintain that the qualities of the elements are their respective specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*).
Alternatively, sound is the quality of space;
sound and touch are the qualities of air;
those two, along with form, are the qualities of fire.
According to the Sāṃkhyas, those [qualities] are with taste in water,
and with smell in earth— these five;
this very point is expressed by the statement that they each reside in a single substratum.
And it has been said by Īśānaśiva: "Space has sound as its sole quality; wind has the qualities of sound and touch;
fire is held to have the three qualities of sound, touch, and form."
Water possesses four qualities through its attributes of sound, touch, form, and taste;
earth possesses five qualities through sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Thus [ends verses 20–22].
The orb of the sky is marked with six dots;
that of the wind is triangular and endowed with a svastika; and that of fire is joined with a half-moon. || 23 ||
The wise know that the mandalas are the lotus for water, the square with a vajra for earth, and each has the appearance of its respective element. || 24 ||
He describes the mandalas of the elements, beginning with "the circle" (vṛttam).
The circle of the sky is that of space (ākāśa).
That very same circle, marked with six dots at equal intervals along the central line of its circular perimeter, belongs to Mātariśvan, the wind.
The triangle has its apex pointing upwards, because it is said: "Fire is above, Śakti is below.
This is also stated elsewhere:
"The fire-mandala [is formed] by the corners of Indra, Rākṣasa, Vāyu, and Agni.
This means that one should extend the lines of intersection of the three triangles so as to be joined with a svastika, and thereby form the shape of a svastika therein.
As it has been said: "In the heart is a triangle, emerging within a svastika of red light.
A *svastika* consists of two lines intersecting at right angles, with their four ends joined together to form four faces directed toward the intermediate directions.
The phrase "of fire" (vahneḥ) connects with the preceding [word].
The connection is: "the lotus joined with a half-moon from the water" (ambhasaḥ). That which is joined with a half-moon is "joined with a half-moon" (ardhendusaṃyutam).
The compound is formed by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) following the rule for the seventh case.

Alternatively, it means that the crescent moon and the lotus are joined—that is, both are combined—into a single orb of water; having thus formed the crescent moon, one should then draw two lotuses on either side of it.
As it was stated by the Teachers: "The watery [mandala] is a disc endowed with a lotus and possessing a half-moon.
And elsewhere as well: "The watery [mandala] is a half-moon, liquid, gentle, white, and joined with a lotus."
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Prayogasāra*: "The lotus-marked [digit] is the half-moon of the waters."
Elsewhere also— it is said that their sequence consists of the lunar disc, followed by a triangle on all sides endowed with six dots and the fire-weapon,
and having a form identical to a pair of lotuses and the crescent moon.
"The mandalas here consist of four corners, are provided with a border, and are infinite.
Also, in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "Or else, the mandala may be half-moon shaped, white, and joined by a pair of lotuses."
In the *Svāyambhuva-nārasiṃha* it is also stated: "The [seat] should be watery, marked with a half-moon and a lotus.
He who says that one should first draw an eight-petaled lotus and then fashion the shapes of half-moons at the tips of its petals is indeed mistaken.
Others, however, say that one should draw a half-moon and write a lotus in its center;
since that too will be explained in the section on the *bhūtalipi* script, it need not be discussed here.
The connection is that the square [mandala] of the earth is "with a vajra."
Some say that one should extend the lines of intersection of the square and fashion eight vajras;
however, those who know the tradition state that the eight vajras should be fashioned directly upon the lines of the square itself.
This is stated in the *Śaunakakalpa*:
"The earth-grasper (bhūgraha) should be square and adorned with eight vajras.
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Hiraṇyagarbhasaṃhitā*: "Furthermore, the auspicious outer [mandala] is four-cornered and adorned with eight vajras."
Thus [it is said].
But the Teachers [state]: "situated upon the eight thunderbolts. The author of the treatise also [states]: "upon the eight vajras."
The *vajra* consists of two lines joined to each other, facing one another, thus forming three faces;
some say it consists of two lines joined at their centers.
He describes the meditation on the mandala with the words "that and that," and so forth.
By this, it is also stated that when drawing a mandala on the ground and so forth, it should be filled with colored powders (rajas) of their respective colors. || 23-24 ||
They say that these are adorned with their own respective colors and enveloped by their own names;
they are known as the *kalās*—Nivṛtti and the others—of the five elements beginning with earth. || 25 ||
Nivṛtti, along with Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and immediately thereafter Śāntyatītā, should be known; they arise from the body of Nāda. || 26 ||
"By the second set of letters" means by the elemental letters (bhūtavarṇa) that will be described hereafter.
This is also the meaning of the phrase "encircled by their own names":
it means they are encircled by whichever mantra is written in the pericarp (*kaṇīkā*) within the diagrams of the elemental scripts (*bhūtalipi*) that will be described.
The traditionalists (*sāmpradāyika*) think as follows:

Since it was previously stated that [the powers] are "of the nature of *kalā*," he says "Dharā" and so forth for the purpose of the ritual application (*prayoga*) and other matters, referring to the powers that have emerged from the *bindu*-tattva and which constitute the causes of the elements (*bhūta*), according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*).
The ellipsis is "the producer of the five elements, beginning with earth.
As it is stated in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
"Śakti was first produced, following the state beyond tranquility (śāntyatīta)."
From that, the state beyond peace (śāntyatītapada) arises from power (śakti), and thereafter, the state of peace (śāntipada) follows in succession.
From that [comes] the stage of knowledge; from that, the synthesis of the stage of establishment.
The stage of cessation arises after the stage of establishment.
Thus has the creation impelled by the Lord been described in brief;
now follows their dissolution in the reverse order.
"From these five steps thus indicated, no other creation is desired,
because this entire world is pervaded by the five *kalās*.
Thus [ends the section on] *nāda*.
"Nādadehasamudbhavā" means those [energies] which originate from the *bindu* whose body is *nāda*. Alternatively, it states their gross designative aspect as "originating from the *nādadeha*.
*Nāda* is the letter *ha*; that from which the body—the origin—of *nāda*, which is sound (*dhvani*), arises is the *nādadeha*, namely the vital air (*vāyu*). By that [air], they are produced.
Because of the non-difference between the property and the possessor of the property (*dharmadharmiṇoḥ*), production is expressed by the word "body" (*deha*).
According to the statement, "The wind moving within the chest produces a deep sound," it is the cause of the production of the *nāda* (nasal resonance).
It is [the letter] *ra*, because it is heated (*raḥ*) by the fire (*samudbhā*), that is, by the fire whose radiance (*bhā*) is fully blazing (*samuddīpyamāna*).
This is its own nature.

In that regard, although the letters *ha*, *ya*, *ra*, and *va* should have been mentioned in their proper sequence, the fact that he has mentioned only these four indicates that the letter *la* is also present.
Furthermore, because the *nāda* (nasal resonance) is mentioned first, it should be understood that the *bindu* (dot) is also joined to them.
These are the seed-syllables of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) in reverse order.
Alternatively, *nāda* is the letter *ha*; its "body" is its essential form. Those whose origin and abiding reside therein are the vowels *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, *e*, and *au*.
It should be understood that these possess the nasal bindu (*m*).
As it is said in the *Trikotottara*: "That supreme seed-syllable called Nāda, which resides within all beings—
this is the supreme, divine form that bestows all accomplishments."
"Peaceful, all-pervading, empty, and established in the five measures. Thus it is said.
Some say that these are joined with *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, and *ha* in sequence; namely: *hrāṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *hrūṃ*, *hraīṃ*, *hrauṃ*.
These are the seeds of the unquintuplicated elements (*apañcīkṛtabhūtabīja*).
Alternatively, *nāda* is the letter *ha*.

Since the body has a predominance of the earth element, it is designated by the word "body" (*deha*), which refers to the letter *la*; that in which its origin and persistence reside is called *nādadehasamudbhava*.
In those [syllables] beginning with *ā*, they are not produced from the body of *nāda*.
Here, they state the conjunction of *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, and *ha* in sequence.
Namely: *hlāṃ*, *hvlīṃ*, *rhlaṃ*, *hlyaiṃ*, *hlauṃ*.
These are the seeds of the fivefold-composed elements (*pañcīkṛtabhūtabīja*).
It should be understood that these very seeds of the elements serve as the cause for the cessation of the ego-identification (*abhimāna*) with them and so forth.
As it was stated by the Teacher: "Consisting of *nāda*, *kalā*, and the rest. (25–26)
This entire world, consisting of the moving and the non-moving, is composed of the five elements.
The non-moving is divided in many ways through distinctions such as mountains, trees, and so forth. || 27 ||
Having thus described the elements, he states that the world consists of them through the word "pañca" (five).
By this, both the theory of *trivṛtkaraṇa* (threefold transformation) and the theory of *pañcīkaraṇa* (fivefold transformation) are indicated.
In that regard, even for those gods who are of the nature of fire (*taijasa*), half of their body is fiery, one-fourth is of earth, and one-fourth is of water.
This is the position regarding the tripartition (trivṛtkaraṇa).
However, according to the position of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa), four parts belong to earth and one-eighth part each belongs to the others;
and so it is for the other elements as well.
As it has been said:
"Having divided each [of the two] into two parts, and then dividing the first part again into four,
those [resulting portions] become five by five through their conjunction with their own and the other second parts."
Alternatively—of fire there are six parts, and of earth, water, air, and ether, there is one-tenth of each part.
Likewise, in our own bodies, which are composed of earth, there are six parts of earth and one-tenth of each of the others.
This should be understood to apply similarly to the watery bodies of those dwelling in the worlds of Varuṇa and the other deities.
As it has been said:
"One should divide each of the elements, beginning with earth, into two parts;
then, taking one part from each, one should further divide them into five."
One should cause each individual part to enter into each element in succession;
thus, for the element of space, there are indeed six parts belonging to itself.
"One should assign the four parts consisting of air and so forth to air and the other elements in this manner;
this is the quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa), so say those who know the reality.
In another place, there is a specific distinction:
Bone, flesh, skin, sinew, and hair as the fifth—
thus is the earth, whose nature is solidity, said to be fivefold.
Saliva, urine, semen, blood, and marrow as the fifth—
these are proclaimed as the five qualities of water in their liquid form.
Hunger, thirst, fear, sleep, laziness, and patience— these qualities,
characterized by heat, are proclaimed to belong to fire.
Running, leaping, eating, contracting, and extending—
these five qualities of wind are established in the form of its functions.
"Passion and hatred, as well as shame, fear, and likewise delusion—these are the five qualities of space, which is called the void and whose nature is hollow. Thus [it is said].
"Moving" means that which is locomotive.
The immobile is stationary.
Since there is much to be said regarding the mobile beings, he sets aside that which was mentioned first and speaks of the immobile, saying "the immobile.
In that regard, he will later state that those mobile beings are born from moisture, from eggs, or from the womb.
Because they have been taught by him, their status as *audbhida* (arising from the earth) has been stated.
As they say:
"The body of a living being is to be known as fourfold, according to the difference in its mode of origin."

"Born from a sprout, born from sweat, born from an egg, and fourthly, born from a womb; that which emerges by breaking through the earth is the 'sprout-born' (audbhida), and that is the stationary being (sthāvara).
The manner of their origin is stated elsewhere as follows:
Immobile beings, such as grasses, shrubs, and the like, are to be known as *udbhijja* (those born from sprouts).
In that regard, the earth, moistened by waters and heated by internal warmth, [produces them].
Being dispersed by the wind, it attains the state of a seed;
likewise, the seeds that have been sown are further moistened by water.
They attain swelling and softness, and reach the state of being a root;
from that root arises the sprout, from which the emergence of leaves occurs; from the leafy nature comes the stalk, and from the stalk, again, the production of blossoms. Thus [it is said]. 27.
Mobile beings are said to be of three kinds: those born from sweat, those born from eggs, and those born from a womb.
Those born from sweat are worms, insects, and the like; those born from eggs are serpents and the like. || 28 ||
He indicates the mobile beings (*cara*) by first providing their classification, saying "the mobile beings," etc.
Showing the connection of each with the root *jan* (to be born), he states their specific types with the words "born from sweat" (*khedaja*), and so forth.
The distinction between "worms, insects, and so forth" is based on whether they bite or do not bite.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), moths and the like are included, as they say: "Worms, insects, moths, and so forth, are the embodied beings known as those born from moisture (*svedaja*)."
The manner of its production is shown elsewhere:
"That which is born from moisture is produced from earth, fire, and water that are being moistened."
Therefore, their non-womb-born nature has been stated.
As it is said in the *Prayogasāra*:
"However, those among these who are born from moisture should also be known as non-womb-born."
"Stable, windless, and divided forty thousandfold.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "serpents and so forth," birds, tortoises, and the like are included.
As they say:
"All birds are egg-born, as are crocodiles, fish, and tortoises.
Thus it is said;
and the manner of their birth is also described as follows:
"From the union of semen and blood that has become a sphere, when it is broken open by time, the fully formed self shall emerge and proceed forth. Thus [it is said]. (28)
Among those born from a womb, such as humans and others, the origin of men is said to arise from the union of semen and blood through the conjunction of the male and female. || 29 ||
The single drop, possessing a dual nature, enters the womb;
in due course, if *rajas* (female constituent) predominates, it becomes a female, and if *retas* (male constituent) predominates, it becomes a male.
When there is equality of both, it is a neuter—such is the established rule. || 30 ||
The *jarāyu* is the womb-cavity in the form of a net.
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "humans and so forth," animals and the like are included.
Their number is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Beings born from a womb are divided into sixty-four thousand types.
The connection [of this statement] is that "the origin of humans among them is now being described."
Since all treatises have human beings as their intended audience,
and by the phrase "joined with blood," its [the mother's] subordinate status is indicated;
therefore, the son is endowed with the caste and other attributes of the father.
And so it is said in the Mahābhārata: "The mother is but a bellows; the son belongs to the father; he by whom one is begotten is indeed oneself.
A *bhastrā* is a bellows, a leather vessel for holding air.
The single *bindu*, consisting of both semen and blood, and therefore consisting of both fire (*agni*) and moon (*soma*), enters the womb.
This "it" is connected with what follows:
"this *bindu*, when the female element (*rajas*) predominates, gradually becomes a woman."
The construction is that a male is produced when the semen is greater in sequence.
Here, "greater" is to be understood in terms of quantity.
It should also be understood that when there is equality of the stated quantities, the birth of a neuter occurs.
As they say:
"Twenty-two parts of *rajas* and fourteen parts of *śukra* arise in males and females at the time of conception."
"A woman occurs when the female portion (rajas) is predominant; a man occurs when the male portion (śukra) is predominant;
when the number of both is equal, the birth of a neuter (napuṃsaka) occurs.
By the word "successively" (kramāt), this is not what is being stated.

Thus, that very drop (bindu), when divided into separate parts by the vital air (vāyu), produces many offspring. As it is said in the Śārīrasthāna of the Vāgbhaṭa: "When the semen and the menstrual blood are repeatedly and manifoldly divided by the vital air according to their respective natures, there is the production of many offspring."
Those with deformed impurities are born with deformed forms and from non-human wombs;
a woman who has reached her sixteenth year, when united with a man who has reached his twentieth, [conceives].
When the womb, the channels, the blood, the semen, the vital air, and the heart are pure, one gives birth to a powerful son; however, if these are deficient, the child will live for fewer years.
"He becomes sickly, short-lived, or unfortunate in the womb, or he does not exist at all. (29–30)
Constrained by the noose of delusion in accordance with past karma, a certain self then attains the state of a living being within that [body]. || 31 ||
Regarding that drop (*bindu*), he describes the movement of the individual soul (*jīva*) with the words "beginning with 'pūrva'":

among the karmas accumulated over hundreds of previous births, there is one— consisting of either merit or demerit— that is powerful, ready to yield its fruit, and which results in both pleasure and pain, being fit for experience within a human body.
That which is bound and fettered by the noose of delusion—which corresponds to its karma and consists of ignorance—is born.
By this, the non-arising of the eternal self is stated;
the meaning is that the self has entered the body as if it were a house.
"Someone" (kaścit) refers to this:
according to the Kaṇāda-sūtra, "The selves are manifold because of their distinct dispositions," and because of the Sāṃkhya statement, "The plurality of puruṣas is established."
In the Vedānta system, however, a distinction imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) must be admitted;
otherwise, if ignorance were destroyed by the knowledge of the Self, then—as it is said:
"O Arjuna, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes."

Because of this statement, since previously accumulated karmas lack the capacity to yield their fruit, there is indeed no "staining" by subsequent karma; for it is said: "He is not stained by karmas, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Furthermore, because of his oneness and his state of liberation, there could be no incarnation at all.
Thus, it has been stated that the cause of [the soul's] descent is the noose of delusion (*moha*).
This was said in the *Adhyātmaviveka*: "Brahman exists, consisting of consciousness and bliss, self-luminous and stainless."
He is all-powerful and all-knowing, and those known as individual souls (jīvas) are His portions.
Just as sparks from a fire are conditioned by beginningless ignorance,
they are differentiated by limiting adjuncts such as length and so forth, through beginningless karmas.
Restrained by merits and demerits which bestow pleasure and pain,
[beings receive] a body, lifespan, and experience born of karma, endowed with their respective species.
They attain [this] in every birth.
Thus [ends the section]. || 31 ||
Then, nourished by food, drink, and other necessities provided by the mother, he who possesses a body of reality grows gradually—day by day, then week by week, and thereafter month by month. || 32 ||
Regarding the word "atha" (now):
the method for this is stated in the *Yogārṇava*:
"Having entered the food that has been eaten, that wind divides it into two parts."
Having entered, it separates the waste matter from the water, each being situated within the interior of the intestines.
Having placed water above the fire and that food upon the water,
one's own vital breath (prāṇa), situated beneath the water, gently fans the fire.
The fire, being fanned by the wind, makes the water extremely hot;
then that food is cooked on all sides by that hot water.
Once it has been digested, it becomes twofold: the waste matter (kiṭṭa) separately and the nutrient essence (rasa) separately.
With that essence, the vital breath (prāṇa) fills those channels once again.
Fully satisfied, they nourish the body from all sides;
the mother’s rasa-carrying channel is pierced by it and is called "supreme."
"Carrying the essence brought by the mother to the interior of the channel situated at the navel.
Regarding the phrase "from the day":
As it has been said:
"A creature [the size of] two *trasareṇu* atoms increases in size in a mere moment;
a louse [the size of] one *nāḍikā* in a measure of time, and a pair [of lice] in a *muhūrta*."
"And for lice, it is the number of Vedas [four] days; from just one day, it becomes two barley-corns.
And in the *Yogārṇava*: "In one night there is the *kalala*; in five nights, the bubble (*budbuda*);
in ten nights, blood; and on the fourteenth, the muscle-flesh (*māṃsapeśī*)."
On the twentieth day, there is thick flesh characterized by a solidified mass;
on the completion of twenty-five days, it becomes a *pala* and all the limbs begin to sprout.
When one month has been completed, he sustains the five elements;
when two months have arrived, the marrow of the head is produced.
The marrow and bones [are formed] in three months; the hair of the head and the fingernails in the fourth;
and the cavities of the ears, eyes, and nose in the fifth month.
"In the sixth month, the cavity of the mouth and the belly [are formed], and in the seventh, the anus;
by the eighth months, all the joints of the limbs are considered complete.
However, there is a specific distinction in the *Adhyātmaviveka*:
In the first month, a state of liquidity called *kalala* is produced;
in the second, however, it becomes a solid mass (*ghana*), then a *piṇḍa*, then a *peśī*, and finally a six-fold thickened *arvuda*.
Generally, these are the successive stages for males, females, and neuters:
in the third [week], the five sprouts of the hands, feet, and head are considered to appear.
At that time, the parts of the limbs and sub-limbs would be minute and simultaneous,
excluding the beard, teeth, and other features that arise immediately after birth.
This is considered by the wise to be the primary nature (prakṛti), while anything else is regarded as a modification (vikṛti);
in the fourth state, the manifestation of those very entities also arises.
His heart, born of his mother, longs for sense objects;
therefore, one should do what is pleasing to the mother for the sake of the embryo's growth.
The wise call that woman who possesses two hearts "one who destroys the body";
by not granting her longings, defects such as deformity may occur in the fetus.
When a mother suffers from the non-attainment of her desired objects, a son is born who is distressed;
if she experiences a longing upon seeing a king, the fetus will be wealthy and enjoyer of pleasures.
He was charming in his ornaments, devoted to righteousness in the hermitage of ascetics,
full of devotion upon seeing the gods, yet cruel when encountering snakes.
By eating iguana one becomes sleepy, but by eating beef one becomes strong;
by [eating] buffalo meat, however, one gives birth to a son with red eyes and hairy body.
In the fifth week, the embryo has fully developed, and there is nourishment by flesh and blood;
in the sixth, there is the distinct formation of bones, sinews, nails, hair, and body hair.
In the seventh month, strength and complexion increase and the limbs reach fullness;
in the eighth month, however, the skin and the sense of hearing are formed, as well as the vital energy (*ojas*) and consciousness (*cetas*) arising from the heart.
The sign in life is considered to be pure, yellowish, or reddish;
yet it runs restlessly back again to the mother and again to the womb.

"Therefore, one born in the eighth month does not live, being deprived of vital energy (*ojas*). Yājñavalkya also says: "The vital energy (*ojas*) of that [child] rushes back again to the nurse and again to the womb; therefore, one born from the womb in the eighth month is deprived of life."
Thus, it should be known that when the *ojas* (vital essence) resides in the fool [the child], then the mother does not live.
When, however, that *ojas* is in the hearts of both, then it should be known that there is no life for either of them.
"Possessing a body of principles" means having a body composed of the twenty-four principles (*tattva*).
He will explain the principles immediately thereafter. || 32 ||
When the *doṣas* (humors) reach the *dūṣyas* (vitiated elements), they easily manifest through one's own sense organs.
The *doṣas* are vāta, pitta, and kapha; the *dūṣyas* are the seven tissues (*dhātus*).
These are known as skin, blood, muscle, fat, bone, marrow, and semen. || 33 ||
Regarding the phrase "by the *doṣas*":
it means that, so as to bring about pleasure (*sukha*), [the embryo] reaches the *dūṣyas* (the bodily constituents) by means of the *doṣas*, and attains manifestation through its own sense organs.
By this, growth up until the eighth month is described.
He states the humors and so forth with the words "vāta" etc.;
"them" refers to the elements (dhātus).
It should be understood that among these, each preceding one is the cause for each succeeding one.
As it is stated in the Suśruta: "The tissues (dhātus)— lymph, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen—
all arise from one another, having been accumulated by the heat of pitta."
If it is asked, "How then can the skin be the cause for the production of blood?"—it is true that the skin and blood are both produced from the nutrient essence (*rasa*).
As it has been said: "The nutrient essence situated within the channels is intensely heated by the bodily heat..."
"It is cooked, and from that which is being cooked, two kinds of cooking occur again;
blood is produced by wrapping it all around with skin.
Also elsewhere: "Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the constituent elements (dhātus)."
It is said that there are seven layers there: skin and blood [are transformed] by the digestive fire.

"In this manner, from the food-essence (*annarasa*) once it has been digested, and likewise from blood and the other [tissues], the bodily constituents (*dhātavaḥ*) are produced in succession by their respective internal fires (*kośāgni*) as they digest them. Thus it is said.
However, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*, after reciting "skin" (*tvak*) and so forth, it is stated that "some read 'plasma-blood' (*rasāsṛk*). (33)
The wise know the organs of knowledge to be the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose;
the objects of the organs of knowledge are traditionally held to be sound and the rest; and there are also the organs of action. || 34 ||
The wise declare that speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals are designated as the organs of action, being associated respectively with speaking, grasping, moving, excretion, and pleasure. || 35 ||
The objects of the organs of action have been fully described; now the internal organ of the self is proclaimed as consisting of mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness. || 36 ||
It has been stated that [the self] attains manifestation through its own senses. In connection with those senses, he also mentions their objects by saying "knowledge," etc.;
in both cases, the word *artha* denotes "object."
"Sound and the rest" refers to sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
It should be noted that while these were previously mentioned among the qualities of the elements (*bhūtaguṇa*), they are here expressed by the word "etc. (*ādi*).
The term *andhu* signifies a mark (*liṅga*).
The phrase "the grasper of the self" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
By this, it is stated that the self is the object of the mind.
Furthermore, he explains the fourfold nature of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) with the words beginning "mind" (manaḥ).
In that context, the mind (manas) consists of volition and conceptualization;
the intellect (buddhi) determines all objects of existence;
and the ego (ahaṅkāra) is characterized by the conceit of being a knower.
The mind is non-conceptual;
such is the distinction between these.
As it has been said:
This supreme power, possessing the aforementioned characteristics, takes the form of the individual soul (jīva);
yet, when it engages in conceptualization and discursive thought, it becomes the mind (manas).
Likewise, that which takes the form of the intellect (buddhi) and effects the determination of all objects,
arising from the conceit "I am the knower," is designated as the ego (ahaṅkāra).
"That very [consciousness], whose nature is non-conceptual, is indeed the essence of the mind;
thus, though one alone, it is perceived in many ways, like a dancer. (34–36)

The ten sense organs, the five elements, and the mind together constitute sixteen; these are the modifications (vikāras). The five elements, the ego-sense (ahaṅkṛti), and the [other] principles are the eight primary natures (prakṛtis). || 37 ||

The knowers of reality recognize seven as the transformations (vikṛti): the unmanifest (avyakta), the great one (mahat), the eight subtle elements (tanmātra), and the great one (mahat) together with the ego (ahaṅkāra). || 38 ||
Thus, having previously mentioned the elements and the sense organs, he states their collective designations as "ten" in two verses.
Alternatively, since it was stated that [the body] possesses the principles (*tattvas*), he mentions those principles as "ten";
it should be understood that the designations such as "modifications" (*vikāra*) and so forth were mentioned by way of that same context.

Alternatively, according to the maxim of the needle and the frying pan (*sūcīkaṭāhanyāya*), having stated the defects along with the things to be corrupted, [the author] mentions the principles (*tattva*) indicated by the phrase "possessing the body of reality" (*tattvadehavān*).
In response to the inquiry "Which are these?", he says "knowledge," and so forth.
The meaning is that the objects of the organs of action are declared to be earth and the other elements.
Thus, the five elements, the ten faculties, and the ten objects of the faculties constitute the twenty-five principles (*tattva*).
As they say:
"The twenty-five principles are enumerated as the elements, the faculties, and the objects of the faculties."

Thus; and furthermore, by treating "visargānandasamyutā" as two separate words— since emission (*visarga*) alone is the function of the anus and the generative organ, whereas [the former] is devoid of bliss— it follows that the principles (*tattva*) are stated to be exactly twenty-four.
As they say:
"By those [factors] including bliss, the twenty-four principles are likewise proclaimed."

By this statement— namely, "mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and consciousness (citta)"— through the exclusion of speech and so forth, it is stated that there are twenty-four principles (tattvas) by virtue of being endowed with these four.
As they say:
"By these [factors] endowed with instruments, the principles (tattvas) are stated, being devoid of speech and so forth. Thus,
while stating the twenty-four principles taught in the Sāṃkhya doctrine, he also mentions some of their well-known designations, saying "ten."

By this, it is stated that there are twenty-four principles (*tattvas*): the ten faculties, the five gross elements, the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*), mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), and primordial matter (*pradhāna*), which is nature (*prakṛti*).
The author himself will state this in the fifth chapter:

"The five elements, the subtle essences (*tanmātra*), the sense organs, as well as the mind, ego (*ahaṃkāra*), intellect (*buddhi*), and primordial matter (*pradhāna*)—the wise know these as the 'friends' (*mitrāṇi*).
They are called 'transformations' (*vikāra*); their status as transformations is due to their nature as eternal effects."

The connection is that there are eight *prakṛtis*. Their status as *prakṛtis* (evolvents) is due to their being the causes for each subsequent member [of the series]. Here, by the word "elements" (*bhūta*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are meant.
This is because the effect is figuratively designated by the name of the cause;
because the elements are described as modifications solely in their capacity as effects;
and because there is a subsequent reference to them as "the subtle elements" (tanmātras).
As they say:
"The seven non-material elements are designated as both 'prakṛti' (evolvents) and 'vikṛti' (evolutes)."
The "unmanifest" (avyakta) means primordial nature (prakṛti), which is synonymous with the term *pradhāna*.
The phrase "the unmanifest is the Great One" (avyaktaṃ mahat) is a transposition [of the terms] for the sake of meter or for the sake of concealment.
The reading may be "sāvyaktaṃ mahat" (the unmanifest and the great), because here the order of dissolution is intended;
as they say: "The twenty-four principles, ending with Prakṛti, have been enumerated."
Thus it is said.
Elsewhere, with reference to the order of emanation, it is stated: "the unmanifest, the great [intellect], egoity, and the elements," and "the subtle elements."

The term "possessing ego" (*sāhaṅkāra*) is a qualifier for that alone; by it, there is a reversal [of the order]. By the word "and" (*ca*), there is a conjunction with the word "primordial natures" (*prakṛtayaḥ*). Therefore, the meaning is that these seven are denoted by the term "both primordial natures and evolutes" (*prakṛtivikṛti*).

Because each preceding element serves as the material cause (*prakṛti*) for each succeeding one, and each succeeding element serves as the modification (*vikṛti*) for each preceding one, these possess the nature of being both material causes and modifications.
As it has been said: "The root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is not a modification; the seven beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) are both material causes and modifications."

"The group of sixteen, however, is a modification; the Puruṣa is neither a primal nature nor a modification. Thus he concludes with the words "the knowers of reality know," the meaning of which is as follows:
This delineation of the principles (*tattva*) which I have provided, beginning with "the organs of knowledge" and ending here, is approved even by those who know the principles.
Alternatively, by the phrase "those who know the principles know," it is indicated that the principles mentioned in the three previous modes are not what we accept;
rather, these twenty-four principles, ending with *prakṛti*, alone are [our position].
There are twenty-five [principles] ending with the Puruṣa; there are twenty-six ending with the Supreme (Parā). This is what is meant by "our own accepted view. This interpretation is traditional.
As it is stated in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā:
"Beyond the twenty-three principles, Prakṛti is said to be supreme;
they declare the Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth, to be beyond Prakṛti."

"For that [Prakṛti] which is dissolved in its own nature, he who is beyond it is Maheśvara, because the activity of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa is dependent upon him. Some, however, interpret this differently.

Having described the creation of the ego (ahaṅkāra) from the *bhūtādi* [tamas], he now speaks of the objects of those senses— which were previously indicated by the statement "from the *taijasa* [rajas] arose the senses"— in connection with that topic,
using the passage beginning with "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and ending with "is proclaimed" (*parikīrtitam*).

Furthermore, as a supplement to the subsequent ritual practice (*vyavahāra*), and as a supplement to the application (*nyāsa*) of the phonemes and principles (*varṇatattva*) for certain mantras, he demonstrates the transformations (*vikāra*) and so forth, beginning with "ten" (*daśa*).
Those who know reality understand this:
because these [categories] are included therein, the knowers of reality have applied these designations; such is the meaning. || 37-38 ||
The body consists of Agni and Soma, for the *bindu* is of the nature of both;
its right portion is known as the Sun, and its left part is the Moon. || 39 ||
Having thus spoken incidentally, he states the subject at hand with the words "Agni...
The body consists of Agni and Soma.
To the question "Why?", he provides the reason: because the *bindu* (the seminal point) is composed of both.
Semen is the form of fire (Agni) and blood is the form of the moon (Soma); he consists of these two.
As it is said: "The moon has sixteen digits (kalās), while the sun has twelve."
Fire, joined with ten parts of *kalā*, consumes thirty-eight parts of *kalā*.
There are thirty-seven (or thirty-eight) [deities] here for the purpose of the conception; therefore, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is sung as being of the nature of Agni and Soma.
"Through the conjunction of a portion of *kalā*, the formation of the embryo occurs.
Thus, the meaning is that [the body] consists of the nature of Agni and Soma.
It has been stated that "the body consists of the nature of Agni and Soma."

He states their established status in specific locations for the sake of conventional usage, based on the distinction between their respective applications and so forth, in the verse beginning with *dakṣiṇāṃśe*.
In this scripture, the southern portion is sometimes referred to by the word "Agni" and sometimes by the word "Sūrya," as indicated by the statement:
"That which is the southern part of Agni."
In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā as well: "The function of the fiery [element] is indeed twofold: that which has the nature of the sun and that which has the nature of fire. (39)
They know there to be ten channels (nāḍīs), among which three are proclaimed as principal:
Iḍā on the left side of the body, Suṣumṇā in the middle, and Piṅgalā on the other side.
In order to establish the positions of the sun and moon mentioned previously, he speaks of the channels (*nāḍīs*) within the body, beginning with the words "the channels.
The syntactical connection is that among those infinite channels, they know ten channels to be the principal ones,
since it will be stated later that "the channels are infinite."
Among those ten, three are proclaimed as the primary ones.
The word "primary" (*mukhyā*) is to be applied by repetition to each of them.
The inclusion of the word "proclaimed" (*prakīrtitāḥ*) is for the sake of clarity, since its meaning would otherwise already be conveyed by the word "known" (*viduḥ*).

And it has been stated therein that the first three [channels] are considered the most important for performing the practice of non-return (*anāvṛtti*). He describes their very state with the words "Iḍā" and so forth.
The word "of the body" (*tanoh*) is connected to three locations.
On the left is *iḍā*, which, arising from the left testicle and being curved like a bow, extends as far as the left nostril—this is the meaning.
In the middle of the body is *suṣumṇā*, situated within the spinal column.
This is because of the statement: "That which has entered the cavity between the base of the head and the end of the staff.
The meaning is that in the other [nostril], the right one, [the breath] arising from the right testicle, curved like a bow, goes as far as the right nostril.
As they say:
That [nāḍī] which is connected to the left testicle, embracing the *suṣumṇā*,
rests upon the right kidney and, curved like a bow, is situated in the heart.
"From the left shoulder, passing between the collarbones, it should go to the right nostril;
and likewise, arising from the right testicle, it should go to the left aperture of the nose. Thus it is said.
Also in another tantra: "That which is fashioned as the Suṣumṇā, having gone there, rests upon the right testicle."
Situated in the heart, it rests upon the middle of the collarbone of the left side.
"O Daughter of the Mountain, one [nāḍī] reaches the right nostril,
while the other, arising from the left groin, likewise reaches the left nostril.
The nature of these two is described in the *Yogārṇava*:
"The *iḍā*, resembling a conch or a jasmine flower, is situated on its left;
the *piṅgalā*, with a white-red luster, rests upon the right side.
By this, the presence of the sun and the moon in the *piṅgalā* and *iḍā* respectively is stated.
"Because it is said: 'The moon moves in the iḍā, and the sun in the piṅgalā. — [40]
Among those [channels], the central channel (nāḍī) should be of the nature of Agni and Soma. || 41 ||
Stating that the *suṣumṇā* is the principal [of the channels], he describes its nature with the words "in the middle.
By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "among those also," the term "principal" (*mukhyā*) is understood to carry over.
Among those three, the *suṣumṇā* in the middle is the principal one.
Because of the statement, "And the *suṣumṇā* alone is the channel among them," it is of the nature of Agni and Soma; this should be applied as the reason for its primacy.
Because the previously mentioned *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, which take the form of Soma and Agni, dissolve right here;
as it has been said: "having entered the mouth of Rāhu.
By this, it is also stated that her station extends as far as the *brahmarandhra*.
As they say:
"Between those two, the Suṣumṇā is situated, resting against the spinal column as far as the Brahmarandhra. || 41 ||
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Supūṣā, Alambuṣā, Yaśasvinī, Śaṅkhinī, and Kuhū are considered to be the seven nāḍīs. || 42 ||
He states the names of the remaining seven as "Gāndhārī" and so forth. Their locations and essential natures are described in the *Yogārṇava*:
"On the back of the *iḍā* is Gāndhārī, resembling the throat of a peacock."
Gāndhārī is proclaimed as extending from the left foot up to the eyes.
A channel resembling an elephant’s tongue and a blue lotus stands before it,
extending from the head on the left side down to the big toe of the foot.
Pūṣan, however, is on the back of Piṅgalā; resembling a dark blue cloud, she extends from the corner of the eye of the southern side as far as the soles of the feet.
Alambuṣā is yellow in color and is situated in the middle of the throat;
Yaśasvinī is conch-colored and resides in the eastern region of Piṅgalā.
The Śaṅkhinī is considered to be situated between Gāndhārī and Sarasvatī;
it is golden-colored and extends from the feet to the ears on the left side.
"From the big toe to the top of the head on the southern side, it is considered to be Kuhū.
By others, however, Vāraṇā, Sarasvatī, Viśvodarā, and Payasvinī are also mentioned as being primary.
As they say:
"And those [channels] are very numerous; among them, fourteen are declared to be the principal ones:
Suṣumṇā, Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Kuhū, and Sarasvatī..."
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, the illustrious Vāraṇā,
Viśvodarā, Śaṅkhinī, and then Pūṣā and Payasvinī.
Alambuṣā. Thus. Also elsewhere: "In this body, fourteen channels (nāḍīs) are traditionally held to be primary."
Thus [it is said].
Their meditations and forms have not been described here for fear of making the book too voluminous;
they are indicated by the very term "principal" (mukhyāḥ). || 42 ||
Infinite channels have arisen from the five joints of the Suṣumṇā;
the vital breath (prāṇa), having risen from the Mūlādhāra, pervades that body by means of them. || 43 ||
Having thus described the principal channels, he speaks of the general ones with the words "the channels.
From the five joints of the *suṣumṇā*, infinite channels have arisen.
The five joints are those ending with the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, *maṇipūraka*, *anāhata*, *viśuddha*, and *ājñā*.
In this context, the completion of a joint (*parva*) occurs from each lower knot (*granthi*) up to the next upper knot.

Although the lexicon states, "A *granthi* is a joint (*parva*) or a knotty fiber (*paruṣī*)," and common usage refers to it as "the limit of a sugarcane joint," nevertheless, because there are six knots here, it is explained in this manner.

Because the author of the *Āśvalāyana-Śrautasūtra-Bhāṣya* has explained the word *parvan* in this manner in the passage, "One should mutter [the mantra] on the *parvan*," he will likewise state with this very intention: "On the joint of the thumb and the finger.
It should be understood that at these joints of the *suṣumṇā*, there occurs a conjunction (*yoga*) of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*.
"Infinite" (*anantā*) means infinity because they are impossible to count;
as it is said: "O fair-eyed one, [they are within] the previously mentioned *suṣumṇā* situated in the center."
They arise from the navel, the heart, the throat region, the space between the eyebrows, and the joints.
Some vessels have their openings facing downward, some likewise face upward,
and others have their openings directed horizontally; there are more than three hundred thousand such vessels,
while those declared to be principal are said to number fifty thousand.
In all of them, the powerful vital breath, Vāyu, is present on every side.
"It is eternally established and all-pervading.
However, there is a distinction in the *Adhyātmaviveka*:—
The number of bones in the body is three hundred and sixty;
however, Dhanvantari has declared that there are exactly three hundred bones here.
In this body, there are two hundred and ten bone-joints;
the joints of the muscles, ligaments, and vessels are considered to be two thousand.
There are nine hundred ligaments and five hundred muscles;
in women, there are twenty additional ones in the breasts and ten in the womb.

"Regarding the veins and arteries, there are twenty-nine lakhs [29,000,000], as well as nine hundred and fifty-six. Thus it is said. He states the result of those channels beginning with the word "mūla":
The primary wind called *prāṇa*, which is distinct from those to be described hereafter, is the sustainer of the body;
as they say:
"The *rājasa* [wind] known as *prāṇa* is the primary sustainer of the body."
"Those divisions are renowned as ten, by which the body is pervaded.
That is the aforementioned body, "sā cāsau tanuḥ," meaning that very body. (43)
Here, ten winds are proclaimed and ten fires are remembered;
the five vital airs beginning with prāṇa, as well as nāga, kūrma, and dhanañjaya. || 44 ||
These ten fires, which are said to be named Kṛkala, Devadatta, and so forth, reside within embodied beings when they are afflicted by the defects of the bodily constituents. || 45 ||
While describing its divisions, he mentions the fires as well by way of context, saying "the winds are here.
He states their names themselves as "prāṇa and the rest. By the word "and the rest" (ādi), apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna are included; they are mentioned first because they are well-known.
Regarding this, the specific detail is given in the *Yogārṇava*: "The form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is proclaimed to resemble a sapphire;
it resides in the middle of the mouth and nose, in the center of the heart, and in the middle of the navel."
Some say that the *prāṇa* resides even in the big toe;
this *apāna*, however, carries away food and waste products.
The apāna wind carries out semen, urine, and excrement;
it resembles an indragopa insect and is like a twilight cloud.
And it resides in the penis and the anus, in the thighs, the groins, and the knees;
in the shanks, the belly, the nape of the neck, and at the root of the navel.
Vyāna circulates the food and provokes all diseases;
it resembles great silver and is the cause of rejection and acquisition.
And it remains there continuously between the eyes and the ears, at the waist and also at the ankles, as well as in the nose, the throat, and the region of the buttocks.
The vital air named Udāna causes the lower lip and the face to quiver, provokes agitation in the limbs and eyes,
and agitates the vital points (marmas).
Having the color of lightning or fire, he causes one to rise from bed or leave one's seat;
he abides in the joints of both the feet and the hands.
The wind named Samāna brings into equilibrium the blood, bile, phlegm, and wind that have been drunk, eaten, or inhaled, as well as the limbs of the body.
Residing throughout the entire body, its form is like cow's milk;
in the act of belching, it is called Nāga, resembling a dark blue cloud.
The *kūrma* [vāyu] is situated in the opening of the eyes and has a luster like crushed collyrium;
the *kṛkara*, however, is in the act of sneezing and resembles the *javā* flower.
In yawning, Devadatta is like pure crystal;
likewise, in the sound, Dhanañjaya has the color of great gold.

"On the forehead, the chest, the shoulders, the heart, the navel, and in the skin and bones—the five winds, beginning with Nāga, are firmly established together. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the teacher named Dhanañjaya states: "In this body, one should produce various kinds of sounds."
"But because it is worldly air, it does not leave the dead.
However, others have stated that there are four additional winds:
Vairambhaṇa, Sthānamukhya, Pradyota, and likewise Prakṛta.
"The Vairambhaṇas and others there have all come under the power of the winds.
Thus he describes the abiding state of the fires with the words "the fires.
Their names are stated elsewhere as follows:
All those Jātavedas were Kalmāṣa, Kusuma,
Dahana, Śoṣaṇa, and the mighty Tapana.
"Piṭhara, Pataga, Svarṇa, Agādha, and Bhrāja.
However, elsewhere other names are mentioned:
Jṛmbhaka, Dīpaka, Vibhrama, Bhrama, Śobhana,
Āvasthya, Āhavanīya, and likewise Dakṣiṇāgni.
"In the *anvāhārya* [fire] and the *gārhapatya*—these are the ten carriers (*vahni*s).
Thus it is said. Others have stated them differently: "The radiant (*bhrājaka*), the coloring (*rañjaka*), the moistening (*kledaka*), and likewise the lubricating (*snehaka*)."
The supporter, the cooker, and the seventh is called the dissolver.
The pervasive, the purifying, and the phlegmatic is recorded as the tenth.
Thus, the humors (doṣas) are wind, bile, and phlegm.
It has already been stated that the seven constituents (dhātus) are subject to corruption. || 44–45 ||
Hunger and thirst belong to the vital breath (prāṇa); memory belongs to the mind (manas);
grief and delusion belong to the intellect (buddhi); and old age and death belong to the body—these are the six waves. || 46 ||
Having thus spoken of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he describes its specific states; and in this context, he also speaks of the mind and the body, beginning with "hunger" (*bubhukṣā*).
A "wave" (*ūmi*) is a particular state that produces affliction. (46)
Tendons, bones, and marrow arise from semen; skin, flesh, and blood arise from blood.
This body of six sheaths (ṣāṭkauśika) is said to exist in all the bodies of embodied beings.

In speaking of the sixfold sheath (*ṣāṭkauśika*) as a consequence of the six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*), he explains the products of semen and blood by distinguishing them: "sinews," etc.; from the father's semen come sinews and so forth;
from the mother's blood come skin and so forth.
As it has been said: "Three from the mother, three from the father.
But elsewhere: "The marrow, blood, fat, flesh, spleen, liver, and rectum [are from the mother]."
States such as the heart, the navel, and so forth, are considered to be born of the mother.
"The beard, body hair, head hair, sinews, veins, arteries, nails, teeth, semen, and so forth—these stable elements are derived from the father. (47)
Being thus situated in the womb, remembering the good and evil deeds of his previous birth, he remains there, miserable in nature, his body covered by the fetal membrane.
He describes the manner of its abiding in the womb with the words "thus situated" (*itthambhūta*).
The meaning is that, thus situated—with hands placed between the thighs and ears covered—leaning against the mother's back, he meditates upon the means of liberation.
As they say:
Covering the openings of his ears with his hands placed between his thighs,
he remains in the womb, agitated by his dwelling there and filled with fear.

"Remembering the various births and torments previously experienced, and contemplating the means to liberation, he remains devoted to practice. In another place, there is this distinction: "With palms joined at his forehead, he rests upon the back of his mother."
With his limbs contracted, he dwells within the womb, situated on the right side.
A woman leaning toward the left side is considered to indicate a eunuch; one leaning toward the middle is likewise considered so.
Thus [ends verse 48].
In the course of time, even while causing distress to his mother,
that infant is then born with his body curled up and his face turned downwards.
He stands motionless for a moment, wishing to weep out of fear. || 50 ||
Regarding the phrase "in the course of time," Yājñavalkya states the sequence of time as follows: "In the ninth or even the tenth [month].
Elsewhere it is also said: "The time for birth is then in the ninth month and so forth."
Thus, with his body contracted, his limbs shriveled, and his face turned downwards— that is, facing down— he is born, meaning he is produced,
impelled by the winds of childbirth; this is the understood sense of the passage.
As they say:
"In the ninth or tenth month, by powerful winds of labor,
the creature is expelled through the opening like an arrow, accompanied by feverish distress."
Elsewhere it is also said: "Then, with his head downward, the infant is forced out through the opening of the womb by powerful birth-winds, his limbs pained.
He remains motionless on the ground for a moment; this is the implied meaning. (49-50)
Then she, whose nature is consciousness, all-pervading, and possessing the form of the universe,
having attained the presence of Śiva, became the source of the qualities of eternal bliss.

Having thus described the creation of objects up to the formation of the body, he now speaks of the creation of sound— which was mentioned generally in the verse, "Having attained that" (1.14)— by analyzing it.
Stating that one desires to weep out of fear, and explaining the manner in which phonemes arise since even the aforementioned weeping consists of unmanifest phonemes,
he says "Then," etc., describing how all mantras arise in general from the Kuṇḍalinī.
As it has been said:
"The state that first arises from the *mūlādhāra* is called *parā*; thereafter, that which goes to the heart and is joined with the intellect is called *paśyantī* and *madhyamā*."

Then, as this living being desires to weep, the *vaikharī* [speech] arises in the mouth; from that, bound by the *suṣumṇā*, the collection of phonemes (*varṇasaṅgha*) comes forth, impelled by the vital air (*pavana*).
"Because the channel-path is undivided, there is no manifestation of phonemes therein. Thus,
after the arising of the body from that [source], that Goddess Kuṇḍalinī— the Supreme Deity— is of the nature of consciousness and, for that very reason, consists of the Śabda-Brahman.

Multiplied by all her limbs, and therefore awakened—that is, having attained consciousness—by the Universal Self (Viśvātman), the All-Self (Sarvātman), she gives birth to the world consisting of mantra;
this is the connection [of the sentence] at a distance.
In that regard, within the Mūlādhāra, there exists a channel (nāḍī) coiled like a serpent.
The movement of this [power] within that [space] by the force of the vital air (vāyu) is itself its "repetition" (guṇana).
In that context, the phrase "consisting of consciousness" is a description of her essential nature (svarūpa). She is well-known.
"Omnipresent" indicates general pervasion;
"possessing all forms" indicates pervasion of the objects of experience.
The remainder is: "she remains having attained proximity to Śiva."
By this, it is stated that in the Śaivasiddhānta, she is denoted by the word "Śakti.
The term "proximity" (sannidhi) is used figuratively,
because in that system there is non-difference between Śiva and Śakti.
As it has been said by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta:
"Power does not seek separation from the nature of the possessor of power;
there is an eternal identity between these two, just as between fire and its capacity to burn."
Alternatively, "perfect treasure" (samyannidhiḥ) means having attained one's own nature, which is the nature of Śiva; for he will say: "The body (piṇḍa) becomes Kuṇḍalinī, whose self is Śiva.
She is that in whom there is the arising (udaya) of the qualities (guṇas)—namely, sattva, rajas, and tamas.
She is both eternal bliss and the source of the qualities (*guṇa*).
By the term "eternal bliss," her nature as Kuṇḍalinī is expressed;
by the term "source of the qualities," she is said to be that which is denoted by *prakṛti* according to the Sāṃkhya system.
As they say: "That which they call *pradhāna* is what is described as *śakti*. || 51 ||
Unconditioned by space, time, and the like, auspicious, and pervading all bodies—
this is remembered as the Supreme Power (paraśakti), distinguished by the division of the higher and the lower.
She dances eternally and effortlessly within the heart-lotus of yogins, flashing like lightning in the foundational support (ādhāra) of all beings. || 53 ||
The Goddess stands encompassing everything in the manner of a conch-spiral,
having assumed the graceful beauty of the limbs of serpents coiled into rings.
The Goddess consists of all the gods; she is auspicious and consists of all mantras;
she is manifest as the essence of all principles (tattvas), subtler than the subtle, and all-pervading.

Now, he describes its pervasiveness according to the sequence of the internal (ādhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), the qualities (adhiguṇa), the objects (adhiviṣaya), and the celestial (adhijyautiṣa): "Direction and time," etc.
"Following all bodies" refers to its pervasion of the body.
This is the division into the higher and the lower.
She is a certain supreme power (paraśakti), and even through her differentiation, she remains this very same supreme power.
As they say: "Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, and intellect..."
This nature of mine, called egoism, is divided eightfold.

"Know that this lower nature of Mine is distinct from another, higher nature, O mighty-armed one, which is the living soul (jīva), by which this world is sustained. Alternatively, "para" refers to the gross, and "apara" to the very gross, such as the Mahat-tattva and so forth; through that distinction, there is the supreme power (para-śakti) and the gross power (sthūla-śakti).
Because of the statement, "from the gross, the gross," this indicates pervasion by Mahat and the other principles.
Alternatively, by the phrase "pervading all bodies," the pervasion of the masculine, feminine, and neuter genders is shown both by word and by meaning.

In terms of terminology, she is called Śiva, she is called Kuṇḍalinī, and she is called Pradhāna. Yet, even though she is of such a nature, she is designated specifically as female; thus he says, "She is both Parā and Aparā. Parā is Prakṛti, and Aparā is the male and neuter Prakṛti. By means of that distinction, or by the abandonment of that [distinction], this Supreme Power (Paraśakti) is so remembered.
This is the meaning:

although she is denoted by the three genders, nevertheless, because she is the wish-fulfilling creeper that instantly satisfies every desire of the devotees who are exhausted by the burden of their unwavering devotion,
she is denoted by the term "Paraśakti" (the Supreme Power).
For this very reason, she is auspicious and delightful;
as the teachers have said:
"Though equal to both males and neuters, she excels among women."
Thus it is said; and also in the *Nityaklinnāmnāya*:
"For she resides everywhere, especially within passionate women."
"Then [the reality] shines forth; therefore, one should not cause them to transcend it.
"Añjasā" means by way of its true nature (*tattvena*).
By the phrase "dancing eternally in the lotus-heart of yogins," the meaning is that it is known by those very [yogins] through the instruction of the Guru.

Because it is said, "She is visible to those taught by the Teacher," the specification of her location is given by the phrase "throbbing in the *mūlādhāra-cakra*, the support of all beings— that is, all living creatures.
By the phrase "having the form of lightning," the method of meditation (*dhyāna*) is described.

As they say: "Resembling ten million flashes of lightning, with a luster that surpasses the glow of the fire of cosmic destruction by its own radiance. Alternatively, it is stated that she possesses manifold splendors because she is the cause for the production of numerous sounds.
The meaning is that just as the spiral within a conch shell remains encircling the conch and is known as "glory" (yaśas), so too is this Goddess.
This intermediate sentence is indeed distinct.
The connection between the words "conch" (śaṅkha) and "Kuṇḍalinī" is established through a relationship of cause and effect.
"Of those serpents that have become coiled, having attained the form of a coil"—
some explain *kuṇḍalī* as a separate word;
[they say] the meaning is that these beings and serpents likewise have such crooked movements, and this [speech] is like that.
That is not so;
for [the phrase] "the one with earrings is the supreme deity" would be a tautology.
The expression "consisting of all deities" refers to the pervasiveness of the gods.
She "shines" (divyati), thus she is the Goddess (devī), meaning she is of the nature of splendor; by this, her pervasion as splendor is indicated.
She is "consisting of all mantras," which indicates her pervasion as mantra.
"Śivā" means having the form of Śiva;
or alternatively, "śivā" means having an auspicious form.
By this, the pervasion of auspiciousness is indicated.
"Manifestly consisting of all principles" refers to the pervasion of the principles (*tattva-vyāpti*).
Regarding the apparent contradiction in the statement "the pervasive one is subtler than the subtle," the resolution is that "subtler than the subtle" means difficult to perceive;
or else, it is subtler even than a *trasareṇu* (a mote of dust), being more subtle because it resides within, and thus more minute.
By this, the pervasiveness [of consciousness] down to the atom and so forth is demonstrated.
As it has been said:
"That which [is perceived] by a single part of a hair-tip split a thousandfold..."
"Because of her subtlety, she is like [the infinite] mother of the three worlds.
Thus, she is all-pervading (*vibhu*), incapable of being known by means of measurement (*iyattā*). (52–55)
The Goddess, the mother of the three abodes, whose nature is the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), consists of forty-two letters and takes the form of fifty letters. || 56 ||
The Kuṇḍalinī, the supreme deity, pervading all the limbs, when awakened by the Universal Self, gives birth to the world consisting of mantra. || 57 ||
"Tridhāma" means having the form of the moon, sun, and fire;
alternatively, "tridhāma" refers to the three locations,
namely the netherworld (pātāla), the earth, and heaven.
By this, the pervasion of the locations (sthāna) has been shown.
"Consisting of the essence of forty-two phonemes" means she is composed of the *bhūtalipi* mantra; "having the form of fifty phonemes" means she is composed of the *mātṛkā*. (56–57)
The Śakti, multiplied by one, is the impeller of the entire universe;
it is the seed-syllable of the Vedas, the seed-syllable of Śrī, the seed-syllable of Śakti, and that of Manobhava (the god of love). || 58 ||
Prāsāda, Tumburu, Piṇḍa, Cintāratna, Gaṇeśvara, Mārttaṇḍabhairava, Daurga, and that which is born of Nārasiṃha and Varāha. || 59 ||
He then certainly produces Vāsudeva, Hayagrīva, the seed-syllable of Śrī Puruṣottama, and other seed-syllables as well. 60.

Having thus described the general process of manifestation, he begins to explain the creation of sound (*śabda-sṛṣṭi*) through its specific forms—such as single or dual—as well as, by occasion, the subsequent creation of objects (*artha-sṛṣṭi*) indicated by the sounds of that world, starting with the words "ekadhā" and so forth.
The entire universe consists of the form of word and meaning; *tatpravartinī* is the power that brings them forth, their producer.
The connection is that when multiplied by one, it produces the seed-syllable of the Vedas and so forth; this should be understood likewise in what follows.
He will explain the seed-syllable of the Vedas, namely the *praṇava*, later on.
The seed-syllable of Śrī is in the eighth;
the seed-syllable of Śakti is in the ninth;
and the seed-syllable of Manobhava is in the seventeenth.
The *prāsāda* [tune] is in the eighteenth;
*tumburu* in the nineteenth;
and *piṇḍa* in the penultimate.
The Cintāratna is in the nineteenth;
Gaṇeśvara is in the thirteenth;
and Mārttaṇḍabhairava is in the fourteenth.
The Daurga [Purāṇa] in the eleventh;
the Nārasiṃha in the sixteenth;
the Vārāha in the fifteenth.
"Glauṃ" is Vāsudeva;
this is extracted as the seed-syllable (bīja) of Gopāla,
and it is expressed by the word "Vāsudeva."
That [is taught] in the seventeenth [chapter].
The seed-syllable of Vāsudeva, which is merely the ether (viyanmātra), is taught in the Nāradapañcarātra;
Hayagrīva is [taught] in the fifteenth.

Because it is stated that "Śrīpuruṣottama" means "the Puruṣottama endowed with Śrī," and because of the non-difference between power (śakti) and the possessor of power (śaktimān), the seed-syllable of the power of Puruṣottama is expressed by the term "the seed-syllable of Śrīpuruṣottama. That [is described] in the seventeenth [chapter].
In this context, the seed-syllable of Kāma itself is stated to be the seed-syllable of Puruṣottama.
As they say: "Brahmā, embraced by Dharā and adorned with Māyā and the Bindu, is here the deity known as Puruṣottama, whose form is that of Manmatha."
"Others as well" refers to the seed-syllables of the moon, the seed-syllables of the image, and so forth. (58–60)
When that consciousness becomes doubled in form, it consists of the two—
the Supreme Self and the individual self, as well as sound and meaning— resembling swans during day and night.
Then this supreme goddess creates both Prakṛti and Puruṣa;
whatever other pairs exist in this world, all that was born from her. || 62 ||
With all her limbs tripled, she whose form is consciousness, the consort of Śiva, gives birth to the Traipura mantra, the mantra of the three cavities, and the Caṇḍanāyaka. || 63 ||
The solar mantra, the Mṛtyuñjaya, the Śaktisambhava, the Vinatāsuta, the three-syllabled mantra of Vāgīśī, and the Nīlakaṇṭha which destroys poison. || 64 ||
"In the fourteenth [verse], the two syllables 'haṃsa' [are mentioned].
