This is connected with the phrase "the two syllables denoting the Supreme Self. The meaning is that they are expressive of the Supreme Self (paramātman).
Those two,
Prakṛti and Puruṣa, are of the nature of "I" (so'ham) and "That" (tat).
Although Puruṣa is beginningless, his manifestation here is figuratively attributed to him due to his being colored by Māyā.
The connection is that whatever other pair was born in the world from her presence—
that is the light, the mantra, and so forth;
the two mantras of Tripura are in the twelfth [chapter].

On the thirteenth [day], Śaktivināyaka. Although it subsequently becomes twelve syllables through the addition of nine syllables, it nevertheless consists of three seed-syllables (*bīja*), because the triad is predominant by virtue of being composed of seed-syllables; or else, as stated in another tantra, it is *hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ*.
The first [mantra] beginning with *pāśa* is in the ninth [chapter].
"Three-syllabled" refers to two *trikaṇṭakī*s in the tenth [chapter],
or else it denotes the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified.
Traipuṭa is in the tenth;
Caṇḍanāyaka and Caṇḍeśvara are in the twentieth;
Saura is in the fourteenth.
The *Mṛtyuñjaya* [mantra] is in the eighteenth [chapter];
the two mantras arising from Śakti are in the ninth.
Regarding the reading "the Śākta and the Śāmbhava," the Śāmbhava is that which is taught in another tantra, consisting of the *praṇava*, the *māyā-bīja*, and the *prāsāda*.
"Cast [it] at the son of Vinatā, Oṃ"—this is stated in another tantra.
The three-syllabled mantra of Vāgīśī is in the seventh [position].
In the reading "Vāgīśa," the three-syllabled [mantra] is the single Śākta [mantra] located in the ninth position.
In the nineteenth [chapter], [there is] the Nīlakaṇṭha [mantra], which removes poison. || 61–64 ||
The Yantra is the triple-folded Goddess; it is the three worlds, the three qualities (guṇas), the three abodes, the triad of the Vedas, and the auspicious triad of letters. || 65 ||
The Goddess is the three Puṣkaras, the vowels, and the triad of Brahmā and the other gods;
she is the fire, the three times, the triple power, the great triple state, the three channels, the three aims of life, and whatever else is considered to be threefold. || 66 ||
The *yantra* is in the ninth [chapter].
The three qualities (*guṇatraya*) and the three abodes (*dhāmatraya*) are in the fourth.

Although the *Atharvaveda* exists, it is nevertheless called the "three Vedas" because the sacrifice is accomplished through the three constituent elements consisting of the *hotṛ*, *adhvaryu*, and *udgātṛ*.
The Śruti also states: "This very Trayī-vidyā [is present] in the sacrifice.
The three phonemes of the Praṇava are the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*.
Tripuṣkara refers to the triad of sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
Its threefold nature is due to being eldest, middle, and youngest. The vowels are the acute (udātta), the grave (anudātta), and the circumflex (svarita).
The goddesses are Gāyatrī, Sarasvatī, and Sāvitrī.
The triad of Brahmā and the others—namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—is in the ninth [verse].
The word "Devī" is a separate term serving as an epithet for Kuṇḍalī.
The triad of fires consists of the Dakṣiṇāgni, Gārhapatya, and Āhavanīya.
The three times consist of the past, present, and future, or alternatively, the forms of morning, midday, and evening.
The three powers (śakti) consist of Raudrī, Jyeṣṭhā, and Vāmā, or alternatively, they consist of majesty (prabhāva), energy (utsāha), and mantra. These [powers] exist in the first [of the three].
The three modes of livelihood consist of sacrificing, teaching, and receiving gifts, according to the traditional injunction: "Three activities constitute one's livelihood.
Alternatively, the three modes of livelihood may be agriculture, animal husbandry, and trade.
In the reading "mahat," the word "mahat" should be construed as an adjective qualifying the triad of channels.
The triad of channels consists of *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumṇā* in the first [verse].
The "threefold group" (*trivarga*) refers to virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*).
As it is said, "The triad [of goals] consists of dharma, kāma, and artha.
"Anything else" refers to the three defects and so forth. 65–66.
The Śāmbhavī [mudrā], which bestows happiness, is multiplied by fourfold;
at that time, it produces the four-syllabled [mantra] of the Lord of the Padminīs. || 67 ||
The four oceans are the fourfold reality of the Goddess belonging to Mahādevī; they are the four internal organs [of the senses]. || 68 ||
Regarding the phrase "of the friend of the lotus-lake":
this refers to that which consists of the syllables *praṇava*, *māyā*, and *haṃsa*, as stated in another tantra;
it belongs to the eighth [chapter] of Mahādevī, the Great Lakṣmī.
The fourfold reality of the Goddess consists of the reality of the self (ātmatattva), the reality of knowledge (vidyātattva), the reality of Śiva (śivatattva), and the reality of all (sarvatattva).
Regarding the phrase "the four oceans," this refers to a quartet in relation to the directions starting from the east; however, in actual fact, it is one.
The internal organs consist of the forms of mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and consciousness (citta). || 67–68 ||
The four states beginning with the subtle (sūkṣma) are the fourfold forms of Viṣṇu;
the fourfold group of Gaṇeśas is the fourfold group beginning with the Self (ātman). || 69 ||

The sacred seats (pīṭhas) beginning with Ojāpūka, the fourfold group beginning with Dharma, the elephants beginning with Damaka, and whatever other tetrad exists—[all these belong] to the Goddess. || 70 ||
Regarding the phrase "the subtle and so forth" (*sūkṣmādīn*): in the first [verse], "subtle" (*sūkṣmā*) refers to *parā*.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī* are included. As it has been said: "Vaikharī, madhyamā, paśyantī, and also sūkṣmā."
"These [states] arise out of order, starting from Kuṇḍalinī in sequence.
Thus, "states" (bhāvān) refers to the specific conditions of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turīya);
or it refers to the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified.
The eighth [verse] is for the forms of Viṣṇu;
"of the Gaṇeśas" is for the thirteenth;
and "of the Self and so forth" is for the fourth.
"Seat" (pīṭha) refers to Oḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, Pūrṇagiri, and Kāmarūpa.
"Of dharma and so forth" refers to the fourth [tetrad];
it is also indicative of adharma and the others.
Or [the initiation] for the sake of dharma, wealth, and so forth, at the beginning of that;

"of elephants" refers to the eighth [chapter]; "other" refers to the initiation into the maṇḍala of Siddha and others, the mantra of Heramba, the seed-syllables of the Goddess and the Dūtīs, and so forth. (69–70)
The consort of Śambhu, who bestows all goals, is multiplied fivefold;
she is Tripurā, the five peaks, and her two groups of five syllables.
The five-jeweled mantra of the Great Goddess bestows the fruit of all desires;
the five-syllabled mantra of Maheśa [is likewise], as is the five-colored [mantra] of Garuḍa. || 72 ||
The five objects of desire which cause delusion, the five arrows of the celestial tree,
the five vital breaths beginning with prāṇa, and the five colors of the Great Lord.
This Supreme Power, whose form consists of the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas, sequentially creates the five forms, the five Kalās, and the five Brahma-Ṛks. || 74 ||
"In five ways" means that she emits [the phonemes] beginning with the five peaks (pañcakūṭa) in sequence;
the sequence, however, will be explained later as beginning with the power (śakti) and the resonance (dhvani).

Likewise, in the subsequent [passages] as well, the words "according to the sequence of six" (*ṣaṭkramāt*) should be joined with the creation of sound, and this same meaning should be explained for them.
Regarding the term "five-peaked" (*pañcakūṭam*): *ha*, *sa*, *ka*, *la*, and *ra*—these five phonemes, when unified, are designated by the word "peak" (*kūṭa*).
Regarding her, there are two groups of five syllables:
one consisting of the five objects of desire (*pañcakāma*), and the other consisting of the seed-syllables of the arrows (*vāṇabīja*); these constitute the twelve [syllables].
This has been stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
O Maheśvarī, the five arrows are said to be within the mantra of Tripureśī;
by means of those very five arrows, the five-syllabled [mantra] is to be known.
"By means of the five desires previously mentioned, one becomes Pañcakāmeśvarī.
Thus [ends the section on] the "Five Jewels."
The fivefold mantra stated in another tantra is: *gluṃ*, *śluṃ*, *mluṃ*, *pluṃ*, and *nluṃ*.
[These correspond to] Siddhā and the others: Vijayā, Śyāmā, Vārāhī, and Sundarī.
"Of Maheśa" refers to the eighteenth [chapter];
"of Garuḍa" refers to the twenty-fourth;
and "the deluders" (*samohanān*) is in the plural to include the deluders and others.
In the twelfth [chapter], he describes the arrows as sensual pleasures, and the celestial trees as the *mandāra*, *pārijāta*, *saṃtāna*, *kalpadruma*,
and *haricandana*.
The winds in the first [circle],
and the colors, white and so forth, in the third;
[this refers to] the Great Lord.
It is connected with what follows:
the forms [are described] in the eighteenth [chapter],
and the kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, in the first.
In the eighteenth [chapter], the *brahmaṛcas* beginning with Īśāna and others are to be known;

"the rest" refers to that which, through the distinction between the *bhūta* and the *praṇava*, maintains, ordains, and performs the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth, along with the solar form—this is the meaning. (71–74)
Multiplied sixfold, that Goddess bears the six-syllabled mantra;
she bears the six-peak Tripurā-mantra and the six-syllabled Gāṇapatya-mantra. || 75 ||
The six-syllabled [mantra] of the moon, the six-syllabled Nārasiṃha, the six seasons headed by spring, and the lords of the Gaṇas beginning with Āmoda. || 76 ||
The Supreme Goddess produced the treasuries (kośa), the waves (ūrmi), the flavors (rasa), the powers (śakti), the six paths beginning with Śākinī,
the sixfold machine (yantra) of Śakti,
and the six supports (ādhāra); whatever is sixfold in this world, all that is the Supreme Goddess.
The six-syllabled Rāma-mantra is [taught] in the fifteenth [chapter].
"Six-peaked" (ṣaṭkūṭa) is as stated in the Tripurārṇava;
the "six-peaked" refers to the central seed-syllable (madhyabīja).

As it has been said: "The syllable *daṇḍi* (DAM), accompanied by the eyes of the beloved (*kāntā*), the end of the beloved (*antā*), the one agitated by the end of the beloved (*vāntākulalānta*), and the left (*vāma*), together with sound (*sanāda*)—this six-peaked mantra, declared in the *Tripurārṇava*, is the most secret; remember it as the manifest God of Love himself. Thus.
The *gāṇapatya* [mantra] mentioned in another tantra consists of *vakratuṇḍa* ending in the dative case and followed by the *varma* [seed-syllable].
The six-syllabled Śaiva mantra is in the eighteenth [chapter],
and the six-syllabled Kṛṣṇa mantra is in the seventeenth.
Or there is the relationship of qualifier and qualified.
The six-syllable [mantra] of Himaruci is in the fourteenth [chapter],
and the Nārasiṃha [mantra] is in the sixteenth.
The six-syllabled Pāśupata weapon is mentioned in the twentieth [chapter];
alternatively, there is the relationship of qualifier and qualified.
The seasons are mentioned in the twenty-third [chapter].
"Āmoda and the others" refers to the thirteen [qualities] in the thirteenth [chapter]. "Treasures" refers to the waves in the first [chapter]. "Flavors" refers to the sweet and so forth.
In the thirteenth [chapter], there is [the description] of the powers (śaktis) beginning with Āmodā;
in the twentieth, [there is the description] of the Śākinīs and so forth.
Alternatively, there may be a relationship of qualifier and qualified between "power" (śaktiḥ) and "Śākinī and so forth" (śākinyādyāḥ).
The six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) are in the fifth;
the yantra is in the ninth;
the supports (ādhāra) are in the fifth.
Whatever exists in the world, all that—consisting of the sixfold [system], the six limbs, the Sītā-mantra, the six rites (ṣaṭkarma), the seats (āsana), and so forth—[is contained herein]. (75–77)
The eternal Goddess, who forms half the body of Śaṅkara, is multiplied sevenfold;
she is the seven-syllabled Tripurā-mantra and the seven-syllabled Vināyaka. || 78 ||
That Sudarśana [mantra] consists of seven syllables and is composed of the seven vyāhṛtis;
it [governs] the worlds, mountains, vowels, elements, sages, islands, and even the planets.
The fuel-sticks are reckoned as seven, and there are seven tongues that consume the oblation;
whatever else is of sevenfold variety, all that has been produced from her.
"Seven-syllabled" refers to the seven-syllabled mantra of Padmāvatī in the tenth [chapter].
"Tripurā-mantra" refers to the Bhairavī-mantra beginning with the Māyā-bīja, arranged in both direct (anuloma) and reverse (viloma) order.
In the seventeenth [chapter], the seven-syllable Śaṅkha-mantra and Vināyaka-Subrahmaṇya [mantras] are [taught] in the thirteenth.
Alternatively, there is the qualifier-qualified relationship: "the seven-syllable Tripurā-mantra" and "Vināyaka as the seven-syllable [mantra]."
"Of the *vyāhṛtis*" refers to the twenty-first [chapter];
"seven-syllabled" refers to the *aṅkuśa* mantra in the seventeenth;
and "Sudarśana" is in the sixteenth.
Or rather, there is the relationship of qualifier and qualified.
[He traversed] the worlds, beginning with Bhūr; and the mountains: Vindhya, Pāriyātra, Sahya, Ṛkṣa, Malaya, Mahendra, and Śuktimat.
The notes are Ṣaḍja, Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Madhyama, Pañcama, Dhaivata, and Niṣāda.
In the first [manvantara], the bodily constituents are the skin and so forth.
The sages are Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Atri, Jamadagni, Gautama, Viśvāmitra, and Bharadvāja; because they belong to the Vaivasvata Manvantara, they are thus known as the seven Ṛṣis.
The continents—Jambū, Plakṣa, Śālmali, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara—and the planets.
According to the view of some, since Rāhu and Ketu do not possess the status of planets, seven are mentioned; these are placed in the sixth [house].
And likewise, by the teacher Varāhamihira:
"Because of the excellence of its tasting the nectar, this head of the Asura, though severed, was not indeed deprived of life; thus it does not attain the state of a planet," and so forth.
Thus has this cause of eclipses been stated by the teachers possessing divine vision;
that Rāhu is not the cause in this matter—this is the true essence of the scriptures.
To that asura Rāhu, a boon was granted by Brahmā in the past:
"At the time of an eclipse, you shall receive nourishment from the portion of the oblation offered."
By this and a great deal of textual material beginning with these words, the status of Rāhu and Ketu as planets is refuted.

Due to the word "api" (also/even), the verb "ajījanat" (gave birth) is understood to carry over [from the previous context]. The subsequent word "samidhaḥ" (fuel-sticks) connects with the following action.
There are seven fuel-sticks for the consumer of oblations, as declared in the Śruti.
Thus says the Śruti:
"O Agni, you have seven fuel-sticks, seven tongues, seven Ṛṣis, and seven beloved abodes."
Thus [it is said].
Or, for the seven planets: the Arka, Palāśa, Khadira, Apāmārga, and Pippala; and—
"Audumbara is *śamī*.
In that case, [the word *audumbara*] is not connected with the term "consumer of oblations" (*havirbhuj*).
The seven-tongued [fire] is also threefold in the fifth [chapter].
"Other" refers to the primordial nature (prakṛti), its transformations (vikṛti), the Tripura-tattva, the Garuḍa-mantra, the Yantra-paṭala, the two mantras, the Vaivasvata-mantra, and so forth. 78–80.
The Śaiva mantra consisting of two sets of eight syllables is the Power (Śakti) multiplied eightfold;
[and] for Viṣṇu, the supreme eight-syllabled mantra named Śrīkara. || 81 ||

The eight-syllabled mantra of Hari, the pair of eight-syllabled mantras of Śakti, the eight-syllabled mantra of Bhānu, the eight-syllabled mantra of Durgā, and that of the Supreme Self (Paramātman). || 82 ||
The eight-syllable mantra of Nīlakaṇṭha, whose essence is Vāsudeva;
the divine Kāmārgala yantra, and the Devī-yantra known as Ghaṭārgala. || 83 ||
This auspicious eightfold incense is heart-pleasing to the goddesses and gods;
it [reaches] Brahmā and the others, the Bhairavas, the serpents, the Mūrtis, the quarters, and the Vasus as well. || 84 ||
The great goddess has eight seats, accompanied by the eight groups of eight;
she [bestows] the eight primary forms, beginning with Vighna and Vakratuṇḍa, in due order. || 85 ||
When he expands everything eightfold in this world—the qualities beginning with *aṇimā*, the serpents, the forms of fire beginning with Yama, and so forth—then [he manifests all]. || 86 ||
Both [mantras] pertaining to Śiva are in the nineteenth [chapter].
Viṣṇu’s supreme eight-syllabled mantra named Śrīkara and both [mantras] of Kṛṣṇa are in the seventeenth.
"Of Hari" is in the fifteenth.
The pair [of verses] beginning with "śakteḥ" is in the ninth;
that beginning with "bhānoḥ" is in the fourteenth;
and the two verses beginning with "daurga" are also in the eleventh.
"Of the Supreme Self" refers to the sixth [chapter].
"Of Nīlakaṇṭha":
by the word *nīlakaṇṭha*, the mantra of Kṣetrapāla is understood; that is in the twentieth [chapter].
Or else, as stated in another tantra: "Oṃ nīlakaṇṭhāya svāhā.
This is the mantra whose essence is Vāsudeva.
In the scriptures of the Āgamas, the word *manu* is a designation for a mantra.
"Oṃ namo vāsudevāya"—this is stated in another tantra. Regarding the *Kāmārgala*, it is found in the seventeenth [chapter];
since it is not well-known as a *Kāmārgala* within that [specific] work, it is the *Kāmārgala* as stated in another tantra.

One should write the syllable *vyoma* (ha), along with Brahmā, Indra, the Lord of the World (Yama), Agni, and the left eye (u) with a bindu (m), within the pericarp; and one should write the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the beloved woman upon the eight petals.

One should write the root mantra, differentiated by vowels, upon the leaves of the month and the digits; and upon the teeth-leaves, it should be written with the consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *sa*, distinguished by their respective colors.
"One should enclose this with a temple [mandira], and outside with the power (śakti) and the goad (aṅkuśa);
they know this yantra, which is equal to the 'jar-bolt' (ghaṭārgala), as the 'bolt of desire' (kāmārgala).
This means it is the divine "bolt of Yama" (yamārgala).
According to the statement, "The divine machine is the bolt of Yama," this [bolt] is in the twenty-fourth [chapter]. The Goddess is Bhuvaneśī.
Because it is stated that "the goddess Śakti is named Hṛllekhā," her yantra is the Ghaṭārgala in the ninth [chapter],
and the threefold Gandhāṣṭaka is in the fourth.
The god Viṣṇu and the god Śiva are two gods; the goddess and the two gods are "the deities" (devāḥ). Of them. In some places, the reading is "divyam."
Then, "of the gods" refers generally;
[the mantras] beginning with Brāhmī are in the sixth [chapter],
and the eight Bhairavas are in the ninth.
The serpents in the twenty-third [section]; the eight forms (of Śiva) in the twenty-eighth;
the quarters, namely the directions beginning with the east.
Regarding the Vasus: "Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa—these eight are remembered as the Vasus. Thus it is said.
The eightfold seat (aṣṭapīṭha), endowed with eight groups of eight, consists of sixty-four varieties as follows:
Māyā, Maṅgala, Nāga, Vāmana, Mahālakṣmī, Caritra, Bhṛgu, Chāyā, Chatra, Hiraṇyahastina, Mahendra, Uḍīśa, and Campāpura.
Ṣaṣṭhakṣīraka, Mañjaneśvara, Purailā, Candrapūḥ, Śrīgiri, Kolākullaka, Pūrṇaparvata, Kurukṣetra, Ekaliṅga, and Arbuda.

Kāśmīra, Ekāmraka, Kāñcī, the excellent Malaya mountain, Eka-randhūta-devī, Koṭṭa, Āmrāteśa, Jālandhara, Surabhimanīṣā, Adrikā, Śrī, Prayāga; Trisrotas, Kāmakoṭṭa, Ujjayinī, Mathurā, Kośalā, and Kānyakubja.
From here, passing through Dyāna, Aṅkāra, Aṭṭahāsa, Aviraja, and then Kuṇḍina, one reaches Rājagṛha.
Nepāla, Puṇḍravardhana, Mālava, Parasīka, Kāmarūpa, Kedāra, Vindhya, Mahāmaṭha, Gośruti, Kāmpilya, Śrīpīṭha, Maru, and Īśa—
these are the primary *prakṛtis*.
In the thirteenth [chapter], one should worship the Vighnas and Vakratuṇḍas.
Regarding "aṇimā and so forth":
aṇimā, mahimā, garimā, and likewise laghimā.
"Sovereignty, mastery, irresistible will, and attainment"—thus [it is said].
"Nāgas" refers to elephants in the eighth [house];
"of fire" refers to the fifth [house].
At the end [of the sequence], one should worship Yamādi and the others.
"The other" refers to the mantra of Dhūmāvatī, who is dear to the Lord of Speech and Passion, and so forth. (81–86)
The eternal [Goddess], multiplied ninefold, gives birth to the nine-syllabled mantra;
Maheśvarī, whose form is the principles (tattva), is the ninefold essence of the principles of power (śakti). || 87 ||

She possesses the ninefold group of the powers of the seats (pīṭhaśaktis), the nine aesthetic sentiments beginning with the erotic (śṛṅgāra), and the nine gems beginning with ruby (māṇikya), joined with the nine classes [of letters]. || 88 ||
The auspicious mandala of the nine breath-messengers is ninefold; whatever in this world consists of a group of nine, all of that arises from her. || 89 ||
"Ninefold" means that it produces whatever mantra consisting of nine principles or nine syllables exists in the world,
such as the nine-syllable Gopāla mantra accompanied by the Śārṅga bow, and so forth.
The first half-verse is connected with the preceding action, while the second verse is connected with the subsequent action.

Regarding "the principles of the powers" (*śakti-tattvānām*): *prakṛti*, *nāda*, and *bindu*; *bindu*, *nāda*, and *bīja*; and *raudrī*, *jyeṣṭhā*, and *vāmā*—these are the nine principles of power in the first [category].
Others hold that there are ten principles to be mentioned later, excluding *sadāśiva*, thus making nine.
Regarding "of the powers of the seats" (pīṭhaśaktīnām), this applies to their respective mantras as well in various places.
[The rasas] beginning with the erotic:
the erotic, the heroic, the pathetic, the marvelous, the comic, and the terrifying.
"The loathsome, the furious, and the peaceful—these nine are remembered as the aesthetic sentiments (rasas) in poetry.
Thus [it is said]. "The nine jewels and the six classes" is in the sixth [chapter];
"of the life-breaths and messengers" is in the twenty-third.
In the third [chapter], there is a mandala with nine centers.
Regarding the phrase "whatever it may be":
this refers to the nine sacrificial pits, the nine planets, the tortoise-chakra, the nine squares, and so forth. (87–89)
The tenfold transformation of Śambhu’s consort is the destroyer of the suffering of worldly existence;
the ten-syllable mantra of Gaṇapati and the ten-syllable mantra of Tvaritā. || 90 ||
The ten-syllable mantra of Sarasvatī, the ten-syllable mantra of the Yakṣiṇī, the mantra consisting of Vāsudeva, and the ten-syllable mantra of Aśvārūḍhā. || 91 ||
The ten-syllabled mantra of Tripurā is the ten-peak [mantra] of Tripurā;
by name it is the Padmāvatī-mantra, the ten-syllabled Ramā-mantra. || 92 ||

The tenfold group of Śakti-tattvas is Maheśvarī, whose nature is that of the principles (tattva). She sequentially [manifests] the ten channels (nāḍīs), the ten incarnations (avatāras) of Viṣṇu, the ten guardians of the world (lokapālas), and whatever else she creates. || 93 ||
Regarding "of Gaṇapati":
[this applies] to the thirteenth [chapter], which concerns the swift propitiation.
Regarding "of Tvaritā": [this applies] to the tenth [chapter], which is devoid of *māyā*.
As it has been said: "The armor (va), the sky (kha), and its last letter (m); joined with Śiva (h) is the final [syllable]; the first of the women (a), the moon (u), the earth (la), and the void (v).
The last [syllable] with its source (m); ending with the weapon (pha); together with the stars (u)—this is the ten-syllabled mantra.
Regarding the word "armor" (varma): it refers to the syllable *va*.
Varma Huṃ! Khe Svarūpa! Ca Svarūpa!
The last of those is *cha*, joined with the letter *i* and the *yuga* (the pair) of *śiva* (the letter *ha*), thus forming *che*.
The final [letter] is *kṣa*.
*Aṅganā* means woman.
The syllable *huṃ* consists of the letter *ha* with the *dyu* (the letter *i*), followed by the *sāvīlavaṃ* (the letter *u*) joined with the *anusvāra*.
The final letter is *kṣa*, joined with the *sayoni* (the letter *e*), resulting in *kṣe*. The weapon-mantra is *phaṭ*, which follows at the end of that.
"With the star and joined with the Praṇava at the beginning"—
thus is the extraction of the ten syllables of Tvaritā.
This is also stated in the Nārāyaṇīya:
Bhuvaneśa, Bhūtadaṇḍī, the final letter at the end of Kalā, together with the Yoni;
the fifth of those, its end, together with Rudra, and the abode at the end of Sāmanta.

"The one called Vāmā, the first long vowel, the principle of wrath (Kopa-tattva) joined with the end of Hara—know this ten-syllable mantra to begin with Tārā and end with Phaṭ. Thus [it is said]. "Bhuvana... [etc.]

*Bhuvaneśa* is *ha*; *bhūta* is *u*; the staff (*daṇḍa*) is the anusvāra; thus, *huṃ*. The *kalās* are the vowels; that which is at their end is *ka*; the one following it is *kha*; joined with the *yonikam*, which is *e*, it becomes *khe*. The fifth from that is *ca*; that which is at its end is *cha*.
Together with Rudra, it consists of eleven thousand [recitations]; by that, "che" is formed.
It ends with the *sāmanta* and ends with the *visarga*.
The *ālaya* is the letter *kṣa*.
The woman called Vāmā;
the first *huṃ*, its long form *hūṃ*; the principle of wrath (*kopatattva*) is *kṣaḥ*.
Joined with *hareṇa*, *ekāreṇa*, and *ante yuk kṣe* at the end—
this ten-syllable mantra begins with *praṇava* and ends with *phaṭ*.
"Of Sarasvatī" refers to the seventh [chapter].
Regarding the Yakṣiṇī, that which is stated in another tantra is: "Śrī ĀḤ Śrī ĀḤ Yakṣiṇi Haṃ Haṃ Haṃ Svāhā.
Regarding the one whose essence is Vāsudeva, [the mantra] is for Gopāla in the seventeenth [chapter].
Regarding the one mounted on a horse, [the mantra] is in the tenth [chapter], excluding the three seed-syllables.
Because it has been extracted from another tantra as the ten-syllable mantra itself,
it is said:
"The first is the thirteenth [letter] with the staff (ṃ), and after that, the eleventh."
The third [syllable] of the eighth [group] should be joined with the first of the third group.
The first of the sixth, the second of the seventh, and the fifth of the sixth;
joined with the first and the eleventh, followed by the seventh and the fifth.

"Then, joined with *tūrya* [the fourth letter], the second of the seventh [group], conjoined with the first and third [letters], and *dviṭha* [the second of the sixth group]— this is declared to be the ten-syllabled mantra. Thus, regarding the "ten peaks" (*daśakūṭa*), there are six peaks for the middle seed-syllable, and two peaks respectively for the initial and final seed-syllables.
Regarding the phrase "two peaks," when combined, these constitute the ten-peak mantra of Tripurā as stated in another tantra: *eṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ śrauṃ tripurāyai namaḥ*.
The Padmāvatī mantra, as stated in another tantra, is: *oṃ hneṃ padme padmāvati svāhā*.
The *rāmamantra* is in the eighth;
in the reading *rāmamantram*, it is in the fifteenth;
and the *śaktitattvas* are in the fifth.
"In the [chapter] beginning with 'of the channels' (nāḍīnām)" refers to the first;
"the incarnations" (avatārān) refers to the seventeenth;
and "of the world-protectors" (lokapālānām) refers to the fourth.
"Other" refers to the consecration by fire-mantras, the Jayadurgā-mantra, and so forth. (90–93)
Consciousness, multiplied elevenfold, becomes identical with the universe. From the primordial power of the eleven Rudras, there arises the eleven-syllabled [mantra];
through the eleven-syllabled speech, the eleven Rudras emerge in succession. || 94 ||
Regarding the term *rudraikādaśanī*: it refers to the recitation of the Rudrādhyāya eleven times with each of its six ancillary parts (*ṣaḍaṅga*); such is the *rudraikādaśanī*.
Alternatively, it refers to eleven repetitions of the Rudra [mantra] itself; thus it is called *rudraikādaśanī*.

The Rudra with six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgarudra*) consists of: the six verses beginning with *yajjāgrataḥ*; the twenty-two verses beginning with *sahasraśīrṣā*; then the two sections (*anuvāka*) beginning with *āśuḥ śiśānaḥ* and *vibhrāt*, which together comprise one hundred verses;
and the second [section] consisting of the sixteen verses beginning with *sahasraśīrṣā*.
The third [rite] is with six [verses].
"A hundred"—
this refers to the weapon [rite] performed with the Śatarudrīya.
As for the Śatarudra:
the Ṣaṭṣaṣṭi, the Nīlasūkta, and again the recitation of sixteen Ṛg-verses; "eṣa te" and "he," "namaste" in two [verses], and also "nataṃ vidma" and "yameva."
The four [verses] beginning with *mīḍhuṣṭama* constitute the Śatarudrīya.
Thus, the eleven-syllable [mantra] of Sarasvatī, the primordial power (*ādyaśakti*), is in the seventh [position].
Alternatively, regarding the *Nityaklinnā* of the Primordial Power (*Ādyaśakti*), it is stated in another tantra:
"Hrīṃ nityaklinne madadrave svāhā. In the reading *Ādyā*, it is an epithet of the Goddess.
This [deity] is also in the seventh [finger] by way of speech.
Regarding the Rudras:
Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, and Aparājita.
Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu, Kapardin, and likewise Raivata;
"Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, and Kāpālī are considered to be forms of Śiva.
Here too, it should be understood that there is something else.
And that consists of the mantras of Śakti, Vināyaka, and so forth. 94.
The soul of all, multiplied by twelve in sequence, is the eternal mantra of Maheśānī, the mantra whose essence is Vāsudeva. || 95 ||
The zodiac signs, the suns, and the forms of Hari—the twelvefold yantra and everything else of that kind was born from her. (96)
The verb "emits" (*samudgirati*) is connected to both the preceding and the following sentences by way of the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣigolakanyāya*).
Because the final [word] and the first [word] are restricted, the portion ending with "other" (*anyat*) is connected to every subsequent sentence.
From here on, the sentences are indeed distinct.
The *nityāmantra* of Maheśānī and Vajraprastāriṇī is in the tenth [chapter];
Vāsudeva is in the fifteenth;
and the zodiac signs (*rāśi*) are in the eighth.
In the fifteenth [chapter], the suns and the forms of Hari;
in the ninth, the yantra;
"the other" refers to the sword-mantra and so forth.
By the phrase "of such a kind," this is what is meant:
the mantra of Vāgīśvarī mounted on a horse, beginning with Viśvedeva, multiplied thirteenfold;
and the mantra of Lakṣmī-Vāsudeva-Gopāla, beginning with Bhuvana, multiplied fourteenfold.
The fifteenfold [category] consists of the Nityā, Śūlinī, mantra, lunar day (tithi), and so forth;
the sixteenfold [category] consists of the cakra, mantra, vowel, and kalā, and so forth;
the seventeenfold [category] consists of the Laghupañcamī, Tārā, and other vidyās, mantras, and so forth.
The rites beginning with the fire-consecration (*agni-saṃskāra*) for the *kṛṣṇavāmana-mantra* are eighteenfold;
those beginning with the *kṛṣṇadharā-mantra* are nineteenfold;
and those beginning with the *haladharomāmaheśvara-mantra* are twentyfold.
In twenty-one ways are the mantra and yantra of the one named Vaṭuka;
in twenty-two ways are the mantra and others of Kṛṣṇa, Annādhipati, and Sumukhī;
and in twenty-three ways are the Laghuśyāmā, the Puruṣottama-hṛdaya-aṅga-mantra, and so forth—thus says the Sūta. (95–96)
When that [Gāyatrī] becomes beautiful with twenty-four principles—namely the Gāyatrī of Savitṛ, the Gāyatrī of Śambhu, and the Gāyatrī whose essence is Madana—[then she is perfected]. || 97 ||
The Gāyatrī of Viṣṇu, the Gāyatrī of the three-footed Self, the Gāyatrī of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and the Gāyatrī of Śambhu’s consort. || 98 ||
The twenty-four principles were situated within that Supreme Self.

Although the Goddess has indeed produced the creation consisting of the thirteen Viśvedevas, the fourteen worlds, and the fifteen lunar days (tithis), nevertheless, because she exists until the end of the *parārdha* and because it is impossible to name all her many forms, he speaks of her as "fourfold" (*catur*) to indicate those that are primary.
The meaning is that she is multiplied twenty-four-fold, her self having the nature of the twenty-four principles (*tattva*).
In the twenty-first [verse] of Savitṛ;
"of Śambhu" is stated in another tantra.
That [mantra]: "We know Maheśa; we meditate upon Him who is pure in speech."
"May that auspicious one impel us"—thus [it is said].
She whose nature is passion is in the seventeenth [chapter]. || 97 ||
The Viṣṇugāyatrī is also [recited] in the seventeenth [chapter], as is the Puruṣottamagāyatrī; or rather, it is referred to by the term "Viṣṇugāyatrī" as stated in another tantra:
"We know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva."
"May that Viṣṇu impel us.
This [verse] belongs to Tripurā, who consists of three feet, in the twelfth [chapter].
As for [the verse beginning with] "Of Dakṣiṇāmūrti":
"We know Dakṣiṇāmūrti; we meditate upon Him who is established in contemplation.
May that Ghorasiva inspire us. Thus [ends the mantra].
"O Consort of Śambhu," etc.
"May we know her who deludes all; may we meditate upon her, the mother of the universe;
may she, the moist one, inspire us.
Thus [are the mantras] for the first [set of] principles (tattvas).
These *gāyatrīs* are also the principles (*tattvas*) that were produced within her;
here too, it should be understood that there are others.
These include the Agnisamṛddhā, Agnidakṣiṇā, Mūrtīcī, Ṛtumatī, Mantravatī, Kratuṇḍā, Durgā, Tvaritā, Agninṛsiṃha, Garuḍa, Hayagrīva, Gāyatrī, and so forth. (97–99)
The all-pervading Lord, who consists of all mantras multiplied by thirty-two varieties, generates the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra and the great mantra of Nārasiṃha. || 100 ||
The mantra of the high-souled Varuṇa known as Lavaṇa, the Hayagrīva-mantra, the Daurga-mantra, the Vārāha-mantra, and the Vahnināyaka-mantra. || 101 ||
She [is] the great mantra of Gaṇeśa, the mantra of the Lord of Food (Annapūrṇā), the mantra of Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and the garland-mantra of the Mind-born One (Kāmadeva). || 102 ||
The Triṣṭubh mantra of Vanavāsinī, the great mantra named Aghora, the Bhadrakālī mantra, the Mālā-mantra of Lakṣmī, and that which has Yama as its essence. || 103 ||
She [recited] the mantra of the son of Devakī, the mantra of Śrī Puruṣottama, the Śrī Gopāla mantra, the mantra of Bhūmi, and the Tārā mantra in succession. || 104 ||

She gives birth to the great mantra of Mahālakṣmī, the mantra of Bhūteśvara, the mantra consisting of Kṣetrapāla, and the mantra that wards off calamities; she gives birth to the Mātaṅginī-vidyā, the perfected lore of auspicious origin. || 105 ||
The Vedic Mṛtyuñjaya [is recited] in the twenty-third [chapter];
the Nārasiṃha in the sixteenth;
and the Mahāmanu, the King of Mantras, is the aforementioned qualification.
The one named Lavaṇa is in the twenty-second [chapter]. "Of Varuṇa" is as stated in the Śruti.
"Of the Great Soul" (mahātmanaḥ) is an epithet; by that, the meaning is "Mahāvāruṇa."
The Hayagrīva [mantra] is in the fifteenth [chapter]. The Durga [mantra] is that which is declared in the Śruti,
beginning with "ambike ambālike," and so forth.
The Vārāha [mantra] is in the fifteenth [chapter].
The mantra for the worship of Agni (Agnisthāpana), beginning with Vahnināyaka, is in the fifth [chapter].
Of Gaṇeśitu, that is Haridrā-Gaṇeśa: "Oṃ huṃ gaṃ glauṃ, to Haridrā-Gaṇapati, the bestower of boons, [who captivates] the heart of all people..."
"Stambhaya stambhaya svāhā! The follower of the Atharvaveda [should worship] Vakratuṇḍa,
who is considered the bestower of the increase of wealth, the giver of treasures, and the granter of jewels.
To the slayer of demons, the slayer of Vala, the one with the curved trunk, Hūṃ! Salutation!

Because it is called the "Great Mantra" (*mahāmantra*), it refers either to the mantra of Mahāgaṇapati which will be described right here—since, according to tradition, it consists of thirty-two syllables—or to the mantra of the Lord of Food (*annādhipa*) mentioned in another tantra: "Oṃ hrīṃ! O you who are the form of food, the form of the four tastes, salutations, salutations! To the Lord of Food, grant me food."
"svāhā"—thus [it is stated] in the nineteenth [chapter] of the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtti[-tantra]*.
The thirty-two-syllable garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*) of Manobhuva is taught in another tantra.
It is called "Triṣṭubh" because it is designated as such by way of the secondary application (*upacāra*) mentioned within that context; thus, it is said to consist of thirty-two syllables.
This is because seventy-two mantras have been extracted from within it,
and because thirty-two syllables also exist therein;
that which is called Aghora is mentioned in another tantra.
Because the author of the work has stated that it consists of fifty-one syllables.
As he said:
"Then the letter *na*, followed by the sound of a tooth-bite (*dantasambhinna*), then at the end of *bhaga*, and then at the end of that."
Then follows the form of Aghorā at the end of the letter Ya, consisting of two "han" syllables and two "daha" syllables.
Having stated the practice of the two *pacas*, one should likewise rotate [the mantra] ending with the head (*śiraḥ*), the armor (*varma*) and so forth, and the word *phaṭ*.
Thus [ends the section on] the letter *na*.

"Oṃ namo bhagavate aghorarūpāya hana hana daha daha paca paca bhrāmaya bhrāmaya huṃ phaṭ svāhā. This thirty-four-syllable mantra is Aghora; it is in the Anuṣṭubh meter, and its deities are Aghora and others. [The syllable count is: 6, 6, 8, 10, 2, 2 = 34. The six limbs are formed accordingly.
The Bhadrakālī mantra consists of twenty-four syllables.
The mantra "mahālakṣmyā" is in the tenth [chapter];
the two mantras beginning with "sarvatobhadrarūpaṃ yamātmakam" are in the twenty-fourth;
and the mantra beginning with "devakīsūnoḥ" followed by "sukīrttyādi" is in the seventeenth.

The mantra of Śrī Puruṣottama as stated in another Tantra is: "Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya puruṣottama āyurme dehi viṣṇave prabhaviṣṇave namaḥ. In the seventeenth [chapter], the mantra of Śrī Gopāla and both the yantra and its limbs are also [described].
O Earth,
you were lifted up by the boar Kṛṣṇa with his hundred arms;
O Clay, take away my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me.
Thus it is stated in another tantra.
The mantra of Tārā as stated in another tantra is: "Oṃ hrīḥ hauṃ hūṃ, homage to Tārā, to Mahātārā; ferry across, ferry across all those who have not crossed over; cross, cross! Svāhā! Thus.
The great mantra of Mahālakṣmī is characterized by the Śrīsūkta.
The mantra of Bhūteśvara, as stated in another Tantra, is: "Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed Rudra, the lord of all beings; destroy, destroy the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and ḍākinīs!"
The form of the Kṣetrapāla as described in another Tantra is as follows: "Come, come, O wise one, O face-averted one! Make dance, make dance!
O Vighnamahābhairava Kṣetrapāla, accept this offering, accept it! Svāhā! Thus.
The warding off of calamities is taught in another tantra;

however, since twenty-one syllables will be mentioned here, [the mantra] for Mātaṅginī as taught in another tantra is as follows: "Oṃ hrīḥ eḥ śrīḥ, obeisance to the Blessed One, O Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī, O Śrīmātaṅgeśvarī."
"O you who bring all people under your control, svāhā!
This refers to the *siddhavidyā* mentioned in another tantra,
or else it refers to the two qualifiers, "accomplished" (*siddha*) and so forth, belonging to the very [mantra] previously mentioned.
It should also be understood that there is something else;
and that consists of the Vaiṣṇava-tattva, the pervasive Śaiva-mantras, and so forth. (100–105)
Multiplied by this sequential method, she, the beloved of Śiva, arranges the thirty-six principles (tattvas) of the Śaivas. || 106 ||
"By this" means: multiplied by this sequence of application; that is to say, multiplied thirty-six times.
"Of the Śaivas" refers to the fifth [chapter]. || 106 ||
She brings forth other auspicious mantras and yantras;
Viśvanāyikā is multiplied by forty-two at the root. || 107 ||
"Other mantras" refers to the Ucchiṣṭagaṇapati, Puruṣottama-vyāpaka, and other mantras mentioned in other tantras.
As previously [stated]: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the single-tusked one, the elephant-faced one, the pot-bellied one, the Great Soul of the Residue; Kroṃ Hrīṃ Hūṃ."

"Ghe ghe svāhā. This is the third [mantra] in the seventeenth [chapter]. Regarding the phrase "yantrāṇi" (yantras): these refer to the yantras consisting of grids as taught in the Yantra-paṭala, such as the Mahālakṣmī-yantra and others taught in the eighth chapter.

By the general statement "by this sequential method" (*anena kramayogena*), and by the similar mention of "mantras" and "yantras," it is indicated that she gives birth to the thirty-eight *kalās* multiplied by thirty-eight—
namely, the mantras such as their seed-syllables (*bīja*) and so forth;
and the yantras such as those of Navadurgā, Puruṣottama, Netrodaka, and Aṅga-mantra, as well as the yantras of Vṛddhaśyāmā, Varāha, and Nṛsiṃha.
"Forty-two":

at the root, in the *mūlādhāra*, Viśvanāyikā Kuṇḍalinī, multiplied by forty-two, creates in this sequence the garland of phonemes (*varṇamālikā*) consisting of the earthly script (*bhūtalipi*), which is composed of forty-two [phonemes] from *a* to *sa* and is of the nature of mantra; such is the connection. || 107 ||
She gives birth to Kuṇḍalinī, who is all-pervasive and consists of the Śabdabrahman;
from her comes Śakti, from that Dhvani, from that Nāda, and from that Nirodhikā.
From that arose the half-moon, from that the point (bindu), and from that the Supreme (Parā);
then followed the Visionary (Paśyantī), the Intermediate (Madhyamā), and the Articulate (Vaikharī) speech, which is the birthplace of sound.
She consists of will, knowledge, and action; she is of the nature of light and composed of the qualities (guṇas). || 109 ||
By this sequence, Kuṇḍalinī emits the garland of phonemes, consisting of forty-two elements, beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'sa'. (110)
Multiplied by fifty gates, she gives birth to a garland of fifty phonemes;
from those phonemes, the Kalās, beginning with Rudra, emerge in succession as non-different from them. || 111 ||
He states that very sequence as "the power" (*śakti*). That *kuṇḍalinī* gives birth to power.
(The author of the *Gūḍhārthadīpikā* says: "Power is the state of the primordial cause, sound, being oriented toward manifestation.")
From that [Unstruck Sound], there is the resonance (dhvani);
from that resonance, and so forth—this should be understood.
Furthermore, although this sequence was stated by the author at the very end of the entire work, it is also to be applied to the production of each successive syllable.

In that context, the power of consciousness (cicchakti) entered into *sattva* is denoted by the term *paramākāśa*, which is its state as such; that same [power], when entered into *sattva* and permeated by *rajas*, is denoted by the word *dhvani* and is its state as the syllable (*akṣara*); that same [power], when permeated by *tamas*, is denoted by the word *nāda* and is its unmanifest state (*avyaktāvasthā*);
that same [power], due to the predominance of *tamas*, is denoted by the word *nirodhikā*; and that same [power], due to the predominance of *sattva*, is the crescent moon (*arddhendu*).
That which is denoted by the word "Sound" (śabda) [becomes] denoted by the word "Bindu" through the conjunction of those two.
As they say:
"Exalted by the power of the will (icchā-śakti), it illumines the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti)."
"And that power, in male form, the Lord creates what is called action.
This very *bindu*, having moved to another location, becomes known as *parā* and so forth.
"From that" means from the *bindu*.
*Parā* is at the root (*mūlādhāra*), *paśyantī* is in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, *madhyamā* is in the heart, and *vaikharī* is in the mouth.
As it has been said:
"The subtle *kuṇḍalinī*, whose nature consists of pure light, resides in the center."
Therefore, it rises upward, moving upwards beyond the range of hearing.
Self-luminous Paśyantī, having resorted to Suṣumṇā,
becomes Madhyamā in the form of sound upon reaching the heart-lotus.
Then, through mere internal discourse, she becomes undivided and moves upward;
she resides in the chest, throat, and palate, and is situated in the head, nose, and teeth.
"Vaikharī speech is that which grasps all phonemes emitted from the root of the tongue and the lips;
it is the progenitor of the manifold expansion of sound and is perceived by the ear. Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Kādima-tantra*: "By the striking of the power of one's own will, through the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa-vāyu*)."
The supreme Nāda, known as Parā, has arisen in the Mūlādhāra.
That very [vital energy], led upward by that [power] and expanded within its own seat (svādhiṣṭhāna), attains the name Paśyantī; by that same power, it is led upward ever more slowly.
Accompanied by the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva), it is called the Middle Path (madhyamā) in the unstruck (anāhata) [cakra];
likewise, being impelled upward from those two, it reaches the region of the throat in the Viśuddhi [cakra].
Then, that which is called *vaikharī* proceeds sequentially through the throat, head, palate, lips, and teeth,
as well as the root, tip, and back of the tongue, and finally the tip of the nose.
The letters, from 'a' up to 'kṣa', have arisen in succession from the throat, palate, lips, throat-and-lips, and the two [upper and lower] teeth-and-lips.
"The state of being syllables (akṣaratva) is declared for these [sounds] from 'a' to 'kṣa'.
And so says the Śruti:
"Speech is measured in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them."
Three [quarters] of speech are hidden in the cave and do not stir; humans speak only the fourth.
Thus it is said.

Alternatively, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) itself, known as the Supreme (*parā*), is the illuminator characterized by the manifestation of consciousness; it is the quiescent state of Māyā, meaning the Supreme Speech (*parā vāk*).
The states involving vibration (*saspaṇda*) are Paśyantī and the others.

In that context, he speaks of Paśyantī as being of the nature of the common vibration (*sāmānyapraspanda*) and light (*prakāśa*), consisting of the principle of the Bindu (*bindutattva*), and manifesting within the locations starting from the Mūlādhāra up to the navel.
It is called "Paśyantī" because its essence is knowledge; this is the meaning.

He speaks of the *madhyamā* as that which consists of the external and internal organs, whose form is Hiraṇyagarbha, which is composed of *nāda* and *bindu*, whose place of manifestation extends from the navel to the heart, and whose essential nature consists of specific volitions (*saṅkalpa*) and so forth.
The analysis of the compound is: "that in which the intellect (*mā*), located in the middle (*madhye*), resides."

He speaks of *vaikharī*—which has the form of the Virāj, consists of seed-syllables (*bīja*), is manifested in the locations from the heart to the mouth, and whose essence is the generality of sound—in the phrase "in speech" (*vāci*).
The meaning is that it is called *vaikharī* because of its specific clarity (*viśeṣeṇa kharatvāt*).
Regarding the phrase "according to those phonemes" (*tadvarṇataḥ*):
She gives birth to those phonemes (*varṇa*) and those parts (*kalā*) which are non-different from them;

she gives birth to Rudra and the others. By the word "and the others" (*ādi*), [are included] their Śaktis, the Viṣṇus and the Śaktis of Viṣṇu, the fifty medicinal herbs, and the fifty Kāmas and their Śaktis.

"Thus have been declared the medicinal herbs according to the sequence of the letters beginning with 'A', which grant all accomplishments through their various forms as pills, decoctions, and ashes. Furthermore,
another application of these herbs is stated in the *Kādimata*:
Whichever mantra it may be, pills prepared from the medicinal herbs corresponding to its syllables,
in a number equal to those syllables, grant the accomplishment of the mantra.

"Through her, there shall be initiation, the wearing of her [symbol], the tasting of her, the anointing with her, and likewise worship; this leads to the attainment of accomplishment (*siddhi*), and not otherwise.
As for the fifty desires and their powers, they are as follows:
Kāmakāmadakānta, Kāntimān, Kāmagas,
as well as Kāmācāra, Kāmī, Kāmuka, and Kāmavardhana.
Rāma, Rama, Ramaṇa, Lord of Rati, Beloved of Rati,
Lord of the Night, Consort of Ramā, the Delighting One, and the Wanderer of the Night.
Nandaka, Nandana, Nandī, and furthermore Nandayitā;
the five-arrowed one, the friend of Rati, the flower-bowed one, and the wielder of the great bow.
Bhrāmaṇa, Bhramaṇa, Bhramamāṇa, and another, Bhrama;
Bhrānta, Bhrāmaka, Bhrāntācāra, and Bhramāvaha.

he is Madana, Manmatha, Mātaṅga, and the leader of the bees.

Having the luster of pomegranate flowers, they are joined by their Śaktis on their left sides;
all are gentle, clad in red garments, and hold flower-arrows and sugarcane bows.
Adorned with all ornaments and richly decorated, the fifty Kāmas are proclaimed:
Rati, Prīti, Kāminī, Mohinī, and Kamalapriyā.
Vilāsinī, Kalpalatā, Śyāmalā, Śucismitā, Vismitākṣī, Viśālākṣī, Lelihānā, and Digambarā.
Vāmā, Kubjā, Dharā, Nityā, Kalyāṇī, Mohinī,
as well as Madanā, the best of goddesses, Lāpinī, and Madinī.
Kalahapriyā, Ekākṣī, Sumukhī, Nalinī, Japinī, Pālinī, Śivā, Mugdhā, Rasā, and Bhramā.
Cārulolā, Cañcalā, Dīrghajihvā, Ratipriyā, Lolākṣī, Bhṛṅgiṇī, Pāṭalā, and likewise Mādanī.
And Mālā, Haṃsinī, Viśvatomukhī, as well as Nandinī;
likewise Ramaṇī, Kānti, Kalakaṇṭhī, and Vṛkodarī.
"These fifty Śaktis are described as dark as a cloud, intoxicated with passion, resembling saffron in hue, adorned with all ornaments,
holding blue lotuses in their hands, and capable of attracting the three worlds— thus they are to be meditated upon."
The fifty Gaṇeśas and their Śaktis are as follows:

Gajavaktra, Nirañjana, Kapardin, Dīrghajihvaka, Śaṅkukarṇa, Vṛṣabhadhvaja, and Gaṇanāyaka.
Gajendra, Sūrpakarṇa, and the one known as Trilocana;
Lambodara and Mahānanda—these are the four forms of Sadāśiva.
Āmoda, Durmukha, Sumukha, Pramodaka,
Ekarada, Dvijihva, Śūra, Vīra, and Ṣaṇmukha.
The Bestower of Boons, Vāmadeva, Vakratuṇḍa, Dviraṇḍaka,
the Commander of the Army, the Village Leader, the Intoxicated, the Excessively Drunk, and he whose vehicle is the Intoxicated Elephant.
He with matted hair, the shaven-headed one, the bearer of the sword, the most excellent, he whose banner is the bull,
the lover of food, the lord of the Gaṇas, and the one known as Meghanādaka.
The pervasive Lord of the Gaṇas has declared these fifty to be the leaders of the Gaṇas.
(Meditation: Resembling the young morning sun, they have elephant faces and three eyes.
Holding nooses, goads, boons, and gestures of fearlessness in their hands, they are endowed with their respective Śaktis.
(The fifty Śaktis are: Śrī, Hrī, Puṣṭi, Śānti, Svasti, and Sarasvatī.

likewise there are Bhrūkuṭi, Lajjā, Dīrghaghoṇā, and Dhanurdharā.
She is known as Yāminī (the Night) and Rātri (Night), blinded by passion and radiant as the moon;
she has tremulous eyes, she is flickering light, auspicious yet ill-fated, and she is Śivā.

"Blazing with all ornaments, seated on the laps of their beloveds, with beautiful eyes, holding red lotuses in their hands, and robed in red garlands and garments— thus they are to be meditated upon.
The fifty Kṣetrapālas will be described in the Kṣetrapāla mantra [verses 108–111].

The fire would be the *nirodhikā*; the half-moon would be the moon; the sun would be [the other half]; and in the union of both, there is the essence of the *bindu*, the treasury of splendors. || 112 ||

Since the castes (varṇas) were born from the Bindu, which consists of Śiva and Śakti, they must be of the nature of Agni and Soma; for they have arisen from that Sun which consists of Śiva and Śakti, having attained their existence as the forms of Moon, Sun, and Fire. || 113 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the Śāradātilaka composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇa Deśikendra. || 1 ||

Since the fact that the castes consist of Agni and Soma, as well as their nature as Soma, Sūrya, and Agni, will be useful later on, the author intends to explain this and says: "The Obstructress" (*nirodhikā*).
Because the Obstructress has the nature of Agni, she is the very essence of Śiva. Because the Half-moon has the nature of Soma, it is the very essence of Śakti.

For this reason, they have attained their origin from the Sun, who consists of Śiva and Śakti. The Sun possesses the nature of both Śiva and Śakti, as it is said: "The Arka [Sun] arises from the union of the two."
Therefore, they take on the forms of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire, because of the non-difference between cause and effect. || 112-113 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter:
Thereafter, I shall explain the manifestation of the phonemes within the mouths of men, which are constantly impelled by the vital breath and emerge through the aperture of the *suṣumṇā*. || 1 ||
The phonemes manifest sequentially through the organs of articulation, such as the throat and so forth.
Among these, the vowels are said to belong to the Moon (Saumya), while the consonants (sparśas) belong to the Sun (Saura) and bring about auspicious results. || 2 ||
All these pervaders belong to the fire-god; they have the Moon, the Sun, and Fire as their deities.
The sixteen vowels are well-known, and the consonants (sparśas) are twenty-five. || 3 ||

Having thus described the creation of meaning and the creation of sound up to the level of *madhyamā*, he makes a formal promise (*pratijānīte*) to describe the creation of *vaikharī* by first restating what has been said, beginning with the words "Then...
and "The wind is impelled...".
Impelled by the *maruts* in succession, they are brought to the station of *paśyantī*, meaning they are made ready for emergence.

Therefore, the connection is that the phonemes (*varṇas*), having exited through the aperture of the *suṣumṇā*, manifest in sequence through the articulatory organs (*karaṇas*) such as the throat and so forth.
The apertures of the *suṣumṇā* are located in the *anāhata* and *viśuddhi* [cakras].
Because there is no simultaneous utterance [of phonemes], it is said that they occur "in sequence.
This was stated by the venerable Bhartṛhari:
"The self, having come together with the intellect, joins the mind to objects through the desire to speak."
"The mind strikes the fire of the body; it impels the wind.
The wind, moving within the chest, produces a deep tone.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "throat and so forth," the palate and other [articulatory sites] are included.
As it has been said:
"The eight places of articulation for the phonemes are the chest, the throat, the head, the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate. (Vākyapadīya).

Regarding that which was stated—that all phonemes (varṇas) possess the nature of the Moon, Sun, and Fire—it is now said, for the sake of their practical application and for the conventional usage of the thirty-eight kalās and so forth, that they are threefold according to a systematic arrangement.
Among these phonemes, the vowels (svaras) range from 'a' to the visarga; the stops (sparśas) range from 'ka' to 'ma'; and the pervaders (vyāpakas) range from 'ya' to 'kṣa'.
Thus, all these deities—Soma, Sūrya, and Agni—are the sources of auspiciousness.
Among them, he will explain the arising of the vowels immediately hereafter;
however, it should be understood that the arising of the others occurs through the "arising of the elements" (bhūtodaya) which will be taught in the final chapter.
"Arising from the *bhūtakalās*," according to the statement of the Teacher (*ācārya*).
He will indicate this very point by describing the phonemes of the elements (*bhūtavarṇa*) right here, in the manner that will be stated later: "without vowels" (*vinā svaraiḥ*, Śāradātilaka 2.8).
In response to the inquiry as to how many vowels and so forth there are, he says: "the vowels" (*svarāḥ*).
"Especially renowned" means they are well-known as independent;
as they say: "Among those, the vowels shall be independent. (1-3)
The tactile sensations are known to have *tattva* as their essence, since the letter *ma* is the *puruṣa*;
those ten are all-pervasive and bestow desire, wealth, and dharma. || 4 ||
Regarding the phrase "tattvātmānaḥ" (having the principles as their essence):
this is a statement of their essential nature, meaning they consist of the twenty-four principles beginning with *prakṛti*.
Now, one might object: since their number is twenty-five, how can it be said that they consist of twenty-four principles? To this, he says: "because the *puruṣa* is the letter *ma*."
For this reason, the letter *ma* signifies the Puruṣa and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), meaning the one whose form is the universe (*viśvarūpa*).

The letters beginning with *bha* represent Prakṛti, the intellect (*buddhi*), the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the mind (*manas*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the sense organs such as hearing and speech, along with ether and the rest; these are the other letters.

It has been stated that this is useful for the ritual depositions (*nyāsa*) of the principles of power (*śakti-tattva*) and so forth, and it is also indicated that among the twelve solar digits (*kalā*) mentioned in the sequence of two-by-two letters, the last one is to be omitted.
Thus, these [letters] consist of the twenty-four principles (*tattva*).
As the Teacher has stated: "The final [letter], the Self (*ātman*), is remembered as the Sun (*ravi*).
For this very reason, because of the union with the vowel *a* in the form of the *bindu* within all seed-syllables (*bīja*), it should be understood that they possess identity with the Puruṣa.

Because the letter *ma* has the form of a *bindu*, and because it will be stated later that "the *bindu* is said to be the male, the Sun," [the letters *ka* and so on] are called *sparśas* (contacts). This is because they are followed through by their own constituent parts beginning with *ka*, and because they are touched by the letter *ma*, which is the *bindu* in the form of the Sun; for this very reason, they are solar (*saurāḥ*).
Alternatively, the construction is as follows:
The letter *ma* is the Puruṣa; the other consonants (*sparśas*) have the principles (*tattvas*) as their essence.
This is connected with what follows by the word "since" (*yataḥ*).
Since from the letter *ya* there are ten pervaders (*vyāpakas*).
Because they reside within these defects (*doṣa*) and the objects of corruption (*dūṣya*), they possess pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*).

Since fire (*agni*) is also present therein, they are called "fiery" (*āgneya*); alternatively, they should be understood as "fiery" because they end with the syllable *kṣa*, which has the form of the Time-Fire (*Kālāgni*) known as Nṛsiṃha.
Their fruits for the three [classes] are, respectively, the granting of desire, wealth, and dharma.
For this very reason, he will state further on: "The vowels are the bestowers of desires," and so forth. || 4 ||
Among the vowels, those previously mentioned are short, while the subsequent ones are long;
these [vowels] consist of Śiva and Śakti, ending respectively with the nasal bindu and the visarga. || 5 ||

Demonstrating the distinct manifestation of the vowels themselves, he states "short" (*hrasva*) and so forth, describing two modes for the purpose of expressing their eight forms and their powers, as well as for subsequent practical usage.
Although the vowels *e* and *au* are long in this context, they possess a technical shortness (*pāribhāṣika-hrasvatvam*).
These short and long vowels are, in sequence, composed of Śiva and Śakti.
The short vowels—a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ, e, o—are composed of Śiva; the meaning is that they are of masculine form.

Intending to state that in the *avajāpā* (the unstruck sound), these two—bindu and sarga—are distinct as the forms of Puruṣa and Prakṛti, he says: "They are those whose conclusion consists of bindu and sarga."

Those [vowels] that are short are joined with the nasal drop (bindu) at the end, and those that are long are joined with the visarga at the end; the meaning is that the nasal drop is the eighth among the short vowels, and the visarga is the eighth among the long vowels. || 5 ||
The Bindu is declared to be the male, the Sun, and Emission (sarga) is the female, the Moon. That which is the middle of the vowels is the group of four neuter sounds. || 6 ||
For this very reason, it says: "The Bindu is the Puruṣa.
The expression "the Moon-maker" (Niśākara) is used because the other vowels consist of its digits (kalās) and are of the nature of lunar days (tithis).
The Visarga, which has the form of the Moon, serves as the cause for completing its own sixteenth number.
They are called *svaras* because they sound (*svarante*) or speak; for this very reason, they are gentle (*saumya*).

This is precisely the position favored by the author of the treatise, since we observe such usage as "by the *ṣa*-groups, which are included among the non-neuter short and long [vowels]," at the occasion of describing the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the *mātṛkā*.

However, some maintain that among the vowels, *a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ*—as previously mentioned—are short (*hrasva*) with one *mātrā*, while the others—*ā, ī, ū, ṝ, ḹ, e, ai, o, au*, as well as those followed by a *bindu*, a *visarga*, at the end of a word, or followed by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*)—are long (*dīrgha*). Such a person is merely to be pitied. As for "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*), it is a property (*dharma*); they possess this quality, hence [the term] "neuter."
The suffix *ac* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *arśas-ādi* group.
The short [vowels] are situated in Piṅgalā; the others are joined in Iḍā. Those four which are neuter should be known as residing in the middle of Suṣumṇā. || 7 ||
Regarding the statement "the arising of the vowels is taught in the Piṅgalā," [it refers to] the short vowels *a, i, u, e, o*;

the subsequent ones are the long vowels *ā, ī, ū, ai, au*. Since the arising [of these vowels] has already been stated by the very line "the sun and the moon [arise] at the points of the bindu and the visarga," [this is merely a restatement].
This purpose has been stated by Gautama:
"The rites arising from the *Ṣaḍsvarodaya*, such as killing and so forth, are well-known;
they yield results quickly when performed with short vowels, and otherwise when performed with long vowels."
Regarding the term *suṣumṇā*:
therein, at the moment the bodily wind begins its entry from the northern part into the southern part, it flows through both for a certain period of time;
that is the time of the commencement of the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*).
Then the pair of short vowels consisting of *ṛ* and *ḷ* arises.
Thus, at the time of beginning the entry of the [bodily] wind from the southern part into the northern part, the bodily wind flows in both directions for a certain period;
that is the time of the transit (*saṃkrānti*) of the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*).
Then the pair of long vowels, *ṛ* and *ḷ*, arises. As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Starting from the seventh vowel, there are four which are neuter."
"When the vital breath (prāṇa) has resorted to the Suṣumṇā, they arise at the transition of the solstices.
Others, however, think otherwise: that the short vowels are *a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ*, while the long ones are *ā, ī, ū, ṝ, ḹ*.
This has been stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
When the vital breath (prāṇa) is situated on the right, then it is the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana);
there, five short vowels consisting of the five elements arise.
"When the *prāṇa* rests on the left [nostril], then it is the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*).
At that time, the five elements are elongated and they emerge individually.
Also elsewhere: "When the *prāṇa* is situated in the right channel, there is indeed the *parā* and the *recikā* [breaths]."
And Indhikā, Vidyā, and Nivṛtti, respectively.
"Pratiṣṭhā, Śānti, Dīpikā, Mocikā, and Sūkṣmā— these vowels, O Dear One, arise within the vital breath (prāṇa) resting in the iḍā.

According to their view, although the arising of the vowels beginning with *e* (ekāra) has not been explicitly stated, nevertheless, because they are *sandhyakṣaras* (diphthongs), their arising should be understood as occurring simultaneously with the arising of those [component vowels].
The teacher Padmapāda, however, states: "An internal *ayana* [is measured] by five external *ghaṭikās*.
Since even the delay mentioned in the prescribed method is untenable, one should understand that the production of temporal divisions is based on inhalations and exhalations (*śvāsocchvāsas*).
Among these, those consisting of a day-and-night (*ahorātra*), a fortnight (*pakṣa*), or an *ayana* are to be known according to one's will. (7)
Without vowels, the manifestation of other [consonants] does not occur clearly;
therefore, the wise declare that the phonemes consist of Śiva and Śakti. || 8 ||
Demonstrating the etymological derivation of the term *vyañjana* (consonant), he states that they too consist of Śiva and Śakti with the word "vinā" (without).
Without vowels (*svara*), the manifestation (*vyakti*) of others—the consonants beginning with *ka*—does not occur through direct clarity (*añjasā*).
Therefore, all phonemes (*varṇa*) consist of Śiva and Śakti.
The etymological derivation of *vyañjanam* as "that which colors (*rañjayati*) the individual" has been shown.
As they say: "From being manifested (*vyaṅgyāt*) by them, it becomes the manifestor (*vyañjanam*).
This is what is meant.
It has been stated previously that the vowels consist of Śiva and Śakti;
since it is impossible to pronounce consonants without vowels, they possess the nature of Śiva and Śakti when pronounced together with vowels.
Thus, because the consonants are subordinate to them, their emergence (udaya) should be understood as occurring solely through the emergence of the vowels.
And it is said in the Mantramuktāvalī: "And the mantras have that as their primary object. (8)
Others, however, interpret it differently. Regarding what was stated—that [the bindus] have the forms of the Moon, Sun, and Fire—he analyzes that with the words "among these" (*eṣu*).
Here, because the bindu in the form of the Sun is all-pervasive, the term "arising of auspiciousness" (*śubhodayāḥ*) is used as a qualification of the solar [bindu].

Now, one might object: if this is the division, then the previously mentioned reason—"by which"—which was stated as applying to all phonemes in general, would not be tenable. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "all" (*sarve*).
"Regarding the deities Soma, Sūrya, and Agni":
if it is argued that even so, the contradiction remains exactly as it was,
we say no.
However, it should be understood that while this [classification] is ultimate, the division [into groups] is for the sake of practical application and so forth.

Regarding the question—"What are those [sounds] called *svara*, *sparśa*, and *vyāpaka* that were mentioned, and how many are there?"—the author says "The vowels" (*svarāḥ*), etc. By this, the statement that "the vowels are twenty-one," which is heard in other sources such as the *Śikṣā*, is refuted.

The phrase "twenty-five" (pañcaviṃśati) serves to dispel the doubt that, since [the elements] are all-pervasive, there might be a perception of the knower even when he is conjoined with them. || 1-3 ||

Speaking of that Puruṣa who was mentioned in the previous chapter as "possessing the body of the principles" (*tattvadehavān*), [the author] states "the principles are the self" (*tattvātmānaḥ*) in order to indicate that the arising of the principles beginning with *Prakṛti* occurs precisely through the arising of this [Puruṣa]. By the word "ten" (*daśa*), he indicates the inclusion of the retroflex *la*.
The word "kāma" (desire) refers, in sequence, to the fruit of the three.
He explains further what was stated—that all [vowels] are the deities Moon, Sun, and Fire—with the words "the short" (*hrasva*).
Because the short vowels have the form of the Puruṣa, they possess the nature of Fire and the Sun; because they are vowels (*svara*), they possess the nature of the Moon.
For the long vowels, their nature as the Moon arises from being vowels, while their nature as the Sun and Fire arises from being produced from the short vowels.
Thinking that, according to other treatises, these two designations might apply only to the ten [vowels], he says "they would be" (*te syuḥ*).
He states that they possess that nature by means of another method with the words "of the vowels" (*svarāṇām*).
By the term "situated in the middle" (*madhyagam*), it is indicated that their origin is from the letter *ra*.
As the teachers have said: "The four vowels beginning with ṛ are traditionally held to be produced from the letter r and followed by the letter l."
By this [it is shown that] the group of six short vowels arises from the letter *ha*, and the group of six long vowels arises from the letter *ī*.

In that regard, because the letter *ha* has the form of the male (*puṃs*), it possesses the nature of the sun (*arka*); because the letter *ī* has the form of power (*śakti*), it possesses the nature of the moon (*soma*).
Because the letter *ra* has the nature of fire (*agni*), it possesses the nature of fire.
Although we do not explicitly state here the distinction that the letter *ha* is the cause of the six short vowels,
nevertheless, since it is impossible for it to be the cause of their production in isolation, the persistence of both [the *ha* and the *ra*] must necessarily be required.
In this same way, the same should be understood for the other two as well.
Thus, each one possesses the nature of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni.
As it has been said in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*:
"Since an effect is never produced when only one [of the three] is manifested [in reality], therefore a state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) is established among all things.
Thus, *sāmarasya* is the existence of the triad. (5–6)
He states the same thing in another way with the words "in Piṅgalā":
since both Iḍā and Piṅgalā are included within the Suṣumṇā during the emergence of the neuter [state], their respective phonemes are also included therein;
for without those two, that emergence cannot occur.
Therefore it was said previously: "She whose nature is that of Agni and Soma. (7)
He demonstrates that each of the consonants (*vyañjana*) has the nature of the Moon, Sun, and Fire by the phrase "without vowels" (*vinā svaraiḥ*).

Having begun with the words, "By whom [the phonemes] have attained their existence from the Sun consisting of Śiva and Śakti," he concludes what was stated in the passage beginning with "All are deities of the Moon, Sun, and Fire" with the word "Śiva."
"Therefore" is a restatement of the three previously mentioned reasons.
Śiva is of the nature of the sun and fire, while Śakti is of the nature of the moon;
or else, that which is Śiva is indeed Śakti herself.
Because there is no difference between Śiva and Śakti, she is also said to be of the nature of the seed-syllable (bīja) of Bhuvaneśī.
As the Teachers have said:
"Just as the letters divided into the six groups cannot be other than the vowels..."
"Thus it is woven by Savitṛ.
In this way, by indicating the process of tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) and the emergence from the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśī, the creation from the three luminaries (*tejas*) has been described. (8)
Since the Mātṛkā has arisen from the five elements as its cause, therefore the phonemes (varṇas), which consist of the elements, are fivefold each according to their division. || 9 ||

Now, indicating the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) and the origin from the *praṇava*, he speaks again of the division of phonemes for the purpose of their separate application, beginning with the words "From the cause" (*kāraṇāt*).
Alternatively, in response to the inquiry— "Which are those phonemes" regarding what was stated as "joined with their respective phonemes"— he says, "From the cause."
From the cause, which is the bindu arising from the union of Śiva and Śakti;
"mātṛkā" is the designation for the collection of phonemes beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'. As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"That well-known garland of letters is called the supreme Mātṛkā.
Thus [it is said]. By way of five-fifths—that is, ten divisions—and furthermore, according to the previous sequence, there is even the repetition "five by five" (*pañcato'pi pañca*). || 9 ||
The elements of air, fire, earth, water, and space correspond respectively to the fifty letters.
Five are short, five are long, ending with the nasal bindu, and they arise from the junctions [of vowels and consonants]. || 10 ||

The consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṣa*, *kṣa*, *la*, *sa*, and *ha* are declared to be fivefold, arising from the letters of the Mātṛkā through the divisions of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire. || 11 ||
He explains that very [point] which was indicated by the words "wind" (*vāyu*) and so forth.
Because wind and space are mentioned as being at the beginning and the end [of the sequence], they are stated out of their natural order (*vyutkrama*).
This is for the purpose of highlighting their primary importance in the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*).
In that regard, there are fifty [phonemes] so that those whose letters are fixed may be included within their respective elements (*bhūta-tattva*).
Since the *visarga* is not included therein, it does not possess a secondary status.
It is well known that there are five short vowels and five long vowels.
Since those [vowels] that can arise from *saṃdhi* are mentioned separately here, there is no inclusion of the technical (*pāribhāṣika*) short and long vowels.
The phrase "ending in *viṃdu*" is a qualifier for those that can arise from *saṃdhi*;
these are *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*.
The manner in which their formation through euphonic combination (*sandhi*) occurs has been stated by the Teachers as follows: "Through the union of *a* and *i*, the phoneme *e* is desired;
then, through the union of that very *e* with *a*, the syllable *ai* arises."
In conjunction with the letter *u*, that very [vowel] becomes the vowel named *o*;
in conjunction with the letter *ū*, that same [vowel] becomes the vowel named *au*.
"The four diphthongs are the mantras that accomplish all aims.
Now, one might ask: why is the visarga not counted here?

It is said: impelled by the vital breath (*prāṇapavana*) through an effort produced by the desire to speak arising from the *mūlādhāra*, and emerging from the throat itself without reaching another articulatory site (*sthāna*), this [sound] consisting of *prakṛti* is not counted among the elements (*bhūta*) in this creation.

For this very reason, the Teachers have stated the production of the letters beginning with *ka* from the creation itself in the passage starting with "The creation emerging from the throat" and ending with "the creation would indeed be perishable.
In the *Kādimata* as well, it is said:
"The five pentads are proclaimed to consist of breath, fire, air, water, and ether."
The creation called the power of illusion (māyā-śakti) is the Lord who consists of all beings.
"Therefore, its placement here is not in a single location within the self of Śiva.
The remainder [of the phrase] is "the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *śa*.
By this [it is shown that]: *a, ā, e, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, ṣa* belong to the region of Vāyu.

In this manner, *i*, *ī*, *e*, *kha*, *cha*, *ṭha*, *tha*, *pha*, *ra*, and *kṣā* belong to the fire element (*āgneyāḥ*). In the same way, it should be understood for the [vowels] beginning with *bhū* as well.
As it was said by the Teachers:
The vowels beginning with *ū* and *a*, scattered with the fourth letter (*ṇa*), are the days;
the second protection (*rakṣā*) is by sight alone; the years of Fire (*vahni*) are those beginning with the non-dual (*advandva*) and *yonika*.
The winds (*marutaḥ*) are the letters of the cheek (*kapola*) and the dot (*bindu*), along with the fifth letter (*ma*); likewise for Space (*vyoman*) in the case of *śa-hau*.
Thus [it is said].
Here, in this section on the purification of mantras, the method of purification characterized by one's own *kula* and other *kulas* has not been explicitly stated;
it is indicated by the description of the elemental phonemes (*bhūtavarṇa*).
The results are as stated by Piṅgalāmata:
"The number of syllables is proclaimed to be forty-five."
The group (gaṇa) should be known as consisting of nine in the five [categories] beginning with the earthly (pārthiva).
In this context, because long vowels are grasped by short ones alone, there is the statement "by nine.
If the first letter of both the mantra and the practitioner is of the earth element (pārthiva), then that is declared to be his *kula*; one should observe other cases in the same manner.
In the Pārthiva [circle], the Vāruṇa is the friend; likewise, in the Āgneya, the Māruta is the friend.
In the circles of Indra and Varuṇa, the Māruta is proclaimed to be the enemy.
An enemy of the watery element is the fiery one, and likewise, the fiery element is the enemy of the watery;
however, that which arises from space is common to all elements indeed.
"Where there is a conjunction of mutually contradictory phonemes, that mantra kills the practitioner, or at least it does not become favorable toward him. Thus it is said.
Also in another Tantra: "I shall describe the division of phonemes established according to four measures."
One's own family, a friend, a neutral party, and an enemy as the fourth.
The winds, fires, waters, and the earth are proclaimed;
they bring about progressively higher accomplishment, as well as equanimity, disease, and death.
Having approached them, the ministers attain [their goals] here; understand these [results]:
success is declared when [the king is] a friend, but nothing at all when he is neutral.

Death, disease, and enemies [occur] within one's own family; however, there is supreme success when the first letter of the name of the practitioner follows that of the person to be accomplished, in due order.
Having drawn [the diagram] with upper and lower positions, one should determine the degrees;
the fire element is the friend of the wind element, while the water element is neutral.
One should know the Pārthiva as the enemy of the Vāyava, and the Vāyava as the enemy of the Taijasa;
furthermore, the Vāruṇa is the enemy of the Taijasa, while the Pārthiva is neutral toward the Rudra.
The Vāyavya is declared to be a friend, while the Taijasa is one's own kinsman;
