the Pārthiva is a friend in the Vāruṇa state, whereas the Vāyava is neutral.
One should know that the fiery (taijas) is the enemy, while the watery (vāruṇa) is one's own kin;
in the case of the earthy (pārthiva), the watery is a friend and the fiery is declared to be the enemy.

"Vāyu is neutral, while Pṛthu’s lineage is its own [dominant] family. This has been described to you as the 'division of castes' (varṇāṃśaka) together with its ancestral lineages. Thus [ends verses 10–11].
The thirty-eight *kalās* are established within their respective maṇḍalas:
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, and Dhṛti. || 12 ||
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā, and Pūrṇāmṛtā—these are the digits born of the vowels that bestow all desires. || 13 ||
The initial division was made for the purpose of the thirty-eight *kalās* and so forth. He states those very *kalās* with the words "Soma," etc.
By this, it is stated that the production of the thirty-eight *kalās* arises precisely from the three divisions of the *praṇava*: the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*.
In this context, the first syllable possesses the nature of the Moon because it takes the form of the *visarga*.
The vowel *u* has the nature of Fire, since the *visarjanīya* arises from the letter *r*.
That the letter *m* has the nature of the Sun is well known.
If it is asked, "How can the first and second [syllables] have the nature of Soma and Agni?", it is replied:
In the final chapter, he will explain the origin of the *praṇava* from the *ajapā*.
In that context, when reversed, the *ajapā* becomes *so 'ham*. When the letters *sa* and *ha* are elided as before, the *praṇava* is established.
Therein, the first syllable consists of the *visarga*.
As it is said: "The *sarga* (visarga) is power (*śakti*) and the moon (*niśākara*).

When the *visarga* of that very [syllable] undergoes the substitution of *sakāra* and the substitution of *utva*, the substitution of the letter *u* occurs; thus, it possesses the nature of fire (*agnitva*).
Alternatively, because it will be stated later that "the *praṇava* consists of three letters" derived from the sun, moon, and fire, those [letters] possess such a nature.
Therefore, this is what is meant:
the production of thirty-eight *kalās* from the three divisions of the *praṇava*, and the production of fifty *kalās* from its five divisions.
However, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*—
For the sake of the activity of worldly existence, the three elements— taking the form of fire, sun, and moon— move about by relying upon space and wind.
That fire which consists of the essence of Rudra is known as the three-fold *tejas*;
its qualities became ninefold when divided by the attributes of *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*.
The ten digits of Fire, together with the Bindu, are said to bestow merit;
that essence which is of the nature of Brahma is the Sun, and it possesses four qualities.
Those qualities, through their further differentiation into sub-qualities, become twelve;
thus, the twelve digits (kalās) of the Sun are renowned as bestowers of wealth.
It is not shown as "nāda," "kalā," and so forth, because it is formless;
and that earth which is of the nature of Viṣṇu is Soma, consisting of the five qualities.
"Those qualities also became fifteen through their individual divisions;
those sixteen digits (kalās) of the moon, together with the seed-syllable (bīja), bestow the body of love.
Thus, "in those respective maṇḍalas" refers to the lunar maṇḍala, the solar maṇḍala, and the fire maṇḍala.
By the phrase "born from its own vowel" (*svaraja*), it is stated that in the worship of Amṛtā and the others, one should perform the worship by placing the vowel at the beginning.
The practical application there is as follows: *aṃ amṛtāyai namaḥ*, and so forth. (12–13)
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumṇā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā. || 14 ||

The twelve [calories] beginning with Kābhā and ending with Sauryāṣṭhā are proclaimed as the givers of wealth (vasudā). They are Dhūmrā, Arciḥ, Uṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and also Havyavahā and Kavyavahā. || 15 ||
These digits (kalās) of the ten vowels, beginning with *a*, bestow righteousness;
they should be meditated upon as white, yellow, and red, respectively, while granting fearlessness and desired boons. || 16 ||
"Beginning with *ka*," etc., means:
twelve letters in direct order from the letter *ka* up to *ṭha*, and twelve letters in reverse order from the letter *bha* up to *ḍa*.
The application therein is as follows: *kaṃ bhaṃ tapinyai namaḥ*.
*Khaṃ baṃ tāpinyai namaḥ*, and so forth.
Regarding *havyakavyavahe*: it is a *dvandva* compound of the two words *havya* and *kavya*, which is then compounded with the word *vaha*.

By the maxim that "a word heard after a *dvandva* compound is connected with each member individually," there are two powers: *havyavāha* (bearer of oblations to the gods) and *kavyavāha* (bearer of oblations to the ancestors).
By the phrase "of *yā* and the others," it is stated that *dhūmrārcis*, *cīra*, and so forth, possess the nature of *yā* and the rest.
The ritual application (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: "Obeisance to you, O *dhūmrārcis*," and so on. (14–15)
Regarding "abhayeṣṭa": "iṣṭa" means a boon.
In this regard, those who know the tradition maintain that the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) is in the right hand and the gesture of granting a boon (vara) is in the left hand.
And it has been said:
"The right hand raised and extended is the *abhaya-mudrā*;
the left hand turned downward and extended is the *vara-mudrā*."

In the tenth chapter, regarding the meditation on Bhuvaneśī, it is said: "The right hands are described as holding a goad and the gesture of fearlessness; the left hands hold a noose and grant desired boons."

In another tantra, regarding the meditation on Sarasvatī: "Her two upper arms hold a rosary and a water-pot, while her lower pair display the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*); in one hand she holds a book. Thus it is said.
In the *Sautrāmaṇītantra*, in the fifth chapter:
"She holds in her right hands a wheel, a sword, a mace, and the gesture of fearlessness; and she bears in her left arms a conch, a shield, a plow, and the gesture of granting boons."
In another tantra, regarding the constant meditation: "Holding a skull-cup and likewise the gesture of fearlessness with her right hands," and so forth.
In another [text] as well: "She holds in her hands a noose, a banner, a shield, the Śārṅga bow, and a boon-granting gesture, while on her left side she is adorned with all ornaments."

"Holding an elephant goad, a staff, a sword, and an arrow, as well as the gesture of fearlessness, with her right hands, she is seated upon a lotus pedestal. Thus it is said. Also in the *Kādimata*: "Speak, O God Maheśāna, regarding the gross and subtle forms."
The accomplishment of various actions in the two meditations through their connection with results.
Now, O Maheśānī, listen as I describe in due order the weapons for their respective hands that have been mentioned; indeed, you shall hear them now from the remainder.
In the two-armed form, the left and right hands should display the gestures of boon-granting (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*);
in the four-armed form, they hold a noose (*pāśa*) and a goad (*aṅkuśa*); and in the six-armed form, they hold a bow and an arrow.
"Leather shield and sword in eight arms, mace and trident in ten declared.

Therefore, wherever the meditation on Śakti involves the gestures of boon-granting (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), it should generally be understood that the *abhaya* is in the right hand and the *vara* in the left.
As for that which is stated in the latter hexad:
"With the left [hand] joined in the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), and with the right, however, in the gesture of granting boons (varada)."
Elsewhere as well:
"The goddess, intent on granting boons, holds a book and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and a rosary in her right."
Thus.
This should be understood as applying to each specific deity according to the respective tradition of one's own guru; enough said on this point.
Regarding the phrase "in due order":

The colors of the gentle digits (saumyakalā) and so forth are white and the like; by this, the inclusion of color, clothing, garlands, and ornaments is intended. This should be understood in the same way for what follows as well. || 16 ||
From the five divisions of Tāra, there arise the fifty phonemic energies (kalās).
He indicates those *kalās* for the sake of which the division among the five elements was stated;

or rather, he points them out with the words "of the *tāra*" (*tārasya*), as they were previously indicated at the end of the preceding chapter [1.111] by the statement, "the *kalās* are non-different from its phonemes.
The five divisions of the *tāra*, that is, the *praṇava*, are the letters *a*, *u*, *m*, the *bindu*, and the *nāda*.
Although the sixth and seventh divisions of the *praṇava* are "Power" (*śakti*) and "Peace" (*śānti*), nevertheless they are not included among these [sixteen],
because they are transcendent (*paratva*).
As it has been said:
"Since the two subsequent [letters] of the sevenfold Tāra are themselves further [extensions],
therefore those called Śakti and Śānta are not recited together with the others.
Here, the word "fifty" (pañcāśat) is used figuratively (lākṣaṇika).
The ellipsis is "the arts (kalās) were produced in sequence.
By the maxim of the crow's eye and the eyeball, the word "in sequence" is connected to both [contexts]. || 17 ||
Creation, intellect, memory, intelligence, splendor, fortune, steadfastness, stability, and accomplishment—these are declared to be the kalās of the *ka*-group in their respective order. (18)
Born from the syllable *A*, these goddesses possess the luster of molten gold;
they hold in their hands a rosary, two lotuses, and a water-pot. || 19 ||
Jarā, Pālinī, Śānti, Īśvarī, Ratikāmukā, Varadā, Āhlādinī, Prīti, and Dīrghā are the goddesses born from the *ṣ* and *t* groups [of consonants]. || 20 ||

From the syllable *U*, those born of Viṣṇu are proclaimed to be dark like the leaf of the *tāla* tree, with their arms displaying the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*), the lotus, and the discus. || 21 ||
Tīkṣṇā, Raudrī, Bhayā, Nidrā, Tandrī, Kṣut, Krodhinī, Kriyā, Utkārī, and Mṛtyu—these are said to be the [deities] born from the *pa* group. || 22 ||
Born from the syllable *māṃ* by Rudra, they possess a luster like that of the autumnal moon;
with their arms, they hold the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), the trident, the skull-bowl, and the boon-granting gesture (*vara*). || 23 ||

He states that very sequence with the words beginning "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) and ending with "thus the fifty have been explained. It should be understood that they are produced from the letter *a*, which is a part of the *praṇava*, and also produced by Brahman, who is denoted by that [letter].
This is because of the non-difference between the signified and the signifier.
As it was said by the Teachers: "The [letters] originate from the syllable *a* and are born of Brahman. The same applies hereafter as well.
"Akṣasrak" means a rosary of beads.
The visualization of the weapons extends from the lower right hand to the lower left hand.
"Āhlādinī" is the division of the word.
*Dara* means a conch shell.
*Nibhā* refers to the splendor or luster of the autumnal moon; those [garlands] possess such a radiance.
Alternatively, the word *nibha* signifies "resembling. (18–23)
Spoken by Īśvara, [the letters] from the *bindu* are yellow, white, reddish-brown, and black;
and those situated in the *ṣa*-group are infinite and resemble the color of the hibiscus flower. || 24 ||
Holding the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), the deer, and the axe in her arms, she grants boons;
she is Nivṛtti, along with Pratiṣṭhā, Vidya, and immediately after, Śānti. || 25 ||
Indhikā, Dīpikā, Recikā, Mocikā, and the supreme [Parā];
likewise Sūkṣmā, Sūkṣmāmṛtā, Jñānāmṛtā, and Āpyāyinī. || 26 ||
Pervasive and of the nature of space, they are infinite and conjoined with their own essential sounds; born from Nāda by Sadāśiva, these possess a white luster. || 27 ||
Their lotus-like hands are enriched with a rosary, a book, a string of beads, and a skull-cup;
one should first employ the sixteen digits born of the vowels during the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Thus, the fifty digits that bestow all prosperity have been declared. || 28 ||
Bindukalā says: "By Īśvara.
Regarding the word "bindoḥ," there is a word-division (*padaccheda*) as *asita*.
"Hariṇam" refers to the mark of a deer;
others consider it to be a young fawn.
"Ṭaṅkaḥ" means an axe.
"Sapratiṣṭhā" means accompanied by the *pratiṣṭhā*-kalā;
"parā" is the name of a *kalā*;
"sūkṣmāmṛtā" is one [kalā], and "jñānāmṛtā" is another.
Ananta is the sixteenth digit (kalā).
Guṇa is the trident (śūla).
"Hand-lotus" (*karāmbuja*) is a simile-compound (*upamā-samāsa*).
Regarding the first [verse], the visualization of the weapons is "upward" in the right and left [hands], while in the latter, it is "downward. Some, however, maintain that the order is reversed.
This sequence has been stated for the worship of the conch.
Regarding the sequence of placement upon the body, he says "In the placement," where "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction from what preceded.
"Bestowing all prosperity" is the fruit of the ritual placement (nyāsa). || 24–28 ||
Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, and Amareśvara. || 29 ||
Arghīśa, Bhārabhūtīśa, Tithīśa, Sthāṇuka, Hara, Jhiṇṭīśa, Bhautika, Sadyojāta, and Anugraheśvara. || 30 ||
Akrūra, Mahāsena, and the sixteen forms of the Svaras;
and thereafter Krodhīśa, Caṇḍeśa, Pañcāntaka, and Śivottama. || 31 ||
Then there were Ekārdraka, Kūrma, Ekanetra, Āhvaya, and Caturānana;
likewise Aja, Īśa, Sarva, Someśa, as well as Lāṅgalin and Dāruka. || 32 ||
Ardhanārīśvara, Umākānta, Aṣāḍhin, Daṇḍin, Adri, Mīna, Meṣa, Lohitāśva, and Śikhin; || 33 ||
Chagalaṇḍa and Dviraṇḍeśa, those known as Mahākāla and Vālin, as well as those called Bhujaṅgeśa, Pinākīśa, and Khaḍgīśa, are likewise [the lords of the faces]. || 34 ||
Śvetabhṛgu, Īśala, Kulīśiva, and Saṃvarttaka—these are remembered as the Rudras; they are red in color and hold tridents and skull-bowls. || 35 ||
The phrase "the Rudras and others" refers to the Rudras previously mentioned; he identifies them as Śrīkaṇṭha and so forth.
Regarding "Sthāṇuka," the suffix *ka* is used in the sense of the base itself, thus it is the name Sthāṇu.
"Ekarudra, Kūrma, Ekanetra, and Caturānana" is a copulative compound (*dvandva*).
The word *āhva* is not included within the category of technical names (*saṃjñā*). The same applies to *ākhyā* and the others that follow.
[As in the examples] *chagalaṇḍa* and *dviraṇḍa*.
The word "īśa" (Lord) is connected to both [sides].
The visualization of the weapons is for the left and right [hands].
The same applies hereafter as well.
This is the general rule.
What is to be stated hereafter, beginning with "bandhūka" and so forth, should be understood as applying when there is a fusion with the *śakti*.
The same applies to the Viṣṇus as well.

As for the expression "shining like molten gold" found in certain places, it should be understood that this is due to the predominance of the power (*śakti*) within the non-difference of the power and its possessor (*śaktimān*). || 29-35 ||
Pūrṇodarī, Virajā, and Śālmalī follow after that; Lolākṣī, Vartulākṣī, and Dīrghaghoṇā are likewise proclaimed. || 36 ||
Sudīrghamukhī and Gomukhī, as well as Dīrghajihvā; Kuṇḍodarī and Ūrdhvakeśī, and likewise Vikṛtamukhī. || 37 ||
Then Jvālāmukhī is to be known, followed by Ulkāmukhī; then Suśrīmukhī and Vidyāmukhī—these are the powers of the vowels (svaraśaktis). || 38 ||
Mahākālī and Sarasvatī are endowed with all supernatural powers;
Gaurī is the knowledge of the three worlds, and beyond that is the power of mantra.
Ātmaśakti, Bhūtamātā, and likewise Lambodarī are considered [the powers]; furthermore, Drāviṇī, Nāgarī, Khecarī, and Mañjarī. || 40 ||
Rūpiṇī, Vīriṇī, and then Kākodaryā as well as Pūtanā;
there may also be Bhadrakālī and Yoginī, as well as Śaṅkhinī and Gajīnī. || 41 ||
Kālarātri, Kubjinī, Kapardinī, and Vajriṇī; Jayā, Sumukheśvarī, Revatī, and likewise Mādhavī. || 42 ||
The Vāruṇī and Vāyavī [powers] are proclaimed, followed by Rakṣovidāriṇī;
thereafter comes Sahajā Lakṣmī, all-pervasive and endowed with Māyā. || 43 ||
These [goddesses] are seated upon the Rudrāṅka-pīṭha, their bodies crimson with vermilion;
the lotuses of their hands are adorned with red lotuses and skull-cups. || 44 ||
He indicates these powers denoted by the initial words with the verse beginning "pūrṇedari.
This same principle should also be applied to Viṣṇu and the powers of Viṣṇu.
In the expression "sudīrghamukhigomukhyau bhadrakāliyoginyau," the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (optionally) in the rule "ṅyāpoḥ saṃjñācchandasorbahulam" [Pāṇini 6.3.63] accounts for the form.
The first member of the compound takes its short vowel;
however, in actual usage, it remains long.
"Endowed with all perfections" (*sarvasiddhisamanvitā*) is an epithet of Gaurī.

Therefore, the name of the Śakti is *Sarvasiddhigaurī*, as stated by the author of the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā* and others; likewise, it is said elsewhere: "Gaurī is designated by the name Sarvasiddhi."
Of the Rudras, beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha;
"aṅka" means the lap. (Verses 36–44)
Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Mādhava, Govinda, and Viṣṇu;
another is known as Madhusūdana, and then Trivikrama and Vāmana. || 45 ||
Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and thereafter Dāmodara, Vāsudeva, and Saṅkarṣaṇa—these are thus proclaimed. || 46 ||
Pradyumna and Aniruddha are, in order, the personified forms of the vowels;

thereafter [the forms] are the wielder of the discus, the wielder of the mace, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the wielder of the sword, the wielder of the conch, and again the wielder of the plow. || 47 ||
Muṣalī is known as Śūli; another is Pāśī, and then Aṅkuśī.
Mukunda, Nandaja, Nandī, Nara, Narakajit, and Hari. || 48 ||
Kṛṣṇa, Satya, Sātvata, Śauri, Śūra, Janārdana, Bhūdhara, Viśvamūrti, Vaikuṇṭha, and Puruṣottama. || 49 ||
Bali, the younger brother of Bala, Bāla, Vṛṣaghna, and again Vṛṣa;
Siṃha, Varāha, Vimala, and Nṛsiṃha—these are the forms of Halāyudha (the wielder of the plow). || 50 ||
These [deities], Keśava and the others, are dark-complexioned, holding discs, conchs, and lotuses in their hands;
they are Kīrti, Kānti, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Dhṛti, Śānti, Kriyā, and Dayā. || 51 ||
Medhā, Saharṣā, Śraddhā, Lajjā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Prīti, and Rati—these are declared to be the powers of the vowels in their respective order. || 52 ||
Jayā, Durgā, Prabhā, Satyā, Caṇḍā, Vāṇī, Vilāsinī, Vijayā, Virajā, Viśvā, Vinadā, Sunadā, and Smṛti. || 53 ||
She is supernatural power (ṛddhi), prosperity (samṛddhi), purity (śuddhi); she is devotion (bhakti), intelligence (buddhi), mindfulness (smṛti), and forbearance (kṣamā).
She is delight (ramā), Umā, the moistening one (kledinī), the drenched one (klinnā), the giver of wealth (vasudā), and the earth (vasudhā) who is beyond compare. || 54 ||
Parā, Parāyaṇā, Sūkṣmā, Sandhyā, Prajñā, Prabhā, Niśā, Amoghā, Vidyutā, and Kīrti—these and others grant all desires. || 55 ||
Seated upon the laps of their beloveds with smiling faces, these [goddesses] have limbs resembling streaks of lightning and hands that grant boons and protection like lotuses. || 56 ||
He also mentions Keśava and the others, as well as their Śaktis, who are included by the word "etcetera," in the passage beginning with "Keśava.
The term "halām" refers to consonants according to the technical terminology of grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇaparibhāṣā*).
The meditation on the weapons is performed in the left and right [hands].
The same applies in the subsequent cases as well. The compound *vasudhāparā* is to be analyzed as *aparā vasudhā*; *parā* is the name of a *kalā*. (45–56)
From the various phonemes of the *mātṛkā*, all mantras were born;
through the division of mantras and vidyās, there are three types of mantra lineages. || 57 ||
All mantras are declared to have the nature of male, female, or neuter. Mantras are to be known as male deities, while Vidyās are remembered as female deities. || 58 ||
Then, from the words "Consciousness" (*caitanya*) up to "consisting of fifty letters" (*pañcāśad-varṇarūpiṇī*), the nature of Kuṇḍalī as the Mātṛkā is described;

it is also stated that the mantras have arisen from her alone. He introduces this as the reason for the threefold classification of mantras that will be explained for the purpose of their practical application (*prayoga*).
Regarding the term "mātṛkā":
the word "yataḥ" (from which) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Its origin was previously stated by the phrase "consisting of Śiva and Śakti."
He demonstrates that very same principle regarding mantras as well with the word "mantra.
The term "mātṛkā" is to be construed with "from that" (tataḥ).
By this, it is stated that all [mantras] possess the nature of both the Moon and the Sun.
As stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Those mantras are said to be of two kinds, according to the division between the lunar (*saumya*) and the solar (*saura*). The solar mantras have male deities; they are proclaimed as [the] mantras."
"Likewise, those known as the Vidyās are gentle and have women as their presiding deities.
By the rising of these two, the rising of all [the other planets] is also said to occur. || 57 ||
He states that mantras are of three kinds—masculine, feminine, and neuter—for the sake of accomplishing specific applications (*prayoga*).

Here too, because the middle group of four consists of Śiva and Śakti, it is neuter; thus, among the threefold nature of the vowels, since there is no utterance of others apart from them, their causality should be understood by way of their being of that same nature.
Because the word "all" (*sarva*) is used here, the term "mantra" is not to be understood in its technical sense;
this applies likewise in what follows.
If it is asked, "How can there be a conceptualization of male, female, and so forth for a mantra that denotes partless consciousness and indivisible bliss?"—this is true.
In reality, it does not exist at all;
it is a mere mental construction for the sake of lay practitioners (upāsakas),
as they have said:
The conceptualization of forms for Brahman— which is composed of consciousness, non-dual, partless, and bodiless— is intended for the sake of the practice of its worshippers.
Regarding the deities of the form realm (rūpadhātu), there is the conceptualization of three genders, beginning with male, female, and neuter. Thus,
male mantras are considered to end in *huṃ phaṭ*, while those of females are held to end in the two *viṭhas* (*oṃ svāhā*).
The neuter ones end with "namaḥ"; thus the mantras have been described as being of three kinds. || 59 ||

According to the intention of Gārgya, he states their characteristics as "pum" and so forth. According to the tradition, "ending in huṃ phaṭ" means that they end in those [syllables] either individually or collectively. "Ending in dviṭha" means ending in svāhā.
By the word *ṭha*, the *bindu* is expressed either through similarity or by implication;
for according to the lexicon, "Ṭha is in the void (*śūnya*) and in the great wind.
The void is indeed of the nature of the *bindu*.
Its doubling results in that visarga, and that is of the nature of Śakti. Thus, by the word *dviṭha*, the fire-śakti is called *svāhā*.
In the *Prayogasāra*, however, it is stated: "Mantras ending in *vaṣaṭ* or *phaṭ* are masculine; those ending in *vauṣaṭ* or *svāhā* are feminine;
and those ending in *huṃ* or *namaḥ* are neuter—thus mantras are remembered as being of three kinds."

The mantras are also inferred by means of the *tāra* [the syllable *oṃ*], from their beginning, end, and middle, according to their proximity to the nature of male, female, and neuter, just as [gender is determined] by the presence of the nasal drop (*bindu*), the visarga, or the crescent moon (*indukhaṇḍa*) at the end; thus they are proclaimed. (59)
These three types of mantras are taught for the purposes of subjugation, pacification, and malevolent rites;
the mantras should be understood as having the nature of Agni and Soma, corresponding respectively to the cruel and the gentle. || 60 ||
The *mantras* of the two [classes of] *karma* are said to consist mostly of fire, stars, the letter *m*, and space;
those of the *āgneya* class abound in the syllable *m*, while those of the *saumya* class abound in the immortal syllable *u*.
When the vital breath moves in the southern channel, the fires awaken;
and when the breath is situated in the other part, the lunar elements attain awakening.
When the vital breath has entered both channels, all [deities] attain awakening;
once awakened, they always bestow their fruit upon the practitioners of mantra. || 63 ||
He states the purpose for the three types in sequence with the words "are praised" (*śastā*).
It is said in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"The remaining males are praised; they are especially [effective] for subjugation (*vaśya*) and eradication (*uccāṭa*)."
"When the destruction of the subtle activity (kṣudrakriyā) occurs, women [attain it], and elsewhere, those who are neither male nor female.

Since the prior arising of the Mātṛkā-Kuṇḍalī has been stated, and because she consists of the nature of fire and moon (agnīṣoma), he shows that the mantras likewise possess that nature with the word "agnī" (fire).
The phrase "of the two actions" (karmaṇoḥ) connects back to what precedes.
Vahni is the letter *ra*.
Tāra is the syllable *oṃ*.
Antya is the letter *kṣa*.
The letter *ha* represents space (*viyat*).
The word *prāyaḥ* generally signifies abundance;
as Amarasimha states: "The word *prāyaḥ* is used in the sense of majority, in the sense of 'mostly,' and in the sense of 'slowly'."
The term "belonging to Agni" (āgneyāḥ) is connected with what precedes; that is the Moon (indu).
This is because, in the ritual placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa), the lunar orb is placed beginning with the letter *sa*.
"Amṛtam vaḥ. Here, when one [term] occurs in plurality, it denotes the essence (tattva). This has been stated by Īśānaśiva:
The letters beginning with *tāra* (om) and *kāśa* (ka), and ending with the final and initial letters [of their respective groups], are fiery (*āgneya*); the others are lunar (*saumya*).
A lunar mantra may become fiery if it ends in *namaḥ*, and a fiery mantra may become lunar if it ends in *phaṭ*.
Through fiery mantras, one achieves success in cruel rites; through lunar mantras, one should perform gentle rites in the prescribed manner. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "A mantra whose final syllable is 'tāra' (om), 'agni' (ra), or 'viyat' (ha), is generally considered fiery;
the remainder is lunar. These two are praised for fierce and gentle rites respectively."

"An Āgneya mantra should generally be Saumya, accompanied by 'namaḥ' at the end; likewise, a Saumya mantra becomes Āgneya when it is joined with 'phaṭ' at the conclusion. Thus it is said. Also in the Piṅgalāmata: "Even a Raudra mantra attains a state of tranquility when it is endowed with a peaceful (Saumya) class [of syllables]."
"Even a peaceful mantra, if it is sprouted with *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*, becomes fierce.
Regarding this, there is a specific detail in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"One should recite two mantras known as 'fiery' and 'lunar,' having the *tāra* (om) at the beginning and end respectively, for the two [types of practice]."
Thus it is explained in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*:
one lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) consists of four degrees (*aṃśaka*).

Among those, for the asterisms belonging to Agni, the two eastern parts constitute the head and the other part the tail; for those belonging to Soma, the two northern parts constitute the head and the other part the tail. Gārgya maintains that no ritual application should be performed during the time of the tail.
The lunar mansions belonging to Agni and Soma will be explained in the "Snake-Wheel" (*ahicakra*). Among those, the solar mansions are the fiery mansions (*agninakṣatra*).
Regarding the fruit of awakening, he says: "they bestow."
Otherwise, because faults are observed,
as it is said in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"A mantra that is either asleep or merely awakened does not bestow accomplishment."
The time of sleep is when [the breath] flows through the left [nostril], and waking is when it flows through the right.

"The reversal of this [sequence] for the fire-mantra and the moon-mantra—one should know it to be the time of awakening; both flow for both. Also elsewhere: "But at the time of sleep, the recitation of a mantra does not bestow its intended fruit."
Thus [it is said].
Elsewhere, the time of sleep is stated otherwise,
as they say:
"From the union of the breath (prāṇa) [and the downward flow] (apāna), there is the meeting of Śiva and Śakti;
this is to be known as the time of awakening, and the time of sleep follows thereafter.
Elsewhere, however, another method for the sake of awakening is stated:
Having carefully encapsulated the letters beginning with *la* and ending with *na*, together with the bindu, and again ending with the visarga, one should recite the letter *kṣa* alone.
If thus recited as instructed, it bestows swift accomplishment upon the awakened one. Thus [it is said].
By describing their essential natures as male, female, and so forth, their mutual opposition is also indicated.
As they say:
"Those whose presiding deity is female are generally enemies of one whose presiding deity is male."
In matters concerning women as deities, there shall be mutual conflict between those who are gentle and those who are cruel.
The same applies to the male deities.
Thus, the connection with the subsequent [section] is by way of the reversal of the preceding. || 62–63 ||
Those mantras that are defective—such as being "cut" (chinna) and so forth—do not protect the practitioner.
They are described as being cut, obstructed, devoid of power, or turned away. || 64 ||
Deaf and blind, as well as paralyzed and immobilized;
burnt, terrified, frightened, soiled, and insulted—(65)

Furthermore, one who is divided, one who is fast asleep, one intoxicated by passion, one who has fainted, one whose vitality is stolen, one who is deficient, one who is ruined, and again, a child. || 66 ||
Furthermore, [the types of mantras are]: the Kumāra, the Yuvan, the Prauḍha, the Vṛddha, the Nistriṃśaka, the Nirbīja, the Siddhihīna, the Manda, and the Kūṭa. || 67 ||
He is partless and devoid of essence; he is squint-eyed and seedless. He is enveloped in smoke, deluded, and afflicted by hunger. || 68 ||
One who is excessively arrogant, one who is physically deficient, one who is said to be excessively angry, one who is excessively cruel, one who is bashful, and one whose mind is tranquil; || 69 ||
One who has fallen from his position, one who is incapacitated, and one who is very old are proclaimed [as unfit].
I shall now describe the characteristics of those who are devoid of affection and those who are afflicted. || 70 ||
In this regard, since it has been stated that mantras arise from the *mātṛkā* which consists of Śakti and Śiva, the defects such as *āṇava* and so forth serve as the causes for their arising.
Consequently, mantras associated with internal defects such as being "severed" (*chinna*) yield contrary results; thus he says, "severed," etc.
That mantras corrupted by defects such as being severed do not protect the practitioner is the general result applicable to all.
The specific results for each [case] that will be described later should be understood accordingly.
He explains the meaning of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) with the words "severed" (*chinna*).
Furthermore, by the phrase "likewise again," he indicates that the *kūṭa* itself is the indicator of the indivisible (*niraṃśa*).
"Extremely aged" (*ativṛddha*) is a qualification of "devoid of oil" (*niḥsneha*); therefore, after being devoid of oil, one becomes extremely aged, and subsequently afflicted. (64–70)

That mantra whose beginning, middle, and end contain the seed-syllable *ā* (the wind), whether conjoined or unjoined, and further [characterized by] being mounted by a consonant (*khara*), is of four or five types; such is known as the "severed" (*chinna*) mantra. || 71 ||
Regarding "of *manu*":
it refers to the syllable *yaṃ*.
The phrase "at the beginning, middle, and end" indicates a conjunction.
Whether conjoined with another syllable, disjoined, or solitary—each of these is connected twice.
The grammatical construction is: "that which has a distinguished wind or a distinguished seed is designated as *sacchinna*.
Here, "seed" (*bīja*) refers to the seed of power (*śaktibīja*).
"Svarākrānta" means "conjoined with a long vowel.
Those who know the tradition say that it is conjoined with these vowels: ā, ī, ū, e, and au.
If it is asked how the word "bīja" (seed-syllable) refers to the *māyābīja*, it is stated in the Śaiva [scriptures]:
The names of the seed-syllable of Māyā are: Mālinī, Śivavallarī, Vātāvartī, Kalā, Vāṇī, Bīja, Śakti, and Kuṇḍalī.
As it is said in the Piṅgalāmata: "That mantra at whose beginning, middle, and end [the syllable] is seen..."
"Divided fourfold, fivefold, twofold, and as the solitary hero (*ekavīra*), accompanied by the vowels—
this is proclaimed as the wind-seed (*vāyubīja*) mantra when it is split.
In that very same [text], having begun with "Now, the exposition of the seed-syllables of the mantra-fragments," it is explained as follows:
The seed-syllable of wind is the letter *ya*.
The solitary hero is *hnaḥ*.
"Overpowered by vowels" means joined with a long vowel.
The sequence of *hrāṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *hrūṃ*, *hraim*, and *hrauṃ* has been demonstrated in that very same place by way of illustration:

"To those who are not terrible, *hrāṃ*; to those who are terrible, *hrīṃ*; to those who are most terrible, *hrūṃ*; to all, O Śarva, from every side, *hraim*; salutations be to you in your forms as Rudra, *hrauṃ*. Thus it is said.
And in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "Or [it may be] a single hero (ekavīra), especially when pervaded by vowels.
But in another text it is said: "The mantra is severed at the half-verse. Here, "half-verse" (*ardhagraha*) means being interrupted in the middle of a *ṛc* or a *śloka*.
But elsewhere it is said: "They are severed by the omissions of the seed-syllables at the beginning, middle, and end. || 71 ||

That mantra which is marked by the pair of earth-seeds (la-la) at its beginning, middle, and end, should be known as "obstructed" (ruddha), and it is devoid of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 72 ||
The conjunction "ādityaiḥ" refers to these [elements].
"Bhū-bīja" is *laṃ*.
"In each pair" means for each one individually.
Experience (*bhukti*) is the fruit pertaining to this world.
As it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"In the beginning it is twofold, in the middle threefold, and again at the end it becomes twofold."

"This mantra, having the seed-syllable *Indra* (HŪM), is called 'obstructed' (*ruddha*). And elsewhere: "O Dear One, that mantra which is joined with the Vajra (HŪM) is proclaimed as 'restrained' (*niruddha*), [occurring] twice at the beginning, thrice in the middle, and again twice at the end."
The syllable *la* is the *vajra*;
the phrase "in both cases" implies "in three ways.
By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), the conjunction of both is also indicated.
By this, the claim made by some that the seed-syllable of the Earth (bhū-bīja) is *glauṃ* is also refuted.
However, in another text, a different method is given: "That which is obstructed is known as 'without euphonic combination' (*niḥsandhika*).
That in which the euphonic combinations of vowels (*svarasandhi*) and consonants (*vyañjanasandhi*) as taught in grammar do not occur is "without euphonic combination."
In another tantra: "They are obstructed, together with their retinues. (72)
That mantra which is devoid of the three principles of Māyā, the Śrī-bīja, and Rāva is said to be "devoid of power" (śaktihīna), provided that these do not occur within it. || 73 ||

The seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) is at the mouth, Māyā (Hrīṃ) is at the head, and the goad (Aṅkuśa, Phreṃ) is likewise [at the feet]. This [syllable] is said to be Parāṅmukha, consisting of the letter Ha joined with the Bindu. || 74 ||
If the moon [the vowel *i*] does not exist at the beginning, end, or middle, it is traditionally said that one is deaf.
"Māyā" refers to the seed-syllable (bīja) of Bhuvaneśī.
"The three principles" (tritattva) refers to either the syllable *hūṃ* or the *praṇava* (*oṃ*).
The sound is the *phreṃkāra*.
There is no conjunction of these.
As it has been said:

"Where the seed-syllable of Māyā, the three principles (tritattva), or even the sound RĀVA, or the Śrīgṛha does not exist, that mantra is proclaimed to be devoid of power. Thus it is said. Also in the Piṅgalāmata: "If the seed-syllable of Māyā, the three principles, or the Śrīgṛha are not present..."
"One who is known as 'devoid of power' destroys the capability of his ministers.

Thus [it is said]. Now, beginning with the "Exposition of the Seed-syllables of the Mantra-portion," it is explained in that very same place: *tritattvaṃ hūṃ śrīgrahaṃ śrīmiti* ("the three principles, hūṃ, the seizer of Śrī, and śrī").
Regarding the word *yasya* ("of whom"):
At the beginning, in the mouth;
at the end, on the head.
The goad is the syllable *kroṃ*.
The word "vā" (or) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
There is also a reading "kvacideva ca" (and only in some cases).
This has been stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
That in which the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma*) is not in the middle, and the goad (*aṅkuśa*) is at the end of the *māyā*,
is declared to be "turned away" (*parāṅmukha*).
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"He in whose [mantra] the seed-syllable of Kāmakalā is not found in the middle position,
and in which Māyā is at the beginning and the Aṅkuśa at the end— this should be known as 'parāṅmukha' (turned away)."
Regarding the letter *ha*: that is the moon (*indu*). It is also connected here with the phrase "joined with the bindu."
The phrase "in the beginning, middle, and end" does not imply a conjunction.
As it has been said:
"The void (śūnya), conjoined with the bindu, [is placed] at the beginning and end, or else in the middle."
"Or he in whom the seed of life does not exist is known as deaf. By this, the claim made by some that the word *indu* denotes the letter *ṭha* is also refuted. (73–75)

A mantra that possesses five vowels but is devoid of the letter *ra*, the sun (the letter *r̥*), and the moon (the letter *u*), should be known as "eyeless"; it bestows suffering, grief, and disease. || 76 ||
Regarding "five":
the letter *ha* is [the seed-syllable] of the Sun (*arka*).
This is because, in the Vaiṣṇava Great Principle (Bṛhattattva) assignment, the principle of the solar orb (*arkamaṇḍala-tattva*) is assigned as beginning with the letter *ha*.
Because the letter *ha* has the form of a male, it is the sun;
the moon is the letter *sa*.
The phrase "five," and so forth, refers to both as the seeds of defects.
The result is, respectively, the bestowal of suffering, grief, and fear;
for since the three eyes consist of fire, sun, and moon, one should understand that there is even partial blindness due to the loss of one or two [of these elements].
As it is said in the Piṅgalāmata:

"The five-syllable mantra, however, which is devoid of fire (ra), moon (sa), sun (ha), and thunderbolt (kṣa), should be known as 'eyeless' (netrahīna); it brings about suffering, grief, and disease. Thus [it is said].
Now, beginning with the "Exposition of the Seed-Syllables of the Mantra-Parts," it is explained in that very same work: "The moon is *sa*; the sun is *ha*. (76)

At the beginning, middle, and end [of the mantra] are Haṃsa, Prāsāda, and Vāg-bhava; the letter *ha* with the bindu is the *jīva*, or else the sound consisting of four *kalās*. The word "I bow" (*namāmi*) and the word "Māyā" do not exist in that which is *kīlita*. || 77 ||
Regarding "ādi":
this refers to a collective group of these [sounds], not a collective group beginning with *haṃsa*,
because it has been stated as "or the sound (*rāvaṃ*)."
In another text as well: "Or even the *haṃsa* consisting of *māyā*. Here, *haṃsa* is the essential nature (*svarūpa*). The seed-syllable of the *Prāsāda* mantra is *hauṃ*.
Vāgbhava is *eṃ*.
The letter *ha* with a bindu is *haṃ*.
Jīva is *saḥ*.
The sound *rāva* is *phreṃ*.
That which lacks the four-mora *hūṃ*, the seed-syllable of *māyā-śakti*, and the word *namāmi* is called *kīlita* (pierced).

In this context, "hakārobindumān" is one word, and "jīvaḥ" is another. Therein, what is the nature of the *jīva*? It is that which possesses the letter *ha*, the letter *a*, the letter *u*, and the *bindu*.
By that, *śoṃ* is established.
Here, by the sequence *a*, *u*, and *bindu*, the syllable *oṃ* is formed, as in the rule: "The vowels *a*, *u*, and *m* should be [the components]."
And so it is stated in the Piṅgalāmata:
"That whose self is seen neither as the ninth vowel joined with the letter *jī* (ya), mounted upon *ā*, and accompanied by the bindu, nor as the four-part sound (*rāva*)..."
"Wherever the *prāsāda*, the *vāgbhava*, the *haṃsa*, or the *māyā* is seen—at the beginning, middle, or end—it is called 'staked' (*kīlita*). Thus it is said.
Now, having begun with "the exposition of the seed-syllables that are parts of the mantra," it is explained in that very same place: "The ninth vowel is the syllable *o*."
The self is *haḥ*.
The sound is *phreṃ*.
The four-part [syllable] is *hūṃ*.
In another tantra, however, having read "or even that which consists of *haṃsa* and *māyā*," it is explained as *hrīṃ*.
Others say that even in the statement of Piṅgalā, "the *haṃsa* is *māyā*," this is the very same meaning.
Elsewhere, however, it is said: "That which is pervaded by another seed-syllable within is called 'staked' (*kīlita*)."
Thus [it is said].
In another text: "The seed-syllable is fixed as a stake. (77)
That mantra in which there is one [syllable] in the middle and two at the head, and in which the weapons Indra and Purandara are found, is paralyzed and obstructs success. || 78 ||
"One" means at the end of the head;
"astra" refers to the syllable *phaṭ*.
Puraṃdara consists of *la*.
In the middle there is one *phaṭ* or *la*;
at the end there are two *phaṭ*s or two *la*s.
Some explain that there is the syllable *phaṭ* in the middle and two *la*s at the end; that is incorrect,
because it contradicts other texts.
And so it is said in the Piṅgalāmata:
"If the seed-syllable of Śakra (Ś) occurs once in the middle and twice at the end,
the wise who know mantras declare that such a mantra is 'paralyzed' (stambhita)."

And in another text: "Where [the syllable] is seen at the end of the mantra in two ways, three ways, eight ways, or six ways, that mantra is proclaimed by the Lord Śrīśa as the 'Paralyzed Great Weapon' (mahāstra-stambhita)."
This is because of the contradiction between these two texts.
The reading "na vidyete sa mantraḥ" ("that mantra does not exist") is a scribal error;
however, "vidyete sa tu mantraḥ syāt" ("that mantra indeed exists") is the traditional reading.
But elsewhere it is said:
"He who is appointed to an action but does not perform it is paralyzed. (78)
If fire and wind are joined together at the head of a mantra and are seen there seven times, the knower of mantras should consider that mantra to be burnt. || 79 ||
Regarding "vahniriti": *vahni* is the letter *ra*; *vāyu* is the letter *ya*. It is joined with that, either below or above, or at the head—that is, at the beginning.
As it is stated in the Piṅgalāmata:
"When the syllable of fire (RA) is ignited by the seven seed-syllables of the winds (HA) situated at the beginning, the noble ones declare that mantra to be 'burnt'."
In another treatise, it is stated in a different manner: "Those who have been heard by six ears are burnt.
But elsewhere, it says: "Those who exceed the seed-syllable of fire (RA) are burnt. || 79 ||
The Astra-mantra is seen to consist of two, three, six, or eight syllables.
He in whose mouth the Praṇava does not reside is called "terrified" (trasta);
whether it be Śiva or Śakti, he is proclaimed as one named "frightened. || 80 ||
Regarding the term *astra*: that [mantra] in which the *phaṭ* syllable of the weapon (*astra*) is seen with two, three, six,
or eight syllables is called the *Bhīta* (the Frightened) in the *Piṅgalāmata*.
"If the mantra, joined with the weapon-syllable (astra), is [present] at the beginning, middle, and end,
it is called 'frightened' (bhīta) in the Tantra. Thus [it is said].
Others, however, did not read the text as "trastaḥ so'bhihito mantraḥ," but rather as "trāsitāḥ siddhibhīṣitāḥ" in another tantra. Regarding the word "yasya":
"At the beginning" means at the start.

"Śiva is *ha* and Śakti is *sa*"—so say the traditionalists (*sāmpradāyikāḥ*). Some, however, say that by the word "Śiva" they mean the *bindu* (the nasal dot) and by the word "Śakti" they mean the *visarga* (the two dots).
That is incorrect,
because in the mantras and so forth, neither the solitary bindu nor the solitary visarga exists.
If it is argued that [the bindu] should be understood as being joined with another syllable:
Therefore, it is better to follow the traditional meaning.
At the end of the work, the author will state:
"Those two are called *puṃs* (the male) and *prakṛti* (nature); *haṃ* is the male, while *saḥ* is nature."
Thus it is said.
This very same defect has been stated under another name in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "That mantra at the beginning of which there is no Śiva, Śakti, or the syllable Oṃ [is defective]."
"They say that [a mantra] devoid of the *mātṛkā* bestows inferior accomplishments. Thus it is said.
Now, beginning with the "Exposition of the Seed-syllables of the Mantra-fragments," it is explained in that very same place: "Śiva is *haṃ*, and Śakti is *saḥ*. (80)
If a mantra has four instances of the letter *ma* at its beginning, middle, and end, it is impure; a knower of mantras should avoid such a one. || 81 ||
"Ādi" (and so forth) refers to their conjunction. "The four groups ending in *m*" is also a conjunction.
Therefore, by combining [these] three places, four *mātras* are required.
As it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"Where [the pause] is seen in four ways at the beginning, middle, and end."

"One who knows mantras should abandon that mantra which contains the letter *ma* as a stain. Elsewhere, however, it is said: "That mantra in which the letter *ma* is seen in three places—at the beginning, in the middle, and at the heart—is declared by the Lord to be stained (*malina*)."
The difference arises from being a different opinion;
the word *hṛdaya* signifies the end (*anta*).
However, elsewhere it is said: "They are defiled by the three impurities known as the innate, the adventitious, and that called māyā. (81)

That mantra in whose middle there is the letter *da*, or at whose head there is a *krodha* [seed-syllable] in two ways, and which stands as a weapon (*astra*), is declared to be "obscured" (*tiraskṛta*). || 82 ||
Regarding the phrase "of which":
*hūṃ* is the seed-syllable of anger; there is an option between the letter *da* and the syllable of anger (*krodha*) in the middle;
[the syllable of anger] is at the top, that is, at the end.
The connection is that "the weapon [is] twofold.
There is a conjunction of the middle and the end.
As it has been stated in the Piṅgalāmata:
"He whose [mantra] has the letter *da*—the seed-syllable of wrath—or who has it situated in the middle, and at whose end the two *phaṭ*s are situated, that individual is disregarded.
Also elsewhere: "He in whose middle the letter *da*, the seed-syllable of wrath, is situated in the heart..."
"And that [mantra] which has the syllable *phaṭ* at both ends is 'disdained' (*tiraskṛta*).
Thus it is said; and in another tantra: "Those who are defeated are disdained. (82)
If there are two *bhyos* at the heart, *vaṣaṭ* at the head, and *phaṭ* in the middle, that mantra has been corrupted and should be abandoned by the wise in their pursuit of accomplishments. || 83 ||
The two syllables *bhyo* are at the beginning and the head;
*vaṣaṭ* and the weapon-syllable (*astra*) are in the middle. Thus, *vaṣaṭ* is at the end of the head, and the weapon-syllable *hraḥ* is in the middle.
As stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"That mantra in the midst of which there are two syllables of the weapon (*astra*) and likewise at the end of *vaṣaṭ* is to be known as 'divided' (*bhinna*), and it is devoid of success."

In the *Piṅgalāmata* as well: "The two syllables of the weapon-mantra (*astra*), with *vaṣaṭ* at the end and likewise at the beginning, preceded by *oṃ*, constitute this mantra; it is proclaimed as being thus differentiated.
Then, having introduced the section on the explanation of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the mantra-parts, it is explained in that very same place:
The weapon-mantra is *hraḥ*.
*Oumāḥ* refers to the syllable *oṃ*.
Some read: "Bhyo-dvayaṃ in the heart, *vaṣaṭ* on the head, and *ābū* in the middle."
And others read: "Vaṣaṭ and Vauṣaṭ are in the middle.
Elsewhere it says: "They have been brought to a state of division; they are differentiated. (83)
That which is devoid of the three colors and the *haṃsa* is declared to be deep sleep (*suṣupta*). || 84 ||
Regarding "three-colored" (*trivarṇa*):
the state of being three-colored belongs to a single [entity] alone, namely its being devoid of the *haṃsa*.
As it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"Wherever there may be three syllables devoid of the *haṃsa*, that is declared by Śambhu in the Siddhānta to be 'deep sleep' (*suṣupta*), which bestows desired fruits.
Also, in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "That mantra which consists of three syllables but is bereft of the *haṃsa*..."
"But he who is fast asleep should be known as one who robs [the practitioner] of the fruit of all accomplishments.
Regarding this, some say: "The 'asleep' state is that in which the lamp is unknown.
In another place, however, it is said: "Those whose capacities have been destroyed by *māyā* are 'asleep'."
But elsewhere it is said: "One may sleep without [the use of] a seat. || 84 ||
Whether it be a mantra or a vidyā consisting of seventeen syllables, beginning with five *phaṭ* sounds, that which has been proclaimed by Madonmatta; || 85 ||

He whose mantra has that same weapon situated in its middle is said to be "fainted" (mūrchita). He whose [mantra] resides in a place of pause (virāma) is called "deprived of vitality" (hṛtavīrya). || 86 ||
Regarding the term "mantra": that which consists of seven, eight,
and ten syllables is thus eighteen syllables in total.
The term "pañcakamādau" (five *phaṭ*s at the beginning) is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that in which there are five *phaṭ*s at the beginning.
As it has been said:
"Whether it be a *vidyā* or a *mantra*, if it consists of eighteen syllables..."

"Preceded by five *phaṭ*-utterances, it is called *Madonmatta* (Intoxicated with Pride). Also in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Whether it be a Vidyā or a King of Mantras that consists of seventeen [syllables], if it has five *phaṭ*-utterances at the beginning, it is proclaimed as *Unmatta* (Intoxicated)."
Here too, there is a fault in [the definition] being qualified by two qualifiers.
The phrase "in that same way" occurs five times.
In another text, there is a different formulation: "Furthermore, those who have fainted are devoid of consciousness."
"Virāma" refers to that at the end of which there is an *astra* (weapon-syllable); the meaning is "at the conclusion of which an *astra* occurs."
In some places, the reading is: "The mantra which has *virāma* [as its final element] is not feminine.
This is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "That mantra which has the *astra-mantra* [phaṭ] in its middle and at its end by Śambhu..."
"That mantra which is known as 'stolen of its potency' (hṛtavīrya) does not grant success at all.
And elsewhere: "That [mantra] which reaches a point of pause is called 'stolen of its potency' (hṛtavīrya)."
Some also maintain that there are five types;
however, this is contradictory.
Others, however, say: "One who possesses capability is indeed one whose vigor is not inferior."
But elsewhere it is said: "That which is devoid of potency and has extra syllables. (85-86)
A mantra that is joined with squares at the beginning, the middle, and likewise at the head, yet is deficient—namely, one consisting of eighteen syllables—should be known as such. || 87 ||
A mantra of nineteen syllables that is joined with the *tāra*, enriched by the seed-syllables of *hṛllekhā* and *aṅkuśa*, is declared to be "destroyed" (*pradhvasta*). || 88 ||
"At the beginning" implies a conjunction;
"the fourfold weapon" likewise refers to the four weapons combined together in the three locations.

In another tantra, however, this is called by the name Bhīta: "Bhairava declared that eighteen-syllable mantra to be Bhīta, which is joined with the weapon-mantra (astra) four times— at the beginning, at the end, and likewise in the middle."
There is a distinction regarding the state of having eighteen syllables.

Here too, the phrase "yaḥ syādaṣṭādaśākṣaraḥ" (that which consists of eighteen syllables) is connected to both [the preceding and following contexts] by way of the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣigolakanyāya*).
In some places, the reading is "jñātavyo bhīta ityeṣaḥ."
In another treatise, however, there is a different method:
"Now, those that have been subtracted are deficient by the portions known as *susiddha*, *siddha*, and *sādhya*.
In yet another place, it says: "That which is obtained from a defective [calculation] is deficient."
"Yaḥ syāt" means "he who may be.
*Tāra* is the *praṇava*.
Some say that *tāra* is "preṃ."
That is incorrect,
because it contradicts other texts.
As stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"Any mantra consisting of nineteen syllables that is endowed with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and joined with the *mahāmāyā-aṅkuśa* is declared to be 'destroyed' (*pradhvasta*). Thus it is said.
Also in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "If it consists of eighteen syllables..."
"Or, with nineteen syllables, provided it is endowed with the *māyā* (hrīṃ), the *oṃkāra*, and the *aṅkuśa* (kroṃ);
this is the mantra declared by Lord Śambhu as 'Pradhvasta'. To avoid this [interpretation], some read the text as: "The mantra which is endowed with the *praṇava*."
Hṛllekhā is Māyā.
As it is stated in the Bhuvaneśīpārijāta:
"This seed-syllable of Māyā is declared to be the imperishable [syllable] of the three worlds."
"And she is Hṛllekhā, the Mistress of Yoga (Yogeśī), the Mistress of the World (Bhuvaneśī), and the Yoginī. Thus [ends verses 87–88].
A mantra of seven syllables is a child; that which consists of eight syllables is a youth;
a mantra of sixteen syllables is a young adult; and a mantra of forty syllables is a mature man. (89)
Regarding the term "seven-syllabled":
it consists of forty scripts and forty phonemes.
As it has been said:

"The child (bāla) consists of seven syllables, the youth (kumāra) of eight syllables; the mature (prauḍha) consists of forty syllables, and the adolescent (taruṇa) of sixteen syllables. Thus [it is said]. Elsewhere: "The child consists of short syllables."
But in another text it says: "Children are not firm in their duties. Elsewhere it says: "Even from a guru, [one may act] without following the injunctions when one has reached the age of youth."
In another text, however, it says: "The young are excessively intoxicated"; elsewhere, however: "The mature are dominated by their lords. (89)
A mantra of thirty syllables, one of sixty-four syllables, one of one hundred syllables, and even one of four hundred syllables is designated as "vṛddha" (the aged). || 90 ||
Regarding "thirty":
it consists of four hundred syllables; the term *caturadhikaśatākṣaraḥ* (four-hundred-plus-syllable) is a compound with the middle word elided (*madhyapadalopī*).
Some explain *catuḥśatākṣaraḥ* as meaning "that which has four hundred syllables" (*catvāri śatāni akṣarāṇi yasya*).
That is not so,
because it contradicts other texts:
"Whether it be thirty syllables, a hundred syllables, or likewise sixty-four syllables..."

"Or even four hundred and more is designated as 'vṛddha' (grown). Thus it is said. Also in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Where there are thirty, or fifty, or sixty-four, or four hundred syllables, that mantra is known by the name 'vṛddha'."
As he himself will state later regarding the characteristics of extreme old age:
"Starting from four hundred [years] up to a thousand years of age," and so forth.
And thus there would be no contradiction;
for it is said in another text: "The elders perform only minor actions."
Thus [ends verse] 90.
The nine-syllable mantra joined with the *dhruva* is declared to be the "Sword" (*nistriṃśa*).
At its conclusion is the Heart mantra, and the Head mantra is in the middle. || 91 ||

If the *śikhā* and *varma* mantras are absent, as well as the syllables *vauṣaṭ* and *phaṭ*, or if it is devoid of the syllables of Śiva and Śakti, that [mantra] is known as "seedless" (*nirbīja*). || 92 ||
"Nine":
the *dhruvā* is the syllable *oṃ*. The state of having nine syllables belongs to that single [verse] by virtue of its being joined with the *dhruvā*.
*Nistriṃśa* means "cruel" (*dhātuka*).
In the *Piṅgalāmata*: "The nine-syllable *nistriṃśa*, when joined with the *dhruvaka*, brings about untimely death."
"Of which" refers to:
*namaḥ* is the heart mantra;
*svāhā* is the head mantra.
Śikhā vaṣaṭ. Varma huṃ. Śivo ’ham.
"Śaktyarṇaḥ saḥ" means "that [letter] is the phoneme of Śakti.
This occurs precisely between the two alternatives.
Here, the reading "saṃsyātām" is a scribal error.
"They would not exist," so says the traditional teacher.
As it has been said:
"At the end of the heart and head [mantras] comes the crest (śikhā); the armor (varma) is in the middle; or else, the eye (netra) and weapon (astra) are at the end."
"The King of Mantras, in which those two phonemes consisting of Śiva and Śakti do not exist, is proclaimed as 'seedless' (nirbīja) and is employed in all rites.
However, in another Tantra it is said: "That which is devoid of the syllable Oṃ at the beginning is designated as 'seedless'."
Thus [ends the section on] verses 91–92.
In these positions, if the syllable *phaṭ* is seen six times, that mantra will be devoid of success; a mantra consisting of ten syllables is considered weak. || 93 ||
"In these" refers to those characterized as being without seed (*nirbīja*), and is intended to indicate the inclusion of other [practices] mentioned in other tantras.
Thus he says "in these": this is a collective reference to the beginning, middle, and end of these.
Regarding the term "sixfold" (*ṣoḍhā*), there are six [syllables] combined across these three positions.
Regarding "slow" (*manda*):
it consists of ten syllables, starting with the *paṅkti* [meter].
As it has been said: "That which consists of ten syllables is *manda*";
and in another tantra: "Those devoid of radiance are *manda*. || 93 ||

A *kūṭa* is a mantra consisting of a single syllable; it is said to be partless (*niraṃśaka*). A two-syllabled mantra is devoid of essence (*satvahīna*), while a four-syllabled one is called *kekara*.
Regarding the term *kūṭa*:
it has been said—"A *kūṭa* is either a single-syllabled mantra or one that is partless.
Regarding the term *dvivarṇa* (two-syllabled):
As it has been said:
"Those who possess the two syllables [Sa and Ta] are those conquered by *sattva*.
But elsewhere: "Those conquered by *sattva* are those in whom *tamas* is predominant."
"Caturvarṇa" means having four seed-syllables. According to the *Piṅgalāmata*, there is this distinction:
"One devoid of the *dhruva* [syllable], but possessing four or six seed-syllables, is considered *kekara*."
Thus [ends the verse]. 94.
A six-syllabled mantra that lacks a seed-syllable, or one of seven and a half syllables,
or one of twelve and a half syllables, is considered "smoky" (dhūmita) and is therefore censured.

Likewise, there is one with three and a half seed-syllables, one consisting of twenty-one phonemes, and one of twenty phonemes; that which consists of thirty phonemes is embraced [by the former]. || 96 ||
The mantra consisting of thirty-two syllables is proclaimed as "deluded";
likewise, that which consists of twenty-four syllables and that which consists of twenty-seven syllables. || 97 ||
That [mantra] afflicted by hunger should be known as having twenty-four syllables;
or it may have eleven syllables, or even twenty-five syllables. || 98 ||
A mantra consisting of twenty-three syllables is declared to be "proud" (dṛpta). || 99 ||
Regarding the term "six-syllabled":
elsewhere it is stated, "those [mantras] devoid of seed-syllables and the syllable *oṃ*.
Regarding the term "with half-": [this refers to the half-measure].
In this context, the state of having six and a half syllables and twelve and a half phonemes should be understood as being due to the presence of a consonant at the end.
"Likewise, three and a half seed-syllables" means that a *bīja* (seed-syllable) is a phoneme (*varṇa*).
The meaning is that it is "smoky" in that same way.
As it has been said:
"The mantra consists of six and a half syllables, or twelve and a half phonemes."
"He is declared to be 'smoky' (dhūmita), or else [consisting of] three and a half syllables.
Likewise, there is the state of being "aged" (vṛddha) and "embraced" (āliṅgita) for that which consists of thirty syllables.
"Proud" (dṛpta) [is as follows]:

One should not think: "Since the excessively arrogant person was already mentioned during the occasion of the enumeration (uddeśa), how can the definition of the arrogant person be formulated during the occasion of the definition (lakṣaṇa)?
For even when a prefix is present, there is a difference in meaning.
As it has been said:
"One [prefix] subverts the meaning of the verbal root (dhātu), another conforms to it,
yet another qualifies that very same meaning, and another is employed as being devoid of meaning.
Thus it is stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"Alternatively, the mantra may consist of twenty-four syllables, or eleven syllables, or twenty-three syllables; they know that [mantra] to be 'intelligent' (matidṛpta). (95–99)
A mantra of twenty-six syllables, as well as one of thirty-six letters, or one of twenty-nine letters, is said to be deficient in its limbs (aṅga). || 100 ||
One who has twenty-eight syllables or even thirty-one is said to be excessively angry; he is censured in all ritual actions. || 101 ||
A mantra of thirty syllables, or even thirty-three, is said to be excessively cruel and is censured for all ritual activities. || 102 ||
"Twenty-six":
this is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning those [mantras] which have one less than thirty.
It is also stated in the fourth chapter of the *Mantramuktāvalī* regarding the deficient limb: "consisting of thirty-eight syllables. (100–102)
Starting from forty up to sixty-three, that number of mantras is declared to be designated as "with shame" (savrīḍa). || 103 ||
Regarding the phrase "forty":
beginning with forty syllables and increasing by one syllable at a time, there are twenty-four varieties of the *sabrīḍa* [mantra].
As stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "Up to sixty-four syllables. (103)
Those mantras that consist of sixty-five syllables are peaceful in nature;
[this applies] from sixty-five syllables up to ninety-nine syllables. || 104 ||
Those mantras which consist of thirteen or fifteen syllables are designated by the wise as "fallen from their place" (sthānabhraṣṭa). || 105 ||
"Ekona" means that which has sixty-five syllables as its beginning; this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the quality included (*saguṇasaṃvijñāna*).
Alternatively, the analysis of the word may be "from this [point] of sixty-five syllables."
His state of mental tranquility was previously described.
Also, in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"Those [verses] which are sixty-five up to ninety-nine..."
Thus, by shifting its position and increasing by one syllable at a time, it consists of thirty-four varieties. (104–105)
They are said to be deficient by one hundred, or one hundred and fifty, or two hundred, or ninety-two, or even ninety-nine. || 106 ||
Or those [mantras] numbering three hundred are said to be without oil;
then, beginning from four hundred up to a thousand syllables. || 107 ||
Those who are excessively advanced in their applications should always be avoided by the wise.
Mantras consisting of more than a thousand syllables are known as *daṇḍakas* and are called "afflicted. ||108||
These mantras, consisting of two thousand syllables, have been divided into a hundred sections;
these mantras, as they stand, should be understood as being in the form of hymns. || 109 ||
"One hundred," "two hundred," "ninety-two"—this is one; "two hundred and fifty," "ninety-two less one," "ninety increased by one," and "three hundred.
Thus, there are five types [of each].
But in the Piṅgalāmata, it is said:
"Those whose functions are devoid of moisture are endowed with one, two, or thirty-one phonemes."
It is indeed of three types.
In the *Mantramuktāvalī*, a sixth type is also mentioned: "Three hundred, however, as a single collection.
Some maintain that two hundred is one type.
"Another says it is ninety-two; another says that, minus one, it is ninety-one"—thus they have stated this alternative method.
That is not correct.
Because it has been stated that those numbering from sixty-six up to ninety-nine are designated as "fallen from their station" (sthānabhraṣṭa).
If it is argued that, just like the thirty phonemes, a single [category] will be corrupted by two defects, that is not so;
for in that case, it is stated that there are only those exceeding one hundred, up to three hundred.
The phrase "of which the number" is connected everywhere.
The connection is as follows: those mantras whose number exceeds one hundred are "without oil" (niḥsneha).
Among the yogas and applications, those which are *daṇḍakas* and are in the form of hymns (*stotra*) should be known by the name "the afflicted" (*pīḍita*).
The connection [between the two]. || 106–109 ||
In the same way, practitioners (mantrins) must understand the vidyās in rites performed for specific desires.
That dull-witted person who applies a mantra without recognizing these defects will not achieve success even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. || 110 ||

Now, one might raise the objection that these defects have been stated only for *mantras*, whereas *vidyās* are faultless; anticipating this, he says: "These are *mantras*. Just as these *mantras* exist as being defective, so too should the *vidyās* be understood by the practitioners (*mantrins*).
As it has been said: "Just like the *mantras*, the *vidyās* are mutually distinguished by their differences."
"These [impurities] are to be known by the lord of teachers as they have been described in various tantras.

By the phrase "in rites for specific desires" (kāmyakarmasu), it is implied that since these defects do not exist when reciting mantras for the sake of liberation (mukti), even the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) need not be performed.
This is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa).
Therefore, for the sake of liberation, one should not perform purification and the other [rituals] whose characteristics will be described hereafter. || 110 ||
One should apply those mantras, which are corrupted by such defects, to oneself;
one should purify them with the upward-moving breath while binding the *yonimudrā*.

By the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*), one should understand defects such as *mīlita* (obscured), *vipakṣastha* (situated in the opposite side), *dārita* (torn), *mūka* (mute), *nagna* (naked), *bhujaṅgama* (serpentine), *śūnya* (void), *hata* (struck down), and others.
Their definitions are as follows:
"The mantras, though employed by the practitioner, are *mīlita* because they are exceedingly dull in their effect. And so on.
"Those situated in the enemy's opposition have taken refuge in the side of the foe.
And: "He for whom no fixed [position] exists at the beginning, middle, or end, is known as 'the torn one' (dārita) in this Tantra by the One Clad in Skin (Kṛttivāsas)."
"Without the ritual placement (nyāsa), one becomes mute;
without the 'sprout' (pallava), a mantra is proclaimed to be naked."
"A serpent-like mantra is one that is abandoned by its seer (ṛṣi), deity (daivata), and meter (chandas).
And: "That mantra which another hears while it is being recited is called 'void' (śūnya)."
"One who is headless is said to be slain.

Regarding the method of purification, he says: "The mantras within oneself," and so forth. The contemplation that the effect is indeed non-different from the cause is what constitutes "yoking" (yojanā) within the self.
In some places, the reading is "one should join the mantras within one's own self. He describes purification by another method with the words "one should purify":

having bound the *yonimudrā* characterized as will be described hereafter, one should cause the syllables of the mantras, arisen from the *mūlādhāra*, to perform movements of going and returning as far as the *brahmarandhra*.
They say that the method of purification is as follows: having meditated and performed the retention of breath (*vāyudhāraṇa*), one should recite the mantra a thousand times.

As it has been said: "Having bound the *yoni* and, by means of the path beginning with the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the drop (*bindu*), having reached the state beyond mind (*unmanī*), one should recite the mantra a thousand times there; then that mantra becomes awakened."
The characteristic of *yonimudrā* is as follows:
having firmly pressed the perineum and the anus together, one draws the *apāna* upward;
this is called *mūlabandha*.
"One should contract and bind that which is between the anus and the penis; even an old man becomes young through constant practice of the *mūlabandha*. Thus it is said.
Because it seals the location of the *yoni*, it is called *yonimudrā*.
Regarding this, they say:

"This very Yonimudrā has indeed been described by me; its binding is difficult even for the gods to attain. By means of this binding, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished for the preeminent practitioner."

Those who are cut down, obstructed, pinned, or paralyzed; those who are asleep, intoxicated, or unconscious; those whose vigor has failed; those who are burnt, terrified, or standing on the side of the enemy; and those who are children, the elderly, or arrogant in their youth—[all these are to be avoided].

Those mantras which are seedless, those which are deficient in essence, those that are fragmented, and those lacking limbs or syllables—all these mantras become powerful through the binding of the mudrā in the womb. Thus [it is said]. 111.
The ten consecrations of mantras, which bestow accomplishment, are now described: birth, life-giving, striking, and likewise awakening; || 112 ||

Now, consecration (abhiṣeka), purification (vimalīkaraṇa), nourishment (āpyāyana), satiation (tarpaṇa), illumination (dīpana), and concealment (gupti)—these ten are the purificatory rites for mantras. || 113 ||

Thus, for those practitioners who are unacquainted with the *yonimudrā* and lack the power of breath-retention (*pavanadhāraṇā*), he speaks of the purification of mantras by means of the ten sacraments (*daśasaṃskāra*). Also in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"The *āṇava* [mantras] of practitioners should be known as being joined with such defects," and so forth.
Therefore, a certain method is being declared for the destruction of those defects.
Birth, life, awakening, striking, purification, nourishment,
and consecration— these are the seven rites performed with certainty by means of the ritual limbs.
"Indeed, all mantras become granters of desires when purified.
Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "Then, at an auspicious moment, one should impart the consecrated mantra to him."
These seven purificatory rites of mantra are difficult for men on earth to obtain.
By the words "birth," "life," and so forth;

it should be understood that here, setting aside the three generally well-known purificatory rites (saṃskāras) characterized by satiation (tarpaṇa), illumination (dīpana), and concealment (gopana), the statement "seven" is made. || 112-113 ||
The extraction of mantras from the midst of the Mātṛkā is known as their "birth. (114)
Regarding the phrase "of the mantras":
by the expression "from the midst of the *mātṛkā*," this is what is meant.

Having drawn the lotus of the *mātṛkā* with saffron, *rocanā*, or other substances upon an auspicious seat or similar surface, each individual syllable of the mantra to be given should be extracted from that *mātṛkā* lotus.
As it has been said: "Having drawn the lotus of the letters, one should extract this birthplace of mantras.
The wise one should recite the syllables of the mantra with the Praṇava (Om) interspersed between them;
those learned in the Mantras and Tantras call this "the life" of the mantra. || 115 ||
Regarding the term "praṇava":
therein, the state of being interspersed with the *praṇava* is as follows: *oṃ rāṃ oṃ rā oṃ mā oṃ ya oṃ na oṃ maḥ*.
By the word "sudhīḥ" (the wise one), it is stated that this is performed one hundred times.
As it has been said:
"One should recite the syllables of the mantra together with the *praṇava* one hundred times;
this is called 'liberation while living' (*jīvanmukta*)."
Thus [it is said].
By the phrase "those expert in mantra and tantra," it is meant that others call its name "the Seed" (bīja).
As stated in the Piṅgalāmata: "The Praṇava is called the seed; one should apply it at the end of the seed."
"Having placed another syllable in between, this mantra is considered to be 'seeded' (bījita). || 115 ||
Having written out the syllables of the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should strike each one with sandalwood water using the Vāyu [seed-syllable]; that is declared to be "striking" (tāḍana).
He recites the mantra.
By the word "mantrī" (the mantra-practitioner), it is stated that one should inscribe the letters of the mantra upon birch bark using saffron, gorocana, or similar substances.
[The syllable] "yam" is by means of the seed-syllable of Vāyu.
One should strike each [leaf] one hundred times.
As it has been said:
"Having inscribed the syllables of the mantra upon birch bark, one should [strike] each one even a hundred times with sandalwood water."
One should strike with the seed-syllable of air (Yam); this is declared to be "striking. Thus [ends verse 116].

Having written that mantra, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should perform the awakening with *karavīra* flowers, numbering as many as the syllables of that mantra, ending with the syllable *ya*. || 117 ||

Regarding the phrase "having written": by the word "mantrī" (the practitioner), it is stated that the writing is to be done on birch bark (*bhūrja*) with saffron (*kuṅkuma*), yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and so forth.
By the phrase "born of *karavīra*," it means with the flowers of the red *karavīra*.
[It is] being carried [there] by means of the seed-syllable *ram*.
As it has been said:
"In this [mandala], one should draw [the design] with red karavīra flowers, the number of which corresponds to the syllables of the mantra."
This awakening has been described as that which should be struck by means of the fire-seed (vahnibīja). Thus [ends verse 117].

According to the procedure taught in the *Svatantra*, the mantra-practitioner should consecrate the mantra with asvattha sprouts, equal in number to the syllables of the mantra, for the sake of purification. || 118 ||
Regarding the term "independent" (*svatantra*): it means according to the procedures taught in the independent [tantras].

It should be understood that in the case of a Śaiva mantra, it is according to the Śiva-tantra; in the case of a Śākta mantra, according to the Śakti-tantra; and in the case of a Vaiṣṇava mantra, according to the Vaiṣṇava-tantra.
As before, having written the syllables of the mantra upon birch bark, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣiñcet*).
By the word "mantrin" (the mantra-practitioner), the practical application is stated as: "I consecrate such-and-such a syllable of this mantra; *namaḥ*.
Thus it has been said:
"One should consecrate [the disciple] with a sprout of the *pippala* tree according to the path set forth in one's own tantra;
this consecration consists of writing the mantra on birch bark (*bhūrja*) one hundred and eight times. Thus it is said. In the *Piṅgalāmata*, there is a specific distinction:
"Having placed the mantra-syllable upon the pericarp with *mālatī* buds,
one should perform the consecration with pure *aśvattha* sprouts equal in number to the syllables of that mantra, as prescribed in the *Svatantra*. Thus it is said.
Having written the syllables of the mantra with *mālatī* buds, one should perform the consecration. || 118 ||

Having intentionally contemplated the mantra with the mind, the practitioner of mantra should burn away the three impurities within the mantra by means of the Jyotirmantra; this is the purification. || 119 ||
Regarding the phrase "having reflected":
by means of the *jyotis* mantra which is about to be described;

by the word "mantrin," it is stated that one should raise the *kuṇḍalinī* from the *mūlādhāra* and, through its [the *kuṇḍalinī*'s] fire (*tadvahninā*), perform the burning away of defects (*doṣadāha*).
The three impurities are the innate (*sahaja*), the adventitious (*āgantuka*), and that which consists of illusion (*māyīya*).
It is also stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "One should burn away the [impurities] known as the innate, the adventitious, and that called illusion by means of the form of light."
The practitioner of mantra [removes] the three impurities from the mantra; thereby, he becomes stainless. Thus [it is said]. || 119 ||
The *jyotirmanu* is considered to be *tāraṃ* (oṃ), followed by the sky (0), fire (3), the moon (1), and the pair (2), ending with the staff (daṇḍī).
With this mantra, one should perform a sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) syllable by syllable using water infused with *kuśa* grass after it has been consecrated by recitation (*japta*). || 120 ||
This nourishing [of the mantra] with water according to the prescribed rule by means of that mantra is considered [the rite];
the satiation of the mantra with water by means of the mantra is known as *tarpaṇa*. || 121 ||
He states the mantra of light as "tāra":
*tāra* is the *praṇava*;
*vyoma* is the letter *ha*.
The letter *ra* is Agni;
*au* is Manu.
"This pair, staff-bearer, joined with the *anusvāra*" is an epithet of the mantra.
In the reading "daṇḍī," it is an epithet of Vyoman.
As it is stated in the *Nighaṇṭumātṛkā*:
"Akrūreśaka, Daṇḍī, Binduka, Kāma, and Guhyaka."
"The bodice and the Prācīnayoni are the continuous stream of pleasure and pain.
Thus, even further on, it should be understood that the *bindu* is denoted by the word "staff" (*daṇḍa*).
Regarding the word "kuśā":
"Recited one hundred and eight times"—
the writing is exactly as before.
The word "by that" (tena) is connected to both instances.
As it is said in the Piṅgalāmata: "If the mantra is sprinkled syllable by syllable with water purified by Kuśa grass and consecrated one hundred and eight times, it becomes nourished."
"According to rule" means seven times for each syllable.
