Some explain "with that mantra" as meaning "with the Jyotir-mantra";
that is incorrect.
Because it contradicts other texts.
As it has been said:
"The nourishment [of the mantra] should be performed with water and *kuśa* grass, recited syllable by syllable."
Thus;
the meaning is "by means of that root mantra. In this regard, the procedure is as follows:
Having recited the deity-mantra, one should perform the libation with water, saying: "I satisfy this mantra, namaḥ.
This is precisely what is meant by "mantra-libation" (mantratarpaṇa).
As it has been said:
One should apply the word *tarpayāmi* at the end of the mantra when the names [of the deities] are in the nominative case;
however, when they are in the accusative case, one should do so again.
Thus it is said.
This same method should be observed everywhere else as well, in all acts of libation (tarpaṇa).
This too [is repeated] one hundred and eight times. (120–121)
The illumination of the mantra is said to be the conjunction with Tāra, Māyā, and Ramā;
the concealment of the mantra being recited is its non-disclosure. || 122 ||
Ten ritual preparations (saṃskāra) are proclaimed, which are kept secret in all mantras;
by performing them according to the oral tradition, the mantra-practitioner attains his desired goal. || 123 ||
*Tāreti*: *Tāra* is the *praṇava*, *oṃ*; *māyā* is *śakti*.
"O Ramā Śrī!
It is held that at the end of the mantra there should be the application of the name for the purpose of eradication (*proccāṭana*).
Since this definition of the yoga has been stated, here the mantra itself stands in the place of the name.

"Therefore, having first placed these seeds [into the vessel], one should recite the mantra seven times"—so say the teachers. Regarding the phrase "according to tradition" (*sampradāyena*): the tradition for each specific consecration (*saṃskāra*) that I have mentioned must be kept in mind. (122–123)

One should employ a mantra that is favorable to one's own star, lunar mansion, and zodiacal sign; for out of greed for gain, even a clever man might accept a vast offering from Rudra, yet Ruru accepted only a mountain.

When the syllables *lo*, *ka*, *lo*, *pa*, *ṭu*, *grā*, *ma*, *kha*, *lau*, *dyo*, and *bhe* are distributed among the asterisms in sequence, and the two vowels *sa* and *ta* fall within the portion of Revatī, then [the result is as follows]. (125)
Now, he shows the intermediate investigation for one who has engaged in saguṇa-upāsanā, which is an ancillary to nirguṇa-upāsanā, with the words "svatārā" etc.
"Sva" means his own name; its "tārā" is the lunar mansion (nakṣatra). The same applies hereafter as well.
A wise person, having carefully and thoroughly examined a mantra that abounds in syllables corresponding to malefic asterisms, zodiac signs, spirits, or enemies, should diligently avoid it.

Because of this statement, in order to provide knowledge regarding the stars (tārā) and their friendship (maitrī), the author speaks of the constellations (*nakṣatras*) within the syllables, beginning with "prāpa.
Here, the intended convention (*saṅketa*) of the author Vāraruca is meant; as follows:

"In this system, numbers are known from the letters belonging to the *ka*, *ṭa*, *pa*, and *ya* groups, using the final letters of each group; furthermore, when the negative particle *nañ* is used, it should be understood as zero, and likewise when a vowel alone is mentioned.
Here, the two letters *ka* and *ṭa* represent nine; *pā* represents five; *yo* represents eight; and *hā* represents the end (zero).
A *piṇḍa* consists of conjunct consonants.
In that regard, the number is determined by the final letter:
2 la, 3 ka, 1 lo, 3 pa, 1 pa, 1 ṭu, 1 prā, 2 pa, 1 kha, 2 lau, 3 dyo, 1.
In this manner, Aśvinī and the other lunar mansions are to be known from the aforementioned syllables beginning with two.
The meaning is that the letters are divided according to their respective asterisms (nakṣatras) in due order;
this is to be connected with the word "tadā" (then) which follows later.
Here, because the letters *gha* and *ya* are identical in the Nāgarī script, the reading *ghakāra* is the result of an error.
By that, the single syllable *dya* is comprised.
The final two vowels, *aṃ* and *aḥ*, have entered the portion of Revatī;
therefore, in Revatī there are three syllables: *aṃ*, *aḥ*, and *la*.
Because it is already stated by the phrase "situated in the portion of Revatī," it is not included among the numerical figures (aṅka),

just as in the forthcoming description of the letters of the zodiac signs, where [the letter] *va* is [used for] "bāla" and "gaura," and *kha* for "khura. By means of the letter *ra*, only two syllables are expressed for Virgo (Kanyā).
Since for others it is stated by the very word "śādaya" regarding the daughter,
it should be understood that the same applies here as well.
In the lunar mansion Uttarabhādrapada, the number three is taken by means of the letter *la*.
Thus, there are six syllables. Since the letter *ṣa* is a constituent part of the letter *kṣa*, the letter *kṣa* is also included by that very [letter *ṣa*].
Therefore, there are four syllables here.
As it has been stated by the Teachers:
"From that, the letter *kṣa* was born; its presiding deity is Nṛsiṃha.
That, moreover, together with the letters *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha*, proceeded to the constellation Proṣṭhapadā."

In the *Īśānaśiva* as well: "The beloved is charming with a small lizard; the venerable beloved is the night; another is a female from the troop of birds; and she is numbered among the vessels and children.
Thus it is said.

In the *Nārāyaṇīya*, however, after stating the letters for the twenty-six asterisms beginning with Rājya and so forth, the letters *ama* are stated for the final two asterisms (*Aśleṣā* and *Maghā*).
Regarding this, some read *lvau* and explain that the letter *la* represents the number three and the letter *va* represents the number four.
That is incorrect.
Because it contradicts the convention (*saṅketa*).
For in the convention it is stated that "the digits are [indicated] by the final letters of the groups.
It is precisely with this intention that the assumption of the dual number is made.
That too is merely due to delusion;
for, in order to establish the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the letters of the convention, the nominative singular alone is appropriate,
and not the dual formed by joining [the two].
This is because it is not seen anywhere else [in this context].
For this very reason, this reading has been disregarded by commentaries such as the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*.
Others, however, read *bavau* and say: "By the letter *ba* belonging to the *pa*-group (*pavarga*), there are three numbers; by the following semivowel (*antasthīya*) *va*, there are four numbers."
That too contradicts the *Prapañcasāra* and other texts beginning with the *Śāna*;
therefore, this very reading is also found in the *Nārāyaṇīya*,
though there was an error on the part of the commentator in that regard.

The first semi-vowel (*antastha*) is *va*, which signifies the number four; the second is the *pavarga* letter [the first of which is *pa*], which signifies the number three. Thus, everything is consistent. However, in order to avoid contradiction with the *Prapañcasāra* and other texts, some have read the word as *phullā*; in that case, it is explained that the first *la* represents the number three and the subsequent *la* also represents the number three.
That too contradicts the convention, because in the convention, two marks were not grasped by means of a single cluster (*piṇḍa*).
By this [it is meant]: *a*, *ā*, *aśvinī*.
*i* is Bharaṇī; *ī*, *u*, *ū* are Kṛttikā; and so forth should be understood. (124–125)
Birth, prosperity, adversity, security, enemy, benefactor, death, friend, and great friend—these [houses] beginning with birth recur again and again. || 126 ||
The phrase "beginning from the first letter of one's own name," which will be mentioned later, should also be applied here.

Therefore, the syntactical connection is as follows: "Then, when there is a difference in letters, one should repeatedly count the [stages] beginning with birth and so forth, in a clockwise direction, starting from the first letter of one's own name up to the first letter of the mantra"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

The meaning is that one should calculate by proceeding clockwise from the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) containing the first letter of the practitioner's name up to the lunar mansion containing the first letter of the mantra, and then consider the result.
As it has been said:
"The wise one should count [the syllables] in a clockwise direction starting from the syllable known as the name of the practitioner."

Elsewhere it is also said: "One should consider the fruit to be as many [units] as there are syllables of the mantra, preceded by one's own name and so forth, beginning with one and ending with nine. And elsewhere: "Having thus assigned the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) among the divided syllables..."
Starting from the birth asterism and ending with the asterism of the mantra,
this [calculation] should be understood to apply when there is identity between the name of the zodiac sign and the well-known personal name.
O Rāma, having divided [the total] by nine, [one obtains] the arrows (five), the mountains (seven), and the mantras.

"The remaining [positions] are to be avoided; those that are auspicious bestow the accomplishment of desired goals through recitation (*japa*) and other practices. Thus, having excluded the first, third, fifth, and seventh [houses], the remainder is auspicious.
As it has been said: "Having abandoned the third, fifth, first, seventh, and ninth stars.
And elsewhere: "The sixth, eighth, and ninth are auspicious, as are those occurring in pairs;
the others are not auspicious—this should be known by those skilled in the Tantras."
Some even desire auspiciousness for the first [year].
As it has been said:
"Calamity, death, and the enemy year are to be avoided by the wise."
Thus [it is said].
This, however, refers to one's first birth.
In this consideration of *tārāmaitrī* (friendship by star), *yonimaitrī* (friendship by birth) and *gaṇamaitrī* (friendship by group) must necessarily be examined as well.
Because even those two consist of constellations (*nakṣatra*).

The consideration of one's own family (*svakula*) and the other family (*anyakula*) is also stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Likewise, a constellation belonging to a single group is indeed one's own family (*svakula*), while the other is the alien family (*akula*)."
Thus it is said.

Likewise, in the *Mantramuktāvalī*, in the description of the division between one’s own family (*svakula*) and another family (*anyakula*), even a single lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) belonging to the same group is stated to be one’s own family.
In that regard, the friendship of the womb (*yonimaitrī*) is as follows: horse, goat, two snakes, dog, bull, eater [of dogs], ram, seasons, and mouse.
The horse, the cow, then successively the buffalo, the tiger, again the buffalo, the tiger and the deer,
the two spotted deer, the monkey, then the two brown ones, the monkey, the lion and the horse,
the king of beasts (the lion), and the elephant— this is the birth-order of the signs. Thus it is said.
Including Abhijit as well, there are twenty-eight [nakṣatras].
[The animals corresponding to them are: 1. horse, 2. elephant, 3. ram, 4. serpent;
5. dog, 6. cat, 7. ram, 8. cat, 9. mouse.
11. Cow; 12. Buffalo; 13. Tiger; 14. Buffalo; 15. Tiger; 16. Deer; 17. Dog;
18. Monkey; 19. Mongoose;
20. Monkey; 21. Lion; 22. Horse; 23. Lion; 24. Cow; 25. Elephant.

As for the enmities: "The cow and the tiger, the elephant and the lion, the horse and the buffalo, the dog and the deer, the mongoose and the snake, and likewise the monkey and the ram, as well as the cat and the mouse—these are great natural hostilities.
Thus it is said.
"O Maheśvarī, the methods of killing according to the birth star (*janmanakṣatra*) and the womb (*yoni*) truly grant success without delay. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, its utility for other purposes is also stated elsewhere:
Regarding the friendship of groups (*gaṇamaitrī*):

therein, the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) belonging to the group of humans and so forth will be explained in the twenty-first [chapter]. As for the result (*phala*), it is considered as follows: the state of being a victim and an executioner.

There is enmity between human *rākṣasas* and divine *rākṣasas*; there is affection between gods and humans; and there is equality even among those of their own respective kind. Thus [it is said]. 126.

In the [twelve] zodiac signs, the letters are divided in order as follows: *vā* (white), *laṃ* (yellow), *gauraṃ* (fair), *khuraṃ* (red), *śoṇaṃ* (crimson), *śamī* (peaceful), and *śobhā* (splendor). In the sign of Virgo (*kanyā*), the letters beginning with *śa* are prescribed.
Now, he states the division of the syllables into the zodiac signs (*rāśivibhāga*) with the verse beginning "vālam":

*vā* 4, *laṃ* 3, *gau* 3, *raṃ* 2, *khu* 2, *raṃ* 2, *śo* 5, *ṇaṃ* 5, *śa* 5, *mī* 5, *śo* 5, *bhā* 4. Thus, the letters are distributed among the signs; they have been stated according to their respective divisions. In Virgo (*kanyā*), the two final vowels (*svara*) reside, as do the letters beginning with *śa*.
Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the letters śa, ṣa, sa, ha, and la are included.
The letter kṣa enters into Pisces (mīna). As the teachers have said: "A girl born from the letters a, ma, and the groups beginning with śa is considered to be a virgin."
Thus it is said:
"Likewise, the letter *kṣa*, situated in Pisces, is together with the four beginning with *y*."
By this [method], it should be understood that "a ā i ī" corresponds to "meṣaḥ" (Aries), and so forth. || 127 ||
The ascendant, wealth, siblings, kinsmen, sons, enemies, wife, death, dharma, action, income, and expenditure are the twelve zodiacal signs. || 128 ||
"The twelve zodiac signs" is stated because of the metaphorical identification of the fruit and the bearer of the fruit. Here is the method:
one should count starting from whichever sign the first letter of the practitioner’s name falls into, up to whichever sign the first letter of the mantra falls into.
The sixth, eighth, and twelfth positions are censurable.
As it has been said:
"One should count from the letter of the practitioner up to the end of the numerical total of the letters of the name of the person to be accomplished."
"Those classes [of planets] that are subject to the eighth, sixth, and twelfth houses are not auspicious.
As for the verse: "The first, fifth, and ninth houses are known as those of kinsmen; the second, sixth, and tenth are servants;
the third, seventh, and eleventh are providers of sustenance; and the twelfth, eighth, and fourth are destroyers."

If this statement is read within the section on the results of the zodiacal signs (*rāśiphala*), then one must count starting from one's own birth sign up to the sign of the mantra; thus, it is indeed a different method.
As it has been said:
"Having examined the signs and debts of the mantras starting from the birth sign up to the sign of the mantra, one should recite the mantra that is free from enemies.

This is the secret: if [the method] is not found among those read in the section on signs (*rāśi-prakaraṇa*), then it should be explained as having the fruit of the *akaḍama-cakra* which will be described hereafter. || 128 ||
One should write the letters within a square divided into four compartments,
starting from the first letter of one's own name and proceeding from 'a' to 'kṣa'.
The practitioner of mantras should determine the [status of] the *siddha* and others, and should again act by means of the *siddha* and others:
the *siddha* bestows success through recitation (*japa*), the *sādhya* through burnt offerings (*huta*) and so forth;
the *susiddha* [bestows success] merely by being encountered, while the *ari* (enemy) devours the practitioner. ||130||
The *siddha* vowels are said to be kinsmen; the *sādhya* vowels are remembered as servants.
The *susiddha* vowels should be known as nourishers, while the *śatru* vowels are considered destroyers. (131)
He describes the method for purifying the *siddha* and other [categories] of mantras with the words "square" (*caturasra*).
The "mantrin" is one who is well-versed in the tradition of the science of mantras (*mantraśāstra*).
Since it will be stated later, "one should again [classify] the *siddha* and others by means of the *siddha* and others," the extraction of sixteen squares (*ṣoḍaśakoṣṭha*) is indicated.
Therein, one should draw five lines extending east-west, north-south, and south-north;
thus sixteen squares are produced.
Therein, one should write the syllables.
The phrase "separated by one" is to be understood as the remainder [of the instruction].
As for the method of writing: the first [syllable] is placed in the first of the first group of four;
the second is placed in the first of the second group, proceeding clockwise.
By proceeding clockwise, one places the third [syllable] in the first square of the third [row],
and the fourth [syllable] in the first square of the fourth [row]. Likewise, by proceeding clockwise, one places the fifth [syllable] in the second square of the first [row].
In the second of the second [rounds], the sixth;
in the third of the second, the seventh;
in the fourth of the second, the eighth.
Thus, by moving clockwise, the first and third [steps] form the ninth;
the second and third, the tenth;
and the third and third, the eleventh.
The twelfth [syllable] is in the fourth and third [lines];
likewise, the thirteenth is in the first and fourth;
the fourteenth is in the second and fourth.

In the third and fourth [cells], one should place the fifteenth; in the fourth and fourth, one should place the sixteenth. Having thus completed the writing of the vowels, one should likewise write the consonants beginning with *ka* in that same sequence.
Thus it is said in the Kādimata:

"In the first of the first [cycles], one should place the first [letter]; likewise in the first of the second, the second; and from elsewhere, the others; and in the same way, one should arrange the rest."
"One should write the respective fifth letter in each of those squares.

And in another tantra: "One should write four [letters] within the four groups of four squares starting from the northeast (Īśa) and ending with the southeast (Īśe). Likewise in the southeast (Āgneya), similarly in the southwest (Nairṛtya), and again in the northwest (Anila)."
The wise one should likewise write the letters beginning with *ka* in those very same compartments;
the intelligent one should complete it by the fourth enclosure in the southwest and northeast.
Whichever letter constitutes the first syllable of a name within a group of four, that [group] beginning with it belongs to that very person.
From that, one should understand that each successive group of four consists of Siddha and the others in due order.
"And thus, among the four [categories] beginning with *siddha*, it should be understood that they are *siddha* and so forth.
He states the purpose of this [verse] with the words "one's own name" (*svanāma*).
The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "starting from the square of the first letter of one's own name up to the square of the first letter of the mantra."
"Regarding 'the Siddhas and so forth' etc.: he himself will reveal this on the occasion of explaining the words, meanings, and results. As for the word 'should imagine'..."

Thus, in whichever tetrad the first letter of its own name occurs, that is the tetrad of the *siddha* [category]. Following that, in clockwise order, are the three tetrads beginning with the *sādhya* and so forth.
The practitioner of mantra should again perform [the rites] by means of the *siddha* and other categories.
In whichever four-square grid one’s own initial syllable appears, that is the "Siddha-Siddha" square.
Then, in those same four squares, proceeding clockwise through the next three squares, one should designate them as "Siddha-Sādhya," "Siddha-Susiddha," and "Siddha-Ari.
If the initial syllable of the mantra also occurs within this very same four-square grid, it is then established as "Siddha" according to this very calculation.

If, in this first tetrad, one begins from the first letter of one's own name and proceeds clockwise to find the first letter of the mantra in the second tetrad, then— starting from whichever square in the first tetrad contained the first letter of the name— one should likewise assign [the positions] in the second tetrad as follows,
proceeding clockwise: *sādhya*, *siddha*, *sādhyasādhya*, *sādhyasusiddha*, and *sādhyārī*.

If, however, the first syllable of the mantra is in the third group of four [cells] proceeding clockwise from the first four syllables of one's own name, then, as before, one should assign from that very cell, proceeding clockwise, the [results] beginning with *susiddha-siddha*, *susiddha-susiddha*, *sādhya-susiddha*, and *susiddha-susiddha*. If, however, the first syllable of the mantra is in the fourth group of four [cells] proceeding clockwise from the first four syllables of one's own name, then, as before, from that very cell...
One should arrange them in clockwise order as: *arisiddha*, *arisādhya*, *arisusiddha*, and *aryarī*.
Now, if it is asked what determines that the counting in the second and subsequent groups of four begins from that very same square, it is said:
the natural sequence itself is the determining factor.
And that [discussion] occurs in the first section of the fifth chapter:
"For it is the sequence of items already obtained in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) that is considered;
and those [items] are obtained here through the original injunction (codaka) as possessing sequence itself."
"Because there is no further desire [for more], no other sequence for them is conceived," and so forth, as it has been stated.
In that regard, when the question arises as to what exactly is to be grasped, it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*:

"Whatever name may be well-known, or what may be his birth-name, or whatever name may have been given by the Guru through the ritual of casting flowers for ascetics— one should cause the letters of that very name to be divided. Thus it is said.
Elsewhere also it is said: "Furthermore, a name well-known in the world is given by the mother or likewise by the father.
And elsewhere also: "By means of which he sleeps and by which he wakes, and by which he speaks even while standing at a distance."
"One should grasp that name even if one is distracted by another thought.
And elsewhere: "The name given by the mother or father should be purified with great effort."
Others, however, have stated that in this context only the name given at birth should be taken.
As it has been said:
"Having examined the first syllable of the mantra in relation to the syllable of the birth-star (janmarkṣa), [one should proceed]."
"One by means of four squares" refers to a group of four squares.
Furthermore, within the squares of the grid, starting from the letter of birth to the right, the wise should know the sequence as *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari* (enemies). Thus:
at birth, that is, at the time of birth, whatever asterism it was—Aśvinī and so forth—their letters are "cu ce colā aśvinī proktā" and so on; starting from that [letter], [the sequence proceeds].
The meaning is: "beginning with the first syllable of the name of birth.
This should be understood to apply similarly to the phrase "from the syllable of birth" as well.
Furthermore, this should be known as an option between the name of birth and a well-known name.
Or rather, as it is said, "What is this [mantra]?"—
it is the "bestower of success" (siddhida) because it is perfected through recitation;
it is the "bestower of success" when it is accomplished through oblations and other such means.

The connection is that [the mantra] is "well-perfected" (susiddha) merely by being attained, and thus it "bestows accomplishment" (siddhida). By the word "etc. (ādi), offerings of libation (tarpaṇa) and so forth are included. The results for the "perfected-of-the-perfected" (siddhasiddha) and other categories are as stated in the Piṅgalāmata: [The text continues with the verses: "The *siddhasiddha* bestows the fruit of knowledge; the *siddhasādhya*, the fruit of wealth; the *siddhasusiddha*, the fruit of power; and the *siddhaduṣṭa*, the fruit of death. The *sādhyasiddha* bestows the fruit of wealth; the *sādhyasādhya*, the fruit of knowledge; the *sādhyasusiddha*, the fruit of power; and the *sādhyaduṣṭa*, the fruit of death. The *susiddhasiddha* bestows the fruit of liberation; the *susiddhasādhya*, the fruit of knowledge; the *susiddhasusiddha*, the fruit of power; and the *susiddhaduṣṭa*, the fruit of death. The *siddha-siddha* [mantra] is accomplished from what has been described; the *sādhya* is accomplished by doubling the recitation (*japa*).
The *susiddha* is accomplished by half that number of recitations, while its enemy destroys one's kinsmen.
If the mantra is mastered after twice the number of recitations, it is "to be accomplished" (sādhya); however, that which is "difficult to accomplish" (sādhya) is useless.
That which is "well-accomplished" (susiddha) is mastered with half that number of recitations, while its "enemy" (ari) destroys the merit born of recitation.
A *susiddha-siddha* [mantra] is accomplished by half the recitation; a *sādhya* by double that recitation;
a *susiddha* [mantra] is mastered from the very first glance; its enemy destroys one's kinsmen and caste.

"One that is *arisiddha* (conquered by the enemy) kills the son; one that is *arisādhya* (to be conquered by the enemy) kills the daughter; one that is *susiddha* (well-accomplished) kills the wife; and its enemy (*ari*) destroys the practitioner. Thus it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*, where the calculation of the *siddha* and other categories is given for each individual syllable.
Having analyzed the name given by the mother and father, as well as that bestowed by the lineage-elders,
by separating its syllables according to the distinctions between vowels and consonants.
In that very manner, one should then begin the purification of the seed-syllables of the mantra,
which arise from the bindu, the double-bindu, the upadhmānīya, and the tongue and feet.

Having abandoned the four neuter vowels, as well as syllables resulting from combined pronunciation, those with extra syllables, and corrupt (apabhraṃśa) syllables, [one should practice] one hundred thousand times.
One should purify each letter of the name together with the syllables of the mantra:
consonants with consonants alone, and likewise vowels with vowels.
Having purified the first [syllable] with the first [mantra-syllable] and the second with the second,
if the syllables in either the mantra or the name should be unequal—
Then, having commenced the mantra, one should apply it evenly;
O fair-faced one, in whichever mantra there are two accomplished syllables at the beginning and the end.
In a very short time, he shall become the bestower of all accomplishments;
however, one who possesses [the mantra] beginning and ending with the *sādhya* attains success only with great difficulty.
That which is well-established at both the beginning and the end bestows the power of all desires;
however, that mantra whose beginning and end are hostile must be abandoned.
That which is established at the beginning and to be accomplished at the end is perfected by doubling [the recitation];
that which is established at the beginning and well-accomplished at the end is perfected through the recitation as prescribed.
The last letter that is a *siddha* [in the alphabet] should be abandoned by those most skilled in mantras;
likewise, one beginning with *sādhya* and ending with *siddha* is accomplished through threefold recitation.
One who is initially *sādhya* (to be won over) becomes well-accomplished at the end through the prescribed method;
however, one who is initially *sādhya* but ultimately an enemy should be avoided with great effort.
One who is "well-accomplished" (susiddha) and so forth, ending with "accomplished" (siddha), achieves success from that which has been described.
However, one who is "well-accomplished" and so forth, ending with "to be accomplished" (sādhya), requires four groups [of mantras].
A name that begins with a "well-accomplished" (susiddha) letter and ends with an "enemy" (ari) letter is declared to be mediocre;
likewise, one that begins with an "enemy" letter and ends with a "well-accomplished" letter is also to be abandoned in this ritual practice.
Established at the beginning, middle, and likewise at the end, it bestows auspicious results;
it is declared by the Self-Existent One in the Tantra to be effective for all objectives and neutral.
One who has successfully mastered the three positions certainly accomplishes all objectives;
however, a mantra whose enemy resides in those three positions is death itself—of this there is no doubt.

That which begins with *siddha* and ends with a pair of *sādhya*s is called "useless" by the wise; that which begins with *siddha* and ends with two *susiddha*s accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings.
A mantra beginning with a Siddha letter and ending with a pair of Ari letters is proclaimed to be destructive.
When it begins with an Ari, has a Siddha in the middle, and ends with a Sādhya, it becomes an enemy.
The accomplishment of his task will come with great difficulty, and its fruit will be very small;
if there is an enemy at the end, there will be a pair of attainable results at the beginning and in the middle.
The task will be delayed and will perish very quickly in the end;
when the goal is to be accomplished at the beginning and the end, it becomes accomplished in the middle.
When that which is established at the beginning and end becomes the object to be accomplished in the middle,
both that which is to be accomplished and that which is already accomplished are indeed perfected through an abundance of recitation.
If the Siddha is encircled by the Ari, the Susiddha will likewise become so;
it should be known that this brings about the destruction of everything for the practitioner—of this there is no doubt.
Whether the object of accomplishment is separated by a *siddhānta* or even well-established by a *siddhānta*, this mantra is quickly perfected; so the Lord himself has declared.
If a mantra has its enemy neutralized by the Siddha state, even if it is itself well-perfected, that mantra does not become an enemy; rather, it attains success with difficulty.
But if even one who is well-accomplished has his success obstructed by another object of attainment,
he will achieve it with extreme difficulty for the practitioner, and not otherwise.
If a Siddha or even a Susiddha is obstructed by an enemy,
one should see such a characteristic and avoid him from afar.
"A mantra corrupted or intercepted by an enemy must never be given.
Also, in the Nārāyaṇīya: "A mantra that abounds in corrupt syllables is censured."
This has been explained in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*.

Therein, having written the letters of the alphabet as before, one writes the mantra and the name near them; having purified the first letter with the first letter, and again having purified the second letter with the second letter, one writes the name once more at the conclusion of the name.

The meaning is that one should purify [the mantra] until its completion; however, if in a given mantra the letters of the *sādhya* (the object to be accomplished) and the letters of the enemy (*vairin*) are more numerous than the others, then one should avoid that mantra.
Regarding this, some say that there is no purification for certain letters.

"O Goddess of the Suras, one should perform the counting while strictly excluding the syllables *namaḥ*, the *praṇava* (oṃ), their combinations, and corrupted (*vapabhraṃśa*) syllables. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, by the author of the *Tattvasāgara*, another method for the conceptualization of the *siddha* and other categories is stated in that very same work.
Alternatively, on a twelve-spoked wheel,
one should write the letters from the beginning (A) to the end (Ha), excluding the *kūṭas* and *ṣaṇḍhas*, starting from the east and proceeding as far as the northeast.
One should write the numbers starting from one and ending with twelve in order, beginning from the east;
thus the fourfold nature of the mantra—as *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, or *ari*—will become clearly manifest.
In the [houses] of nine, one, and five, [the planet] is established (siddha); in six and ten, it is to be accomplished (sādhya);
in three, seven, and eleven, it is a friend; and in four, eight, and twelve, it is an enemy.
Alternatively, I shall speak briefly of another portion of the mantra:
the collection of letters of the Mātṛkā, beginning with the letter 'A' and ending with the letter 'Ha'.
Having placed each syllable in sequence within the four squares,
the knower of mantras should count them in order as *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *vairin*.
Wherever the phonemes (varṇas) arise from the name-mantra,
one should prescribe the mantra by means of those phonemes, according to the distinctions such as *siddha*, *sādhya*, and so forth.

Alternatively, having added the numerical values of the mantra and the name, when divided by four, the mantra becomes *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, or *ari* starting from one. Thus it is said. However, in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
Mantra is said to be of three kinds: *siddha*, *sādhya*, and *susiddhaka*.

That which consists of few syllables is *siddha*; the *mālā* and *ardhamālā* types are *sādhya*; and that which exceeds these is *susiddha*, which is highly praised for poetic composition. Thus it is said.
There is yet another distinction: one who is pure should worship the mantra that bestows both visible and invisible fruits—the *sakala*, the *niṣkala*, the *sūkṣma*, and likewise the *sakalaniṣkala*.
Śiva has declared that the sixfold mantra is differentiated by its parts (kalā) and transcends those parts;
know that the "with-parts" (sakala) resides in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and that which is below it is "without-parts" (niṣkala).
"The mind is named Sūkṣma; it resides in the heart, possessing both parts and being partless. It is situated in the Bindu, undivided from the Kalās, yet beyond the Kalās above that.
That very Kalā is Kuṇḍalinī, the power of Nāda, as declared by Śiva. Thus [it is said].
A mantra contemplated upon these six locations remains fixed in its place and bestows fruit; it is not otherwise.
As it is said in the *Mālinīvijaya*:
"Mantras that abide in their proper place grant boons, and those that abide in meditation bestow fruit."
"Even those well-accomplished [mantras] become enemies when they are separated from their meditative stations. Thus it is said.
If, through ignorance, one should take up an enemy mantra, then the method for its abandonment is stated:
"Now, the ritual for the complete abandonment of an enemy mantra is clearly explained."
Having become pure and composed, one should begin on an auspicious day.
For the destruction of all suffering without exception, the Teacher [prescribed] the supreme rite;
therein, first, in a beautiful hall, [he established] the ritual jar according to the sequence of the initiation procedure.
The wise one should place [the vessel] within the maṇḍala and fill it with auspicious water;
having invoked the deity there by reciting the mantra in reverse order.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and having worshipped [the deity], one should worship the surrounding deities (āvaraṇas).
Thus, having worshipped the deity of the mantra along with its attendants, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) [proceeds].
Having offered oblations with clarified butter and the *viloma* mantra,
the wise twice-born man should likewise offer eight hundred or one thousand and eight oblations even for a cow.
Then, with the mantra "brahmārpaṇam," he should likewise gratify the Lord at the end;
thereafter, he should duly offer an oblation (bali) of milk-rice to the deities.
Likewise, from the intermediate directions and the cardinal directions, [I summon you] with the following supreme mantras:
"Come, O Indra, Lord of the Gods, O Śatamanyu, Lord of Śacī!"
Salutations to you; accept this offering of flowers, incense, and the like.
Come, O Lord of splendors, O carrier of oblations, O bestower of boons!
Accept these well-offered flowers, incense, and other offerings, as well as this bali; O King of Pretas, come hither, you who possess a luster like that of crushed collyrium!
Having accepted this offered oblation, be well-pleased and grant me boons;
salutations to you, O Lord of the Rakshasas, Nirṛti, who have come here.
Accept this offering, worship, and so forth, presented by me with devotion;
come, O Guardian of the Western Quarter, Lord of the Water-world (Loka), homage be to you!
Accepting this worship offered with devotion, may you find pleasure;
O Prabhajana, Lord of Life, come here together with your retinue.
"Accept with respect this offering prepared by me according to the prescribed rites;
may Kuvera and the Lord of the Stars (Rudra), the two best of gods, come hither!"
May you two, the bestowers of boons, be pleased by these flowers, incense, and other offerings for my sake.
O Lord, O Blessed One, O Sovereign who is the refuge of all knowledge! You alone are the Lord.
Honored with flowers, incense, and other offerings, be pleased for the sake of prosperity! Come, O Brahmā, Lord of all worlds, to this worship.
Accept [this offering], turn back all my obstacles; salutations be unto you!
Come, O bestower of boons, O Unmanifest One, O Viṣṇu, Leader of the Universe!
Worshipped with supreme devotion, may you be the bestower of happiness upon me;
thereafter, one should worship the deity of the mantra along with his retinue.
Then, with the mantra recited correctly and with offerings of flowers and lamps,
the wise one should pray to the deity of the mantra who has been worshipped.
O Lord, without considering what was favorable, I, with a fickle intellect,
have accepted and worshipped that which is the very nature of the mantra.
By this, may you completely dispel the agitation of my mind;
may my sin be destroyed, and may there be eternal welfare.
"May devotion to you alone, which is purifying [and auspicious], extend my welfare"—
having thus prayed to the Mistress of Mantras, he wrote the mantra in reverse order upon a leaf.
Having written it, one should worship it with *amalaka*, camphor, and sandalwood,
placing it upon a water-pot while endowed with supreme devotion.
Then, having tied that leaf upon his own head,
the wise man should bathe with the auspicious waters from the consecrated pitcher, which are imbued with mantras.
Furthermore, having filled another jar with water while remaining self-controlled,
one should place the mantra-leaf within it and then perform worship.
One should place that jar on the bank of a river or in another pure reservoir of water,
and then one should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability.

For one who has performed the ritual in this manner, the afflictions arising from the mantras of enemies are destroyed without a doubt; gradually, clarity of mind arises, and his family, becoming exceedingly prosperous, flourishes in due course. Thus it is said.
Now, the method for calculating the balance of debts and assets as stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī* is written here:

Multiply the years to be calculated by fourteen (Indra), twenty-seven (stars/ṛkṣa), twelve (eyes), twelve (suns/ravi), fifteen (pañcadaśa), six (seasons/ṛtu), four (Vedas), six (fires/vahni), eight (weapons/āyudha), eight (aṣṭa), and nine (navabhiḥ).
Then, multiply the letters of the practitioner's name by ten, one, seven, four, eight, three, seven, five, four, six, and three respectively.
Subtracting the name-number from the year-number, and vice versa, the remainder for both should be understood; the greater remainder shall be the debt or the wealth.
A mantra with a debt is auspiciously fruitful, whereas one with wealth is inauspicious.
"When they are equal, it is said by the lords of sages to have equal results.

Regarding that, the method is as follows: one should separate and set aside the letters of the name of the mantra to be accomplished, the practitioner, and the disciple, categorized by their vowels and consonants.

Then, having formed the four groups of the *mātṛkā* consisting of eleven syllables each— namely *a-ka-ṭha-pa*— one should count the mantra syllables, distinguished by their vowels and consonants, using the numbers assigned to Indra and the other deities.
One should likewise count the syllables of the practitioner’s name, distinguished by their vowels and consonants, using the numbers assigned to the directions and so forth.

In that regard, the method of multiplication is as follows: whatever letter is in a particular position, one should multiply that letter by the numerical value of that position; the meaning is that one should multiply it by the number corresponding to that place-value.
For example: the letter *a* situated in the first square should be multiplied by fourteen; there, one multiplied by fourteen is fourteen itself.
Likewise, the letter *i* situated in the second square should be multiplied by twenty-seven.
Therefore, twenty-seven multiplied by two is fifty-four.
Likewise, the letter *u* situated in the third position is doubled to become six.
In this manner, one should also multiply the letters of the practitioner's name by ten and the other [coefficients].

Regarding the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*): among the syllables of the mantra, the numerical values for *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, *ṝ*, and *ḹ* are to be understood as belonging only to short vowels. Then, all these numerical values are to be added together and divided by eight.
Whatever remainder is left over is the debtor (*ṛṇī*), the one in arrears (*adhamarṇa*).
A deficient heap belongs to the creditor, the superior debtor;
if there is a mantra [of protection] therein, it belongs to the inferior debtor, and in that case it should be accepted.
If not, it should not be accepted.
Now, the method for calculating the balance of debt and credit as taught in the *Kādimatatantra* is as follows:
"Starting from the first letter of the name up to the first letter of the mantra, divide [the count] by three and multiply by the vowels; the other [calculation] is the reverse."
The meaning of this is as follows:
having counted from the first letter of the practitioner's name up to the first letter of the mantra according to the sequence of the Mātṛkās, that numerical value is multiplied by three.
"Having performed [this], one should divide by seven vowels.
This is the practitioner's heap (*sādhakarāśi*).

Thus, having counted from the first letter of the mantra up to the first letter of the practitioner's name according to the sequence of the *mātṛkā* alphabet, one should multiply that numerical value by three.
"One should divide by seven" refers to the aggregate of mantras;
the rest is as before.
Or, the method for clearing debts and assets as stated in another tantra is as follows:

"The name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), doubled and joined with the name of the practitioner (sādhaka), should be divided by eight; the remainder is [the result], while the other case is the reverse.
This is the meaning of this [verse].
One should double the syllables of the mantra, having separated them according to their form as vowels and consonants.
One should then add the syllables of the practitioner’s name, likewise separated according to their form as vowels and consonants, to those [syllables].
Thereafter, one should divide by eight.
This is the mass of mantras.
In this way, the syllables of the practitioner's name,
having been separated into the forms of vowels and consonants, are doubled in the form of vowels and consonants.
One should remove [the letters] joined with eight [others], separated by the mantra-syllables;
such is the heap of the practitioner.
The rest is as before.
When these [defects] have been mentioned, the clearing of the debt or the wealth must necessarily be performed regarding the mantras.
In that regard, how do the mantras possess the state of being a debt? That has been stated in the *Kādimata*:
"Due to practice performed in a previous birth, it causes the non-attainment of results because of sin."
When evil has perished, there is the attainment of fruit; at the proper time, through the dissolution of the body, one is free from debt.
By the mere attainment of the mantra, the former [mantra] becomes effective for the sake of accomplishment;
that man who has received the mantra from a guru whose own mantra is perfected shall partake in success.
"He who, disregarding [the mantra] due to the intoxication of wealth (lakṣmīmada), has obtained the enjoyment of the mantra, that mantra should be known as his creditor;
its worship is the prerequisite.
Therefore, the purification of this debt must be performed by everyone in every way. Thus it is said.
In another treatise, an alternative method for the purification of mantras is stated:

"Having drawn a six-petalled wheel, one should write the letters beginning with 'a'— one by one— in the petals starting from the east, excluding the neuter (*niṣṣaṇḍha*) and compound (*kūṭa*) syllables."
One should investigate starting from the first letter of one's own name;
when that letter is in the rising sign, prosperity is indicated, while in the second sign, there is the destruction of prosperity.
"In the third [year] one should know wealth (or stability), in the fourth there is conflict with kinsmen;
in the fifth one will be of a doubtful nature, and the sixth is the destroyer of all.
Regarding this, the exception concerning the purification of *siddha* and the other [categories] is stated in another treatise and applies everywhere.
There is no fault in [the use of] the Piṇḍa, Tāra, Svapnalabdha, the six-syllable mantra, Prāsāda, Ārka, Traipura, Nārasiṃha, Mālā, Māyā, Mātṛ, Vārāha, Kāmāstra, Strī, Āpta, Veda, or Ratna mantras.
Thus it is said.
The nature of the *mālāmantra* is described in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
"Those mantras which consist of many syllables are known as *mālāmantras*."
A garland of more than ten syllables is a *mālā*; one of more than five is a *ardhamālikā*.
A garland consisting of five [beads] is not for the elderly, the aged, or children;
a garland bestows success in old age, while a half-garland does so in youth.
"In childhood, however, a mantra of five syllables is the bestower of success. Thus it is said.
In the *Prayogasāra*, however: "Those mantras ending in nine syllables are proclaimed as seed-mantras (*bījamantra*);
furthermore, those mantras ending in twenty syllables are likewise declared to be [seed-mantras]."
Mantras with more syllables than that are proclaimed as *mālāmantras*.
Seed-mantras (*bījamantras*) bestow success in childhood, while [other] mantras [bestow it] in youth.
"And *mālāmantras* bestow success especially in old age.
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Mantras consisting of more than twenty syllables are known as *mālāmantras*."
Mantras consisting of more than ten syllables, and those of fewer than that, are designated as "seed" (bīja) mantras.

"Mālā-mantras grant success in old age, while [ordinary] mantras grant success in youth; those consisting of more than five syllables grant success in childhood, and others always grant success at all times. Thus it is stated in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*: "In states other than those mentioned, for the sake of accomplishing seed-mantras (*bīja-mantra*), mālā-mantras, and [other] mantras..."
"One should recite it twice.
Likewise:
"In the same way, for the eight-syllable *haṃsa* mantra as well as for the five-syllable one..."
One should not purify the *siddha* and other [categories] of a seed-syllable that consists of one, two, three, or more [consonants].
Likewise: "In mantras consisting of one, three, five, seven, nine, eleven, six, thirty-two, or twenty-six syllables, no division into parts is reckoned."
In the Gāruḍa and other solar tantras, in those of Viṣṇu, and in the Buddhist and Jain traditions,
as well as in mantras of the Mahākūṭa class, there is no purification of the Siddhas and so forth.
"A mantra consisting of more than forty syllables, increasing by one syllable at a time up to sixty-three seed-syllables, bestows manifold fruits.
And likewise: "Those mantras which are perfected through the Command (ājñā) by the grace of the Yoginīs..."
"Whatever mantras have been obtained, they bestow the fruit of all desires. Thus it is said.
For those [mantras] other than these, purification is mandatory.
As it has been stated:
Whether it be a mantra, or a vidyā, or a hymn of praise, or even a sūkta,
it becomes the destroyer of the body of Arthabandhu in an instant.
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid the wicked everywhere—not only in the case of mantras, but especially among embodied beings.
One should examine the relationship between them; otherwise, it will not come to pass. Thus it is said.
However, regarding a mantra that does not harmonize with the Siddhas and others, another method has been taught.
As they say:
"In all these defects, one should employ either Māyā or Kāma."
"Having first cast [the seed-syllable], one should bestow Śrī for the sake of liberation from its defects.
Likewise: "Or even a defective mantra becomes effective when encapsulated by the Tāra;
moreover, whichever mantra a person has devotion for, that very mantra becomes effective for him."
Likewise, in the *Bhuvaneśīpārijāta*:
"Combined with the seed-syllable of Māyā, it becomes a bestower of swift success;
the *piṇḍa* mantra alone, when illuminated by the seed-syllable of Māyā [is likewise effective]."

"From the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ) arises Prāṇa; the seed-syllable is endowed with the potency of consciousness. Thus it is said. Likewise: "When arranged in both direct and reverse order by means of the garland of phonemes, the mantras joined with each individual phoneme, when recited, bestow swift accomplishment."
"If even the mantras of enemies [are ineffective] for men, what need is there to mention other mantras?

Thus [it is said]. Ahead, for the sake of practical usage, he states the alternative names for the perfected (*siddha*) and other letters, beginning with "the perfected syllables" (*siddhārṇā*). (129–131)
An action performed by relying upon a lamp-stand yields its fruit. || 132 ||
Since the fruit has already been mentioned, he states the location for the recitation of the mantra with the word "dīpa" (lamp).
The meaning of the term "dīpa" is stated elsewhere:
"That place where the person shines is called the 'dīpasthāna' (lamp-location)."
Thus it is said.
Likewise: "I shall now fully explain the multitude of lamps as taught in the *Brahmayāmala*, by which temples, villages, houses, and so forth are to be known as auspicious or inauspicious."
"The letters from *ka* to *kṣa* are known as 'lamps' (*dīpa*).
The sixteen vowels should be understood by the best of practitioners as being called 'seats' (*pīṭha*).
Likewise: "The vowels are designated as the seats, while the consonants are indeed the lamps."
The place where the syllable of the lamp resides within a particular square shall become that [result].
"This shall be the location of the lamp in the Kūrma-cakra; of this there is no doubt.
Regarding "its location of the lamp":
its activity consists of recitation (*japa*) and so forth.
Therefore, he will say: "The means for accomplishing the success of mantras. || 132 ||
Having divided the ground into a square, one should draw a grid of nine compartments;
starting from the eastern compartment, one should write the seven groups [of consonants] in successive order.
He states the tortoise-diagram (*kūrma-cakra*) for the purpose of knowing the location of the lamp, beginning with the word "four.
Therein, one should draw two lines extending from east to west and two extending from south to north in the center of a square;
thus, nine compartments are produced.
In those nine squares, the nine Kṣetrapālas are to be worshipped.
As it is said:
"These nine Kṣetrapālas are the lords of the lamps within the nine squares."
Amṛta, Vṛṣabha, Śailarāja, Vāsuki, and Arthakṛt.
"Śaktikṛt (the Citadel), Padmayoni, and Mahāśaṅkha—these are the nine.
One should worship them, accompanied by their retinues of shadow and parasols, starting from the center and proceeding from the east.
This means beginning with the eastern compartment and so forth.
"The seven groups" refers to *ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa-ya-śa*. One should write them in sequence up to the end of the north (*uttarāntam*).
Here, as far as possible, one should begin from the center and proceed into each square.
As it has been said: "In the eastern square, the five-fold *ka*-group is placed in order from the center;
likewise, the *ca*-group is placed in the same manner from the center elsewhere, specifically in the southeast. (133)
In the central square of the Lakṣmī-īśa [grid], one should write the vowels in pairs;
in the directions starting from the east, where the first letter of the name of the field (kṣetra) is situated. || 134 ||
One should know that his face is [there], with two hands situated on both sides;
the two cavities are the belly, the two [remaining parts] are the feet, and what is left is said to be the tail.
According to this sequence, one should divide even that which stands in the middle into its respective portions. || 135 ||
"One should write the vowels in pairs in the central square.
Regarding that, the method of writing is stated elsewhere:
"In the central square, one should write two *a*-sounds in the front portion."
One should know there are two fire-syllables (Āgneya) and should draw two upward-facing syllables (Ud) in the southern direction.
One should find two *ṛ* vowels in the southwest, and likewise two *ḷ* vowels in the west;
one should find two *e* vowels in the northwest, and two *o* vowels are prescribed in the north.
"And one should know the final pair in the Īśa [corner]; having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should investigate.
This sequence of writing is indeed indicated by the phrase "one should divide according to this sequence," which will be stated hereafter.
Regarding the term "known as a field" (*kṣetrākhyā*):
here, the word "field" (*kṣetra*) is indicative of villages and so forth.
As it has been said: "The sacred seat (*pīṭha*), the field (*kṣetra*), the city (*pura*), the town (*nagara*), and the village (*grāma*)."
Thus it is said.
Its definition is stated elsewhere: "The field (*kṣetra*) consists of the letters from *ka* to *na*; the village (*grāma*) consists of those from *pa* to *ma*;
and the city (*pura*) correctly consists of those from *ya* to *ṣa*, as declared by the best of teachers."
"Sahānta" is said to be the city; this is the characteristic of the field (*kṣetra*).
As for the characteristic of the seat (*pīṭha*), it was stated previously: "The sixteen vowels are called the seats.
However, in some places it is also said: "In forests, mountains, towns, villages, temples, rivers, and so forth."

The phrase "situated on both sides" applies respectively to the hands, the flanks, and the feet. Thus, the first [part] is on both sides of each [limb], while the tail is the remainder situated adjacent to the subsequent [parts]. (134–135)
Situated in the mouth, one attains success; situated in the hand, one has a short life;
situated in the belly, one remains indifferent; situated at the feet, one shall experience suffering. || 136 ||
The practitioner situated in the tail is afflicted by imprisonment, eradication, and other such calamities.
This is declared to be the Kūrma-cakra, the means for accomplishing the success of mantras. || 137 ||
He states its fruit [with the words] "situated in the mouth. The word "mantrī" (the mantra-practitioner) is drawn in [from the previous context].
The meaning is: one for whom the mantra has been accepted according to the method of initiation taught in the Tantra.
In the two words "agre'pi mantriṇām" as well, this same meaning is to be understood.
That by which one lives is "jīvana," meaning enjoyment; he whose enjoyment is slight is "svalpajīvanaḥ.
As it has been said: "When situated in the mouth, it is known to grant auspiciousness; when situated in the hand, it possesses little enjoyment."
By such [statements] as these;
and likewise— "In the mouth there shall be the accomplishment of all aims; on the two hands, it brings about minor accomplishments," and so forth.
Likewise: "Therefore, one should undertake all ritual action by resorting to the mouth;
in its absence, one may resort to the hand, but one should not resort to any other part of the tortoise.
Regarding this, a specific detail is stated in another text:
Wherever enmity exists between the names of the site and the practitioner,
one should understand that specific [factor] from the scriptures and properly abandon it.
The mutual enmity of the two *ṛ* vowels is stated by means of the letter *ga*;
that of the pair of *ṛ* vowels is stated by the letter *ṭha*, and that of the letter *ṭha* is also [stated] by means of that [same *ṭha*].
The two *ḷ* vowels are [substituted] by the letter *pa*, and the letter *pa* is also [substituted] by the two *ḷ* vowels;
the pair *o* is [substituted] by the letter *ṣa*, and the letter *ṣa* is [substituted] by the pair *o*.
The letter *ja* is [substituted] by *ṭa*; the letter *jha* (*ū*) by *kha*;
the letter *u* by *ta*; and the letter *pha* by *dha*.
The letter *bha* is an enemy to the letter *ra*, and the letter *ya* is an enemy to the letter *sa*;
for these letters there is enmity, while for others there is the state of friendship.
"The practitioner should diligently avoid the position of the enemy in the *kūrmacakra*.
An illustration of this is shown in that very same [work]: "For example, Aṭṭahāsa, the great city, would be the enemy of Garga."
In this manner, one should apply [the mantra] of Gayāmreśvara to the letters beginning with 'A'.
He made Ākhyam for Ṛṣabha and Padmakam for Ḷtaka;
Oḍḍiyāna for Ṣaṇmukha and Auḍra for Ṣaṅguṇaka.
Jayantī is the enemy of Ṭaṅkana; Khaṇḍhāra comes from Jhañjabhaṭṭa; Taraṇi (known as Tārā) belongs to Ḍakadeva; and Dhūma belongs to Phaṇjaka.
"Ramya is the enemy of Bhaṭṭa, and the lake is indeed the enemy of Yajñamitra.
Having thus purified them in sequence, the wise man should abandon the place of the enemy.
Likewise: "One should apply the first letter of each of those [names] to the preceding paths."
If that is the mass of its consonants, and if it is the first [vowel] joined with the seat (pīṭha).

One should avoid all the syllables of the name when they are joined with the *pīṭhas*. Having taken those [syllables] beginning with that [first one] according to the path, one should then discard the vowel.

"Having omitted the initial, middle, and final letters among the syllables of the village name, the square in which the second syllable resides is its mouth. Also elsewhere: "In whichever [square] the second syllable of that respective name resides, that is the mouth."
Thus [it is said].
However, this refers to names beginning with vowels.
Regarding names and so forth, when there is a conjunct consonant (*saṃyogākṣara*), he states a specific rule:
Wherever among the names of villages and so forth there are three syllables,
and where the vowel is situated mounted upon the middle syllable, that is the "mouth" (mukha).
"If you have two syllables clearly [beginning] with the names of villages and so forth, that wherein the first vowel resides is desired as the 'face' (vadana).
And likewise: "For the mantras that accomplish the sacred field (kṣetra), there is only one initial syllable."
"If it should exist, that mantra will certainly bestow the fruit of all accomplishments.
Thus [it is said]. Another [text] states the specific fruits:
"One should perform [the rite] for liberation in the mouth, but for malevolent magic (ābhicārika) in the right [hand]."
One who desires prosperity should be in the west, and one who bestows peace should be in the north.
In the northeast there shall be the destruction of enemies; in the southeast, it bestows enemies.
In the southwest there shall be fear of enemies; in the northwest, however, there is flight.
"Whoever performs a sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) without understanding the *kūrmacakra* gains no fruit from that recitation; rather, it leads to misfortune.

Regarding this, there is a specific rule in the *Kādima-tantra*: "Having increased the length and width [of the mandala] and divided [the result] by eight, [one determines the directions] from the remainder."
Having discerned one of their groups as the first, he should assign it a name.
When the forms of the sites (vāstu) are unknown, they should be known by their names;
the consonants belong to the Deśakūrma, and likewise the vowels belong to the Gṛhakūrma.
Thus [ends the section]. 136–137.
A field of merit, the bank of a river, a cave, a mountain peak, sacred sites, the confluences of rivers, and a purifying forest. || 138 ||
Secluded gardens, the foot of a bilva tree,
a mountain slope, a temple, a seashore, and one’s own home— these places are praised for the practitioners of mantra. || 139 ||

While describing the locations for the *puraścaraṇa* recitation, he speaks regarding the subject of the *kūrma-cakra* (the tortoise diagram), beginning with the word "puṇya" (sacred). "The bank of a river" means the bank of a sacred river,
because the bank of an ordinary river is prohibited.
In the phrase "the purifying forest" (*pāvanaṃ vanam*), there is a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*).
This also applies to the expression "secluded and pure gardens" (*udyānāni viviktāni pūtāni*);
for the lexicon states: "The words *vivikta* and *pūta* both mean 'solitary' (*vijana*)."
By the phrase "these are the locations," that which is taught in other tantras is also indicated.
As they say:
"In the place of Śiva facing west, devoid of the bull and so forth..."
"In a grove of Aśvattha, Bilva, and Tulasī trees, or one covered with various flowers;
in a cow-pen, at the root of an Aśvattha tree, or in sacred fields—it is thus recommended.
Also, in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
Recitation is praised when performed in the presence of the sun, fire, a preceptor, the moon, a lamp, water, brahmins, and cows.
Alternatively, one should dwell wherever the mind finds serenity.
Regarding that very specific location, a distinction in the fruit has also been stated:
"Recitation performed at home is said to be ordinary, but in a cow-pen it is a hundredfold."
And likewise in a grove or a forest, it is said to be a thousandfold.
"Ten thousandfold on a holy mountain, but a hundred-thousandfold by a river;
they say it is ten-millionfold in a temple, and infinite in the presence of Śiva.
Thus, in the case of mantras possessing specific powers, the eight groups of eight sacred seats (pīṭhas) and so forth should also be understood accordingly.
Otherwise— in a place free from the fear and distress caused by barbarians, wicked people, wild beasts, or serpents; or in a secluded forest that is beyond reproach and filled with devotion.
One should dwell in a beautiful region, in a righteous kingdom that is well-provided with food and free from calamity;
one should reside in a delightful place where devotees gather, and never in a state of dependence on others.
The path along which kings, ministers, royal officials, and powerful men travel— that is a place where one who knows the truth should not dwell.
One should not dwell in ruined temples, gardens, houses, or at the foot of trees; nor on riverbanks, in mountain thickets, or in cavities in the earth and similar places.
Thus [ends the section]. 138–139.
Alms-food, sacrificial offerings, vegetables, prescribed fruits, milk, roots, and barley-based preparations—these are the foods permitted for practitioners of mantra. || 140 ||
Regarding the foods permitted for the performer of *puraścaraṇa*, he says "alms" (*bhaikṣya*).
This refers specifically to the student (*brahmacārī*) and the ascetic (*yati*). The nature of alms is described elsewhere as follows:
"Alms should be received from the houses of twice-born men who are endowed with Vedic conduct, pure, prosperous, and born of a noble lineage.
Here, "fit for sacrificial oblation" (*haviṣya*) refers to food suitable for a vow (*vrata-haviṣya*), and not to food suitable for a funeral rite (*śrāddha-haviṣya*) and the like.
And regarding that, another Smṛti states: "Winter grains, white rice, steamed rice, paddy, mung beans, barley, sesame, peas, *kaṅgu*, *nīvāra* millet, *vāstuka* greens, and *hilamocikā*."
Sixty-day rice, black pot-herbs, radish, and varieties of *kemuka* other than that; bulbous roots, rock salt, sea salt, and cow's curd and milk.
Milk from which the cream has not been removed, jackfruit, mango, harītakī,
tamarind (or pippalī), cumin, and orange.

"Plantains, lavalī, and dhātrī fruits, along with jaggery and sugarcane juice not fried in oil—sages declare these to be *haviṣya* food. Here, the phrase "fruit, milk, and roots are prescribed" is to be supplied [from the preceding verse]. (140)

For the attainment of the goals of human life, a true disciple should take refuge in a guru—one who is pure by birth from both mother and father, possessed of a pure disposition, and one who has conquered the senses. (141)
It has been stated that a true disciple should take refuge in a guru. Therefore, he describes the characteristics of a guru with the words beginning "from the mother," and so forth.
"Pure from the side of the mother and the father" means born of a pure father and mother.
That purity is to be understood both through worldly renown and by an investigation of his character.
As it has been said:
"The sons, devoid of moral conduct and abandoning their own duty, reveal that secret deed which was committed by their mother while she was blinded by intoxication during her youth."
"Pure disposition" means having pure mental activity;
otherwise, due to wickedness, one would not even be worthy of service.
"One who has conquered the senses."
Because one whose senses are unsubdued is turned away from the deities. || 141 ||
He knew the essence of all scriptures and understood the true meaning of all treatises;
he was devoted to helping others and intent upon recitation, worship, and other such practices. || 142 ||
He knows the essence of all scriptures;
otherwise, there would be a lack of familiarity with the various traditions such as Śaivism and others.
He is a knower of the reality of the meaning of all treatises.
Otherwise, the investigation of the scriptures and the treatises would be untenable;
he is devoted to the welfare of others,
for otherwise there would be no compassion toward his disciples.
Without that compassion, even a mantra becomes averse [to its goal],
despite one being intent upon recitation, worship, and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), meditation and fire-offerings (homa) are included.
Otherwise, because there is an absence of the deity's presence for one who has violated the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*),
it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"A mantra does not become propitious— even if it is well-accomplished— unless it is meditated upon and recited."
One that has not been recited does not desire to grant success, nor does one that has not been offered oblations become a giver of fruit.
"Therefore, the practitioner who desires success for himself should daily perform this fourfold ritual: worship, meditation, recitation, and fire-oblation. (142)
His speech was unfailing; he was peaceful and had reached the further shore of the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas. He followed the path of yoga and had entered the heart of the deities. || 143 ||
Thus endowed with such qualities, the Guru is approved by the Āgamas. || 144 ||
His speech is unfailing, he is capable of bestowing grace,
and he is peaceful;
otherwise, that which is held in high esteem by the world would be unfit for service.
"Having reached the further shore of the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas.
By this, his steadfastness in his own proper conduct is expressed,
as it has been said:
"By a person who follows the conduct of their caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama), the Supreme Person Viṣṇu is propitiated; there is no other path that causes Him satisfaction.
Also elsewhere: "Whatever worship of deities or the like is performed apart from one's own duty (svadharma)..."
"For it would fall away from that very moment, like a palace made of sand.
Thus, one must pursue the path of yoga;
otherwise, there would be an incapacity even for bestowing initiation and other rites.
"Captivating to the heart of the deity" means captivating to the heart like the deity itself; that is to say, its appearance is serene.
Just as there is satisfaction in the mind upon seeing the deity, so too is satisfaction produced in the mind by seeing it [the image].
As it has been said:
"The conduct of men follows their actions, and the mind follows their conduct; physical form follows the mind, and for the most part, virtues follow physical form.
And wherever there is satisfaction of the mind, there the attainment of the fruit is certain.
As it has been said: "In that which the mind and the eyes find delight, there is prosperity.
Likewise, there is the recollection of the learned Kālidāsa: "For the mind knows the connections of previous births.
By the word "etcetera," that which is stated in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra is included:
Neither too young nor old, neither lame nor emaciated;
neither with extra limbs nor deficient in limbs, neither bald nor with protruding teeth.
"One who is grateful, eloquent, brave, one who has reached the further shore of established scriptures,
who has practiced the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*), who is discerning in extracting and removing [impurities such as] *śalya*,
who knows the sequence of ritual procedures (*kriyānukrama*), and who is discerning in the *mudrā* and *tantra* [traditions]. Thus it is said.
Pure, well-attired, youthful, with an equanimous mind toward all beings,
wise, of unassuming intellect, grateful, affectionate toward his disciples,
endowed with faith, and free from malice— such a householder is called a guru.
And one should also consider what is stated in other texts beginning with these words:
"The teacher, the maternal uncle, the officiating priest, the paternal uncle, the father-in-law, and the king—
these six are also gurus."

Because it is stated elsewhere, the qualification "accepted by scripture" (*āgamasammata*) is used here. He who rescues embodied beings submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra by providing the raft of reality (*tattva*) is alone remembered as the Guru in this world.
Because of this statement.
However, there is a specific rule regarding the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasvata*: "Whether born in Āryāvarta or elsewhere, [the officiant] must be devoid of the eight letters beginning with 'ka'."

"One who is proficient in the Śaiva Siddhānta and has mastered the mantras for consecration (pratiṣṭhā). And in the Vīrāgama: "A learned man born in a region between Kumārī and Himavat, which is naturally inhabited by black deer, is worthy of the office of an Ācārya."
Also in the *Yogaśivapaddhati*: "The most excellent gurus are those born in Madhyadeśa, Kurukṣetra, Nābhī, Ujjayinī, Antarvedī, Pratiṣṭhāna, and Āvantī."
The Caulas born in the Gauḍa country, as well as the Māgadhas, Keralas, Kauśalas,
and Daśārṇas, are considered to be the Madhyama Gurus.
"Those born in Karṇāṭaka, Koṅkaṇa, Ākīra, as well as Kacchati, Kāliṅga, Kāmarūpa, and Kāmboja are considered the lowest.
And in the Devīmata: "The preceptor should be a knower of the Śaiva scriptures, born in the land of Śiva..."

"Whether a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) or a householder (*gṛhastha*), one who is devoted to the worship of Śiva and whose birth occurs under an asterism favorable to the patron (*yajamāna*) is called a *deśika* (preceptor). Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "One who is a householder or established in celibacy, and who is free from the eight defects beginning with the letter 'ka' (*kakārāṣṭaka-vivarjita*)."
"One should always make as one's teacher one who is devoted to the vows of fasting.
Likewise: "That twice-born man who perceives the Self as distinct in all things—even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks—is a teacher; of this there is no doubt."
But one who has awakened through the Pañcarātra and knows the reality of the meaning of the Siddhānta is declared to be an Ācārya, even if he is devoid of all [other] characteristics.
"He who possesses supreme devotion toward Viṣṇu as he does toward his guru—he alone is to be known as a true teacher; I tell you this truth. Thus it is said.
Regarding the Śaiva initiation, there is a specific detail in the Atītāgama:
Whether he has matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot, he should be born in an auspicious region,
a twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Śiva scriptures, and is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct.
"He who always takes refuge in Śiva alone through the actions of speech, mind, and body—he is designated as the true *ācārya* in rites such as the initiation (*dīkṣā*) into Śiva.
And regarding the rite for pacification (*śāntika*): "One who is learned in the Vedas, whose soul is serene, and who has been consecrated by the initiation into Śiva..."
One who knows the Śiva-āgamas, possesses intelligence, and is devoted to the worship of Śiva.
"One who wears a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, whose body is marked with the trident,
who is born of a pure region and lineage, who is endowed with good character and conduct,
and who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and Shastras— such a person is called a wise Guru. Thus it is said.

Also, in the *Pratiṣṭhāpaddhati*: "One who possesses the characteristics of a *liṅgin* (or *liṅga*), who knows the defining marks, who is skillful in the sequence of rituals, who knows the reality of the pervasion of the deities, and who is proficient in the sixfold path (*ṣaḍvidhādhvan*)."
"Or rather, what is the use of detailed knowledge regarding auspicious and inauspicious signs?
He who possesses the correct thorough knowledge of birth, conduct, and the first three qualities—that teacher is the most excellent, bestowing the fruits of all desires. Thus it is said.
The status of the ascetic (*yati*) as a teacher is also stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*:

"A mantra-practitioner who has observed the vows of the sacred sites, who possesses knowledge, is well-composed, and is constantly devoted— such an ascetic is renowned as a teacher, even if he is merely a householder."
Also in the Bātulottara: "Having obtained such a Guru—one who bestows fearlessness through Vidyā and is free from greed and fickleness—who would not be liberated from bondage?
And in the Pauṣkara: "Even if he lacks all [other] characteristics, one who possesses knowledge is called a Guru."
"And knowledge is the realization of reality, which rests upon the knowledge of the six paths. (143–144)
The disciple should be of noble birth, pure in soul, devoted to the goals of human endeavor, one who has studied the Vedas, skillful, and far removed from the power of passion. || 145 ||
Always seeking the welfare of living beings, ever a believer who has abandoned atheism, devoted to his own duty with devotion, and striving for the benefit of his father and mother. (146)
He is devoted to serving his gurus with the wealth of speech, mind, and body;
he has abandoned pride toward his gurus on account of [superiority in] birth, learning, wealth, and so forth. || 147 ||
Indeed, for the sake of obeying the guru’s command, he is intent on even sacrificing his life; having set aside his own affairs, he is always devoted to the service of the guru. || 148 ||
A disciple who always dwells with his guru like a servant, performing his commands day and night, remains devoted to the service of his guru. || 149 ||
A disciple who obeys the commands of the guru through the actions of mind, speech, and body—he alone should be accepted at that time by one desiring auspiciousness, and no other. || 150 ||
He who always conceals the secrets of mantra and worship, and he who, knowing the true essence of the scriptures and proper conduct, pays homage at the three times of day; || 151 ||
Only such a person should be made a disciple, and no other whose life is meager;
endowed with such qualities as these, one becomes a disciple, and no other. || 152 ||
He states the characteristics of a disciple with the word "disciple": one who is of noble family (*kulīna*) is born of pure parents;
otherwise, because those such as the *kuṇḍa* and *gola* are impure, they must never be touched.
He is of pure self and non-cruel mind,
because knowledge is not to be imparted to one who is cruel;
as the Śruti says:
Knowledge indeed came to a Brahmin, saying:
"Guard me; I am your treasure.
Do not speak of me to one who is envious, nor to one who is dishonest, nor to one who is unrestrained."
"May I likewise be possessed of vigor.
Thus, he is one who is devoted to human effort (*puruṣārtha*).
By this, his freedom from addiction is expressed.
Otherwise, the instruction would be purposeless. By the phrase "one who has studied the Veda," his purity is expressed;
as it has been said:
"The twice-born who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself elsewhere, quickly becomes a Śūdra even while living, along with his progeny. Thus [it is said].
"Skilled" means not deluded.
Because one who is deluded lacks the capacity to be awakened by the mantra;

because one whose mind is far removed from the god of love (Manobhava) is a lustful person, and due to being possessed of sin— that is, having an impure mind— lacks the qualification for the propitiation of the mantra.
"Always seeking the welfare of living beings.
Otherwise, the sin of one who is intent on performing malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) and the like based on mantras taught by someone else would touch even the teacher.
"A believer" (*āstika*) is one whose conviction is that the next world exists.

Otherwise, in the state of nihilism (*nāstikatā*), because one would not propitiate the mantra-deities, the deities would become enraged with the guru. One must abandon nihilism and avoid association with nihilists;
otherwise, there would be the fault born of such association.
Devoted to his own duty and possessed of right conduct;
for one who lacks proper conduct has no entitlement [to this].
He is intent on the welfare of his mother and father through devotion, and not out of hypocrisy or the like.
This alone has been declared by Vyāsa and others to be his supreme duty.
By the words "speech, mind," and so forth, non-deceitfulness is expressed;
and by the phrase "of such a kind," [this quality is further characterized].
"Youthful, with all his faculties disciplined, an abode of compassion"—
thus one should observe what is stated in other texts. As it says in the *Prayogasāra*:
In that regard also, for one who is devoted and who bestows wealth upon his son—
thus it is said in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Performing service to the teacher through the actions of mind, speech, and body."
