One who possesses pure disposition and great enthusiasm is known as a disciple, a bodhisattva.
"But neither the son, nor the husband, nor the one who has transgressed, nor likewise the one who bestows wealth [is to be instructed].
By the phrase "nor another," the prohibition of anyone else is stated.
And likewise, elsewhere, after describing the faults of a disciple, it is said: "One should not accept as a disciple one who lacks such qualities as these;
for if one were to accept him, his faults would likely infect the teacher as well."

Just as the fault of a minister reaches the king, his lord, or the fault committed by a wife reaches her husband, so too the fault committed by a disciple reaches the teacher; of this there is no doubt.
"If one accepts [a disciple] through initiation out of affection or even out of greed, a curse from the deity shall fall upon that guru together with his disciples.
Therefore, a guru should always accept a disciple only after having thoroughly tested him. Thus it is said.
In the *Bhuvaneśīparijāta* it is also stated: "He who would speak [the teachings] to one who is not a disciple becomes a perpetrator of a great sin.
However, in another text there is this distinction: "When the Guru is speaking words, one should then speak these words:"
"Be gracious, O Lord, O God," he said with reverence, "and likewise, 'So be it.'"

Having prostrated, one should sit at his side; likewise, one should move about with his permission. One should attend upon him while looking toward his face and carry out whatever he commands with reverence.
One should not speak untruth before him, nor should one engage in excessive chatter;
likewise, one should avoid lust, anger, greed, pride, laughter, and flattery.

"A disciple who desires to prosper should never, under any circumstances, engage with his teacher in frivolous or deceitful activities, nor in lamentation; likewise, he should not enter into the giving or receiving of debts, nor the buying and selling of goods. Thus it is said.

In the *Prayogasāra* as well: "The guru is the mother, the father, the master, kinsmen, and friends; Śiva [is he]. Having thus fixed the mind, one should always worship the guru with one's whole being."
One should not speak untruth to the guru, nor should one cause him to be censured.
One should turn others away from what he has undertaken; if unable to do so, one should abandon that position.
One should practice the same service toward the wives of the guru as one does toward the guru himself;
one should look upon elder brothers as one would the guru, and upon younger brothers as one would oneself.
Whatever has been commanded by the guru, whether it be desirable or undesirable,
one should immediately abide by it with a mind free from guile.
"One should always worship the future guru through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
Thus it is said. Also, in the Devyāgama, there is this statement of Śiva: "One should avoid performing separate worship and displaying arrogance in the presence of the guru."
"One should avoid [using] the initiation, the exposition, the authority, and so forth, in the presence of the Guru.
In that same [text]: "One should worship the seat, the bed, the garment, the ornament, the sandals, as well as the shadow, the wife, and whatever else has been touched by him."
Elsewhere also it is said: "As it is with the deity, so it is with the mantra; as it is with the mantra, so it is with the guru;
as it is with the guru, so it is with one's own self—thus is the sequence of devotion traditionally taught."
Thus [ends the section] from verses 145 to 152.

In one year a Brāhmaṇa becomes fit, in two years a Kṣatriya, O King, a Vaiśya in three years, and a Śūdra in four years under a Guru. Such a devoted servant should be accepted for initiation, sacrificial rites, vows, and other observances. || 153 ||
Thus ends the second chapter in the Śāradātilaka composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇa Deśikendra. || 2 ||
He states the duration of time for the examination of the disciple with the word "one" (*ekā*). The phrase "should be [the time] for the guru" is to be connected everywhere.
Regarding the Śūdra, it is "with four."
If it be asked, "How then can a Śūdra have the entitlement for initiation and so forth?",
do not say so; for the Smṛti establishes the lack of entitlement only with respect to the study of the Vedas and the rituals prescribed therein, while his entitlement exists elsewhere.
Therefore, in the section concerning Śūdras, the Smṛti states: "One should not omit the five sacrifices by means of the mantra of salutation."
The mantras were indeed proclaimed by Īśvara; therein, the Blessed One himself has shown the respective eligibility [of practitioners].
As the Blessed One said in the section on mantras concerning the temple:
"For women and Śūdras, this mantra ending in 'namas' is auspicious."

"Having understood this, O Mahāsena, one should initiate even Cāṇḍālas. Thus it is said. Also in the Piṅgalāmata: "The knower of mantras should perform initiation for the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas."

Elsewhere it is also stated: "Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, possessing pure intellects, who are devoted to the worship of the Guru, the Deity, and the twice-born, shall be qualified for the worship of the Image.
Therefore, [this applies] even to the direct Vedic mantras, such as the six-syllabled mantra of Rāma, the eight-syllabled Saura mantra, the King of Mantras, and those beginning with the *praṇava*.
And he has no entitlement [to such practices].
Likewise, it was stated by the teacher Padmapāda in his *Praṇavavyākhyāna*:
"By the phrase 'consisting of the letters A, U, and M,' it is shown that only those belonging to the three *varṇas* have entitlement to the *praṇava* and other mantras, not women or *śūdras*."
Thus it has been indicated, as it was said.
And so it is stated in the *Nṛsiṃhatāpanīya*:
"They do not desire the Sāvitrī, the Praṇava, the Yajus, or Lakṣmī for women or Śūdras."
"If a woman or a Śūdra should know the Sāvitrī, Lakṣmī, the Yajus, or the Praṇava, it is traditionally held that they go to a lower state.
Thus it is stated in the Mahākapilapañcarātra with reference to the eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa.
The Veda does not exist apart from the *praṇava*, and the mantra is the very summit of the Veda;
therefore, the mantra is considered supreme to the Veda, and the *āgama* is known as a limb (*aṅga*) of the Veda.
Desirable rites such as subjugation and attraction, which bestow both seen and unseen fruits,
are all accomplished through the Veda by means of planetary sacrifices and other such rituals.
Without the Veda there are no sacrifices, and sacrifices are not devoid of Vedic mantras;
therefore, the Veda is the supreme mantra, and a mantra is not one that has abandoned the Veda.
"There is no entitlement for Śūdras to the mantras; this is a supreme rule.
Due to the absence of mantras, indeed every ritual action is performed without mantra.
Thus it is stated in the *Nāradapañcarātra* concerning the eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa:
"A five-night [period of study] is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas;

it does not even reach the path of the ears of Śūdras and others. Likewise, regarding the Veda, [it is said]: "Upon hearing it, one's ears are to be filled with molten tin and lac; upon reciting it, the tongue is to be cut off; and upon retaining it, the body is to be destroyed."
There is no need for further elaboration regarding the instruction on punishment found in his Smṛtis.

Elsewhere, it is stated in general terms that the status of either being a teacher or a disciple is established by living together for one year: "The state of being a guru or a disciple arises from residing with each other for a year."
In the *Sārasaṃgraha* as well: "The true guru should examine the disciple who has sought refuge for one year.
Some have said that this refers specifically to Brāhmaṇas.
In the tenth chapter, however, it is said: "Having examined [the disciple] for a year, or half a year, but never otherwise."
But in the *Prayogasāra* it is said: "The examination of a Brahmin is recommended after three years, that of a king after six years, and that of a Vaiśya after nine years."
"Even among those twelve [castes], there are those such as the *vṛṣala*s," etc.
A specific detail is given in the *Siddhāntasārasaṃgraha*:
"A Brāhmaṇa and likewise a Kṣatriya should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as prescribed;
the best of Vaiśyas should give it doubled, and the most excellent of Śūdras threefold.
One desiring the accomplishment of the mantra according to the rules should bestow it fourfold. Thus [it is said]. 153.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition.
Now begins the third chapter.
Thereafter, I shall explain the subsidiary rite of initiation (dīkṣāṅga), preceded by the Vāstu sacrifice,
by the performance of which the knower of mantras enjoys the fruit of initiation.
Thus, initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the means for receiving the mantra whose nature has been elaborated according to the previously stated method and which bestows all human goals.
To explain that [initiation], he promises to elaborate upon the sacrificial rites of the site (*vāstuyāga*) and so forth, which constitute its ancillaries—beginning with the words "Then" (*tataḥ*).

Relying on the principle of Bhaṭṭa—that "the primary transcendental result (*pradhānāpūrva*), when assisted by the subsidiary transcendental results (*aṅgāpūrva*), produces a capacity for the fruit"—he says: "By what has been performed" (*kṛtena*).
In this context, by way of digression, certain other ancillaries of initiation (*dīkṣāṅga*) mentioned in another tantra are stated:
failure, attainment of the [sacred] ground, death, destruction of kinsmen (or intellect),
increase of lifespan, destruction of progeny, prosperity, and accumulation of jewels.

The attainment of a virtuous son, loss of position, intelligence, wealth, and subjugation—these are to be known as the results for the months beginning with Caitra; however, one should avoid the intercalary month (malamāsa).
Elsewhere, however, the month of Āṣāḍha is also said to yield excellent results:
"The commencement of a mantra in the month preceding Vaiśākha is very difficult to endure (causing suffering);
in Vaiśākha it bestows wealth, and in Jyeṣṭha it would bring about death."
In Āṣāḍha, it is considered to grant the attainment of a son; in Śrāvaṇa, it is held to bestow auspiciousness;
and in Bhādrapada, the loss of knowledge is proclaimed by the wise.
"In Āśvina there is complete success; in Kārttika, it bestows the attainment of knowledge;
in Mārgaśīrṣa, it shall be auspicious; Pauṣa brings about suffering;
in Māgha, there is an increase in intelligence; and in Phālguna, there is mastery over all. Thus it is said.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara, however, there is this distinction:
"Initiation during the autumn season and in Vaiśākha bestows the most excellent fruit;
initiation in Phālguna, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Jyeṣṭha is middling."
"The months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and Māgha are declared by the wise to be the most excellent;
however, the month of Caitra, as well as Pauṣa and Bhādrapada, are censured.
Even during these censured months, initiation is said to be auspicious when it occurs during an eclipse."

In that regard, Āṣāḍha is prohibited because it is not included within the *uttamā* [period], yet it is accepted because it is included within the *kaṣṭā* [period]. Likewise, it should be understood that Jyaiṣṭha is also prohibited for the very same reason—that it is not included within the *uttamā*.
And so it is stated in the Kālottara:
"The conjunction of autumn and spring is prescribed for the ritual procedure of initiation (*dīkṣā*). In the absence of those two, it is recommended at other times, excluding the rainy season.
Also, in the *Kriyākāṇḍaśekhara*: "Initiation shall not take place except on a festival day (*parvan*), nor during the rainy season, nor in the months of Caitra and Pauṣa."
Thus [it is said].
The prohibition regarding Āṣāḍha and Śrāvaṇa is because they are not included among the superior or middling [months].
In the *Kāraṇa* [Tantra]: "In the month preceding Āṣāḍha, in Āṣāḍha, and in Mārgaśīrṣa..."
"The wise man should not perform initiation in [these months], but he may perform it in other months.
Thus, it should be understood that the prohibition of Mārgaśīrṣa is due solely to its not being included among the "excellent" months.
In the Agastyasaṃhitā—
"Whether in the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, initiation brings all auspiciousness.
However, the *Kālottara* states: "By those desiring prosperity, it should be in the bright fortnight; by those desiring liberation, in the dark fortnight."
Such is the distinction.
In the *Saṃhitā*: "The full moon, the fifth, the second, the seventh, as well as the thirteenth and the tenth—these are praised as granting all desires."
But elsewhere it is said: "On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on the fourteenth, or on one of the five festival days (parva).
Also, in the *Mantrasārasaṃgraha*: "Especially on the second, the fifth, or even the sixth [lunar day]."
"It should be performed on the twelfth day, or even on the thirteenth.
However, in the *Mantraratnāvalī* it is stated: "The fourth, ninth, sixth, eighth, and fourteenth days—excluding the full moon—are said to be beneficial for those seeking liberation."
In the *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā*, however, it is stated: "Having carefully considered each respective lunar day (*tithi*), one should initiate those who are devoted to that [deity] on that day.
Indra asked: "O Nārada, tell me specifically which lunar day is prescribed for whom?
Nārada replied: "The full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) is declared for Brahmā, and the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) for the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu)."
The fourteenth day is said to belong to Śiva, while the thirteenth day is said to belong to Speech.
"The second is declared to belong to Śrī, and the third to Pārvatī;
the fourth belongs to Gaṇanātha, while the seventh is declared to belong to Bhānu; among the paths of Pārvatī, the eighth and the fourteenth are constant. Thus it is said.
In the *Pañcarātra*, however, there is a specific rule regarding the initiation of Viṣṇu: "On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, as well as during the sun's transit (*saṃkramaṇa*).
Here, the transits refer to those other than the [specific] Viṣṇu-padas.
And in the Kālottara: "Excluding the intercalary days, those [lunar days] which touch three solar days [should be avoided]."
In the *Ratnāvalī*, however, it is said: "For the sake of prosperity, one should avoid the days of Āditya (Sunday), Maṅgala (Tuesday), and Sauri (Saturday).
And in the *Saṃhitā*: "It should be performed on the days of Ravi (Sun), Guru (Jupiter), Śita (Venus), Soma (Moon), Budha (Mercury), and Śukra (Venus)."
Thus;
the meaning is "in the bright fortnight.
Elsewhere: "The three Uttaras, Rohiṇī, Revatī, Puṣya, and Vāsava (Jyeṣṭhā)."
"Dhaniṣṭhā, Vāyu (Svātī), Mitra (Anurādhā), Āśvin (Bharaṇī), Pitrya (Maghā), Tvāṣṭra (Citrā), Nairṛta (Mūla), Aiśa (Abhijit), Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇa), and Hasta—these are auspicious for initiation.
Thus [it is said]. "Vāsava" refers to Jyeṣṭhā.
Vāyu is Svātī; Mitra is Anurādhā;
Aśvin is Aśvinī.
Maghā belongs to the Pitṛs; Citrā belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ;
Mūlā belongs to Nirṛti.
Ārdrā belongs to these [deities].
Śravaṇa belongs to Viṣṇu.
Also in the *Saṃhitā*: "And in the asterisms of Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Svātī, Viśākhā, and Hasta..."
"In this manner, one should perform the mantra-consecration during the three Jyeṣṭhās, the three Uttarās, and [the other aforementioned asterisms]. Thus it is said.
In the *Ratnāvalī*: "The three Uttarās, Rohiṇī, Puṣya, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Hasta, Svāti, Anurādhā, Maghā, Mūla, and Revatī."
Abhijit and Śravaṇa. And as for the cause: Pauṣṇa, Rohiṇī, Āditya, Śravaṇa, and likewise Aśvinī.
The [mantras] dedicated to Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Indra, and likewise to Nirṛti;

"Tiṣya (Puṣya), the three [asterisms] following Uttarā-Ārdrā, Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), and the birth asterism of the disciple—these constellations are praised for the rite of initiation, O observer of good vows. Thus [it is said]. Pauṣṇa is Revatī.
The Āditya [offering] is in Punarvasu;
the Sāvitra [offering] is in Hastā;
the Saumya [offering] is in Mṛgaśiras.

In the *Nīlatantra* as well: "Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Ārdrā, Dhaniṣṭhā, the three Uttarās, Puṣya, and Śatabhiṣā are declared to be the asterisms for initiation (*dīkṣā*). However, in the *Ratnāvalī*: "The first lunar day (*pratipad*), Pūrvāṣāḍhā, the fifth lunar day, and likewise Kṛttikā..."
Pūrvabhādrapadā is the sixth, and likewise Rohiṇī is the tenth.
"The twelfth [tithi] with the Sarpa (Āśleṣā) asterism, and the thirteenth with Aryaman (Pūrvaphalgunī)—
these are called 'asterism-deficient' (nakṣatraluptā), and they bring destruction even to the gods.
Other instances of the defectiveness of lunar days and asterisms resulting from their conjunction with weekdays and so forth are to be understood from the science of astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra).
Likewise: "In all auspicious conjunctions (*yoga*), initiation bestows all that is auspicious. In the *Ratnāvalī*: "The conjunctions are Yoga, Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, Śobhana, and Śubha."
And Sukarman, Dhṛti, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Siddhi, and Harṣaṇa.
"Varīyān, Śiva, Siddha, Brahmā, and Indraka are the sixteen.
Likewise: "They say that the [lunar] days are auspicious for initiation, especially so."
"One should especially avoid Śakuni and the other [yogas], as well as Viṣṭi. Thus it is said.

In the Saṃhitā: "On a day when the five-fold limbs [of the calendar] are pure, during its own rising, when the lunar day (tithi) and the weekday are auspicious, during the rising of Jupiter and Venus, and when the ascendant (lagna) is purified by the subtraction of twelve [signs]."
"When Venus and Jupiter are waxing and conjoined with strength,
when there is an auspicious conjunction with the Moon, and when one is in an auspicious division (*varga*) at an auspicious rising (*udaya*)—
in such circumstances, the collection of all mantras brings about every happiness. Thus [it is said].
And so it is stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*: "When a planet is in its sign of debilitation, or in retrograde motion, or in extreme velocity, or when it is immature, aged, or set;

or during the renunciation of worldly life, a pilgrimage to a deity, the performance of vows and observances, the piercing of the ears, initiation (*dīkṣā*), the tying of the sacred thread (*mauñjīvandha*), the marriage ceremony of the Gaṇas, or the consecration of a temple or deity—[these should not be undertaken]."
"The wise should avoid [certain actions] with great effort when Jupiter, the preceptor of the thirty gods, is situated in the sign of Leo.

Likewise: "A movable sign (cara-rāśi) should be avoided by all; a fixed sign (sthira-rāśi) bestows happiness. Malefic planets (pāpa-grahas) situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses, and benefics (saumya-grahas) situated in the angles (kendras) and the trine (trikoṇa), [are auspicious]."
"In initiation (dīkṣā), however, [planets] situated in the auspicious [houses] are declared [to be beneficial], while those situated in the eighth house (randhra) cause total destruction.
Here, "gain" (āya) refers to the eleventh house. By the term "angular" (kendrāṇi), the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth houses are indicated.

"Trikoṇa" refers to the fifth and ninth houses; "randhra" is the eighth house. Likewise: on the day of the disciple's birth, at the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), at the equinoxes (viṣuva), and at the solstices (ayana).
"In other meritorious conjunctions, during the eclipses of the moon or sun, or at a time favorable to the disciple, the purification of the body brings auspiciousness. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "In this [regard], on a day of the lunar mansion, the lunar day, and so forth, or on a day of a [specific] yoga or karaṇa..."
"The instruction in mantras by the Guru and the performance of propitiatory rites bring about auspiciousness. Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Kriyākāṇḍaśekhara*, after stating everything regarding the lunar days and so forth, it is stated:
"Having carefully examined [the disciple] in this manner and other ways, the preceptor should perform the initiation (*dīkṣā*)."
"For one desiring liberation, no restriction of time or other factors is prescribed.
And in the *Ratnāvalī*: "All those [actions] are to be censured, except for those praised for the sake of liberation."
And this [rite] should be performed on a day after observing the fire-wheel (agnicakra) that is about to be described.

There is also an exception: "During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, at the birth of a disciple, during the transit of the sun into Capricorn (makarasaṃkrānti), and at a time when the Guru is moved by compassion—these are not required for initiation regarding the constellations and so forth. Thus it is said.

Likewise: "On the days of a disciple's birth, at the sun's passage into a new sign (*saṃkrānti*), during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, or when joined with an auspicious conjunction (*puṇyayoga*), the supreme accomplishment of the mantra for men is declared.
Also, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "At the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), at the two solstices (*ayana*), on the full moon of Āṣāḍha (at the *saṃkrānti*), and during the festival of Damanaka..."
"Initiation (dīkṣā) must be performed at the [proper] times during the rite of the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa).
And in the *Kālottara*: "During initiation, consecration, as well as the formal acquisition of mantras, upon the taking up and release of vows, and during the ritual involving ritual substances."
On the full moon day of Kārttika and Vaiśākha, during an eclipse of Rāhu (Svarbhānu),
during solar and lunar eclipses, and at the commencement of the Ṣaḍaśīti periods;
"In conjunctions of planets and constellations, at the equinoxes, during festivals, and at all solstices, a ritual union (yoga) grants the accomplishment of all goals. Thus it is said.
Also in the Rudrayāmala: "At a sacred pilgrimage site, during an eclipse of the sun or moon, and on the two Dāmana festivals..."
"One performing the initiation of mantra (mantradīkṣā) need not purify [the time] by means of the month, asterism, and so forth.
And in the Agastyasaṃhitā: "At the time of a solar eclipse, nothing else need be sought;
there is no other time equal to the time of a solar eclipse."
In that regard, whatever is performed there all becomes the giver of infinite fruit;
on the occasion of a solar eclipse, there is no need for purification based on the month, lunar day, or weekday.
Whatever desired [gift] is given to the Guru by men at that time,
the mantra becomes effective with speed and without effort.
"This must be performed with every effort by those desiring the accomplishment of mantra.

Likewise, it is stated elsewhere: "At a holy pilgrimage site, at Kurukṣetra, at the four seats of the Goddess (Devīpīṭha), at Prayāga, and with a venerable Guru in Kāśī, one need not distinguish between the proper and improper time."
In the *Tattvasāgarasaṃhitā*: "Listen to the special occasion for initiation even without regard for the lunar day (*tithi*):
when a rare and singular opportunity to meet a true Guru has presented itself."
"When permission for that is obtained, it is the great occasion for initiation.
Whether in a village or a forest, in a sacred field or by day or night, whenever the Guru arrives by providence, then the initiation shall take place. Thus it is said.
Likewise: "Whenever there is the desire [to be initiated], then initiation occurs according to the command of the Guru;
there is no specific lunar day, no vow, no fire-oblation, no ritual bathing, and no recitation of mantras.
Rather, the cause of initiation is simply the attainment of one's own chosen True Guru. (1)
Having slain the Rākṣasa named Vāstu and occupied his body, the fifty-three deities remain; one should first offer an oblation to them. || 2 ||
He states the origin of the Vāstuyāga with the words "having killed the Rākṣasa," etc.,
as it has been said:—

"Kaśyapa’s wife Siṃhikā gave birth to Rāhu and Vāstu as her sons; the elder was decapitated by Hari, and the younger was struck down by the gods. Thus it is said. Also, in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra: "Formerly there was Mahānagra, who caused terror to all beings."
Struck down by the gods upon the earth, he is known as Vāstupuruṣa.
As long as the earth remains firm in the world, so long does Vāstu-asura remain;
but at the time of dissolution, he goes to rest along with the gods, all the planets, and the rest.
Its extent all around is one hundred crore yojanas;
it stands pervading the earth and is described as being black in color.
The knees and elbows are at the corners [of the mouth], while the wrists are at the southeast and northwest;
this [mudrā] has the feet at the northeast and the hands joined at the heart, with the head directed toward the northeast.
"With hair standing erect, very corpulent, with round eyes, and the form of an asura.
Elsewhere, however, his downward-facing nature is mentioned:
"The asura named Vāstvīśa, who possesses a massive body, was granted boons by the gods in ancient times and is to be worshipped."
He always lies upon the ground with his feet and hands outstretched, his face turned downwards.
"The head of this Vāstoṣpati was placed in the northeast; his two hands were in the northwest and the southeast; and his pair of feet was situated in the direction of the night-stalkers (the north).
Thus [it is said].

The true nature of the *vāstu* is stated elsewhere: "In ancient times, during the battle with the demon Andhaka, the terrifying sweat-water of the enraged Trident-bearer fell from his forehead onto the earth."
Somaśambhu, however, has stated the following rule: "In acts of worship, one should visualize the Vāstu deity with its hands contracted, face upwards, and having the form of a demon;
but when constructing walls and so forth, it should be visualized with its face turned downwards."
"His knees are pressed against his elbows in the directions of wind and fire;
his two feet are in the direction of the ancestors (northwest); his head is in the direction of Rudra (northeast); and his hands are joined in *añjali* at his heart.
Thus [he stands], out of fear of rising again.
As it is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
"One should worship all the gods established in the site (vāstu) during their respective rites;
otherwise, he shall perish unless [the rite] proceeds by the command of Mādhava."
"One should offer an oblation (*bali*) to them first.
As it has been said: "Furthermore, those who are averse to their worship shall take away the merits performed by them and shall incur their misdeeds."
"Therefore, for those virtuous ones who perform their worship every year, only auspicious things quickly arise, and not even a mention of anything inauspicious.
Thus it was also said by Maya: "In the construction of houses and such, where the deity Vāstu is not worshipped..."
In that case, everything would become empty, destroyed by demons, obstacles, and the like.
"Therefore, those who desire perfect success should perform the worship of the Vāstu deity correctly.

And likewise: "The Vāstu-bali offering is prescribed for auspicious rites, initiation, the construction of pavilions, and the rituals for houses and so forth; it serves for the pacification of obstructive spirits (rakṣas) and impediments, and for the attainment of prosperity."
Also in the Mahākapilapañcarātra: "Prior to the acquisition of land and likewise when establishing stones, one should especially worship Vāstu for the sake of water reservoirs and houses."
In other rites as well, such as sacrifices and fire-offerings,
the Guru should prepare the Vāstumaṇḍala by drawing it out with lines on level ground.
A site that is level brings happiness, whereas an uneven one does not bring happiness.
From Brahmā down to Aditi, there are fifty-three [deities].
Indeed, the presiding deities of all dwellings have been proclaimed;
for without worshipping (or taking leave of) them all, one should not cause temples and other structures to be built.
There would be the non-arising and destruction of both the property and the property-bearer.
Thus [it is said]. (2)
The maṇḍala for these offerings is now described correctly: one should lay down a thread extending from east to west according to the stated measurement. || 3 ||
Regarding the phrase "pūrva" and so forth, he speaks of the production of sixty-four squares for the sake of the mandala in its entirety and according to the rule.
As for the word "vinyaset," this is the usage of the root *as* belonging to the Bhuvādi class, meaning "to go, to shine, and to take."
"According to the stated measurement" means by that measurement which has been stated in the *Vāstuśāstra*.
In some places, the reading is "according to the measurement of a cubit (*hasta*)."
In the Mahākapilapañcarātra, however, there is this distinction:
"For houses, palaces, wells, pavilions, and water-reservoirs, a Vāstu-maṇḍala measuring eight cubits should be prepared, and not otherwise. (3)
Taking a small portion from the center of that, one should draw two fish on either side;
then, one should lay a thread between them, situated in the north-south direction. || 4 ||
"Among those, the middle" means:
having taken some point as the center, one should take a mark slightly beyond that middle.
To the question "Why?", the ellipsis is supplied with "from the tip of the thread."

In this manner, one should produce two fish-marks—that is, two points—at both ends, north and south, of the east-west line (prācīsūtra); this is the remaining [instruction]. The method for doing so is as follows:
Having placed the beginning of the thread at the eastern end of the eastern line, one should rotate the tip of the thread from the central mark;
likewise from the western end as well.
From this, one fish-mark is formed.
The same applies elsewhere; thus is the second fish.
As it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Then, for the sake of establishing the *somasūtra*, there is the rotation of the tip of the thread."
Having placed one's hand on both the front part of the lap and the back part of the lap, one should perform [the rite].
The fish moves northward and southward along the line;
it is drawn with its mouth at the head, its tail at the end, and its body spread across the central mark.
The Soma-thread should be on all sides.
Thus [ends the section]. 4.
One should draw crocodiles in the corners using each pair of lines as well as the two outermost ones;
then, one should drop threads there so that their tips rest in the middle of the fish. || 5 ||
"By means of two each": therein, by means of two tips each, one fish is [placed] as before. That is to say:
With a cord measuring half the eastern cord (prācīsūtra) and fixed at the tip of the eastern cord, one should draw a semicircle in the northeast and the southeast.
Then, with that same cord fixed at the tip of the northern cord, one should draw a semicircle in the northeast and the northwest.
In this way, a fish-figure (matsya) is produced in the northeast.
Likewise, as before, using that same thread positioned with its tip facing west, one should draw a half-moon in the northwest and the southwest; thus a fish is produced in the northwest.
Using that same thread positioned with its tip facing west, one should again draw a half-moon in the northwest and the southwest; thus a fish is produced in the northwest.
Using that same thread positioned with its tip facing south, one should draw a half-moon in the southwest and the southeast.
Then, in both cases as well, two fish-figures arise.
As it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"One should mark the directions with a cord measuring half the area."
"Having relied upon the marks in the cardinal directions, one should draw the numbers in the corners with a thread measuring half the field, in both reverse and direct order.
Thus, when the four "fishes" (matsya) have been produced, he says "the fishes," etc., meaning that one should apply four threads from their middles to their tips. || 5 ||
There, it should be a square provided with four compartments;
the practitioner of mantra should then further divide that so as to consist of sixty-four squares.
"Square" (caturasra) is said because the body of the site (vāstu) is square.
As it has been stated:
"A certain demon of destructive nature has a four-cornered form."
Thus it is said;
and also in the Mahākapilapañcarātra: "That Vāstupuruṣa was established by the gods as a square."
The teachers also say: "This [Vāstupuruṣa] is situated in a square form.
And in the *Prayogasāra* as well: "That Vāstupuruṣa should be known as being situated in a square form."
Thus:

"provided with four outer compartments. This means that within the square and at the four lower corners, another set of four compartments is prescribed for the purpose of worshipping Guru, Gaṇeśa, Durgā, and Kṣetreśa.
Regarding the word "tat" (that):
the syntactical connection is that one should divide it in such a way that it becomes sixty-four parts. || 6 ||
From Īśāna to Rakṣas, and from Agni to Prabhañjana—one should thus, with a concentrated mind, lay down two threads as the ear-thread (karṇasūtra). || 7 ||
Regarding the phrase "from Īśāna":
the wind is *prabhañjana*, and the corner having that deity is denoted by that term; [the line] extends as far as that.
In this manner, one should lay down two threads known as *karṇasūtra* (ear-threads).
In the treatises on architecture (*śilpaśāstra*), the diagonal line (*karṇasūtra*) is designated as the "corner-line" (*koṇasūtra*).
The term *samāhita* is connected to both [the practitioner and the thread] according to the maxim of the crow’s eye.

In this context, the practitioner (*mantrin*), being composed and attentive, and being conversant with the mantra scriptures through tradition, should lay down the thread extending from east to west, and so forth.
It follows as the agent in seven ritual acts, because it has been consecrated at the end.
In that regard, the method for producing the sixty-four squares is as follows: one should draw four diagonal lines across four squares to form another set of lines.
Upon the fish-shaped figures produced in the center of that [grid], one should drop two threads extending from east to west and two threads extending from south to north.
In this way, sixteen squares are formed.
Then, one should again draw four diagonal threads (karṇasūtra) within the four corner squares.
Upon those [lines] where fish-figures have arisen, one should drop two threads extending east-west and two extending north-south.
When this has been done, fish-figures arise within the two central squares; upon those fish-figures, one should lay two threads extending east-west and two extending north-south.
In this way, sixty-four squares are produced.
In this regard, one should erase the diagonal lines (karṇasūtra) other than the two primary diagonal lines mentioned in other texts.
Regarding this, there is a specific rule stated by Īśānaśiva:
"The sixty-four squares are to be worshipped by Brahmins; the eighty-one squares by kings and others."
Thus [it is said].
However, in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra* it is stated: "A site-plan (*vāstu*) of eighty-one squares is recommended for the construction of houses;
a site-plan of sixty-four squares is praised for temples."
Somaśambhu also states: "One should construct the Vāstu-maṇḍala with sixty-four compartments for a temple;

for a house as well, one should perform the Vāstu rite, but with eighty-one compartments. In the Mahākapila-pañcarātra it is said: "For a temple, sixty-four [compartments], and likewise eighty-one for a house."
Thus it is said; likewise elsewhere: "Having divided the site into eighty-one squares for houses and the like, the Vāstu deity is recorded by Brahmā as occupying sixty-four squares in a temple."
Having spoken thus, he said: "I shall now describe the excellent pavilions (maṇḍapas) in accordance with the proportions of the temple.
Thus it was said by him; this Vāstu-maṇḍala is for the pavilion of the preceptor.
One should first worship Brahmā in the center; then, in the four intermediate squares, one should worship Āryamā and the others, starting from the east, in the four cardinal directions. || 8 ||
Then Vivasvat, then Mitra, and after that Mahīdhara;
[then] Brahmā—thus it is said.
The connection is that one should worship Brahmā, who is composed (*samāhita*), first and in the middle within the four squares (*koṣṭha*).
The meaning is that when the four compartments have been measured out in a single form, one should draw a lotus there.
As it is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "In the center of the twenty-five squares, one should worship Brahmā upon the lotus."
Thus it is said.
Also in the Kādimata: "In the very center, one should properly worship Brahmā, who is seated upon a lotus, golden-hued, four-faced, and distinguished by the study of the Vedas."
By the word "at first," the association with Sarasvatī is expressed.
By the phrase "composed in mind" (samāhita), this is meant:
having first worshipped the pedestal (pīṭha), one should afterwards worship Brahmā therein.
There, having worshipped [the deities] from Maṇḍūka up to Paratattva, and having worshipped the nine Pīṭha-śaktis beginning with Aṇimā and ending with Sarvasiddhi, one should recite the Pīṭha-mantra:
*Oṃ sarvajñānakriyāvyaktakamalāsanāya yogapīṭhāya namaḥ*.
Then the Mūla-mantra is: *Oṃ namo brahmaṇe*.
Prajāpati is the seer;
Paṅkti is the meter;
Brahmā is the deity.
The limbs [of the body] are represented by the syllables.
Brahmā should be meditated upon as holding a rosary, a *sruk* and *sruva* ladle, a staff, and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
The meditation on the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest is described in the *Kulaprakāśatantra*:

Aṇimā, residing in the Sindhu region, is to be worshipped; she is yellow in color and has four arms, holding a boon-granting gesture and a vajra in her right hands, and bearing the gestures of fearlessness and a treasure-vessel in her left hands.
One should worship Mahimā, who is mounted upon a buffalo, possesses a blazing radiance,
holds a staff and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands, and a spear and a rosary in her right hands.
Stationed on a lotus stalk, she is light-bodied, dark-complexioned, worthy of worship, and four-armed;
she holds a serpent-noose in her right hand, while in her left are the gesture of fearlessness and a lotus.

Resembling a mountain of gold, she is worthy of worship; Garimā likewise stands upon a tortoise, holding a mace and the gesture of granting boons in her right hands, and bearing the gestures of fearlessness and the bestowing of treasures in her left.
The goddess to be worshipped, who has gone to the realm of the pretas, is seated upon a blue mass of lightning;
she holds an excellent sword in her right hand, and in her left, she displays the gesture of fearlessness along with a chisel.
The venerable Vaśitā is smoke-colored, seated upon a deer, and possesses four arms;
she holds a lotus and a banner in her right hands, while her left hands display the gestures of boon-granting (*vara*) and holding a lotus (*sarojinī*).
Seated upon a goat, her limbs should be exceedingly red; she should have a great desire for worship.
She holds a rosary of beads in her right hand and a water-pot in her left.
The worshipful Prāpti is mounted upon a bull and resembles snow;
she holds a trident and a varada-mudrā in her right hands, while her left hands display the abhaya-mudrā and a lotus.

"Complete success (Sarvasiddhi) has the luster of a ruby; she is four-armed and should be worshipped. She holds a rosary and a lotus, as well as a citron and a lotus. Thus [ends the section on] the directions.
One should worship in the four directions, beginning with the east; the phrase "in a clockwise direction" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
This same [rule] also applies here to the four squares.
The meaning is that he is worshipped in a single form.
By that [principle], the Ārya is in the eastern direction, Vivasvat in the southern direction, Mahīdhara in the western direction, and Pūjya in the northern direction.
As it has been stated by the Teachers:
One should worship in the four squares of the eastern, southern, western, and northern directions.
Thus [ends the eighth section].
Furthermore, in the pairs of half-cells at the corners, surrounding [the center] starting from the southeast (vahni), again— || 9 ||
The wise one [should worship] Sāvitra and Savitṛ, Śakra and Indrajaya, Rudra and Rudrajaya, as well as Āpa and Āpavatsaka. || 10 ||
Regarding the word *koṇe*: it means in the corner of the *brahmapada*, specifically in the lower and upper squares of the corner portion,
because they are divided by the diagonal line (*karṇasūtra*).
In that [space], there is a half-cell; in the pairs thereof, beginning with the southeast (āgneya) and so forth, one should worship Sāvitra in the upper cell and Savitṛ in the lower cell.
"Around" means in the four directions.
As it has been said:

Somaśambhu states: "In the center is Brahmā with nine squares; the others are recorded as having one square each. Marīci and the rest occupy six squares each, positioned in order in the directions starting from the east.
The eight lords of the corners are situated there within the eight half-squares of the corners."
Although the phrase "above or below" is not present here, nevertheless,
an upward progression is obtained through the description of the abode and the body as taught in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*.
It is as follows:
Rudra is established on his head, Parjanya and Aditi are situated in his two ears,
and the waters are well-established in his mouth.
Āpavatsa is stationed at the throat, and Jayanta likewise;
Diti is on the shoulders, while Pañcārgalā and others are on the two arms, as are Mahendra and others.
Rudra and Savitṛ are situated on his chest, while Savitṛ likewise is the servant;
Brahmā is established in his heart and at his navel.
Pṛthvīdhara and Marīci are on her breasts,
while Vivasvān and he named Mitra, the Pitṛs, are stationed on her feet.
"Pāpa and the others, as well as Pūṣan and the others—these seven [are located] on the seven-arched shanks;
Indra is situated in the penis, and Jaya is established in the testicles.
Thus, Rudra is Īśāna.
Dāsa Rudrajaya; Pṛthvīdhara Mahīdhara; Marīci Ārya.
The Pitṛs are Nirṛti; evil is disease;
Indra is Śakra.
Thus it should be understood.
As it has been said: "He who is Īśa is this Īśāna-Rudra; his conqueror is Rudradāsaka. He is known as Marīci and Āryaka, and he shall be the father of the lord of the Rākṣasas."
"Pāpa" is known as "disease. Furthermore, elsewhere it is said: "Having relied upon Dhātṛ and Vahni, and having placed three feet below..."
There, in the step known as Vāsava, one should worship the deity Savitṛ.
Between Vidhi and Savitṛ, having placed Savitṛ upon two footprints, and having positioned Pitṛ and Dhātṛ below those two footprints.
One should worship the highly fortunate Indra in the station known as Loka;
likewise, Indrajaya is to be worshipped, situated between Brahmā and Śakra.
Having relied upon the two wind-elements and having established three steps below,
one should worship the god Rudra there in the step known as Bhuvana.
Likewise, between Īśa and Vedha, there is its victory in three quarters;
in the northeast is the Āpaka, well-situated in the three quarters of Kāma.
"Then, in the middle of that *āpavedha*, one should worship Vatsa in the three squares.
Also in the *Somaśambhu*: "In the square of Savitṛ, one should offer red flowers in the corner cell below the fire;
and in the cell below that, one should give water with *kuśa* grass to Savitṛ."
One should offer rice cooked with turmeric to Indra in the bottom-left corner,
and sweet food to Indrajaya below Indra.
One should offer food prepared with ghee to Rudra on the square below the southwest corner;
beneath that, one should present raw meat to Rudrajaya.
Then water [is placed] below the auspicious corner (śivakoṇa), and likewise for its calf (tadvatsāya) on that same level.
Thus it is said.
"At the front, on both sides of that ear-line"—because of the functional purpose of the ear-line (*karṇasūtra*), it is stated here as "the square of half the corner" (*koṇārddhakoṣṭha*). (9–10)
On both sides of that ear-line, within the pairs of squares, the preceptor [should place] Śarva, Guha, Aryaman, Jṛmbhaka, and Pilapicchaka. || 11 ||
One should worship Carakī, Vidārī, and Pūtanā in sequence;
one should worship these in the directions starting from the east, in the positions at the beginning and end of each half-verse. || 12 ||
The best of teachers [should worship] eight gods each, according to their divisions:
in order, Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Śakra, and Bhāskara; || 13 ||
Satya, Vṛṣa, and Antarikṣa are situated in the eastern direction;
as well as Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, and Yama the guardian of the house. || 14 ||
Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛga are situated in the southern direction;
then come Nirṛti, Daurvārika, Sugrīva, and Varuṇa. || 15 ||
Puṣpadanta and Asura, Śoṣa and Roga are situated in the western direction;
Vāyu, Nāga, Mukhya, Soma, and Bhallāṭa, as well as those named Argala and Diti and Aditi, are situated in the direction of Kuvera (the north). || 16 ||
Regarding the word "tad" (that):
one who instructs (*diśati*) or teaches mantras to disciples is a *deśika*, that is, a mantra-expert (*māntrika*).
In all cases, the sequence (*krama*)—meaning "surrounded by fire and the other [elements]"—is to be understood accordingly.

Regarding the phrase "sārddhādyanta" (with the halves at the beginning and end): it refers to those words which exist together with the halves (ardha) that are at the beginning (ādya) and the end (anta). This is obtained from the corner square that has been halved by the diagonal line (karṇasūtra). || 11-16 ||

Having filled the footprints of the aforementioned deities with the five previously mentioned substances, one should then offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa) to them using those very materials. || 17 ||
This is declared to be the *vāstubali*, which bestows the abundance of all prosperity. || 18 ||
He states the performance of the bali offering with the words "of those mentioned.
The fifth [layer] is with the powders (*rajas*) to be described for the *sarvatobhadra* mandala;
therein, one should fill in the lotuses in the very manner that will be described.
In that [mandala], the central lotus is white and the others are red.

As it is stated in the *Divyasārasvata*: "Having cleared away nine squares in the center, one should fill them with white powder; furthermore, [one should do so] in the four directions surrounding it."
Having swept away the six squares, one should fill them with dust and blood;
and the remaining squares here should be arranged according to their proper positions.
"Then, in the center of the variegated [squares], one should worship Brahmā. Thus [it is said].
The boundary lines of the squares are white, and the squares themselves are variegated.
The meditation (*dhyāna*) on the Vāstu deities as described in another Tantra is written here: "The essential forms of all the aforementioned deities are now declared."
In her right hands she holds a rosary and a sacrificial ladle; in her left, a staff and a water-pot.
One should worship the eight-eyed one seated upon a lotus in the center;
all the gods stationed within the body of Vāstu have four arms.
With palms joined in reverence and holding swords and shields in their hands,
they all gazed intently at Brahmā, facing toward his face.
When they remain each in its own place, it is described as "common" (sādhāraṇa).
Marīci is white in color, and Vivasvān is the color of a red cloud.
Śātakumbha is like the sky, while Nabhomitra is black in color; Bhūdhara is the color of the sun, Sāvitrī has the luster of blue, and Sāvitra has a smoky form.
Indra has the luster of a reddish-brown color, and Indrajaya is white;
Rudra resembles coral, and likewise Rudraya is yellow.
Āpa is white as cow’s milk; Āpavatsa has the luster of a japā flower;
Īśāna is white as milk; Parjanya is like collyrium in appearance.
Jayanta is like the color of collyrium; Mahendra has a dark-blue luster;
Āditya is red in color; and Satyaka is of variegated colors.
Vṛṣa has the luster of the bandhūka flower, and Antarikṣaka has the luster of the kunda flower;
Agni has the brilliance of the rising sun, and Pūṣan resembles a red lotus.
Gṛhakṣata is false, appearing like a rainbow and having the color of lightning;
Yama is like collyrium in appearance, and Gandharva is like a ruby.
Bhṛṅgarāja is the color of a bumblebee, Mṛga resembles a cloud,
Nirṛti has the luster of fire, and Dauvārika is known to be yellow.
Sagrīva has the luster of a peacock's neck, Puṣpadantaka has the luster of the moon,
Varuṇa possesses the brilliance of crystal, and the Asura is considered to have the appearance of a bumblebee.
Consumption (śoṣa) resembles a blue lotus, and the evil disease of consumption (pāpayakṣma) is like sapphire;
wind (vāyu) should be of a blackish hue, and the serpent (nāga) is like a conch shell or the moon.
Mukhya is like a pearl, Bhallāṭa is like a white lotus,
Soma is like crystal, and Argala has the luster of a red lotus.
Diti is remembered as white as a jasmine flower or the moon, while Aditi is tawny;
Carakī resembles a conch shell, and Vidārī has the brilliance of fire.
Pūtanā is like snow in appearance, with the luster of a cloud;
Pilapicchikā likewise holds a sword, a drinking vessel, a knife, and a pair of scissors.
These Rākṣasīs are proclaimed to be of terrifying form;
Skanda and the other Grahas are white, red, yellow, and black.
"Holding a vajra, a spear, a sword, and a noose, with distorted faces, they are declared to be terrifying; those are the Grahas, beginning with Skanda.
Thus, the eighteen lines should be meditated upon as both channels (*nāḍī*) and as those respective deities.
As it has been said: "Lakṣmī, Yaśovatī, Kāntā, Supriyā, Sukalā, Śivā, Subhagā, Sumukhī, and Nandā—these are the channels (nāḍīs) that emerge from the eastern direction."
"Dhanyā, Prāṇā, Viśālā, Sthirā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Niśā, Virajā, and Vibhavā—these channels are known to have gentle faces. Thus it is said.
In the phrase "with milk-rice dishes" (*pāyasānnaiḥ*), the plural number is used for the sake of including other similar items.
By this, the substances such as parched grain (*lāja*) and others to be mentioned are included.
In that regard, the specific offerings for the *bali* and the mantras for each respective deity have been stated in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*:
"With milk-rice, boiled rice, and parched grain, combined with incense and flowers..."
O Brahmā, accept this bali offering, consisting of unbroken rice grains mixed with sesame seeds and adorned with black gram, cooked rice, and other items; destroy the defects of the site.
O you named Āryaka, accept this cake with sugar and fragrant substances placed upon milk-rice; destroy all defects.
O Lord, accept this offering consisting of sandalwood and other substances, adorned with camphor and agallochum;
O Vivasvat, please destroy all defects.
O Protector, accept this pleasing offering of milk-rice with jaggery, accompanied by flowers and other items; O Friend, grant me peace.
O Lord of the Earth, accept this rice mixed with black gram and meat, combined with perfumes and milk; destroy all defects.

Having thus offered the internal oblation (antarbali), although the worship of all the others begins with the southeast (āgneya) and so forth, one should nevertheless offer the oblation starting from the northeast (īśāna),
in accordance with the scriptural injunction.
The scriptural statement is as follows:

"The offering (bali) for all things is generally described as proceeding from Īśa [the northeast] in a clockwise direction; however, there is indeed a distinction regarding the determination of the locations for all objects. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, worship is also stated to begin with Īśa and so forth in other places.
"And one should worship the deities in the corners beginning with the northeast according to the prescribed rule.
Also elsewhere: "The wise man should worship those situated in the four corners beginning with the northeast."
Thus it is said:
"O Water, accept this pleasing oblation consisting of milk mixed with sugar and adorned with flowers and other offerings; grant me peace."
O child, accept this offering of curd mixed with jaggery and adorned with fragrant substances and other items; dispel all obstacles here.
O Sāvitrī, accept these flowers, kuśa grass, water, and the fragrance of camphor and agallochum; grant me peace in this matter.
O Lord Sūrya, accept this offering of flour-cake with jaggery, adorned with red perfumes and other ornaments; destroy all obstacles here.
O Lord Śakra, accept this pleasing offering consisting of cool food and flowers endowed with saffron and other ingredients; salutations be unto you!
O Indrajaya, accept this pleasing oblation of rice mixed with ghee and adorned with garments, perfumes, and other offerings; homage be unto you!
O Lord Rudra, accept this pleasing offering of meat, both cooked and raw, combined with cloth, flowers, and other items; I bow down to you.
Heart-flesh (or meat) cooked with ghee and combined with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings—
accept this *bali* offering, O Rudrajaya, and grant me well-being!
O Vidārī, accept this red flower together with meat, accompanied by red garments and other offerings; destroy this obstacle of the Rākṣasa!
O Pāpī (Pūtane), you who are joined with bile, blood, and bone, and adorned with the scent of blood and the like—accept this offering; destroy the obstacle of the Rākṣasa!
O Śarva, accept this bali-offering consisting of rice mixed with beans (or meat), clarified butter, and adorned with garments, perfumes, and the like; destroy these obstacles caused by the Rākṣasas.
O Skanda, accept this offering of meat combined with flowers and the like, and adorned with black gram cakes; destroy the obstacle of the Rākṣasa.
Dog meat (delicious), combined with flour-cakes and accompanied by cooked meat and water—O Aryaman, accept this; destroy the obstacle of the Rākṣasas.
O Jṛmbhaka, accept this offering of blood, meat, rice, fish, along with perfumes and incense; destroy the obstacles caused by Rākṣasas.
O Pilipiccha, accept this meat provided with goat's ears, along with cloth, perfumes, and other offerings; destroy this obstacle of the Rākṣasa.
O Carakī, accept this meat prepared with ghee and provided with garments, perfumes, and other offerings; destroy this obstacle caused by the Rākṣasa.
O Lord, accept this bali offering— consisting of unbroken rice grains with ghee, adorned with garments, perfumes, and other ornaments— which removes the defects of the site (vāstu).
O King of Devas (Clouds), accept this pleasing offering consisting of blue lotuses, milk-rice, and garments; homage be to you!
O son of Jiṣṇu, accept this five-cubit, bright yellow banner adorned with flowers and other offerings; take this pleasing bali; salutations be to you!
O God, King of the Devas, accept this pleasing offering of cooked rice filled with clarified butter and adorned with the five jewels and other gems; homage be to you!
O Bhāskara, accept this pleasing oblation consisting of cooked food mixed with red flowers and prepared with red perfumes and other offerings; homage be to you!

O Satya, accept this canopy, which has the luster of smoke-colored [saffron], beautifully adorned with perfumes and other offerings, provided with cloth [and red flowers]; accept this bali; salutations be unto you!
Indeed, this meat-offering, honored with garments, perfumes, and other articles—
accept this bull-sacrifice and destroy the defects of the site.
But this grassy ground is well-provided with meat, offerings, and the like;
accept this pleasing oblation, O Vyoman, and grant me peace.
O Seven-Tongued One, accept this gold, flour-cake, and cloth, along with perfumes and other offerings mixed with clarified butter; salutations be unto you!
O Lord Pūṣan, accept this pleasing offering of milk mixed with parched grain and adorned with red flowers and other ornaments; homage be to you!
O Vitatha, accept this offering endowed with the scent of curd and other fragrances, accompanied by yellow flowers; destroy the obstacle here.
O Lord Yama, accept this pleasing offering of rice mixed with honey, adorned with red garments and other ornaments; salutations be unto you!
O Guardian of the House, accept this pleasing offering of cooked meat, rice, fresh butter, and ornaments such as garments; salutations be unto you.
O Gandharva, accept this offering combined with various perfumes and accompanied by red flowers and the like; destroy all defects.
O Bhṛṅgarāja, take this offering consisting of the tongue of a bird placed upon a meal of black gram; grant me peace.
O God of the Deer, accept this pleasing offering of barley mixed with ghee and sesame seeds, combined with perfumes, flowers, and other such items; homage be to you!
O King of Rākṣasas, accept this offering of sweets mixed with sugar, adorned with cloth, incense, and other gifts; we pay homage to you.
O Gatekeeper, accept this pleasing offering consisting of sandalwood, aguru wood, and fragrant flowers; homage be to you!
O Lord Sugrīva, please accept this milk-rice offering adorned with perfumes, flowers, and other ornaments; grant me peace.
O King of Waters, accept this pleasing offering of barley-grains, cow’s milk, and food that has been steeped in liquor; homage be to you!
O Puṣpadanta, accept this bundle of kuśa grass mixed with black gram and anointed with ghee, perfumes, and other substances; destroy all defects.
O Lord of Asuras, accept this offering prepared with honey, ground [grains], and adorned with perfumes and other [substances]; destroy all defects.
Accept this offering (bali) consisting of ghee combined with food, well-scented with camphor and other fragrances; grant me the pacification of all remaining afflictions.
O Lord, accept this offering of barley and rice, adorned with perfumes, flowers, and the like; O Disease, destroy all afflictions and faults.
O Lord who has a deer as your vehicle, accept this pleasing oblation consisting of *maṇḍaka* (sweetmeat) with clarified butter, adorned with various foods; salutations be unto you!
And this kṛsara food, adorned with flowers, perfumes, and so forth—O Lord of Pātāla, accept this; may every obstacle here be destroyed.
O Chief One, accept this offering consisting of coconut water, cooked rice, and yellow garments;
destroy the defects of the site.
O Soma, accept this offering of milk-rice mixed with honey and adorned with various flowers; destroy all defects.
O Bhallāṭa, accept this pleasing offering of boiled rice mixed with clarified butter and accompanied by fragrant flowers; homage be unto you!
O you named Argala, accept this pleasing offering of black gram cooked with rice, anointed with ghee, and adorned with flowers, perfumes, and other ornaments; salutations be unto you!
O Mother of the Daityas, accept this milk combined with sugar and adorned with various offerings of flowers; destroy all defects.
O Mother of the Gods, accept this palanquin joined with honey and adorned with perfumes, garments, and other offerings; accept this pleasing oblation; salutations be unto you.
May those deities who dwell in heaven, the netherworld, and the mortal realm, and who reside in this site, accept this pleasing offering; being satisfied, may they depart for their own abodes.
May the Mothers, the Bhūtas, the Vetālas, and others who desire offerings,
as well as those who belong to the retinue of Viṣṇu, accept this bali offering.

"Having offered the *bali* to the ancestors and the guardians of the fields according to one's desire, one should worship with *kuśa* grass, flowers, and so forth, in the absence of the prescribed path. By the phrase "all prosperity," the *bali* offering to the directions is also indicated.

As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "The offering to the quarters (*digbali*) is proclaimed here as that which consists of the remaining rites of the site, which brings about all protection and prosperity, and which bestows satisfaction upon the spirits."
That which is intended for all beings, including the assembly of the guardians of the quarters, by means of their names,
and which concludes with worship and dismissal, should be known as the *diśāṃ bali*.

One should offer oblations in the various directions according to their respective order, using curd, water, blue lotus, flowers, parched grain, flour, sesame seeds, and boiled rice as the sacrificial materials.
Furthermore, that which belongs to the gods, to the radiant ones, to the spirits, to the progeny, and even to the Rākṣasas;
as well as to the waters, to the vital breaths, and to the lunar mansions.
Having uttered those names of the Vidyās and the Lords of the Vidyās as previously stated, one should offer the bali-oblation;
having pronounced the word "with vehicle" (savāhana), [one offers] to the retinue and to the Śakti.
Then, having joined [the mantra] with "and to all those attendants," one should further offer the bali-oblation to the spirits (bhūtas) in sequence, proceeding clockwise.

This rite, performed with offerings to the guardians of the directions, provides protection from the fear of enemies, piśācas, vetālas, and rākṣasas, and especially bestows the abundance of all prosperity.

"At the time of building a site or a house, when there is injury to living beings, at the entry into a new home, and during the performance of a peace-offering (śāntihoma), the offering to the quarters (diśāṃ bali) should be employed for the sake of success. Thus it is said.
Therein, the ritual procedure is written down according to the instruction.
Then the patron (yajamāna) should choose the preceptor (ācārya).

Thereupon, the preceptor, having selected a site with the characteristics to be described, and having performed its purification according to the method to be described, should sprinkle the ground with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the five Brahmans.
In the center of that [mandala], with a golden needle or a jewel— or in their absence, with silver, fruit, flowers, or grain— one of any [of these]—
[the nine lines]: Śāntā, Yaśovatī, Kāntā, Viśālā, Prāṇavāhinī, Satī, Sumanā, Nandā, and Subhadrā is considered the ninth.

Having thus drawn nine lines extending from east to west, beginning from the south and ending in the north— [the rivers] Hiraṇyā, Suvratā, Lakṣmī, Vibhūti, Vimalā, Priyā, Jayā, Kalā, and Viśokā are remembered by the wise as the ninth.

Having thus drawn nine lines extending from south to north, beginning at the west and ending at the east, and having properly prepared them with a cord of thread (*śulka-doraka*) and so forth, one should construct a variegated mandala adorned with five powders (*pañca-rajas*) according to the previously mentioned method, provided with the four corner squares as described before. To the west of that, one should prepare either a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or a leveled altar (*sthaṇḍila*) measuring one cubit and possessing three enclosures (*trimekhala*).

Then, outside [the central area], one should invoke all fifty-three deities situated in their respective squares and limbs as previously described—namely, Guru, Gaṇeśa, Durgā, and Kṣetrapāla located in the corner squares; Brahmā occupying four squares at the navel; Āryaka occupying four squares to the east of him and situated at his left breast; and so forth, ending with Aditi occupying half a square and Karṇa occupying a square—by means of the *padārthānusamaya* method, using the formula "O Brahmā, come here! Stay here! for each, preceded by the *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*.
One should worship [the vessel] with the respective mantras ending in the dative case, using the ritual services (upacāras) such as water for the feet (pādya) and so forth.

Then, in the northeast corner of the mandala, one should place a jar that is free of blemishes, not uprooted from its base, adorned externally with curd and consecrated rice (akṣata), its mouth covered with the sprouts of mango, holy fig (aśvattha), banyan (nyagrodha), cluster fig (udumbara), and plakṣa trees, and wrapped in a pair of cloths.
One should place a firm water-pot, filled with pure water and containing various fruits and the five precious gems inserted within, upon unbroken grains (akṣata).
Then, one should invoke Varuṇa into the pot with the Varuṇa-gāyatrī mantra beginning "imaṃ me varuṇa.
[One should also invoke: "All rivers such as the Gaṅgā, all oceans, and all lakes."
May they come, bringing about the destruction of the sacrificer's misfortunes.

Having thus invoked the sacred fords (tīrthas) by bringing seven types of earth from a horse-stable, an elephant-stable, an anthill, a river-confluence, a lake, a cow-pen, and a road, and having placed them into the pitcher, one should worship Varuṇa in that pitcher with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) using the mantra: "vaṃ varuṇāya namaḥ.
Then—
One should add murā, māṃsī, vacā, kuṣṭha, śaileya, the two types of rajanī,

śaṭī, campaka, and musta— these being all the medicinal herbs. Then, having approached the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and performed the rites beginning with the consecrations (saṃskāra) up to the end of the "mouth of fire" (agnimukha), [one should offer] to the fifty-three deities beginning with Brahmā.

One should offer oblations one thousand and eight, one hundred and eight, twenty-eight, or eight times each, using either barley or black sesame seeds, or with sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) made from any one of the following: the *udumbara*, other milk-exuding trees, *palāśa*, *khadira*, *apāmārga*, *kuśa*, or *dūrvā* grass.
Some, however, say that there should be one hundred oblations for Brahmā and ten oblations for each of the others.

Then, with the mantra "Oṃ vāstoṣpataye namaḥ" or with five Vedic mantras containing its indicative marks, one should offer five bilva fruits or bilva seeds into the fire. Then, having completed the subsequent ritual procedure (*uttaratantra*), one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with either the Agni-mantra or the Varuṇa-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, using the substances prescribed in the Tantra.

Having offered *bali* to the fifty-three deities with their respective mantras and having performed the *bali* for the directions, the preceptor, facing westward, should perform the auspicious consecration (*maṅgalābhiṣeka*) upon the candidate— who faces eastward— using the water from the *śānti-kalaśa* with the mantras beginning with "Oṃ, may the gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara consecrate you," as stated in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*, along with Vedic mantras; thereafter, he should bathe him with waters containing all medicinal herbs.

Then the preceptor, having again worshipped the gods beginning with Brahmā with the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra), thereafter [recites]: "May all the hosts of gods depart, taking with them this earthly worship,
for the sake of accomplishing desired wishes and for the purpose of returning once more."
Thus one should recite.
Then the disciple should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*ācārya*).

Then the preceptor, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) on the western side of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), should place the object of the rite (*sādhya*) upon it and [protect] it with either the *Sudarśana* or the *Aghora* [mantra].

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon himself, having become those very forms, and having adorned himself with a red turban, upper garment, garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth, he should stand facing north on the southern side of the person for whom the rite is intended. Taking a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or another such material, he should place the sacrificial balls (piṇḍas) offered to the deities beginning with Brahmā therein according to their respective positions.
Having established those respective deities together with Vāstupuruṣa right there, he should place a lamp of ghee upon each of the sacrificial balls.
Having placed [the vessel], adorned it with red flowers, and sprinkled the person to be protected (sādhya), one should take that vessel with both hands and recite:
"Whatever beings dwell here, having taken this bali-offering duly presented, may they seek residence elsewhere; may they forgive us for our presence here. Homage be to them!"

Having performed the *nīrājana* (lustration) of the object to be accomplished with this mantra, one should prepare blood-water (*raktodaka*) and *bhūtakrūra* in another vessel measuring one *āḍhaka*. Having placed nine lamps there as well, and having performed the *nīrājana* with that [mixture], one should— sword in hand, surrounded by many others with swords in their hands and surrounded by hundreds of torches,
with the quarters of the sky resounding with the sound of five kinds of musical instruments and the recitation of *svasti* hymns— proceed to a crossroads or the foot of a great tree.

Or, having gone to any one of these places—a pond, a river, or a temple—and having smeared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) there with cow dung, facing east, he should install the respective deities and place the ritual balls (*piṇḍas*) here and there. Having offered oblations (*bali*) to the spirits in the four directions with the previously mentioned mantra using *bhūtakrūra*, and having poured blood-water there, he should circumambulate it clockwise. Then, having washed his hands, feet, and eyes, he should repeatedly look back at all that [ritual] without looking at his attendants.

Having dispatched [the ritual assistant] ahead, one who is himself established in meditation should approach the object to be accomplished and provide protection for it; this is the primary method. As they say: "One should perform the pacification of the site with sacrificial fuel sticks and the offering of oblations."
The fire sacrifice should be performed in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit in size and having three tiers.
Likewise, with barley and black sesame seeds, and with sacrificial fuel-sticks made from milk-exuding trees—
whether from the palāśa, khadira, apāmārga, or udumbara trees.
Alternatively, it may be performed with kuśa and dūrvā grasses combined with honey and clarified butter,
or else with five bilva fruits or even with bilva seeds.

"At the conclusion of the *homa*, one should offer a *bali* in the site of the *vāstu* with various kinds of food and edibles; one should present these specific offerings in their proper sequence," and so forth.
Elsewhere, it is stated that this should be performed every year at a specific time.
As they say:
"Thus, when the sun has entered Leo, on the full moon day every year,
one should perform the worship of Vāstu in one's own home within a mandala, accompanied by the sequence of burnt offerings."
For one who acts in this manner within the home, nothing inauspicious ever occurs.
There shall be no untimely death, nor affliction from diseases, spirits, ghosts, and the like; there shall be no harm from serpents, nor mutual quarrels, nor any inauspicious events.
Possessing abundance of sons, grandsons, wealth, health, cattle,
and female slaves, he remains free from disease, victorious, renowned, and lives for a long time in that house.
Everywhere in the royal palaces, as well as in the quarters of the queens,
in the residences of the ministers, counselors, and generals, and likewise throughout the city.

The preceptor should perform [the rite] every year for the sake of the success described; otherwise, there will be constant suffering through results contrary to what was stated. Thus [ends verses 17–18].
On an auspicious day favorable to the lunar mansion, the zodiac sign, and the day of the week, [he should perform the rite] upon a pure patch of ground free from husks and charcoal. || 19 ||
Regarding the construction of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the text says "under a lunar mansion" (*nakṣatra*).

The connection is as follows: according to the methods prescribed in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*, one should construct the pavilion on an auspicious day, under a lunar mansion favorable to the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*), in a zodiac sign favorable to that person, on a favorable weekday, and on an auspicious lunar date (*tithi*) as specified in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*.
And so it is stated in the *Rājamārttaṇḍa*:

"By means of the Sun, the two [Punarvasu], Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Hasta, Dhaniṣṭhā, the three Uttarās, Puṣya, Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa), Maghā, Anurādhā, and Svāti— when these are pure and endowed with auspicious stars..."

"On days of the Saumya planets, in a yoga free from malefic influences, on a lunar day that is 'virikta' (cleansed), and on a day devoid of *viṣṭi*, the sages declare that building a house and other such works are auspicious.
Thus [it is said]: "on pure ground."
Regarding that, the examination of the ground is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
"In that regard, one who is expert in the science of architecture (*vāstu*) should examine the ground;
[one should avoid ground that is] cracked, containing debris, an anthill, or 'red' (*rohiṇī*)."
Ground that is far removed [from water] takes away the lifespan and wealth of the builder;
ground that is cracked causes death, while saline soil destroys wealth.
Accompanied by a thorn, it constantly causes affliction; uneven, it brings fear from enemies.
Yet, when floating in the northeast corner, it certainly bestows prosperity upon the doer.
The earth with a flood in the east brings prosperity and bestows boons (or strength);
with a flood in the north, it causes enmity, death, and disease; and with a flood in the southeast, it brings about calamity.
That ground which slopes toward the south (the direction of the Lord of Dharma) constantly brings the fear of death;
and that ground which slopes toward the southwest (the direction of Nirṛti) causes the destruction of one's home.
Land flooded by Varuṇa is said to cause the loss of wealth;
likewise, land flooded by wind always causes great anxiety.
The white [earth] is known as Brāhmaṇī, the red as Kṣatriyā;
the yellow should be understood as Vaiśyā, and the black is proclaimed as Śūdrā.
A Brāhmaṇī woman should have the scent of ghee; a Kṣatriyā woman produces the scent of blood;
a Vaiśyā woman should have the scent of milk; and a Śūdrā woman has the scent of excrement.
The earth that is sweet is known as Brāhmaṇī; that which is astringent is remembered as Kṣatriyā;
the Vaiśyā should be understood as bitter, while the Śūdrā earth is pungent.
The earth covered with *kuśa* grass belongs to a Brāhmaṇī; it belongs to a Kṣatriyā if it is thick with *śara* grass;
it belongs to a Vaiśyā if it is thick with *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass; and it belongs to a Śūdrā if it is overgrown with all kinds of grass.
White, yellow, red, and likewise endowed with a black color;
firm, stable, and smooth—the earth brings all happiness.
"In the time of heat, cool touch is auspicious; at the onset of winter, the touch of fire; and during the rains, both touches are auspicious. Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Hayaśīrṣa-pañcarātra*: "Where there is pleasure among cows with their calves together with bulls..."
O best of men, it is there that beautiful women take their pleasure with men.
Fragrant with the scent of Kāśmīra sandalwood, and possessing the aroma of camphor and agallochum;
smelling of lotus and water-lily, and bearing the fragrance of jasmine and campaka.
She has the fragrance of the *pāṭalā* and *mallikā* flowers; she smells of *nāgakeśara*;
she has the scent of curd, milk, and clarified butter; and she has the fragrance of wine and spirits.
"And that which has the fragrance of fragrant rice and is endowed with auspicious scents is considered the common ground for all castes. Likewise:
"Having understood [the requirements], one should examine the ground, which is auspicious and slopes toward the east or the north."
It was free from danger, well-concealed by grass, and flooded with water.
When the pit is being filled with auspicious soil that remains even more abundant than before, and likewise when a heap of flowers placed therein does not wither; |||
In that manner, the lamp does not go out, and the water does not quickly decay;
white, reddish, yellow, and black [colors] are praised for the Brahmins and the other castes respectively.
That which possesses a scent equal to clarified butter, blood, fragrance, or wine,
and which is sweet, astringent, sour, and pungent;
"Whatever [altar] is prepared with *kuśa*, *śara*, *kāśa*, and *dūrvā* grasses.
Also, in the *Prayogasāra*: "Having fashioned a cavity in the ground one *vitasti* in width..."
He should cast that earth into it; this is auspicious when those [other] waters remain.
One should know that [the ground] is middling if it is level, and it is called inferior if it is low;
having thus examined with effort and abandoned inferior ground, [one should proceed].
"Having cleared the ground of charcoal, husks, hair, and bones," and so forth;
[the word] "husks" (tuṣa) [is used].
Husks are the outer skins of grain; embers are extinguished firebrands.
By the word "etcetera," one should understand other such thorns as bones, hair, stones, ashes, and so forth, because otherwise defects would be observed.
As it is said in the Vāsiṣṭhī: "When a stone is encountered in the earth while the pit is being dug, then there is untimely death; and with bones, hair, or charcoal, there is loss of wealth."
"It is said that there will be danger from fire due to ashes, and poverty due to husks.
In this regard, the knowledge of hidden defects (śalya) is to be understood from the Ahibala-cakra as described in the Ādiyāmala.
It is as follows:
I shall explain the snake-wheel (ahicakra) just as it was spoken by the Omniscient One,
by which practitioners come to know substances, thorns, and likewise emptiness.
Eight vertical lines and likewise five horizontal lines should be drawn;
thus, in the snake-wheel (ahicakra), there are twenty-eight squares.
In that [table], the asterisms of Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Aśvinī, Yāmya (Bharaṇī), Kṛttikā, Maghā, Bhāgya (Pūrvaphalgunī),
and Uttarāphālgunī— this fixed group of seven— should be written in a row.
One should draw Ahibudhnya, Ajapādārka, Śatabhiṣaj, Brāhma,
Āśleṣā, Puṣya, and Hasta, situated in the second row.
Abhijit, Viṣṇu, Dhaniṣṭhā, Saumya, Raudra,
Punarvasu, and Citrā— these seven constellations are in the third row of the Dhiṣṇya.
Having placed Viśvarkṣa (Śatabhiṣaj), the water asterism (Pūrvāṣāḍhā), Mūla, Jyeṣṭhā, Anurādhā, Viśākhā,
and Svātī in the fourth row, one should examine the wheel.
Revatī, Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, and Uttaraphalgunī are in the first row;
Uttarabhādrapadā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, Śatabhiṣā, Rohiṇī, Āśleṣā, Puṣyā, Hastā, and Citrā are in the second row;
Abhijit, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, and Svātī are in the third row.
Then, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Mūla, Jyeṣṭhā, Anurādhā, Viśākhā, and Svātī are in the fourth row.
In this way, the arrangement in the form of a serpent is produced in the diagram.
