Maghā is considered the southern door-jamb, and Kṛttikā is held to be situated at the door.

The three asterisms beginning with Aśvinī, the five beginning with Pūrvāṣāḍhā, the four beginning with Revatī, and those beginning with Pūrvabhādrapadā belong to the Moon; the remaining ones belong to the Sun.
The nadīs elapsed since sunrise, when divided by sixty, yield a remainder;
this [remainder], added to the moon’s motion for the day, becomes the moon at that specific time.
One should calculate the sun, situated in its asterism at the time of the event, in the same manner as for the moon;
subsequently, one should observe whether those two are situated in their own asterisms or in other asterisms.
When the Sun and Moon are in a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) belonging to the Moon, then a treasure is certain;
if they both reside in a lunar mansion belonging to the Sun, then there is a thorn (a hidden obstacle), and not otherwise.
"The second [period] is to be known as occurring in its own sign; there is nothing [of consequence] in the opposite case.
The extent of the ground is determined by the measure of the degrees traversed in the zodiacal sign, using twelve *kāmbika* fingers.
And likewise: "A treasure is to be known in the place of the Moon, but a thorn in the place of the Sun."
Thus it is said:
having learned this wheel from the mouth of the Guru, one should perform the extraction of the thorn (*śalyoddhāra*).
And this should be performed only once on ground measured by the distance of a *nivartana*.
And the nature of the *nivartana* is as follows: "A staff (*daṇḍa*) shall be ten cubits (*hasta*) long; thirty staffs make one *nivartana*."
In the middle of that, another wheel should be drawn twice;
above that, it should not be done—so say those who know the tradition.
Alternatively, the extraction of the thorn (śalyoddhāra) should be performed according to the method taught in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra.
For example:
at the time of beginning the construction of a palace, and especially in the case of a house and so forth,
one who desires his own welfare must perform the extraction of the splinter (śalyoddhāra).

And at the time of commencing the construction of a palace, the wise man should know that whatever limb of the body of Vāstu a person touches, there is a firm splinter (śalya) located in that very spot.
If a man scratches his head, one should extract a splinter from the head;
it should be understood that a bone is the splinter there, located at a depth of three hand-spans when digging.
Fire, disease, and loss of wealth arise;
one should extract the thorn with effort if one desires one's own welfare.
If one scratches the arms, it indicates an iron chain;
it will remain bound by both hands—this characteristic has been described to you.
One should know that it portends the death of the master or likewise his departure to a foreign land;
therefore, one who desires success for oneself should carefully extract the thorn.
If one scratches the thighs, however, one should indicate a splinter of bell-metal;
it will remain with only one hand [engaged]. Thus has the characteristic been described to you.
An unchaste wife brings about the loss of one's reputation;
therefore, if one desires one's own welfare, one should diligently extract this thorn.
If the two hands itch while digging, one should indicate a skeleton;
and it will be found at a depth of three cubits, and not otherwise.
There may be fire, burning, disease, and death accompanied by a thorn;
one who desires his own welfare should extract the thorn with effort.
If he scratches his back, one should indicate the presence of an arrow in the arm;
it will remain there with only one hand—of this there is no doubt.
In that case, there will be the destruction of the master, or the wife becomes unchaste;
however, when she scratches her feet, one should predict a splinter in the hand.
The characteristic described for you is that it should stand at one and a half cubits;
[otherwise] there occurs the destruction of cattle, royal punishment, and loss of crops.
One who desires his own success should extract the thorn with effort;
however, when the belly itches, one should point out a stone there.
The characteristic mark has been described for you as measuring two cubits;
a snake-bite may occur there, therefore one should extract the dart.
If there is itching on the knees, one should apply ashes there; it will remain for two months. Thus has the characteristic been described to you.
It causes the burning of fire, mental anguish, and the fears of affliction and suffering;
since it performs such actions, one should indeed uproot it.
The cow-horn, yellow frog, conch, mother-of-pearl, tortoise,
and śambuka shell are recommended, as are other varieties of gems.
One should remove charcoal, husks, hair, bone, and splinters; as long as one examines the water while it is being strained, the defect caused by the splinter is destroyed.
Water situated far below cannot be reached by digging;
one must dig down five cubits to pacify the defects caused by the arrow.
"Then, having extracted the *śalya*, one should fill it so that it is perfectly level.
Also, in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "In a temple, a *śalya* may cause defects as far as the water's edge;
therefore, the ground for a temple should be purified as far as the water's edge."
"Until it reaches the stage of stone, or gravel, or until it attains purity. (19)
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should construct a beautiful pavilion with an interior space measured by five,
seven, or nine cubits.

"Having caused [the officiants] to recite 'an auspicious day' (puṇyāha)" means that the recitation for an auspicious day is most well-known among the Bahvṛcas. Alternatively, it means: "May you all declare this to be an auspicious day for this sacrificer; likewise, may you all pronounce 'well-being' (svasti); likewise, may you all pronounce 'prosperity' (ṛddhi)."
The declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) is performed three times.
As stated by Baudhāyana:
"Having caused [the officiants] to pronounce each blessing (*āśis*) three times, preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*, with the formula 'Auspicious day! Hail! Prosperity! (*puṇyāhaṃ svasti ṛddhiḥ*)."
In that regard, one should construct the pavilion and so forth only after first ascertaining the knowledge of the directions, such as the east;
for otherwise, faults are observed. As it has been said: "If one should act according to what is merely seen [without such ascertainment], one who has failed will go to hell."
"Having determined the directions by the movement of the sun, the preceptor should perform the rites.
Also elsewhere: "Where the direction is not correctly known due to irregularities in the site, one should determine the position of the pure directions by fixing a gnomon there."
The means for knowing that [direction] is stated in that very same work: "Listen, I shall explain according to the rule how the knowledge of the directions is attained through that movement:
having drawn a circle on a perfectly level ground by means of rotation..."
One should place a gnomon twelve finger-breadths long at the center-point of that;
by means of the two shadows at its tip, one determines the east and west lines within the circle.
Having made marks to the east and west, and likewise on both sides of that [central point],
one should then draw two circles by rotating [the cord] equally around them.
One should first lay down a thread in the middle between those two points where they meet, situated to the south and north,
and then place another thread in the middle of the two junctions, extending east and west.
"One should first lay out the Sūtra-Dakṣottara for them, starting from the east," so it is said.
Also in the Kriyāsāra: "Having made the ground level there, one should fashion a circular area measuring one cubit, and a gnomon (śaṅku) made of Khadira wood, twelve finger-breadths in height."
If such wood is not available, the wise man should install a sacrificial tree there;
the point where its shadow touches is considered the middle of that site.
One should extend the cord diagonally; the middle [cord] is known as being between south and north.
By the extension of four cords, the other four corners are formed.
"Thus has the thorough knowledge of the directions been clearly explained;
having understood this, the wise man should properly construct the pavilion and other structures.
In that regard, however, there is a specific distinction in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*:
When the sun has reached the equinox, one should perform the measurement with a gnomon;
one should set up a gnomon made of khadira wood, twelve finger-breadths in width.
Having made it steady and grasped with an iron mallet, one should strike it oneself eight times; this is recommended, proceeding gradually and lightly.
When the mallet falls from the hand while striking the stake,
then a great and insurmountable grief arises for the striker.
One should wrap the cord around the peg; the cord may be made of muñja grass, silk, cotton, or even from the hair of an animal, and its thickness should be equal to four barley grains.
When the thread being wound around releases the peg at that very moment, one should know it portends the death of a son; if it snaps, it indeed indicates one's own destruction.
"In that case as well, the destruction of inauspiciousness occurs through the *nārasiṃha* oblation. Thus it is said.
Maya also stated: "The sacrificial stake (*śaṅku*) is prescribed to be made of heartwood; its tip should be fashioned with various circular carvings.
Having prepared it properly at the beginning of the day, one should plant it in level ground."
With a measurement double that of the gnomon, one should draw a circle in its center;
when the shadows of the forenoon and afternoon enter into the interior of that mandala, [one should mark them].
The thread passing through those two points is intended for the eastern and western directions;
it passes between the two points and follows the tails of two fish drawn within that interval.
In this manner, one should lay down two threads, one running from south to north and the other from east to west.
Then, one should cast further threads from their respective ends toward the opposite corners;
the wise architect should lay these threads facing east, north, and so forth. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "Having made the ground level with water, resembling the surface of a mirror, one should draw a circle there with a measurement of twelve finger-breadths."
Having fixed an immovable gnomon in the center, one should observe its shadow;
for the circular line is that which is delineated by the external shadow of the gnomon.
One should observe the entry and exit of the shadow of the gnomon upon that [line];
from the two marks made by the tips of the gnomon's shadow, one should determine the east and west directions.
When the sun has moved toward the east or the west, one should determine the north and south;
at the equinox, when the sky is clear, one should determine the direction by means of a gnomon.
In this manner, during autumn and spring, one should determine the direction from the sun.
"Either toward the east by means of the conjunction with Puṣya, or between Citrā and Svātī.

Also elsewhere: "Just as the specific knowledge of the divisions of the eastern and western directions has been taught here, having analyzed that subject in brief, one should perform the ritual acts as instructed."
As for the method for determining the east at night, it is as follows:
"The interval between Kṛttikā, Śravaṇa, Puṣya, Citrā, and Svāti—this is the form of the eastern direction when the sun has risen to the height of a yoke. Thus it is said.
In the *Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana* it is also stated: "The East is [defined] by the rising of Śravaṇa, and likewise by the rising of Kṛttikā;
it is between Citrā and Svātī that the East lies, but it is not the East for the Moon and the Sun.
The calculation of the subtle East should be performed by means of the rule of three (*trairāśika*).
For example: on the second day as well, having fixed the gnomon in the same manner, one should mark the points for the forenoon and afternoon.
Therein, one should divide the ground between the marks of the two days—the preceding and the following—with sesame seeds and so forth.

Then follows the calculation by the rule of three (*trairāśika*): if this interval is obtained by means of sixty *ghaṭikās*, then what is it by means of the *ghaṭikās* contained within the interval between the preceding and succeeding marks of the previous day?

This is the rule of three. Regarding that, the formula for the rule of three is as follows: "The first and last terms are of the same kind and constitute the measure (*pramāṇa*) and the requirement (*icchā*)."
"The fruit, being of a different kind, should be divided by the first [value] with the last quality in the middle.

By this method, one should increase the intermediate ground— which has arrived as a measure of sesame seeds and so forth— toward the north during the northern solstice (*udagayana*) and toward the south during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*), right at the eastern mark (*prāgaṅka*).
Therein one should draw a line;
this is the subtle eastward line.
By the phrase "one should construct the pavilion," the threefold pavilion—distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior—is indicated.
Regarding that, the threefold nature of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"Now we shall describe the construction of the pavilion as proclaimed by Brahmā;
it is considered to be of three kinds according to superior, middling, and inferior measurements."

By this, the avoidance of the defects mentioned in the *Kriyāsāra*, such as "excessive in measurement" or "deficient," is indicated. He states the measurement for all three types of pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) with the words "by five [parts]" (*mañcabhiḥ*). Regarding that, the literal explanation is as follows: the smallest pavilion has a width and length of five cubits (*hasta*), resulting in a total area of twenty-five cubits.

The medium [mandapa], however, measures seven cubits in width and length, with a ground area of forty-nine cubits. The superior [mandapa] measures nine cubits in length and width, with a ground area of eighty-one cubits.
Among these, we shall first consider the superior mandapa.
The author himself will describe the nine-pit (navakuṇḍīya) system in this very mandapa further ahead.
And in those pits, according to the method to be described, one, three, or five girdles (mekhalā) should be made, leaving a space equal to a quarter of the altar (vedi).
This is stated in the Piṅgalāmata:
"O beloved, there should be one girdle, or three, or five according to the number of elements.
Also in another Tantra: "O Goddess of the gods, there may be five girdles, or three, or even one."
Thus it is said.
Also, in the Siddhāntaśekhara: "For all fire-pits (kuṇḍas), there should be either one, three, or five girdles (mekhalās)."
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*: "Five girdles (mekhalā) should be made.
In that case, regarding the option of five girdles, there is no inclusion of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) themselves.
The position of the three girdles (*trimekhala*), however, is that stated by the author of the treatise.
According to that view, the fire-pits (*kuṇḍas*) alone are accommodated in some manner or other;
there is no place at all for the movement of the performer of the oblation and others, because of extreme overcrowding.

Furthermore, there is no possibility of accommodating the sacrificial ground (*sthāṇḍila*) intended for the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice—which is to be described later—within the altar (*vedi*), nor is there room for the bed which is also to be described later.
Even when there is an increase in the number of fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*) due to other rites or an abundance of oblation materials, even then there is no accommodation within the pits;
what then can be said of the middle and lowest sizes?
In that case, since even the position of five sacrificial pits (pañcakuṇḍīpakṣa) is untenable,
the author has proposed the position of nine sacrificial pits (navakuṇḍīpakṣa) there as well; however,
that too would be utterly inconsistent.
Therefore, it is not an explanation according to the literal text.
However, some say that the term "middle" (*antara*) refers to the meaning of the "knowable" (*vedya*) which will be described later.
According to their view, the smallest pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) has a width and length of fifteen cubits and a ground area of two hundred and twenty-five square cubits.
The medium [size] has a length and width of twenty-one cubits and an area of four hundred forty-one karas;
the superior [size], however, has a length and width of twenty-seven cubits and an area of seven hundred twenty-nine karas.
Even that is not approved by the virtuous.
Because such a measurement is not mentioned in other texts; however, in the *Mantramuktāvalī* and other works, another measurement is also given:
"Or twenty-four cubits, or likewise twenty cubits."
Thus it is said;
and elsewhere as well: "The pavilion and the temple-shrine should be twenty cubits in measurement."
It is stated to be twenty cubits or indeed twenty-four cubits;
therefore, the meaning of this autumnal verse should be explained as follows:
"by five and by seven" is a collective expression.
Therefore, the smallest pavilion has a length and width of twelve cubits and an area of one hundred and forty-four cubits.
Following the sequence "by five" and "by nine," the middle pavilion has a length and width of fourteen cubits and an area of one hundred and ninety-six cubits.
And then, it follows [the phrase] "by seven and nine.
Thus, the best pavilion (maṇḍapa) has a length and width of sixteen cubits and an area of two hundred and fifty-six cubits;
in this way, the pavilion is described as being of three kinds.
Thus it is stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*: "This [smallest] is twelve cubits; from that, it increases by two each step in sequence.
By this, the medium size is stated to be fourteen cubits, and the largest sixteen cubits.

In the *Siddhāntaśekhara* as well: "The pavilion may be twelve cubits, or even ten; other pavilions should be constructed, increasing by two cubits each. Somaśambhu also says: "The pavilion may be twelve cubits, or [ten]."
"The remaining auspicious pavilions (*maṇḍapas*) should be increased by two cubits each. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "Starting from twelve cubits, increasing by two at each step..."
Elsewhere as well: "A wise man should have a pavilion constructed in the northeast portion of the house, measuring twelve, eight, six, or sixteen cubits on all sides.
Also in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Now, a pavilion with a width of twelve [cubits] is known as the smallest."
Thus it is said. Also in the Pañcarātra: "In this case, the pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be sixteen cubits [in size] for the best [type]."
Also in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "They say that the best measurement is sixteen cubits.
Furthermore, this pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) should be made square.
As stated by Kātyāyana in the *Pariśiṣṭa*: "The [shape] is a square, unless otherwise specified.
Also in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "It is a square with four doors.
However, its perfect squareness must be established according to the procedure prescribed for the *vāstumaṇḍala*.
In this regard, the specific detail is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The site of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is said to be twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in height from the ground.
Furthermore, concerning the pavilion, it is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
"The height should be one cubit, perfectly level and very beautiful," so it is said.
Also elsewhere: "The pavilion (maṇḍapa) on the ground should be elevated."
Now, one might object: "Since the accomplishment of the fruit is achieved by the smallest of these three mandapas alone, there would be no performance of the middle and largest ones.

This is not so; for according to the principle that "since the fruit arises from the action, as in the world, there shall be a distinction of fruit based on their magnitude," it is not a fault, as a gradation of fruits is thus postulated.

For instance, heaven is heard in scripture as the fruit of both the Agnihotra and the Jyotiṣṭoma; although that [heaven] is accomplished by the first alone, no one would fail to perform the second, the larger, [sacrifice].
Anticipating the objection that [the ritual] might proceed [in this way], the *Ākara* (the *Tantravārttika*) has refuted the assumption of gradations in the fruit by means of the principle:

"Or rather, because it is a part of the conceptualization, it follows from the sense" (*arthāt*); for by this, even conceptualization is stated to be a single part of the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
Furthermore, the author of the *Vārttika* has stated that this is also established through the authority of position (*sthāna-pramāṇa*).

"Regarding actions, whether small or great, and their fruits within their own respective spheres, although there is no distinction because of the commonality of their locus, [the result] is impelled [by the specific nature of the action].
This establishes the explanation: that the [result] of actions is declared [to arise] due to the commonality of their locus.
Just as she [the moon] is in the midst of her own collection [of digits], so too is she in the midst of the fruits;
because of the commonality of measurement, even though it is not stated specifically.

As for what was stated by someone else— that a twelve-cubit [image] may be of two types, namely that the two middle ones are considered to have a height and span of ten cubits each, while the two flanking ones have a height and span of twelve cubits each—
that is incorrect.
Because this would result in a confusion of the measurements for the pillars and other elements.

(The literal explanation [of the previous verse] should also be applied according to the circumstances in the case of a single *kuṇḍa* or five *kuṇḍas*, but not to the nine *kuṇḍas* mentioned by the author of the text. || 20 ||
It should be provided with sixteen pillars; among them, four are to be placed in the center, eight-hasta in height, and twelve are to be established around the perimeter. || 21 ||
He describes the method for installing the pillars in the pavilion with the words "sixteen" and so forth.
Regarding the four [pillars], among those pillars, four situated in the middle should be placed at the corners of the altar.
As it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"In the center there should be a group of four pillars, and in their midst a pedestal (vedikā) is prescribed.
Also elsewhere: "One should place pillars, which have the nature of the Vedas, at the corners of the pedestal."
"In the very sequence beginning with Āgneyī.
By this, it should be understood that the installation of the twelve external pillars also follows the sequence beginning with Āgneyī.
As it has been said:
"The commencement [of the rite] takes place when the pillar is raised, when the stone is laid, when the cord is fixed to the peg,
when the pit is dug and consecrated, and when the fire-altar is prepared."
And those [pillars] are eight cubits in height.
By stating the height of the pillars, the author of the text has indicated that sixteen cubits is indeed the maximum [height].
As it is said in the *Pañcarātra*: "One should erect pillars half the height of the pavilion, numbering four, and likewise provided with capitals."
Thus;
"on both sides" means on both sides of the central pillars.
As it is said in the *Kriyāsara*: "Having leveled the ground and demarcated it with a cord, one should set up the pillars evenly."
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Pañcarātra*: "Furthermore, there are twelve pillars on the exterior as well, according to the stated proportions, distributed here and there. (21)
Measuring five cubits, they should be without gaps, straight, and auspicious;
the best of those skilled in the art of weaving should bury one-fifth of them in the earth. || 22 ||
What are the sixteen pillars like?
They are without holes, meaning they are free from perforations;
by this, their solidity is expressed.
"Upright" means straight; "not crooked" means not bent in any way. "Neither thick nor thin" means that they are therefore auspicious.
Furthermore, such a quality as this is not possible unless they originate from a tree of excellent substance (*sāra-vṛkṣa*).
This also is stated by implication that [the pillars] should be made from heartwood;
as it says in the Pañcarātra: "One should make the pillars firm, straight, and even, produced from heartwood."
In the *Kriyāsāra*, however, there is this distinction: for the work of constructing pillars, one may use sacrificial wood, bamboo, or the *kramuka* tree;
or other pure trees may be used, but never any other species of plant.

"A pillar that is itself dry, crooked, ancient, or produced from inauspicious ground must be rejected in the work of erecting pillars. Thus it is said. For the medium and inferior [types of houses], the measurement of twelve pillars should be calculated by means of the rule of three (trairāśika).
"Five parts of that" means: having divided the height of the pillar into five parts, one should bury one-fifth part into the ground; this is the meaning. || 22 ||
One should cover it on all sides with coconut leaves and bamboo;
at the doors, there should be arches made from milk-exuding trees in due order. || 23 ||
Regarding the phrase "on all sides of that":
on all sides of that pavilion, everywhere except for the doors, one should cover it with bamboo and coconut leaves;
in the absence of coconut leaves, one should enclose it with mats.
As stated in the *Vāstuśāstra*: "The pavilions, such as the Vijaya and others, should be well-covered with mats.
And in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "One should decorate the pavilion on all sides with fresh branches."
As for the statement in the *Kriyāsāra*, "having constructed a wall all around," that should be understood as referring to pavilions containing permanent images and the like,
because it will be stated in that very same work: "This rule is declared for rites involving permanent *liṅgas*."
He speaks of the installation of the arches (*toraṇa*) with the words "at the doors" (*dvāreṣu*).
Now, one might ask: since the doors themselves have not yet been mentioned, how can there be this statement "at the doors"?
True.
By the very phrase "at the doors," the doors are implied. Their measurement and location are stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"One should construct four doors in the cardinal directions, [measuring] one-fifth [of the width]."
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Kriyāsāra*: "The wise man should place the doors in the cardinal directions, and the arches (toraṇas) in those very same doors at the center."

In the *Pañcarātra*, the measurement is stated as follows: "For the smallest [image], it should be two cubits; for the medium and largest, it should be increased by four finger-breadths per category. Thus it is said.
"One should deposit" means one should bury it with exactly a fifth part.
As it is stated in the Vāstuśāstra: "One should deposit a fifth part in the ground; this is the rule common to all."
In the Siddhāntaśekhara, concerning the pillars of the archway (toraṇa), it is said:
"The excavation for all [pillars] should be one-fifth [of their height]; this has been declared by Śiva."
"Successively" means in the directions of the east, south, west, and north.
"Of milk-yielding trees" refers to the *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *plakṣa*.
This is because of the technical definition: "The *nyagrodha*, *uḍumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *plakṣa* are the milky trees.

As it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "A *nyagrodha* archway is prescribed for the east, an *uḍumbara* for the south, one produced from an *aśvattha* for the west, and a *plakṣa* archway for the north."
"Or [the tree] produced from the *plakṣa* in the east, and the *nyagrodha* is held to be in the north.
Also, in the *Kriyāsāra*: "The *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, *bodhidruma*, and *vaṭa* are, in order, the four archways starting from the east."
Thus [says] Somaśambhu as well: "The archways made of Plakṣa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees should be constructed in order starting from the east;
or else, there may be a reversal of the beginning and the end."
"Out of necessity, one should place only one of these in all directions.
Also, in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "Then, with the mantra 'agnimīle', one should install the eastern arch;
with the mantra 'iṣetvorjetvā', one should install the southern arch."
"By the mantra *agna āyāhi*, one should [place] the western arch;
by the mantra *śanno devīḥ*, one should offer the northern arch. Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "The gods are stationed in the form of arches within the sacrificial pavilion (*yajñamaṇḍapa*)."
For the purpose of destroying obstacles and for the protection of the sacrifice.
One should place a nyagrodha tree in the east, likewise an udumbara in the south,
a pippala in the west, and a plakṣa in the north.
The Suśobhana [image] is in the east, consecrated with mantras from the Ṛgveda and other Vedas; the one named Subhadra is in the south, with the mantra "iṣe tvorje tvā."
"One should place that called Sukarma in the west with the Sāmaveda and so forth, using the mantra 'śanno devī'; one should place Suhotra in the north.
As for what was stated by someone else regarding the placement of these [trees]—the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Jaṭī, and Vaṭa—in the east and other directions, that is irrelevant.
This is because it contradicts various written statements.
Furthermore, this installation of the gateway pillars (toraṇastambha) should be understood as being at a distance of one cubit (hasta) from the pavilion (maṇḍapa).
As it has been said: "Outside the door of the pavilion, according to the measurement of the altar (vedi), in the sequence of the directions..."
"One should install an archway made from the Plakṣa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees.
And in the Vāstuśāstra: "One should cause these doors of the pavilion to be constructed in each direction using branches of the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa trees."
Because they are constructed at the gates, the term "gate" (dvāra) is used to refer to the archways (toraṇa).
However, it should be understood that these are located in the west, south, north, and east, either proceeding counter-clockwise or starting from the western gate.
Regarding this, there is a specific detail in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"If one of these is unavailable, it may be [another wood]; in its absence, the *śamī* tree is prescribed.
For the archway (*toraṇa*), the heartwood of the *jambu*, *khadira*, or the *tāla* tree is traditionally taught.
However, in the *Kriyāsāra*: "The auspicious poles for the archway should be straight, with their bark intact, and fresh."
Thus [ends the section]. ||23||
The height of each of those pillars is recorded as seven cubits;
their circumference is stated to be ten finger-breadths [per cubit]. || 24 ||
Regarding the word "stambhaiḥ" (pillars):
"with seven cubits" refers to the best pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), since the author of the text states all measurements for the best [pavilion] alone.
"Separately, separately" means that the measurement for the middling and inferior [pavilions] is distinct from one another.
Therefore, in the medium [size], they are six cubits;
in the inferior, five cubits.
Regarding the pillars of the archway, it is stated in the Vāstuśāstra:
"They are five cubits in measure, two cubits in width;
they increase by six finger-breadths, and thus the best are seven cubits. Here, "in width" refers to the measurement of the horizontal plank.
Although the six-cubit measurement for the middle [size] is not explicitly stated, it is understood through logical necessity.

This was stated by Kātyāyana: "The dimension [is determined] by suitability according to the purpose. The circumference—the width—of those arch-pillars (*toraṇastambha*) is to be known by means of calculating the perimeter.
In that regard, the calculation of the rough circumference was stated by Bhāskarācārya:
"Alternatively, [the circumference] multiplied by twenty-two and then divided by seven shall be a rough [value], suitable for practical use."
Vyāsa multiplied by twenty-two is 220; divided by seven, the quotient is 31. This is the circumference of that wooden [object] whose diameter is ten finger-breadths. || 24 ||
The measurement of the horizontal beam (tiryakphalaka) should be half the measurement of the pillars.
One should fashion the spikes (śūla) in the middle of the archway (toraṇa) according to the measurement of one cubit. || 25 ||
Regarding the term "tiryak" (horizontal):

the measurement of that horizontal plank which is positioned above, in the form of a lintel, between the two pillars, is half the measure of the pillars— that is, of the five-cubit pillars that serve as the archway supports.
By this, the measurement of two and a half cubits is stated.
Regarding the plural "of the pillars" (*stambhānām*), it should be understood that because there are many doors, there are likewise many arch-pillars (*toraṇastambha*).
By this, it is also indicated that in the smallest pavilion (*kaniṣṭhamaṇḍapa*), there may be five-cubit arch-pillars.
This measurement for the horizontal plank (tiryakphalaka) applies only to the best [type of image];
for the other two, a reduction of six angulas each should be understood,
as it is stated thus in the Vāstuśāstra.
The plural form "śūlāni" (spears) refers to the number four;
the singular form "toraṇe" (at the archway) is used in the sense of a genus.
Therefore, one spear should be made for each individual archway.
And that [pillar] is one cubit in measure;
therein, the insertion is three finger-breadths and the circumference is six parts. This is the same for the three pavilions.

In that regard, the nature of the trident (*śūla*) is as follows: there is a central pin (*madhyakīla*) with a sharp point and straight; flanking it on both sides are two curved [pins] with sharp points.
These refer to the curved portions situated at the level of the central pin.
As it is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Having thus constructed the archway (*toraṇa*), one should place three tridents above."
"Their tridents shall extend the length of an arm.
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "The door-frames should be marked with tridents at their own tops."
The central shaft should indeed be straight, while the two sides are slightly curved.
"Both of those have been fully described; at that time, one should plant a finger-breadth [of earth].
However, when the singular number is intended in the word "toraṇe" (on the arch), then the plural "śūlāni" (stakes) is used according to the principle of the *kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa*.
It culminates in a state of threefoldness.
"By the measure of the hand" means the measurement of the three combined.
As it is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Having thus constructed the archway, one should place three spikes (*śūla*) above the head."
"The length of the trident is nine finger-breadths (aṅgulas), and its width is one-fourth of that;
for the remaining [limbs], the increase is two finger-breadths, and the insertion (veśa) increases by one finger-breadth.
Thus, in the case of the smallest [trident], the insertion is two finger-breadths.
Also in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"And in the middle portion between the two tips, [one should draw] tridents upon the band."
It should be understood that these [emblems], being made of the same wood as the [liṅga], must be fashioned by a Śaiva artisan alone.
However, there is a specific rule regarding the Vaiṣṇava [liṅga]:
according to the Vāstuśāstra— "On the top [of the liṅga], with a twelfth part [of its height], [one should fashion] the conch, discus, mace, and lotus."
"One should install those [tridents] made of one's own wood according to the sequence beginning with the east.

Because it is stated here that these are "made of one's own wood," it follows by logical necessity that the tridents occupying these positions in the Śaiva tradition must likewise be made of one's own wood.
In that context, the twelve-fold division applies specifically to the pillars of the archways (*toraṇa*).

In the preceding supplementary statement, "likewise, seven cubits for the best [size]," since those very [trees] are the subject under discussion, by that [rule], fourteen and twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) are respectively the measurements for the branches and so forth in the best and other sizes;
however, the width is indeed by one-fourth of its own [length].
As for the claim made by someone that the measurement of four finger-breadths and so forth is derived from one-twelfth of the plank, that is incorrect;
for that [measurement] is not the subject under discussion.
And because it is stated that the measure of the trident is nine finger-breadths (*aṅgula*),

the arrangement of these [elements] should also be understood as being as before. Then, one *kalaśa* should be placed at each archway (*toraṇa*), two on each side of every door, and one in each corner.
As it has been said:
"One should place jars provided with perfumes, flowers, and garments;
one should worship Dhruva, Dharā, Vākpati, and Vighneśa within them."
In the pitchers situated at the corners of the pavilion, these [deities] are to be placed in sequence:
Amṛta, Durjaya, Siddhārtha, and Maṅgala.
"Indra and the others are to be worshipped in the jars placed at the doors with their respective excellent mantras. Also elsewhere: "One should place two jars at each door within the pavilion."
"Filled with filtered water and adorned with mango sprouts. Thus [ends verse 25].

One should fasten banners in the various directions that possess a splendor equal to that of the world-protectors, and one should adorn the pavilion with canopies, garlands of darbha grass, and other ornaments. || 26 ||
"Flags in the directions" refers to the nature of the flags as described in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*:
"The flags are recorded as being five cubits in length and colored yellow, red, and so forth."
"They are considered to be joined with staffs made of bamboo, measuring two or five cubits.
That is, measuring ten cubits (two times five).
Also elsewhere—
"Five cubits long, the banners should be made; alternatively, they may be two cubits. The staff should be ten cubits long, and one should place them in the eight directions.
However, in the *Kriyāsāra*, there is a specific distinction: "The characteristics of the banners are now correctly described exactly as they are."
Outside the pavilion, together with poles ten cubits in length.
One should install eight banners in sequence in the eight directions starting from the east;
their width is two cubits, and their middle [circumference] is equal to one's own cubit.
The half of the width is the crest and the tail, measuring three cubits;
the crest has the appearance of a fish, while the tip of the tail is triangular.
Between those two, one should likewise fashion a quadrangular area marked with banners,
[depicting] an elephant, a goat, a buffalo, a lion, a fish, a deer, and a horse.
One should draw a bull in the middle of the banner according to the rule,
or else the eight elephants of the quarters, headed by Airāvata.
"One should draw well-defined [images] upon the banners using the aforementioned pigments;
thus has been described the auspicious characteristic of the banners. Thus it is said.
The necessity of the banners is stated in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme consecration of the banner (dhvajāropaṇa),
by performing which properly a person shall obtain the fruit of all [meritorious deeds].
The Yātudhānas, Guhyakas, Kuṣmāṇḍas, and those who roam the sky—
these foremost of Asuras— were contemplating the abode of the gods, now bereft of its banner.
O Brahmin, in a pavilion devoid of a banner,
all the worship, fire-oblations, recitations, and other rites performed by the wise would be in vain.
Just as a field perishes for its owner without protection,
so too a temple would utterly perish without its banner.
The cruel attendants of Viṣṇu, such as the Kuṣmāṇḍas and others who are remembered,
seize the offerings and the like if they see the deity unprotected.

"Having seen the banners of the God in the pavilion, blazing with the brilliance of fire, they all perish like darkness dispelled by the rays of the sun. Thus [it is said]: "possessing a splendor equal to that of the World-Protectors."

The colors of the world-protectors (lokapālas) will be described in the fourth [chapter]. The installation of the banners has also been stated in the *Sārasaṃgraha*: "Banners for each and every pit (kuṇḍa) have been prescribed by those learned in the meaning of the scriptures."
The banners should be seven cubits long and one-seventh as wide.
"The ninth [digit] has the appearance of the world-protectors and the luster of snow.
Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "It is joined with banners and flags."
Thus [says] Somaśambhu as well: "The banners should be seven cubits long and twenty finger-breadths wide;
the poles for the banners should be ten cubits long and wrapped around at one-fifth [of their length]."
"Flags and weapons-marked [objects], provided with flowers and perfumes.
Thus he describes the decoration of the pavilion, beginning with the word "canopy."
A canopy is moonlight.
A *darbha* garland consists of *darbha* grass tied together with a cord.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one should understand such things as the wrapping of pillars with fine silk (*dukūla*) and the binding of garlands of mango sprouts.
As it is said in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Abounding with garlands of mango sprouts, adorned with canopies, covered with variegated cloths, and decorated with pillars [weighing] a *tulā*;
[it is further adorned] with plantain trunks bearing fruit, as well as *kramuka* nuts and coconuts."
With various kinds of fruits, offerings, mirrors, and even chowries.
"One should construct the pavilion adorned and radiant with jewels and flowers.
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "One should decorate the pillars with mirrors, chowries, bells, and cloths."
"By means of water-jars (*kalaśa*), hour-glasses (*ghaṭikā*), supports (*sādhāra*), and likewise by pebbles (*karkara*). Thus it is said.

Regarding the defect that arises when the pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) are otherwise, it is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "If they are constructed with unmentioned materials, or if they have a crooked shape..."
A pavilion that is either too large or too small brings destruction to its builders.

That pavilion which is well-constructed with the means prescribed by the verbal roots, which is beautiful, symmetrical, pleasing, and brings auspiciousness to the agent of the action—thus [it is said]. || 26 ||
Then, on that field measuring three parts, one should prepare a square altar (vedī) of one cubit (aratni) for the sake of the mandala. || 27 ||
He speaks of the "emanation of the Veda" with the word *tat*.
In a field measured by that third part—that is, the third portion—of the thread in the middle of the pavilion;
otherwise, if one were to take a third part of the area of the field, it would result in something quite arbitrary.
As it has been said: "Then one should fashion the thread for the pavilion as threefold; by its middle portion, the altar (vedikā) is established in due order starting from the east.
Consequently, the altar consists of the ninth part.
As it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Having made the pavilion nine parts, the altar is considered to be in the central part."
One should prepare a square altar (*vedi*) in the middle of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), either three *aratnis* high or one *hasta* high,
for the sake of the mandala— the *Sarvatobhadra* mandala to be described later.
This has been stated in the description of the pavilion:

"Then, in the center of that [mandala] which is provided with four entrances, the wise one should construct an altar—one-third of a part [of the whole], measuring one *aratni* in height, resembling the interior of a mirror, and captivating to the mind. Thus it is said.
By many authors, the word *aratni* is also employed in the sense of a "hand" (*hasta*).

As stated in the *Kādima-tantra* after describing the characteristics of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*): "From four of those [finger-breadths] comes a fist (*muṣṭi*); a span (*vitasti*) is formed by three times that; an *aratni* is made from two of those; and a cubit (*hasta*) is from two of those, O Śivā. Furthermore, in many places in the *Śulba-sūtra*, Kātyāyana also employs the word *aratni* to mean a cubit (*hasta*).

In the *Mantramuktāvalī*, regarding the description of a two-cubit (*dvihasta*) sacrificial pit for the purpose of ten-thousand-fold oblations (*ayutahoma*), it is stated: "An *aratni* is [a measure] exceeding ten finger-breadths (*daśāṅgula*). In that same work, regarding the four-cubit pit for a hundred-thousand-fold oblation (*lakṣahoma*), it says: "An *aratni* is [a measure] exceeding twenty-four finger-breadths.
Therefore, here too, the word *aratni* is explained as being equivalent to a single cubit (*hasta*).
As it is stated in the Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā:
"It should be elevated at the hands and wide, measuring four cubits on all sides."
Also in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "A sacrificial altar (*vedi*), resembling a mirror, should be made of bricks or even of clay, with a height of one *rājahasta*, by a wise person desiring success.
Here, a *rājahasta* is the length from the tip of the middle finger [to the elbow].
In the *Pañcarātra* as well:
"The altar [should be] one-third of the pavilion;
its height is one-fourth of that."
Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Having divided the pavilion into three parts, the middle portion shall be the altar (*vedikā*);
its height should be one cubit, and it should be square and level."
The excellent altar should be constructed as firmly as possible with bricks, either baked or unbaked; or, in their absence, even with clay.
"Having straight sides, very smooth, and resembling the surface of a mirror.
Here, *utsedha* means height.

In the Siddhāntaśekhara, however, there is this distinction: "The altar (vedī) therein is of four kinds— the Caturasrā, the Padminī, the Śrīdharī, and the Sarvatobhadrā— for initiations (dīkṣā), installations (sthāpana), and so forth."
A square altar with four corners bestows all fruits;
for the consecration of tanks and similar works, it should be like a lotus-pool, resembling a lotus.
"For kings, the altar for the consecration should be the Sarvatobhadra or the Caturbhadrā;
for a wedding, the Śrīdharī altar, provided with twenty corners, resembling the surface of a mirror and free from depressions or elevations. Thus it is said.
The fault in the improper construction of the altar (vedikā) is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "An altar that is crooked on its sides, damp in the middle, rough, or unpleasant to look at,
and one that is deficient or excessive in measurement, destroys the work of the builder."
In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā, however, after describing the pavilion and other structures, it says:
"Having performed everything previously mentioned, either with or without the pavilion and so forth, one should prepare the maṇḍala as before, and especially the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). (27)
Even before the day of initiation, one should perform the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) on seven ritual days for the sake of attaining all auspiciousness. || 28 ||
Regarding the rite of depositing the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), he says "previously" (*prāg eva*).
It is stated that this should be performed seven days prior to the day of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth, in such a way that the initiation becomes the eighth [day].
By the term "according to rule" (*vidhivat*), it is indicated that it may be done with nine, five, three, or even immediately.
As it is stated in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
"In the rites of installation, initiation, consecration, and likewise in festivals;
in the sprinkling for the sake of pacification, in marriage, and in the binding of the sacred thread."
"In all auspicious rites,
one should perform the ritual sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) nine, seven, five, three days, or immediately prior to the day of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā). Thus it is said.

In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* as well: "Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made by means of Brahmins, the Preceptor (*deśika*) should perform the sacrifice of the auspicious sprouts (*maṅgalāṅkura-yajña*) on that very same day."

"Either on the seventh or the ninth day, and certainly before the sacrificial rite. Also elsewhere: "In various festivals, such as initiations, installations, and the rite of the *pavitra*, the performer of the ritual first plants auspicious sprouts; from that, the rite becomes auspicious."
"On the seventh or ninth day before the auspicious day for the performance of the rite,
or on the fifth day at a favorable moment (*muhūrta*), one should perform the ritual for the auspicious sprouts (*maṅgalāṅkura*).
Regarding this, having fasted on the preceding day and performed the *nāndī-śrāddha* according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, one should begin the offering of the sprouts.

As it has been said: "One who is already purified by his guru should, on the seventh day prior to the day of purification, form a resolve and fast; then the auspicious rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) should be performed."
"One should perform the Nāndīmukha-śrāddha on the preceding day and the Svastivācana; one should indeed carry out this according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra. Thus it is said.
Also in the Saṃhitā: "In all cases, there is the Abhyudaya-śrāddha as well as the production of the sprouts (aṅkura)."
"One should perform [the preliminary rite] at the very outset of an action whose nature is prosperity. || 28 ||
To the north of the pavilion, one should construct a secret hall extending from east to west; then, within it, the wise practitioner should fashion the mandala.
Regarding the hall (*śālā*):
therein, a measurement of twenty cubits in length and ten in width is the supreme dimension for a hall.
Since there is no purpose for such a large size, the hall should be constructed with half of this [measurement], according to the middle measurement.
Therefore, it should be made here ten cubits long and five cubits wide.
He states that very same thing: "extending from east to west."
One should construct a hut that is long and square in shape, concealed, surrounded on all sides by a wall and so forth, provided with a single door on the south side, and free from drafts.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Having made that firm hut situated toward the southwest, one should ensure it is free from drafts."
Upon that [ground], one should construct the mandala that is about to be described. || 29 ||
One should lay down five threads, each measuring five cubits;
among these, they should extend from east to west with an interval of twelve finger-breadths.
In that same manner, one should lay down eleven north-south threads;
forty squares are produced there, which one should then wipe clean. || 31 ||
In the row, there are four paths at the ends on both sides of the central square;
thus, two paths remain, and three squares are left here.
The wise one should color those squares with white, yellow, reddish-brown, and black powders;
then, he should fill the pathways with dark blue powder. || 33 ||
He describes the mandala itself as follows: "Five cubits," etc.

Having laid down a single cord measuring five cubits extending from east to west in the middle of the hall's width, one should lay two cords each at a distance of twelve finger-breadths on both the southern and northern sides of that central cord.
Then, one should lay down eleven threads intersecting those five threads;
"in that manner" means with intervals of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
In this way, all five cubits (*hasta*) are encompassed.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Having stretched out the cord, one should snap it so that it extends from south to north;
with a measurement of five cubits, one should drop two [lines] on each side."
"In the same way, according to the previously mentioned measurement, one should successively lay down eleven threads from east to west, each twelve finger-breadths apart and level;
then, upon those lines, [one should mark] the interval between the previous threads."
The word "should wipe" (pramārjayet) connects with what follows later.
One should wipe four paths in rows;
the meaning is "on the outside."
Because it will be stated [later] that "in the interior," one should clear away one path of four squares on the east, a southern path of eight squares, another path of four squares on the west,
and a northern path of eight squares.

Then, on both sides—on the two flanks—of the inner four-square (antaścatuṣka) and the middle four-square (madhyacatuṣka), one should erase two paths (vīthīs) consisting of two squares each; the phrase "one should erase" is to be supplied here.
From this, he states the resulting conclusion: "Thus... [iti].
In this mandala, three sets of four squares remain;
these remaining twelve squares situated in the three groups of four should each be colored with powders, beginning with white.
Therein, [the color] is white at the station of Vāyu,
yellow at the station of Agni, and ruddy at the station of the Rakṣases.
That "it is black in the station of Īśa" has been stated by the term *sudhīḥ*.
As it was said by the Teachers:
"Yellow, red, white, and black—each step [corresponds] to fire and the others, ending with Śarva."
Thus.
Immediately thereafter, one should fill the pathways with dark green [pigment]. (30–33)
Regarding the vessels for the ritual of planting the sprouts, they say there are three types:
the *pālikās*, the five-faced ones, and the shallow bowls (*śarāvas*), arranged in four successive stages. || 34 ||
Those consisting of Hari, Brahmā, and Śiva have been declared by the knowers of all Tantras;
their height should be inferred as sixteen, twelve, and eight [units] respectively. || 35 ||

Regarding the vessels for depositing the sprouts, he says "vessels" (*pātrāṇi*). Large, high shallow bowls (*śarāva*) themselves are referred to by the term *pālikā*. Those same *pālikās* when slightly lowered and provided with five openings are called *pañcamukhī*.
The *śarāva* vessels are well known.
By the phrase "by those who know all the tantras," it is stated that there is no distinction of vessels in rites such as the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of the five deities.
The first [group] has the form of Hari.
The second [group] has the form of Brahmā;
the third has the form of Śiva.
By this, it is stated that Hari, Brahmā, and Īśa are to be worshipped in these vessels.
Thus it is stated in the Sārasvata-mata: "One should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva in those vessels that have been mentioned."
Also in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "One should worship Rudra with sandalwood and flowers in shallow bowls (*śarāva*), Viṣṇu in *pālikā* vessels, and Brahmā in small jars (*ghaṭikā*). (34–35)
Having gradually wound auspicious threads around those [spots] with fingers' breadth intervals,
the preceptor, after washing them, places rice grains upon those locations.
One should place [the vessels] upon bunches of fragrant darbha grass, starting from the west;
one should fill the vessels with dried cow dung, sand, clay, and husks. || 37 ||
"Gradually by finger-breadths" is connected with what precedes.
However, there is a specific detail in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
"The width of the mouth of the *pālikā* is said to be sixteen finger-breadths."
It may be the throat-passage, which is eight finger-breadths in width.
The width of the footstool is declared to be six finger-breadths;
its height is four finger-breadths, and the joint between them should be one finger-breadth.
And at its junction, there should not be "I" (the letter *a*), nor even half of the footstool (*pādapīṭa*);
thus the five-faced *ghaṭikā* shall be the granter of all desires.
They say that the five faces indeed have a width of four finger-breadths:
four in the four directions and one above, according to the rule.
The width of the *ghaṭikā* is said to be twelve finger-breadths;
some teachers, however, state that it should be sixteen finger-breadths.
"The opening of the *śarāva* is said to be twelve *aṅgulas* in width;
its base at the bottom is stated to be four *aṅgulas* in width.
Also elsewhere: "In this [practice], the *ghaṭikā* should have five openings, measuring one *tāla* in both width and height."
There is one set of four faces toward the cardinal directions, while another equal portion is situated in the center.
The shallow bowl has a mouth as wide as a palm tree, with its height being half of its width;
its handle is four finger-breadths in circumference, and its neck is raised, excluding the opening.
"Alternatively, they may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even of clay, according to availability.
However, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, it says: "One should prepare the *pālikā* and other vessels according to what is available."
"Thus.
"Those" refers to the vessels.
"Auspicious" means free from black discoloration, scars, and the like.
"With thread" means with a triple-stranded cord.
In this regard, it should be understood that the washing comes first, followed by the wrapping with the thread.
"A bunch of *darbha* grass" is what will be described later.
Regarding "in the west and so forth":
one should place four small bowls in the western group of four, four five-faced vessels in the central group of four, and four shallow cups in the eastern group of four.
It should be understood that the installation begins with the southeast (āgneya) among those [corners].
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "One should place the vessels in them, individually in each of the four [corners], starting from the southeast and ending with the northeast."
Regarding "karīṣa": *karīṣa* is the powder of dried cow dung.
With these [substances], one should fill all the vessels in successive order.
And it is said in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "One should fill them in successive order.
Also in the *Prayogasāra*: "One should fill the vessels from above with earth, sand, and cow-dung."
Thus it is said.
Regarding this, there is a specific detail in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"On another day, having worshipped the spade with perfumes and other offerings..."
Accompanied by song and dance, and provided with elephants and horses.
The preceptor and the others, some mounted on chariots and others likewise mounted on elephants,
went to the bank of a pond, a river, or a flower grove.
There, having swept a pure portion of the ground with *darbha* grass while reciting the *astra-mantra*,
and having sprinkled it with *arghya* water while recollecting the respective mantras;
Having invoked the Earth with the heart-mantra, one should worship her with perfumes and flowers;
then, having dug the earth with a spade while reciting the weapon-mantra, [one should take] the soil.
Having taken [the earth] with the Vāmadeva mantra, one should fill a bronze vessel;
having cleansed the clay with the Hṛdaya mantra and wiped it with a cloth, one should hold it.
Then the preceptor, having performed a circumambulation of the city or the residence with the sounds of all auspicious instruments, should lead [the image] to the pavilion.
A wise person should perform this rite during the day and not at night.
Thus [ends verses 36–37].
The knower of the tantras, having washed the seeds with milk using the Sudhā-bīja mantra, should consecrate them with the root mantra, preceded by the five sounds. || 38 ||
Preceded by auspicious customs and the benedictory words of the twice-born,
the preceptor, with a restrained mind, should offer [the oblation] into those vessels.
Regarding the sowing of seeds in those [vessels], he says "with nectar" (sudhā): that is, with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*. "With milk" means with cow's milk; "having washed" [is the sense].
In the Mahākapilapañcarātra, however, there is this distinction:
"Having washed [the vessel] with water using the twelve-syllable mantra."
In the *Sārasvata-mata* as well, it is stated: "Having washed those seeds with water and milk in succession.
This is indicated by the phrase "one who knows the Tantras."
"By the root-mantra" means they should be consecrated one hundred and eight times with the root-mantra and the mantra to be given.
As it is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
"When no number is specified for recitations and the like, there should be one hundred and eight or one thousand."
Thus [it is said]. The five sounds, however, are the kettledrum (*paṭaha*), the *ḍhakkā* drum, the clay drum (*mṛdaṅga*), wind instruments (*mukhavādya*), and the conch (*śaṅkha*).
"Auspicious custom" (*maṅgalācāra*) refers to that which is well-known in various regions, preceded by the sound of *ulūlu* and so forth.

By the phrase "the teacher with a restrained mind," it is stated that having unified those seeds, he should, at night, facing either east or north, cast them into the *pālikā* vessels and so forth while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
This is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
Facing either the east or the north, one should sow all the seeds in order within the *pālikās* and other vessels, using the primary root-mantra as the seed-syllable.
Since Soma is the lord of seeds, one should perform the sowing at night. Thus it is said.
In the opinion of Sārasvata as well: "Since he becomes radiant from the seeds and the deities during the night, therefore the Guru should sow the seeds only at night. (38-39)
Rice, black gram, pigeon pea, mung bean, sesame,
flat bean, mustard, horse gram, millet, and kidney bean— these are the seeds for the rite of producing sprouts.
He states the seeds, beginning with "śāli": *śāli* refers to winter rice; *śyāma* is *śyāmāka*, which is well known as *sāvā* in the Kānyakubja dialect.
Āḍhakī is the same as tūvarī; niṣpāva is the same as rājamāṣa,
because it is explained thus in Śrīdhara’s commentary on the Viṣṇupurāṇa.
"One should avoid *niṣpāva* and *rājamāṣa* seeds while the deity is asleep," because of this separate statement, there is no sublation [of the general rule] in that case.
In the *Sārasvata-mata*, the worship of deities for each individual seed is prescribed:
"One should worship Skanda in *priyaṅgu*, Vāyu in *niṣpāva*, and Agni in *kulatthaka*."
One should offer Nirṛti in āḍhakī, Soma in mudge, and Vaivasvata in sesame.
"One should worship Prajāpati when the grain is rice (*śāli*), Ananta when it is mustard (*sarṣapa*),
Indra when it is black (*śyāma*), and Varuṇa when it is black gram (*māṣa*), O Daughter of the Mountain. Furthermore, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, the daily worship of Soma is also prescribed.

"One should worship Soma daily until the day of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa). When the day of the preliminary consecration arrives, the Guru should perform the dismissal (udvāsana) of Soma. Thus [it is said]. (40)

Having sprinkled [the site] with water mixed with turmeric and covered it with cloths, the preceptor should offer oblations (bali) into three types of vessels in the directions, starting from the east. || 41 ||
Regarding *haridrā* (turmeric):
the mantra for that is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"To Tryambaka, to Śarva, to Śaṅkara, and to Śiva..."
Homage again and again to the eternal one, the foremost in all the worlds.
"Having scattered [the seeds] with this mantra, one should rain down water mixed with turmeric powder; one should sprinkle those [seeds] with water day after day.
This is indicated by the phrase "this, O Teacher."
"With garments" means with new garments; the plural number, according to the *kapiñjalādhikaraṇa* principle, results in a limit of three.
"Having covered"—that is, the four vessels, each with one [garment]. The syntactical connection is: "one should cast the offering at night."
In the morning, having again performed the sweeping of the ground and other rites, one should offer the bali-oblation at the beginning of the second night.
At night, one should worship with names beginning with *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*, using the names of the Lords of Night:
Bhūtas, Pitṛs, Yakṣas, Nāgas, Brahmā, Śiva, and Hari. (42)

Regarding the phrase "beginning with the Praṇava": the mantra for that occasion is: *Oṃ, obeisance to the spirits; may they accept this bali-offering, together with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and betel-leaves—svāhā*.
The mantra is to be formulated in the same way for other occasions as well.

In the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*, however, there is this distinction: "Then one should sprinkle [the seeds] with pure water mixed with fragrance for three nights, or even for five nights, according to the rule. In the *Sārasvata-mata*, it is said: "Another person should never look at the sprouts once they have fully emerged."
"Only the teacher or his disciple, by his command, should enter. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Having carefully covered them with cloths, one should cause them to be well-guarded. (42)
The deities for all seven nights have been proclaimed;
for the Bhūtas, there should be parched grain, sesame seeds, turmeric, curd, and barley meal.
Rice mixed with sesame seeds is prescribed for the ancestors;
parched grain mixed with karambha and coconut water is for the yakṣas. || 44 ||
To the Nāgas, flour mixed with parched grain; to Brahmā, lotus-shaped unbroken rice (akṣata);
to Śarva, food accompanied by cakes; and to Viṣṇu, rice cooked with jaggery. || 45 ||
Regarding the sacrificial materials for the *bali* offerings on each of the seven nights, he says: "To the *bhūtas*...
up to the end of "sānnāḥ" constitutes six [offerings] on the first night;
this very [set] is named the *bhūtakrūra*.
As it has been said:
"The food consisting of parched grain, sesame, red powder, curd, and barley meal is called *bhūtakrūra*.
*Karambha* refers to curd and barley meal.

*Akṣatāḥ* refers to unbroken grains of rice. When the offering of oblations (*balidāna*) takes place over nine nights, then the materials for the oblation and the deities for each of the two-night periods have been stated by the teachers: "The Vaiṣṇava [oblation] is milk-rice (*dugdhānna*), and the Vaiṣṇaveya is *kṛśara* (rice and sesame), if the oblation is prescribed to be performed sequentially throughout the nine nights. (43–45)
Then, one should offer bali according to the rules even to the Lords of the World (Lokeśvaras).
For the sake of prosperity during initiations, consecrations, the entry into a new house, and festivals, one should perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa). || 46 ||
Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then):
in each respective direction, an offering (*bali*) consisting of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and so forth should be presented.
Among them, the offering for Ananta is between the southwest (*nairṛtya*) and the west (*pratīcī*), and that for Brahmā is between the northeast (*īśa*) and the east (*pūrva*).
By the phrase "according to rule" (*vidhivat*), it is indicated that the *bali* offering to the directions mentioned previously should also be performed here.
The application (*viniyoga*) of these vessels will be explained later.
The examination of the sprouts (*aṅkura-parīkṣā*) is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "One should examine the sprouts for the sake of the prosperity of the patron (*yajamāna*)."
They have grown straight upward, tender, and white.
One should avoid those that are smoke-colored, incomplete, or similarly distorted; as well as those that are dark-green, crooked, and inauspicious.
A black comet with a smoky luster causes drought,
strife, incomplete harvests, the destruction of people, famine, and dark sprouts [of calamity].
If the sprout points horizontally, there will be disease; likewise, if it is crooked, there is fear of enemies.
When an inauspicious sprout has arisen, one should perform a propitiatory fire sacrifice (śāntihoma).

"The Guru, together with those bearing the [divine] forms, should perform the oblation with the root mantra, or with the Aghora-weapon mantra or the Astra-mantra, one hundred or even a thousand times. Thus it is said. Also, in the Sārasvata-mata: "One should indicate the auspicious or inauspicious results for the patron by means of well-developed sprouts."
"With dark green sprouts there is loss of wealth; with those growing horizontally, disease; with those swaying, [unrest]; with those bent, suffering;
with those poorly formed, death; with those curved, diseases; and with those [growing] in the wrong place or region, the loss of what is desired. Thus [it is said]. (46)
In the previously described pavilion, the wise man [should divide] the area outside the altar into three parts.
Having divided the field, one should designate the eastern and other directions within the central portion;
then, in the eight directions, one should construct sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) of beautiful form in due order. || 48 ||
He states the location of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) with the words "in the east," and so forth.

The connection is as follows: having divided the area outside the altar on all sides—dividing the line through the center of the field into three parts—one should, in due order, fashion beautiful-shaped pits in the eight directions starting from the east, following the sequence clockwise at each respective central portion.
"Vidvān" (the learned one) means one who knows even the five girdles and so forth.
"Āśāsu" (in the quarters) means in the directions ending with Īśāna;
for according to the technical rule: "Because of the exclusion of the limits mentioned starting from the east, the specific sequence alone is intended."

The meaning is that by him the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be constructed after leaving aside one-quarter of the altar (vedi) and leaving aside the space there suitable for the girdle (mekhalā) which is to be described later.
Thus it becomes complete.
This was stated by Somaśambhu: "Having left aside the interval of one quarter of the altar..."
Thus it is said.
Also in the Siddhāntaśekhara: "Having abandoned one-fourth of the Veda.
Thus.
In the Nāradīya [Tantra] as well: "The space between the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the altar (vedī) should be one and a quarter cubits.
Here, the word "quarter" (pāda) indicates something slightly more than that.
Therefore, this belongs to the scope of the medium and superior pavilions (*maṇḍapa*).
It is also stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "The distance between the altar (*vedikā*) and the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be two cubits."
This concerns the subject of a pavilion (maṇḍapa) measuring twenty-four cubits.
However, in the Vāsiṣṭha-saṃhitā it is said:
"Having left a space of thirteen finger-breadths on each of the four sides of the altar (vedikā)..."
"The wise man should duly construct the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) as prescribed in his own tradition.
Here, "sacrificial pits" refers to those equipped with girdles (mekhalās). (47–48)
The square, the half-moon, the triangle, the perfect circle, the hexagon, the lotus-shaped, and the octagon—these are their names. || 49 ||
He states that very sequence as "quadrangular" (caturasram).
This has been said in the Āmnāyarahasya:
"In the procedure for the nine pits (kuṇḍas), when the eight pits are situated in the cardinal directions..."
Thus [ends the verse]. 49.
The preceptor’s sacrificial pit (ācāryakuṇḍa) should be in the middle between Gaurīpati and Mahendra;
one should prepare a piece of ground measuring one cubit, as previously described. || 50 ||
This sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be square on all sides, which brings auspiciousness;
those learned in the Tantras know it to be one cubit (hasta) in measure, consisting of twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas). || 51 ||
The measurement of a finger (mānāṅgula) is declared to be the length of the middle joint of the middle finger of the right hand of the artisan. || 52 ||
Regarding "the preceptor’s pit" (ācāryakuṇḍa):
between Gaurīpati and Mahendra, in the intermediate direction between the northeast and the east, there should be the preceptor’s pit.
This is stated in that very same [text]:
One should cause the ninth fire-pit (kuṇḍa) to be made in the intermediate direction between the east and the northeast;
it may be either circular or square.
Thus it is said.
As it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Between Purandara and Īśa, [the site] should be circular or square;
that is prescribed for the preceptor."
Elsewhere it is also said: "Some scholars say that the space between the directions of Gaurīpati (the North-East) and Surapati (the East) is circular.
And in the *Kriyāsāra* as well: "The central space of the two lords of the Bull (the North-East) may be either circular or square."
Thus [it is said].
In that regard, because it serves as the archetype for all sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), he first states the characteristics of the square pit, beginning with the word "one cubit" (*hasta*).
The phrase "as before" refers to the method of constructing the square of the *vāstumaṇḍala*.

The connection is that one should imagine [the fire] on all sides in the four directions. Since the measurement of a square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) was stated in *hasta*s, he also states the measurement in *aṅgula*s for the purpose of establishing those characteristics. "Of the performer" refers to the disciple who is to be consecrated, and not the preceptor (*ācārya*).
Because the word "agent" (*kartṛ*) is applied to the disciple as well, by virtue of his being the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*).
Now, one might ask: why is the teacher (*ācārya*) alone not taken here as the one denoted by the primary sense of the word "agent"? To this it is replied:

"Regarding the acts of giving, reciting, undertaking, choosing a boon, choosing a bridegroom, vows, and measurements, one should rely upon the sacrificer"—this is because of the statement of Kātyāyana.
Now, if it is asked: "This [rule] pertains to the Śrauta ritual, while the present context pertains to the Tantric; how then can there be syntactic unity?"—that is not so.
This is because of the statement: "And that which is spoken by others [is authoritative] provided it is not contradictory.
For example, in the case of the Soma sacrifice and other Vedic rites, it is said:
"The rite must always be performed by one wearing the sacred thread (yajñopavītin) and with the topknot tied."
"An action must be performed by one who is pure"— since such [injunctions] are not contradictory, even the Smārta tradition is accepted here as well. It is the same in this case too.
For this very reason it has been said: "The ritual action is one and the same as recognized across all branches (*sarvaśākhā-pratyaya*).
By the phrase "those who know the *tantras*," it is meant those who are experts in the various characteristics of finger-measures (*aṅgula*) described in their respective *tantras*.
Regarding the phrase "of the middle finger joint":
By the word *parva*, the middle joint (*madhyamaparva*) is intended. The measurement of the length of that [joint] is one *aṅgula*.
Alternatively, the connection is that the measurement of the length of the middle joint of the middle finger is one *aṅgula*. (50–52)
The measure-finger (mānāṅgula) is declared to be fashioned from eight barley grains;
a wise man should divide a square field into five parts. || 53 ||

In order to establish the conventional usage of the *yava* (barley-corn) which the author will employ later in the passage beginning with "in the sequence of two *yavas," he states "of the *yavas*" (*yavānām*), meaning that a *yava* is one-eighth of an *aṅgula*.
The term "measuring *aṅgula*" (*mānāṅgula*) is merely another name for that very same [unit]; it is not a separate definition of an *aṅgula*.
Or [it is so] because of the absence of the employment of words such as "or" (*vā*).
And in another text:
"The subtle particle of dust that is seen when the sun has passed through a lattice window..."
First, they declare that to be the *trasareṇu*, the smallest unit of measurement.
Eight of those atoms (paramāṇu) should be known as one mote of dust in a sunbeam (trasareṇu); eight of these motes of dust are traditionally remembered as one particle of dust (reṇu).
Eight of those dust particles are known by the wise as a *bālāgra* (the tip of a hair);
eight *bālāgras* are a *likhyā*, and eight *likhyās* are known as a *yūkā*.
They say eight *yūkās* make one *yava*, and eight *yavas* make one *aṅgula*. Twenty-one finger-joints (*aṅgula-parvan*) are to be known as one *ratni*.
"Twenty-four fingers indeed shall constitute one *hasta*.
Thus, two fingers are spoken of as a single unit.
This is also stated in the *Trailokyasāra*:
"The measure of a finger (aṅgula) is the middle joint of the middle finger of the maker;
[it consists of] eight horizontal barley-corns (yava-udara) or three grains of rice (vrīhi) with their tips pointing upwards. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, it is stated that the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) must be constructed using the *mātrā-aṅgula* measure alone.
For example:
according to the measurement prescribed by Śiva for the dimensions of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), a cubit (hasta) consists of twelve finger-breadths (mātrāṅgula);
furthermore, the best [measurement] is determined by the length of the middle joint of the middle finger.
"By this same measurement in finger-breadths (mātrāṅgula), the girdle, the neck, the navel,
and the womb of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍayoni) are to be made.
Thus it is said.
According to the *Maya* [Tantra] as well— beginning with the passage, "That which has increased by the sequence of atoms is called the *mānāṅgula*," and so forth—
it is stated that eight *yavas* constitute one *aṅgula*.
"An *aṅgula* shall be one *mātra*, and a *vitasti* is twelve *aṅgulas*," and so on, up to that point.
Also, in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "Eight *yavas* shall constitute an *aṅgula*; twenty-four *aṅgulas* make a *kara*."
"And another [measure] is twenty-four finger-breadths, measured by one's own thumb. Thus it is said.
In that context, there is likewise equality between the thumb and the middle joint of the finger.
Now, if it is argued: "Even though the use of the word 'or' (*vā*) and so forth is not present here, a choice will nevertheless arise from the very words *mātrāṅgula* and *mānāṅgula* themselves."

That is not so; for even further on, there is no usage [of the term] as distinct [from the others]. However, where in the *Pañcarātra* the definition of the five types of *aṅgula* is stated, there their specific arrangement is also explained.
But here, since no specific restriction has been stated, it is merely a synonym;
as it is said in the *Pañcarātra*:
"Those rays of the sun which reach the path of the window..."
Within them, subtle particles called *trasareṇus* move about.
Eight of those atoms (paramāṇu) make one speck of dust (reṇu);
eight of those make a tip of a hair (bālāgra); eight of those make a nit (likṣā); and eight of those make a louse (yūkā).
Eight of those barley-corns are declared to be one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*);
