that [finger] with seven barley-corns is the best, while the same [with eight] is the middle.
Six barley grains with their husks are declared to be the measure of the *mānāṅgula*;
by placing eight such barley grains across, the *mānāntarāṅgula* is defined.
The length between the two joints in the middle of the middle finger of the disciple’s right hand is declared to be a *mātrāṅgula*.
A fist is formed by the remaining fingers excluding the thumb;
one should divide this into four parts, and one such part is known as a *muṣṭyaṅguli*.
Having divided any given human height into ten parts,
and then having divided one of those parts into twelve, one such part constitutes one finger-breadth (aṅgula).
One should know that the "finger-measure obtained from the body" (dehalabdha-aṅgula) is its [the body's] measure;
furthermore, the height of the image should be based on the "great finger-measure" (mahāmāna-aṅgula).
That which is the finger-measure of the great standard (mahāmāna) is called the measure-finger (mātrāṅgula);
one should fashion the limbs of the image using precisely this measure-finger of the other standard.
One should construct the palaces and other structures using that same measurement or by another measurement;
furthermore, the procedure for the altars, pedestals, palanquins, chariots, and so forth is as follows.
It should be measured by the *mānāṅgula* alone and not by any other;
indeed, one should prepare the ritual implements here according to the *mānāṅgula*.
"The implements for the oblation, such as the *sruva* ladle and others, and the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) are based on the *mānāṅgula* finger-breadth;
one may also fashion the pit and other elements using the *dehalabdha-aṅgula* (the finger-measure obtained from one's own body).
In many manuscripts, the reading "mānāṅgulam" appears in both instances.
In one instance, the term *mānāṅgula* is technical (pāribhāṣika); in the other, it is to be explained etymologically (yaugika) as "an angula by means of measurement" (*mānena pramāṇena*).
The area of the quadrangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) has been stated according to its definition;
since that [area] consists of angulas, and because it is impossible to state it without knowing them, it is now being discussed.

Regarding this, Bhāskarācārya states in the *Līlāvatī*: "In the case of an isosceles triangle, an equilateral quadrilateral, and likewise a rectangle, [the area] is the product of its base and height."
In the *Triśatikā*, Śrīdhara Ācārya also states: "The rule for generating [the area] arises in the case of an equilateral trapezoid and in a triangular field:
one should multiply half the sum of the base and the face by the middle perpendicular."
In this manner, twenty-four multiplied by twenty-four yields five hundred and seventy-six finger-breadths as the area;
this very area is to be understood for all eight types of fire-pits (kuṇḍa).
Therefore, this alone is the fundamental form (prakṛti) for all fire-pits.

The types beginning with two cubits are now described:

In that context, the root and its respective extension-line (āyāma-sūtra) are synonyms for the "line through the middle of the instrument" (karaṇī-madhya-sūtra) and so forth.

For example:

Having subtracted the square from the last odd number, one should double the square root if it is even; having subtracted that square from the first odd number, one should set down twice the quotient obtained.

"One should place double that amount in each row; thus, repeatedly, the square of the row shall be the area.

for a five-cubit square, it is forty-nine minus one-third.

By this [measure], there are 53 *aṅgulas*, 5 *yavas*, 2 *likhyās*, and 4 *yūkās*; such is the cord for five cubits (*pañcahasta-karaṇī*). When nineteen is subtracted from sixty-four, it is fifty-five; by this [measure], there are 58 *aṅgulas*, 6 *yavas*, 3 *likhyās*, and 4 *yūkās*; such is the cord for six cubits (*ṣaḍhasta-karaṇī*).
In a seven-cubit [square], the diagonal (karaṇī) is considered to be sixty-three minus half;
in an eight-cubit [square], it is sixty-eight minus twice seventeen.

By this [calculation], the measuring cord (karaṇī) for eight cubits is 67 aṅgulas, 7 barley-corns (yava), 7 louse-eggs (yūkā), and 4 nits (likhyā). For nine cubits, the cord should be made 72 aṅgulas,
minus 19 in two directions and 76 in one direction.

By this [calculation], there are 75 finger-breadths (aṅgulas), 7 barley-corns (yavas), and 2 louse-eggs (yūkas) in the measuring-line (likhyā); such is the measuring-line for ten cubits (daśahasta-karaṇī). Having fashioned the desired square according to the method prescribed for the yoni and other parts, thus have I clearly stated the measuring-lines for sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) up to ten cubits in size. (63–65)
The depth of the excavation is said to be equal to the width of the pit.

Now, regarding the excavation of the pit (*kuṇḍa*), he says "yāvān" (as much as). The meaning is that the excavation should be made with a measurement equal to the extent of the pit's width, which is its middle cord (*madhyasūtra*). Having stated that all pits are one cubit (*hasta*) in measure—
In the Kādima[tantra]: "The *aratni* is the standard measure for all the aforementioned fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*).
The synonymy between *aratni* and *hasta* has been explained by that very same [text] as previously demonstrated.
Elsewhere also it is said: "Whatever the measurement of the width of the *kuṇḍa* has been stated, that same measurement is prescribed for the excavation as well.
And the Teachers say: "With twenty-four finger-breadths..."
Then, having measured out the area of the ground with a cord, he should dig it to that same depth with those [spades].
Thus it is said.
In the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā* as well: "The sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is deep according to its width.
And in the *Divyasārasvata*: "Having first drawn lines to form a square divided into four compartments, as before..."

"In the middle of that, one should dig a pit as deep and long as the measurement of a cubit. Thus it is said. Also in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*: "Twenty-four finger-breadths in length, provided with a corresponding excavation."
Others, however, say that the pit should be dug together with the girdle (mekhalā).
This is stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"One should dig a pit one cubit deep horizontally and upwards, together with the girdle."
Thus [it is said]. Also in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*: "Having ascertained the height of the five triple girdles, one should dig the remainder below.
Viśvakarman also says: "The depth of the excavation is declared to be one-eighth of the width, while the depression [at the bottom] is fifteen finger-breadths."
"Or it may be elevated by nine finger-breadths.
Thus he himself will say.
In the *Prathama* [Tantra] as well: "The pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be measured in *jināṅgula*s crosswise and upward, together with the girdle (*mekhalā*).
Also, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The excavation of the pit should be equal in measure to the pit itself, including the girdle above."
Thus,
between these two positions, it is the first position alone that appears to be logically sound; for:

"One should know the true nature of the *kuṇḍa* as the supreme body of *prakṛti*," and so forth; for by such statements, the status of the girdles (*mekhalā*) as constituent parts (*aṅga*) is declared.
Since they constitute ornaments, it is not logical for one to bathe with them.
If it is argued that "if they were merely ornaments, there might be occasions when they ought not to be used," we say no;
for that which is devoid of erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) brings about the destruction of the sacrificer.
Because of this statement, the wearing of ornaments is also necessary. Furthermore, it is said: "Death [occurs] when the girdle is broken," and likewise: "The sacrificial pit has a worn-out girdle."
If it is argued that [the girdle] is an auxiliary because its deficiency is stated to be a defect in such passages as, "When the girdle is excessive due to pride, diseases increase," and so forth—
let it indeed be an auxiliary; nevertheless, bathing with it is untenable,
because it is a logical principle that the performance of the action is understood to apply to the primary rite.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for the essential nature of the pit (*kuṇḍa*) to be attained without the act of digging, it is also illogical for that [digging], which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) contributing directly through a visible means (*dṛṣṭadvārā sannipatyopakāraka*), to be established as an auxiliary contributing indirectly through an invisible means (*adṛṣṭadvārā ārādupakāraka*) along with the girdle (*mekhalā*).
And it is said in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:

"The digging [of the pit] is declared to be equal to the act of measuring the pit; its status as an auxiliary [to the sacrifice] is established through direct assistance (sannipatyopakāra), while the girdle (mekhalā) and so forth remain [as auxiliaries in that same manner]. Thus it is said.
Nor should it be argued that the girdles (*mekhalā*) are subsidiary parts of the pit (*khāta*), as is the case with the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites for rice grains;
for by such statements as "the pits have three girdles," they are prescribed specifically as parts of the pit.

Furthermore, if the application of the ritual effect were not accepted as occurring in the primary element, then even in the case of pits measuring two cubits and so forth, the doubling of the area would not be attained.

In that case as well, the doubling and so forth of the result of the cubit-cubed excavation for one cubit and so on would constitute its *karaṇī* (the diagonal) based on the measure of its square root;
and that is undesirable, for it would follow that, according to your view, the excavation would not conform [to the prescribed dimensions].
Furthermore, in the case of the three-tiered altar (*trimekhalā*), there would be a separate excavation.
In the case of five girdles, it is one way;
in the case of twelve-finger-width girdles, it is another.
Furthermore, there is the statement of Viśvakarman: "The depression should be fifteen finger-widths, while the elevation and so forth should be nine finger-widths."
Also in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*:
"Having determined the height of the three girdles as five [parts], one should dig the remainder below."

By means of the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of these two specific statements with the phrase "above the girdle," other general injunctions must necessarily be explained. This is just as, regarding the scope of a specific injunction such as "he divides the *āgneya* cake into four parts," there exists a corresponding general rule: "he divides the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) into four parts."
As stated by the author of the Vārttika: "A general rule that is unclear should be restricted by means of a specific one.
Therefore, even against your will, you must accept that a single girdle (*mekhalā*) is to be worn in the *kuṇḍa*, and that it is to be dug out without a girdle;
for there is no injunction prescribing [the digging] together with a girdle.

Therefore, the established conclusion is that the pit should be dug even without a girdle (*mekhalā*). As for the scriptural injunctions regarding digging the pit together with a girdle, these apply to sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) measuring four *aratnis*, one *hasta*, and so forth;
it should be understood that they pertain to such cases because there is no purpose for an excess in the depth of the pit when performing oblations (*homa*) numbering fifty or more.
For it has been said: "Where there is a conflict between two Vedic texts (śruti), both are remembered as dharma;
but where there is a conflict between two Smṛtis, their respective scopes must be determined separately.
It is with this very intention that it was stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"One should have three girdles made, measuring four, three, and two finger-breadths respectively;
or else, one may make a single girdle in abbreviated rites.
As for what was stated by that same author—namely, that since the plural number is used here, it is logical to favor the inclusion of many [girdles]—that too is not correct.
Since our own position has been stated more extensively, that very view should be accepted.
And it was said by Jaimini:
"In a conflict between properties of equal status, the property belonging to the majority shall prevail."
Thus, in that regard, according to the first position, the result for its cubic cubits is 13,824; according to the latter position, it is 14,724. || 66 ||
Whatever is the form of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), such is the form of the girdles (mekhalās).

The three girdles of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be known, in sequence, as being one, two, and one-and-a-half finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in height and length, measuring approximately one fist in circumference.
In a pit measuring one *aratni*, they should be three, two, or one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) in size;
in a pit measuring one cubit (*hasta*), they should be four, three, or two finger-breadths.
Then Mekhalā said: "Regarding the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*).

The meaning is that the form of the sacrificial pits—such as the square, the womb-shaped (*yoni*), and so forth—is the same as the form of the girdles (*mekhalās*); that is, on a square pit, the girdle should be square in form, and on a womb-shaped pit, the girdle should be womb-shaped.
By this, the girdles should be made in the shape of a circle.
It has been stated that there is no loss of their squareness regarding the actual form of the girdles.
"Three" refers to the middle position.
The position of five girdles is the best;
the position of one girdle is the least.
However, according to the author's own statement, the position of three girdles alone is the superior position.
In that case, the position of two girdles is the middling one;
the position of a single girdle is the inferior one.
As it is stated in the *Vāyavīya-saṃhitā*: "Or there may be three girdles, or two, or even one."
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Kriyāsāra*: "A sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) joined with the navel and the womb, and having three girdles (*mekhalā*), is excellent;
a pit with two girdles is middling; it is inferior if it has only one girdle."

Elsewhere also— "Three girdles for the pit, or two girdles, or else the wise man may use a single girdle. But in the *Somaśambhu*, it says: "The pit of a twice-born man has three girdles; that of a Kṣatriya has two girdles."

"But for a Vaiśya, there is only one girdle. Thus, since it has been stated that "the [girdles] are four, three, and two finger-breadths" with reference to the one-cubit pit (*ekahastakuṇḍa*), which serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*) for all pits, this applies everywhere.
It is understood that the girdles (mekhalās) should be made with portions of one-sixth, one-eighth, and one-twelfth [of the total height] respectively,
according to the Bhaṭṭa principle that "the modification (vikṛti) should be performed like the archetype (prakṛti).
This has been stated by Somaśambhu:
"The twenty-fourth part of the pit (kuṇḍa) is designated as one finger (aṅgula);
by this [unit] the girdle (mekhalā), the neck (kaṇṭha), and the navel (nābhi) are to be divided. Thus it is said.
In the Mahākapila-pañcarātra, however, it is stated even more clearly:
The first [line] is said to be one-sixth of the pit (kuṇḍa), the second one-eighth,
and the third one-twelfth.
Thus it is taught.
Also in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*: "O Goddess, hear from me concerning the girdles (mekhalās), especially regarding those starting from two cubits;
they should be measured by portions of six, eight, and twelve [aṅgulas], and thus established, they are auspicious.
As for what the author of the treatise has stated regarding the fist-sized and other altars, even when they are two cubits or more, that should be understood as being according to gross measurement.
Regarding the phrase "but [a size] of only one fist": the expression "in height and length" applies in all cases up to the limit of one cubit (*hasta*).

In this context, according to the stated measurement of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), a *muṣṭi*-sized pit is twenty-one *aṅgulas* in measure, since *muṣṭi* and *ratni* are synonyms. In that *muṣṭi*-pit,
the first [line] is three and a half *aṅgulas*,
and the middle [line] is four *aṅgulas* plus five barley-corns (*yava*).
The third [measurement] is one and three-quarter *aṅgulas*.
The pit (*kuṇḍa*) is said to be the measure of an *aratni*, which, according to the measurement of *aṅgulas*, is twenty-two and a half *aṅgulas*.
This is because it is stated: "An *aratni* is a hand together with the little finger, that being the hand minus its sixteenth part."
Among those, the first is three and three-quarter *aṅgulas*;
the middle one is six and a half *yavas* long;
and the third is two *aṅgulas* minus one *yava*.
Herein is the method for fashioning the girdle (*mekhalā*).
On the first tier, a girdle should be made with a height of two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and a width of nine finger-breadths, starting from the neck.
Above that, the second [girdle] should have a height of three finger-breadths and a width of seven finger-breadths.
Above that, it is four finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths in width;
thus, by its fruit, it indeed possesses the dimension of four, three, two, and one finger-breadths.
And it has been said:
"Whichever girdle was previously mentioned, each of those is declared to be a 'ground' (bhūmi).
By this, the first [girdle] is nine finger-breadths high internally and four finger-breadths wide, while it is four finger-breadths high externally.
The second [line] is five finger-breadths high and three finger-breadths wide internally, while externally it is three finger-breadths high.
The third, however, is two finger-breadths high and two finger-breadths wide on both sides.
As it is said in the *Mohaśūrottara*: "With four [fingers] at the corners, three at the Rāmas, and two at the Yamas"—here, "corners" (*koṇa*) refers to the four [corners].
Elsewhere it is also said: "Alternatively, three [lines] measuring four, three, or two finger-breadths are auspicious in all cases.
Viśvakarman also says: "The elevated [line] and the others [are measured] by nine finger-breadths."
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Kriyāsāra*: "In this [context], the height of the primary girdle is stated to be nine finger-breadths;
the height of the outer girdle is traditionally recorded as five finger-breadths."
"The height of the outer girdle is two finger-breadths in sequence;
its width is four, three, and two finger-breadths, provided with three girdles.
Also, in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*: "The first [girdle] is two finger-breadths in length and nine finger-breadths in height."
"The middle [line] is three finger-breadths on the outside, while the third is by two finger-breadths.
Also, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The twenty-fourth part of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) is traditionally known as one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*)."
Furthermore, having established the definition of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), it is said: "The upper [line] consists of four, three, and two [units];
the middle and lower [lines] are likewise declared to be three [units each], both in width and in height.
By this, it is meant that the first [line] is four *aṅgulas*, the one above it is three *aṅgulas*, and the one above that is two *aṅgulas*.
The two interpretations—that [the width] is four *aṅgulas* on the outside, three *aṅgulas* in the middle inside, and two *aṅgulas* touching the neck—are refuted.
As for the definition of some:
"When the diameter is divided into twenty-four parts, [the widths] are four, three, and two parts respectively."
"Outside the neck on all sides, a girdle is considered appropriate, with a height equal to nine or eight parts of the *rāma* garment.
Here, the heights of the second and third [sections] are stated as six parts and three parts respectively;
that is inconsistent.

This is because it contradicts many written texts and because there is an absence of any statement establishing this. Furthermore, that which was stated by that very same person— namely, "Some have said that these [lines] are equal in width and height"— is merely a manifestation of ignorance,
due to a failure to understand the meaning of the specific scriptural passages cited.

Furthermore, the claim that statements such as "by means of fingers [measuring] Koṇa, Rāma, and Yama" (i.e., nine, three, and four) result in [the measurement of] the width alone is also a sign of ignorance.
For the Teachers have stated:
"Endowed with qualities preceded by Sattva, they are respectively twelve, eight, and four fingers in height."
"Girdles (mekhalā) four finger-breadths wide on all sides are considered to bestow all supernatural powers (siddhis).
Following that opinion, others have also stated the measurement for all girdles as "eight vitastis and half of that" (i.e., four vitastis).
However, since that [latter] is explicitly stated to "bestow all supernatural powers," it should be understood as referring to a specific result.
There too, first, the outer neck-ring (*kaṇṭha*) is twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width and four finger-breadths in height.
Above that, the second [ring] is eight finger-breadths in width and four finger-breadths in height.
Above that, it should be understood that [the third ring] is four finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths in width.
Thus, in the case of a *kuṇḍa*, the height of the first girdle (*mekhalā*) shall be twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
As it is stated in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*:
"Therein, the first girdle is twelve finger-breadths in width."
Its height and its width are both four finger-breadths on all sides.
And above that, there should be a parapet (vapra) four finger-breadths high,
and it should be properly extended all around by eight finger-breadths.
Furthermore, above that, a rampart (vapra) should be constructed; it is the third [element], four fingers wide and likewise elevated.
Thus, regarding the position of five girdles (mekhalā), its measurement is stated in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*:
"Or five girdles should be made, measuring six, five, four, three, and two [finger-breadths]," so it is said.
Also, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "There should be five girdles, measuring six, five, four, three, and two [finger-breadths]."
Thus it is said.
Regarding the view of two girdles (*mekhalā*), their characteristics are stated in another Tantra:
"The pair of girdles is considered to be [one] sixth and one eighth [of the width of the base]."
Thus it is said.

Even in the case of a single girdle, the author of the text has already indicated this by stating the characteristics of the *yoni*: "Possessing a length, width, and height of six, four, and two *aṅgulas* respectively."
Its measurement is stated in the Piṅgalāmata:
"A single girdle is considered to be six finger-breadths in height and width."
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* as well: "Or rather, a single girdle is prescribed; its width is one-fourth [of the circumference].
In the *Prathama* too: "A single girdle of six finger-breadths should be made outside the neck-finger."
Thus it is said.
Also in the Siddhāntaśekhara: "One should make the girdle (mekhalā) of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas); if there is only one, it should be six finger-breadths [in height]."
Somaśambhu also says: "And one [mekhalā] consists of six finger-breadths.
Elsewhere it is also stated: "The girdle (mekhalā) has a width and height of six parts, or it may be a single unit."
Thus it is said.
However, in the *Kāmika*, there is this distinction:
"The width and height of the girdle (mekhalā) shall be one-sixteenth part [of the pit]; and the girdle shall have the same shape as the pit."
"But for all of them, only a single girdle should be made here for the sake of simplicity. (Verses 67–69)

The end of the Mekhalās (girdles) should be at a distance of one finger-breadth all around from the rim (nemi). A wise man should increase that measurement progressively for a pit (kuṇḍa) of one cubit up to ten cubits; for others, it should be increased separately according to half-finger-breadths. || 70 ||
Regarding the measurement of the neck (*kaṇṭha*), he says "of the girdles" (*mekhalānām*).

The connection is that the rim (*nemi*) of a pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit (*hasta*) should be [formed] from the inner edge of the girdles, extending all around by a measure of one finger-width (*aṅgula*) at a time.
The meaning is that it should extend, covering one finger-width after another.
The fifth case ending is used in the sense of "nearby" (lyablope).
In some places, the reading is *aṅguli*;
in that case, it should be construed as being in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
By this it is stated that the rim (*nemi*) is one twenty-fourth part of the diameter of the pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Even in the case of [pits] measuring two cubits and so forth, the rim is likewise one twenty-fourth part of its corresponding radius (*karaṇī*).
It has been stated that for others, up to ten cubits, one should increase it gradually by half a finger-breadth (*ardhāṅgula*) according to the sequence.
That, however, is with the intention of [measuring] two cubits (dvihasta).

And in those two cubits, there are one finger-breadth (aṅgula), three barley-corns (yava), two louse-eggs (yūkā), four nit-dusts (likhyā), five minute particles (reṇu), and four triad-particles (tryasareṇu).
As it is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "The neck is indeed proclaimed to be one twenty-fourth part.
By this, the neck is seven *yavas* in a span (*ratni*) and seven and a half *yavas* in a cubit (*arati*).

This has been stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "In sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) measured by one cubit (*hasta*), the neck [of the fire-pit] is eight barley-corns (*yava*); in those measured by one forearm (*aratni*), it is seven and a half barley-corns; and in those measured by one forearm, it is seven barley-corns."
Thus it is said.
However, in the Kāmika, it is stated otherwise: "Its lip [is determined] by one-twelfth of the field.
Thus.
Somaśambhu also states: "The neck is one finger-breadth externally; in some scriptures, it is two finger-breadths.
However, the traditionalists accept only the first position, as it is agreed upon by many tantras.
As it has been said, beginning with the one-cubit [measurement]: "The neck is one finger-breadth outside the excavation; outside of that, the girdles follow in sequence."
In the *Piṅgalāmata* as well: "One should leave a space of one finger-breadth from the edge; such shall be the placement of the girdles.
Elsewhere also: "The neck [of the vessel] should be made one finger-breadth outside [the girdles]."
Thus it is said.
Also in the Siddhāntaśekhara: "In a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit, one should then make the neck (kaṇṭha) one finger-breadth wide."
And in the *Kālottara*: "The neck [of the fire-pit] is one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) outside the excavation; this is the rule for all fire-pits.
One should calculate one finger-breadth as the twenty-fourth part [of the pit].

This has been explained by the commentators [of that text] by means of the well-known conventional usage of fingers on a cubit, beginning with the statement: "Eight *yava*s make one finger-breadth," and so forth.

The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) has been described according to the [specific] fire-oblation (homa). However, this technical definition (paribhāṣā) is now established for the purpose of stating the measurements for the excavation and other dimensions:
one should divide the area of the pit intended to be constructed into twenty-four parts and designate the measure of one twenty-fourth part as one *aṅgula*.
Therefore, it is said that this rule applies to all sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*).
It is also stated elsewhere: "The neck (*kaṇṭha*) should be eight barley-corns (*yava*) in measure when the pit is one cubit (*kara*) in size."
Elsewhere also it is said: "The rim of a single-hand-sized bowl should be one finger-breadth all around on the outside. (70)
In a two-cubit pit, those [lines] should be known as measuring sixty-four finger-breadths;
in four-cubit pits, they measure sixty-eight finger-breadths. || 71 ||
In a *kuṇḍa* that produces mercury (*rasakara*), they should be provided with ten, eight, and six finger-breadths [respectively];
in a *kuṇḍa* measured by eight cubits, they should be eight finger-breadths for each row of the sun.

In a sacrificial pit measuring ten cubits, the wise should know that the girdles (mekhalās) are to be understood on all sides as being ten finger-breadths in width and height, according to the [specified] digits.
Indicating the width and length of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) measuring two cubits and so forth, he speaks of the girdles (*mekhalā*).
In all these cases, the girdles should be constructed as previously described using sixth, eighth, and twelfth parts.
The phrase "to be understood according to their width and height" connects with everything that follows, as before.
Regarding the phrase "rasa-veda-guṇa-aṅgulas" (six, four, and three finger-breadths):
the teachers have disregarded the small difference of five barley-corns and two minute particles (*yūkās*); this is the first [measurement].
The middle [measurement] consists of four finger-breadths and two barley-corns.
Two finger-breadths, six barley-corns, and five louse-eggs constitute the final [measurement].
Although the girdles for sacrificial pits measuring three, five, seven, and nine cubits are not mentioned here, it is nevertheless stated further on:
"A pit measuring one cubit is prescribed for a single hundred-thousand-fold recitation."
One should increase it by the hand for as long as ten lakhs [of repetitions].
Thus, the application for altars of three cubits and so forth has been stated.
Therefore, the measurement of its girdle (*mekhalā*) should also be understood as before, being the sixth, eighth, and twelfth parts [of the altar's height].
In that regard, for an altar of three cubits, it is six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), seven barley-corns (*yava*), three louse-eggs (*yūkā*), and three *likhyā*s; this is the first [measurement].
Five *aṅgulas* make one *yava*; four *yūkas* and four *likhyās* plus half a *likhyā* constitute the middle [measure].
Three *aṅgulas*, three *yavas*, five *yūkas*, and six *likhyās* minus one-third constitute the smallest [measure].
Thus it is said: "four cubits."
The Vasus are eight, the Tarkas are six, and the Yugas are four.
Here, the fact that these represent the sixth, eighth, and twelfth parts has been made manifest by the author himself.
In this same manner, it should be understood for [temple sizes] of five cubits and so forth as well. (71–73)
In front of the Hotṛ priest is their source, shaped like an aśvattha leaf above. || 74 ||
Regarding the phrase "the *yoni* of the *hotṛ*": above these girdles (*mekhalā*), at their midpoint, a *yoni* should be fashioned in front of the *hotṛ* like an *aśvattha* leaf.
This has been stated by Somaśambhu:
"Above them, the *yoni* should be situated in the middle, like the leaves of the *aśvattha* and *palāśa* trees.
And this aforementioned *yoni* should be made in the shape of a *kuṇḍa*.
By the phrase "in front of the Hotṛ," this is what is meant:
the altar should be positioned such that it does not fall behind [the priest], and so that the Hotṛ faces either eastward or northward;
furthermore, the *yoni* (the sacrificial cavity) should be placed by some on top of the western girdle (*mekhalā*), and by others on top of the southern girdle.
As it is stated in the *Svāyambhuva*: "The fire-pits (kuṇḍa) situated in the east, south, and southeast have their openings facing north;
the remaining ones are recorded as facing east, arranged according to what is aesthetically pleasing.
Also, in the *Trailokyasāra*: "That situated in the south faces east and south; that situated in the water [northwest] faces west and north."
"Even for the ninth *kuṇḍa*, the *yoni* is situated in the south and in the water [direction]. (Here, by the word "east," [the directions] are Agni, Water, Nairṛta, Vāyu, North, and Īśāna.
Also, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The *yoni* of the *kuṇḍas* in the directions of Indra, Agni, and Yama is traditionally held to face north."
"The womb [of the fire] is traditionally held to face east among the others; [it may also face] northeast or north.
Also, in the *Kriyāsāra*: "The performer of the oblation should place [the fire] in front, or to the south, or even to the west."

Somaśambhu also states: "The fire-pit (kuṇḍa) for the east, southeast, and south should have its opening facing north; those for the remaining directions should face east; and for those two [the northeast and northwest], it may be either. Here, by the mention of "northeast" (*aiśānya*), the ninth pit is included as a partial reference.

By this [rule], the eastern, southeastern, and southern fire-pits, as well as the ninth pit, are oriented with their openings facing north; the other five pits have their openings facing east. || 74 ||
The yoni of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) measuring one muṣṭi, three aratnis, or one hasta is said to possess a length,
width, and height of six, four, and two aṅgulas respectively.
He states its measurement as "muṣṭi" (a fist).

Since all fire-pits (*kuṇḍas*) have one cubit as their basic unit, the *yoni* must everywhere be made with a length, width, and height consisting of four, six, and twelve parts [of that unit] respectively.
As it is said in another Tantra:
"By [increasing] the length of the pit by one-fourth, one-sixth, or one-twelfth [of its original size], it becomes elongated;
[it is] broad and high, and its tip is one-fourteenth [of that].
Thus, in the *Kriyāsāra*: "Its length is six finger-breadths and its width is four finger-breadths."
Thus [it is said].
This, however, refers to the position of having a single girdle;
others, on the other hand, describe it otherwise.
Regarding the phrase "six, four, and two finger-breadths in length":
this means it is twelve finger-breadths in length (six times two), six finger-breadths in width (three times two), eight finger-breadths in width, and two finger-breadths in height.
As it has been said:
In the *Svāyambhuva*: "The womb (*yoni*) is situated in the middle of the girdle (*mekhalā*), with a width equal to one and a half parts of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Also, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "By means of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) [in length], the womb is eight finger-breadths in width."
"Her elevation [is] two finger-breadths.
Also, in the *Prayogasāra*: "The vulva, three parts wide, should be twelve finger-breadths in length at its center."
"One should make the height one-twelfth [of the pit], slightly less than that of the water-pot (kumbha).
In some places, even a height of one finger-breadth is mentioned;
as stated in the Nāradīya: "The width of the yoni is one-third of the pit, and its height is one finger-breadth."
"It should be as long as half the *kuṇḍa*.
Also, in the *Trailokyasāra*: "The *yoni* is twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length, but less than one-third in width."
"However, its height is one finger-breadth.
Also, in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "The width of the *yoni* is eight finger-breadths, and its height is measured at one finger-breadth."
Thus it is said;
and elsewhere as well: "The height is one finger-breadth.
By this, there is an option between a height of two finger-breadths and a height of one finger-breadth.
The width at the base is eight finger-breadths;
since it is said that it should be like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree due to its tapering toward the tip, the center of the *yoni* should be made slightly depressed.
This is stated in the *Trailokyasāra*: "In the middle, however, there is the support for the clarified butter (*ājya*)."
The traditionalists also consider the womb (yoni) to be of this very same kind.

Others, however, connect the phrase "six, four, and two finger-breadths" with the height, width, and so forth; thus they say that the womb should be made twelve finger-breadths in width, twelve finger-breadths in length, and twelve finger-breadths in height.
As it is stated in the Pañcarātra: "One should fashion a vulva (yoni) twelve finger-breadths in height and of the same extent in length."
Elsewhere also it is said: "Because it has the form of the twelve vowels, the *yoni* should be twelve finger-breadths [in size]; it is equal in height and length."
Both of these two positions should be understood according to the tradition of one's own guru.
However, the aforementioned measurement applies to the position of three girdles;
when the position of twelve-finger-width girdles is adopted, the *yoni* is described according to that system.
In the *Prayogasāra*: "The first girdle is of the nature of *sattva*, twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in width;
thereafter, the second is said to be of the nature of *rajas*, [eight finger-breadths]."
The third belt is known as the Tāmasī, measuring four finger-breadths [in height];
the width of each of these is four finger-breadths in measure.
Situated in the western direction, it is exactly fifteen finger-breadths in length,
five finger-breadths wide at both ends, and six, four, and two finger-breadths [in width] respectively.
"One should fashion the *yoni* of the pit, having the shape of a distinct *aśvattha* leaf, concave, placed within the pit, and thirteen finger-breadths in height.
Regarding the phrase "in the west," it should be understood as being according to the view that there is only a single pit. || 75 ||
One should make the tip of the *yoni* one finger-breadth wide and slightly downward-facing.
In other sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*), one should increase the width of the *yoni* by one finger-breadth for each successive pit;
likewise, one should increase the tip of the *yoni* by a sequence of two barley-grains at each step.
"One finger" (ekāṅgula):
by this, it is stated that at every [corner], the tip of the *yoni* should also be made slightly downward-facing and enter into the pit (*kuṇḍa*) by means of this twenty-fourth part.
As it is said in the *Nāradīya*: "The two lips of the pit are like the leaves of the Bodhi tree."

The "lip" (oṣṭha) refers to the tip of the vulva, meaning the front part that has entered the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). It is also stated in the *Trailokyasāra*: "Likewise, having entered within, it is considered to be joined with two jars and shaped like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree."
In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā as well: "One should fashion a girdle in the middle, or on the west or the south;
it should be beautiful at the front, slightly depressed, and gradually tapering away."
"With the front [of the altar] facing the *kuṇḍa*, with the girdle (*mekhalā*) slightly released.
Here, for fear of excessive length in the text, the measurement of the *yoni* and its front and so forth has not been stated for each [type of *kuṇḍa*] up to the ten-cubit *kuṇḍa*.
Nevertheless, something is said: the length is [calculated] by half the width plus one-sixth;
the width is [the same]; the height should be half the width; and the tip [of the spire] should be half the height.
In other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should increase the length of the vulva (yoni) by one finger-breadth for each subsequent pit;
likewise, one should also increase the tip of the vulva by a sequence of two barley-grains at each step.
Thus, this has been stated regarding those unskilled in calculation by means of measurement on the ground;
it does not, however, intend to convey the meaning of an exact calculation. || 76 ||
Starting from the ground, the stalk should extend to the center of the *yoni* and be provided with a hollow;
the one most skilled in the tantras should not place that *yoni* within the corners of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). || 77 ||
Regarding the phrase "the stalk from the ground":
the stalk should extend from the ground up to the womb.
By the expression "starting from the ground," it is stated that the stalk must be made so as to be attached to the outer girdle.
The meaning is that one should construct an altar (*vedi*) four finger-breadths high and wide, joined with an outer rim (*mekhalā*), and place the stalk (*nāla*) upon it.

How so? It means that there should be a hole in the middle; thus, having made a hole in the center above the middle rim for the purpose of laying the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and spreading the sacrificial grass (*paristaraṇa*), the other central portion is to be filled.
As it is stated in the Pañcarātra:
"Starting from the base (sthalā), the womb (yoni) should be equal to the outer girdle (bāhyamekhalā)."

As for the one who stated that "having a hole in the middle" (*sarandhraka*) is a qualification of the stalk (*nāla*), he is indeed mistaken; for the word "stalk" (*nāla*) denotes precisely that which has a hole, and because if it were described as having a hole, it would result in the postulation of an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

Nor should it be said that the placement of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and other items occurs outside the stalk (*nāla*); for there is no sublation of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) by the seen (*dṛṣṭa*), and furthermore, there would be no space for the enclosing sticks and the ritual strewing (*paristaraṇa*).
But in the *Prayogasāra*: "To the west of the yoni, the stalk should be four finger-breadths in length;
its width is desired to be three, two, and one finger-breadth respectively, tapering toward the tip. (77)
One should fashion a navel within the fire-pits (kuṇḍa) resembling a lotus;
its measurement is declared to be in proportion to each respective pit. || 78 ||

In the case of single-handled [vessels] with a fist-sized opening, the navel should be two or three finger-breadths in height and width; in other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should increase these measurements accordingly.
The one of noble intellect should mark the navel at a distance of two barley-grains [from the center];
he should avoid placing the yoni in the *kuṇḍa* of the yoni and the navel in the *kuṇḍa* of the lotus.
Having divided the navel-field into three parts, one should fashion the pericarp in the center;
with two outer portions, one should arrange eight petals.
Regarding the phrase "the navel of the pits":
one should fashion a navel within the pits.
The meaning is that, having made the navel either in the shape of the pit or in the shape of a lotus, one should place it in the middle of the excavation.

The word *nābhi* is also masculine, as stated in the rule: "The word *nābhi* occurs in two genders when referring to the sun (*ātapa*) or a Kṣatriya; it is also [masculine] when referring to a part of a living being.

Regarding its height and breadth—that is, its elevation and width—it is said that here too, as previously, since the one-cubit measure is the archetype for all fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*), the [central] depression is broad by a sixth part of the pit's width and its height is half of that.
He describes the very resemblance to a lotus with the words "the navel," etc.; the phrase "one should make" implies "with a portion.
And it is said in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "In a pit dug at the side of the sacrificial ground, the navel and the girdle [should be made] in the sacrificial fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*)."
Thus [ends the section on verses] 78–81.
A sacrificial pit measuring one fist is prescribed for fifty oblations;
for a hundred oblations, it should be one *aratni* in measure, and for a thousand oblations, one *hasta*.
For ten thousand [bow-lengths], it is said to be two cubits; for a hundred thousand, four cubits;
for one million, six cubits; and for ten million, it is traditionally held to be eight cubits.
He states the application of the *muṣṭi* (fist) and other types of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) with the passage beginning with "muṣṭi" and ending with "koṭyām aṣṭakarām.
Regarding the hundred-fold oblation (*śatahoma*), the word division is "aratnimātram.
As it has been said:
"A fist-measure [of area] for fifty [lakhs], and an aratni-measure for a hundred [lakhs]," so it is said.
Furthermore, in the *Saṃhitā*: "And for a crore-homa, as well as for half a crore, the pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be eight cubits [in measure]."
Thus [ends the section]. 82–83.
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit is prescribed for a single hundred thousand oblations (lakṣa).
One should increase the size by one cubit for each subsequent hundred thousand, up to ten million.
A pit measuring ten cubits is prescribed for a crore of oblations. || 84 ||
He states another alternative with the word "eka" (one).
This, however, refers to objects consisting of small materials such as flowers or clarified butter, or it concerns a *homa* performed by a single agent, up to a limit of five hands.
Beyond that, it should be understood as referring to large-scale materials or to cases involving multiple agents.
By the phrase "eight cubits at ten million," the alternative view of "ten cubits" is negated.
However, there is a specific distinction in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "At half a lakh [of oblations], the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is three cubits; at one lakh oblations, it is four cubits."
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is prescribed as five cubits in size for a sequence of ten lakhs of oblations.
"Six cubits [in length] for twenty lakhs, and seven cubits for fifty million.
Also elsewhere: "Some say one cubit for a hundred thousand oblations, two cubits for two hundred thousand, and three cubits for three hundred thousand."
They say that for one hundred thousand [recitations], the sacrificial pit at home should be four cubits; for five hundred thousand, it should be five cubits.
At one hundred thousand recitations, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shall be six cubits; at seven hundred thousand, it shall be seven cubits;
at eight hundred thousand, eight cubits; and at nine hundred thousand, nine cubits.
"For ten lakhs [of oblations], the pit should be ten cubits; indeed, even for a crore-homa, it should be ten cubits.
For on this earth, there is no pit greater than ten cubits. (84)
The quadrangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is declared to bring about all accomplishments;
the yoni-shaped pit bestows sons, and that which resembles a half-moon bestows auspiciousness. || 85 ||
A triangular pit causes the destruction of enemies; for rites of pacification (śāntika), it should be circular;
for rites of cutting (chedana) and killing (māraṇa), the pit should be hexagonal and resemble a lotus. || 86 ||
The eight-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is said to bestow rain and pacify diseases;
for Brahmins it should be square, while for kings it is desired to be circular.
For Vaiśyas, it is said to have the luster of a half-moon; for Śūdras, it is described as triangular. Some Tantrikas desire it to be square for all classes.
One should know that the form of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is the supreme body of Prakṛti. || 88 ||
The head is said to be in the east, the arms in the south and north;
the pit is called the belly, while the yoni and the feet are in the west. || 89 ||
Now, he states the specific results of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) with the words "all," etc.
"Cutting" (*chedaḥ*) means destruction (*ucchedaḥ*), that is to say, eradication (*uccāṭanam*).
And this specific result is to be understood as occurring only when the pit is constructed in the respective directions previously mentioned.
As it is said in the Kāmika: "In the east, for paralyzing (stambha), it is square; in the south-eastern quarter, for the vulva-shaped [rite], it is triangular;
in the south, for killing (māraṇa), it is a half-moon; and in the south-western corner, for hatred (dveṣa), it is a triangle."
"In the west, for pacification (śāntika), a hexagonal [pit] is prescribed; in the northwest, for eradication (uccāṭana);

in the north, for nourishment (pauṣṭika), a lotus-shaped one; and in the northeast, an eight-sided [pit] which bestows liberation. Thus it is said. Also in the Piṅgalāmata: "In the north, for the rite of subjugation (vaśya), the pit should be shaped like a lotus."
In the rite of eradication, it is on the six-pointed [vajra] in the northwest; for killing, it is on the half-moon in the south.
"A four-cornered [pit] for paralyzing in the east; shaped like the *bhaga* (vulva) in the southeast for attracting;
circular in the west for pacification; and eight-cornered in the northeast, which bestows liberation.
Thus it is said. Also, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "The pit called the *yoni* is said to be in the southeast, facing north."
In the case of an increase in progeny or in affliction, the "Half-moon" (ardhacandra) mudrā is then described.
In the south, for that purpose of killing, it is always recommended to face north;
in the southwest, there should be a triangular pit (kuṇḍa) facing east for the rite of inciting enmity.
Next, I shall describe the circular pit (vṛtta-kuṇḍa), which is beneficial for rites of pacification (śāntika) in the western direction;
the hexagonal pit (ṣaḍasra-kuṇḍa) is said to be effective for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana) in the northwestern direction.
"Now I shall describe the lotus-shaped pit (padmakuṇḍa) in the north; it increases prosperity. Next, I shall describe the eight-cornered pit (aṣṭāsra-kuṇḍa) in the northeast; it grants all desires.

Here, by the principle of "separateness-in-conjunction" (saṃyogapṛthaktva), it should be understood that the accomplishment of the specific fruits mentioned for each respective pit is also attained through the eight-pit arrangement performed as an ancillary part of the initiation (dīkṣā).

Also in the *Kriyāsāra*: "The sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics and measuring one palm (*tāla*) in size, is prescribed for the worship of mobile [deities], but not for the four-faced [stationary] one."
Having constructed a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the path described here and endowed with its proper characteristics,
a Kṣatriya, a wealthy person, or even a Śūdra should have it bound with copper.
If those are unavailable, however, one should construct it very firmly by binding it together with bricks,
and likewise coat it with clay according to the previously described method.
One should have this pit (kuṇḍa) made of copper, endowed with the proper characteristics, or even of clay;
one may employ it for the worship of a mobile image, but not for the worship of a stationary one.

And here, by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit with the preceding statement, it should be understood that the measurement is one *tāla*. O bull among immortals, one should thoroughly cleanse a copper vessel with acid, an earthen vessel with cow-dung water, and a stone mansion with lime.
"One should decorate earthen pits, along with their joints on all sides,
with red clay and rice-flour paste, making them as pleasing to the eye as possible. Regarding this,
he states the fault that arises if the pits are deficient, excessive, or otherwise deformed:
Viśvakarman: If the pit is too deep, there will be disease; if it is too shallow, there is loss of cattle and wealth.
In a curved pit, there is suffering; in one with a broken boundary-line (mekhalā), death occurs.
If the girdle is omitted, there will be excessive grief and the loss of wealth;
a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) made without a yoni is said to cause the destruction of one's wife.

"It is declared that a *kuṇḍa* whose neck is deficient [in measure] causes the destruction of offspring. Also, in another *Āgama*: "If it exceeds the proper measure, death occurs; if it is deficient in measure, poverty results," and so forth.

In the *Kriyāsāra* as well: "A sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) that is deficient or excessive in measurement, one with a cracked girdle (*mekhalā*), or one lacking aesthetic beauty, brings about the destruction of the patron (*yajamāna*).
Also, in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*: "If the sacrificial pit here is deficient or excessive, it bestows many defects."
"Therefore, having examined this thoroughly, it should be performed by one who desires auspiciousness.

Also, in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "If [the measurement] is deficient, there is a great disease; if excessive, an increase in enemies; if the vulva is deficient, epilepsy; and if the neck is deficient, punishment by speech."
Also in the *Jayadrathayāmala*: "Enmity toward friends occurs when the thread is excessive; poverty when it lacks honor;
suppression of speech when it lacks a throat; and failure results from a deficient excavation."
If it is excessive, there is demonic enjoyment; if the girdle is too high due to pride, diseases increase greatly, and in the case of a division [of the waist], epilepsy occurs.
"In a cracked [fire-pit] or one crowded with fissures, there will be censure; thus it is said.
Regarding this, its necessity is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*: "That fire which is devoid of [the proper] direction, location, and sacrificial pit is indeed merely worldly."
Therefore, one should select the directions, locations, and sacrificial pits according to the characteristics previously described.
"Such a *kuṇḍa* may not exist, or one should resort to a *sthaṇḍila* (an earthen altar).

Thus, the author’s statement is made with the intention of referring to the *nitya* [daily] rite and with the intention of referring to a single *kuṇḍa*, wherein the *kuṇḍa* is of the nature of a pit and the *yoni* is at the western side. (85–89)

One should perform the daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites either on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or by means of very beautiful sand; that [mound] should be made one cubit in size. || 90 ||
A square [pit] on all sides with a height equal to one finger-breadth—thus the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) have been described; next, the large and small sacrificial ladles (sruk-sruva) are explained.
He states an alternative for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the words "always" (*nityam*).
It is joined with a height of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*);
the finger-breadth has the characteristics previously described.
Alternatively, it is that which possesses the height of the four fingers, meaning the fingers of the hand.

As they say: "The wise call that [sacrificial ground] a *sthaṇḍila* which is one *ratni* in length, raised by the thickness of a thumb-joint, well-proportioned, or even leveled with sand, quadrangular, and two fingers in height; others say it should be one cubit in width."
It should be understood that this refers to the scope of a minor *homa*.
As it is stated in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*: "In a concise *homa* ritual, the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) shall be the measure of an arrow."

In the *Kriyāsāra*, however, a specific location for the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) is also stated: "The place for the homa is in the eight directions; it should have its tail (the rear end) facing east, or be sloping toward the northeast, or have its tail facing north; such a region is remembered as the site for the sacrificial mound."
In the *Piṅgalāmata*, however, there is this distinction: "For the fire-oblation (*homa*), a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*), or a small hearth (*hasantikā*) is recommended.
Also, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*: "Now I shall describe the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), whether performed in a sacrificial pit or on a leveled mound."
"Either on an altar, or in an iron vessel, or in a new, auspicious earthen one.
Regarding this, the *Kriyāsāra* specifies: "Or [on] a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) made of sand, or even with the dust of red clay."
The *agnicakra* of the house should also be examined.
As it is stated elsewhere:
"Having first drawn a grid of nine squares, then [starting] from the northeast (Īśa) and the southwest (Nirṛti) in sequence..."
One should place [the syllables] of Varuṇa and Indra in the west and east, and those of Vāyu and Agni in the south and north.
Having placed the Sun and the others in the central square, one should predict the results;
under the Sun there will be sorrow, and under Mercury there will be the acquisition of wealth.

In the house of Venus, there shall be gain of wealth; Saturn would cause loss. One should know that in the house of the Moon there is profit, and in the house of Mars, there is killing and imprisonment.
Jupiter brings about the attainment of wealth, while Rahu is considered to cause loss;
indeed, through Ketu, one always meets death in the circle of fire.

"One should count three and then three [houses] starting from the solar asterism up to the house of the day; however, one need not consider this in the case of daily (nitya) or occasional (naimittika) rites, such as the homa for Durgā.
Concluding what has been said, he introduces what is to be stated next with the word "evam" (thus).
Since the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) is also stated to be a substitute for the fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*), it should be understood that the summary refers specifically to the fire-pits. || 90-91 ||

One should fashion the *sruk* for the sacrifice according to the method to be described; it should be made from one of the following: *śrīparṇī*, *śiṃśapā*, or a milky-sap tree, and it must be heavy. (92)
Having taken [the measurement], one should again divide it by thirty-six to obtain a span (hasta).
With twenty parts there shall be the staff (daṇḍa), and with eight of those parts the altar (vedī) shall be formed. || 93 ||
The neck is measured by one part, and the mouth is measured by seven parts;
the width of the neck is proclaimed to be three parts of the pedestal. || 94 ||
He states the definition of the *sruva* ladle with the words "one should fashion":
*śrīparṇī* is the *kāśmarī* tree;
*kṣīraśākhinaḥ* refers to the *nyagrodha* and other trees that produce milky sap.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "The *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *plakṣa* are the milky trees.

Regarding the phrase "by one-third of the altar" (*veditryaṃśena*), the meaning is that the *viṣkambha* (the pillar) stands at the end of the neck (*kaṇṭha*) by three-quarters of one-third [of the altar].
And that [distance] is to be known by means of calculating its circumference. || 92–94 ||
The tip [of the nozzle] should be level with the throat; one should fashion the passage at the mouth according to the measurement of the little finger, for the exit of the medicinal paste. || 95 ||
"Agra" means the front; it is at the level of the neck and has a width equal to one-third of the altar (vedi),
since the length for all [the altars] has already been stated.
Because it is said, "for the sake of the exit of the clarified butter," [the word] "path" refers to that which pierces the enclosure of the throat-ledge.
As it is stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"The wise one should cause a path for the exit of the clarified butter to be made below the throat."
"And one should perform the piercing with a heated iron rod from the front," so it is said.
Also, in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*:
"There should be a perforation in the region of the neck, reaching as far as the little finger."
Thus [ends the verse]. 95.
The pericarp (kaṇīkā) should be fashioned in the center of the altar with one part;
one should fashion a pit (avaṭa) all around it with one part on the outside. || 96 ||
Of that [pit], the circular part should be made with three parts, and the semi-circular [portion] with half a part;
one should fashion the petals all around with one part. The girdle (mekhalā) for both the mouth and the altar (vedi) should be of the measure of half a part all around. || 97 ||
He describes the method of constructing the altar (vedi) that has been indicated with the word "vedi.
The central hub (kaṇīkā), however, must be kept elevated in the middle of the excavation.
Outside of that hub, on all sides—that is, everywhere around it.
By this, two parts are comprised.
*Avaṭa* means a pit.
"By three parts" means by two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The word "outside" (bahiḥ) means around the pit (avaṭa); thus, by the phrase "around the [pit]," two parts are included.
The syntactical connection is that the girdle (mekhalā) should be made with a measurement of half a part (ardhāṃśa) around both the mouth and the altar (vedi).
Therefore, with that same half-part, the girdle must also be constructed at the mouth.
And that [mandala] is circular in shape.
In this regard, one part is for the pericarp (*kaṇīkā*), two parts for the pit (*avaṭa*), one part for the circle, and two parts for the petals; with one part, a rim (*mekhalā*) is made.
That is to say, by means of half a portion, a square boundary should be constructed all around.
As it is said in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"The decorative border (*śobhā*) should be half a finger [in width], whether it be uniform or even painted."
Here, the word *aṅgula* signifies a part (*aṃśa*).
Thus, all eight parts are employed. According to the instruction, decorative patterns such as folds (*vali*) and the like should be made at the corners of the boundary (*sīman*). (96–97)
At the base and the tip of the staff, there should be two *kumbhas* (vases) measuring three and four finger-breadths respectively;
the pair of *gaṇḍīs* (bosses) should consist of four parts (*yamāṃśa*), and this is declared to be the circumference of the staff.
The back portion of the altar should be shaped like a tortoise with six parts;
one should draw the face of a swan, an elephant, or a boar.
This is declared to be the characteristic of the *sruc* ladle on the back part of its face. || 99 ||

Regarding the term *daṇḍa*: here, due to the context of parts (*aṃśa*), the word *aṅgula* denotes a part. Therefore, at the base it should be made with one-third [of the length], its face directed toward the base; but at the top, it should be made with one-fourth [of the length], its face joined to the altar (*vedi*).
The word "gradually" (kramāt) also applies to what follows.
In that regard, two parts attached to the base of the jar (mūlakumbha), and even two parts attached elsewhere, should be made into a *gaṇḍī* shaped like a bracelet (*kaṅkaṇa*).
Since the word *yuga*—according to the lexicon stating "yuga means a pair, [the Kṛta age,] etc."—can denote the meaning of duality in its expressed sense; [it refers to two parts].
Because there is no authoritative evidence for accepting [the presence of] characteristic marks;
as it was stated by Somaśambhu:
"At the base and at the tip of the staff, the *gaṇḍī* should be like a bracelet."
Thus, eleven parts are produced.
In the middle, a staff measuring nine parts remains for the purpose of support.
As it is stated in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra: "The staff (daṇḍa) shall consist of six parts (rasāṅgulaiḥ).
In this context, if the word *aṅgula* were taken to mean [standard] finger-breadths (*aṅgulāni*), then three and a half parts would remain for the staff.
Consequently, there would be no space at all for its support.
The width of the base of the staff should be made with six parts.
The rear portion of the altar is shaped like a tortoise; this is distinct [from the other parts].

However, those who connect "the non-extension of the staff" (*daṇḍasyānāha*) with "the length is stated" as separate items, and who further connect [it] with "the back part of the altar is six parts and shaped like a tortoise," are indeed wandering in error;
for the word *ānāha* does not denote length, and length has already been mentioned previously.
Thus it is stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"The circumference of the middle of the staff is declared to be six finger-breadths."

Regarding the phrase "in the form of a tortoise," because the mention of "with six parts" would otherwise be redundant, the connection is that one should draw the face of a swan or similar creature on the back part of the mouth of this *sruk* ladle.
"Potrin" refers to the boar (*varāha*). (98–99)
One should fashion the *sruva* ladle with twenty-four parts;
its handle is said to be measured by twenty-two parts. || 100 ||
The circumference [of the pit] is four parts; it should be capable of holding one *karṣa* of clarified butter—that is its head.
One should bury it two parts deep in the mud in the shape of a deer's footprint. || 101 ||
The gaṇḍī should be at the base and tip of the handle and adorned with a ring;
thus the rule for the sruva has been declared, and now the maṇḍalas are described. || 102 ||
He states the characteristics of the *sruva* with the words "the *sruk*":
the circumference (*ānāha*) is the width [measured] by four parts;
this is the connection with the word "of this" (*etasya*).
As stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "The staff (*daṇḍa*) shall consist of four finger-breadths (*vedāṅgula*).
Regarding the term "karṣa": the definition of a *karṣa* is as follows—
"A *māṣa* shall consist of ten *guñjās*, and sixteen *māṣas* are declared to be a *karṣa*. Thus [it is said].
One should fashion its head with two parts.
The connection is that one should dig in the mud a shape like a deer’s footprint so that it may hold the drawn-out clarified butter (*karṣājya*).
Because it is said they are "adorned with bracelets," the word *gaṇḍī* here is a synonym for a water-jar (*ghaṭa*).
As it is stated in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "One should have two very beautiful jars made at the root and the tip."
Thus it is said.
And those two should be performed as before, since no specific distinction is mentioned.
The bracelet (kaṅkaṇa) should also be performed as before.
There is a distinction elsewhere:
"In the absence of that, the oblation is offered with two leaves of the *palāśa* tree."

In this context, it should be understood that "with two leaves" refers to the two middle leaves, according to the Vedic injunction: "He offers with the middle leaf. This is also stated in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made of fire-purified metal, not of bell-metal, iron, or lead;
they may also be made of sacrificial wood, as approved by craftsmen, according to the requirements of either Tantric or Smārta rites.

"Or on a leaf of a sacred tree (*brahmavṛkṣa*) such as the *parṇa*, which is without holes and has risen up in the middle. But elsewhere it is said: "In the absence of *palāśa* leaves, however, one may use leaves produced from the *pippala* tree."
Thus it is said.

Also in the *Saṃhitā*: "O Sage, one should place the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles upon a flawless, beautiful leaf of the *palāśa* tree, or upon a small leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, when performing the abbreviated fire-sacrifice (*homakarma*). (100–102)
In a square divided into four compartments and provided with diagonal lines, one should likewise draw four corner-lines within all four of those compartments. || 103 ||
At intervals, he should cause them to fall so that they form fish-patterns;
the practitioner of mantra should [draw] two lines each extending from east to west and two extending from south to north.
Upon those fish-marks, one should drop four threads equally;
as before, one should drop the diagonal threads (karṇasūtra) in the corner squares. || 105 ||
One should lay down four lines upon the fish that have arisen therefrom;
then, within the resulting squares, one should drop further lines upon those fish. || 106 ||
Now, he describes the construction of the *sarvatobhadra* and other mandalas upon the altar (*vedikā*) with the words "square" (*caturasra*).
The meaning is that one should construct a square, provided with four corners and two diagonal lines (*karṇasūtra*), according to the method stated for the *vāstu-maṇḍala*.
With two verses, he explains the method for producing sixteen squares, beginning with the words "fourfold" (*catuṣvī*).
In the four quadrants, one should likewise draw four diagonal lines such that fish-shaped figures (*matsya*) are formed in each center.
The practitioner of mantra should cast four equal lines upon those fish—two extending east-west and two extending north-south; this is the connection [of the instructions].
In this way, it becomes composed of sixteen squares.
He states the method for producing sixty-four squares in a verse and a half, beginning with "as before.
This applies to three locations; therein is the method.

In the four corner squares, having laid down four diagonal threads as before, one should lay down this set of four threads— two with their tips pointing east and two with their tips pointing north— upon the four fish-figures produced by those [diagonals] as before. Furthermore,

upon the four fish-figures in the intermediate squares produced by the intersection of these four threads, one should again lay down two threads with their tips pointing east and two with their tips pointing north.
In this way, sixty-four squares are produced. || 103–106 ||
Up to two hundred [and] fifty-six steps, the mantra-practitioner should likewise lay down the lines there according to that very same procedure. || 107 ||
The meaning of "by that very same procedure" is as follows:

having laid down four diagonal lines (karṇasūtra) in the four corner squares as before, one should lay down two threads— one with its tip pointing east and one with its tip pointing north— upon the four fish-figures produced by those lines.
Then, one should lay down six threads with their tips pointing east and six with their tips pointing north upon the fish-shaped intermediate squares produced by this fourfold grid of lines;
in this way, two hundred and fifty-six squares are formed. || 107 ||
One should draw a lotus with excellent characteristics in the center using thirty-six squares;
the pedestal (pīṭha) should be formed by one outer row, and the pathway (vīthikā) by a pair of rows. || 108 ||

The practitioner of mantras should fashion the door-decorations and secondary ornaments with the two remaining [parts] according to the procedure taught in the scriptures; thereafter, he should draw a lotus.
He states the application of the compartments with the words "thirty-six.
He will describe the method of drawing the lotus immediately thereafter. The word "outside" (bahis) applies to three locations.
Outside, one should construct a pedestal (*pīṭha*) consisting of twenty-eight squares surrounding [the center] in a row, according to the method to be described.
Outside that, one should construct a pathway (*vīthikā*) consisting of eighty squares surrounding [the center] in two rows, according to the method to be described.

Outside that, using the remaining two rows consisting of one hundred and twelve squares surrounding [the center], one should fashion the gates, the *śobhās*, the *upaśobhās*, the weapons (*astras*), and the corners.
One should perform [this] according to the method that will be described. 108–109.
Having set aside one-twelfth of the lotus-field on the outside, the wise one should divide its center into three equal circular sections. || 110 ||
The first [space] should be the location for the pericarp; the second is for the filaments;
the third is for the petals of that lotus, with the tips of the petals [formed] by the aforementioned proportion. || 111 ||
He describes the method for constructing the lotus with the words "In the lotus" (*padme*).

Therein, the lotus-field consists of thirty-six squares; it is divided eightfold by two lines in that direction and by two diagonal lines (*karṇasūtra*). Those very lines are the central lines of the petals.
Regarding the method therein: having divided the length of the lotus-field into twelve parts, one should discard one part on the outside from all sides.
Then, having divided those ten parts into six, one should fix the beginning of the cord in the center; with two parts, one circle is made, and above that, another with two parts.
Above that, one should construct three circles using two parts each;
it should be noted that the mention of "the first" and so forth is intended to indicate the locations for the limbs, enclosures, and other elements to be described later.
Regarding the phrase "by the pearl-part," this refers to the twelfth part, as he will explain the circle there later on. (110–111)
Having measured the space between the outer boundary and the interior according to the prescribed rule, the wise one should place half-moons at the tips of the filaments all around. || 112 ||
Having drawn the lines for the joints, one should then drop the threads there.
Regarding the word "bāhya" (external):

the wise person, by means of the measurement of the space between that which is the external petal-circle, having fixed [the thread] at the tips of the filaments—that is, at the edge of the filament-circle—the remainder of the sentence being "the thread and so forth";
according to the rule, on both sides all around—this refers to the threads in the middle of the lotus.
The connection is as follows: having drawn four half-moons situated at the junctions—meaning four half-moons situated at the junctions—one should cast the threads there.
Regarding the reading "by which rule" (*yadvidhinā*), the meaning is: by that rule, by that measurement, which is the measurement of the space between the outer circle.
In this regard, the procedure is as follows:

having fixed a thread measuring the interval between the circles at the intersection of the filament-circle and the cardinal-direction threads, one should draw two half-moons, each touching the leaf-circles on both sides of that cardinal-direction thread and ending at the points where they meet the filament-circle.
Thus, when the four lines for the cardinal directions and the four lines for the corners have been drawn, eight half-moons are produced.
This is understood from the plural number in the phrase "at the tips of the filaments" (*keśarāgreṣu*);
since there are eight locations for the filaments in the midst of the eight petals, the formation of the eight petals follows accordingly.
Then, at the eight junctions formed by the mutual intersection of the two half-moons, one should draw a single line between each pair of facing halves.
In this way, eight boundary lines for the eight petals are produced.
The crescent-shaped portions situated on both sides of the boundary lines running below the junctions are to be erased.
As it has been said:
"To achieve the perfection of a petal, one should place a thread at the junction between the centers of two petals so as to span the interval between them;
then, by means of half-moons produced from two rotations around both sides of that interval, the petal shall be perfected."

Elsewhere also: Having established the previously mentioned field along the diagonal line (diksūtra) and having wiped away the rest, one should extend two corner-lines (koṇasūtra) according to the measurement of the fish-figures at the cardinal points of the circle.
Having placed the junctions of the petals upon the tips of the filaments, one should mark them;
then, having dropped the threads, one should draw the eight petals there. Thus [ends verses 112–113].
One should draw a circle with the same measurement as that of the tips of the petals.
Within that space, on both sides of the central line, the wise one should, using the outer hand, draw the tips of the petals all around. || 114 ||
He states the fourth circle with the words "dalāgra" and so forth.
Having excluded from the outside that measurement which belongs to the tips of the petals—namely, the form of the twelfth part—one should construct the fourth circle with that measurement.
He explains the method for forming the tips of the petals with the word "tat" (that).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: within that interval—that is, within the interval of the circle drawn at the tips of the petals—one should skillfully draw the tips of the petals in all directions and intermediate points (vidiś) using the outer hand on both sides of the central line, which is the line through the middle of the petals.
The method for this is as follows:

For the fourth [petal], having placed the beginning of the thread at the tip of the junction-thread on both sides of the central petal-thread within the inner circle, one should apply two threads from the middle circle to the point where the petal-tip circle intersects the central petal-thread;
among these, one end of the thread touches the petal, and the second touches the intersection of the petal-tip and the central petal-thread.
And so that the two upper portions of the lines may face each other, it is said "with the outer hand.

Then, having omitted the circle of the pericarp (*kaṇīkā*), one should properly erase the three circles situated outside and the lines in the middle of the lotus petals, so that an eight-petaled lotus is seen, pleasing to the eye. || 114 ||
One should arrange the filaments in pairs at the inner bases;
this is declared by those who know the Tantras to be the general lotus design. || 115 ||

He describes the arrangement of the filaments (*kesara*) with the word "dalaiḥ": one should fashion two filaments on each petal— on both sides of the central line of the petal, within the space between the lines marking the edges of the petals located at the joints— which touch the circle of the pericarp (*karṇikā*), have their bases attached to the circle of the pericarp, have their tips touching the circle of the filaments, are slightly thick at the tips, and face one another.
He summarizes this as follows:
he will state that one should make a lotus anywhere; in that regard, this method is to be understood. || 115 ||
One should sweep three squares for the purpose of the feet at the corners of the pedestal;
with the remaining squares, one should fashion the limbs of the twice-born [deities]. || 116 ||
One should sweep the squares arranged in rows without breaking their alignment;
then, one should construct doors in the cardinal directions using two or four squares each.
Regarding what was stated, "one should construct the pedestal," he explains that procedure with the words "the squares" (*padāni*).

For the sake of the pedestal, one should erase three squares: each corner square from the row established for the pedestal, along with the two squares situated on either side of it; thus, these three squares are to be cleared for the purpose of the feet.
One should fashion the limbs of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) with the remaining four squares.
The clearing for the sake of the pathway (*vīthī*) should be performed by unifying the two rows established for that purpose.
He describes the doors with the words "in the directions" (*dikṣu*).

For the sake of the doors, one should erase the two cells situated on both sides of the central line within the inner row— located between the two rows established all around for the purpose [of the mandala]— as well as the four cells situated on the sides of the central line within the outer row, for the purpose of the four doors in the four directions.
In this way, there should be four gates. || 116-117 ||
Then, there should be three squares and one square for the *śobhās* on both sides of the door;
immediately thereafter, the *upaśobhās* should consist of one square and three squares;
and with the remaining six squares, the four corners (*koṇas*) are formed. || 118 ||
Regarding the phrase "Śobhā says with words":
one should erase the three squares located on each side of the door within the inner row, as well as the single square located on each side of the door in the outer row.
In this way, there will be eight *śobhās*.
Regarding the *upaśobhās*:
one should erase each single square situated within the row and connected on both sides to a *śobhā*, as well as three squares from the outer row on each side.
Thus there shall be eight secondary ornaments (*upaśobhā*).
Regarding the "remaining" [cells]:
