one should erase the three cells located in the inner row that are joined to the secondary ornaments on both sides, as well as the three cells located in the outer row.
In this way, there shall be four corners. || 118 ||
One should color that enchanting maṇḍala with five colors:
yellow should be made from turmeric powder, and white from rice flour. (119)
Red is the powder of safflower; black is that produced from burnt husks;
and dark-grey is said to be that produced from the leaves of the bilva tree and others—thus the five colors are described. || 120 ||
The auspicious white boundary lines should be one finger in height and width;
the pericarp should be yellow in color, and the filaments red.
The practitioner of mantra should color the petals with white pigment and their joints with dark blue; alternatively, the pericarp may be yellow.
The filaments should be yellowish-red, and the petals should also be reddish;
the joints should be black or white, or alternatively, yellow or black. (123)
One should color the interiors of the pedestals; the feet should have a reddish luster, and its limbs, as well as those in the four pathways, should be white. || 124 ||
One should draw wish-fulfilling creepers endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruits,
variegated with various colors and captivating to the sight of all.
The doors are white in color, the primary ornaments (śobhā) are said to be red, the secondary ornaments (upaśobhā) are yellow in color, and the corners are black. || 126 ||
Regarding the phrase "one should dye," he mentions five colors for the purpose of coloring the mandala.
As for "safflower" (*kusumbha*),
elsewhere another red pigment is mentioned.
Likewise, blood is said to be the dust of defects combined with alkali.
"Born of *pulāka*" means born from worthless grain.
"Pulāka refers to chaffed grain," according to the *Trikāṇḍa*.
Its preparation is as follows:
at the time of half-burning the chaffed grain, one should sprinkle it with milk or similar liquids, and then reduce it to a powder after straining it through a cloth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), other things such as green leaves are meant.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Dust arising from dark-green foliage is prescribed for one's own ritual acts."
Thus;
here, by the word *śyāma*, the yellowish-green color (*haridvarṇa*) is understood.
However, in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, its necessity is stated:
Earth is to be known as yellow, and water is proclaimed to be white;
fire indeed has the color red, and wind is proclaimed to be dark blue.
And the fifth, O Great Sage, is the black-colored Ākāśa;
Rudra is the presiding deity of the white [element], and Brahmā is the presiding deity of the red.
When yellow, the presiding deity is Viṣṇu; when black, he is remembered as Acyuta;
and when dark-blue, O sinless one, the presiding deity is declared by me to be Nāga.
They milk the white [milk] for the planets, the red arising from the host of cruel spirits,
the black for the incitement of all the asuras, and likewise the blue for Vaināyaki.
Green dust destroys both the Paiśācī and Rākṣasī [influences].

Therefore, during fire-offerings (homa), consecrations (abhiṣeka), and especially during sacrifices, one should employ that [green dust] to form a maṇḍala which causes the deities to be satisfied. Thus it is said.

However, there is a specific distinction in another tantra: "If one who is capable desires fierce accomplishment (*siddhi*), he should adorn the mandalas here with gems of those colors—with pearls, topaz, rubies, sapphires, and emeralds. Thus it is said.
"All" refers to the boundary lines (*sīmārekhā*).
Having previously mentioned the white lotus, he speaks of the red lotus with the words "or else.
However, in the case of initiation (*dīkṣā*) according to the Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, or Śaiva traditions, it should be understood that there is an option determined by the specific system.
The phrase "it is indeed yellow" applies even to the second alternative.
Having concluded the other alternative, he states the subject at hand with the words "by the yellow [color]";
this option is according to one's own preference.
"Pīṭhagarbhāṇi" refers to the corners of the lotus-field (*kamalakṣetra*). Here, "garbha" means that which has these [corners] as its interior; thus, "garbha" refers to the location of the corners.
The suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule beginning with *arśas*.
Then follows the state of being neuter.
The drawing of the *kalpalatikā* for that *pīṭha* is to be understood from the oral instruction. (119–126)
One should draw three lines on the outside, white, red, and black in sequence;
this is known as the Sarvatobhadra mandala, which is common to all.
"Outside" means outside the boundary line established on the outermost edge.
However, there is a specific detail in the *Vaśiṣṭha-saṃhitā*:
"Yellow [powder] should be applied in the east, white in the west, and likewise in the north."
The red [lotus] is on the right, the black is in the south, and the pale-red is situated in the southeast.
In the southwest, blue in color; in the northwest, smoke-colored; and in the northeast, fair (gaura)—this is the sequence prescribed for the eight petals. Thus [ends verse 127].
Having divided the square ground into twelve parts from each direction, the wise one should cast threads there; thus, a hundred squares are seen. || 128 ||
One should subsequently fashion a pedestal consisting of forty-four squares and a lotus of thirty-six squares; there are no pathways here in the row. 129.
The secondary decorations at the door-ornaments are not seen as they were before.
The knower of the tantra should form the corners with the remaining six squares;
he should perform the rest as previously described, and thus the auspicious mandala is completed. || 130 ||
He states another type of mandala with the words "square" (caturasrām).
Since the method for producing the fish-designs is not possible here, there is the statement "twelvefold from the directions.
In that case, one should divide the ground twelvefold in the four directions and then drop the lines therein.
The method for that is as follows:

having prepared sixteen squares as before, one should divide one of those squares into three equal parts; then, at the two points of that division, one should lay down two threads with their tips pointing eastward.

In the pairs of fish formed at each intersection produced by the meeting of these two lines, one should lay down two lines each with their tips pointing east; thus, one should lay down six lines with their tips pointing east.
In this way, one hundred and forty-four squares are produced.
The word "by squares" connects back to what precedes.
In the same manner as the lotus was released;
the pedestal (pīṭha) in the row is just as before.
"By the remaining [syllables]" means:
In that [mandala], one square is situated within the row, while five squares are situated in the outer row;
such is the meaning of "by six.
The word "the rest" refers to the application of colors, the drawing of the three outer lines, and so forth. (128–130)
The wise one should arrange sixty-four squares in a square grid;
with four squares in the center, there shall be a lotus, and again around that [are the remaining squares]. || 131 ||
One should draw four paths ending at the edge of the mandala;
in the four squares situated in the cardinal directions, one should paint lotuses.
Having divided the four intermediate squares into sixteen parts, the wise one should erase them into the form of a svastika, using white, yellow, red, and black [colors]. || 133 ||
One should fill those svastikas with powders starting from the northeast (śiva), following the very path previously described; one should complete the rest in the same manner.
This mandala, known as the nine-naved (navanābha), is said to bestow all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). || 134 ||
He describes the nine-naveled maṇḍala with the words "square" (*caturasra*).
Therein, having first divided it into sixty-four squares as before, one should place a lotus in the central group of four squares as previously described.
Then, in the four cardinal directions, one should construct four paths (*vīthī*) consisting of eight squares each.
In this way, eight groups of four squares remain in the eight directions. Having divided those into sixteen parts, one should erase them as before.
As for the method of erasure: in the sixteen squares, each square of the central group of four is [to be erased] in a direction opposite to its respective neighbor.

Having swept [the area], one should sweep three squares beginning from the corner square of the outer path (*bāhyavīthī*) adjacent to that, in the very same direction. In this way, by sweeping four squares each in the manner of an *upaśobhā*, they become formed as *svastika*s.
Some, however, describe the sweeping differently.

Having cleared away two squares from the eastern direction belonging to the central group of four, one should clear away two squares situated on the outer path connected to them, extending as far as the southern direction. Likewise, having cleared away two squares from the southern direction belonging to the southern group, one should clear away [two squares] situated on the outer path connected to them, extending as far as the western direction.
One should erase two squares.
Likewise, having erased the two western squares in the western direction, one should erase the two northernmost squares situated in the outer path that are connected to them.
Then, having erased the two northern squares in the northern direction, one should erase those connected to them situated in the outer path extending as far as the eastern direction.
One should cleanse two squares. Both wings are likewise traditional.
[The sequence] begins from Śiva, proceeding either from Īśāna to the end of Vāyavya, or [alternatively].
The remainder refers to the dyeing with lotus-paste and so forth, the drawing of wish-fulfilling creepers (*kalpalatikā*) in the walkways (*vīthī*), and the three lines. || 131–134 ||
This five-lotus mandala, adorned with svastikas and vajras, has been described.
For the purpose of worshipping the deity during initiation, this set of four mandalas, which bestows all prosperity, has been taught in accordance with all tantras. || 135 ||
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śāradātilaka* composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇa Deśikendra. || 3 ||
The phrase "the svastika-vajita" means that one should sweep away the four svastikas.
Regarding the term "fourfold," their scope has been stated in the *Prayogasāra* after describing the nine-navel [mandala]:
This supreme state has been declared for the nine jars;
likewise, having first conceived a lotus in the previously mentioned location as before, [one should proceed].
Likewise, having joined the paths in each set of four,
one should draw svastikas in the cardinal directions and erase the corner squares.
This supreme position for the five jars should be established;
likewise, one should draw a lotus in the square space that has been described.
"The single deity of the *kalaśa* is said to have a common locus.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, according to the tradition of the true lineage. || 3 ||
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Now, out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners of mantra, I shall expound initiation (dīkṣā),
without which the fruit of all mantras cannot be obtained.
Whichever mantra-practitioner accomplishes one [mantra] through recitation, fire-offerings, worship,
and other manifold rites, for him the others are accomplished with little effort.
For one who has correctly mastered even a single mantra, there is nothing here that cannot be accomplished;
what then need be said of a man who possesses many mantras? He is indeed Lord Hari himself.

Thus it is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* and the *Nārāyaṇīya*, and elsewhere as well: "O beautiful one, for him by whom a mantra written from a book is recited, no success arises; rather, there is loss at every step."

Likewise, it is stated elsewhere: "Just as those twice-born who have not undergone initiation have no entitlement here to their own duties, such as Vedic study and the like, so too [they gain it] following the initiation ceremony."
"Likewise, those who are uninitiated have no entitlement to the worship of the deity through mantras and so forth; therefore, one should make oneself consecrated by Śiva.
And in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "A mantra heard by chance, whether by deception or without deception..."
"Or one should recite that which has been seen in a manuscript or found in a verse, if it is not harmful.

Regarding this very point: "Having entered the initiation according to the rules, ending with the consecration, and having heard the Tantra obtained from the Guru, one should accomplish the desired mantra."
Elsewhere it is also said: "All rituals, when performed with the Guru as the primary guide, bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Therefore, for the sake of liberation, one should always serve the Guru with a well-composed mind;
for all rituals not instructed by the Guru will certainly be fruitless."
Elsewhere also it is said: "Recitation, the ritual of worshiping the deity, and other duties should be performed by men who possess initiation;
for those self-controlled ones, there is neither sin nor impurity due to birth."

Since it has been stated [in the passage] beginning with "ityādi" that the fruit of the mantra is obtained through initiation (*dīkṣā*), and because the fruit is not accomplished from those [mantras] acquired without the prescribed method in the absence of that [initiation], he makes a formal promise to state the initiation which must necessarily be explained, saying: "Now" (*atha*).
Now, following the description of the mandala, I shall proclaim the initiation of the mantras.
The ellipsis is "out of a desire for the welfare of the disciples previously mentioned";
or alternatively, the ellipsis is "of the Vedic people.
This alone is the traditional reading.
By this, it is stated that initiation by means of mantras (mantradīkṣā) is said to have the nature of all [levels of] generality.
As it was said by Īśānaśiva:
"That [initiation], however, is fourfold due to the distinctions of Mantra, Śiva, Śakti, and Viṣṇu."

"Indeed, initiation through mantra is traditionally held to be common to all groups of mantras; likewise, O twice-born one, it applies to the ancient [castes], as well as to the Śaiva, Śākta, and Vaiṣṇava traditions. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Prayogasāra*: "Having directly perceived one's chosen deity according to the path of mantra..."

"And the Guru should awaken the disciple; that is called mantra-dīkṣā. Also, in the *Ṣaḍanvaya-mahāratna*: "That initiation (dīkṣā) is of three kinds: first is the āṇavī, the supreme is the śākteyī, and the other is the śāmbhavī, which bestows immediate liberation."
Initiation performed through the means of mantras, worship, postures, locations, meditation, and so forth,
according to the form prescribed in the scriptures, is called the āṇavī initiation.

Having perceived her own power in the accomplishment [of the goal], she performed for the disciple an initiation by that power alone, without external means; this is celebrated as the Śākteyī initiation.
Even without a specific underlying intention, for both the teacher and the noble disciple,
it brings about the manifestation of Śiva-nature solely through the grace of the instructor.
"Let this initiation of Śambhu be received, which effects the immersion into Śiva.
For this very reason, the author of the text will state in the Bhairavī-paṭala: "Having received initiation" (12.26).
There, the meaning is "having received the initiation of Śakti."
Likewise, regarding the twelve-syllable mantra, it says: "Initiated and having conquered the senses.
Here, the meaning is "initiated by way of the Vaiṣṇava path.
Similarly, regarding the five-syllable Śiva-mantra as well, it says: "Initiated by way of the Śaiva path."

In this regard, the initiations (dīkṣā) of Śakti, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are to be understood according to their respective Tantras. Regarding the reading "of the practitioners of mantra" (mantriṇām), they say that because the word *mantra* was uttered in the phrase "the fruit of all mantras" in the second half of the verse, it is connected here as "of the mantras. Thus, [the meaning is: "I shall proclaim initiation out of a desire for the welfare of the practitioners of mantra."
However, because there is no connection with the principal mantra-word itself, even that which is a mantra-word is submerged within the compound; thus, the reading is not correct.
The Teachers also say:
"Now I shall duly proclaim the procedure for the initiation of the Manus for the welfare of the world.
Thus [it is said] in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā.
In the Śiva-āgama, initiation is taught by Śiva, the Supreme Self, as being threefold: that of Śāmbhavī, that of Śāktī, and that of Māntrī.
By the mere sight, touch, or even conversation with the Guru, consciousness arises immediately in the person; that initiation is considered Śāmbhavī.
The initiation of power (*śāktī*) is that which possesses knowledge; having entered the body of the disciple, it is performed by the Guru through the path of yoga with the eye of wisdom.
Initiation consists of mantra and ritual action, preceded by the sacrificial pit (or vessel) and the mandala;
this is because of that reason.
Without that initiation,
all those mantras and whatever fruit belongs to them are not obtained— that is, they are not attained.
By this, the following has been stated:

Any mantra whatsoever must be received from the gurus by the disciple through initiation alone, because there is no rule that it would otherwise yield its fruit. Furthermore, while through initiations such as those of Śiva and others only their respective mantras yield fruit, through this [initiation], all mantras do so.
And this phrase, "and all that is the fruit of those mantras," should also be explained as a qualification of the fruit.
By that [previous method], the entire fruit is not obtained merely through instruction and so forth;
however, by this [method], everything is obtained—this is the meaning.
This is because instruction (*upadeśa*) is also prescribed in other tantras.

The etymology of the word *mantra* is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "Because he who has attained perfection brings about the contemplation (*manana*) of the complete knowledge of the universe and protection (*trāṇa*) from the bonds of saṃsāra, he is therefore called a *mantra*."

And in the Rudrayāmala: "O Dear One, because of contemplation (*manana*), because of protection (*trāṇa*), and because of the awakening to my own form through my presiding presence (*madadhiṣṭhāna*), it is correctly called *mantra*. Also elsewhere: "A *mantra* is so called because of secret instruction (*guptopadeśa*), and also because of contemplation and protection."
Thus [ends the first section].
Because it bestows divine knowledge and brings about the destruction of sin, it is therefore called *dīkṣā* by the teachers who are knowers of the Tantras. || 2 ||
That [power] is declared to be fourfold, according to the divisions of *kriyāvatī* and so forth:
it is *kriyāvatī*, *varṇamayī*, *kalātmā*, and also *vedhamayī*.
These, which bring about prosperity, are described in this tantra in their proper sequence.
Having bathed according to the rules and performed his morning rites, the preceptor, adorned and observing silence, should proceed to the sacrificial pavilion for the sake of the sacrifice. || 5 ||
He states the etymological derivation of the word *dīkṣā* with the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and so forth.
This is the etymology derived by taking the first syllable of the two words "should give" (*dadyāt*) and "destruction" (*kṣaya*).
This is in accordance with the statement of Yāska: "One may also provide an etymological explanation based on the similarity of syllables."
As it has been said:
"Because it bestows here a divine state, because it consumes the impurity of *māyā* and *karman*,
and because it yields the fruit arising from the four aims of life, it is therefore designated as 'initiation' (*dīkṣā*)."
In the *Prayogasāra* as well: "The true nature of knowledge is bestowed, and the accumulation of sins is destroyed;
therefore, that should be known as *dīkṣā*, the rite called the severing of bonds.
Here, because it will be stated that even the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) is performed by means of the *tantra* within this very *dīkṣā*, it is indicated by the word "by the teachers" (*deśikaiḥ*).
Prior to the bath, some of the daily duties (*nityakṛtya*) are briefly described:

having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, and having performed purification (*śauca*) and bodily cleansing according to the rules prescribed in the *Smṛtis*; having discarded one's night-garment and put on another garment; having performed the ritual bath with mantras (*mantra-snāna*); having arrived at the temple and performed sweeping, smearing [with cow dung], and other such tasks; and having removed the remains of the previous offering (*nirmālya*) from the deity—
One should worship with the leaves and other materials remaining from the previous day and then offer salutation;
for otherwise, a fault is observed. As they say: "A beast bound while overcome by thirst, and a maiden who is menstruating..."
"And a deity with [worn] flower-offerings destroys previously accumulated merit.

Thus it is said in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "Having properly performed purification according to the procedure prescribed in the Smṛtis, having washed one's feet, sipped water (ācamana), and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one who is self-restrained—"
Having entered the place of the deity and removed the faded flowers (nirmālya),
the wise man should offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), as well as the respectful water-offering (arghya) and the water for washing the feet (pādya).
"One should offer water for washing the face, one should indeed offer a tooth-stick, one should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya), and one should offer a pure, auspicious garment. Then,
having sat upon the seat as prescribed, one should meditate on the Gurus at the crown of one's head.
In the morning, one should remember the Guru upon a white lotus on the head—having two eyes, two arms, a serene countenance, and peaceful—preceded by his name:
"I am the Divine, I am none other; I am indeed Brahman, not subject to sorrow."
I am of the nature of truth, consciousness, and bliss, possessing an eternally liberated essence.
Having thus meditated upon the identity of the Guru, the Deity, and the Self,

one should pray: "O Primordial God, O Śrīnātha Viṣṇu, who consist of the consciousness of the three worlds, by Your very command, having risen at dawn, I shall follow the course of worldly existence for the sake of Your pleasure."
"I know what is Dharma, yet I have no inclination toward it; I know what is Adharma, yet I have no aversion to it.
Whatever I am directed to do by whichever deity resides in my heart, that I perform.
In this [verse], the substitution of "O Śrīnātha Viṣṇu" should be made for "O Śiva," and so forth.
Saying "O Caṇḍīśa, O Śambhu," and so forth, one should then proceed to a river or similar place for the purpose of bathing while reciting the names and qualities of the deity.
The instruction regarding bathing and so on is given here in order to state the proper sequence;
for the deities do not preside over a person who wears impure clothes, has not bathed, or is without ornaments.
Thus it is said.
By this, it is stated that one who is unable to perform the immersion bath (majjana-snāna) may perform other types of bathing as well.
As they say:
"In times of prosperity, [the bath] is performed with cow-dust, or in times of adversity, with mantras alone. Furthermore,
having bathed according to the rules and performed the morning rites, one performs the mantra-bath (*mantra-snāna*), the mantra-sandhyā, and the mantra-libation (*mantra-tarpaṇa*).
It has been indicated that this must be performed.
Now I shall proclaim the auspicious bath which removes all sins;
by performing it correctly, the practitioner becomes fit for all rites.
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* and other such texts,

as well as in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*, the procedure for the mantra-bath and other rites is stated as follows: "Having first performed the Vedic bath, one should thereafter perform the Tantric [bath]," and so forth.
In that regard, mantra-bath is of two kinds: internal and external.
Among these, the internal Vaiṣṇava bath is described in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*:
"One should [meditate upon] Vāsudeva, who has four arms and resembles infinite suns..."
Wearing a crown and adorned with a garland of forest flowers, he holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.
One should contemplate the stream born from the water of His feet falling upon one's own head,
entering one's own body through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
By means of that [water], one should wash away all the impurity residing within this body;
at that very moment, the practitioner becomes free from passion (viraja), resembling a crystal.
"This bath is considered superior to a thousand recitations of mantras.
Thus, the internal Śākta bath has been described in the *Śrīpañcamīmata*.
The method of bathing is twofold, distinguished as external and internal;
the internal bathing, though extremely secret, [is described here] with due reverence.
I shall speak for the sake of destroying worldly existence and for the attainment of the fourfold goals of human life,
having recollected the threefold consciousness from within the midst of the three steps.
A flowing stream of existence, consciousness, and bliss, within the range of contemplation,
it is the means for men— especially yogins— to attain liberation through mere remembrance.
One should meditate upon oneself as being bathed by that [water] for the sake of the pacification of existence. Thus is the internal bath.
So it is said.
In the Śaiva Āgama, the internal bath (ābhyantara-snāna) is described as follows:
"Preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the mental bath (mānasa-snāna) with the root mantra (mūlamantra) in the mind; this is prescribed for all occasions."
Now the external procedure is described:

having bathed according to the rules prescribed in one’s own Vedic branch (*śākhā*), preceded by breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs upon the body—[one recites]: "O Sun, the sacred fords within the belly of the cosmic egg have been touched by your rays."
By that truth, O God, O Maker of Day, grant me a sacred ford.
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu,
and Kāverī, please be present in these waters.
I invoke you here for the purpose of bathing, O beautiful goddess;
come, O Gaṅgā, salutations to you who are endowed with all sacred fords.

Thus, having drawn forth the *tīrtha* from the solar orb (*ādityamaṇḍala*) with the mantra and the goad-mudrā (*aṅkuśamudrā*), having invoked it and joined it to the water with the syllable *vaṃ*, having visualized there the orbs of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, having consecrated it twelve times with the nectar-seed-syllable (*amṛtabīja*) *vaṃ*,
having veiled it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), protected it with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and consecrated it eleven times with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*)—
Oṃ! You are the support of Viṣṇu, who possesses incomparable splendor and whose form is all things;
and from him those waters were born, which share his very nature—to them I bow.
Having thus performed the worship, one should immerse oneself;
for it is stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "Having worshipped with this [mantra], one should immerse oneself in the sacred ford while meditating upon Hari."

There, having visualized the root mantra and the form of the deity, and having emerged [from meditation], one should consecrate oneself seven or twelve times with the root mantra using either the conch mudrā or the flask mudrā.
As he repeatedly desires to emit the entire universe, the pure seed is produced;
may the divine waters, the mothers of all beings, purify me.
One should recite this, encased by the seed-syllables *tāra* (oṃ) and *vāruṇa* (vaṃ):
"May the waters— which, through their very touch, wash away the misfortune existing in all beings in the form of impurity— purify me eternally."
Having thus consecrated her with these two mantras:
"Whatever misfortune is in my hair, at the parting of my hair, or on my head;
whatever is on my forehead, in my ears, or in my eyes—may the waters destroy that! Salutations to you!"
May long life, health, sovereignty, the destruction of the enemy faction, happiness, contentment, forbearance, faith, and knowledge be yours; salutations to you!
Thus one should consecrate.
This is the external mantra-bath.
Then one should consecrate oneself with the root-vidyā of Varuṇa.
Thus it is stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"Having performed the necessary rites, one should perform purification, sipping water, and cleaning the teeth."
Having performed the rinsing of the mouth and other preliminary rites, one should perform the bath.
Having drawn the sacred water from the mandala by means of the heart-mudrā (or mantra) and the hook-mudrā,
one should invoke it into the water and unite it with the mandalas of the moon, sun, and fire.
Having reflected thus, the mantra-practitioner, being well-composed, should immerse himself in its midst;
having recited the root mantra, he should mentally delineate the form.

Having risen and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should thereafter perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) upon himself with the root mantra and the mudrā known as the "vase" (kalaśa).
"Then, having sprinkled [it] seven times with water consecrated by the mantra," thus [it is said].
Also in the Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā:
Having performed the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon his body preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*),
he should draw forth the sacred water (*tīrtha*) from the orb of the glorious Sun using the hook-gesture (*aṅkuśamudrā*).
Having bathed [the object] with the syllable *vaṃ*, one should veil it with the *kavaca* (armor mantra);
having protected it with the *astra* (weapon mantra), one should consecrate it with the root mantra twenty-one times.
Having immersed oneself therein, one should meditate upon the glorious deity while reciting the mantra according to one's ability;
then, having emerged and formed the *kumbha-mudrā*, one should bathe twelve times.
Having placed the water from the Śālagrāma stone, mixed with the fragrance of Tulasī,
into a conch shell, one should whirl it three times and then pour it over one’s own head.
He who, without drinking the water from a Śālagrāma stone, merely pours it upon his head,
is declared to be a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa.
One should drink the water from the feet of a Brahmin before the water from the feet of Viṣṇu;
he who, out of delusion, acts contrarily is called a destroyer of his own self.
Whatever sacred fords exist upon the earth, they are all present in the ocean;
yet all the sacred fords, including the oceans, reside in the right foot of a Brahmin.

Then, having briefly satiated the gods and humans, and having offered libations to the ancestors, he should carefully wash his feet and thighs, put on his garment, and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
One should wear two pure garments, an undergarment and an upper robe, which are uncut, well-appearing, and white; then, seated upon a seat, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
"Having made either the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* or the *tripuṇḍra*, one should perform the *saṃdhyā*.
As for the definitions of the *aṅkuśa*, *kumbha*, and *śaṅkha* mudrās, they are as follows:
[the *aṅkuśa* is formed] by taking the middle finger of the left fist held by the right fist...
Extending the index finger and then contracting it—this is the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*.
Placing the right thumb upon the left thumb with both hands, one should form a fist with space between the fingers; this is the *kumbha* mudrā.
Having grasped the left thumb with the right fist,
one should turn the fist upward and then extend the thumb.
The remaining fingers of the left hand are joined and well-extended, touched by the right thumb;
this is declared to be the conch mudrā.
In that regard, there is a specific rule for the Vaiṣṇava tilaka: "A mace (gadā) should be made on the forehead, a bow and arrow on the head;
Nandaka [the sword] in the middle of the heart, and a conch and a discus on the two arms."
"O Nārada, if a Brahmin marked with the conch and discus should die in a cremation ground, he attains that same destination which is proclaimed for one who dies at Prayāga.
According to the Śaivas, however, the application of the *tripuṇḍra* with ashes must be performed immediately after wearing the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*.
Therefore, the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) is mandatory for the twice-born.
As it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"He upon whose forehead a straight and gentle vertical mark is seen..."
Even that Cāṇḍāla, being pure in soul, is indeed worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt.
Even a man who is impure, lacking in good conduct, and committing evil with his mind,
shall always remain pure if he is marked with the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra).
"O Four-faced One, for my pleasure, for the sake of auspiciousness, or for protection,
my devotee should always wear the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* without negligence.
Regarding that, the procedure for wearing the *tripuṇḍra* is as follows:
The wise one should bring ash produced from the *agnihotra* fire that has been purified;
or else, having brought cow-dung that has not touched the ground with the *sadyojāta* mantra.
Having dried [the vessel] with the left hand, one should burn it away with the Aghora mantra;
having lifted it up with the Tatpuruṣa mantra, one should purify it with the Īśāna mantra.
Having thus consecrated the ashes with the mantra beginning with "agniriti," one should rub them over the limbs and touch them; then, taking them up again with the mantra.
One should recite the mantra "tad rudrāya" [from the Yajurveda] as many times as the number of Rudras,
using the names of the deities preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ), in the dative case, ending with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), and including their respective portions (*aṃśaka*).
One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead, shoulders, and belly with the five-colored syllables and so forth, and on the head with the five-syllable mantra.
"The practitioner who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is like another Śiva in person.
As for the mantra:
"Fire is ash, wind is ash, water is ash, earth is ash, space is ash; indeed, all this is ash."
"The mind is ashes; these senses are ashes. Therefore, one should declare this vow: 'This is the Pāśupata vow, that one should touch the limbs with ashes.
Therefore, that is Brahman; this is the Pāśupata for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu).
This means by means of the five-syllabled Yajus mantra.
Or in another way: Brahmā is to be known on the forehead, Havyavāhana (Agni) in the heart, Skanda at the navel, Pūṣan in the throat, and Rudra in the right arm.
Āditya is in the middle of the right arm, and Śaśin is at the wrist;
Vāmadeva is on the left arm, and Prabhañjana is in the middle of the left arm.
"At the wrist-joint are the Vasus; Hara is said to be in the region of the back;
Śambhu is proclaimed to be at the hump [of the neck]; and the Supreme Self (Paramātman) is said to be in the head.
Thus, in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, the wearing of the *tripuṇḍra* is described as being entirely without mantras.
"Furthermore, the practitioner of mantra, having performed the ritual placement of the hands (nyāsa), should draw the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) with ashes.
Thus it is said;
the taking up of the ashes is also mentioned in that very same place.
The ashes of the Śiva-fire should be collected, or those produced from the Agnihotra fire, or even those arising from the nuptial fire;
they should be well-burnt, pure, and fragrant.
The dung of a tawny cow is recommended when it has fallen from the sky while being carried,
neither moist nor too hard, neither foul-smelling nor dried up.
If it has fallen, one should discard what is above and below and take up the remainder;
having formed it into a ball, one should cast it into the Śiva-fire while reciting the root mantra.
Having discarded both the uncooked and the overcooked portions, one should take the white ash,
stir it with a cloth, and place it in an ash-receptacle.
"One should collect the ashes only when the deity has not been dismissed;
for once the dismissal has been performed, the ashes become *caṇḍabhasma* (impure ashes).
Thereafter, having performed the *sandhyā* as prescribed in one's own Vedic school (*śākhā*), one should perform the *mantra-sandhyā*.
For example:

having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), one should take water from a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) in the right hand, recite the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) over it three times, and perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) three times with that same root mantra. Then, placing the sacred water from the right hand into the left hand, one should consecrate it three times with the root mantra and [sprinkle] it seven times with the drops of water falling therefrom.

Having cleansed oneself with the root mantra (*mūla*), one should take the remaining water in the right hand, bring it near the nose, and draw it into the interior of the body through the *iḍā* [left nostril].

Visualizing that water as black in color due to the accumulated sins being washed away, one should expel it through the *dakṣa-nāḍī* [right nostril] and pour it onto the previously visualized adamantine stone (*vajra-śilā*) while reciting the mantra.
This is the *aghamarṣaṇa*.

Again, taking water with both hands joined in the añjali gesture, one should offer arghya three times with the respective Gāyatrī or the root mantra (mūlamantra), saying: "I offer this arghya to the Deity residing in the solar disc.
Then, meditating upon the Deity situated in the solar disc and performing the upasthāna with the root mantra, one should recite the respective mantra-Gāyatrī or the root mantra twenty-eight times.
Then, having recited the root mantra and offered libations twenty-eight times with the thought, "I satisfy the deity," one should visualize the deity within the solar disc,

offer the *arghya* to the Sun, dismiss the sacred water (*tīrtha*) with the *saṃhāramudrā*, pay homage to the Sun and other deities, and proceed to the sacrificial pavilion while reciting a hymn of praise to the deity.

As it has been stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "Having performed the twilight worship (*sandhyā*) and recited the hymn (*stotra*), one should indeed proceed to the sacrificial hall (*yāgamandira*).
Likewise: "Having performed the Tantric bath according to the very procedure already described..."
Having performed the Vedic and Tantric twilight rituals (sandhyā) as well as the libation (tarpaṇa),
"By reciting hymns and the names [of the deity], one shall go to the abode of the gods. By the word "silent," the prohibition of conversing with other people is intended.
The characteristic of the *saṃhāramudrā* is as follows: having placed the right hand, with its face upward, upon the left hand which is turned downward,
one should join the fingers together with the fingers [of the other hand] and rotate them.
"This is declared to be the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, and it is highly praised for the act of offering.
Thus it is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:

Having sat down in a clean place, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) in succession; having performed this by means of the Supreme Reality (paratattva), one should indeed perform the purification (mārjana) within the body.
Then, having embraced them with water,
the recitation of the entire Aghamarṣaṇa hymn is prescribed as an auspicious offering of Arghya that removes all sins.
Then, the knower of mantras should perform the ritual attendance according to reality,
having recollected the high-souled Viṣṇu, who consists of light and resides within the maṇḍala.
Afterwards, the practitioner should perform the recitation (japa) with the root mantra,
or with the Gāyatrī or the Vaiṣṇavī mantra, having the syllable Om (praṇava) at both the beginning and the end.
Having seated himself in a pure place, he should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the deities beginning with Viṣṇu, as well as for the ancestors and human beings.
One should diligently offer libations to them and then ask forgiveness from the sacred site;
reciting the root mantra, one should proceed until reaching one's own home.
Having reached both hands and feet, one should diligently wash them and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
"Having reached the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa), one should enter after performing a circumambulation.
Also elsewhere: "Having sipped water again and performed the assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) as before, taking water in the left hand, with drops of water trickling [from it]..."
Having performed the sprinkling seven times while reciting the mantra over his head,
the wise one should take the remaining water in his right hand.

Having drawn [the water] into the interior of the body through the *iḍā* [left nostril], that black-colored water— [representing] the accumulated sins washed away— is expelled through the *dakṣa-nāḍī* [right nostril].
Then, the mantra-practitioner, having visualized the form of sin in his right hand,
should cast it onto a vajra-stone in front of him while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Standing, one should offer three handfuls of water to Dineśa;
then the wise person should recite the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having prostrated before the deity situated within the solar disc, one should ask for forgiveness;
then, having dismissed the sacred water (tīrtha) with the saṃhāra-mudrā and sipped water (ācamana), one should remain restrained in speech.

"Having thus completed the twilight ritual (sandhyā), one should then commence the rite of ritual placement (nyāsa). Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the Śaiva Āgama: "Then, having made the sacred water (tīrtha) consist of the nature of Śiva by means of mantras whose essence is Śiva, one should perform the sprinkling (mārjana) with that water using the Saṃhitā mantras."
Pouring water from the left hand while holding it with the right hand, one should perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) on the head in sequence with the mantras; this is what has been taught.

Having led that white water, which is the form of consciousness, situated in the hollow of the right hand up to the tip of the nose, one should draw it in with the left [nostril] and perform breath-retention (kumbhaka).
That sin, appearing like collyrium, should be expelled through the path of Piṅgā (the Viṣṭi breath) and cast upon a diamond-stone; by this, there shall be the expiation of that evil.

Having offered a handful of water as an *arghya* to Śiva with the auspicious mantra ending in "svāhā," accompanied by *kuśa* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, one should recite the Gāyatrī according to one's ability.
"Having sipped water according to the rule with three handfuls, one should offer the *arghya* to the Sun with red flowers and other substances, using the root mantra. Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*: "One should perform the libations to the gods and others, and having completed the *brahmayajña*, one should proceed [with the remaining rites]."
"Having meditated upon Mahādeva situated within the maṇḍala and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite, one should then offer the arghya to that Śiva in the form of the Sun. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, in the *Śivasamhitā*: "The mantra known as *Vyomavyāpin* and those which are the five Brahmans..."
Those mantras [beginning with] "śivagāyatryā" and "rudraṃ ca" respectively.
"This knowledge, the Śivasaṃhitā, is declared to be the destroyer of all sins.
Thus it is said.
One should then proclaim "ĀM ĪM ŪM ĀDYATAḤ VYOMAVYĀPINE CA" (to the one who pervades the sky from the primordial source).
"This [mantra], enclosed at the beginning and end by the Praṇava, is proclaimed as the Vyomavyāpin.
This is the general rule.
Regarding specific mantras for acts such as ritual sipping (ācamana) and so forth, the particular mantras mentioned in their respective ritual manuals (kalpas) should be applied.
And this twilight ritual (saṃdhyā) should be performed at the three times of day;
as stated in the Agastya-saṃhitā:
"Having meditated upon Rāma as one's own self and one's guru, one should then perform the Rāma-saṃdhyā."
"In the evening, in the morning, and at midday.
Thus it is said.
Also in the Śaiva Āgama: "The knower of mantras should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) in the morning, at midday, and in the evening."
Thus [ends the section]. 2-5.
Having sipped water according to the rule and prepared the general offering (sāmānyārghya) there,
one should sprinkle the door with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) and perform the worship of the door.
"Ācamya" means:
in that regard, in the area outside the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*),
because it is stated thus in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*.
"By the prescribed rule" means by the rule stated in the Smṛtis and by the Vaiṣṇava and other rules.
As they say:
"Facing east or north, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, having tied his topknot, and with his arms placed between his knees..."
Then, looking at the water while seated comfortably, he should remain silent, not stooping, with a one-pointed mind, desiring to consume it.

One should perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana) with pure water that is not hot, which is free from foul tastes, smells, and the like, and devoid of insects, froth, or bubbles; it may even be water that has merely been looked upon.
Water reaching the heart, the throat, and the mouth respectively purifies the various twice-born castes;
even for a *vṛṣala* (śūdra) and his wife, it does so by being drunk three times, while for those born of inverse unions (*kuṇḍa*, *anuloma*, etc.), it does so once.
Having sipped water (*ācamana*) three times, the waters please the three Vedic Persons (*trivedapuruṣa*); as for that which one wipes away (*nirmārṣṭi*), [it purifies] the exterior.
Twice with the Atharvaveda, the six-limbed sacrificial Puruṣas shall be pleased from the thumb.
By touching the ring fingers and eyes with the thumbs, one pleases the Sun;
likewise, the index fingers joined with the thumbs, held evenly over the two nostrils, [please] Vāyu;
the little fingers with the thumbs over the ears [please] the Directions; and from the navel, the Vasus.
"One should place the *ātman* at the heart, the *ṛṣis* at the shoulders, and all the [deities] at the head with all the fingers.

Alternatively, the Vaiṣṇava method of sipping water (*ācamana*) is as follows: "Having drunk [water] three times with [the mantras beginning with] Keśava and the others, one should wash the hands twice;
one should wipe the lips twice, and likewise cleanse the mouth twice."
Having washed one hand with one [portion of water] and likewise the feet with another,
he should then sprinkle his head with one [portion], followed by [the worship of] Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others.
One should touch the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, navel, chest, head, and arms;
having performed the *ācamana* in this manner, one becomes Nārāyaṇa himself.
Keśava and the others were described previously; now I shall describe Saṅkarṣaṇa and the rest:
Saṅkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
"Puruṣottama, Adhokṣaja, Nṛsiṃha, as well as Acyuta, Janārdana, Upendra, Hari, and Viṣṇu—these are indeed the twelve. Thus [it is said].

Regarding the Śākta *ācamana*, the Piṅgalāmata states: "Having performed the sipping of water (*ācamana*) with the principles beginning with Ātmatattva, preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with *svadhā*..."
Then, by means of mantras, one should [purify] the face, nose, eyes, ears, navel, and heart in three ways.
"One should touch the head and shoulders; the salutation to the ears is said to be performed with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
*Ātman*, *Vidyā*, and *Śiva* are considered the *tattvas*; the *praṇava* and *vāgbhava* are likewise held [to be the mantras].
Regarding this, in the Śaiva Āgama: "Having gazed [at the water], one should drink it three times with the *brahmatīrtha* while reciting the *śambhara* [mantras]."

"One should know the three principles (tattvas) consisting of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, respectively, through those [syllables] ending with *svadhā*— namely *hrāṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *hrūṃ*— which are the *śambaras* in their respective order. Thus, having prepared the general *arghya* offering, this is done outside [the maṇḍala].
The general *argha* is described in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"Having purified the vessel with the *astra-mantra*, one should fill it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having invoked the sacred waters (*tīrtha*), one should then deposit the perfumes and other offerings with the *praṇava*."
"And one should display the *dhenumudrā*; this is declared to be the general *argha*.
Here, it should be understood that by the word "praṇava," all five *praṇavas* are to be included as appropriate. The method for that is as follows:

Having placed the common vessel facing the door and recited, "Oṃ hraḥ, I prepare the water offering for the door," one should follow the sequence stated in the verse beginning with "the vessel [is purified] by the weapon-mantra" (*pātramastreṇa*). Thus,
"the door."
Having recited the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should sprinkle the door with the water of the general *arghya*.

The general weapon-mantra and so forth will be explained further on. Here, in all instances, even at the beginning, one should append the general weapon-mantra—*astrāya phaṭ*—at the end of the mantra to be employed, such as the weapon-mantra under discussion.
Thus it is with all the mantras of the limbs; some, however, claim that in the case of the weapon-mantra (*astra*) and others, there are only the seed-syllables such as *phaṭ*.
Above the Udumbara tree, one should worship Vighna, Mahālakṣmī, and Sarasvatī;
then, on the southern branch, Vighna, and Kṣetreśa elsewhere.
On their two sides, one should worship Gaṅgā and Yamunā with flowers and water; at each door, one should worship the Astra-mantra on the threshold, following this sequence.
He explains the worship of the door itself with the words "above" (*ūrdhva*) and so forth.

The *ūrdhveḍumbaraka* is the horizontal beam situated above the two door-posts; the term *ūḍumbara* is applied to the threshold (*dehalī*). Since that [threshold] is also situated above, the word *ūḍumbara* is used there by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) due to this similarity.
In that [mandala], one should worship Mahālakṣmī in the center—that is, Dvāraśrī—with flowers and water; the connection is that one should worship her with *arghya* water and flowers.
As it has been said: "Having worshipped Dvāraśrī above."
Elsewhere it is also said: "Above the door, [one should worship] 'Salutation to Door-Glory' (dvāraśrī), and on its right and left, Vighna and Sarasvatī.
Thereafter, one should worship Vighna and Sarasvatī in the two upper corners, starting from the south.
"In the southern branch" means beneath the southern branch;
here some say it refers to the worship of Durgā.
"From the other" means beneath the northern branch.
The connection is with the term "Kṣetreśa.
As it has been said:
"In the corners, one should worship Vighna, Durgā, Vāṇī, and Kṣetreśa."
Thus [it is said].
"Of those two" refers to the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa) and the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapāla).
By the phrase "the Gaṅgā and Yamunā situated at their sides," the worship of the doors and so forth is indicated, as previously described.
That very [deity] is mentioned later by the words "in due order.
Water refers to the general *arghya* water.

The mantras for these [deities] consist of their respective names preceded by the syllable *tāra* (oṃ), the seed-syllable, and the nasal bindu, ending in the dative case (*ṅe*), and followed by the word *namaḥ*.
The ritual application is as follows: *oṃ dvāṃ dvāraśriyai namaḥ*, and so forth.

This is stated in the *Ḍāmara*: "The first syllable of the name, situated between the syllable *oṃ* and the bindu (*m*), is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the deities; that bestows prosperity and accomplishment (*siddhi*) in worship."
The author himself will also state: "beginning with the first letter of one's own name.

This should be understood as applying to those cases where the seed-syllable (*bīja*) has not been explicitly mentioned. Regarding the phrase "on the threshold" (*dehalyām*): *oṃ hnaḥ astrāya phaṭ namaḥ* is the worship of the weapon (*astra*).
It is simply with "flower-water.

As it has been said: "The wise man, having uttered 'ha' and 'ra' together with the *visarga* and followed by the word 'astra' (*phaṭ*), should then release mustard seeds or unbroken grains, or flowers, into the midst [of the water]."
Others, however, desire only the worship of the Vāstupuruṣa here;
as it has been said:
"The Vāstupuruṣa is to be worshipped there, at the entrance and in the middle of the pedestal."
Thus [it is said].
The meditation on these [deities] is to be understood from their respective contexts;
for this very reason, the term "Mahālakṣmī" is employed here.
By the phrase "at each door," this is what is meant:
as they say— "Now,
at a beautiful door, on the right and left branches..."
To Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Gaṅgā, and Yamunā, [one should offer] in the east.
Oṃ! To Bhadra and Subhadra, the cow Godā and the black cow are offered as sacrificial fees in the south;
to Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, the rivers Revā and Tāpī are offered in the west.
"Oṃ, to the treasure-vases Śaṅkha and Padma; likewise, Vāṇī and Veṇī in the north. Thus [it is said].
Somaśambhu also states: "Two by two of the rivers, with their own names in the dative case ending."
But elsewhere: "One should worship Bhadra, Subhadra, Gaṅgā, and Yamunā at the two door-posts;
[their names] ending in the dative case and followed by 'namaḥ', one should worship at the eastern door."

One should worship at the southern gate those possessing the power of consciousness (cicchakti) and likewise the power of illusion (māyāśakti), using [mantras] ending in the dative case and concluding with "namaḥ."
One should worship Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Gaurī, and Śrī on the two door-panels in the west,
using [mantras] ending in the dative case and the word "namaḥ."
"One should worship Jaya and Vijayā, as well as the Śaṅkha and Padma treasures,
ending with the dative case and followed by 'namaḥ', in the north.
Some authorities state that the worship of the door-keepers (dvārapāla) to be described hereafter is also obligatory.
All of this should be understood as being the same even for the daily worship (nityapūjā).
As they say: "This is to be performed everywhere, especially in the case of [deities] who have been installed."
Regarding the initiation (*dīkṣā*), however, there is a specific detail mentioned in another tantra:
one should worship the door-keepers according to the various divisions such as the Vaiṣṇava and others,
with two on each side of every door, making eight in total in due order.
Nanda, Sunanda, the one named Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa,
the one named Bala, Prabala, the one named Bhadra, and Subhadra are considered Vaiṣṇavas.
Then Nandi and Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa and the Bull;
after them, Bhṛṅgiriṭi, Skanda, and Pārvatīśa as the seventh.
Caṇḍeśvara is the eighth; these are the eight Śaiva door-keepers in sequence:
Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadaṃṣṭra, Mahodara, and Gajānana.
Lambodara, Vikaṭa, and Vighnarāja as the seventh;
Dhūmrarāja is to be known as the eighth—these are the Gāṇapatyas in their respective order.
"The Mothers beginning with Brāhmī are proclaimed [as the deities], and the Śākteya ones are the door-keepers.
Others, however, speak of other door-keepers, Gopāla and Rāmacandra—
Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa in the east, and Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ in the south.
Jaya and Vijaya are in the west, while Bala and Prabala are in the north.
Thus [ends the section]. (7–8)
Immediately thereafter, the Lord of Teachers, by means of his divine vision, should dispel the celestial obstacles with the Astra-mantra and those that move through the atmosphere. || 9 ||
And this [process] is indicated by the phrase "immediately thereafter.

By the term "Lord of Teachers" (*deśikendra*), it is stated that one should contemplate oneself as Sadāśiva. The very act of beholding oneself in the form of Sadāśiva through one's own vision is what constitutes the divine gaze (*divyadṛṣṭyavalokana*).
"With water" means with the general *arghya* water. || 9 ||
With three blows of the heels, one should ward off the terrestrial obstacles. || 10 ||
Regarding "with blows from the heels," the mantra for that occasion is as follows:
"May those beings depart who are beings dwelling upon the earth."
May those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva.
"May the spirits and *piśācas* depart in all directions; without causing offense to anyone, I shall commence this rite of Brahman.
Thus it is said in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*, after reciting "apasarpantu" and so forth.
"Having struck [the ground] three times with the heels while reciting this mantra, the wise knower of mantras, having expelled the hosts of spirits, should sit upon his seat. Thus [it is said].
In the *Somaśambhu*, however: "With three strikes from the right heel, [one should expel] the three types of beings situated on the earth."
Thus;
in this manner, [he removes] even the three kinds of obstacles. || 10 ||
Touching slightly with his left hand the branch [of the door], the Guru should step over the threshold;
contracting his body, he should enter within with his right foot.
"A limb" refers to the left limb. "Contracting" means [doing so] in order to provide space for emerging obstacles.
As it has been said: "While clearing away obstacles, one should grant a path on the left."
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, elsewhere: "By the gesture of contracting the left limb, he gives way to those obstacles that arise for those departing."
Thus; and likewise elsewhere: "Having expelled the host of obstacles from the left. Thus.
The triad beginning with "touching within" has a visible purpose, because the deity is also worshipped at the threshold. || 11 ||
One should worship the Lord of the Site (Vāstveśa) and Brahmā in the south-western direction;
one should then sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion with the five products of the cow and water for the arghya offering.
"Vāstvīśam" refers to the Kṣetrapāla of each respective field;
these shall be described by me in the Kṣetrapāla mantra.
The section beginning with "divyadṛṣṭi" and ending with the worship of Brahmā is common even to the daily ritual (nityapūjā).
Regarding "pañcagavya":
the varieties of the five products of the cow will be explained in the twenty-first [chapter].
"Arghyatoya" refers to the water for general offerings.
"One should sprinkle" means with the mantra to be given.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "One should sprinkle the site of initiation with cow-products, purified by the mantra. (12)
One should perform the purification of that area up to the crossroads by means of inspection and other rites.
Inspection is performed with the root mantra, and sprinkling is considered to be done with the *śara* mantra. || 13 ||
Striking with those very [blades] and sprinkling with the armor-mantra is prescribed;
the wise one should fumigate the interior with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor. || 14 ||
There, one should scatter the offerings (vikirān) seven times consecrated with the weapon-mantra (śarāṇu):
parched grain, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, dūrvā grass, a goad, and unbroken rice grains. || 15 ||
Addressing them with the mantra "Vikirā," which destroys the entire multitude of obstacles, one should sweep them away with a handful of darbha grass consecrated by the Astra-mantra. || 16 ||
The phrase "up to the crossroads" (catuṣpathāntam) is connected with what precedes it.

In that context, the area outside the pavilion (maṇḍapa), extending for the distance of one cubit (hasta) from the gateway pillars (toraṇastambha), is designated by the term "crossroads" (catuṣpatha).
One should perform its purification—along with the purification of the pavilion—by means of the four rites beginning with inspection (vīkṣaṇa).
Here too, the phrase "up to the crossroads" (catuṣpathāntam) applies.
He states the very acts of gazing and so forth with the words "gazing" (vīkṣaṇam).
"With the root mantra" (mūlamantreṇa) means with the mantra to be given.
"By the arrow" means by the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*);
"by the armor" means by the armor-mantra (*kavaca-mantra*).
The nature of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and ablution (*abhyukṣaṇa*) will be explained further on.
And those [offerings] are made with the common *arghya* water alone.
"In the interval" (*antaram*) means the middle of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
"The wise one" (*sudhīḥ*) is connected with what follows.
And by this, the specific detail mentioned by Somaśambhu is indicated:
"there" means in the middle of the pavilion;
"with the arrow-mantra" means with the *astra* mantra.
In the scriptural treatises (*āgama-śāstra*), the word *aṇu* is a synonym for mantra.
*Siddhārtha* refers to white mustard seeds.
*Bhasman* refers to cow-dung ash.

"Destruction of the entire flood of obstacles" refers to the meditation (*dhyāna*). The word "seven," mentioned in the phrase "with [mantras] recited over the weapon (*astra*)," is to be supplied here.
By the particle "ca" (and) in the phrase "one should sweep (*mārjayet*)," the word "scattered offerings (*vikirān*)" is to be supplied.
The word "those" (tān) is connected with what follows.
However, there is a specific distinction in the *Somaśambhu*:
"The scattered offerings (*vikirān*) should be either pure parched grains (*lājān*) or [grains] consecrated seven times with the weapon-mantra (*śastra*)."
These [offerings], sprinkled with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra and enveloped by the Kavaca-mantra, [should be presented].

One should wipe away [the impurities] with that fistful of *darbha* grass— which has the form of various weapons, wards off floods of obstacles, is made from thirty-six blades each the length of a palm tree,
and has been consecrated seven times with the *Śivāstra* mantra— [thereby obtaining] the supreme sword of awakening.
Thus; [this] scattering and wiping away should be performed with the mantra to be recited. 13–16.
One should prepare a seat for the Vardhanī vessel in the direction of Īśa (the northeast), after having had the Brahmins recite the Puṇyāha formula and having satisfied them with gifts. || 17 ||
Among the mandalas described, he should draw one upon the altar;
the mantra-practitioner should enter and sit upon a soft seat, facing either east or north.
Regarding "of the Lord" (īśasya):
the vessel with its stalk is the *vardhanī*; for its seat, [it is placed] in the direction of the Lord, that is, in the northeast (*aiśānī*).
The connection is that one should "arrange" (prakalpayet), meaning "place," those scattered offerings (vikirān).
Regarding the term "puṇyāha": the recitation for an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) is as described in the third chapter. || 17 ||
"One" refers to the maṇḍala;
this much [is required] in the initiation alone. "Should enter" means he should sit down.
"A soft seat" means for the sake of non-distraction; this is for the sake of a visible purpose.
For when there is distraction, the mind goes toward that very thing and not toward recitation, worship, and so forth.
By the word "mantrin," this is what is meant.
Having recited "Homage to Anantāsana!
Homage to Vimalāsana!
Homage to Padmāsana! and placed the consecrated *kuśa* grass upon the seat, one should worship the seat.
For the seat-mantra (*āsana-mantra*): Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Sutala is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Kūrma is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for sitting upon the seat.
Oṃ! O Earth, the worlds are supported by you; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu.
Therefore, support me eternally, O Goddess, and make this seat pure.

Thus, one should sit with the seat-mantra (*āsana-mantra*). As it has been said: "The seer of that seat is Kūrma; its meter is likewise Sūktatṛṣṭubh; its world is Sutala; and its presiding deity is Sudhīśa."
It is said that the Earth is indeed its deity, and its utility for practices such as recitation (japa) has been stated.
In that regard, the seats mentioned in other tantras are as follows:
"Whether it be silk, or cotton cloth, or even leather, or woolen."
A seat made of cane, or palm leaves, or of kambala grass, or of darbha grass.
The practitioner of mantra should avoid a seat made of bamboo, stone, wood, earth, grass, or leaves, for such a seat bestows poverty, disease, and suffering.
"The attainment of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa occurs upon a seat covered with cloth, deerskin, and kuśa grass.
Regarding wooden seats and others, a specific rule has been stated: "For ascetics (yatīs), one should have a smooth seat made in the shape of a tortoise."
But for others, one should have it made with four sides and four corners.
A wise person should always avoid a seat made of cow dung or clay that is broken, as well as one made of Palāśa or Pippala wood, or one pierced by metal, or one that has been exposed to the sun.
One should not perform giving, sipping water for purification, fire-offerings, eating, worship of the deities, Vedic study, or libations while sitting with one's feet raised.
"One who has placed his feet upon a seat, or upon his knees, or even upon his shanks, having performed the *avasakthikā* posture, is called *prauḍhapāda*. (18)
Seated in the lotus posture, observing silence, with mind composed and senses subdued, the preceptor should place the articles of worship on the right side. || 19 ||
Regarding the phrase "having assumed the lotus posture" (*baddhapadmāsana*):
the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) will be described later.
The portion stating, "one should bind the two big toes with the hands," is utilized only in the context of *yoga*; that [portion] is not present here.
Because the definition of the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) is stated in exactly the same way in another tantra: "Taking the left foot, one should place it upon the right;
likewise, one should place the right foot above the left."
Pressing the heels against the hips with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose—
this is the lotus posture (padmāsana), honored by all.
The term "lotus posture" (*padmāsana*) is an illustration;
as they say:
"Seated in a single posture, such as the lotus, the svastika, the hero (*vīra*), or others..."
"One should perform recitation, worship, and so forth; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
By the word "silence" (mauna), there is a prohibition of conversation as prompted by worldly attachment.
As it has been said:
"One should not speak even with those present in the assembly during recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth.
This is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) consisting of the attributes "concentrated" (*samāhita*), "vigilant" (*sāvadhāna*), and "one who has conquered the senses" (*jitendriya*).
The "articles of worship" (pūjādravyāṇi) are the flowers and so forth.
This is connected with the word "deśika" (the preceptor) in the following verse.
By this, it is stated that one should also place the vessels for arghya, pādya, ācamana, madhuparka, and the second ācamana on the left side. || 19 ||
To the left, one should place a beautiful jar filled with well-perfumed water;
afterwards, one should set down a vessel for the washing of the hands. || 20 ||
One should place auspicious lamps ignited with ghee all around,
as well as a beautiful mirror, a fly-whisk, an umbrella, and a charming palm-leaf fan.
The preceptor, having joined his palms in reverence, should place the vessels containing the sprouts of auspiciousness on the left and right sides.
Having bowed to the gurus and Gaṇeśāna, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having accomplished the purification of the hands (karaśuddhi), one should thereafter perform the three claps (tālatraya). || 23 ||

The preceptor should also perform the binding of the directions with the *Urdhvordhva-astra-mantra*. He should then provide protection on all sides using the splendor generated by that mantra. || 24 ||
"Suvāsitaṃ" means [perfumed] with camphor and other such substances. || 20 ||

"Manoharam" (captivating) is an adjective qualifying all four items, beginning with the mirror. The syntactic connection is as follows: "one should place the mirror," and so forth; "one should enter," and so forth.
This much is the same even in the case of the daily worship (nityapūjā). || 21 ||

Regarding the term *maṅgalāni*: one should place in the various directions those auspicious vessels (*maṅgala-rūpāṇi aṅkura-pātrāṇi*) in which seeds have been sown according to the aforementioned method.
By the word "the Preceptor" (*deśika*), this is what is intended: [that the Preceptor himself should perform this].
In the manner previously described, one should perform this three times starting from the eastern direction and so forth.
This very rite of reception (*pratipattikarma*) for them occurs precisely at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Having joined the palms in reverence, [one should place them] on the left and right sides.
The connection is: "having bowed to the Guru Gaṇeśāna.
In that regard, the ritual application is:
*Oṃ guṃ, salutations to the Gurus*.
Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati.

As it has been stated by the Teachers: "In the sacrifice (or as limbs of the rite), the mantras beginning with the Guru and ending with the Lokapālas should end in the dative case followed by 'namaḥ'.
In the act of worship they should be thus; however, in the fire-ritual (vahnikārya), they should end in the seed-syllable 'svāhā' (dviṭha)."
Thus [it is said].
Here, because it is stated that "the [mantras] ending with *dviṭha* (svāhā) are for the rite of fire," there is an inclusion of the tongues of Agni and so forth which are to be described later;
for immediately after that, the procedure for the gold [offering] is performed with the mantras of the world-protectors (*lokeśa*). || 22 ||
By the use of the plural "gurus," the guru, paramaguru, parāparaguru, and parameṣṭhiguru are included.
As they have said:
"Therefore, beginning from the very beginning, one should pay homage to the lineage of gurus."
Thus,
one should then recite this verse:
"Oṃ, salutations to the great ones, salutations to the small ones, salutations to the young, and salutations to the aged."
"Let us sacrifice to the gods if we are able; may I not cut off the blessing from one who is superior—O gods, look upon me! Thus [is the mantra for] the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*).
In this context, the phrase "with the weapon-mantra" (astramantreṇa) is connected to the three [acts] beginning with the purification of the hands (karaśuddhi).

Therein, "purification of the hands" refers to the placement (nyāsa) of the weapon-mantra by way of pervasion upon the fingers beginning with the thumbs, on the interior of both hands, on the exterior of both hands, and on both sides of both hands.
As it has been said:
"The mantra is within the two hands—the pervaded and the pervader—on the inner and outer sides. (23)
Regarding "digbandha" (the binding of the directions):
it is the placement of the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) in the ten directions using the index finger drawn up from the *nārāca-muṣṭi* (arrow-fist) grip.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Having covered the directions with the index finger, whose tip is made to flick against the tip of the thumb..."
Thus it is said.

Also elsewhere: "If the tip of the thumb should touch the tip of the middle finger, while the other fingers remain unjoined, then there shall be the mudrā of the supreme weapon named Nārāca, the destroyer of the elements. Thus it is said.

There is a distinction elsewhere: "At the conclusion of the *praṇava* and the heart [mantra], having likewise uttered the word 'Sudarśana' with the dative case-ending and ending the mantra with *phaṭ*, one should fashion the ten ramparts (*daśaharit*) by means of this mantra.

By the word "the Preceptor" (*deśika*), it is indicated that one should construct the rampart of fire both with the Sudarśana mantra and also with the mantra for the rampart of fire to be described later.
The mudrā of the fire-enclosure is described in the *Prayogasāra*: "Having placed the two hands with their tips like tridents, one should move them crossed over on both sides;
this is declared to be the *astramudrā*, characterized as the fire-enclosure."
"It pacifies the malice of others and removes the fear of serpents and thunderbolts.
Thus it is said: "Then, having purified [the site] with the Astra-mantra, [one performs] the hand-clapping, the binding of the directions, and the fire-chamber."
He states their fruit with the words "by that. || 24 ||
One should unite the self with the Supreme Self by means of the path of the *suṣumṇā*, being composed and employing the method joined with yoga and the *cin-mantra*. || 25 ||
One should contemplate the principles (tattvas) of all beings within the Cause (kāraṇa), as they are dissolved in the form of seeds within the Supreme Self (paramātman) in reverse order. || 26 ||
Regarding the term *suṣumṇā*:

the connection is that one who is concentrated (*samāhita*) should, by means of the path of the *suṣumṇā*, unite the self (*ātmānaṃ*)—that is, the individual soul (*jīvātmānaṃ*) residing in the heart-lotus—with the Supreme Self (*paramātmani*) through the method joined with yoga and by means of the "consciousness-mantra" (*cinmantreṇa*). This is the sense.

As they say: "The individual soul (jīva), which is the size of the tip of a needle, should be meditated upon by the wise within the heart-lotus, which has its root in Brahman and possesses the stalk of knowledge.
This is the meaning of the phrase "by means of the method joined with yoga."

Having raised Kuṇḍalinī by means of the syllable *HŪṂ* along the path taught by the Guru, and having visualized her as having reached the heart-lotus, one should then seize the life-force (*jīva*) at its opening and visualize it as having reached the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*).
For this very reason, there is the expression "one who is concentrated" (*samāhita*).
By the *cinmantra*, which is the *ātman-mantra* to be described hereafter.
As they say: "The supreme, white [deity] is to be led to the *dvādaśānta* by means of the *haṃsa-mantra*."
Elsewhere also: "Having drawn up the individual soul (jīva) from its own abode by means of its own channel through the *haṃsa* into its own lotus.
And elsewhere also: "Then, having joined the soul via the path of the central channel, which is difficult to traverse, into the extremely subtle Śiva seated in the lotus (*puṣkara*)."
"By the swan" means: when [the mind] has reached the pericarp of the thousand-spoked [lotus], that is, the Supreme Self (paramātman). || 25 ||
Regarding the term "in the cause":

the syntactical connection is that one should meditate upon the principles (tattvas), beginning with earth, as being dissolved by way of reversal into the Supreme Self—the cause of all beings—in the form of a seed.
In this context, "reversal" refers to the order of dissolution in relation to the process of creation.
In all cases, the dissolution of the effect into its cause is observed;
for this very reason, the description of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) occurs in the first chapter,
because without emanation there would be no knowledge of the relationship between cause and effect.
For this very reason, there is the qualifying expression "the cause of all beings.
By the word "also" (api), it includes the phonemes as well.
As it has been said: "Having thus formed a mental resolve, one should then withdraw the phonemes from their positions of placement."
And that sequence is stated in the Tantra:
"By the reverse order, the *kṣa* [syllable] dissolves into the letter *la*;
this [*la*] into the letter *ha*; the letter *ha* into the letter *sa*; and then the letter *sa* into the letter *ṣa*."

"Having diligently brought about dissolution in sequence up to the letter *a*, one should place that *a* in the *brahmarandhra* at the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*). The word "ca" (and) serves to include the preceding [elements]. || 26 ||
Then, one should dry up the body with the wind through the wind-seed;
by that same fire-seed, one should dissolve the entire physical form. || 27 ||

Then, one should separate the humors with nectar, that is, with ambrosial water; having thus prepared them, one should drench and repeatedly bathe the body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head. || 28 ||
"Then" means by means of the seed-syllable of air, the letter *ya*;
the meaning is: by the wind arising from that.
By this, the inhalation (pūraka) is described;
by means of the seed-syllable of fire, the letter *ra*.

With that very [syllable], by means of the fire arising from the seed-syllable of fire, one should burn the entire body together with the personified sin (*pāpapuruṣa*), which consists of one's own impurities.
The meditation on the personification of sin is as follows:
having the murder of a Brahmin for its head, the theft of gold for its two arms,
the drinking of intoxicants joined with its heart, and the violation of the Guru’s bed for its two hips.
The pair of feet joined with that [body] was the cause of the downfall of limbs and minor members;
its hair were minor offenses, and its beard and eyes were red.
"One should contemplate [the sin] as holding a sword and shield, the size of a thumb, face-down, and black in color, in the right side of the abdomen.
By this, the *kumbhaka* (retention of breath) is described. || 27 ||

Then, when the burning has occurred, by the statement "one should separate the impurities from the ashes of the personified sin (pāpapuruṣa) which is the very nature of the impurities," the exhalation (recaka) is described.
In that context, it should be understood that the separation of the ashes is also effected by means of the seed-syllable of air (vāyubīja).
As the Teachers have said: "One should release [the breath] according to the previous rule."
Thus [it is said].
Nāgabhaṭṭa also says: "By means of the wind from his mouth and so forth, he removed that entire heap of ashes."
Also in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*: "Having scattered that entire heap of ashes with the wind produced from the seed-syllable of Vāyu.
Thus it is said.
Elsewhere also it is said: "His body burnt by the fire of that rising mass of wealth, his ashes were scattered by the wind.
Regarding this, some maintain that in these three locations, the sequence follows the numbers sixteen, sixty-four, and thirty-two.
Others say that the number is fifty-two and twenty-five.
This is stated in the *Saṃhitā*:
"By means of the seed-syllables of the Maruts, Agni, and the Moon, there are fifty measures (mātras)."
