Thus it is said. And the Teachers [state]: "Alternatively, once the body has been purified through the processes of drying, burning, flooding, and piercing, one should properly restrain the vital breaths by means of the fifty distinct measures (mātrās)."
"Furthermore, although consisting of fifty [letters], the *tāra* (the syllable Om) is taught as being divided by its *kalās*.
By means of that very measure, the *kalās* are maintained by the knower of reality (*tattvavid*).
Some, however, maintain that there is a threefold *prāṇāyāma* for each of the three locations as well.

The connection is as follows: with the nectar, by means of the seed-syllable of nectar "vaṃ," one should flood, that is, completely drench, the body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head with the nectar arising therefrom, which is the water of immortality. || 28 ||
Then, one should cause the principles (tattvas) dissolved in the self to reach their own respective places;
one should then bring the self into the lotus of the heart of the Supreme Self. || 29 ||
"Own place" (svasthāna) means according to the sequence of emanation, in the manner described in the first chapter.
By the word "then" (tadā), it is stated that one should likewise cause the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa' to reach their own places by way of the sequence of emanation.
As it has been said:

"Having brought down from that [Amṛta] the form consisting of all the phonemes by means of the recitation of the letter *la*, one should fashion with it a complete body as a rain of a flood of nectar.
Having thus fashioned the body "with half of a hundred phonemes," [one proceeds].
The connection is as follows: by means of the mantra of Haṃsadeva, one should bring the self from the presence of the Supreme Self (paramātman) into the lotus of the heart.
The "Lord" (deva) of the "Haṃsa"—that is, the individual soul (jīva)—is the Supreme Self because He is the object of worship;
[this is accomplished] by that mantra, namely "So 'ham" (That am I).
Alternatively, "by Manu" is connected with "of the Supreme Self," as it was previously stated that one should "join [it] to the Supreme Self";
thus, the word "from that" is obtained by implication.
"Of the Swan-God" (haṃsadevasya) is connected with what follows.

As it is stated in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*: "Having thus sounded that primordial [Maṇvī]— who has been realized by the Siddhas at the end of the Nāda— with the mantra 'So'ham,' one should place the digit of the individual soul (*jīvakalā*) from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) into the heart."
Also in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*: "Having brought that self-consciousness from the sky of consciousness by means of the thought 'I am He'...

Regarding this, the procedure is set forth according to the teacher's instruction: "For the sake of attaining the qualification for the worship of the venerable Deity and so forth, I shall perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other rites."

Having visualized Kuṇḍalinī—arisen from the Mūlādhāra, radiant with the brilliance of a thousand flashes of lightning, and in the form of a lotus fiber—having reached the heart-lotus via the path of the Suṣumṇā; and having grasped the individual soul (jīva) from the heart-lotus in the form of a lamp-flame and visualized it proceeding from the twelve-petaled lotus to the thousand-petaled lotus;
there, one should unite the individual soul with the Supreme Self by means of the *haṃsa* mantra.
Then, from the feet up to the knees, one should visualize a yellow square, the earth-maṇḍala;

there, having recollected the action of moving with the feet, the object to be reached, smell, the sense of smell, the earth, Brahmā, the *nivṛtti* [kalā], and the *samāna* wind, one should recite this: *oṃ hrāṃ brahmaṇe pṛthivyadhipataye nivṛttikalātmane huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Having recited the mantra, one should dissolve all those [elements] into water through the door of Kuṇḍalinī, thinking "I dissolve them," and thus withdraw them into the locus of water.
One should contemplate the water-maṇḍala, white and semi-circular in shape, extending from the knees up to the navel;

therein, one should remember the hand, the object to be taken, the tongue, the taste, the water, Viṣṇu, the *pratiṣṭhā* [kalā], and the *udāna* breath, and [recite]: *oṃ hrīṃ viṣṇave jalādhipataye pratiṣṭhākalātmane haṃ*.

Having uttered this mantra, *phaṭ svāhā*, one should dissolve them all into the fire through the gateway of Kuṇḍalinī, withdrawing them into the locus of fire with the thought, "I dissolve them in the fire. One should contemplate the triangular fire-mandala, red in color, extending from the navel to the heart; therein, one should recollect the anus, the organ of excretion, the visarjanīya sound, the eye, fire, Rudra, Vidyā, and Vyāna. Then, one should utter: *oṃ hrūṃ rudrāya tejo'dhipataye vidyākalātmane huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

Having recited the mantra, one should dissolve all those [elements] into the wind through the door of Kuṇḍalinī, thinking "I dissolve them into the wind," and thus withdraw them into the station of the wind.

Then, from the heart up to the eyebrows, one should contemplate the circular wind-maṇḍala, which is black and marked with six dots; therein, one should meditate upon the presiding deity Īśāna, bliss, its object, touch, the tangible, the wind, the Lord (Īśvara), peace, and the downward breath (apāna), while reciting: *Oṃ hnaiṃ īśānāya*.

Having recited this mantra, "To the Lord of Wind, whose nature is the power of pacification, *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*," one should dissolve all of them into the space through the door of Kuṇḍalinī, withdrawing them into the locus of space with the thought, "I dissolve them into space.
Then, from the center of the eyebrows up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), there is the clear, circular mandala of space; therein—
Having recollected speech, the face, the inexpressible, sound, the ear, space, Sadāśiva, Śāntyatītā, and the vital breath (prāṇa), one should utter this mantra: "Oṃ hnauṃ!

To the Lord of Space, Sadāśiva, whose self is the Śāntyatītā-kalā, huṃ phaṭ svāhā! Having thus dissolved all of them into the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra) with the thought, "I dissolve them into the ego," one should then dissolve that ego into the principle of Mahat.

Having dissolved the principle of Mahat into Prakṛti— which is the meaning of the *hṛllekhā* [mantra], whose nature is the Śabdabrahman known as Mātṛkā— thinking, "I dissolve it," one should then dissolve that [Prakṛti] likewise into the Self-luminous Reality,
which is of the nature of eternally awakened and pure consciousness, and is characterized by existence, knowledge, infinity, and bliss.
One should dissolve [the elements] with the thought, "I dissolve them into the Supreme Cause, the Parabrahman.
Thus it is said in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"One should dissolve earth—along with its fragrance and other qualities and conjoined with the sense of smell—into water."
One should dissolve the tastes and so forth, together with the tongue, into the water within the fire.

The wise one should dissolve form and the other [objects] along with the eye into fire within the wind; then he should dissolve the wind into space, together with touch and the other [objects] along with the skin.
One should dissolve the sky, together with sound, into the ego; that [ego] into the Great Principle (mahat);
and the Great Principle into the Unmanifest, the supreme cause of all powers.
"One should contemplate that everything, beginning with the earth, is dissolved therein—that supreme Vaiṣṇava station which is of the nature of Sat-Cit-Ānanda.

Then, for the purification of the embodied person of sin: Śarīrasyāntaryāmī (the Inner Controller of the Body) is the Ṛṣi; Satyam (Truth) is the Devatā; and Prakṛti-Puruṣam (Primal Nature and Spirit) is the Chandas.

Having stated the *viniyoga*, one should contemplate the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) of white form situated in the right side of the abdomen; then, having stated that for the seed-syllable *yaṃ* (Vāyu), Kiṣkindha is the *ṛṣi*, Vāyu is the deity, and Jagatī is the meter, and that its *viniyoga* is for the purification of the personification of sin together with the body,
one should contemplate *yaṃ* at the root of the navel within the circle of six dots.
That seed-syllable of wind is smoky in color and joined with a flickering banner;
accompanied by the sounds "dhūṃ dhūṃ," it is the purifier of all, having Īśa as its presiding deity.

Having meditated thus, one should rotate the seed-syllable sixteen or twelve times by means of the practice of inhalation (*pūraka*), and visualize the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) together with his body as being dried up by the wind arising from that seed-syllable.
Then, having stated: "For the seed-syllable *raṃ*, the seer is Kaśyapa, the deity is Agni, the meter is Triṣṭubh; its application is for the burning of that [sin],"—
One should contemplate within the heart a red triangular fire-mandala,
which is said to be endowed with the Vidyā-kalā and has Rudra as its presiding deity.
Having meditated thus, one should rotate the seed-syllable sixty-four or fifty times by means of the practice of *kumbhaka* (retention).
One should visualize that [the body] has been reduced to ashes by the fire arising from that seed-syllable.

Then, by means of *recaka* (exhalation) for thirty-two or twenty-five *mātrās*, one should rotate the previously mentioned wind-seed-syllable and exhale the ashes of the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*).

Then, having said: "The seed-syllable *vaṃ* belongs to Varuṇa; Hiraṇyagarbha is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Haṃsa is the deity (*devatā*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chanda*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for immersion (*plāvana*)."— "The *vāruṇa* [mantra] is the white mandala of Varuṇa, resembling the crescent moon, situated upon a pair of white lotuses, and its presiding deity is Varuṇa."
Having meditated thus, one should visualize the ashes of that body becoming a solid mass through the nectar flowing from its seed-syllable.

Then, having stated: "For the seed-syllable *laṃ*, which is the seed of Earth—Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Indra is the deity (*devatā*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of solidification"—one should [visualize] the Earth-mandala marked with a vajra within the Foundation-mandala (*ādhāramaṇḍala*).
One should meditate in the mind, as before, upon a square and firm [seat] of yellow color, presided over by Indra, and joined with the seed-syllable *laṃ*.
Having meditated thus, one should contemplate the body as firm through the solidity arising from that seed-syllable.

Then, having stated: "For the seed-syllable *haṃ* of space, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Space is the deity (*devatā*), the Paṅkti is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is in expansion"—one visualizes the orb of space as circular, radiant with the syllable *haṃ*, at the end of the twelve fingers.
One should meditate upon the deity of space, who is joined with the Śāntyatītā and Kalā kalās.
Having meditated thus, one should conceive of space by means of the ether arising from that [seed-syllable].
As it has been said:
"With the earth-seed-syllable *glauṃ*, one should lead that [space] to a state of endurance."
"By means of the seed-syllables *oṃ*, *haṃ*, and *vaṃ*, the process of reintegration (*avayavīkaraṇa*) occurs.

Thus, having meditated upon one's own body in this manner, one should cause the principles (*tattvas*) to reach their respective locations through the sequence of emanation from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Then, by means of the mantra "So 'ham" (That am I), one should bring the individual soul (*jīva*) from the presence of the Supreme Self into the heart-lotus; this is the summary.
And this purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) is essential.

Worship performed by one devoid of the purification of the five elements—just like malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), as well as recitation (*japa*) and so forth—will yield a contrary result; likewise for worship performed without devotion.
Indeed, for those who are devoid of the ritual procedure (*vidhi*), it destroys the fruit of their actions;
yet, by the command of Śaṅkara, it bestows the sovereignty over the night-stalkers (*niśācara*).

Thus it is stated in the Śaivāgama. Also elsewhere: "The purification of the elements that have taken the form of the body, through contact with the imperishable Brahman—this is considered *bhūtaśuddhi* (purification of the elements)."
"Without the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), all rites such as recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), worship (arcana), and so forth,
will be fruitless even if performed in every possible manner.

Following this, the installation of one's own vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) must necessarily be performed immediately thereafter using the mantra for the installation of the vital breaths that is about to be described.
This is known from tradition and the instruction of the guru.
Regarding this, there is a specific detail in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*:
"Having placed the hand upon the heart, one should perform the stabilization of the vital breath (*prāṇasthāpana*)."

Then, for the sake of accomplishing the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the eightfold actions beginning with birth, one should perform sixteen repetitions of the *praṇava* and meditate upon the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*). Thus [it is said]. (29)
Then, according to Manu, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and other rites for Haṃsadeva;
the knower of mantras should then assign the seer (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas), and the deity (daivata) of the mantra. || 30 ||
Having placed [the mantras] upon one's own head, face, and heart in due order, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to the rule with the root mantra. || 31 ||
He states what must be done immediately next with the words "of Haṃsadeva.

The connection is as follows: then, having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) according to rule with the root mantra, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and so forth for Haṃsadeva.
In this context, the meaning of the phrase "according to rule" is as follows:

When it is the *ajapā* placement (*nyāsa*), then by means of the *ajapā*; when it is the *praṇava* placement, then by means of the *praṇava*; when it is the external *mātṛkā* placement, then by means of the *mātṛkā*.
Likewise, when it is the placement of Bhuvaneśī, then by means of her; when it is the placement of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), then by means of the mantra being recited.
In that regard, there is a specific rule for the *prāṇāyāma* of the *mātṛkā*.
As they say:
"One should fill the breath through the *iḍā* with the vowels (*svaras*), and retain it (*kumbhaya*) with the consonants (*sparśas*);
then one should exhale (*recayet*) through the *piṅgalā* with the sibilants (*ūṣmas*) beginning with *ya*."

In the same manner, there should be filling, retention, and then exhalation of the breath through the *iḍā*; thereafter, the triad of filling and the other two [retention and exhalation] should again be performed through both nostrils.

"Having performed three *prāṇāyāmas*, one should thereafter perform the pervasive [recitation] (*vyāpaka*) with the letters beginning with 'A' and ending with 'KṢa', from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
Regarding the mantra being recited, the *prāṇāyāma* should be performed with the single primary seed-syllable (*bīja*) of that mantra.

Or by all [of them]. In that regard, if by one [breath], there are sixty-four repetitions; if by eight syllables, thirty-two times, and so forth—this should be understood. As they say: "One should recite a ten-syllable mantra twenty-eight times for the sake of desired results."
"One should not restrain the well-praised wind with the eighteen-syllable mantra;

rather, a person skilled in the practice of exhalation (recaka), while practicing the 'nine-fold deliberation' (navavicāra) of the sage and muttering the mantras according to their respective syllables, should perform the application of breath (prāṇaprayoga). Thus it is said.
The ritual placement (nyāsa) is as follows:
the first [syllable] of the ajapā-mantra is at the root, the next at the head,
and likewise on the right and left sides.

In this regard, the practice is as follows: "Haṃ, obeisance to the Self that is the Puruṣa; Saḥ, obeisance to the Self that is Prakṛti; Haṃsaḥ, obeisance to the Self that is both Prakṛti and Puruṣa. This is the pervasive [mantra].
In that same manner, the internal placement of the *mātṛkās* (*antarmātṛkānyāsa*) is also performed.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the offering of the previous day's recitation (*pūjā-pūrvadinajapa-nivedana*) and the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for the recitation of that day are included.
Following this, the placement of the *praṇava* is performed, because it originates from the *haṃsa-mantra*.
He too should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) in the locations of the *mātṛkās* with "Oṃ Aṃ, salutation to Brahmā; Oṃ Āṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu," and so forth.
I shall explain their names in the final chapter during the discussion on the origin of the *praṇava*.
The placement of the ninety-four *kalās* produced from that has also been indicated.
The locations for that placement are as follows: one should place the fire-born kalās within the three triangles of the *mūlādhāra*;
the twelve solar kalās upon the petals of the heart-lotus.
In the center of the sixteen petals of the head [cakra], there are the digits (kalās) born of the Moon;
those born of Nāda reside in the place of the vowels, while those born of Bindu reside in the five faces.
In the east, south, and north; facing west and upward;
in the heart, throat, and shoulders; at the navel and the abdomen; and on the back and chest.
One should also place the digits born from the syllable *mā* upon the two breasts;
those born from the syllable *u* are placed on the feet, the secret organ, the thighs, the knees, the shanks, and the buttocks.

One should place the five secret digits born from the syllable *A* upon the soles of the feet, the palms of the hands, the nostrils, the two arms, and the two sides of the feet. One should install them thus.
"On the heart, the secret place, and the feet.
Thus, he states the general placement of the seers (*ṛṣi*) and so forth for those [mantras] already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned, beginning with the word "seers" (*ṛṣi*).
For this very reason, there is the general mention of "of the mantra. Since the deity is also applicable here, the specific mention of "of the self" (ātmanaḥ) is made.

Consequently, in the placement of Ajapā, it is of Ajapā; in the placement of Praṇava, it is of Praṇava; in the external placement of Mātṛkā, it is of Mātṛkā; and in the placement of Bhuvaneśī, it is of her.
Regarding the phrase "in the placement of the root mantra" (*mūlamantranyāse*), this refers to the mantra being recited.
By the expression "the knower of mantras [placing them] in due order," the placement of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and powers (*śakti*) is also indicated;
some say this refers to the right and left corners (*koṇa*) of the seat.
Others say it is on the secret parts;
others say it is on the breasts.
The necessity of performing the nyāsa of the ṛṣis and so forth has been stated elsewhere:

"When this [mantra] is recited without the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the seers (*ṛṣi*), meters (*chandas*), and deities (*devatā*), even if it has been mastered, its fruit will be insignificant. (30–31)

One should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa immediately followed by the Mantra-nyāsa; one should place [the mantras] on the fingers beginning with the thumb, along with their respective limbs (aṅgas) and seed-syllables (jāti). || 32 ||
Having placed the Astra-mantra upon the two palms, one should perform the triple clapping (tālatraya) and so forth;
with concentrated mind, one should bind the directions by means of that very [mantra] using snapping sounds (choṭikā). || 33 ||
He states the external *mātṛkā*-nyāsa with the words "one should perform" (*vidadhyāt*).
The meaning is that one should elaborate upon the *mātṛkā*-nyāsa ending with the *prapañca-yāga*, which is about to be described.
The connection is that immediately thereafter, one should perform the *mantra*-nyāsa and the *bhuvaneśī*-nyāsa.
As it is said: "The Praṇava, the Goddess Mātṛkā, and Hṛllekhā—these three are the nectar that is the illuminator of all mantras; so says the Blessed Lord Śiva.
And in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā: "In that regard, first is the Haṃsanyāsa, and indeed the Praṇavanyāsa as well."
The third is the placement of the Mātṛkās, and after that follows the placement of Brahman.
"The fifth is described by the virtuous as the *nyāsa* consisting of five syllables;
among these, one should perform either one or all in rites such as worship.

Thus [it is said]. Immediately following this, he describes the *karanyāsa* (hand-assignment) for those already mentioned and those yet to be mentioned, beginning with the words "the thumb... (*aṅguṣṭha*).
By the word "immediately" (*anantaram*), it is stated that the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) must be performed with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
For this very reason, he will say in the *Lakṣmīpaṭala*: "Having purified the two hands with the mantra.
This has been stated as follows:
"The wise one [should place] the Tāra and Rudra mantras on the inner and outer sides of the two hands, which are the pervader and the pervaded.
Thus,
"with the limbs" means with the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) prescribed for each respective ritual manual (kalpa).
In that regard, having uttered the heart-mantra, the application is "namas" with both thumbs, and so forth.
As it was stated by the Teachers: "One should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the fingers in sequence with the [five] limbs, beginning with the thumbs."

The phrase "by those of the same kind" (sajātibhiḥ) is connected with what follows. Regarding the expression "of the *tattala* [beats]," the word "those" (*tat*) refers to the fingers because they are the subject under discussion; by means of them, the hand is indicated.
By the word *tala*, both the inner and outer surfaces are included.
Therefore, having recited the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one says "namas" with the palms and backs of the hands; such is the application of the weapon-mantra.
As it has been said:
Homage to the two thumbs with *hrāṃ hrīṃ*; then homage to the two index fingers with *hrūṃ hraiṃ*;
then homage to the two middle fingers with *hrūṃ hraiṃ*; then homage to the two ring fingers with *hrūṃ hraiṃ*.
"Oṃ hrauṃ, salutation to the two little fingers; hraḥ, salutation to the backs of the palms.
Thus one should perform the triple clapping and so forth; this is the application of the limbs and the weapon-mantra.
Its essential nature has been described elsewhere:
"One should utter three *tāla*s with the palms extended."
He clarifies what is indicated by the word "and so forth" in the phrase "three claps of the hands, etc. with the words "the directions.
"By that very [means]" refers to the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*).
"A snap of the fingers" takes the form of the *nārāca-mudrā*.
The *nārāca-mudrā* is the snapping sound produced by the tips of the thumb and forefinger;
this is according to its definition.
The word "composed" (*samāhita*) is to be connected with what follows.
The connection here is as follows:
"Then, being composed and wise, one should place the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) upon the heart and other [limbs] by means of the jāti-mantras.
The word "ca" (and) serves to include the previously mentioned [placement] on the thumbs and other fingers.
The word "tataḥ" (then) means immediately after the placement (*nyāsa*) of the respective mantras as prescribed in the various *kalpas* that are about to be described.
As they say: "First is the placement of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth; after that, the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*);
then the placement of the fingers (*aṅgulivyāpaka*), and the placement of the heart and other limbs (*hṛdādinyāsa*)."

Three *tāla* strokes constitute the binding of the directions (*digbandha*). Thus it is said. Furthermore, elsewhere: "Having first performed the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), one should thereafter perform the ritual placement on the body (*dehanyāsa*)."
"Then one should perform the *aṅganyāsa*; this is the general rule.

Thus [it is said]. The Teachers also, having stated [the procedure] up to the end of the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), say: "For at the commencement of the recitation (*japa*) of the mantras, this is indeed the common method of preparation."
Thus,
by the words "composed" and "wise," the six-limbed mudrās are indicated.
As it has been said in another Āgama:
The heart is touched with the palm of the hand spread out;
the head is likewise [touched]; the crest-lock (śikhā) is properly [touched] with the fist, the thumb pointing downwards.
With such hands, touching the armor, the shoulder, and so forth,
the index, middle, and ring fingers are said to correspond respectively to the three eyes.
"When the two eyes are indicated, then [the gesture is formed by] the index and middle fingers.
Here, the phrase "with the palm extended" means with the four fingers excluding the thumb.
As it has been said:
With the four fingers excluding the thumb at the heart, and at the head;
at the crest-lock (śikhā), there should be a fist with the thumb forming a tube.
"All fingers [should be joined] up to the navel; this is the binding of armor on the two hands.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the six-limbed mudrā of Śakti in another tantra: "The heart is known to be formed by the middle, ring, and index fingers; the head [is formed by the same]..."
The crest-lock (śikhā) is known to be formed by the middle and index fingers together with the thumb.
"The armor (kavaca) is said to be with ten [fingers], the eye (netra) is declared with three;
the weapon (astra) shall be formed by the two [remaining] fingers—this is considered the arrangement of the limbs.
Thus, the six-limbed mudrās of Śiva are described in the Śaiva Āgama.
Having formed the hands into hollowed fists, one should place the two thumbs at the heart;
this is declared to be the Heart Mudrā, and the Head Mudrā is now described.
Placing both hands with clenched fists together at the forehead,
one should extend the tips of the two index fingers upward, with the thumbs positioned on the outside.
Joining the two hands at the crown of the head in the form of hollowed fists, the index fingers are bent downward with their tips touching,
and likewise the little fingers are directed upward.
This is the Śikhā-mudrā, which destroys all calamities;
it is formed by joining the tips of the two thumbs and making the two index fingers like a triangle.
Having turned the head backward, one should lead [the hands] from both sides;
with the two hands reaching as far as the heart, this is the mudrā of the armor (kavaca) that bestows fearlessness.
Having made the hand face upward with the thumb and little finger joined,
one should extend the middle finger slightly and bend the other fingers.
This is declared to be the Netra-mudrā, which destroys Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and elephants;
one should then forcefully clasp the two palms together against each other. (32–33)
Then, the wise practitioner should assign the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) to the heart and other parts:
first, "Oṃ Hṛdayāya Namaḥ," and for the head, "Vahnivallabhā" (Svāhā). || 34 ||
"Vaṣaṭ" is said for the crest-lock (śikhā), "Hum" is uttered for the armor (kavaca), "Vauṣaṭ" is for the three eyes, and "Phaṭ" is for the weapon (astra) in due order. || 35 ||
One should apply the six-limbed mantras as previously described to the six limbs;
however, for that mantra which has only five limbs, one should omit the mantra for the eyes. || 36 ||
In response to the inquiry as to what those "castes" (jātis) are, given that they were mentioned [in the previous verse], he says "hṛdaya... and so on.
The meaning is that first one should recite the initial mantra for the head, and immediately after this, one should utter "vahnivallabhā svāhā. || 34 ||
The phrase "to the three-eyed one" (*netratrayāya*) is an elliptical expression;
therefore, for two-eyed deities such as Viṣṇu and others, the formula used is "to the two eyes, *vauṣaṭ*. (35)

Having combined the six-limbed mantras as they are described in their respective ritual manuals (kalpa) with the birth-mantras (jāti-mantra) mentioned in this manner, one should apply them to the six limbs—the heart and so forth—by means of the prescribed mudrās; that is to say, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa). || 36 ||
For a mantra that is deficient in its constituent parts, one should supply those very parts oneself;
one should perform the various ritual placements (nyāsa) according to the procedures prescribed in the respective ritual manuals (kalpa).
Regarding the word *aṅga*: "deficiency of limbs" (*aṅgahīnatva*) refers to the absence of the extraction of mantras (such as the eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa) [from the body].
This occurs either through repetition by oneself or through [the cutting off of] a portion.
By this, the necessity of the auxiliary limbs (aṅga) has been stated.
As they say:
"Even for those who have perfected their mantras, worship, recitation, adoration, and fire-offerings [require them]."
"Deprived of the proper arrangement of the limbs, these [mantras] will not yield their fruits. Thus it is said.

Gautama has also stated the purpose of employing the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga): "When this self consisting of consciousness is being worshipped by means of the heart, it becomes present within the heart as the conscious essence."
Thereafter, one should perform the state of being intent upon that [deity] by means of the heart-mantra and the supreme self.
In the Supreme Self, which is of the nature of consciousness and endowed with qualities such as omniscience and loftiness,
the wise practitioner performs the intake of sense objects by means of the Śiraḥ-mantra.
A firm meditation, consisting of the nature of the abode of consciousness in the heart, head, and body,
is performed with reverence for one's own deity by means of the *śikhā-mantra*.

The accumulation of the ritual placement (nyāsa) is performed for the deity whose essence is mantra, by means of the armor-mantra (varma-mantra) which pervades [the body] with the splendor expressed by that mantra.
That which bestows supreme knowledge upon the Supreme Self, whose nature is pure consciousness, is the light consisting of the heart and other centers; this is what is designated as the "eye."
"That weapon which destroys whatever internal or external form belongs to the practitioner, born of ignorance—that is declared to be the supreme abode.
Thus [it is said]. Previously, the word "then" (*tataḥ*) was explained as meaning "after the ritual placement of the mantra" (*mantranyāsānantaram*).
In response to the question, "What is the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) therein?", he says "those respective [mantras]".
By "placements" (*nyāsān*), he means the ritual placements of mantras. The necessity of these as well has been stated elsewhere:
"The wise declare that recitation (japa) without the ritual placement (nyāsa) is demonic and fruitless;
having become one with that [mantra] through nyāsa, and having become a god, one should worship it.
Also, in the Kulaprakāśatantra: "He who daily performs the nyāsas according to the path taught in the Āgamas..."
One attains the state of a deity, and the accomplishment of mantra arises.
The foolish-minded person who, without performing the various ritual depositions (*nyāsa*),
should employ the mantras, will be afflicted by all obstacles, just as a young deer is by tigers.
"O Dear One, when one who is shielded by the armor of the ritual placement (nyāsa) recites the mantra, obstacles flee upon seeing him, just as elephants flee upon seeing a lion. Thus it is said.
Also, in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā: "One who is not Śiva himself should not practice Śiva; one who is not Śiva himself should not worship Śiva."
"One who is not Śiva should not meditate upon Śiva, nor shall one who is not Śiva attain Śiva.
Thus [it is said]. The author of the work also states: "One should place the syllables of the mantra for the sake of accomplishing the state of being the deity."
By this, it is stated that even in those cases where the arrangement of syllables in a mantra is not explicitly mentioned in the recitation, it must nevertheless be performed. || 37 ||
The wise preceptor should fashion a seat within his own body, beginning with Dharma and the others in sequence,
by means of the two shoulders and the pair of thighs, proceeding in a clockwise direction.

Having sequentially deposited Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya on the face and the two sides of the navel, one should likewise arrange Adharma and the others on the mouth, the sides, and the sides of the navel.
Dharma and the others are remembered as the feet; others are the limbs of the pedestal.
Ananta is in the heart, and within this [lotus] are the sun, moon, and fire.
Regarding the phrase "one should conceive" (*kalpayet*), he states the conception of the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) within the body for the sake of the sacrifice of the Self (*ātmayāga*).
The meaning is that one should conceive the sacred seat by means of the [qualities] beginning with Dharma, which have been deposited within the body of the Self.
By the word "in sequence" (*kramāt*) here, the following is intended:
"Salutation to Maṇḍūka" in the Ādhāra;
"Salutation to Kālāgnirudra" in the Svādhiṣṭhāna;
"Salutation to Kūrma" at the navel.
Then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of Ādhāraśakti and the others in the heart, one subsequently performs the placement of Dharma and the rest.
As they say:
"One should place Ādhāraśakti, Prakṛti, Kūrma, Śeṣa, the Earth, and the Ocean of Milk."
And the White Island (Śvetadvīpa), the great pavilion resplendent with jewels and honored [by all], and the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) [are to be meditated upon] in the region of the heart.
Thus it is said.
Regarding the word "shoulder" (*aṃse*):
by the term "clockwise," meaning in the order of a rightward rotation,
it is stated that the wise preceptor performs the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) beginning from the right shoulder and ending at the right thigh.
This is the traditional position.
As it was stated by Īśānaśiva: "One should worship the power called Ādhāra in the heart and on the right shoulder;
Dharma and Jñāna on the left shoulder and on the two thighs."
"Sovereignty is the perception of dispassion.
Thus [it is said]; this is connected with the subsequent word "in sequence" (kramāt).
Regarding the word "mukha" (mouth):
here too, the phrase "in a clockwise direction" (*prādakṣiṇyena*) is to be supplied.
By the word "kramāt" (in sequence), this is what is stated.
Then the mouth, then the left side, then the navel, then the right side.
As it has been said:
"In the mouth, in the left side, in the navel, and in the right side."
"And likewise unrighteousness (adharma), ignorance (ajñāna), lack of dispassion (avairāgya), and lack of mastery (anaiśvarya).
Thus it was said by Īśānaśiva: "Then unrighteousness is in the mouth;
ignorance is on the left side, and [the others] are at the navel and the right side."
"Absence of dispassion and absence of sovereignty.
As for the statement of the Teacher— "by means of the mouth, the navel, the root, and the two sides"— that too [refers to] the mouth and the sides, according to the commentators on that [work].
This has already been explained by the words "the base of the navel and the sides.
The meaning is that those very same [elements], such as non-dharma (adharma) and so forth, are preceded by the negative particle (nañ).
"Others" refers to non-dharma and so forth.
"In this" means in the infinite.
"Lotus" refers to that which will have its characteristics described below.
By this [statement], it is stated that each preceding element serves as the substratum for each subsequent one.
In this lotus, the sun, moon, and fire are to be joined [as the three centers]. (38–40)
In these [parts], the best of gurus should assign the respective arts, preceded by their initial letters; likewise, he should assign the three qualities, beginning with sattva. || 41 ||
Having properly assigned the Self, the Inner Self, the Supreme Self, and the Knowledge-Self here, one should then assign the mantra of the seat (pīṭha). || 42 ||
"In these" refers to the three maṇḍalas.
Regarding "the letter at the beginning of the name," such as *ka*, *bha*, and so forth—the word "beginning" (*ādi*) being repeated—it means those preceded by that [initial letter].
The sequence therein is as follows:

Having placed the solar maṇḍala there, one should place its digits (kalās) therein; then the lunar maṇḍala, and therein its digits; then the fiery maṇḍala, and therein its digits—one should place them in this manner.
"In that same way" means upon each preceding [maṇḍala].
The word "preceded by the first letter of the name" (*nāmādyakṣarapūrvakān*) is drawn over here from the previous section.
Therefore, one should place [the syllables] preceded by whatever is the first letter of the name.
Here, this is connected with the following phrase, "the supreme guru."
Then follows the ritual application beginning with *oṃ saṃ sattvāya namaḥ* and so forth.
As it has been said: "The qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are [denoted] by the initial syllables.
And this is merely an illustration of the direction.
Because it has been stated as such everywhere previously;
here, however, the word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction with respect to the Supreme Self.
Therefore, this is the meaning:
In the triad beginning with the Self (ātman), the first syllable alone is the seed-mantra (*bīja*).
However, regarding the Self of Knowledge (*jñānātman*), it is stated by the term "supreme guru" that the seed-mantra is *māyā*.
By the phrase "then one should deposit the seat-mantra (*pīṭhamantra*)," this is what is being expressed.

One should worship: *māṃ*—salutation to the principle of Māyā; *kaṃ*—salutation to the principle of Kalā; *viṃ*—salutation to the principle of Vidyā; *paṃ*—salutation to the Supreme Principle (*Paratattva*).
One should install the nine seat-powers (*pīṭhaśakti*) at the center and at the bases of the eight petals starting from the tip of the heart-lotus.
As it has been said: "The principle of Māyā, the principle of Kalā, the principle of Vidyā, and likewise the Supreme."
"Having installed the powers of the seat (pīṭhaśaktis), one should then install the mantra of the seat.

Thus [it is said]. Also elsewhere: "Then, having installed the nine powers in the eight directions all around and in the center, one should duly install the great mantra of the seat located in the middle of its pericarp. (41-42)
Thus, one should meditate upon the chosen deity within the seat consisting of the body;
having displayed the mudrās according to the rule, one should perform the ritual placement of the arghya offering. || 43 ||
Regarding "mudrās": the specific mudrās for each [deity], as taught in their respective ritual manuals (*kalpas*), will be described by me in their respective chapters.
By the word "according to rule" (*vidhivat*), it is stated that one should request the deity after performing mental worship immediately following this.
Therein, the mantra for invitation is as follows: "Oṃ, welcome, O Lord of the gods of gods! O Keśava, be present here.
Accept this mental worship, contemplated according to its true nature.
In this context, at the word "Keśava," one should perform the appropriate substitution with the names of the respective deities.
As it has been said:

"Having thus meditated upon himself, with an intellect that was sharp and clear, he [perceived] the son of Nanda before him through his very consciousness alone, and [honored him] with blameless offerings such as the *arghya* and so forth."
"One should sacrifice.
Thus [it is said].
Also elsewhere: "Having meditated upon the deity and then displayed the mudrās according to the ritual injunctions..."
One should perform mental worship, and thereafter one should carry out the placement of the arghya offering. Thus [it is said]. (43)
"Oṃ, welcome, O Lord of the gods of gods; O Keśava, be present before me! Accept this mental worship, which has been contemplated according to its true meaning.
In this mantra, the name of the respective deity should be substituted in place of the vocative address "Keśava. (43)

Having sprinkled the conch with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), the wise practitioner should place it upon its stand to the left of the fire-mandala, filling it with nectar-like drops flowing from the lunar point (bindu). || 44 ||
One should fill that [vessel] according to the prescribed rite with water, fragrant flowers, and other offerings;
[one should contemplate] the support as fire, the conch as the sun, and the water as consisting of nectar. || 45 ||
One should meditate upon the digits (kalās) of Fire, Sun, and Moon in their respective order;
then, touching [the body], the knower of the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) should mutter the root mantra and perform the placement (nyāsa). || 46 ||

Having worshipped thoroughly with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra) and covering [the vessel] with both hands, the preceptor, perceiving [the water] as the deity, should recite the vidyā according to the rule. || 47 ||
It has been stated that one should perform the placement of the *arghya* (offering water).
He describes its procedure with the words "the conch," etc.
It should be understood that "to the left" means on the left side, in front of oneself.
As it has been said: "A conch before oneself.
The grammatical connection is that the conch, together with its stand, is [placed] upon the fire-mandala, which is a triangle with its apex pointing upward.
By the word "the wise one" (*vidvān*), it is indicated here that "fire-mandala" is an elliptical designation (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, it should be understood that [the site] is in the form of a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square, secured by the *śaṅkhamudrā* (conch-gesture), and with its six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) worshipped.
As it has been said:
"Having first drawn a triangle, and then a hexagon outside of that..."

"Having drawn a circle and a square in the center and written the *māyā* [syllable] therein, one should then display the conch-gesture (*śaṅkhamudrā*) and perform the worship of the limbs in the corners and directions. Thus it is said.
Also elsewhere: "One should fashion a triangle, a hexagon, a circle, and a square."
"Having assumed the conch mudrā, one should worship the six limbs. Thus [it is said].
"Bindu" refers to the space between the eyebrows; some say it refers to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
In that regard, because of the presence of the lunar disc (*candramaṇḍala*),
the meditation on the ocean is performed with [the visualization] "consisting of nectar flowing from the drop" (*bindusrutasudhāmaya*).
As it says in the *Somaśambhu*:

"Having filled [the vessel] with water in the form of nectar produced from the *bindu*, along with unbroken rice and other substances, one should worship it with the *hṛdaya* mantra and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and then consecrate it.
By the phrase "one should fill it according to the rule," this is what is meant.
"Reciting the Mātṛkā in reverse order ending with the Bindu, as well as the root mantra in reverse order.
As it has been said:
"The wise one should fill [the vessel] with pure water using the syllables in reverse order, ending with the Śiras [mantra]."
Thus:
"The support" means the support [of the body] as the solar disc (*pāvaka-maṇḍala*), the conch as the solar disc, and the water as the lunar disc (*indu-maṇḍala*).
In those mandalas, one should also remember the respective digits (kalās);
some even perform their worship.

The procedure for this is as follows: having drawn a square, a circle, a hexagon, and a triangle mandala in front of oneself to the left, and having stabilized it with the conch-gesture (śaṅkhamudrā).

Having worshipped the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) according to the sequence of worship with flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and having washed the base (*ādhāra*) with the *astra-mantra*, one should install the base with the mantra: "Oṃ, salutation to the seat of the *arghya* vessel for such-and-such [deity], which consists of the ten digits (*kalā*) of the fire-mandala (*vahnimaṇḍala*). Then, one should worship the ten digits of fire starting from the east.
Thereafter, having washed the conch with the conch-mantra (the conch-mantra as stated in the *Puruṣottama-paṭala*), one should [worship] with: "Aṃ, to the sun-mandala..."

Having placed the vessel upon the base with the mantra: "Obeisance to the vessel for [the deity] named so-and-so, whose self consists of twelve digits," one should worship the twelve digits of the Sun in the twelve locations in a clockwise direction. Then, while reciting the *mātṛkā* in reverse order and the root-mantra in reverse order, one should fill the conch with pure water and worship it with: "Oṃ, obeisance to the lunar orb, whose self consists of sixteen digits, the nectar for the arghya-vessel of [the deity] named so-and-so. Thereupon, one should worship the sixteen digits of the Moon there in a clockwise direction.
Then, having invoked the *tīrtha* from the solar orb by means of the *aṅkuśa-mudrā* with the mantra "Gaṅge ca," he should also invoke the Deity from his own heart-lotus;
for it will be stated later that the Preceptor is the presiding deity of the [invoked] divinity.
As it has been said:
In that regard, one should cause the sacred water (tīrtha) to descend from the orb of the sun,
just as one brings Lord Hari from his own heart-lotus.
Thus it is said.
The characteristics of the goad mudrā (aṅkuśamudrā) were explained in the context of the ritual bath. Or rather, this is the goad mudrā,
as they say:

"Direct in the middle, with the middle joint pressed down, and the index finger pointing downward—this should be known as the *aṅkuśa* (goad) mudrā, when the [index finger] is bent at the middle joint. Thus it is said: "having touched... and so forth.
The word "in water" (apsu) is connected with "one should place" (nyaset); the word "of that" (tasya) refers to the root mantra.

By the phrase "one who knows the limb-mantras," it is stated that the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed precisely by means of the worship according to the sequence of directions to be described hereafter.
The connection with the word "having fully worshipped" (*abhisampūjya*) is with the word "water" (*apaḥ*).
By the phrase "covering with both hands," it is indicated that this is done by means of the *matsya-mudrā* (the fish-gesture), as implied by the term "the instructor" (*deśika*).
The characteristic of that [mudrā] is as follows:
both hands are placed facing downwards upon one's own [lap], with the thumbs positioned on both sides; this is declared to be the Matsya-mudrā (Fish Mudrā).
In this context, regarding the injunction beginning with "evam-ādi," it is stated that the distinction between male and female deities is not intended by the terms *mūlamantra* and *vidyā*.
Otherwise, if only one were mentioned, the inclusion of the other would not occur.
"According to the rule" (*yathānyāyam*) means either seven or eight times.
This enumeration (or arrangement) should also be understood from what was stated previously:
"Touching [the object], one should mutter the mantra eight times."
Thus [ends the section on verses] 44–47.
Having protected it with the Astra-mantra and veiled it with the Kavaca-mantra, and having performed the Dhenu-mudrā, one should seal it with its own specific mudrā. || 48 ||
"Having protected"— this is the connection. And that protection should be understood as being performed with snapping sounds (*choṭikā*).
In the phrase "having veiled," the word "that" is also connected here; and that [veiling] is effected by means of the *avaguṇṭhana* mudrā and the seed-syllable of nectar (*amṛtabīja*).
"With one's own mudrā" means with Sannirodhinī.
The Avaguṇṭhana, Dhenu, and Sannirodhana mudrās will be described in the twenty-third [chapter].
Then, above the conch, one should display the Śaṅkha, Musala, Cakra, Mahāmudrā, and Yoni mudrās.
As they say:
"One should contemplate the sacred site as consisting of consciousness and bring it [there] with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*;
and having displayed the *dhenu-mudrā*, [one brings it] from the sacred sites within the belly of the universe."
"One should display the conch mudrā, the discus mudrā, and that called the mace;
having made [the deity] supreme with effort, one should indeed display the one called the secret.
Thus, specific details such as the display of the *gālinī* mudrā in the mantra of Kṛṣṇa and the display of the *garuḍa* mudrā in the mantra of Rāma should be investigated.
The characteristics of the conch mudrā have been described previously.
As for the characteristics of the others, however:
having formed fists with both hands, place the right hand over the left.
One should perform this mace-mudrā, which destroys all obstacles.

Having joined the two little fingers together, the two index fingers [should be placed] upon the ring fingers; the two middle fingers, being long and joined, should extend upward from below the ring fingers;
one should place the tips of the two thumbs [upon them]. This is declared to be the *yonimudrā*. Thus it is said.

Having inverted the palms of the left and right hands, one should interlace the two thumbs between the little fingers and the ring fingers; this is declared to be the auspicious *cakramudrā*, which bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*). Thus it is said.
The twenty-third [chapter] will explain the characteristics of Mahāmudrā:
The little fingers and thumbs of the two hands are joined to one another;
the index, middle, and ring fingers are pressed together and bent like a vajra.
"This is declared to be the Gālinī mudrā, moved above the conch.
Having brought the two hands face-to-face and having joined the two little fingers together,
the two index fingers are likewise joined, as are the two thumbs.
One should bend the two middle fingers and the two ring fingers as if they were two wings;
this shall be the Garuḍa-mudrā, which destroys all poisons. Thus [it is said]. (48)
Having placed the *prokṣaṇī* vessel to the south, one should fill it with water;
having taken a little of the *arghya* water, one should add it to the water in the *prokṣaṇī*. || 49 ||
"Southern" refers to the vessel made of copper or similar materials,
as they say:

"Gold, silver, lotus, copper, clay, wood, bell-metal, the *pādma* [lotus-leaf], and the *pālāśa* [palāśa-leaf]—these are the excellent vessels for the worship of Acyuta when no specific mantra is used.
Among all of these, copper and conch are superior; however, for the *arghya*, the lotus is highly praised. Thus [it is said]. (49)
To the north of the *arghya* water, the *pādya* and *ācamanīya* waters should be prepared;
the Guru should then sprinkle himself, the sacrificial materials, and the mandala with them. || 50 ||

Then, with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, one should worship Dharma and the other [deities] in due order upon one's own body by means of the mantra, according to the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*). || 51 ||
"Of the *arghya*" means of the *arghya* vessel. When there is the capacity [to do so], these [vessels] should be separate; when there is no capacity, everything is done with just one.
As they say: "Alternatively, one should prepare the water for washing the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and so forth, in a single vessel.
The connection is that one should sprinkle [the items] with the root mantra (mūlamantra) according to Manu.
This is the general rule;
however, in other instances, a specific mantra for sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) has been stated. In those cases, it should be understood that the sprinkling is to be performed with that very mantra.
By the word "guru," it is stated that this sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is to be performed three times.
As they say:
"Then one should sprinkle one's own body three times with this [liquid] by means of the hand and the mantra, and likewise the whole [of the ritual objects]."
The *sādhana* consists of flowers, sandalwood, and so forth.
Thus,
the connection is that one should consecrate by sprinkling (*prokṣayet*) the other sacrificial items and materials for worship in their proper order.
He speaks of the internal sacrifice with the words "one should deposit" (*nyaset*).
As it has been said:
"The worship of the *manu* who has attained [realization] is of two kinds: external and internal."
"The distinction between renunciants (nyāsins) has been declared; for others, both [types of worship] are likewise prescribed. Thus it is said.

Also in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā: "Having first performed the internal sacrifice (antar-yāga), ending with the fire-rite (agnikārya), a person should thereafter perform the external sacrifice (bahir-yāga)."
Likewise, there is also a statement by Śambhu in the *Saṃhitā*:
"O moon-faced one, a householder does not attain auspiciousness either in this world or in the next through mere knowledge alone, without [the performance of] gifts,
fire-offerings, and so forth."
O Goddess, if a householder were not to offer oblations, nor give gifts,
nor worship according to the prescribed rite— who indeed would perform this daily?
O beautiful lady, one who observes the vow of celibacy has no authority to give;
for even among all gurus, who indeed would give away what is desired?
In the Kali age, forest-dwellers possess no power, nor do they exist; the wandering mendicant possesses nothing but knowledge, being devoid of rituals such as giving gifts or offering oblations.
One becomes liberated from all the demons of suffering, and not otherwise—
whether one is a wandering mendicant free from passion, or likewise a householder free from passion.
O lotus-faced one, both virtuous women and householders who seek auspiciousness through auspicious rites shall sink into the Kumbhīpāka hell.
With the requisites for worship, they should perform [rites], give gifts, and offer honors;
and if forest-dwellers and ascetics likewise perform these daily, [they shall attain the same fruit].
"They do not turn back from saṃsāra due to the fault of transgressing the injunction;
for these, having ascended to the state of a *yati*, would indeed become vessels of suffering.
By the phrase "by the sequence of renunciation" (*nyāsakrameṇa*) here, this is what is meant.

One should worship Maṇḍūka, Kālāgni, Rudra, and Kūrma in the regions of the Ādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, and Nābhi; then, having worshipped Ādhāraśakti and the others in the heart, followed by the eight [qualities] beginning with Dharma in their respective places, one performs again in the heart the worship starting from Śeṣa and ending with Paratattva.
This is stated in the Rāmapūrvatāpanīya:
One should worship Māyā and Vidya in the two principles (tattva) beyond Kalā, as well as the powers (śakti) beginning with Vimalā.
Thus [ends verses 50–51].

With flowers and other offerings, up to the end of the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra), one should then, with undistracted mind, present five handfuls of flowers to the Supreme Deity within that [seat]. || 52 ||

One should worship [the deity] in sequence at the head, the heart, the base (the feet), and all the limbs, using offerings such as fragrances and so forth, even without the offering of food (naivedya). || 53 ||
The fragrance is the primary [quality] of the flower.
The plural number is used in the sense of "and so forth" (*ādi*); thus, the meaning is "by means of fragrance and the rest.
Such a construction serves the purpose of including the flower itself by means of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*).
Alternatively, "with flowers and so forth" (*puṣpādyaiḥ*) refers to flowers and the first [item], fragrance (*gandha*).
This is because, among the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), flowers are specified immediately after fragrance.
Thus, it concludes with the *pīṭhamantra*.
The meaning is: "up to the seat-power (pīṭhaśakti) and the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra).
Regarding the word "in that" (tasmin):
the connection with the subsequent [text] is that one should worship the Supreme Deity with offerings such as perfumes and so forth upon such a seat consisting of the body.
By the first [verse], the flower is [indicated]. Regarding that, he states the specific detail with the word "five.
By the phrase "with undistracted mind," the thirtieth [verse] is implied.
As it has been said by the Teachers:
"One should offer handfuls of flowers upon one's own body five times or even thirty times."
"Without the food offering (naivedya)"— this is the intended meaning: having presented the services beginning with the seat and ending with the lamp, the food offering should not be given externally.

Then, having raised Kuṇḍalinī according to the procedure taught by the Guru and led her to the *dvādaśānta*, one should cause her to unite with Śiva residing there and gratify the Deity with the stream of nectar arising from that union. || 52-53 ||
One should complete the remainder according to the procedure taught by the guru.
One should employ all of this with the water contained in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel. || 54 ||
Having poured out the water from the *prokṣaṇī*, he should refill it as before;
then the practitioner of mantra should properly worship that mandala with perfumes and other offerings. || 55 ||

"Taught by the Guru" means that the remainder— namely, mental incense and lamps, mantra recitation, the offering of the recitation, the dedication to Brahman, the request for forgiveness, and so forth— is to be performed, with the exception of the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*). As they say:
"Having meditated, one should worship with mental offerings such as sandalwood paste, incense, and lamps;
at the time of eating, having performed some recitation, one should offer [the food].
Regarding one who is incapable, he says "all."
The passage beginning with "Having bowed to the gurus" and ending with "thus" is the same for the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) as well.
However, this is the specific distinction regarding the daily worship:
one should pour this very water from the conch into the *vardhanī* vessel.
Then, having performed three *prāṇāyāmas* and the daily recitation (*nityajapa*) one thousand and eight times, one should again perform three *prāṇāyāmas*.
For it is said: "One should cast [the water] into the *vardhanī* vessel," and because of the statement: "The wise have prescribed that triad both before and after the recitation.
This has been stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
Having performed the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) with devotion one thousand and eight times,
that which is recited daily is known as the obligatory recitation (nitya-japa).
During the solstices, the equinoxes, the eclipses of the moon and sun,
on the twelfth lunar day, and on the full moon— on these occasions, there is the occasional (naimittika) recitation.
"Then, from that which is eternal, it is tripled; and likewise, there is the worship of Hari.
Having thus described the internal sacrifice (*āntarayāga*), he speaks of the external sacrifice (*bahiryāga*) with the word "tataḥ" (then).

"Tataḥ" means immediately after that; the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) [should perform it] properly, meaning in a beautiful manner, as it has been described as being auspicious in every respect (*sarvatobhadra*).
The connection is as follows: one should worship with perfumes and other offerings that *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala, which has been drawn in the center of the altar (*vedi*).
By the word "and others" (*ādi*), flowers are intended.
By the term "the mantra-practitioner" (*mantrī*), it should be understood that the worship mantra, "Obeisance to the Śrī-sarvatobhadra-maṇḍala," is indicated. (54–55)
Having filled the center of the *kaṇīkā* with *śāli* rice and decorated it with *taṇḍula* rice on top, the knower of the ritual procedure should then spread *darbha* grass over them. || 56 ||
One should place a *kūrca* (bundle of grass) together with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) upon them;
then, beginning with the *Ādhāraśakti*, one should worship the pedestal (*pīṭha*) consisting of mantras. || 57 ||
"By means of śāli rice" means having adorned the top with rice and having placed grains of rice thereon; "again" means immediately thereafter.
Regarding those rice grains,
that measurement is stated elsewhere:
"Having placed śāli rice, measured by an āḍhaka, within the husk."
"And one should place rice grains and an eight-part portion of them, along with a *kūrca* (bundle of grass), upon it. As for the definition of an *āḍhaka*: "A *kuḍava* consists of four *palas*;
a *prastha* consists of four *kuḍavas*."
"Four *prasthas* make one *āḍhaka*.
Thus,
"one-eighth of that" refers to a measure equal to two *kuḍavas*.
Eight *tolakas* as stated in the scriptures constitute one *pala*.
A *kūrca*, also known by the synonym *viṣṭara*, consists of twenty-seven fresh blades of *darbha* grass tied together in the shape of a braid.
As it is said in the *Ḍāmara*: "Twenty-seven *darbha* blades, adorned with a knot at the tip of the braid..."
"The characteristic [of the seat] has been fully described in all sacrifices on the *viṣṭara*.
Regarding this, those who know the tradition maintain that one should worship the Deity with the three principles beginning with the Self (*ātman*) and then commence the external worship.
[The text says: "The Support-Energy" (*ādhāraśakti*), etc.
In this regard, one should first perform the worship of the Guru and Gaṇapati.
As it has been said:
"First, there is a row of venerable [deities] to the north of the seat of worship, extending from the northwest to the northeast."
"Ambikēya (Gaṇeśa) is to be worshipped elsewhere as well, holding in his lotus-like hands the noose, the staff, the goad, and the gesture of fearlessness. Thus it is said.
Elsewhere also: "The knower of mantra should worship the lineage of gurus on the northern part of the seat, beginning from the northwest corner up to the northeast corner."
"Then, having likewise worshipped the two— the Guru and the Paramaguru— as well as the Parameṣṭhiguru,

one should worship the Paramācāryaguru, the Ādisiddhiguru, and then one's own Guru. Here, after the Paramācāryaguru, it should be understood that the Parāparaguru and the Paramasiddhiguru are also to be included.
Their meditation is described in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"The preceptors are white-complexioned, wearing white garments, and holding books;
they are either joined with the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyānamudrā*) or meditating upon their own respective Hari."
"They should be meditated upon during worship and other rites; through such meditation, one becomes possessed of knowledge.
Regarding the Śākta and other systems, however, there is this distinction in another tantra:
"They [the deities] are adorned with red garlands, garments, perfumes, and ornaments; they are well-decorated and seated upon lotus thrones."
"And all [these] have reached the culmination of yoga with an object, having attained the goal of the eight qualities of sovereignty.
Thus [it is said]. In that regard, the formula begins with "Salutations to the venerable Gurus" (śrīgurubhyo namaḥ) and so forth:
"The Deity, the Guru, the place of the Guru, the sacred field (kṣetra), and the presiding deities of the field..."
One should utter "Siddham," followed by the titles of the Siddhas, and then the word "Śrīpūrva."
Because of this statement, it is said that "one should worship. (56–57)
Below, one should worship Ādhāraśakti, who stands upon a tortoise-stone, possesses a luster like the autumnal moon, and holds two lotuses.
One should worship a dark-blue tortoise mounted upon its head;
above that, one should worship Ananta, who resembles a jasmine flower, seated upon the Brahma-stone.
One should worship the Holder of the Discus (Viṣṇu) on the crown of the head, supporting the earth;
and there [one should worship] her who is dark as a tamāla tree and who bears blue lotuses.
One should worship the Earth, girdled by the shimmering oceans;
upon her, an island made of jewels, and within that, a pavilion of gems.
One should worship the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpataru) therein, which grant the desired accomplishments of the practitioner;
below them, one should worship the altar-platform, radiant with its pavilion.
Thereafter, one should again worship the pedestal upon it with Dharma and the other [Tattvas].
[One should worship] those whose forms are the feet, possessing the luster of red, dark-blue, yellow, and sapphire.
He says that very thing with the word "below" (adhaḥ).
By this, the following is stated:
one should worship a large-bodied red frog in the pericarp [of the lotus] with the mantra, "Salutation to Maṇḍūka."
Above that is the ten-armed, five-faced Kālāgnirudra, whose right and left sides are red and black; [one should worship him with] "Obeisance to Kālāgnirudra.
Above that is the massive-bodied tortoise; [one should worship him with] "Obeisance to the Tortoise.
This has been stated in the Śaunaka-kalpa:
"One should worship Maṇḍūka, Pṛthivī, and the others in the pericarp (kaṇīkā) in due order.
Thus it is said.
Also, in the Nārasiṃhakalpa: "In an eight-petaled lotus, one should worship Maṇḍūka, ending with the Supreme Reality (paratattva)."
Thus:
"the tortoise-stone" (*kūrmaśilā*) means a stone in the shape of a tortoise; [she] is mounted upon that.
The tortoise that was previously worshipped should be understood as the "tortoise-slab" (*kūrmaśilā*);

however, the tortoise to be described hereafter is indeed distinct from that. As it is stated in the *Tāpanīya*: "The power (*śakti*) and the one called the support (*ādhāra*), [along with] the tortoise and the serpent (*nāga*)."
The meaning of "autumnal moon" (śaraccandra) is to be understood as before.
"Brahmaśilā" is the designation for the stone slab situated beneath the primary image (mūlapratimā).
As it is stated in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā:
One should cast the purified Brahma-stone, smeared with sandalwood paste, into the pit;
then, having performed the deposition of the jewels (or principles), by means of the nine names of the Śaktis.
"Haritāla and other minerals, as well as seeds, fragrances, and medicinal herbs,
should be placed upon the Brahma-stone according to the procedure prescribed in the Śiva-śāstra. By such statements [it is established that] "the Liṅga is upon the Brahma-stone."
Up to the words "slightly sloping toward the northeast," [the description continues].
Regarding "Ananta":
its essential form is described as "having a human shape above the navel and a serpent shape below, with a single hood and a thousand hoods."
Elsewhere, that meditation is described as follows:
"The splendor of Viṣṇu, indeed honored by its own thirty-two principles beginning with Earth and ending with Vidyā, is called Infinity;
it constitutes the seat, and that serpent Ananta is of the form of the pedestal. Thus it is said.

Elsewhere also it is said: "In this system, by means of the thirty-two principles beginning with Earth (Dharā) and ending with Knowledge (Vidyā), Ananta takes the form of the sacred seat (pīṭha); thus he is called the 'Seat of Ananta' (Anantāsana)."
The compound means "one who wears blue lotuses.
He will state later: "two *indīvaras*.
By the phrase "the earth girdled by the shimmering ocean," the meaning is that after the Earth, the Ocean is to be worshipped with the mantra "Obeisance to the Ocean" (*sāgarāya namaḥ*).
In that regard, in the mantra of Sarasvatī, there is the ocean of knowledge; in the mantra of Lakṣmī-Viṣṇu, the milk-ocean; in the mantra of Gaṇeśa, the ocean of sugarcane juice.
Elsewhere, it should be understood as the ocean of nectar, and so forth. In that distinguished [ocean]... 58–63.
One should worship the principles beginning with Dharma, which have assumed the forms of a bull, a lion, and an elephant;
one should worship them on the limbs, preceded by the negative particle (nañ), as described by their characteristics. || 64 ||
Regarding "vṛṣa": *keśarī* means a lion; *bhūta* refers to a class of divine beings (*devayoni*).
Their nature is described elsewhere:
"The Rākṣasas are of terrible form, wearing red garments, black in color, possessing claws and fangs with formidable tusks, and holding a curved knife and a skull-topped staff in their hands."
Likewise, the beings were dejected-faced. "Ibha" means an elephant.
[The deities] preceded by the negative particle (nañ) are Adharma, Ajñāna, Avairāgya, and Anaiśvarya;
they possess the characteristics already described, meaning they have colors such as red and forms such as a bull, and so forth.
And it has been said:

Dharma is red and has the form of a bull; Jñāna is dark blue and has the form of a lion; Vairāgya is white with the form of an elephant; and Aiśvarya is yellow and has the form of a wicked spirit—these are, in sequence, the legs of the pedestal.
"Adharma and the others who are the four lords of the pedestal (pīṭha) are indeed beautiful with the forms described above. || 64 ||
Then one should worship the lotuses in the corners beginning with the southeast and in the cardinal directions;
first the "Root of Bliss" (Ānandakanda), and immediately after that the "Stalk of Consciousness" (Saṃvinnāla).
Regarding the phrase "in the Āgneya and others":
by the word "others" (ādi), the corners of Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśa are included. "In the directions" refers to the east, south, west, and north.
The particle *ca* is used for conjunction (*samuccaye*).
This is because of the technical definition (*paribhāṣaṇāt*): "The four quarters are obtained by the word 'direction' (*dik*), as are Vṛṣa and the others.
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
"And [the directions] beginning with Adharma (South) and ending with Uttara (North) in sequence.
Here, the teachers maintain that the "eastern" direction is that which faces the front of the deity.
And thus it is said in the Āgama:
"The direction situated between the deity and the practitioner is here called the East."
Elsewhere it is also said: "The teachers declare that the east is [defined] either in front of the deity or in front of oneself;
however, the east is designated as the true east only when excluding the worship of the deity.
And in another Tantra: "Wherever the sun rises in the sky, the knowers of the Vedas call that the east."
"Thus, those who know the true scriptures always proclaim [the worship] of both the worshiper and the object of worship.
Furthermore, on another occasion regarding the worship of the door: "Starting from the face of the deity, one should designate the eastern direction;
the arrangement of the limbs and other enclosures for the retinue begins from that point."
There is also a logical justification for this:
at the occasion of the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the deities of the sacred seats (pīṭha) upon the body, the placement of the lower lip (adharmanya) is prescribed for the mouth;
and that [mouth] is the foremost part [of the face].

On the occasion of the worship of Mahāgaṇapati, the author of the work, having stated that one should worship [the deities] in the four directions starting from the east outside the triangle, further specified, "beneath the bilva tree in front.
Likewise, in the second enclosure of the Rāma-pūjā, he mentions: "Hanumān together with Sugrīva."
Having said this, he spoke again: "Hanumān, holding a book, was reading before him.
Furthermore, worship has also been prescribed by facing the north.
Furthermore, regarding the other rites, there is the facing toward the west and so forth;
and therein, the worship of Adharma and the others, as well as the worship of the limbs (aṅga) and so forth, might sometimes occur according to one sequence,
while at other times it might occur according to another sequence— such [alternations] are contradictory.

And in another tantra: "The eastern portion is prescribed for the Hotṛ priest; the left portion is [prescribed] by those who know the Āgamas as the southern; the right should be known as the foremost northern portion by the wise; and the western portion is said [to belong to the Adhvaryu]. Thus it is said.
And in the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*: "Now, in the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*), one should designate the east as being in front;
then follows the worship of the attendant deities (*parivāra*) in a clockwise direction.
Also in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The Śaktis, beginning with Lakṣmī, holding chowries, [are to be worshipped] on the petals starting from the front."
Thus, for this very reason, it will be explained that in the worship of the powers of the seats (*pīṭhaśakti*) and so forth, one begins from the foremost petal and so on.

Therefore, even when performing worship while facing north and so forth, one should understand that the worship of the qualities (*dharma* etc. and the limbs (*aṅga* etc. proceeds by designating one's own front side as the east.
Therefore, it should be understood that even when writing syllables on the petals of a yantra or similar diagram, one must begin writing from the foremost petal;
this is the general direction for the worship of mobile deities.
Now, as for the statement "one should worship the lotus," it is according to the sequence that will be described.
In this context, the word "atha" (then) indicates that one should first worship Ananta with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to Ananta," before the lotus.
As it has been said: "Then [one worships] Śeṣa, the lotus in the heart."
At the occasion of the deposition [of the mantras] upon the body, the author himself has also stated:
"In this heart-lotus is the infinite. || 65 ||

Immediately after worshipping the lotus that embodies all principles (tattvas), the practitioner of mantra [should worship] the petals consisting of the primary elements (prakṛti) and the filaments consisting of the transformations (vikāra). || 66 ||
Then one should worship the pericarp enriched with the fifty seed-syllables;
therein, one should worship the Sun, Moon, and Fire together with their digits (kalās). || 67 ||
Then, with the three syllables of the Praṇava, one should worship the qualities beginning with Sattva, as well as the Self, the Inner Self, and the Supreme Self.

And [one should worship] the Self of Knowledge according to the rule, ending with the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra). One should worship the powers of the seat (pīṭhaśakti) upon the filaments and in the center, together with Varā and Abhayā. || 69 ||
Regarding the phrase "with the digits" (*kalābhiḥ*):

some explain the meaning of this as being "together with the digits" [referring to] the solar mandala consisting of twelve digits, the lunar mandala consisting of sixteen digits, and the fiery mandala consisting of ten digits.
Others, however, describe it otherwise:
although not explicitly stated, the state of possessing twelve digits and so forth is obtained.
Thus, having worshipped the solar mandala, one worships the twelve digits therein; then the lunar mandala and its sixteen digits; then the fire mandala.
"One should worship its ten digits"—
this is the traditional view.
"In it" means in the pericarp.
The connection is that one should worship the Sun, Moon, and Fire together with their respective digits (kalās) by means of the three syllables of the *praṇava*—namely, *a*, *u*, and *m*.
As it has been said: "One should [worship] the Sun, Moon, and Fire as joined with the parts of the *praṇava*."

By this it is indicated that the presiding deities of those respective maṇḍalas—namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa—are to be worshipped in their corresponding maṇḍalas. As they say: "In the solar orb, Brahmā should be meditated upon as having four faces, wearing a crown, seated upon a swan, and holding with his four hands a water-pot, a white umbrella, a rosary, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, clad in white garments."
On the left side of the image is Garuḍa, dark as a rain cloud, bearing a discus, a conch, a mace, and a lotus;
he wears necklaces, a garland, bracelets, and a beautiful crown, while Viṣṇu wears yellow garments and the Kaustubha gem.

"On the orb of fire, [is] Śiva, moon-crested, white, Rudra, ten-armed and three-eyed; holding in his hands the *ṭaṅka*, deer, fire, trident, skull, mudrā, rosary, garland, the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*).
Also elsewhere: "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara are indeed to be worshipped in sequence within the three mandalas."
Thus [it is said].
Now, regarding "those beginning with sattva":
they are of white, red, and black forms.
As it has been said:
"The qualities white, red, and black are declared to be situated upon the seat."
By the phrase "according to rule," this is what is meant:
immediately after this, one should worship Māyā, Kalā, Vidyā, and the Supreme Principle (Paratattva).
Having worshipped [the deities] beginning with the Self (Ātman) and ending with the Supreme Principle, one should fully worship the Śaktis.
Thus it is said; and also in the *Vaihāyasī-mantra-prakāśa*:
"Sattva, rajas, and that which is called śārvara, as well as the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire."
"One should worship the fourfold group beginning with Vidyā and the fourfold group of principles (tattvas) at the end of the fourfold group of selves.
Also, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*: "The seat consists of the triad of principles beginning with Ātman, situated above the three circles."

By the phrase "ending with the seat-mantra" (*pīṭhamantrāvasānakam*), the author indicates the place of worship for the seat-powers (*pīṭhaśakti*) implied therein; he states this with the word "seat" (*pīṭha*).
"In the filaments" means in the filaments of the lotus that has already been worshipped.

Therein, having performed the worship of the seat-powers in the eight petals beginning with the front petal, proceeding clockwise, and in the center, one performs the worship of the seat-mantra—this is the meaning.
"Where no specific distinction is stated by means of the left [hand], the sequence is understood to apply everywhere"—
according to this technical rule (paribhāṣā).

For this very reason, on the occasion of the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the deities of the seats (pīṭha-devatā) within the body, I have described the ritual placement of the powers of the seats (pīṭha-śakti).
The powers of the seats (pīṭhaśaktis) and the mantras of the seats will be explained in their respective mantras.
Their visualization is "bestowing boons and fearlessness.
The colors of these [powers] have also been stated by the teachers:
"White, black, red, yellow, dark-blue, fire-like, and white—these powers (śaktis) are said to have forms of light resembling collyrium and the japa flower.
Thus, from Maṇḍūka up to this point, it is the same even for the daily worship (nityapūjā). (67–69)

A pot fashioned from gold or other precious materials, its interior washed with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra, fumigated with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, and possessing a beautiful form; || 70 ||
Its body is completely enveloped by a triple-stranded thread, closely wound without gaps;
