it is not yet worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and it is provided with a *kūrca* grass-bundle and unbroken grains of rice. || 71 ||
When the pedestal has been thus worshipped, he states the placement of the water-pot (*kumbha*) with the words "gold and so forth" (*hemādīti*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), silver, copper, and earthen vessels are to be understood according to one's capacity.
*Kumbham* means the jar (*kalaśam*).
Thus it is stated in the Mahākapilapañcarātra: "A beautiful pitcher made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay—
provided it is flawless and smeared with sandalwood paste."
Elsewhere it is also said: "O Goddess of the Gods, one should properly wash a pitcher—whether made of gold, silver, or clay, as prescribed—with the Astra-mantra.
Furthermore, elsewhere, the etymology and authoritative proof regarding the word *kalaśa* (pitcher) have been stated:
Since this was fashioned by Viśvakarman from the gods by taking a portion (kalā) from each of them,
it is therefore called a *kalaśa*.

"The width [of the body] of the pitchers is fifty finger-breadths, their height sixteen finger-breadths, and their mouth shall be eight finger-breadths. Thus it is said. However, the teacher Padmapāda has provided the etymological derivation: "The *kalās* (digits) lie within them" (*kalāḥ śerate*).
With waters consecrated by the Astra-mantra;
with their limbs encircled by a triple-stranded thread—that is, a thread consisting of the three qualities (guṇas) such as sattva and the rest;
for that reason, they perform the wrapping of a cord around the neck.
"Sealed" (*nīrandhra*) is an adjective qualifying the water-pot (*kumbha*).
This has been stated in the *Vāyavīya-saṃhitā*:
"It may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay."
"Strewn with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, covered with sprouts of *kuśa* and *dūrvā* grass,

its neck encircled by a white thread, and wrapped in a pair of new cloths. Some, however, interpret this as meaning that the body [of the image] should be wound with thread so as to be completely without gaps.
In that view, every jar would be wrapped in threads; consequently, the word *aṅga* (limb/part) here would be redundant.
Elsewhere, there is a distinction:

"With a thread spun from a virgin, tripled through ritual action, and consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), one should wrap it evenly all around. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), incense is meant. (70–71)

The mantra-knower, an expert in the ritual procedure, should place [the vessel] whose interior contains the nine gems while uttering the syllable *Tāra*; having conceived the oneness of the jar and the pedestal.
Regarding the phrase "having a belly of nine gems":
the nine gems will be described in the sixth [chapter]. The grammatical connection is that one should place such a jar while uttering the syllable *tāra*.
In this context, it should be understood that by the word *tāra*, the five *praṇavas* within their respective mantras are also included.
By the term *mantrī*, the recitation of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) is also indicated.
By the phrase *vidhānavit*, it is stated that one is capable of producing the resulting power even without the decoctions of the fifty medicinal herbs. || 72 ||

With a decoction of milk-tree bark, or with that produced from the bark of the *palāśa* tree, or with water from a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), well-scented with camphor, fragrant substances, and flowers. || 73 ||
Chanting the Mātṛkā in reverse order as prescribed, identifying it with one's own self, and likewise chanting the root mantra while perceiving it as the deity, one should fill [the vessel]. || 74 ||
Regarding the word "kṣīra" (milk): this means with a decoction of milk-trees—that is, a decoction of the barks of the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *vaṭa*.
According to the method prescribed in Āyurveda, the decoction should be taken when reduced to one-fourth.
"According to rule" means with the nasal bindu.
"In that manner" means in reverse order.
The connection is that one should fill [the vessel] with the thought of the deity as non-different from oneself.
The meaning is that one should constantly contemplate the identity of the self, the deity, and the water. || 73-74 ||
In a conch filled with the scum of the decoction, one should stir the eight fragrances which grant all desires; having invoked all the *kalās* therein, one should worship them. || 75 ||
First, there are ten digits (kalās) of Agni; then twelve of the Sun (Dvādaśātman);
sixteen of Soma; and thereafter fifty digits [of the Earth]. || 76 ||
Having recited the root mantra in reverse order, the knower of mantras, with a concentrated mind, should meditate upon the deity of the mantra. || 77 ||
"In the conch" means in one other than the conch that has been established.
Therein, the ritual up to the establishment of the conch should be performed as before.
"With decoction water" refers to [the vessel] being filled with what remains after the filling of the *kalaśa*.
Having stirred the eight fragrances with the Heart mantra together with its root, this is the "grounded eight-fragrance" (*piṣṭagandhāṣṭaka*).
As it has been said:
"And having stirred the ground eight-fragrance, which consists of the nature of the Eight Forms (*aṣṭamūrti*)."
Thus:
by the phrase "bestowing the desired," the recitation of the mantra *gandhadvārām* is indicated;
and by the instruction "one should worship," it should be understood that one should display the *dhenumudrā* with the head.
All together there are ninety-four;
"of twelvefold nature" refers to the Sun.
By the word "subsequently," this is what is stated.
Immediately after the portion produced from the letter *a* is "haṃsaḥ";
immediately after that produced from the letter *u* is "pra tad viṣṇuḥ";
and immediately after that produced from the letter *m* is "tryambakam".

Immediately after the Binduja [mantra], one should recite the *tatpādika* and so forth; for the Nādaja, one should recite the verse beginning with "viṣṇuryoniṃ". There are fifty-one kalās produced from the fivefold divisions of the Tāra.
Here, the thirty-eight *kalās* are worshipped; then the fifty-one *kalās*, followed by the five secret *kalās* in the water of the conch.
These consist of Will (*icchā*), Knowledge (*jñāna*), Action (*kriyā*), Consciousness (*cit*), Self (*ātman*), and Bliss (*ānanda*).
Thus, there are thirty-eight *kalās*, fifty-one *kalās*, and five secret *kalās*, which together constitute the nature of ninety-four deities.
As the teachers have said: "First is the *haṃsa* [mantra] of Prakṛti; immediately after that is *pratad viṣṇu*;
the third should be *tryambaka*; and the fourth begins with *tat-pada*."
Let the fifth mantra, beginning with "viṣṇuryoniṃ...", be conceived;
having invoked the deity consisting of the ninety-four mantras, let him be worshipped.
"In this context, the five *ṛc* verses that have been proclaimed are joined individually with each of the five divisions of the digits (*kalā*) of Tāra.
Also elsewhere: "And having invoked the digits in sequence, numbering ninety-four..."
Thus:

"With a concentrated mind" means that while meditating upon the deity of the mantra with a concentrated mind, one should recite the root mantra in reverse order, and having invoked that very deity, perform worship; such is the connection [of the words].
This is also obtained from the words "the knower of mantras" [in the verse].
As they say: "Having recited the root mantra and invoked the deity, the knower of mantras, having performed worship, should pour the water from the conch into the divine pitcher. Thus it is said.

The phrase "with a concentrated mind" was stated here in connection with the context; however, this qualification should be understood as applying to all meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), for otherwise, meditation itself would be impossible to perform. (75–77)
The wise one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of vital breath) in each respective place;
he should pour the decoction, which consists of the [sixteen] digits (*kalā*) and is situated within a conch, into the jar. || 78 ||
Regarding the term *prāṇa*: the etymology of the word *pratiṣṭhā* is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*—
the successful derivation of the word *pratiṣṭhā* is from the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *prati*.
Because particles have multiple meanings, the prefix *prati* is established in the sense of "refinement" (*saṃskāra*) and so forth.
This very point is expressed by those who are experts in grammar:
that a proximity to a particular [word] is indeed established for that which is otherwise all-pervasive.
"The ritual installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the image of the True Being (*sanmūrti*) by means of mantras and meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*) is thus defined.
Regarding this, the practical application (*prayoga*) is as follows:

Having invoked her with "O Dhūmrācī, come! and having displayed the eight mudrās, one should worship her with "Obeisance to Dhūmrācī, the Mistress" (dhūmrācīṣe namaḥ). Then, in the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra, one should perform the installation of the vital breaths by substituting the word "Dhūmrācī" in the sixth case for the word "amuṣya" (of such-and-such).
This same procedure applies to all the *kalās*.

Alternatively, having performed the invocation and other rites for all ten fire-energies (*agni-kalā*) simultaneously, and having performed the worship of each individually, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* while reciting the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra; in place of the word *amuṣya*, one should utter the name of all [the energies] in the genitive case.
The visualization of the *kalās* should be understood as described in the second chapter.

The meaning of the phrase "in each respective place" (*tatra tatra*) is as follows: first, [the mantras] of the ten digits of Fire (*vahnikalā*); then those of the twelve digits of the Sun (*sūryakalā*); then those of the sixteen digits of the Moon (*somakalā*); then the *ṛc*s born from the syllable *da*; then the *ṛc*s born from the syllable *u*; then the *ṛc*s born from the syllable *ma*, ten of them; then the *ṛc*s born from the five *bindu*s; and then the sixteen digits of Sound (*nādakalā*).
Then, for the five *guptakalās*, [the verse] beginning with "vicakṣaṇa" is used; by this, it is stated that one should recite the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra three times everywhere.
Others, however, apply the phrase "in reverse order" (*pratilomena*) to every instance.

As for that which pertains to the consecration for malevolent rites (*ābhicārika*), then first there are the *nāda*-kalās of such a kind; then the *bindu*-kalās of such a kind; then the *makāra*-kalās of such a kind; then the *ukāra*-kalās of such a kind;
then the *akāra*-kalās of such a kind; and then those of the Moon, Sun, and Fire.
As they say:
"Having filled a conch placed upon a sacrificial mound with that water,
and having stirred together flour representing the eight forms [of Śiva] along with the eight fragrances..."
Having performed the placement of the limbs of Hṛllekhā according to the sequence of the Kalānāda, joined each with its own respective name, one should employ them individually.
Here, at the end of the *nāda-kalā*, one should properly invoke and worship Viṣṇu as the *kalā* beginning with *yenī*, which pervades and is itself pervaded by all [the other *kalās*].
Having touched [the disciple] with the right hand while reciting the *Susthāpana-mantra* beginning with "yuktanādakalānāmnā" and so forth, one should join [him] three times.
"Having likewise invoked the digits (kalās) of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire— distinguished by [the mantras] beginning with Bindu and Tāra— one should worship them in sequence.
The phrase "one should cast [them]" implies [casting them] with the root mantra (mūlamantra).
As it has been said:
"Then one should utter the root mantra over the water, which consists of the [five] digits (kalās), and cause it to be present within the pitcher."
Elsewhere also it is said: "The knower of mantras, having uttered the root mantra, should cast that [substance] into the jar. (78)
That eightfold fragrance is threefold, consisting of the natures of Śakti, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
it consists of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, cora, saffron, and gorocana. || 79 ||
They know the eight fragrant substances of Śakti to be jaṭāmāṃsī, māṃsī, kapi, candana, aguru, hnīvera, kuṣṭha, kuṅkuma, and sevya. (80)
They know *jaṭāmāṃsī*, *mura*, and [the others] as the eight fragrances of Viṣṇu.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, *tamāla*, water, saffron, combined with *kuśīta* and *kuṣṭha*, is remembered as the eight fragrances of Śiva. (81)

Regarding what was stated as "having stirred the eightfold perfume," he says "the eightfold perfume. By the statement that it consists of Śakti, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, its extreme dearness is indicated. "Cora" and "bhaṭīra" are terms in the Kānyakubja dialect.
Rocanā is *gorocanā*.
*Kapi* is well known as *gaṇṭhivana*.
*Hrīvera* is *vālaka*.
*Kuṣṭha* is well known as *kūṭha*. *Sevyaka* is *uśīra*. *Jaṭāmāṃsī* and *mura* form a collective dvandva compound, which is neuter by virtue of being a singular aggregate.
Surā is well known by its own name; tamāla is that which is produced from leaves;
jala is vālaka.
Kuśīta is red sandalwood (*raktacandana*).
These [substances] should be taken in equal parts.
In the *Gaṇapatisaṃhitā*, the "Eightfold Incense of Gaṇeśa" (*gaṇeśagandhāṣṭaka*) is also mentioned:

"Svarūpa, sandalwood, cora, rocanā, aguru, the two kinds of musk, and kastūrī combined with camphor— these are declared to be the eight fragrances (aṣṭagandha) for the great and all-pervading Gaṇeśa. (Verses 79–81)
At the end of the three-syllable mantra beginning with *pāśa*, there should be the word "of this one" (*amuṣya*).
Then, in sequence: "the vital breaths here," "the vital breaths likewise," and "the individual soul (jīva) is situated here. || 82 ||
All the sense organs of that person shall once again become his own state;
then there are the states of speech, mind, sight, hearing, smell, and breath. || 83 ||
"Having come here afterwards, may they remain happily for a long time—thus is the pair of *ṭha*s.
This is declared to be the life-mantra (*prāṇamanu*), which bestows life upon all living beings. (84)
It has been stated that one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the rite of vitalizing the breath); therefore, he states the mantra for that [rite] as "pāśādi" and so forth.
The three-syllabled mantra beginning with "pāśa" will be explained in the ninth chapter.
The *ātman* is the *jīva-mantra*.

Regarding this, those who know the tradition maintain that by the phrase "the three-syllable mantra beginning with *pāśa* and ending with the *ātman*," these eight seed-syllables— *yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hauṃ*— which are to be taught in the twenty-third [chapter],
are included. Furthermore, in this context, it should be understood that there is a repetition of each word from *pāśa* to *ātman*.
This is because it will be explained thus in the twenty-third [chapter].
The meaning of the word *amuṣya* is as follows:
the name of the deity to be accomplished (sādhya), such as a yantra, should be employed in the genitive case.

And likewise, regarding the application of this Vedic text—"This man, the son of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so, is your king, O Kurus"—Kātyāyana states in his *Kalpasūtra* (Śrautasūtra): "'Asau' [is used] for the purpose of removal.
Its commentary explains: "The meaning of 'removal' is that the word 'adaḥ' (that one) should be removed and the [proper] name should be employed."
Also in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"Whatever form the word 'so-and-so' takes when seen in mantras,
one should employ that form in place of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in that position."
In the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā* commentary on that [text], it is stated as follows:
"And this is to be understood as applying to instances other than the mantra of Puruṣottama;
for in that case, the word 'durita' or the word 'alakṣmī' is employed in place of the word 'amuka'."
The meaning is that one should utter the word "amuṣya" (of such-and-such) preceded by "tathā.
The expression "speech, mind, and eye" is an indicator for the word "eye," which is a synonym for the word "nayanam";
it is taught in that manner solely for the sake of metrical requirements.
And likewise, in the twenty-third [chapter], that very same [text] states: "At the end of this [process], all the senses [dissolve], and finally speech and mind.
Even in the instruction of those who know the mantras, the word "eye" alone is found taught by those who know the tradition.
And thus is the statement of the Teacher in the Dīkṣā-paṭala:

"Likewise, having raised speech and mind, [one should say] 'let them come here, following after that breath'"; thus the commentator Padmapādācārya explained: "The mention of speech and mind is for the purpose of indicating the eyes, ears, nose, and vital breaths.
Likewise, the teachers [state] in the *Prāṇapratiṣṭhāpaṭala*:
"Likewise, speech, mind, sight, hearing, and also smell together with breath. Regarding this, the commentators have explained: "By the word *dṛk* (sight), the word *cakṣus* (eye) is understood."
If this were not the case, then in one place there would be the word *nayanam*, in another the word *cakṣuḥ*, in another the word *dṛk*, and likewise in another the word *locanam*.
But that is incorrect;
for a mantra that is uttered as a synonym does not become that very mantra; otherwise, the very verses used for extracting mantras (*mantroddhāra*) would themselves be the mantras.
Therefore, it is established that the word *nayana* is indicative of the word *cakṣus*.
Regarding the words "nose" (*ghrāṇa*) and "vital breath" (*prāṇa*):
in this mantra, it should be understood that the term *prāṇāḥ* ends in the plural.
This is due to the formation of a *dvandva* compound from the many words beginning with speech (*vāk*).
He will state this in the twenty-third [chapter]: "The breaths are in the words 'speech,' 'ear,' and 'nose.
*Ṭha-dvayaṃ svāhā*.

Now, if it is asked: "In this mantra, since there is the insertion of the name of the deity to be propitiated (sādhya-devatā) or of a yantra and so forth in place of 'amuṣya' (of such-and-such), how can it possess the status of a mantra?
We reply: it is established by the settled conclusions (siddhānta) of the Mīmāṃsā topical discussions (adhikaraṇa).

For instance, in the second chapter (*adhyāya*), in the section concerning the meaning of verbal roots (*bhāvārtha-caraṇa*), in the topical discussion beginning with the sūtra: "In the case of those not recorded [in the Vedic canon], there is no status as a mantra; for the distinction [between mantra and non-mantra] applies only to those that are recorded," it is stated regarding *ūha* (modification)—
Regarding the doubt as to whether *pravara* names constitute mantras or are non-mantras, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that they are non-mantras.
In connection with that, it was also deliberated whether, upon the insertion of *ūha*, *pravara*, and *nāmadheya*, the entire [formula] becomes a non-mantra, or only the inserted portion.
In that regard, the established conclusion is that only the inserted portion is a non-mantra.
In connection with that very topic, this further point has been considered:

regarding those mantras such as "This one is the son of so-and-so, the son of so-and-so; he is the king of this people," where words like "king" (*rājan*) are used in place of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-sthāna*), is there an absence of *mantra*-status or is there indeed *mantra*-status?
In that case, when a pronoun recited in the text is used together with words such as "king" (rājan),
its function is merely to convey authority.
Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it lacks the status of a mantra, just like the *ūha* (modification) and other such elements.
The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows:
this would indeed be the case if the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) as it is recited were to confer authority upon the employment of words such as "king" (*rājan*);
but rather, pronouns merely serve to introduce another word in their place.
For instance,

in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the mantra is heard as "I offer what is pleasing to Agni" (*agnaye tvājuṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*). However, in the modified rite (*vikṛti*) involving an oblation for the deity Sūrya, the word "to Sūrya" (*sūryāya*) is substituted by logical principle (*nyāya*).
Let it be that this [part] is not a mantra.

Thus, by the word *pravara*, the recitation of the words denoting the *pravara* lineages—such as Asita, Devala, and Śāṇḍilya—is intended; and by the word *nāmadheya*, the recitation of the name denoting the sacrificer, such as Viṣṇuśarman and so forth, is intended.

Furthermore, because these [names] are not mentioned in the Veda, and because there is no mention of them in their specific form as items to be employed in mantras by the injunction, "One should proclaim the *pravara* and the names," they do not possess the status of mantras.
As for the mention of pronouns (*sarvanāman*), it is due to the impossibility of mentioning the specific names of kings and others, given their infinite number.
This is for the purpose of conveying specific meanings such as "king" and so forth.
Since this [word] lacks the inherent capacity to convey such meanings on its own,
being itself unfit for usage, it indicates only those specific words that are fit for usage.
As in the case of "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*) and so forth;

therefore, [the author] demonstrates that only those words which have as their object specific meanings such as "king" (*rājan*), whose forms are intended to be expressed, are to be employed within the mantra-texts.

It is for this very purpose that the pronominal word (*sarvanāmapada*) was taught by the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayanavidhi*), which has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*); thus it is determined.
Therefore, since names such as "king" and so forth are also frequently found in the traditional recitations (āmnāta), they indeed possess the status of mantras. || 82–84 ||

Afterwards, having covered this cup with the tender sprouts of the *aśvattha*, *panasa*, and *cūta* trees tied together with *indravallī* vines— mistaking them for celestial trees— the Guru rendered the vessel fruitful by placing it upon the mouth of the jar. (85)
One should duly establish [the images] of the wish-fulfilling trees with the thought of their fruit;
thereafter, one should wrap the water-pot with a pair of stainless linen cloths.
*Indravallī* refers to the specific creeper known as *indravāruṇī*.
A *caṣaka* is a vessel of the type consisting of a jar, a shallow bowl, or the like.
By the term "according to rule" (*vidhivat*), the recitation of the root mantra is indicated.
"Kṣauma" refers to that which is produced from flax;
in its absence, silk cloth and the like may be used.
Elsewhere, even being wrapped in a single garment has been mentioned.
"One should wrap the jar with a cloth that is exceedingly subtle, pure, and new, having the nature of the *māyātattva*. (85–86)
Having fashioned an image within this shade of the wish-fulfilling trees by means of the root mantra, the practitioner of mantra should invoke and worship the deity of that mantra therein. || 87 ||
"In the initiation for a single mantra, one should [invoke] the deity of that mantra.

Regarding the procedure for the initiation of the five abodes (*pañcāyatana*), it is stated by the term "the mantrin" that one should install five jars and invoke the respective deities into each jar.
As it has been said by the Teachers: "Thus, according to the prescribed rule for the jar-rite, whether with a single jar or with multiple jars..."
Thus, the sequence for the installation of the deities in the initiation of the five shrines (*pañcāyatana-dīkṣā*) is stated in the *Jñānamālā*:
"When one should worship Śaṅkara in the center and Śrīpati in the northeast..."
Likewise, one should place Haṃsa in the southeast and the son of Pārvatī in the southwest.
And Bhavānī, who is affectionate toward her devotees, should always be worshipped in the northwest;
however, when Govinda is in the center, one should worship Śaṅkara in the northeast.
The practitioner, composed and concentrated, should worship Gaṇanātha in the southeast, Tapanas in the southwest, and Ambikā in the northwest.

When [the sun] is in the middle, one should worship the Thousand-rayed One (Sahasrāṃśu) in the northeast, the Lord of Pārvatī (Pārvatīpati) in the southeast, the Single-tusked One (Ekadanta) in the southwest, and Acyuta in the northwest.
One should worship the Goddess in the northwest, who is the sole ground for both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
but when Bhavānī is in the center, one should worship Mādhava in the northeast.
The preceptor should worship the Lord of Pārvatī in the southeast, Gaṇanāyaka in the southwest,
and Pradyotana in the northwest.
When Heramba is in the center, one should worship Acyuta in the northeast,
Pañcavaktra in the southeast, and Jagadambikā in the southwest.
The practitioner, remaining vigilant, should indeed worship the Sun in the northwest. For deities who have departed from their own places bestow sorrow, suffering, and fear;
consequently, the king and the practitioner situated within that mandala perish. Thus it is said.

Elsewhere as well: "When Śambhu occupies the center, Hari, Naha (Nirṛti), Hara, and Bhūdevī [are placed]; when Harī is in the center, Śaṅkara, Āsyenāgasutā (Sarasvatī), Ravi, Hara, Gaṇeśa, Aja, and Ambikā are established; when Devī is in the center, Viṣṇu, Hara, Ekadanta, Ravi, Lambodara, Aja, and Īśvara [are established]."

"Those [syllables] beginning with Śaṅkara (Śa) from the northeast (Īśāna) quarter grant great auspiciousness, but when transposed, they cause loss. Thus it is said. The learned scholars also state: "Śaṃ, Nā, Ra, Ga, De, Ma, Dhyān, Nā, Śaṃ, Ga, Ra, Bhe, Śataḥ, Sū, Śaṃ, Ga, Nā, De, De, Nā, Śaṃ, Ga, Ra, Ga, Nā, Śaṃ, Bha, Sū—these are to be worshipped in the intermediate directions. Thus it is said.
Elsewhere, installation is said to follow the sequence beginning with Āgneya (Agni).
[The deities are]: Sūrya, Ekadanta, Acyuta, Śakti, Rudra, Vighneśvara, Īśa, Adrisūta (Gaurī), Arka, Kṛṣṇa;
Śrīnātha, Vighneśa, Bhaga, Ambikeśa, Caṇḍīśa, Heramba, Pataṅga, and Kṛṣṇa.
"Śrī, Śambhu, Sūrya, Khuratha, Amba, and Kṛṣṇa are to be worshipped clockwise in the center and the intermediate directions.
Abiding in their own places, they grant the attainment of all desires; however, if they are situated elsewhere, they destroy one's wealth.
Also elsewhere: "Having worshipped Hari in the center, [one worships] Gaṇeśa, Pārvatī, and Śiva; then Gaṇeśa in the center..."
"Śambhu, Āryā, Aravi, Viṣṇu, Ravi, then Vighna, Aja, Śakti, and Īśvara;
in the center, Śakti; then Īśa, Vighna, Ravi, and Viṣṇu in the center;
and Hara, Sūrya, Ibha, Asya, Śiva, and Acyuta are indeed placed starting from the southeast corner. Thus it is said.
In both cases, there is indeed equality in terms of the result regarding the sequence of installation.
However, the worship begins with Gaṇapati;
it should be understood that where Gaṇapati holds the primary position, the worship begins with Sūrya.
As they say:
"Having offered a handful of flowers to the principal deity, the worship of Gaṇeśa and others should take place;
however, if Gaṇeśa himself is the principal deity, it should occur according to the sequence of the Sun."
They provide this explanation in two ways:

according to the primary view, one first performs merely the *puṣpāñjali* (handful of flowers), and afterwards, having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa and others, one performs the "principal worship" (*mukhyapūjā*).
Others, however, maintain that by the word *puṣpāñjali*, that handful of flowers which occurs at the conclusion of the worship is included.
Therefore, after the worship of the principal deity, there is the worship of Gaṇeśa and the others;
this should be understood according to the specific tradition of one's own guru.
This very sequence for the installation of the deities is the same even in the daily worship (*nityapūjā*).
In that regard, the daily worship (nityapūjā) should be performed upon a Śālagrāma stone, a jewel, a yantra, or an image made of stone and so forth.
As it is stated in the Jñānamālā: "The gods became intent on obstacles for the sake of the pleasure of the Mountain-Daughter’s lover;
having heard that conduct of the Goddess, a most terrible curse was pronounced."
Afflicted by the curse of Pārvatī, the gods—
including Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, and other foremost deities— were transformed into stone.
O gods, though she has become stone, she has been praised as a granter of boons;
those who worship her in her own place shall attain the four aims of human existence.
"He alone is capable of granting [boons] according to my word; therefore, this very one is the chosen boon.

For that reason, worship must be performed even toward stone images. Thus it is said in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "An image made of clay, fashioned from wood, born of metal, or likewise born of jewels..."
It is known to be of seven kinds: that born of stone, that born of fragrance, and that born of flowers.
"An image made of flowers, of fragrant substances, or of clay is beneficial;
when worshipped at that very time, these grant the fruit of all desires. Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*: "Whether made of stone, or metal, or gems, or wood..."
And that made of clay; these five types of images are thus proclaimed.
For all the gods, the Mahānīlā bestows fame;
the one made of wood is said to grant desires; and the golden one bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
A silver vessel bestows the fruit of heaven; a copper one indeed increases longevity; a bronze one destroys many calamities; and a brass one is the destroyer of enemies.
An image made of stone bestows all enjoyments; one made of crystal brings forth radiance;
indeed, one made of clay is renowned for bestowing great enjoyment and is truly auspicious.
"A statue in a home should be worshipped according to the measurement of the *mānāṅgula*, consisting of fifteen fingers; indeed, one exceeding that is not praised.
Also elsewhere: "Starting from the joint of the thumb up to a span (*vitasti*)."
"In the home, however, an image should be made; one that is larger than that is not recommended by the wise.
As for the statement: "A gentle image, one cubit in measure, bestows wealth; one two cubits high leads to security and abundance;
and one three or four cubits in height [brings about prosperity]."
That should be understood as referring to an installed image.
Regarding an earthen image, a specific rule is stated therein: "I shall describe the earthen image; learn it from me exactly as it is."
An earthen image is said to be of two kinds, according to the sequence: baked and unbaked.
All people do not praise an image made of burnt clay;
an unbaked image is praised, and that alone should be fashioned by the wise.
It should never be made with lime nor ever with stone powder;
one should fashion it from clay alone, according to the rules and in the proper sequence.
"The clay for a Brāhmaṇa is remembered as white and soft; for a Kṣatriya, it is red; for a Vaiśya, it should be yellow and soft; and for a Śūdra, it is declared to be black.
Elsewhere, there is this distinction: "If the clay has extra limbs, there is fear of the king; if it has missing limbs, there is lack of capacity for the maker."
If she has a thin waist, there is fear of hunger; if she has a slender body, there is loss of wealth.
One should indicate death by the falling of a weapon upon a woman who has been wounded;
if she is bent to the left, it destroys the wife, but if bent to the right, it destroys the life-span of the doer.
"If the gaze is directed upward, it causes blindness; if downward, it causes anxiety.
One should understand the auspicious and inauspicious results for all images as stated by the Sun. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, elsewhere: "A deity should never be fashioned with either an extra limb or a missing limb."
An excessive [debt] would destroy the artisan, and one that is too small would cause the loss of wealth.
A woman with a thin belly portends famine; one who is fleshless brings the loss of wealth;
one with a crooked nose leads to suffering; and one with contracted limbs is terrifying.
A flat nose leads to suffering and grief; lack of eyes destroys the vision;
a sunken face brings misery, as does being thin in the hands and feet.
O King, one with drooping shoulders and weak shanks causes delusion and madness;
one with a parched mouth and a sunken waist kills the king.
A great hell arises for one who is deprived of hands and feet;
and a form devoid of shanks brings about the welfare of one's enemies.
That which is deficient in its chest leads to the destruction of sons and friends;
however, that which possesses complete limbs always bestows longevity and prosperity.
"Having thus attained the [proper] characteristics, the supreme images should be fashioned.

Elsewhere, there is this specific instruction: "When [the image] is broken, cracked, fallen, burnt, abandoned by humans, devoid of sacrifice, or defiled by remnants, or when it has fallen upon impure grounds..."
Furthermore, when another mantra was recited or when [the site] was defiled by the touch of a fallen person—
among these ten instances, the gods did not grant their presence.

"Thus Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent, gave this instruction. Elsewhere it is said: "One should carefully avoid an image that is broken, cracked, decayed, scorched by fire, shattered, or fallen away from its own characteristic marks."
"One should cast an image made of wood into fire, and likewise cast another into water.
And similarly: "If the worship for one day is omitted, one should perform double the worship;
if for three nights, however, a great worship (mahāpūjā) is required; beyond that, a ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa)."
If the worship is interrupted for many days beyond one month,
some authorities require a re-consecration (pratiṣṭhā), while others prescribe the procedure of sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa).
The characteristics of the ritual sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*) are as follows, in that very same [text]: "As for the sprinkling of the deity, having dismissed the deity as before,
one should bathe him five times each in sequence with clay and water."
Having bathed [the image] with the products of the cow and purified it with water from *darbha* grass,
one should sprinkle it one hundred and eight times with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel while reciting the root mantra.
Placing his hand, adorned with flowers and kuśa grass, upon the head of the deity,
he should recite the root mantra five times and then one hundred and eight times.
Then, one should touch [the body] from the head down to the seat with the root mantra;
one should perform the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa), the placement of the letters (lipinyāsa), and the placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa).
One should perform the installation with the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra and conduct a grand worship according to the rules as prescribed in one's own Tantra.
"In cases such as when a sacrifice has been omitted, the procedure of sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) is generally prescribed.
Also elsewhere: "The daily worship of Hari should be performed at a Śālagrāma stone, a gem, a yantra, a maṇḍala, or in an image, but never on bare ground alone."
In the *Rāmapūrvatāpanīya* as well: "The form of this God, who is both [immanent and transcendent], is the construction of the Yantra;
without the Yantra, the deity is not pleased by worship.
Also, in the *Saṃhitā*: "They say the Yantra consists of Mantra, and the deity has the form of Mantra."
A deity who has not been worshipped with a yantra does not become propitious all of a sudden.
Likewise: "The worship of all mantras is praised when performed upon a yantra.

Thus it was also said by Īśānaśiva: "One should perform the sacrifice to Śakti with the sense of one's own identity within the wheel (cakra), or on a painting, or on a cloth, but not upon the ground."
"If out of delusion he should worship one situated on the bare ground, he would fall from the three goals of life"—so say those perfected in mantra.
As for the worship of Śiva, it should be performed upon a form of Śiva, whether a fixed or a mobile Śivaliṅga.
In that regard, concerning a mobile liṅga made of stone or other materials, the characteristics such as the five lines (pañcasūtra) and so forth that have been described must necessarily be observed.
However, there is no fault even if the specific characteristics are absent in the case of a *liṅga* made of gems and the like.
As it is said in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*:
"One should not perform the extraction of [auspicious] marks for those made of gems or for movable [images]."
O twice-born one, this is their characteristic of self-luminosity, even though they are born of gold.
Therefore, one should not perform the removal of marks on [an image] like a stone liṅga;
however, in some cases, the marking of immovable [images] made of metallic substances is permitted.
"The marks (lakṣaṇa) should be fashioned according to the rules upon a stationary linga;
on a mobile linga, the Guru should fashion the marks with the tips of kusha grass (or fingers), or he may even contemplate the marks situated upon the linga in his mind. Thus it is said.
Somaśambhu also says: "The extraction of characteristics applies to [liṅgas] made of gems, but not to those made of metal or those originating from rivers;
nor has it been seen anywhere in the scriptures regarding liṅgas made of metal."
"Their essential nature is their defining characteristic, and their radiance is stainless among jewels.
However, there is a specific rule elsewhere: "Two lingas and two Gaṇeśas should not be worshipped in a single house."
Likewise, it is marked with the three powers, the conch, and the ten [signs] beginning with the fish.
A wise person should not worship two conch shells, nor two *śālagrāma* stones,
nor two discs of Dvārakā, nor likewise two suns.
"By constantly worshipping these, a householder shall experience perpetual anxiety.
Having recited the root mantra, the wise one brings forth the light from its own place through the path of the *suṣumṇā*, as it emerges from the aperture of the nose.

Having united the consciousness within the cluster of flowers with the *mātṛkā* residing in the hand, the wise one should invoke it into the image through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). || 89 ||
It was stated that one should worship after having invoked [the deity]. Regarding that, he describes the method of invocation with the words "from the root" (*mūla*):
from its own place, namely, from the heart-lotus.
Others say [he comes] from the solar orb.
As it is stated in the Vaihāyasī-mantrakoṣa:
"Then, either from the sun or from the lotus of the heart, one should invoke the son of Nanda, who is beautifully attired."
Thus it is said. Furthermore, elsewhere: "One should invoke the Great Goddess from the cavern of the heart-lotus, or from the solar orb, or from one's own *dvādaśānta*."
"By means of the *brahmarandhra*" means through the aperture of the *brahmarandhra*.
"In the hand-held lotus of the *mātṛkās* amidst a collection of flowers" refers to two locative cases in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
The wise one, having recited the root mantra, brings the radiance from its own place via the path of the *suṣumṇā*, and having emerged through the nostrils by way of the *brahmarandhra*—
The connection is as follows: having joined that consciousness, which resides in the hand, with the collection of flowers upon the lotus of the *mātṛkā*, one should invoke it into the image.
As it has been said:
"Having brought the Deity through the path of the *suṣumṇā* to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*)."
"Having meditated on [the deity] emerging from the left nostril while situated within one's own joined palms,
one should offer that flower and place it upon the image or other object.
Here, *āvāhana* means "invocation."
By means of the invocation mantra (*āvāhinī*). And that [invocation] is performed by saying "Be invoked, *namaḥ*" at the end of the root mantra, or else at the end of the verse taught in the Āgama;
or rather, it is stated by the word "sudhīḥ" (the wise one) that one should recite the Āgama verse at the end of the root mantra.
This indeed is the primary method.
Even in the *Saṃhitā*, after stating the incense mantra:
"In this manner, thus, at the end of the seed-syllable, the incense mantra is proclaimed."
This has been stated by such passages as these.
In the same manner, [the procedure for] installation and so forth should be inferred in what follows as well.
The verse, however, is as follows:
"O Supreme Lord, I invoke you— who abide within the self, unborn and pure— into this physical form, just as one invokes the consumer of oblations (Agni) into the sacrificial fire-drill.
This invocation and the subsequent rites are not to be performed for the Śālagrāma stone and similar objects.
As they say:
"In the case of the Śālagrāma or a stationary [liṅga], there is no invocation nor dismissal;
for Hari is eternally present in the Śālagrāma stone and such."
Elsewhere also: "In the worship of a permanent [image], there is neither dismissal nor invocation;
in the worship of a non-permanent [image], there may be an option; however, in the case of a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), both should take place."
"In the worship of the Śālagrāma, there is indeed neither invocation nor dismissal.
Regarding this, in the case of the *pañcāyatana* (five-deity) arrangement, there is an invocation for each deity individually, followed by the installation of each deity individually.

There arises a doubt as to whether there should be *padārthānusamaya*—that is, performing the rites from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the food offering (*naivedya*) for all deities in one place before proceeding likewise with another—or *kāṇḍānusamaya*.
On this point, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is *kāṇḍānusamaya*;
for it is said: "Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the principal deity, the worship of Gaṇeśa and the others should take place."
Thus it has been stated.
In that context, the word *arcana* denotes worship (*pūjā*), and that [worship] extends from the invocation (*āvāhana*) up to the offering of food (*naivedya*).

This was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the section titled "But because of the scriptural statement, [the rite] ends with the encircling" (*vacanāt tu parivyāṇāntam*) in the second quarter of the fifth chapter. (88–89)
One should perform the stabilization, the placement, and the immediate cessation;
thereafter, one should perform the sakalīkaraṇa and the veiling. || 90 ||
Having performed the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa), one should perform the rite of supreme transformation (paramīkṛti).
Composed in mind, one should perform these [rites] in sequence with their respective mudrās. || 91 ||
The connection is that the wise one should perform the installation (*saṃsthāpana*);
*saṃsthāpana* means establishing.
That [should be done] with the *Sthāpinī* [mantra].
The verse, however, says:
"O Lord (Vibhu), this is Your majestic form; within it, I establish You, the omnipresent One, drawn by the oil of devotion like a lamp."
By the word "sudhīḥ" (the wise one), it is stated that one should sit upon the seat;
as follows, at the end of the root mantra:
"O God, inner controller of all, [I offer] this auspicious [seat] consisting of all seeds."
I prepare a supreme, pure seat for you who abides in your own self.
"Accept the seat; obeisance.
Then, at the end of the root mantra:
"O God, whose nature is the Imperishable, seated comfortably upon this excellent seat..."
May you be established; be gracious, O Supreme Lord.
"Be seated, obeisance!
[This refers to] the prayer for the deity's presence, that is, for its remaining in close proximity;
therefore, it is [accomplished] by the *sannidhāpinī* [mudrā].
The verse, however, says: "O Lord of Gods, O Master, this power of yours is non-different from you;
O you who are intent upon favoring your devotees, please manifest your presence within her."
Complete cessation is the act of ceasing, the absence of longing for any other state of mind;
that [is achieved] by means of complete cessation.
As for the verse:
"By your command, O Lord of Gods, O ocean of mercy, O ocean of virtues, I restrain you—who are satisfied solely by the bliss of the Self—from departing, O Father, O Guru. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, in the *Siddhāntasāgara*, the definitions of the rites beginning with invocation (*āvāhana*) are stated differently.
The respectful manifestation of the reality that is already inherently full, facing [the practitioner] during its worship and other rites, is called "invocation" (āvāhana).
In the worship performed with devotion, the stabilization of this Śiva who has been invoked within the body of knowledge (vidyādeha) is prescribed as the rite of installation (sthāpana).
When worship is being performed, the capacity of the deity to accept it and bestow grace and so forth— that, in this context, is what is called "presence" (sānnidhya).
"Indeed, that presence of Śiva which lasts until the completion of the worship is designated as *sannirodha* (the complete withdrawal) of this Lord, by virtue of His power," and so forth.
By the word "immediately thereafter" (*anantaram*), both the act of making [the deity] face [the practitioner] and the prayer are expressed through two mudrās.
The two verses state:
"Whether due to ignorance, dejection, or a deficiency in the ritual implements,
when the rite remains incomplete, even then, remain present before me."
"O Maheśvara, filling the sacrificial altar with your glance that showers nectar, remain firm as the personified fulfillment of the sacrifice.
Thus is the description of the mudrā: "The two thumbs, held in fists, facing each other and interlocked..."
One should join them together with the tips raised; this is the *sammukha-mudrā*.
"With the fingers extended, the two hands joined together and facing each other, one should place them at one's own heart; this is the mudrā known as 'Prayer' (prārthana).
Thus, *sakalīkaraṇa* is the prayer for [the deity] to abide in its complete form."
And that [is accomplished] through the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) upon the body of the deity.
"Enveloping" (*avaguṇṭhana*) means rendering [the deity] invisible to the gaze of the unworthy;
this is done by means of that *avaguṇṭhanī* [mudrā].
The verse, however, is as follows:

As it is said: "One whose intellect is exceedingly clear should [visualize] from the visible [object] up to the feet, rising high.
In the case of the *bahuvartī-dīpa* (multi-wick lamp), an uneven number of wicks should be taken.
As they say: "The *ārātīka*, however, is endowed with an uneven number of many wicks."
Thus [it is said].

However, in the *Prayogasāra*: "One should display a lamp on high, provided with a wick and an oily substance such as sesame oil, tawny-colored clarified butter (*kapilājya*), beeswax, or another kind of fat. Thus [it is said].
In this regard, the traditional teaching is that if the lamp is with ghee, it should be on the right; if with oil, then on the left.
And likewise, if the offering is white, it is on the right; if red, it is on the left. || 107–108 ||
The practitioner of mantra should offer [the oblation] together with plantain fruit and clarified butter;
at each interval between the ritual services, he should offer water there.
By the word "mantrī" (the practitioner), this is what is meant: one should sprinkle the food offering with water over which the Astra-mantra has been recited.

However, in the Śaiva Āgama it is said: "Then, having recited [the mantra] seven times with *darbha* grass placed in a conch shell, ending with 'vauṣaṭ', one should sprinkle it with drops of that water using the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra itself."

Then, having protected it with the *cakramudrā*, one should sprinkle the oblation (*havis*) with water consecrated twelve times with the wind-seed syllable (*vāyubīja*). Having dried up its defects with the wind arising therefrom, one should contemplate the fire-seed syllable (*agnibīja*) on the palm of the right hand; placing the left palm against its back and displaying it toward the food offering (*naivedya*), one should burn its defects with the fire arising therefrom. Then, contemplating the nectar-seed syllable (*amṛtabīja*) on the palm of the left hand, one should place the right palm against its back.

Having prepared the food offering (naivedya) and presented it, one should visualize it as being bathed by the stream of nectar arising from it; having sprinkled it with water consecrated by the recitation of the root mantra (mūlamantra),

meditated upon all of that as being of the nature of nectar, touched it while reciting the root mantra eight times, displayed the cow-mudrā (dhenamudrā), worshipped it with water, fragrance, and flowers, and offered a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) to the deity, one should meditate that light has emerged from the mouth of the deity.
Touching the primary food-offering vessel with the left thumb and taking water in the right hand, one recites the root mantra ending with *svāhā*:
"I offer this, prepared in a worthy vessel and consisting of various kinds of excellent foods for the sacrificial fire, to the God together with his retinue; please accept it."

Having recited this verse, one should offer water with the words, "I offer the food-offering (naivedya) to the God, together with his limbs and retinue; obeisance," and then display the food-offering mudrā.
Then, lifting the food-offering vessel three times with both hands holding flowers, one should say: "I offer this to You; may You enjoy it."
One should recite: "havirhare.
In that context, the word "hare" should be replaced by the name of the respective deity.
As they say:

Having protected that [water] sprinkled with stars by means of the seal of the Enemy (Arimudrikā), having dried it with the Vāyavya-water, and having burnt away the defects of fire with the right hand, one should fill the left hand with the essence of nectar (Saudharasa), consecrate it with the mantra as nectar (Amṛtīkṛta), and then, touching it, recite the mantra.
Let him worship the one who is completely filled with the fragrance of a hundred-fold *manu* incense using a fragrant seal, with the finest perfumes;
then, having offered his joined palms in prostration, let him worship Hari, and from His mouth let him emit the Great Radiance.
Then, reciting the root mantra ending with "vītihotradayitā," he should pour water;
lifting it up along with flowers, he should offer that oblation, which is of the nature of nectar, with joined palms.
"This is the mantra for the offering of the oblation (nivedyārpaṇa) in all forms of worship, using one's own name.
Then, displaying the *grāsamudrā* with the left hand and the *prāṇa*-mudrās and so forth with the right hand, one should mutter the mantras beginning with "To Prāṇa, Svāhā" (*prāṇāya svāhā*).
As they say:
"Displaying with the left hand the *grāsamudrā*, which resembles a full-blown blue lotus, one should display [the gestures] of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth with the right hand."
One should touch the little finger and the ring finger with the tips of one's own thumbs; this is the first mudrā.
Likewise, the others are formed by the index and middle fingers, and the ring and middle fingers respectively.
The ring finger, the index finger, and the middle finger should be [joined]; likewise, the fourth [mudrā] consists of those same fingers together with the little finger.
Similarly, the fifth is taught here; these are the mudrās of Prāṇa and the others, to be employed in conjunction with their respective mantras.
"Prāṇa, apāna, udāna, vyāna, and samāna are joined with the fourth [vowel] in sequence;
if they are the guardians of the path of Kṛṣṇa by means of the bride who is the stream of stars (tārādhārā), these are the mantras.
And the characteristics of the mudrās for the flowers and so forth are as follows:
The thumb and the forefinger are prescribed for the flower; the middle finger and the ring finger for the incense; and the middle finger and the ring finger are proclaimed for the food offering.
Through the joining of the other fingers, the five mudrās are proclaimed;
these mudrās should be displayed even when the various offerings, such as perfumes and so forth, are presented.
"The ritual action performed with a mudrā bestows imperishable fruit.
Regarding the word "therein":
the Supreme Gurus maintain that one should offer handfuls of flowers at intervals during the services, offer water, and wash one's own hands.
Now, the specific details mentioned in other tantras are recorded here:
worship is traditionally held to be of two kinds—without remains (*anirmālya*) and with remains (*sanirmālya*).
[The former is performed] with divine substances born of the mind, such as perfumes, flowers, garlands, and so forth.
Worship of which is without faded garlands and bestows divine enjoyments as well as liberation,
[is performed] with delightful sacrificial substances produced from villages, forests, and other sources.
Whatever worship is properly performed by devotees, that includes the offering of the *nirmālya* (remnants of the offering).
Regarding the nature of *nirmālya*, it is stated in the *Tattvasāgara-saṃhitā*:
"Flowers, as soon as they are produced, are naturally [considered] already smelled."
And likewise by the five great elements, by the sun, and by the moon.
And by living beings such as bees and others, [the offering] is made of flowers alone; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, it is called *nirmālya*.
Thus [it is said].
Anticipating the objection, "If it is *nirmālya* (remnant of an offering), how can there be a fruit [from it]?", it is stated in that very same [text]:
"The fruit accomplished from a flower already smelled is small, unlike that which comes from one offered with the mind (*mānasa*).
Therefore, because it cannot be avoided and because otherwise there would be no means [to attain the goal]."
"Because of the limited intelligence of men, ritual action may be performed with external flowers.

Likewise: "Furthermore, worship is considered to be threefold—superior, inferior, and middling. It is further divided a hundredfold according to the qualifications and the causal conditions [of the practitioner]."

Worship performed with all the complete requisites of sacrifice is considered supreme; however, worship performed with whatever materials are available, even if they are merely visible objects, is middling.
Worship performed with leaves, flowers, and water is designated as the lowest;
it is [the form] practiced by stainless Brahman-sages who have understood the entire meaning of the Vedas.
But that worship which is performed with a sattvic disposition bestows liberation;
it is practiced by those devoted to austerity and by those who know the true nature of the Blessed One.
That worship which is performed correctly by women, children, the elderly, the ignorant, and others who are devoted yet of limited minds, is of the nature of passion (rājasa) and bestows happiness.

That worship which is performed constantly is declared to be *tāmasī* (of the nature of darkness); it is likewise afflicted, impure due to birth or death, fearful, and performed with a distracted mind.
And it is further divided into five types, including that which arises from practice;
this is so if a disease reaching the limit of jumping is observed within oneself.
At that time, worship should not be performed upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or in images;
nor should one perform bathing, the use of a tooth-stick, or even the fire-oblation (homa).
Having gazed upon the solar disc or else upon the image,
one should recite the root mantra once and cast forth a flower accompanied by unbroken grains of rice.
Exhausted by extremely severe diseases and worn out by fasts,
or even by his own ritual commitments, he should nevertheless complete what is his own duty.
Having bathed and praised the God, as well as the fires and the gurus, and having worshipped the Brahmins, [I declare]:
"By your grace, this worship which had been interrupted for so long [is now restored]."
Having prayed, "May there be no fault for me," one should perform the rite again as before.
Now, I shall describe the worship for those in a state of impurity (sūtakin), as enjoined by the Āgamas.
Having bathed and performed the daily mental rites,
one should worship according to the sequence of external worship through the yoga of visualization (*sthāna-dhyāna*).
If one is not desirous, or even if one is desirous, one should always act as previously described;
the worship for those who are fearful will now be explained exactly as enjoined by the Āgamas.
Whether obtained or not obtained, the means such as the arghya-vessel and so forth—
It should be performed with water for worship; however, if water is not available, [one should use other substances].
If one should worship the God with flowers of meditative visualization and other such offerings,
I shall now describe the *daurvidhikī* rite of worship as enjoined by the Āgamas.
Fools, women, children, the elderly, and others are considered to be of dull intellect;
[the deities are] Ratna, Maṇḍapa, Dharma, and so forth—the fourfold group—along with Uraga and Ambuja.
In the same way, the limbs of the primary form are worshipped;
this is prescribed as the abbreviated rite for all other [deities] as well.

"Nārada has said: 'Indeed, when all the required materials for ritual practice are unavailable, the mere mental visualization [is sufficient]; even with water that is not from a pure source, there is fullness [of the rite].
Thus it is said.
Regarding one who is unable to perform worship: "If one is unable to propitiate [the deity], one should give the means for worship;
if one is not even able to give those, one should at least behold the act of worship."
He who does not possess even one [of these] goes downward indeed, and not otherwise;
but he who, with devotion and effort, has himself accomplished them all—
The wise person should worship with the ritual requisites; he shall obtain the complete fruit.
Whoever worships according to the rules with devotion, using requisites brought from others, [attains the same].
"He shall obtain only half the fruit of the worship; he does not receive the full fruit.
Thus [ends verse 109].
One should also worship the enclosures, beginning with the limbs (aṅga) and ending with the world-protectors (lokapāla).
One should worship the heart-mantra and the others in the filaments, starting from the southeast corner. || 110 ||
It has been stated that "one should worship the limbs and so forth again.
Regarding this, it says "at the beginning and end, [the two] general [limbs].
He summarizes once more in order to explain the meditation, location, and application for those two, as well as to clarify the meaning of the word "beginning" (*ādi*).
He states its essential nature as "beginning with the limbs" (*aṅgādi*).
Since the occasion for worship has been mentioned previously, he will therefore say: "Having thus worshipped according to the rule, ending with the *nivedya* offering" (4.118).
That in which the limbs (*aṅga*) and the enclosure of the limbs (*aṅgāvṛti*) come first is [the *aṅgādi*].

"Where there is a covering by the world-protectors at the end"—this refers to the sequence beginning with the limbs (*aṅga*) and ending with the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). This is an adverbial phrase (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
It should be understood that by the word "world-protector" itself, the covering by their respective weapons is also included.
And this [instruction] is intended as a possibility, since it is observed to be so in many instances; it is not a mandatory rule.
Because of the word "api" (also/even), the phrase "one should offer water at intervals" is to be supplied here as well.
He states the worship-place common to all for the worship of the limbs: "in the filaments," and so forth.
By the word "beginning with the southeast corner" (*agnikoṇādi*), the southwest, northwest, and northeast corners are intended.
As it has been said:
"The limbs, beginning with the heart and ending with the armor, [are assigned] from the southeast to the northeast."
"One should worship the Netra-mantra in front, and again in the directions outside.
Also elsewhere: "In the directions of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Śiva [the North], one should worship from the Hṛdaya-mantra up to the Varma-mantra."
Others, however, explain it as being in the corners of Agni, Īśāna, Nairṛta, and Vāyu;
as they say:
"Having sacrificed to the heart in the southeast, one should sacrifice to the head in the northeast."
The Śikhā should be worshipped in the southwest, and one should worship the Kavaca in the northwest.
"Having worshipped the Eye (Netra) in front, one should then worship the Weapon (Śastra) in the cardinal directions.
Also elsewhere: "The worship of the limbs (Aṅga) is performed in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center."
Thus it is said;
and the determination is according to the teacher's instruction.
Here, the [directions] beginning with Āgneya are in relation to the previously conceived east, and not according to the conventional [east]. || 110 ||
The deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās) are to be meditated upon: the Eye in front and the Weapon-mantra in the directions;
they possess tongues that are white as frost, crystal, dark, blue, black, and reddish-brown respectively.
The word "netram" (the eye) refers to the center of the eye, which is the *kaṇīkā*, situated in front of the deity.

In the mantras for worship, beginning with those for the head (*śiras*), it should be understood that they end with "namaḥ. However, in the fire sacrifice (*homa*), the mantras for the heart (*hṛdaya*) and the other limbs should end with "svāhā."
In the first and second [sections], there is no employment of that [term] precisely because they are already endowed with that genus (*tajjāti*).
Furthermore, this matter is established by the context (*adhikaraṇasiddha*).

For instance, in the section beginning, "In a mantra, there may be the status of being a supplement to its own sentence because of the instruction of a quality," it is stated regarding the *svāhākāra* or *vaṣaṭkāra*: "to the gods..."

Since the rule "one offers the oblation" is enjoined in a general sense by means of the suffix *svāhākāra*, there is no subsequent sublation (*bādha*) of that [rule] in mantras such as "To the Earth, svāhā! or "To the Atmosphere, svāhā! etc.; nor is there sublation in other mantras, because—as in the case of the seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses—there is no restrictive application (*upasaṃhāra*). Thus it is established. 111.

The principal female forms, bearing the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, should be worshipped next; they are the retinues mentioned in the ritual manuals (kalpa), to be worshipped in their proper sequence. || 112 ||
The teacher Padmapāda maintains that there are two positions: that women are either subordinate bodies or [the deities] themselves.
And it has been said: "The presiding deities of the limbs, who bear the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, are to be worshipped in the form of women."
He states the position of those things called "obstructions" with the word "afterwards" (*paścāt*). This means immediately after the "enclosure of the limbs" (*aṅgāvṛti*);
this too is generally the case.
Because those [obstructions] existed even prior to that. || 112 ||

First, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas), together with their primary retinues and accompanied by their weapons, classes, and presiding deities, in the directions starting from the east in due order. || 113 ||
Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Pavana, Vidhu, Īśāna, the Lord of Serpents, and below and above, the Grandfather (Brahmā). || 114 ||
Yellow, red, white, smoky-grey, white, and smoky-grey—both;
fair-complexioned and ruddy: these are described in order according to their colors. || 115 ||

"End" (anta) refers to the exterior, because it was previously stated that the enclosure (āvaraṇa) belongs to the reality-level (tattva) of the square; and this interpretation is so because it is seen accordingly in the Vaihāyasī-mantrakośa and the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā.
And because of the established tradition (*satsampradāya*),

one should worship Indra, Agni, and the other world-protectors (*lokapāla*) at the end, in sequence starting from the east and so forth in the various directions; such is the connection [of the text].

In this regard, since the general application such as "Obeisance to Indra" (*indrāya namaḥ*) would otherwise be obtained, he states the specific rule with the words beginning with "at the root" (*mūla*).
The word "at the end" (*ante*) is also connected here. Therefore, the meaning is that this word must indeed be placed at the very end of all [the names].
And this will become clear in the written ritual manual (*prayoga*).
The meaning of the phrase "accompanied by their primary retinues" (*mūlapāriṣadānvitān*) is as follows:

when Indra and the others are worshipped in the enclosure of the Śaktis, then it should be understood that the epithet "together with their respective retinues of Śaktis" applies as a qualifier to each of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and the [world-guardians] such as Vajra.

Thus, in the worship of Śiva, [one offers] to each [deity] with the formula "to the attendant of Śiva" (śivapāriṣadāya). Thus, in the worship of Gaṇeśa, [one offers] to each [deity] with the formula "to the attendant of Gaṇeśa" (gaṇeśapāriṣadāya). Thus, in the worship of Sūrya, [one offers] to each [deity] with the formula "to the attendant of Sūrya" (sūryapāriṣadāya).
Thus, in the worship of Viṣṇu, for each [offering], one should say "to the attendants of Viṣṇu" (viṣṇupāriṣadāya).
The transposition of the word order has been made for the sake of concealment.
In the phrase "heti," the word "end" (anta) is also to be connected.
The meaning is that [the sequence] ends with "indrāya" and so forth.
In this ritual application as well, the lords of the classes (*jātyadhipas*) are pronounced first, followed by the *hetis*.
However, in the root text (*mūla*), the word *heti* is placed first because it consists of fewer syllables.
The *hetayas* are weapons.
The *jātayas* are the worlds of gods, radiant beings (*suratejas*), *pretas*, *rakṣasas*, water-beings, living creatures, constellations, spirits (*bhūta*), and *nāgas*.
It should also be understood that they are accompanied by their vehicles and their retinues.
The vehicles, however, are Airāvata, goat, buffalo, man, makara, deer, horse, bull, chariot, and swan.
As it has been stated by the Teachers:
"The deities should be worshipped in sequence according to their caste, presiding deity, weapon, vehicle, and retinue."
Thus [it is said]. And he himself will state in the Nityā-mantra:
"At the end, one should worship the world-protectors together with their vehicles and weapons."
Thus it is said;
they should be understood as being accompanied by their powers (*śakti*).
This has been stated in the *Vaihāyasī-mantrakośa*:

"The practitioner of mantra should worship the Lords of the World (Lokeśvaras) within the terrestrial mandala— equipped with their weapons, powers, vehicles, and retinues— with sandalwood, flowers, and incense for the sake of his own desired goal.
It should also be understood that they are preceded by their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*).
The seed-syllables (bījas), however, are: Laṃ, Raṃ, Maṃ, Kṣaṃ, Baṃ, Yaṃ, Śaṃ, Haṃ, Naṃ, Kaṃ.
As it is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
"The third [vowel] in forward order, and the second [vowel] in reverse order."
The fourth is in forward order, and the eighth is in reverse order.
The third [syllable] is obtained in forward order from the reverse;
the fourth is the seventh letter, established in reverse order from the [first] vowel.
The fourth [syllable] is in direct order, and the third is in reverse order;
all of these are indeed differentiated by the vowel preceding the penultimate letter and by their own names.
"The seed-syllable, beginning with Vāsava and ending with Brahmā, is arranged in ascending order.
Regarding this, some say that these [syllables] are also long.
Others say that for Ananta and Brahmā, there is the seed-syllable of the *māyāpāśa*.
As it has been said:
"They are to be worshipped with the [syllables] of Earth, Fire, Wind, and so forth, ending with Varuṇa, Anila, and Seseśvara, joined with Ananta and Bindu, by means of the noose of Māyā."
In that regard, "Rakṣas" refers to Nirṛti; "Pavana" to Vāyu; "Vidhu" to Soma; "Pannagādhīśa" to Ananta; and "Pitāmaha" to Brahmā.
These are to be placed in the directions starting from the East in successive order. Here, the well-known directions beginning with the East are to be understood.
As it has been said:
"One of pure intellect should worship [the deities] in their respective directions, accompanied by their own caste-lords, weapons, vehicles, and retinues."
And in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "And [he should worship] Indra and the others in their respective directions.
The author of the work also states: "One should worship Indra and the other guardians of the world (lokapālas) in their own respective directions."
Thus it is said.
Therein, eight [deities] are to be worshipped in the eight directions; Ananta is to be worshipped between Nirṛti and Varuṇa.
One should place Brahmā between Indra and Īśāna.
As it is stated in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
"Viṣṇu in the southwest (Nairṛta) and Vidhi (Brahmā) in the northeast (Aiśvara)."
Outside the lotus are also the weapons, beginning with the vajra and ending with the lotus.
"One should worship the Lords of the World (lokeśas) in their well-known directions in sequence.
Here, the mention of "Nairṛta" and "Īśvara" should be understood as indicating their proximity [to the respective directions].
In this context, the sequence wherein one worships Brahmā first and then worships Ananta is to be understood as belonging to the Purāṇic tradition, not the Tantric,
because it contradicts many Tantras such as the Mahākapila-pañcarātra, the Hayaśīrṣa-pañcarātra, and the Prapañcasāra.
And likewise the Teachers [state]:
"The fifth [wheel] is considered to consist of Indra and the others, ending with Ananta-Brahmā;
the sixth consists of Vajra and the others, ending with Cakra-Padma."
The ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows: *oṃ laṃ indrāya surādhipataye sāyudhāya savāhanāya saparivārāya saśaktikāya viṣṇupāriṣadāya namaḥ*.
In the same way: *oṃ raṃ agnaye tejo'dhipataye*, and so forth.
In the worship of these, the mudrās of the World-Protectors (lokapāla) should be displayed. As it is said:
"With the bases of the hands well-joined, all the fingers are extended."
"This is the mudrā of the Lords of the World; one should display it during their worship. (113–115)
One should know their weapons in sequence as the vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, the goad, the mace, the trident, the discus, and the lotus. || 116 ||

Yellow, white, sky-colored (blue), lightning-like, red, white, and black; and with the luster of a Karavinda flower or pale-red—these are described as the colors of the thunderbolt and the other [regents]. || 117 ||
Having thus worshipped according to the rules up to the offering of the food oblation (naivedya), the Guru then prepares a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the south and establishes the fire there.
Having performed the purificatory rites according to the rules, the learned man should perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice;
there, he should worship the deity whose form has been described with perfumes and other offerings.
"Vajra" means a sword or scimitar;
"ākāśa" is blue in color.
Karavinda is a tree that generally has blue flowers like those of the atasī plant; the meaning is that [the color] is like the hue of its flowers.
This was stated by the Teachers: "They are the reddish-brown color of the karavinda."
Thus.

In that regard, the ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows: *Oṃ, homage to Viṣṇu’s attendant, who possesses a vajra, whose crown is marked with a vajra, who is accompanied by his weapons, his vehicle, his retinue, and his power*—and so forth, as should be inferred.
As it has been said by the Teachers:
"The images are externally endowed with their own well-defined crowns, and their lotus-hands are raised, holding their respective weapons and the gesture of granting fearlessness."
Thus,
the procedure beginning with "having fashioned the image with the root mantra" and ending with "having offered [the oblation]" is the same for the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) as well.

By the phrase "the wise one, having consecrated according to rule," the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*)— beginning with *vīkṣaṇa* (inspection)— and the purificatory rites of the clarified butter (*ghṛtasaṃskāra*) are indicated through the sequence of offering oblations of clarified butter into the fire.
It is thus stated that the purificatory rites (saṃskāras), beginning with conception (garbhādhāna), must be performed. || 116–119 ||
Having offered oblations with the *tāra* and the *vyāhṛti*s, the knower of mantras, using the root mantra, should offer milk-rice mixed with honey twenty-five times. || 120 ||
Having offered oblations again with the *vyāhṛti* mantras, one should worship [the deity] once more with perfumes and other offerings.
Having united that [deity] with the image situated on the pedestal, one should dismiss the fire.
With the remaining oblation, one should scatter a bali offering all around for the attendants of the deity, accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata). || 122 ||
Regarding the phrase "with the Tāra and the Vyāhṛtis":
here, the first four [oblations] are with the Tāra and the Vyāhṛtis, and one is with the whole [formula].
The connection is that subsequently one should offer again with the Vyāhṛtis.
It should be understood as being "as before.
Furthermore, immediately thereafter, one should worship that deity with perfumes and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings are intended.
"Having joined her to the image situated on the pedestal"—this is to be supplied [to the preceding]. (120–122)
Then, having removed the offering and purified the water once more,
and having worshipped with the five services (pañcopacāra), one should display the parasol and the fly-whisk.
One should offer betel leaf mixed with a piece of camphor, having recited the root mantra one thousand times with undistracted mind;
that which has been consecrated by the mantra should be offered to the deity for the sake of all prosperity. || 124 ||
By the word "then" (tataḥ), this is what is meant:
one should give water for the purpose of drinking at the end of the root mantra.
The verse is as follows: "O Lord of all the lords of gods, supreme bringer of satisfaction to all, filled with unbroken bliss, accept this excellent water.

Then, having offered the water remaining from the meal and having withdrawn the divine luster (*tejas*) back into the mouth of the deity, one should give a portion of the food offering (*naivedya*) to Viśvakseṇa and the others.
As it has been said:
"From the vessel of the primary Īśāna, one should take a portion of the *naivedya* offering for the Supreme Parameṣṭhin, who is the embodiment of all deities."
Salutations to you, Viṣvaksena, who are joined with the army of Śrī Rāma.
"One should offer [the remnants] to Gaṇeśa as Vakratuṇḍa, to Sūrya as Caṇḍāṃśu,
to Śakti as Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī, and to Śiva as Caṇḍeśvara. Thus,
even in the phrase "to the attendants (pārṣada) of the deity," by the word *pāriṣada*, these very ones are intended to be included.
"for the sake of all prosperity, for the deity"—these two dative cases are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
Regarding "one should offer":

here, in the daily worship (*nityapūjā*), having offered betel, an umbrella, a mirror, and chowries—[one offers] the intellect together with its latent impressions as the mirror, and the auspicious objects.
The various fluctuations of your mind have been fashioned into the form of a dance.
O Lord, sounds in the form of songs and musical instruments of various kinds,
as well as nine umbrellas fashioned like lotuses, have been prepared by me.
The *suṣumṇā* nerve is in the form of the banner, while the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and others are in the form of chowries;
the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) is the elephant, and speed is fashioned as the chariot.
The senses are in the form of horses; sound and the other objects are the path of the chariot;
the mind is in the form of the reins; the intellect is in the form of the charioteer;
and everything else is likewise fashioned as your various implements.
Having recited these verses and having chanted the root mantra according to one’s ability, [one should say]: "O Protector of the most secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us!
O God, may success be mine through your grace, for you abide within me."
With this [verse], one should offer that recitation (*japa*) to the deity.

As it is stated in the Śaiva Āgama: "Having recited the verse, the practitioner of mantra should, with his right hand and water for the *arghya* offering consecrated by the root-mantra, present it to Śambhu with his right hand."
Then, having offered the *arghya* with its face turned away, one should worship the conch.
As it is stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"A wise person should indeed worship the conch like a deity with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings."

Thus it is stated elsewhere as well: "O best of Brahmins, by the command of Vāsudeva, all the sacred fords (tīrtha) that exist in the three worlds abide within the conch; therefore, one should always worship the conch."
Then one should perform a circumambulation.
Regarding that, there is a specific rule in another Tantra:
"One [circumambulation] for Caṇḍī, seven for the Sun, and three one should offer for Vināyaka."
"One should offer four [circumambulations] to Keśava and half a circumambulation to Śiva.
Thereafter, having offered praise and bowed down, one should perform the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*).
Regarding this, there is a specific rule in another tantra:
"The rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) do not exist in the obligatory daily oblation (*nityahoma*).

Thus, [one should offer] with water from the *culuka* [cupped hands], [reciting]: "From this point forward, by virtue of my authority over life, intellect, body, and dharma, in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, through mind and speech..."
"Whatever has been thought with the two hands, the feet, the belly, and the genitals; whatever has been spoken, and whatever has been done—may all that be an offering unto Brahman, Svāhā!

I offer myself and everything belonging to me to Hari, Oṃ Tat Sat. Having thus offered oneself with this *brahmārpaṇa* mantra, the specific procedure is that one should dissolve the Deity within the lotus of one's own heart by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*.
The characteristics of the *saṃhāramudrā* have already been stated.
