Regarding the acceptance of *prasāda*, a devotee of a particular deity must indeed accept the *prasāda* of that specific deity.
However, in the worship of the five deities (*pañcadevatā*), it is only Viṣṇu who [is worshipped] through contact with the *śālagrāma* stone, while for the others, it is otherwise.
And likewise, in the *Bahvṛca-pariśiṣṭa*: "The food offered to Viṣṇu is considered pure by the gods, Siddhas, and Ṛṣis;
having eaten the food offered to another deity, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."
"The offerings made to Śiva—leaves, flowers, fruits, and water—are ungraspable [as ordinary objects];
through contact with a Śālagrāma stone, everything attains purity. Thus it is said.
There is another distinction in another Tantra: "Now, due to distraction or foolishness, there may be an interruption in the recitation, fire-oblation, or worship."
When he rises, he should then again perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). Thus [ends verses 123–124].
Then, [he should offer] in the northeast of Śambhu, in the space strewn by the Guru, that which was previously collected. || 125 ||

Having placed a water-pot (karkarī) filled with water and adorned with golden cloth and other ornaments, [one should visualize] within it [the goddess] seated upon a lion and bearing a sword and a shield.
One should worship the deity of the weapon in the western face, who has a terrible form;
having worshipped her with the moving seat, the Guru should then take hold of her. || 127 ||
Saying "Protect! to the world-protectors with water released from the mouth of the vessel, he announced the command of the deity while turning around inside in a clockwise direction. || 128 ||
Having recited the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should install [the deity] as before;
having worshipped the weapon again there with perfumes and other offerings upon a firm seat. || 129 ||
"Śambhodīśī" means in the northeast.
"Karkarī" refers to a water-vessel with a spout and a handle.
The syntactical connection is that one should worship the weapon-deity (astradevatā) of such a nature within that *karkarī*.
"With a moving seat" means with a seat that has been raised high.
"That"—

the preceptor, taking up that water-jar (*karkarī*), while proclaiming the divine command, "Protect the world-guardians with the water released from its mouth," [stood] within the inner altar of the inner pavilion.
The connection is that, having turned around in a complete circumambulation from left to right, one should settle her as before.
In that regard, "in the water-pot" (*karkarī*);
the meaning is: seated upon a firm seat, that is, a motionless seat. (125–129)
Then, once the fire has been consecrated, one should cook the *caru* with cow’s milk in a new vessel made of copper or another material, which has been washed with the *astra-mantra*. || 130 ||
Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then):
"in the consecrated fire" means in the fire consecrated by the preceptor in his own sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

This is a reference back to the ritual for generating the fire which the preceptor has already performed at this very time, as will be described in the subsequent chapter; thus it says, "in the consecrated fire."
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Having sprinkled the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) and having placed the fire therein,
one should then duly worship the deity, beginning with the preparatory rite of *anvādhāna*."
"Having performed the pouring of rice, one should cook the *caru* in that milk. Thus it is said.

Also, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "There, having gathered the necessary materials and worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rule, [one should perform] the pouring of rice and so forth with the root-mantras, the mantras of the forms, the limb-mantras, and the knowledge-mantras (*vidyās*)."

Having prepared the *caru*, one should cook it in milk and then divide it into three parts. Having offered one part and performed the oblation with another, the Guru, together with his disciples, should consume the remaining portion. Thus [it is said]. 130.
Having cast fifteen handfuls of rice grains produced from the *śāli* variety, which have been consecrated with the root mantra, one should recite the weapon-mantra (*astramanu*). || 131 ||

Having washed the mouth of the vessel and covered it with the armor-mantra (kavacāṇu), the preeminent teacher, facing east, should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the root-mantra (mūlamantra). || 132 ||
"Rice grains" (taṇḍulān): the ellipsis is "measured by fifteen handfuls" (prasṛtīnām).
The connection is: "having washed the rice grains and thrown them in while reciting the Astra mantra."
The definition of a *prasṛti* will be explained further on. || 131-132 ||
When it has been thoroughly heated, one should offer the hot sprinkling of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle;
then, with the root mantra, one should subsequently lower that vessel [from the fire] while reciting the *kavaca* mantra. || 133 ||

On the mandala strewn with kusha grass over which mantras have been recited, the Guru, according to the prescribed rite, should divide it into three parts and assign one portion to the deity. || 134 ||

"With the *sruva* ladle": the connection is that once the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) has been properly steamed, one should perform the sprinkling of hot clarified butter (*ājya*) over it using the *sruva* ladle while reciting the root mantra.
By the phrase "the guru according to rule," it is stated that an equal division [of the materials] should be made with *kuśa* grass using this root mantra. || 133-134 ||
The preceptor himself should offer another oblation into the fire, and then, having performed the prescribed sipping of water (ācamana), he should eat together with the disciple. || 135 ||
Regarding the word "anyeti":

by the phrase "in the fire," it is meant that the preceptor should offer oblations into the fire of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍāgni). This refers back to what was stated in the subsequent chapter: "with *caru* mixed with clarified butter"; thus, the oblation performed twenty-five times with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) as mentioned there should be understood to apply here as well.
"One should eat.
Regarding that, there is a specific detail in the *Somaśambhu*:
"The third part of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), measured as three morsels (*grāsa*)."
Or it may be the size of eight mouthfuls, free from the desire for sight or touch.

"Having placed [the food] in a cup made of *pālāśa* leaves for the sake of liberation, or in one made of *pippala* leaves for the sake of enjoyment, the practitioner should feed [the deity] with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and cause them to sip pure water. Thus [it is said]. (135)

Having brought the disciple who has sipped water and performed the ritual purification of the limbs (sakalīkaraṇa), the teacher [should offer] a staff the size of a palm tree, produced from a milk-tree or similar source, over which the heart-mantra has been recited. 136.
Then he should give a tooth-stick to the disciple who is self-restrained;
having cleansed his teeth and then washed that [stick] himself, he should discard it. || 137 ||
"Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa" means having placed the six limbs of the mantra upon his own limbs.
Regarding "tāla": *tāla* is the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the middle finger of an outstretched hand.
As it has been said:
"The wise declare that the distance between the tips of the thumb and the middle finger when the hand is extended is one *tāla*."
By the phrase "the preceptor should give," the mantra for giving is stated.
As it says in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"One should give that [offering] with this [mantra]: Māyā (Hrīṃ), followed by Daṇḍin, and then the pair of Ṭha-s (Ṭhaṭhaḥ)."
Thus [it is said].
By the words "one should dismiss," it is stated that the examination of that [object] must be performed immediately after the dismissal.
Having washed it, one should place it on the ground with the left hand on the left side.
Thus it is said. There is a specific detail in the *Prayogasāra*, as follows in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
Having consecrated a tooth-stick produced from a milky tree or similar source by reciting the heart-mantra over it,
one should clean the teeth with it, then break it off, rinse it, and cast it upon the ground.
In the directions starting from the east, including the zenith and nadir, its falling on the head occurs in sequence, resulting respectively in:
growth, shame, death, loss of wealth, decay, peace, disease, and wealth.
"The increase of happiness is supreme suffering; these are the fruits of doubt.
Also elsewhere: "In the case of intellect, fortune, heat, separation, untimely death, auspiciousness, misfortune, peace, sovereignty, and so forth..."
"When the first fall of the tooth-washing twig bears an inauspicious fruit, one should offer a root-oblation with sesame seeds.
Also elsewhere: "Now, in this case, a tooth-stick twelve finger-breadths in length should be given to the mango tree; its tip should be rubbed against his teeth."
One should cast the upper face there into that mandala and raise the pedestal;
a fall toward the west, north, Rudra (north-east), or Indra (east) is auspicious, while otherwise it is inauspicious.

"One should offer a hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra for the destruction of ill omens. Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā: "If that discarded tooth-stick is seen by the Guru, its tip pointing toward the east, north, west, or the northeast is auspicious; otherwise, it is inauspicious."
"In that face of an inauspicious quarter, the Guru, for the sake of pacifying its defect, should perform one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five oblations with the root mantra. (136-137)

Having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth for him according to the rules and having protected him by tying the topknot, the preceptor should lie down upon that same altar on a bed of darbha grass together with her; this is declared to be the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) for that night. || 138 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Śāradātilaka* composed by the venerable Lakṣmaṇa Deśikendra. 4.

The connection is as follows: "having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to rule and having protected [the head] by tying the topknot (śikhābandha) according to rule. Regarding that, the procedure for the ritual sipping of water has already been stated by me previously;
however, concerning the tying of the topknot, it is by the phrase "according to rule" that this is expressed.
One should bind the topknot with the root mantra together with the crest-mantra (*śikhāmantra*) of the same class, or with the Aghora mantra and so forth.
Regarding the word "he should lie down":
the connection is that the Guru should lie down for that night upon a bed of *darbha* grass on that altar together with this disciple.
The word "vedyām" (on the altar) indicates proximity as the sense of the locative case.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"Then, that disciple, having sipped water and being protected by the tying of the topknot..."
"Having done so on the altar together with him, the Guru should sleep upon a bed of *darbha* grass.
By the word "Guru," it is stated that he should cause the disciple to sleep on the right side of the deity with his head toward the east.
Relying on the *māṇava* dream, he should cause [the disciple] to sleep with his head to the east.
Thus it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*. However, in the *Somaśambhu*, it says: "The householders, protected by the Astra-mantra, should be placed on beds of Darbha grass with their heads to the east;
the ascetics (yatins) should be placed on beds of pure ashes with their heads to the south."

In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, however, it is said: "On the southern side of the deity, the preceptor, being pure, should cause that disciple to undergo the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) upon a clean bed spread with an unwashed cloth and covered with Darbha grass."
Having consecrated it with mantras and meditating on Śiva, he should sleep at night with his head toward the east;
then the Guru, using the tip of a thread tied to his own topknot, [should bind] his [the disciple's] topknot.
Having wrapped it with a new cloth and covered it with armor,

and having drawn three lines all around with ashes mixed with sesame and mustard seeds consecrated with the Astra-mantra, one should offer an oblation to the guardians of the directions outside of that. Thus it is said.

Regarding the *svapnamāṇava* mantra among the Vaiṣṇava mantras, as revealed in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the heart [of all], the sovereign lord of all worlds, the universe itself, whose form is the universe, and the master of dreams.

"This is the Svapna-māṇava mantra as taught by Nārada and others. Furthermore, in the Śaiva and Śākta traditions, the Piṅgalāmata states: "The Tāra (Om), followed by 'hili' twice, then 'to the Trident-bearer,' and ending with the Dviṭha (Svāhā)—this is the Svapna-māṇava mantra proclaimed by Śambhu."
The specific detail mentioned in another tantra is as follows: "Homage to the unborn, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul;
homage to the Left-handed one, whose form is the universe (Viṣṇu), the Lord of Dreams."
"O Maheśvara, tell me the truth in my dreams regarding all matters without exception; by your grace, I shall accomplish the success of my undertakings."
Having thus prayed to the Lord at the time of sleep with this mantra, one should go to sleep;
and in the morning, the examination of the dream must be performed.
As it is said in the Piṅgalāmata:
In the morning, the Guru should ask the disciple about whatever auspicious or inauspicious things were seen in the dream.
If it was auspicious, he should declare it to be auspicious for him; if inauspicious, he should perform one hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra.
Thus has the procedure for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the disciple been described in due order.
Elsewhere it is also said: "If [the dream] is cruel, it is the lowest; if it is not seen, it is middling; but if it is clearly seen, it is the highest of the high.

And in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* as well: "Having performed the worship of the Guru's feet, fasting and with senses subdued, one should lie upon a bed of *darbha* grass at night and, having seen a dream, report it."
A maiden, an umbrella, a chariot, a lamp, a palace, a lotus, a river, an elephant,
a bull, a garland, the ocean, a serpent, and a tree.
Having seen a mountain, a sacrificial horse, raw meat, liquor, spirits, and all such things as these, one shall attain success.
A Caṇḍāla, a young camel, a craftsman, a pit, an empty place, an inauspicious thing,
a man smeared with oil, a naked man, a withered tree, and a eunuch.
"Having seen a palace on fire, a person may incur disease;
and having seen an evil dream, one attains success through the performance of a *homa*.

In this context, the term "one who has fasted" (*upavāsī*) refers to a prohibition against eating that follows from natural inclination (*rāgataḥ*), but it does not refer to a prohibition against eating the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) prescribed by the scriptural injunction.

Also, in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "Then, having risen in the morning and reflected upon the dream he has seen—if it is auspicious, one should know it as auspicious; if inauspicious, one should perform a hundred oblations," and so forth. In the *Nārāyaṇīya*, however: "In the morning, the disciple should report the dreams he has observed to the guru."
"Through auspicious [deeds], there is supreme accomplishment and devotion.
Thus is the consecration (adhivāsa) described; that is, on the day prior to receiving the mantra.
In the Piṅgalāmata, however, immediate consecration (sadyo'dhivāsa) is also mentioned: "Or else, one should perform the immediate consecration according to the prescribed rule."
Also in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "A wise practitioner should not perform the rite of initiation over two days;
if it is to be done on a single day, he should perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*) immediately."

The meaning of the word *adhivāsa* is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "When the root *vas* (to dwell) is preceded by the prefix *adhi*, and the suffix *ghañ* is applied to form the abstract noun (*bhāve*),
this usage— namely *adhivāsa*— is established."

"Dwelling together with the guru and others at night, according to the prescribed rules—this is indeed considered the meaning of 'hi' (for/indeed), owing to the polysemous nature of particles. Thus [ends verse 138].
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Thereafter, I shall describe the generation of the fire in accordance with all the tantras,
within the preceptor’s sacrificial pit that has been duly consecrated according to the path of the scriptures.

On the very day of the consecration (adhivāsa), immediately after the worship of the weapon-deities (astradevatā), he states the rites to be performed by the preceptor (ācārya), such as the purification of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍasaṃskāra) and so forth, beginning with the word "tataḥ" (then).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "I shall describe the generation of the fire according to all tantras, duly performed in the consecrated preceptor’s fire-pit (ācāryakuṇḍa) by way of the path of the scriptures. || 1 ||
There should be eighteen consecrations for the sacrificial pits as enjoined in the Tantra:
inspection with the root mantra and sprinkling with the Śara mantra are prescribed. || 2 ||
He states that very procedure [with the words] "eighteen," etc.
By "with the arrow" (śareṇa) is meant with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra).
Here, in all instances, the mantras beginning with the weapon-mantra are to be understood as belonging to the mantra to be bestowed.
Regarding the statement that "the inspection is performed with the root mantra," some say it refers specifically to the *jāti-mantra*;
this is the traditional practice.
"Sprinkling" (*prokṣaṇa*) is done with the tips of the hands turned upward.
For it is stated in the Sūtra: "One should sprinkle with the palm turned upwards. || 2 ||

Striking with that same [mantra] is prescribed, as is sprinkling with darbha grass using the armor-mantra (varma). Dug with the weapon-mantra (astra), it is filled with the heart-mantra (hṛd). || 3 ||
"Sprinkling" (abhyukṣaṇa) means pouring water everywhere while maintaining a closed fist.
"Excavation" (uddhāra) is the filling of the earth dug out with other earth; sprinkling is indeed the same as pouring.
This is because the suffix follows the root meaning of the verb *abhi-vas*, as it is said that "sometimes [the suffix] follows that [root]. || 3 ||
Leveling is considered to be performed with the weapon-mantra (astra), and sprinkling with the armor-mantra (varma);
pounding with the missile-mantra (heti), and sweeping with the armor-mantra (varma). || 4 ||
Anointing, the fashioning of the artistic forms, and immediately after that, the drawing of the three lines; thereafter, worship with the heart-mantra is prescribed. || 5 ||
"With the *hetimantra*" means with the *astra-mantra*.
The phrase "with the *varma-mantra*" is connected to the four [mantras] that follow.
As it was stated by Somaśambhu:

"Performing the sweeping, the smearing [of the ground], the fashioning of the forms of the digits (kalās), the donning of the triple-thread (trisūtrī), and the worship with the Armour-mantra and the Heart-mantra. Thus it is said. "Fashioning of the forms of the digits" refers to the fashioning of the forms of the digits of the Moon, Sun, and Fire.
"Making it three-stranded" means wrapping it with three threads. || 4-5 ||

One should perform the vajrīkaraṇa with the Astra-mantra, [the sprinkling] with auspicious kuśa grass using the Hṛdaya-mantra, the drawing of a boundary at the crossroads with the Kavaca-mantra, and the clearing of the ground with the Astra-mantra. || 6 ||
In the sacrificial rite, one should consecrate the fire-pits with these aforementioned purificatory rites;
or otherwise, one should consecrate them by means of the four [rites] beginning with inspection (vīkṣaṇa).
"Vajrīkaraṇa" means contemplating [the site] as firm as a vajra.
"Catuṣpatha" means making four paths in the four directions from the center using kusha grass.
"Tanutreṇa" means with the armor mantra (*kavaca-mantra*).

Some say that *akṣapāṭana* means the eradication of the senses (*indriya-uccāṭana*). Others, however, hold that *kṣapāṭanāḥ* refers to *rākṣasa*s; thus, it means "that in which *kṣapāṭanā*s do not exist.
The meaning is that one should effect the warding off of *rākṣasa*s by means of the syllable *huṃ*.
But other traditionalists [explain] as follows: *aṭa-paṭa* means "going"; "going" is knowledge. It is the piercing (*pāṭana*) and pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*.
He says "or else" (*athavā*) with reference to those who are incapable. (6–7)
One should draw three lines each, directed toward the east and the north, with the heart-mantra.
Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Indra are said to be the presiding deities of those lines whose tips point toward the east.
Of the lines with their tips pointing northward, [the spaces] are for Brahmā, Vaivasvata, and Indu;
or else, one should draw a triangle there surrounded by a hexagon. || 9 ||
"Three":
one should draw three lines each.
By the word "cows," this is what is meant.
The blades with their tips pointing eastward are arranged from south to north, and those with their tips pointing northward are arranged from west to east;
furthermore, according to tradition, all of them are one span (prādeśa) in length.
This has been stated in the Sautrāmaṇitantra:
"One should draw [the lines] facing east, arranged from north to south, beginning from the south; one should draw them facing north, arranged from front to back, beginning from the west.
Having drawn three lines each in this manner, one should sprinkle [them] with the Vāgbhava [syllable]. Thus it is said.
Alternatively, one should draw a triangle surrounded by a hexagon.
Regarding this, some have read the text as "a circle with a hexagon and a triangle" (*ṣaṭkoṇavṛttatrikoṇam*);
that is merely the manifestation of their ignorance.
And likewise, the teachers [state]: "Alternatively, [it is] upon a triangle surrounded by a hexagon, according to the instruction of the gurus."
And likewise in the *Yāmala*: "O Goddess, one should draw a triangle here surrounded by a hexagon. Also elsewhere: "Having drawn the lines from the center..."
A hexagon and a triangle.
Thus [ends verses 8–9].
Having sprinkled all [the items] with the *tāra* (om), one should then worship the Yoga-pīṭha, [visualizing] Vāgīśvarī, who has bathed after her menses and resembles a blue lotus. || 10 ||
One should worship [the fire] joined with Vāgīśvara using ritual offerings;
it should be produced from a sun-crystal or the like, or else obtained from the house of a learned Brahmin (śrotriya). || 11 ||
Having brought the fire in a vessel, one should set aside the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters;
then the preceptor should consecrate it according to the rule by means of inspection and other rites. || 12 ||
Regarding the word "all":

having sprinkled these with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), and having worshipped the Yoga-pīṭha—beginning from Maṇḍūka up to the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*) as the Yoga-pīṭha of Vāgīśī—and having worshipped the nine Pīṭha-śaktis mentioned previously, one should worship the Yoga-pīṭha with the mantra: *hrīṃ vāgīśvarayor yoga-pīṭhāya namaḥ*.
In this context, it should be understood that by the word "tāra," the five praṇavas are to be included within their respective mantras.
Regarding the phrase "one should worship": one should worship Vāgīśī on the seat with the seed-syllable of Śakti, and Vāgīśa with the sādhya-mantra.

This has been stated in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*: "One should [worship] Vāgīśī with the seed-syllable of Śakti, and Vāgīśa with the mantra of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*). It is also stated elsewhere: "That deity with the mantra of the one to be accomplished," and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "from the sun-gem and so forth," fire produced from the fire-drill (*araṇi*) is included.
As it has been said:
"Fire produced from the sun-gem, or from the fire-drill, or born in the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*)."
Thus:
"born in the house of a *śrotriya*.
Being a *śrotriya* consists in the study of the Vedas and the performance of their prescribed rites.
Therefore, the intended meaning refers to the state of possessing the sacred fires (*sāgnitva*).
As it is stated in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*:
"Having forcibly [taken] the fire even from the house of one who has maintained the sacred fires, according to the prescribed rule..."
"And having brought it, one should place it therein. "With a vessel" means with a vessel made of bell-metal or similar material.
"It should be covered by another vessel," say the teachers.

However, elsewhere it is stated: "Whether produced in the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), or born from a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*), or even produced from a fire-drill (*araṇī*), [the fire] should be placed in a vessel made of gold or other precious materials."

Atri also says: "One should perform the bringing of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) when an auspicious vessel such as a copper bowl is covered by another vessel, or even in a similar earthenware dish (*śarāva*). Also elsewhere: "Having taken [the fire] from the sacred site (*kṣetra*), one should place it in a vessel made of excellent gold or even in a copper vessel."
"Or having covered it in an earthen vessel, one of pure and vast intellect.
As for that which is stated in the *Smṛtisāra*: "In a shallow dish, or in a broken vessel, or in a potsherd, or even on a firebrand..."
One should not perform the bringing forward of the fire, for it brings about the fear of loss of health.
The meaning of this statement is that when a primary vessel is available, a shallow earthen dish (śarāva) should not be accepted.
Regarding the instruction "one should discard the portion for the flesh-eaters," it should be understood that this is done toward the southwest (nairṛtya) using the weapon-mantra (astramantra).

As it has been said: "O Dear One, having taken up the fire with the Astra-mantra and covered it with the Kavaca-mantra, one should cast away the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda) toward the southwest using the Astra-mantra.
In another tradition, the casting away of the flesh-eater's portion is performed with the seed-syllable of Fire (vahni-bīja).

As it has been said: "The practitioner, by means of the fire-seed syllable (*vahnibīja*), should discard the portion consisting of raw flesh, and thereafter purify it with the weapon-mantra (*astraka*).
However, there is a specific distinction in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"Having brought [the fire] with the *astra-mantra*, one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyād*) in the southwest;
the wise one should establish the portion belonging to the gods in front with the root-mantra.
By the phrase "according to rule," it is stated that sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and moistening (*abhyukṣaṇa*) should likewise be performed so that the fire, once brought, remains stable.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "by gazing and so forth," the three purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are intended. || 10-12 ||

Meditating on the unification of the earth element with the fire of the belly and the bindu, one should then unite the consciousness with the seed-syllable of fire within the sacrificial fire. || 13 ||
Regarding the term "audaryā":
the *bindu* is well known as the essential nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*),
because it possesses the nature of both fire (*agni*) and the moon (*soma*).
The fire born from that is the *bindava* fire;
others say *bindu* refers to the space between the eyebrows. Of the terrestrial, that is, the earthly [fire].
Of Agni, the possessor of wealth. || 13 ||

The practitioner, having consecrated it with the *tāra* mantra, rendered it nectar-like by means of the *dhenumudrā*, protected it subsequently with the *astra* mantra, and veiled it with the *tanutra* mantra. || 14 ||
Then the preceptor, having rotated the fire three times around the vessel in a clockwise direction, preceded this by the loud recitation of the *tāra-mantra*. || 15 ||
With his knees touching the ground, he should cast the fire facing himself into the womb of the Goddess, perceiving it as the seed-syllable of Śiva. || 16 ||
Regarding "by Tāra": the meaning of the word *tāra* is as before.
The teachers state that "made into nectar" means by means of the seed-syllable of nectar (*amṛta*).
As it has been said: "Then one should perform the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) by means of the seed-syllable of water, together with the bindu of fire.
It is "protected" by means of the binding of the directions (digbandha).
The term "circumambulation" (pradakṣiṇam) is connected with what precedes it.
Regarding "the utterance of the Tāra mantra": this refers to the utterance of the Tāra, which is the Praṇava, as the root mantra.
As it has been said:
"The practitioner should place this [vessel] facing him with its opening toward himself, and afterwards [place] the fire with the root mantra.
Here too, the meaning of the word *tāra* is as before.
"Raṃ, obeisance to the consciousness of fire," thus say the teacher Padmapāda.
Others, however, state that by the word *tāra* [the syllable] *hūṃ* is meant, and by the word *mantra*, "obeisance to the consciousness of fire.
As it has been said:
Having first uttered the mantra "Hūṃ" followed by the word for consciousness (caitanya) in the dative case and joined with "namaḥ," the preceptor should thereafter raise that fire.
Having knelt with both knees on the ground, one should circumambulate three times above the *kuṇḍa* there,
within the sphere of the womb of Vāgīśī.
"Having meditated upon it as the seed-syllable of Śiva, one should quickly cast the fire [into it].
Thus [it is said]. "With the thought that it is the seed-syllable of Śiva"—this [is stated] in the Śaiva [tradition].
For it is stated thus in the Śaiva Tantra;
and he himself will say: "One should conceive of him even by the name 'Śivāgni'."
Also in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Having produced the auspicious fire.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Saṃhitā*: "There, Lakṣmī, being in her courses, [united] with the Lord Nārāyaṇa."
"One should contemplate the fire produced by the village-rite (grāmyadharma) as being there.
For this very reason, the author of the work will also state generally: "The parents of the fire," and later:
"One should offer oblations into the Vaiṣṇava fire."
Thus [it is said].
The analysis of the compound is: "one by whom the surface of the earth has been touched with the two knees.
However, in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā—
Having uttered the seed-syllable of fire (raṃ), one should place the fire upon the seat, either through the path of the yoni or likewise facing oneself. (Verses 14–16)
Thereafter, one should offer water for sipping (ācamana) and other services to the God and the Goddess;
then the preceptor should kindle that fire with this mantra. || 17 ||

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "ritual rinsing and so forth," the inclusion of the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) and the subsequent offerings (*upacāra*) is intended, because of the statement: "One should worship with the offerings.
[The word] "one should kindle" (*jvālayet*) [is used].
By this which is about to be stated.

In that regard, the specific rule is as follows: Whether one is about to offer oblations or has already offered into the fire, one should not blow upon the fire with the hands, a winnowing basket, a dipping-spoon, or similar implements; nor should one do so by means of a fan or other such devices.
"One should blow upon the fire with the mouth alone, for it was born from the mouth;
however, the injunction 'one should not blow upon the fire with the mouth' applies to the worldly [fire]. (17)
Having uttered "cit piṅgalam hanadaha pacaya yugmāni," and then "sarvajña ājñāpaya svāhā," this mantra was previously proclaimed. || 18 ||
I worship Agni, the blazing one, the knower of all beings, the consumer of oblations—pure, golden-hued, kindled, and facing in every direction. || 19 ||
In the mantra "citpiṅgalam," the accusative case is used for the object of the verbal action; however, in the ritual manual (mantra), it is connected as the subject.
The phrase "han" and so forth consists of three pairs.
The meaning is that this mantra which was previously mentioned and indicated by the words "one should cause to blaze with this mantra" is now explicitly stated.
In some places, however, the reading is simply "samudīritaḥ.
Here, one should display the Jvālinī mudrā for the kindling of the fire. Its characteristic definition is as follows:
Having made the two wrists level, with the fingers of both hands extended,
one should join the two middle fingers and place the two thumbs in between them.
This is that supreme mudrā, Jvālinī, for the rite of homa.
Thus [ends the section]. (18–19)
One should attend upon the fire according to the rule with this mantra of Manu;
one should then assign the tongues of the fire-eater within one's own body by means of mantras. || 20 ||
In the penis, anus, head, mouth, nose, and eyes, everywhere:
[the letters] from *sa* to *ya*, joined with *vahnirārghīśa* (the fire-vowels *ṛ* and *ū*) and accompanied by the bindu (*m*). || 21 ||
The phonemes are declared by the instructors of the seven tongues to be the mantras.
Those tongues are said to be threefold, according to the distinction of qualities in ritual actions. || 22 ||
By the phrase "according to rule" (vidhivat), this is what is meant: having risen and joined one's palms in reverence, one should mutter the mantra.
By the passage beginning with "this fire," etc., [it is shown].
"Everywhere" (sarvataḥ) means in all limbs; that is, the seventh location.

"And tongues on all the limbs," according to the statement of the Ācārya. And this is the locus for the ritual placement (nyāsa), because the worship of Bahurūpā is commenced in that manner. And it has been said: "In the linga, the anus, the head, the mouth, the nose, and the eyes, in sequence."
"One should place that multiform goddess, who is intensely red, upon all the limbs.
It should be understood that this sequence of enumeration is for the sake of facilitating the extraction of the seed-syllables (*bīja*).
Regarding the word *vahnī*: the letter *ra* is the "fire" (*vahni*); the letter *i* is the "lord of half" (*ardhīśa*), namely the vowel *ū*; these are joined together.
[The letters] beginning with *sa* and ending with *ya* means those starting with *sa* and ending with *ya*.
In reverse order, these syllables, together with the bindu, become mantras. || 20–21 ||
"Of the tongues" refers to all three types as well.
In that regard, the ritual application is: "Oṃ Hiraṇyāyai namaḥ" on the linga, and so forth. || 22 ||
Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Bahurūpā, and Atiraktā are considered the Sāttvika [energies] in sacrificial rites. || 23 ||
Padmarāgā, Suvarṇā, and the third, Bhadralohitā; following Lohitā are Śvetā, Dhūminī, and Karālikā. || 24 ||
The tongues of the Rājasa fire, impelled in rites for desired objects, are of smoky color, swift as thought, and possess sparks in the form of the universe. || 25 ||
Lohitā, Karālā, and Kālī are said to belong to the Tamas quality;
these seven are employed by practitioners in rites of a cruel nature.
The tongues of Kalyāṇaretas are equal in luster to their respective names.
The immortals (gods), Pitṛs, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Nāgas, Piśācas, and Rākṣasas are declared to be the presiding deities of the seven tongues. || 27 ||
Regarding the fire of auspicious seed (*kalyāṇaretas*),
he states that its presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) is "the immortal" (*amartya*).
Here, the mention of the presiding deities of the tongues is for the purpose of performing the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in their respective locations.
Therefore, [one should recite] "Obeisance to the gods" (*surebhyo namaḥ*) and so forth;
others, however, say "Obeisance to Hiraṇyā, the mistress of the gods" (*surādhipataye hiraṇyāyai namaḥ*) and so forth.

Furthermore, having perceived each respective deity as residing in the center of the tongue, while that specific rite is being performed, one should offer those respective substances into each of them.
This is for the purpose of demonstrating the accomplishment of the fruit.
And so the Teachers [have said]:
"Upon the tongues of the gods and others, for the sake of completing their respective tasks..."
"One should offer oblations; those deities composed of *maya* will grant the desired accomplishment. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, specific materials are mentioned in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*:
"Fuel-sticks, gold, [the substance] called *gaganā*, sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and clarified butter (*ghṛta*)."
For the accomplishment of one's purpose, one should likewise offer barley into the red Bahurūpā fire.
"One should offer parched grain (lāja) into Kṛṣṇā, flour-meal (saktu) into Suprabhā, sesame seeds into Atiraktā, and always gold (kanaka) into Kanakā;
the practitioner should offer all substances in all rites. Thus it is said.
Regarding the ritual actions as well, another tantra states: "The fruits of these [mantras] are proclaimed in sequence according to the distinction of their desired aims:
the first is for subjugation and attraction; Gaganā is considered for paralyzing."
"Red for causing hatred and delusion, black for the rite of killing; Suprabhā is considered suitable for pacification and nourishment, while Suraktā is intended for eradication.
Though she is but one, she possesses many forms and bestows the fruits of all desires. (23–27)
One should assign the limbs of the Fire-god to the body according to the method previously stated;
then again, [one assigns] Sahasrācī, Svastipūrṇa, and Uttiṣṭhapuruṣa. || 28 ||
Dhūmavyāpin, Saptajihva, and Dhanurdhara—these are declared to be the six-limbed mantras (ṣaḍaṅgamantra) in sequence, conjoined with their respective seed-syllables (jāti). || 29 ||
Regarding the phrase "of fire":
"in the body" means in one's own physical form; the word "of the self" is to be supplied as a complement.
The same applies to what follows. By "as stated," it is meant as stated in the preceding chapter.
The fact that Sahasrārcis and the others are in the dative case is according to the traditional teaching (sampradāya).
The ritual application (prayoga), however, is as follows: "Obeisance to the thousand-rayed one for the heart," and so forth. || 28–29 ||
The preceptor should then assign the eight forms of Jātavedas upon his own body:
first on the head, shoulders, sides, and hips; and again on the hips, sides, and shoulders. || 30 ||
One should assign [the mantras] by way of circumambulation; they are stated in their proper order as follows:
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, and the one named Havyavāhana. || 31 ||
Another is known as Aśvodaraja, and then again the one called Vaiśvānara;
Kaumāratejas, Viśvamukha, and Devamukha are recorded [as others]. || 32 ||
The forms of the Fire-god (Vahni-mūrtis) begin with Tārā, Agni, and Pada, and end with Namaḥ.
Regarding the "forms":
they are on the left shoulders, sides, and hips.
The anus and the rectum;
some call it the *liṅga*.
[These are located] behind, on the right sides of the waist and the shoulders. (30–32)
Regarding "tārāgnayaḥ":
the analysis of the compound is that those mantras which have the *tāra* (the *praṇava*) and the word "agnaye" at their beginning.
This applies both in the *nyāsa* ritual and in worship (*pūjā*), according to the rule "natyantāḥ."

It has been stated that in the *home* formulas the word ends in *svāhā*. Because these [mantras] are joined with *namaḥ*, they end in the dative case. The ritual application (*prayoga*), however, is: *huṃ agnaye jātavedase namaḥ mūrdhni*, and so forth. || 33 ||
Having prepared a seat, one should meditate upon the form of that fire.

One should meditate on the beloved [deity], who is the color of the hibiscus flower, adorned with golden ornaments, seated upon a lotus, possessing three eyes, and holding aloft his spear, the svastika, and the gesture of fearlessness with his long arms.
One should meditate upon the Fire-god, whose head is bound with matted locks.
Then, one should sprinkle pure water upon the girdle;
with *darbha* grass that has no inner core, one should spread it across the middle of the girdle.

"Having prepared the seat"—the word "on the body" (*tanau*) is to be supplied here. [One should perform this] preceded by the worship of the *pīṭha* powers as described in the fourteenth chapter, beginning with Maṇḍūka and ending with Paratattva, [reciting]: "Oṃ *raṃ*, obeisance to the fire-seat (*agnyāsana*). [This is done] upon their bodies.
The ritual placement (nyāsa) and the preparation of the seat (āsana). ||33||
He speaks of meditation (*dhyāna*) with the words "the desired" (*iṣṭam*).
"The desired" means the boon (*vara*).
From the lower right hand up to the lower left hand, the desired [objects] and so forth are to be meditated upon.
"Abhīti" (fearlessness) joined with "svastika" is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (*madhyapadalopī samāsa*).
"Ākalpa" means ornamentation. ||34||
"Tataḥ" (then) means:
having worshipped the fire within one's own heart by means of the sequence of the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*).
"Paristaret" (he should strew around) means: [he should strew the sacrificial grass].
With the tips pointing eastward and northward.
As it is stated in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*:
"One should surround the fire with *darbha* grass having its tips pointing eastward and northward."
Thus it is said.
Also elsewhere: "Then, having strewn the sacrificial pit with *darbha* grass whose tips point toward the direction of Hari (the West) and Dhana-da (the North)," so [it is stated].
The most excellent of gurus should place the enclosing sticks (paridhis) in the cardinal directions, excluding the east;
having worshipped them in a clockwise direction, he should install the forms of Brahmā and the other deities within them. || 36 ||

By the phrase "O supreme guru," it is stated that the ritual strewing (*paristaraṇa*) and other rites must be performed even in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with a single rim (*ekamekhala*), and so forth.
As they say:
"In a pit with one rim, one of sharp intellect should perform the strewing below the rim; in a pit with two rims [the strewing is done] between them."
One should place [the sticks] upon the second girdle in the case of three girdles, or upon the girdle situated between them; this is the meaning.
One should deposit the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) in the directions, excluding the east.
As for the enclosing sticks, they are described by Kātyāyana.
"He places the enclosing sticks (paridhi) around [the fire]: they should be fresh, from a single tree, arm-length in size, and made of Palāśa, Vaikaṅkata, Kāśmarya, or Bilva wood.
Thus it is said.
Even on a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila), the placement of the grass-strewing and the enclosing sticks must necessarily be performed.

Because it has been stated that "the girdle is situated in the middle," one should not think that since there is no girdle on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), the ritual strewing (*paristaraṇa*) and so forth should also not be performed;
for that [girdle] is an ancillary part of the installation of the fire, not an ancillary part of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

However, when the author of the treatise anticipates the question of where the ritual strewing (*paristaraṇa*) and other rites should be performed within the *trimekhala* pit he himself has described, he states: "in the middle enclosing-line.
As they say:
"Then, on the outside, there is the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) provided with three enclosing lines (*paridhi*), with *darbha* grasses pointing eastward and northward."
Thus it is said.
Also elsewhere: "Then, one should place three enclosing stones (paridhis) three times on the outside of the sand-pile. ||36||
Having meditated upon the fire, one should worship it in the center with perfumes and other offerings using this mantra:
"O Vaiśvānara, O Jātavedas, come here [āvaha] after these words. (37)
Accomplish all rites at the conclusion of the word *lohitākṣa*.
This mantra, beloved of Agni, is said to end with the wife of fire (*svāhā*). || 38 ||
"In the middle" means in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that has been worshipped with the mantras beginning with Maṇḍūka and ending with the Pīṭha-mantra.

As it is stated in the Sautrāmaṇi-tantra: "The knower of the ritual procedure [should worship] in the center of the pit, in sequence, with the mantras beginning with Ādhāra-śakti and ending with Padmāsana."
"Having worshipped [the deities] one above the other, the powers of the seat (āsana-śaktis) are to be worshipped in sequence at the bases of the petals starting from the east, and in the center.
Thus [it is said]. He states the mantra for Agni as "vaiśvānara".
The wife of fire is Svāhā. || 37-38 ||
In the center and in all six corners, one should worship the tongues, radiant with flames;
and upon the filaments, one should worship the deities of the limbs according to the stated method.
He describes the worship of the enclosure of fire (*agnyāvaraṇapūjā*) with the words "in the center" (*madhye*).
By this, the fire-seat (*agnipīṭha*) consisting of a six-cornered pericarp and eight petals is indicated.
"Radiant with flames" (*jvālārucaḥ*) refers to the visualization of the tongues [of fire].
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "All tongues should be fully known as having the nature of a blaze in their essential form."
Alternatively, there is a transposition of the sequence.
In that regard, the connection is that one should worship the tongues both in the six corners and in the center.

There, having worshipped the six tongues in the six corners—starting from the northeast (Īśāna) and ending at the northwest (Vāyu)—according to the ritual arrangement, one should then worship Bahurūpā in the center, as she was installed.
"One should worship"—thus say those who know the tradition.
As it is stated by Somaśambhu: "O Rudra, Indra, Vahni, Māṃsāda, Varuṇa, Anila, and Gocara!"
The six tongues of fire, beginning with Hiraṇyā, are situated in their proper sequence.
"But in the middle, she is Bahurūpā.
Thus it is said; and also in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*:
Then one should worship the tongues in the center and in the six corners:
Hiraṇyā, who has the luster of molten gold, is situated in the direction of the Trident-bearer (the northeast).
The tongue of the color of lapis lazuli is situated in the eastern direction in the sky;
the red tongue, resembling the rising sun, is located in the southeastern direction.
Kṛṣṇā, resembling a blue lotus, is situated in the south-western direction;
Suprabhā, with the luster of a ruby, is situated in the western direction.
Exceedingly red, with the luster of the Javā flower, she is situated in the northern direction;
multiform and appearing according to her true nature, she is established in the south and north.
"These flames are yellow in luster and endowed with the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness.
Also elsewhere: "The tongues [of fire] are in the six corners and in the center; the limbs [of the deity] are in the filaments."
Thus it is said. Also in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā: "Hiraṇyā has her tongue directed toward the northeast; Kanakā is situated in the east;
Raktā is in the southeast; Kṛṣṇā is in the southwest; and the other is considered to be Suprabhā."
The tongue of the Maruts is intensely red, with a luster corresponding to its own name;
it is the middle tongue, three-pointed, and called Bahurūpā.
"One [flame] with that crest blazes on the right, while another is on the left;
it should be recited immediately after its own seed-syllable.
Thus it is said.

Some, not respecting the sequence of the recitation as it was heard [in the scriptures], say that one should worship the six tongues as they have been installed: first in the middle, then starting from the northeast (śivakoṇa) and proceeding clockwise until the northwest (vāyukoṇa).
This is their intention.
Having worshipped that particular [tongue] situated in the center for each respective rite, one should worship the others among Īśā and the rest.
As it has been said:
"Now, in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the tongue named Hiraṇyā is praised on earth at the beginning of the ritual."
The one named Kanaka is considered for rites such as immobilization (stambhana), while the red one is indeed considered for rites such as causing hatred (dveṣaṇa).
On this earth, the wise ones have declared that Kṛṣṇā is for killing, Suprabhā for pacification,
and Atiraktā for expulsion.
However, those who know the tradition have stated that [this mantra] belongs specifically to the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of Bahurūpā, because she bestows the fruits of all desires.
And it has been said: "She always spreads auspicious things in the midst."

But in another tantra, however—other wise ones who have reached the further shore of the scriptures and possess pure intellects declare that the radiance of the enemy of Vṛtra (Indra) is brilliant white when situated in the eastern quarter; it is black for the Lord of the Ancestors (Yama); furthermore, it is golden in the west; it is multiform for Varuṇa; and it is red for the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva) when situated in the north.
"And one should place a slightly reddish gold [image] of Agni situated in the middle of the *kuṇḍa*.
Following this, the worship of the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*) is also to be understood as taking place in these same locations.
"By the stated path" refers to that which was described in the previous chapter.
In that regard, the manner of worship is as follows:
"Obeisance to the thousand-rayed one for the heart; svāhā obeisance to the one full of well-being for the head," and so forth. (39)
On the petals, one should worship the forms bearing the Śakti and the Svastika;
thereafter, one should worship the world-protectors (Lokapālas) in the directions, possessing the characteristics previously described. || 40 ||
"One should worship the forms as they have been assigned.
Following this, the teacher Padmapāda also desires the enclosure of the Mothers and Bhairavas.
In some places, there is even an additional reading: "The Mothers are to be worshipped on the tips of the petals, along with the Bhairavas beginning with Aghora (Asitāṅga)."
"In the directions" refers to the *darbha* grasses placed upon the girdle; it should also be understood as referring to the well-known cardinal directions, beginning with the East.
As they say: "In the center, in the six corners, on the tongues, and also on the filaments;
then outside with the limb-mantras, and subsequently in order with the eight forms."
"Upon the darbha grass resting on the girdle, [one should worship] the lords of the directions in order, starting from the east"—thus [it is said].
"Having the aforementioned characteristics" means having the nature described in the preceding chapter. (40)
Thereafter, taking up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with both hands and holding them face downwards,
the preceptor, having taken *darbha* grass, should heat them three times in the fire.
One should purify their tips, middles, and bases respectively with those [mantras];
having grasped them with the left hand, one should sprinkle them with the right. || 42 ||

The specific details mentioned in other tantras that must necessarily be performed, which were indicated by the word "afterwards," are now written down: Having spread *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing eastward on one's left side, and having placed upon them the *praṇītā* and *prokṣaṇī* vessels, the *ājya-sthālī* and *caru-sthālī*,

the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with their *kuśa*-roots hanging down, five fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood, and likewise all other aforementioned vessels, placing them in pairs face-down, [one should proceed] with the root mantra.

Having sprinkled the vessels with the *pavitra* and turned them face upwards, having filled the *praṇītā* vessel with water, having invoked the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) therein, and having placed the *pavitra*, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and other items into it, one should purify it and place it in the northern direction. Having poured a little of that water into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, one should sprinkle all the materials intended for the oblation with that water, using either the *namaḥ* mantra or the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Then [one should say]: "In this rite, you shall be the *brahmā*, acting as the supervisor of what has been done and what remains to be done."
"Having invoked Brahmā and worshipped him, one should seat him upon the throne.
This is stated in the Saṃhitā:
"The knower of mantras, having arranged the vessels in pairs according to the rule..."
Having sprinkled those [vessels] with water using the strainer and having placed them face upwards;
One should wash the vessel again, fill it with pure water,
offer unbroken grains (akṣata) and a purifier (pavitra), and after purifying that [water], set it aside.
In the northern direction, that vessel is called *praṇītā* by the wise;
then, having taken a little of the *praṇītā* water into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, with those waters—
"One should sprinkle the collection of materials for the sacrifice with the root mantra;
then, having invoked Brahmā, one should also worship him with the root mantra. In this context, sprinkling (*avokṣaṇa*) is the act of pouring [water] with the hand turned downwards.
For it is stated in the Sūtra: "One should sprinkle with the hand turned downwards.

Furthermore, elsewhere it is said: "Having spread Darbha grass with its tips pointing toward the direction of Indra (the east) upon the left side, and having placed the vessels in pairs above that—first with their openings facing downward and then likewise with their openings facing upward—"
Then, having filled another vessel with water purified by mantras,
one should sprinkle all the sacrificial materials placed on the left side, along with the kūrca-grass, using the heart-mantra.
Elsewhere also: Having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward upon his own left side, he should place vessels made of gold or other materials according to his means,
turned face down in pairs, for the ritual.

"Having turned the vessels face upwards, one should fill them with water and other substances. Also elsewhere: "Then, having spread *darbha* grass on the left side with their tips pointing toward the direction of the beloved of Pulomā’s daughter (the west), the wise man should place all the vessels above that in pairs, with their openings facing downwards."

"Then, when these vessels have been turned face up, the wise one, having filled one with water and having well-visualized the sacred waters (*tīrtha*) therein, should sprinkle the collection of materials situated on the left side with those [waters] using *darbha* grass blades (*kūrca*), reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*. Thus [it is said].
He describes the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, beginning with "Having taken... and so forth.
It should be understood that the taking up [of the breath] occurs only when the two faces are turned upwards,
because it is stated that one should heat them while they are facing downwards.
This is done with both hands, the right and the left.

"One should purify" applies to each [part] respectively. The meaning of "in due order" is as follows: with the roots of the *darbha* grass one purifies its root; with the middle parts of the *darbha* grass its middle part; and with the tips of the *darbha* grass its tip.
"With the right hand" means with the right hand.
"One should sprinkle" means with the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel. || 41-42 ||
Having heated those two again, the minister should cast the darbha grasses into the fire;
he should then place them on a bed of kuśa grass to his own right side. || 43 ||
By the phrase "again thus," it is stated that the two hands, placed facing downwards, [are to be rotated] three times.
"In this way, one should cast the *darbha* grasses into the fire" refers to the concluding rite (*pratipattikarma*).

By the word "mantrin," the placement (*nyāsa*) of the powers of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*) is to be performed in sequence upon the root, middle, and tip [of the blades].
It should be understood that one should assign Śakti to the *sruc* with the *namaḥ* mantra and Śambhu to the *sruva*.
In the Śaiva tradition, however, there is the triad of principles beginning with the Self (*ātman*).
As they say: "Having taken up the *sruc* and *sruva*, facing upwards and downwards respectively in due order..."
Having heated it over the fire, one should touch it three times with the roots, middle, and tips of *darbha* grass.
Again, having heated thirty blades of kuśa grass with their tips pointing downward in the fire,
one should place the powers— beginning with Icchā— in order at the root, the middle, and the tip.
"One should place Śakti in the *sruc* and Śambhu in the *sruva* with the heart-mantra.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, in the Śaiva Āgama: "Having taken up the *sruc* and *sruva*, facing upwards and downwards respectively,"
Having heated it over the fire, one should touch it three times with the roots, middle, and tips of *darbha* grass.

Having sequentially deposited the three principles (tattva) consisting of the Self, Knowledge, and Śiva in the regions of the Kuśa-grass portions, using the syllables *hāṃ*, *hīṃ*, *hūṃ*, and *śaṃ* in order.
Having assigned Śakti to the *sruc* ladle and Śambhu to the *sruva* spoon with the Heart-mantra,
their necks should be wrapped with three threads and worshipped with flowers and other offerings.
"Having placed those two upon the kuśa grass to his own right.
Thus, the eight purificatory rites (saṃskāra) for the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles have been described.
The word "tāv" (those two) refers to the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles; everywhere, the sequence of recitation should be understood according to their masculine gender. || 43 ||

Then, taking the vessel for the clarified butter (ājyasthālī), one should sprinkle it with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astra). Having poured the clarified butter into it, it should be purified through the rites of inspection (vīkṣaṇa) and so forth. || 44 ||
He states the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the words "the clarified butter.

"With the water of the weapon" means with the *prokṣaṇī* water over which the weapon-mantra has been recited. The syntactical connection is: having poured the clarified butter, which has been consecrated by the rites of inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, into that vessel for the clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*).
In this context, clarified butter (ājya) derived from cows and other such sources is to be understood.
As it is stated in the Piṅgalāmata:
"Clarified butter from a cow is to be known as the best; clarified butter from a buffalo is middling."
"The birth of the goat is the lowest; therefore, that which comes from the cow is praised.
For this very reason, the author will state here and there: "with cow's milk," "drenched with buffalo ghee," and "anointed with ewe's ghee. (44)
Having extinguished the embers with the Vāyavya mantra, one should place them upon those [embers] while reciting the Hṛdaya mantra;
this is declared as *tāpana* by the preceptors who are knowers of the Tantras. || 45 ||

Regarding the word "niruhya" (having removed): having separated [the vessel] from the fire in the *kuṇḍa*, one should place it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*; the word "the clarified butter vessel" (*ājyasthālīm*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The meaning is that this heating (*tāpana*) has been taught by the masters who know the *tantras* after [the previous procedure] was described.

By this, two purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are indicated: first, the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) with the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), and second, the contemplation of one's own body as being composed of Brahman.
As they say: "Having taken cow-ghee and consecrated it with the root-mantra itself, one should contemplate one's own body as consisting of Brahman and heat it over the fire."
Also in the Śaiva Āgama: "Having taken cow's clarified butter consecrated with the root mantra, and having meditated upon one's own body as consisting of Brahman... and so forth.
In the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā it is also stated: "Having deposited the mantra into the clarified butter, one should display the mudrā known as the 'Cow' (dhenu-mudrā).
Thus, there are these two purificatory rites (saṃskāras), as well as the six purificatory rites to be described hereafter.
In the same way, there are eight purificatory rites for the clarified butter as well.
As it is stated in the Piṅgalāmata: "According to the Śiva scriptures, eighteen purificatory rites are to be known for the sacrificial pit;
there are eight for the clarified butter, the large ladle (sruc), and the small ladle (sruva)."
Thus [ends the section]. 45.
Having ignited a pair of darbha grass blades and cast them into the clarified butter, one should throw them into the fire;
this is the purification performed by the Guru with the heart-mantra. || 46 ||

Having performed the lustration ceremony with ghee using a pair of blazing *darbha* blades while reciting the *varman* mantra, he should cast the *darbha* into the fire; this is declared to be the "illumination" (*abhidyotana*). || 47 ||

Having displayed blades of darbha grass blazing in clarified butter while reciting the Astra-mantra, the Guru should cast them into the fire; this is considered the rite of illumination (udyotana). || 48 ||

"Having kindled": the syntactical connection is that, having kindled a pair of *darbha* blades and cast them into the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the Heart Mantra, one should cast them into the fire.
"Having performed the lustration" (*nīrājya*) means having rotated them all around.
"He" refers to the preceptor.
"With the armor" means with the armor-mantra (*kavaca-mantra*).
The connection is: "having performed the lustration (*nīrājana*) of the clarified butter with that armor [mantra]."
"Darbha" refers to a pair of *darbha* blades.

In these three purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), as well as in the two rites to be described hereafter, the disposal of the *darbha* blades into the fire is a ritual of final application (*pratipattikarma*).

For this very reason, there is an absence of mantras therein; consequently, if by some cause those *darbha* blades should be destroyed, the rite consisting of their disposal into the fire [must still be performed].
The darbha grasses are not the instigators [of the action].
This has been established in the fourth chapter.
Regarding the phrase "in the fire, those... [it means they are offered].
The same applies to the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles as well. || 46-48 ||
Having taken the clarified butter and having pushed back the embers, one should touch water in the fire;
then, with the thumb and the ring finger, one should hold two *darbha* blades measuring a span (*prādeśa*). || 49 ||

Having taken [the vessel], one should purify the ghee with the Astra mantra; this purification of the ghee should likewise be performed with two Kuśa blades facing oneself, using the Hṛdaya mantra. || 50 ||
One should perform the immersion in ghee; thus the six purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are declared.
A pair of darbha blades with a knot, measuring a span (prādeśa), should be placed within the ghee. || 51 ||
Having set aside two portions and divided them into the two wings— the white and the other—
one should visualize the *iḍā* channel in the left portion and the *piṅgalā* in the right;
then, having meditated on the *suṣumṇā* in the center, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the prescribed rule.

"Having taken the clarified butter" means having placed the vessel of *ājya* on the fire; "having pushed back" means having joined [the portions]. He should perform the touching of water immediately after this.
Regarding the term *aṅguṣṭha*: *upakaniṣṭhā* refers to the ring finger (*anāmā*).
The phrase "by means of the thumb and the upakaniṣṭhā" implies that this is done with both hands.
It should be understood that one should purify [the ghee] facing the fire.

And it is said in the Śaiva Āgama: "With two blades of *darbha* grass, each a span long, held between the tips of the thumb and ring finger, one should perform the purification (*utpavana*) of the ghee facing the fire with the *astra-mantra*."
"Similarly" means that one should hold [the kuśa grass] with the tips of the thumbs and ring fingers of both hands.
Here too, in the two purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), the ritual of disposal (*pratipattikarma*) consisting of the throwing of the two kuśas into the fire is to be understood.
He states the procedure for the fire sacrifice (*homavidhi*) with the words "prādeśa" and so forth.
"In the midst of the ghee" means within the ghee.
"The white and the other" refers to the bright fortnight on the left and the dark fortnight on the right.
Having meditated thus, all three [mantras] are indeed [to be recited] with clarified butter. || 49-52 ||
Taking the clarified butter from the southern portion with the *sruva* ladle, the Guru [offers it] with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. || 53 ||
One should offer oblation to Agni with "Svāhā" into the right eye of the Fire; likewise, taking [the offering] from the left, one should offer it into the left eye of the Fire. || 54 ||
Then, taking clarified butter from the center [of the fire], one should offer it into the eye on the forehead of the Fire-god with the Heart-mantra, saying: "Svāhā to Soma! || 55 ||

One should offer oblations to Agni and Soma with the mantra "Svāhā," using the Heart-syllable (Hṛdayāṇu) and the Heart-mantra (Hṛnmantra), taking the clarified butter from the southern portion with the dipping-spoon (sruva). || 56 ||
One should offer oblations to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the mantra "Svāhā" into his mouth;
thus one should pour the remnants of the clarified butter into the portion according to the sequence of the subsequent offerings. || 57 ||
Regarding the phrase "according to the rule," he states the rule as "with the *sruva*. The connection is: "in that manner, with the *sruva* and the Heart-mantra, taking [the ghee] from the left.
The connection is: "with the Heart-mantra, taking the clarified butter (*ājya*) from the center."
Some read the text as *hetiṃ sampātayed bhāgam*; in that case, *heti* refers to the remainder of the oblation (*āhuti-śeṣa*).
However, for those who read it as *iti sampādayet*, according to their interpretation, *iti* signifies completion.
Having performed the *svāhā*-ending oblation, the Guru should perform the opening of the faces of the fires and the eyes.

Regarding those who read "ye tu heti saṃpātayet," in their view, having performed the oblation ending with *svā*, at the end of the syllable *hā*, one should pour the remainder (*saṃpāta*) of that very portion from which the clarified butter offering was taken back into that same portion; such is the connection.
The traditionalists accept this very reading.
*Anvāhuti* means following each oblation (*āhuti*).
As it is stated in the Śaiva Āgama: "Having taken [the substance] with the *sruva* ladle, one should offer it as a homa."
One should sequentially cast the remnants of those portions of clarified butter into the fire with the mantras "svā" and "he. (53–57)
Thus the Guru should perform the opening of the eyes, the lead, and the mouth;
he should again offer oblations with clarified butter, accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis* together with the *tārā*. || 58 ||
The most excellent preceptor should offer oblations three times with the fire-mantra;
he should thus perform the rites for the fire, beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna), in their proper sequence. || 59 ||
"Thus, 'to Agni'":
by that fourfold oblation, there is the opening of the three eyes and the faces;
the meaning is "in sequence."
"With the *vyāhṛtis* together with the stars" means [with them] both individually and collectively;
for this very reason, it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "One should offer oblations with the five *manus*.
Furthermore, the word "subsequently" (*anantaram*) is connected with what follows.
"By the mantra of Agni" refers to the previously mentioned "O Vaiśvānara";
"by the Praṇava" means that all five Praṇavas are included.
By the phrase "O best of teachers," it is stated that the application (viniyoga) of each respective mantra should be understood according to its own specific context. || 58-59 ||
With eight oblations of clarified butter, each accompanied by the *praṇava* (Om) individually, one performs the *garbhādhāna*, the *puṃsavana*, and the *sīmantonnayana*. || 60 ||
Immediately thereafter, the birth-rite (jātakarma) should take place, as well as the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa);
after that, the first outing (upaniṣkramaṇa), and then the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) is prescribed. || 61 ||
The Caula and Upanayana rites, followed again by the Mahānāmnī and the Mahāvrata;
then the Upaniṣad, and subsequently the Godāna, the marriage, and death. || 62 ||
Those rites ending with marriage are prescribed for auspicious acts; those ending with death are declared for cruel deeds by those who know the Agamas of fire.
He states "garbhādhāna" (conception) as that which is included by the word "etcetera" in the phrase "beginning with garbhādhāna," and so forth.
Furthermore, the connection is as follows: immediately after [conception] comes the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), and immediately after that, the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) should take place.
This is the meaning of the word "immediately after."

Having performed the rite of removing the stalk as characterized by the five oblations of fuel-sticks (samidh) which will be described hereafter, and having thus purified the birth-impurity (sūtaka), one should perform the naming of the fire according to the names of those respective deities;
for example, Kṛṣṇāgni, Nārāyaṇāgni, or Durgāgni.
Then, having united the two parents within himself, he should perform the purificatory rites beginning with the departure [from the womb];
the word "etc. (ādi) is mentioned as a single unit for the purpose of indicating those [subsequent rites]. This has been stated in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
Having meditated upon the newborn as having this very form, one should perform the birth-rite (jātakarman);
then, having removed the umbilical cord and purified the impurity of birth (sūtaka).
Having given him the name Śivāgni, preceded by the offering of oblations,
and having performed the dismissal of the parents, as well as the tonsure, the initiation, and other rites;
"And having performed the purificatory rite for him at the conclusion of the marriage," thus [it is said].
Also in the *Sautrāmaṇi-tantra*: "The rites beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*)," and so forth.
The rites concluding the birth-ceremony [are performed] with fire, separately for each, by means of the Vāgbhava [syllable].
Having performed eight oblations of clarified butter and having given the fire the name "Vārāhyagni," he should then proceed with the first feeding of solid food for the fire.
"Up to the end of the marriage ceremony, [the rites are performed] with the Vāgbhava [syllable], according to the previously mentioned sequence of eight oblations.
Regarding this, the teachers maintain that although the *samāvartana* (the rite of returning home) is not explicitly mentioned after the gift of the cow (*godāna*), it must nevertheless be performed.
As it is stated in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*: "The return home (*samāvartana*), marriage (*udvāha*), and thereafter the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*).
Also elsewhere: "With that very [mixture], one should offer oblations for both the return home and the marriage."
Thus it is said.
Also elsewhere: "One should perform the return home (samāvartana) and marriage by that same rite."
However, some read "tathopaniṣadam snānam" and explain *snāna* as *samāvartana*.
According to their view, the *godāna* ceremony follows after the *samāvartana*.
The ritual procedure, however, begins with: "Oṃ, I perform the *garbhādhāna* sacrament for this fire; svāhā," and so forth. (60–63)
Then, having worshipped his parents, he should unite them with himself;
he should offer five fuel-sticks (samidh) drenched with ghee from both their roots and tips. || 64 ||
Regarding the word "tataḥ" (then): immediately after the naming ceremony, one should offer five fuel-sticks (*samidh*) into that aforementioned fire for its two parents.
The meaning is that it is for the purpose of removing the umbilical cord immediately after the birth-rite (*jātakarma*).
As it is stated in the Śaiva Āgama:
"Then, for the removal of the umbilical cord, [one should perform the rite] for the faces with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*)."
"Five fuel-sticks (samidh) should be offered at the edge and the root, drenched in clarified butter.

Thus [it is said]. However, in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā: "They should be made of Palāśa wood or other sacrificial woods, twelve finger-breadths long, straight, not naturally dry, with their bark intact, free from blemishes, and uniform."
"Alternatively, they are prescribed as being ten finger-breadths long, resembling the little finger;
or, if these are unavailable, even those measuring a span (prādeśa) may be offered in their entirety. Thus [it is said]. (64)
The best of those who know the tantras should offer one oblation each, in due order and according to the rule, for the mantra, the tongue, the limbs, and the form of the fire. || 65 ||
"By mantras" refers to those mentioned in the context of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). "In sequence" means according to the order of the *nyāsa*.
By the phrase "according to the rule," he recalls what was stated regarding the *homa* sacrifice—that it must end with *svāhā*.
The practical application (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: *styūṃ hiraṇyāyai svāhā*, and so forth.
Immediately after this, in the *adhidevatā* oblation as well, [one recites] "Oṃ surebhyaḥ svāhā" and so forth;
likewise, "To the thousand-eyed one, to the heart, namaḥ svāhā" and so forth;
and "Oṃ agnaye jātavedase svāhā" and so forth.
By the phrase "the best among those who know the tantras," the inclusion of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), their weapons (*astra*), and their enclosures (*āvṛti*) is to be understood.
As it is stated in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*:
"One should offer oblations once each with the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) and so forth, preceded by the syllable *TĀR*."
"In those respective places, one of clear intellect [should offer oblations] with [mantras] ending in *svāhā*, according to the sequence. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Prayogasāra*: "All mantras should be employed in the rites of fire-oblation (*homakarman*) ending in *svāhā*. (65)

Having taken up clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle and having poured it four times into the *sruc* while holding it, the preceptor, standing and with a restrained mind, offers it into the fire with the *sruva*. || 66 ||
One should offer oblations with the fire-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* for the sake of success;
one should offer ten oblations with the mantra of Vighneśvara. || 67 ||

Regarding the term *avadāya*: the teacher, with a disciplined mind, having placed clarified butter (*ājya*) four times into the large ladle (*sruk*) by means of the small dipping-spoon (*sruva*), and having covered that *sruk* with the *sruva*, should offer it into the fire while standing still, using the fire-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*; such is the syntactical connection.
By the phrase "the teacher with a restrained mind," the state of having even feet and eyes fixed on the tips of the horns and so forth is described.
By the phrase "ending with *vauṣaṭ*," it is meant that the word *vauṣaṭ* is to be substituted in place of the word *svāhā*.
However, there is a specific distinction in the Śaiva Āgama:
Having placed the *sruva* ladle face-down into the *sruc* filled with clarified butter,
and having fixed a flower upon the tip of its prong, he should then [proceed] with his left hand.
Again, holding those two with the left hand in the mudrā resembling a conch shell,
he rose up with his upper body elevated and his feet together.
"Placing the root of that [the penis] at the navel, with eyes fixed on the tip of the horn,
and bringing it to the space between the left breast and its root without weariness"—
thus [it is said] regarding Vighneśvara.

It should be understood that [this applies] to Mahāgaṇapati, divided tenfold and interwoven with each preceding [form]. It should also be known that one should offer four oblations using the entire [mantra] together.
As it is said in the Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī:
By means of the Mahāgaṇeśa mantra, joined with each preceding one,
and by means of the six seed-syllables beginning with Tāra (Oṃ), using the syllables of the mountain (seven) as the instruments.
"O Goddess of the gods, having offered [the oblation] tenfold when [the deities] are divided, one should offer it with the whole [mantra] when they are united.
And likewise, the Teachers [state]:
With the tenfold divisions beginning with Tārā, combined with each preceding one,
and with the Gāṇapatya mantra, one should offer ten oblations.
"And one should offer oblations four times with that [mantra] in its entirety. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, elsewhere: "O Goddess of the Gods, having offered oblations ten times separately with the Mahāgaṇeśa mantra joined with each preceding [mantra], and then generally [with the whole]," so it is stated. (66–67)
This opening of the fire (agnimukha) is considered common to all ritual systems.
Therefore, having worshipped the pedestal within the fire for the deity, [one should proceed]. || 68 ||
One should worship that deity, the bestower of desired fruits, who is in the form of fire;
the practitioner of mantra should offer oblations into her mouth twenty-five times. || 69 ||
With clarified butter and the root mantra, this is the unification of the faces;
contemplating the identity of the fire and the deity together with the self. || 70 ||
"Of the deity" means of the deity of the mantra to be offered in the present context.
"The deity" refers to [the deity] together with its retinue (*sāvaraṇa*).
Regarding "the unification of the faces," it is stated in the Śaiva Āgama:
"Thus, within the desired face, there is the inclusion of all faces and their oneness."
Alternatively, one should remember the measurement of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as being like that of the desired face.
"The faces are to be internalized; their unification with that [central face] is considered [the process]. (68–70)
One should offer eleven oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra;
this is declared by those who know the scriptures to be the "joining of the channels" (nāḍī-sandhāna). || 71 ||
