The best of teachers should properly offer one oblation at a time, mixed with honey, to the principal limbs and the surrounding enclosures in their proper sequence.
Regarding "the joining of the channels" (*nāḍīsandhāna*): it is the unification of the three channels belonging to the deities of fire and the self.
"Of the subsidiary and primary enclosures" (*aṅgamukhyānām āvṛtīnām*) means of the deity of the mantra to be offered in the present context.
In this context as well, the phrase "O limb" (*aṅga*) and so forth is intended to indicate the possibility [of such repetition].

By the word "correctly" (*samyak*), it is stated that where there is no primacy of the repetition of the limbs (*aṅga-vṛtti*), the repetition applies to those repetitions beginning with that [limb] according to its occurrence. By the term "supreme teacher" (*deśikottama*), it is stated that ten oblations are to be offered with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
As they say:
"One should offer ten oblations for each individual goddess of the retinue. (71–72)
Then, once the other sacrificial pits have been consecrated according to the rules,
the preceptor, with a concentrated mind, should cause the fire to dwell in the eastern and other directions.

Regarding the phrase "in the consecrations" (*saṃskṛteṣu*): the word "by the officiating priests" (*ṛtvigbhiḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Therefore, the officiating priests shall perform the eighteen consecrations in their respective vessels according to the prescribed rule.
The teacher should perform the ritual transfer of the fire (agniviharaṇa) everywhere; this is the meaning.
[This refers to] the directions starting from the east and ending with the northeast (īśāna).
By the word "concentrated" (samāhita), the uninterrupted performance of the fire-transfer is indicated. || 73 ||

Having worshipped the deity mentioned in the Tantra— accompanied by the limbs (aṅgas) and the surrounding enclosures (āvaraṇas)— with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, the officiating priests (ṛtvijas) should perform oblations twenty-five times with clarified butter (ājya) using the root mantra, and likewise with sacrificial porridge (caru) mixed with clarified butter. || 74 ||

Regarding the phrase "having sacrificed to the deity": it should be understood that here, after the worship, one should offer one oblation each for the limbs (*aṅga*) and so forth of each respective deity as before, and then offer ten oblations to the root deity.
Likewise, [one should offer] with the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*).
In the previous chapter, it was stated that the sacrificial food (caru) which has been prepared is divided into three portions:
one portion is offered to the deity,
and another should be offered as an oblation (homa) into the fire.
This is the oblation for that very [deity].
Likewise, [it is performed] twenty-five times with the root mantra. || 74 ||
Having risen in the morning, they should again offer oblations with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter,
or with substances prescribed by the ritual manuals, one thousand and eight times for each separately.

He states the duties for the second day with the words "In the morning" (*prātaḥ*). The teachers and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) each should perform the oblations (*juhuyuḥ*). Regarding this, there is a specific detail in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
"Ghee is to be offered with the *sruva* ladle, fuel-wood with the hand, and the remainder with the *sruc* ladle or by hand;
therein it should be offered through the divine or likewise the ṛṣi-tīrtha.
Thus, one thousand and eight oblations for each [deity] are to be offered individually into that kindled fire.

Otherwise, because faults are observed, it is stated in the *Bahvṛcapariśiṣṭa*: "If one who considers himself wise should offer oblations into a fire that is smoky, the sacrificer, along with his sons, shall become blind; such is the Vedic revelation."
Also in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*: "The man who offers oblations into a fire that lacks flames or one that is without embers is born with weak digestion, prone to disease, and impoverished."
"Therefore, one desiring health, long life, and ultimate prosperity should offer oblations only when the fire is well-kindled, and never when it is not kindled.
Thus it is said in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "One should not offer oblations when the fire is not blazing, nor in a fire that is merely middling, nor in one that is censurable."
"When the blazing, licking fire is kindled, one should offer oblations for the accomplishment of the ritual act. Thus [it is said]. 75.
Then, having made the disciple— who has washed his teeth, bathed, and is composed—
drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should lead him to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having beheld that consciousness within the heart-lotus with his divine vision,
the Guru, having united it with his own self, should perform the purification of the paths (adhva-viśodhana).
After the *homa*, he describes the duties of the Guru with the word "then" (*tataḥ*).
Regarding the phrase "having made [the disciple] drink the five products of the cow" (*pañcagavya*), this takes place outside the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) itself.
The specific procedure for the five products of the cow, however, he will explain in the twenty-first chapter.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Having drunk the five products of the cow as prescribed and having sipped water according to the rule,
one should then cause [the disciple] to enter the place of sacrifice by the southern door."
Regarding the phrase "that consciousness":

the meaning is that one should draw that consciousness from the heart through the channel (nāḍī) by means of the goad-mudrā (aṅkuśamudrā), and then join it to one's own heart via the path of one's own central channel.
As it has been said:
"Taking that consciousness residing in the heart, which has the form of a shimmering star, one should place it in one's own heart by means of the goad-mudrā.
Thus [ends] the purification of the paths (*adhvaviśodhana*).
This has been stated in the *Ṣaḍanvayamahāratna*:
"Purification (śodhana) consists of contemplating the unity of the cause of the principles (*tattvas*);
therein, one contemplates the oneness of the bindu of the phonemes (*varṇas*) and the digits (*kalās*). (76–77)
It has been stated that there are three paths: the path of the parts (kalādhvā), the path of the principles (tattvādhvā), and the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvā);
and another triad: the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvā), the path of the words (padādhvā), and the path of the mantras (mantrādhvā). || 78 ||
Regarding the phrase "it has been said":
the word "iti" occurs twice.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "the other triad has been stated by those who know the Tantras."
The first three are of the nature of meaning (artha), while the latter three are of the nature of sound (śabda).
As it is stated in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
"In that regard, three are declared to be sounds (dhātu) and three to be meanings (artha)."
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, elsewhere: "The path of mantra, the path of word, and the path of phoneme are [the paths] from the perspective of sound;
the path of world, the path of principle, and the path of aspect are [the paths] from the perspective of meaning, in their respective order."

However, it should be understood that here the statement is given according to the order of withdrawal (saṃhāra-krama), whereas in the root [text] it is according to the order of emanation (sṛṣṭi-krama). || 78 ||
The five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, are proclaimed as the path of kalās (kalādhvan). The path of principles (tattvādhvan) is divided in many ways according to the different Śaiva Āgamas. || 79 ||
There are thirty-six Śiva-tattvas, thirty-two Vaiṣṇava-tattvas, and twenty-four Maitra-tattvas belonging to Prakṛti. || 80 ||
The ten principles and the seven [principles] of that which consists of three parts have been stated;
[these are further elaborated] in many ways, namely fivefold. These are the Maitra and Sāṃkhya [teachings].
As it is stated in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
"There are certain principles belonging to the Purāṇas and to Tripurā,
as well as certain principles well-known from Sāṃkhya and Yoga."
"Then, having performed [the rites] in their entirety, [one should worship] those other [deities] as well that are renowned in the Śiva scriptures.
Thus [ends the section on] Tripurā, whose nature consists of three parts. (79–81)
The Śaiva principles are said to be Śiva, Śakti, and Sadāśiva. || 81 ||
Indeed, these five pure principles together with Īśvara and Vidyā are as follows:
Māyā, Kāla, Niyati, Kalā, and Vidyā is remembered as the last. || 82 ||

"Pure" means that they are pure because they are free from the three impurities (*mala*): the individual (*āṇava*), the karmic (*kārmika*), and the cosmic (*māyīya*). Among these, the so-called *āṇava* is Sadāśiva’s own lack of self-reflection (*anavamarśa*).
The *kārma* [avidyā] is the notion, "I am a possessor of merit and demerit.
The *māyīya* [avidyā] is the cognition of the self in egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth.
And it is said in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
Śiva, Śakti, from that the Nāda, from that the Bindu and Sadāśiva; from that Maheśvara was born, and from Maheśvara arose Pure Vidyā. Thus [it is said]. 82.
Passion is the person; these seven—both pure and impure—are as follows:
primordial nature (prakṛti), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), mind (manas), and the organs of knowledge (jñānendriya). || 83 ||
The organs of action, the subtle elements (tanmātras), and the five gross elements—these, O Teacher, are declared in the Āgama to be the twenty-four impure principles. || 84 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the Śaivas," the classification of the principles (*tattvas*) is demonstrated here as being "pure" and "impure. They are pure by virtue of being causes and being free from the three impurities (*mala*); they are impure by virtue of being effects and being possessed of those [impurities].
As it is stated in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
"She is the sovereign power of speech belonging to the trident-bearing Lord known as Vāgīśa;
she manifests as Mātṛkā in the form of the phonemes."
Then, from the union with Ananta, he emitted Māyā and Kāla;
from Kalā, Niyati; from Kalā, Vidyā; and from Kalā, Rāga and Puruṣa—and so forth. Thus, endowed with the number thirty-six, [the principle] consists of both the pure and the impure.
Thus ends [the section] with verses 83–84.
The individual soul, the vital breaths, the intellect, the mind, and then the organs of knowledge and action. || 85 ||

The five subtle elements (tanmātras), the five gross elements (bhūtas), the heart-lotus, the triad of fires, and Vāsudeva and the others—these are the principles (tattvas) belonging to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. || 86 ||
The wise know the five elements, the subtle essences, the senses, as well as the mind, ego, intellect, and primordial matter (pradhāna) to be the eight friends. || 87 ||
The five kalās beginning with Nivṛtti, then Bindu, Kalā, Nāda, Śakti, and Sadāśiva preceded by [Sadāśiva], they know as the nature of Prakṛti. || 88 ||
Self-knowledge is Śiva, and thereafter Śiva is knowledge itself;
furthermore, all principles (tattvas) are said to be the principles belonging to the threefold Self. || 89 ||
The ten are the organs of knowledge and the organs of action;
the word "five" is connected to both.
The triad of luminaries consists of fire, the moon, and the sun.
The four [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva will be described in the eighth [chapter]. || 85-86 ||
The ten faculties; pride is the ego (ahaṅkāra);
and intellect is the principle of the Great One (mahattattva).
*Pradhāna* is *prakṛti*.
It is the Self itself. He dispels the suspicion that it is a mere fabrication of his own imagination by stating "by those who know those respective scriptures. (87–90)

This is indeed called the path of reality (tattvādhvan) by those who know the various scriptures; it is declared as the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) by the wise, consisting of the worlds themselves. || 90 ||
The wise declare that the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*) consists of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*.
The collection of phonemes is the path of words (*padādhvan*), and the multitudes of mantras constitute the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*). || 91 ||
The worlds (*bhuvana*) are five: those consisting of ether, air, fire, water, and earth.
However, in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*, the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) is proclaimed as extending from Ādhāra up to Unmanī.
Thus [it is said].
"The collection of phonemes" refers to the phonemes together with the bindu.
However, in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā—
The path of words, consisting of a collection of words, is divided into many varieties;
it exists as the constituent parts of great mantras and secondary mantras.
"Because it consists of the primary limbs, that path is composed of five steps.
Thus, the collections of mantras are the seven mantras: *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and *ya*. (90–91)
The most excellent of gurus should gradually purify these six paths;
he should likewise contemplate them in the feet, the navel, the heart, the forehead, and the head of the disciple. || 92 ||
At the head, in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
Therein, this is the method of purification:

having recollected the path of the *kalās* in the feet, and having placed the *kalās* beginning with their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*) upon the feet, the secret parts, the heart, the mouth, and the head, one subsequently performs the purification of the path of the *kalās*.

Thus, having recollected the path of principles (*tattvādhvan*) in the navel, one should project them into the preceding locations in reverse order; thereafter follows the purification of the path of principles.

Likewise, having recollected the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) in the navel, one should project [the deities] beginning with their own seed-syllables (*bīja*) into the immediately following locations; thereafter follows its purification.
Similarly, having recollected the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*) in the heart, one should project the pure phonemes into that body; thereafter follows the purification of the path of phonemes.
Thus, having recollected the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) on the forehead and performed the placement (nyāsa) of the letters along with the bindu, there is the purification of that [path].

Likewise, having recollected the path of mantras (mantrādhvan) on the head and pervaded the seven mantras in their respective locations, the purification of that path follows; this is what was stated by the "best of gurus" with the words "thus...". (92)

Then, the Guru should touch him with the *kūrca* according to the prescribed rule and perform oblations in the preceptor’s fire-pit (*ācāryakuṇḍa*) using purified sesame seeds saturated with clarified butter.
"I purify this path; svāhā!"—with these words, one should offer eight oblations individually for each path, beginning with *TĀRĀ*, and thereby lead them sequentially into dissolution. || 94 ||
By the phrase "according to rule," it should be understood that [the subject] is the disciple.
"He should touch that guru" is a separate sentence.
This has been stated in the Nārāyaṇīya:
"Having withdrawn that disciple into his own self through meditation by means of the process of dissolution,
and having generated him again, he should place consecrated *darbha* grasses into his hand.
Some read the text as "touching him" (*taṃ spṛśan*).
In that context, by the phrase "according to the rule," it should be understood that [the offering] is performed with the left hand.
The connection is that the Guru should offer eight oblations, beginning with the *tāra* (oṃ), separately for each path (*adhvan*).
The phrase "I purify" means "of such-and-such a person."
"By those that are thoroughly purified" means having removed the refuse, washed, and dried them.
The ritual application (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: *Oṃ, I purify the path of the digits (*kalādhvan*) of such-and-such a person, svāhā*, and so forth. (93–94)
O Śivā, one should generate from Śiva those who have dissolved [into him] by means of the path of emanation. || 95 ||
Beholding that child with his divine vision, the supreme teacher should again unite that consciousness, which resides within himself, with the disciple. || 96 ||
"In Śiva, residing in the thousand-petalled [lotus]" is connected with what precedes;
"in succession" refers to what follows;
and "in the previous" means up to Śiva.

The connection is that one should generate them from Śiva by way of the path of emanation (*sṛṣṭimārga*). "By way of the path of emanation" means that one should apply the subsequent [element] according to the preceding one;
the meaning is: exactly as it was brought forth, so it remains.
By this purification of the paths, the purification of the body is accomplished;
for the body consists precisely of the six paths.
As they say:
Her head is the kalā beyond peace (śāntyatīta), her facial hair is peace (śānti);
her knees and shanks are cessation (nivṛtti), and her hair is the paths of the worlds (bhuvana-adhvan).

"O Śivā, the path of mantra consists of flesh and blood, joined with the channels [of the body] that are the feet, syllables, and head; the path of the principles (tattva) consists of marrow, fat, bone, the bodily constituents (dhātu), and semen. (95–96)

Having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*) by means of the root mantra, the Guru, who knows the mantras, should dismiss the deity—along with his limbs (*sāṅga*) and retinue (*sāvaraṇa*)—into the water-pot (*kumbha*). || 97 ||

Having again offered oblations with the vyāhṛtis, and having offered one oblation each for the tongue and other parts of the Fire, he should sprinkle water around [the fire] and then into himself. || 98 ||

Having prepared the fire and arranged his own enclosing sticks and the surrounding grass, the practitioner of mantras should burn these in the case of an occasional rite; however, in the case of a regular rite, he should not burn them.
Regarding the phrase "with the root mantra," by the word "preceptor" (deśika), it is implied that [the mantra] ends with *vauṣaṭ*.
This has been stated in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā: "Then, having filled the *sruva* ladle with the clarified butter remaining from the *homa*..."
Having placed a flower before it, [he should offer] that [libation] with the sruva ladle turned downwards.
Having covered [the vessel] with a bunch of Darbha grass, standing up with palms joined at the base [of the grass],
one should offer a stream of water the thickness of a barley grain, ending with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*.
Having thus performed the *pūrṇāhuti* offering;
that is to say, having performed the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) from the fire, one should bring [the deity] into the water-pot (*kumbha*).
By the phrase "the teacher is the guide," it is stated that after offering one oblation for each of the deity’s limbs, circumambulations, and so forth, the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) takes place.
This is done with the *vyāhṛtis*, both individually and collectively.
However, the traditionalists say that here the term *vyāhṛti* refers to the *mahāvyāhṛtis*.
And they are as follows: Oṃ bhūr, svāhā to Agni, to the Earth, and to the Great One.
Oṃ bhuvaḥ, svāhā to Vāyu, to the Atmosphere, and to the Great One.
Oṃ, svāhā to the Sun, to the sky, and to the Great One!
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, svāhā to the Moon, to the constellations, to the quarters, and to the Great One!
And it is said: "One should again complete the oblation, preceded by the Mahāvyāhṛtis."
Thus [it is said].

By the word "and so forth" (*ityādi*) in the phrase "the tongues of Vibhāvasu and so forth," one includes the limbs of the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*), their forms (*mūrti*), the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), and their weapons.
The term "having sprinkled around" (*pariṣicya*) is to be connected with the word "the fire" (*pāvakam*).
"By waters" means by the water in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.
"Having joined the purifier within one's own self"—
in that regard, after having offered prayers with the prayer-mantra (*prārthanā-mantra*), the dismissal (*udvāsana*) follows. This has been stated in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*:
"O Fire, O you of great power, accomplisher of all rites!
Even when another rite has arrived, grant your presence with respect.
Having thus prayed with this mantra, one should also dismiss the fire. Thus [ends verses 97–99].
One should bind the eyes of the disciple with a cloth using the Netra-mantra;
then, taking that disciple by the hand, one should lead him from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to the mandala. || 100 ||
Having again filled his joined palms with flowers according to the rule, he should cast them into the jar while reciting the root mantra, for the pleasure of the deity. || 101 ||
"With a garment" means with a new, white one.
As it is said in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "Having bound the eyes with a new white cloth."
In the Piṅgalāmata, however, there is this distinction: "One should bind his eyes with the cloth from one's own eyes, using the Netra-mantra.
In the Mantratantraprakāśa as well: "Then the preceptor, having bound his eyes with the Netra-mantra..."
Thus [it is said].
But in the Nārāyaṇīya, however, it says: "One should bind the eye with the eyes, and the eye with the eye."
"One should lead [the disciple] to the maṇḍala" means by way of circumambulation (prādakṣiṇyena) to the western gate; this is the implied meaning.
As it has been stated in the Nārāyaṇīya:
"Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the body of the disciple, one should lead him clockwise around [the mandala].
Having brought him to the western door, one should cause him to cast a handful of flowers.
By the phrase "one should cause him to cast according to the rule," the specific detail mentioned in the *Piṅgalāmata* is summarized.
Having filled his joined palms with flowers, he should offer them upon the yoga-pīṭha;
a fall of flowers toward the west, north, north-east, or east portends good fortune, whereas in other directions it is inauspicious.
"One should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the Astra-mantra for the sake of pacification. (100-101)

Having removed that blindfold from him as he sat upon the bed of *darbha* grass, the Guru, according to the sequence of the self-sacrifice (*ātmayāga*), again withdraws and then generates [the disciple]. || 102 ||
Then, one should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) on the body of the child using their respective mantras;
having worshipped the chosen deity residing in the water-pot with the five types of offerings (pañcopacāra). || 103 ||
Regarding the phrase "by means of the sequence of the sacrifice to the self" (*ātmayāgakramāt*),

some maintain that it refers to the sequence of the elaborate sacrifice (*prapañcayāga*) which will be described later. However, the traditionalists hold that the "sacrifice to the self" (*ātmayāga*) is the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*).
"By that sequence" means by the sequence of the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) as taught therein; for both the dissolution and the creation of the elements have been described there.
The syntactical connection is: "having dissolved the body, and then immediately having produced it again."
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"One should cause the elements, beginning with earth, to dissolve into their respective qualities (*guṇa*),
properly established within the body, by means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*)."
"Then, one should contemplate the body according to the very order of emanation.
Also, in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "Having sat upon a divine seat, one should dissolve its physical form;
one should dissolve the earth, which is conjoined with smell and the other [sensory objects] and the sense of smell, into water."
By means of these and other passages, ending with the words, "one should then meditate upon that which has arisen.
Also elsewhere: "Then, [the disciple] seated comfortably on a throne in the consecration pavilion..."
"The Guru should purify this [disciple] as before, by means of drying and other [practices].
Also, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The Guru should awaken him there while he is seated comfortably, by means of drying and so forth."
Regarding this, the teachers state the prayer to the deity as follows:
"O Goddess, abode of compassion! O refuge of all prosperity!
O Mother, who loves those who seek shelter! Bestow Your grace upon this child."
O Goddess of the gods, O support of compassion! Show mercy to this wretched one who is bound by the fetters headed by the *āṇava* bond, O Sovereign Lady.
"May he be nourished even by worldly and otherworldly enjoyments; and let all true devotion be bestowed upon him who takes refuge in the Partless. (102-103)
One should perform the ritual of sakalīkṛti for her according to the method taught in the Tantra;
then, once the maṇḍala has been adorned, one should seat the disciple upon another [seat].
"In another mandala" means outside the mandala, in the northeast. This was stated by Somaśambhu:
In a bathing pavilion constructed in the northeastern direction from the sacrificial hall,
one should prepare an altar measuring two cubits in length and eight finger-breadths in height.

"Having placed Ananta upon a seat made of *śrīparṇī* wood and other materials, and having seated the disciple there facing east, one should perform the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) and worship him. Thus it is said.
In the *Prayogasāra*: "Then, in the northeastern direction, [one should worship] the disciple whose body has been arranged with mantras as prescribed."
Seated upon the pedestal on a square altar, with the tips of darbha grass in his hand.
"One should personally consecrate the disciple who follows the reality of the Self.
Regarding the instruction "one should seat [him]," it should be understood that for the purpose of eating he is seated facing east, and for liberation (mukti) facing north.
As it is stated in the *Somaśambhu*: "For bathing, one faces north; for eating, one faces east; and for liberation, [one faces north]."
"Having raised the upper body," thus [it is said].
Also elsewhere: "In the mandala, having established the direction of Īśa (the northeast), one should place those seeking liberation facing north."
For the sake of the meal, he should seat the disciples there facing the east. Thus [ends verse 104].
While the five musical instruments resounded, the Guru, together with the benedictions of the Brahmins, duly lifted up the water-pot and [removed] the celestial trees situated at its mouth. || 105 ||
Having placed the Mātṛkā on the head of the child while mentally reciting it, the knower of the Self should sprinkle him with water consecrated by the root mantra. || 106 ||

Having again taken up the *vardhanī* vessel, which has been worshipped and embodies the form of the weapon, one should swiftly sprinkle [the disciple] with its well-consecrated waters for the sake of protection. || 107 ||

The connection is that one should mentally recite the *mātṛkā* according to the rule and consecrate [the disciple] with the root mantra; there, "according to the rule" means reciting the *mātṛkā* in reverse order and the root mantra in that same form.
As it has been said by the Teachers:

"Just as in the past a jar was filled with nectar-like syllables, so too should the excellent preceptor fill the body of the disciple with those [syllables] and consecrate him for the swift attainment of his desired perfections. Also elsewhere: "A person of good intellect who recites the mantra should consecrate [the disciple]."
Thus it is said.

Also elsewhere: "One should perform the consecration according to rule, using the letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *a*, as well as the letters of the mantra repeated three times in their entirety."
The phrase "well-prepared" (*susādhitaiḥ*) is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) in both cases;
likewise, "honored" (*pūjitām*) is also a restatement.
[The word] *añjasā*.
In reality. || 105–107 ||
With the remaining water, the Guru should cause the disciple to sip;
then, the knower of the Self should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon him, making him one with the deity. || 108 ||
Having risen and put on two clean garments, and having sipped water and become silent, the disciple should sit in the presence of the teacher. || 109 ||
The supreme teacher, contemplating the oneness of those two, should worship the deity who has been transferred into the disciple with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. || 110 ||
"By what remains" means by that which is situated in the consecration-vessel remaining after the consecration;
"the self of the deity" [is consecrated] by means of the consecration;
"in the presence" means in the vicinity.
"Transferred" means by means of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
By the word "supreme teacher" (*deśikottama*) and the word "now" (*adya*), it is stated that only incense and lamps are to be taken.
"Of those two" refers to the disciple and the deity.
By the word "tataḥ" (then), it is indicated that one should place the hand upon the head of the disciple and recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
This has been stated in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*:
"Then, having placed his own hand upon the disciple's head, he should recite [the mantra] one hundred times."
"Then one should give the mantra one hundred and eight times, preceded by water. Also elsewhere: "Then, while placing his hand upon the head, he should empower the mantra;
saying 'May there be equality,' he should offer unbroken rice-grains (akṣata)."
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"The Preceptor himself, the soul of the universe, should place his own hand upon the head of that [disciple]."
Thus [ends the section on verses] 108–110.
Then, preceded by the offering of water, the wise one should impart the knowledge to that humble disciple;
furthermore, he should recite eight times the knowledge received from his own guru.
One should give [the mantra] into the right ear three times, or as many times as it takes to recite;
as it has been said:
"Then, the excellent mantra, complete with its seer and other attributes, according to the rule..."
The Guru should say three times into the left ear, "It is priceless.
The phrase "preceded by water" refers specifically to the case of a Brāhmaṇa.
"In this interval,
may it yield equal fruit for both of us"— thus the eminent sage, with a serene countenance, should speak to that disciple.
The Guru should visualize the knowledge, consisting of light, departing from himself;
the disciple should visualize it as having arrived.
Thus [it is said].

In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, however, it is said: "Then, by the command of the Guru, the disciple, in the presence of Śiva, the fire, and the Guru, shall utter the words of initiation (dīkṣāvākya) after having formed this intention with devotion."
"Better is the abandonment of life or even the cutting off of one's head,
than that I should eat without having worshipped the three-eyed Lord.
Following the gift of the Vidyā, the Guru should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times.
As it has been said: "One should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times in order to avoid the loss of one's own power.
Also, in the *Nārāyaṇīya* and the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*:
"Having imparted the mantra, the preceptor should indeed recite it a thousand times for his own success."
Thus [ends the section]. 111.

Contemplating with his intellect the identity of the Guru, the Vidyā, and the Deity, he should prostrate himself like a staff upon the ground before that Guru, who is the very essence of the Deity. || 112 ||
One should place his pair of lotus-feet upon one's own head;
one should offer to him one's body, wealth, and life—everything. || 113 ||
"One should prostrate," [it is said].
"O Lord, by your grace I am fulfilled in every way;
I am liberated from the great snare of illusion and death, and I am Śiva."
It should be understood that this means while reciting the mantra;

therein, a prostration consisting of either eight limbs or five limbs is to be performed. As they say: "With both arms, with the two feet, with the knees, with the chest, with the head, and with the eyes..."
With both mind and speech, the eight-limbed prostration is thus described.
"With both arms, the knees, the head, the speech, and the intellect—this is the five-limbed prostration; these two are the most excellent in all cases.
By the phrase "one should announce the matter," it is stated that one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the guru, as well as the water-pot (*kumbha*) and other items.
As they say:
"One should give half of one's wealth to the guru, or else half of that as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)."

In the *Mantratantraprakāśa* it is also said: "A mantra that has not been received from a preceptor, or one that has been received but for which the ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has not been given, does not attain accomplishment even if it is recited constantly."

"Having given the teacher a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of either one's entire wealth or half of it, while avoiding stinginess regarding one's riches, the reception of the mantra is then considered appropriate. Thus it is said.
And in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*: "One should give the pavilion, together with the implements of sacrifice, to the teacher."
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, elsewhere: "Having abandoned stinginess regarding wealth and having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), the wise man should offer up his own body as well."
Thus it is said.
Also elsewhere: "Having accomplished his purpose, the disciple, whose mind is drawn toward the guru through devotion, should report everything to him—whatever it may be and however much."
Cows, land, abundant gold, and many houses, fields, and so forth—
whether it be half of that, or half of that again, or even a tenth part thereof.
"One should give food, clothing, and so forth, without distress, according to one's wealth.
Likewise: "And having offered everything, including the water-pot and other items, to the guru."
Elsewhere it is also said: "A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to one’s own guru according to one’s means;
one of pure intellect should not practice stinginess regarding wealth toward the one who has granted the gift of life.
Thereafter, the duties of the guru as stated in other tantras are written down.
The Guru should instruct the disciple regarding bathing, the twilight rituals, right conduct, as well as the obligatory and optional rites, and the methods for attaining success through mantras.
Thus it is stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*.
Elsewhere also: "Then, having prostrated, let him listen properly to the pledges (*samayas*), with his body bowed down by the weight of devotion."
Regarding this, proper conduct (*sadācāra*) has been stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"In the presence of a deity, in the presence of a guru, in a cremation ground, or at a crossroads,
one should avoid shoes, sitting, excrement, urine, and sexual intercourse."

One should utter the words "Śrī" (the Auspicious One) first before [mentioning] the deity, the Guru, those in the position of Guru, the sacred field (kṣetra), the presiding deities of the field, the Siddhas, and those with authority over the Siddhas.
One should not revile a maiden who is intoxicated, of low birth, in her menses, with drooping breasts, deformed, with disheveled hair, or afflicted by lust.

One should not look upon a maiden’s private parts, nor engage in animal play, nor gaze at a woman clad in a single garment with her breasts exposed; one should avoid the property of others and the wives of others.
One should never stretch one's feet toward grain, cattle, teachers, deities, fire, knowledge, a treasury, or a king; nor should one step over them.
One should avoid laziness, intoxication, delusion, deceit, backbiting, and strife; one should also avoid envy, self-conceit, and the censuring of others.
One should not find fault with a Brahmin who bears the marks of his order and observes his vows, nor with the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, the Saṃhitās, the Purāṇas, the Āgama scriptures, or the Kalpas.
A pair [of tongs], a pestle, a stone, a rope, a hearth, a mortar, a winnowing basket,
a broom, a staff, a banner, and a vaidūrya weapon.
The water-pot, the chowrie, the parasol, the mirror, and likewise ornaments,
as well as other articles suitable for enjoyment and whatever sacrificial materials there may be.
Objects located in great sacred places or in temples,
as well as those things declared divine, which are indeed possessed by spirits.
One should never leap over these, nor should one touch them with one's feet:
a social gathering that is despised by the world, and one that spreads according to its own whims.
One should never engage in that which consists of harming others,
nor should one accept gifts out of a desire for personal enjoyment.
One should acquire wealth with effort for the sake of honoring the deities and guests;
one should maintain straightforwardness, truthfulness, good character, equanimity, and fortitude.
For one who always maintains patience, compassion, detachment, and divine power— these qualities mentioned here that are appropriate for both this world and the next—
"One who has been initiated should practice proper conduct and thereby attain peace.
Likewise: "One should not take shelter in the shade of the *vibhītaka*, *arka*, *kārañja*, or *nīhī* trees."
Of pillars, lamps, humans, and likewise of other living beings.
"One should avoid from afar the touch of the tips of nails, hair, phlegm, bathing water, and the water used for washing clothes, as well as the dust raised by donkeys and dogs. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, in the *Mantratantraprakāśa* by Somaśambhu: "One should not revile the Primordial Deity (Kāraṇadeva), nor the scripture composed by Him."
One should not step over the shadow of the Guru, the practitioner, or the Liṅga.
"One should not step over [the offerings], nor should one give away the *nirmālya* to one initiated by Śiva. Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Ṣaḍanvayamahārātra*: "One should not transgress the command of the Guru, nor should one speak back;
day and night, one should observe his command like a servant."
One should likewise abandon untruth, impurity, excessive talk,
that which is unpleasant, as well as laziness, and especially lust and anger.
One should never speak with an uncovered face in the presence of a guru;
nor should one harbor pride on account of wealth, caste, stage of life, or other such factors.
One must never consume the property of a guru if it has not been given by him;
if it is given, it should be accepted as a grace, and never out of greed.
One should renounce non-duality, the worship of deities, and the emblems of the guru— such as sandals, the yogic belt, and other implements of practice— in the presence of the guru.
One should never leap over it, nor even touch it with one's feet; one should always bow down before it. Likewise, one should not sleep on a couch, nor stretch out one's feet toward it.
One should not perform stretching of the limbs or playful gestures in the presence of the guru;
when going out or returning, one should do so after bowing to the guru’s sandals.
Having deliberated, one should perform one's duties; being gracious, one should attend to the teacher's business.
One should not step over the teacher’s shadow, nor should one walk ahead of the teacher.
One should depart from the teacher's house with the right foot first, having offered salutations;
one should not display one's own power or attempt to gather disciples in the presence of the teacher.
A wise person should not harbor egoism, nor should they maintain an arrogant physical posture; furthermore, in the presence of one's superior, one should not prostrate before one's own guru.
"Seeing one intent on prostration, the Guru should restrain him.
Likewise: "One should not carry out the Guru's command, nor should one speak with 'you' (yuṣmad)."
Thus [ends the section]. 112–113.
From that time forward, with a single-minded focus, he should do what is pleasing to his guru;
having given the full sacrificial fee to the officiating priests, he should do so with a joyful heart. || 114 ||
Thereafter, one should gratify the Brahmins with various kinds of food and edibles along with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
This is declared to be the "Kriyāvatī" initiation, which bestows all prosperity. || 115 ||

By the statement "one should do what is pleasing to the guru," the primacy of the guru’s satisfaction is expressed. As it is said in the *Daśapaṭalī*: "The disciple must also always perform service to the guru;
without such service, knowledge will not be fruitful."
"When the Guru is pleased, Śiva is pleased; when Śiva is pleased, the three worlds are pleased.
But when the Guru is angry, O Maheśānī, neither I nor you can protect [one].
Therefore, with every effort, one should not provoke the anger of the Guru. Thus it is said.
"To the officiating priests" (*ṛtvigbhyaḥ*) means to those beginning with the *brahmā*.

In that regard, it should be understood that after performing the purification of the *praṇītā* water, having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the *brahmā*, and having dismissed the *brahmā*, one should cause [the priests] to consume the remainder of the cooked oblation (*caru*) that was offered.
This is stated in the *Saṃhitā*:
Having performed the purification with water, one should give a gift to the Brahmins according to one's own means,
free from greed and delusion.
Then, having dismissed Brahmā, one should feed the Brahmins;
increasing through the words of blessing from those learned in the Vedas, one shall become happy.
Then, having consumed the remainder of the oblation in a portion the size of a hen's egg,
which has been consecrated with the Gāyatrī mantra.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore: "One should apply the sacred ash with the mantra *tryāyuṣaṃ yamagne*.
One should sprinkle oneself with water from a full vessel that has been consecrated seven times, using those waters along with *dūrvā* grass and *tulasī* leaves. (114-115)
Now I shall describe the initiation consisting of phonemes (varṇa), as known from the Āgamas.
Phonemes consist of the Puruṣa and Prakṛti; the body is likewise of such a nature. || 116 ||
Therefore, the preceptor should project the phonemes onto the body of the disciple;
he should then withdraw those phonemes, joined with their respective locations, in reverse order. || 117 ||

Then, by his own command and through the deity-state according to the ritual, the best of teachers causes this disciple—whose constituent principles have dissolved—to become possessed of a divine body. || 118 ||
Having united that consciousness with the Supreme Self, the supreme guru should then bring forth those phonemes from it and install them once more within the body of the disciple. || 119 ||
One should duly unite consciousness according to the sequence of emanation;
thus, the state of the deity, consisting of supreme bliss, arises in the disciple. || 120 ||
He speaks of the initiation consisting of phonemes (*varṇātmikā dīkṣā*), which follows in sequence, with the word "Now" (*atha*).
Regarding the phrase "that and that":
the supreme teacher, having united that consciousness—the consciousness of the disciple—with the Supreme Self, [does so] because of the state of being the deity, since he himself is the deity.
Therefore, because it is established by [the Guru's] command:

by one's own command according to the ritual procedure, through the reverse order—namely, the reverse order of both the phonemes (*varṇa*) and the positions (*sthāna*)—one should absorb the phonemes joined with their respective positions.
The meaning is that one should absorb the subsequent position and phoneme into the preceding position and phoneme.
The term "supreme guru" (*gurūttama*) is connected with what follows. "From that" means from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
"According to rule" (*vidhivat*) means the subsequent position and letter from the preceding position and letter.
By the word "ca" (and) in the phrase "caitanyaṃ ca," the term "in the body of the disciple" (*śiṣyatanau*) is to be supplied.
This has been stated by the Teachers:
"For the phonemes, transformed through the union of fire and moon, are indeed created..."
With these [mantras] recited in reverse order, one should thoroughly pervade this entire body—
which consists of the elements and is composed of skin, blood, and so forth—
according to the rule, by means of the method of sharp intelligence.

Having sequentially withdrawn the final letters from the consonants, those respective [letters] from the four groups of letters in the scripts, these from the nasalized syllables (*anunāsika*), and likewise from the following vowels, he—
having contracted [the breath] together with its place of articulation and having dissolved his entire body— abides within the forehead at the end.
May he, who has pervaded the twenty-two worlds with his attainment, enter into my very being.
Rising from the *mūlādhāra* with a radiance like a flash of lightning, subtle in form and reaching to the crown of the head, she is the most minute root of all splendors;
skilled in traversing the path of the *suṣumṇā*, she is permeated by the Sun.
Then, while meditating, one should immediately cause the nectar to flow from the Sun together with the Half-Moon.
May that stream of nectar falling upon the head,
which consists of syllables, fashion with those [syllables] the entire body, beginning with the face; and may the splendor fallen within [the heart] likewise do so.
Like fire with clarified butter, he should kindle his own spiritual splendor.
Having thus withdrawn and then produced a body composed of light that pervades all the worlds,
he should conceive his own form as consisting of the power (śakti).
One should also apply that mark to oneself. Thus [ends verses 116–120].
This initiation consisting of the phonemes (varṇa), which bestows consciousness, has been declared.
Thereafter, the initiation consisting of the digits (kalā) is described according to the rule. || 121 ||
Since the five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, are the powers of the elements, one should pierce the disciple by meditating upon them within the body composed of those elements. || 122 ||
Nivṛtti is situated beginning from the soles of the feet up to the knees; Pratiṣṭhā stands pervading the space from the knees up to the navel. || 123 ||
The Vidyā-mantra pervades from the navel up to the throat; beyond that is the Śānti-mantra.
From the throat up to the forehead it is pervaded by the Śāntyatīta-mantra, and from there up to the crest (śikhā). || 124 ||
The *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatītā*) is to be known; it is declared to be the pervasion of the *kalās*.
By means of the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), the Guru [moves] from one station to another station. (125)
Having united them, the wise one should pierce them by means of the Command (ājñā) up to the limit of Śiva;
this is declared to be the initiation of the Kalās, which bestows a divine state. || 126 ||
He describes the sequence of Kalāvatī’s initiation with the word "tataḥ" (then).
Regarding the phrase "having meditated," that meditation which was indicated is explained by the passage ending with "the cessation [of the world]," and so forth.
"From the sole" means from the soles of the feet.
The connection is that [one should begin] from the knees, the navel, the throat, and from there the forehead.
Having joined them from one place to another by means of the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), one should pierce the body of the disciple; this is the connection.
Withdrawal, as before, occurs into their respective causes.
"Up to Śiva, ending with Śiva.
Although the origination from Śiva via the path of emanation (*sṛṣṭimārga*) has not been explicitly stated, it is to be understood as before. 121–126.

Next, I shall describe the initiation consisting of piercing (*vedha*), which liberates one from the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). One should meditate within the body of the disciple, at the four-petaled *mūlādhāra*. || 127 ||

In the center of the triangle, O stainless one, where the threefold radiance unfolds, she is joined with three encircling bands and possesses a splendor equal to ten million flashes of lightning. || 128 ||
Having swiftly pierced the six chakras, one reaches the Goddess who consists of Śiva and Śakti, whose form is pure consciousness alone, the subtle and most subtle Power. || 129 ||
As she proceeds along the middle path toward the divine Supreme Śiva,
one should withdraw the letters situated on the petals from Va to Sa while seated upon the lotus throne.

Having joined that [energy] within the Svādhiṣṭhāna, which is a six-petaled lotus endowed with the letters beginning with *ba* and ending with *la*, the Guru should pierce it by means of the Command (*ājñā*). || 131 ||
The Guru should dissolve those phonemes into Viṣṇu, and him again into the navel-lotus;
there, upon the ten-petaled lotus enriched with the phonemes from *ḍa* to *pha*, he should unite [the self]. || 132 ||

The Guru should withdraw those phonemes into Rudra, and then, having joined him into the heart-lotus—which is enriched by the twelve solar phonemes from *ka* to *ṭha*—he should unite him with Īśvara. || 133 ||
One should draw those letters into this [lotus], and again into that sixteen-petaled lotus of the throat which is enriched with vowels; having joined the vowels there once more, || 134 ||
Having withdrawn them into Sadāśiva, the Guru then joins him once again between the two eyebrows, upon the two-petaled lotus that is white with the letters *ha* and *kṣa*. || 135 ||

The Guru should dissolve that [vowel] into its corresponding consonant, and join that [consonant] into the Bindu; he should join that [Bindu] into the Kalā, and subsequently join that Kalā into the Nāda, and finally join the Nāda into the Nādānta. || 136 ||
Having united that [power] with Unmanī, and that within the mouth of Viṣṇu, the best of teachers should again unite it with the mouth of the Guru. || 137 ||
Together with his own self, he should pierce the power (śakti) into the Supreme Lord;
then, by the command of the Guru, the disciple, with his bonds severed, shall fall to the earth. || 138 ||
Having attained divine awakening, he realizes everything at that very moment;
he becomes Śiva manifest—there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 139 ||
This initiation consisting of piercing bestows all forms of consciousness;
the fourfold initiation has been correctly described in this tantra according to its sequence. || 140 ||
He describes the initiation consisting of piercing (*vedhamayī dīkṣā*) with the word "then" (*tataḥ*).
The locative cases in the phrase "in the middle of the body," "at the *mūlādhāra*," and "in the middle of the triangle" are used in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
The connection is as follows: one should meditate upon such a Śakti in the middle of the triangle at the four-petalled *mūlādhāra* within the body of the disciple.
What kind of power? Endowed with three coils (*valaya*).

Although, in this context, the coils of the Power (*śakti*) are indeed immeasurable, it is nevertheless so described because she arises from the three coils of the primary creation, such as the three Vedas. Furthermore, what kind [of power]?
Having pierced the six chakras by way of the central path, the *suṣumnā*, it proceeds as far as Paraśiva.
The six chakras are known as Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūraka, Anāhata, Viśuddha, and Ājñā. "In the Lotus-seated One" refers to Brahmā, the presiding deity of the *ādhāra*.

In this manner, Viṣṇu and the others are to be understood as the presiding deities of the Svādhiṣṭhāna and the other centers. One should join that Brahmā with those letters from *ba* to *la*, and that Viṣṇu with the lotus of the navel, the Maṇipūraka.
Then, the word "should pierce" (vedhayet) is to be supplied [to the verse].
Those letters from *ḍa* to *pha*;
that Rudra.
Having joined them in the heart-lotus, which is rich with twelve petals—[the lotus] of the *anāhata* [cakra]—one should pierce it; this is the syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*).
The Guru should dissolve those letters, from *ka* to *ṭha*, into the Lord (*īśvara*); such is the construction.
Immediately thereafter, having joined the Lord (Īśvara) into this lotus-throat (the Viśuddhi-cakra), one should pierce it—this is the syntactical connection.
Having withdrawn those vowels into Sadāśiva, such is the construction.
Having joined that Sadāśiva into the "hair-leaf" (bhrūsaroruha) of the Ājñā-cakra, one should pierce it—this is the syntactical connection.
The phrase "one should employ at the beginning" and so forth means that one should pierce;
its two syllables are *ha* and *kṣa*.
[One should place them] in the *bindu*, which is Śiva.
Because it is said that "the *bindu* has Śiva as its essence," [he refers to] that Śiva.
These six cakras, beginning with *kalā*, are situated one above the other starting from the middle of the eyebrows.
For this very reason, the *sahasrāra* is the *dvādaśānta*.

Thus, according to the previously mentioned sequence, the connection is that one should pierce the power (*śakti*), namely Kuṇḍalinī, into the Supreme Lord Śiva by means of the self—the individual soul of the disciple.
This is because it is impossible to perform the piercing without the power.
For this very reason, there is the instruction that one should first meditate on Śakti in the Mūlādhāra.
Consequently, it should be understood that the piercing (*vedha*) in the Svādhiṣṭhāna and other centers is also performed by Śakti alone.
"With severed bonds" (*chinnapāśaḥ*) means being liberated from the three bonds (*pāśatraya*).
As stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"The bond (*pāśa*) is defined as the fixation upon actions, whether they be virtuous or non-virtuous;
that bond, which is the sole means of bondage, should be understood as being threefold."
"The first is the innate bond (*sahaja-pāśa*), and the other is the adventitious (*āgantuka*); the third is the incidental (*prāsangika*). Thus, the triad of bonds is remembered.
Just as, through the piercing (*vedha*) performed by the author’s supreme guru, Ācārya Somānanda, the author’s gurus, Utpalācārya and others, became one with Śiva.
The lineage of the author’s gurus is shown in the commentary on the third verse.
Thus, through the piercing (*vedha*) performed by Caṇḍeśvarācārya, Śivasvāmin became one whose very self is Śiva.
Likewise, the venerable Śrīkaṇṭhācāryas said:

"Knowledge of time, as well as the deception of time in another body, entry [into another body], piercing, and so forth, are obtained when Śiva is propitiated. Thus he concludes with the word "gradually" (kramāt).

In the *Ṣaḍanvayamahāratna*, it is stated that this individual initiation (*āṇavī dīkṣā*) is of ten kinds. As follows: "The individual initiation is manifold, while the initiations of power (*śākteyī*) and of Śambhu (*śāmbhavī*) are each single; thus it is recited by the learned who are experts in the scriptures."
The *āṇavī* [power] has been described as being manifold; its divisions are now stated:
the *smārtī*, the *mānasikī*, the *yaugī*, the *cākṣuṣī*, and likewise the *spārśanī*.
The consecration (ābhiṣecikī) is of four kinds: vocal (vācikī), mantra-based (māntrikī), pertaining to the Hotṛ priest (hautrī), and scriptural (śāstrī).
Recalling the disciple who resides in a foreign land, the Guru [severs] the three bonds (pāśatraya) in succession.

Having separated [the soul] through the procedure involving dissolution (*laya*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and the limbs (*aṅga*), this [process] consisting of perfect union within the supreme Śiva is called the "Smārta initiation" (*smārtī dīkṣā*).
Having perceived with the mind one who is pure and seated in her own presence,
that [power] which liberates from the three impurities by means of the methods is indeed the mental [power].
Having entered the body of the disciple according to the sequence taught in yoga, the yogin takes hold of that disciple's self and performs the union with his own self.
That is declared to be the initiation of yoga, which destroys the three impurities;
it consists of gazing while firmly resolving "I am Śiva," with a heart moistened by compassion.
That initiation by sight (*cākṣuṣī-dīkṣā*) is the destroyer of all sins;
having himself become Supreme Śiva, the Guru, with a mind free from doubt, [performs it].
With the hand of Śiva, one should touch the head of the disciple while reciting the mantra;
this is called the initiation by touch (sparśadīkṣā), which effects the manifestation of Śiva.
(Regarding the characteristics of the Hand of Śiva, Somaśambhu states:
"One should fashion a mandala with perfumes on one's own right hand;
there, one should worship the Lord according to the prescribed rite—thus shall the Hand of Śiva be formed. )
Having visualized his own mouth as the mouth of the Guru, the Guru, with reverence,
[bestows] the divine mantras and so forth upon the disciple through the application of the Guru’s mouth.

Together with the placement of mudrās (mudrānyāsa) and other rites, one should bestow this, for it is indeed the supreme oral initiation (vācikī dīkṣā); likewise, [the disciple's] body becomes conjoined with the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).

Having himself become the embodiment of the mantra, he should reverently bestow the mantra upon the disciple in its proper sequence; that is the Mantra-initiation (māntrī-dīkṣā), which destroys impurity.
Having deposited the fire according to the prescribed rule either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a sacrificial mound (sthāṇḍila),
one should proceed through each path (adhvan) in due order, following the sequence of dissolution and enjoyment.
This initiation pertaining to the Hotṛ priest, consisting of oblations, is proclaimed for the sake of purification [of] the mantra, syllable, part, principle, word, and world.
For a worthy disciple who is devoted and intent upon service and worship,
the initiation performed together with the threefold words of the scripture is called the scriptural initiation (śāstrī-dīkṣā).
Having respectfully worshipped both Śiva and the consort of Śiva in the pitcher,
that initiation which results from the consecration with the pitcher of Śiva shall be known as the *ābhiṣecikī* (consecratory) initiation.
Now, the measurements for the substances used in the oblation (homa) are stated here:
one karṣa of clarified butter is prescribed for the oblation, and milk is recorded as being one śukti in measure. || 141 ||
The five products of the cow have been described by the wise as being equal [in merit]; honey, milk, and cooked rice in the measure of an akṣa are declared to be equal to those.

The curd should be the measure of a handful (prasṛti); the parched rice grains (lāja) should be the measure of a fist; the flattened rice (pṛthuka) should be of that same measure, and the groats (śaktu) are likewise declared to be so.

Jaggery should be half a *pala* in measure, and sugar is considered to be the same; the quantity of sacrificial oblation (*caru*) should be half a mouthful, and sugarcane is considered to be measured by the joint. || 144 ||
One should arrange each leaf and flower, as well as each cake;
they know that the plantain fruit and the orange fruit should likewise be offered one by one. || 145 ||
The mātuluṅga fruit is divided into four pieces, the jackfruit into ten;
the wise know that coconuts are cut into eight pieces. || 146 ||
The bilva fruit is to be divided into three parts, and the kapittha fruit is to be cut into three pieces;
likewise, the urvāruka fruit is prescribed to be cut into three pieces for the homa.
Other fruits should be cut into pieces, and the sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) should be ten finger-breadths long;
three blades of dūrvā grass are prescribed, and the guḍūcī should be four finger-breadths long.
The rice should be one handful; likewise, the mung beans, black gram, and barley;
the grains should be half that amount, while the kodrava should be measured at one handful. || 149 ||
Wheat and red rice are prescribed by the measure of a handful;
sesame seeds should be the size of a palmful, and mustard seeds are of that same measure. || 150 ||
Salt measuring one *śukti*, twenty-one *marīca* peppers, one *pura* of *vadarā* (jujube) size, and *rāmaṭha* (asafetida) of equal measure are prescribed. || 151 ||
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron—each the size of a tamarind seed—are prescribed by the masters. || 152 ||
"Only one karṣa" means that the definition of a *karṣa* has been stated previously;
it should be understood that this same measure applies to oil as well.
"Only a śukti" means two karṣas constitute a śukti;
"only an akṣa" means one karṣa.
"A handful" (*prasṛti*) is the measure of two *palas*.
"Measured by a fist" (*muṣṭisammita*) means measured by a *pala*.
"Puffed rice" (*pṛthuka*) refers to flattened grains.
Half a *pala* is two *karṣas*.
Half a mouthful (*grāsārddha*) is eighty *raktikās*.
As it has been said:
Ten *guñjās* make one *māṣa*; four *māṣas* make one *śāṇa*.
Two *śāṇas* make a *ghaṭaka*, which is also known as a *kāla*, a *badara*, and a *drakṣaṇa*.
Two of those [tindukas] make one pāṇitala; two pāṇitalas make one karṣa; two karṣas make one suvarṇa; two suvarṇas make one kavalagraha;
two kavalagrahas make one picu; two picus make one vīḍālapadaka; and two vīḍālapadakas make one tinduka or akṣa.
"Śukti is eight māṣakas; two of those are one pala. Bilva is four fourths [of a pala]. A muṣṭi is an āmra; a prakūñca is likewise two palas, as is a prasṛti."
*Mātuluṅga* is the citron;
*urvāruka* is the cucumber. Regarding the term *samidhaḥ* (fuel sticks): [they are as follows].
In this regard, the specific characteristics [to be avoided] are as follows:
those that are shattered, split in two, short, crooked, thick, thin,
worm-eaten, long, or devoid of their husks should be rejected.
A split [line] causes the destruction of one's lifespan; a bifurcated one gives rise to disease;
in a short line one meets death, and likewise, a crooked one creates obstacles.

If the lines are thick, one's fortune is lost; if they are thin, there is the exhaustion of the officiating priest. If they are of two kinds (uneven), eye diseases will arise; and if bitten by insects, it destroys wealth.
Those that are long, skinless, and known to be life-destroyers produce hatred;
sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) that possess milk, and are neither too large nor too small, grant all desires.
[One should take a stick] with moist bark, cut evenly, and as round as the index finger.
"A wise person should offer such [fuel-sticks] and attains abundant prosperity.
The fuel-sticks (samidh) prescribed for the Śrauta, Smārta, and Tantric rites have thus been described.
Regarding another specific detail, it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"One should collect sacrificial fuel-sticks from other trees, avoiding the *śleṣmātaka* and *piśāca* trees.
Thus [it is said].
They should be the size of a handful, weighing one *pala*.
Half of that amount consists of two *karṣas*.
"A mere handful" (*culukamātra*) means a measure of one *karṣa*,
since the term "palm of the hand" (*pāṇitala*) refers to a handful.
A *śukti* is two *karṣas*.
*Pura* is *guggulu*.
The measure of a *badara* is eighty *guñjās*.
*Rāmaṭha* is asafoetida (*hiṅgu*).
However, in the *Śaiva-āgama*:
"One should offer as oblation three pieces of roots and five fine [fibers]."
"The eighth part for the bulbous roots, and two finger-breadths for the creepers. (141–152)

The preceptor should meditate on Vaiśvānara as standing during the offerings of fuel-sticks (samidh), as lying down during the offerings of clarified butter (ājya), and as seated during all other matters. || 153 ||
One should offer oblations into the mouth of the fire, O wise one, in all ritual acts.
Fire with smoke should be known as the head, while smokeless fire is indeed the eye. || 154 ||
The ear becomes like a burning black flame, and likewise the nose like wood on fire;
the tongue is like a blazing fire—this indeed is the characteristic of fire. || 155 ||
If the oblation is offered at the ear, disease occurs; if at the eye, blindness is declared;
if at the nose, mental anguish arises; and if at the head, the loss of wealth follows. || 156 ||
"Stationed" means arisen.
"Within the mouth" refers to the definition of the mouth and so forth, which has been stated elsewhere:
Fire with smoke should be known as the head, and smokeless fire as the eyes;
the blazing, slender flame is the ears, and the wood of the fire is the nose.
"Where the fire flickers like pure crystal, that should be known as the mouth [of the fire], measuring four finger-breadths.
Furthermore, in the *Vanadurgākalpa* proclaimed by the Guru: "For the sake of accomplishing all undertakings, one should perform the oblation there upon the tongue [of the fire]."
Having recognized the eyes, ears, and other [limbs], the most excellent of preceptors should perform the fire oblation.
If one makes an offering in the ear of Agni, there will be fear from disease;
if in the nose, great suffering; and in the eyes, blindness shall occur.
It is declared that [a flame] on the hair brings poverty; therefore, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) upon the tongues [of the flames].
Where there is wood, that is in the ears; where there is smoke, that is in the nose.
"Where there is a slight glow in the eyes, that is its head;
where the fire blazes, there the tongue is said to be.
By the word "Vipaścit," this is what is meant.
In the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) for the destruction of enemies, by offering oblations into these specific parts of the fire, the corresponding limbs of the enemy are destroyed.
As they say: "If one should offer oblations into the head of the fire, the nose, the ear, or likewise the eye, then it will swiftly destroy those very limbs. (153–156)
The beautiful color of Suvarṇaretas is described as resembling gold, vermilion, the morning sun, saffron, and honey. || 157 ||
*Kṣaudra* means honey.
A complexion resembling gold, saffron, and honey is considered beautiful;
this should be understood to apply to the stage of *ākṛṣṭi*.
As it is said in the venerable *Matangapārameśvara*: "The attraction of both divine and non-divine beings is always desired;
[the one who is] like molten gold and like yellow orpiment."
"The color of turmeric or realgar, as well as that resembling gorocanā, is praised. Thus it is said.
It should be understood that "the color of vermilion or the morning sun" is for the sake of victory (*jayārtha*).
That which has the luster of a ruby (*padmarāga*) or is like the juice of lac is excellent.
A fire with the color of the rising sun is praised by the wise for the sake of victory.
For it is stated there [in that context]:
"But regarding another rite, in that very same place:
'The fire resembles an *indragopaka* insect, or has the appearance of blood.'"
It is praised when resembling a rainbow, and likewise when resembling saffron water.
A color equal to that of red varieties of flowers is praised. Thus [it is said]. (157)

The sound of fire that resembles the roar of kettledrums, rain-clouds, or lordly elephants is auspicious; likewise, a scent resembling nagakesara, campaka, punnāga, pāṭala, or yūthikā flowers is auspicious. || 158 ||
Resembling the scent of the padma, indīvara, kahlāra, and sapī flowers, as well as guggulu resin—this is declared by those who know the tantras to be the auspicious fragrance of fire. || 159 ||

The phrase "the drum" and so forth is an illustration; for the sake of success, the sound of fire is known to grant accomplishment when it is like the resonance of clouds, a lute, a conch, or a mṛdaṅga drum, and not otherwise.
The term "nāga" and so forth is indicative [of other fragrances as well], for it is said:
"The fragrance of aromatic substances and the fragrance of ghee are auspicious.
The fragrance of the lotus leads to long life, while the fragrance of the blue water-lily (*indīvara*) and others leads to good fortune.
As it has been said: "A fragrance equal to the blue lotus is immediately commended for good fortune;
the scent of the lotus leads to longevity, and the scent of the *bilva* fruit, O virtuous lady, [is likewise beneficial].
There is also a specific distinction: "In this context, a pungent odor is always praised for the practice of *abhicāra* (malevolent magic). (158–159)
The flames of the sacrificial fire, which move clockwise, are free from flickering, and resemble the luster of an umbrella;
they bestow auspiciousness upon the sacrificer, and especially so upon his kingdom. || 160 ||

Smoke as white as a jasmine flower or the moon is declared to be auspicious for fire; however, smoke that is black in color portends the destruction of the patron, even if he possesses a dark complexion. || 161 ||
A white fire, resembling the sound of a crow, quickly destroys the kingdom; a sound like the braying of a donkey brings about the total destruction of the fire. || 162 ||
The term "resembling an umbrella" (*chatrābhā*) is an illustration;
for it is said: "An arm shaped like an umbrella is excellent, as is one resembling a banner or a chowrie.
Thus, a black [arm] destroys the sacrificer, while a white one destroys the kingdom.
It should be understood that this applies specifically to the ritual action involving colors such as red or yellow, and not in a general sense.
As they say: "Having understood that particular suitability which corresponds to each respective ritual action..."

"One should always accept [the time] for an action or reject it according to its opposite. Regarding this, the specific detail is stated in that very same work: "In this rite of killing, expulsion, and destruction, the color of black flowers and the color of fire are desired here as most auspicious."

"White and auspicious, even whiter than conch, crystal, jasmine, or the moon—such a fire is always prescribed for rites of pacification (śāntika) or nourishment (pauṣṭika). Thus it is said. By that same authority, the blackness [of the fire] is also declared to be avoided:
"Equal to a bee, collyrium, or a sword, it does not bestow success in terms of color.
There is also another distinction: "That which resembles the eye of a cat or the plumage of a parrot is not to be accepted."
"Resembling the neck of a peacock, with the luster of a variegated pigeon. (160–162)
If the fire has a foul odor, it will bring suffering to the sacrificer;
if its flame has broken curls, it will cause death and the depletion of wealth. || 163 ||
Smoke resembling the color of a parrot’s wing, or possessing a luster like that of a pigeon, soon brings about the loss of horses and cattle. || 164 ||
When such defects have occurred, the preceptor should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra as an act of expiation. || 165 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Śāradātilaka composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇa Deśikendra. || 5 ||
"Pūtigandha" means a foul odor.
"Death," and so forth, follow in their respective order.
By the phrase "of such a kind," this is what is meant:
A fire that resembles a bull or an elephant in its movement always bestows prosperity;
this applies to those fires that arise from celestial chariots, canopies, or palaces.
Furthermore, by its shape, it is praised as being like a swan or a peacock;
however, the fire that always has the form of a lion is remembered as one that grants immediate success.
The forms of the remaining fanged creatures are not recommended for the rite of homa;
the forms of donkeys, camels, buffaloes, and the like do not lead to success in this matter.
That which is smooth, turning to the right, and possesses a pleasant sound should be recognized as leading to the accomplishment of one's goals; otherwise, it causes obstacles.

"O best of sages, one who is harsh, makes a crackling sound, always moves in a counter-clockwise direction, scratches the earth, or has hair pointing downwards— such a person is not accepted in this scripture of the Supreme Lord."
Regarding the phrase "twenty-five":

according to the principle that for every occurrence of a cause, the corresponding effect recurs—whether one perceives two defects or three defects—the oblations must be offered twenty-five times. || 163-165 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition. 5.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Next, I shall describe the form consisting of the [five] colors, which brings about universal awakening;
for if this is not perceived, this entire world remains inert.
After the description of initiation (*dīkṣā*), the mantras must be taught; therefore, he promises to explain the *mātṛkā*, which is their source, with the word "Now" (*atha*).
He refers to the *mātṛkā* as "the body of phonemes.
It is the generative cause of all cognitions—which consist of the expansion of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*)—and which exist in the forms of *parā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*.
The meaning is: "that power," namely the power that ordains and unfolds. || 1 ||
The Seer is declared to be Brahmā; Gāyatrī is said to be the metre;
and Sarasvatī is proclaimed as the deity by the best of teachers. || 2 ||
By the word "samuddiṣṭa" (pointed out), there is a connection with the term *vidhi* (rule); by the word "īrita" (uttered), there is a connection with the term *devī* (goddess);
and by the word "samākhyāta" (designated), there is a connection with the term *mātṛkā* (matrix).
This is the view of the teacher Padmapāda.
By the phrase "by the supreme teachers," it is indicated that the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and powers (*śakti*) are also to be mentioned.
In this regard, some hold that the consonants are the seeds and the vowels are the powers.
As it is stated in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
"O Supreme Goddess, the consonants are the seeds (bījas), and the vowels are the powers (śaktis)."
It should be understood that these very *bīja* and *śakti* [mantras] apply to all *mātṛkā* mantras, from the *lipi* of the ground (*bhūtala*) up to those distinct from the *prapañcayāga*.
Elsewhere, other *bīja* and *śakti* mantras are mentioned,
as they say:
"The letter *a* together with a *bindu* is proclaimed as its seed-syllable (*bīja*);
the letter *a* together with two *bindus* is designated as the Power (*śakti*).
As for the application (*viniyoga*), it is "the application in the recitation" at the time of reciting the *mātṛkā* mantra.

It should be understood that, except in cases where it is performed as part of a mantra, its application (*viniyoga*) is in the rite of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as a constituent part of that specific mantra. || 2 ||

The six limbs, conjoined with their respective seed-syllables (jāti), should be assigned by the teachers in due order using the six groups of consonants, beginning with the neuter and ending with the short and long vowels. || 3 ||

Regarding the term *aklība*: "eunuchs" (*klība*) refers to the neuter vowels *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*; those devoid of these are *aklība*. Among these, the short vowels are *a*, *i*, *u*, *e*, *o*, and *aṃ*—these six being the short ones—and the others are the long ones; [the text refers to] those included within or situated among them.
And those six groups (varga) are which? The plural number is used for the sake of including the first [of each group].
By "kādayaḥ" (the ka-series and so forth)—namely ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya—one [should understand] the heart and the other [limbs] in their respective order.
"Endowed with seed-syllables" means they are joined with "Hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth.
The practical application (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: *aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and so on.
By the phrase "by the teachers," the following is intended:

here, having performed the purification of the hands (*kara-śuddhi*) with the four neuter [mantras], one should assign the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) from the palms and backs of the hands to the thumbs and other fingers according to the statement: "One should assign [the mantras] to the thumbs and other fingers along with their respective classes. Thus, having assigned the limbs starting with *aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ* as "salutation to the two thumbs" (*aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*), and so forth, then—

Having placed the sixteen vowels upon the palms and backs of both the right and left hands—starting from the little finger of the right hand up to the thumb of the left hand—one should then place the consonants from *ka* to *sa* in sequence, four letters on each joint starting from the left index finger up to the right index finger, and the letters *ha* and *la* on the two thumbs. Finally, one should place the letter *kṣa* on all the fingers; this is to be known as the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* of the hands.

Thus it should be understood in all cases. As stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Then, by means of the respective [finger], its back, and its pervasion, one should place the six [syllables] and so forth, beginning with the little finger on the right-hand fingers."
Having placed [the mantras] ending with the left thumb, one should then place the consonants as well,
starting from the left index finger, four by four.

Just as in the sequence of the fingers, up to the right index finger, one should place [the mantras] on the two thumbs; this is declared to be the *karanyāsa* (placement on the hands). Thus [ends verse 3].
Her face, arms, palms, waist, and chest are adorned with the fifty letters; she wears a radiant crown bound with the crescent moon, possesses full and lofty breasts,
and holds in her lotus-like hands a mudrā, a rosary, a jar brimming with nectar, and the Goddess of Knowledge.
I take refuge in the Goddess of Speech, who bears a radiant white luster and possesses three eyes. || 4 ||
"Fifty" [refers to the fingers].
The state of being divided will become clear through the description of the locations for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) that is about to be stated.
The *mudrā* is the *jñānamudrā*, consisting of the union of the thumb and forefinger, facing sideways.
As they say:
"The thumb and index finger joined at their tips, with the other fingers extended,
facing sideways— this is proclaimed as the *jñānamudrā*."
"Vidyā" means the book and its seal;
"the book-seal is formed by binding the left fist facing oneself.
[She is] of clear radiance and white complexion.
This is an illustration for garments, body-unguents, and garlands; likewise, in all subsequent instances, this should be understood for all terms denoting colors.
Regarding the visualization of the weapons: "upward and so forth" means [the first] on the right, and the others on the left.

Here, immediately after the meditations, one should display the weapon-mudrās. In the same way, it should be understood that this applies up to the end of the mantra of Sarasvatī in what follows. The meditation on each individual syllable, as taught in another tantra, is as follows:
(a) Resembling gold, with eight arms resplendent with tridents and maces,
four-faced and of immense body, he whose vehicle is the tortoise is the letter *A*.
