White in complexion, holding a noose and a goad in her hands, seated upon a lotus with an elephant as her vehicle,
she measures sixty yojanas in height and is adorned with ornaments of pearls.
(i) Yellow in color, holding a lotus-hand, a vajra, and an axe, it destroys enemies;
measuring two or one yojana, it is the letter *I* situated upon a tortoise.
This [letter] *Ī* is five yojanas long and two and a half yojanas wide;
she has a swan for her vehicle, bestows nourishment, is white in color, rich with pearls, and has a white face.
Holding a mace and a goad in his hands, having a crow as his vehicle, adorned with black ornaments,
he is two thousand yojanas in height and is the imperishable one.

The two Ṛ-letters, which are red in color, have nooses and spears as their arms, are mounted upon camels situated within the orb of fire, possess the previously mentioned dimensions, and are destroyers of Time. They should be visualized as such.
Seated upon a swan atop a four-cornered lotus, possessing a luster equal to a topaz,
with hands holding a noose and a vajra, the fierce pair of *ḷ* and *ḹ* brings about restraint.

(e) The great syllable *E* shall be dark-complexioned, seated upon a ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), adorned with necklaces and ornaments, and its hands enriched with a mace, a fruit, an enemy, and a lotus.
(e) Resembling a fresh jasmine flower, with tridents and vajras in her arms, standing upon an elephant,
and measuring ten million yojanas— this is the form of Aīm, the bestower of poetic skill.
Consisting of consciousness, all-pervading, tranquil, and blazing with two thousand rays,
it is yellow in color, seated upon a bull, possesses the form of a boar, and is the essence of Śrīkara.
Resembling molten gold, she bestows the power of the noose and the discus upon her arms;
for a thousand *yojanas*, she is of golden hue and immeasurable splendor.
Having the luster of fresh saffron, seated upon a lotus, adorned with red ornaments,
four-armed, and golden-hued, he bestows prosperity and destroys enemies.
One should meditate on [the deity] who holds a vajra-spear, who is minor, who bestows the fruit of battle, who has a donkey as his vehicle,
who measures one thousand yojanas, whose name ends in a vowel, and who has two arms.
Seated upon the earth-disk and an elephant, resembling fresh saffron in color,
holding a trident and a vajra, he is black and measures two thousand yojanas.
(kha) With a noose and a spear in his hands, he is mounted upon a ram; he is the Restrainer, black and terrifying, measuring a thousand yojanas in extent.
The letter Ga is red in luster, stands upon a lotus, rests on a serpent, is adorned with snakes, holds a noose and a goad in its hands, and extends for a hundred yojanas.
(gha) He stands upon a camel and an owl; he holds a mace and a vajra; he is immeasurable, possesses two faces, extends for a thousand yojanas, and is dark-colored.
(Ṅa) The syllable Ṅa should be black, with blazing radiance, two-armed, and mounted upon a crow; it is ten million yojanas in length and half a yojana in width, and it bestows minor fruits.
(ca) He should be situated upon a lotus at the tip of the cosmic age, possessing four arms and white radiance;
he has matted hair, is richly endowed with fragrance, and extends for ten million *yojanas*.
(Cha) He is white, of that same size, four-armed, and of a pale-white complexion;
(Ja, Jha) and there are two others, each measuring ten million [yojanas], four-armed, and possessing a white radiance.
(Ña) The vehicle of the crow should be measured at thousands of yojanas;
it causes enmity, is marked by the syllable Ña, is black in color, and has two arms.
Seated upon a curlew, he has two arms, is bound by serpents, and possesses a great sound;
in the syllable *ṭha*, he stands upon the earth, a lotus, and a lordly elephant, radiant with two hands.
The pervasive Lord, who destroys poison, measures one hundred thousand yojanas;
in the letter *ḍa*, he likewise has eight arms, four faces, and is beautifully adorned.
(Ḍha) Measuring a thousand *yojanas*, he stands upon the earth;
born from the orb of fire, he has ten arms and a blazing radiance.
He would indeed be a thousand *yojanas* in measure, seated upon a tiger;
he would possess sixty years of age, have four arms, and be well-adorned.
Measuring a thousand [yojanas], rich in fragrance, with the luster of saffron, and consisting of those syllables;
he should be ten million yojanas in measure, possessing eight arms and four faces.
(Tha) Yellow-colored, mounted upon a bull, and terrifying even in his own form;
(Da) two-faced, six-armed, possessing a crore-fold measure, and seated upon a buffalo.
(dha) Siṃhavāha has four arms and measures four hundred thousand [in size]. (na) Dvibhuja, who rides upon a crow, should be one thousand [in size].
(Pa) The letter *pa* is twenty-armed, ten-faced, and stands upon a peak (*koṭi*), measuring one *koṭi* [yojanas].
(Pha) The letter *pha* measures ten *koṭis* of *yojanas* and possesses two arms.
(ba) Seated upon a lotus that is the seat of a lion, he is restless, white, six-faced, and two-armed; the syllable *ba* is ten crores [in extent] and ruddy.
(bha) He whose vehicle is a swan shining amidst blue lotuses, the bestower of nourishment;
he who has three hands, three faces, a tiger as his vehicle, and a terrifying form.
The letter *ma* is worth ten lakhs of gold coins; it has a smoky luster and possesses great power. It is four-armed and resembles a venomous serpent.
Adorned with garlands of skulls, resplendent with the crescent moon,
pervasive, four-faced (or four-armed), smoke-colored, and seated upon a deer— such is the syllable YĀṂ.
Seated upon a triangle, a lotus, and a ram, she possesses four arms;

(Ṣa) then Ṣa, which in the rite of subjugation (kārmaṇa) is blackish in appearance, has the measure of a thousand, and possesses two arms.
He who measures ten million [in size] is white, possessing a body as radiant as a swan, and endowed with two arms.
He whose form is the syllable *ha* is white, has three arms, and is crowned by the all-pervading moon.

The forms of the syllable *ḷh* hold a noose and the gesture of fearlessness; they are white, mounted on elephants, and reside upon the orb of the earth and mountains. The syllable *kṣo* has ten arms and possesses the luster of jewels.
(ksa) Thus, the various manifestations of the phonemes have been expounded by me here. || 4 ||
On the forehead, the face, the circular eyes, the ears, the nose, the two cheeks, the lips, the teeth, the head, the mouth, and on the joints and tips of the arms and legs; || 5 ||

In the two sides, in the back, in the navel, in the abdomen, and in the heart; likewise in the shoulder-blades, in the hump, in the shoulders, starting from the heart, and similarly in the pair of hands and feet. || 6 ||

One who has been initiated should, with a concentrated mind, perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of [the mantras] beginning with *vā* and ending with *sā*, preceded by the knowledge of oneself and the Supreme, according to the path described, reciting them one hundred thousand times. || 8 ||
The wise one should mutter [the mantra] ten thousand times with sesame seeds soaked in honey;

On the two sides, beginning with the right;

"The wise one should place [the letters] beginning with *sā* and ending with *kaṣ* upon the heart and so forth, the pair of feet, likewise upon the belly and so forth, and upon the head and so forth. Some explain the term "upper shoulder" (*uttarāṃsa*) as referring to both armpits.

According to their view, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is as follows: two syllables on each of the two shoulders, one on the hump, two syllables on each of the two flanks, one on the pair of hands, and one on the pair of feet.

As it is stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
Having deposited [the mantras] at the heart, the two arms, and the two roots of the thighs, one should likewise deposit them on the back of the neck;

then, beginning from the heart, one should deposit them on the two armpits, as well as on the pair of hands and feet, and by way of pervasion on the belly and the face—one should thus deposit that which consists of the phonemes. Thus it is said.

Regarding that, the application is as follows:

And it is said: "Beginning with Om and ending with Namah—or alternatively, ending with Namah—accompanied by the bindu and the two dots (the nasal and the visarga), the placement of the fifty syllables is prescribed in their proper sequence."
By the phrase "in due order," this is what is meant:
the arrangement of letters should be performed during the rites of settling in a good location (*sausthānika*), setting out on a journey (*autthānika*), bathing, and eating.
Among these, in the rite of settling in a good location, the placement of the fifty-one letters is to be done according to the method already described.
In the *autthānika* [rite], there is a placement (*nyāsa*) by way of pervasion upon the face, the two arms, the two feet, the navel, and the heart for the seven groups of consonants.
Their respective deities are Brahmā, Sarasvatī, Viṣṇu, Śrī, Rudra, Umā, and Sarveśvara.
In the rite of bathing (*snāna*), there is a placement of the three groups beginning with *a*, *ka*, and *ca* upon the face, the middle [of the body], and the feet.
The deities of this [mantra] are the Moon, the Sun, and Fire.
At the time of eating, the placement (*nyāsa*) is performed from the head down to the feet for the entire body.
It should be employed everywhere in accordance with the requirements of place, time, and other factors.

"By that number" means by the number one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*).

As it has been said: "Having thus meditated upon that very form consisting of fifty letters within the beautiful body, and having sequentially deposited [the letters] in the previously mentioned locations, one should recite the syllables."

others, however, explain it otherwise,

Having invoked her, one should worship the Goddess upon that [seat] together with her enclosures;
the first enclosure consists of the limbs (aṅgas), and the second consists of the vowels in pairs. || 13 ||

The third [wheel] consists of the eight groups (aṣṭavarga); immediately after that, the fourth is by their powers (śakti). The fifth is said to be by the Mothers (mātṛ), and the sixth is remembered as being by the Lords of the World (lokeśvara). || 14 ||
Then, the seventh [deity] is proclaimed by the weapons of the world-protectors, beginning with the thunderbolt;

Vyāpinī, Pālinī, and thereafter Pāvanī, Kledinī;

1. Holding a staff, a water-pot, and then a rosary and the gesture of fearlessness, Brāhmī has the luster of gold and is radiant with a black antelope skin.
Carrying a trident, an axe, a small drum, and a human skull-cup, the auspicious Māheśvarī, resembling snow in hue, is to be meditated upon. || 20 ||
Holding a goad, a staff, a khaṭvāṅga, and a noose in her hands, Kaumārī resembles the bandhūka flower and is the bestower of desires. || 21 ||
Holding a discus, a bell, a skull-cup, and a conch in her hands, Vaiṣṇavī—dark as the tamāla tree and radiant with grace—is to be meditated upon. || 22 ||
Holding a pestle, a sword, a shield, and a plough with her four hands, Vārāhī, who has the complexion of a dark cloud at the end of time, should be meditated upon. || 23 ||
Holding a goad, a javelin, lightning, and a thunderbolt in her hands, Indrāṇī, who resembles a sapphire, should be meditated upon as the bestower of all prosperity. || 24 ||
25. Cāmuṇḍā, who has a red body and is adorned with a garland of severed heads, should be meditated upon as holding a trident, a sword, a human head, and a skull-cup in her hands.
Holding a rosary of seeds, a citron, a skull, and a lotus in her hands, Mahālakṣmī is described as resembling gold in complexion. || 26 ||
In this manner, the best of practitioners should worship the Mātṛkā daily. || 27 ||
The meditation on the weapons of Brāhmī and the others:
for Brāhmī, the meditation on the weapons proceeds from the upper left hand down to the lower left.
For Māheśvarī, it begins with the upper right hands and ends with the lower ones.
In the case of Kaumārī, [the worship proceeds] from the upper left up to the upper right;
in the case of Vaiṣṇavī, from the upper right up to the upper left;
and in the case of Vārāhī, from the lower right up to the lower left.
In the case of Indrāṇī and Cāmuṇḍā, [the sequence begins] from the upper right and left [hands] respectively;
in the case of Mahālakṣmī, it begins from the upper right hand and extends to the upper left. Their respective vehicles (vāhanas) should also be meditated upon.
It should be understood that these belong to their respective deities:
in the case of Brāhmī, it is the *haṃsa*;
therein, in the case of Vārāhī, it is the buffalo.
As it has been said: "I shall now describe Vārāhī, who is seated upon a buffalo.
In the case of Cāmuṇḍā, it should be understood that she is on a *preta*.
Vārāhī has the face of a boar;
Cāmuṇḍā is to be meditated upon as fleshless.
Among these, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Indrāṇī, and Mahālakṣmī have two eyes, while the others have three eyes.
The seed-syllables of these [goddesses] are stated in another tantra as follows:
"The eight long vowels, the eight consonants beginning with *kṣa*, and the letter *sa* together with *na*, joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*)."
"Indra, conjoined with Ākāśa, one should know as the seeds of these [vowels] in sequence.
By the phrase "the best of practitioners," it is stated that one should employ the Mātṛkā, thus accomplished, as a subsidiary part of another mantra. (19–27)

Having meditated upon the Goddess according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the letters accompanied by the *sarga* (visarga) through the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
Then, having performed the placement of the letters beginning with *ḍa*, ending with the *bindu* (anusvāra), by way of maintenance (*sthiti*). || 28 ||
The wise one should know the previously mentioned Ṛṣis and others, together with their limbs;
he should meditate here upon Varṇeśvarī, accompanied by her beloved. || 29 ||
He describes the placement by way of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa) with the words "one should place" (nyaset).
When one places [the mantras] by way of emanation—that is, by the path of creation—then they are "endowed with emanation" (sargānvitān).
The connection is made by supplying the correlative pronouns "yat" and "tad."
The same applies to what follows.
By the phrase "according to the rule," this is what is meant:
here, the deity is the Sṛṣṭimātṛkā.
As before, the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed with the phonemes ending in the *visarga*.
The sage (*ṛṣi*), the meter (*chandas*), the meditation (*dhyāna*), and all other rites such as worship are exactly as previously described.
The locations for the assignments (*nyāsasthānāni*) are also precisely those mentioned before.
The ritual application (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: *aḥ* homage to the hairline;
*āḥ* homage to the face, and so forth.

He states the *sthitinyāsa* with the words "beginning with emission" (*sarga*), etc. "Beginning with the letter *ḍa*" means up to the letter *ṭha*. "Ending with emission and the bindu" [means ending with the letter *ṣa* and the nasal dot].
It should be understood that every syllable is accompanied by the *bindu* and the *sarga*.

By the word "the learned one" (*vidvān*), this is what is meant: the six limbs of the deity Mātṛkā in her state of stability (*sthitimātṛkā*) are also to be formed with the letters preceded by the *sarga* and ending with the *bindu*, just as before.
The application therein is as follows.

Having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) up to *kṣāntam* as follows: *ḍaṃḥ namaḥ* on the right ankle; *ḍhaṃḥ namaḥ* at the base of the toes of the right foot, and so forth; one should then perform the placement beginning with *aṃ namaḥ* at the hairline (*keśānta*) and ending with *ṭhaṃḥ namaḥ* on the right knee.
As it is stated in the Śaiva [Tantra]: "One should join the Supreme Deity beginning with the letter *ḍa* and ending with the letter *ṭha*.
Regarding this, some perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) during the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), starting from the letter *a* up to the letter *ṭha*.
In the *sthiti* [phase], it consists of the letters beginning with *ḍa* and ending with *kṣa*.
This is delightful when not subjected to critical analysis,
because it constitutes the ritual deposition (*nyāsa*) of the entire *mātṛkā*.
In this regard, it concerns the ritual placement of stability (*sthitinyāsa*). || 28–29 ||
I bow to the goddess who possesses the luster of vermilion, is adorned with infinite ornaments, and has three eyes;
she holds a book, a rosary, and the excellent young deer,
while the golden-limbed Bhagavatī stands by her side.
One should meditate on her holding a book and a rosary of beads in her lotus-like hands. || 30 ||
The left side [is as follows]:
the meditation on the weapons begins from the top;

holding a garland of letters and a rosary of beads—this [he holds] in the right hand, while knowledge is in the left.
The compound *karābja* is a simile-compound (*upamā-samāsa*).
Thus [ends the section]. || 30 ||
One should perform all [rites], beginning with worship, according to the previous method;
one should then install this [mantra] joined with the *bindu*, having withdrawn it in reverse order. || 31 ||
The learned one should know the previously mentioned [deities], such as the Ṛṣis and others, together with their limbs.
He describes the *saṃhāranyāsa* (dissolution-assignment) with the words "endowed with the Bindu";
that is, in reverse order, from the letter *kṣa* down to the letter *a*.
The locations, however, remain the same.
By the word "the knower" (vidvān), this is what is meant:
the six limbs of the deities of the Saṃhāra-mātṛkā should also be performed with the phonemes ending in the bindu, just as before.
As it has been said:
"Then, in the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the bindus, the seer (ṛṣi) and the meter (chandas) are as before;
the six-limbed rite (ṣaḍaṅgaka) consists of the goddess Saṃhāraśāradā together with the letters accompanied by the bindus."
The ritual application, however, is as follows: "Kṣaṃ namaḥ" from the heart and so on at the mouth; "Laṃ namaḥ" from the heart and so on at the stomach, and so forth. (31–32)
The auspicious Goddess Vāgvallabhā is to be meditated upon on a pedestal composed of colors. || 32 ||

What indeed are emission, maintenance, and withdrawal?
Emission is the manifestation outside of that which is internal;
maintenance is the manifestation within Śiva.
Destruction is the remaining in an intermediate state as mere residual formations (*saṃskāra*).
As they say:
"Of the conscious Self, the Lord and Master of all worlds..."
O Sovereign Lady, manifestation is the appearance of the manifold variety of the grasped and the grasper.
"In this state, the manifestation of the worlds is said to be their persistence; when only the latent impressions remain, that is destruction, which is withdrawal (saṃhṛti) in Śiva.
Thus, the meaning is that the threefold placement (nyāsa) should be performed through meditation. || 33 ||

The best of practitioners should perform all [rites], such as the ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship, according to the previously mentioned method; he should perform the placement with the digits (kalā) arising from the Tāra mantra. || 34 ||
The letters and so forth, joined with the *tāra* (om) and followed by "namas," are to be placed [as mantras].

Regarding the placement of the *kalās*, he says "arising from the *tāra*" (*tārotthābhiḥ*).
This means that one should place that *mātṛkā* along with the *kalās*—namely *sṛṣṭi* and the others—which arise from the five divisions of the *praṇava*, in the locations previously mentioned.
By the phrase "the best of practitioners" (*sādhakasattama*), it is also implied that the sequence begins with the three *praṇavas*.
"Beginning with the vowels" means beginning with the vowel *a* and so forth.
Being of such a nature, they are joined with the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*).
By this, the following sequence is established.

For this very reason, according to the tradition that "words joined with the first [syllable] are followed by *namaḥ*," there is the state of being in the dative case due to the connection with *namaḥ* at the end.

Although the requirement for the verb "one should install" (*nyaset*) is already satisfied, he says "they are to be installed" (*nyastavyāḥ*) in order to indicate that the installation of the fivefold *kalās* occurs at the beginning.

In that regard, however, because it has been stated: "In the ritual of placement (nyāsa), one should first employ the sixteen digits (kalās) born of the vowels," first there is the placement of the digits of sound (nādakalā), namely Nivṛtti and the others; afterwards, the placement of those born of the letters *a*, *u*, and the *bindu*, namely Sṛṣṭi and the others.
The ritual application (prayoga), however, is as follows: "Oṃ aṃ, salutation to Nivṛtti at the hairline," and so forth.
"The deity is Śāradā, whose essence is the Kalās and who gives birth to the phonemes.

"Situated between short and long [vowels]" means situated among vowels that are neither neuter (e/o/ai/au) nor short or long.

Therefore, the teacher Padmapāda says: "Everything is everywhere. || 37 ||

one should install her preceded by the third [syllable], ending with "namas," and joined with Rudra. || 38 ||
He speaks of Śrīkaṇṭha and Mātṛkā as "the third," meaning the third [syllable] of Bhairavī,
which will be described in the twelfth [chapter].
Some say that it is devoid of the letter *ra*.
This alone is the traditional position,
because the seed-syllable (bīja) of the pericarp of the lotus of the Mātṛkā is thus correctly comprised.
Among the thirty divisions of the Bhairavī, the third division of one of them indeed consists of the letter *ra* joined with the vowel *ī*.
The author himself will state this very point at the occasion of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), saying: "with *ha* joined to the six long vowels.
"One should place" means in the locations already mentioned.
However, the traditionalists (*sāmpradāyika*) maintain that there should be a conjunction with the *praṇava*, *śakti*, *prāsāda*, and the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*).
"Accompanied by Rudra" means together with Śrīkaṇṭha and the others along with their Śaktis.
By the phrase "ending with *namaḥ*," the application of the dative case is also indicated.
The practical application is as follows: *hsau aṃ śrīkaṇṭheśapūrṇodarībhyāṃ namaḥ keśānte* (Hsau Aṃ, salutation to Śrīkaṇṭheśa and Pūrṇodarī at the hairline), and so forth.
This is the traditional position.
In this regard, the author has omitted the word *īśa* in some instances due to metrical constraints;
however, it must certainly be included at the time of the ritual assignment (*nyāsa*).
Some, however, say "Salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha together with Pūrṇedārī," while others say "Salutation to Pūrṇedārī and Śrīkaṇṭha.
In both of these views, they maintain that the Rudras are the primary entities.
Some also desire [the mantra] as "pūrṇedarīśrīkaṇṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ. However, all three of those positions are non-traditional (*asāmpradāyika*).
In the first position, there is the use of the word *sahita*, which is both unstated [in the source] and redundant.
In the second alternative, the dative case is inappropriate in both instances;
for in one case it would be required by its connection with *namaḥ*, while in the other there is no such governing factor.
Furthermore, in all three alternatives, because it is stated that [the mantra] is "joined with Rudra," the Mātṛkā does not achieve a direct, uninterrupted conjunction with the Rudras.
Therefore, the traditional position alone is superior.
However, the author of the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā* stated the usage: "Obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭheśa, whose glory is complete.
That too is incorrect.
Because in the *Dhyāna* [section], the status of being a deity is understood only for those combined together, like Agni and Soma;
yet in this particular application (*prayoga*), there is a combination of two deities,
since their status is understood as being independent of one another through the separate mention of the dative case.
Furthermore,

in the case of the injunction, "One offers in the evening to Agni and to Prajāpati," although there is no connection of each [deity] with the action individually due to their mutual dependence created by the two words, the conjunction of the deities is nonetheless intended.

In this case, however, because the word *namaḥ* is connected with each [name] individually in the absence of that [conjunction], there is an even clearer cognition of their collective conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Therefore, even in the *homādi* (fire-offering and so forth), there is only a single oblation (*āhuti*) with "svāhā" following both Śrīkaṇṭheśa and Pūrṇodarī.
This should be understood likewise in the case of the *nyāsas* of Keśava and the rest, as well as Kāmagaṇeśa.
As for the fact that in some places there is an insertion of the words "and to Keśava" and "and to Kīrtti," it should be understood that this is for the sake of conforming to the meter. || 38 ||
Those [mantras] beginning with *ya* are respectively endowed with the *sad-dhātu*, *prāṇa*, *śakti*, and *ātman*.
Their seer is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and the meter is said to be Gāyatrī. || 39 ||
The deity Arddhanārīśvara is proclaimed by those learned in the Tantras;
the preceptor should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa) using the syllable *ha* joined with the six long vowels. || 40 ||

Regarding "with the elements" (sadhātu): those Rudras are to be known as being joined respectively with the ten pervasive [letters] beginning with *ya* and so forth; the elements (*dhātavaḥ*) are skin, blood, fat, bone, marrow, semen, breath, power (*śakti*), and the self (*ātman*).

In this context, although the word *rudra* is embedded within a compound, it is nevertheless referred to by means of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), according to Vāmana’s sūtra: "A pronoun may refer back to that which has been concealed by a compound. The usage, however, is as follows:
"Hsauḥ yaṃ, salutation to Vālīśa and Sumukhīśvarī, who are the essence of the skin, at the heart," and so forth.
Here, the word *ātman* is employed according to tradition.
In another text, having stated that the word *krodha* (wrath) should be used in place of the word *ātman*, it is said that the word *ātman* should be employed everywhere.
Likewise: "The [energies] beginning with Yā, which are the life-force, power, wrath, and so forth, united with the Self.
Also elsewhere: "The individual soul (jīva), power, and wrath—these too [are united] with the Self."
Thus [it is said].
But the Teachers [state]: "O Ambikā, those two elements as well, beginning with *ya*, the seven vital breaths (*samīraṇa*), and *kṣa* together with *pa-ra*, are Krodha."
Here, because the letter *kṣa* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Narasiṃha, it is designated by the word "wrath" (*krodha*).
In the commentary on the first verse by Padmapādācārya, the mention of the "place of the Mother" (*mātṛkāsthāna*) is explained by the words beginning with "composed" (*viracita*).

Since they are "named" (*ākhyāyante*) by these [syllables], the seven constituent elements (*saptadhātu*) are indicated; by the word "heart" (*hṛt*), both the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the power (*śakti*) are denoted.
It has been stated that by the word *ka*, which signifies bliss, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is expressed; thus it was said, "the places for the *yādi*-nyāsa.
Following that doctrine, the author of the root text has here employed the term "Self" (*ātman*).

Now, one might ask: since the deity-self, beginning with the skin and ending with the Supreme Self, is already present within the practitioner's body through the *yādi*-nyāsa alone, what remains to be accomplished by the nyāsa of the remaining syllables?

We say that it is the conceptualization of the arrangement of the specific parts of the deity. Furthermore, there is no fixed rule that a general conceptualization must first occur and only then a specific conceptualization,
such that the placement of the script would necessarily begin with the letter *kṣa*.
The body of the deity is indeed eternally and universally composed of both general and specific forms.
Its presence within the body of the practitioner is brought about through ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in first recollecting the presence [of the deity] in specific limbs by means of the placement of the letters beginning with *A*.

Furthermore, in the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), there is no lapse in the proper order by asserting that the general withdrawal occurs first and the specific withdrawal follows later;
for both are withdrawn into the Self alone. Nor is the separate withdrawal of the particulars redundant, on the grounds that they have already been withdrawn by the general withdrawal.
Because one must perform the contemplation of the sequence of the specific withdrawal (*viśeṣasaṃhārakrama*), [it is said:
"the six long vowels" are *ā, ī, ū, e, au, aḥ*. It is stated that this is combined with the *hasa*, namely the letter *ha* and the letter *sa*, together with the word "the teacher" (*deśika*).
The ritual application (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: "To *ha-sāṃ*, the heart, *namaḥ*," and so forth.
Others, however, desire that the limbs of the Mātṛkā begin with *ha-sāṃ* and so on.

The traditionalists (*sāmpradāyikāḥ*), however, [employ] the Praṇava, Māyā, Lakṣmī, the five-syllabled mantra, Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, and Indrāṇī, preceded by their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*).

[The mantra is formed as follows: "Rakṣa-yugmāntā" (ending with two *rakṣa*s), "Amuka-vāhane-pramukha-rakṣa-yugmāntā" (beginning with the name of the vehicle and ending with two *rakṣa*s), "Amuka-haste-pramukha-māṃ rakṣa-yugmāntā" (beginning with the name of the hand-gesture and ending with two *rakṣa*s after the word *māṃ*). Then, one should recite the limbs (*aṅga*) of the Mātṛkās, which are encircled by the three long vowels and encapsulated by the syllable *Māyā* (the *hrīṃ*), followed by the third [seed-syllable] and the *Sañjīvanī*. Then, having twice uttered the words "Ūrdhva-keśini, Jaṭila-keśini, Viśva-rūpiṇi, Tārākṣiṇi, Māraya," one should utter the Heart-mantra and the others. As for the application (*prayoga*): *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ namaḥ śivāya namaḥ haṃ brahmāṇi rakṣa rakṣa haṃsa-vāhane rakṣa rakṣa padma-haste māṃ*.
"Protect, protect! Hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ! Aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ! Āṃ hrāṃ hrūṃ hsauḥ! To the heart, Sañjīvanī, obeisance," and so forth. The seed-syllables (bījas) are: māṃ kaṃ kroṃ huṃ haṃ.
The weapons are the lotus, trident, spear, discus, mace, and thunderbolt.

The pervasive mantra (vyāpakamantra), however, is as follows: *Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ namaḥ śivāya hūṃ cāmuṇḍe rakṣa rakṣa vetālavāhane rakṣa rakṣa pāśahaste mama sarvāṅgaṃ rakṣa rakṣa hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ*— having uttered the six short vowels (*hrasvaṣaṭka*) and the six long vowels from *ā* to *kṣa* (*dīrghaṣaṭka*), [and then] *hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hsauḥ sarvāṅgavyāpinī svāhā*— having thus performed the pervasion (*vyāpaka*), one should perform the placement of the Śrīkaṇṭha-mātṛkā.
In this regard, the other mantras that pervade the eight [faces] and so forth should be understood according to the oral tradition (*sampradāya*). As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"The eight Mothers have arisen, and they are the presiding deities (*nāyikā*) of the [eight] classes of consonants."
The goddess Vyāpinī, Pālinī, Pāvanī, and again Kledinī.
"Dhāriṇī, Mālinī, further Haṃsinī, and likewise Śāntinī;
these are declared to be the eight Bhairavas who are the leaders of the [consonant] groups.
Thus, the eighth is the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*): having uttered [the consonants] from *a* to *kṣa*, one should say, "Salutation to Saṃhārabhairava and Śāntinī on all limbs. (39–40)
Resembling the Bandhūka flower and gold, holding a beautiful rosary,

and adorned with the crescent moon as an ornament— [the three-eyed one].
We constantly take refuge in the body of the Lord of the Mother of the World (Śiva). || 41 ||

the visualization of the weapons begins from the upper right [hand] with the goad and the rosary, while the other two are on the left. || 41 ||
One should worship him according to the rules by the very same path as previously described;
one should install the Mātṛkā beginning with *smara* (the letter *ka*), accompanied by "Obeisance to Keśava" and so forth. || 42 ||
By the phrase "according to the rule," the following is meant:
one should install the Kāmamātṛkā, beginning either with *smara* or with *vālā*.
The practical application is as follows: "Oṃ *klīṃ* aṃ, obeisance to Kāma and Rati" at the hairline (*keśānta*), and so forth.
This meditation is as follows:

[He] whose body is red, who wears garments dyed with the hue of glowing coals, who is adorned with ornaments, and whose lap is beautifully graced by a spear held in his hand and richly decorated with blue lotuses.
"One should meditate upon the form of Ananga, who possesses a bow of sugarcane with arrows of flowers, and who shines with the luster of a beautiful pomegranate flower.
Thus, one should perform the nyāsa of the Gaṇapati-mātṛkā, beginning either with the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati or with the six seed-syllables.

And the visualization (*dhyāna*) is:
[He whose] body-unguents and garments possess a beautiful, shimmering red luster from the intoxication of youth...

"I shall meditate upon the auspicious Gaṇeśa, who has the face of a lordly elephant, who is illuminated by three eyes, and who holds a boon-granting gesture, a goad, a noose, and the gesture of fearlessness with his lotus-like hands; he is embraced on his left lap by a woman holding a beautiful red lotus in her hand. Thus.
In this context, the connection with the skin and other [elements] should also be considered for both pervasive [mantras].
Regarding the placement of the Mātṛkās beginning with Keśava, he says "beginning with Smara," meaning beginning with the Kāma-bīja (the seed-syllable of desire).
However, the traditionalists maintain that it involves the union of the three-fold [mantra] and the eight-syllabled Nārāyaṇa mantra.
Some [advocate] the conjunction of three *praṇavas*, others the state of being encapsulated by three *praṇavas*,
and some the conjunction with the *śrībīja*;
such is the practice according to their respective traditions.
The ritual application (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: *klīṃ aṃ keśavakīttībhyāṃ namaḥ keśānte* (and so forth).
Some, moreover, desire the formula: *keśavāya kīrttyai namaḥ*. (42)
In the [mantras] beginning with *ya*, the Viṣṇus are endowed with the elements, the vital breath, power, and the self;
Prajāpati is declared to be the seer (*ṛṣi*), and the Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (*chandas*). || 43 ||
Hari, who is half of Lakṣmī herself, is declared here to be the manifest deity.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using the seed-syllable joined with the long vowel. || 44 ||
"Along with the elements" (*sadhātu*) means:
"Obeisance to Puruṣottama, whose nature is the skin, and to Vasudhā," at the heart, and so forth.
"Endowed with the long [vowels]" means...

The six [syllables] previously mentioned are long; they are to be understood as being joined with the initial seed-syllable (*ādibīja*), which is the *kāmabīja* (the syllable *klāṃ klīṃ*, etc.), for the heart and the other limbs. Others, however, maintain that these are simply the limbs of the *mātṛkā* beginning with *klām*.

But the traditionalists (*sāmpradāyika*) hold that the limbs, such as the heart, consist of the consonants from *ka* onwards, each encased by the sounds of the *māyā*, *nārāyaṇa-aṣṭākṣara*, *ajapa*, and *paramātman* mantras, and joined with the goddesses Padminī, Viṣṇupatnī, Varadā, Kamalarūpā, and Śūlinī.
The ritual application (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: *Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya haṃsaḥ sohaṃ aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya haṃsaḥ sohaṃ devyai hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and so forth. (43–44)
With her hands she bears the lotus, mace, conch, and discus; [she holds] knowledge, the lotus-mirror, and a golden pitcher, flashing like lightning amidst clouds.
With her left hand, out of a longing for embrace, she clings to the high breast of [her consort], which is adorned with dense ornaments.
May the form manifested by Puṇḍarīkākṣa and Lakṣmī protect you. || 45 ||
"With hands," etc.;
"cloud-like," and so forth, are adjectives qualifying the body (*vapuḥ*).
*Ākalpa* means ornamentation (*bhūṣā*).
The meditation on the weapons begins from the lower right hand and extends as far as the lower left hand.
By this, it is established that the weapons of the male deities are on the right and the weapons of the female deities are on the left;
this is the view of the teacher Padmapāda.
And it has been said:
"His hands are beautified by the mirror of knowledge, the jar of nectar, the lotus, the mace Kaumodakī, and the Sudarśana disc.
Thus.
In this case, the sequence should be understood as starting from the upper left and ending with the upper right.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the meditation on the four-armed form in this ritual placement (nyāsa) pertains to Viṣṇu alone, not to him when accompanied by Lakṣmī.
This [placement] is also essential.
As they say:
"This installation beginning with Keśava grants imperishability to embodied beings merely by the act of installation; this is the truth, the truth, and not otherwise. (45)
Here, the practitioner of mantras should perform all rites, beginning with worship, as previously described;
the most excellent knower of mantras should then project the Mātṛkā, preceded by Śakti, upon his own body.
The seer is remembered as Śakti, the meter as Gāyatrī, and the deity is declared by the wise to be the Mother of the Universe, the bestower of all auspiciousness. || 47 ||
The wise one should form the limbs with the Māyā-formula joined with the long [vowel] and the half-moon. || 48 ||
The seer (ṛṣi) is Śakti, the son of Vasiṣṭha.
"Bestower of all prosperity" is stated as the application (viniyoga).
[Regarding the word] "long" (dīrgha):
The long vowels are the six long ones; [the seed-syllable] consists of the half-moon and the bindu.
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "by means of the seed-syllable whose nature is *māyā* endowed with these.
As for the ritual application (*prayoga*), it is: *hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and so forth.
Some maintain that the syllables *hrām* and so forth are indeed the limbs (*aṅga*) of the Mātṛkās;
the same applies hereafter as well. (46–48)
She possesses lofty, broad, and full breasts that rival the rising sun at its zenith;
she is resplendent with a crown, necklaces, a girdle, and anklets adorned with many crescent moons;
and she holds in her lotus-like hands a rosary, a noose, a goad, and a book.
May the three-eyed Mistress of the World, seated upon a lotus, grant you a face [of beauty]. ||49||
"Rising," etc. *Mañjīra* means an anklet. *Japavaṭī* means a rosary of beads.
The meditation on the weapons is as follows: the goad and the rosary are in the right hands, while the other two are in the left.
And it has been stated by the teacher Padmapāda: "She should be meditated upon with her hands holding a rosary, a goad, a noose, and a book. (49)
One should worship the Goddess every day according to the previously mentioned procedure;
one should install the Mātṛkā, endowed with the Śrī-bīja, upon one's body according to the prescribed rite. || 50 ||
The sage is remembered as Bhṛgu, the meter as Gāyatrī, and she is remembered as the deity;
she is the source of all prosperity and is known by the wise as the mistress of the worlds. (51)
The practitioner should form the limbs [of the mantra] by means of the seed-syllable previously introduced. || 52 ||
The phrase "the source of all prosperity" is a statement regarding its application (*viniyoga*).
"By means of what was previously introduced" means by the path previously described, namely, that which is joined with the six long vowels.
"By the seed-syllable" means by the *śrī*-bīja.
By that, "śrāṃ śrīm" and so forth constitute the six limbs;
or these and others are the limbs of the Mātṛkā. (50–52)
She possesses a radiance equal to a streak of lightning and is being sprinkled by four elephants resembling the snowy mountains, which hold jars of nectar lifted upon their trunks;
she bears a rosary of *japavaṭa* seeds, two lotuses, and a book in her lotus-like hands.
One should meditate upon the Mistress of the World, whose breasts are curved and resplendent with shining jewels. ||53||
"Lightning"—this refers to the meditation on the weapons from the lower right hand up to the lower left hand. || 53 ||
One should propitiate this [goddess] with flowers and other offerings according to the prescribed method;
one should place the auspicious Mātṛkā, beginning with Smara, upon the body. || 54 ||
The seer is declared to be Sammohana; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī;
and the deity is declared by the practitioners of mantra to be the Supreme Mother of all beings. || 55 ||
One should perform the arrangement of the limbs with the [mantra] of Smara, joined with the long [vowel]. || 56 ||

By the phrase "smarādyām" (beginning with Smara), it is stated that one should also install Kāma, Śrī, Śakti, and so forth. Their seers (*ṛṣi*) and other [constituent parts] are the same as those [of the previous deities].
The limbs (*aṅga*) are formed by the twice-repeated seed-syllables (*bīja*).

She has eight hands holding a five-arrowed lotus, a goad, a rosary, a noose, a bow made of the lotus-stalk of the qualities of knowledge, and is three-eyed.
May she who is richly adorned with red and dawn-colored garments, unguents, and ornaments, the mother of the castes, and who bears the moon upon her crest, protect you.
"Bestowing auspiciousness" is the statement regarding the application (viniyoga). "Joined with the long [vowels]" means joined with the six long vowels. || 54-56 ||
Holding in her lotus-like hands a rosary of crystal, a bow made of sugarcane, the five arrows of Smara, and a lore, she who possesses three eyes is resplendent like ten million rising suns.
One should meditate upon the Mother of all beings, who has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
All rites, beginning with worship, have been declared according to the previously stated injunctions.
One should worship the Goddess, whose body consists of the phonemes and who is preceded by the seed-syllables of Śakti, Śrī, and Kāma. || 58 ||
"Bāla" refers to the book of knowledge (*vidyā*).
In the right [hands], starting from the bottom, [he holds] the rosary (*akṣamālā*) and the five arrows.
In the left [hands], a book and a bow.

They should be meditated upon as holding a rosary, an arrow, a bow, and a book. || 57-58 ||

One should meditate upon her who is ruddy in hue, afflicted by the weight of her breasts, holding in her own hands a rosary, a bow of sugarcane, a noose, two lotuses, a goad, arrows, and a boon-bestowing book.
She who deludes, who has three eyes, and whose crest is the young moon.

One should worship [the deity] together with the enclosures (āvaraṇas) and the most beautiful ritual offerings (upacāras).
I shall now describe the Prapañcayāga, which bestows the perfection of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda). || 62 ||
The beginning of the Vedas, Śakti, Ajapā, the Great Mantra of the Supreme Self, and the Consort of Fire—these five mantras are said to bring auspiciousness. || 63 ||
"Prapañca" refers to the statement of application (*viniyoga*): "bestowing the attainment of Being-Consciousness-Bliss.

The ajapā is "haṃsaḥ. The great mantra of the Self is "so 'ham. The wife of Agni is "svāhā."

"Even when independent, the eight-syllabled mantra brings about accomplishment;
therefore, a wise man intent on liberation should recite it according to the rules. Thus say the traditionalists regarding the encapsulation by *vāgbhava* and *hṛllekhā*. (62–63)

The knower of the ritual procedure should install the Mātṛkā, beginning with Tāra (Om), Śakti (Hrīṃ), and so forth, ending with Ajapā (Haṃsaḥ) and the two Viṭhas (Hauṃ), according to the prescribed path of emanation upon the body.
The seer is Brahmā, the metre is declared to be Gāyatrī;
its deity is the supreme splendor pervading all the letters. || 65 ||
Regarding the phrase "beginning with the power of Tārā":
the *ātman* is the mantra of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*),
because the *ajapā* has already been mentioned previously.

*Dviṭhaḥ svāhā*. At the beginning of each syllable is *Tāra* (Oṃ) and *Māyā* (Hrīṃ); at the end are *Ajapā* and the rest (*Haṃsaḥ so'haṃ*). The application is as follows: *Oṃ hrīṃ aṃ haṃsaḥ so'haṃ svāhā* at the hairline (*keśānta*), and so forth.

Since the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) will be described later, the term "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) is used here. By the expression "knower of the ritual procedure" (*vidhānavit*), the following is meant: having meditated upon Mahāgaṇapati along with his retinue, preceded by the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one should recite the seed-syllable of Gaṇeśa forty-four times and [the mantra] *gaṇānāṃ tvā* once.

Having thus recited the Mahāgaṇapati mantra four times, and having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the pure Mātṛkā as previously described three times, one should also place the [groups] beginning with *a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya* upon the seven locations: the faces, arms, feet, belly, and heart. || 64–65 ||
One should assign the five limbs using the five mantras beginning with *svāhā*;
the wise one should further place the weapon-mantra in the directions using the syllables of Hari and Hara.
"By *svāhā* and so forth in reverse order" means the following application:
*svāhā hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *sohaṃ śirase svāhā*, and so on.
"In the directions" means by means of snapping the fingers.
"Furthermore, immediately after" means from the sixth limb.
"By the syllables of Hari and Hara" means according to what is heard [in the scriptures].
As it has been said:

"The heart of the *jāyāgni* (the fire of the wife), and likewise the head; 'so'ham' is the self (*ātman*), and 'haṃsa' is the crest-lock (*śikhā*). That which is 'sva' is the armor (*varma*); the one called 'tārā' (the syllable Om) is the eye (*īkṣaṇa*) when combined, and the weapon (*astra*) is said to be the color of Hari and Hara (white and black). Thus [is the assignment of the limbs]. Some say [the weapon is] "hri" and "hra. (66)
That which is being measured by the five mantras beginning with *Tārā*, yet is eternally inaccessible to the means of knowledge; the sole root of the universe;
existence, consciousness, and all-pervading, imperishable, and infallible—that [is the Supreme].
Devote yourselves to that supreme splendor, which is like a dense mass of nectar and moonlight.
"Tārādī" means:
worship that well-known supreme light, Brahman, incessantly and at all times.
Its supremacy is due to the fact that all other lights are pervaded by it.
"Like a mass of thick nectar-moon water"— this is a *vyastarūpaka* (an inverted metaphor).
By this, the fault of the masculine gender is also avoided,
just as in the expression "the fingers were the young shoots."
By this, its nature as consisting of bliss (*ānandamayatva*) is implied.
It is *acyuta*, meaning immutable;
it is *avinaśvara*, meaning indestructible.
"Samasta-ga" means all-pervasive.
"Cit" means having the nature of self-luminous consciousness.
"Sat" means having the nature of existence.
"By faith alone all this is real, real"—and from the Śruti: "By consciousness alone all this shines. That is the single root of the world, because the world is of the nature of its transformation;
it is inaccessible to the means of valid cognition (māna).
This is because of the Vedic scripture: "From which words turn back.
For this very reason, he says: "Being comprehended by these [mantras], it is to be attained through their recitation"—this is the meaning.

In that regard, because the five-limbed *Tāra* (Om) has all modifications dissolved within it, and because the limbs of the Goddess’s *Tāra* likewise culminate in the realization of the bliss of non-difference from its own limbs.

This is because even the *ajapa* mantra and the *ātman* mantra consist in the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*), and because even the five and two syllables of the *praṇava* have as their referent the consciousness that pervades everything.
Regarding the *saṃhitā*, however, it is said:
"The *praṇava* should be known as a digit of consciousness (*citkalā*), whose nature is the pervasion of *māyā*."
O Goddess of the gods, by means of the word *haṃsa*, she is directly the very nature of the Self.
From the three points (*bindu*) located therein, she who consists of emanation, maintenance, and dissolution was born;
this Vāmā, whose form is Brahman, was produced by the primordial point (*bindu*).
Then, by means of the second *bindu*, she protects the three worlds;
O beloved, she is this primordial Vaiṣṇavī Māyā, the eldest, characterized by the quality of *sattva*.
With the *bindu* at the tip of the antenna, everything is pervaded by the *rasanā* and enveloped in darkness;
then, O Goddess, Raudrī gives birth to the three *bindus*, and Ambikā likewise.
When this withdrawal known as Haṃsa reveals the Self,
then it takes the form of a mirror and subsequently becomes composed of light.
"O Dear One, by placing the two phonemes [Ha and Kṣa] after the wife of Fire (Svāhā), one says 'the Supreme Light' (*paraṃ jyotiḥ*).
The practitioner who contemplates in this way shall become Brahman manifest.
Here, the worship of the form of the *Prapañcayāga* has not been mentioned; it is as described in another Tantra: [The worship of the Prapañcayāgamūrti is as follows:]...
On the seat proclaimed by the Mātṛkā-mantra, which is a lotus composed of excellent syllables,
one should invoke the form of the Prapañcayāga and worship it.
The first enclosure is said to consist of the vowels; the second, of the forms beginning with 'ka';
and the third is designated as belonging to Bhāratī, consisting of sixteen powers.

The fourth [enclosure] is together with the Mothers and the Bhairavas such as Asitāṅga; the fifth is with the lords of the directions, starting with Indra (Vāsava); and the next is with their weapons. Thus [it is said]. (67)
The letters, consisting of the five elements, were previously described according to their groups;
therefore, they know that the sense organs are of the nature of knowledge and that the phenomenal world is composed of them. || 68 ||
It was stated, "I shall explain the Prapañcayāga.
In that context, the Prapañcayāga is so called because it is therein that the *prapañca* (the manifold) is worshipped (*ijyate*) and offered as oblation (*hūyate*).
While describing that very method of oblation (*homaprakāra*), he also indicates another form of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by saying, "consisting of the five elements" (*pañcabhūta*).
"In the second [chapter], 'previously'...
This is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for "having the nature of the sense organs of cognition";
by this, they are of the color of space.

Those whose nature consists of the organs of knowledge and action are the color of air; those whose form is their respective objects are the color of fire; and those whose form is the ten vital airs beginning with prāṇa—these and other such points are to be inferred.
"Consisting of that" means consisting of the five elements. || 68 ||

The body is also like that; the mantra-practitioner should place the syllables in reverse order within it, joined with their respective locations, and offer them as oblations into the supreme radiance.
"Of such a kind" means consisting of the five elements (*pañcabhūtamaya*).
Regarding that, "one should assign the phonemes":
the method for this is as follows; having uttered the ten phonemes of earth as in the *prapañcayāga*, one should assign them from the soles of the feet up to the knees.
In this manner, one should perform the placement up to the element of space (*ākāśa*).
Regarding the phrase "in reverse order":
one should again perform the placement of the letters beginning with space in their respective locations, down to the element of earth (*bhūmi*).
"Tattad" refers to meditation during the reverse placement;
having performed meditation in this manner, one should perform the reverse placement. (69)

Having thus performed the oblation consisting of these colors, the practitioner of mantra, having duly deposited the Mother of the Universe upon his body, shall become possessed of a divine form. || 70 ||
One who possesses single-minded devotion should recite mantras, worship the deities, and sacrifice to the fire;
and as a knower of mantras, one should offer oblations into the fire with substances prescribed by the tantras. || 71 ||
The phrase "in this manner" (evam) extends the previously mentioned procedure to the *prapañcayāga* as well.
The method for that is: one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) up to the end with the mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ kṣaṃ haṃsaḥ so'haṃ svāhā*.

The essential meaning is that one should perform the *saṃhāranyāsa* (the ritual placement of withdrawal) while meditating: "I offer the letter *kṣa*, its presiding deity, and its respective location, along with the consciousness delimited by them, into the fire.
This is the traditional position.
As it has been said: "Of the beloved one, who arises from the *bindu* of the power exerted in the *ādhāra*, and who devours the moon at her head and mouth,
one should cause the letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *a* to fall [into] fire and moon."

"The practitioner, having performed [this], is liberated from all kinds of diseases. Thus it is said. Regarding the necessity of performing the aforementioned various types of *mātṛkā-nyāsa* at the beginning of other mantras, he says "having performed" (*nyasya*).
By the phrase "the practitioner according to rule" (*mantrī yathānyāyam*), this is what is meant:

One who is unable to perform all the *mātṛkā*-nyāsas should install the *kalāmātṛkā* and so forth in the Śākta [tradition], the *śrīkaṇṭhamātṛkā* and so forth in the Śaiva, the *keśavamātṛkā* and so forth in the Vaiṣṇava, and the *mātṛkā* of the *śuddhaprapañcayāga* everywhere.
As it has been said:

"Know that all recitations and the like of every mantra performed without the placement of the letters (*lipi*) are fruitless; therefore, one should first place the *lipi*. Thus it is said. Also in the *Kādimata*: "The six limbs of the *mātṛkā* and the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* itself..."
"Having first performed [the placement] for all [the goddesses], one should afterwards place those prescribed in the Tantra.
And the teachers say: "[One should perform] the placements of the scripts and so forth, together with their limbs (aṅgas)."

And in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "One should place all the limbs [of the mantra]; for mantras accompanied by their limbs grant success. Also elsewhere: "He who, at the commencement of ritual action, should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Mātṛkā, either joined with the Rudras or alone, [attains success]."
The mantras bring him immediate success, and both his sins and his old age go to destruction together.
Thus.
By the phrase "with undistracted mind," it is stated that the accomplishment of the mantra (*mantrasiddhi*) occurs through recitation encased within the *mātṛkā*.
As it has been said:

In the Kulaprakāśatantra: "The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra encapsulated by the letters of the Mātṛkā, one hundred times each in forward and reverse order; after one month, that person becomes accomplished."
"By the mere recitation of the Mātṛkā, tens of millions upon tens of millions of mantras become perfectly accomplished; of this there is no doubt, for everything originates from it. Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Prayogasāra*: "When the Mātṛkā is mastered, all classes of mantras become mastered."
"Since all mantras are submerged here and there within the Mātṛkā. (70–71)
The wise know that the eight substances are fuel-sticks of the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Nyagrodha trees, sesame seeds, white mustard, milk-rice, and clarified butter.
With these [mantras], one who is composed should offer oblations a hundred thousand times, or half of that;
he attains all desires and finds supreme accomplishment. || 73 ||
He states the rites for desired results (*kāmyakarmāṇi*) of all *mātṛkā* mantras with the words "with substances" (*dravyaiḥ*).
He states the substances with the words "of the *aśvattha*" (*aśvattha* etc.). One should offer one hundred thousand—that is, twelve thousand five hundred—oblations with each individual substance.
"Or half of that" means:
six thousand two hundred and fifty for each individual substance.
By the word "concentrated" (*samāhita*), it is indicated that even half of that [amount] may be used.
As it is said: "The minister [should give] half of that, or even half of that.
Then, with each individual substance, there are three thousand and one hundred and twenty-five. (71–73)
Having offered thousands of oblations with these [mantras], the practitioner shall destroy enemies, malevolent planets, spirits, fevers, curses, and serpents. || 74 ||
Regarding the phrase "thousands of suns":
at that time, each [sun] is accompanied by fifteen hundred [rays].
By the word "mantrin," this is what is meant.
Having considered the smallness or greatness of the knowledge (*vidyā*) and other factors, the fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed as double or fourfold.
And it is said:
"One should offer twelve thousand oblations, or twice that, or even four times that."
Thus, at that time, there are three thousand or six thousand for each one.
The same applies hereafter as well.
It should also be understood that when the [defect] is extremely slight, one may perform the recitation even only once up to a hundred times.
As it has been said:
"Observing each respective transformation, let the practitioner of mantra offer oblations by increasing the count from one, two, three, four, up to a hundred."
Thus,
the "minor" [rites] spoken of by Nārāyaṇa are as follows: paralysis, hatred, destruction, expulsion, delusion, killing, and disease— these are known as the minor rites.
Thus [ends the verse]. 74.
This oblation has been proclaimed as that which swiftly destroys the distortions arising from the improper practice or realization of mantras. || 75 ||
He states another application [of the mantra] with the words "of mantras.
"Improper conduct" refers to the pronunciation of the phonemes in a manner other than [the prescribed one].
"Non-comprehension" is the lack of knowledge that this mantra is defective (*kalada*).
The modifications arising from that [ignorance] are as follows:

among them, a modification resulting from non-regular functioning (*ayathāvṛtti*) consists of wind-diseases, leprosy, and so forth; a modification resulting from non-comprehension (*apratipatti*) consists of insanity (*unmāda*), as explained in detail in the *Nārasiṃha*.
Therefore, "regular functioning" (*yathāvṛtti*) and "comprehension" (*pratipatti*) form the compound *yathāvṛttipratipattī*, which is subsequently connected with the negative particle (*nañ*).

The statement "the homa is thus proclaimed" should be understood as referring to a thousand repetitions, because of the scriptural declaration: "One should pacify [it] quickly by means of a thousand repetitions. || 75 ||
One should offer oblations with these [mantras], accompanied by the three sweets, a hundred thousand times with devotion;
before long, he shall become a veritable Indra upon the earth.
"With the three sweets" means with these eight [substances]. Milk, honey, and clarified butter constitute the "three sweets."
As it has been said: "Clarified butter, milk, and honey—these are called the 'three sweets' (madhuratra-ya).
Alternatively, sugar may be used in place of milk. || 76 ||
Having offered oblations with these, the practitioner may accomplish subjugation and other rites as well.
By offering one hundred thousand pure sesame seeds, he is liberated from all sins.
The practitioner of mantras should offer oblations of milk-rice for the sake of all prosperity;
by the homa of one hundred thousand lotuses, he shall attain great fortune. || 78 ||
One should offer oblations with ghee one hundred thousand times; one shall attain supreme renown.
By offering oblations of jasmine flowers, one shall bring all the world under one's control. || 79 ||

Having purified them and made them into pills smeared with the three sweets, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations while measuring by weight; thus, one will swiftly bring everyone under control.
By these eight [substances]. By the term "practitioner" (*sādhaka*), it is stated that [the rite] is performed with fifty thousand oblations (*lakṣārddha*) within three years.
As they say: "One should offer these, combined with the three sweets, either one hundred thousand or half of that."
"Within three years, he brings the entire three worlds under his control.
"With pure [materials]" means having removed refuse and washed them until they are thoroughly dried;
this is connected with the phrase "he should offer a hundred thousand oblations."
The word "by means of *homa*" is connected with "measured by a hundred thousand" (*lakṣamānataḥ*).
The connection is: "having made pills from purified salts from which dross has been removed.
The number beginning with "having offered a hundred thousand" and so forth applies to a great undertaking.
"And one should offer oblations after observing the gravity or lightness of the task, using an appropriate quantity," as it has been said. (77–80)
Having written the letters of the alphabet individually upon slips of paper, one should worship them and offer oblations into the fire while reciting the letters from those slips. || 81 ||
The fire-oblation (homa) removes malevolent magic and bestows all forms of protection and success;
for a thousand oblations, one should bestow a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) measured in gold coins (niṣkas). || 82 ||
Regarding the phrase "having written":

having written the letters of the *mātṛkā* individually and separately upon pieces of bark such as palm leaves, and having worshipped each one separately, one should offer oblations into the fire while reciting the syllables of that mantra after having worshipped the *mātṛkā*-pedestal in the fire; such is the connection [of the words].

In that regard, the sequence of worship is as follows: having pronounced the seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), deity (*devatā*), power (*śakti*), and seed-syllable (*bīja*) for each individual syllable, and having performed meditation (*dhyāna*), one should offer perfume and other articles with that very syllable.
Regarding the seers and so forth therein: in the middle of the *Arjunyāyana*, there are two *Bhārgavas*; they are the *Pratiṣṭhikās*.
Agniveśya has three [syllables], Supratiṣṭhā has four, and Gautama has three.
The Gāyatrī belongs to Bharadvāja; the Uṣṇih is [the seer] Ekāraka;
the Anuṣṭubh is Lohityāyana; and for two [verses], the Bṛhatī belongs to Vasiṣṭha.
Māṇḍavya and Daṇḍaka are for the vowels; Muni and Chandas for the *pa* and *ya* meters;
Mauhāyana for the *paṅkti*; Ka, A, and Ja for the *triṣṭubh*; and Gha and Ṅa for the two [subsequent] types.
Yogyāyana is the Jagatī meter, the sage is Gopālyāyanaka; Atijagatī is the meter, Chennaṣaka is the Śarkarī, and Aja is the [sage].

Śarkarī is [the son] of Kāśyapa; Atiśarkarī is [the son] of Jhañaya; Śunaka is [the son] of Aṣṭi; Saumanasyā is [the daughter] of Aṣṭi; Ḍe is [the daughter] of Kāraṇa; and Dhṛti is [the daughter] of Kāraṇa.
In the three [sections] beginning with Ḍhaṇo, Māṇḍavya, Atidhṛti, Sāṃkṛtyāyana, and Kṛti, there shall be Kātyāyana; however, in the Napaka sections, Prakṛti shall be used.
The Dākṣāyaṇa and Vyāghrāyaṇa forms are considered modifications (vikṛti) of Bha; Śāṇḍilya and Saṃkṛti are the modifications of Ma; and Kāṇḍalī and Atikṛti are the modifications of Ya.
Dāṇḍyāyana and Utkṛti, as well as Jātāyana and Daṇḍaka;
Lāṭyāyana and Daṇḍaka, Śeṣa and Sahaja, and Jayadaṇḍaka.
Māṇḍavya and Daṇḍaka are at the target; for the letters beginning with *ka*, the sages and meters are [assigned].
When this has been stated, the deities, beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha, are also proclaimed.
"Her seed-syllable is [Hrīm], while her powers are considered to be Pūrṇeśvarī and the others. Thus, the meditation is as previously stated;
that which was said should be reflected upon.
A *niṣka* consists of four *suvarṇas*. || 81–82 ||
Or one may give half, according to one's capacity, and thus obtain the fruit as described.
Having consecrated it seven times with this [mantra], one should drink it every day at dawn. || 83 ||
"By this [method]" means: the sequence of practice here is as follows.

Having oneself become the form of the deity, one takes water upon the lotus of the letters (*lipipadma*) and recites the ten-syllable *Bālā* mantra, then the reversed ten-syllable mantra, and the *Bālā* mantra again; thus it is endured.

Having thus recited [the mantra] from *a* to *kṣa*, including the nasal bindu (*m*), and having again recited from *a* to *kṣa* along with the bindu and the visarga (*ḥ*), one should drink [the nectar] while meditating on the pervasion of these syllables between the eyebrows like the flame of a lamp.
Meditating on the emergence of the phonemes within the mouth and their exit from the mouth in the form of the scriptures and so forth, one should drink it a second time. || 83 ||
He becomes eloquent and attains supreme poetic skill.
One should cook ghee with the juice of *brāhmī*, a paste of *vacā*, and milk. (84)
The word "water" (salilam) is to be connected with what precedes.
It should be understood that the phrase "it may be so" refers to "after twelve months.
Even one who is mute and speech-impaired, if he possesses the cow of poetic genius, attains supreme perfection after twelve months.
Because of this statement.
Regarding "the juice of *brāhmī*":
here, the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) should be taken only from a cow that has a calf still living and is of a single color.
The milk is also of that same quality.
And the cooking of ghee is according to the method prescribed in Āyurveda.

In that regard, it is stated as a general rule that "the unctuous substance (sneha) is four times the amount of the paste (kalka)," meaning the paste constitutes one-fourth part of the unctuous substance.

In this case, however, considering that it is a "natural decoction" (*svarasapāka*), one should take a paste (*kalka*) equal to one-eighth of the oil. As it has been said: "The oil is prepared successively with pure water, a decoction, and a fresh juice; one should add a fourth, a sixth, or an eighth part of the paste."
In this context, "brāhmī juice" refers to the fresh juice (svarasa).
As it has been said: "They know the fresh juice to be the liquid obtained by crushing a moist substance and filtering it through a cloth."
Regarding the term *kalka*: "A *kalka* is that which has been ground upon a stone. In this regard, the procedure is as follows.
Two *prastha*s of ghee, two *pala*s of the paste of white vacā,
four times as much *brāhmī* juice as the ghee, and four times as much milk;
for in the preparation of an unctuous substance (*sneha*), there should be five or more liquid ingredients.
In that regard, they say there is a commonality of oiliness, and it should be fourfold in quantity compared to the preceding.
Because it has been stated thus:
water four times the quantity [of the other ingredients] should be added. As it has been said: "In some cases, where cooking with milk, curd, and sour gruel (āranāla) is prescribed..."

"In that [process], one should employ four times as much water for the purpose of infusing potency. And regarding the knowledge of cooking: "When the medicinal paste cannot be grasped by the fingers, when there is no crackling sound in the oil or the fire, and when the color and other qualities are perfected—at that time, one should quickly remove it from the heat."
Likewise, elsewhere it is said: "In the cooking of an unctuous substance (*sneha*), the paste (*kalka*) should be reduced until it becomes as thick as a wick (*vartī*).
And similarly: "The cessation of froth for clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and its emergence [of froth] for oil (*taila*);
for a linctus (*leha*), the presence of threads and sinking in water, yet not flowing."
"This ghee is for the purpose of drinking.
In this case, the cooking must be exactly equal (sama).
As it has been said: "Oil becomes fit for its purpose when cooked; for internal consumption, the cooking should be equal."
It is rough for massage and mild for nasal administration; this is the general rule. || 84 ||

Having recited the Mātṛkā-mantra ten thousand times and accumulated it according to the prescribed rite, that wise man should drink it in the morning; he shall become like the Lord of Speech. || 85 ||
Or one should drink vacā root, consecrated a thousand times with the Brāhmī mantra, along with milk;
he shall obtain great intelligence before long—of this there is no doubt. || 86 ||
"According to the prescribed rite" means:

then, having removed the ghee from the fire and cooled it, one should visualize the seat of the Mātṛkās (*mātṛkāpīṭha*)—over which the mantra has been recited ten thousand times—as being within the ghee; having worshipped it according to the procedure taught for the Mātṛkās, one should drink it.
"It shall come to pass" should be understood as occurring after one year.
For it is said: "One becomes a poet after a year.
However, there is a specific detail in another tantra: one *pala* of white *vacā* powder and one *karṣa* of *turagagandhī*.
Kṛṣṇā, haridrā, sindhūttha, dhātrī, rug, and viśvabheṣaja.
Having separately ground them, one should cast them into a prastha of ghee and cook it over a gentle fire,
skilled in the art of cooking, with four prasthas of brāhmī juice.
This is declared to be Brāhmī-ghṛta; having consecrated it ten thousand times with this mantra, one should drink it during a solar eclipse and shall attain omniscience.
Or, at the beginning of the day, one should always lick [the medicine] consecrated fifty times;
thus, he shall attain a playfulness of speech that is esteemed among the assemblies of poets. Thus [ends verses 85–86].

Having fashioned the lotus as previously described and having established the water-pot as before, the practitioner of mantra should fill it with the decoction of milky trees according to the prescribed rule. || 87 ||
Having stirred the eight fragrances within this vessel endowed with the nine jewels, one should invoke and worship the Goddess Mātṛkā according to the path previously described. || 88 ||
One should sprinkle the beloved man with waters consecrated a thousand times;
on a Sunday, at an auspicious moment, one should also feed the Brāhmaṇas. || 86 ||
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor according to one's own ability, endowed with devotion;
for this specifically provides protection and brings about the pacification of malevolent spells (kṛtyā) and malice. || 90 ||
They say that this consecration bestows sovereignty upon men, grants the accomplishment of all auspicious fortunes, and provides the power to enchant the entire world. || 91 ||
"Previously mentioned" means that which was stated on the occasion of the worship of the Mātṛkās.
"As before" means according to the method described in the Fourth [Āhnika].
"With decoction" means with a medicinal extract (*kaṣāya*).
"Properly" means that one should fill [the vessel] while reciting the *mātṛkā* along with the nasal bindus, using [the decoction] reduced to one-fourth [of its original volume].
"Of the milk-bearing trees" means [the decoction] of their bark.
"Aṣṭagandha" refers to the Śākta [tradition]. The nine gems will be described later. "Accomplished a thousand times" means consecrated a thousand times with mantras.
The connection [of the sentence] is that one should consecrate with waters on a Sunday at an auspicious *lagna*;
it should be understood as "for a month," because of the statement, "And for that month as well."
In the word *nara*, the masculine gender is not intended to be significant, as it is said:
"Even a barren woman (*nārī*) may give birth to an excellent son who is the abode of various virtues.
*Sambalanam* (or *sammohanam*) means subjugation (*vaśyam*). || 87-91 ||
Having constructed the previously described maṇḍala consisting of nine squares,
the mantra-practitioner should place nine jars in those squares, beginning with the center.

The practitioner of mantras [should place] pure [vessels] wrapped with threads, smeared externally with sandalwood paste, perfumed with excellent incense, and provided with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains. || 93 ||
Having filled them with pure water, one should surround them with silken cloths;
[one should place] pearls, rubies, lapis lazuli, gomedas, diamonds, and corals. || 94 ||
Ruby, emerald, and sapphire—these are called the nine gems in their respective order; one should place them into those jars. || 95 ||
One should cast Viṣṇukrāntā, Indravallī, Devī, and Dūrvā [into the jars],
and place tender mango sprouts upon the mouths of the jars.
The practitioner of mantras, having worshipped the Goddess in the central jar starting from Taurus, should place cups filled with unbroken rice and fruits.
One should worship in the jars placed in the directions the goddesses previously mentioned, beginning with Vyāpinī;
accompanied by their respective group-mantras (varga-mantras) and possessing the characteristics described, they bestow all perfections (siddhis). || 98 ||
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with sugar and ghee;
having touched the jars with kuśa grass, one should recite [the mantra] over a hundred and more times for each. || 99 ||
"Endowed with nine parts" means having nine centers (*nābha*).
"Pure" means free from wounds, blackness, and so forth.
"Perfumed with excellent incense"—up to this point—it says "one should deposit them in order," meaning all [the items] everywhere, starting from the center.
"Devī" refers to Sahadevī.
"One should deposit" means all [of them] everywhere.
"The bull Indra, from that beginning" means from the eastward beginning.
"Vāsava, Vṛtrahā, Vṛṣā"—this is from the lexicon (kośa).
"In the directions" and "in the jars" are locative case endings in different grammatical relations (vyadhikaraṇa).
The "groups" (varga) are those beginning with 'a' and so forth, both individually and collectively; these themselves are the mantras, as well as those joined with them or preceded by them.
The "vidyā" is the Mātṛkā;
"a little over one hundred" means one hundred [repetitions] for each jar. (92–99)
One should perform the consecration in reverse order for that candidate who has offered the ritual fee;
this rite causes the destruction of all sins, bestows auspiciousness, and grants the accomplishment of peace. || 100 ||
They know this consecration to be the pacifier of sorcery, malice, and the like; it bestows good fortune, prosperity, and victory, and grants sons even to those who are barren. || 101 ||
Standing before one afflicted by fever, one should recite [the mantra] more than a thousand times;
his fever will perish quickly, as will even minor spirits and planetary influences. || 102 ||
"In reverse order" means with the jars situated starting from the northeast (īśāna) and so forth.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Furthermore, one should consecrate the beloved woman [by sprinkling] from the end to the beginning, from the middle to the end."
Thus, it is understood that even the seizing spirits of minor diseases are destroyed. (100–102)

Having meditated upon the moon, which is white and composed of flowing nectar, within the supreme splendor, the practitioner of yoga should recite the mantra; this brings about the destruction of poison and disease.
It destroys wrinkles and graying hair, eliminates hunger and thirst, bestows nourishment, grants all forms of prosperity, and confers auspicious fortune. || 104 ||
In the supreme Śiva, who resides in the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus within the Supreme Radiance (paratejas), the moon is that very [moon] located there. 103–104.
The letters shall have the forms of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire; likewise, there are three metals:
silver is remembered as the Moon, gold as the Sun, and copper as Fire. || 105 ||
The proportions of the metals have been clearly specified by the number of the letters beginning with 'Sva' (the vowels);
with those alloys, one should fashion a mudrā that is well-proportioned and harmoniously joined. || 106 ||
Having recited the mantra a full thousand times, the practitioner should then touch it and offer oblations;
he should pour the remnants of the mantra-recitation into that [substance] along with the flour-mash, according to the previously stated number. || 107 ||
He speaks of the *triśaktimudrā* with the words "soma" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the three metals":
since it has been stated that "all metal is fiery (*taijasa*)," the term "metal" (*loha*) is used here to designate silver, gold, and copper.
"So be it" means having the form of the moon, the sun, and fire.
He states that very point: "silver is the moon," and so forth.
"Svara, etc. [refers to the following].
Silver 16, gold 25, and copper 10.
However, some say that because the [other] metals consist of twelve parts, there are twelve parts of gold;
this very position is the traditional one.
Also in the Śaiva Āgama: "By means of copper, silver, and gold [in the proportions of] twelve, sixteen, and one."
Here, it is explained that the number follows a reverse order.
Regarding the term *asaṅkalitā*: it means not yet combined or joined, but subsequently brought together and united.
In that regard, the method is as follows: having fashioned three rings from each of those three metals according to their respective proportions, one should subsequently join them together.
"Exceeding by one" means exceeding by eight.
"Having recited the Mātṛkā"—this is the ellipsis.
Then the mantra-practitioner, with the previously mentioned number—namely, one thousand and eight—should offer oblations with honey; such is the connection [of the sentence].

"One should pour it into that" means: "pouring" (sampāta) refers to the pouring of the remnants of the clarified butter from the *sruva* ladle into the ring-finger (*mudrikā*) for each offering. (105–107)

Having placed that seal (mudrā) into the jar according to the procedure prescribed for consecration, one should, with a concentrated mind, invoke the Goddess and worship her with the ritual offerings (upacāras). || 108 ||
Having consecrated him, the Guru should give that ring to the disciplined disciple:
"This [ring] is the destroyer of demons, minor ailments, poisons, and fevers. (109)
One should provide special protection against beasts of prey, thieves, wild animals, and the like;
by wearing this, a lord of men attains victory in battle. (110)
"Stated in the context of the consecration" means by that which is taught regarding the single vase.
"Having invoked" refers to [the invocation] into the jar.
"Having consecrated" refers to the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
"Vyāla" means a serpent;
"mṛga" means a tiger. (108–110)
