The mantra-practitioner should divide the Mātṛkā into nine groups in their proper order:
eight vowels, eight consonants (sparśas), and five pervasive [semi-vowels]. || 111 ||
The nine groups have arisen, and the planets are the lords of these nine groups: the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu. || 112 ||
He speaks of the nine-jewel ring with the words "one should divide.
By the word "mantrin," the placement of the nine planets (navagrahanyāsa) is also indicated. The method for that is as follows:

Having uttered the vowels, one should perform the placement [of mantras] over the entire body from the head to the throat with "Oṃ, obeisance to the lunar orb (somamaṇḍala). Having uttered the consonants from *ka* to *ma*, one should place it from the throat to the heart with "Oṃ, obeisance to the solar orb (sūryamaṇḍala). Having uttered the consonants from *ya* onwards, one should place it pervasively from the heart to the feet with "Oṃ, obeisance to the fiery orb (vahnimaṇḍala)"; this is the placement of the three orbs (*maṇḍalatrayanyāsa*). Then, having uttered the consonants from *ā* to *ṭha*, one should place it from the head to the heart with "Oṃ, obeisance to the lunar orb. Having uttered the consonants from *ā* to *kṣa*, one should place it with "Oṃ, obeisance to the fiery orb."

One should perform the placement [of mantras] from the heart down to the feet; this is the *agnīṣoma-nyāsa*. Having uttered the letters from *ā* to *kṣa*, one should perform the placement as a pervasive [covering] with the mantra "Haṃsaḥ puruṣātmane namaḥ"; this is the *haṃsa-nyāsa*.
These placements are indicated by the phrase "in due order" (*yathākramāt*).

Then, having performed the placement (nyāsa) starting from "aṃ āṃ iṃ īṃ uṃ ūṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ [ḷṃ ḹṃ eṃ aiṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aḥ] namaḥ to the Blessed Sun" and ending with Ketu in that sequence, one should again perform the three previously mentioned nyāsas in reverse order; this is the grahanyāsa.
In that regard, Soma is associated with the remaining eight vowels, Aṅgāraka with the *ka*-group, Budha with the *ca*-group, Bṛhaspati with the *ṭa*-group, and Śukra with the *ta*-group.
Saturn is [assigned] with the *pa*-group, Rāhu with the *ya*-group, and Ketu with the *ṣa*-group.
This is the sequence of placement (*nyāsakrama*) here.

The locations, however, are the root-support (*mūlādhāra*), the generative organ (*liṅga*), the navel, the heart, the throat, the uvula, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, and the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
The pervasive [syllables] begin with the letter *ya*.
By the word "also" (*api*), the term "five by five" (*pañcaśaḥ*) is also connected here.
He states the sequence of the graspers (*graha*) with the words beginning with "arketi."
Rakta is Maṅgala;
Jña is Budha; Manda is Śanaiścara.
Ahi is Rāhu. || 111-112 ||
Garnet, pearl, beautiful coral, and again emerald; topaz, glittering diamond, sapphire, and auspicious hessonite. || 113 ||
One should fashion an auspicious seal from these nine gems, including lapis lazuli;
one should perform all [rites] such as recitation and fire-offerings according to the previously described method. || 114 ||
For whoever wears this mudrā, the planetary spirits (grahas) shall come under his control;
his good fortune increases, and his prosperity shall be unimpeded. || 115 ||
Malevolent spells and treachery perish; all calamities vanish.
Rakshasas, spirits, piśācas, and the like, overwhelmed by fear, do not even look upon him. (116)
Wealth, jewels, and other riches increase higher and higher;
by the grace of the ring, royal fortune remains forever stable. || 117 ||
By the word *cāvi*, the inclusion of extremely red coral is stated.
By the word *lasat*, the inclusion of the six-pointed vajra itself is stated.
"By the previously mentioned path" means by the method previously described for the mudrā. (113–117)
It has the radiant seed-syllable of the third [vowel] as its pericarp, with filaments manifesting through pairs of vowels;
it possesses petals in the form of the flourishing vowels of the consonant groups, is encircled by the abode of the Earth (the square),
and is beautified by a triangle shining with the color of the lord of stars (the letter *va*).
The Yantra of the colored body is declared to be supreme, the highest destroyer of all diseases. || 118 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Śāradātilaka composed by the venerable Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra. || 6 ||
Regarding the statement "the third," it refers to the seed-syllable of the pericarp mentioned previously. This is the dhāraṇayantra.
The letter *ṭha* is the Lord of Tārās (*tārādhīśvara*),
because of the similarity of their forms (*ākārasāmyāt*) and because such a form is written in the Gauḍa script.
The letter *va* has the color of water (*vāri-varṇa*).
It is beautified by those two diagonal directions (*dik-koṇa*) that shine forth from them.
Therefore, this alone is the distinction here from the previously mentioned yantra.
It is stated in the *Kādimata*: "Ṭhaṃ vaṃ [should be placed] in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The teachers have declared that the very worship-diagram mentioned previously is the retention-diagram (*dhāraṇayantra*).
Some also explain this verse in accordance with that [interpretation].
It is beautified by those two shining corners of the directions;
thus, "vidik" comes to mean "corner" (koṇa).
Then, the syllable *ṭha* is placed in the intermediate directions (*vidikṣu*).
By the word "corner" (vikoṇa), the directions are meant;
therefore, the meaning is that the letter *va* is in the directions.
This has been stated by the Teachers:

And the lotus of the letter [Haḥ], encircled by the orb of the earth together with the seven oceans in all directions, is remembered upon the head as the conqueror of death, which utterly destroys poison and disease.
Thus [it is said]. (118)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition. 6.
Now begins the seventh chapter. Next, I shall explain the script of the elements (*bhūtalipi*), which is most secret and extremely difficult to obtain.
Having attained which, the sages obtained all their desires from Śambhu.
Now, he speaks of the specific *mātṛkā* known as the *bhūtalipi* mantra, beginning with the word "atha. The grammatical connection is: "that which [he] obtained from the presence of Śambhu.
By the phrase "all desires," the ritual application (*viniyoga*) is stated. || 1 ||
The five short vowels are the phonemes of conjunction: space, air, fire, water, and earth;
[these correspond] respectively to the last, the first, the second, the fourth, and the middle [consonants]. || 2 ||
The letters of the five groups, together with the final [consonant] and the white moon (the visarga), constitute what is called the *bhūtalipi* (earth-script) consisting of forty-two letters. || 3 ||
He extracts the mantra with the words "five," etc.
The first group consists of the five short vowels: a, i, u, ṛ, and ḷ. The second group consists of the conjunct (sandhi) vowels: e, ai, o, and au.
Vyoma is *haḥ*;
Īra is *yaḥ*;
Agni is *raḥ*.
Water is *va*;
Earth is *la*;
this is the third.
He states the sequence of the letters of the five groups with the words "the last," etc.: the last is *ḍa*, the first is *ka*, the second is *kha*, the fourth is *gha*, and the middle one is *ga*.
This same sequence applies to the [next] four groups as well.
Thus is the group of eight.
*Vānta* is *śa*.
White is *ṣa*.
Because of the reading "Śrīkaṇṭha" and so forth, that [deity] is Indu;
this is the ninth [chapter]. 2-3.

The fifth letters of the groups beginning with *ā*, *ya*, *ma*, *ra*, and *ṇa*, when joined with the letter *śa*, are to be known as the first letters of their respective groups; these nine groups are thus remembered. || 4 ||
He states the first letters of the nine groups with the words *āyambarārṇāḥ*.
This is a *dvandva* compound consisting of *a*, *e*, and *ambarārṇa* (the letter of the sky).
Therein, when the *vṛddhi* [substitution] is applied to *a* and *e* by the rule *vṛddhireci*, the result is *ai*.
Then, by this [rule], when *eco'yavāyavaḥ* applies subsequently, *āy* is substituted [for *ai*], and thus *āyambarārṇa* is established.
In *ambarārṇe*, there is *ha*. [This refers to] the groups of consonants: *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*. || 4 ||
The wise know the letters of the groups [of consonants] to be distinct from the categories of ether, air, fire, water, and earth.
In the second group, there is no earth; in the ninth, there is no water, nor is there earth.
He states that the letters of the groups consist of the elements with the words "space" (*vyoma*) and so forth.
The meaning is that the first letters of each of the nine groups individually have the nature of space and the other elements.
In some places, there is a reading: "they know the nine letters as distinct."
In this context, "nine" should be understood as a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*).
The construction is: they know the nine syllables to be distinct and individual, consisting of ether, air, and so forth.

To the question, "Since the last and the penultimate [groups] consist of seven and eight syllables respectively, how can there be nine syllables?", he says: "In the first recitation, for each of the syllables of the groups..."
It has been stated that [the syllables] consist of the five elements (*pañcabhūtātmakatva*); however, this does not apply to the second and ninth [syllables]. Therefore, he says "of the second," etc.
The intention is that both [sets of syllables] are possible in both cases.
Since the second group consists of four syllables, there is no syllable consisting of the element earth (*bhū*).
Because the ninth [syllable] consists of three phonemes, there is an absence of both [the preceding and following vowels]. || 5 ||

Viriñci, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the Aśvins, Prajāpati, and the Lords of the Directions, accompanied by the powers of action (kriyā) and the rest, shall be the presiding deities of the classes [of consonants] in their respective order. || 6 ||
The sage is Dakṣiṇāmūrti; Gāyatrī is declared to be the metre;
and the deity is said by the wise to be the supreme Parā, the Mistress of the Letters herself. || 7 ||
The deity of the nine groups said: "Viriñci.
The lords of the directions are Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Soma.
What are they all like?
They are endowed with the powers of action and so forth, being possessed of the threefold powers of action, knowledge, and will repeated thrice.
Some, however, maintain that there are nine deities: one as the Lord of the Directions (Digeśvara) and three each for the powers of action and the rest. || 6-7 ||

One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the six groups of consonants together with their respective seed-syllables. One should meditate upon the Goddess at the root of the tree of letters, within the lotus that is identical with Her. || 8 ||
"Hādī" refers to the heart by means of the third group [of consonants].
Likewise, the others are formed by the remaining [consonants] ending with the eighth [of each group].
The application is as follows: *haṃ yaṃ raṃ vaṃ laṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and so forth.
Regarding the instruction "one should meditate":
[one should meditate] upon the lotus consisting of those [syllables], the varṇābja. || 8 ||
The wise declare that the tree is eternally auspicious and composed of phonemes;
it has the great seed of supreme consciousness and the great root of *bindu* and *nāda*. 9.
With the branches of its syllables spread across the earth in all directions, and with the leaves of its own syllables covering the three worlds like water, it flourished. || 10 ||
He was radiant with sprouts the color of fire, like the celestial tree adorned with jewels;
he was illuminating the splendor of his body with flowers as brilliant as the color of the wind-god.
Bowing low with fruits that are as vast as the sky, the supreme refuge of all beings, he sprinkles the Supreme Goddess with the nectars known as the highest immortality. || 12 ||
Fashioned by the Vedas, Agamas, and other scriptures, it is exalted and enchanting; it is composed of Śiva and Śakti, and the three worlds directly take refuge in its shadow. || 13 ||
Relying upon this, the sages shall attain all their desires. || 14 ||
Regarding the statement "of the tree of speech" (*lipitara*), he describes its essential nature with the word "eternal" (*nitya*);
this is because, according to the systems of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) and the Bhāṭṭas, phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal.
"Supreme consciousness" (*parasamvit*) refers to Kuṇḍalinī.
Some say it is the Supreme Brahman. "Śiphā" means the root.
If it is said to be eternal, how can its production from a seed occur?
It is metaphorically designated as a "seed" by virtue of its being a manifestor.
By the word "their own," there is an exclusion of the elements and phonemes mentioned in the second [chapter].
This [explanation] should also be applied to earth and the other [elements].
"Vedāgama" means that the height of the tree is of such a form [as described]. || 9-14 ||
With breasts full and high, resembling ten million crescent moons,
her head adorned with the half-moon, her three eyes rolling from the intoxication of honey-wine— she who incessantly holds in her hands a boon, a rosary, a sacred knowledge, and a skull-cup.
I take refuge in Vāgīśvarī, who today is praised for her youth and whose body is inscribed with letters. || 15 ||
It was stated that "one should meditate," and he now describes that meditation with the words "on the lap" (aṅke).
"Lap" (aṅka) means a mark or stain; she is "freed from" (unmukta), meaning abandoned by it.
Regarding the meditation on the weapons: the first two are in the first pair of hands below the left [side], and the others are in the second pair above them.
Others, however, say that [the sequence] begins from the top on the right, and then on the left for the subsequent ones. || 15 ||

The best of teachers [should place the consciousness] in the locus of support—the foundation—at the navel, the heart, and again at the throat; then in the *bindu*, then in the *nāda*, then in the *śakti*, and finally in Śiva. || 16 ||
Having duly placed the nine vowels upon the nine seats, the wise practitioner should place the letters beginning with *ha* upon his body, starting from the face and proceeding upwards. || 17 ||
"Ādhāra" means:
in the location of the support, which is the space between the anus and the genitals;
in the substratum, which is the *liṅga*.
In the *bindu* at the center of the eyebrows;
in the *nāda* at the end of the hair;
in the *śakti* in the region above that.
"In Śivā" means at the *dvādaśānta*.

"In the nine supports" (*navādhāreṣu*) refers to the nine cakras beginning with the *ādhāra* as previously described. By the phrase "according to the rule," it is meant that one should perform the meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*) of each respective support.
For this very reason, although it was stated previously beginning with "in the support" (*ādhāra*), the expression "in the nine supports" (*navādhāreṣu*) is repeated.
The meditation on the supports (*ādhārabhāvanā*) will be explained in the final chapter.
By the term "the best of teachers" (*deśikasattama*), the fact that the phonemes are accompanied by the nasal bindu (*sabinduka*) is indicated. (16–17)
The best of teachers, being composed, should place the letters of the five groups upon the arms and feet, in the directions of upward, east, south, north, and west;
and [he should place them] in the sequence of the tip, the base, the middle of the base, the middle of the tip, and the middle of the space, beginning with the letter *kṣa*.
Concentrated on the belly, the pair of flanks, the navel, and the back. || 19 ||
One should place the three letters beginning with *śa* in sequence in the secret place, the heart, and the space between the eyebrows.
In the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), it ends with emission; in the process of maintenance (*sthiti*), it consists of fire, wind, and water.
One should deposit [the mantra] through the sequence of the stages of space (viyat), ending with the emission of the bindu;
for the withdrawal, one should deposit it in reverse order, adorned with the bindu.

The supreme practitioner, initiated by means of the path taught in the scriptures, should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) one hundred thousand times, recite [the mantra] that many times, and offer oblations with sesame seeds ten thousand times. || 22 ||
He explains what was stated as "from above and so forth" with the word "ūrdhva.
The wise one has stated that the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed by conceiving of oneself as having five faces.
By the term "composed" (*samāhita*), the presence of the *bindu* (anusvāra) for the phonemes is indicated.
Regarding "doḥpaditi":

the best of teachers should place the letters of the five groups [of consonants] upon the arms and feet—in the sequence of the tips, roots, middle, and bases of the upper parts and lower parts, starting from the abdomen and ending at the back; this is how it connects with what follows.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "root" (*mūla*) and "tip" (*agra*) constitute "root-and-tip" (*mūlāgra*); that which is near those two is "near-root-and-tip" (*upamūlāgra*).
Thus, [the term] "tip, root, near-root-and-tip, and middle region" (*agramūlopamūlāgramadhyadeśa*) is the analysis.
Here, "tip" (*agra*) refers to the end of the finger.
The root is the base of the thighs. Near the root are the elbows and knees. Near the tip are the first joints of the fingers and toes.
The "middle region" (madhyadeśa) refers to the middle joints, namely the wrists and ankles.

By the term "composed" (samāhita), it is stated that he is a seer who, through his dedication to meditative absorption (samādhi), does not deviate from the proper placement [of the letters]. By the term "best of teachers" (deśikasattama), it is indicated that the phonemes are accompanied by the nasal bindu.
"Bhrūvile" means in the middle of the eyebrows.
"In sequence" (kramāt) is connected everywhere, beginning with the vowels; here, it means according to the sequence stated in this mantra.
Regarding the phrase "in creation":
the ellipsis is that the *bhūtalipi* (earth-script) ends with *sarga*.
The connection is that one should sequentially place that [script], which ends with *bindu* and *sarga*, during the state of maintenance (*sthiti*).
In response to the inquiry as to what the sequence is, he says "fire" (*vahnī*) and so forth.
Therein, having placed each individual syllable of fire and the others, one should place them again in that very same order.
This is the sequence therein:

uṃḥ iṃḥ ṛṃḥ aṃḥ ḷṃḥ oṃḥ eṃḥ auṃḥ eṃḥ auṃḥ eṃḥ, and so forth; as declared in the Āgamas and as stated in the *Kulaprakāśatantra*. "One who has been initiated" (dīkṣita) refers to the definition [of the practitioner].
In this regard, the sequence consists of one placement (*nyāsa*) and one repetition (*āvṛtti*); this is what is stated by the phrase "the best of practitioners. (18–22)
The wise one should worship the Goddess every day on the seat previously described;
he should offer a seat consisting of a lotus of letters and fashion the form [of the deity] with the root mantra. || 23 ||
One should worship the Goddess therein together with the primary limbs and the surrounding enclosures;
first the enclosure of the limbs, and afterwards that consisting of Ambikā and the others, so it is taught.
The second is said to consist of the Mothers; the third, of sixteen powers (dvyaṣṭa-śakti);
and the fourth and fifth are further said to consist of twenty-two powers.
The sixth enclosure is known to consist of the sixty-four Śaktis, the leaders of the worlds;
furthermore, the seventh [enclosure] shall be with their weapons, and the eighth enclosure [is formed by them]. || 26 ||

Thus is the venerable Śrībhūtalipidevatā, the sustainer of the world, to be worshipped according to the rules in the aforementioned locations; one should worship her limbs [the ancillary deities] as well. || 27 ||
Ambikā, Vāgbhavī, Durgā, and Śrīśakti are to be understood according to the characteristics previously mentioned;
Brāhmī and the others are to be worshipped as before, along with Karālī, Vikarālī, and Umā.
Regarding the instruction "one should worship":

here, someone has said that because of the statement "on the previously described pedestal," the worship of the thirty-two Śaktis (by repeating the sixteen twice), the sixty-four (by repeating them four times), and the one hundred and twenty-eight (by repeating them eight times) must take place on an eight-petaled lotus; otherwise, the phrase "on the previously described pedestal" would be contradicted.
That is not according to tradition;
for in their view, the state of having eight coverings (*aṣṭāvṛtitva*) would be contradicted.
A "covering" (*āvṛtti*) is defined as worship by way of surrounding [the deity] on all sides.
That [first enclosure] is formed solely by the worship of the eight powers (*aṣṭaśakti*). If a second enclosure distinct from that is worshipped, it constitutes a different enclosure altogether;
it is not included within the former.
This has not been seen previously in other mantra systems.
However, according to the traditional school (*sāmpradāyika-pakṣa*), the meaning of the phrase "on the seat previously mentioned" is as follows:
one should worship here also the seats, the powers, and the mantras of the seats that were mentioned previously.
This is to be applied everywhere.
Accordingly, the author will state at the occasion of the worship of Mahāgaṇapati: "One should worship on the seat previously described.
In that context, if the previously mentioned single-syllable Gaṇapati is intended, and only a lotus-seat with eight petals is taken, then as for the worship in the hexagon and other [enclosures]:
That which is to be stated would be untenable;
furthermore, the statement regarding the pedestal (*pīṭha*) consisting of a triangle, a hexagon, and the lotus of the *mātṛkā*s within the meditation (*dhyāna*) would also be inconsistent.

If it were argued that "on the previously mentioned pedestal" means "as described in the section on meditation," then [that too would fail], because there is no statement that establishes the worship of the pedestal's power (*pīṭhaśakti*) or the pedestal-mantra (*pīṭhmantra*).
It is enough to say that otherwise there would be no worship at all.
Therefore, having constructed here an eight-petalled lotus, a sixteen-petalled lotus, and a four-gated *bhūpura*, one should worship the previously mentioned *pīṭha-śaktis* therein;

then, having offered the seat with the *varṇābja* (the lotus of letters), having conceived the form (*mūrti*) by means of the root mantra (*mūla*), and having worshipped the Goddess there, one should worship the limbs (*aṅgas*) upon the filaments as before.

Above that, one should worship the four goddesses beginning with Ambikā on the petals of the directions; in front of them, the goddesses beginning with Brāhmī; and on the sixteen-petalled lotus and the others, the goddesses beginning with Karālī.
Regarding the phrase "with the lotus of letters" (*varṇābjena*): the formula is *hsauḥ varṇābjāya bhūtalipiyogapīṭhāya namaḥ*.
Regarding that form:
he explains the word "etcetera" in the phrase "limbs, etc. with the words "at the beginning," and so forth.
He states the place of worship for the covering of the limbs with the words "in the locations."
Regarding the phrase "in those mentioned" (*ukteṣu*), it refers to those [deities] already enumerated. By the expression "according to rule" (*vidhivat*), the meditations (*dhyāna*) are indicated.
He explains the word "beginning with Ambikā" (*ambikādyādi*) by saying "one should worship" (*pūjayet*).
The meditation (*dhyāna*) for these [goddesses] should be investigated in their respective sections.
Regarding the meditation for the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛpūjādhyāna*), he says "the aforementioned" (*ukta*).
This means those whose characteristics have been stated, namely, those whose meditations were described in the previous chapter (*prākpaṭala*).
"As before" means in the previously mentioned locations. (23–28)
Sarasvatī, Śrī, Durgā, Lakṣmī, Śruti, Smṛti, Dhṛti, Śraddhā, Medhā, Mati, Kānti, and Āryā—these are the sixteen Śaktis. || 29 ||
Holding swords and shields, dark-complexioned, well-adorned, and worthy of worship, they are Vidyā, Hrī, Puṣṭi, Prajñā, Sinīvālī, and Kuhū. || 30 ||
Rudrā, Vīryā, Prabhā, Nandā, Poṣā, Ṛddhidā, Śubhā, Kālarātri, Mahārātri, Bhadrakālī, and Kapardinī. || 31 ||
Vikṛti, Daṇḍinī, Muṇḍinī, Śikhaṇḍinī who holds a crescent moon, the destroyer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, and she who is not distressed by the demon Mahiṣāsura. || 32 ||
Indrāṇī, Rudrāṇī, who forms half the body of Śaṅkara, Nārī, Nārāyaṇī, the wielder of the trident, and the protectress. || 33 ||
Ambikā and Hlādinī are indeed remembered as the thirty-two Śaktis;
they have discs in their hands, faces like Piśācas, and are to be worshipped with beautiful ornaments. || 34 ||
He explains the words "dvyaṣṭa-śakti" and so forth with the word "karālī.
The phrase "are to be worshipped" refers to [the goddesses] on the sixteen petals.
The reading is "rudrā vīrya."
By that, Rudrā is the seventh, Vīryā the eighth, Prabhā the ninth,
and Nandā the tenth.
"Śubhā" is an adjective, not the name of a Śakti.
As it is stated in the Saṃhitā: "Rudrā, Vīryā, Prabhā, Nandā, Poṣiṇī, and likewise Ṛddhidā."
Regarding the phrase "Daṇḍinī and Muṇḍinī":
these refer to two powers (śakti), namely Daṇḍinī and Muṇḍinī,
because it is stated that "Daṇḍinī is indeed the transformation (vikṛti)."
"Niśumbhaśumbhamathanī" is one [deity];
"they are to be worshipped" refers to [the deities] at the tips and the junctions of the sixteen petals.
This is stated in the Saṃhitā:
They are to be worshipped in order starting from the east, upon the tips of the petals and at the joints.
Thus [ends verses 29–34].
Piṅgalākṣī, Viḍālākṣī, Samṛddhi, Vṛddhi, Śraddhā, Svāhā, she known as Svadhā, Māyā, and Vasundharā. || 35 ||
The sustainer of the three worlds, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, the sovereign of the thirty gods; she of beautiful form and manifold forms, the mother of Skanda, and the beloved of Acyuta. || 36 ||
Vimalā, Āmalā, and thereafter Aruṇī and Punarāruṇī;
she is nature (prakṛti), transformation (vikṛti), as well as creation, maintenance, and withdrawal. || 37 ||
Sandhyā, Mātā, Satī, Haṃsī, Madīkā, Rañjikā, Parā, Devamātā, Bhagavatī, Devakī, and Kamalāsanā. || 38 ||
She has three faces, another has seven faces; she intoxicates both gods and demons.
She has hanging lips, upturned hair, many heads, and a belly like a wolf’s. || 39 ||
After that was the one named Ratharekhā, then Śaśirekhā, followed by Gaganavegā and Pavanavegā. || 40 ||
Then there is the one named Bhuvanapālā; from her comes Madanāturā; likewise Anaṅgā, Anaṅgamadanā, and Anaṅgamekhalā. || 41 ||
Anaṅgakusumā, Viśvarūpā, Asurabhayaṅkarī, Akṣobhyā, Satyavādinī, Vajrarūpā, and Śucivratā. || 42 ||
Varadā and Vāgīśā are proclaimed as the sixty-four [deities];
all of them hold bows and arrows, possess flaming tongues, and are of great splendor. || 43 ||

Those with fangs, those with wild beasts [as ornaments], and those with hair standing erect—whose minds are intent on the commencement of battle, all blazing with every ornament—should be worshipped with great effort. || 44 ||

The analysis of the compound is as follows: she whose designation (abhikhyā) is *svadhā* and whose name (*saṃjñā*) is *māyā*. Accordingly, the Teachers [state]: "She who is known as Māyā is Vasundharā."
Elsewhere also it is said: "Śraddhā, Svāhā, she who is called Svadhā, Mātṛkā, and Vasundharā.
Regarding the phrase "sthitiḥ saṃhṛtireva ca," there is a variant reading in some places: "saṃsthitiḥ sthitireva ca."
This alone is the traditional view. "Parā" is a name for Śakti; "Surā" is one [name], and "Asuravimardinī" is another.
As it has been said:
"The army of the gods, led by the seven chiefs, as well as the host of the Asuras."
Likewise, "apare" is the name of Śakti;
immediately following that, it is connected with "pavanavegā.
The word division is "asurabhayaṅkarī."
The analysis of the compound is: "Akṣobhyā" (the Unshakeable) and "Satyavādinī" (the Truth-Speaker).
"They are to be worshipped with effort" means [starting] from the inner square and so forth, proceeding clockwise.
As it is stated in the Saṃhitā: "One should worship these Śaktis."
In the very order of circumambulation.
Thus [ends the section] 35–44.
The Lords of the World (Lokeśas) are to be worshipped as before, and likewise the [deities] beginning with Vajra;
the mantra-practitioner who thus worships the deity of the Śrī Bhūtalipi is [successful]. || 45 ||
He shall become the ground upon which the two Śrīvāṇīs reside, and he is saluted even by the gods.
By offering ten thousand lotuses into the fire, one may bring a king under one's control. || 46 ||
Likewise, by offering oblations with blue lotuses, great fortune (Mahālakṣmī) arises;
and by sacrificing with Palāśa flowers, one becomes a poet within a year. || 47 ||
By means of an oblation of *rājī* and salt, one should bring a woman under one's control;
the practitioner should perform here also those rites spoken of by Mātṛkā. || 48 ||
"As before" means as described in the Fourth [chapter].
That has been stated in the Saṃhitā:
"O Dear One, one should worship the guardians of the worlds outside that, upon the orb of the earth."
Thus;
"tadvat" (in that manner) is like the fourth case-ending suffix *vat*. || 45 ||
The statement "it is like that" is incorrect;
for in both subsequent applications as well, this very same number [of members] applies. (46–48)
The man who worships the mantra by encasing it with the *bhūtalipi* (earth-script) one hundred times, both in direct and reverse order, for him the mantra shall become perfected. || 49 ||

He states that even other mantras achieve success by this very method with the words "bhūta... etc. The grammatical connection is: "having encapsulated [the mantra] in forward and reverse order," it becomes a perfected mantra (*siddho manuḥ*).
The meaning is that his mantra will be accomplished;
this should be understood as occurring within just one month.
As it is stated in the *Kulaprakāśatantra*: "One should recite the mantra for only one month, encapsulated by the letters of the *bhūtalipi*."
"By reciting it a thousand times either in direct or reverse order, his mantra becomes perfected.

Alternatively, the meaning is that one who has fallen into a position of being "to be accomplished" (sādhya) or "hostile" (ari) bestows the fruit of a mantra situated in a "perfected" (siddha) position. || 49 ||
O knower of the vital breath, unite Kuṇḍalinī—who is coiled like a sleeping serpent—along the central path with the supreme abode by means of the supreme nectars. || 50 ||
One should flood [the body] from the crown of the head down to the base; this yoga bestows all perfections.
Indeed, one whose body is thus consecrated by this [mantra] becomes like the sun in splendor. || 51 ||
Having understood the specific operations of the yantras, one should accomplish the ritual acts. || 52 ||

"By the middle path" means by way of the central channel, the *suṣumṇā*; "lead to the supreme abode" means lead [the soul] to the supreme station, the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*), the abode of Śiva, by means of the sequential piercing of the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*). By the term "knower of breath," the yogi is indicated.
"Up to the root" means reaching as far as the *mūlādhāra*. The connection is that one should "flood [it] with the supreme nectars.
He states that this [mantra] is a limb (*aṅga*) of another mantra with the words "by this" (verse 52).

The sky (the letter *ha*) enriched with the drop (*bindu*), joined with Śiva (*i*), conjoined with the fourth vowel (*ū*), and ending with *namaḥ*— this is the mantra prescribed for the middle [of the diagram] for the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), using the letters of his name. On the petals, one should write the letters representing his elements, each enclosed within the letter *ha*.
Having written the remainder on the final petal, the wise one should encircle it with a circle.
Regarding the "space-machine," he says "bindu" and so forth:
"gagana" is *ha*; enriched with the *bindu*, it becomes *haṃ*. That very same "gagana" is thus endowed with the *bindu*.
Śiva is the letter *e*; joined with that, it becomes *heṃ*. Here, by the word "Śiva," the number eleven is indicated, as there are eleven Rudras.
By that [number], the eleventh vowel is meant; thus, the letter *e* is what is expressed by the word "Śiva."
The word *jñānī* joined with the dative case—that is, joined with the singular dative ending—means "to Jñānin.

This mantra, ending in *namaḥ*, is prescribed for the middle [of the diagram], meaning it should be written in the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Regarding the "syllables of the kinsmen" of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*)—such as Devadatta who is afflicted by poison—it is said: "The Siddha-syllables are declared to be the kinsmen" (2.131).

Together with the syllables of the Siddhakoṣṭha, one should write the elemental letters (*bhūtavarṇa*) of those [syllables] upon the petals— namely, the elemental letters of space (*vyoma*) mentioned in this chapter— letter by letter, each enclosed within the letter *ha*.
On the ninth petal, which is the last, one should write the two elemental letters of space, each individually enclosed within the letter *ha*, on that eighth petal.
By the word "intelligent" (matimān), it is stated that all syllables are accompanied by the bindu.
"All syllables are accompanied by the bindu"—so say those who know the tradition.
The action, "O Hara, remove the poison of Devadatta," should be written in the middle [of the mantra]. 53.
This "sky-machine" (viyadyantra) is said to be fashioned from lac and sandalwood;
when offered at the rising of Rāhu on the day of Rohiṇī, it destroys poison and grants all peace. || 54 ||
*Lākṣā* is lac-dye (*alaktaka*).
Regarding the phrase "at Rohiṇī, at the rising of Rāhu":
here, at the specific *muhūrta* of the lunar mansion at that time, and upon the rising of the respective elemental planet, the corresponding yantra should be drawn.

On that day, it was the ninth *muhūrta* of Rohiṇī, and at night, it was the eighth *muhūrta* of Rohiṇī. At that time, there was the rising of Rāhu; specifically, the rising of Rāhu occurred during the rising of Vāyubhūta.
Since the rising of the five elements is fixed within each individual sign, the rising of the nine planets also certainly occurs therein.
As it has been said: "The vital breaths (prāṇa), fire, wind, water, and ether are the winds [of the planets] in their respective order:
Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Saturn, Mercury, the Sun, and the Moon and Rāhu."
"In due order, among the four elements, space becomes the soul of all.
Thus it is said elsewhere: "The Guru [Jupiter] is in the northwest; Venus and Mars move in fire [the southeast];"
On the earth, Mercury and the Sun are to be known; in the water, the Moon and Saturn.
One should know that space along with the planets is thus present in all the zodiacal signs;
three hundred and sixty breaths constitute one nāḍikā.
One zodiac sign is said to consist of five nāḍikās; a day consists of twelve signs, beginning with Aries and ending with Pisces.
Within these zodiac signs, the risings of the planets are to be understood;
in each individual sign here, there are five elements.
Wind, fire, earth, water, and space as the fifth—
indeed, within each of these, five subtle elements arise.
For all the zodiacal signs (rāśis), the first breath-moment (nāḍikā) is said to belong to Vāyu and the others;
the second breath-moment belongs to Agni, and the third is considered to belong to the Earth (Pṛthivī).
The fourth is to be known as Vāruṇī, and the fifth is remembered as Vyomā;
in all cases, those on the preceding day are auspicious, while those immediately following are inauspicious.
Rāhu, Mars, the Sun, and Saturn—these are auspicious when situated to the south; Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon—these gentle planets bring good fortune when situated to the left.
Thus has the rising of the planets among the signs and elements been described.
The rising of the elements (bhūtōdaya) will be explained in the final chapter.
The asterisms and auspicious moments have been declared in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra):
Ārdrā, Aśleṣā, Anurādhā, Maghā,
Dhaniṣṭhikā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Abhijit, and Rohiṇī.
Jyeṣṭhā, Viśākhā, Mūla, Śatatārakā,
and the two Uttarā-Phalgunīs are the fifteen moments of the day.
Ārdrā at night, as well as the eight beginning with Pūrvabhādrapadā,
Punarvasu, Kṣaṇa (Aśleṣā), Puṣya, Śruti (Śravaṇā), and the three beginning with Hasta.
*Śruti* means *śravaṇā*.
*Karādikāḥ* means those beginning with Hasta; the three [asterisms] are Hasta, Citrā, and Svātī—this should be understood in the same way for the subsequent cases as well.
Others, however, say that it should be performed when Rāhu is in the Rohiṇī asterism. || 54 ||

One should fashion the two [seed-syllables] that bear the crescent moon upon their heads, ending respectively with the dative case-ending and followed by "namaḥ," in the center; then, having inscribed the syllables of Vāyu enclosed by 'ya' according to the rule on the eight petals, one should place the remaining syllable on the final petal.
This yantra, situated upon a palm leaf, should be encircled by the house of Vāyu. || 55 ||

He states the Vāyavya yantra with the words "the two which... Here, *akṣi* refers to the vowel *ī*. This is because of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating: "When no distinction is specified, [the term] refers to the left."
The letter *e* is the lower lip;
the crescent moon is the bindu.

"Eye and lower lip" (*akṣyadhara*) refers to these two; "accompanied by those" is *sākṣyadhara*; and "those [two] having the crescent moon as their head" (*indukhaṇḍaśiras*) is the analysis of the compound.
Because it exists in sequence, [the syllables] are "yiṃ" and "yeṃ. To Kopeśa joined with the dative suffix (ṅe) is "Kopeśāya.
One should fashion—that is, write—this mantra accompanied by "namaḥ" (namoyuktam), namely "Namaḥ Kopeśāya," in the center of the pericarp (kaṇīkā).
One should enclose these syllables—the colors of the Vāyu-beings mentioned in this chapter—within *yapuṭas* according to the prescribed rule; that is to say, letter by letter.
Furthermore, they should end with the *bindu*.

One should surround them with a circle marked by six *bindus*, as stated in the description of the abode of Vāyu: "The circle of the sky belongs to Mātariśvan (Vāyu) and is marked with six *bindus*. Thus, one should envelop them with a circle adorned by six *bindus*.
Here too, as before, the ritual action (karma) should be written down. || 55 ||
If one buries a mechanical device at the entrance of an enemy's house during the rising of Saturn in the Svāti nakṣatra, it will certainly cause his expulsion or even his death. || 56 ||

"Under Svāti, at the rising of Mandi" means: when the rising of Mandi, that is Śanaiścara (Saturn)—meaning the rising of water and earth—occurs during the muhūrta of the Svāti asterism, one should bury a Vāyavya (north-western) yantra at the gate of the enemy; this is the syntactical connection. || 56 ||

The pair of seed-syllables of Fire, joined respectively with the ear (Ś), Sadyojāta (S), and the half-moon (Ū), followed by the two vowels (Ā and Ī) and RĪ, and ending with PHAṬ HRŪM— this is the mantra prescribed for the center.
One should inscribe upon the petals the letters born of Fire, constricted by Fire, nourished by the syllables of the target (sādhya).
And the final [syllable] is placed on the final petal, situated within the interior of the birch-bark, following the path of fire. || 57 ||
Regarding the mantra of Agni, it says "of fire":
in the Śravaṇa [nakṣatra], there is the letter *u*, followed by a crescent moon (*ardhendu*) and a bindu.
Joined with these in sequence, this is the pair of seed-syllables of fire, namely the two *repha*s; thus, *ruṃ* and *roṃ*.
The other essential form consists of the word *namaḥ* at the heart.
This mantra is the one prescribed in the middle, situated within the *kāṇīkā*.
It should be understood that each syllable is enclosed by the letter *ra*, being constricted by fire (*vahni*).
In this context, because it consists of a single syllable, the *rodha* (enclosure) results in a *sampuṭa* (encasement).

By the words "with the syllables of the *sādhya* which nourish," it means "with the nourishing syllables of the *sādhya*"; since it is stated that "the nourishing [syllables] are to be known as those that are well-accomplished" (*susiddha*), the meaning is "with the syllables from the *susiddha* square.
The meaning of "situated in the fire-vehicle with a svastika and a triangle in the center, mixed with the syllable of the slayer" is that it is the location of the nourishing syllables. || 57 ||
When there is a conjunction of an auspicious day and a favorable constellation, this fiery yantra, composed of lac and saffron, is declared to be a protector against all malevolent beings. || 58 ||
If that [name] is mixed with "killer-syllables" (ghātakākṣara) and written upon a cloth with funeral ashes during the rising of Mars in the asterism Kṛttikā, it shall destroy the enemy. || 59 ||
According to the statement, "The letters of the enemy's house are considered killer-letters," the letters of the enemy's house are the killer-letters.
In Kṛttikā—that is, during the auspicious moment (muhūrta) of the Kṛttikā constellation—at the rising of Mars (Maṅgala), meaning at the rising of the fire-element and the earth-element;
in that garment, namely the shroud-garment (citāvastra).
"One should destroy" refers to [an object] buried in a house or elsewhere. || 58–59 ||

The number of syllables in the Vāruṇa-mantras is said to be one hundred and fifty (150), joined with that same number (150) plus half a moon (1/2) [making 300.5], and ending with half a moon (1/2) and a moon (1).
In the middle of these, the syllables of the earth (Bhū) are recited.
Within the leaf-cells, one should place the syllables of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), along with the syllables of their kinsmen, arranged in the form of a bird.
Having drawn this yantra encircled by a water-mandala, it becomes one pertaining to Varuṇa.
He states the Varuṇa Yantra: "Nāsā" means *ṛ*; joined with the half-moon (*ardhendu*) and the bindu, it becomes *ṛ̃*. "Ambu" means *va*; by that, it is *vṛ̃*.
That "ambu" (*va*) joined with "manu" (*au*) and the half-moon and bindu becomes *vauṃ*.
Here, by the word *manu*, the number fourteen—referring to the fourteen Manus—is indicated. By that [number], the fourteen vowels are meant; thus, the vowel *au* is denoted by the word *manu*.
[The rule] "ending in *ṅ*, *vidhu*, and *vīdhava*" applies.
"Vidhvante vidhuśabdānte bhuve tena vidhubhuve namaḥ"—
this mantra is declared, that is, stated as something to be written, in the center of the pericarp (*kaṇīkā*).
[One should write] the syllables enclosed by the letter *va*, with each syllable accompanied by the nasal bindu.
[It is] with a water-city [consisting of] a half-moon accompanied by two lotuses on both sides. || 60 ||

One should write this on birch bark with red sandalwood water; when the diagram is drawn under the constellation of Śatabhiṣaj during the period of Venus, it will bring about subjugation and other such effects. || 61 ||
The asterism of Varuṇa is Śatabhiṣā; at that muhūrta, when Kāvya (Mercury) or Śukra (Venus) has risen, and when the rising occurs in the signs of Vahni (Aries) or Bhū (Taurus)—this is the meaning.
By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "subjugation and so forth," attraction, enchantment, and the like are included. || 61 ||

The *gaṇḍa* [syllable] is adorned with a dot; such would be the *vasumatī*. However, the two *jagas* situated between the two *gaṇḍas* are *luke*; one should write this mantra in the center with a bow (*natim*). One should write the letters ending in *la*, enclosed by the letter *la*, upon the petals of the *vasumatī*.
One should encircle the earth with houses according to the rules, provided with service-roads and varṇas. || 62 ||
He states the terrestrial yantra: "Gaṇḍa" refers to the letter *ḷ*, adorned with a bindu (*ḷ̐*).
"Vasumatī" is the letter *la*; being likewise possessed of a bindu, it becomes *laṃ*.
The two letters *ja* and *ga* stand between the two syllables *gaṇḍa*.
Regarding the phrase "between the two *gaṇḍas*":
here, first there is merely the letter *ga*, and subsequently there is the letter *ṇḍa* joined with the *parasavarṇa*; thus, the form *gaja-gaṇḍa* is established.
The nature of the syllable LU is salutation (namas).
One should write this mantra in the center, within the pericarp (kaṇīkā).
In this context, it is stated that they "end with *la*" because of the deficiency of one syllable;
therefore, the meaning is that three *la* characters accompanied by the bindu (anusvāra) should be written on the eighth petal. [This applies to] each syllable enclosed within the letter *la*.

"Those who possess the letters of the *sevāvara* are known as the *sādhya-sevakas*" (Śāradātilaka 2.131); by this statement, the meaning is that they are formed with the letters from the *sādhya*-box. "According to rule" means that they are accompanied by the nasal bindu. || 62 ||
When the moon has risen in the constellation Jyeṣ�terā and the ground is soft, a mechanical device made of earth mixed with red ochre will,
before long, act as a pillar everywhere.
He who constantly worships the deity of the Śrībhūtalipi, who is more secret than the secret, shall be filled with auspicious sons, wealth, and grain. || 64 ||
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the auspicious moment (muhūrta) of the Jyeṣṭhā constellation, when Mercury has risen— that is, at the rising of the earth—

in clay, meaning in a clay vessel; in all cases, "one who causes paralysis" (stambhakṛt) should be understood as one who effects the paralyzing of wind, fire, water, semen, the edge of a sword, armies, and so forth.

In that regard, retention [of the seed] during the phase of semen and so forth, and burial in the army and so forth, should be understood by the wise according to their respective contexts. || 63-64 ||
The mountain is obstructed by Varuṇa; two *ṭha*s are in *davāgvādini*;
this ten-syllable mantra of Vāgīśvarī bestows the power of speech. (65)

Having thus stated the *mātṛkā* mantras, and desiring to state the *Sarasvatī* mantras which are their derivatives, he extracts the ten-syllabled mantra of Vāgvādinī with the words "adrir" and so forth.
"Adri" is the letter *da*; it is "constrained" (*saṃruddha*)—that is, encapsulated—by "Varuṇa," the letter *va*. From this, "vadava" is produced. "Da-vāgvādini" is its essential form.
"Ṭha ṭha svāhā. He bestows the power of speech (*vāgvibhava*) preeminently; thus, he is "Vāgvibhavaprada" (the Bestower of the Power of Speech).
By indicating its ritual application (*viniyoga*) through this [mantra], many variations are suggested.
As it is stated in the Sārasvata-mata: "This [mantra], encapsulated by the Tāra and Māyā, bestows the great Sarasvatī."
The seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbīja) preceded by Māyā is extracted here for the praise of the Teacher.

Having uttered the Seed of Speech, Bhuvaneśvarī, and "vadavada," one should meditate upon the Eternal Speech as follows: "O Vāgvādinī, svāhā! I meditate upon the Goddess who has eternally shattered the mass of my sins through her very syllables."
Thus [it is said]. Some say that the seed-syllable of speech is enclosed by Māyā;
others say that Māyā comes first.
In another tantra, even the Vāgbhava syllable alone is extracted;
some say that this itself is the union of Śiva and Śakti,
while others maintain the opposite.
In the *Prayogasāra*, even the *Bālā* [mantra] and others are extracted.
One [form] is encased by five *praṇavas* at the beginning; another is joined with the seed-syllable of *Bālā* in the middle and at the beginning of *svāhā*;
and another has the vocative form encased by the *vāgbhava* syllable.
The other [mantra] has the invocation enclosed by the *bālā* and *tārtīya* [syllables]. The fifth has the invocation enclosed by the seed-syllable of *kāma*.
The sixth is joined with *balā* at the beginning of *svāhā*.
Thus, many other divisions of this [tradition] have not been mentioned here for fear of making the text too voluminous;
they are to be understood from the respective lineages of one's own gurus.
As it was said by the Teachers in their hymn:

O Sovereign of Wisdom, distinguished by the five *praṇavas* at the beginning and end, with a blazing trident in hand—O *Pratyaṅgirā*, you destroy the magical spells and mechanical devices of those who hate your devotees; be victorious!

O Goddess, at the end of the repetition [of the mantra] I am joined with the *Sama-sāyaka*, and at its beginning likewise with the *Vāgbhava*; at the end of the vocative, I am joined with the two moons (*anu-dvicandra*); O Supreme One, I bow before You.

O Vāgīśī, I bow to that [power] which forcibly bestows poetic skill even upon one who is mute by birth— whether it be situated between the two seed-syllables of Vāgbhava, or encapsulated by the essence of Your name, Sārasvata.
O Mistress of Speech, eternal salutations be to you, the Goddess whose very name is the Lord, who— encased within the mantra of Kāmeśvarī— is the constant deluder of both women and men.

"Or rather, I offer my salutation to that jewel of your name which, though it sprouted from a child—a mere infant of the dull-witted—now shines resplendent upon the tongues of the wise through the radiance of their abundant compositions of poetry.
Others, however, say that there is an additional vocative at the end: "O Vāgīśvarī" (Goddess of Speech).
The specific details of these meditations are to be learned from the mouth of the Guru. || 65 ||

The seer is Kaṇva, the metre is Virāj, and the deity is Speech as it is uttered. Having assigned these syllables to the head, ears, eyes, nose, mouth, anus, and genitals as previously described, one should fashion the limbs as taught by the Mothers. || 66 ||
Regarding the term "ṛṣi":
the ṛṣi is to be known as Dhiṣaṇa. This has been stated by Īśānaśiva:
"The seer is considered to be Dhiṣaṇa, and others know him as Kaṇva.
Thus,
"Vāk" is the seed-syllable (bīja) and "Svāhā" is the power (śakti).
Brahman is the seed and Māyā is the power; the individual soul (jīva) is the seed and the intellect (buddhi) is the power;
Udāna is the seed and Kuṇḍalinī is the power.
This triad of subtle seeds and so forth is to be known in all mantras.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"The Lord is the seed of the worlds, while the unborn Śakti consists of the qualities (*guṇas*)."
The Supreme Self, as well as the intellect, the vital air, and Kuṇḍalinī.
"In the fourfold seed-power, this triad is indeed common.
Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "One should contemplate the fourfold seed-power in all mantras."
Among those, the triad is common; that is now being examined.
The Lord is the primordial seed of the worlds; He is called Brahman.
His power, which consists of the qualities (guṇas), is known as Māyā.

That very Lord, the God who is the witness of the intellect (*buddhi*), is declared here as the second seed; the intellect (*buddhi*) is cited as its power (*śakti*). Udana, conjoined with consciousness (*cit*), is called the third seed.
The power there is Kuṇḍalinī; these three are common [to all].
"It should be known that within all mantras, there are one's own seed-syllables (bīja) and powers (śakti).
Here, "andhi" refers to the linga.
"As before" means in the manner described in the fourth [chapter].
These are joined with their respective seed-syllables: *aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and so forth.
However, those who know the tradition maintain that the limbs [of the mantra] are otherwise.
Oṃ hrāṃ, speak! O Ṛgveda, you are the heart. Oṃ hrīṃ, speak! O Yajurveda, you are the head.
Oṃ hrūṃ, speech! O Sāmaveda, you are the crest-lock (śikhā).
Oṃ hraiṃ vādini, the armor of the Atharvaveda.
Oṃ hrauṃ svāhā, the eye of the six limbs.
Having uttered the entire mantra: Oṃ hraḥ, the weapon consisting of the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Dharmaśāstra, Itihāsa, Kalpas, Gāthās, and Nārāśaṃsīs.

As it is stated in the *Sārasvatamata*: "One should fashion the limbs of the mantra in sequence with the syllables 'ya', 'ma', 'na', 'dha', 'ra', 'va', 'hi', 'ya', 'ga', 'la', 'rṇa', preceded by 'hnam' and likewise by those beginning with 'veda'."
The teacher Padmapāda, however, stated that they are the limbs of the Mātṛkā, beginning with "Salutation to the Mother" (mātṛ), "Salutation to the Heart" (hṛdayāya), and so forth. || 66 ||
Bearing a crescent of the young moon, radiant with white splendor,
her limbs bent by the weight of her breasts, she sits upon a white lotus;
the beauty of her own lotus-like hands holds a pen and a book.
May the Goddess of Speech protect us for the attainment of all prosperity. || 67 ||
Regarding "taruṇa":
*taruṇa-śakalam* means a young fragment or piece.
*Karakamala* is a metaphorical compound (*upamita-samāsa*).
The visualization of the implements is as follows: a pen in the right hand and a book in the left. || 67 ||

One should recite the mantra one million times and then perform the fire oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that amount, using white lotuses smeared with milk or sesame seeds soaked in honey. || 68 ||
On the seat (pīṭha) proclaimed by the Mother, the wise one should worship Vāgīśī;
he should offer a seat consisting of the lotus of letters and fashion the form with the root mantra. || 69 ||
By the word *sudhīḥ*, the application of the feminine gender in the verses concerning the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth is indicated.
He extracts the *pīṭha-mantra* with the words "in the lotus of letters" (*varṇābje na*).
The practical formula is: *hsauḥ vāgvādinīyogapīṭhāya namaḥ*. || 68-69 ||
Having first worshipped the limbs, one should afterwards worship these powers:
Yoga, Satya, Vimalā, Jñānā, Buddhi, and again Smṛti. || 70 ||

Medhā and Prajñā, holding seals and books in their hands, should be worshipped according to the ritual procedure upon the petals, and Brāhmī and the others likewise at the tips of the petals. || 71 ||
The world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be worshipped on the outside, and their weapons outside of them;
thus the mantra-practitioner, intent upon recitation, fire-oblations, and so forth, should perform the worship. || 72 ||
Delighting in celibacy, pure, with teeth, nails, and so forth clean, he should constantly remember all women with the thought that they are deities. || 73 ||
"Then the powers (śaktis)" means that "then" refers to the fourth enclosure;
therefore, first there is the enclosure of the limbs (aṅga) within the pericarp (karṇikā).
The second [wheel] is with the eight pairs of vowels;
the third with the eight groups of consonants;
and the fourth with the powers such as Yoga and so forth, starting from the right.

Their meditation has been described by Īśānaśiva as follows: "The Śaktis, who possess books and rosaries for recitation, who wear spotless necklaces and are exceedingly radiant, whose splendor resembles that of the moon, and who are situated upon each petal."
"One should worship those [deities] located in the fourth enclosure, beginning with the direction of the prescribed sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)," so it is said.
But the Teachers [state]: "In the syllable-lotus according to the procedure taught in the Mātṛkā."
"According to the rule" refers to the meditations mentioned in the preceding chapter.
Outside, in a square [mandala]. (70–73)
The wise man certainly attains the power of poetic composition within twelve months by drinking water consecrated with that mantra and reciting it one thousand times every day. || 74 ||
Within one year, he will undoubtedly become a great poet and a minister, provided he stands in water reaching only to his chest while meditating upon the orb of the sun. || 75 ||
One should recite the mantra three thousand times daily while the Goddess remains present;
through the mandala, one obtains on earth an incomparable mastery of speech. || 76 ||
One should offer oblations with *palāśa* and *bilva* flowers moistened with honey, or with fuel-sticks produced from those same trees; thus one attains the fame of the Lord of Speech.
This person shall become a bestower of all auspicious fortune and power over others, by means of flowers produced from the rājavṛkṣa tree, soaked in honey. || 78 ||
And having kindled that [fire], one should offer oblations; thus one shall obtain incomparable poetic skill.
In this way, the ten-syllable mantra has been declared for the success of those who desire speech. || 79 ||
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "The wise man, having drunk that water consecrated with the mantra, will certainly attain poetic skill within twelve months.
By the term "the wise man" (*dhīmān*), it is indicated that there should be sevenfold consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) by hand, covering [the vessel] seven times, and drinking it seven times.
Regarding the drinking, one should keep in mind the meditation previously described.
"Within forty-nine days from the mandala" is the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "bestowing all fortune (*saubhāgya*), prosperity (*lakṣmī*), and subjugation (*vaśya*)," it should be understood that for *saubhāgya* and *vaśya*, the mantra begins with the *bālā* [mantra], while for *lakṣmī*, it begins with the *śrī* seed-syllable; likewise, for liberation from sin (*pāpavimukti*), it should be known that it begins with the *nṛsiṃha* seed-syllable.
Thus say the teachers Padmapāda.
Rājavṛkṣa is the Śyonāka tree. From the Kalpa, the yantra is described as follows:
Draw the *vāgbīja* (AIM) in the center of a yantra consisting of rows of human figures on the leaves;
it is surrounded by the letters of the mantra and all the consonants from *a* to *kṣa*,
and it bestows the desired fruit.
"The yantra shall be held in the hand, and it is a source of poetic inspiration. Thus [ends verses 74–79].
At the end of *hṛdaya*, [one should utter] "O Blessed One" (*bhagavati*) and then the pair of words "speak" (*vada*).
Thereafter, one should extract the syllable of speech (*vāgbhava*) at the beginning, ending with the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*), followed by "O Goddess of Speech" (*vāgdevi*). || 80 ||
One should [worship] Manu, who is enriched with sixteen syllables and bestows the fruit of mastery over speech;
one should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) of the mantra using its six parts along with their respective seed-syllables. || 81 ||
He extracts another mantra with the words "hṛdaya" and so forth: at the end of "hṛdaya," followed by the end of "namaḥ.
"Bhagavati" is the essential form.
Here, it should be understood that when the visarga of the word "namaḥ" undergoes the *rorutva* and *guṇa* changes, it becomes the vowel *o*.
"Speak, speak the pair of words 'vada'—
O Goddess of Speech, [reveal] your own form. The word "speak" (vada) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
What is the mantra like?
It is that which has *svāhā* (the wife of Fire) at its end and the *vāgbhava* (speech-born) seed-syllable at its beginning.
Some maintain that there is also the conjunction of *ha* and *sa* here.
Others say it is the reverse.
By stating that it bestows the fruit of mastery over speech (*vāgaiśvarya*), the author indicates its application (*viniyoga*) and also suggests that it begins with the *Śrī-bīja*.
Here, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the power-syllable (*śakti*) should be understood as those previously mentioned.
The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details are exactly as previously stated.
Regarding "with six words": the first word is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the fourth is *vadavada*.
Others, however, say that the two words *vada vada* constitute a pair, and that the speech-seed (*vāgbīja*) is joined to the beginning of each individual word. (80–81)

I bow to the Goddess of Speech, seated upon a lotus, radiant with a gentle smile, her breasts slightly bowed; she is brilliant white, adorned with pure unguents, garlands, and garments, and shines with a crescent moon; holding in her lotus-like hands a book, a rosary, a vessel brimming with nectar, and the goddess of knowledge.
I bow to the three-eyed goddess, who bestows the power of speech and grants the wealth of good fortune. || 82 ||
"Śubhrāmiti" refers to the Vyākhyāna-mudrā (the gesture of exposition). Its characteristic is as follows:

"With the tips of the thumb and index finger joined, one should extend the others and display them facing forward; this mudrā, known as Vyākhyāna (Exposition), is to be employed. Thus [it is said]. "Akṣaguṇa" means a rosary of beads.
The *vidyā* is the book. The visualization of the weapons extends from the upper right hand to the upper left hand. "Seated upon a lotus" means she resides on a white lotus. || 82 ||
Eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should recite [the mantra] correctly ten lakṣas with undistracted mind;
at the end, one should offer oblations with sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter, numbering one-tenth of the recitation.
One should worship the Goddess on the seat (pīṭha) according to the sequence previously mentioned as told by one's mother;
day after day, at the time of dawn, one should drink water consecrated with that mantra. || 84 ||
A learned minister shall perform this for a year; there is no doubt about it. During the rite of bathing, he should sprinkle himself with waters over which mantras have been recited.
One should satisfy her with pure waters and thereby attain supreme intelligence;
the wise person should wear all flowers, perfumes, and the like over which it has been recited. Thus, one is honored by the virtuous in assemblies and becomes victorious in debate. || 86 ||
"Correctly" refers to the previously mentioned rule for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*). "Eight hundred thousand" means eight lakhs.
"With undistracted mind" means having focused one's attention on the meaning of the mantra.
As it has been said:
"One should recite the mantra according to the prescribed rule, with no other thought in mind."
"Previously mentioned" refers to the method associated with the ten-syllable mantra.
"One should drink" is to be understood as previously described.
In the phrase "flowers, perfumes, and so forth," it should be understood that these possess the nature of desire and the rest.
"Recited over that" means seven times.
From "one should consecrate" up to "shall obtain" constitutes one application (prayoga). || 83-86 ||
*Tāra* (Om), *māyā* (Hrīṃ) as the lower part, *bindu* (ṃ), *śakti* (Svāhā), and *tāra* (Om) [again], followed by *sarasvatī* in the dative case ending with *namaḥ*:
this is declared to be the eleven-syllable mantra. || 87 ||

The practitioner of mantra should sequentially place the syllables of the mantra at the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), between the eyebrows, and in the nine apertures; the assignment of the limbs [of the deity] is performed with the Vāgbhava syllable. || 88 ||
He extracts the mantra of Haṃsavāgīśvarī with the words "tāra" and so on.
*Tāra* is the *praṇava* (om).
*Māyā* is the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśī.
The vowel *a* and the *bindu* (dot) constitute the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable].
*Sarasvatī* ending in the feminine suffix *ṅi* becomes *sarasvatyai*. That which ends with *namaḥ* is called *namo'nta*.
Regarding this, some say there is a conjunction with *hsa* in the Vāgbhava [syllable];
others desire a conjunction with *sa*.
The Vāgbhava is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and Māyā is the power (*śakti*).
Others say that the seed-syllable is *praṇava*.
The seer is as previously stated;
the meter is *triṣṭubh*.
The deity is Haṃsavāgīśvarī.
It is stated by [the author] that the practitioner [should worship her] in sequence within the nine apertures: the two ears, the two eyes, the two nostrils, the mouth, the penis, and the anus.
The supreme gurus say that "by the Vāgbhava" means by the Tāra and Māyā enclosed together;
others, however, say it means by the Māyā-bīja joined with the six long vowels beginning with the Vāgbhava. || 87-88 ||
I bow with devotion to Vāṇī, whose face is as radiant as the full moon, who possesses the luster of camphor and jasmine,
and whose head is marked by the crescent moon; she holds with her own hands a lute, a rosary, a jar filled with nectar, and the Goddess of Learning, while her breasts are full and high.
I worship her whose body is adorned with divine ornaments and who is mounted upon a swan. || 89 ||
Regarding the word "vāṇīm" (the speech):
in some places the reading is "mudrām" (the mudrā). When the reading is "vidyām" (the vidyā), then the meditation on the weapons is as before.
In the second recension, the rosary and mudrā are in the upper right hand and so forth; elsewhere, they are different. 89.
The best of practitioners should recite the mantra twelve hundred thousand times, and then perform a fire sacrifice with white lotuses or with nāgacampaka flowers, one thousand times each.

By the term "supreme practitioner," it is stated that one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) while remaining established in the observance (*niyama*), without interrupting the recitation (*japa*).
Regarding "with the lotus of the phonemes" (*varṇābjena*), the practical application is: *hsauḥ haṃsavāgīśvarīyogapīṭhāya namaḥ*. || 90 ||
As stated by the Mother, one should worship her on the seat according to the sequence to be described;
one should prepare the seat with the lotus of the [respective] letter and fashion the form with the root mantra. || 91 ||

Thereafter, the refined (saṃskṛta) speech-form of the Goddess should be worshipped on her right, and the vernacular (prākṛta) speech-form, which bestows all accomplishments, should be worshipped on her left. || 92 ||
"Saṃskṛtā is to be worshipped.
Regarding these two, their meditation is described in the Sārasvata-mata:
"On the right, Saṃskṛtā is to be worshipped, with both hands in the gesture of yoga (yogamudrā)."
And another [nostril] on the left side has a mouth from which a sound constantly issues forth. Thus (ends verses 91–92).
Having performed the sacrifice as before, one should then worship the limbs, beginning with Prajñā:
Prajñā, Medhā, Śruti, Śakti, Smṛti, Vāgīśvarī, and Mati. || 93 ||

Immediately after that, one should worship Svasti, followed by the goddesses beginning with Brahmi; furthermore, one should worship the Lords of the Quarters (Lokapālas) and their weapons outside of them. || 94 ||

Thus one should worship the Goddess; one will become the very embodiment of the beloved of Speech (Vāgvallabha). One should also accomplish here the rites mentioned in connection with the ten-syllable mantra.
The best of practitioners should perform the worship here as well, according to the previous procedure. || 95 ||
"As before" means according to the method stated previously for the filaments (*kesara*).
By the phrase "beloved of speech," the ritual application (*viniyoga*) is indicated. (93–95)
One should recite "vācaspatemṛte bhūyaḥ plavaḥ plava" again;
this mantra, beginning with "vāk," is declared by the sages to consist of eleven syllables. || 96 ||
One should duly form the limbs with the five words beginning with *vāk*;
first, one should install the Mātṛkā as before, according to the prescribed rule. || 97 ||
He extracts another mantra with the words "vāca" and so forth. "Vāgādi" means beginning with the *vāgbhava* [syllable].
Because it is stated to consist of eleven syllables, there is a sandhi (euphonic combination) between "amṛte" and "pare" with the preceding word, but not within the mantra itself.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"Speech is the tortoise, joined with the two sides; O Śukra, at the end of your hair is the raft when one has died.
This ten-syllable Vidyā, ending with 'plu', is the preeminent Sarasvatī. Thus it is said.
The seed-syllable is *eṃ* and the power is *pluḥ*.
One should perform the [assignment of] seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth as previously described.
Here, the heart is formed with the *vāgbhava* syllable, and the four limbs are formed with the other four words.
Regarding the phrase "according to rule" (*vidhivat*):
by this entire expression, it is stated that [the mantra] is the *astra*.
Now, some maintain that because it is said, "one should perform the limbs with five words," there are only five limbs (*pañcāṅga*) here.
This is not the essence;

for by the injunction "one should perform the limbs," it is established that there are exactly six limbs. When there is a desire for their specific enumeration, the statement "by five words" [is made].
The phrase "by speech and so forth" (vāgādyaiḥ) is for the sake of indicating the sequence.
If only the word "by words" (padaiḥ) were stated, there would certainly be doubt as to what those six are.

In that context, the expression "according to rule" (vidhivat) is used to indicate them both individually and collectively through concealment; furthermore, this is because it is impossible for the primary [number] to be sublated by the word "by five" (pañcabhiḥ).
Furthermore, in whatever case it is intended to be so, he will establish it exactly in that way,
by means of the passage beginning with "one should conceive of the five limbs of the mantra" (96–97).
Seated upon a lotus, holding a rosary, two lotuses, and a book in her hands;
wearing a crown bound with the young moon; possessing a luster like that of pearls, the moon, and jasmine;
with eyes half-opened by her brow; and weighed down by the weight of her breasts—may she bring about your prosperity.
May the goddess of speech be ever-present, who is incessantly served by hosts of sages. || 98 ||
"Kamale" means white.
The visualization of the weapons extends from the lower right hand to the lower left hand. || 98 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for Rudra and perform oblations with clarified butter ten times that amount;
then, upon a pedestal fashioned according to the Mātṛkā, one should worship her as previously described. || 99 ||
By offering oblations with *palāśa* flowers, one shall attain supreme accomplishment;
likewise by using *kadamba* flowers or fruits produced from the *śrīvṛkṣa* tree. || 100 ||
Before long, one obtains eloquence by offering oblations with jasmine flowers or with *nandyāvarta* blossoms; thus, one becomes a master of speech. || 101 ||
"Rudra-lakṣa" means eleven lakhs.
"Just as before" refers to the method associated with the eleven-syllable mantra.
"In that same way" means that one shall attain the accomplishment of speech (vāk-siddhi).
The connection is that one soon attains the glory of speech, that is, excellence of speech.
In the *nandyāvarta* [design], there is *gandhatagara*. The word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative with the phrase "arising from *kunda* flowers. (99–101)
While reciting [mantras], one should cook Kapila ghee with the juice of *brāhmī* and a paste of *vacā*;
by drinking that regularly at the beginning of the day, one will become a knower of the meaning of all scriptures. || 102 ||
Having recited this vidyā, one should consume the leaf of the Brāhmī plant;
the wise person will not forget the Vedas and Āgamas they have heard. What more need be said? This vidyā is a wish-fulfilling gem for those who recite it. || 103 ||
Regarding "the juice of *brāhmī*":
here too, since it is a cooking by means of the fresh juice (*svarasa-pāka*), the paste of the drug itself is one-eighth part of the ghee, and the *brāhmī* juice is four times the amount of the ghee.
The rest is as before.
In some places, the reading is *vacākalpa*. The connection is that one should cook while reciting [the mantra].
The ellipsis is that [the food] should be consecrated with this vidyā for seven days.
"One should drink daily at the beginning of the day" refers to a period of three or five years.

Everything beginning with "by means of this vidyā" should also be applied to the *brāhmī* leaf. Both the phrase beginning with "all" and that beginning with "intelligent" are the results of both [practices], according to the distinction in the duration of the observance (*samaya*).
Thus it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:

"He who drinks at dawn for three years a mouthful of the juice of the *brāhmī* plant mixed with the ghee of a tawny cow, having chanted [the mantra] over it—indeed, he retains what is spoken once; after five years, he does not forget what is spoken thrice, even when held in his mouth."
Thus, even the eating of its sprouts is recorded in this way.
"The wish-fulfilling gem" (kāmada-maṇi).
By this, the following is indicated:
"This, when recited, removes eye disease, even that which is born of a 'suvīra' [poison]."
Having consumed urine and recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times on the lunar days (tithis), one should offer oblations of *yoṅkolla* sap;
or eight thousand times. He [will know] the past, the present, and the future—thus and so forth. (102–103)
The bed of Viṣṇu situated in the water consists of the absolute four-faced one (Brahmā), joined with Bindu and Arghīśa; [the syllables] Vahni, Bindu, Sadyojāta, Ambumān, and Bhṛgu. || 104 ||
The wise have declared three seed-syllables for Sarasvatī and Ārthī;
one should fashion the limbs with these twice-spoken seed-syllables conjoined with the [respective] classes. || 105 ||
He extracts another mantra with the words "situated in water" (*toyastham*).
Ananta is the form of Viṣṇu’s resting place;
[the word] "situated in water" means situated in the letter *va*, or by that [letter].
The letter *ka* with four faces (*caturmukha*) is [the syllable] *ka* alone, devoid of vowel; by that, [it represents] speech.
Some say that this very portion is the mantra.
As it is said in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:

"The Lord of the Sword (Khaḍgīśa), who is tall (prāṃśuka) and possesses peaceful piercing (sāntavedhā); the serpent (bhujaṅga) situated at the end of the ear (karṇāntastha) together with the staff (daṇḍa);
and the tooth (danta) accompanied by Ambā (Ambhā) and possessing the Bindu (bindumān)—these are the three seed-syllables (bījas) of Vāgīśvarī, which is Bhṛgu. Thus it is said.
The commentator has stated that "vāk" is a portion of the mantra.

Others, however, say: "Who is the four-faced one? He is 'ka' together with the pure [vowel] and the bindu; by that [suffix], 'kāṃ' [is formed]. In this way, the status of being a seed-syllable (bīja) is established for that which possesses the bindu."
Those who know the tradition, however, say that the word "vāk" which was previously extracted is what characterizes the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable;
thus its status as a seed-syllable (*bīja*) is established, and it becomes associated with Sarasvatī.
Others, however, extract the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable by means of another method.

The word *ka* refers to Viṣṇu’s reclining posture situated in the water; by that [word] *ka*, the letter *a* is meant, which is his essential nature (*svarūpa*). In the compound of *ka* and *i*, the word *ke* is formed. Of what kind is the reclining? It is "with hair" (*sake*), meaning accompanied by hair (*kesa*). When there is a joining (*vala*)—that is, a union (*sammelana*)—the four-faced one (*caturmukha*) is *ka*; by that, [he is] the head.
Then, "Bindu" [is as follows]: Arghīśa is *ū*, Vahni is the letter *ra*, Sadyojāta is the vowel *o*, Ambu is the letter *va*, and Bhṛgu is the letter *sa*.
By the phrase "of Sarasvatī and the others," the application (*viniyoga*) is stated.
The first is the seed-syllable (bīja), the last is the power (śakti), and the seer (ṛṣi) and other [limbs] are as previously stated. || 105 ||

I meditate upon the Sovereign Goddess, who is as radiant as a string of pearls, adorned with a crescent moon upon her head; who holds in her own arms the *Vyākhyā*, the rosary of letters, a jeweled pitcher, and a book;
and whose waist is bent by the weight of her full and lofty breasts.
I praise for eternity her who is praised by speech, who is bowed to by the three worlds, and who is seated upon a lotus. ||106||

"Muktā" (the Liberated One). The explanation is as previously stated regarding the *vyākhyāna-mudrā*. The visualization of the weapons extends from the upper right hand to the upper left hand. || 106 ||

One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times and perform oblations with milk-rice (pāyasa) sprinkled with clarified butter (ājya) into the consecrated fire, using one-tenth of that number as the portion for the burnt offering.
The best of practitioners should worship Vāgīśī on the seat according to the rite proclaimed by the Mother, following the path previously set forth, every single day. || 108 ||
Having offered oblations with *vyāghāta* flowers, one shall obtain incomparable mastery of speech;
likewise by offering *jāti* flowers and white lotuses sprinkled with sandalwood water. || 109 ||

By offering auspicious *nandyāvarta* flowers and *kunda* blossoms, one attains mastery of speech; by reciting the three seed-syllables (*bīja*), the practitioner of mantra gains victory in the assembly.
If one eats white vacā or brāhmī that has been consecrated with mantra recitation day after day, the practitioner attains the desired power of intelligence; of this there is no doubt. || 111 ||
When these mantras have been thus spoken, one who is initiated and possesses a restrained mind—
whosoever worships in this manner with devotion— shall partake in both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"According to the rite" means by means of white perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as will be described;
"as previously introduced" means by the path consisting of the eleven-syllable mantra;
"the best of practitioners" means one who abides by the observances (*samaya*) of a worshipper of Sarasvatī.
*Vyāghāta* is the *rājavṛkṣa*; according to the lexicon: "The *āragvadha*, the *dīrghaphala*, the *vyāghāta*, and the *caturaṅgula* [are synonyms]. *Nandyāvartas* are *gandhatagaras*.
"Auspicious" (*śubhaiḥ*) means fragrant; this is an epithet for *kundas*.
"At will" means excessively.
"Initiated" means according to the method stated by the author of the text. || 107-112 ||
In the ritual for Sarasvatī, worship is performed with fragrant flowers that are well-washed;
likewise, there is dūrvā grass, sprouted seeds, and flowers produced from the rājavṛkṣa tree. || 113 ||
One who constantly resorts to Sarasvatī should always avoid blue lotuses and the sprouts of the sindhuvāra plant. || 114 ||
The āmrāta, gṛñjana, bilva, karañja, and likewise garlic;
oil, onion, oil-cake, and even the meat of a porcupine—these [are forbidden] in one's diet. || 115 ||
Those who desire the grace of Sarasvatī should always avoid stale food;
they should not consume betel at night, nor should they approach a woman during her menstrual period. || 116 ||

One should never sleep during the two twilights, nor utter anything while impure; one should remain silent during the evening watches and should not gaze upon a woman clad only in a lower garment. || 117 ||
A wise man should not approach a woman in her menses, nor should he revile a beautiful-eyed woman; he should not speak falsehood, nor should he step over a book. || 118 ||
