One should neither neglect nor step over leaves that are rich in syllables (inscribed with mantras), especially on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, on festival days, and during the first day of the lunar fortnight or during eclipses. || 119 ||
A wise person should never recite the Vidyā during any of the transitional periods (saṃkrama). Furthermore, during the exposition, one should abandon sleep, laziness, and yawning. || 120 ||
He states the conventions for the Sarasvatī [rite] with the words "with very white" and so forth.
*Bījāṅkura* is a barley sprout;
*sindhuvāra* is *nirguṇḍī*.
The connection is that one should avoid these [items] which are about to be described at the time of eating.
*Āmrāta* is known as *avāra* in the Kānyakubja dialect;
*guñjana* is commonly known as *gājara* (carrot).
*Kalañja* is a specific kind of fruit, the *kṛṣṇabīja*, known as *kaliṅgaḍa* in the Gujarati language, *kharbujā* in the Gauḍa (Bengali) language,
and *roḍa* in the Kānyakubja (Kannauji) language.
*Taila* refers to oil that is visible and unmixed with condiments or other ingredients.
*Śārṅgāṣṭa* is *siṅghāḍa* in the Kānyakubja dialect;
*sāṅguṣṭha* is a corrupt reading, because eating with the thumb is prescribed.
As they say:
"Giving, receiving, burnt offerings, eating, and even the offering of bali must always be performed with the thumb; otherwise, it belongs to the asuras.
Thus, everything becomes stale, even that which has been cooked in ghee.
The meaning of the injunction "one should not consume betel at night" is as follows: having placed betel in the mouth, one should not go to sleep at night.
There is also a Smṛti text: "One should discard the betel from the mouth."
Even one's own [wife] who is naked and has the directions as her garment. || 113-120 ||
Likewise, anger, spitting, and touching the lower parts of the body [are causes for impurity], as are humans, snakes, cats, frogs, mongooses, and the like. || 121 ||
If people should pass between [the teacher and the listeners], one should then cease the exposition;
and if a lamp goes out during the nights, one should immediately cease the recitation. || 122 ||
Having correctly understood these defects, he who worships Bhāratī with devotion attains perfection of speech, like a second Vācaspati. || 123 ||
Śrīṃ Hrīṃ.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Śāradātilaka* composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇa Deśikendra. || 7 ||
"Low-limbed" (nīcāṅga) refers to those who dwell below the navel.
By the word "etc. (ādi), animals and so forth are included. || 121-123 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Next, I shall declare the mantras of Śrī, which bestow the fruits of prosperity and good fortune.
By whose mere sidelong glance the three worlds flourish. || 1 ||
Now, since it was necessary to explain the mantras according to one of the five methods, and since the *śakti*-mantras are the subject at hand here, the author—

desiring to speak of them starting with the *śakti*-mantras— first states the *Sarasvatī* mantras which denote the power (*śakti*) of Brahmā, and then begins to state the *Lakṣmī* mantras which denote the power of Viṣṇu, saying "Now" (*atha*).

"Śrīsaubhāgya... is the statement regarding the ritual application (*viniyoga*). By the term "the three worlds" (*trailokya*), those who dwell in the three worlds are indicated through metaphorical extension (*lakṣaṇā*).
As stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "He is praiseworthy, he is virtuous, he is blessed, he is of noble birth, and he is wise."
"He who has been beheld by you, O Goddess, is both a hero and one of great prowess. || 1 ||
The letter *va* mounted upon fire (*ra*), conjoined with the moon (*i*) from the left eye—this is declared to be the seed-syllable of Śiva, like another wish-fulfilling gem. || 2 ||
The sage is Bhṛgu, the metre is Nivṛt, and the deity is declared to be Śrī.
One should perform the six limb-prostrations in sequence using the seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels.
He extracts the mantra as "vāntam" (the vomited).
"Vāntam" is *śa*; "vahni" is the letter *ra*; "vāmanetra" is the vowel *ī*; and "indubīndu" is the nasal bindu (*m*).
By the term "cintāratna," this is what is meant: that it begins with the *praṇava* (oṃ), or with *śakti*, or with *vāk*, or with *kāma*, according to their respective conjunctions.
And there is the subordination of various deities:

just as when [the mantra] begins with *praṇava*, the deity is Śrī whose nature is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), so too when it begins with *śakti* and so forth, the deity is Śrī whose nature is Śakti, and so on.
The letter *śa* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the letter *ī* is the power (*śakti*).
"Six long [vowels]" refers to those excluding the neuter [vowels].
"Vauṣaṭ with the two eyes" is the application for the fifth limb.
Therefore, it should be understood that wherever there are two eyes, this application is to be used there.
In another ritual manual, five limbs are prescribed:
"To Mahāśrī Mahāvidyutprabhā, svāhā" is the heart;
"To Śrī Vijayā, svāhā" is the head.
"O Gaurī of great strength, bind, bind, svāhā"—this is the *śikhā*.
"Firmness, svāhā"—this is the *varma*.
"O you of great body, lotus-handed one, hūṃ phaṭ"—this is the *astra*.
In another ritual procedure, however: *śriye svāhā* is the heart;
*śrīṃ phaṭ* is the head;
*śrīṃ namaḥ* is the crest-lock.
"Śriye prasīda, namaḥ varma; Śrīṃ phaṭ astram. Thus is the five-limbed [mantra].
And it is said in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Its limbs are declared to be twofold; one should resort to one of these two.

By the word "successively" (*kramāt*), it is indicated that there is a long application when joined with *Śakti* and so forth, whereas when preceded by the *praṇava*, there is a conjunction with that [short form]. (2–3)
[He saw] Śrī, who by her splendor resembles gold, being sprinkled by four elephants resembling the snowy mountains with golden jars of nectar uplifted in their trunks;
she bears a boon-granting gesture and a pair of lotuses in her hands, and is radiant with a crown.
I bow to her who dwells upon the lotus, her broad hips radiant with a silken garment bound around them. || 4 ||
By the word "splendor" (*kānti*),
height and whiteness [of the Himalayas] are indicated;
by the word "lotus" (*aravinda*), whiteness [is indicated].
All of this should be understood according to the *Śrīmantra*.
The visualization of the weapons extends from the lower left [hand] to the lower right [hand].
This is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"Four-armed, with a golden luster, her two upper hands holding lotuses,
her right hand in the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), and her left hand bestowing boons (vara).
Following this meditation, the Lakṣmī-mudrā should be displayed.
Having likewise formed the *cakramudrā* and extended the two middle fingers, one should bring the two little fingers together and place the two thumbs at their tips;
this indeed is the supreme *lakṣmīmudrā*, which bestows all prosperity. Thus it is said.
And it should be understood that this [mantra] is common to all the Lakṣmī-mantras. || 4 ||
Having been initiated and having conquered his senses, he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
he should also daily worship Śrī with fragrant flowers and other offerings. || 5 ||
One should offer that thousand-fold oblation with lotuses smeared with honey;
at the conclusion of the recitation, the practitioner of mantra should offer sesame seeds drenched in honey.
The best of practitioners should offer oblations with bilva fruits, or even with three of them;
here, he should properly worship the seat (pīṭha) endowed with the nine powers (nava-śakti). || 7 ||

Vibhūti (prosperity), Unnati (elevation), Kānti (splendor), Sṛṣṭi (creation), Kīrti (fame), Sannati (humility), Puṣṭi (nourishment), Utkṛṣṭi (excellence), and Ṛddhi (abundance) are declared to be the nine powers. || 8 ||
"Bhānulakṣa" means twelve lakhs.
By the word "mantrī" (the practitioner of mantra), it is stated that there should be a recitation of one-tenth [of the main mantra] as a subsidiary to the eight-syllabled Nārāyaṇa mantra.
For this very reason, he will later state: "A devotee of Viṣṇu, firm in his vows."

By the phrase "at the end of the recitation" (*japānta*), it is stated that the oblation (*homa*) must be performed by one who remains within the observance of that [recitation] without interruption from the recitation.
The phrase "or with three" refers to the fourth alternative as a combination;
even in that case, four thousand oblations are to be offered with each individual substance.

Alternatively, by the statement "the best of practitioners should offer oblations with the three," it is meant that after offering once each with the *Kamalavāsinī*, the *Mahālakṣmī*, and the *Śrīsūkta* mantras, one should subsequently offer with the root mantra (*mūla*).
The term "best of practitioners" (*sādhakottama*) is connected to both [the preceding and following clauses] according to the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣigolakanyāya*).
By the phrase "the best of practitioners here correctly," this is indicated:

having worshipped [the deities] from Maṇḍūka up to the Supreme Reality (Paratattva) in the Śrīpūjā according to the method described in the fourth chapter, the nine Pīṭha-Śaktis preceded by the Śrī-bīja should be worshipped in the directions starting from the east and in the center. || 5–8 ||
Having invoked the Goddess here together with her retinue, one should worship her;
having offered a seat beginning with the seed-syllable, one should fashion the form [of the deity] by means of the root-mantra. || 9 ||
Here, on an eight-petalled lotus with the seed-syllable *śrīṃ* in its pericarp;
as it was stated by the Teachers: "Then there is a beautiful eight-petalled lotus."
The teacher Padmapāda has explained that "the beautiful Śrībījayoga is in the pericarp.
Also, in the Saṃhitā: "One should draw an eight-petaled diagram adorned with a circle on the outside;
having placed the seed-syllable (bīja) in the center..."
Thus [it is said]. He extracts the *pīṭha-mantra* as "beginning with the seed-syllable" (*bījādyaṃ*), namely:
*Śrīṃ sarvaśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ*.
It should be understood that the *pīṭhamantra* is common to all *Śrīmantras*.

However, the teachers beginning with Padmapādācārya have stated the two mantras for the *pīṭha* and the *mūrti* as follows: "OṂ ŚRĪṂ, obeisance to the seat of the Goddess Śrī; OṂ ŚRĪṂ, obeisance to the form of the Goddess Śrī.
Here, a white lotus is to be meditated upon.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Having mentally conceived a pure lotus, one should worship Śiva in its pericarp.
One should sacrifice as before; then one should worship the limbs on the petals of the directions:
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. || 10 ||
Having the luster of snow, the most intense tamāla, and sapphire, they wear yellow garments;
they possess four arms, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus. || 11 ||
"As before" means according to the method described in the fourth chapter;
the meditation on the weapons of Vāsudeva and the others should be understood as I have explained it in the Nārāyaṇa-mantra. (10–11)
On the petals situated in the intermediate directions, one should worship the elephant-keepers and others;
[namely] the keeper (damaka), water, guggulu, and kuruṇṭaka. || 12 ||
"In those situated at the intermediate directions" means with respect to the imagined directions.
As for what is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "On the petals starting from the southeast (āgneya), there are guggulu and kuruṇṭaka..."
Damaka and Salila are the elephants with the luster of silver.
They are to be meditated upon as holding golden jars;
it should be understood that this is stated with reference to the southeast direction as established therein. || 12 ||
One should worship the deity Śaṅkhanidhi on the right side of the Goddess, accompanied by his beloved;
their faces are like lotuses with slight smiles, and they resemble pearls and rubies. || 13 ||
Intent on embracing one another, they hold conchs and lotuses;
their heads are marked by two conchs from which streams of excellent jewels are pouring forth. || 14 ||

One should worship him who has a protruding belly and holds the treasure of the conch, whose breasts are like thick clouds, and who, on his left side, is accompanied by his beloved and holds the treasure of the lotus. || 15 ||

Resembling vermilion, their arms were locked in embrace; they held red lotuses and blue water-lilies, and their heads were marked by two lotuses from which streams of jewels were pouring forth. || 16 ||
One should worship Tundila, Paṅkajanidhi, and the slender Vasumatī upon the tips of the petals; and Balākī and the others all around them. || 17 ||
"To the right and left of the Goddess" refers to the pericarp.
"With pearls and rubies" indicates, respectively, the colors of the Śaṅkha-treasure and the Vasudhārā-treasure.
"Holding a conch and a lotus" applies to both [deities] in both places.
The same applies to what follows.
Their weapons and meditations begin with the right hand (dakṣa) and so forth.
Kambukanidhi means the Śaṅkha-nidhi (the conch-treasure).
"Vasudhārā" refers to the name of the Śaṅkhanidhi-Śakti. The portion ending with "ghanastanīm" constitutes the preliminary visualization (*pūrvadhyāna*). "Paṅkajanidhim" means the Padmanidhi.
"Vasumatī" refers to the one named Śakti, who holds a lotus and a treasure-vessel (nidhi).
By the use of the word "api" (also), it is implied that she is "one with thick breasts" as well.
These constitute the deities of the second enclosure, because it is stated that there are others [in the third enclosure] consisting of four groups of treasures (catuṣkanidhiyugaiḥ). || 13–17 ||
Balākī, Vimalā, Kamalā, Vanamālikā, Vibhīṣikā, Mālikā, Śāṅkarī, and Vasumālikā. || 18 ||

One should worship the Lords of the World (Lokeśas) at the end, holding two lotuses and possessing a luster equal to strings of pearls; outside of them, one should worship the weapons beginning with the Vajra.
Regarding Balākī:
their meditation is described in the Nārāyaṇīya [section] as follows—
"Balākī is short and dark-complexioned, holding a white lotus."
One should meditate on Śrīdūtī at the eastern gate, with both arms raised upward.
One should meditate on Vanamālā at the southern gate, white-bodied and holding a red lotus with her hand raised upward.
One should meditate with devotion upon Śrī’s messenger Vibhīṣikā at the western door, who is green in color and holds a white lotus aloft with her two arms.
"Likewise, the Śāṅkarī [form] should be meditated upon elsewhere as holding a lotus garland and having the luster of honey.
Thus it is said in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Vimalā, Kamalā, Mālikā, and Vasumālikā—
these messengers (dūtīs) are to be worshipped externally in the intermediate directions.
Thus it is said.
In this case, however, the reversal between Kamalā and Vanamālī is to be reconciled by treating it as belonging to another Kalpa. || 18-19 ||
In this manner, the best of practitioners who worships the Goddess according to the prescribed rite shall attain an abundance of wealth and grain, and he shall obtain irreproachable fame. || 20 ||
By the phrase "the best of practitioners according to the rite," the application of the feminine gender in the verses concerning the invocation and so forth has been stated. || 20 ||

Standing in water reaching up to his chest, the practitioner of mantra, being self-restrained and meditating upon the Goddess in the solar orb, should recite this mantra three hundred thousand times. || 21 ||
That knower of mantras, having taken his stand at the root of a *bilva* tree within the temple of Viṣṇu, shall become a stable abode for Ramā in a short time. || 22 ||
By reciting the mantra three hundred thousand times, one obtains the desired wealth.
By the phrase "the practitioner, being self-restrained," it is indicated that the recitation of the mantra "Obeisance to the Illustrious Ratnagarbhā" should be performed one hundredth of that number.
Having meditated [on her] within the solar orb, she should be visualized as red, holding the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons, and bearing a vessel of treasures and a jar of jewels.
This is to be known.
As it has been said: Standing in water reaching only to her breasts, she beholds Śrī seated upon the pedestal of the solar disc, resembling fresh lac and adorned with ornaments of rubies.
"A person who performs three hundred thousand recitations [of this mantra] over two jars filled with great jewels and treasure-vessels shall, before long, become a lord of wealth. (21–23)
One should offer oblations in the fire of Aśoka with rice grains mixed with clarified butter. || 23 ||
The knower of mantras brings even the three worlds under his control before long;
by offering a million pure grains of rice into the fire of the sun, he shall bring [all] beings under his sway. || 24 ||
A prince shall obtain even greater royal splendor;
he should offer oblations in a fire of khadira wood with rice grains smeared with honey. || 25 ||
The king will quickly become submissive and great fortune will increase, for he dwells in the shade of a Bilva tree, subsisting on sacrificial food mixed with Bilva. || 26 ||
Having offered oblations for two years with those fruits or with lotuses, the supreme practitioner will certainly behold Mahālakṣmī with his own eyes. || 27 ||

Having offered oblations of clarified butter-sprinkled sacrificial food, milk-rice, and sesame flour, the best of mantra-knowers obtains prosperity by means of a hundred thousand [recitations]. || 28 ||
"In the fire of the aśoka" means in a fire kindled with aśoka wood.
"One should offer oblations" is connected with the word "one million" (niyuta).
By the phrase "the knower of mantras," it is indicated that in this ritual application, one possesses the power of desire and so forth.
"By pure ones" means having removed the refuse, washed, and dried;
this is also to be applied to the phrase "mixed with clarified butter.
"In the fire of the sun" means in a fire kindled with fuel-sticks of *arka* wood.
A *niyuta* is a *lakṣa*.

And so says the Śruti: "One, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand (*ayuta*), a hundred thousand (*niyuta*), a million (*prayuta*), ten million (*arbuda*), a hundred million (*nyarbuda*), a billion (*samudra*), ten billion (*madhya*), a hundred billion (*anta*), and a trillion (*parārddha*)."
Thus it is said in the *Trikāṇḍī*: "Beyond ten million (koṭi), there are other numbers such as a hundred [million], a lakh, and a niyuta."
"One should offer a hundred thousand oblations" is the connection.
"Made of khadira wood" means in a fire made from its wood.
By the word "quickly," it is indicated that a specific desire (*kāma*) is also to be associated here.
Having offered one thousand and eight oblations with bilva fruits; or,
in their absence, with lotuses.
With the verse beginning "haviṣā," [he offers] with the *caru* oblation. || 23–28 ||
One should diligently offer a hundred thousand oblations with honey-smeared red lotuses;
Lakṣmī shall not abandon his lineage until the dissolution of all beings. || 29 ||
Regarding "Madhurā" and so forth: therein, a specific visualization is described in another Tantra:
"Holding a citron and a vessel of treasure upon a lotus..."
[One should meditate on] the beautiful, red Śrī, seated at the foot of the celestial tree (suratara).

"Having visualized [the goddess] adorned with great jewels and clothed in red garments, one offers a hundred thousand oblations of lotuses with sweet-smelling petals for the attainment of Indirā (Lakṣmī).
Thus [it is said] until the dissolution of all beings, that is, for the duration of a kalpa. (29)
The Vāgbhava (AIM), Vanitā (HRĪM), Viṣṇu’s Māyā (HŪM), and Makaraketana (KLĪM)— this mantra,
consisting of four seed-syllables, bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
The knower of the mantra should perform the limb-protection rites using the Ramā-bīja (HRĪM) enriched with the long vowels.
He extracts another mantra with the words "vāgbhavam" (the source of speech).
The consort of Viṣṇu is the Śrī-bīja (the seed-syllable of Śrī).
Makaraketana is the Kāma-bīja (the seed-syllable of Kāma).

By the statement "bringing the fruits of the four aims of life" (caturvargaphalāvaha), the application (viniyoga) is being stated; this means that for the sake of *dharma*, the mantra begins with the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable; for the sake of *artha*, it begins with the *lakṣmī* seed-syllable; for the sake of *kāma*, it begins with the *kāma* seed-syllable; and for the sake of *mokṣa*, it begins with the *māyā* seed-syllable. The seers (*ṛṣi*) and other [limbs] are as previously mentioned.
The second is the seed-syllable (bīja) and the third is the power (śakti).
Regarding the phrase "the limbs":
it means by that Ramā-bīja which is enriched with the long vowels, that is, conjoined with the six long vowels. || 30 ||
She whose radiance resembles a ruby, who is constantly being sprinkled by four lofty elephants white as snow with water from jeweled jars held at the tips of their trunks, and who,
with her lotus-like hands, bestows boons upon Hari while displaying the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*) along with a pair of lotuses.
I salute the beloved of Brahmā, who desires the pārijāta creeper. || 31 ||
The term "hastābjaiḥ" (with lotus-hands) is a *upamita-samāsa* (simile compound).
"Varadānam" (the granting of boons) is one [attribute]. The visualization of the weapons is as before. ||31||

Eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; at the conclusion, one who has conquered the senses should offer one thousand blossoming reddish lotuses into the fire. || 32 ||
One should worship on the pedestal fashioned for Ramā according to its prescribed ritual; the practitioner should perform the various applications situated therein with that mantra. || 33 ||
He is eternally served by the treasures (nidhis) standing before him in embodied form.
He is the long vowel 'Ā', beginning with 'A' and ending with the Visarga; he is Brahmā, the Sun, and the Earth. || 34 ||
The ten-syllable mantra of Vahni, beginning with "vānte sinyai," is declared to have Dakṣa as its seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ as its meter (chandaḥ), and Śrī as its deity (devatā). || 35 ||
He states another mantra with the words "dīrgha" and so forth.
Among the kalās arising from the Praṇava, the long vowel is the letter *na*;
that which begins with *ya* is *ma*.
"Ending in visarga and accompanied by visarga" is an epithet of the letter *ma*. *Brahmā* is *ka*; *bhānu* is the syllable *maṃ*.
Therefore, because of the statement, "The self is remembered as the sun," or alternatively, Mahākāla is the embodiment of the letter *ma*, and [he is] also the poison denoted by the word Mahākāla;
that [poison] resides in the right nostril.
Therefore, the Sun is *ma*.
As it has been said:
"The Sun moves within Piṅgalā; therefore, the right side is declared by the lords of sages to be the seat of poison."
Thus,
by this, it is also explained why the letter *ma* is sometimes taken as being denoted by the word "poison" (*viṣa*).
*Vasundharā* is *la*.
Or its own form;
for Śinī, the own form;
for Vahni, the beloved Svāhā.
In this mantra as well, the teachers beginning with Padmapāda maintain that there is the nature of *praṇava*, *śakti*, *vāk*, *kāma*, and so forth;
and as before, there is the subordination of the names of the respective deities.
*Śrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*). (32–35)
The Heart has been declared for the Goddess; the Head is proclaimed for Padminī;
the Topknot is spoken of for Viṣṇupatnī; and the Armor for Varadā. || 36 ||

The weapon-mantra (astra) is for the one whose form is a lotus; these mantras, preceded by the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ," are declared to be the limb-mantras (aṅgamantras). One should meditate upon the Goddess with undivided mind. || 37 ||
He states the five-limbed mantras [for the goddess] as follows:
"Oṃ, obeisance to the Goddess; obeisance to the heart," and so forth.
Because there are only five limbs, there is no mention of the eyes. || 36-37 ||
Seated upon a lotus, her face smiling,

she holds with her lotus-hands the gestures of generosity (*dāna*), the pair of lotuses (*padma-yuga*), and fearlessness (*abhaya*); resembling a flash of lightning in her form, she shines with broad, high breasts adorned with strings of pearls.
May Kamalā protect you, gladdening Hari with the splendor of her sidelong glances. || 38 ||
"Seated," it is said;
the boon is the granting of gifts, while the meditation on the weapon is as before. || 38 ||
The knower of mantras who has conquered his senses should recite the mantra one million times;
the practitioner of mantra should then perform oblations with lotuses smeared with honey, numbering one-tenth of that amount. || 39 ||
One should worship the Goddess in the Śrīpīṭha; first, one should sacrifice to the limbs (aṅgas).
Thereafter, Balākā and the others are to be worshipped, as well as the world-protectors (lokeśas) and the two enclosures (āvṛtis). || 40 ||
Thus one should worship the Goddess; one shall become an abode of prosperity.
Standing in a river flowing to the ocean with water reaching up to the neck, || 41 ||
The practitioner of mantra should recite it three hundred thousand times, and he shall become Vaiśravaṇa in person.
By the phrase "the knower of mantra," it is indicated that there should be a recitation of one-tenth as many times for the eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa as a subsidiary practice;
furthermore, a recitation of the Ratnagarbhā-mantra one-hundredth as many times is also implied.
"Sweet" means the three sweets (*trimadhura*).
By the word "of riches," there is a statement of its application (*viniyoga*).
The phrase "in the river flowing to the ocean" implies "directly" as the ellipsis (*śeṣa*).
Vaiśravaṇa is Kuvera. || 39-42 ||
Having propitiated the Goddess under the Uttarā constellation with garlands, sandalwood paste, and other offerings. || 42 ||
Then, one should offer a thousand oblations with flowers produced from the *nandyāvarta* plant;
on the full moon day, one should offer oblations with *bilva* fruits soaked in honey.
On the fifth lunar day, during the Friday, with fragrant white lotuses or other pure flowers, one of vast intellect should worship every month;
by doing so for just one year, he shall always become a treasury of all prosperity.
"Having propitiated," and so forth, ending with "a treasury of perfections," constitutes one application [of the formula].
Regarding "the Uttarā constellation," it should be understood as referring to all three of the Uttarās.
The words "having propitiated" and "one thousand" are to be connected with every instance.
"With those soaked in honey and moist with the three sweets," etc.
The word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "or by others" is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

When both [substances] are present in one [offering], there is no single performance (*tantra*) for the two separate oblations, because the substances are distinct and the causes [for the oblations] are distinct. (42–44)
Vāgbhava, Śambhuvanitā, Ramā, and Makaraketana;
and the third [syllable], blazing with the fire-seed (vahni-bīja), is on the side of the world. || 45 ||

This twelve-syllable heart-mantra of Mahālakṣmī, beginning with the syllable Om and preceded by the seed-syllables Arghīśa (Hrīm) and Bhṛgu (Sakala), is declared to bestow all spiritual accomplishments. || 46 ||
The seer is Brahmā, the meter is declared to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is Mahālakṣmī, the primordial source of the worlds. || 47 ||
He extracts another mantra with the words "vāgbhava" and so forth: "śambhuvanitā" is the seed-syllable of Māyā;
the third [syllable] belongs either to Vālā or to Bhairavī.
Some say that [the name] Bhairavī is devoid of the letter *ra*;
this alone is the traditional position. The world is her very nature.

Pārśva is the letter *pa*. Blazing with the seed-syllable of fire (*vahni-bīja*) means joined with the letter *ra*; thus, *pra*. Arghīśa is *ū*; enriched by that is Bhṛgu, which is the letter *sa*; thus, *sū*.
This is its essential form:
"Hṛn namaḥ. It begins with the Tāra (Om) and begins with the Praṇava (Om); the remainder is that it consists of thirteen syllables.
By the phrase "bestower of all accomplishments" (sarvasiddhida), the application (viniyoga) is stated.
The Praṇava is the seed-syllable (bīja); the third [syllable] is the power (śakti). || 45-47 ||
Having purified both hands with the mantra beginning with *Tāra* and ending with the *hṛdaya*, one should place the five seed-syllables upon the fingers in their proper order. || 48 ||
The practitioner of mantra should place the remainder of the mantra upon both palms;
then, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) with the mantra from the head down to the feet. || 49 ||
One should place the five seed-syllables on the head, face, chest, private parts, and feet;
one should place the remaining seven syllables in the heart upon the seven constituent elements (dhātus).

The limbs [of the mantra] are formed by the five seed-syllables, and the weapon-mantra (astra) by the remaining syllables, joined with the qualities such as knowledge and sovereignty, ending in the dative case, and accompanied by their respective seed-syllables. || 51 ||
Knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and splendor—these six, beginning with knowledge and sovereignty, are declared to be the deities of the limbs in their respective order. || 52 ||
Regarding the meditation on the hands, he says "having purified the two hands";
the meaning is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the root mantra upon the two hands as a pervasive [mantra].
"With the mantra" means with the root mantra.
The phrase "from *tāra* up to the heart" is an adjective qualifying the remainder of the mantra as well.
"In the fingers in due order" refers to the thumbs and so forth.
In the case of the placement (*nyāsa*) on the head and so forth, the phrase "from *tāra* up to the heart" is likewise connected [to that].
In the phrase "the limbs" (*aṅgāni*),
here too, [the term] "endowed with knowledge, sovereignty, and so forth" (*jñānaiśvaryādibhir yuktaiḥ*) is a third-case instrumental used in a non-concordant construction (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
[The limbs] are the seeds (*bījaiḥ*) which consist of those [mantras] ending in the dative case, such as "endowed with knowledge, sovereignty, and so forth."
The phrase "with the remaining syllables" qualifies both [the preceding and following parts].
"Limbs" refers to those ending with the eyes. *Eṃ* for knowledge, *to the heart, namaḥ*.
The application is as follows: *Śrī Ā aiśvaryāya śirase svāhā*, and so forth.
Some, following their own tradition, also pronounce the word *ātmaneśa*.
According to that view, the formula for use is "Oṃ, obeisance to the heart, the self of knowledge," and so forth. (48–52)
Thus, having cast off his body, he should remember that supreme garden,
adorned with *campaka*, *aśoka*, *punnāga*, and *pāṭala* trees.
With *lavaṅga*, *mādhavī*, *bilva*, *devadāru*, and *nameru* trees, and with well-flowered *kalpa* trees such as the *mandāra* and *pārijāta*; || 54 ||
With sandalwood trees, *kaṇīkāra* trees, *mātuliṅga* citrons, and *vañjula* reeds;
with pomegranates, *lakuca* fruits, *aṅkola* trees, betel-nut palms, and *kuravaka* flowers as well. || 55 ||
It was adorned with plantains, kunda, mandāra, and coconut trees,
and embellished by clusters of other trees rich in fragrant blossoms.
With *mālatī*, *mallikā*, *jātī*, *ketakī*, and *śatapatraka*; and also with *pārantī*, *tulasī*, *nandyāvarta*, and *edamaka*. || 57 ||
It was adorned by bowing bees endowed with flowers of every season,
and its quarters were filled with the fragrance of blossoms scattered by the gentle breeze.
In its center, it was filled with ever-blooming white water-lilies, blue lotuses, and red lotuses, as well as fragrant kahlāras and fresh blue water-lilies. || 59 ||
It was graced by swans, cranes, ducks, bees, and birds known as cakravākas, as well as other birds making a tumultuous clamor. || 60 ||
In the middle of that great lake, upon an exceedingly beautiful sandbank, was a pavilion with jeweled floors, surrounded by *pārijāta* trees. || 61 ||
The *nameru* is the *rudrākṣa*. In its center is a great lake;

in the middle of that, on the sandy bank, one should mentally conceive a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), and within that, one should contemplate the *pārijāta* tree—this is the connection with what follows. (53–61)
Resplendent like the rising sun, yet cool as the moon,
it was provided with four gates and adorned with golden ramparts.
It was endowed with eight doors beautified by the arrangement of jewels,
and possessed lofty gate-towers and archways fashioned from the nine precious gems.
It was adorned with rows of banners fastened to golden staffs,
and it shone with rows of pillars set with the nine precious gems.
It was resplendent with lamp-stands joined by a thousand lamps,
and enchanting with windows fashioned from refined gold.
It was adorned with hundreds of millions of golden ornaments fastened with cloth of various colors,
and with banners equipped with rows of tinkling bells.
Made of gold, variegated with various jewels, and exceedingly vast,
they were adorned with rows of garlands of rubies, diamonds, lapis lazuli, and gold.
It was adorned with canopies of various colors and diverse patterns, beautified by jewels set at intervals that were pleasing to the sight.
It was joined with all kinds of jewels, with a brilliant golden floor,
and adorned with ketaki, mālatī, jātī, campaka, utpala, and kesara flowers.
The surface of the earth was adorned with these and other flowers, such as jasmine, tulasī, jasmine, nandyāvarta, and kadamba.
The quarters of the sky were made fragrant by ambu, saffron, musk, tamālaka, sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.
Having thus reflected with his mind upon a most beautiful pavilion, the practitioner of mantra should visualize a lovely *pārijāta* tree in its center. || 72 ||
Beneath that, the practitioner of mantra should visualize a great jeweled lion-throne;
upon it, he should contemplate the goddess Mahālakṣmī, who is enchanting to the mind. || 73 ||
"Adorned with cloths of various colors" is an epithet of the banners (*patākā*).
"Made of gold," and so forth, are epithets of the canopies (*vitāna*).
And thus, following the earth [is the ocean], then the Ocean of Milk, the island, the garden, the great lake, the sandbank, the pavilion, and the *pārijāta* tree.
One should worship the jewel lion-throne;
the rest is the same. (62–68)
Regarding the word *kuṭṭima*: the lexicon states, "A *kuṭṭima* is a paved floor; it is not feminine. *Ambu* refers to fragrant substances.
*Kumkumā* is a term in the Kānyakubja dialect; its etymological analysis (*vigraha*) is "the navel of the musk deer.
Having thus reflected in his mind, he says "the pavilion" (*maṇḍapa*); this is a restatement of what was previously called "the pavilion."
Because the connection with the word "in the middle of that" (tanmadhye) is present in the mind due to its being separated by qualifiers [from the preceding context]. || 69–73 ||
Resplendent with the luster of the rising sun, her crest-jewel shining with a crescent moon and her necklace radiant,
adorned with jeweled ornaments, she bears the beauty of a mango blossom upon her breasts;
holding a lotus in one hand and the Kaustubha gem incessantly in the other, she smiles ever so sweetly.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Deity, who possesses three eyes like full-blown lotuses. || 74 ||
The *koṭīra* is a crown;
the meditation on the weapons is as before. || 74 ||
She was resplendent with lotus-feet beautified by tinkling anklets,
and adorned with a girdle-string studded with clusters of the nine gems.
Its waist-band was set with pearls, rubies,
and lapis lazuli, and it shone brilliantly in the middle, adorned with three folds.
Her navel was adorned by a whirlpool of the river Jāhnavī,
and her breasts were embellished with sandalwood paste, camphor, and saffron.
She bore an upper garment fashioned from fine silk, which was heavier than a string of pearls released from a rain-cloud. || 78 ||
Adorned with armlets of lapis lazuli set in refined gold,
her lotus-like hands were enriched with golden bracelets shimmering with rubies.
Adorned with rings set with fragments of rubies,
and graced by necklaces and armlets fashioned from refined gold.
Her neck resembles a conch shell adorned with various and diverse ornaments;
she is decorated with jeweled earrings that have the appearance of rising crescent moons. || 81 ||
Pāṭīra is sandalwood. Graiveya is an ornament for the neck. Kamba is a conch shell. (77–81)
Adorned with golden earrings shimmering with inlaid jewels,
her sprout-like lower lip was lovely with the beauty of hibiscus and coral.
Her rows of teeth shone like the seeds of pomegranate fruit,
and her face resembled the autumn moon, free from both blemish and waning.
Beautiful with three eyes shaped like the petals of a white lotus,
her creeper-like eyebrows surpassed the grace of Cupid’s bow.
Her nose was uplifted like the beauty of a blooming lotus flower, and she surpassed the half-moon with the splendor of the radiance on her forehead. || 85 ||
Her lotus-face was marked with a tilaka of musk endowed with intense fragrance, and her hair was richly adorned with the playful movements of swarms of intoxicated bees. || 86 ||
Her braided hair bore the beauty of *pārijāta* blossoms,
and her head was adorned with a crown fashioned from priceless jewels.
That Mahālakṣmī, the abode of all loveliness, the dwelling place of the splendor of grace, and the birthplace of all radiant energies, is truly captivating to the mind. || 88 ||
The analysis of the compound is: "those whose locks of hair shine like a row of intoxicated bees. (82–88)
Reflecting thus upon the Goddess, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) and having conquered his senses,
he should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times and offer oblations with clarified butter ten thousand times.
Then, one should offer ten thousand oblations each with bilva fruits and lotuses;
thereafter, one should perform libations with pure, fragrant waters twenty thousand times. || 90 ||
When the seat has arisen from the seed-syllable of Śrī, one should worship Mahālakṣmī.
One should offer the seat with the Śrī-bīja and fashion the form with the root-mantra. || 91 ||

One should worship the son of Śaṅkara on the right side of the Goddess, and on the other side, one should worship the Flower-Bowed One (Kāmadeva) with his hands joined in a handful of flowers. || 92 ||
The oblation (homa) is performed with clarified butter (ghṛta) in a quantity equal to one-tenth [of the total recitation];
however, an additional twenty thousand oblations may be offered.
This is done upon a pedestal (pīṭha) consisting of an eight-petaled lotus, a twelve-petaled lotus, and a square with four doors.
Some [identify him] as Śaṅkaranandana, Gaṇeśa, or Skanda; the visualization for both [forms] is that he holds a handful of flowers in his hand. (89–92)
One should worship the limbs according to the prescribed rule in the locations previously mentioned;
one should worship the eight Śaktis, beginning with Umā, situated in the middle of the petals, in their proper order. || 93 ||
Then Umā, Śrī, Sarasvatī, Durgā together with Dharaṇī, Gāyatrī, and the goddess Uṣā—all holding lotuses in their hands and beautifully adorned—[appeared]. || 94 ||
The two daughters of Jahnu and Sūrya, worthy of worship, were intent on washing his feet;
the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, were worshipped as they held chowries at his sides. || 95 ||
Then one should worship Varuṇa, who holds a parasol, in the west;
having worshipped him, one should then sacrifice to the nine planets surrounding the zodiac signs.
One should worship the elephants of the quarters in their respective directions, adorned with four tusks:
Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, and Añjana.
One should worship Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka in sequence;
then one should worship Indra and the other [directional deities], as well as their weapons outside of them.
One should daily worship the Goddess with devotion, using fragrant and most enchanting perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures. || 99 ||
A person seeking long life should offer oblations of dūrvā grass sprinkled with clarified butter into a well-kindled fire for ten nights, one thousand and eight times.
He who, for seven days, should offer oblations of guḍūcī sprinkled with ghee one thousand and eight times, shall live for a hundred autumns. || 101 ||
Regarding those previously mentioned [mantras] excluding the fourth:

"according to rule" refers to the application of *namaḥ* to the limbs beginning with the head, as has been stated. Alternatively, it is said that they should be used together with the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) according to their respective ritual arrangements.
She who has lotuses in her two hands is Padmahastā.
Subsequently, the plural form should be understood as resulting from the retention of one term (*ekaśeṣa*) among the eight instances of the word *Padmahastā*.
The third enclosure begins with Jahnu and ends with Paścima.
"Having worshipped" refers to the twelve petals.
Regarding "the zodiac signs," their respective colors have been stated by the teachers as follows:
The twins, Virgo, and Cancer are yellow;
these others—Libra, Capricorn, Aries, and Scorpio—are of a reddish luster.
"The four remaining [spheres] of movement stand as white and are considered distinct.
Thus, their essential natures should be understood in accordance with their respective names.
This is the fourth enclosure.
Now, one should worship the nine planets all around;
their colors and their forms will be described in the mantra of the Moon.
"The world-elephants" (diggajān) refers to the white ones.
"In the directions" (dikṣu) means in their respective directions.
"One thousand and eight" (aṣṭottarasahasrakam) applies to both [the offerings and the recitations] every day. || 93-101 ||
Having offered sesame seeds smeared with ghee, one shall obtain long life;
beginning on a Sunday, the practitioner of mantra should perform this day after day for ten nights.
By offering oblations of fuel-sticks from the *arka* tree smeared with clarified butter, one certainly obtains freedom from disease.
Standing in water reaching up to the neck and meditating upon the Goddess within the sun, [one attains this]. (103)
Raising his arms, the knower of mantras should recite this one thousand and eight times;
he immediately obtains health in this mortal world, as well as all his desires.
By constantly offering oblations of *śāli* rice one thousand and eight times, [he attains the same].
Before long, great prosperity will certainly arise. || 105 ||
The mantra-practitioner should offer oblations with flowers produced from the Lakṣmī-vallī creeper, or with Nandyāvarta flowers, or with white mustard seeds soaked in clarified butter. || 106 ||
One attains great prosperity and is honored by all living beings.
Having offered one thousand and eight [oblations],
this is also the subsequent application.
On Sunday is the day of Āditya.
One should offer oblations one thousand and eight times.
The Lakṣmī-vallī plant has leaves shaped like betel leaves, with a red dot in the center and white flowers.
The word "vā" (or) is used in the sense of conjunction. || 102–107 ||
Mixed with black pepper and cumin, and combined with the powder of coconut; || 107 ||
One who knows the mantra, has conquered his senses, and subsists on milk-rice (pāyasa) should offer oblations of cakes mixed with molasses, cooked in clarified butter, and drizzled with ghee. 108.
By offering one hundred and eight oblations daily from the maṇḍala, one becomes a giver of wealth;
by sacrificing with clarified butter mixed with jaggery, one shall become possessed of food.
One should offer one thousand and eight hibiscus flowers (javāpuṣpa) as oblations;
then, taking the ashes mixed with the juice of betel leaf, one should recite the mantra over them. || 110 ||
One should apply a tilaka with that [substance], and by doing so, it shall bring everything under control;
one who possesses self-mastery may subjugate Brahmins using sacrificial fuel and flowers from the Brahmavṛkṣa tree. || 111 ||
The wise one, the best among those who know mantras, having offered *jātī* flowers for a king, red lotuses for Vaiśyas,
and blue lotuses for Śūdras, shall bring them under his control.
By offering oblations of madhūka flowers, one brings women under one's control within forty-nine days from the beginning of the maṇḍala;
[he becomes] Kubera, the giver of wealth.
"One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times," and so forth.
"Ashes" refers to the ashes of burnt *javā* flowers.
The "Brahma-tree" is the *palāśa*.
For there is a Vedic revelation stating, "The Palāśa tree is indeed Brahman. (107–113)
Having fashioned the mandala consisting of nine squares, adorned with a yantra. || 113 ||
One should perform the consecration according to the ritual for the sake of all accomplishments;
one should place jars possessing auspicious characteristics upon those positions. || 114 ||

One should fill these [vessels], whose entire bodies are smeared with sandalwood paste, which are provided with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains, and which are wrapped in fine silk, with water from sacred fords (*tīrtha*). || 115 ||
The best of preceptors should place a lotus, set with the nine gems and fashioned from refined gold, adorned with a mechanical device, into the central pitcher. || 116 ||
Having ground together equal parts of sandalwood, uśīra, camphor, jasmine, kaṅkola, saffron, kuṣṭha, aguru, tamāla, and cardamom; || 117 ||
Having stirred [the contents] within all the jars, one should also cast jewels [into them].
Regarding the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), it says "having performed" [the following]:
the self consisting of nine parts, which was described in the third [chapter], possesses nine centers (*navanābha*).
The meaning is that one should draw the diagram (yantra) to be described hereafter within the central seed-syllable (kaṇīkā) adorned with the yantra.

Regarding the phrase "according to the rule," he states the prescribed procedure beginning with "the jars" and so forth. "Fashioned from drawn gold" means fashioned from gold weighing one hundred and sixty *raktikās*.
"Rich in yantras" means endowed with the yantras that will be described hereafter;
by this, the meaning is "the lotus-yantra. *Jātī* refers to the nutmeg (*jātīphala*).
"By way of division" means by way of equal distribution.
"Jewels" refers to the nine [jewels] mentioned in the chapter on the *mātṛkā*.
"In all the jars" [is the phrase].
The word "also" (api) here is connected with this as well. 113–118.
Lakṣmī, dūrvā, sadābhadrā, sahadevī, and madhuvratā. || 118 ||
Muśalī, śakravallī, krāntā, and the leaves of apāmārga;
likewise priyaṅgu, mung beans, wheat, rice, sesame, and barley. || 119 ||

Having washed the rice grains and the beans, one should place them into these [liquids], along with [the juices of] the dhātrī, lakuc, and bilva, as well as those of the kadalī and the coconut. || 120 ||
Having also offered fruits, one should cast these flowers:
the lotus, the saugandhika, the jasmine, the mallikā, and likewise the bakula.
The leaves arising from the Campaka, Aśoka, Punnāga, Tulasī, and Ketaka, as well as those of the Vaṭa, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, and Udumbara trees. || 122 ||

Lakṣmī (as previously defined), 1. dūrvā grass, 2. sadābhadra (bhadramustā), 3. sahadevī, 4. madhuvrata (bhṛṅgarāja), 5. muṣalī (the muṣalī tuber), 6. śakravallī (indravāruṇī), 7. krāntā (viṣṇukrāntā), 8. and apāmārga leaves, 9.—having washed these, one should place them individually into these nine jars; this is the syntactical connection with what follows.
"Priyaṅgu" is *kaṅgu*.
"One should cast [them]" applies to each [ingredient]. (118–120)
"Also fruits" and "also sprouts" [are to be placed] in all the jars. || 121 ||
Having poured the Brahmakūrca [mixture] and covered the openings of the jars with cups containing fruit and unbroken rice, one should then cover them with linen cloths. || 123 ||
Having invoked Mahālakṣmī, one should worship her in the central pitcher;
one should then worship Umā and the others, in due order, in the remaining eight pitchers.
Having offered pleasing perfumes, flowers, along with incense and lamps, and having presented various kinds of food and edibles, one should touch them and mutter the mantra. || 125 ||

At the conclusion of three thousand recitations, having brought the subject to be accomplished under control and having established a seat upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should cause him to sit down upon it. || 126 ||
Having respectfully adorned him with beautiful ornaments and garments, he was accompanied by auspicious women who scattered flowers and unbroken grains of rice. || 127 ||
While the twice-born recited blessings preceded by auspicious words, and while the five musical instruments resounded, at that auspicious moment, the wise one [proceeded]. || 128 ||
Having lifted the central pitcher while recollecting the mantra of Mahālakṣmī, the preceptor should consecrate [the disciple] in due order with the other pitchers as well. || 129 ||
Touching his head with his hand, the preceptor should pronounce a blessing:
"May there be prosperity; may there be auspiciousness; may Mahālakṣmī be gracious."
The *brahmakūrca* is that which is described in the chapter on initiation (*dīkṣāpaṭala*).
"Having touched them" means simultaneously with [a blade of] *kuśa* grass or the like. "With auspicious women" means with young maidens (*ciraṇṭī*).
He utters a blessing itself, saying, "May it be auspicious. (123–130)
"May the gods protect you always; may prosperity attend you at all times.
Then, having risen and being consecrated, he put on two garments. || 131 ||
Having sipped water according to the prescribed rule, he should prostrate like a staff before the guru,
honoring him with garments, ornaments, grain, wealth, perfumes, cattle, buffaloes, and so forth.
One should satisfy the male and female servants according to the prescribed rules, regarding them with the thought that they are deities;
afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins along with the poor, the blind, and the wretched.
He should hold a great festival in his home together with his kinsmen;
then that best of men considers himself to have achieved his life's purpose. || 134 ||
A king who has been consecrated conquers his enemies before long;
a prince desiring the turban obtains the turban—of this there is no doubt. || 135 ||
Having been consecrated, even a barren woman gives birth to a son of great intelligence;
he becomes a guide when great diseases arise and when there are malevolent acts of sorcery. || 136 ||
In the event of ill omens concerning living beings and the like, one should perform an ablution;
it bestows all prosperity upon men and grants the attainment of all good fortune. || 137 ||
It pacifies all diseases, wards off all calamities, provides protection for the fetus of women, and is supreme in generating long life. || 138 ||
He is the protector of the maternity chamber for women who have given birth, and the guardian of the flower-wombs of those whose flowers and wombs have perished. || 139 ||
Those learned in the meaning of the scriptures declare this consecration to be the destroyer of kings who are terrified by approaching enemies. || 140 ||
The name of the person for whom the rite is intended, preceded by "Oṃ" and followed by "Śrī Śaktimāra," should be placed in pairs upon the filaments.
Outside of that, there is a lotus with twelve petals shining with the syllables of the mantra;
its filaments consist of the consonants, and it possesses sixteen petals radiant with the vowels, [surrounded by] the earth-element.
One should draw the yantra encircled by the two *bimba* mantras and the *tvaritā* mantra ending with *vaṣaṭ*.
The letters *ha* and *kṣa* should be written repeatedly in the corners of the two square enclosures;
this is the Mahālakṣmī yantra, which bestows the fruit of all sovereignty. || 142 ||
It pacifies all suffering and wards off all calamities; what more need be said here? There exists nothing superior to this. || 143 ||
Regarding the yantra, he says "vedādī" (beginning with the Vedas).
The connection is that one should draw a lotus-shaped yantra.
Of what kind is it?

The *praṇava* (oṃ) is at the beginning of the Vedas; that in which the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the name of the action of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) reside should be known as being in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), because it will be stated [later] that [the names] are on the filaments (*kiñjalka*). Furthermore, of what nature is it?
In the filaments—that is, in the positions of the stamens—one should place [the deities] in pairs, accompanied by Śrī, Śakti, and Māra.
According to those who know the tradition, the sequence is as follows: in the first filament, Śrī and Śakti; in the next, Māra and Śrī; and in the one following that, Śakti and Māra.
By this method, there are eight repetitions of the three seed-syllables.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
It is that wherein the syllables of the mantra shine upon the petals of the Sun—that is, upon twelve petals.
Again, what are its further qualifications?

Outside of that is the filament of consonants (*vyañjana-kesara*); this means that where the consonants, beginning with *ka*, are located upon the filaments, two consonants must be written in each position of a filament because there are two filaments. Furthermore, how is it? It is joined with the shimmering vowels (*svara-lasat*) and possesses sixteen petals, being a pair of eight-petaled [circles].
It is encircled by two *dharā* disks that are mutually interpenetrated;
this is to be connected with the phrase "together with *tvaritā*.
And this [description] begins from above.
Having first wrapped it quickly with that [thread], one should subsequently wrap it with two ground-level chambers (*bhūgṛha*).
Here, the mutual interpenetration [of the layers] is obtained by implication;
for when squares are made one above the other, the wrapping of the *yantra* is accomplished directly by means of a single square alone.
But the encircling by another is done only by a square, not by the mantra.
If it is argued that this constitutes the encircling of the yantra through a traditional succession, we say no;
for if the two were distinct, both would indeed be directly encircled by the yantra.
Of what kind of *tvaritā*? [It is] that which ends with *vaṣaṭ*; in this regard, the traditionalists (*sāmpradāyikāḥ*) say that the word *phaṭ* is replaced by *vaṣaṭ*.
Others, however, say that *vaṣaṭ* is an addition.
The syllables *hakṣau* [occur] in an eightfold repetition. || 141–143 ||
The consort of Śambhu, Śrī, Ruddhā, Kamā, Bhagavatī, Mahī;
Brahmā, Āditya, Dharā, Dīrghā, Laḥ, Kṣādi, Bhagavān, and Marut. (144)
"Prasīda-yugalam," followed by "Śrī-uddhā Bhuvaneśvarī," ending with "Mahālakṣmi" and preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ)—this is the mantra. || 145 ||
Abounding in twenty-seven syllables, it is declared to bestow all prosperity.
The heart-mantra is said to be "kamale," and the head-mantra should be "kamalālaye. || 146 ||
One should perform the *śikhā* with "prasīda," the *kavaca* with those same [syllables], and the *astra* with these words, each individually enclosed by the three seed-syllables. || 147 ||
He states another mantra, beginning with "Śambhu": "The consort of Śambhu" refers to the seed-syllable of Māyā; "enclosed by Śrī" means it is flanked by the seed-syllable of Śrī.

Because it consists of a single syllable, the enclosure (*sampuṭa*) results in *rodha*. In *kama*, the letters are *ka* and *ma*. *Bhaga* is the vowel *e*; the earth (*mahī*) joined with that is *la*, hence *le*.
In the Nāgara script, because the letter *e* has the form of a vulva (*bhaga*), it is denoted by the word *bhaga*.
The letters *ka* and *ma* represent Brahmā and Āditya, respectively;
the letter *la* represents the Earth (*dharā*).
The long [vowel] is joined with a long [consonant]; therein, because there is no reason for skipping the first, it is joined with the *ākāra* (the letter *ā*), and thus [the result is] *lā*.
The meaning is that *la*, beginning with *kṣa*, is a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*). *Marut* is the letter *ya*.
The Blessed One is joined with the letter *e*; by that [suffix], it becomes "Mahālakṣmī," which is the essential form. Some maintain that this word may also end in the dative case.
However, because the letter *ya* functions as a *kīlaka* (stake) in these [mantras], it is not extracted in that manner.
Others, however, having extracted the distinction at the beginning of the doublets and so forth, state that there are twenty-eight letters.
"Sarvasamṛddhi" is the statement of the application (*viniyoga*).
The seed-syllable *Śrīṃ* is the power of Māyā;
Kamalavāsinī is its seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth.
"By that very [means]" refers to the word "be gracious" (*prasīda*).
"By means of four-syllable [units]" refers to the term *mahālakṣmī*.
"Encased by three seed-syllables" refers to the three seed-syllables distinct from the *praṇava* (oṃ) situated at the beginning of the mantra.
The ellipsis is that one should perform the limb-protections (*aṅga*) individually, that is, for each one separately.
The application therein is as follows: "Śrī Ā Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Kamale Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance to the heart," and so forth. (144–147)
[I bow to] the Supreme Goddess, whose splendor is as red as vermilion, who dwells in the lotus, who is a treasure-trove of the waters of beauty,
adorned with a crown, armlets, necklaces, earrings, waist-bands,
and other ornaments; she who, with her lotus-hands, holds a vessel of eight petals, a pair of lotuses, and a mirror.
One should constantly meditate upon the beloved wife of Śārṅgin, who is surrounded by her female attendants.
The meditation on the weapons extends from the lower right hand to the lower left hand. || 148 ||

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with bilva fruits smeared with honey in a consecrated fire, using a tenth part [of the recitation], according to the very path previously described. || 149 ||
One should worship her upon the seat (pīṭha) using the seed-syllable of Śrī, according to the sequence to be described hereafter;
outside the enclosure of the limbs (aṅgāvṛtti), the forms beginning with Śrīdhara are to be worshipped. || 150 ||
Hṛṣīkeśa known as Śrīdhara, Vaikuṇṭha, Viśvarūpaka, Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. || 151 ||
Having worshipped [the deities] at the inner bases, one should perform sacrifice among the petals to Bhāratī, Pārvatī, Cāndrī, Śacī, and Damakā and the others. || 152 ||
On the tips of the petals, one should worship these arrows of Mahālakṣmī in sequence:
Anurāga, Saṃvāda, Vijaya, Vallabha, and Mada.
Immediately after the Lords of the World, the best of practitioners should worship joy, strength, and splendor, as well as their weapons, on the exterior. || 154 ||
For those who worship the goddess Mahālakṣmī according to this rite, Lakṣmī herself shall dwell among them, forgetting her own abode. || 155 ||
If one performs a hundred thousand oblations with blue lotuses soaked in sandalwood water, a king shall obtain the sovereignty over his enemies without having to engage in battle. || 156 ||
The limb-worship (aṅgāvṛtti) is outside [the petals], on the filaments (kesara).
By that, the worship of the limbs is performed upon the pericarp (kaṇīkā).
For this very reason, there is the statement: "one should worship at the bases of the petals."
"In the middle of the petals" means in the middle of the petals of the directions.
"The [deities] beginning with Damaka" refers to those in the middle of the petals of the intermediate directions.
"In front of them" means on the tips of the petals.
The connection is: "those who worship as the best of practitioners.

By the term "the best of practitioners," this is what is meant: those who are established in the observance (*samaya*) of the worshippers of the Goddess Lakṣmī, characterized by truthfulness and other such qualities. (149–156)
A man who goes to the royal assembly would be honored by it;
[therein are found] Dūrvā grass, the goddess Mahālakṣmī, Viṣṇukrāntā, and Madhuvratā. || 157 ||
Muśalī, śakravallī, sadābhadrā, añjalipriyā, haricandana, karpūra, candana, aṅkola, and rocanā. || 158 ||

Having ground together *mālūra*, *kesara*, and *kuṣṭha* with the juices of *niśā*, one should perform the rite of the forehead mark (*tilaka*) while reciting the mantra one thousand and eight times. || 159 ||
All [attendants] remain under the control of the minister who acts [thus], day and night.
The minister should resort to the mantra of Śrī and should also recite the Śrīsūktas. || 160 ||
*Tayā* means "with fear.
*Devī* refers to *sahadevī*.
*Madhuvratā* refers to the *bhṛṅgarāja* (royal bee).
*Sadābhadra* is *bhadramustā*.
*Añjalipriyā* is *añjalinī*.
*Hātājoḍī* is a term in the Kānyakubja dialect.
Haricandana is yellow sandalwood;
mālūra is the bilva fruit;
kesaras are nāgakesaras.
*Niśā* is turmeric.
The *Śrīsūkta*, consisting of fifteen verses, is well known among the Bahvṛcas (Ṛgvedins). Its ritual procedure is as follows:
The Ṛṣi of the first [verse] is declared to be Śrī; thereafter are Ānanda, Kardama, Cilkīta, and Indirāputra—these are proclaimed as the Munis.
The meter for the first fourteen [verses] is Anuṣṭubh;
for the next three, it is Bṛhatī; and for the fourth, fifth, and sixth, Triṣṭubh is declared.
In the seventh [section] and those following, the *anuṣṭubh* of eight [syllables] is proclaimed;
the *prastāra* and *paṅkti* are mentioned, and Agni and the two gods are proclaimed in the final [verse].
The seed-syllable and the power-syllable are at the beginning and the end; the ritual application is for the attainment of wealth.
[The nyāsa is performed] on the head, eyes, ears, and nose, as well as on the mouth, neck, and both hands.
One should place [the mantras] upon the heart, navel, genitals, anus, thighs, knees, shanks, and feet;
likewise, with a garland made of gold, moonstone, silver, and so forth.
With the verses beginning with "suvarṇā," "srajā," and "hiraṇyā" as the fifth,
and "hiraṇyavarṇā"— these ending with "namaḥ"— one should then perform the limb-worship (aṅganyāsa).
Seated upon a red lotus, with eyes like lotuses, adorned with various many ornaments,
her complexion the color of a mass of pollen from a crimson lotus, and wearing a crest-jewel of fine gems.
The preceptor should thus meditate upon the Goddess, the mother of the three worlds, who holds a pair of lotuses and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with her own arms.
One should recite the mantra from the first day of the bright fortnight until the eleventh day,
offering one thousand oblations of fuel-sticks, bilva fruits, lotuses, and clarified butter.
Then one should offer oblations ten times the amount [of the main offering] with milk-rice (pāyasa) soaked in the three sweets (trimadhu);
thereafter, one should worship Śivā upon the Śrīpīṭha according to the procedure previously described.
Having conceived the form [of the deity] by means of the root mantra, one should perform the sixteen services using the fifteen mantras, both individually and collectively.
Then, in the worship of the enclosure, there is the worship of the limbs upon the filaments:
Padmā, Padmavarṇā, Padmasthā, Ārdra, and Turīyakā.
Tarpayantī, Tṛptā, Jvalantī, and likewise Saptamī; the eighth is Svarṇaprākārā—one should worship these upon the petals.
Thus, the worship together with the weapons of Lokeśāna has been described.
Now, at the end of all the Śrī-mantras, the Śrī-yantra as taught in another tantra is written:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the Yantra of Śrī; listen, O beloved!
This Yantra bestows all accomplishments and is the supreme means of enchanting all.
It bestows energy, nourishment, prosperity, and fame;
it grants immortality to men and provides the fruit of all desired objects.
It effects the destruction of enemies, the supreme increase of friends,
the gathering of one's own army, and the withdrawal of the enemy's forces.
O Maheśvarī, when one is constantly afflicted by enemies through mantras such as those of the Atharvaveda, there is protection against the supreme mantras and the cutting of their power.
The practice of dhāraṇā bestows longevity, health, prosperity, good fortune, and wealth;
it is like a great eight-petaled lotus, complete with a pericarp and filaments.
One should inscribe the Śrī-bīja joined with the name in the pericarp;
one should inscribe the Vāruṇa [bīja] adorned with a bindu on the eastern petal ten thousand times.
The meaning is that it is the letter *va*, joined with the vowel *a* and accompanied by the nasal dot (*bindu*), consisting of the consonant alone;
thus it becomes *vaṃ*.
This seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Viṣṇu, possessed of the *bindu*, is on its petal in the southern direction.
It becomes "aṃ.
The letter *na* joined with the final consonant (*ya*) and provided with a bindu is on the petal belonging to Varuṇa;
*na* here refers to the letter *pa*.
The letter *ya* becomes *repha*. Thus, it becomes *praṃ*.
One should write Viṣṇu, conjoined with the *bindu*, on the northern petal of the lotus.
The meaning is "aṃ.
The letter ending in *ja* (i.e., *jha*), conjoined with fire (*ra*) and possessing a bindu, is located on the petal in the direction of fire.
"Ending in *ja*" refers to the letter *jha*.
Vahni is the letter *ra*.
Thus, it becomes *jhraṃ*.
The letter *va* at the end, joined with Viṣṇu and provided with a bindu, is on the petal of Nairṛta.
The letter *śa* is that which has been vomited forth;
*Viṣṇu* is the letter *a*.
Thus, it becomes "śam."
One should write the twelfth seed-syllable of Brahmā, conjoined with the fifth vowel, and endowed with the bindu and nāda, upon the purifying petal.
Brahmā is *ka*; therefore, the twelfth letter is *ṭha*.
The fifth vowel is *u*. Thus, it becomes *ṭhuṃ*.
One should place the first letter of the class, conjoined with the *śānta* vowel (ṛ), endowed with the eleventh [vowel],
and joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, upon the petal in the northeastern direction.
The first of the class is the letter *ka*.
The peaceful one is *ṣa*. The eleventh is the letter *e*.
The syllable *kṣeṃ* comes to be [there]. Outside of that, the practitioner should place the Śrī-bīja in the first enclosure all around;
the Kāma-bīja in the second, and the Śakti-bīja in the third.
Then, having drawn a subterranean chamber (bhūgṛha) and facing east with a very serene mind,
he should diligently worship the Guru with garments, grain, wealth, and other offerings.
O Dear One, one should worship the yantra with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth;
and having performed a thousand recitations, O Dear One, it brings about all spiritual accomplishments.
One should write it on a silver plate, or a copper one, or on birch bark, and then wear it.

Having written the name within the Śrī-bīja, one should write the letter ending in *ṭha* (ṇa) outside of it; then, having surrounded it continuously with the letter ending in *la* (ḷ) joined with the nasal dot (*bindu*).
Furthermore, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus, writing "Śrī Ā Hnī" on each petal.
Then, having encircled Mahāmāyā with two triangles from the outside, for one who constantly wears this, prosperity increases—of this there is no doubt. (157–160)
Desiring greater prosperity, one should always be a speaker of truth;
one should eat facing the west and speak pleasant words preceded by a smile. || 161 ||
Restrained and pure, he should adorn himself with perfumes, flowers, and other such things;
he should sleep on a clean bed with a young woman, and not with any other. || 162 ||
One should not descend into water naked, nor should one eat while smeared with oil;
one should not smear turmeric on the face, nor should one ever sleep while impure. || 163 ||
One should not draw on the ground in vain, nor should one carry a bilva fruit, a droṇa measure, or a lotus upon the head; nor should one eat salt or oil alone.
One should never be impure, nor should one eat contemptible food;
one should never step over a *droṇa* measure, a lotus, or a *bilva* fruit with one's feet. || 165 ||
One should always wear on one's head sahadevī, indravallī, śrīvallī, viṣṇuvallabhā, kanyā, jambu, and pravāla. || 166 ||
He speaks of the many qualities of the devotee of Kamala:
"facing the western direction" means one whose face is turned toward the west; "with a youthful [appearance]," and so forth.
Nor [is it caused] by old age;
for it is said: "Old age, however, produces fever.
For women, old age occurs after fifty-five years.
By the phrase "not by another," this is what is meant:
as they say— [a woman] who is wicked, of a miserable lineage, defiled by quarrelsomeness, corrupt in her conduct, and undesirable.

"One who desires wealth should not touch a woman who is attached to many men or unattached, whose limbs are exceedingly emaciated, who is very short or very tall, afflicted by disease, fond of sensual pleasures, fickle toward every man, beloved by kings yet herself unlovely, with eyes like a crow's or the gait of a frog, and adorned with house-flowers. Thus it is said.
*Droṇa* is *gūmā* in the Kānyakubja dialect;
*śrīdevī* is *śrīlatā*;
*viṣṇuvallabhā* is *viṣṇukrāntā*.
The maiden is Ghṛtakumārī. || 161–166 ||
Thus, one who is constantly devoted to right conduct, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and firm in his vows, attains great prosperity that is difficult even for the gods to obtain. || 167 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Śāradātilaka* composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇa, the Lord of Teachers. 8.
*bth* " *bi* means 'he practices';
this refers to the adoption of the conduct taught in other tantras."
As it is stated in the Nārāyaṇīya:
"One should not urinate, nor step upon a lotus, nor eat its seed;
one should not be impure, nor cut a bilva fruit, nor sleep on the bare ground."

Salt and *āmalaka* fruit should be avoided on the days of the Nāgas and Ādityas respectively; on the fifth lunar day and during the northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*), women should be avoided; and one should avoid eating while facing westward.
One should not clean one's teeth with *bilva* fruits, and one should bow down to them at the three junctions of the day.
Sesame seeds should be consumed by him in the morning, and he should wear [them] and consume *lakṣmī*.
"One should wear that flower upon the head during the Uttarāyaṇa and eat sweet food;
on the full moon day of the bright fortnight, one should consume milk-rice and bilva seeds. Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Prayogasāra*:
One who desires prosperity should not sleep upon grain, nor over fire, nor on weapons; nor should one sleep with the head toward the south or west, nor naked, nor with hands and feet wet.
Furthermore, one should not apply oil for massage at night, nor should one smear it on the face. Thus [it is said]. 167.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Now I shall describe Bhuvaneśvarī, the mother of the world, who sustains the universe.
Even Brahmā and the other gods, having known her, attained exalted prosperity.

Having thus stated the mantras of Sarasvatī and Śrī, [the author] begins to state the mantras of Bhuvaneśī immediately thereafter because they are contained within them, starting with the word "atha" (now).
By the phrase "having known which," the various divisions of this three-syllabled mantra are indicated.
Among those, the author himself will explain the encasing by *vāk* (speech), the encasing by *vāk-śrī*, the encasing by *śrī-kāma*, and the encasing by *kāma-śrī*.

In this way, the four variations—namely, being encapsulated by desire (*kāma*), being encapsulated by Śrīvāk, being encapsulated by speech and desire (*vāk-kāma*), and being encapsulated by desire and speech (*kāma-vāk*)—should be inferred by oneself.
As it has been said:
"When she, the Sovereign of all desires (*sarvakāmeśvarī*), manifests with desire at the beginning and end..."
Through the Vāgbhava [syllable], one attains fortune from beginning to end, the fruits of sons and wealth, and the bestowal of speech.

"Thus, when the petals are arranged separately, that power indeed becomes the granter of desires. Also elsewhere: "Or, O beautiful one, the practitioner of mantra, having encapsulated [the mantra] with the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja)..."
"By practicing with restricted diet, one may bring the three worlds under one's control. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, the teacher Padmapāda has mentioned two other variations: being enclosed by the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) and being enclosed by the four *śrī-bījas*.
"May Śrī worship me"—this indicates the ritual application (*viniyoga*). || 1 ||
Nakulīśa is mounted upon fire, possessing a left eye and a half-moon;
his seed-syllable, as it has been declared, is practiced by those desiring spiritual perfection. || 2 ||
The sage is Śakti, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity of the Mantra is said to be Bhuvaneśvarī, who is served by the assembly of vowels. || 3 ||
He extracts the mantra as "nakulīśa.
Nakulīśa is the letter *ha*; Agni is the letter *ra*; the left eye is the letter *ī*; and the half-moon is the nasal bindu (*m*).
Thus, when combined, they form a single seed-syllable.
By the phrase "served by those desiring spiritual success" (*siddhikāṅkṣibhiḥ sevitām*), it is indicated that even this [mantra] alone is a means for accomplishing all human goals (*puruṣārtha*).
Thus, it is said in the *Bhuvaneśvarīpārijāta*:
"There is no man equal to me, and there is no woman equal to you."
"A mantra equal to the seed-syllable of illusion has never existed, nor will it ever exist. Thus [it is said].
Śakti is the son of Vasiṣṭha; as it is stated in the Saṃhitā: "The seer Śakti is the son of Vasiṣṭha. Ha is the seed-syllable (bīja), and Īṃ is the power (śakti).
As it is stated in the Daśapaṭalī:
"Haṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), īṃ is the power (śakti); its application is for the sake of one's desired goal. (2-3)

One whose body has been consecrated with the Mātṛkā should perform the six limbs in sequence using the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels, according to the path of both withdrawal and emanation.
Then one should perform the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa) for the sake of attaining the state of the deity:
[placing] Hṛllekhā on the head and Gaganā in the lotus of the heart. || 5 ||
One should visualize the red Karālikā at the secret place and Mahocchuṣmā on the two feet;
[and the other goddesses] in the upper, eastern, southern, northern, and western faces.
Regarding the phrase "six long [vowels]":
here, however, only the extraction of the six-limbed mantra has been performed;
he will explain the ritual placement (nyāsa) at the appropriate occasion for nyāsa.
Regarding the phrase "by way of dissolution and emanation":
here, because the word *sṛṣṭi* (emanation) has fewer syllables, it ought to have been placed first [according to grammatical rules].
That was not done; therefore, one should perform the emanation-arrangement (*sṛṣṭinyāsa*) after having performed the dissolution-arrangement (*saṃhāranyāsa*).
As it is stated in the Saṃhitā:
"One should first install the Mātṛkā according to the method of the Guru’s instruction, in reverse order, beginning with the letter 'A' and ending with the final phoneme."

"The placement of the *saṃhāramātṛkā* (the alphabet of withdrawal) is radiant with the essence of the bliss of Brahman. Thus [it is said]. The teachers also state: "Having thus withdrawn and then generated the body..."
Thus.
Regarding "in the two feet":
it should be understood that this is done with one hand at one and the same time; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to repeat the mantra. (4–6)
One should place [the syllables] enriched with short seed-syllables such as *sa* and others, together with the elements and their splendors;
thereafter, one should place the six limbs, joined with the [five] birth-mantras, in due order.
Regarding "sadyādi":
*sadya* is the vowel *o*; those beginning with it are the five short vowels. By this method of reverse order, the five short vowels—excluding the neuter (*m*)—are taken.
The masters of the tradition maintain that the seed-syllable (*bīja*) which possesses the short vowels *o*, *e*, *i*, *a*, and *sadyādi* (the first of the *sadyojāta*-mantras) is thus enriched;
by this, the seed-syllables become *hroṃ*, *hreṃ*, *hruṃ*, *hriṃ*, and *hraṃ*.
However, the author of the *Gūḍhārthadīpikā* has stated these five short vowels as *o*, *e*, *ḷ*, *ṛ*, and *u*.
That is not so;
for even when "Sadyojāta" and the others are employed at the beginning of all [mantras] according to tradition, it is only those excluding the neuter [seed-syllables] that are taken.
As for the claim made by some that the mere vowel constitutes the seed-syllable, that too is incorrect.
Because the inclusion of the word "seed" (bīja) would otherwise be purposeless.
And it is said in the *Daśapaṭalī*:
"The knower of mantra, having pierced the [deity] on the seat with the lips, ears, eyes, and so forth, which are the objects of knowledge..."
"One should place Hṛllekhā and the others," it is said.

"Together with the elements and their splendors" means in the sequence beginning with earth; thus, Hṛllekhā is yellow, Gaganā is white, Raktā is red, Mahocchuṣmā is red, Karālikā is black, and Svacchā is transparent.
Regarding the term "limbs" (aṅgāni):
it means by means of the limb-mantras belonging to their respective classes as previously mentioned.
For this very reason, [it says] "subsequently."

As it has been said by the Teachers: "One should place Hṛllekhā, Gaganā, Karālikā (who is red), and Mahocchuṣmā on the head, the face, the heart, the secret place, and the feet, along with their limbs. (7)
One should place Brahmā, conjoined with Gāyatrī, on the forehead;
one should place Viṣṇu, conjoined with Sāvitrī, on the right cheek. || 8 ||
One should place Maheśvara, joined with Vāgīśvarī, on the left cheek;
then, one should again place the Lord of Wealth (Dhanapati), accompanied by Śrī, at the tip of the left ear. || 9 ||
Having placed Rati upon the face, one should place Smara; having placed Puṣṭi, one should place Gaṇapati on the left ear.
One should place the two Nidhis on the ear and within the space between the ear and the cheek.
One should place the root mantra on the face; furthermore, one should place these [syllables] on the body:
at the base of the throat, on the pair of breasts, on the left shoulder, and in the lotus of the heart. || 11 ||

The instructor [should place the syllables] on the left shoulder, on both sides, at the region of the navel, on the forehead, shoulder, side, and abdomen, on the other side and shoulder, and on the heart. || 12 ||
Then, one should assign the Brahmāṇīs and the others according to the prescribed rite and their stated characteristics;
