having performed the pervasive assignment (vyāpaka-nyāsa) over the body with the root mantra, one should meditate upon the Goddess. || 13 ||
He states the *yoninyāsa* with the words "Brahmāṇam" and so forth. In that context, *hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ* are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of Gāyatrī and the others;
*haṃ hiṃ huṃ* are those of Brahmā and the others.
For others, there are their respective seeds.
It should be understood that the first syllable of a treasure (nidhi) is its seed.
Regarding this, the application is as follows:
"Hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā together with Gāyatrī," and so forth.
The fact that the name of the Śakti comes first in the worship will become clear later. "At the tip of the left ear" means upon the left ear.
Because it is treated like a tree in the treatise;
[it is] above the left ear and above the right ear,
since the left was mentioned first.
The two treasures (nidhi), whose nature is described in the *Śrīpaṭala*, together with their powers,
are located in the regions between the ears and the cheeks— that is, on the right and left sides.
"Root" refers to the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
The word "face" (*vadana*) indicates the chin, which is a part of it.
"These" refers to [the deities] beginning with Brahmā and ending with Mūla.
This alone is the traditional reading.
Some read "one should place this upon the body.
According to that view, one should place this Bhuvaneśī in nine locations beginning with the throat: on the pair of breasts, right and left; and so forth.
"On the left shoulder and on the right shoulder.
Although the lexicon states, "In the body, *vāma* should be the left," nevertheless, in this context, by the word *savya*, the right alone is intended.
Because "vāma" was previously stated separately [from "savya"].

Thus, there is usage in many places in the Śaiva Āgamas such as: "One should perform the placement (vinyaset) on the right and left. Furthermore, another lexicon states: "Savya refers to the right and the left."
"On the pair of sides" means on the right and left.
By the word "deśika," the state of possessing seeds (sabījatva) is indicated.
"Bhālāṃsa" refers to the locations for the placement of the Mātṛkā letters.
The left shoulder and side;
the right side and shoulder;
and the other [part], the hump.
Although the term *apara-gala* refers to the hump (*kakud*), its usage here is like that of *Bhīma* for *Bhīmasena*.
As the Teachers have stated:
"In the forehead, shoulders, flanks, and belly; and in the flanks, shoulders, *apara-gala*, and heart, [the measurements are] in successive order."
The eight Mothers, beginning with Brahmāṇī, should be installed according to the rules by those proficient in mantra.
"According to the rule" means beginning with one's own seed-syllable (*bīja*). "Possessing the stated characteristics" means having the meditations described in the *Mātṛkāpaṭala*.
"Pervasive" means [the placement] from the head down to the big toes of the feet by means of both hands. (8–13)

One should worship Bhuvaneśī, who possesses the splendor of the rising sun, who wears the moon as a crown, whose breasts are full, who is endowed with three eyes, whose face is smiling, and whose hands hold the gestures of granting boons, the goad, the noose, and the protection. 14.
He speaks of the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) with the words "rising," etc.
*Inaḥ* means the sun.
There is also the phrase "seated upon a red lotus."

Those who know the tradition state that the weapon is in the lower left hand, the boon-granting gesture (*vara*) in the upper right, the goad (*aṅkuśa*) in the upper left, and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) in the lower right. This is stated in the *Mahāsammohana*:
"One should place a goad in the right [hand] and cause a noose to be given in the left;
one should place the boon-granting gesture on the left and the gesture of fearlessness in the right hand. Thus [it is said]. (14)
The knower of mantras should recite the mantra thirty-two hundred thousand times according to the prescribed measure;
he should perform oblations with the eight substances mixed with the three sweets, numbering one-tenth of that amount. || 15 ||

"One should recite" means that this mantra, preceded by an investigation into the meaning of the mantra, is the expounder of the Primordial Śakti who exists in the form of both Nature (prakṛti) and Spirit (puruṣa), whose essence is Hari and Hara;
for this very reason, her name is Bhuvaneśī.

As it has been said: "Because of the qualities of greenness (*haritva*) and because of the act of seizing (*haratva*), this word, which is uttered as a *śleṣa* (double entendre) regarding the two—masculinity and primordial nature (*puṃprakṛti*)—is declared to be of that very form.
Furthermore, in the *Saṃhitā*: "O Maheśānī, within the seed-syllable of space (*vyomabīja*), Kailāsa and other [mountains] are established."
O Dear One, gold and other such substances are produced in many ways from the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ).
Therefore, he exists in this world, established upon the circle of the earth;
by means of the fourth vowel, he is sustained in the netherworld (pātāla) in the form of Śeṣa.
Therefore, she is the mistress even of Pātāla, the great circle of the earth;
for this reason, O Dear One, she is Maheśānī, the sovereign of the world.
In the syllable *ha*, there is space (*vyoma*) through the fourth vowel;
when the modification occurs with the letter *ra*, she is manifestly of the nature of fire.
The potency of fire is to be known as wealth; therefore, the letter *ra* is the earth.
For this very reason, O Maheśānī, it is considered identical with *la*.
From the nectar of the bindu-cakra, the Goddess, flooding the three worlds, becomes liquid;
therefore, she flows as a half-mora.
Therefore, she is called Maheśānī and Bhuvaneśī.
By the phrase "knower of mantras," the union with the *hasakalā* is indicated.
The yoga of the *praṇava* for the sake of liberation has also been indicated;
or else, there is the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) as described in other tantras,
as follows:
Resorting to the southern image in a temple of Śiva at Ekaliṅga,
he sat in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), smeared with ashes, and seated upon a mat of kuśa grass.
Beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until its fourteenth day,
one should daily worship Śiva and Śakti and recite the mantra one thousand times.
"One should offer oblations of *vyāghāta* fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
thereafter, one should meditate upon Umā, the Sovereign of All, for more than a thousand times.
[This is done] with [offerings] joined by the three sweets (*tri-svādu*) and endowed with the three honeys (*trimadhura*).
Thus it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Milk, honey, and ghee— these three in equal measure are known as the 'three sweets' (*trimadhura*)."
Others say that sugar should be used in place of milk:
"One should then perform oblations amounting to one-tenth of the recitation with eight substances sprinkled with jaggery, honey, and ghee.
Thus it is said.
The commentators have explained that "guḍa" means sugar;
"by eight substances" refers to those mentioned in the Mātṛkāpaṭala. || 15 ||
Having meditated there upon Pārvatī, one should offer the *arghya* to the Lord of Day;
[the mandala] has an eight-petaled lotus on the outside and a circle with sixteen petals. || 16 ||
One should draw a most beautiful hexagon in the center of the pericarp;
then, one should worship the pedestal endowed with the nine powers.
Jayā, Vijayā, then Ajitā and Aparājitā;
Nityā, Vilāsinī, Dogdhrī, Aghorā, and Maṅgalā—these are the nine. || 18 ||
"One should give" refers to [the offering] with the root mantra.
"Therein" means in the solar mandala.
Considering this to be the solar power (*saurī śakti*), it is mentioned here because the primary focus is the offering of the *arghya*.
However, it should be understood that among all mantras, one must visualize the respective deity of each mantra within the solar disc and offer the *arghya* to the Sun within that solar disc;
this was stated by me on the occasion of explaining the *sandhyā* rites.
In this context, immediately after meditation, one should display the weapons, the book, the knowledge-source (jñānayoni), and the seed-syllable mudrās. As it has been said:
"Having thus meditated upon the supreme Śakti, one should correctly display the mudrās."
"The noose, the goad, the gestures of fearlessness and granting of boons, the book, and the source of knowledge.
Regarding that, the definition of the noose-mudrā (*pāśamudrā*) is as follows: [it is formed] by the index finger of the left fist [grasping] the index finger of the right fist.
"Having joined the tips of the two thumbs, one should place them upon the tips of the two index fingers;
this is proclaimed by the wise as the *pāśa* (noose) mudrā.
Thus [it is said]. The characteristics of the remaining mudrās have been described by me previously.
The seed-syllable mudrā (bījamudrā) is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru.
Here, this mantra for sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) during one's own ritual worship (pūjāsādhana) should be known:
Oṃ, Vāgbhava, Māyā, Śrībīja, and Paramāmṛta.
Having addressed the Blessed One in form, [she said: "O dweller in the lunar disc!"
Filling the two [vessels] with the nectar of the moon is also called "the substance.
This pair is the purifier; thereafter follows the venerable *māyā*, *vāk*, and *dviṭha*.
"Having sprinkled oneself and the ritual implements with that nectar," it is said.
He describes the worship diagram as "the lotus."
"Six-cornered" means that two triangles, one above and one below, are mutually intersecting.
By the phrase "extremely beautiful," it is stated that it should be constructed in such a way that it becomes symmetrical.
Regarding that, the method for achieving the symmetry of the triangles and so forth is now described:
"Having abandoned the long [line] with its eastern qualities in the form of a circle, two others are placed transversely on the two sides;
likewise, there are six spokes from another side, and thus there are twelve spokes even in the northern direction.
Having drawn a straight line toward the east and taking its center as a reference, one should draw a circle of the desired size and divide that eastern line into four parts.
Having set aside one-fourth from one end, one should drop a single horizontal thread;
by applying two threads on the sides, a triangle is formed.
When this is likewise done from the other side as well, a hexagon is produced.
Thus, by drawing [lines] from north to south, the meaning is that there are twelve lines.
The measure for the circle has been stated by the Teachers: "The practitioner should draw a circle with a measurement of six finger-breadths."
One should cause it to proceed outside that with a space of six finger-breadths.
One should draw a circle of that same size, and further, a third one outside of it;
then, in the center of the middle circle, one should inscribe the *hṛllekhā* seed-syllable.
The second [circle] is joined to the first; it is a slightly conjoined hexagon, folded into a mandala of fire that does not touch the central circle.
"One should draw [the diagram] ending with Indra, Agni, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Īśa,
and Antaka. Here, it should be understood that even the two upper circles are intended solely for the purpose of making the hexagon symmetrical.
Above this, it should be known as a square,
because it is so stated in the context of the yantra for the worship of the mantra of the final Śakti;
it is also described as having four doors.

Because that [practice] is common [to all], it is not mentioned here. "Then" (tataḥ) means immediately after the constant recitation (nityajapa), since that has been performed following the internal sacrifice (antaryāga). ||16-18||
Having offered the seat beginning with the seed-syllable (bīja), one should fashion the form by means of that very [syllable];
therein, having invoked the Goddess along with her attendants (āvaraṇas), one should worship her. || 19 ||
In the center, the east, the south, the north, and the west, one should worship Hṛllekhā and the others in due order; they possess a radiance equal to the five elements. || 20 ||

Holding a boon-granting gesture, a noose, a goad, and the gesture of fearlessness, and adorned with immeasurable ornaments, one should worship the deities of the limbs in the previously mentioned locations. || 21 ||
He extracts the *pīṭha-mantra* as "beginning with the seed-syllable" (*bījādya*).
The application therein is as follows:
having uttered the root seed-syllable, [one says] "Obeisance to the lotus-throne of all powers" (*sarvaśaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ*).
As it has been said:

"Having uttered the word *sarvaśakti*, followed by *kamalāsana* in the dative case (*ṅe-anta*), one should worship the seat with the word *namaḥ*; O Śivā, [one should likewise worship] each respective seed-syllable (*bīja*) and so forth."
It should be understood that this seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra) is common to all the mantras of the Sovereigns of the Worlds (bhuvaneśīs).
Her lotus is to be meditated upon as red.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
Having placed a red lotus upon a jeweled lion-throne,
one should invoke the Goddess there with the heart-mantra.
Thus it is said.
"By that very [means]" means that these, starting from the center, are to be worshipped in due order; this is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*).
He states the meaning of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) with the words "in front," and so forth.
"Hṛllekhā and the others" refers to them as they have been installed. The visualization of their weapons is like that of the Goddess.
[This applies] to those previously mentioned, namely Āgneyī and the others, as stated in the fourth chapter.
It should be understood that those [deities] beginning with Āgneya are situated within the pericarp (*kaṇīkā*).
As for the statement by the author of the text that "the limbs (*aṅga*) are on the filaments (*kesara*)," this is a restatement of what was stated generally;
the intention is that elsewhere it has been said, "the limbs are on the filaments."
But here, one worships in the pericarp alone;
thereafter, Hṛllekhā and the others, as well as the limbs (aṅgas), are to be worshipped as before.
Thus it is said.

Some, however, say that the worship of the limbs (aṅgapūjana) occurs in both places—that is, at both locations for the sixfold ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa). But that contradicts the *Prapañcasāra* and other such works. (19–21)
In the six corners, the practitioner of mantra should worship the deities of the couples;
first, in the northeast corner [he should worship] her who holds a shining staff, a water-pot, a rosary, and displays the gesture of fearlessness.
The practitioner of mantras should worship Gāyatrī and likewise Brahmā;
in the southwest corner [he should worship her] bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
One should worship Sāvitrī, dressed in yellow garments, and likewise Viṣṇu;
in the north-western corner [one should worship her] holding an axe, a rosary, and displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons. || 24 ||
One should worship Sarasvatī in this manner and Rudra with such characteristics;
one should worship a jewel-pitcher and a jeweled casket in the southeast corner. || 25 ||
[One should meditate on] the pot-bellied Lord of Wealth (Dhananāyaka), who holds a yellow [garment] with both hands;
[the practitioner] embraces him with the right hand, while the left hand holds a lotus [toward] her. || 26 ||
One should worship Mahālakṣmī, mounted upon the shoulder of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera);
and in the western quarter, Madana, bearing arrows, a noose, a goad, and a bow. || 27 ||
One should worship her who is adorned with jewel ornaments, holding a garment dyed with saffron; embracing her husband with her right hand and holding a blue lotus with her left. || 28 ||
One should properly worship Rati, who sits upon the lap of her lover, with one's hand;
and in the northeast, one should duly worship Vighnarāja together with his beloved. || 29 ||
Holding a goad and a noose, with fingers touching the exquisite limbs of his beloved, enriched by a skull-cup filled with honey, the King of Obstacles is clothed only in the directions. || 30 ||
In Puṣkara, [he saw him] holding a shimmering cup from which jewels were dripping; she possessed a form like vermilion and was intoxicated with unrestrained passion. || 31 ||
With her other hand holding a red lotus that touched her banner, she embraced her beloved; she was ruddy, radiant, naked, and full of splendor. || 32 ||
Now, regarding the method of worship:

having first described the worship in the corners of the upward-pointing triangle, proceeding clockwise from the west to the northeast, he describes the worship in the corners of the downward-pointing triangle, proceeding clockwise, with the words "in the six corners."
Hence the expression "ataeva" (for this very reason).
Regarding the visualization of the weapons: in the first [form], they begin from the upper left, and in the other, they begin from the upper right;
in the Gāyatrī form, they are on the upper right and left hands in the first case, and on the lower right and left hands in the other.
In the case of Sāvitrī, [the worship extends] from the upper left to the lower left;
in the case of Sarasvatī, a jewel-pot is on the left and another on the right;
in the case of Dhananāyaka, [it extends] from the lower right to the lower left.
In the case of Madana, there are the goad and the noose in the upper left and right hands;
"touching the lower body of his beloved" refers to the lower left hand;
and "honey," etc., refers to the lower right hand in the case of Vighnarāja.
*Puṣkara* refers to the tip of an elephant’s trunk.
"Uddāma" and so forth describe the visualization of the *śakti*.
"Holding a red lotus" refers to [the hand] on the right.
"By the other" means by the left. || 22-32 ||
The two treasures (Nidhis) should be worshipped in the pericarp; then, the limbs (Aṅgas) on both sides of the hexagon;
these [deities] in the filaments; and afterwards, one should worship them upon the petals. || 33 ||
Anaṅgakusumā was later Anaṅgakusumāturā; Anaṅgamadanā likewise became Anaṅgamadanāturā. || 34 ||
Bhuvanapālā and Gaganavegā, followed by Śaśirekhā and Gaganarekhā—these are the eight Śaktis. || 35 ||
Holding a noose, a goad, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, they possess ruddy complexions.
Then, upon the sixteen petals are Karālī, Vikarālī, and Umā.
Sarasvatī, Śrī, Durgā, Lakṣmī, Śruti, Smṛti, Dhṛti, Śraddhā, Medhā, Mati, Kānti, and Āryā—these are the sixteen Śaktis. || 37 ||
The dark-colored Mothers, bearing swords and shields, are to be worshipped;
the attendant Śaktis are to be worshipped outside the lotus. || 38 ||
The first is Anaṅgarūpā; after that is Anaṅgamadanā;
then Madanāturā, Bhuvanavegā, and Bhuvanapālikā. || 39 ||
She may be entirely afflicted by the pangs of love in the cold season; she may possess a girdle of love, a drinking cup, a palm-leaf fan, betel, and a bright parasol. || 40 ||
Holding chowries, silken garments, and flowers with her lotus-like hands, she should worship the world-protectors, resplendent with all their ornaments, outside [the mandala]. || 41 ||
One should likewise worship the goddesses external to her, beginning with Vajrā;
she is worshipped by all the gods, so what need be said of the best of men? || 42 ||

The minister, having offered oblations with the best fuel-sticks of the Aśvattha tree mixed with the three sweets, shall quickly bring Brāhmaṇas under his control; by means of the lotus-oblation, he shall likewise subjugate kings. || 43 ||
Day after day, his wives and the minister should perform their ablutions with water over which the *palāśa* flowers and *kumuda* lilies have been consecrated twenty-five times.
He who sprinkles himself [with this water] shall possess all good fortune;
a man should drink water over which the mantra has been recited twenty-five times in the morning. || 45 ||
Having attained great wisdom, one becomes the foremost among poets;
it is like well-prepared saffron blended with camphor and agallochum. || 46 ||
Having taken [these], one should apply a forehead mark (tilaka) which is unsurpassed for subjugating kings.
Having fashioned a doll made of rice-flour and mixed with sweet substances... || 47 ||
Having recited [the mantra] and established the vital breath (prāṇa) within it, one should consume it on a Sunday;
this brings under one's control a king, a woman, or even a man. || 48 ||
Standing in water reaching up to the neck and gazing at the sun reflected in the water, a person should recite the mantra three thousand times; he shall obtain his desired maiden.
The practitioner of the mantra should eat food consecrated with that same mantra for the attainment of prosperity. || 49 ||

Having written the *māyā* mantra together with the name of the person to be influenced (*sādhya*) upon a wooden board or similar surface using ashes, one should display that yantra at that time; thus, a pregnant woman will give birth easily.
"In the pericarp" means in the pericarp of the lotus.
"The two treasures" refers to those deposited as previously described.
"These" refers to Anaṅgakusumā and the others who will be mentioned immediately hereafter.
The meditation on these [deities] is to be understood as being like that of the Goddess.
"Kheṭaka" means "pharī" in the Kānyakubja dialect.
Up to the word "śyāmā," this is the meditation on the previous Śakti.
The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and [they] are to be worshipped" (*pūjyāś-ca*) is displaced;
it should be understood as following the word "mothers" (*mātaraḥ*). By virtue of this "and," the powers (*śaktayaḥ*) to be described hereafter are also included along with the mothers.
Therefore, the Mothers should be worshipped as they were assigned, outside the lotus;
likewise, the attendants are also [to be placed] outside the lotus in the eight directions.
These [deities] have two arms: in the left hand a red utpala lotus, and in the other hand a cup (caṣaka) and so forth.

As it is said in the *Prayogasāra*: "The beautiful attendants are to be meditated upon as red, adorned with garments blazing with red, possessing large eyes with reddish corners, and holding red lotuses in their hands."

Since all these auxiliary elements, such as libations (*tarpaṇa*) and others, are present here throughout, the fact that he mentions only meditation (*dhyāna*), worship (*pūjā*), recitation (*japa*), and fire-oblation (*homa*) indicates that these are to be performed regularly (*nitya*).
As it is said in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
A mantra, even if well-perfected, does not become gracious if it is neither meditated upon nor recited;
it has no desire to grant success if it is not recited, and it will yield no fruit if it is not offered in oblation.
Therefore, if the practitioner desires success for himself, he should perform daily these four rites: worship, meditation, recitation, and fire-offering.
"One weary from recitation should meditate on Śiva; weary from meditation, one should recite again.
Endowed with both recitation and meditation, the knower of mantras attains success quickly.
Thus, from "the practitioner of mantra should worship in the six angles" up to this point, the agentive term "the practitioner of mantra" (mantrī) is understood to carry over.
And by this, it is indicated precisely through the knowledge of the conduct of the samaya:
as they say—
"The Lord of Yoga, seeking accomplishment, should observe the excellent vows."
One should not eat without honoring the Goddess, nor should one remain with a soiled appearance.
One should never speak anything untrue, nor should one ever approach a widow;
one should daily wear beautiful red ornaments on all parts of the body.
On the day of the *rakta* [tithi], one should worship the maiden who is red in color, while recollecting the Goddess;
being impure, one should not wander about, but should sleep on a secluded bed.
"One should never revile a woman, especially a maiden.
By the statement "one should worship the Goddess in this manner," the following is intended:
among the enclosures (*āvaraṇas*), after the sixteen powers (*śaktis*), thirty-two powers, and subsequently sixty-four powers are to be worshipped.
And these [syllables] are to be understood as they have been stated in the *bhūtalipi* mantra.
He states the very fruit of that [practice]: "He is worshipped by all the gods.
By the phrase "how much more so by the best of men," this is what is intended: [that he is worshipped by them even more].
That which was stated by him in the middle—the enclosure of the eight Śaktis beginning with Anaṅgakusumā—is the fruit of that [lower stage].
Regarding the word "manuja" (human):
thereafter, that which is the enclosure of the sixteen Śaktis is the fruit of this [higher stage], indicated by the words "by the best ones."
As it is said in the Mahāsamohana:
"Whether by four, or by three, or again by two,
or even by one— by all these obscurations in this manner, one who desires enjoyments should perform extensive sacrifice."
Likewise, the womb-enclosure (*garbhāvaraṇa*) is for those who are external, and their worship is performed in the center; this is stated in that very [text].
By this, it is indicated that her worship begins with seven enclosures and ends with eleven enclosures.
Thus, by the phrase "the practitioner (*mantrī*) [should perform] the five-enclosure [or] even the six-enclosure [rite]," this is what is meant:
He is accomplished, renowned, majestic, renunciant, a yogi, and one who has conquered his senses;
he is omniscient, fortunate, illustrious, free from anxiety, and pleasing to behold.
No fear arises for that embodied being who has mastered the mantra from thieves, wild beasts, vetālas, guhyakas, asuras, or dānavas.
"In a village or even in a city, in an assembly or in the presence of a king,
one who is well-known is honored by the virtuous and obtains his desired welfare.
By the phrase "the minister quickly," it is stated that there is a *ayuta-homa* (ten-thousand-fold oblation).
As stated in the *Prayogasāra*:

"For the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), one should offer oblations of *aśvattha*, *rājīva*, sesame, and milk, respectively, for the [castes] beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, in the same manner, ten thousand times (*ayuta*) each."
"Excellent, well-prepared"—thus it was recited one thousand and eight times.
"The effigy" refers to one twelve finger-breadths in length.
"One should devour" means from the big toe of the right foot up to the big toe of the left foot.
In the case of a woman, however, it is the reverse.
"With ashes" means with cow-dung ashes.
It should be understood as being square.
Regarding the production of a son, *palāśabhasma* (ash of the *palāśa* tree) is mentioned in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"The *hṛllekhā* [mantra] written with ash, directed toward the goal, in the abode of Indra..."
Thus [ends the section] from verse 33 to 50.

The ritual act to be accomplished is situated within the *śakti*; it is surrounded by *śaktis* outside in the corners, joined with the syllables of Hari and Hara that are yellowish-white on their cheeks;
thereafter, it is further encircled by those same syllables joined with *ī* and *lī*. This bestows the desired object.
The yantra situated within a square enclosure (bhūpura) and tripled in its lines bestows good fortune and prosperity.
Regarding the statement "within the Śakti," he describes the triple-layered yantra:
the syntactical connection is that such a triple-layered yantra bestows the wealth of good fortune. What is it like?
In the upward-pointing triangle within the abode of the peacock (varhiṇa),
situated in the midst of the seed-syllable of Śakti at the end of Śakti;
"sādhya" here is an indicator for the practitioner (sādhaka).
In a rite where there is an object to be accomplished and a means of accomplishment, the application is as follows:
"Subjugate Yajñadatta for Devadatta; do, do!"
As it is stated in the *Rāmapūrvatāpanīya*:
"One should write the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) ending in the accusative case, and likewise the practitioner (*sādhaka*) ending in the genitive case;
and one should place two 'kuru' [mantras] at its sides."
Thus it is said.
Therein, the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) is in the portion of the *bīja* and the letter *ra*;
the name of the practitioner (sādhaka) is in the portion of the fourth vowel.
Between those two, one should write the ritual action within the portion belonging to the practitioner.
As it is stated in the Saṃhitā:
"In the portion of the letter *repha* (r) of that [mantra] which belongs to its power (*śakti*), one should write the syllables of the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*)."
"Bring the practitioner under control within the portion of the fourth vowel;
for the sake of all success, one should write it touching the top of the target.
And the Teachers say: "On both sides of the *hṛllekhā* situated within the central circle..."
One should write the letter of the name of the person to be accomplished below, and that of the practitioner above.
"One should draw the ritual action between the fire and the glory within the portion of the practitioner.
By this, it is also stated that one must necessarily draw the narrative and the power (*śakti*).
Elsewhere also it is said: "having encircled it with the letter *ṭha*.
This refers to the outer parts at the tips of the triangles.
Regarding the plural form "by the powers" (*śaktibhiḥ*), by the principle of the *kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa*, it results in the number three.
It is surrounded by those three seed-syllables of power (*śakti-bīja*).
Furthermore, the enclosure is on the outer side of the syllables of Hari and Hara written on the two lobes.
As it has been said: "One should write *Parā* at the tips of the corners."
Thus [it is said].
And the Teachers [state]: "The syllable *viḥ*, which is to be accomplished by means of *śakti*, is pierced by the seed-syllables of Indra, Anila, Nirṛti, and Agni within the city of Fire."
The enclosure here is as follows:
having caused each seed-syllable to be circumambulated clockwise by the tip of a *repha*, one should lead it beneath the next [syllable] and bind the tip of its *īkāra* [to the following].
This is stated in the *Saṃhitā*:
Bondage at the three locations is said to bestow accomplishment;
one should encircle the tip of the *repha* of those three seed-syllables in a clockwise direction.
"One should surround its lower triad with the tip of Māyā;
this bond of power (*śaktibandha*), delightful through its mutual interconnection, has been described.
Thus, one should write *īṃ* within the corners situated at the corners of that triangle.
As it has been said: "In the intervals of the triangle, the left eye with the bindu.
It is characterized by the yellow letters *ha*, *ri*, *ha*, and *ra* on the cheeks.
On the two triangular corners of the cheeks, one says "hari" on one side and "hara" on the other;
some say "hri" and "hra," but that is not correct.
Because there is no authoritative evidence [to the contrary].
And so it is stated in the *Saṃhitā*: "On each side of the corners, the syllables 'ha' and 'rya', as well as the syllables 'ha' and 'ra'."

Afterwards, immediately following that, by those [syllables] Hari and Hara joined with *īṃ*—that is, by the syllables *ha-ri-īṃ* and *ha-ra-īṃ*—it is surrounded. As it is stated in the Saṃhitā: "Furthermore, between these two, the fourth [vowel] itself, along with the bindu."
"One should encircle it with the vowels; then one should draw a circle on the outside.
Also, in the Gaurītantra: "The seed-syllable of Hari (the letter *ha*), the letters from *ha* to *na*, and the letters from *kṣa* to *a* [should be placed] on the outside."
And the Ācāryas [state]: "They should be joined together in the middle.
However, Padmapādācārya maintains that each one of these is a separate yoga.
"Hari īṃ, Hara īṃ.
By means of the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa';
the word "api" (also) serves to include the preceding [elements].
*Āvītam* means "encircled.
The meaning is that one should draw a *bhūpura* (circumscribed square) outside of that [central figure].
This very same [diagram], provided with eight petals, has been described by the teachers as the *pūjāyantra*. || 51 ||
The name of the practitioner to be accomplished is situated within the seed-syllable, encircled by the syllables of Māyā (Hrīṃ), Ramā (Śrīṃ), and Manmatha (Klīṃ) shot five times;
it is enclosed within two fire-purifiers (the letter Ra), and within the six-fold enclosure (the six vowels) are the three seed-syllables enriched with their respective names.

This is joined with the Self and the Non-Self (the letters A and Ha), topped with the letter Ī, and its sides bound by Hari and Hara (the letters La and Sa). Outside of this, [it is surrounded by the letters of the alphabet].
It is encircled by the six seed-syllables joined by ligatures, and by the two houses of the earth. || 52 ||
One should draw this divine yantra, which has sixfold corners shining with the Cintāmaṇi and Nṛsiṃha; when worn, it bestows all spiritual accomplishments. || 53 ||
Regarding the statement "within the seed-syllables" (*bījāntaḥ*) concerning the sixfold yantra:
the connection is that one should draw this sixfold yantra.
Of what kind is the yantra?
In the two fire-purī-s (triangles), which are mutually interpenetrating, there are two triangles.

This is done as follows: having drawn a circle of the aforementioned dimensions and stretched a thread from east to west, one should fix a thread at its two ends and, using a thread measuring half the diameter of the circle, form two fish-marks (matsyas).
When this is done, a set of four fish-marks (matsya) is produced.

Having struck two threads running north-south through the first pair of fish-marks and the second pair of fish-marks, one should place the beginning of a thread at the eastern tip of the eastern thread and strike two transverse threads across the bellies of the two western fish-marks.

Again, having placed the beginning of the thread at the western tip of the previous thread, one should strike two horizontal threads across the bellies of the two fish located in the eastern direction.
One should then erase the eastern thread and the circle.
When this is done, two joined fire-walls (vahnipura) are produced.
In that regard, "seed" refers to the seed-syllable of power (*śaktibīja*); "wherein the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is situated within it" means [the mantra] is thus.
The writing of the names of the object to be accomplished, the practitioner, and the ritual action is exactly as before. "By fives" means fivefold, like arrows.
There, within the hexagon itself, there is one enclosure with five *māyā* seeds;
in the space between those, there is a second enclosure with five *śrī* seeds;
and in the space between those, there is a third enclosure with five *kāma* seeds.
Thus, one enclosure is completed with fifteen seed-syllables.
This has been stated by the teacher Padmapāda: "In that regard, one enclosure is formed by the *māyā*-seed-syllable (*hrīṃ*) repeated five times;
again, within that very space, [another is formed] by the *śrī*-seed-syllable (*śrīṃ*)."
In the same way, in that interval, [it is filled] with the seed-syllable of Māra.
Thus it has been said:
Having drawn the fire-diagram (vahni) in its folded form, one should place the Śakti in the center;
having surrounded it with the letter *ṭha*, one should then place the Śakti five times on the outside.
"Having written that [diagram] outside in the same manner, one should write the Śrī-bīja and the Kāmarāja-bīja.
Thus it is said.
The Teachers also state: "The five syllables *Ha-ra-mā-yā* should be placed five times around the outer circle of the womb."

"Outside of that are the *śara-māyās* and outside of those the *kala-māyās*. Therefore, in this case, having written the *śakti-bīja* and the *māyā-bīja* within the inner circle, one subsequently surrounds them with the three *bījas* in the six corners of the hexagonal enclosure (*rasapuṭa*).
The three seed-syllables enriched with names.
Here, by the word "name" (ākhyā), the names of the object to be accomplished (sādhya), the practitioner (sādhaka), and the ritual action (karman) are denoted.
The three seed-syllables are those previously mentioned: Śakti, Śrī, and Mānmatha.
As it has been said:
"In the three corners of the fire [triangle], one should write the triad of the Śrīmat-pakṣīya [mantras]—
the seed-syllables of Śakti, Śrī, and Kāma— along with their stems (daṇḍas), together with the syllable of the practitioner."

The word "likhet" (he should write) occurs twice. And that [twofold nature] is obtained from the very words "sātmaka" (with soul) and "anātmaka" (without soul). In this context, "sātmaka" means with the *bindu* (anusvāra), while "anātmaka"—by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—means with the *visarga*.
In that regard, the sequence of writing is as follows:

within the three upper corner-segments situated upon the vowel *ī*, one should write the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) accompanied by the *bindu* (anusvāra) and containing the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*).

Then, proceeding clockwise within the three lower corner-segments situated upon the letter *ra*, one should write [the three seed-syllables] accompanied by the *visarga* and containing the name and the ritual action (*karman*) of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*).
As it has been said: "One should inscribe three seed-syllables accompanied by the bindu in the six corners of the two fires and in the upper portion."

"In the same way, one should write those [syllables] in the lower sections joined with the name of the practitioner (sādhaka), accompanied by the visarga, and joined with the name of the target (sādhya) and the ritual action. Thus,
one should write "ĪM" at the tip of the interior corner of the eastern direction.
"Having Hari and Hara bound to the *gaṇḍas*.
By the word *gaṇḍa*, the two sides of each corner of the hexagon are meant.
Therefore, as before, one should write the syllables of Hari and Hara there.

Outside, at the tips of the six corners, the joints are connected by six *māyā* seeds (*hrīṃ*). Although the meaning is already established by the phrase "joints are bound" (*baddhasandhi*), the author uses the expression "joints are interconnected" (*anubaddhasandhi*); by this, the author intends to convey that the binding of the joints occurs at intervals of one [corner].
Regarding this, the Teachers say: "Those [lines], separated by single intervals, should be connected with one another;
the outer [lines] with the inner [lines] by means of their inner 'crests' (śikhā), and the inner [lines] with the outer [lines].
Also in the *Saṃhitā*: "The binding of the powers (śakti-bandha) is as before, but here it is performed due to the state of being separated by a single interval."
Thus it is said.
In other works as well, such as the *Mantramuktāvalī*, it is stated that the joints are bound by skipping one [syllable] at a time.
The reasoning here is that in the case of binding with an interval of one, there occurs a binding of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) situated within their respective triangles.

In this regard, the method is as follows: having circumambulated each respective seed-syllable with its own *svara* and *repha*, one should lead it beneath the next and bind it at the tip of the vowel *ī* of the seed-syllable separated by one interval.
Those who know the tradition maintain this very view.
Others, however, state that the seed-syllables should be written at the junctions;
as it has been said: "One should write the six *hṛllekhā* syllables within the six intermediate spaces of the corners."
This also applies to the Uttara-yantra,
because of the general statement "with syllables" (lipibhiḥ).
The encircling is performed both in regular order and in reverse order.
As the teachers have said: "The letters in their forward order are auspicious, as are those in reverse order outside of that.
And in the *Saṃhitā* as well: "In the middle of that meter, there are fifty syllables in forward order."

"Likewise, the Mātṛkā [should be placed] outside that square in reverse order. One should enclose it with two squares of the earth, intersecting each other at the cardinal and intermediate directions. As the Teachers have said: "Then one should draw two circles of the earth, intersecting one another."
From here, the sequence of writing begins with Cintāmaṇi and Nṛsiṃha starting from the northeast (Īśāna).

Therefore, the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha is in the cardinal directions, while the Śaiva seed-syllable of Cintāmaṇi is in the intermediate corners. As it has been said: "The syllable of Nṛsiṃha situated in the major directions, having its essence resting upon the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāratna)."
Thus it is said.
And this specific detail is stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*:
"Then, having drawn tridents in the corners and at the junctions..."
Thus [it is said].
And the Teachers state: "Externally, it is marked with sixteen spikes. (52-53)

One should write the seed-syllable of Durgā, surrounded by the *vyāhṛtis*, situated in the corner of the "dwelling" (the square) between two pairs of syllables; immediately following that, one should write the seed-syllable bound by pairs of letters forming its cheeks. Then, one should write the *Gāyatrī* with its gaps filled by the solar powers (*sūrya-śakti*), and surround that with the *Triṣṭubh*.
In the pair of cities on earth, [this work] is accompanied by the Mātṛkā and contains the true Cintāmaṇi of the lion. || 54 ||
The Yantra, multiplied by twelve (the number of the Sun), is said to bestow protection and success;
it generates all forms of good fortune and wards off all enemies. || 55 ||

Now he describes the twelvefold yantra—beginning with the word "seed" (bīja). The "pair of houses of Vasu and Agni" refers to a hexagon; when those two are joined, it becomes a twelve-cornered figure.
In some places, the reading is *guhamukhadvandva*. In that context, *guha* is Skanda; his faces are six, and their pair (*dvandva*) refers to the twelve-angled figure.

Therein, having constructed a hexagon according to the previously mentioned method, one should strike a line from south to north across the two fish (*matsya*) produced there, [extending] to their two tips.
Taking hold of the [central] thread, one should form four fish-marks using a thread equal in length to half the circumference of the circle.

Therein, having stretched two threads running east-west through the pair of eastern fish-marks and the pair of northern fish-marks, one should place the beginning of a thread at the tip of the eastern-northern thread and stretch two transverse threads across the bellies of the two northern fish-marks.

Again, having placed the beginning of the thread at the second end of the north-south thread (dakṣottarasūtra), one should strike two horizontal threads across the bellies of the two right-side fish-marks.
One should then erase the north-south thread.

Thus, when the twelve corners have been formed, one should write the seed-syllable of Śakti together with the goal, the practitioner, and the ritual action as before, and surround it with the seven vyāhṛtis in reverse order.
As it is stated in the *Saṃhitā*:
"The practitioner of mantra should wrap [it] in reverse order with the seven *vyāhṛtis*."
And the Teachers [state]: "One should cause the Śakti, who resides within, to enter by means of the *vyāhṛtis* in reverse order.
This was explained by the teacher Padmapāda as: "by means of the seven *vyāhṛtis*."
Regarding "koṇagam":
having written the seed-syllable of Durgā, *duḥ*, in the twelve corners, one should write *īṃ* in the interior portion at the tip of each corner.
As it is stated in the Saṃhitā: "In the twelve-spoked [wheel], one should place the *duḥ*-natured syllable with the bindu and the fourth vowel (*ī*) as well."
Thus it has been said by the Teachers: "In the corner is the seed-syllable of the *duṃ*."
Likewise: "Then one should write the Māyā-bīja, ending with *ra* (the sun) and *va* (the corner), provided with a *bindu*.
And in the Nārāyaṇīya: "The mountain (*adri*) is its seed-syllable, possessing Śiva and Śakti."
Thus,
the seer and other details have been stated in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*:
Kāśyapa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chanda*), and Durgā is the deity (*devatā*).

One should meditate upon her as being dark-green like *dūrvā* grass, with three eyes, seated upon an eight-petaled lotus, and holding— in order from the lower right— a trident, an arrow, a sword, a discus, a conch, a shield, a bow, and a skull-cup.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
The oblation with sesame seeds should be one-tenth of the number of recitations (*japa*).
Worship and other rites are to be understood as being like those for Vanadurgā.

For the well-known *gāyatrī*, the syllables are bound in pairs by means of pairs of letters; each [pair] is placed in reverse order on the sides of the corners of the *gaṇḍa* (the central square) of each syllable of the *gāyatrī*.
The meaning is that one should write each pair twice.
By the separate mention of *ṇiya*, there are twenty-four syllables;
this is according to the *Piṅgala-sūtra*: "and so forth, as in the *Puraṇa*."
As it is stated in the *Saṃhitā*: "One should write the syllables of the *gāyatrī* in reverse order, two by two.
And the Teachers also say: "One should write the *gāyatrī* in reverse order upon the cheek of the Fire."
Thus [it is said]. He will describe the *gāyatrī* in the twenty-second [chapter].
It is "one whose openings are bound" by the twelve seed-syllables of the powers (*śakti*) situated externally at the tips of the corners, along with the powers of the sun (*ravi*).
Here too, as before, the binding is performed by skipping one [vowel] at a time.
As it is said in the *Saṃhitā*: "O Dear One, one should perform the binding of the powers (*śakti*) in twelve ways as before;
each one, separated by an interval, is beautiful."
Thus [it is said]. And the Teachers [state]: "Those powers, separated by one [position] at a time, are mutually connected. Thus.

The *triṣṭubh* metre is encircled by the verse beginning with *triṣṭubhā jātavedase* in reverse order. As it has been said: "Outside that, on the sides of the corners, one should place the *āgneya* mantra in reverse order."

He will explain the *triṣṭubh* meter in the twenty-second [chapter]. It is pervaded by the *mātṛkā*, from *a* to *kṣa*, in both direct and reverse order. As it is stated in the *Saṃhitā*: "One should encircle the outside with the *mātṛkā* in both direct and reverse order."
Thus [it is said].
The Teachers also [state]: "And those who have reached the phonemes.
Thus.
As before, one should draw a pair of cities on the ground with mutual interpenetration.

With "Satsiṃhacintāmaṇi," starting from the east, the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha is placed in the cardinal directions and corners, while the Śaiva Cintāmaṇi seed-syllable is placed in the intermediate corners.
This is multiplied by the number of the sun, that is, twelvefold.
It should be understood that, compared to the previous yantra, its fruits and other benefits are twofold. || 54-55 ||
One should draw a lotus flower endowed with six petals;
having written the *māyā* (the syllable Hrīṃ) in the center and on the petals,
this diagram is surrounded by the vowels for women.
Bestowing sons, situated within an underground chamber. || 56 ||
He describes another yantra—beginning with "one should write":
it should consist of six petals made of mercury-leaf (rasapattras).
One should write the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the seven locations.
"Enveloped by vowels" means surrounded by the vowels beginning with *a* and ending with the visarga.
However, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*, a square is not mentioned here:
"In the center of a six-petaled lotus, one should draw the Goddess, and [the letters] upon the petals."
"A woman desiring a son should wear this yantra, which is surrounded by the vowels. Thus [ends verse 56].
Having inscribed the Śakti in the center of a hexagon, and having inscribed that same [Śakti] again in the corners,
[one should place it] within the womb containing the object of accomplishment (sādhya), situated in front of the city of the earth (vasudhāpura).
This yantra shall bring men under one's control. || 57 ||
He states another yantra with the words "six," etc. "Containing the object of attainment within" means [it is placed] in seven locations. || 57 ||

The practitioner of mantras should extract the mantra consisting of the three seed-syllables—Vāgbhava, Śambhuvanitā, and Ramā—which is the means for accomplishing the fruits of the three aims of life. || 58 ||
He extracts another mantra with the words "vāgbhavam" and so forth. Vāgbhava is the twelfth vowel (au) with the bindu (m).
Śambhuvanitā is the seed-syllable of Śakti (hrīṃ).

"Trivarga" is a statement regarding the application [of the mantra]; the first [syllable] is the seed (bīja) and the middle is the power (śakti). The seer (ṛṣi) and the meter (chandas) are as previously stated.
For this very reason, in the Pāśādi-mantra, the seer and the others were mentioned earlier.
This has been stated according to the sequence of withdrawal (pratyāhāra). || 58 ||

The knower of mantras should fashion the six limbs of this mantra, joined with their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*), using the middle portion beginning with the *vāgbhava* syllable, which possesses the six long vowels. Furthermore, the practitioner should perform here the nyāsas previously described in exactly the same manner. || 59 ||
"Six long [syllables]" refers to the application beginning with *eṃ hrāṃ hrat eṃ hrīṃ śiraḥ* and so forth. This is connected with the following word, "one who knows the mantra. || 59 ||
Her body is crimson with vermilion, she has three eyes, and her crest-jewel is the shimmering leader of the stars (the moon) upon her ruby crown; her face is smiling,
her breasts are full, and with her two hands she holds a goblet filled with jewels and a red lotus.
One should meditate upon the supreme Mother, who is gentle and has her right foot placed within a jeweled jar.
He describes the meditation: "Sindūra... and so forth.
*Mauli* means a crown;
*śekhara* means a head ornament.
A jar full of jewels is a "jewel-jar" (ratnaghaṭaḥ).
[The phrase] "seated upon a red lotus" (raktapadmasthām) is also [to be understood]. || 60 ||

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; the practitioner of the mantra should offer oblations with milk-rice soaked in sweet substances ten times that number, and worship on the pedestal previously described.

Having offered oblations to the Goddess with most beautiful perfumes and other substances according to the previously mentioned method, as well as with *palāśa* flowers, one shall obtain great eloquence and prosperity.
"Ravilakṣa" means twelve lakhs. "As previously stated" refers to that which was spoken by Bhuvaneśī.
"With perfumes and so forth" means with those [substances] mentioned in the fourth [chapter].
"By means of those that are exceedingly beautiful" means: by means of those [mantras] which have been separated from the deities of the protective enclosures (āvaraṇa). || 61–62 ||
One should drink consecrated *brāhmī* ghee; after one year, the power of poetic composition will arise.
By offering white mustard seeds mixed with salt into the fire, the practitioner of mantras shall bring others under his control. || 63 ||
In this matter, no deliberation need be made regarding men, women, or kings;
[one should worship] with flowers grown from four-finger-widths, sprinkled with sandalwood water. || 64 ||
Having offered [the oblation], the practitioner quickly brings even the three worlds under his control.
He should offer ten thousand red lotuses soaked in honey. (65)
One obtains the glory of sovereignty likewise with sesame seeds and rice;
furthermore, one should accomplish the previously mentioned rites by means of this mantra. || 66 ||
Regarding "Brāhmī-ghṛta":
here, one should cook ghee in four times the amount of Brāhmī juice.
And it is said: "A medicinal paste (kalka) may also serve as the fat (sneha) when a medicated oil or ghee is to be prepared with a liquid alone."
Thus [it is said].
Other matters should be understood as stated in the *Mātṛkāpaṭala*. "Siddhārtha" refers to white mustard seeds (*gaurasarṣapa*).
The *rājavṛkṣa* tree is four fingers [in height]. || 63–66 ||

This three-syllable Vidyā is considered to be Māyā encased within the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbīja). One should fashion it by enclosing the middle syllable with the long vowel and the enclosure of Speech. || 67 ||
The knower of mantras, the most excellent of men, should perform the ancillaries (aṅgas) joined with the [mantra] syllables in their proper sequence, according to the methods previously observed. 68.
He states another mantra beginning with "vāk. The seed-syllable (bīja), the power (śakti), the seer (ṛṣi), and the meter (chandas) are as before.
The phrase "in the middle" refers to the Māyā-bīja.
"With the long [vowel] and with the six long [vowels].
The ritual application (*prayoga*), however, is: *eṃ hrāṃ eṃ hṛt eṃ hrīṃ eṃ*."
"Head," and so forth.
By the term "knower of the mantra," the state of being encapsulated by speech (*vākpuṭatva*) at the beginning of the seed-syllables such as *hṛllekhā* is indicated.
"The root" refers to this mantra. (67–68)

I bow to the eternal Goddess Śyāmāṅgī, who bears the crescent moon upon her crest; she holds with her own hands the gesture of generosity, a red lotus, and a supreme jeweled chalice that wards off all fear;
she is radiant with a pearl necklace, her breasts are slightly bent, and she shines with three eyes.
I bow to the consort of Hara, worshipped by the gods, who rests upon a red lotus. || 69 ||
He speaks of the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) with the words beginning "śyāmāṅgīm" and so forth.
"Giving" (*dāna*) means a boon (*vara*). "Removing fear" (*bhayahara*) means fearlessness (*abhaya*).
And "supreme" is an epithet of the particular cup.
"Seated upon a red lotus"—the visualization of the weapon is as before. || 69 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with a tenth part of that number, using *palāśa* flowers mixed with honey or flowers from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree. || 70 ||
The "tattva-lakṣa" consists of twenty-four lakṣas;
[these are offered] with sweet words, drenched in the three sweets. || 70 ||
One should worship the Supreme Goddess on the seat established by Hṛllekhā;
the practitioner of mantra should worship Hṛllekhā and the others, as previously described, beginning from the center. || 71 ||
The practitioner of mantras should worship the couples in the six corners as before;
the worship of the limbs is performed on the filaments, and the Mothers are to be worshipped on the petals. || 72 ||
This is prescribed in the *Hṛllekhā* and proclaimed by Bhuvaneśī.
As it is stated in the *Bhuvaneśīpārijāta*:
"This seed-syllable of Māyā is proclaimed as the imperishable [syllable] of the three worlds."
"And this Hṛllekhā is the Mistress of Yoga.
Thus [it is said];
"as previously mentioned" means they are conjoined with their respective seed-syllables (bīja).
"As before" refers to the names of the deities together with their respective powers and so forth. || 71-72 ||
Mounted upon the lap of Bhairava, with smiling faces and languid with passion, they are Asitāṅgī, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and the one known as Unmatta. || 73 ||
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhārī are the eight Bhairavas at the rear;
they carry a trident, a skull-cup, a corpse, and a small drum.

The Mothers are said to begin with long vowels and are adorned with curly locks of hair; the Bhairavas are remembered as beginning with short vowels and are formidable, naked, and elephant-like. || 75 ||
The sixteen goddesses beginning with Karālī, previously mentioned, are to be worshipped upon the sixteen petals;
outside of those are Anaṅgarūpā and the others, and further outside are the world-protectors (lokeśas) along with their weapons.
In this way, one should propitiate the Goddess by the very path prescribed in the scriptures;
thus, one brings kings under control as well as women languid with passion. || 77 ||
By offering clarified butter with the *manu*, one obtains the desired wealth;
by offering fragrant flowers, one attains the desired prosperity. || 78 ||
One should eat food every day that has been consecrated with this mantra;
one will certainly become free from disease and attain a long life. || 79 ||
A specific visualization has been described by the passage beginning with "Bhairavāṅga" and so forth;
other details should be understood as stated in the *Mātṛkāpaṭala*.
A *kṣudradundubhi* is a small hand-drum (*ḍamaru*).
The meditation on the weapons of Bhairava begins from the upper right and extends down to the lower right.

The eight long vowels beginning with *ā* are the eight Mothers (*mātṛ*) corresponding to those [weapons] in sequence. Other matters, such as the earth element (*kṣamā*) and so forth, should be understood as previously stated.
The same applies here to the rule "evam hrasvādyāḥ" (and so on, starting with the short vowels).
Here, the technical designation of "short" (*hrasva*) refers to *a*, *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, *ḷ*, *e*, *o*, and *aṃ*. However, in actual usage:
Aṃ, obeisance to Brāhmī, who resides on the lap of Asitāṅga-Bhairava, and Āṃ Kṣāṃ, and so forth. (73–79)

The three-syllabled mantra beginning with *pāśa* consists of Ananta joined with the Bindu (*An*), Māyā (*Hrīṃ*), Brahmā (*Om*), Agni (*Ra*), and Tāra (*Oṃ*). It bestows the fruit of bringing all under one's control.
The Seer and other [limbs] have been stated previously; the ritual of the limbs is considered to be performed with the seed-syllable. || 80 ||
He states another mantra: "Ananta. Ananta is the letter Ā; joined with the bindu, it becomes ĀṂ.
Brahmā is the letter *ka*;
Agni is the letter *ra*;
Tāra is the Praṇava.
Joined with those two, it is *kroṃ*. The name of the first seed-syllable is "noose" (*pāśa*), and that of the last is "hook" (*aṅkuśa*).
As the teachers have said:
"The sages have declared that *pratiṣṭhā* near the *bindu* is the seed-syllable of the fetter (*pāśabīja*).
The goad (*aṅkuśa*) consists of one's own earth (*nijabhū*), fire (*dahana*), the nourisher (*āpyāyin*), and a fragment of the moon (*niśaśadharakhaṇḍa*)."
Therefore, the three-syllable mantra begins with *pāśa* (the noose) and so forth. "Of all" (*sarvavaśya*) is the statement of its application (*viniyoga*).
The seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the power (*śakti*) are as before.
"By the seed-syllable" means by the seed-syllable of Māyā (*hrīṃ*).
"Joined with the six long vowels and encased by the noose and the goad" refers to the supreme gurus.
The ritual application (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: *āṃ hrāṃ kroṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and so forth.
The installation (nyāsa) of the mantras beginning with Hṛllekhā, preceded by the seed-syllables enclosed within the noose and goad, should also be performed. || 80 ||
Holding a boon-granting gesture, a goad, a noose, and the gesture of fearlessness, as well as the Vidyā,
she is seated upon a lotus throne;
she resembles ten million rising suns and possesses three eyes.
I worship her, the primordial Mistress of the World.
Regarding meditation, he says "vare" and so forth.
"Abhītimudrā" means the gesture of fearlessness. "Seated upon a lotus throne" means seated upon a red lotus throne.
The meditation on the weapon is as before. || 81 ||

Eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) and with his senses subdued, he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the true principle; at the conclusion of the recitation, the best of those who know mantras should perform one thousand oblations.
Then, one should offer oblations with as many fuel-sticks of milk-tree wood smeared with curd, honey, and ghee,
followed by pure sesame seeds sprinkled with water, in that same number.
"Twenty-four lakhs" means twenty-four hundred thousand.
As it has been stated by the Teachers:
"Thus, being well-restrained, one should properly recite this supreme mantra twenty-four lakhs of times."
Thus:

"eating sacrificial food and having conquered the senses" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the duties of the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*). "A thousand of those" means twenty-four thousand.
He says that there are six thousand for each.
In some places, the reading is simply "six thousand.
This was stated by the Teachers:
"And six thousand pieces of wood from milk-exuding trees, sprinkled with curd, honey, and ghee.
The phrase "at the end of the recitation" (japānte) means that the rule applies specifically without any interruption by the recitation.
By the term "the best among those who know the mantras," it is indicated that the *svāhā* ending is required for the fire-oblation (*homa*).
"Honey, nectar, and the milky trees" refers to the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *vaṭa* trees; for each of these, there is a fire-oblation (*homa*) of six thousand [offerings].
By that count—that is, by the number twenty-four—[the total is reached]. (82–83)
Upon the seat fashioned by Hṛllekhā, which is endowed with the nine powers, one should worship that Supreme Goddess according to the sequence to be described. || 84 ||
One should first worship Hṛllekhā and the others in the pericarp according to the rule;
the limbs [of the mantra] should be on the filaments, and the Mothers should be stationed on the petals in their proper order.
Furthermore, Indra and the others are to be worshipped, and their weapons outside of them.
By worshipping the Goddess in this manner, one indeed becomes Vaiśravaṇa in person. || 86 ||
He is worshipped by all the worlds, equal in splendor to the sun;
a house presided over by him is filled with the flames of lamps even at night. (87)
By the power of this mantra, it is seen by all living beings.
One should offer oblations at night with mustard seeds mixed with lac and anointed with clarified butter. || 88 ||

The practitioner shall instantly bring the king under his control, as well as the king's wife. By offering oblations of food, he becomes possessed of food; by offering lotuses into the fire, he becomes glorious. || 89 ||
By offering flowers produced from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree, one becomes a poet;
by an oblation of sesame seeds, one becomes free from disease; and by an oblation of clarified butter, one attains long life.
The best of practitioners should also accomplish the rites previously mentioned. || 90 ||
The meaning is that in this [mandala] prescribed by Hṛllekhā and proclaimed by Bhuvaneśī,
the powers of that pīṭha are also to be worshipped.
By the phrase "endowed with the nine powers," the distinctness of the pīṭha-mantra is indicated.
Therefore, it is stated that there is a conjunction of three seed-syllables in the *pīṭha-mantra*.
Here, the *pīṭha* consists of a six-cornered pericarp and an eight-petalled lotus;
there is no sixteen-petalled [lotus].
In that regard, since no specific mode of worship has been mentioned,
it is said that [the mantras] begin with a seed-syllable enclosed between two seed-syllables according to the prescribed rule.
The term "Mothers" refers to those seated upon the lap of Bhairava.
By the accusative case ending in "pūjyata" (is worshipped), the favor of the gods is expressed.
[He is] directly like Vaiśravaṇa Kubera.
[The word] "vaśayet" (should subjugate) [is used].
The method of recitation therein is stated in another tantra:
"One should prefix the syllable *hrīṃ* to the names of those two, and likewise append *āṃ* and *kroṃ*. (84–90)
Having drawn the eight "bolts" (digargalas) and the three-syllable mantra beginning with *pāśa* within the center, one should write the limb-mantras (*aṅgamanus*) in the [remaining] squares,

and in the others, the two eight-syllable mantras. One should place the letters *a*, *ca*, and so on, in the first and last groups of six, along with *yu*, *la*, *ya*, and *va*, upon the seat of space (*vyomāsana*) at the bolts.
Having written [the letters] starting from Śva, Li, Kha, Indu, Jala, Adhipa, and so on, according to their qualities, one should then write two rows.

In the eight inner compartments, one should write the syllable *māyā* (hrīṃ) together with the self-syllable, enclosed within pairs of vowels; on the petals, one should write the root mantra in three rows according to the sequence.
It should be encircled three times by nooses and goads, and surrounded by the letters in both direct and reverse order.
It is surrounded on the outside by a lotus-mouthed jar resting upon a lotus. || 92 ||

From the center to the middle of the ear, there are two marks for each thread;
within the square, one should enclose it with threads as desired by doubling those pairs.

Having constructed a single square according to the method described for the *vāstumaṇḍala*, provided with lines toward the east and north, one should mark it from the center toward the east and north using a measurement equal to half the diagonal line.
By applying cords between each pair of marks, another square arises within the first, intersecting it at the corners located at the cardinal directions.
Then, having performed the expansion of the eight enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) according to one's desire, one should fashion them in the shape of bolts (*argala*).
In all cases, the diagonal lines (*dikkarṇa*) should be erased.

Having thus drawn the eight directional bolts and made a circle in the center, one should inscribe there the three-syllable mantra beginning with *pāśa* (namely, *Pāśapāśitāya*) within the junctions between the two squares.

Having drawn a circle, one should write the *hṛdaya*, *śiras*, *śikhā*, *kavaca*, and *aṇu* mantras in the eight squares according to the method of worship, starting from the southeast corner of the intermediate directions;
one should write the *netra* mantra in the center at the front portion and the *astra* mantra in the cardinal squares.
As it has been said:
The best of mantra-knowers should inscribe the six limbs in the eight corners in their proper order,
in the corners of Agni, Īśa, Asura, and Vāyu.
"Having inscribed [the syllables] ending with the *kavaca*, the wise one should draw the *netra* (eye) in the center;

O Dear One, he should inscribe the *astra* fourfold in the four cardinal directions and the intermediate corners. Thus it is said. Above that, having written the eight-syllable mantra beginning with *pāśa* in the eight squares starting from the top, and then again having drawn a circle at the external junctions, [one should place them] in those resulting [sections].

Having written the eight-syllable mantra of Kāminī within eight compartments, one should bind [the diagram] at the junctions of the eight surrounding enclosures; having drawn a circle outside the [original] circle, one should write the sixteen-syllable Śākta mantra—consisting of eight pairs of syllables—within the sixteen compartments produced therefrom. Some maintain that this connects with what precedes.

Others, however, having caused two circles to be drawn at the inner and outer junctions of the two squares, cause a circle to be drawn outside the circle at the junctions of the eight surrounding enclosures.

Regarding this, some say that one should write the sixteen syllables within those compartments. Others, however, construct a single circle above the outer junctions of the square and cause a second circle to be made at the junctions of the eight perimeters.
All three of these positions are untenable.

Because the sequence prescribed by the Śruti is sublated, and because the eight square cells— which are attached to the circle of the *kaṇīkā* and shaped like downward-facing triangles— are empty. Furthermore, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the postulation of three circles, as well as the postulation of two circles in the other two views, is devoid of scriptural authority (*aprāmāṇika*).
One should postulate only as much as is necessary for the explanation to proceed, and nothing more.
Therefore, only a single *vṛtta* (metrical foot) needs to be postulated;
for it is accepted by all that the subsequent *vṛtta* constitutes the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the lotus.
Therefore, it is best to follow the meaning according to the tradition that is about to be explained.

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: having written "tatparam acpūrva" and having written the sixteen syllables (aṣṭayugārṇa) in the squares, one should write the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) in the filaments (*kesara*).
"Of the vowels" (*acām*) refers to the vowels, excluding the neuter vowels.
The state of being distinct from the neuter [vowels] is obtained by the term "the two preceding and following groups of six.
The first group of six is *a, ā, i, ī, u, ū*; the second group of six is *e, ai, o, au, aṃ, aḥ*.

A *bahuvrīhi* compound should be formed as follows: those in whom the state of being seated (*āsana-sthiti*) in the void (*vyoman*) consists of the excellent dissolutions (*layavara*) joined with these [vowels] are "those whose seat is the void" (*vyomāsana*).
"Syād āsyā tv āsanā sthitiḥ"—this is the lexicon (koṣa).

One should write two rows [of letters] upon the bolts (argaleṣu), according to the sequence of the three syllables, starting from Indra, Jala, Ādhipa, etc., and from the east, west, etc., in accordance with their qualities;
all of these [syllables] are accompanied by the bindu.
Regarding the method of drawing there:
beginning from the circle formed at the junction of the line added to the eastern bolt (pūrvārgalā), one should write "hlaṃ hlāṃ hliṃ" extending to the end of the bolt toward the north;
then, starting again from the tip of the southern bolt, one should write "hlīṃ hluṃ hlūṃ" extending to the end of the circle toward the south.
In this way, the circumambulation is accomplished.
As it is stated in the Saṃhitā:
"Make the [seed-syllable] consisting of power (śakti), water, and fire, conjoined with the point (bindu) and space (vyoman)."
That seed-syllable, joined with its own vowel and excluding *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*, should thus be made twelvefold; therein, O beautiful one, arrange it fourfold.
O beloved, one should write from the circle up to the eight corners, ending with the circle.
"O Dear One, one should write the first triad, facing east, to the north;
the wise one should then write the second triad, facing east, to the south.
Thus, having written from the westward bolt (argalā), starting from the circle to the south, the sequence *hleṃ hlaiṃ hloṃ* up to the end of the bolt, one should again [proceed] to the north—
Starting from the *argalāgra*, one should draw the sequence *hlauṃ hlaṃ hlaḥ*.
As it has been said:
"One should likewise write the third [syllable] in the western part and in the south."

"Likewise on the fourth bolt, but at the end of the north in the western [bolt]. Thus, having written *hyam*, *hyām*, and *hyim* on the eastern side of the southeast bolt as before, one should write *hyīm*, *hyum*, and *hyūm* on the western side as before.
As it has been said:
"Having abandoned the earth [element], one should apply the wind [element] there among the seeds of the sun;
one should draw the first triad on the eastern side of the bolt of fire."
"Likewise, O Dear One, one should also inscribe another triad to the west.
Thus, having inscribed *hyeṃ hyaiṃ hyoṃ* to the west of the wind-barrier (*vāyvargalā*) as before, one should [inscribe] *hyauṃ* to the east as before.
One should write "hyaṃ hyaḥ.
As it has been said:
"In the same manner, one should write a triad to the west in the Mārutārgalaka."
"And also from the east, O Queen of the Gods," thus [it is said].
In this manner, having written *hvaṃ hvāṃ hviṃ* as before on the eastern side of the southern bolt (*yāmyārgalā*), one writes *hvīṃ* on the western side as before.
One should write "hvaṃ" and "hvūṃ.
As it has been said:
"Leaving aside Vāyu (ha), one should place Varuṇa (va) there among the seed-syllables of the Sun."
"A triad in the south, but the second [triad] from the east goes to the western end.
Thus, in the northern bolt, one should write *hveṃ hvaiṃ hvoṃ* from the west as before, and as before, one should write *hvauṃ hvaḥ hvaḥ* from the east.
As it has been said:
"Then, in the northern bolt (uttarārgalā), one should write a triad from the west;
the fourth, O Goddess, from the east."
Thus,
in the same manner, having written *hraṃ hrāṃ hriṃ* on the south of the *kanyā*-bolt (the southwest bolt) as before, one should write *hrīṃ hruṃ hrūṃ* on the north as before.
As it has been said:
"Having removed the vowel *ī* from the seeds of the Sun (*arka-bīja*), one should place the letter *ra* there.
The practitioner of mantra should write the first triad and the subsequent triad within the *Rākṣasārgalā*, from south to north."
Thus, having written "hreṃ hraiṃ hroṃ" in the north as before, one should write "hrauṃ hraṃ hraḥ" in the south as before, according to the Śaivārgalā.
As it has been said:
"Furthermore, in the Śaivārgala,
O Goddess, [the sequence is] first from the north, and afterwards from the southern path."

The teacher Padmapāda, however, states: having drawn an eight-cornered figure consisting of two squares, one should extend two straight lines passing through the eight corners so that the two lines meet each other at the center, forming the shape of a small drum (*dundubhi*). Having thus extended them and formed two circles on both sides of the center of the drum, one should fashion eight petals with tips like bolts (*argala*), starting from the two lines at the tips of the eight drums of the outer circle.
Outside the three circles, one should fashion a jar encircled by lotuses; this is the method for constructing the body of the yantra.

Due to its connection with the square, one should write the *aṅgas* in the eight squares, the eight-syllable mantra beginning with *pāśa* in the subsequent squares, the eight-syllable mantra beginning with *kāminī* in the following squares, and the sixteen-syllable mantra in the form of drums (*dundubhi*) within the pairs of intermediate squares starting with *a-c*.
In this way, even the Vedic sequence for the writing of the mantra is upheld;
and this position is traditional.
As it is stated in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
Then, having joined the two earth-disks together in a hollowed-out union,
O Goddess, one should arrange them so that an eight-cornered figure arises, beautiful to the sight and pleasing to the mind.
O Goddess, having stepped upon those two lines at their tips toward the eight directions, the mantra-practitioner should fashion a beautiful bolt-like shape with the two lines.
A wise person should construct the eight-fold bolt (argalāṣṭaka) using a single measure alone;
at its tip, he should fashion a circle like the orb of the moon.
Then, having drawn it back inside, the best of practitioners should again draw the previously mentioned supreme [diagram],
marking it with a pair of eight-square grids in sequence.
"O Goddess, so that it may become manifest, there should be two *vasus* [sixteen] for the corners,
and the beautiful *argalas* should indeed be properly arranged.
Then, above that, upon the petals of the eight-petaled lotus, [one places] Māyā residing in the filaments.
The fourth vowel is denoted by the word *māyā*.
Thus it is stated in the *Nighaṇṭumātṛkā*:
"The three forms of the goddess *Ī*, the left eye, the crest, and likewise the crooked one (*kauṭila*)."
"The eloquent and pure one named Jihva, Māyā-Viṣṇu, is revealed.
Thus, one should write the *ātman* mantra "Haṃsa" joined with those two on both sides of the *saṃhitā*, situated between the letter 'a' and the letter 'ā'.
By this, the meaning is as follows:
One should write the seven syllables: *pra*, *ti*, *ke*, *sa*, *ra*, *m*, *aṃ*, *haṃ*, *saḥ*, *īṃ*, *haṃ*, *saḥ*, *āṃ*.
As it has been said:
"The word *haṃsa* [consists of] the left eye (*ī*) adorned with the dot (*bindu*) and the crescent (*indu*)."
Furthermore, one should write this five-syllable mantra, which is the "Hamsa" word.
"The seven-syllable [mantra] situated within the interior of the pair of vowels shall become eightfold.
And the Teachers say: "Likewise, one should place Māyā, conjoined with the vowels of the dyads, upon the filaments of the lotus."
Thus [it is said]. The teacher Padmapāda, however, states that *aṃ*, *haṃ*, *īṃ*, *saḥ*, *āṃ*, and so forth, should be written upon the filaments (*kesara*).
One should write the root mantra upon the petals in a sequence of three rows.
Regarding this, those who know the tradition say that one should draw two rows horizontally and then draw one row above them;
others, however, state that one should draw three rows from bottom to top.
"Three times" [refers to this].
In that regard, the meaning is as follows: one [circle] is with the noose and goad, the second is with the letters in regular order, and the third is with the letters in reverse order.
As it has been said:
"Outside of that, one should encircle it in the form of a circle with the noose and goad."
O Dear One, the encircling of the Mātṛkā is performed in the manner of direct order (anuloma).
In the same manner, one should write the encirclement of the *mātṛkā* in reverse order.
And the teachers [state]: "One should encircle the exterior of the lotus with the two seed-syllables of the noose (*pāśa*) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*)."
"One should cause [the breath] to enter by means of syllables moving in forward and reverse order on the outside of that.

Thus, it is surrounded by a jar situated upon a lotus, with its mouth facing upward, located in the position of the pericarp of the upward-facing lotus, and having the face of a downward-facing lotus.
This is the "offering" (*prābhṛta*), which takes the form of a secondary element (*upapada*). (91–93)
The noose, the glorious Śakti, Kandarpa, Kāmaśakti, Indirā, and the goad. || 93 ||
The first mantra consists of eight syllables; then follows "Kāmini Rañjini," and another eight-syllable mantra ending in "svāhā" has been proclaimed by the virtuous. || 94 ||
He states the eight-syllable mantra as "pāśa" and so forth: *pāśa* is *āṃ*; *kandarpa* is the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*); *indirā* is the seed-syllable of Śrī; and *aṅkuśa* is *kroṃ*.
This too is an independent mantra.
The seer and other components of this [mantra] are as follows:
the seer and so forth are declared to be Ajagā, Gayatrī, and Śakti; the limbs are formed with the six long vowels and the Māyā-bīja (Hrīm); by all authorities, it is held that there are eight limbs.

One should contemplate in one's heart the goddess who is the embodiment of bliss, who is ruddy in complexion, who holds a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows in her hands, and who is distressed by the weight of her breasts.
One should recite [the mantra] eight hundred thousand times and perform oblations with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter in the quantity of one-tenth [of the recitation].
One should worship the Goddess on the Śākta seat with the limbs beginning with Hṛllekhā.
"The fifth enclosure consists of the Mothers, the Lords of the World, Vajra, and the others;
its application is declared for such purposes as bringing women under control and summoning.
