Thus [it is said]. He extracts the second eight-syllable mantra with the words "tataḥ" (then).
This mantra is also independent.
Its seer and other details are as follows:
the seer is Samohana, the meter is declared to be Nivṛt, and this is its deity.
The limb "Sarvasammohinī" consists of words repeated twice.
Dark-limbed, adorned with beautiful ornaments, playing the lute with her two arms,
and wearing the moon as her crest-ornament, she gladdens the world with her various songs.
First, one should offer twenty thousand oblations as a tenth-part;
thereafter, by means of Madhūka flowers smeared with the three sweets, one deludes the entire world.
Worship [is performed] at the Mātaṅginī-pīṭha; Rati and the others are in the triangle.
In the pentagon are the five arrows, and the worship of the limbs is in the filaments.
Anaṅgakusumā and the others are on the petals, while the Mothers are at the tips;
together with the World-Protectors and those beginning with Vajra, this is considered the sevenfold enclosure.

In the *Nārāyaṇīya*, however, it is said: "When written with lac on the left hand upon an eight-petalled lotus, the mantra recited ten times shall bring subjugation through the previously described ritual as well."
Having written [the mantra] on birch bark upon an eight-spoked [diagram], one who desires to bring others under control should wear it.

Having inscribed this mantra on a secluded wall or similar surface, the practitioner, remaining silent and gazing [at it], should recite it; then the desired [person] will quickly arrive. Thus [ends verses 93–94].
*Hrīṃ ā gauri rudradayite yogeśvari savarṇa phaṭ svāhā*.
This sixteen-syllable mantra, ending with *svāhā*, has been proclaimed by the virtuous. (95)
He extracts the sixteen-syllable mantra as "hrīṃ"; the armor-mantra is "huṃ".
This also is an independent mantra.
Its seer and other details are as follows: the seer is declared to be Aja, the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Gaurī Caṇḍakātyāyanī, who bestows the power of subjugation and prosperity.
O Manoratha, one should perform the six limbs with the six long vowels;
she who possesses a golden luster holds a mirror and collyrium in her hands for the sake of accomplishment.
I always worship that Gaurī, who holds a noose and a goad and is adorned with every ornament;
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with clarified butter ten times that amount.
On the seat (pīṭha) imagined as Dharma and the other [principles], one should worship these powers of the seat (pīṭhaśakti):
Prabhā, Jñānā, Vāk, Vāgīśvarī, Jvālinī, and Parā.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Guhyaśakti—these are the nine;
they are enriched by the vowels excluding the three short ones and the neuter [vowels], and are joined with the letter *bhṛ* (Bh).
"Gauṃ Gauri" is for the form (mūrti), and "Hṛt" is conceived as the seat-mantra (pīṭhamaṃtra).
Thus, one should worship the Goddess upon the seat with pleasing substances such as sandalwood paste and the like.
And for Subhagā, at the end of "vidma" there should be "he," and at the end [of that] "kāmamāli";
for Nyai, there should be "dhīmahi," and "tanno gaurī" should be followed by "tat pracodayāt."
One should arrange all the ritual services with this Gāyatrī mantra;
having first worshipped the limbs, one should then worship Subhagā and the others.
Bhṛgu, Sāmbu, Sadviti, Yaṣa, Ṣaṣṭā, and Kendu— these and others beginning with them are Subhagā, Lalitā, Kāminī, and Kāmamālinī.

In other directions as well, one should draw weapons with the weapons of the world-protectors; and at night, on the left thigh of a woman with beautiful eyes, one should inscribe her name during the night.
"Covering [the organ] with the left hand, one should recite the mantra with focused mind;
by a hundred or a thousand [recitations], one shall bring a fickle-eyed woman, infatuated by desire.
However, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*, there is this distinction: "They know the right [hand] to be used for subduing men."
Incense, flowers, water, and so forth, consecrated with this mantra and offered or used, bring all people under one's influence.
The Caṇḍakātyāyanī vidyā is difficult to obtain in the three worlds. Thus [ends verse 95].
Having written this yantra according to the prescribed rule on birch bark or similar material, one should wear it on the left arm, or around the neck, or upon one's own head. || 96 ||
One shall bring all mortals under control, and kings in particular;
having written this on a blue cloth and then fashioned it into a pill. || 97 ||
One should place [the effigy] in the heart of a representation of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) fashioned from beeswax,
having deposited it according to the prescribed ritual into a vessel filled with the three sweets (trimadhura).

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having cast forth the bali-oblation during the nights, the practitioner of mantra should daily recite the root mantra eight thousand times. || 99 ||
Within seven days, one shall attract the desired woman, who will be overwhelmed by passion;
having written this on birch bark and then fashioned it into a pill. (100)
By the phrase "having written according to the rule," it is stated that one has observed fasts and other observances on an auspicious day such as Puṣya or Sunday.
Since it is said "in the eighth part of Puṣya-Sunday," this [mantra] is to be written on a blue cloth with substances such as the blood of the ring finger.
As it has been said: "One should write it with the blood of the ring finger, together with lac and the impurities of the eye."
Thus:
*siktha* means beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*).
"Having worshipped according to the injunction" means with red perfumes and other substances, in a pit one cubit deep.
And it is said in the Nārāyaṇīya: "Having placed her beneath sour gruel (kāñjika), one should worship her with red flowers.
The term "offering" (bali) refers to milk-rice (pāyasa) and the like.
Having deposited [the deity] by means of the three-syllabled mantra itself— that is, having offered it— one should attract [the essence] by means of the three-syllabled root mantra,
or else by another method.
As it is said in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"One should heat the effigy in the fires so that it does not dissolve. (96–100)
One should wrap [the vessel] in sequence with lac, copper, silver, and gold;
having placed the Goddess Bhuvaneśvarī within that jar and worshipped her according to the rules. || 101 ||
Having touched him, one should mutter the mantra a thousand times as many as the suns;
having consecrated the beloved person to be accomplished, one should bind the yantra up to the crest-lock.
A person obtains beauty, nourishment, wealth, health, and fame by writing that mantra on a wall and worshipping it daily with devotion. (103)
Even ghosts, spirits, and demons are not able even to look upon him.
A warrior who, having had this [mantra] written on his helmet, wears it when accomplished, slays many enemies in battle and attains victory like Arjuna. || 104 ||
"Tāmra" means by the aforementioned authorities;
"yathāvat" means by the path explicitly stated in the three-syllable [mantra];
"taṃ kumbham" refers to that jar.
"Mantra" refers to that which is situated within the pericarp.
"Divākara" means twelve. "Having written on the wall" means with red chalk (gairika).
As it has been said:
"O fair-faced one, one should draw the yantra with red ochre on the wall of the house;
it brings about the destruction of all malevolent planets as well as of enemies."
Having drawn it there, it is worshipped; all fools, thoroughly deluded, come under his control and no longer undergo transformation.
All those wicked enemies who are difficult to conquer become his servants;
indeed, no one wicked, harmful, or obstructive arises against him.
And the planets, yakṣas, and piśācas, as well as bhūtas, vetālas, and daṃṣṭriṇas. (101–104)
In the two fire-purified [triangles] marked with vajras, one should place her,
enriched with the *paśa* and *aṅkuśa*, with the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) situated within her belly;
then, in the center, in the corners, and on the outer circle.
One should scratch that repeatedly all around. || 105 ||
This, when written on birch bark, shall bring all men under control;
it generates health and sovereignty, and bestows victory in battles. (106)
He states another yantra with the words "vajerati":
within two fire-purī-s (triangles) intersecting each other to form a hexagon,
at the location of a svastika marked by a vajra.
"In the middle of the two cities of fire" refers to two locative cases in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). "That" refers to *māyā*.
"That" consists of three syllables. (105–106)
Upon a birch-bark or lotus leaf, rich with golden filaments and possessing eight petals representing the eight classes of consonants, situated in the city of the earth,
[one should place] that which is bound by means of ropes and goads according to their respective qualities.
One should draw Māyā situated in the center, together with the person to be accomplished (sādhya).
This most excellent yantra, when worn by men, constantly bestows health, sovereignty, good fortune, victory, and other such blessings. (108)
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Śāradātilaka* composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇa Deśikendra. 9.
Furthermore, regarding another method of the yantra, he says "on birch bark" (*bhūrje*).
The connection is that one should write the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) three times, bound by a noose and a goad, according to its qualities.
"Prabaddhāṃ" means "nibaddhām" (bound).

When the reading is simply "likhet," then it should be read as: "one should draw a lotus rich with its own filaments, having eight petals corresponding to the [eight] groups of consonants, situated in front of the earth.
Others, having read simply "likhet," supply the word "yantram" (the diagram) as the object of the verb "likhet" (should draw).
When the question arises as to what that [form] is like, they say: "One should draw Māyā within the lotus. (107–108)
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition. || 9 ||
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Thereafter, I shall describe Tvaritā, who bestows her fruit swiftly.
The Tāra, the Māyā, the Varma-bīja, and Ṛddhi joined with the vowel of Īśa. || 1 ||
The Tortoise is the final syllable therein, the Blessed One *kṣaḥ*; the Woman is the long-extended garment (*saṃvartī*).
The Blessed One Māyā is followed by *phaṭ*; this is the twelve-syllabled mantra. || 2 ||
The sage is said to be Arjuna, the meter is declared to be Virāj, and the deity is proclaimed to be Tvaritā, who bestows the fruits of the goals of human existence. || 3 ||

Having thus stated the mantras of Bhuvaneśvarī, [the author] begins to speak of other mantras, such as Tvaritā and others, by the word "tataḥ" (thereafter), because the mantra of Pāśa and so forth belongs to the category of Nityā mantras.
The etymology of the word *tvaritā* is shown by the phrase "bestowing swift fruit" (*tvaritaphaladāyinīm*).
As it has been said:
"For those endowed with devotion, she brings about accomplishment with speed;
thus the Goddess shall be known as Tvaritā to the practitioner, because she swiftly removes poison, seizing spirits, and other afflictions."
He extracts the mantra as follows: "Tāra" means the Praṇava (Oṃ). Māyā is the seed-syllable of Śakti. Varma-bīja is Huṃ.
In the ritual placement of the Kalās, Ṛddhi is Khaḥ. Īśasvara is the eleventh vowel (Ū). Conjoined with this, it becomes Khe.

The tortoise is the letter *ca*; at its end is *cha*. *Bhaga* is the vowel *e*; that which possesses it is the "Lord" (*bhagavān*), meaning it is joined with *e*. By that [letter], *cha* becomes *kṣa*, which is the very form of the Woman (*strī*).
Here, the letter *kṣa* should be understood as being accompanied by the *visarga*.
Because it is said, "the surrounding garland," [there is] *hūṃ* for the long body-covering.
*Kṣaḥ* is the dissolution; the Blessed One is endowed with the letter *e*.
Therefore, [it is said] "kṣe.
It is well known that this goddess possesses a curse;
for this reason, some consider the syllable "kṣe" to be a *kīlaka* (stake).
For that purpose, one first utters the syllable *kṣe* and then utters the syllable *hūṃ* at the end.
However, in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*, it is stated: "The two seed-syllables *strīṃ* and *mīṃ* are proclaimed to be the armor and the pin."
Some [teachers] hold that the syllable *hūṃ* comes first and the syllable *kṣe* comes after; thus there is a great disagreement among the masters.
In this regard, just as knots occur in certain places on trees and the like, so too do the knots called "stake" (*kīla*) occur in mantras by their very nature.
Consequently, defects such as delay in time and lack of accomplishment arise;
and that [defect] occurs only when [the mantra] pertains to a specific syllable.
In that regard, for certain mantras, they extract that particular syllable and perform the recitation after completing it with some other syllable prescribed by the scriptures.
In some cases, they perform the recitation by omitting those [syllables] entirely and inserting other syllables instead.
In certain instances, even the presence of what is called a "kīla" (a flaw) does not bring about any defect;
just as knots found in trees and such things may be harmful in some cases, yet in others they actually serve as a source of excellence.
As it is said:
"Of sandalwood, there are three excellent types: the knotted, the cloth-like, and the hollow."
As they say: "A defective *kīlaka* (stake) is known to be an obstacle to success; however, a non-defective *kīlaka*, when known, bestows excellent accomplishment.
In that regard, the mantra accompanied by the two *māyās* has been extracted for the purpose of removing the defects of that *kīlaka*.

As it has been stated by the Teachers: "The practitioner of mantra should employ the seed-syllable of Māyā at the end of *Tārā* and also at the beginning of the *astra* [mantra]. For by that means, the desired accomplishment shall come to those who know the mantra before long.
Also, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "That which begins with *phaṭ* and *tārā*, joined with those two goddesses, bestows all accomplishments."
Thus: the *praṇava* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and *māyā* is the power (*śakti*).
The teacher Padmapāda maintains that *huṃ* is the seed-syllable.
The phrase "for the sake of human goals" expresses the application [of the scripture]. 1-3.
One should place the letters, excluding the vowel *mā*, upon the head, the forehead, the throat, and the heart;
and upon the navel, the private parts, the pair of thighs, the knees, the shanks, and the feet.
Having performed the placement (vinyāsa), the practitioner should perform the pervasive assignment (vyāpaka) with the entire mantra,
using the seven syllables beginning with Kūrma, each progressively deprived of its preceding vowel.
The most excellent practitioner should arrange the six limbs by means of two [syllables] each.
Regarding the placement of the syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*), he says "māyā" and so forth. By this, the placement of exactly ten syllables is intended.
In that regard, there is the placement of one syllable each in the two locations beginning with the pair of thighs.
"In the steps" means in the two feet.
By the word "practitioner," the utterance accompanied by Māyā is stated for the pervasive [deity].
He states the six limbs with the words "beginning with Kūrma."
The word *kūrma* (tortoise) is the first [letter] of that [group], namely *kha*.
The plural number is used in the sense of "beginning with" (*ādi*); thus, it means "by the seven letters beginning with *kha*," which here refers to the seven letters beginning with *kūrma*.

Since the primary action requires a connection with the preceding [words], and there is an expectancy for such a connection, the phrase "by two and two" is connected to each pair according to the principle of the *aruṇādhikaraṇa*.
"Khe ca" is the heart; "ca che" is the head; "che kṣaḥ" is the tuft (śikhā), and so forth. This has been stated in the Nārāyaṇīya, after extracting the ten-syllable mantra:

"The seven vowels beginning with *a* belong to the third [set] of words ending in the ninth; by means of those, the limbs (aṅgas) consisting of two syllables each are to be formed according to the oral instruction.
Some, however, explain it as: "by those seven syllables of which the first is the letter *ca*, [forming the word] *kūrma*."

In that system, one should apply the word *māyāvivajītān* by carrying it over (*anuvṛtti*) and subsequently changing its case ending to *māyāvivajītair*, and then join it to the present context; thus, with the six limbs beginning with *cakāra* and ending with *phaṭ*.
This has been stated in the *Kādimata* after extracting the ten-syllable mantra:
"The Vidyā consists of the fourth vowel and so forth, along with seven syllables;

one should form the limbs (aṅgas) with pairs of syllables in the sequence of six for both the hands and the limbs. And in the Saṃhitā: "Ca-che is the pair for the heart, ta-che for the head, and then che-kṣo is the pair for the crest-lock (śikhā)."
*Kṣaḥ* is the pair of women and the armor; *strī* is likewise the pair of *hum* and *ātman*.
"Having placed *hūṃ* and *kṣe* in the eyes, *kṣe phaṭ* is proclaimed as the weapon (*astra*). Thus it is said.
Both of these two positions are to be understood according to the respective traditions of one's own guru.

By the term "supreme practitioner," the application of the *kuṇḍalinī* seed-syllable *hlīṃ* and the *māyā* seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels within the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) is indicated.
Therefore, there is the statement in the *Nārāyaṇīya* that [it is] "from instruction. (4-6)
Dark-complexioned, her head adorned with a crest of many peacock feathers, wearing a garment of woven leaves,
her full breasts shining with a necklace of *guñjā* berries, she bears eight serpents which have been made to produce the sweet tinkling of earrings, armlets, girdles, and anklets.
I worship the goddess Kairātī, who has three eyes and whose hands are raised, granting boons and fearlessness. || 7 ||
He speaks of meditation with the words "śyāmām" (the dark-complexioned one).
"Kalāpa" means a peacock's tail-feather;
this is an elliptical expression for bracelets and other ornaments.

As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "She has bracelets of peacock feathers, a crest of peacock plumes, and garments of young sprouts; she sits upon a lion-throne, with a peacock-umbrella and a banner of a peacock-feather.
She bears the eight lordly serpents, such as Tāṭaṅka and others, whom she has brought under her control.

In that regard, the two Ananta and Kulika, having become earrings (*tāṭaṅka*), Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla, having become armlets (*aṅgada*), Takṣaka and Mahāpadma, having become waist-bands (*mekhalā*), and the two Nāgas Karkeṭaka and Padma, having become anklets (*nūpura*), are to be meditated upon.
As it is said in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"The Brāhmaṇas have snakes for earrings, O King, and are endowed with snake-armlets;
the Vaiśyas have snake-girdles, and the Śūdras have snake-anklets. Thus it is said.
Regarding their visualization, it is stated: "The two Brāhmaṇas, Ananta and Kulika, are described as having the color of fire."
Each, moreover, was adorned with a thousand hoods.
Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla are Kṣatriyas of yellow complexion,
each resplendent with seven hundred hoods.
Takṣaka and Mahāpadma are known as these two Vaiśya serpents;
they are blue in color, with five hundred hoods upon their lofty heads.
"Padmaka and Karkeṭaka are Śūdras, white in color, and possess three hundred hoods.
Thus say those who know the tradition regarding the visualization of the weapons in the left and right [hands]. (7)

Having recited this mantra one hundred thousand times, the knower of mantras, with his senses subdued, should perform a fire sacrifice with ten parts—namely, one-tenth of that number—using excellent *bilva* wood sticks smeared with the three sweets (*madhura*). || 8 ||
By the phrase "one who knows the mantra," it is meant that there should be a recitation of ten parts of the mantra *oṃ hrīṃ namo nitye svāhā*.

Furthermore, there should be a recitation of one hundredth part of the five-syllable Śiva-mantra (*pañcākṣara*) and of the servant-mantra (*kiṅkaramantra*): *oṃ hrīṃ namo bhagavate śavarāya mahākirātarūpāya kaṅkāladharāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. || 8 ||
Upon a seat fashioned by Hṛllekhā, endowed with the nine powers,
one should worship the goddess Tvaritā according to the procedure to be described.

In the world conceived by Hṛllekhā as proclaimed by Bhuvaneśī, the Śaktis of that seat (pīṭha) are also to be worshipped here; this is the meaning. By the phrase "endowed with nine Śaktis," he indicates that the mantra of the seat is distinct [from the previous one].
In this case, the pedestal (*pīṭha*) consists of eight petals only,
because the deities to be worshipped on sixteen petals have not been mentioned.
This has been stated in the *Saṃhitā*:
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus and draw a circle around it outside;
on each of the eight petals, one should write the armor-mantra (kavaca) eight times.
In the center, one should place Bhuvaneśānī, and surround her on the outside with the Mātṛkā;
this is declared to be the wheel named "The All-Protecting."
"Having invoked the Goddess here once more, one should worship her with the ritual offerings (upacāras).
And the teachers say: "Having invoked the Goddess upon the lotus-seat [of the heart], which is the lion-throne held by the eight lords of the directions..."
Thus [ends the ninth].
The *saṃvartaka* [letter] joined with the *bindu*, the armor, the entire void, the *vajradeha*, the many pairs, and indeed the two *hiṅgulu*s. || 10 ||

The pair of thunderclaps (ga-ra-ja), the sky (i), the moon (u), the armor (va), the last [consonant] (ha) with a long vowel and a bindu (hūṃ)—this is proclaimed as the heart-mantra for Pañcānana, which is the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra). || 11 ||

One should offer a seat with this [mantra] and fashion the image with the root mantra. One should worship Gāyatrī, who has been brought forth by the limbs [of the deity], in sequence upon the filaments. || 12 ||
He extracts the mantra for the seat with the words "saṃvarttaka.
Saṃvarttaka joined with the bindu (dot) is *kṣaṃ*; the armor-mantra is *huṃ*.
"Sakala" means together with the bindu; by the word "kalā," the half-moon is indicated, and thus it denotes the bindu.
"Viyat haṃ" refers to the form of the person with a vajra-body;
the connection is that it is uttered quickly. "Sendu" means together with the dot (bindu); thus, "viyat haṃ" is [the mantra] with the bindu.
The armor-syllable is *huṃ*; the final letter is *kṣa*, which possesses a long vowel *ā* and a nasal dot (*bindu*), thus forming *kṣāṃ*. The heart-mantra is *namaḥ*.
Regarding the worship of the limbs (*aṅgapūjā*), he says "with the limbs" (*aṅgaiḥ*).

Concerning the word "in sequence" (*kramāt*), those who know the tradition maintain that one should worship the six limbs on the first six filaments, and then worship the *praṇītā* and the *gāyatrī* on the [filaments] of Kubera and Īśāna.
As it has been said by the Teachers: "One should worship Gāyatrī, together with her limbs, in the sequence of the directions.
This very point has also been explained in the same way by Padmapādācārya.
Elsewhere also it is said: "On the eight lion-thrones, one should worship, in order, on the petals starting from the east, Aṅga, Praṇītā, and Gāyatrī."
In the Trotalāmata as well: "One should worship the deities of the limbs on the eight petals there, beginning from the eastern direction;
one should worship Praṇītā in the north and Gāyatrī in the northeast.
This alone is the consensus of the author of the Mantradevaprakāśikā and others. (10–12)
On the petals, one should worship these [goddesses], beginning with Śrībīja, well-adorned:
Huṅkārī, Khecarī, Caṇḍā, Chedanī, and the woman Kṣepaṇī. || 13 ||
Hūṃkārī and Kṣemakārī, adorned with the weapons of Lokeśa, are in front; outside, Phaṭkārī holds a bow and arrow.
On both sides of the door, the two [deities] holding golden *vetra* staffs and lotuses are to be worshipped. Regarding the phrase "on the petals":
this is an explanation of the term "well-adorned," referring to these powers (*śakti*) of the mantra-syllables which are about to be described.
Regarding "Lokeśa":
the word "ornament" (bhūṣaṇa) is an indicator for [their] color, vehicle, and so forth.
Therefore, the meaning is that their colors, weapons, ornaments, and vehicles are like those of Indra and the other [deities].
And it is said in the *Trotalāmata*:
"They are equal to Indra and the other world-protectors in their colors, vehicles, and weapons."
"In front" refers to the Goddess.
Some do not perform the worship of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and their weapons here, on the grounds that the *śaktis* themselves possess those forms.
Others worship them in the form of women.
As it is stated in the Trottalāmata:
"One should worship the lords of the directions, who have become women, in that outer enclosure."
Others, however, say that the Mothers, seated upon the laps of the Bhairavas, should be worshipped on the tips of the petals.
And it is stated in the Trotalāmata:
"Outside of that, one should worship the eight Bhairavas together with the Mothers of the sacred seats (pīṭhas). (13–14)
Then [the names] Jayā, Vijayā, and Kiṅkarā, followed by the word *pada*. || 15 ||
At the end of the word "rakṣa rakṣa," one should utter "tvaritājñā sthiro bhava.
Then, with the mantra ending in the weapon-syllable (phaṭ), one should worship the servant outside of that. || 16 ||
Kṛṣṇa, bearing a staff, with dark and curly hair, was adorned with fragrant, reddish wild flowers of the atimukta variety. || 17 ||

One should worship with incense, lamps, and other offerings, as well as with delightful dances and songs; thus the practitioner, having perfected the mantra, is honored by women, men, and kings. || 18 ||
Within a year, he is honored as one who has surpassed Kubera in wealth through his prosperity;
having prepared a Yoni-kuṇḍa here, he should perform the fire-oblation according to his own desire. || 19 ||
By offering oblations with jasmine flowers (mallikā), one may bring the entire world under control;
by offering oblations with palāśa flowers, one pacifies malevolent spirits, enmity, and other such evils.
By offering auspicious pieces of sugarcane, one attains great prosperity;
by the oblation of dūrvā grass, the practitioner obtains a long life. || 21 ||
"On both sides of the door" means on the outer sides of the door, as indicated by the statement "situated outside the door.
These two [deities] also have two arms and their color is the same as that of the presiding deity.
And it is said: "The capable ones are like that.
He extracts the *kiṅkara* mantra as *kiṅkarāya*. The armor is *huṃ*.
*Astraṃ phaṭ*. The one named Kiṅkara is a particular type of spirit who has become a servant of the Goddess;
he too has exactly two arms.
Outside that, on the outer part of the door, [is one] with barbarian hair—meaning with disheveled hair or, as it were, curly hair.
There is a specific detail in the *Trotalātantra*: "[He is] seated upon a corpse-seat at the exterior of the doorway, most terrifying."
Thus.
One who recites the mantra of Tvaritā should recite the Gāyatrī of Tvaritā,
as they say:
At the end of the word "Tvaritā Devī," one should utter "vidmahe";
having spoken "vidyāṃ dhīmahi," one should say "tanno devī pracodayāt."
"By the recitation of the Gāyatrī Tvaritā, she brings about her presence.
Thus [it is said]. "By her own will" means:
By this it is stated:

in the ritual applications to be described hereafter, the number for the *homa*—whether it be a thousand, the ten-thousand (*ayuta*) to be mentioned, or that increased by three—is determined by the gravity or lightness of the task;
the same applies to the *japa*.

As it has been said: "The number of oblations is one thousand, or three thousand, or up to ten thousand; for as many times as there are oblations, so many times should the mantra be recited by the practitioner. And elsewhere: "The number of oblations is one thousand, extending up to three thousand."
"Having considered lightness and gravity regarding the task at hand, one should act with skill. Thus it is said.

It should be understood that in all ritual applications, an oblation (homa) should also be performed for the five-syllable mantra and the servant-mantra (kiṅkara) by means of a tenth part of this [primary] oblation.
In the phrase "one should bring under control," there is the nature of Kāmādi;
in the phrase "from sorcery, malice, and so forth," there is the nature of Nṛsiṃhādi;
and in the phrase "great supernatural power," there is the nature of Śaktyādi.
"One attains a long life" refers to the state of being a conqueror of death (*mṛtyuñjaya*) and so forth.
By the word "practitioner" (*sādhaka*), it is stated that one has performed the preparatory rite (*puraścaryā*) three times. (15–21)
By offering washed grains as an oblation, one shall attain desired prosperity;
with barley, there shall be abundance of grain, and with wheat, the accomplishment of one's wishes.
Through rice offerings, there shall be inexhaustible success; through sesame seeds, great prosperity.
By offering blue lotuses, the practitioner of mantra shall bring the king’s wife under his control. || 23 ||
By offering blossomed lotuses, one brings the earth under one's control;
through Aśoka flowers, one obtains a son; and through Madhūka flowers, one shall attain what is desired. || 24 ||
By offering fruits produced from the jambu tree, one obtains the desired wealth;
by flowers born of the pāṭali tree, one attains a beloved beautiful woman. || 25 ||

The term "washed" (*prakṣālita*) is an adjective qualifying everything up to the sesame seeds (*tila*). "Desired prosperity" (*śriyam iṣṭām*) refers to the attainment of *śrī*; "obtains a son" (*putram āpnoti*) refers to the attainment of *kāma*.
The word *medinīm* (the earth) indicates the people dwelling upon the earth;
the plural sense is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
The phrase *iṣṭām sundarīm* (the beloved beautiful woman) refers to the union with the young girl. (22–25)
By offering flowers produced from the bakula tree, one’s fame shall be imperishable;
by means of mango blossoms, one obtains a long life; and by campaka flowers, one obtains gold. || 26 ||
A wise person should fashion a golden image of an enemy using mustard seeds;
by offering oblations of bakula leaves, one shall swiftly destroy the foes. || 27 ||
By means of an oblation of *śālmalī* leaves, one will certainly destroy rivals;
likewise, with *kodrava* grains or *kaṇḍana* seeds, or with *nimba* leaves, one may cause mutual enmity. || 28 ||
It should be understood that the practice of *ajapā-yoga* is for the sake of attaining fame (*kīrti*).
[The word] *anapāyinī* means imperishable. As for the form "labhet," since the root *labh* is conjugated in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), how can it be used here?

"Lābha" means "that which is obtained"; it is derived from the root *labh* with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac). [The form] "lābhavat" is formed by adding the suffix *kvip* to the verb in the sense of "acting like" (*ācāre*), according to the rule *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*, whereby it attains the status of a verbal root (*dhātutva*).
Therefore, the resolution is that the *liṅ* [suffix] takes the *parasmaipada* [ending].
In some places, the reading is simply "bhavet" (it may be).
Regarding the word "āmraiḥ":
Here, the word "with flowers" (puṣpaiḥ) is to be supplied.
"Should destroy" (utsādayet) refers to the nature of the seed-syllable of Vāyu and so forth. "Sapatnān" means enemies.
"By means of threshing" refers to the chaff and husks;
the meaning is that one should destroy [the afflictions] in that same manner.
"By means of nimba trees" means by means of nimba fruits. (26–28)
By a homa of black gram (māṣa), one becomes mute; by [a homa] with dice, one becomes insane; and an enemy shall be destroyed.
The number of oblations (homa) should be ten thousand (ayuta), and the recitation (japa) is declared to be of the same amount. || 29 ||
With dice made from the fruits of the *bībhītaka* tree. || 29 ||
Bathing with water consecrated by those mantras is known to remove all diseases; a mouthful of water over which that mantra has been recited, when cast into the mouth, destroys poison. || 30 ||
One who knows the mantra should give medicine to the afflicted with this mantra;
by the power of this mantra, he shall be liberated from disease. || 31 ||
"Destroying poison" refers to the application of the *garuḍa* seed-syllable (*bīja*). By the phrase "knower of mantras," the application of the *nṛsiṃha* seed-syllable is indicated. (30–31)
A ring made of the three metals, properly consecrated with this mantra, pacifies malevolent magic, treachery, and the like, and destroys all diseases. || 32 ||
Regarding "trilohī" (the three metals):
this has been properly prepared, consecrated with the recitation of this mantra, and subjected to the ritual sprinkling (*sampāta*).
Here, the author of the *Apekṣitārthadyotikā* states that equal portions of each of the metals should be used. || 32 ||
She is considered the eternal bestower of all prosperity and the one who brings everything under control;
whatever the knower of mantras desires is accomplished by means of this [mantra]. || 33 ||

By the phrase "whatever the knower of mantras desires," it is indicated that [this practice] brings liberation when joined with the *praṇava* (OM), produces dharma and knowledge when joined with speech (*vāk*), and accomplishes everything when joined with *śakti*. || 33 ||
In the center of a lotus with ten petals, one should write the Māyā-bīja (Hrīṃ) containing the desired object of attainment;
then the ten syllables beginning with Tāra (Oṃ), situated within the mantra, and the seed-syllable of the hexagon located in the city of the earth (La).
This *Tvaritā* yantra, when worn, pacifies black magic, treachery, and the like; it removes the fear of wild beasts and thieves, and especially bestows victory. || 35 ||
He states the yantra: "In the center," etc.
The two locative cases in "in the lotus in the center" (*madhye saroje*) are in different grammatical relations (vyadhikaraṇa).
"Desired" refers to subjugation (*vaśyādi*) and so forth; "and that which is to be accomplished" (*sādhya*) is that which is within its interior.
"Regarding 'Tārā and the others'": this refers to those [mantras] distinct from Māyā.
By the phrase "especially bestowing victory," it is indicated that the object of accomplishment (sādhya) should be written within the Māyā-bīja, which is the seed-syllable of Durgā. || 34-35 ||
One should write "Tāre Huṃ" within the hollow of a lotus, accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*);

having written eight syllables of the mantra upon the eight petals, it should be encircled three times by the *śakti* [syllable] on the outside. This [yantra], situated in a jar and resting upon a lotus, belongs to the Lotus-faced One.
This yantra brings about subjugation, removes fear from planets and other such sources, bestows prosperity, and grants fame. (36)

He states another yantra with the words "tāra" (the syllable Om) and so forth. "In the hollow of the lotus" means in the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus. "The mantra-syllables" refers to those [syllables] excluding the two *māyās*, the *tāra* (Om), and the *varma* (Hum).
Because they are employed elsewhere.
Regarding the phrase "lotus-face":
the mouth of the jar itself is metaphorically designated as such [a lotus] because it possesses those qualities within the yantra.
Regarding "this fame": it should be understood that the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) is [inserted] in the ajapā [mantra]. || 36 ||
Having divided the grid into one hundred and twenty-one squares, the knower of mantras should place the *dhruva* (OM) in the center,

followed by the *sādhya* (the name of the practitioner), and then write *Tvaritā* starting from the auspicious syllable *Śiva* (HA), omitting *Māyā* (HRĪM). Having repeatedly recited the mantra, he should strike it with a trident shining at the ends of the lines.
This yantra pacifies poison and great malevolent rites, brings about subjugation, and bestows prosperity. || 37 ||
He states another yantra with the words "of the squares" (*koṣṭhānām*).
By twelve lines extending south to north and twelve lines extending east to west, one hundred and twenty-one squares are produced.
The word "in the middle" (*madhyataḥ*) uses the suffix *tasi* in the sense of the locative case.
Therein, one should write the mantra twelve times in a clockwise sequence starting from Śiva (the northeast) and proceeding to Īśāna (the east).

In this context, for the neutralization of poison (*kṣveḍa*), the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*) is written within the *garuḍa* seed-syllable; for the neutralization of great malevolent magic (*mahābhicāra*), it is written within the *nṛsiṃha* seed-syllable.

In the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*), [one should use] the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*); for prosperity (*śrī*), the seed-syllable of Śrī; for all purposes (*sarvārtha*), the power-syllable (*śakti*), and so forth—this is how it should be understood.
However, the traditionalists (*sāmpradāyika*) explain it otherwise:
"One should write the syllable of Śiva and the rest in the center of the fixed [syllable]."
Here, the suffix -tasi is used in the sense of the ablative case.
By the word "etc. (ādi), the [offerings] dedicated to Agni, Nirṛti, and Vāyu are included.
Thus, this is the meaning:
Having written the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the center, one should then write five *praṇavas* in the five corner squares located toward the northeast (*īśa*).
Likewise, one should do so in the five corner squares starting from the southeast (*āgneya*) as well.
The knower of mantras should write the goddess Tvaritā in such a way that she is accompanied by the object of attainment (*sādhya*) but without the *māyā* (hrīṃ).
Here, by the term *mantraviccha*, the sequence of writing is indicated.
By the phrase "endowed with the sādhya," it is meant that one should write the letters of the sādhya one by one in each square starting from the *dhruva* (the central pivot),
and that the sādhya for all rites should be written in the central *dhruva*.

The sequence for writing the syllables here is as follows: In that regard, within the five groups of five starting with Īśāna, one should first write the four syllables beginning with *huṃ* and ending with *che* in the four squares located in the eastern direction for the first *praṇava*;

then, having written *kṣaḥ* in the square to its south, one should write the remaining four syllables ending with the middle *praṇava* in the four squares following that—this constitutes one round (*āvṛtti*).
Then, having written "huṃ khe" in the first three syllables of the second *tāra*, the second [line] is formed by reciting what was previously written.

Likewise, having written "huṃ khe" in the first two syllables of the third *tāra*, the third [line] is formed by relying upon what was previously written. Similarly, having written "huṃ" in the first syllable of the fourth *tāra*, the fourth [line] is formed by the presentation of what was previously written.

Again, beginning with the fifth *praṇava*, the fifth repetition is performed by reciting exactly as written before. In this same manner, beginning with the five *praṇavas*, there are five repetitions of the preceding words.
Thus, there are ten repetitions in one corner.
The same applies to the three corners beginning with the southeast (āgneya).

Accordingly, in the words of the Ācārya: "Or one should trace [the mantra] after each," the word *vā* is taken as a disjunctive particle (*cheda*) used in a collective sense (*samuccaya*), and it is explained that one should write it ten times.
And in the Nārāyaṇīya: "On birch bark, within a case of *sakāraka*, blazing with the javelin and the trident..."
"In the corners, the name placed within the center [should be surrounded by] *tāra* (OM);
*phaṭ* should be in the directions. Just as it is written, this *mālārṇayuk* [mantra], for every leaf, removes the affliction caused by planetary spirits. Thus it is said.
*Kāraka* is 121; *javeti* is 48.
The rest is clear.
Another yantra mentioned in another tantra is as follows:
Having drawn twelve lines from east to west and twelve from south to north,

the *sādhya* (the name to be inscribed) should be placed in the central squares, while the *dhruva* (the fixed seed-syllable) should be in the squares located in the direction of the Lord of Asuras (the southwest). Afterwards, the weapon-syllable (*astra*), other mantra-syllables, and the remaining letters should be written in the remaining squares.
Even the gods cannot harm a man who is equipped with a mechanical device, so what need be said of the multitudes of mortals? Thus [it is said]. (37)
In the eighty-one squares, one should write the *sādhya* (the name of the person to be accomplished) in the center of the opening between the letters ending in *ṭ*.

Then, in the lines extending toward the cardinal directions, one should write the syllables *jūṃ saḥ* up to the end of the *śikhā* (the crest-mantra). In the remaining squares, starting from the northeast and moving toward the southwest, one should write the mantra of Lakṣmī line by line.
With the *śastrāvi* mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ*, recited swiftly, he scattered [the offerings] in all four directions. || 38 ||
He states another diagram: "One," etc.
One should draw ten lines extending east-west and ten lines extending north-south.
In this way, eighty-one squares are produced.
There, having written the letter *ṭha*—the final letter of the *ṭha*-group—in the central square, one should write the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) in its center.
The term "object of accomplishment" is illustrative and includes the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and others as well.
Regarding the phrase "in the rows extending toward the directions":

From the central square, within the four rows consisting of the four squares each in the east, west, south, and north, one should write the syllables *jūṃ saḥ* as their essential form, ending with *śikhā* and ending with *vaṣaṭ*; thus, according to the sequence of individual letters, one should write the mantra *jūṃ saḥ vaṣaṭ*.
The *lakṣmī-mantra* to be spoken next is that which begins with "Śrī" and so forth;
the weapon is "Phaṭ," and that which manifests within it is "Vaṣaṭ. She who has this at her end is [the goddess] Tvaritā; by means of that *Tvaritā-mantra*, in each of the four directions...
One should encircle it with each repetition individually.
As it has been said: "The mantra consisting of the words for the weapons and so forth, beginning with the directions and ending with *vaṣaṭ*, should be placed in each respective direction."
Elsewhere also it is said: "Vaṣaṭ at the end, Bahiḥśīghrā in the directions, Ṭhaṃ, the jar, and Vahni.
Regarding this, some explain it otherwise.
And regarding the statement, "The weapon-mantra (astra) appears where there is an excess of *vaṣaṭ*," it is argued that one should utter the *phaṭ*-sound and then utter the *vaṣaṭ*-sound;
however, that is incorrect because it contradicts other tantras.
As it has been said: "Tvaritā should end with *vaṣaṭ* and be devoid of the syllable *phaṭ*.
In this case, for the encircling and at the front, the mantra is accompanied by *māyā*. (38)

One should properly visualize the wheel called Anugraha, fashioned from gold and other materials, encircled by the syllables *lānta* (the labials), surrounded by the lotus-seated [Brahmā], and presided over by the lotus-seated [Viṣṇu]. ||39||
With *la* sounds and *va* sounds;
"wreathed with excellence" means by a garland-maker.
As it was said by the Teachers: "A bimba fruit encircled by a garland of fat."
Thus:
one should place or maintain [it] according to the measure as previously stated.
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "gold etcetera," silver and copper are meant. || 39 ||
He shall overcome sorcery, untimely death, disease, and the like, as well as poisons, spirits, and great planetary afflictions;
he shall live for a hundred years and rejoice with sons, grandsons, and prosperity.
In that regard, its fruit has been stated: "The machine was formerly held by Yama, by Brahmā, by Viṣṇu, by Budha, by Bhairava, by Heramba, and by Guha."
By the grace of this vidyā,
all those sufferings that exist in the three worlds— whether artificial or natural— come under one's control.
By the power of the Queen of Knowledge (Vidyārājñī), these [obstacles] are undoubtedly destroyed.
Having drawn this supreme Wheel of Grace upon a flat wall with chalk, one should worship it.
There, the entire circle of people belonging to one's family becomes [subdued], and one brings the world of men under control here by means of one's whole being.
Thus [ends the section]. 40.
That which is Śrī is Māyā; that which is Māyā is known as Śrī. In the sacrifice, she is not to be known as "us.
Māyā is Līlā, and Lālī is Yāmā; in the sacrifice, Lālī is to be known as Līlā. || 41 ||
The wise man should write the mantra of Ramā, beginning with Īśa (the northeast) and starting from Kanyā (the west), within sixty-four squares;
it should be surrounded externally as prescribed by Tvaritā and further encircled by the letters beginning with La, residing in excellent gold.
Whether in a country, a town, a city, or a house, one should duly install this wheel;
there, cattle and buffalo will certainly increase, and there shall be the perfect prosperity of subjects and crops. (43)
He describes another yantra with the words "one should draw":
having drawn nine lines extending east-west and north-south, one should form sixty-four squares. [The sequence begins] from Kanyā (Virgo) starting from the southwest (nairṛtya).
"Ramāmanuṃ śrīse," etc.
"Properly" means that with the *vaṣaṭ* ending, it is done in all four directions.

Here, having written the syllable *ṭha* in the four central squares, one should write the names of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and the ritual action (*karman*) in their midst.
"One should deposit it as prescribed" means that it is said to be deposited and worshipped within a space measuring one cubit (hasta). || 41-43 ||

The Lord Caṇḍa, Meru, and Sarga combined constitute what is known as the Trikaṇṭakī Vidyā, consisting of three syllables. It is taught that the arrangement of the limbs (aṅgas) is performed by repeating the syllables of the mantra twice. || 44 ||
He states another mantra:
"The armor (kavaca) is *huṃ*; Caṇḍa is *khaḥ*; the Blessed One joined with the letter *e* is *khe*."
*Meru* is *kṣa*.

Here, because the fifty letters beginning with *a* and ending with *la* constitute the rosary (*akṣamālā*), the letter *kṣa*, which occupies the position of Mount Meru, is denoted by the word "Meru. It is "endowed with emission," meaning it is joined with the visarga.
This very point—that this [syllable] is accompanied by the *visarga*—is also indicated in the preceding mantra.

As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The second seed-syllable of the ten-syllabled *Tōtalā*, together with the third and the sixth, is called *Trikaṇṭakī*; by that, one shall be perfectly accomplished."
Thus: the first is the seed (bīja), the last is the power (śakti). || 44 ||
Her body is blue below the navel, reddish in luster from the region of the throat downward, and white above the face;
with four faces, her limbs are terrifying due to mouths with formidable fangs turned toward her belly;
she holds two lamps, a conch, and a discus in her lotus-like hands, and within her matted locks—
May the three-eyed deity, whose crescent moon shines brilliantly, be the remover of fear.

One should recite this mantra three hundred thousand times; at the end, having offered oblations of clarified butter in the previously mentioned manner according to a tenth part [of the recitation], one should worship that Trikaṇṭakī. || 46 ||

"Blue" (nīlā): the connection is that she is white from her mouth. "Terrifying-limbed" (bhīṣaṇāṅgī) is to be construed with "four mouths," which are formidable with fangs and encompassed by her belly.
"Surrounded by bellies" means having four bellies on the sides.
"Kambu" refers to a conch shell.
Regarding the visualization of the weapons: they are in the first pair of hands, starting from the right, and in the last pair, starting from below those. || 45-46 ||
Having formed the triśūla-mudrā with both hands and meditating upon oneself as Trikaṇṭakī, one should touch and recite [the mantra]; the seizing spirit will immediately release the victim. || 47 ||

Regarding the *triśūlamudrā*: it is defined as "by the joining of the little finger and the thumb, and by the extending of the remaining fingers. These two final syllables of this mantra, when joined with *che* at the end, are to be known as *viṣahā trikaṇṭakī*.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"The fifth and third petals of that [lotus] are for poison-removal, and the sixth is likewise."
The seer and all else for this triad are the same as previously stated. || 47 ||
This three-colored plant, known as Trikaṇṭakī, is a vidyā that subjugates women;
one should perform the six-limbed nyāsa (aṅga-ṣaṭka) using the mantra syllables repeated, just as previously described. || 48 ||
Meditating upon the deity mentioned previously, one should recite the mantra three million times.
Having offered a tenth part of that as oblations with honey and flour-cake (sapiṣā), one shall bring women and men under one's control. || 49 ||
He states another mantra: "kṣe. The word "vaśya" expresses its application (viniyoga).
The first [syllable] is the seed (bīja), and the middle [syllable] is the power (śakti).
By the repetition of these two verses;
"triniyutam" means three hundred thousand (three lakhs). || 48-49 ||
*Tāra*, *māyā*, followed by *vāgbhava*; then *nityaklinne madadrave*;
ending with *vāṅ*, *māyā*, and *vahnijāyā*—this is the fifteen-syllable mantra. (50)
Again, with two, two, two, and five syllables, one should perform the six limbs, even without speech, by means of the entire [mantra]. || 51 ||
He states the mantra of Nityā as "Tāra" (Om).
"Vāgbhava" is *eṃ*.
Here, one should understand the meters, sages, and so forth mentioned for the mantra of Nityā that will be described immediately hereafter.

The *praṇava* (oṃ) is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*). For the sake of prosperity (*śrī*), it begins with the seed-syllable of Śrī; for the pacification of diseases and the like, it begins with the seed-syllable of Durgā; and for the pacification of suffering and misfortune, it begins with the seed-syllable of Kāma.
The state of being the seed-syllable of Durgā and so forth pertains to the pacification of old age and death;
the state of being the seed-syllable of Kāma pertains to the pacification of suffering and misfortune;
and the state of being Mṛtyuñjaya and so forth pertains to the pacification of old age and death.
Before the word *madadrave*, there is also the employment of the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya-nāma*).
This should be understood to apply to the two mantras that will be mentioned hereafter as well.
The phrase "without speech" (*vācaṃ vinā*) is connected with both instances.

The meaning is that by means of those thirteen syllables, one should form the five limbs (*pañcāṅga*) according to the aforementioned method, and with the remainder taken as a whole, the weapon-mantra (*astra*) is formed.
Then, immediately after this, one should again perform the limb-assignments using the *vāgbhava* [syllable].
This has been stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "By means of one's own phonemes, numbering the [total] syllables of the night and the cruel [aspects], and by oneself, excluding the *vāgbhava*."
Having performed the placement of the six limbs with speech alone, one should again place the limbs.
Thus [ends verses 50–51].
The island was triangular, vast, and enchanting with celestial trees; it was rich with the warbling of cuckoos and gently caressed by the breeze. || 52 ||
Having recollected [the Lord] situated in the midst of the ocean of nectar, amidst bees, flowers, and creepers, with the rising moon and sun, within that pavilion of rubies; || 53 ||
One should contemplate the Goddess, who visibly fascinates the three worlds, seated upon a lotus placed on a jeweled lion-throne with a brilliant triangular base. || 54 ||
Regarding the word "continent" (dvīpa):

the syntactical connection is that one should visualize the Goddess upon a lotus on a jeweled throne within a ruby pavilion, on that continent which is remembered as a triangle situated in the midst of the ocean of wine.
The locative cases are used in a non-co-referential sense in both instances.
"Triangle" refers to one facing downwards.
By the phrase "ocean of wine," this is meant: immediately after the earth [layer] comes the ocean of wine, then the triangle, the island, the ruby pavilion, and the jewel throne.
"One should perform the placement" (nyasyet) refers to the placement of the seats (pīṭha-nyāsa).
The remainder is the same.
This should also be understood for the subsequent mantra.
By the phrase "trailokyamohinīm," the statement of the application (viniyoga) is expressed. || 52-54 ||

One should worship that eternal goddess, who has the young moon as her crest-jewel; she is red in hue, possesses three eyes, and holds in her hands a noose, a goad, a wish-fulfilling creeper, and a skull-cup; she is striking a sweet-toned lute.
By the phrase "striking the *kalavallakī* lute," it is indicated that she has six arms;
the visualization of her weapons, however, is as before. || 55 ||
One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times and then perform oblations with clarified butter;
thereafter, one should worship the pedestal endowed with the four powers for one-tenth of that number.
One should worship Āṃpūrvā Drāviṇī Vāmā in the northeast corner (Śambhukoṇa), and Jyeṣṭhā Āhlādakāriṇī, preceded by the syllable Īṃ, in the southeast (Hutāśana). || 57 ||
One should worship Kṣobhiṇī Raudrī, beginning with the syllable *ūṃ*, in the northwest;
the wise practitioner should worship Guhyaśakti, beginning with the syllable *vāgbhava*, in the center (the northwest wind). || 58 ||
"Endowed with four powers" refers to the four *pīṭha*-powers (*pīṭha-śakti*).
In this context, the terms beginning with "Drāviṇī" are qualifiers for Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī.
The meaning here is that one should install the triad of powers in the corners starting from the northeast (Īśa) and place the fourth in the center.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "One should install these Śaktis in the corners starting from Īśa and in the center.
There is a reading: "In the center, one should worship Guhyaśakti."
The reading "vāyau" should be understood as corrected by [the authority of] knowledge. || 56–58 ||
Having offered an āsana consisting of illusion (māyā) and the rest, one should fashion the image from clay with the root mantra;
there, one should worship the Goddess according to the sequence that will be described. || 59 ||
One should perform the worship of the limbs upon the filaments and worship these [deities] upon the petals:
the first is Nityā, the next Subhadrā, then Maṅgalā, and Naravīriṇī. || 60 ||
Subhagā, Durbhagā, and further Bhūyas; the seventh is Manonmanī. The eighth is Rudrarūpā, and they are all intent upon playing the lute. || 61 ||
Regarding the phrase "beginning with Māyā":
it is stated that after uttering the seed-syllable (bīja) of Bhuvaneśī, the worship of the sacred seat (pīṭhapūjā) is performed with the mantra beginning with "sarvaśakti" and so forth. ||59-60||
Regarding the word "ādyā": the first [of the vowels] is eternal (*nityā*).

Regarding the word "ādau": those which are the first and last among the vowels, as well as the pairs and the neuters—excluding these, the other eight [vowels], when joined with the *bindu*, are the mantras of those [goddesses]. (60–61)
The messengers (dūtīs) are red, enchanting, well-attired, and languid with passion;
they are vowels devoid of initial and final pairs, excluding the neuter ones. || 62 ||
The names of these [five] end with the syllable *bindu* (m); they are Anaṅga, Smara, Manmatha, Kāma, and Māra, who bear five arrows, a noose, a goad, and a bow. || 63 ||
The worship of the five [deities] beginning with Anaṅga is performed all around upon the eight petals;
the visualization of the weapons extends from the lower right to the lower left. || 63 ||
Richly adorned with side-ornaments, red in color, and beautifully decorated, they are to be worshipped;
their seed-syllable is declared to be that of the god of love (Mānmatha), enriched by the emission from the void (vyoma). || 64 ||
Abounding with quivers attached to their other limbs, they have arrows in their back-quivers;
"mānmatha" refers to the seed-syllable of Kāma (klīm); "endowed with the creation of space" means it is joined with the letter *ha* and the *visarga*. || 64 ||
Rati, virati, prīti, aprīti, mati, durmati, dhṛti, vidhṛti, tuṣṭi, and atuṣṭi are recorded as the ten [mental faculties]. || 65 ||
Red in color, holding lutes in their hands, two are stationed on each side of Kāma;
endowed with all ornaments, they should be worshipped, their lotus-faces smiling. || 66 ||
"Rati," and so forth, are the names of the ten Śaktis. (65–66)

The seed-syllable of these [goddesses] consists of the four-faced one (Ga), enriched by the harsh sound (Ra) released from the two lips of the eunuch (E), and possessing the drop (M); outside of these are the Lords of the World (Lokeśvaras) in their proper sequence. 67.
Thus one should worship the Goddess, who is difficult even for the gods to attain;
he obtains supreme sovereignty and is sought after by women.

Regarding "klība": the four neuter vowels are the two *e*s (*ee*). Enriched by these—that is, joined with them—is the four-faced one, the letter *ja*. By means of that, [the seed-syllables are] *jaṃ*, *jāṃ*, *jiṃ*, *jīṃ*, *juṃ*, *jūṃ*, *joṃ*, *jauṃ*.
The mantras are "jaṃ jaḥ" and so forth. The word "respectively" (kramāt) connects back to the preceding [verse].
Even though not explicitly mentioned, the world-protectors (lokeśas) and their weapons (astras) are also to be worshipped.
Because it was stated in general terms in the fourth chapter [of the *Guhyasamāja-tantra*], verses 67–68.

The seed-syllable of Vāgbhava, the seed-syllable of Mānmatha, "Nityaklinne," followed again by "Madau," "Drave," and the mantra of the Consort of Fire (Raktā)—this is declared to be the twelve-syllabled mantra. || 69 ||
The seer is Sammohana, the metre is Nivṛt, and the deity is Nityā.
Having performed the six limbs (of the ritual) with speech, one should meditate upon Nityā, the bestower of one's own desired goals. || 70 ||
He states another mantra: "Vāk" (Speech).
The two "madas" are the letters *ma* and *da*.
*Klīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*).
"Vācayet" means "with the Vāgbhava [bīja]. "Joined with the six long Kāmabījas" is the statement of the supreme gurus.
"The bestower of one's own desired [object]" is the statement regarding its application (viniyoga). || 69-70 ||
I bow to her who has the crescent moon upon her head, who is crimson in hue, who is worshipped by the immortals, who holds a lotus, a noose, a goad, and a full skull-cup in her hands,
whose body, garments, and ornaments are red, and who possesses three eyes.
One should meditate upon the consort of Śiva, her limbs overwhelmed by intoxication.
Having recited [the mantra] four hundred thousand times, one should at the end offer ten thousand oblations with Madhūka flowers smeared with honey, and thus satisfy one's own preceptor. || 72 ||
"Half-moon" refers to the crescent;
"goad" refers to the hook;
"full" refers to [the vessel] filled with wine.
The meditation on the weapons is as before. || 71–72 ||
One should worship the Goddess at the Śaktipīṭha according to the method that will be described;
one should worship the limbs as before, and thereafter worship these Śaktis.
Nityā, Nirañjanā, Klinnā, Kledinī, Madanāturā, Madadravā, Drāviṇī, and Draviṇī—these are the eight powers (śaktis). || 74 ||

One should worship the world-protectors (Lokapālas) in the outer [circle], endowed with their respective mounts and weapons; they have eyes like red lotuses and hands adorned with blue lotuses and skull-cups. || 75 ||
The practitioner of mantra, lying upon his bed, should recite the perfected mantra one thousand times;
whatever woman he contemplates during the night, she arrives at that very moment.
Regarding "Śaktipīṭha":
the meaning is that the nine Śaktis mentioned in the context of the Śaktipīṭha are to be worshipped here.
"As before" means according to the method described in the fourth [chapter].
Regarding the phrase "raktāmbujekṣaṇā," one may also read it as "raktāmbujaprabhā. (73–76)

Following *vāṅmāyā*, [the mantra] consists of the syllables *nitye bhūyo klinne madadrave*, ending with *dviṭha* (svāhā), totaling twelve syllables; this mantra bestows subjugation (*vaśya*). || 77 ||
The sage is said by the sages to be Aṅgiras, the metre is Triṣṭubh, and the deity is declared to be Vajraprastāriṇī, the bestower of desired boons. || 78 ||
He states the Vajraprastāriṇī mantra as "vāk" and so forth;
"vāk" means the source of speech (vāgbhava).
Others apply the terms in this same manner.
After *māyā*, [the word] *klinne* again; afterwards, the word *vāk*.
Then *nityā*; this is a case of an indeclinable (avibhaktika) reference.
Then *madadrave*.
Ṭhaḥ is the bindu, dviṭhaḥ is two bindus, and visarga is the emission (sarga). Since it is said that "emission is Śakti," this is the seed-syllable (bīja) of Bhuvaneśī.
Since it is stated that "the number of syllables of the sun" means twelve syllables, the *aṅkuśa* seed-syllable follows the *vāgbhava*.
By this, the following is expressed:
first *māyā*, then *klinne*, then the *vāgbhava* and the *aṅkuśa*, and then *nityamadadrave*.
Then follows the seed-syllable of Māyā.

As stated by the Teachers: "Smara (s), Dīrgha (ī), Adhara (u), Arka (ra), Agni (ra), Ūm (ū), Dīrgha (ī), It (i), Pakṣa (ya), Mad (ma), Dad (da), Ra (ra), Lānta (la), Śiva (ha)—this twelve-syllabled mantra is said to be restrained on both sides by Śakti. Thus it is declared.

Also in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "In the *klinna* [state] are speech and the goad; in the *nitya* [state] are sound and time; in the *dadrava* [state] are the wife, the mistress, and power—this is obstructed."
Others say that [the mantra] beginning with *māyā* consists of eleven syllables, excluding *vāgbhava*.
This is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The two *sākṣitvacau*, *klinne*, *kāla*, *atri*, and *drave śiraḥ*."
And the Teachers [state]: "Between the two *nīdrās*, there are the *madās* and the *śiras*;
likewise, there is the *māyā* and so forth."
Both mantras are indeed traditional. The procedure to be described hereafter is the same for all.
In the first mantra, *vāk* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*).
In the second mantra, *vāk* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and *māyā* is the power (*śakti*). In the third, *māyā* is the seed-syllable and *svāhā* is the power.
The terms *vaśya* and *abhīṣṭada* express the application (*viniyoga*). || 77-78 ||
The best of mantra-knowers should perform the six-limbed ritual with the Vāgbhava syllable;
thereafter, with a concentrated mind, he should meditate upon Vajraprastāriṇī.
Regarding the phrase "by means of Vāgbhava," the supreme teachers maintain that it is joined with the Māyā-bīja [Hrīm] along with the six long vowels.
However, in the case of the second mantra:
"Or with two, one, two, and again two;
the mantra-practitioner should apply the ritual of the limbs (aṅgavidhi) by means of the mantra-syllables conjoined with the [seed-]classes.
In this view, "with the Vāgbhava [syllable]" is the understood supplement for "the head."
Thus is the application of the verse regarding the six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*). By the phrase "the best of mantra-knowers," the ancillaries mentioned in other tantras are indicated.

They are as follows: *āhlādinī* at the heart, *klinne* at the head, *kledini* at the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *nitye* for the armor (*varma*), *mada* for the eyes (*netra*), and *drave* for the weapon (*astra*). (79)
Seated upon a red lotus with eight petals in the midst of a red ocean and a red boat,

she has a red body, a crescent moon shimmering upon her red crown, a smiling face, and three eyes; in her hands, she holds a citron, an arrow, a noose, a goad, a beautiful bow of love, and a skull-cup.
We take refuge in Ambikā, who bears [the crescent moon], whose limbs are bent low, and who is bowed down by the weight of her breasts. || 80 ||

The practitioner of mantras should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; at the conclusion of the recitation, he should then perform ten thousand oblations with excellent sacrificial fuel-sticks made from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree and sprinkled with clarified butter. || 81 ||
By the phrase "in the red ocean," this is what is meant:
immediately after the earth, one should place the red ocean, the red boat, and the sun-petal lotus during the ritual placement of the seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*).
The remainder is the same.
The arrow is the shaft;
the bow of Madana is the sugarcane bow.
Regarding the visualization of the weapons: from the upper left [hand] proceed the noose, the bow, and the skull-cup; from the upper right [hand] proceed the goad, the arrow, and the citron.
Some say that in the second mantra, a pomegranate (*dāḍima*) is to be substituted for the citron (*bījapūra*).
"Bearing the weight of her breasts" means possessing an abundance of them; because of that, she has limbs bent low. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), red fragrance is implied.
He himself was likewise dressed in such attire.
As it has been said:
"The Goddess is to be worshipped at the Śaktipīṭha with flowers and red unguents."
"He himself also has his limbs adorned.
Thus, in the third [act], the limbs and the meditative absorption (dhyāna) are as follows:
The ritual procedure for the limbs is prescribed with pairs of colors.
[She is] as previously described, holding the gesture of fearlessness, a noose, a goad, and a skull-cup.
With the best of sacrificial fuels, that is, with the most excellent pieces of wood. || 80-82 ||
One should worship the Goddess at the Śaktipīṭha with red flowers and other offerings;
the limbs (aṅgas) are to be worshipped on the filaments (kesaras), and these [deities] on the petals (dalas). || 82 ||
Hṛllekhā, Kledinī, Klinnā, Kṣobhiṇī, Madanāturā, Nirañjanā, Rāgavatī, and the seventh, Madanāvatī. || 83 ||
Mekhalā, Drāviṇī, and after them Vegavatī are remembered as the others.
These Śaktis, bearing skull-bowls and lotuses, possess bodies of red hue. || 84 ||
He speaks of the offering to the limbs (*āvaraṇapūjā*) with the words "the limbs" (*aṅgāni*).
Those limbs which have been mentioned in general should be placed upon the filaments (*kesara*);
the remainder [of the location] is "in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) above the triangle."
For it is stated thus in the *Nārāyaṇīya* regarding meditative absorption (*dhyāna*): "She who dwells in the Red Ocean, who moves upon a boat, and who resides in the lotus born from the moon."
And it has been said: "She is to be worshipped in sequence with these limbs (aṅgas), powers (śaktis), and lords of the directions (āśādhipas).
Furthermore, in another Tantra, after describing the pedestal (pīṭha) as having a triangle, a hexagon, and twelve petals—
First, one should worship the limbs; then, one should worship those situated within the triangle. After that, one should worship those known as Will, Knowledge, and Action within the hexagons.
"One should worship the Ḍākinīs and others, as well as Hṛllekhā and others, in the twelve [petals].
Thus,
there are twelve Smaras.
The appearance of two dots as lines in manuscripts is due to the error of the scribe.
And it is stated in the Nārāyaṇīya: "Mekhalā, Drāviṇī, Vegavatī, and Kāma—these are remembered [as such]."
The teachers also have stated: "Twelve [forms] are declared to be with memory.
For this very reason, they are called "powers" (śaktis).
Otherwise, he would have spoken merely of meditation (*dhyāna*). Therefore, the intention is that this is the meditation on the *śaktis*,
whereas Smara is the well-known [conventional] meditation.
"Red-bodied" means having a reddish-hued body. || 82-84 ||

The Mothers should be worshipped in the cardinal and intermediate directions, and the lords of the directions should be worshipped again; the practitioner of mantra should daily revere the mantra with devotion through worship and other rites. || 85 ||
Freed from poverty and disease, he shall live for a hundred autumns;
the practitioner devoted to this mantra shall bring the entire world under his control. || 86 ||
The wise man should daily perform the rinsing of his mouth with mantras;
the intelligent one should wear consecrated collyrium and the meritorious *tilaka*. || 87 ||
The practitioner who should consume consecrated betel-leaf will become beloved by the world.
"The Mothers in the cardinal and intermediate directions"—
this is merely a specification of the location outside the twelve petals.
By that [method], beginning from the front (purobhāga) and proceeding clockwise, the worship of the Mothers is performed within the square in the eight directions.
"The lords of the directions" (digīśvarāḥ) is an indicator for their weapons.

In the third [enclosure], however, is the worship of the retinue (āvaraṇapūjā), first with the limbs (aṅgaiḥ), then with the eight powers mentioned in the previous mantra, the world-protectors (lokapāla), and their weapons.
"Having been initiated, one should mutter this mantra a hundred thousand times;
thereafter, one should perform oblations ten thousand times with Madhūka flowers mixed with honey, or else with clarified butter. (85–87)
The practitioner of mantra, consisting of the three seed-syllables, is proclaimed by Śrī, Māyā, and Madana. || 88 ||
The seer is Sammohana, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Manu.
The six limbs are assigned in sequence by repeating those same seed-syllables in the form known as Tripuṭā. || 89 ||
He states the Traipuṭa mantra with the word "Śrī.
The term "Sammohana" is illustrative;
it should be understood that Bhṛgu, Śakti, and Sammohana are the seers (ṛṣis).
The first is the seed-syllable (bīja), the second is the power (śakti). || 88-89 ||

One should meditate upon the Goddess seated beneath the Kalpavṛkṣa tree in the delightful Pārijāta grove, within a pavilion with jeweled floors, upon a gentle throne of gems, and on a lotus adorned with six angles. || 90 ||
Regarding the word *pārijāte*:

the grammatical construction is that one should meditate upon the Goddess seated upon a lotus on a jeweled throne (*ratnasiṃhāsana*) on a jeweled floor (*maṇikuṭṭima*), beneath a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) in a pavilion within the Pārijāta grove.
The locative cases here are used with different substrata (*vyadhikaraṇya*).
On a four-petalled and an eight-petalled lotus;
therein, the four-petalled [lotus] is in the pericarp of the six-cornered [figure], and the other [eight-petalled one] is in its pericarp.
And it is said in the Nārāyaṇīya: "One should worship her on the four-petalled [lotus] and her on the lotus situated within the six-cornered [figure]."
Thus it is said. Furthermore, this is what is meant:
immediately thereafter, one should worship the Golden Ground, the Pārijāta Grove, the Jewel Pavilion, the Jeweled Terrace, and the Jewel Lion Throne.
The rest is the same.
"On a jeweled floor fashioned from the earth, radiant with fresh gold, beneath a wish-fulfilling tree"—so it is stated by the Teacher [Ācārya]. (90)
Holding a bow, a noose, lotuses, and a goad, as well as flower-arrows in her lotus-like hands; she wears a jeweled crown, has three eyes,
possesses the luster of a golden lotus, is bent by the weight of her breasts, and is adorned with jeweled anklets and a girdle.
One should meditate upon the primordial Śakti, whose body shines with necklaces and other ornaments. || 91 ||
The bow is a sugarcane bow.
The visualization of the weapons extends from the lower left hand to the lower right hand.
As it has been stated by the Teachers: "One should meditate [on the deity] holding a pair of lotuses, a noose, a goad, and a sugarcane bow."
[She who holds] a bow with flower-tipped arrows, possessing the color of fresh gold. Thus [ends verse 91].
She was surrounded by female messengers who carried fly-whisks, mirrors, betel-boxes, and small caskets, their breasts heaving with emotion;
she gazed upon the practitioner with a look that rained down the nectar of compassion. || 92 ||
"Tāmbūlakaraṇḍaka" is one [item].
"Samudgaka" is a casket, a small box, a vessel for storing perfumes and the like.
"By female messengers" (dūtībhiḥ).
Ghṛṇinī, Sūryā, Ādityā, and Prabhāvatī— these four reside upon the four petals starting from the northeast (saumya). They too possess two arms.
In the right hand there is a fly-whisk and so forth, and in the left hand the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*).
As it has been said:
"The boon-granting gesture (*vara*) is always declared to be the common [gesture] for a hand that is unarmed."
"And fearlessness.
Thus it is said.
However, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*, the state of having joined palms is mentioned: "And those female messengers with joined palms..."
"Saumyā, Ghṛṇinī, Sūryā, Ādityā, and Prabhāvatī.
Thus [ends verse 92].
One should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times, or ten thousand times, while offering excellent sacrificial fuel-sticks made from *bilva* and *āragvadha* wood, smeared with honey. || 93 ||
One should offer oblations with *japā* flowers and satisfy the Guru with wealth;
one should worship her according to the prescribed rite upon a pedestal (*pīṭha*) established for Hṛllekhā. || 94 ||
One should worship Lakṣmī and the others in the six triangles beginning with the southeast:
Lakṣmī, who has the luster of gold, is slender, and holds a lotus, a jewel, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. || 95 ||
[One should meditate on] Hari, who resembles gold and holds a discus, conch, mace, and lotus;
and Gaurī, who is as red as the hibiscus flower and holds a noose, goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons. || 96 ||
[He beheld] Hara, who holds a deer, a skull-topped staff, the gesture of fearlessness, and his desired [objects], resembling gold;
and the gentle Rati, golden-hued, holding a blue lotus in her hand. || 97 ||
One should worship Smara, who is reddish-brown and holds a noose, a goad, a bow, and five arrows;
on both sides, as before, one should worship the pair of treasures.
"Bhānulakṣa" means twelve hundred thousand.
"Āragvadha" is the *rājavṛkṣa*.
By the phrase "according to the procedure," the drawing of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) within the yantra as taught in other tantras is indicated.
As it is stated in the Saṃhitā:
"Having first drawn a hexagon, the wise one should write the Vidyā in the center;
he should then write it repeatedly in the corners of the hexagon in successive order."
"On the outside, one should make an eight-petaled lotus adorned with the long vowels;
one should draw a square mandala adorned with four doors. Thus [it is said].
*Ṭaṅka* means an axe.
The archer is the bow. The meditation on weapons should be understood according to their respective categories [as described in verses 93–98].
Having fully worshipped the external [deities], one should worship the Mothers upon the petals;
one should worship the World-Protectors in female form, with gentle appearances. || 99 ||
"As before" refers to meditation together with the Śakti.
"On both sides" means on the sides of the hexagon. This concludes the enclosure (āvaraṇa).
"Outside" means on the filaments of the eight-petaled lotus [surrounding] the hexagon.
By the phrase "of gentle form," it is implied—as stated in another tantra—that they are "those praised for the propitiation of the Goddess who is intoxicated with exalted youth. (99)
Thus, he who constantly worships the Goddess, endowed with devotion, shall attain divine poetic talent and obtain boundless prosperity. (100)
"Having obtained incomparable good fortune, may one sport for a very long time on earth"—
here, *kavitām* (poetic skill) signifies the primacy of the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable (*aiṃ*). "Having attained prosperity" (*lakṣmīm*) signifies the primacy of the *śrī* seed-syllable (*hrīṃ*).

As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The mantra that bestows fortune (*śrī*) and brings about subjugation (*vaśya*) consists of the seed-syllable of the power (*śakti*) of the desire for fortune (*śrīkāma*).
Here, "fortune" (*saubhāgya*) refers to the state of beginning with the syllable of desire (*kāma*) and having the syllable of *māyā* in the middle.
If, however, [the mantra] ends with Māyā, it is included within the Tripurā-mantras.
Thus, when it consists of both Śakti and so forth, it should be known as "glorious" (yaśaskara).
One should also perform the ancillaries (aṅgas) beginning with the same seed-syllable (bīja) as the mantra begins. (100–101)
The noose, the goad, the hollowed palms, the spear, the jhīṇṭīśa, the sky, and the eye. || 101 ||
Ending with the word *parameśvarī*, followed by two *ṭha*s (the syllable *svāhā*), and preceded by the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), this mantra of Aśvārūḍhā is said to consist of thirteen syllables. || 102 ||
With two, one, and one; with two and five syllables—one should form the six limbs with these two [groups], and thereafter one should meditate upon the Goddess. || 103 ||
He states the mantra for the one mounted on a horse as "pāśa," etc.
"Pāśa" is *aṃ*, the "goad" is *kroṃ*, and "power" is the seed-syllable of Māyā (*hrīṃ*). Thus, it consists of three syllables beginning with "pāśa.
Since it is stated that there are thirteen syllables, it should be understood that the mantra is not enclosed by two "pāśas" at the beginning and end.
*Jhiṇṭīśaḥ* (the letter *jha*), *e*, *gaganaṃ* (the letter *ha*), and *haḥ* together with *sadṛk* (*sa*) and *ikāra* (*i*). Therefore, it is so.
The traditionalists state that there is a repetition of this word *ehi* and that it begins with the speech (*vāk*, i.e., *ai*).

Others, however, having recited three quarters of a verse from the numbers four (*abdhi*), five (*śara*), and five (*bāṇa*), conclude with *dviṭha* (*kṣa*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*, *u*), *māyā* (*ī*), the noose (*pāśa*, *pha*), and the *praṇava* (*oṃ*).
"O slayer of Vṛtra, whatever the sun has risen over today,
all that is under your control, O Indra"— this is the Ṛgvedic verse.
Its seer is Brahmā, its meter is Virāṭ, its seed-syllable is Om (Praṇava), and its power is Svāhā.

Others consider the ten-syllabled mantra to be that which was previously mentioned: "One should place the syllables in sequence upon the head, forehead, eyes, tip of the nose, mouth, throat, heart, navel, the base of the *dhvaja*, and the feet.
The placement of the thirteen syllables is as follows: "Upon the head, forehead, *ājñā*, ears, eyes, tip of the nose, mouth, fingers, and [the rest]."
