"One should place the syllables at the heart, navel, base of the banner (the genitals), and the feet. Thus [it is said].
With the ten-syllable mantra containing the six long vowels, one performs the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
The traditionalists (*sāmpradāyika*) state that even for the six-footed mantras mentioned in the *Grantha*, there should be the application of the six long vowels.

The meditation on the ten-syllable mantra: [One should meditate upon] the auspicious Śivā, who is ruddy, seated upon a ruddy lotus, clad in ruddy garments and ornaments, four-armed, three-eyed, and possessing a gracious countenance.
She holds a sword, a shield, and a staff in her right and left hands;
below [the staff] there should be a golden cane, and above it is situated a noose.
Then, having bound the victim with a noose around the neck and seized him with a cane,
he was made to wander in the sky with hands joined in *añjali*, and finally cast down at the practitioner's feet.
One should meditate upon her as drawing [it] toward herself.
Thus [ends the section on verses 101–103].
Mounted upon a red horse, wearing a crescent moon as her crest-ornament, three-eyed,

she binds the victim with a noose and leads him away with her right hand while he is rendered helpless by the arrows of Love; with her other hand she holds a beautiful staff made of excellent gold— thus one should meditate on her who is so enchanting.
One should meditate incessantly upon the Goddess, who is bent by the weight of her breasts and made beautiful by divine necklaces. 104.
He describes the meditation on the thirteen-syllable mantra with the words "raktām" (red) and so forth.
"Aśva" means a red horse.
It should be understood that the practitioner binds the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—who is overwhelmed by the arrows of the God of Love—by the neck with a noose.
"Having bound her by the neck with a noose," so it is said. Furthermore, she is being led away by another hand—the left one. Again, how is she qualified?
Holding a cane in her right hand;
as it has been said: "Mounted upon a horse, holding a staff made of fresh gold at the tip of her hand, she leads [the way] with her other right hand."
Thus [ends the verse]. 104.
One who has conquered the senses should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with clarified butter at the end;
he should perform oblations amounting to one-tenth of that number and worship the Goddess in the Śaktipīṭha. || 105 ||

By means of the ritual procedure described for the three-syllable mantra beginning with *pāśa*, the practitioner, being composed in mind, obtains his desired fruit by offering oblations of rice enriched with clarified butter. ||106||
One should subjugate kings with salt sprinkled with honey and gold;
by that same procedure, the mantra-practitioner may also subjugate a woman. || 107 ||
"Bāṇalakṣa" means five hundred thousand [repetitions].

Regarding the ten-syllable mantra, however: "Eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should recite it one hundred thousand times according to the number of its syllables, and perform a fire-oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth that amount."
"O Dear One, one should perform [the rite] with *palāśa* leaves, or with *javā* flowers, or with safflower, or with clarified butter, or with other red flowers.
As for the worship: it consists of a pair of five-petaled lotuses, joined with a hexagon and an eight-petaled lotus.
O Dear One, it consists of two squares joined by two doors.
Having fashioned the maṇḍala, one should invoke that Goddess here and worship her with the limbs [of the mantra],
the arrows, sound and the other objects of sense, and with the supreme rites of attraction and union.
And by means of the senses beginning with hearing and ending with the intellect, as well as the final ones— attraction and so forth—
one [perceives] the vital breath, the self, power, consciousness, mind, ego, and the states of being.
"And the body [is placed] upon the eight petals, followed by the words of the *ākarṣaṇī* mantra;
then the world-protectors beginning with Brāhmī, and their weapons outside of that.
And as for the yantra: "Having constructed a yantra consisting of a triangle, a hexagon, and a circle, together with an outer circle..."
In the center of that, one should first draw the Vidyā and then the rest.
One should place the three colors within the triangles and the six syllables within the hexagons;
then, one should encircle the Mātṛkā in sequence along the path of the outer circle.

Thus, by arranging them in the middle, one should fashion ten yantras; through the performance of recitation (japa), worship, and ritual offerings (sampāta), one shall accomplish subjugation (vaśya), attraction (ākarṣaṇa), wealth, women,
the earth, jewels, fame, good fortune, treasures, and beauty.
Thus [ends the section]. 105–107.
Having drawn squares numbering the transformations within a central group of four, one should write the Praṇava together with the name of the person to be accomplished;
in the other [squares], one should write the twelve syllables of the mantra—this is the Yantra that brings all under control.
Regarding the yantra, he says "having written" (*ālikhya*).
The modification (*vikāra*) is sixteenfold.
"One should write" means starting from the tip and proceeding clockwise. || 108 ||

One should utter the word *māheśvari* at the end of *bhagavati* preceded by *māyā* (hrīṃ). Then, for *annapūrṇe*, one should say the pair of *ṭha*s (ṭhaṭha). This mantra consists of seventeen syllables.
One should perform the limb-protections (*aṅga*) with *māyā*, and thereafter meditate upon the Goddess. || 109 ||
He states the mantra of Annapūrṇā as "māyā" and so forth.
"Hṛt" means *namaḥ*.
Here, it should be understood that when the letter *s* of the word *namaḥ* undergoes the *ru*-substitution (*rorutva*) and the subsequent *guṇa*, the result is the vowel *u*.
*ṭha-yugalaṃ svāhā*.
Since it is stated here that there are seventeen syllables, the *yaṇ*-substitution does not apply to *ri-a*. Some authorities say that this [mantra] begins with the *praṇava* (oṃ).
Brahmā is the seer, Anuṣṭubh is the meter, Māyā is the seed-syllable, and Svāhā is the power;
[the mantra] is formed with "Māyayā" joined with the six long vowels. || 109 ||
Beholding her— red-complexioned, clad in variegated garments, with a crescent moon as her crest-ornament,
intent on bestowing food, and bowed by the weight of her breasts—
as she dances while gazing upon him who is adorned with a crescent moon;
One should worship the joyful Goddess, the destroyer of the suffering of worldly existence.
"Devoted to the giving of food"—this is the statement regarding the ritual application (viniyoga). [He meditates on] Śiva, whose ornament is the crescent moon. || 110 ||
One should recite the mantra according to the prescribed rule eight thousand times;
immediately thereafter, one should offer oblations of food mixed with ghee in a quantity equal to one-tenth of that number. || 111 ||
One should worship the Goddess at Śaktipīṭha with the weapons of Maṅgalalokeśvara;
every morning, one should daily recite this mantra one hundred and eight times. || 112 ||
The abundance of food for this [practitioner] shall be even greater than that of Śiriyā;
"according to rule" means by the path described in the *puraścaraṇa*.
"A pair of eight thousand" means sixteen thousand.
Of this practitioner. || 111-113 ||
Māyā, the word Padmāvatī, and then the beloved of Agni (Svāhā). || 113 ||
The mantra consisting of seven syllables is declared to bestow control over all;
one should perform the ritual applications (aṅgas) with the Māyā-bīja and meditate upon the Enchantress of the Three Worlds. 114.
He states the mantra of Padmāvatī as "māyā.
"Sarvavaśyā" is the statement of its application (viniyoga).
"Trailokyamohinī" is also [a name].
Brahmā is the seer, Gāyatrī is the meter, Māyā is the seed-syllable, and Svāhā is the power.
Here too, "by means of Māyā" is as before. (113–114)
I worship Padmāvatī, who sits in the lotus posture, holding two red lotuses with her lotus-like hands, possessing three eyes, adorned with ornaments, red in hue, and having a face like a lotus. (115)
He states the meditation on Padmāvatī with the words "Padme" and so forth. || 115 ||
One should recite the mantra for one hundred thousand repetitions and perform a fire sacrifice with clarified butter ten times that amount;
one should worship the Goddess upon the Śaktipīṭha together with her limbs and the surrounding retinues. || 116 ||
The worship of the limbs (aṅgapūjā) should take place upon the filaments; the Mothers are to be worshipped on the petals;
the world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be worshipped outside, and their weapons (astras) further outside.
Thus, he who worships the mantra through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, shall become fortunate among all women, like another Kāmadeva. || 118 ||
One hundred thousand is a *pakṣa*; two hundred thousand is a *lakṣa*. || 116–118 ||

Having inscribed the Śakti-mantra in the center of a hexagon and the remaining six syllables in its corners, this Padmāvatīyantra is highly praised when surrounded externally by the Mātṛkā-letters. ||119||
He describes the yantra: "Having six spokes," etc. (119).
Having placed the *tāra* (om) on the head and meditated upon the goddess Bhāratī,
one should place the seed-syllable of Śakti on the forehead while recollecting Bhuvaneśvarī.
Having meditated upon the Sun and Fire, one should place *Ama* (the letter A) upon the two eyes;
then, recollecting the Moon, one should place [the letters] ending with *Ṭa* (Ṭha) upon the face using the mouth-circle. || 121 ||
One should place the seed-syllable of Ramā upon the tongue while meditating upon her;
the wise practitioner should then place the two syllables of Svāhā on the cheeks with the thought that they are the lordly elephants of that goddess.
A man who performs this daily placement known as Amaṭha will certainly become a beloved of fame, fortune, beauty, and intelligence. || 123 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Śāradātilaka* composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇa Deśikendra. 10.
Regarding the *amathanyāsa*, he says "tāra" and so forth: *aṃ* is the nasal drop (*bindu*), and *aḥ* is the emission (*visarga*).
"By means of the *mukhavṛtta*" means "in the *mukhavṛtta* [meter]";
in some places, the reading is "*mukhe vṛttena*". This means that one should place [the syllables] in the mouth by means of the *vṛtta*, that is, in the form of a *vṛtta*.

"Ending in *ṭa*" means the letter *ṭha*. "With the thought of that lordly elephant" means with the perception of Lakṣmī’s lordly elephant. Because it is stated thus, the respective meditations for each instance should be understood according to their specific context.

In that regard, this ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed by contracting the index, ring, and little fingers, while joining the middle fingers and thumbs so that they take the form of an elephant's trunk.
"One should perform [this meditation]"—such is the instruction of the traditional teachers.

As for the meditation on Gajendra: "I worship the two elephants, white as a star, a jasmine flower, or the moon; fierce with rutting ichor flowing from their temples; enriched by the beauty of their shimmering trunks; and possessing gleaming tusks."
Thus [ends the section]. 120–122.
By the phrase "Kīrtiśrī," its independence is expressed.
Regarding that, the ritual application is as follows: Oṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī;
Hrīṃ, salutation to Umā.
Aṃ, to the solar maṇḍala; Aḥ, to the fiery maṇḍala;
Vaṃ, to the lunar maṇḍala.
Śrīṃ, svāṃ to Śrī;
hāṃ to Dantin. The meter, seer, and other details for this [mantra] are as follows:
For the *amaṭhaśrī* mantra, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is the seer (*ṛṣi*),
Bṛhatī is the meter (*chandaḥ*),
and Amaṭhaśrī is the deity (*devatā*).
*Hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *śrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*). The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of bringing all under control. *Oṃ śrīṃ* is the heart.
Śrīkari is for the head;
Dhanakari is for the crest-lock;
Dhānyakari is for the armor.
The eye is the producer of supernatural power; the weapon is the producer of nourishment. 120–123.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition. 10.
Now begins the eleventh chapter. Next, I shall declare the mantra of Durgā, which bestows both seen and unseen fruits.
Māyā (ī), joined with Atri (u) and enriched by the Bindu (m), becomes this [syllable] "mū" once again, which possesses creation. || 1 ||

Ending with the word *pañca*, established in the wind (*māruta*), and seated upon the element of earth (*bhautika*), this mantra consists of eight syllables, beginning with *tāra* (om) and ending with *hṛdaya* (namaḥ). || 2 ||
The seer is Nārada, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Manu’s Durgā, who is proclaimed by the virtuous as the remover of misfortunes. || 3 ||

Having thus stated the eternal mantras, and because the twelve-fold mantra of Durgā’s seed-syllable has been mentioned, he begins to state the Durgā mantras with the word "tataḥ" (then). He extracts the mantra with the word "māyā": *māyā* is the seed-syllable of Śakti.
The letter *da* belongs to Atri, the letter *u* is Karṇa, and the *bindu* is the *anusvāra*; by the word "endowed with this" (*etadāḍhya*), *duṃ* is indicated.
Furthermore, that same letter *du* is "possessing emission" (*sargavān*), meaning it is joined with the *visarga*.
By this, it is suggested that such is also the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
It is for this very reason that the expression "possessing creation" (sargavān) is used;
however, in the mantra, there is only the letter *ra*,
because the prefix (*upasarga*) has such a form.
The letter *ga* is the ender of the five [vowels]. It is endowed with stability (*pratiṣṭhā*) and joined with the vowel *ā*.
Thus, it becomes *gā*.

The letter *ya* is Māruta (the Wind); the letter *e* is Bhautika (the Elemental), and its seat is that [Wind], hence *yai*. As it has been said: "The seed-syllables of Tāra, Māyā, and Svāhā, followed by 'to Durgā' and ending with the Heart-mantra."
Thus say the traditionalists; they state that after the seed-syllable of Māyā comes the seed-syllable of Kāma.
*Duṃ* is the seed-syllable, and *Māyā* is the power (*śakti*).
With the words beginning with "durita," the statement of the application [of the mantra] is made. || 1-3 ||
The practitioner, using the root mantra devoid of the *namaskāra*, should perform the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) according to the rule, together with *hrām* and the other syllables. || 4 ||

"Namaskāra" means with the root mantra devoid of the word "namaskāra. The connection is that one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) together with *hrāṃ* and so forth— that is, with *hrāṃ hrīṃ* and the rest.
The ritual application (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: *Oṃ hrīṃ duṃ durgāyai hrāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*;
*Oṃ hrīṃ duṃ durgāyai hrīṃ śirase svāhā*, and so forth. As it has been said:
"Tāra and Māyā [are for] Durgā; [the assignment of the limbs] begins and ends with Hrām and so forth.
Regarding this, the commentators have explained that by the word "ca" (and), there is an inclusion of the seed-syllable of Durgā.
As it says: "vidhi" etc.
This indicates the six-limbed mudrā of Śakti. || 4 ||
Seated upon a lion, crowned with the moon, and adorned with three eyes, she holds a conch, a discus, a bow, and an arrow in her four arms which resemble emeralds;
she is graced by armlets, necklaces, bracelets, jingling girdles, and tinkling anklets.
May Durgā, who removes misfortune and whose earrings gleam with jewels, be for your protection. || 5 ||

Regarding the phrase "siṃhasthā" (seated upon a lion): the meditation on the weapons is as follows—[the first two] in the upper [hands] starting from the left, and [the remaining two] in the lower ones.
The analysis of the compound is: she by whom armlets (*aṅgada*) and other ornaments are "āmukta" (fastened) and "dhṛta" (worn).
An evil destiny is a wicked rebirth and poverty.
Among all the mantras of Durgā, this mudrā should be displayed immediately after meditation:
having formed a fist with both hands, place the right hand over the left.
"Having placed [it] upon the head and worshipped, this is declared to be the Durgā-mudrā. Thus [ends the section on] the display of the weapon-mudrās. 5.

One who has conquered the senses should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, or, being self-controlled, should offer oblations of sesame seeds mixed with honey or milk-rice in that same number of thousands.
In this manner, one should properly worship the Pīṭha, endowed with the nine Śaktis:
Prabhā, Māyā, Jayā, Sūkṣmā, Viśuddhā, and again Nandinī. || 7 ||
Suprabhā, Vijayā, and Sarvasiddhidā—these are the nine Śaktis. One should worship them with the vowels, excluding the three short vowels and the neuter (visarga). || 8 ||
A hundred thousand is eight lakhs;
with milk-rice (*payodhas*), that is, with *pāyasa*;
a thousand of those is eight thousand.
"In this manner" means by the method that will be explained hereafter. "Bestower of all accomplishments" (*sarvasiddhidā*) is a name for Śakti.
The visualization (*dhyāna*) of these [goddesses] is described elsewhere as follows:

These [deities] are all red in color like the hibiscus flower, with smiling faces, and consist of six syllables beginning with *e* (ekāra) joined with the first vowels (*ādi-svara*) and the moon (*indu*).
"Holding bows, arrows, and joined palms, adorned with white garlands and unguents, they should be worshipped in sequence within the petals at the end of the three-fold self.
Thus [it is said]. "Ajmi" means...
The three short vowels are *a*, *i*, and *u*, along with the neuter [vowels]. This means by the nine vowels consisting of the vowel-letters (*aj*) excluding those.
As for the application:
"Āṃ, obeisance to Prabhā," and so forth. (6–8)

After the *praṇava*, [the mantra] "to him whose weapons are diamond-claws and fangs, to the Great Lion," followed by the armor-mantra (*varma*), the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and prostration (*nati*)—this is considered the Lion-mantra (*siṃhamanu*). || 9 ||
One should offer a seat with this [mantra] and fashion the image with the root mantra;
having invoked the Goddess into that image, the knower of mantras should worship her. || 10 ||

He states the lion-mantra: "With the Praṇava," meaning that after [the initial] Praṇava, one should utter the Praṇava again. "To the one whose weapons are diamond-claws and fangs" and "to the Lion" constitute the essential form [of the mantra].
The armor is *huṃ*, the weapon is *phaṭ*;
the word of salutation is *namaḥ*. || 9-10 ||
Having first worshipped the armor of the limbs (aṅgāvṛti), one should worship the Śaktis upon the petals:
Jayā, Vijayā, Kīrti, Prīti, and then Prabhā. || 11 ||

Faith (śraddhā), intelligence (medhā), and sacred learning (śruti) are proclaimed [as the first three]; beginning with the initial letter of each of their own names, one should worship the eight weapons in due order upon the tips of the petals. || 12 ||
The discus, conch, mace, sword, noose, goad, arrow, and bow;
then the Lords of the World (Lokeśvaras) on the outside, and immediately after them their weapons. || 13 ||
"Having worshipped" is according to the fourth method.
"Victory! Regarding these, their visualization is described elsewhere:

Resembling shining emeralds, all of them adorned with the moon, holding in their hands an arrow, a trident, a bow, and a threatening forefinger—Jayā and the others should be worshipped, joined with the syllables beginning with *jaṃ* and so forth. Thus [ends the section]. 11–13.

In this manner, once the mantra has been mastered through recitation and other means, the practitioner of mantras who is skilled in the ritual procedures should perform the applications he desires by means of this mantra. || 14 ||
"One who knows the ritual procedures should perform the applications.
By this it is meant:
[the mantra] beginning with the seed-syllable of Śrī is for the sake of prosperity (śrī).
The Mṛtyuñjaya mantra and others lead to long life;
the Nṛsiṃha seed-syllable and others lead to victory over enemies;
and when all [mantras] are encapsulated, there is the attainment of all desires.
Regarding the phrase "the attainment of sons through desire and so forth":
this application of the seed (bījayoga) is to be understood as occurring immediately after the power (śakti). || 14 ||
Having installed nine beautiful jars according to the prescribed rite—filled with jewels, gold, and other precious substances, and placed within the nine positions. || 15 ||
If [the astrological configuration] is neutral, one should worship the Goddess; in other cases, one should worship Jayā and the others.
Having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should consecrate the lord of men. || 16 ||
The king conquers his enemies; the practitioner attains the glory of victory;
and the sick person becomes long-lived, freed from all diseases. || 17 ||
A barren woman consecrated according to the rite obtains an excellent son.
Ghee consecrated with this mantra removes minor fevers;
likewise, ashes and other substances consecrated by recitation are especially beneficial for pregnant women. || 18 ||
"Having installed according to the rule" means by the procedure taught in the *Mātṛkāpaṭala*.
By the word "gold and so forth," the eightfold offering (*gandhāṣṭaka*) pertaining to the Śakti is intended.
"In the nine squares" implies, as the ellipsis suggests, that this refers to the nine-petalled lotus mandala (*navanābha-maṇḍala*).
In the phrase "with perfumes, flowers, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes incense, lamps, and food offerings (*naivedya*).
The term "having worshipped" (*sampūjya*) is illustrative;
by it, one should understand that [the mantras] have been recited (*japta*) along with the *sampāta* [offering].
As they say: "Having filled jars with the water of the *kaṣāya* decoctions according to the rule, one should recite the mantra three thousand times, accompanied by oblations of clarified butter."
Consecrated by them, the king— pure in soul and having fasted on the preceding day—
shall conquer his enemies in an instant and attain victory and prosperity.
"The sick person, however, is liberated from the afflictions of the planets as well as from diseases"—
the remainder [of the sentence] is "having consumed the clarified butter."
"Ashes and so forth" means that ghee is the remainder;
by the word "and so forth," scents, flowers, and the like are included. "Likewise" means it wards off minor planetary influences (kṣudragraha). || 15-18 ||
Having written the seed-syllable *tāre* in the center with the object of the rite (*sādhya*) situated within it, and having inscribed the eight syllables of the mantra upon the petals,
one should encircle it with the *triṣṭubh* verse and surround it with the letters of the *mātṛkā*.
One should fashion the diagram of Durgā situated within a city-diagram (bhūpura). || 19 ||
It wards off minor spirits, great diseases, thieves, and serpents;
it bestows victory and glory upon men, and grants happiness to pregnant women. || 20 ||
He states the yantra: "In the center," etc.
The two locative cases in "tāre" (in the seed-syllable) are in different grammatical relations (vyadhikaraṇa).
"In the center" means in the pericarp (kaṇīkā).
The syllable *tāre* refers to *praṇava* (OM).
*Bījaṃ daurgam* means the seed-syllable of Durgā.
The connection is that one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the middle, together with the name and the action of the practitioner (*sādhaka*).
The *triṣṭubh* meter and *jātavedas* [deity] will be explained in the twenty-second [chapter]. || 19-20 ||
"Bhāntaṃ viyat sanayanaṃ śveto madīni ṭhadvayam"—this eight-syllable Vidyā is declared to be Mahiṣamadīnī. || 21 ||
"Huṃ phaṭ" is proclaimed as the heart-mantra for the slayer of the buffalo;
"O enemy of the buffalo, Śārṅgin! Huṃ phaṭ" is declared as the head-limb mantra. || 22 ||
The mantra for the crest (*śikhā*) consists of the pair "mahipaṃ bhīṣaya" ending with *huṃ phaṭ*.
O Goddess, the armor (*kavaca*) consists of "mahiṣaṃ hana" at the end of the pair, followed by *huṃ phaṭ*. || 23 ||
At the end of "mahiṣānte" and "sūdani," the weapon-mantra ending in "huṃ phaṭ" is proclaimed;
with these mantras joined by their respective seed-syllables (jāti), one should fashion the five limbs (pañcāṅga). || 24 ||
He states the mantra for Mahiṣamardinī, beginning with "bhāntam": *bhāntam* is the letter *ma*; *viyat* is the letter *ha*; together with the eye (*ikāra*), it becomes *mahi*.
*Śvetaḥ* is *ṣa*.
*Madīni* is the essential nature (*svarūpa*). *Ṭha-dvayaṃ svāhā*.
For it is said in the Nārāyaṇīya: "Poison, marrow, time, fire, and that which abides in the night—these are *Ṭha-dvayaṃ*."
Thus: *maṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*).
Its seer (*ṛṣi*) is named Śākavatsa.
The meter is *prakṛti*.
Others say that Mārkaṇḍeya is the seer (*ṛṣi*).
In the mantra for the *śikhā* and *varman*, the word *mahiṣa* should be understood as being in the accusative case. (21–24)
I bow to her who resembles a *gāruḍa* gem, adorned with a jeweled crown and earrings, possessing an eye in her forehead, seated upon the head of Mahiṣa,
and holding a discus, a conch, a sword, a shield, arrows, a bow, and a trident.
She who bears the threatening gesture with her own arms and is crowned by the moon. || 25 ||
He describes the meditation with the words "gāruḍa" and so forth.
*Gāruḍopala* means the gem vomited by Garuḍa.
The weapons [are placed] in the first two upper hands starting from the right, and in the other two lower hands starting from the left.
"Tarjanīm" refers to the *tarjanī-mudrā*. Its definition is as follows:
"The index finger alone is raised upward, while the remaining fingers are joined together below."
"This mudrā is called the tarjanī; it causes fear to both the speaker and the listener. Thus [it is said].
Thus it is said in the Īśānasaṃhitā:
"One should meditate upon the great Durgā, dark-hued and adorned with all ornaments,
enriched by the splendor of her crown of matted locks and endowed with the shimmering crescent moon."
The Goddess, wearing yellow garments, with two full and elevated breasts,
holding a discus and a chain in her excellent hands, and below those, a sword and a shield.
And below that, the arrow and the bow; and below, the threatening gesture (tarjanī) together with the trident.
Thus [ends verse 25].

One should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times; having offered a thousand oblations of auspicious sesame seeds, one should worship Mahiṣamardinī upon the previously described pedestal. || 26 ||
On the previously mentioned, uninterrupted seat of Durgā. || 26 ||
Having worshipped the limbs upon the petals, one should worship the one named Durgā of excellent complexion, the third called Āryā, and the fourth, Kanakaprabhā. || 27 ||

The practitioner of mantra should worship the fifth [mudrā] known as Kṛttikā and the sixth, which bestows fearlessness, as a beautiful maiden, using the long vowels in their respective order. || 28 ||
"One should worship the limbs"—the word "in the filaments" (kesareṣu) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
This is connected with the subsequent phrase "in the petals" (patreṣu).
"With long vowels"—the ellipsis is "excluding the two neuter [vowels] at the end."
By the word "long" (dīrgha), the technical designation is intended;
thus, the meaning is "by these eight," namely: ā, ī, ū, e, ai, o, au, and aḥ.
This is stated in the first chapter of the Nārāyaṇīya:
Having stated, "And Ananta is to be recited first," it was said in the subsequent chapter, "in sequence with the initial vowels.
It is precisely with this intention that it is explained in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*: "with the initial vowels, namely ā, ī, ū, e, ai, o, au, and aḥ. (27–28)
One should worship the weapons in the front [petals]—the discus, conch, sword, and shield—with the arrows, bow, trident, and skull, and so forth, in due order. || 29 ||
"At the tips" means at the tips of the petals;
"by those beginning with *ya*" means by those ending with *ha*. || 29 ||
Furthermore, the world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be worshipped, and after that, their weapons;
by means of an oblation of sesame seeds, one may bring under control men and even kings.
The mantra-practitioner should offer oblations with *siddhārtha* seeds; he is instantly liberated from diseases.
By offering lotuses, one conquers enemies; by offering *dūrvā* grass, one attains peace. || 31 ||
Through oblations of *palāśa* flowers one attains nourishment, and through grains, the prosperity of grain;
an oblation performed with crow feathers spreads hatred among men. || 32 ||
"Should subjugate" indicates that it begins with the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma*).
By the term "mantra-practitioner," it is indicated that it begins with *mṛtyuñjaya* and so forth. "Should conquer" indicates that it begins with one's own seed-syllable.
"Peace" refers to having *nṛsiṃha* and so forth at the beginning; "prosperity" refers to having the third [syllable] and so forth at the beginning;
and "the glory of grain" refers to having the seed-syllable *śrī* at the beginning. (30–32)
By performing oblations of *marīca* (black pepper), the enemy certainly meets his death;
having visualized the Goddess, one should destroy minor enemies, thieves, spirits, and the like. || 33 ||
Regarding the word *marīca*: there is also a form of the word *marīca* with a long vowel in the middle. Thus it is stated in the *Śabdabhedaprakāśa*: "Marīcaṃ and likewise maricaṃ."
Death is the state of having one's own seed and so forth. || 33 ||

The syllable *tāra* (oṃ), the pair *durge*, the red one (*ra*), the final letter of the series ending in *ḍha* (*ṇa*), together with the eye (*i*), and ending with *dviṭha* (*svāhā*)—this ten-syllabled mantra, "O Victorious Durgā," is to be known. || 34 ||
He states the mantra of Jayadurgā: "Tāra" refers to the Praṇava (Om).
"Durgeyugam" means "Durge Durge."
The letter *ra* is red;

the last [letter] is *kṣa*; the one ending in *ḍha* is *ṇa*; and "with the eye" means accompanied by the vowel *i*. These two [terms] are qualifiers for both [the preceding letters]. Thus, [the mantra is] *kṣiṇi*.
It ends with *dviṭha* and concludes with *svāhā*.
As it is stated in the Nārāyaṇīya:
"The *tāra* (oṃ), the two *durgā*s, fire (*ra*), the final letter ending in *ḍha*, the *sadṛś* (the letter *sa*), and the *śiras* (phaṭ)."
Thus it is stated.
This has been explained in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*:
the word "similar" (*sadṛk*) is an adjective qualifying both.
"Kṣiṇī" is its name;
the sage is Mārkaṇḍeya, the metre is Bṛhatī, the seed-syllable is Oṃ (Praṇava), and the power is Svāhā. || 34 ||
"Tārā" and so forth is the Heart mantra for Durgā; "Durge" is declared to be the Head. "Durgāyai" is the Topknot (Śikhā), and "Bhūtarakṣiṇi" is proclaimed as the Armor (Varman).
The pair beginning with Tārā and Durgā is proclaimed as the two Rakṣiṇīs; the pair beginning with Tārā and Durgā is proclaimed as the two Rakṣiṇī-Weapons. || 36 ||
The phrase "beginning with Tārā" is connected to the end of the *varma* [mantra]. || 35-36 ||

Having the luster of a dark cloud, inspiring fear in the hosts of enemies with her sidelong glances, with a crescent moon bound upon her crest, bearing in her hands a conch, a discus, a sword, and a trident, three-eyed,
seated upon the shoulders of a lion, filling the entire triple world with her splendor— [I bow to her].
One should meditate upon Durgā, known as Jayā, who is surrounded by the thirty gods and served by those desiring spiritual accomplishments.
"Kāla" refers to the three-pronged trident.
The meditation on the weapon is like that of the eight-syllable mantra.
"By those desiring success"—this is the statement of the application (viniyoga). || 37 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and then offer oblations of clarified butter;
one-tenth of that number should be offered into the consecrated fire, and one should also feed Brahmins. || 38 ||
On the seat described as having eight syllables, the wise one should worship as before;
while reciting the mantra, he may enter into battle and especially slay his enemies. || 39 ||
One should recite this mantra at the beginning of legal disputes and the like; therein too, one shall be victorious.
One who desires victory should worship weapons and missiles with this vidyā. || 40 ||
"Bāṇalakṣa" means five hundred thousand [recitations].
By the statement "one should also feed Brāhmaṇas," those ten types of preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*) are indicated.
As it has been said:
Japa, fire sacrifice (homa), libation (tarpaṇa), one’s own consecration (svābhiṣeka), the rite for effacing sins (aghamarṣaṇa),
offering water to the Sun (sūryārghya), drinking water, prostration, and the worship of the deity.
"And the feeding of Brahmins [should be done] in a ratio of one-tenth for each preceding stage.
This is to be understood as applying to the preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*) for all mantras.
Some say there are only five types:
recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), libation (tarpaṇa), worship (pūjā), and feeding of Brahmins (brāhmaṇabhojana).
Thus it is said.

In the phrase "everywhere by means of recitation and so forth," this very [method] is to be understood as the meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). "In that which is proclaimed for the eight-syllable [mantra]" refers to that which is proclaimed for the eight-syllable Durgā mantra.
"The wise one" (*sudhīḥ*)—thus [it is said].
By this, it should be understood that even in this application, after the *praṇava*, there is the insertion of one's own seed-syllable (*bīja*) and so forth.
"Weapon" (*astra*) refers to arrows and the like;
"armament" (*śastra*) refers to swords and the like. (38–40)
At the end of the word *jvalajvala*, one should utter the word *śūlinī*.
The mantra ends with *huṃ phaṭ* following *duṣṭagrahaṃ*, concluding with the wife of fire (*svāhā*). || 41 ||
It is declared to consist of the elements, the senses, and the imperishable; it is the destroyer of seizing spirits, minor ailments, and the like.
Dīrghatamas is said to be the seer (ṛṣi), and Kakubh is cited as the meter (chandas). || 42 ||
The goddess Śūlinī is proclaimed as the one worshipped by all the gods. "O Durgā, O giver of boons" is the heart-mantra; "O dweller of the Vindhyas" is the head-mantra. || 43 ||

The mantra for the one who delights in battle preceded by combat is *asurānte madīni*. Furthermore, the armor (*varma*) for the one highly honored by gods and siddhas consists of two terrifying [syllables]. || 44 ||
O Mahāyogeśvarī, the pair of syllables *rakṣa* should be placed in sequence for Nandinī;
these five-limbed mantras, beginning with *śūlini* and ending with *haṃ phaṭ*, are traditionally taught. || 45 ||
He states the mantra of Śūlinī-Durgā with the word "jvala" and so forth.
Here, the elements (bhūtas) are five;
the sense organs (indriyas)—both the organs of cognition and the organs of action—are ten.
When these are totaled, the number becomes fifteen.
However, the counting of the mantra syllables should not be performed according to the rule "the movement of digits is from left to right";
for if that were done, the number of syllables would be one hundred and five.
With the fifteen syllables consisting of the elements (bhūta), the senses (indriya), and the imperishable (akṣara); *huṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*).
"Graha" and so forth constitute the statement of the application (*viniyoga*).
Of the eighteen planets;
of the minor [afflictions], namely paralysis, hatred, eradication, expulsion, delusion, killing, and disease;
and by the word "etcetera," of spirits, ghosts, ḍākinīs, and so forth.

By stating the application (*viniyoga*) with the word "destroyer" (*nāśaka*), it is indicated that [the mantra] is encased by the *praṇava*, the seed-syllables of Nṛsiṃha and Durgā, and ends with *vaṣaṭ*.
"O Durgā, [this is] the heart" (*durge hṛt*) is the heart-mantra;
likewise for the head as well.
*Tacchikhā* means that it is the *śikhā-mantra* of that [mantra]. *Yuddhapūrvapriye* means "O you who are fond of battle."
"Devī" and so forth, ending with "mahāyogeśvari";
the word "astra" (weapon) is to be understood as the remainder [of the mantra]. "Varma" (armor), followed by "asurānta," "madīni," and again "yuddhapūrvapriye."
Or there is the reading: "and the two weapons that terrify.
The connection is as follows: the five limb-mantras of Śūlinī and the others are traditionally taught to be recited in sequence, each ending with *hūṃ phaṭ*.
The practical application (prayoga), however, is as follows: *śūlini durge huṃ phaṭ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and so forth.
Those following the tradition, however, state that the limbs (aṅgas) are interwoven with each preceding one;
therefore, the application is: *śūlini durge varade huṃ phaṭ śirase svāhā*, and so forth.
Others, however, state that the limbs are otherwise according to specific desires:
"The heart is declared to be in *Durgā*, the head in *Varadā*, the crest (*śikhā*) in *Vindhyavāsinī*, the armor (*varma*) in *Varma*, and the eyes (*netra*) in *Asurāntā*."
When joined with *yuddhapriye*, the weapon-mantra becomes one that terrifies both [parties].
At the beginning of these, one should utter the word *śūlinī* preceded by the *tārā* (the syllable *oṃ*).
At the conclusion of all [these], O Goddess, well-worshipped by the Siddhas—
Nandinī, the pair of Rakṣās, and Mahāyogeśvarī as well.
"These armor (*varma*) and weapon (*astra*) seed-syllables indeed provide protection against the planets;
through the placement (*nyāsa*) repeated fifty times, even a severe fever is destroyed.
Thus [it is said]. The ritual application (*prayoga*) therein is as follows:
"Oṃ, O Śūlinī Durgā, well-worshipped by gods and siddhas, O Nandinī, protect, protect, O Mahāyogeśvarī! Huṃ Phaṭ! and so forth.
With this very intention, the teachers [have said]:
"And likewise, O you who are fond of battle, [the mantra] beginning with *varma* (the armor) and ending with *asuramardini* (the slayer of asuras)."

Having recited "and the two-fold weapon for protection from fear," and having recited "O Devī," and so forth, it is stated: "The ritual of the limbs alone is declared to provide protection and ward off the seizing spirits.
Thus it was recited.
In this case as well, everything is consistent in the reading written by Malli;
by the word "in sequence" (kramāt), it is also indicated that there is a continuous interweaving of preceding [elements] according to the tradition. || 41–45 ||
Mounted upon a lion, dark as a water-laden cloud, she bears in her lotus-like hands a trident, an arrow, a sword, a lotus, a mace, a bow, and a noose;
she is adorned with the moon as her crest-ornament, possesses three eyes, and is surrounded on all sides by four goddesses bearing bucklers.
I meditate upon the wielder of the trident, who is served by maidens and who strikes terror into her adversaries. ||46||
"Adhyārūḍhām" means mounted upon.
"Mṛgendram" means a lion.
"Arāṇi" refers to that in which spokes (ara) exist.
The wheel of the noble ones;
the conch, born of water;
and the teachers—
Holding in her lotus-like hands a trident, arrows, a noose, a sword, a mace, a bow, and a lasso.
Thus [it is said].

And the author of the work, at the time of worship, will speak specifically of the worship of the conch, stating: "On the tips of the petals are its weapons—the discus, the conch, and again the sword.
Regarding the phrase "with four [goddesses]":
this means with those known as Jayā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, and Śūlakātyāyinī.

The word "asmin" (in this) is in the instrumental case in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*), even though there is no actual conjunction [of the weapon with the hand], just as in the expression "an elder [is seated] with a youth.
The visualization of the weapons extends from the lower right to the lower left. || 46 ||
The wise practitioner of mantra should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times;
the fire oblation (homa), however, should consist of food with honey and be performed in a measure of one-tenth that amount. || 47 ||
"Varṇalakṣam" means a hundred thousand repetitions measured by the syllables of the mantra.
"Vicakṣaṇaḥ" means one who knows the rules (niyamas) that apply during the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa). || 47 ||
One should worship on the previously mentioned pedestal according to the method to be described;
having performed the worship of the limbs, the Śaktis are to be worshipped upon the petals. || 48 ||
Durgā and the others—Varadā, Vindhyavāsinī, Asuramardinī, and Yuddhapriyā as the fifth—are well-worshipped by gods and siddhas. || 49 ||
The seventh is declared to be Nandinī, the supreme Mahāyogeśvarī.
Upon the tips of the petals are her weapons: the conch, the discus, and the sword once again. || 50 ||
Having placed the sword, arrow, bow, trident, and noose [in the directions], and then the lords of the quarters,
one who has attained perfection through such recitations and other means may perform whatever action he desires.
Whoever should daily offer one thousand and eight oblations of sesame seeds soaked in the three sweets, his power shall become superhuman. || 52 ||
A person should daily offer one hundred and eight oblations with honey;
within a year, he shall obtain his desire and attain great prosperity.
"In the previously mentioned [mantra] of the eight syllables of Durgā" means as stated before.
"Having performed the worship"—the word "in the filaments" (kesareṣu) is to be supplied. "The other" refers to the eighth [syllable].
The meditation on these has been stated elsewhere: "One should worship Durgā and the others, who have the appearance of clouds and hold a bow and arrows in their hands.
[One should offer oblations] with substances soaked in the three sweets—that is, saturated with milk, honey, and ghee.
Some say that "sugar" (śarkarā) should be substituted for "milk" (payaḥ).
It should be understood that "supernatural power" (śaktiḥ syād atimānuṣī) occurs before a year has passed.
As it has been said: "His power shall be unimpeded even before a year."
Thus [ends the section] 48–53.
The oblation of dūrvā grass grants the fulfillment of all desires for men;
likewise, weapons such as the churikā become consecrated when recited over with this mantra. || 54 ||
Offerings smeared with the ghee from the final oblation bestow the glory of victory.
A fire sacrifice performed with fuel-sticks of *aśvattha* or *arka*, or with sesame seeds soaked in honey, swiftly brings the desired men who are practitioners of mantra under one's control. || 55 ||
Regarding the "durvā-homa":
it should be understood as one hundred and eight [oblations].
As it has been said:
"By offering dūrvā grass joined with *trika* [three] one hundred and eight times, one shall obtain one's desire correctly.
Regarding the phrase "churikā and so forth," by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), items such as swords, claws, and the like are to be understood.
The connection is that [the items] are smeared with the *sampāta* clarified butter and then consecrated by this mantra.
The *homam* for the sake of the *sampāta* consists of five thousand [oblations]. Thus it is said, "consecrated."
Ten thousand [oblations].

As it has been said: "Having invoked the goddess into a sharp sword and worshipped her with perfumes and other offerings, one should offer five thousand oblations of clarified butter according to the prescribed method."
Smeared with the ājya-drops from the oblation and having recited this mantra one thousand times in five sets of two hundred, he becomes empowered as a knower of the specific mantra.
"Then, with a sword in hand, he shall be a warrior who crushes the enemy army.
In this context, "sword" is an illustration for any weapon.
As stated by the Teacher: "The knife, the sword, and the claws.
Regarding the word *aśvattha*:
the number of oblations (*homa*) should be known as twelve thousand.
As it has been said:
"The mantra-practitioner, with a most lucid mind, should offer oblations twelve thousand times with *arka* wood smeared with the three sweets, or with *aśvattha* wood, or with sesame seeds."
Thus [it is said].
By the word "quickly" (kṣipram), this is what is meant:

having meditated upon the goddess as red in color and holding a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows, the practitioner should contemplate the binding of the target with the noose and the drawing [of him] in with the goad; such is the sixth [instruction].
In the word "narān" (men), the gender is not intended to be significant.

Having meditated upon oneself as that Goddess, with weapons raised in her hands and possessing the splendor of the God of Death (Kāla), one should recite the mantra; by touching [the afflicted person], the seizing spirit (graha) is released. || 56 ||

One who knows the mantra, by means of this mantra and according to the prescribed rite, perceiving [the deity] as the divine essence, shall swiftly destroy the poison of snakes, rats, scorpions, and the like. (57)
"Rising," etc.: the connection is that, having meditated upon oneself in the form of the Goddess as described, and having touched the afflicted person, one should recite the mantra.
"The seizure is released."
"Having caused [him] to enter, he was made to abandon"— this is the ellipsis.
Because it is stated "having caused him to enter for a moment as it were," the mention of a "seizing spirit" (graha) is not intended to be significant.
Therefore, the meaning is that there are eighteen grahas.
As for the manner of their possession: having correctly identified the eighteen grahas by means of the characteristics previously described...
One should contemplate these [deities] with their heads devoured, possessing two arms and drooping eyes.
The reciter of mantras, using water from his cupped palms [visualized] as consisting of flames,
shall cause the possessed person to cast off all seizing spirits (grahas) in a mere moment.
Thus it is said.
As for the method of abandoning [the state]:

having meditated upon Durgā in the form described above between oneself and the afflicted person, one should firmly clench the fist by pressing the three fingers starting with the little finger with the thumb, extend the index finger toward the side of the right ear, and rotate it very rapidly like a wheel; by means of this *cakramudrā*, one should effect liberation.

As it has been said: "Furthermore, by meditating upon Ambikā, who is surrounded by her own weapons, between oneself and the afflicted person while reciting [the mantra] with the *ari-mudrā*, the seizing spirits (*graha*) flee, their bodies rendered powerless."
"Sarpeti" (he moves); by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), dogs and other such animals are included.
"With the thought that it is a deity according to the rule prescribed in the mantra"—the word "of himself" (*ātmanaḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
The connection is that one should destroy the poison by means of this mantra according to the prescribed rule (*vidhi*);
"according to the prescribed rule" refers to the visualization of the deity through a specific form of meditation.
As it has been said:
"Whether it arises from snakes, rats, scorpions, and the like, or from many-legged creatures, dogs, or spiders—
that Vindhyavāsinī destroys the poison of men instantly through her very presence alone.
A specific visualization (dhyāna) is described elsewhere as follows:
Resembling the autumnal moon, radiant with a face like a blooming lotus,
her auspicious hands— those lotuses— holding a discus, a conch, and a pair of jars of nectar.

"By meditating upon this Durgā—who is adorned with white ornaments, who is moist with nectar, and who is sprinkling the bewildered poison with this [nectar]—a person shall destroy the poison. Thus [ends verses 56–57].
Having taken arrows consecrated with this mantra, the practitioner should discharge them at the opposing army;
it will then quickly flee. || 58 ||
Regarding the phrase "consecrated arrows":
it should be understood that one must meditate upon that goddess at the tip of the arrow.
As it has been said:
Having fixed a sharp arrow and having recited this mantra for the goddess Kṣemaṅkarī—thus [it is said]. || 58 ||
Having meditated upon himself as the Goddess holding a trident and a noose,
one who enters the field of battle undisturbed shall emerge victorious and free from wounds.
"One should enter"—
the remainder is "while reciting the mantra.
As it has been said:
"Having transformed oneself into the Noble One (Āryā) equipped with a trident and noose, and having entered the enemy force while reciting the mantra,
one quickly seizes their weapons and robs them of their consciousness.
It should be understood that the state of being unscarred results from the performance of the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the generation [of the deity], as well as from the seizing of the weapons.
But in another tantra:
"She is dark-complexioned, of massive body, with eyes like blazing fire;
she holds a noose, a hand-drum, a trident, and the powder known as 'the deluder'."
Bearing [weapons] with her four hands and adorned by lordly elephants,
she was surrounded on all sides by an army and by exceedingly long, flowing tresses of hair.
"Covering [the enemy] with her dark [forms], devoted to loud laughter, when meditated upon, Durgā will in no time indeed delude the army of the foe. Thus [it is said]. (59)

One should perform oblations with sesame seeds and white mustard seeds one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rite, while reciting the mantra joined with the [victim's] name; for him, death shall come.

The connection is that one should recite the mantra joined with the *nāma* (name) according to the rule and perform the *homa* sacrifice; "according to the rule" means in the manner of the *pallava*, that is, during the recitation (*japa*) and the *homa*, at the beginning of the word *svāhā* and so forth.
As it has been said:
"In the 'pallava' [rite], the sequence of mantra words begins with the name of the person to be accomplished;
this is prescribed for the rite of killing (māraṇa). Thus it is said.
But this [procedure] applies to the rite of recitation (*japa*); however, in the case of an oblation (*homa*), the name is to be uttered before the word *svāhā*. And it has been stated by Gautama:

"In all the mantras of the various classes of beings, one should insert the names therein; [the name] before the word *svāhā* in the fire-oblation (*homa*), and at the end of the mantra in the rite of recitation (*japa*).
Thus it was said by the Teachers:

If a practitioner of mantra offers one hundred thousand oblations of sesame seeds and white mustard seeds while reciting the name of an enemy, that person, his body struck by disease, will meet death; of this there is no doubt. Thus [it is said]. (60)
By offering pellets made from cow dung one hundred and eight times,
the practitioner of mantra creates enmity between two affectionate persons within seven days.
Having taken cow dung, one should then recite [the mantra] three thousand times in the sky;
for those who are about to depart, it will become a paralyzing spell when buried at the gateway. || 62 ||
What is the use of saying more? One may accomplish everything by means of this mantra.
"Aṣṭaśata" means one hundred and eight. In the context of "vidveṣam" (enmity), "viyogam" (separation) may also be substituted.
"Two who are hostile toward each other become separated," so it is said.
A specific type of meditation [is described] elsewhere:
"Holding a pestle, a trident, and two skull-cups in her hands, she is dark-complexioned, naked, and should be meditated upon as the one who causes hatred for the Mūrti. Thus [it is said].
Regarding "cow-dung" and so forth, it is because of the instruction that it refers to the dung of a bull.
"Having taken cow-dung from the sky"—the meaning is that cow-dung touching the ground is not to be taken. As it has been said: "The cow-dung untouched [by the earth] is in the atmosphere. (61–62)
Having uttered the word "uttiṣṭha" (arise), there should then be the word "puruṣi" (O man). || 63 ||
O Grandfather, you who possess the sun and the moon as your eyes, if it is possible, please speak immediately after uttering [this], for fear has come upon me.
Or, O Blessed One, tell me that which is impossible;
then the mantra of thirty-seven syllables, consisting of the fire-wife (Śamaya), shall be [revealed]. || 65 ||
The seer is Āraṇyaka; the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh;
the deity is Vanadurgā, the liberator from all miserable states. || 66 ||
He states the mantra of Vanadurgā with the words "uttiṣṭha" and so forth.
The grammatical connection is that after that, there should be the word "puruṣi.
The Grandfather (Brahmā) is the letter *ka*; "with the eye and the moon" means accompanied by the vowel *i* and the bindu (*m*).
"What is the point of that? "And there is fear for me"—the word "and" (ca) is not in the middle of the mantra.
"Whether it is possible or impossible."
The very nature [of the mantra] is *amanta* (ending in *-am*).
In the word "bhagavati," the accusative case is used for the object of the verbal action; however, in the mantra, it is in the vocative.
Or, in this context, those syllables of mine are the *kīlakas* (stake-mantras).
The words "huṃ durgai" are the *akīlakas*.
As it is stated in the *Īśānasaṃhitā*:
"Having extracted the seed-syllable of the quality (*guṇabīja*), then the word 'uttiṣṭha' (arise)."
Having extracted the syllable *puruṣī*, one should join it with Brahmā and the subtle [syllable].
Having uttered [the mantra] together with the nasal bindu, one should say the word "svapiṣi" (you sleep).
Then, having addressed [it as] "bhayaṃ me" (fear for me), it likewise becomes present.
Having said "if it is possible" and having declared "it is impossible," one should extract the seed-syllable of the armor and [the name] "Bhagavatī" in the difficult [position].
Having extracted "śamaya," one should likewise utter the word "svāhā.
Thus is this Great Goddess Niṣkīlā, the bestower of all accomplishments.

At the end of the *guṇa* [mantra], one should join the seed-syllable of Durgā, the Mistress of the World (*bhuvaneśānī*). Having uttered one's own seed-syllable at the end of the *varman* (the armor-mantra), one should then recite it in reverse order at the very end.
"One should join the previously mentioned triad of seed-syllables with *krauñcadāraṇā*;
then the Vidyā is inflamed, free from obstacles, and bestows all accomplishments. Thus it is said.
The syllable *U* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*).
"Dur" is the seed-syllable, according to the teacher Padmapādācārya;
"sarva" and so forth is the statement regarding the ritual application (viniyoga). || 63–66 ||
In the eight joints of the feet, in the anus, the genitals, the *ādhāra*, and the abdomen;
again, in the sides, the heart, the breasts, and the throat, as well as in the eight joints of the arms. || 67 ||
One should place the syllables of the mantra upon the face, nose, cheeks, eyes, ears, the space between the eyebrows, and the crown of the head, for the sake of attaining the state of the deity.

The arrangement of the limbs [of the maṇḍala] should be made by means of six, four, eight, and eight mantra-syllables joined with the [five] seed-syllables (jāti), corresponding respectively to the six sense-faculties. (69)
He states the arrangement of the syllables with the words "pāda" and so forth. There are four joints for each of the feet and arms.
In this context, one should take the pairs of locations for the sides, breasts, nose, cheeks, eyes, and ears.
By the five sense organs. By the phrase "in due order," this is what is meant:
for each [deity], the limb [of the mantra] consists of "rakṣa rakṣa" followed by the final syllable [of the name].

As it is stated in the Īśāna-saṃhitā: "One should perform the limb-rites (aṅgas) with mantras consisting of syllables numbering [the seasons] (six), [the Vedas] (four), [the days of the week] (seven), [the Vasus] (eight), and [the limbs of the body] (sixteen), joined with the words 'durgāyai rakṣa rakṣa'. (Verses 67–69)

Seated in the center of a golden lotus, three-eyed and resembling a flash of lightning, she holds a discus, a conch, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, while bearing a digit of the moon; adorned with necklaces,
armlets, strings of pearls, and earrings, she is praised by Indra and the other gods.
One should meditate upon her who dwells in the Vindhyas, whose face is like the moon, and who has a lion standing at her side.
The meditation on the weapons is performed from the right upper [hand] to the two upper [hands] in the first case, and from those two lower [hands] to the two lower [hands] in the last;
others, however, say it proceeds from the right upper [hand] down to the right lower [hand]. (70)

Having meditated thus, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times; then, as a tenth part of that, he should offer oblations of sacrificial food, rice with honey, and sesame seeds.
"By a tenth part of that" means forty thousand [recitations].
In that context, the meaning is that each of the four substances is joined with one [of the others];
"with the oblation" means with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
With winter rice,
with ghee along with milk,
and with sesame seeds.
By four. || 71 ||
One should worship the Goddess together with her limbs and other attendants upon the previously mentioned pedestal.
The limb-worship is as before; one should worship these [deities] at the bases of the petals. || 72 ||
Āryā, Durgā, she named Bhadrā, Bhadrakālī, then Ambikā, Kṣemā, another named Vedagarbhā, and Kṣemaṃkarī— these are the eight Śaktis.
One should worship the weapons— the conch, discus, sword, and shield— along with the arrows, bow, and trident, ending with the skull, within the petals.
The [goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī should be at the tips of the petals, and after that, the world-protectors (lokapālas).
With a perfected mantra for the ritual applications, one should thus meditate upon the Goddess. || 75 ||
"As before" means in the directions starting from the southeast (āgneya) and so forth, as well as in the front directions.
And this worship is performed within the filaments at the end of the pericarp, because the worship of Śakti has been taught [to take place] there first.
Regarding the "eight powers": their visualization is described elsewhere as follows—
"The noble powers and the others hold shields, swords, and bows."
"Those who have their limbs adorned with serpents, though terrifying, are to be worshipped.
Thus it is said. "Thereafter" refers to the worship of the vajra and other implements as described in the ritual applications (*prayoga*).

Due to the plural number, in rites such as pacification (*śānti*), there is the encasement within the seed-syllables of Nṛsiṃha; in battle and killing (*māraṇa*), there is the visualization of the sixteen-armed form,
with a dark complexion like a water-laden cloud and standing upon the head of the buffalo-demon.
Regarding protection, it has been stated that one should meditate upon [the deity] as having eight arms, with limbs dark-green like *dūrvā* grass, and standing upon the head of a buffalo.
This was said by the Teachers: "With a discus, mace, sword, shield, arrow, bow, and trident;
with a skull, a double-edged sword (*ṛṣṭi*), pestle (*muśala*), lance (*kunta*), Nandaka sword, bracelet, club (*gadā*), javelin (*bhindipāla*), and spear (*śakti*)."
In Māhiṣaka, she is rich with arms manifesting various forms, resembling a water-laden cloud,
and holding a discus, conch, sword, shield, arrows, a bow, a trident, and a threatening forefinger.
"May Durgā, who stands upon the head of the bull and resembles fresh *dūrvā* grass, be for your prosperity.

Also elsewhere: "One should properly meditate upon her, who resembles blazing fire, who is mounted on the shoulders of a lion, who is awe-inspiring, and who possesses sixteen arms, for the purpose of crushing enemies."
For the attainment of longevity, one should meditate upon her as having dark limbs, eight arms, and standing upon the demon Mahiṣāsura.
Thus [ends the section on] verses 72–75.
Resembling the fire of time, with hair adorned by a crescent moon,
decorated with an eye upon her forehead, seated upon a terrifying lion,
and holding in her hands a discus, a conch, a sword, a shield, a bow, arrows, and a skull-cup—
I worship her who bears the trident in her arms and has conquered the entire army of the asuras.
One who is constantly devoted to the morning bath should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times;
for such a person, riches, grain, and other prosperities will quickly be accomplished. || 77 ||
Kālapāvaka is the fire of universal dissolution.
Karoṭikā is a skull-cup.
As for the weapons, held by the right hands from the top downwards, they are the discus, sword, arrow, and trident.
In the left [hands], conch-shells, shields, bows, and skull-cups are to be meditated upon from above.
It should be understood that this meditation is for the purpose of protection. || 76–77 ||
By this very procedure, one should conquer the seizing spirits, minor ailments, and enemies.
Standing in water reaching the navel and recollecting the Goddess situated in the sun, one should mutter [the mantra] one hundred and eight times; thus one shall obtain great prosperity. || 78 ||
"By this very [means]" refers to the procedure therein,
such as the morning bath and so forth.
The recitation (*japa*) consists of ten thousand [repetitions].
As it has been said:
"For the sake of obtaining the fruits of auspicious actions, one should recite the mantra one thousand times."
"In rites such as eradication (uccāṭana) and other minor operations, one should especially perform it ten thousand times. Thus [it is said].
In this mantra, it should be understood that the word *graha* and so forth are placed before the word *bhaya*.
Thus, *grahabhaya* means fear of planets, *kṣudrabhaya* means fear of minor evils, and *ripubhaya* means fear of enemies.
In the same way, it should be understood that *caurabhaya* and so forth follow later as well.
The meaning of "minor" (*kṣudra*) is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"Stupor, inciting enmity, eradication, destruction, bewilderment, killing, and disease— these are remembered as the minor [rites]."
Thus:
"with water reaching to the navel" refers to [immersion] in a river or similar body of water;
"recalling the Goddess" refers to the visualization described in another tantra.

As they say: "One should meditate upon this Durgā, who holds a conch, a discus, a lotus, and a treasure-vessel in her hands, who is red in color, well-adorned, seated upon a lotus within the orb of the sun, and radiating brilliant light."
"Standing in water reaching up to the navel in a river, one who is self-controlled should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times for the sake of quickly attaining prosperity (*śrī*).
Thus [it is said]: "Great prosperity."
It should also be understood that [the mantra] begins with the seed-syllable of Śrī. || 78 ||
Having kindled a fire with ten thousand thorny twigs from a banyan tree, one should perform a homa sacrifice with the best of sacrificial fuel; this shall destroy the entire multitude of calamities.
One should pacify terrible spells, malevolent rites, spirits, and the like by means of this ritual procedure, using either *apāmārga* wood-sacrificial fuel or wild sesame seeds. || 80 ||

The connection is that one should perform ten thousand oblations (*ayuta-homa*) in a fire that has not been previously consecrated, using excellent fuel-sticks (*samid-vara*) produced from the *vaṭa* tree, complete with their horns and tips.
[One may also use] wild sesame seeds (*kānanodbhava-tila*) or *jattīla* seeds. (79–80)

For the sake of attaining his desired goal, the practitioner of mantras, being self-controlled, should offer a thousand oblations of the best sacrificial wood for ten days beginning from Sunday. || 81 ||
"Mantrī" (the practitioner of mantra)—by this, it is indicated that [the mantra] consists of four syllables beginning with "Sūrya. "A thousand"—meaning every day. || 81 ||
Having taken pure heartwood pieces, one should, with this mantra, offer oblations into the kindled fire for seven nights without weariness. || 82 ||
The best of mantra-knowers shall constantly accomplish every desired goal;
by offering white water-lilies (kumuda), he shall bring Brahmins under his control, and by the oblation of lotuses (padma), kings. || 83 ||

His wife [worshipped] the Vaiśyas with full-blown blue lotuses through the oblation of white lilies (kahlāra), the Śūdras with the oblation of salt, and the assembly hall again with jasmine flowers (jātī). || 84 ||
One should offer oblations daily with rice grains; after a year, one will become possessed of rice.
By offering oblations of dūrvā grass, one attains long life, and by offering honey, one becomes possessed of jewels. || 85 ||
Through grains there shall be an abundance of food; through clarified butter one obtains wealth;
and through cow's milk one attains an increase in cattle—of this there is no doubt. (86)
"Sāra" refers to *khadira* wood.
"Atandrita" (unwearied) also implies a period of three days.
As it has been said:
"With pure heartwood of khadira, for three days or even for seven nights."
"Entirely" means both gentle and fierce.
Regarding that, there is a distinction stated in another tantra:
"The Goddess, resembling a new water-pot, [holds] a trident and a hand-drum with her arms."
Holding an arrow, a bow, and a pair of celestial water-pots, she is supreme.
Having meditated upon Durgā, who has a massive body, a terrifying face, and is beautifully adorned,
one should offer oblations of clarified butter in the center for the rite of nourishment (pauṣṭika).
If, for the rite of subjugation, one should meditate upon the six-armed Goddess as previously described, holding two jars filled with the juice of *kṣvela*.
"The wise and learned one, facing the western direction, should offer oblations with pure heartwood chips mixed with ghee, using the mantra in reverse order.
By the phrase "the best among those who know the mantras," it is indicated here as well that [the fire] originates from the four-syllabled mantra of the Sun. (82–86)
In cases of fever, possession by spirits, poison, or snakes, one should recite [the mantra] while touching the index finger;
by remembering the Goddess who wields the trident, she removes those afflictions in that very instant. || 87 ||
"With the threatening gesture" means with the left [hand];
"those" refers to the fever and so forth. || 87 ||
One should write this mantra, with its syllables beginning with the name of the person to be subdued (*sādhya*), on a leaf;
then, one should place it upon the heart of an image made from the clay of a potter. || 88 ||
Having performed the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) and having worshipped it with flowers and other offerings,
one should place it before oneself and recite the mantra one thousand and eight times.
By worshipping the Goddess in the fire with pungent oil at the junctions of day and night (sandhyās), the knower of mantras certainly attains his desire within a mere fortnight. || 90 ||
Regarding the word "dabhītam":
its specific method will be explained in the twenty-third [chapter].
"Patra" means on birch bark (bhūrja).
Regarding "the potter's clay":

at the time of fashioning a vessel, the potter has clay clinging to his hands; with that, one should place a leaf inscribed with the aforementioned mantra upon the heart of an image twelve finger-breadths in height.
"Having placed it in front" means beneath one's own soles upon a seat or similar object. "During the twilights" (sandhyāsu) means:
The meaning is: "at the evening twilight of the fifteenth day.
In some recensions, the reading is "vaśamāyāti vāñchitaḥ" (the desired object comes under control). || 88-90 ||
Having offered ten thousand oblations and placed thirty sharp arrows before him, he should again discharge them into those [fires];
having touched them, he should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times.
One should pierce the enemy army, which in an instant is destroyed in the ten directions;
having worshipped with wild flowers and sandalwood.
"With sharp oil" means with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*) or, according to some, with mustard oil (*rājikātaila*).
This is to be connected with the word "having offered. By the term "knower of the mantra," the following is intended:

Having placed a seat covered with fine silk upon a svastika and other such designs, and having set down the arrows there, one should invoke the Goddess into them, worship her, and then, having established the fire in a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and worshipped the Goddess therein as well, one should perform the oblation (homa). As it has been said:
One should worship according to the rules upon a pedestal situated in the center of a svastika or located within the wheel of māyā, covered with a fine silk cloth or similar material.
Having placed thirty sharp, gold-feathered arrows,
he should invoke Kātyāyanī and worship her with excellent offerings such as perfumes and the like.

Having invoked that sixteen-armed goddess into the triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) where the fire has been produced according to the previously mentioned sequence, and having worshipped her with sandalwood paste and other offerings;
One should offer a thousand or ten thousand oblations of Siddhārtha oil; there, one should anoint the Linga with a hundred thousand oblations using the residual drops.
Having sent Uddhava away, he should recite the mantra there the same number of times as the oblations;
he should then wrap the jar near its tail with a red thread.
"When those [arrows] have been pierced by that skillful archer, the enemy host, though protected by Indra, flees away with its senses lost. Thus it is said.
A niyuta is a hundred thousand.
"One should pierce"—thus [it is said].

Regarding such a cruel rite, the teacher Padmapāda maintains that it should be performed with a mantra in reverse order (*pratiloma*); or else, with one beginning with its own seed-syllable (*svabīja*) in the natural (*anuloma*) order. (90–92)
Having lost her senses, she would become intent on fleeing. || 92 ||

Having recited [the mantra] over a *kuḍava* measure of white *guñjā* seeds at the rising of the *kulika* [planet], one should remain hidden and scatter them among the enemy army, in marketplaces, and so forth. || 93 ||
Afflicted by fevers, pestilences, and great diseases, and due to mutual discord among the army commanders, that [host] shall perish, go to ruin, and fall into hell. || 94 ||
"A *kuḍava*":
this refers to four *palas*,
according to the statement that "a *kuḍava* shall consist of four *palas*."
"At the rising of Kulika, one should scatter [the offerings]" means: at the rising of Kulika, which is a specific time.
Its definition is given in the *Jyotiṣaratnamālā*:
"Kulikās arise from the sun at intervals of fourteen, twelve, ten, eight, six, four, and two muhūrtas;
during the day they are taken as such, but at night they are diminished by one, for auspicious rites.
Thus: Manu = 14, Arka = 12, Diś = 10, Vasu = 8, Ṛtu = 6, Veda = 4, Pakṣa = 2.
It is simply that [the army] is afflicted by mutual conflict among its commanders;
for the first reason it would perish or fall away,
and for the second reason it would "go"— meaning it would retreat and depart.
The third [alternative] is by way of conjunction. || 92–94 ||
To paralyze an army, the practitioner should offer a thousand oblations with flowers produced from the *kāraskara* tree; he shall turn back that [army] with its leaves. || 95 ||
The term "mantrī" indicates that [the deity] originates from the seed-syllable of the earth (la) and so forth. And the specific visualization is as follows:
[one should meditate on her] as yellow, with excellent arms holding a noose, a mace, a trident, and an iron fist.
"One should meditate on the form of the deity with a cruel face for the rite of immobilization. Thus it is said.
*Kāraskara* refers to the *viṣatinduka* tree;
*kucilā* is a term in the Kānyakubja dialect.
One should prepare it with its leaves.
The meaning is that one should effect the turning back of an army by means of an oblation of a thousand *kāraskāra* leaves. || 95 ||
Having recited [the mantra] on a Tuesday when the moon is in the constellation Kṛttikā, one should cast ashes from a funeral pyre onto the head of an enemy;
thus, the foe shall become estranged and depart from his country. || 96 ||
By means of leaves produced from the *kāraskara* tree that have been blown down by the wind and are mixed with the dust from his feet, one may utterly destroy enemies from a great distance. || 97 ||
*Aṅgārā* refers to Mars (*bhauma*).
In that [lunar day], the tenth *muhūrta* is the *kulika*.
At that time, one should cast ashes upon the head of the enemy; such is the connection [of the text].
"Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times," and so forth;
for it is said: "One should cast upon the head that funeral ash which has been recited one hundred and eight times."
"One should cast [it]" means while meditating on the Goddess. Regarding that, the specific method of meditation is stated in another tantra:
She is black, with a terrifying face, adorned with serpents,
and her many arms are filled with blazing spears that consume the dust of Mārīca and other substances.

"One should meditate upon Mahādurgā as naked (digambarā) in cases of hatred and the like, intent on performing acts of eradication, causing confusion, and expulsion, while rushing about according to her will. Thus it is said.
"By those joined with the dust of his feet": the dust of that enemy's feet is the dust of the left foot, according to the supreme teachers. "One should expel" means:
It should be understood that [the seed-syllables] begin with the seed-syllable of wind (vāyu). || 96-97 ||
Having fashioned an exceedingly beautiful image out of kāraścara wood,
and having consecrated it with recitation and established its vital breaths, one should then cut it limb by limb.
Combined with the fat of a crow and an owl, one thousand and eight oblations should be offered into the sacrificial fire in a cremation ground on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight. || 99 ||
In this very manner, one should offer oblations for three days until the enemy dies;
by offering oblations of *unmatta* wood, enemies shall perish in an instant.
"An image" refers to one ninety-six finger-breadths in length.
As they say:
"For the rite of killing, that image made of wood should measure twelve finger-breadths."
Alternatively, one should fashion it measuring ninety-six finger-breadths according to the sequence of the *mātrā*-finger-measure;
for that which is prepared for the purpose of fire-offerings (*homa*), the supreme procedure has been declared.
For the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), one should fashion it as twelve finger-breadths, as prescribed. Thus [it is said].
"Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
'one should cut' means one thousand and eight times.
'The thumb'..."
From the right thumb up to the left thumb;
"in the cremation ground" and "the bearer of oblations" (havyavāhana) are locative cases in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
"In this very way" [is the meaning].
As it has been said:
[Death occurs] from the falling of trees or walls, from windless conditions,
from enemies or swords, from water or fire, from the bite of a snake, or from a rutting elephant or a warrior.
"By means of yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, piśācas, brahmarākṣasas, or by other causes, the enemy will certainly meet with swift destruction. Thus [it is said]. "Within three days," etc.
The meaning is the three fourteenth days (of the lunar fortnight).
For it is said: "By practicing on the three fourteenth days, the enemy is destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, regarding the specific visualization for the rite of killing (*māraṇa*), it is stated in another [text]:
Durgā, resembling a dark cloud and adorned with serpents,
holds a sharpened sword in her own right hand.
"In the rite of killing (*māraṇa*), the practitioner of mantras should visualize [the deity] seated upon the shoulders of a lion, pulling [the victim] by the hair with her right hand.
There is also another distinction: "In rites of pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), subjugation (*vaśya*), and paralyzing (*stambhana*)," [so it is said].
One should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times for the protection of one's own mantra.

"For expulsion, eradication, inciting hatred, deluding, causing confusion, and killing, the practitioner of mantra should likewise recite the mantra one thousand times. Regarding the word "unmatta" (mad), there is a specific visualization [to be employed].
"Durgā in the form of a Śabarī woman, holding a skull-bowl filled with poison and a powder called *śatabhaṅga*, should be meditated upon for the rite of subjugation (*mādana*). Thus [it is said].
"The mad one" [refers to this].
Dhustūra || 98–100 ||
One should perform a fire-oblation at night in a wilderness with the feathers of an owl and a crow mixed with one's own fat and blood; the enemy shall then become a guest of Death. || 101 ||
"By wings" means by feathers.
"Stained with the blood of its own fat" means stained with the blood of the fat of an owl or a crow.
"In the wilderness" means in the forest. || 101 ||
The minister should place an effigy of the enemy, into which breath has been infused and whose limbs are smeared with poison and pungent substances, into very hot water. || 102 ||
One who is overcome by fever will quickly find relief through the sprinkling of milk.
[She is] terrifying, holding a three-pointed index finger with both her arms. || 103 ||
Having meditated upon the red [deity] within the orb of the sun, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times;
thus, one shall slay one's enemies, together with their kinsmen, before long. || 104 ||

Having meditated upon her as wrathful, equipped with armor, holding a sword and a shield, and situated within the solar disc, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra; he shall destroy his enemies before long. || 105 ||
Regarding the phrase "an image of the enemy":
if the birth asterism (*janmanakṣatra*) of the enemy is known, then [the image] should be made of wood from the tree belonging to that asterism;
if it is not known, it should be made of *kāraskara* wood and twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length.
The "constellation-trees" (nakṣatravṛkṣāḥ) will be described in the twenty-second [chapter].
"Pratiṣṭhitasamīraṇām" means one for whom the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) has been performed.
"Uṣaṇam" means black pepper (marica).
"Marica is said to be *śyāmala*, and that which is produced from a creeper is known as *ūṣaṇa*," thus says Rudra.
He states the remedy with the word "milk" (*dugdha*).
Regarding the word "index finger" (*tarjanīm*):
The *tarjanī-mudrā* is as previously described. "Triśikha" means a trident (*triśūla*). "Sannaddhā" means having donned armor (*kṛtasannāhā*).
The connection is as follows: having meditated upon the solar orb, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times as before.
