Regarding the term "mantrī" (the practitioner of mantra): it refers to one who knows the proper time, such as the specific hour (*velā*) and so forth. || 102-105 ||
[He saw] a terrifying goddess, holding a bow and arrows, mounted upon a lion and resembling a blazing fire;
she was discharging volleys of arrows and rushing toward such an enemy. || 106 ||
Having meditated thus, one should recite this mantra ten million times while standing in the midst of water;
one will certainly and swiftly expel both the enemy and the hostile army. || 107 ||
"Such" means running. "Situated in the midst of water" means up to the lower part of the knees.
"Having made [the image] out of *kāraskara* wood," "with the feathers of an owl and a crow," and "a three-pointed forefinger with both arms."

"Holding a sword and a shield, and clad in armor"—by reciting this and so forth, one will certainly cause [the enemy] to be swiftly eradicated. Regarding such cruel rites: having understood the specific times and seasons, the lunar days (*tithi*), constellations (*nakṣatra*), the *riktā* days, the adverse positions of the planets and asterisms in the *aṣṭavarga*, and the conjunctions such as *pātāla* and others, that which is performed at such a time grants swift accomplishment.
In this context, "velā" refers to the agitation of the ocean beginning from moonrise for a duration of fifteen *ghaṭikās*; that is the lunar *velā*.
At that time, one should not perform cruel rites (*krūrakarman*).
Thereafter, for another period of fifteen *ghaṭikās*, there is no *velā*; at that time, one may perform cruel rites.
Furthermore, immediately following that, the period lasts for fifteen ghaṭikās;
after that same duration, it is no longer present.
As for time—
"The Kulika, the Elder (Sthavira), Yoga, Tārā, Vaināśikī, and Kuja; these, beginning with the eighth sign, are the Tārās used for minor rites. Thus it is said.
"Kalā" refers to the digit of the moon; it increases in the bright fortnight and wanes in the dark fortnight.
One should perform [the rite] starting from the eighth lunar day until the new moon.
The "empty" lunar days (*tithi*) are well known;
the "empty" constellations (*nakṣatra*) are the "poisonous hours" (*viṣanāḍī*).
But in other cases:
having ascertained the life-span of the enemy according to the rules stated for the ascendant,
one should likewise determine the positions of the planets constituting that [enemy] and their *aṣṭakavarga*.
One should perform the rite of exorcism (abhicāraka) in accordance with these three;
for otherwise, the cruel rites will surely destroy the one who performs them.
One should perform those very same actions; otherwise, by acting in opposition to that triad according to one's ability, there will be fruitlessness and self-destruction.
When the eighth house from the Ripu (the sixth) is in the ascendant, and at a time when [the planet] is situated in its eighth sign,
the practitioner should perform inauspicious rites for the destruction of that [enemy].
In the Pātāla yoga, in that called Nīca, in Viṣa yoga, in Mṛtyuja,
in Nāśa yoga, in Dinaja-mṛtyu, and in Krakaca yoga;
And at Caṇḍīśa, Caṇḍāyudhaka, Mahāśūla, and Kāṇaka;
at Raktasthūṇa, the one called Kaṇṭaka, and Sthūṇa known as Pañcārka.
"One should perform ritual applications for the purpose of breaking the enemy's power and for his destruction;
having thus observed [the situation], one should act for the sake of subjugation and shall attain success. Thus it is said. The eighth house will be described in the section on the *cakra-mantra*.
Other yogas are to be known from the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra). || 106-107 ||
By offering oblations well-kindled with *ānityaka* wood, one is liberated from disease and grief; by means of its flowers smeared with honey, one may bring elephants under control. || 108 ||

For protection, one should smear the elephant with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) consecrated by mantra; likewise, one should offer oblations of cow-products, clarified butter, sesame seeds, white mustard, and the excellent *ānityaka* wood. || 109 ||
With milk-rice, the five products of the cow, rice, and ghee—with these individual substances, one thousand and eight [offerings] each. || 110 ||
One should offer oblations into the fire and feed the Brahmins with sweet foods and other delicacies;
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, accompanied by garments and ornaments.
By this rite, the Mātaṅgas and the fourfold armies flourish;
they become entirely free from disease and devoid of minor afflictions. || 112 ||
Regarding the term *anityakam*:
in the Kānyakubja dialect, it is *eracchi*.
*Gavyājyam* is one word.
"With these"— meaning with these eight substances—
"day by day," that is, every single day,
"one should offer oblations separately."
It should be understood that this occurs sequentially: on the first day with the first substance, and on the second day with the second, and so forth.
The term "day by day" (dinaśaḥ) also applies to the phrase "he should feed the Brahmins. (108–112)
One should have the five weapons fashioned from *brahmavṛkṣa* wood by a craftsman:
the conch, the sword, the discus, the *śārṅga* bow, and the *kaumodakī* mace, in their proper order.
"One should have it made" refers to the measurement of a palm tree.
"With a *brahmavṛkṣa*" means with a *palāśa* tree.
It should be understood that this is "fruitful" when performed by one standing on the ground of the twice-born.
Regarding the term "artisan," the word "more skillful" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
This has been stated by the Teachers:
"One who knows the excellent craft.
*Rathāṅga* means a wheel.
The Śārṅga bow;
the Kaumodakī mace.
This is the meaning of the word "in order" (kramāt).

Having marked a large Palāśa tree in the cardinal directions, having cut it with a saw, and having split it into five parts, one should fashion a conch from the central portion and swords and other weapons from the four directional portions starting from the east.
This has been stated by the Teachers:

"Having cut down the great tree of the twice-born and split it further into five parts, the five weapons should be fashioned according to the sequence of the [five] hopes by one skilled in the craft. (113)
Having cast them into the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and touched them, one should mutter the mantra;
then, having properly performed the "sampāta" rite over them five thousand times, one should do so again. || 114 ||
One should offer oblations with clarified butter using their respective mantras and perform worship in due order;
then, having extracted [the substance] from the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) as before, one should recite the mantra.

"Having placed [them] in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)" means: having made a vessel from *palāśa* wood itself and having poured the five products of the cow into its midst, one should place those [mantras] therein;
"Manu" refers to the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
"Five thousand" refers to the total aggregate;
"correctly" means that each [mantra] is recited one thousand times.
While correctly casting [the oblation] into those weapons, one should perform the fire-offering (*homa*) five thousand times.
"Correctly" means according to the manner of one thousand [repetitions] for each individual weapon.
"With their own mantras" refers to those which will be described in the seventeenth [chapter].
"One should worship" means [one should worship] in the vessel itself, preceded by the rite of consecrating the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā). "In sequence" means...
The meaning is "beginning with Śaṅkha who stands in the middle.
"As before" means touching those [points] again that same number of times.
In the Īśānasaṃhitā, however, it is said:
"Having cut down a tree belonging to a Brahmin or the earth that stands upon a Brahmin's land— such as one bearing fruit— and having split it into five equal parts from root to tip on all sides,"
From the middle portion, one should fashion, in sequence, the conch, the Nandaka sword, and the discus;
likewise, one should fashion the Śārṅga bow and the Kaumodakī mace, measuring the height of a palm tree.
Having placed that [substance] into a vessel containing the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and having set it down upon an auspicious svastika,
one should worship it properly and recite the mantra five thousand times.
Having first offered oblations with clarified butter according to the prescribed rite, and having likewise anointed [the image] with the residue of the clarified butter,
the wise practitioner should again recite this mantra.
Having dug pits measuring one cubit in depth in the center and in the directions starting from the east,
one should worship the pedestal there and install it with the root mantra.
Having invoked Mahādurgā into that conch, one should worship her as she stands therein,
along with her respective weapons and forms, which possess the characteristics described for the directions.
One should imagine a rampart all around with the weapon-mantra. Thus [ends verses 114–115].
One should dig five pits in the directions starting from the east and proceeding to the center in sequence.
When these pits have been filled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the practitioner [should proceed]. || 116 ||
The weapons are consecrated with the fivefold sounds;
one should place them starting from the center and perform worship as before. || 117 ||
Having filled it with sand, one should make the ground level with earth;
and there, one should scatter an offering for them with their respective mantras in due order. || 118 ||
Having offered the bali-oblation to the guardians of the directions, one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas;
and one should satisfy the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others with food and other gifts. || 119 ||
"Avaṭān" means "measured by the span of the hand. By the word "sādhaka," it is stated that one should perform the placement (vinyāsa) while reciting the root mantra.
"Arranged" is a restatement;
"one should place" means with the root mantra;
"as before" [refers to the previous arrangement].
With their respective mantras; "in due order" means starting from the center and so forth. (116–119)
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor according to the extent of one's own wealth;
wherever such protection has been thus established, whether in a country, a district, or a city. || 120 ||
In that village or house, prosperity always increases;
yet there are defects such as falling stones, accompanied by spirits, ghosts, and the like. || 121 ||
Sorcery, magical spells, enemies, thieves, and other such calamities do not even look toward that direction; terrified and conquered by him at the command of the deity, they flee. || 122 ||
One should draw a lotus provided with sun-like petals;

then, in its pericarp, one should again place the *tāra* (the syllable Om) together with the seed-syllable containing the *śakti* and accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Then, in sequence, one should place the letters arising from the mantra, two at a time, upon the filaments, and subsequently, the letters belonging to the petals.
Having divided the syllables of the mantra according to the [three] qualities, one should write the final syllable on the final petal.
Enveloped by the letters of the Mātṛkā and situated between two squares of the earth-grid (bhūpura), this yantra of the Goddess dwelling on the Vindhya is said to bestow all prosperity. || 124 ||
It is especially a provider of protection, a destroyer of minor spirits and the like;
it bestows sovereignty upon those who have lost their kingdom, and grants subjugation to those who desire to bring others under their control. || 125 ||
It bestows sons upon those seeking sons and brings peace from disease to the sick;
what more need be said here? This yantra is a wish-fulfilling jewel. || 126 ||
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Śāradātilaka composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra. 11.
Regarding the yantra, he says "lotus" and so forth:
one should draw a lotus provided with twelve petals, corresponding to the twelve suns.

In its pericarp, one should write the Praṇava (Oṃ) together with the goal to be accomplished, preceded by the seed-syllable of Durgā— which resides in the Śakti and contains the Māyā-bīja— and followed by the Visarga. By this it is meant that,
having written the Praṇava in the pericarp of the twelve-petalled lotus, one should write the Māyā-bīja there, then the seed-syllable of Durgā, and then the goal to be accomplished.

"Madīnyā" means those beginning with "mahiṣamadi. By the phrase "in pairs," the threefold repetition of the *mahiṣamadinī* mantra is indicated. "Mantrārṇān" refers to the syllables of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
There are three praises of qualities.
One should write the final single syllable at the end, in the twelfth [position]. (123–126)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition. 11.
Now begins the twelfth chapter:
[It is] the destroyer of the darkness of ignorance, the savior from the ocean of saṃsāra.
May the inconceivable seed of bliss, the great splendor of the Triple City (Tripura), descend. || 1 ||
Now I shall declare the supreme knowledge, which is most secret even from Tripurā;
by knowing which, a man becomes the sovereign lord of all the hosts of Siddhas.
Having thus stated the mantras of Durgā, and because the third [mantra] has been indicated in the *Mātṛkāpaṭala*, he begins to state the mantra of Bhairava with the words "ajñāna" etc.
The etymology of the word *Tripurā* is stated elsewhere:

"Because she existed prior to the creation of the three forms (trimūrti), because she consists of the three Vedas (trayī), and because she fills even the three worlds at the time of dissolution, the name of Ambikā is primarily 'Tripurā'. According to the *Siddheśvarīmata*, however: "In ancient times, she was built by the three gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna."
"In the past, that name 'Tripura' was uttered by the gods.
By the phrase "extremely secret," this is what is meant:
even by me, the true nature [of the goddess] has been extracted while remaining concealed.

Otherwise, having made the promise, "I shall speak of the Vidyā," and then concluding with "the Vidyā is to be known," yet extracting a Mantra [instead], this would be inconsistent; for it has been said: "That which begins with Śakti is called Vidyā, while that which begins with Śiva is called Mantra. As it has been stated: "This is that Śāmbhavī Vidyā, hidden like a woman of noble family."
"It circulates upon the surface of the earth through oral instruction from ear to ear.
The words "siddhi" and so forth constitute the statement regarding the application (viniyoga). || 1–2 ||
The elemental [mantra] situated in space (viyat), Jupiter (bhṛgu), and fire (hutāśa), topped with the bindu;
then the one situated in space, that same [Jupiter], the center (kendra), and fire, possessing the left eye (vāmākṣi) and the bindu;
and the mantra situated in ether (ākāśa), Jupiter, and fire, bearing the crescent moon of creation (sarga). || 3 ||
He extracts the mantra as "viyat" and so forth. *Viyat* is *ha*; *Bhṛgu* is *sa*; *Hutāśa* is the letter *ra*.
These [letters] reside here; thus, by the rule *supi sthaḥ*, the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of location according to the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*).
The first *kūṭa* consists of the element of earth (*bhautika*), the nasal dot (*anusvāra*), and so forth; *viyat* is *ha*, that which begins with it is *sa*;
*ka* is its own form (*svarūpa*).
"Indra-laḥ agnī-raḥ"—
where these are situated is the beginning of the *āhitāgni* [mantra], etc.
"Vāmākṣi-ī" with the nasal dot (*bindu*) as the *anusvāra* is the second *kūṭa*.

The third *kūṭa* consists of: *ākāśa* (the letter *ha*), *bhṛgu* (the letter *sa*), *vahnī* (the letter *repha*, i.e., *ra*), *manu* (the letters *au*), *sarge* (the *visarga*), *indukhaṇḍa* (the crescent moon), and *anusvāra*.
The *repha* at the beginning and end serves as the *kīlaka*.
As it has been stated by the Teachers in the *Bhairavīstava*:
The first [syllable] is the third [vowel] conjoined with fire (R); the seed-syllable is the second [consonant] adorned by fire (R).
Thus [ends the verse]. || 3 ||
The first seed-syllable is Vāgbhava, the second is Kāmabīja, and the third is known as Kāmarāja; thus she is described by means of these three seed-syllables.
The Vidyā consisting of five peaks is Tripurabhairavī, who is to be known. Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (ṛṣi), and Paṅkti is declared to be the meter (chandas). || 5 ||
The deity is said by the teachers to be the goddess Tripurabhairavī;
the knower of the mantra should then place the Vāgbhava mantra from the navel down to the feet.
One should place the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) from the heart down to the navel;
then, one should place the third syllable from the head down to the region of the heart.

One should place the first [syllable] on the two hands, the second on both [feet], and the third on the head, the base, and the heart; one should again place the three seed-syllables in this sequence.
He states the individual names of these as "vāgbhava" and "consisting of five peaks.

It consists of five peaks due to the conjunction of the five consonants *ha*, *sa*, *ka*, *la*, and *ra*; it consists of four peaks by virtue of being devoid of the letter *repha* (r), and it possesses the *nāda* above the *repha*.
The state of having six peaks (ṣaṭkūṭatva) is to be known.
Its thirty variations of expansion (prastāra-bheda) are not stated here for fear of making the book too voluminous;
they should be sought from other tantras.
The first [syllable] is the seed (*bīja*), the middle is the power (*śakti*), or the last is the power.
The fruit of meditating on the seed-syllables individually is stated according to the Sārasvata tradition:
"The Goddess, resembling a fresh jasmine flower, adorned with nets of pearls..."
[She] has great arms bearing a mudrā, a skull-cup, a vidyā-staff, and a rosary.
O Great Goddess, he who, being self-controlled, recites the Vāgbhava mantra one hundred thousand times,
becomes a poet whose compositions are beautiful with various meters and meanings.
Red in color, she stands at the foot of the celestial tree upon a shimmering gem-studded pedestal,
her hands holding a goad, a noose, a skull-cup, an arrow, a citron, and a bow.
Adorned with red flowers, her eyes rolling from intoxication,
she was endowed with playful charm and beauty in the bloom of fresh youth.

Having meditated upon the Goddess, the self-controlled practitioner who recites the middle seed-syllable one hundred thousand times will swiftly agitate the three worlds and, as in the past, become a partaker of supernatural attainments.
She holds a rosary, a jar of nectar, a mudrā, and a book;
she resembles the new moon and jasmine, O King, and is adorned with pearls.

"Having meditated upon the Śakti consisting of consciousness, the self-controlled one who recites the seed-syllable of Sarasvatī finds that his poetic genius becomes continuous upon this earth. Thus it is said.

And in another Tantra: "One who desires knowledge, dressed in white garments and white unguents and adorned with pearl ornaments, should recite the mantra known as Vāgbhava three hundred thousand times in an underground chamber."
Meditating thus upon his own speech as it pours forth prose and verse,
he should offer oblations with *palāśa* flowers alone, drenched in the three sweets (*trimadhura*).
If one desires to bring the three worlds under one's control, that best of poets shall be born as the beloved of beautiful women, provided he recites the second Kāmarāja mantra.
Sweet with the fragrance of musk and saffron, adorned with reddish ornaments,
and wearing garments of red silk, the wise one should mutter [the mantra] three hundred thousand times.
Subduing the world with the corners of her eyes, tremulous with passion—
meditating upon her own form as Ambikā with a joyful heart.
One should offer oblations with *mālatī* flowers saturated with cool camphor;
the worlds become subject to his control—what need is there for much more?
One who desires to attain the playful grace of speech should mutter even a single final seed-syllable a hundred thousand times;
adorned with pure ornaments and garments, he shall become an excellent poet of immeasurable fame,
by means of jasmine buds and falling petals submerged in thick sandalwood water.
"Bringing fortune, having her actions destroyed by flowers, she is likewise considered to be a swift bringer of poetic skill.
Here, because the three seed-syllables (bījas) are extremely well-guarded, the author has not provided the extraction of the illuminating syllables (dīpanī).
Consequently, this Vidyā does not grant success to those who lack it.
Therefore, its extraction is written from the *Siddheśvarī Tantra*:
"In the mantra of Vāgīśvarī, the one known as the Vāgbhava [syllable] resides in the place of the beloved of the Fire-god (RA);
thereafter, the words 'klinne kledini' and 'mahākṣobham' should be joined here."

Therefore, if this [mantra] is uttered as "kuvīti," with its syllables obstructed, there is liberation from the stars within it; and at its end, the word "kuru" should be joined, which is known as Samohana.

Indeed, the mantras herein are the illuminators of the seed-syllables; by means of which the King of Mantras consisting of the three seeds is always perfectly kindled during the rite of recitation, bringing about all prosperity.
He who masters the sciences, agitates the minds of young women, and wanders as a monk—[by this mantra].
The minister shall be like the Lord of Pleasure endowed with all perfections, free from obstacles, and long-lived. Thus it is said.
The liberation through consciousness and bliss mentioned in the commentary on the first verse should be kept in mind.
However, in the latter six [verses], it is said:
"By the first [syllable] she is obscured, but by the middle one she is pinned down."
But if it is cut by the last [syllable], that vidyā is not accomplished.
The first is the beginningless beginning, the middle is the middling-middling, and the end is the endless end; Tripurā bestows swift accomplishment.
"At the beginning and in the middle, and at the end and in the middle;
for the sake of agitation [of the powers], the mantra should be recited by practitioners according to this rule.
Elsewhere, however—
He who recites [the mantra] having joined the first seed-syllable with the middle one, and the last one with the end of the middle one,
shall have the hosts of beings within the three worlds brought under his control and made to share in his sovereignty.
"Having placed the first [syllable] at the beginning and the final seed-syllable at the end, and the middle [syllable] in the middle and at the start,
the best of practitioners who daily recites this mantra becomes liberated while living and attains divine perfection.
Regarding the phrase "of the two hands," it refers to the left and right.
As it has been said: "On the palm of the left hand, and on the second, called the right. (4-8)
One should again perform the placement (nyāsa) consisting of the nine wombs with the three seed-syllables;
[placing them] on the two ears, the chin, then on the two temples, and again on the mouth.

One should place [the syllables] on the two eyes, the nose, the two shoulders, and again on the stomach; then on the two elbows, the two sides of the abdomen, the two knees, and on the head of the penis. || 10 ||
Then one should place Rati and the others on the two feet, the secret place, the two sides, the heart-lotus, the two breasts, and the region of the throat. || 11 ||
He explains that which was stated as "consisting of nine wombs" with the words beginning with "karṇa.
Each womb consists of three positions each.
Regarding this, some maintain that it is the ritual placement (nyāsa) starting from the left limb.
For this very reason, there is the statement regarding the worship [beginning with] "in the left corner" and so forth.
Regarding "the two conchs":
these refer to the regions on either side of the forehead.
In the *Trikāṇḍī* as well: "Śaṅkha refers to a treasure and the bone of the forehead;
nasī refers to the nose;
piṭhara refers to the belly."
Because of its high elevation.
By the word "in the womb" (*kukṣau*), the region of the navel is indicated in order to establish the shape of the yoni, such as that of a tortoise and so forth.
Thus it has been said:
"One should place [the syllables] on the elbows and in the navel-region. In some versions, the reading is "in the navel" (nābhau).
"Dhvaja" means the penis. (9–11)

One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the three *bālā* seed-syllables in these locations in reverse order: *rati* at the base [of the feet], *prīti* at the heart, and *manobhavā* between the eyebrows. || 12 ||

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of these [deities]—Amṛteśī, Yogeśī, and Viśvayoni—in sequence using their seed-syllables in reverse order; thereafter, one should perform the placement of the forms (mūrtinyāsa). || 13 ||
Regarding what was stated as "beginning with Rati" and so forth, he says that very thing: "In the root," etc.
The connection is: "one should place [the syllables] by means of the three Bālā-bījas in reverse order.
This is connected later with the phrase "in these places."
In this context, "reversal" (vilomatva) refers to the following: the first [syllable] of *rati* is the *vāgbhava*; the last of *prīti* is the *manobhava*; and the middle of *madana* is likewise.
As they say:
"The seed-syllable of desire (*kāma*) is taught as the *kāmabīja*, while the seed-syllable of *rati* is the *vāgbhava*."
"The last [syllable], called *samohana*, is the seed of joy (*prīti*), as has been stated.
Regarding the word "in these":
the grammatical connection is that one should install the goddesses beginning with Amṛteśī in the previously mentioned locations together with the *bālā* seeds in reverse order.
In this case as well, the reverse order is exactly as before. || 12–13 ||
First, the knower of the self should place Īśāna, who is the mind-born one (Kāma), with his own seed-syllable and so forth upon the head;
then he should place Tatpuruṣa, who is the dolphin-bannered one (Kāma), upon the face. || 14 ||
Immediately after that, one should place the god of love (Kandarpa) consisting of the Hṛdaya, Aghora, Kumāra, and so forth in the heart;
then, one should install the god of love (Manmatha) consisting of Vāmadeva and the others in the secret region. || 15 ||
Then, one should place Sadyojāta and Kāmadeva at the two feet;
[and likewise] those [deities] upon the faces in the upward, eastern, southern, northern, and western directions. || 16 ||
Regarding the phrase "their respective seed-syllables and so forth":

the seed-syllables of the forms (mūrtis) to be described—the seed-syllables of Manobhava and the others—should be known respectively as the Vanitā, the fourth arrow, the Vāgbhava, the Kāma, and the Māyā seed-syllables.
In both cases, the word "and so forth" (ādi) indicates only that these [syllables] precede them.
Therefore, there is a single verse.
[The word] "tān" refers to Īśāna, Manobhava, and the others.
Thus, this is the formal application (prayoga).
Hsrāṃ to Īśāna, strīṃ to Manobhava, namaḥ, and so forth. || 14–16 ||
One should arrange them as before; Bhṛgu (m), Vyoma (h), and Agni (r) are situated there.
Sadyojāta and the others are established in the five short vowels; this is proclaimed as their seed-syllable.
Regarding the phrase "as before" and the statement "one's own respective seed-syllables, etc.," Bhṛgu extracts those seed-syllables as follows:
Bhṛgu is *sa*; *vyoma* is *ha*; and *agni* is *ra*. It is "properly joined with those two."
In the upper and lower parts respectively, the five short vowels beginning with *sa* (sadyojāta) are [placed] in reverse order: *o*, *e*, *u*, *i*, *a*. || 17 ||
The ritual assignment of the limbs (aṅgakriyā) is considered to be performed with the first seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels.
The practitioner of mantra should assign the five arrows that enchant the three worlds upon his own body.
"Six" refers to the seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels, that is, the middle seed-syllable;
"by the first seed-syllable" refers to the initial seed-syllable of the mantra.
This is according to tradition.
It should also be understood as being by means of the Śākta and other [methods].
Therefore, this is the ritual application.

Hsroḥ hasakala hrāṃ hrīṃ hsrauṃ—[this is] the heart, five times; hrīṃ hrīṃ hsrauṃ—[this is] the head, five times; hrūṃ hrīṃ hsrauṃ—[this is] the crest-lock, five times; hraiṃ hrīṃ hsrauṃ—[this is] the armor, five times; hrauṃ hrīṃ—[this is] the eye, five times; hraḥ hrīṃ hsrauṃ—[this is] the weapon. || 18 ||

One should place Drāviṇī, beginning with *drāṃ*, on the head; Kṣobhiṇī, beginning with *drīṃ*, on the feet; Vaśīkaraṇī, preceded by *klīṃ*, on the mouth; and [the goddess] preceded by the seed-syllable *blūṃ* on the secret organ. || 19 ||
Ākarṣaṇī again in the heart, joined with Bhṛgu at the end of creation;
Sammohanī in this same sequence—this is declared to be the placement of the arrows (bāṇanyāsa). || 20 ||

In the forehead, between the eyebrows, the mouth, the hanging uvula, the throat, and the heart, as well as in the navel and the foundation, there are five [deities] beginning with Tārā and Subhagā. || 21 ||
The fortunate goddesses, Bhaga and Bhagā, should be installed by the mantra-practitioner according to the ritual procedure;
then Bhagasapīṇī, and after that, the supreme Bhagamālinī. || 22 ||
Anaṅgā, Anaṅgakusumā, and again Anaṅgamekhalā;
Anaṅgamadanā—all of them were languid with the intoxication of amorous passion. || 23 ||

Adorned with the colors, ornaments, and other attributes of their principal deities, their lotus-like hands are enriched by holding a rosary, a book, and displaying the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons. || 24 ||
Regarding the phrase "drām-ādyām":
here, in every instance, the teacher has read *ṅa* in place of *ma*;
elsewhere, however, it is said that the arrows begin with *drāṃ*, *drīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *blūṃ*, and *saḥ*.
As it is stated in the *Tripurāsāra*:

"The Lord of Mountains (D) accompanied by the face (U), fire (R), and the vowel 'a' (A)—that is the first seed-syllable; indeed, that same syllable with the staff (M) and the face (U) conjoined with the three forms (Ū) shall be the second."
"Situated within the mouth [of the syllable], mounted by the king of gods (Indra), with a leftward glance, joined with the first of the faces;

preceded by the asterism (Bha), together with the circle (Vṛtta), the enemy (Ari), the sixth vowel (Ū), and half of the lord of the night (Kṣa); the fourth [letter] joined with the letter preceding Ka.
Thus: *Adrīśa* is *da*; the "mouth-circle" (*mukhavṛtta*) is *ā*; *vahni* is *ra*; "with staff" (*sadaṇḍa*) means accompanied by the *anusvāra*.
"This first is *drām*.
That very same [syllable] is the second, *drīm*, which has the form of a face (*ānanavṛtta*) consisting of the letter *ā* conjoined with the letter *ī* of the three forms (*trimūrti*).
Within the mouth is *ka*, the king of gods is *la*, and the left eye is *ī*.
The anusvāra preceded by "vaktra" (the mouth, i.e., *a*) results in *klīṃ*; this is the third [seed-syllable].

"Bha" (the letter *ba*) preceded by "vṛttāri" (the sixth vowel, *ū*), joined with the letter *la*, becomes *blūṃ*; this is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). "Ka" refers to water; its seed-syllable is the letter *va*. Its fourth [vowel] is *sa*; preceded by *ka* and accompanied by *visarga*, it becomes *saḥ*; this is the fifth.
The word "in the heart" (hṛdi) is connected with what follows.
He is Bhṛgu, the end of creation.
Regarding the term "lambikā":
It is a specific location within the mouth.
In some places, the reading is *kaṇīkā*;
in that case, the *Trikāṇḍī* states: "The *kaṇīkā* is an ear-ornament."
Regarding the phrase "according to the rule":

this refers to the fourth case ending (caturthī) terminating in "namaḥ. By the word "by the practitioner" (mantriṇā), it is implied that these [mantras] are to be combined with the preceding ones. || 19-24 ||
The syllables VĀK, KĀMA, BLŪM, STRĪM, and SAḤ—these five are proclaimed as the Tārās;
thereafter, the most excellent practitioner should perform the deposition known as the "Ornaments" (bhūṣaṇa). || 25 ||
He speaks of the *tārās* themselves:
*vāk* refers to the *vāgbhava* [syllable],
and *kāma* refers to the *kāmabīja*.
The other is the *svarūpa* [arrangement]. Regarding the term "called *bhūṣaṇa*":
the *bhūṣaṇanyāsa* is the placement of phonemes in the form of ornaments.
He says that very thing:
"Then the best of practitioners should perform the nyāsa.
The words "the letters of the Mātṛkā" are to be understood as the ellipsis.
By the phrase "O best of practitioners" (sādhakasattama), the presence of the nasal bindu and its visualization as an ornament in each respective location is stated. || 25 ||

One should place [the letters] on the head, on the forehead, the eyebrows, the two ears, the pair of eyes, and the nose; one should place the vowels on the two cheeks, the two lips, the two rows of teeth, and the mouth. || 26 ||
Then on the chin, the throat, the neck, the two sides, the pair of breasts, the two armpits, the two elbows, the two hands, and the region of their backs. || 27 ||
Then at the navel, the secret place, the two thighs, the knees, and the shanks; thereafter, at the two buttocks, the two calves, and finally at the two big toes of the feet. || 28 ||

With a concentrated mind, one should place the letters from *ka* to *ra* in these locations: first on the waist, then on the neck, then on the wrists, and finally on the heart and the private parts. || 29 ||
The best of teachers should thus place these eight syllables— *va*, *la*, *śā*, *ṣa*, *kṣa*, *sā*, *la*, and *ha*— upon the two ear-ornaments and the crown.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon his body, he should meditate upon Tripurabhairavī.
He states the very locations for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the words "on the head," etc. "The throat" refers to the *maṇi* (the pit of the throat), and "the neck" is the region below that.
Here, the placement of two syllables each is performed on the ears and so forth.
One at the location of the eyebrows, one on the two hands,
and one on the region of their backs— so say those who know the tradition.
By the word *sphik* (the buttocks), the two ankles are indicated due to their similarity in height.

The letter *la* is palatal (*mūrddhanya*) on the hip; the letter *śa* is palatal in the heart; and the distinction is that [the letters] are palatal and dental respectively in the two ear-rings—this is what was stated by the "best of teachers. (26–30)

She possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns, wears a crimson silken garment, and is adorned with a garland upon her head; her breasts are smeared with red pigment, and she holds a rosary, the Vidyā, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting mudrā in her lotus-like hands; she bears the beauty of a three-eyed, radiant lotus-face.
I bow to the Goddess, whose jeweled crown is bound with the moon, and who possesses a gentle smile. || 31 ||
Regarding the word "udyat": the analysis of the compound is "that which possesses a garland (*mālā*) of heads (*śirasām*), that is, of severed heads.
Regarding "raktā," it refers to red sandalwood.
The meditation on the weapons is performed with the right upper hand in the first [case] and with the two hands situated below that in the last;
some say it extends from the right upper hand down to the right lower hand.
Here, one should show another meditation preceded by the seed-syllables of the arrows and the five mudrās, which are to be understood from the mouth of the Guru. (31)
Having received initiation, one who has conquered the senses should recite the mantra one million times according to the true principle;
one should offer oblations with flowers from the Brahma-tree (Bilva) ten thousand times for each of the suns (twelve thousand). || 32 ||
"Or with flowers produced from the *karavīra* tree smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*).
Having received initiation— this means having received the initiation of power (*śaktidīkṣā*).
And that [number] is to be understood from other tantras, such as the *Siddheśvarīmata* and others.
Regarding the words *tattva* and *bhānu*, there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) because they are identical in form.
"A hundred thousand *tattvas*" means thirty-six hundred thousand.

The fire-oblation (homa), however, consists of thirty-six thousand oblations with *palāśa* flowers; this is the number for the four-peaked [mantra]. These flowers should be smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), that is, combined with milk, honey, and clarified butter.
Some say that sugar should be used in place of milk;
this applies to both cases.
"A hundred thousand tattvas" means twenty-four lakhs.
The fire sacrifice (homa), however, consists of twenty-four thousand oblations with *karavīra* flowers;
this number pertains to the five-peaked [mantra].
[For the others, it is] one hundred thousand for the *tattva* [mantra] and twelve hundred thousand for the twelve-syllable [mantra].
Because twelve principles (*tattva*) are also taught in another tantra,
it is said in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Therefore, some wise ones declare that there are twelve principles."
Thus [it is said].

In that view, the word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "or with flowers" (*prasūnairvā*) functions as a conjunction (*samuccaya*); thus, the oblation (*homa*) is performed with both combined, totaling twelve thousand.
Furthermore, this number should be understood to apply to the six-peaked mantra (*ṣaṭkūṭa*).
As it has been said by the Teachers:

"Having received initiation from a guru who possesses the marks of excellence and belongs to a true lineage, one who is well-restrained should recite this mantra until half a lakh of its true essence is reached."

And with fresh *palāśa* flowers having sweet-smelling petals, the practitioner of mantras, having properly kindled the fire, should offer oblations equal to a thousand suns, even with the blood of the enemies of horses (elephants). Thus it is said.
In this context, the principles (*tattvas*) are thirty-six, twenty-four, half [of that], and twelve.

They are called "lights" (*bhānavaḥ*) because they shine; thus, the thirty-six principles, the twenty-four principles, and the twelve suns (*ādityas*) have been explained by the teacher Padmapādācārya.
Here too, this same meaning should be understood for the word *bhānu*. (32–33)
A lotus endowed with eight petals and a pericarp enriched with nine triangles. || 33 ||
One should worship the seat of Bhairavī, which is endowed with the powers of will and the rest;
namely, Will, Knowledge, Action, and thereafter Kāminī, the bestower of desires. || 34 ||
Rati, Ratipriyā, Nandā, and Navamī shall be Manonmanī;
these nine Śaktis are declared to be the bearers of the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. || 35 ||
He states the worship-diagram (*pūjāyantra*) with the words "the lotus" (*padmam*).
The remaining sense is that the lotus, having a pericarp consisting of nine wombs (*yoni*) and so forth, is her worship-diagram.
The method for its extraction is now described:

In the second and subsequent divisions of two each, having pierced the womb-circles with the fire of the twilight-sound, one should draw circles with the qualities of three parts, and outside [the center], a lotus together with the earth-house.
The meaning of this is as follows: having made a circle of any desired dimension and divided its eastern diameter into four parts, one should discard one part from the top;

then, starting from the second part and ending at the third part, one should form a downward-pointing triangle. Then, starting from the center and ending at the fourth part, one should form another downward-pointing triangle. Finally, starting from the first part—which separates the junctions of those two—one should form an upward-pointing [triangle].

Having formed a triangle extending up to the third [line], one should form another triangle with its apex pointing upward, starting from the first division that pierces the junction of those two and extending up to the end of the third.
Thus it has been said:
"Situated between the fire-god and the source of the two city-dwellers (Brahmā), with its corners resting upon fire, Varuṇa, and Īśa.
This refers merely to the traditional recollection that [the goddesses] hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
For the meditation on these has already been described in the fourth chapter itself. || 33-35 ||
Vāgbhava, Lohita, Rāyai, Śrīkaṇṭha, Lohita, Anala, Dīrghavān, Yai, Parā, followed by Aparāyai, Hasauḥ, and again [the same]. || 36 ||
"Sadāśivamahāpreta-ṅe'nta-padmāsana-namaḥ. With this mantra, one should offer the seat of the venerable lineage of gurus (śrīgurukrama). || 37 ||
He extracts the *pīṭha-mantra* with the word "vāk": *vāgbhava* is the first seed-syllable of Bālā;
*lohita* is *pa*.
*Rā* is the essential nature (*svarūpa*).
*Śrīkaṇṭha* is the letter *a*; *anala* is *ra*. Being endowed with the long vowel *ā*, it becomes *rā*.
"yai parā" is the original form;
"aparāyai" is the original form;
however, in the case of "parā aparāyai," there is a euphonic combination (sandhi).
*Hsauḥ* is the seed-syllable (*piṇḍa*).
Its essential nature extends up to Sadāśiva Mahāpreta.
The word *preta* is used in the accusative case as the object of the verbal action.
The word *padmāsana* ends in the dative case singular; therefore, [it means] "to the lotus-seat" (*padmāsanāya*). || 36–37 ||
One should worship and further arrange [the ritual] in the space between the eastern and central yonis;
having invoked the deity into that [space], one should [visualize] the form by means of five *praṇavas*.
The connection is that one should worship the lineage of the venerable gurus (śrīgurukrama) in the space between the eastern and central yonis.
Furthermore, the lineage of the venerable gurus is threefold:
the divine host (divyaugha), the perfected host (siddhaugha), and the human host (mānavaugha).
In this regard, the divine lineage (*divyaugha*) consists of Paraprakāśānanda, Parameśānanda, Paramaśivānanda, Kāmeśvaryānanda, Mokṣānanda, Kāmānanda, Amṛtānanda, and others.
The lineage of the accomplished ones (*siddhaugha*) consists of Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadānanda.
As for the human lineage (*mānavaugha*), it is to be known from the respective traditions of one's own gurus.

"One should worship the lineage of gurus on the northern part of the pedestal"—this is an exception to the general rule, which states that [the worship] is "in the space between the front and the center of the yoni. || 38 ||
One should worship with a concentrated mind according to the procedure declared in the Āgamas.
Tārā, Vāk, Śakti, Kamalā, Ha-sa-kha-phreṃ-ha-sauḥ are thus remembered. || 39 ||
In the left corner, one should worship the goddess Rati, whose luster is like that of the moon;
she holds a noose, is gentle, and is overwhelmed by the intoxication of amorous play. || 40 ||
One should worship Prīti, who stands in the southern corner, resembling molten gold, and holding a goad and a gesture of salutation with her two hands.
In front [of her] is Manobhavā, red in color, adorned with red flowers and other ornaments, holding a sugarcane bow and flower-arrows, and possessing a pure smile. || 42 ||
"By what is stated in the Āgama" means by what is taught in the subsequent group of six [chapters].
The etymology of the word *āgama* is stated in another Tantra:
"It has come from the mouth of Śiva and gone into the mouth of the Daughter of the Mountain."
And because this is the opinion of Vāsudeva, it is therefore called *āgama*.
For this very reason, there is the expression "composed" (*samāhita*), meaning "attentive.
Regarding what was stated as "with five *praṇavas*," he specifies those very ones with the word "the *tārās*."
Vāk is the seed-syllable of Vāgbhava; Śakti is the seed-syllable of Māyā;
Kamalā is the seed-syllable of Śrī.
There are two other clusters:
for Rati and Prīti, there is a weapon in one hand and a gesture of salutation in the second during meditation. (39–42)
Thereafter, one who knows the ritual rules should worship the limbs as before;
and first, in the various directions, one should worship the deities of the arrows with their respective mantras.
"As before" means:
in the filaments starting from the southeast (āgneya) and so forth, within the central yoni, and in the four directions;
by the phrase "knowing the procedure," it is stated that this refers to the area outside the central yoni. || 43 ||

One should worship the eight Śaktis, beginning with Subhagā, who possess a radiant luster and offer salutations while holding flowers and arrows in their lotus-like hands, within the eight wombs (yoni). || 44 ||
Regarding the phrase "with lotus-like hands":
there is an arrow in the right hand and a gesture of salutation in the other hand.
As it has been said:

All [the goddesses] beginning with Drāviṇī, in their respective order, are adorned with all ornaments and are full of passion; they hold arrows in their right hands and perform salutations with their remaining hands. Thus [it is said]:
"possessing the splendor of the elements."
The meaning is that their colors are equal to the colors of the earth and the other elements; they are "beginning with Subhagā" as they have been previously arranged. || 44 ||
The two Mothers, seated upon the lap of Bhairava and overwhelmed by the intoxication of passion, should be worshipped duly with flowers and other offerings upon the eight petals. || 45 ||
Then [he saw] the world-protectors in the directions and their weapons outside of them;
having recognized this supreme deity through the merits performed in previous births. || 46 ||
He who follows the prescribed path shall become the abode of all prosperities;
thus, having perfected the mantra, the practitioner of mantras should accomplish his own desired goal. || 47 ||

One should offer oblations with red lotuses that are free from defects and soaked in honey, numbering one hundred thousand or half that amount; or alternatively, one should feed brahmins every day. || 48 ||
One should worship beautiful young women with the thought that they are deities;
at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should satisfy one's own preceptor with wealth, grain, and other offerings. || 49 ||
"Mothers" refers to those ending with Caṇḍikā.
As it has been stated by the Teachers: "One should also worship the group of Mothers, ending with Caṇḍikā, upon the petals together with Asitāṅga and the others."
Thus. By the term "as it truly is" (yathāvat), it is stated that the Mothers are those beginning with the long vowels and the Bhairavas are those beginning with the short vowels.
By the phrase "the station of accomplishments," it is indicated that her name is also "Bestower of Accomplishments" (Sampatpradā). || 45-49 ||

When this is done, the world shall be under one's control, and the abode of Ramā shall be attained—by means of red lotuses smeared with the three sweets, or by red flowers born from the enemy of horses (blue lotuses). || 50 ||
With flowers, milk, food, and ghee, one who knows the golden [mantra] brings the entire universe under control;
through oblations of *palāśa* flowers, the practitioner of mantra attains mastery over speech. || 51 ||
The wise one should offer oblations of guggulu resin combined with camphor and agallochum;
by that very act, he attains divine knowledge and becomes a poet. || 52 ||
An oblation of pieces of *amṛtā* (immortality plant) soaked in milk with gold [as an offering] conquers all untimely death;
an oblation of *dūrvā* grass soaked in milk for three days brings long life.
The term *jaganti-vaśyāni-yasya* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one to whom the worlds are subject.
It is said that this shall become the abode of Ramā.
Regarding that, there is a specific visualization (*dhyāna*): [text follows].
"Having meditated upon Śivā, whose lotus-like hands are adorned with a citron, a rosary, a vessel, and a lotus,
prosperity indeed comes swiftly to one performing rites for nourishment.
Regarding the phrase "born from the enemies of horses," it means born from *karavīra* flowers.
"With ghee" or "with milk products"— this is the third alternative. "He should bring [them] under control."
The specific meditation is as follows:

"The mantra-practitioner, having visualized the form with hands raised holding a noose and a goad, red in color, serene, and her limbs adorned with rubies, diamonds, and emeralds, should perform the previously mentioned rite of making things visible and the eye-ointments. Thus it is said.
"One may become a poet"— this refers to a specific form of meditation taught in the *Saṃvid-śāstra*: "The form consisting of the essence of Sarasvatī, endowed with the primordial form..."
"Whoever should remember [this] at the *dvādaśānta* would, before long, become a master of speech. Thus it is said. *Amṛtā* is *guḍūcī*.
It is called "the conqueror of untimely death" (*apamṛtyujit*).

A specific meditation has been taught by Gautama: "One should perform rites for pacification (śāntika) while visualizing her as wearing white garments and holding the implements of the boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, a jar of nectar, and a book. (50–53)
One may bring Brahmins under control by offering oblations with flowers produced from the *girikarṇī* plant;
kings by means of *kahlāra* flowers; and their wives by means of flowers born from the *kaṇīkāra*. (54)
Having offered oblations with *mallikā* flowers, one shall bring princes under control;
with *koraṇṭaka* flowers, the Vaiśyas; and with those produced from the *pāṭala*, the Śūdras. (55)
Having uttered the mantra, which contains the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) situated at the end of both the forward and reverse orders,
the practitioner of mantra should perform oblations with substances mixed with honey.
With mustard seeds mixed with salt, one may subjugate kings in an instant;
by this very same procedure, one may likewise subjugate their wives and their sons as well. 57 //

With *jātī* flowers and *bilva* fruits mixed with the three sweets (*madhuratrika*), one will certainly bring under control men, women, and kings through the performance of a fire sacrifice (*homa*). || 58 ||
By offering oblations of *mālatī* and *vakula* flowers mixed with sandalwood paste, the practitioner of mantra attains poetic skill within one year. || 59 ||
One should offer oblations with bilva fruits combined with the three sweets; thus one shall subjugate the world and attain the desired prosperity. || 60 ||
He who offers oblations with *pāṭala*, white water-lilies, *kunda*, blue lotuses, *nāgacampaka*, white *nandyāvarta*, and *kṛtamāla* flowers; || 61 ||
Within a year, he shall be born with his sovereignty surpassing that of the lord of the earth;
by offering oblations of food with clarified butter, he shall become a possessor of abundant food.
Girikarṇī is aparājitā;
paṭu is salt;
and nandyāvartas are gandhatagaras.
By the words "with *kṛtamāla* trees, with royal *vṛkṣa* trees, with *pāṭala* trees," and so forth, the word "with flowers" is understood from the qualifying term "in full bloom. (54–62)
One who has self-control should offer camphor mixed with musk and saffron as an oblation;
he immediately attains a beauty even greater than that of Kandarpa. || 63 ||
The practitioner of mantras should offer parched grain soaked in curd, milk, and honey;
having conquered all diseases, he shall live for a hundred autumns. || 64 ||
Two parts of sandalwood, one part of saffron filaments, and one part of gorocanā;
having ground these together with cold water, || 65 ||
One should apply the *tilaka* again; those whom one sees, or who sees one;
those whom one touches, or by whom one is touched—these shall quickly become subject to one's will. (66)
With "himāmbhasā" means with the water of frost. || 66 ||
One should prepare equal parts of camphor, long pepper, and coriander; four parts of jaṭāmāṃsī are prescribed, and an equal amount of rocanā is considered appropriate. || 67 ||
Saffron should consist of seven parts, sandalwood is considered to be ten parts, and agarwood should be nine parts; thus is the sequence of the parts.
Having thoroughly prepared all this ground with snow-water and a maiden, one should take it and apply it as a tilaka on the forehead; by doing so, men shall become lords of the earth. || 69 ||

A man wearing this *tilaka* brings under his control, merely by sight, women full of the pride of intoxication, elephants maddened by rut, lions, tigers, great serpents, and spirits, *vetālas*, and *rākṣasas*. || 70 ||
*Kapi* is red sandalwood (*raktacandana*).
*Coram* is *kacūra*, which is the same as *śaṭī*.
*Digbhāgam* means ten parts.
"Ground by a maiden":
it was ground according to tradition in a cremation ground on the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
"Well-prepared": this means it has been consecrated with the recitation of this mantra. (67–70)

One should inscribe the seed-syllables and the letters of the Gāyatrī three by three within the nine triangles starting from the center; then, having written the alphabet in the openings of the eight petals,
it should be encircled by two earth-mandalas joined with the god of love (Kāmadeva) and wound around the corners.
The Yantra called Traipura has been proclaimed; it agitates the three worlds and bestows prosperity. || 71 ||
He describes the yantra with the words "in the center" (*madhye*) and so forth.
One should draw it in a clockwise direction; thus, there is a threefold repetition.
This refers to the *Gāyatrī* of Tripurā, that is, the *Tripurā-Gāyatrī*.
By means of the script, that is, the Mātṛkā; by means of two earth-mandalas mutually intersecting; [and] the seed-syllable of Manmatha belongs to Bhairavī alone. 71.
Having invoked the deity into this yantra and worshipped it perfectly,
one should perform the *sampāta* rite with oblations, [the yantra] being encased in lac and the three metals.
This instrument, held in the arm, brings victory in battles;
in debate, it shall secure victory through speech and bestow abundant poetic skill.
It shall cause one's lifespan, health, friends, sons, and grandsons to increase. || 73 ||

One may, at will, write this [mantra] in the center of a hexagon; thereafter, in the six corners and subsequently on the petals numbering sixteen, one should surround it with the seed-syllable of space (Haḥ).
Situated within the orb of the earth and written with gorocanā and saffron upon the arms and petals...
This yantra has been declared to bestow good fortune and to bring about incomparable fame for one's poetic compositions. || 74 ||
He states another yantra with the words "kāmaṃ" and so on. "Kāma" refers to the seed-syllable in the center of Bhairavī; [this is] this "kāma."
In those numbered as two times eight— that is, sixteen— this desire; the seed-syllable of space is *haṃ*.
The leaf of the arm is the birch-bark. || 74 ||

One should write the *māyā* (hrīṃ) and the *vāgbhava* (aiṃ) mantras within the house situated between the two fires and in the six corners; then, one should inscribe the syllable *hūṃ* at the junctions and encircle it with the seed-syllable *strīṃ*. Thus proclaimed, this *traipura* [mantra] agitates the three worlds.
This yantra, consisting of the five forms of the Mind-born One (Kāmadeva), bestows the perfection of beauty. || 75 ||
He states another yantra with the words "of fire" (vahneḥ) and so forth.
Madana is well known;
Vāgbhava is well known.
Regarding the phrase "at the joints": this means around the corners in the center of the circle.
By the seed-syllable *strīṃ*, the singular number is intended.
The meaning is that one should write everything within the center of the female seed-syllable (*strībīja*).
As it has been said: "One should cast this very thing into the belly of the Entirety (*sakala*) of the Mind-born One (*manobhava*)."
"Consisting of the five mind-born [deities]" means that the yantra is extracted by means of the five seed-syllables of desire (*kāma*). The mantras of the five desires are as follows:
The fifth [syllable] is joined with the end of the "pure eye" (śuci-nayana); the hand is endowed with the "left eye," the "forest," and the "qualities" (guṇa).
Then there is the "sun-sound" (ravisvara), followed by the "forest" as in the sixth [syllable] of Hari-haya and Viṣṇu; then "tara" joined with "upara," and finally Bhṛgu.
"A wise man should place half-moons upon their heads; thus, indeed, the five Kāmas have been described by me.
Here, *kaṃ* means water, its seed-syllable is *vaḥ*; the fifth of those is *haḥ*.
*Śuci* is the letter *ra*, and "the end of the eye" is *ī*; by that, the Māyā-bīja (*hrīṃ*) is formed.
The syllable *ī* from the left [eye], the third vowel (*guṇa*) *la* from the letter *ya* which is wind (*pavana*),
and the hand (*kara*) which is the letter *ka* joined with that [vowel]— this is the seed-syllable of Kāma (*kāma-bīja*). The solar vowel (*ravi-svara*) is the twelfth vowel, *e*.

Hari-haya (Indra) is *la*; Viṣṇu is *a*. From that [comes] the sixth vowel, *ū*; joined with that is *vana*, which is *ba*. Thus, *blū* is the essential form (*svarūpa*). That from which *u* follows is *ī*; joined with that is *bhṛgu*, which is *sa*. Thus, *strī*.
All [the letters] are accompanied by a half-moon and an anusvāra. || 75 ||
The first [syllable] is the lower one (A) with a bindu (M), situated in Brahma and Indra (AU) and joined with the moon (S);
the second is enriched with Bhṛgu (B) and sarga (H); the third is said to be Manu (E). || 76 ||
She is renowned as Bālā, the one who brings the three worlds under her control;
all rites such as recitation and worship for her should be performed as previously described. || 77 ||
Regarding the statement "by the three seed-syllables of Bālā," he extracts the Bālā mantra as follows: "Adhara" means the letter *e* with a bindu, thus *eṃ*.
"Brahmā" is the letter *ka*; "Indra" is *la*; "Śaśī" (the Moon) is the bindu; and *ī* is its essential form. Thus, [the mantra is] *ka-la-ī-eṃ*.
By that [is meant] *klīṃ*;
*bhṛguḥ* is *saḥ*, and *visarga* in emission is *tena* (the letter *a*), so it is enriched with *manuḥ* (*au*) and *tena* (*sauḥ*).
Elsewhere, it is said to be accompanied by the nasal drop (*bindu*).
As it is stated in the Sanatkumāra:
"The third [letter] of the eighth [varga], joined with the fourteenth,
is indeed called the Daṇḍakuṇḍala, which belongs to Sarasvatī."
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Tripurāsāra*: "This is the curse of this Vidyā.
As for its extraction:
"By that [deity] by whom this primordial Vidyā was previously cursed by the Goddess, she became deprived of her vital breath (*prāṇa*)."
"Therefore, the seed-syllable of Śiva-Śakti was placed by Śambhu above those two preceding seed-syllables;
Akula is above Kula, and below the middle [is] the Fire (dahana). From that point on, she became Ajītā (the Unconquered).
This is because it was stated "as before."
The name of the first seed-syllable is Vāgbhava;
that of the middle is Kāmabīja;
and that of the third is Śakti.
It should be understood that precisely because of this established convention, both [the Vidyās] have been referred to by the terms *vāgbhava* and *kāma* previously and hereafter as well.
For this very reason, their extraction (*uddhāra*) is presented here partially.
The methods of recitation, meditation, and so forth, whether performed individually or collectively, as previously described, should also be applied here.
The final [syllable] with the bindu is the seed (bīja), and the middle [syllable] is the power (śakti).
As it has been said:
"The seed of this mantra, joined with the end of 'ra' (da), together with the daṇḍa and preceded by Lakulīśa."
But the *śakti* [mantra] consists of [the letters] beginning with Indra’s ear-ornament (*ka*), together with the half-born ones (*ja*) up to the three, ending at the face (*na*). Thus it is said.
However, others have also stated that the *nityā* mantra is the seed-syllable of this [Kāma-bīja].
As they say: "Having become *nityā*, one should mutter the Kāma-bīja for the sake of attaining desired goals;
one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the five faces with the five short vowels as the initial seed-syllables."
Having performed the six-limbed ritual with the six long vowels, one should meditate upon the Eternal One, the bestower of one's own desired goals,
seated in the center of a red lotus situated in the midst of the ocean of wine.
The Great Goddess Śivā is beautiful, resembling saffron in hue, with curly hair; she has four arms and holds a noose and a goad.
She holds a skull-cup filled with wine in her right hand,
and she causes the wine from the skull-cup held in her left hand to flow forth.
Having established that [deity] as non-different from oneself, one should slowly recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra, one should offer oblations with *madhūka* flowers amounting to one-tenth of that number.
One who desires to bring under his control a king and a queen should perform worship without weariness according to the path taught by Nityanātha.
Having ascended his chest and becoming one with him in mind,
a person should mutter the eternal Vidyā, having joined it with [the deity's] name.
One should constantly attract her and bring the king under one's control;
having strung together the Mother Goddess (Mātṛkā) with this [mantra], one should recite it one million times.
The entire three worlds remain under his control like servants,
once he has placed the fingers in the *nyasta-mudrā* and bound the abundant *kṣobhiṇī*.
"Having gone to bed, one should always remember [the deity] and mutter the mantra that effects attraction. Thus, the "agitating fist" [is described]. (76–77)
One should utter the word "mānmatham," then "tripurādevi vidmahe," and after saying the word "kāmeśvari," one should then recite "dhīmahi. || 78 ||
At the end of that, one should further recite: "tannaḥ klinne pracodayāt.
This is declared to be the Gāyatrī of Tripura, which bestows all accomplishments. || 79 ||
He extracts the Gāyatrī mantra with the words "mānmatham.
The word *mānmatha* is well known;
the rest is its essential form. ||78-79||
O Tripura, for the attainment of my desired fruit, I shall praise you with this hymn, by which men attain that prosperity which is worshipped even by the gods. || 80 ||
Even Brahmā and the other gods do not truly know her subtle form, whose body is both the beginning of the universe and yet without beginning;
therefore, we bow before her who has the luster of fresh saffron.
We praise Sthūlā, who is the mother of all speech.
He begins the *Tripurāstuti* with the words "by means of praise" (*stutyā*). By which praise? || 80–81 ||
She possesses the splendor of a thousand suns suddenly risen;
her hands bear the emblems of the knowledge-gesture, the rosary, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness;
her lotus-face is adorned with three blue-lotus eyes.
O Tripurā, we worship you, who are radiant with a necklace of large pearls. || 82 ||
"By that necklace which is bright and radiant; 'tāra' may mean 'bright' or 'pure' in the case of pearls," according to Amara. (82)
Resplendent with heaps of vermilion, bowed by the weight of her breasts,
attainable only as the fruit of merit accumulated in previous births—
[she who is] agitated by mutual quarrels and the breaking of pride;
O Mother, what can those of dull intellect know of Your form? || 83 ||
The sages declare you to be the gross,
while the Vedas proclaim you as the subtle; others call you the abode of all speech, O Bhavānī, and yet others say you are the root of the worlds.
We consider him to be an ocean of boundless compassion. || 84 ||
They meditate upon you in their hearts— adorned with a moon as an ornament, white as the autumnal moon, consisting of fifty syllables,
and holding a book, a rosary, and a jar brimming with nectar.
And she is three-eyed, holding the gesture of exposition with her lotus-like hands. || 85 ||
You are Śambhu, whose half-body is joined by the Daughter of the Mountain; you are Viṣṇu, whose form is embraced by Kamalā;
you are the Lotus-born One, the dwelling place of Speech.
And their activities in the world—you alone are they, O Tripurā. || 86 ||
Those measures and standards which are agitated by mutual discord and strife—that is, by their various divisions and specific distinctions—[are the objects of this verse]. || 83 ||

I bow to you, the Supreme Goddess, who, by means of the organs such as the throat, utters the intended meanings within the various words, relying upon the four states— Para and the others— which arise from the Vāgbhava syllable.
I never, at any time, forget her who consists of pure consciousness within my heart. || 87 ||
Because of its similarity in form to the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable (*a*), the triangular foundation-mandala (*ādhāramaṇḍala*) is so called;
those who exist therein are "born from that. Although it is Parā alone who is born there, the same expression is used for the others as well because they possess that gross form.
Alternatively, [the term] *vāgbhava* refers to Kuṇḍalinī, and those [letters] are *tadbhavāḥ*, meaning produced from her;
for it is said: "That which is called Śakti is Kuṇḍalinī, known by the name Āīm.
Such are the four states, beginning with Parā, which take the forms of Parā, Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī.

Resorting in succession to the locations—the foundation, the navel, the throat, and the mouth—and uttering the intended meaning, that is, the desired object, by means of the organs such as the throat and so forth. || 87 ||
Having drawn in the breath and conquered the six enemies,
they gaze at the tip of their own nose with an unwavering mind and meditate upon Him who bears the crescent moon as His crest-ornament upon His head.
O Mother, the form of you, the accomplished one, is like the orb of the rising sun. || 88 ||
Vāyu in the form of prāṇa and apāna;
the group of six enemies consisting of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy. || 88 ||
"O Daughter of the Mountain, the Vedic proclamation that you, having obtained half the body of the enemy of Manmatha, create the manifestation of the worlds is true;
for you are the sole mother of the world."
Otherwise, there would be no stability at all for the entire world. || 89 ||
The presence of that [liṅga] constitutes half the portion of either the Enemy of Manmatha (Śiva), the Supreme Person, or Brahmā;
that is true because it is a Vedic teaching. To state a counter-argument against the opposing view, he says: "If not," and so forth.
The meaning is: "because of the absence of your presiding presence. || 89 ||
O Mother, having performed worship with flowers upon the throne of the celestial trees within the caves of the Golden Mountain,
the wives of the Siddhas sing together with the Kinnarīs.
Their lotus-like eyes were reddened by the taste of the wine they had tasted. || 90 ||
She who bears the splendor of a body shimmering like lightning,
departing from her own abode for the capital city of Śiva,
causing the lotuses of the path of Suṣumṇā to blossom.
I worship the Goddess in my heart, her limbs sprinkled with supreme nectar. || 91 ||

From one's own dwelling place, the *mūlādhāra*, [they go] to Śiva’s capital, the thousand-petalled lotus. Those whose paths are that very *sauṣumṇa*— which arises in the *suṣumṇā* nerve— are called *sauṣumṇa*.
In some places, the reading is "the lotuses of the abode of Suṣumṇā. These lotuses refer to the centers beginning with the Ādhāra and ending with the Sahasrāra. (90–91)
O Mother, I take refuge in You, the source of bliss, the abode of the Vedas, whose body consists of pure consciousness,
and whose lotus feet are praised by Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu.
He [resides] duly in Tripura, the abode of the birth of good fortune. || 92 ||
"Ānandajanmabhavanaṃ śrutīnām" (the birthplace of bliss for the Vedas) constitutes two separate metaphors (*rūpaka*). || 92 ||
She who, in the form of the Moon, creates the universe consisting of word and meaning; she who, in the form of the Sun, sustains it again by her own power;
and she who, in the nature of Fire, withdraws all that at the end of the age.
I never forget that Śāradā in my mind. || 93 ||
She who is Nārāyaṇī, she who carries one across the ocean of hell, she who is Gaurī, she who pacifies all weariness, she who is Sarasvatī, she who bestows knowledge,
and she who is adorned with three eyes.
O daughter of the king of mountains, the wise call you thus. || 94 ||
That in which the existence or being (*bhāva*) of both word and meaning resides is *śāra*;
it is called *Śāradā* because she tears asunder or shatters the fruit of karma (*karmaphala*), that is, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). || 93-94 ||
O Mother of the World, those who praise you in succession with these twelve verses shall attain perfection of speech upon reaching you, and they shall obtain the supreme goal. || 95 ||
"By twelve" refers to the verses beginning with "sadyaḥ" and ending with "vismarāmi.
Since the first two verses serve as an introductory framework (*mukhabandha*), the remaining ones likewise indicate the essential nature and the fruit [of the work].
Furthermore, by the word "twelve," a specific composition named *Dyumaṇimālā* is indicated through a particular classification of poetic treasury (*kośabheda*).
The definition of *tallakṣaṇa* was stated by Bhāmaha: "Now, *dyumaṇimālā* consists of twelve equal verses,
each devoted to manifesting the excellence of a hero."
"A pair of verses is prescribed for the introduction (mukhabandha), and likewise a pair is intended for the conclusion (śeṣa).
This garland of the sun has been composed, which increases the fame of men. (95)
Then, at the end of "namas," one should utter "bhagavati" followed by "śrīmātaṅgīśvari," which captivates the minds of all people. || 96 ||
Beginning with "sarva" and ending with "sukharājye," [the mantra] is "sarvādimukharañjini.
After that, one should cause all kings to be brought under control, and then utter the word "sarva. || 97 ||
Brahmā is under the power of woman and man; again, the eye is the seat of fire.
O you who bring all wicked beasts under control, you are the sustainer of all beings. 98.
"O Śaṅkarī, bring such-and-such a person from all the worlds under my control, O Śivā, O fierce one!"—this mantra of Jāyāgni consists of eighty-eight syllables. || 99 ||
He extracts the mantra of Rājamātaṅginī, beginning with "vāk": *vāk* is the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable], *māyā* is the seed-syllable of Śakti,
*kamalā* is the seed-syllable of Śrī, and *tāraḥ* is the *praṇava*.
"At the end of 'namas' means at the end of the word 'namaḥ'. 'Brahmā' is the letter *ka*. 'The eye' is the letter *i*. 'The seat of fire' is *ri* by that [combination]."

Bhṛgu is its true nature (svarūpa). The Sun is the syllable *ma*, joined with the letter *i* in the pair [of *śiva*]; by that, for me, the sage is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the meter is Gāyatrī, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is Māyā, and the power (*śakti*) is Svāhā. (96–99)
The mantra-practitioner should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) upon his body in the sequence that will be described:
on the head, the forehead, the space between the eyebrows, the palate, the throat, the neck, and the chest. || 100 ||
In the Anāhata [cakra], in the pair of arms, in the belly, in the region of the navel, in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, in the secret place, and in the right and left feet. || 101 ||
One should place eighteen steps in sequence at the *mūlādhāra* and the anus;
[the next] at the throat, the jewel of the throat (*kaṇṭhamaṇi*), the neck, and the region below it;
and at the *anāhata* in the heart.
"In the secret place" means in the *liṅga*.
The sequence "of the right and the other [left]" is stated here because, although it is a universal rule, it must be mentioned in certain instances. (100–102)
By one, two, four, six, eight, six, seven, and eight [syllables]. || 102 ||
This arrangement of words is declared according to the sequence of the syllables of the mantra: ten, five, eight, four, three, one, two, three, two, and two. || 103 ||
He states the division of the words with the word "guṇa" and so forth:
three qualities (guṇas), seven mountains (parvatas), seven rows (paṅktis), ten Vedas (vedas), four fires (agnis), three fires (agnis), one moon (candra), and two eyes (akṣi). || 102–103 ||
The wise one should place Rati and the others at the base of the navel, the heart, and the middle of the eyebrows;
then he should properly install Vākśakti, Lakṣmī, Bījā, and the rest, ending with Mātaṅgī.
By the word "etc. in "Ratī and so forth," [the goddesses] Prīti and Manobhavā are included.
By "seed and so forth" (bījādyāḥ), it is stated that they are the appropriate seeds and so on. The phrase "ending with Mātaṅgī" applies to each [of them] individually.
The application is as follows: *eṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ratyai mātaṅgyai namaḥ*, and so forth; likewise for what follows. || 104 ||
The practitioner of mantra should duly place Hṛllekhā, Gaganā, Raktā, and Karālikā upon the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet. || 105 ||

Then the practitioner should perform the six limbs [of worship], preceded by the seed-syllables consisting of the initial letters of their respective names, beginning with Mahocchuṣmā and ending with Mātaṅgī. || 106 ||
The four castes are divided by twenty; the head by thirteen;
the crest-lock is said to be eighteen; and the armor consists of that many syllables. 107.
The eye is said to consist of thirteen [syllables] and the weapon of two;
having thus assigned the letters of the root mantra according to their divisions, one should then perform the placement of the arrows (vāṇanyāsa). || 108 ||
Regarding the phrase "according to rule":
it has been stated that one should also assign [the mantras] to the five faces.
Those which are the initial syllables of their respective names are themselves the seed-syllables (*bīja*).

The phrase "those preceded by that" (tat-puraḥsarāḥ) means "beginning with that," which is an exception to the previously mentioned seed-syllables (*bīja*). This is to be connected with the subsequent term "ending with Mātaṅgī.
Then, the practitioner should perform the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the letters of the root mantra divided [into six parts]; such is the connection.
By the word "sādhaka" (the practitioner), the union with knowledge, sovereignty, and so forth is indicated.
He states the classification [of the mantra] with the words "by the phonemes" (varṇaiḥ). || 105-108 ||
One should place [the mantras] upon the head, feet, mouth, and private parts, and within the heart-lotus:
Drāviṇī, Kṣobhiṇī, Vardhanī, and again Mohanī. || 109 ||
"The Attracting [Mudrā] begins with the seed-syllable of its own name and possesses auspicious characteristics.
Regarding "its own name":
the connection is that one should install the seed-syllables beginning with those previously mentioned, such as *drāṃ* and so forth, starting from the beginning of its own name, up to *mātaṅgī*.
The meaning is that they are designated by names that correspond to their actual characteristics (*anvarthābhidhāna*). || 109-110 ||
Then, one should assign the Mātaṅgīs and the Manmathas to the face and the shoulders.

The practitioner of mantra should [place] the three seed-syllables and so forth upon the sides, the waist, the region of the navel, and again upon the hips, sides, and shoulders—the god of love, Makaradhvaja. || 111 ||
Madana, Puṣpadhanvan, Pañcama, Kusumāyudha, and the sixth named Kandarpa—these two are beloved by Manobhava and Rati. || 112 ||
The connection is that one should then install the *manmathas* ending with Mātaṅgī.
Regarding "on the face and shoulders," the installation begins from the left shoulder.
"Beginning with the three seed-syllables" means beginning with the first three seed-syllables of the mantra. (110–112)
The knower of mantras should place the bodies of Mātaṅgī and Antakī in these locations:
first Anaṅgakusumā, and then the other, Anaṅgamekhalā. || 113 ||
She was Anaṅgamadanā; likewise, she was Anaṅgamadanāturā;
she was Anaṅgamadanavegā, and furthermore, she was Anaṅgasaṃbhavā. || 114 ||
The seventh is Anaṅgabhuvanapālinī, and then the eighth is Anaṅgaśaśirekhā; these, ending with Mātaṅgī, are proclaimed [as the eight]. 115.
These [mantras], ending with Mātaṅgī, have been proclaimed; the connection is that one should place them upon the body in the aforementioned locations. || 113-115 ||
Then the practitioner should place [the syllables] upon the body: at the base, the foundation, the maṇipūraka, the heart, the throat, the mouth, between the eyebrows, and on the head. || 116 ||
In the first [group] are Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī; Rati, Prīti, and the Kṛttikās; as well as Śānti, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Mātaṅgī, and Pādaśekharā. || 117 ||

The knower of mantras should place the root mantra upon his own head, then on the region of the foundation (ādhāra), the seat (adhiṣṭhāna), the navel, and subsequently on the anāhata [cakra]. || 118 ||
One should place [the mantras] in sequence on the throat, the mouth, between the eyebrows, and the head;
these are the goddesses beginning with Brāhmī as previously described, ending with Mātaṅgī.
In the root, at the *mūlādhāra*;
in the foundation, at the base of the *liṅga*;
in the *maṇipūraka*, at the navel.
The connection is as follows: "These [mantras], which have *mātaṅgī* as their first word and end with *mātaṅgī*, should be placed upon the body by the practitioner.
The word "previously" refers to the sixth [chapter]. Those [mantras] whose final and last word is *mātaṅgī* are so described. (116–119)
In these locations, the practitioner of mantras should place the Bhairavas beginning with Asitāṅga and ending with Mātaṅgī; he should then place the root mantra upon his own head. || 120 ||
The connection is that one should place the nine Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga and ending with Mātaṅgī, as previously mentioned, in these aforementioned locations. || 120 ||
In the foundational place, the locus, at the navel; then in the unstruck (anāhata);
in the region of the throat, in the middle of the eyebrows, and further in the point (bindu), which is the station of the digit (kalā). || 121 ||
Furthermore, [it resides] in the Nirodhikā, in the half-moon, in the beginning and end of the Sound (nāda), in the Unmanī state, in the mouth of Viṣṇu, and in the auspicious Dhruvamaṇḍala. || 122 ||
Beginning from the middle of the eyebrows up to the end of Śiva at the crown of the head, the locations starting from the lower half [of the body] should be known. || 121-122 ||
One should duly assign Mātaṅgī as the final [deity], then Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā after that, Raudrī, Praśānti, the one called Śraddhā, and then again Māheśvarī. || 123 ||
[He created] Kriyāśakti, Sulakṣmī, Sṛṣṭi, Mohinī, Pramathā, Śvāsinī, Vidyullatā, and also Cicchakti. || 124 ||
And then: "One should duly install these [deities], beginning with Sundarānandā and ending with Nandabuddhi, and concluding with Mātaṅgī"—this is the connection.
