Specifically: one is Kriyāśakti, one is named Sṛṣṭi, one is Pramathā, and one is Sundarānandā. (123–125)
These [syllables], beginning with the three seed-syllables, are located in the supports of the head, the forehead, and the heart. || 125 ||
The supreme instructor should duly install Mātaṅgī at the end, that Mātaṅgī who begins with "Mahat" and concludes with the word "Mahālakṣmī. || 126 ||

Having placed that [deity]—beginning with the feet of Siddhalakṣmī and ending with the root [mantra]—in the foundation maṇḍala, the best of teachers should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) by means of that very [mantra].
Thus, having performed the placement of his body, he should meditate upon the deity who is his own self. || 127 ||
"These" refers to those that will be described hereafter.

By the phrase "the best of instructors as it truly is," it is stated— beginning with "the mantra-practitioner [should recite] these mantras starting with the three seed-syllables" and ending with "these [mantras] starting with the three seed-syllables"— and also in the middle where it says "the knower of mantras by means of the practitioner" and "the knower of mantras, the practitioner"— that one should understand that even for those deities who appear in the middle, they likewise possess the nature of beginning with the three seed-syllables.
He states the meaning of the word "etcetera" (ādi) as "Mātaṅgī. She is Mahāmātaṅgī, who consists of Mahat and the other [tattvas].
"By that very [mantra]" means by the root mantra. 125–127.

I would meditate upon her who has a dark-blue body, seated upon a jeweled throne, listening to the recitation of the parrot-cub; she rests one foot upon a lotus, wears a crescent moon, and plays the lute;
she wears a garland bound with white water-lilies, her radiant topknot is tied up, and she is clothed in red garments.
Mātaṅgī, with conch-shell-like ears, overcome by the intoxication of honey, her forehead radiant with decorative paintings; ||128||

The practitioner of mantras should recite the mantra ten thousand times; for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra, he should perform a fire sacrifice with flowers from the *madhūka* tree mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhura*), using a tenth part of that number as the oblation. || 129 ||
"I shall meditate.
*Cūlikā* refers to a topknot of hair;
*śaṅkhapatra* refers to an earring shaped like a conch shell.
*Citraka* is a *tilaka*.
Thus it is said in the *Trikāṇḍī*:
"The *tamāla-leaf*, *tilaka*, and *citraka* are synonyms for *viśeṣaka*."
Here, one should display the intermediate dhyāna and the lute-source mudrā. || 128-129 ||
One should fashion an eight-petaled lotus with a triangular pericarp;
outside the eight petals, there should be a circle consisting of sixteen petals.
On this square seat, which is endowed with symmetry and is captivating to the sight by its splendor,
one should worship these nine Śaktis in their proper sequence.
Vibhūti, unnati, kānti, sṛṣṭi, kīrti, sannati, vyuṣṭi, utkṛṣṭi, ṛddhi, and finally Mātaṅgī. || 132 ||
At the very end, "Obeisance to the one seated upon the lotus of power" (śaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ);
this mantra, preceded by the seed-syllables of Vāk, Śakti, and Lakṣmī, is known as the Seat-mantra (āsana). || 133 ||
Having conceptualized the form with the root mantra and having invoked the deity into it, the knower of mantras should worship according to this procedure which is about to be described. || 134 ||
"Triangle-pedestal" means a pedestal in the shape of a yoni. || 130 ||
The wise practitioner should worship Rati and the others in the three corners as before;
the five goddesses beginning with Hṛllekhā should be worshipped in the center and in the cardinal directions by the mantra-reciter. || 135 ||
"As before" means as they were previously placed, starting from the left corner (*vāmakoṇa*). Likewise, in what follows, the worship is exactly according to the placement.
"As before" refers to the locations mentioned in the Fourth [chapter]. (135)

The knower of the ritual procedure should thereafter worship the limbs, which possess a natural radiance and hold a noose, a goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons, according to the previous method.
One should worship Bāṇa in the southeast; one should sacrifice to the fifth [deity] in front.
Anaṅgakusumā and the others are to be worshipped in the midst of the petals. || 137 ||
Holding a noose, a goad, and displaying the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons, they possess ruddy bodies;
"in the center" (vidhānavit) refers to the pericarp,
and "in the directions" (dikṣu) refers to the filaments of the petals in the cardinal points.
Furthermore, immediately following:
*vallakī* is a lute (*vīṇā*). 136–138.
Furthermore, Lakṣmī and the others, holding lutes in their hands, are to be worshipped at the tips of the petals. || 138 ||
On the eight outer petals, Manmatha and the others, arrogant with passion, should be worshipped;
they are richly adorned with their secondary limbs resting upon their quivers, and they carry flowers as arrows and sugarcane bows.
The Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī and possessing the characteristics previously described, are to be worshipped situated upon the petals;
in front of them, the wise one should worship the Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga. || 140 ||
Furthermore, on the sixteen petals, sixteen Śaktis are to be worshipped;
they are Vāmā and the others, dark-complexioned, singing with lutes and other instruments. (141)
Furthermore, one should worship the four [goddesses] in the four directions of the square: Mātaṅgī and the others, intoxicated with passion, with lutes gracefully held in their hands. || 142 ||
In the eight outer petals, at the bases of the petals;
on the other limb, that is, the back portion;
"niṣaṅga" means a quiver; [those] enriched by that.
Puṣpāstra is he whose arrows are flowers; they possess the characteristics described [in the previous section] and the meditations mentioned in the sixth chapter. (138–142)
One should worship Vighneśa in the southeast corner and Durgā in the southwest;
then one should worship Vaṭuka in the northwest and Kṣetrapa in the northeast. || 143 ||
The world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be worshipped outside, together with their weapons such as the vajra;
once this mantra has been mastered, the practitioner shall accomplish his own desired goal. || 144 ||
"In the southeast corner" (āgneyakoṇe).
It should be understood that this worship is common to all mantras of the Śakti class; for this very reason, it is stated at the end of all such mantras. (143–144)
With Mallikā, Jāti, and Punnāga flowers, one becomes an abode of golden fortune;
or by offering fruits produced from the Bilva tree, or its leaves, one becomes like the sacrificial fire.
Through lotuses, one attains the sovereignty of a prince;
through blue lotuses, a man may bring the entire world under his control; and likewise, through *lakṣmī* flowers, he obtains prosperity.
"Mallikā" should be understood as referring to three types of flowers,
since "with fruits" will be mentioned later [in verses 145–146].

For the purpose of subjugation, the practitioner of mantras should offer oblations of bandhūka flowers, bakula, javā, and kiṃśuka blossoms, mixed with honey, for the attainment of all siddhis. || 147 ||
By offering oblations of salt mixed with honey, one attracts a beautiful woman;
an oblation of kindled *vañjula* wood brings forth rain before long. || 148 ||
With pieces of *amṛtā* smeared with milk, one destroys fever;
with *dūrvā* grass, one attains long life; and with *kadamba* flowers, one achieves subjugation. || 149 ||
By an oblation of food one becomes possessed of food; by rice grains, one becomes wealthy.
Every substance for the oblation is said to be accompanied by the three sweets (trimadhura). || 150 ||
Gold offered with flowers produced from the *nandyāvarta* plant bestows the accomplishment of speech;
one who offers oblations with *nimba* blossoms attains his desired prosperity;
and a man who offers *palāśa* flowers becomes radiant with splendor upon receiving gold. || 151 ||
Regarding the phrase "with bandhūka flowers":

because of the inclusion of the word "flower" (puṣpa) and its proximity [to the other terms], the triad beginning with bakula is also understood as flowers; likewise, "with kadamba" refers to flowers.
The word "all" (sarva) [refers to these].
The aforementioned superior [state] is not obstructed by the qualities of others. (147–151)

For the purpose of subjugation, the mantra-practitioner should perform oblations with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, gorocana, saffron, and other such substances; thus he shall bring the entire world under his control. || 152 ||
Having recited these, one should apply a sectarian mark (tilaka) and become beloved by the world.
By offering oblations with the root of the Nirguṇḍī plant, a person is released from fetters. || 153 ||
"Candana" refers to the eight fragrant substances;
by the word "etcetera," *jaṭāmāṃsī*, *kacūra*, and red sandalwood are included.
"One should subjugate" means...
The fruit of the collective offering of the eight substances:
"These" refers to camphor, *kapicūra*, and the others; "in equal parts" means their proportions are determined according to what was previously stated in the application of the mantra.
"The tilaka" [refers to the mark].
On the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, this [substance] is prepared by a maiden, ground with snow-water and consecrated by the recitation of this mantra. || 152-153 ||
Gold [anointed] with ointments mixed with neem oil destroys enemies;
one should paralyze others with salts mixed with powdered turmeric. || 154 ||
By offering well-ripened fruits that are flavorful and flowers endowed with fragrance, the practitioner who performs the oblation correctly attains everything he desires. || 155 ||
Regarding the phrase "with neem oil":
the method for extracting that oil is as follows—
seeds ground with water in a bronze vessel [should be placed] in the hot sun.
One should place that oil upon it; it will surely flow out, not otherwise. Thus [it is said].
Enemies, that is, adversaries. || 154-155 ||
To attain the desired speech of Mātaṅgī—the primordial deity of the worlds and bestower of boons—one should adorn one's words with a garland of jewels. || 156 ||
He begins the hymn to Mātaṅgī with the words "The deity... The title of the composition is *Ratnamālā*;
because of its connection [to the deity], the name of the hymn is also [the same].
The definition of that [śikhābandha] was stated by Bhāmaha:
"One should compose two auspicious verses marked with the well-known name of the leader;
at the beginning and end of those, one should perform the 'binding of the crest' (śikhābandha) through meditative concentration."
That beautiful Ratnamālā (Jewel Garland) shall consist of nine additional [syllables] through beautiful limbs;
thus, when a garland is composed of the nine jewels and so forth, it proceeds in this order.
Thus, there are eleven verses that bring great joy to the learned. || 156 ||
O Mother, by worshipping your lotus feet, Brahmā and the others attained world-renowned fame,
while other lords of sages attained supreme mastery over speech.
And others [attain] supreme glory through the weight of their devotion. || 157 ||
I bow to the Goddess Mātaṅginī, who bears the crescent moon upon her head and is adorned with the digit of the moon,
whose true meaning is established by the words of the Vedic scriptures.
Awakening Śuka with reverence. || 158 ||
O Goddess, those who worship your lotus-feet, which are illuminated by the jewels in the crowns of bowing gods and asuras, become the lords of the earth.
They proceed with diligence toward perfection. || 159 ||
The connection is that she is the queen-consort of the god who wears the crescent moon on his crest. || 157–159 ||
O Mother, as you move with the grace of an elephant, your tinkling anklets, under the guise of their own jingling,
worship your lotus-feet.
The compositions of unartificial words. || 160 ||
The Vedas are the compositions of uncreated words.
Making every step meaningful with the tinkling of her two anklets as she moved along the path,
she struck that sweet-sounding lute.
May Mātaṅginī gladden my heart. || 161 ||
Her rounded hips were bound with blue silk garments,
her ear-ornaments were fashioned from palmyra leaves,
and her lotus-eyes were rolling from the intoxication of honey-wine.
I bow to the consort of Śambhu, who possesses full breasts. || 162 ||
"Step by step" means at every single step.
"Making [her] fulfilled" implies by her own arrival; "may she gladden" means may she please [him]. || 161-162 ||
I remember with devotion the Mistress of the worlds, who is adorned with priceless ornaments like streaks of lightning, and who is only gradually perceived by the line of fresh downy hair.
Your central orb is marked with three folds.

Sometimes visible and sometimes invisible, beautiful as a flash of lightning, and adorned with priceless ornaments—since it is not produced by any material body, one might wonder how the body can exist; thus he says that it is to be inferred after a long time and is not perceptible to the eye. This is the sense. || 163 ||
She who steals the splendor of blue lotuses with her beauty and the glances of her eyes, like those from beds of lotuses;
she whose mass of hair is adorned with garlands of *kadamba* flowers.
We meditate upon the daughter of Mātaṅga in our hearts. || 164 ||
The connection is as follows: she was taking away the splendor of blue lotuses with her bodily radiance, and she was taking away the splendor of lotus-pools with her side-long glances.
"Mātaṅgakanyām" means having the form of a daughter of the Mātaṅgas. || 164 ||
I would meditate upon Him, whose cheeks are lovely with a rosy hue, who is beautiful with a mark placed upon His bimba-like lower lip,
and whose long eyes are framed by swaying dark locks of hair.
O Great Goddess, your face bears a gentle smile. || 165 ||
Those people who, endowed with devotion, praise Mātaṅginī— the wife of Śaṅkara and the presiding deity of speech— with this hymn;
They constantly resort to supreme glory. || 166 ||
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Śāradātilaka composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra. 12.
It is beautiful because of that special ornament, the forehead-mark (lalāma), which was placed upon her very bimba-like lower lip. 165–166.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, the commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which is based upon the authentic tradition. 12.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Now I shall explain the mantras of Gaṇapati, which bestow the accomplishment of all aims.
Having obtained which, men always accomplish their heart's desires. || 1 ||

Having offered a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to the Principal Deity, there should be the worship of Gaṇeśa—so it is said. Having thus stated the mantras of Śakti, he begins to state the mantras of Gaṇapati, which follow in the sequence, with the words *atha*.
The phrase "bestowing the accomplishment of all aims" (*sarvārthasiddhidān*) is a statement of their ritual application (*viniyoga*). || 1 ||
The seed-syllable of Gaṇapati is "Vīduḥ," which consists of the five final letters [of the five classes] and the bearer of the moon (the letter *u*).
The sage is Gaṇaka, the metre is Nivṛt, and its presiding deity is Vighna. || 2 ||
He extracts the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati with the words "pañcāntaka" (the end of five).
Pañcāntaka is the letter *ga*, and Śaśin is the bindu; joined with that, it becomes *gaṃ*. Furthermore, Śaśin may also be the visarga; joined with that, it also becomes *gaḥ*.
Because it is said, "The creation [is] power, the moon," this extraction is for the sake of concealment. This pair was stated by Uttara-Gārgya.
The ritual procedures for worship and so forth are the same for both.
Some say it is joined with the vowel *au*.
This is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"The seed-syllable [HA] joined with the moon (I) and the letter 'da' (ḌA), and likewise the third [letter 'ka' (KA)]";
thus it is said.
However, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The end of *kha* (HA), the poison (ḌA) ending in *sa* (ḌHA), together with the bindu (Ḥ), the entire [syllable] (HḌHAḤ), and the bindu alone (Ḥ)."
"These five seeds of the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśvara) each produce a distinct fruit. Thus it is said.
But according to the Ācāryas, it begins with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and is uttered in reverse order; joined at the beginning with the *tāra* (oṃ) and the *bindu*,
this Vighna-mantra ends with the *hṛt* (namaḥ) in the ritual of worship (*arcā-vidhi*), and ends with the *dviṭha* (svāhā) in the fire-oblation (*homa*).
The Gaṇaka is the Ṛṣi, the Chanda is Nivṛt, and Vighna is its deity;
the ritual assignment of the limbs (aṅgakriyā) is considered to be performed with the seed-syllable conjoined with the long vowel and the staff (daṇḍin). Thus it is said.
The letter *ga* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the nasal drop (*bindu*) is the power (*śakti*).
In another [tradition], the visarga is the power. || 2 ||
One should perform the ritual assignment of the mantra's limbs (aṅgakriyā) using the seed-syllable accompanied by the six long vowels.
He states the six limbs with the word "six.
In the *Prayogasāra*, even a five-limbed version is mentioned:
"Having first uttered 'Gaṇa' for victory, 'svāhā' is called the heart."
Having addressed Ekadaṃṣṭra, [one recites] "huṃ phaṭ" for the vidyā-mantra and then for the head;
likewise, for the crest-lock (śikhā), one recites "acala" and so forth, ending with "namaḥ" for the ears.
The armor mantra for the elephant-faced one is declared as "namo namaḥ.
And for Mahodara and Caṇḍa, "huṃ phaṭ" is desired as the weapon mantra.
One should place these five limbs as prescribed by the wise;
or, using the seed-syllable along with *prāṃśu*, one may also apply the six limbs. Thus [ends the third verse].
I bow to the one who has the luster of vermilion, three eyes, and a broad belly; who holds a tusk, a noose, a goad, and the gesture of granting boons with his lotus-like hands;

who is beautiful with a citron fruit shining in his great hand; whose crown is illuminated by the crescent moon; who has the face of a lordly elephant, and whose cheeks are moist with the flow of ichor.
Worship Gaṇapati, whose ornaments are bound with the lord of serpents, and who is clothed in red garments and red unguents. || 4 ||
As for the meditation on the weapons: in the upper left and right hands are the goad and the noose;
in the lower ones are his own tusk and the gesture of granting boons.
All these Gaṇapatis should be meditated upon as having a single tusk.
With his teeth complete, on the right side;
as for the second meditation:
one should meditate upon the God, whose body and belly are vast, with a sense of oneness.
"Four-armed, with a single tusk, enriched with a noose and a goad, elephant-faced, ruddy in hue, and holding a tusk and a morsel of food. Thus it is said.
And the *puṣkara* [mudrā] is upon the food held in the right hand. As for the meditation on the seed-syllable joined with the vowel *au*:
one should visualize [the deity] holding a red rosary, an axe, a tusk, and food in his four arms.
"I bow to the golden-hued one, the god of the thirty, who has the face of an elephant, a protruding belly, and a single tusk.
In this case as well, the *puṣkara* (the hand) should be understood as before.
When this very [mantra] is preceded by the seed-syllable *māyā* (*hrīṃ*), then the visualization is as follows:
In the midst of the ocean of nectar, upon a lotus with the radiance of saffron and endowed with petals numbering the seasons (six), one should meditate on Gaṇanāyaka.
The god, who resembles a hibiscus flower, holds a noose and a goad;
he is beautiful-eyed and embraces the goddess who stands at his left side.
The Yoginī, intoxicated with passion, is always drinking from a bright golden goblet filled with honey, holding it in her left hand.
[He saw] the slender-waisted Great Goddess of red complexion embracing [him],
while with one arm she embraced the intoxicated Vighneśa, whose eyes were red.
"The wise one should meditate upon the Gaṇas of that form, in order, starting from the east.
Here, immediately after meditation, this Gaṇapati-mudrā should be displayed: having placed the hand hanging down from the mouth with the fingers contracted.
The middle fingers are positioned with their tips touching the thumb, which is placed below the middle fingers.
"One should perform the mudrā of Gaṇeśa; this which has been declared bestows all accomplishments.
Or else: "The fist with the thumb emerging from the junction of the index and middle fingers, facing downwards and elongated in form, is the Vighna-mudrā (the mudrā of the Obstacle-remover)."
Or else: "The Gaṇeśvarī mudrā occurs when the hand, with its fingertips curled, is applied at the base of the nose. Thus it is said.
It should be understood that this [mantra] is common to all Gaṇapati mantras. || 4 ||

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; thereafter, one should perform a fire sacrifice with a tenth part of that number, using sweetmeats, flattened rice, parched grain, roasted flour, and sugarcane joints.
Coconut, pure sesame seeds, and well-ripened plantain fruits—
these eight substances for Vighna have been declared by the wise.
"Veda-lakṣa" means four hundred thousand.
Regarding "the tenth part":
there, the fire-oblation (homa) is to be performed with eight substances to be mentioned later; one-tenth of ten thousand—that is, five thousand—must be offered with each individual substance.
Some, however, say that there is a combination of eight substances;
that is not correct, because it would lead to uncertainty regarding the measure of the oblation (*āhuti*).
Furthermore, because each [ingredient] at the root is connected with a separate ritual action,
and because it is impossible for a qualified [composite] substance to be a distinct entity that serves as the instrument for an offering of eight substances;
as it has been stated by Bhaṭṭācārya:
"The sacrifice would not be performed with rice alone, nor with barley alone as prescribed;
it would be performed with them mixed."
Likewise, it is because no injunction for mixing [the substances] is observed.
If it is argued that, in this case, even the blending of the three sweets (*trimadhura*) should not be performed,
do not say so.

Because of the statement, "All sacrificial materials for the *homa* are declared to be accompanied by the three sweets (*trimadhura*)," there is no contradiction in their mixing, just as there is none in the case of the mixing of the clarified butter used for the *upastaraṇa* (under-layering) and *pratyupastaraṇa* (counter-under-layering) with the portions of the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) and other offerings.
This has been stated in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*:
"One should offer oblations separately with the eight substances smeared with the three sweets.
[The word] *pṛthukaiḥ* means with flattened cakes (*cipiṭakaiḥ*).
By the word "pure" (*śuddhaiḥ*), it is stated that one should remove debris, wash [the materials], and dry them.
One should perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites over these mantras with the Gāyatrī.
The Gāyatrī is as follows:
"Let us know the one with a single tusk; let us meditate upon the one with a curved trunk;
may that Vighna inspire us.
Thus [ends the verse]. 5-6.
One should worship Vighneśvara on the seat (pīṭha) endowed with the powers (śaktis) beginning with Tīvra:
[the powers] named Tīvra, Jvālinī, Nandā, Bhogadā, and Kāmarūpiṇī. || 7 ||
Ugrā, Tejovatī, Satyā, and the ninth, Vighnanāśinī;
[these are] for the one seated upon a lotus who possesses all primordial powers, ending with the heart. || 8 ||
Regarding the word "intense" (tīvra):
their meditative visualization (dhyāna) is as follows—
bearing nooses, goads, and joined palms in their hands, they resemble fresh saffron in color.
"The powers (śaktis), beginning with Tīvrā, adorned with jewel ornaments, should be worshipped. Thus [ends verses] 7–8.
With this seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra), one should offer a seat to the Lord; having conceptualized the form with the root-mantra, one should worship Vighneśvara within it. || 9 ||
In the four directions of the pericarp, one should first worship these:
Gaṇādhipa, Gaṇeśāna, and thirdly, Gaṇanāyaka. || 10 ||
The Gaṇas, playing together, possess complexions that are respectively yellow, white, red, and blue;
they are all adorned with the ornaments of the lords of serpents and hold lotuses marked with edible offerings.
Regarding the word "of the All-pervasive One" (vibhoḥ):
it has been stated that in the case of the seat-mantra (*pīṭhamantra*) and so forth, they begin with their own seed-syllable (*svabīja*).
"One should worship first" means:

Here, the term "first" refers to its priority in relation to the repetition of the limbs (*aṅga*), since it was stated generally in the fourth chapter that one should worship [the deities] starting from the limbs up to the world-protectors (*lokapāla*).
The statement "first" is made here as an exception to that. On the occasion of explaining this, I, the author of the work, stated for this very reason:
"This statement was spoken with the intention of [indicating] the possibility [of the sequence]. (9–11)
Then, having performed worship as before, one should duly worship the deities of the limbs upon the filaments,
and Vakraṭuṇḍa and the others within the spaces between the petals.
Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadaṃṣṭra, Mahodara, and Gajānana. || 12 ||

Immediately thereafter, one should worship the formidable Vighnarāja known as Lambodara, who is smoke-colored, upon the petals and tips [of the lotus]. Then, one should worship Brāhmī and the other goddesses, as well as the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons; thus one should worship the deity. || 13 ||
One who has mastered the mantra should perform the applications enjoined by the ritual manual;
he should offer libations of pure water to Gaṇanāyaka every day.
"According to the previous method" means in the manner described in the fourth chapter.
"In accordance with the rite" refers to [the recitation of] the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati and so forth.
"One should worship in this way" concludes the instruction.
The worship of the three mantras is indeed the same.
As it was stated by Īśānaśiva:
"Others say that the seed-syllable of Gaṇeśa consists of the five-ending [letter] joined with the bindu and accompanied by the nāda."
"They pronounce [the seed-syllable] ending with the vowel *ū* and the bindu; this rule applies equally to both. This is what has been stated.
However, the distinction is that in the case of the *māyābīja* and so forth, one should worship Āmoda and the others on the six petals.
Furthermore, the procedures for libation (*tarpaṇa*) are common to all mantras.
In the rite of libation (tarpaṇa), however, there is this specific detail for all:
Having descended from his seat upon the golden peak of Mount Udaya, overcome by hunger,
he approaches the golden steps and consumes abundant food such as lotuses and other offerings.

"Having eaten, with a joyful mind, one should remember that Lord of Obstacles (Vighnarāja) as he was worshipped in the past, thinking: 'May he fulfill all desires just as he did before. Thus it is said when remembered at dawn. (12–14)
A diligent person shall obtain forty-four [units] at first, and four hundred before the mandala; thus a man attains his desired goal and more. || 15 ||
Regarding the instruction "one should satisfy":
the practical application is "Gaṃ, I satisfy Gaṇeśa.
"In sequence, four hundred" means as follows.
On each lunar day, one should perform that many oblations with four substances. || 15-16 ||
An oblation performed with coconuts on the fourth lunar day bestows prosperity;
beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, the wise man should perform it daily. || 16 ||
One should offer four hundred oblations, ending with the dative case, of coconut, barley-meal, parched grain, and sesame seeds respectively; thus all living beings shall become submissive. || 17 ||
Regarding the term "subjugated" (*vaśyā*):
therein lies the distinction between the *Prayogasāra* and the *Nārāyaṇīya*.
Having duly brought the object of attainment (*sādhya*) here by means of the noose (*pāśa*) and the hook (*aṅkuśa*), one stands above it.
"One desiring subjugation should recite it; this ritual instantly destroys the anger of one who is enraged. (17)
An offering made with sesame seeds and rice grains brings about the subjugation of Lakṣmī;
an offering made with parched grain mixed with the three sweets bestows a daughter. || 18 ||
Regarding "with sesame seeds":
here too, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight until the fourth day, there is an oblation of four hundred [offerings]. Regarding "with parched grains": [the same applies].
Here too, the four hundred oblations are performed starting from the first day of the bright fortnight (śukla-pratipad) until the fourth day;
the distinction is that it starts from that same first day and continues until the seventh day.
As it has been said:
For seven days, with parched grains sprinkled with the three sweets.
Thus [ends the verse]. 18.
By this rite, a maiden obtains her desired husband;
an oblation of sacrificial food smeared with clarified butter shall accomplish the wishes of men.
"By this method"—by this it is indicated that women also have the right of qualification (*adhikāra*) in such matters. || 19 ||
Just as mercury, when stirred with curd and processed for four days at night, enters into union [with gold], so too does it always bring about subjugation. || 20 ||
"Four days" means from the first day until the fourth day.
"Conciliation" (saṃvāda) is the act of winning over (saṃvanana). || 20 ||
It is made from the root of the white Arka plant, from red sandalwood wood, from Nimba broken by an elephant, or from an elephant tusk. || 21 ||

Having worshipped Vighneśvara during a lunar eclipse, the practitioner of mantra, remaining without food and bearing that [effigy] upon his crest-lock, should perform the recitation while touching it. || 22 ||
One shall obtain the glory of victory in battles, legal proceedings, and so forth.
"One should recite" means from the time of seizure until liberation. (21–23)
Rocanā, consecrated with this mantra and combined with honey, [should be used]. || 23 ||
By the rite of applying the *tilaka*, one brings all men under one's control.
"Mada" refers to the ichor of an elephant. (23–24)
One should write the name within the seed-syllables situated in both direct and reverse order. || 24 ||

Having worshipped the fresh butter and touched it, one should mutter the *prāṇa-mantra* one hundred and eight times; then, having further recited the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) over it, [one should consume it]. || 25 ||
Maintaining silence, one should consume [it] for seven nights during the night;
he will quickly become subject to the practitioner, without a doubt. || 26 ||
It conforms.
One should write the names of the practitioner, the person to be accomplished, and the ritual action between the two seed-syllables upon fresh butter.
By the phrase "in direct and reverse order," it is merely stated that [the names] are enclosed within the two seed-syllables.
"Navanīta" means "new.
It should also be understood as "encased in seed.
As it was said by the Teachers:
"One should write [the mantra] in fresh butter, both in direct and reverse order;
the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) is situated within the belly, encircled by that seed-syllable.
Thus it is said.

The term "fresh butter" (*navanīta*) is an elliptical expression that includes cakes (*apūpa*) and other such items, as stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "This rule applies to the effect [the offering] and also to the cake.
Regarding the phrase "having worshipped thoroughly":

[The phrase] "having further recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times" connects with the preceding [phrase] "to Gaṇeśa, who is the object of accomplishment. The connection is that one should consume that fresh butter (*navanīta*).
"Seven days" means from the first lunar day (pratipad) up to the seventh.
The three diagrams mentioned in another tantra are now described.
Having drawn an eight-petalled lotus,
one should write Gaurī, joined with a bindu and together with the name, upon its pericarp.
One should write the seed-syllables of the [five] forms at the bases of the petals starting from the east;
and on the corner petals, starting from the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, and north.
Then, in sequence, [one should place] the letters beginning with the limbs (aṅga) on the tips of the petals;
thereafter, the letters beginning with the Mother-energies (mātṛśakti) on the exterior of the lotus.
One should write the initial syllables of the world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective directions;
outside, one should draw a [mandala] endowed with sixteen petals and write the vowels upon those petals.
Having encircled the remainder with the Mātṛkā, and likewise with the Pāśa and Aṅkuśa mantras,
one should invoke the Lord of Devas into that Yantra and worship Vighna.
Whoever ties this to a thread of linen or similar material and wears it around the neck or upon the head,
prosperity shall always remain in his hands and eloquence shall ever abide upon his tongue.
"May wisdom, residing in the mind, and fame always increase in every direction.
Thus [is described] the eight-petaled lotus.
"Aṣṭāra" refers to what is above that; "upon the pericarp" means in the center of the pericarp;
"Gaurī" is the letter *ga*.
Regarding "the seed-syllables of the forms": these are the initial syllables of the eight forms (mūrtis) and so forth mentioned in the *Kṣipraprasādanī*.
Regarding "the limb" (*aṅga*): in the system of five limbs, it refers to the fifth [syllable] in the case of Saumya.

The Mothers themselves are the Śaktis; [one should place] their names and so forth, beginning with the first letter, in their respective directions—that is, in the eight petals of their own respective directions. The remainder is [to be done] with the Mātṛkā, beginning with the letter *ka*.
Likewise:

having drawn a hexagon, one should inscribe within its belly the letter "Pa" (the end of the fifth) enriched with a *bindu*, together with the name, upon the bark of a birch tree using *gorocana* and *dūrvā* grass.
Then, one should join the syllable *kāla* (ka) endowed with the vowel *e* (e), followed by the letter at the end of *gā* (ga),
then the syllable of Śakra (ta) bearing the head-vowel (i), and finally, according to rule, the long vowel and the sixth element (ra).

Having written the excellent mantra of Vāyusakha within the *māyā* [triangle], one should then draw a noose and a goad in its corners; outside of that, one should draw an earth-mandala (*bhūmaṇḍala*).
Having worshipped this yantra with fragrant and pleasing flowers, one should worship Vighneśvara.
"The man who wears [this] upon his head shall instantly obtain vast prosperity.
Thus [ends the section]. The mantra is: "To Megholkā, Svāhā!
Likewise—

In the lotus, which has eight petals and filaments of sixteen parts, one should write the seed-syllable *Raṃ* in the center, surrounded by the seed-syllables; then, in the corners, one should write the syllable *Gaṃ*, and on the petals,
which consist of the syllables of the Gāyatrī, one should surround it with the consonants beginning with *Ka*.
Indeed, this yantra, which possesses the seed-syllable *bhūḥ* and the abode of the earth, bestows everything.
Thus [ends the section on verses] 24–26.
One should first utter the seed-syllables of Śrī, Śakti, Smara, Bhū, and Vighna;
thereafter, one should recite "Gaṇapatim" ending in the dative case, followed by "Varadam" at the end of the word "Vara."
Having said, "Bring all these people under my control," twice—this twenty-eight-syllable mantra beginning with Tārā is thus proclaimed. || 28 ||
The seer is Gaṇaka, the metre is Gāyatrī accompanied by Nivṛt, and the deity is Mahāgaṇapati, who is worshipped by the gods. || 29 ||
He extracts the mantra of Mahāgaṇapati with the word "Śrī.
The seed-syllable of the Earth (Bhū-bīja) will be mentioned later.
Regarding the word "Varada," the accusative case is used because it functions as an object in the mantra, yet within the mantra itself, it serves as a vocative.
In the mantra *sarvajanam*, the word ending in the accusative case is also [the object].

Here, some, considering the letter *ya* to be the *kīlaka*, state that the word *gaṇapati* ends in the vocative case. Others state that the word *śrīmahāgaṇapati* ends in the vocative case and that there is also a doubling of the word *vaśam*.
This is indeed the view of the author as well,
since it is stated that "the great mantra of Gaṇeśa" is multiplied by thirty-two varieties.
Others maintain that in the verse of the Ācārya, "Vighna joined with the dative case," the word *vighna* is an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) for the term *Mahāgaṇapati*.
In this case as well, the term *gaṇapati* is used;
and the determination [of its meaning] is according to the teacher’s instruction,
as was also stated by the teacher Padmapāda.
By the statement, "The mantra-practitioner is initiated," it is said that one abandons the dative case and adopts the vocative.
This is because the authors of the *Mantradevaprakāśikā* and others have also extracted [the mantra] ending precisely in the vocative.
The seed-syllable is *gaṃ*, and the power (*śakti*) is *svāhā*.
As it has been said:
"The sixth seed-syllable is dviṭha (the two 'ṭha's), [which are at the end of the seed-syllables]; this is the Śakti. (27–29)

One who knows the ritual procedure should, according to the rules, fashion the six limbs of this mantra by means of its own seed-syllables situated within the six [syllables], provided with their long vowels.
He states the sixfold [rite] with the words "by the six seed-syllables" (*ṣaḍbījastha*).
Regarding the phrase "according to the rule":
it means they are joined with their respective classes [of mantras] and by means of the Śaiva six-limbed mudrās.
By the phrase "one who knows the ritual procedure" (*vidhānavit*), this application (*prayoga*) is indicated:

*oṃ gāṃ* for the heart, *śrīṃ gīṃ* for the head, *hrīṃ gūṃ* for the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), *klīṃ gaiṃ* for the armor (*varma*), *glauṃ gauṃ* for the eyes (*netra*), and *gaṃ gaḥ* for the weapon (*astra*).
This is the traditional method.

Some, however, state that after uttering the five seed-syllables beginning with *praṇava*, one should perform the arrangement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by means of the application of *gām* and so forth; others say that the syllables *gām* and so forth should precede the six seed-syllables. (30)
One should visualize an island made of the nine precious gems in the ocean of sugarcane juice, its shores washed by its waves and fanned by gentle breezes. || 31 ||
It was filled with celestial trees and creepers such as the mandāra and pārijāta, and its ground was reddened by the reflections of the jewels produced therein. || 32 ||

In its center, one should visualize the Pārijāta tree, which illuminates the quarters of the sky with the rising sun and moon, consists of the nine precious gems, and is constantly attended by the six seasons that ever increase delight. || 33 ||
The meaning of the passage beginning with "an island consisting of the nine jewels" (*navaratnamayaṃ dvīpam*) is as follows:

immediately after the earth, one should place the ocean of sugarcane juice (*ikṣusamudra*), an island consisting of the nine jewels (*navaratnamayaṃ dvīpam*), and a *pārijāta* tree consisting of the nine jewels (*navaratnamayaṃ pārijātam*).
The rest is the same.
"Consisting of the nine jewels":
because it originated from an island composed of the nine jewels, the *pārijāta* tree itself also consists of the nine jewels.

Others, however, [describe it] as having a root of ruby (*māṇikya*), sprouts of beryl (*vaidūrya*), branches of sapphire (*indranīla*), young leaves of coral (*pravāla*), foliage of emerald (*marakata*), and peaks of go-meda.
They say that the pearl-bud is the diamond-flower and the ruby is the fruit. Also, in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*:
"With fruits, blossoms, and sprouts known as gems, diamonds, and corals..."
And so forth. || 31–33 ||
Below that, upon a great pedestal fashioned as a lotus of the Mātṛkās, one should meditate on Mahāgaṇapati situated within a triangle inside a hexagon. || 34 ||
The two locative endings in "pīṭhe racitaḥ" (constructed on the seat) are in different grammatical cases (vyadhikaraṇa).
Regarding "situated within the triangle inside the hexagon," here a downward-facing triangle is to be understood.
And this should be understood as being within the pericarp of the lotus of the Mātṛkā. || 34 ||
[I bow to Him] whose face is like that of the lordly elephant, who has the moon as His crest-jewel, who possesses the hue of the dawn, and who is three-eyed;
who is constantly embraced with passion by His beloved, who holds a lotus in Her hand and rests upon His own lap;
and who is equipped with a citron, a mace, a bow, a trident, a discus, a lotus, a noose, and a blue water-lily.
I worship him who carries with his hands the finest rice, his own tusk, and a jewel-filled vase. || 35 ||
He repeatedly warded off with his two ear-flaps the bees whose minds were eager for the abundance of ichor flowing from the hollows of his temples. || 36 ||
He was bestowing showers of jewels from the mouths of ruby jars held in the tips of his hands, gladdening the practitioners while being himself overwhelmed with divine intoxication.
Adorned with a crown of rubies and decorated with jewel ornaments, the practitioner, being composed, should meditate upon [the deity] and recite the mantra four hundred thousand times. || 38 ||
One should offer as oblations the ten-fold portion of four thousand—that is, forty thousand—using the eight substances beginning with ghee (medaka) and so forth. || 39 ||
"Hastī" means the lord of elephants, the best of tuskers.
She holds a lotus in her left hand, while with her right she embraces [him].
The bow is the *ikṣudhanus* (sugarcane bow).
The trident has three prongs (*triśikha*).
The visualization of the weapons proceeds from the lower left hand to the lower right hand.
But the golden pitcher is on the tip of the trunk;
as it has been said—
following the sequence starting from the upper left.

[He is] holding in his hands a discus, a spear, a sword, a bow, a mace, an excellent citron, a conch, a grain of rice, a sprout, a lotus, a noose, and a lotus, with a jar shining at the tip of his trunk. Thus.

In the *Mahāgaṇapatistava* as well, [the deity is described] from left to right, starting from the top: "I take refuge in Mahāgaṇapa, who holds a discus, a lotus, a trident, a noose, a sugar-cane, a blue lotus, a staff, a jar, a cluster of blossoms, a pomegranate, a radish, and a jeweled pitcher."
The Drāviḍas, however, explain it otherwise:
the first two [lines] are at the lower left and right,
and the other two are above them.
In the middle of those two above; at the penultimate of those two above;
at the final of those two above.
And it is said in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*:
"Beginning from the lower right hand and ending at the lower left hand,
[he holds] a mace, a trident, a lotus, a kahlāra lily, and a tusk in his right hands."
With his left hands he holds a rice-ear, a noose, a discus, a sugarcane bow, and a citron;
his lotus-feet are radiant with anklets.
"And having playfully placed a jewel-pitcher on the tip of his lotus-hand.
Others, however, maintain that there is an exchange of the *bījapūra* fruit specifically in the first dhyāna.
Others, however, maintain that there is a transposition of those two [seeds].
By this, the seed-syllables *ra* and *da* appear on the left and right [teeth] respectively.
Regarding the term "mantrī":
The recitation of the nourishment mantra (*puṣṭimantra*) is said to be one-tenth [of the preceding];
that is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru. (35–39)
One should constantly satisfy [the deity] with offerings according to the very path previously described;
one should worship Gaṇanāyaka on the previously mentioned pedestal according to the prescribed rite. || 40 ||
Regarding the phrase "as previously stated":
it means four hundred and forty-four times.
Regarding the phrase "on the previously mentioned seat": [it refers to the seat described earlier].
The meaning is that the *pīṭha-śaktis* and *pīṭha-mantras* mentioned in the previous mantra should also be understood here.
"One should worship Gaṇanāyaka" implies [in] the triangle;
"according to the rule" refers to what will be described below.
The *yantra*, however, has already been described on the occasion of discussing meditation;
the phrase "with its coverings" (*sāvaraṇam*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 40 ||
Outside the triangle, one should worship in the four directions starting from the east;
below the bilva tree at the front, one should worship Śrī and the Lord of Śrī (Śrīpati). || 41 ||
One should worship Padmā, who holds a pair of lotuses, and Hari, who holds a conch and a discus;
to the south, beneath a banyan tree, one should worship Gaurī and the Lord of Gaurī. || 42 ||
Gaurī, holding a noose and a goad, and Hara, holding an axe and a trident;
one should worship Rati and the Lord of Rati beneath the Pippala tree in the west. || 43 ||
Rati, adorned with a blue lotus in her hand, and Smara, bearing a bow and arrow;
under a Priyaṅgu tree in the north, one should worship Mahī and the Boar. || 44 ||
The earth has ears of *śukavrīhi* rice as her hands, and the Lord holds a mace and a discus;
one should worship the Leader of the Gopas together with Lakṣmī in front of the deity. || 45 ||
In the six corners, one should worship Āmoda and the others together with their beloveds.
One should worship Āmoda, accompanied by Siddhi, in the front corner.
One should worship Pramoda, endowed with prosperity, in the southeast corner;
one should worship Sumukha, possessed of splendor, in the northeast corner. || 47 ||
One should worship Durmukha in the southwest corner (Varuṇa’s direction) with Madanāvatī;
one should worship Vighna, accompanied by Madadravā, in the northwest corner (the direction of the night-stalkers). || 48 ||
In the northwest (Vāyavya), one should worship Vighnahartṛ together with Drāviṇī;
they possess reddish bodies and hold a noose, a goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons. || 49 ||
All those obstacles and their women had the lotuses of their faces washed by the streams of ichor flowing from the temples of their cheeks; their eyes were rolling with intoxication.
Holding a lotus in one hand and embracing their beloved with the other, Śaṅkhanidhi and Padmanidhi are to be worshipped in sequence on the two sides of the hexagon. || 51 ||

Accompanied by his two beloveds, whose characteristics were described previously, there shall be worship of the limbs (aṅgapūjā) upon the filaments; Brāhmī and the others shall occupy the spaces between the petals. || 52 ||
The lords of the outer world are to be worshipped, followed by Vajra and the others;
thus, having attained accomplishment through recitation and other means, one may perform the applications as desired by oneself. || 53 ||

One should accomplish [the rite] with eight substances or others prescribed in the ritual manuals (*kalpa*). He describes the worship of the five pairs [of deities] with the words "tri-koṇa" and so forth;
*ṭaṅka* means an axe.
The two hands are joined with blue lotuses; she is enriched by these two.
"Astra" means an arrow; "potrin" means a boar.
[She is located] from the southeast corner.
The meaning is: "in that which is the southeast corner in relation to the eastern direction previously established.
This applies likewise to the northeast corner;
similarly, it should be understood for the west, the southwest, and the northwest corners as well.
As it has been stated by the Teachers:
"Agrāsava and Āmoda, along with Pramoda and Sumukha, are on either side of him at the two corners;
and on his back is the one named Durmukha, while on either side of him are the two who cause obstacles to obstacles."
The term "obstacles" (vighnāḥ) is connected with what precedes. "As previously stated" refers to the eighth chapter.
This concludes the second repetition. ||41-54||
By means of a lotus-homa one [subdues] kings, and by means of auspicious blue lotuses, their wives. || 54 ||
The ministers [honored] the learned with full-blown white water-lilies, the kings with sacrificial fuel-sticks produced from *pippala* trees,
and the lords of men with the finest fuel-wood derived from *udumbara* trees.

By means of *plakṣa* wood, the mantra-practitioner shall bring Vaiśyas under his control; by means of wood from the *vaṭa* tree, he shall bring Śūdras under his control. With honey, there shall be the acquisition of gold; with cow's milk, one shall obtain cows.
By an oblation of clarified butter, a person attains great prosperity;
by curds, there shall be success in all things; and by means of food offerings, one becomes a lord of food.
The connection is with the phrase "the mantra-practitioner shall bring kings under his control" and so forth, beginning with "by means of the lotus-homa.
By the word "mantra-practitioner," it is stated that the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) is to be substituted for the word "all. Regarding the phrase "with the best fuel-sticks":
It is also connected with the three [terms] at the beginning. || 54–57 ||
One desiring rain should offer oblations with the best fuel-sticks of cane;
having offered oblations with safflower blossoms, one obtains garments before long.
Regarding the word "vṛṣṭi": here, it should be understood that the seed-syllable of nectar follows immediately after its own seed-syllable. || 58 ||

At the beginning of each [offering], one should first satisfy [the deities] four times with the root mantra. Śrī, Śakti, Rati, Bhū, and Lakṣmī, preceded by their respective seed-syllables, are accompanied by their beloveds. || 59 ||
He explains the method of the fourfold libation with three verses beginning with "pratyekam" (each one).
First, one should perform the libation four times with the root mantra.
This is the meaning of the word "pratyekam" (each one): [it refers to each individual deity].
Whichever deity is to be gratified in each respective place, one should first perform the libation (tarpaṇa) four times each with the root mantra.

Regarding the phrase "beginning with their own seed-syllables" (svabījādyāḥ): the connection is that one should gratify each [deity] individually, preceded by their respective seed-syllables and accompanied by the word "Priyā" (the Beloved). || 59 ||

The mantra-practitioner should separately satisfy Āmoda and the others, endowed with their respective seed-syllables and powers, four times each; likewise, he should satisfy Śaṅkhanidhi and Padmanidhi. || 60 ||
One should perform the libation for the two [deities] accompanied by their respective seed-syllables (bīja) and joined with their beloved consorts.
Through this libation, one attains one's own desired object from the mandala. || 61 ||
"Beginning with their own seed-syllables" means beginning with the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati.
"Accompanied by their respective consorts four times each" means accompanied by Vasudhārā and Vasumatī.
For example:
Having offered libations four times with the root mantra, saying "I satisfy Mahāgaṇapati," one should then offer libations four times, saying "Śrīṃ! I satisfy Śrī and Śrīpati.
Here, by the word "Lakṣmī," the couple of the fifth stage (*pañcamakrama*) is included, as intended according to the sequence of worship. This has been stated by the Teacher in his hymn:

"Because the pentad of couples performs the five functions through the differentiation of the five causes, one should worship that primary couple. Also elsewhere: "First one should worship the God, and then the pentad of couples."
Elsewhere also, at the conclusion of the ritual placement (nyāsa), it is said:

"One should perform the fivefold placement upon the head, face, heart-lotus, secret place, and feet; [placing] the couples with their own respective seed-syllables and their individual names separately."
Thus, there are thirteen libations for the deities;
there are thirteen root-libations;
and at the very end, there is a libation with the root mantra four times.
Thus, there are one hundred and eight libations (*tarpaṇa*). This is the inferior method (*kaniṣṭha-prakāra*).
According to the teacher Padmapāda, one hundred and twenty-four libations are prescribed in the inferior method.
Namely: *mūla* 4, *mahāgaṇapa* 4, *mūla* 4, *puṣṭi* 4, the five pairs (*pañcamithunāni*) 40, *āmodādi* 64, *mūla* 4; thus it is.
However, the intermediate method is by means of the individual libations (*vyastatarpaṇa*), beginning with "accompanied by the beloved" (*priyānvitā*).
In this context, "separateness" (vyastatva) is obtained from the statement in the root [text]: "Accompanied by the beloved, endowed with power.
For example:

having offered libations four times to the Root [Mantra], one then offers four times [with the mantra]: "OṂ, I offer libations to Śrī together with Śrīpati," and again, "OṂ, I offer libations to Śrīpati together with Śrī."
One should perform the libation four times with the mantra "tarpayāmi.

Thus, there are twenty-six libations for the deities and twenty-six libations with the root mantra (*mūla*). At the end, one performs the libation four times with the root mantra; and at the very beginning, one performs the libation independently four times with the root mantra.
Thus, there are two hundred and sixteen libations (*tarpaṇa*).
As for the "superior method," the remainder is that it applies to each of the libations to be described first;
the meaning is that one should perform the libation four times—once at the beginning and once at the end.
"By the root [mantra]" means for each syllable;
one should satisfy each individual syllable of the root mantra.
For example:

First, the root mantra four times; then the first syllable four times; again the root mantra four times—thus there are twenty-eight offerings of syllables (*varṇatarpaṇa*). Then there are twenty-eight offerings of the root mantra (*mūlatarpaṇa*), and finally the root mantra four times. In this way, there are two hundred and twenty-eight offerings in total.
Then, as in the case of the medium type, there are two hundred and sixteen [offerings].
Thus, there are four hundred and forty-four libations (*tarpaṇas*). This is stated in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarśinī*:
I shall now describe the fourfold libation (tarpaṇa), which bestows all desired objects.
In a solitary, secluded, and delightful place, free from all calamities.
Having performed his ablutions and other rites, the mantra-practitioner, endowed with the previously described ritual placement (nyāsa),
should visualize a forest of flowering lotuses in the middle of the pond.
In its center was a great lotus, resembling the rising sun,
lofty, fragrant, delightful, and captivating to the mind.

The mantra-knower, previously mentioned as one who knows the mantras, should meditate upon [the lotus] as having blossomed instantly from the orb of the sun by means of a flight of stairs made of pure silver.
Having emerged and descended,
the wise one should then meditate upon Mahāgaṇapati together with his retinue as stationed in the center of the pericarp.
Then, having worshipped with excellent fragrant flowers as before,
one should place the mouth of the vessel upon the head of the lord of practitioners.
Having meditated upon the Lord raining streams of jewels upon his head,
[one should bathe him] with waters mixed with moon-pearls, sandalwood, saffron, and musk.
First, having gratified [the deities] four times with the root mantra,
one should likewise satisfy the couples, the six obstacles, and the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma.
The mantra practitioner, using each deity’s respective seed-syllable and so forth, ending with *svāhā*, four times for each,
should separately perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) preceded by the root mantra four times.
Combined, one hundred and eight [recitations] constitute the minimum; this is the sequence.
Alternatively, as before, one may perform them separately with these mantras beginning with the root mantra.
Or the wise one may satisfy [the deities] with mantras according to the method prescribed for worship;
this is the middle procedure, totaling two hundred and sixteen [mantras].
Alternatively, having gratified [the deity] four times with the root mantra,
one should offer four oblations each time with the syllables of the preceding mantra, ending each with "svāhā."
Having first fully satisfied the root mantra four times,
one should thereafter fully satisfy the couples and others as before.
When combined, that would amount to four hundred and forty-four;
thus has the sequence of the eldest been proclaimed by the wise who have reached the further shore of the scriptures.
Having thus satisfied [the deity], thereafter, as before, with the ritual services (upacāras),
the wise one should pray for all desired objects, prostrate, and perform the dismissal (udvāsana).
Whoever thus constantly offers libations shall obtain everything from the mandala;
even in times of drought, in terrible fear, or during calamities such as those caused by kings and thieves.
In cases of high fever, in disputes, in the crisis of extreme poverty,
and especially in all undertakings such as marriages and the like.
In this manner, the lord of men, with a serene mind, should perform the libation;
thus Mahāgaṇeśvara, being pleased, shall become the bestower of great prosperity. Thus it is said.

Others, however, say that by the word *lakṣmī* (glory), the predominance of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) is intended. The sequence of the mantra's enumeration is what is meant. According to that view, first twenty times with the root mantra, then twenty-eight times with the syllables of the mantra, then as many times again with the root mantra, and finally four times with the root mantra up to this point.
Then follow the libations for the twenty-four deities;
that many times [are] the root-libations, and at the end of those, four times with the root mantra.
Thus, there are four hundred and forty-four libations in total.
This has been stated in the *Mūlanārāyaṇīya*, in the *Rahasyapaṭala*:
"Having first performed twenty libations with the mantra-syllables ending in the *dviṭha* (svāhā) and repeated four times according to the Vedas,
one should offer libations to Vighnarāja and likewise to Lakṣmī and the others at each interval."
Elsewhere also: first, twenty times for the couples, the six obstacle-śaktis, and each of the treasure-śaktis, with four repetitions of the root mantra.
Thus, for those letters whose nature is the root-mantra, when they are heated and melted by one of sharp intellect, they become four hundred and forty-four in number. So it is said.

Those, however, who say that the word *mahāgaṇapati* ends in the vocative case (*sambuddhyanta*), state that the number [of offerings] is completed by performing the libation of the syllables (*akṣaratarpaṇa*) as many times as there are syllables [in the root mantra], followed by the libation of the twenty-six pairs (*mithuna*) as many times as those [syllables], and finally four times with the root mantra at the end. Those, however, who say that the word *gaṇapati* ends in the vocative case, [prescribe]: the root mantra four times, *mahāgaṇapati* four times, the root mantra four times, *puṣṭi* four times, and then the libation of the syllables.
First, the libation for the couples is performed as before with the root mantra; at the end, they say that the number is completed by the root mantra.

In the case of a thirty-syllable [mantra], there are libations for each syllable and the root mantra at the end: *mūla* (4), *mūla* (4), *mūlena*—this makes 244. Then, with the eight couples, ending with *mūlena*, it is 68. Then, with the [deities] beginning with Āmoda, ending with *mūlena*, it is 132.
In this way, the completion of the count should be understood.

However, those who maintain that the word *śrīmahāgaṇapati* is in the vocative case and that the word *vaśam* is doubled, [perform] the libation (*tarpaṇa*) consisting of thirty-two syllables for that many times with the root mantra;

likewise, [they perform it] eleven times with the *bījapūra* and others, eighty-eight times with the four pairs (*mithuna*), the six obstacles (*ṣaḍvighna*), and the two treasures (*nidhi*), according to the method described for the youngest [form].
They say that at the beginning and at the end, one should recite the root mantra four times.
As for the mantras of Bījāpūra and others:
"Bījāpūra, the mace, the sugarcane bow, and joined with the trident."
A wheel, a lotus, a noose, and a blue lotus; a stalk of rice with its tip, and joined by two horns.
The five [mantras] beginning with *gaṃ* and preceded by the *praṇava*, ending with *ratnakalaśa* and concluding with the heart-mantra (*hṛd*), and again those beginning with the *śrī*-seed syllable.
The first syllable consisting of six seed-mantras and the final one— these, together with the words to be mentioned hereafter,
are traditionally known as the mantras for the weapons of the Great Obstructors (Mahāvighnas) in their respective order.

The five [deities] beginning with Bījapūra are in reverse order, having the seed-syllables *gaṃ*, *glauṃ*, *klīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *śrīṃ* at their beginning. Furthermore, the five beginning with Rati follow the regular sequence, having the five seed-syllables beginning with *śrīṃ*.
The last one, Ratnakalaśa, means that he has the six seed-syllables beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) at his beginning.

The mantra-arts, the power, the vital breath, the three qualities, the dissolution and destruction of Kālacakra, pervasion, attachment, the ground, one’s own nature, and the Vidyā—all these belong to the Self as the triple world. Thus it is said.
The teacher Padmapāda, however, describes a fourfold repetition of the libation differently,

as follows: with the root mantra divided tenfold, conjoined with the eleven names beginning with Bījapūra— namely Mahāgaṇapati, Kṣipraprasādana, and the eight [others] mentioned therein such as Vighna.
Prior to the mantra "Gaṇapataye," one should perform libations for the twenty-four deities with the root mantra (mūlamantra). Thus, there are fifty-five libations for the deities;
these are performed with the root mantra at the beginning and likewise four times with the root mantra at the end, totaling four hundred and forty-four.
However, in the *Prayogasāra*, it is stated: "The twenty-eight syllables [of the root mantra], joined with ten [syllables] and four words..."
Afterwards, one should satisfy the six Gaṇapas, beginning with Pañcārāma, as well as the two Nidhis.

Having meditated upon the great Gaṇapati, who is composed of jewels and is gracious toward his devotees, on the head of the Lord by repeating this mantra four times for each [syllable], the wise one [should proceed]. Thus [ends verses 60–61].
The seed-syllable of the Earth (Bhū-bīja) is said to consist of the letter 'ma' with a bindu, followed by the letter 'ra', and ending with 'smṛti'.

He extracts the seed-syllable of the Earth (bhū-bīja) as "smṛti": the letter *la* is "māṃsa," situated in *smṛti*; the letter *ga* is its location; and it is joined with the vowel *au* and the nasal drop (*bindu*). Thus, it becomes *glauṃ*. || 62 ||

One should draw the seed-syllable in the center of a six-cornered [figure] within a blazing fire-city, with a star [at its center]; then, in the directions, one should write Lakṣmī, Māyā, and Kandarpa; thereafter, in the six compartments, one should write the six seed-syllables.
In the junctions thereof, one should place the limb-mantras (aṅgamantras), and in the eight-petaled lotus, the letters of the root-mantra.
Let the learned man write the remaining [names] on the other leaves according to their qualities, and the last one on the final Palāśa leaf. ||63||

This yantra of the Lord of the Gaṇas is enveloped by the letters in forward and reverse order, as well as by the noose (pāśa) and the goad (aṅkuśa), and surrounded by two squares representing the earth;
it should be written on excellent birch bark or gold with lac, saffron, gorocana, and musk.
By practicing self-restraint and carrying it out, one may obtain that prosperity which is sought after by all.
Thus has been declared the ritual procedure for Mahāgaṇapati, which is worshipped by the gods, which bestows all accomplishments upon men, and which grants all human goals. || 65 ||
Regarding the yantra, he says "the seed-syllable" (*bījam*).

The grammatical connection is as follows: one should write the seed-syllable *gaṃ*, which is the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati, located within the *tāra* (the *praṇava*), inside a shining triangular fire-palace (*sphuradanalapura*) in the center of a six-cornered figure, upon an eight-petaled lotus (*vasudalakamala*).
In the directions, it should be understood that [the sequence] begins from the front (east) outside the triangle;
in the six corners, which are the "juice-enclosures" (rasapuṭas).
The first six syllables of the mantra constitute the seed-syllable group (*bīja-ṣaṭka*).
One should place the limb-mantras (*aṅga-mantra*) of Mahāgaṇapati at the junctions of the six corners starting from the front.
On the petals, one should write the remaining twenty-two syllables of the mantra, three for each quality, and write the final syllable alone on the eighth petal.
Then, one should encircle it with the letters in both direct and reverse order. Then, one should encircle it with the noose (pāśa) and the goad (aṅkuśa).

According to Padmapādācārya, however: "Having written the eight syllables on the eight petals, and having written the letters of the Mātṛkā, the noose, and the goad within three circles outside of that—"
It has been stated: "One should write the *pāśa* and *māyā* seed-syllables within the two *rbhūpura*s.
*Lākṣā* is the juice of lac;
*kuṅkuma* is that which grows in Kashmir.
Rocanā is cow-bile pigment (gorocanā).
Mṛgamada is musk (kastūrī). || 63–65 ||
One should utter "Māyā" (Hrīm), followed by the pair of feet of Viriñci (Om Namo Bhagavate Vāsudevāya); then one should say "Gaṇapati";
afterwards, one should again say "Khaḍgīśa," "Pāvaka," and finally "Varada. || 66 ||
"Bring all the world under my control at my feet; [this is] the two Ṭhas. This twenty-six syllable mantra is a celestial wish-fulfilling tree for those who worship it. || 67 ||
The Gaṇaka is the Ṛṣi, the metre is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Manu. Regarding the mantra of Virigaṇapati, he says "māyā" and so forth:
Khaḍgīśa is *va*, Pāvaka is *ra*, and the letter *repha* is *ra*.

The seed-syllable (bīja) is *hṛllekhā*, and the power (*śakti*) is *svāhā*. Some, omitting the five syllables beginning with *vara* and the word *lokām*, state that it consists of nineteen syllables. Its meter is *nivṛt*.
The rest is as before. Some read "janapada" instead of "lokapada. Others employ the sixfold seed-syllable of Mahāgaṇapati at the beginning of the word "virīti" and so forth. (66–68)
Virivighneśvara is proclaimed as the bestower of all desires upon those who worship him. || 68 ||
In the Vedas of the internal organ, with five eyes [and] five elements, the arrangement of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) is performed by means of the mantra-syllables beginning with Māyā thus divided;
the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should contemplate this in the place prescribed for Mahāgaṇapati. || 69 ||
Regarding the phrase "the great six-limbed [mantra]":
the four internal organs, the four Vedas, the five arrows, the five elements, and two eyes—
by means of these six words of the second [line], it becomes six-limbed.
The third [mantra] is like that of Mahāgaṇapati. || 68 ||

I worship her who has the luster of vermilion, whose face is like that of an elephant, and who possesses three eyes; she holds a noose and a goad in her hands, and constantly bears a wine-filled skull-cup;
she wears the crescent moon upon her crest, her body is embraced by Puṣṭi, and her hand shines with a lotus while another reaches for the tip of a banner.
With his hand placed upon her lap, which was the source of that [lineage], he held a water-vessel from which a lotus flower shone forth.

One should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times, and perform the fire-oblation (homa) with one-tenth of that number, using the eight substances previously mentioned, smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu). || 71 ||
One should worship on the previously mentioned pedestal, which possesses the nine powers beginning with Tīvrā;
having conceptualized the form by means of the root mantra, one should invoke the Lord there and worship Him. || 72 ||
The *puṣkara* is the tip of an elephant’s trunk.

In the meditation [on this deity], however, there is a noose in the right hand and a goad in the left; below the right is a honey-filled skull-cup, and the left is placed upon the womb of his beloved.
In the same way, Puṣṭi is also four-armed.
In that regard, [the goddess stands] upon lotuses on the right and left.
Regarding the phrase "with hands shining with lotuses" (*padmollasaddhastayā*), the analysis (*vigraha*) is: she whose two hands shine with two lotuses is thus described.
According to those who know the tradition, there is an embrace of the Beloved with the lower right hand, and with the lower left hand, she touches the tip of his *dhvaja*.
However, some say that Puṣṭi has two hands;
[they describe] one hand as holding a lotus and the second hand as touching the tip of a banner.
According to that view, "embracing" (āśleṣa) means proximity, not an embrace with the hand.
In the second mantra as well, this very same meditation applies.
But in the third mantra:
[He holds] a citron, a mace, a bow, and an enemy, as well as a garland, with his right hands—
May Gaṇeśa protect you— he who holds in his beautiful hands arrows, nooses, and lotuses as teeth, a jar rich with jewels,
whose body is crimson with vermilion, who has three eyes, whose trunk is placed upon the Yoni,
and who bears Puṣṭi, whose lotus-hands rest upon his excellent Liṅga.
The worship and other rites for the three are the same. || 70–72 ||

The first [cycle] is the rotation of the couples; the second is with Āmoda and the others, the sky-clad ones (Digambaras); the third is with the limbs (Aṅgas), and the fourth is traditionally known as being with the Mothers (Mātṛs). || 73 ||
The fifth [offering] should be with the World-Protectors, and the sixth is traditionally said to be with the Vajra and other [regents].
Thus, the mantra-practitioner whose mantra is accomplished [should worship] with blossoming lotuses. (74)
One should offer oblations with rice mixed with sesame seeds, and all [beings] will come under one's control.
Having offered oblations with sweetmeats soaked in clarified butter, one attains prosperity;
having offered them, a ruler of the earth attains victory on the fields of battle. || 75 ||

"Previously mentioned" refers to the Mahāgaṇapati-pūjā-yantre. By the phrase "consisting of the nine powers beginning with Tīvrā," the fact that the Pīṭha-mantra begins with Māyā (Hrīm) is stated. || 73–75 ||
By offering oblations with the three sweets (madhutraya), one brings the inhabitants of the earth under one's control;
by offering all kinds of food, both solid and soft, one shall accomplish all desired goals. || 76 ||
"With the three sweets" means with milk, honey, and ghee.
Regarding "edibles such as food":
edible items (bhakṣya) include sweetmeats (laḍḍuka) and the like.
"Edible [substances], mantras, and so forth.
By the word "and so forth," substances such as those to be licked (*lehya*) and those to be sucked (*coṣya*) are included.
Among these, *lehya* refers to *rasālā* (a milk-based confection) and similar items.
The definition of *tallakṣaṇa* is found in the *Sūpaśāstra*:
"Half an *āḍhaka* of curd that has stood for a very long time, sixteen *palas* of sugar as bright as the moon,
one *pala* of ghee, one *pala* of honey, two *karṣas* of black pepper, half a *pala* of ginger, and half a *pala* each of four other [spices]."

"This is the flavorful *rasālā* prepared by Vṛkodara on a white stone slab, ground with gentle hands by his beloved and placed in a vessel made fragrant with an abundance of camphor; it is this very *rasālā* which was tasted by the Blessed Madhusūdana.
Thus [it is said]. As for the four ingredients—cinnamon, cardamom, cinnamon leaf, and saffron—their combined total is half a *pala*.
The yantra mentioned in another tantra is now written down.

I shall describe the yantra that brings about great accomplishment: having inscribed upon a birch-bark leaf, using dūrvā sprouts smeared with the *rocanā* of a sacrificial animal, the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) enclosed within the *virisaṃpuṭa* [mantra], into a pair of earth-houses (*bhūgṛha*) within the *śakti*.
Having written the mantra in the corners according to the Vedic quarters with the remainder of that name, and having encircled it,
one should draw the yantra, invoke Gaṇādhirāja, and worship him with perfumes and flowers.
"By constantly reciting it and wearing it, the entire world comes under his control.
Thus, in the first mantra, "śrutiśaḥ" means three times;
in the final corner, there are two.
In the second mantra, *śruti* means "ear"; therefore, the meaning is "twice.
As it has been said:
"The letters *va* and *ra* are likewise enriched by eyes (*locana*); having extracted them again from the group in that manner, [one obtains] *gaṇapatī*."
Having uttered all [the letters] together, I shall be under control; therefore, the letter *ma* is joined with *aya*, resulting in *maya*.
From the word "śiras" [the head] should come.
Thus, in the third mantra, the *śruti* is fourfold.
In this case, the power situated in the center is external to the mantra;
one should write a single syllable on the final petal. || 76 ||
One should utter one's own seed-syllable constricted by Śakti, followed by Mahāgaṇapati in the dative case;
this twelve-syllabled mantra is said to be "the Consort of Fire" (Agnivadhū). || 77 ||

The seer (ṛṣi) is Gaṇaka, the metre (chandas) is Gāyatrī beginning with Nivṛt, and the deity (devatā) declared in the Tantra by name is Śaktigaṇādhipa. One should determine the limbs (aṅgas) of the mantra using its words, both individually and collectively. || 78 ||
He states the mantra of Śaktigaṇapati with the words "śakti" and so forth.
"Nijaṃ bījam" refers to the seed-syllable *gaṃ*. The phrase "ending in *ḍe*" is to be connected with what follows.
*Hrīṃ gaṃ hrīṃ mahāgaṇapataye svāhā*.
*Gaṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*). [The mantra is formed] with these [syllables] separated.
The five limbs of the mantra are formed by its five words; the sixth is formed by the whole.
I bow to the one who is fair as a pearl, whose face is like a rutting elephant, who has the moon as his crest and three eyes,
and who holds in his hands a lotus, a goad, and a jewel-filled jar; he whose hand rests upon the shoulder of her seated on his lap, who possesses the luster of a lotus and clings to his own banner.
We worship him who has placed his hand upon the womb of the Goddess, and who wears a jewel-encrusted crown. || 79 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with cakes in the consecrated fire ten times that number; thus, one should worship the deity every day. || 80 ||
One should worship on the previously described pedestal according to the very path mentioned before;
by offering pieces of sugarcane, the wise man shall obtain the glory of sovereignty. || 81 ||
Likewise, with coconuts, then with ripe plantains,
and with flattened rice mixed with sugar, one brings the entire world under one's control.
One brings a king under one's control with barley meal (saktu) and Brahmins with auspicious offerings;
by an oblation of clarified butter (ghṛta-homa), one becomes wealthy—of this there is no doubt. || 83 ||
In the meditation [of this deity], however, in the first [form], there are [trunks] above the right and left;
below the right is a jewel-pot, and below the left is the yoni of the Goddess.
According to the tradition, the trunk [of the elephant] rests upon the jewel-pot.
She is so [described] because of the lotus held in her right hand; her left hand touches the tip of the banner. This is according to what was stated previously, without interruption. (79–83)
"Having restrained one's own seed with power, bring it under control with the two syllables *ṭha*. This mantra, preceded by *Tārā* (Oṃ), is said to consist of eleven syllables. || 84 ||
He states another mantra with the words "by power" (*śaktyā*):
"Rudra" refers to the eleventh [vowel].
*Oṃ hrīṃ gaṃ hrīṃ, bring [him] under control, svāhā!*
Gaṃ is the seed-syllable; svāhā is the power (śakti). || 84 ||
The seers (ṛṣis) and other [components] have been mentioned previously; the limbs (aṅgas) are formed by the words of the mantra.
First with one, then with three, two, three, and two; finally, with the whole [mantra], the weapon (astra) is declared. This is considered the arrangement of the limbs. || 85 ||
"Previously" means immediately preceding.
"I [speak] these very words with one [word]" || 85 ||

With his hands he holds a sugarcane staff, the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), a noose, and a goad; embraced by this woman who touches the supreme limb of her own dark-limbed consort with a hand that reaches to the tip of his banner while holding a lotus;
[he is] the three-eyed one, crowned with the crescent moon, [and] glowing like the *japā* flower.
I constantly remember the red-faced Lord, who is ever-intoxicated by enjoyments. || 86 ||

One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times, and for the sake of achieving mastery over the mantra, one should perform a fire sacrifice with ten parts of it using pieces of sugarcane or cakes mixed with clarified butter. || 87 ||
With a joyful mind, one should gratify one’s own guru with wealth, grain, and other offerings;
the worship is prescribed as before, and thereafter one should accomplish the desired goals. || 88 ||
Having offered oblations of cakes smeared with the three sweets, one shall bring kings under one's control on earth;
by offering coconuts on the fourth lunar day, one attains great prosperity. || 89 ||
One may bring women under one's influence with salt mixed with honey.
As for the visualization (dhyāna), it extends from the lower left up to the upper left;
the visualization of the Goddess is to be understood as that which was described in the visualization of Virigaṇapati.
"As before" means as in the case of Viriñcapati; such is the meaning. || 86–90 ||
Saṃvartaka has two eyes and is seated on a fire-altar at his side.
The heart-mantra for the purpose of propitiation consists of ten syllables beginning with its own seed-syllable;
Gaṇaka is its sage, and Virāṭ is declared to be its metre. || 91 ||
The deity of this [mantra] is declared to be Vighna, who inspires swift faith.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual application (ṣaḍaṅga) using the seed-syllable joined with the long vowel. || 92 ||
