He states the mantra for swift faith as "saṃvarttaka. *Saṃvarta* is *kṣa*; *netra* is the vowel *i*. It is joined with that. *Pārśva* is the letter *pa*; it has fire (*repha*) as its seat.
"Preceded by its own seed-syllable" means preceded by *gaṃ*; "to *gaṃ*, the one who quickly bestows grace, obeisance.
Some say it is "preceded by the Śrī-bīja.
*Gaṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *āya* is the power (*śakti*).
"By means of the seed joined with the long [vowel]" refers to the initial seed-syllable. (90–92)
Holding a noose, a goad, a wish-fulfilling creeper, and a tusk,
with a *bījapūra* fruit placed upon his own trunk;
he is red, three-eyed, and has the young moon as his crest.
May Hastimukha, radiant with laughter, protect you. || 93 ||
Regarding "pāśa" (noose):

*viṣāṇa* means tusk. For the meditation on the weapons: in the first case, they are in the two upper right hands; in the last case, they are in the two lower right hands, starting from the upper left hand down to the lower left hand.
Thus say some. || 93 ||

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; at the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform ten thousand oblations with sesame seeds, using substances consisting of the three types of honey or the eight aforementioned items.
"With the three sweets combined with milk, honey, and ghee" is an adjective qualifying the sesame seeds.
As it has been stated by the Teachers: "Then one should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds sprinkled with the three sweets."
Regarding the reading *madhuratritayaiḥ*, it should be understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those [verses] which possess a triad of sweet [qualities]. || 94 ||
On the seat denoted by the single syllable, one should worship Gajānana with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as incense and lamps, according to the method that will be described. || 95 ||
Having first worshipped the limbs, one should then sacrifice to the eight Vighnas:
Vighna, Vināyaka, Vīra, Śūra, and the one known as Varada. || 96 ||

One should then worship the elephant-faced one, the single-tusked one, and the long-bellied one immediately thereafter; subsequently, one should worship them on the tips of the petals, followed by Brāhmī and the others.
The worship of the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons, as well as the propitiation of obstacles (vighnapūjā), has been described.
By offering oblations of clarified butter and cooked food daily, one shall become possessed of abundant food within a year. || 98 ||
A person attains great prosperity by means of milk-rice (pāyasa);
the wise man brings all living beings under his control through an oblation of clarified butter (ājya). || 99 ||
The practitioner of mantra should offer as an oblation every day a ripe coconut fruit together with a clod of earth and a piece of leather; from the mandala, he shall obtain success. || 100 ||
By the word *loṣṭa*, the inner portion of the coconut is meant; the upper part of that, characterized by its husk, is denoted by the word *carman* (skin).
This is an exception to the rule that "the coconut [is divided] into eight parts.
"By this rite" refers to the oblation of the eight substances (*aṣṭadravyahoma*). || 100 ||
One should perform oblations with eight substances combined with the three sweets;
by this procedure, one shall bring all kings and their wives under control.

On the first day of the lunar fortnight and subsequent days, one should offer libations forty-four times with auspicious water upon the head of Vighnarāja for the sake of attaining prosperity. || 102 ||
"With auspicious waters" means with waters in the form of nectar. || 101-102 ||
Holding a noose, a goad, a wish-fulfilling creeper,
and his own tusk in his hands, he is as beautiful as Mount Meru; with a flight of stairs, [he reaches] the orb of the Lord of Day—
Having visualized [the deity] seated upon a lotus at the end of the inheritance (dāyānta), || 103 ||

The practitioner of mantra who knows the ritual procedure should perform, by means of this mantra, the applications previously mentioned for that mantra, or those which have been prescribed for it in this [present] context. (104)
Regarding the libation (tarpaṇa), he describes a specific visualization with the words "pāśa" and so forth:
by means of a silver flight of stairs,
[one descends] from the orb of the Lord of Day, that is, from the solar disc.

"Coming into the water"—this is the ellipsis. Having visualized Gaṇapati as being situated upon a lotus—that is, as standing upon a lotus imagined to be in the water—having placed a lotus (*puṣkara*) upon the head of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and having thus performed meditation; such is the meaning.
The connection [of the ritual] is that one should perform the libation with auspicious waters upon the head of Vighnarāja for the sake of attaining prosperity (*śrī*).
As it has been said: "Having descended from the solar orb like a cloud by means of silver stairs, [the deity] enters the water upon lotus-thrones, holding a creeper, a tooth, a noose, and a goad."

Having placed his nose upon the neck of the person to be accomplished, one should remember Gaṇapati as he sprinkles [the victim] daily with nectar flowing from the openings of that [nostril], and satisfy him with ambrosias. Thus it is said.
Now, regarding the two yantras: one should write the seed-syllable in the center of a hexagon inscribed with the name [of the deity], and then encircle it with the limb-mantras (aṅgamantras).

Then, on an eight-petaled lotus, one should write the vowels in the filaments (kesara) in pairs; and in the petals, one should write the consonants beginning with 'kṣa' and ending with 'ya', omitting the intervening letters.

Having first written the three syllables of the Gāyatrī, surrounded them three times on the outside with the consonants beginning with *ka*, and having enclosed the exterior with two concentric squares (*bhūpura*), one should write the seed-syllable of the Earth (*laṃ*); this yantra is considered to bestow the wealth of spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). Thus it is said.

Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the Great King of Yantras: one should draw a ten-spoked lotus on five petals using dūrvā sprouts sprinkled with the bile of an animal; the seed-syllable of Gaṇeśa, however, should be placed within the heart of the Tāra-mantra.

Then, in the center of that [diagram], one should write the ten mantras and the principal mantra under the name "Rakṣā. Then, having written the syllables of the noose (*pāśa*) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*) on the outside, and having likewise written two images of Indra (*śakra*) on the exterior, one should worship that Gaṇeśa therein with perfumes, flowers, and various other offerings.
"One should wear [this] on the arm or around the neck; it provides protection from all [evils]. Therefore, there is nothing else here that brings such auspiciousness.
And it is said: "Mahāgaṇapati is foremost in quickly bestowing grace;
he is Vighna, Vināyaka, Vīra, Śūra, and Varada as well."
Ibhavaktra, Ekadanta, and likewise Hastimukha are remembered [as the names];
these mantras should end in the dative case and end with "namaḥ," and by means of them, libations (tarpaṇa) and fire-offerings (homa) are performed.
"The mantra-practitioner shall accomplish his desired aim. Thus, from that ritual manual, the root mantra is [placed] in pairs upon the five petals. (103–104)
The end of the five [vowels] joined with the bindu and adorned with the left ear (the letter *u*), beginning with Tārā and ending with the heart—this is proclaimed as the mantra of Heramba. || 105 ||

Consisting of the four castes, he bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life upon men; one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the seed-syllable endowed with the six long vowels. || 106 ||
Regarding Herambamanu, it is said "Pañcāntaka":
Pañcāntaka is *ga*; the left ear is the vowel *ū*. Thus: *oṃ gūṃ namaḥ*.
The seer is Gaṇaka, the metre is Gāyatrī, the deity is Heramba-Gaṇapati;
the seed-syllable is the letter *ga*, and the power is the nasal dot (*bindu*).
[The phrase] "by means of the seed-syllable" [is explained as follows].
By means of what is stated in this mantra. || 105-106 ||
[I bow] to Heramba, who has the luster of pearls, gold, blue *kunda* flowers, and saffron;
who is endowed with three eyes and elephant faces; whose vehicle is Hari (the horse); who bears the moon; who possesses the radiance of the sun;
who is proud, bestows gifts, fearlessness, and joy; and who holds an axe, a head, and the *akṣa*-beads [as his attributes].
I worship Him who holds a garland, a mallet, a goad, and a trident in His hands. || 107 ||
"Muktā" refers to saffron (ghusṛṇa) or safflower (kuṅkuma). These are the colors beginning with "muktā" and ending with "ūrdhva."
It is characterized by elephant faces with the heads of serpents;
"hari" means lion;
"ṭaṅka" means an axe.
"Triśikha" refers to a trident (*triśūla*).
In some places, the reading is "aśoka and triśikha.
In that case, by the phrase "separated from *hretrāṣṭa*," there is a lightness of the syllable *ca*.
By means of an extremely forceful articulation, there is no violation of the meter (*chandobhaṅga*).

The meditation on the weapons consists of the gestures of boon (*vara*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*) in the lower right and left hands, and the other [weapons] in the two hands positioned above them; such is the end [of the description].
In some places, where "dṛptam" (proud/arrogant) occurs, the reading is "kumbham" (the frontal globe).
In that case, "kumbha" refers to the tip of the trunk.
However, when the reading is "dṛptam," it should be understood as the trunk-staff being raised over the sweetmeat.
Some read "pannagam" (a serpent) instead of "mudgaram" (a mallet) here;
as it has been said:
"I worship [the Lord] who holds in his two arms a rosary and a bracelet, and in his other two hands a goad and a *modaka* (sweetmeat)..."

I pray to the Great Gaṇapati named Heramba, who bestows all desired objects upon himself; he who holds a ṭaṅka-axe and a raised skull, whose trunk is adorned with excellent serpent-fangs and golden jars, who stands upon a lion, possesses five faces and three eyes, is crimson in hue, and is clothed in divine garments and grand ornaments. (107)
One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with sesame seeds ten times that number;
then, one should worship the god Heramba upon a pedestal (pīṭha) that has been consecrated with intense offerings.
By the phrase "worshipped with intense [devotion] and so forth," he indicates that the pīṭha-mantra is distinct [from the others]. || 108 ||

The Praṇava, the pair of armor-mantras (kavaca), then "to the Great Lion" (mahāsiṃhāya) followed by "Gāṃ"; then the word "Heramba," and finally "for the seat" (āsanāya) joined with the heart-mantra (hṛt). || 109 ||
He states that very thing: "The Praṇava," "the pair of Kavacas" (huṃ huṃ), and "gām" as the essential form. || 109 ||
This shall be the mantra for the seat; with this, one should offer the seat. One should fashion its form by means of the seed-syllable of Vighna, preceded by *Tāra* (Om).
Having invoked [the deity] therein, one should worship it together with the limbs (*aṅga*) and the surrounding retinue (*āvaraṇa*). || 110 ||
Externally, the Lords of the World (Lokeśvaras) are to be worshipped, and after that, the vajras and so forth.
Thus, one should worship daily and accomplish one's own desired aims. || 111 ||
"Tārādi" means with the root mantra devoid of "namas. || 110-111 ||
One should offer oblations of *modaka* sweets on the sixth and eighth lunar days, and likewise with *kṛsara* (rice and sesame) on the fourteenth day;
one should offer oblations of cakes on the fourteenth day for the attainment of one's desires. || 112 ||
With these substances, the mantra-practitioner should perform oblations even on festival days;
with diligent effort, the adept shall accomplish all his desires. || 113 ||
"In the sixth" applies to both sides [of the fortnight]. The same applies further on.
"Kṛśara" refers to a mixture of sesame seeds and rice.
With these—sour gruel, rice-and-pulse porridge, and cakes—on a festival day, on the full moon, or on the new moon. || 112-113 ||

One should first draw a lotus with eight petals; in its center, within one's own seed-syllable, one should place the name of the person to be accomplished, while it is beautified by filaments shining with the limb-mantras (aṅgamantras).
Then, having divided the remaining beads of the rosary mantra among the petals, one should place them at the center of each petal according to the number of sages (seven).
On the final petal, it is surrounded by the six vowels and by the power (śakti) in the form of the letter Śa. || 114 ||
He describes the *dhāraṇā* yantra with the words "the lotus" (*ambhojam*).
"In the center" means within the pericarp of the eight-petaled [lotus]. "Within its own seed-syllable" means in the middle of this mantra's seed-syllable.
It should be understood that [the mantra] is called "sādhya" (that which is to be accomplished) when accompanied by the ritual action of the practitioner. "Externally" means outside of the pericarp.
"Aṅgamantra" refers to the limb-mantras.
The eye-mantra is at the beginning, as in the ritual of worship;
the sage is sevenfold;
and the garland-mantra is that which will be described hereafter.
In the final [syllable], there is the eighth;
with *śakti* and with *śakāra*, there is a repetition of two. (114)

Having written [the mantra] on birch bark with yellow pigment (rocanā), honey, and saffron, and having wrapped it with a white thread and then sequentially with the three metals, one should wear this yantra on the arm; thus one shall attain all desires. || 115 ||
Intoxication refers to elephant-ichor;
by means of the three linctuses mentioned in the sixth chapter.
"Successively" means by means of copper, silver, and gold. || 115 ||
At the end of *dhruva*, there should be the goad (*aṅkuśa*) of Śakti; then the heart-mantra consisting of one's own seed-syllable.
At the end of "to the Lord of All Obstacles" (*sarvavighnādhipāya*), followed by the dative suffix *-ṅe*, it bestows the accomplishment of all aims. || 116 ||
Then one should proclaim the verse for the pacification of all suffering:
"Come, come, O Blessed One! Paralyze all calamities! || 117 ||
Bhuvaneśī, her own seed-syllable (svabīja), Gāṃ, Nati, and Pāvakavallabhā;
again, Aṅkuśa and Māyā—this is the fifty-five-syllable mantra. || 118 ||
The wise practitioner should accomplish the ritual applications by means of this garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*).
Regarding the garland-mantra, he says "the power" (*śakti*), etc.; "one's own seed-syllable" (*svabīja*) refers to the seed-syllable residing within the mantra.
The seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśī is her own seed-syllable; the seed-syllables of Bhuvaneśī and of oneself are *hrīṃ* and *gūṃ*.
*Gāṃ* is its essential form (*svarūpa*). Because it is stated to consist of fifty-five syllables, there is no sandhi in the phrase "śamanāya ehyehi."

Oṃ hrīḥ kroṃ gūṃ namaḥ! Homage to the Lord of all obstacles, the bestower of the accomplishment of all aims, the pacifier of all suffering! Come, come, O Blessed One! Paralyze, paralyze all calamities! Hrīḥ gūṃ gāṃ naṃ svāhā kroṃ hrīḥ!
By this [mantra], one should accomplish the ritual applications; by this, its status as an independent mantra is also stated.
The procedure for that is as follows: its meter is *amita*; everything else is to be understood as being like [the ritual for] Heramba Gaṇapati. (116–119)
The letter *tā* is Tāra; *khaḍgīśvara* is *kūrmā*; *niḥsvara* is said to be the end of *ṇ*. || 119 ||
The mantra consisting of seven syllables beginning with "bhuve" is the Subrahmaṇyā-mantra;
the ritual assignment of the limbs (aṅgakriyā) is considered to be performed with the fire-seed syllable (raṃ) conjoined with the six long vowels. || 120 ||
He states the Subrahmaṇya mantra as "Tāram" and so forth. Khaḍgīśa is *vaḥ*, Kūrma is *ca*, and *kāra* is *ra*.
*Nisvara* means devoid of vowel (*svarahīna*), that is to say, a consonant (*vyañjana*).
A *ta* following an *ṇa* becomes *da*.
The natural form of the root *bhū* is *bhuve*.
It should be understood that in this case of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), the letter *da* arises from the letter *ta*.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "The mantra 'vacadbhuve' has Subrahmaṇyā as its presiding deity.
However, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*, it is said: "The syllable Om, followed by 'vacat', then 'nābhijale', and joined with 'śivayonaye namaḥ' [is the mantra]."
Thus:
Agni and Gāyatrī are the Ṛṣi and the Chandas;
the Praṇava is the Bīja, and the letter *va* is the Śakti.
Some say it is encapsulated by the *praṇava* (Oṃ);
others, however, say it begins with *māyā*. As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "It is praised as having the *praṇava* at the beginning and end; others have declared it to be preceded by *śakti*."
Thus;
"by the fire-seed" means by the letter *ra*. (119–120)
With a splendor as red as vermilion, a moon-like face, and a body adorned with divine ornaments such as armlets and necklaces, bestowing the bliss of heaven;
holding a lotus, the gesture of fearlessness, a spear, and a cock, and clad in red unguents and garments— (The Lord) [is meditated upon].
We worship Subrahmaṇya, who is ever-ready to destroy the fear of those who bow down to him. || 121 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, and then offer oblations with clarified butter and sacrificial food;
at the conclusion, one should perform the fire-offering ten times that amount and also feed the Brahmins. || 122 ||

The *dhyāna* [mantra], however, is for the two upper [deities] starting with Dakṣa, and for the two lower ones in the first [case]; in the last [case], it is "Subrahmaṇya. This is a name of Kārttikeya.
As it is stated in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*:
The gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) should be in his left hand and a lotus in his right hand;
one should place a cock in the left hand and a spear (śakti) on the right side.
"He is declared to have four arms and one face; he is born from fire. (121–122)

On the seat imagined as Dharma and the other [elements], to the west of the fire-maṇḍala, one should worship the God according to the prescribed rite with the offerings as they have been described. || 123 ||
Regarding the phrase "at the western side of the fire-mandala":
by this, the worship extends only as far as the fire-mandala mentioned in the fourth chapter;
there is no worship of the *pīṭha* or the *pīṭha-śakti*.
Otherwise, he would not have said "behind the circle of fire," since this has already been stated in the fourth chapter itself. || 123 ||
The worship of the limbs (aṅgapūjā) should take place upon the filaments; these [deities] situated within the petals are named Jayanta, Agniveśya, and Kṛttikāputra. || 124 ||

Immediately thereafter, one should worship the Lord of Beings (Bhūtapati), known as Guha, the commander-in-chief, who holds a golden trident, has large eyes, and carries a spear and a vajra-trident in his hands. ||125||
At the tips of the petals in the cardinal directions, starting from the east, [one should place] Deva-senāpati;
then Vidyā, Medhā, and Vajra; and in the corners, Śakti and Kukkuṭī.
One should worship Mayūradvīpa, and furthermore, the Lords of the World (Lokeśvaras) on the exterior;
at the end of those, the weapons should be worshipped as impelled by the rite of Subrahmaṇyā.
On the sixth day, one should satisfy the Lord with sweet foods, both solid and soft, and worship the celibate youths (kumāras) with the thought that they are deities. || 128 ||
May Subrahmaṇya, who is praised by the gods, swiftly bestow upon the practitioner continuity, victory, valor, protection, longevity, prosperity, and fame. 129.
It was stated, "by the ritual rule"; he now states that rule [beginning with] "in the filaments.
The offering of a portion of the food-oblation (naivedya) for him is given to Dhūrtasena. (124–129)

In the performance of recitation, libation, worship, and other rites, one should propitiate Vighneśa, the bestower of all accomplishments, with this hymn of praise for the attainment of all prosperity. || 130 ||
The virtuous declare the syllable *Oṃ* to be the first;
they also praise him whom the Vedas extol as Gajānana, whose feet are bowed to by the hosts of gods.
I worship Him who has made the crescent moon His crest-ornament. || 131 ||

He begins the praise of Gaṇeśa with the words "Oṃkāram. The particle *api* is used here in a different sense. The virtuous ones praise Him as the primordial *oṃkāra* of the Vedas (*śrutīnām*), and even the first of all speech (*vācaḥ*).
That is to say, its nature is the Śabdabrahman (the Word-Brahman). || 130-131 ||
For those intent on worshipping his lotus feet,
it is capable of extinguishing the forest fire of saṃsāra by means of the continuous streams of water flowing from his gifts.
I bow to that Lord of Obstacles, who has the luster of a rain cloud. || 132 ||
Anointing his limbs with fresh saffron,
he was warding off a swarm of intoxicated bees clinging to him with the mud of rut by the rhythmic flapping of his own ears.
Who could forget the son of the enemy of the bodiless one? || 133 ||
Taking up with his lotus-like hand the water of the Gaṅgā residing in the matted locks of Śambhu,
he worships Śiva from nearby with playful gestures.
Those endowed with devotion worship the elephant-faced one. || 134 ||
With his lotus-like trunk-tip (*karāmbujena śuṇḍāgreṇa*).
*Ārāt* means "nearby.
Regarding the phrase "they worship with devotion" (*bhaktiyutā bhajanti*), there is also a reading in some places: "I worship him as my refuge" (*taṃ śaraṇaṃ bhajāmi*). || 132–134 ||
Furthermore, while in the state of childhood, he was washing the breasts of the Mountain King’s daughter with the spray from his own hands for his own sake.
Out of innocence, I worship that elephant-faced one. || 135 ||
"Out of innocence," etc.;
the meaning is that the breasts of the Goddess are always free from being left-over (unchiṣṭa). || 135 ||
Those sprays released from the opening of the trunk by you, having raised your elephantine hand,
wander through the courtyard of the sky as stars.
In its nature as Time, it possesses a luster equal to that of a pearl.
O Elephant-faced One, those sprays released from the cavity of your trunk as you lift it up by you, whose self is Time—those [sprays] are the stars wandering about;
this is a suggested *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), for they are not merely water droplets. (For it is stated in the *Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana*: "The tip of an elephant's trunk is called *puṣkara*.")
"Tārā" means "a poetic fancy (utprekṣā)"; this is the meaning. || 136 ||
While the elephant-faced one was sporting in the ocean as the flood of water transgressed the shore,
the gods, reflecting upon the end of the aeon, [were filled with fear].
They praise the Lord of Kailāsa with hymns of laudation.
"They praise" refers to the compositions made by others at the end of an eon; the "inconsistency of praise" is thus a poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
In reality, however, that praise is due to the fact that [the Lord] cannot be set aside by anyone else. || 137 ||
O you who sport with hosts of divine youths, upon whose serpent-face an upper garment of nāgas is draped,
may you for a moment abandon the course of time.
The two of them arrived like the moon and the sun appearing together with a ball.
The connection is that you, while intent on play, have a garment made by a *nāga*—that is, a serpent—as an upper cloth;
having abandoned the course of time, meaning the subjection to time. || 138 ||
Teaching the meaning of all the scriptures incessantly with his five faces that were smiling,
he is the sole friend of the gods, the sages, and his devoted followers.
I take refuge in Heramba, who is as reddish-brown as the sun. || 139 ||
He who, out of compassion, makes the earth fulfilled by his exceedingly small lotus-feet,
and who is the causeless cause of the words of the authoritative scriptures.
My mind does not abandon that elephant-faced one. || 140 ||
"By virtue of his two feet, there is shortness in comparison to his face, the meters, and so forth;
by this it is indicated that his two feet alone are to be meditated upon as short.
[He is] the cause and the instigator of the Vedas, which are the words of the authoritative ones. (139–140)
By him who formerly drank the Purāṇa from the tip of the horn of the son of Satyavatī— having drawn it out—
and by him who [worships] that son of the Moon-crested Lord through austerities...
I worship that which is attained as a mass of bliss. || 141 ||
The abode of praises and the non-abode of the Vedas,
the playful incarnation of the Supreme Self’s form—
whether in the form of a serpent or in the form of a man.
Worship that indivisible and primordial Lord of Obstacles. || 142 ||
The Purāṇa known as the Bhārata;
the "pada" is the locus,
while the "apada" is that which is beyond the range of perception.
In some places there is a transposition of the words "stuti" and "śruti.
Regarding the phrase "paramātmamūrteḥ," some read it as "paramaṣṭa. (141–142)
Holding a noose and a goad, and his beloved with his broken tusk in his hands,
he [is adorned] by streams of broad spray resembling pearls released from the openings of his trunk.
I worship the body of Śiva and Śivā as they sprinkle [each other]. || 143 ||
Of the two parents, Śiva and Śivā. || 143 ||
The many as one, the elephant with a single tusk, whose form is consciousness, the primordial seed of the universe—
him whom the knowers of Brahman call Brahman.
I take refuge in that son of Śambhu. || 144 ||
His eyes were restless with the sight of the lotus-face of his beloved resting on his own lap,
her own lotus-face smiling through the power of intoxication.
I worship Him, the obstructer, who deludes the entire universe. || 145 ||
Many [appearances] through desire;
one [is real] in truth. 144–145.
For those who, having previously propitiated you, Gajānana, study all the scriptures,
there is nothing further to be learned from them other than from you.
If that exists, then everything is like an unreality. || 146 ||

For those men who study them, there is nothing else to be understood or known apart from You; the word "and" (ca) implies that even for those scriptures, there is nothing else to be propounded apart from You. This is because the Self is propounded in all scriptures; if these scriptures were to propound anything other than You, then—
Everything is a mere construction of the unreal;
the meaning is that those [scriptures] do not even qualify as scriptures, just like the Buddhist scriptures and so forth. || 146 ||
To Hiraṇyagarbha, the Lord of the universe, the ancient seer situated within the solar orb— him,
the elephant-faced one, into whom the virtuous enter.
I take refuge in Him through the yogas appropriate for that time. || 147 ||
"By means of the conjunctions of that time" means that Gaṇeśa alone manifests through his divine play as the incarnations of Hiraṇyagarbha and others;
the sense is that this is because he is the very nature of the Supreme Self. || 147 ||
I worship that Person sung of in the Vedanta,
the Self residing in the heart, a mass of bliss;
by whose splendor people [attain their goal], O Elephant-faced One!
The darkness of obstacles goes to its dissolution. || 148 ||
He states that very same form as "sung by the Vedāntins" (vedāntagītam). || 148 ||
Having observed the crescent moon within the mass of Śambhu’s matted locks with her own trunk,
she reflected out of innocence that her own tusk had been broken.
Desiring to draw [her] forth, may he spread his glory. || 149 ||
"Out of innocence" means by way of sport, because there is never any lapse in his knowledge. || 149 ||
For the purpose of striking down the bolts of obstacles,
they propitiate him whose face is like an intoxicated elephant with coconuts, plantains, and other fruits.
Men attained their desired goal; I worship Him. || 150 ||

Those who, according to the prescribed rite, praise with this hymn the primordial one whose face is like that of the king of elephants— who is to be propitiated through numerous sacrifices and manifold austerities— [attain their goal].
They become repositories of all prosperity. || 151 ||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Śāradātilaka* composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇa, the foremost of teachers. 13.
In the *Bṛhat-tantra*, devotion (*bhakti*) and affection for devotees (*vātsalya*) are expressed by the words beginning with "obstacle" (*vighna*).
The term "men" (*nara*) is used in the plural. (150–151)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition. 13.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Next, the mantra of the Moon is declared, which bestows all prosperity.
The Lord Khaḍgīśa is situated there; [the syllable] Bhr̥gu (Bha) is the seed-syllable of Mercury (Bu), conjoined with the vowel of Manu (U). || 1 ||
This six-syllabled mantra, ending with "to Soma, the heart," is proclaimed;
Bhṛgu is said to be its seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti its meter (chandas), and Soma its deity (devatā). || 2 ||
The mental activity of the limbs is considered to be performed by means of one's own seed-syllable, which possesses long vowels. || 3 ||

Now, desiring to state the solar mantras which follow in sequence, and because that [sun] consists of the three-fold brilliance, he begins to state those mantras while uttering the mantras of the Moon and Fire at the beginning and end; thus,
"Now" (*atha*) expresses the application (*viniyoga*) as "the bestower of all prosperity."

He extracts the mantra: "Khaḍgīśa. Khaḍgīśa is *va*; the *bhṛgu* situated therein is *sa*, which is the fourteenth vowel (*manusvara*), and there is also the nasal dot (*bindu*). Joined with that, it becomes *svauṃ*.
However, in the *Prayogasāra*, the mantra is proclaimed as: "Obeisance to Soma, beginning with *sa*, *va*, *au*, and the *bindu*. (*savau-bindv-ādi-somāya namaḥ*)
Thus [it is said].
In some places, the reading is "the vowel with a bindu" (*bindumānaḥ svaraḥ*).
And in the *Nārāyaṇīya*, the teachers have extracted it as "svauṃ".
Others, however, say that this is the seed-syllable of Mṛtyuñjaya,
and that it was not extracted by the author at the beginning of this work;
the seed-syllable is *svauṃ*.
The power is *āya*.
The power *me* was extracted by the teacher Padmapāda.
But elsewhere—
The seer is Atri, the meter is Virāj, and the first seed-syllable is declared [to be the mantra];
"Namaḥ" is the power (śakti).
Thus it is said.
Some say it should be "encased" (saṃpuṭa) by the Praṇava and the Prāsāda;
others say that those desiring prosperity (śrī) should encase it with the Śrī-mantra.
[The phrase] "with its own seed-syllable" [is used].
Either with the seed-syllable of the mantra and so forth, or with the seed-syllable "Sva. || 1-3 ||
With a face like the orb of the full moon, eternally pure as camphor and crystal,
and with a body adorned by a string of pearls that utterly eradicates darkness; he who, graced by dark-blue locks of hair, holds a night-lotus and a boon-granting gesture in his two hands.
I worship Soma, the ocean of nectar, who possesses the quality of being the refuge for the deer situated upon his own lap.
He speaks of meditation (*dhyāna*) with the words "camphor" (*karpūra*), etc.
In the right and left [hands], there are the *kumuda* and *vara* [lotuses].
In some places, the reading is "wealth" (*dhana*).

Wealth is a vessel for treasure. The meaning is that the mark (aṅka) itself should also be meditated upon, wherein the quality of the substrate— namely, its blueness— has arisen from the deer situated upon it.
As it has been said: "Let the moon be one whose spots are illuminated by your desired [beauty].

Alternatively, the quality of being a refuge (āśrayaguṇa)—that is, the quality of being worthy of service—is proclaimed by the deer situated upon its own lap; for even when the reproach of being "marked" (kalaṅkita) exists, the deer is not abandoned.
The ocean of nectar, whose very nature is immortality. || 4 ||
The practitioner, having conquered his senses, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
he should offer oblations six thousand times with milk-rice mixed with ghee. || 5 ||
"Six hundred thousand" means six lakhs.

By the phrase "the best of practitioners," the recitation of the mantra of the Vidyā ten times its own length (one-tenth) is indicated; this same recitation is also required during the ritual application (*prayoga*).

Regarding this, the teacher Padmapāda states that the Śrī-yoga pertains to the acquisition of wealth, the Vāgbhava-yoga to poetic composition, and the Praṇava-yoga to happiness and other such matters. || 5 ||
On the worshiped pedestal at the edge of the Soma circle, one should worship the Lord of Rohiṇī;
the limbs [of the deity] should be on the filaments, and his goddesses should occupy the spaces between the petals.
Rohiṇī, Kṛttikā, Revatī, and again Bharaṇī;
then Rātri and Ārdrā—these luminaries possess a radiance equal to a necklace of pearls. || 7 ||
Wearing white garlands and garments, adorned with pearl necklaces, burdened by the weight of their breasts, auspicious, and with palms joined in reverence. || 8 ||
With minds attached to their beloveds, languid with the intoxication of passion,
those lotus-eyed women with faces resembling the orb of the moon are worthy of being honored.
Regarding the phrase "ending with soma":
in the fourth chapter, by the words "in that [place] the sun, moon, and fire," worship ending with the fire-maṇḍala was taught.
Here, however, having worshipped the sun and fire-maṇḍalas, the soma-maṇḍala is to be worshipped at the end.
Someone says that worship should not be performed within the fire-mandala, [stating] "up to the edge of the Soma.
That is not so,
because it is not part of the traditional lineage (asāmpradāyika).
Furthermore, this is because it contradicts many texts such as the *Mantradevaprakāśikā*.
Regarding the arrangement of the *pīṭha*, however, [it says] "up to Soma.
In his commentary on the verses of the *Prapañcasāra*, the teacher Padmapāda states that in the worship of the *pīṭha*, one should perform the worship of the solar and fiery mandalas first, and then—
It has been stated that, having worshipped the moon-maṇḍala, one should invoke the Blessed One there.

Regarding the phrase "when the seat (pīṭha) has been worshipped," the remainder is that this is done with the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra), preceded by the worship of the nine powers of the seat (pīṭhanavaśakti).
And those *pīṭha-mantras* should also be understood as they are taught in other tantras,
as follows: Amṛtā, Tārakā, Jyotsnā, Vimalā, and likewise Vyāpinī.
Citrā, Kṛttikā, Kānti, and Śravaṇā are the nine Śaktis.
"Obeisance to you, the seat of consciousness (saṃvitpīṭha), whose essence is the Kalās at the end of Amṛta.
Thus, other powers of the seats (pīṭhaśaktis) have been mentioned by Padmapādācārya.
Rākā, Kumudvatī, Nandā, Sudhā, Sañjīvanī, Kṣamā, Āpyāyanī,
Candrikā, and Hlādinī are the nine Śaktis.

"The practitioner of mantra should worship these [deities], ending with Nati, in order starting from the east. Here, *kalā* is a name for a *śakti*, as it is stated: "The *kalās* on the petals of Īśa."
*Kaścit* refers to the name of a *śakti*, namely Karālī, as stated in the passage: "And these [powers] are, in order, Karālī and so forth.
*Hārasamaprabhāḥ* means they are white, possessing a luster like that of a pearl necklace. (6–9)
The Sun, Mars, Mercury, Saturn, Jupiter, Rāhu, and Venus, along with Ketu—these planets are to be worshipped at the tips of the petals. || 10 ||
Each is endowed with garments of their respective colors and possesses as seed-syllables the initial letters of their own names;
they are red, reddish-brown, white, blue, yellow, smoky-grey, black, and dark-blue.
Āditya; Maṅgala is Aṅgāraka; Manda is Śanaiścara.
Vākpati is Bṛhaspati.

It should be understood that in those [circles], Āditya and the others are to be worshipped in the four cardinal directions, while Bhauma and the others are to be worshipped in the southeast and the other intermediate corners.
As they say:
On the tips of the petals in the east, south, west, and north, respectively, these— Ravi, Candra, Guru, and Śukra— should be worshipped by the practitioners.
"In the corners starting from the southeast (āgneya) are Bhauma, Mandāha, and Ketu.
Thus, those whose seeds consist of the first letters of their own names, together with the bindu (anusvāra).
By this, the mantras of the planets are indicated.
Among them, he will state the mantra for the Sun as part of the planetary sacrifice (grahayajña);
the mantras for the other seven should be understood as "aṃ aṅgārakāya namaḥ" and so forth.
And hereafter, even in the case of worship, this very same procedure is to be followed. || 10-11 ||
With her hand placed upon the left thigh, she grants fearlessness with her right hand;
the Sun has hands adorned with lotuses, and Saturn has a face terrifying with its fangs.
Rāhu should have his face made crooked, and Ketu should have his hands joined in añjali;
thereafter, the world-protectors (lokapālas) together with their weapons, such as the thunderbolt (vajra), are to be worshipped in due order. || 13 ||
Thus, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra becomes an abode of prosperity;
[he visualizes the deity] situated in the center of the heart-lotus, adorned with a necklace of *tāra* beads. || 14 ||
Recalling the Lord of Stars (the Moon), the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra three thousand times;
even if poor, he shall attain royal sovereignty within one year. || 15 ||
Vāma-vīti [is worshipped] with the Sun as his banner, excluding the meditations of others;
for it is said that the Sun has a lotus in his hand, while Ketu has his hands joined in the *añjali* gesture.
This has been stated in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*:
Āditya is described as having two arms, being youthful and endowed with auspicious marks; in his two hands, beautiful lotuses should be fashioned that reach up to his shoulders.
From the *Ketu-tantra*: "He is black, holding a sword and a lamp, or else with palms joined in *añjali*.
Also, in the *Prayoga-sāra*: "The upper half of his body is tawny, his eyebrows are brown, his eyes are red, and he has joined his palms in *añjali*."
Thus:
"tāra" means a brilliant pearl necklace;
"tārāpati" refers to [the moon] accompanied by the heroine (nāyikā). || 12-15 ||
One should recite [the mantra] the previously mentioned number of times while visualizing the Moon upon one's head;
having conquered diseases, untimely death, and miseries, one shall live for a hundred years. || 16 ||
One who delights in the holy life (brahmacarya), being pure, should recite this four-lakṣa mantra;
even one who has not exerted effort shall immediately obtain treasure buried in the earth. || 17 ||
One who has conquered the senses should recite the mantra, especially on the full moon day;
he shall become an abode of good fortune and a supreme treasury of riches. || 18 ||
By means of this mantra, one may destroy terrible fevers, diseases of the head, malevolent spells, complications, and even the aggregate of all poisons. || 19 ||
On the full moon day, fasting, one should offer the arghya at the rising of the moon;
one should draw three circles on the ground, extending from east to west. || 20 ||
Seated upon the prepared throne within the western part of the mandala, the mantra-practitioner should thereafter place all the materials for worship in their entirety at the center. || 21 ||
"Of the previously mentioned number" means three thousand.

By the word "pure," it is stated that one should bathe at the three periods of the day and subsist on milk. As it says in the *Prayogasāra*: "Having performed the bath at the three periods of the day, one should continuously subsist on milk."
One should recite it four hundred thousand times; thus one certainly attains the ritual procedure. So it is said.
"The three mandalas" refers to [those made] with cow dung and so forth. (16–21)
Having worshipped Soma in another mandala provided with lotuses, the wise practitioner should place a silver cup there in front. || 22 ||
Having filled it with cow’s milk and touched it, the preceptor should then mutter the mantra one hundred and eight times using the Vidyā-mantra. || 23 ||
One should offer the arghya to the Moon for the sake of accomplishing all tasks;
one should perform this according to the prescribed rite every month with diligence. || 24 ||
Within six months, the foremost of practitioners attains perfection;
he gains prosperity, even those sons who have been lost, abundant good fortune, and fame. || 25 ||

One obtains a desired daughter, and the daughter shall also obtain a husband. Regarding "in another [place] facing east": the meaning is that having worshipped Soma—having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the seat (pīṭha) and so forth, having performed the sacrifice to the Self (ātmayāga), and having worshipped [the deity] externally upon a lotus-adorned seat.
And it is said:
"Seated with the [deity] situated in the west, one should arrange the ritual substances;
having performed the ritual integration of the self (*sakalīkaraṇa*) and worshipped [the deity], the Lord of Gods, having sipped water (*ācānta*), [should proceed]."
"One should worship Soma in the eastern mandala provided with a lotus.
By the word "wise" (sudhīḥ), this is what is meant:
while reciting the mantra in reverse, one should perform the filling [of the vessel] and the depositing therein of camphor and other substances, as well as flowers such as the white water-lily.
As they say:
"Having placed a silver cup there,
the wise one should fill it with cow's milk while reciting the mantra in reverse order."
And one should respectfully scatter there camphor, cool saffron, unbroken grains (akṣata), knots of kuśa grass, barley, and these flowers.
One should scatter kumuda, indīvara, svarṇaketakī, fresh mallikā, campaka, and śatapatra flowers as they are available.
"One should invoke the Lord from the lunar orb or from one's own heart;
having thus invoked him, one should worship the Moon with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. Thus it is said.
Since it has been stated that "one should offer the *arghya* while fasting," eating at night after the offering of the *arghya* is not prohibited.
By the phrase "a maiden [should drink]," it is indicated that women also have the right to perform such rites as these. (22–26)
What is the use of saying more here? The Lord of Night (the Moon) would give everything. || 26 ||
"Vidye vidyāmālini," followed by "Candriṇī" at the end;
then again "Candramukhi svāhā"—this is declared to be the Vidyā-mantra. || 27 ||
By the statement "the mantra of knowledge has been declared," this is what is meant:
that this very [mantra] consisting of nine syllables and so forth is capable of bestowing a maiden.
As for those nine syllables:
"Having stated the pair of *rakṣa* and the two elephants (*gajau*), there shall be nine syllables for the *kaṇīni*.
Thus, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*, the mantra of the nine-syllable and other vidyās has been extracted.
Having written the mantra, interspersed with its reverse order, upon a leaf and seated upon that,
he who recites it twelve thousand times in a single day;
"Having propitiated Jyeṣṭhā under the constellation Śukra, a maiden is quickly given to him.
Now, the yantra mentioned in another tantra is described:
Having drawn the moon together with its digits within the interior of the crescent moon,
one should write the name surrounded by a six-petaled lotus, adorned with dots made by the tip of a fingernail.

Having written the word "somāya" joined with the word "namaḥ," and having worshipped according to the prescribed rite the [syllables] from 'ka' to 'kṣa' located outside of that, [one should apply it] to the waist, the throat, and the head.
Chanted and bound, this [mantra] instantly destroys poison and bestows nourishment upon it.
Thus [ends the section]. (26–27)
Tāra (Oṃ), Ghṛṇi, Bhṛgu, followed by the left ear (U) as an ornament;
Vahnyāsana (Ra), Maruccheṣa (Ya), with Netra (I), and Atri as the final one. || 28 ||
The eight-syllabled mantra of the Sun is declared to be the bestower of desired objects;
Devanāga is said to be the sage (ṛṣi), and the Gāyatrī is proclaimed as the meter (chandas). || 29 ||
Āditya is declared to be the deity who bestows both seen and unseen fruits;
Satya is said to be the heart, and Brahmā is proclaimed as the Dviṭha. || 30 ||
The crest-lock (śikhā) is for Viṣṇu, the armor (varman) is proclaimed for Rudra;
the eye (netra) is declared for Agni, and the weapon (astra) is said to be for Śarva. || 31 ||

One should again assign the limb-mantras (aṅgamantras), ending with *tejojvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, as they were previously recited individually, and then assign the five forms (pañcamūrti) in their proper order. || 32 ||
One should place Āditya on the head, Ravi in the mouth, the one named Bhānu in the heart, and Bhāskara in the secret region. || 33 ||
One should place the Sun upon the feet with the five [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta, in their short forms. The images of the primary forms should be adorned with all ornaments. || 34 ||

One should place the eight syllables of the mantra, each preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ), respectively upon the head, face, throat, heart, belly, navel, genitals, and feet. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the body, one should meditate upon that treasury of splendors. || 35 ||
He states the mantra of the Sun: "Tāra" (Om).
"Ghṛṇi" is its essential form.
"Bhṛgu" is *sa*; "vāmakarṇa" is *ū*. Adorned with that, it becomes *sū*.
The letter *u* belongs to Indra (*marut*); it is the seat of the fire-syllable *ra*, thus forming *rya*.
"The remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to Ananta; "Atri" is the letter *da*, joined with the eye, the letter *i*, thus forming *di*.
"The westernmost" (*tyapaścima*) is an epithet of the mantra, meaning the syllable ending in *tya*.
By the word "paścima" (western), it is indicated that [the mantra] may also end with "om.
By the phrase "bestower of desired objects," the ritual application (*viniyoga*) is stated.
Since this mantra is recited directly in the Śruti, there is no eligibility for Śūdras and others in this regard.

This is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya Upaniṣad* of the *Taittirīya Śākhā*: "The word *ghṛṇi* consists of two syllables; *sūrya* consists of three; *āditya* consists of three. This, indeed, is the eight-syllabled foot of the Sāvitra mantra, consecrated with prosperity (*śrī*). He who knows this is consecrated with prosperity.
Some call such a person "prosperous" (*śrīmat*).
Others say that it should be "pallavita" (sprouted) by the mantra "śrīkāmahṛllekhāpuṭitaṃ mahyaṃ lakṣmīṃ prayaccha" (encased by Śrī, Kāma, and Hṛllekhā, grant me Lakṣmī).
The seed-syllable is *raṃ* and the power is *yaṃ*. Some say it should begin with the power-seed (*śaktibīja*) and possess the syllable *śrī*.
In that system, the *praṇava* is the seed (*bīja*) and *māyā* is the power (*śakti*).
As it has been said:
"In the Śrībījānta tradition, the root mantra is indeed that of the Yajurveda (or the human lineage)."
This [mantra], encapsulated by Śrī, Kāma, and Hṛllekhā at its end, [says]: "Grant me!"
Thus has the mantra of Lakṣmī been explained according to the view of Śaṅkarācārya; it begins with *hṛllekhā* and ends with *śrī*, as maintained by the school of Viśvarūpa. Thus: *dviṭhaḥ svāhā*.
"Recited" means spoken.
The limb-mantras beginning with "For truth" (*satyāya*) and so forth should be understood as ending individually with each of these [terms].
The practical application therein is as follows:
*Satyāya tejo jvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. "Homage to the heart," and so forth.
Others, however, say that the dative case in *satyāya* and the following terms is not intended to be significant.
The application is as follows: *tena satyatejo jvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and so forth.
This alone is the traditional method, because it has been written in that manner by the author of the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā* and others.

For this very reason, the commentators on the *Prapañcasāra* have explained that the hearing of the vowel ‘a’ in the word “brahma” is for the purpose of precluding the dative case. Furthermore, by the word “again,” the eight-limbed [nyāsa] is also indicated.

Having placed the six syllables of the Sūtra-mantra upon the six locations of the limbs as if they were the six limbs, one should place two syllables ending in “namaḥ” on the belly and the back; this constitutes the eight-limbed [nyāsa].
Regarding the phrase "sadyādi" (beginning with Sadyojāta):

the connection is that one should install the five forms (*pañcamūrti*) in their respective order together with the five short vowels—*o*, *e*, *u*, *i*, and *a*—which are technical terms (*pāribhāṣika*) for the five forms, being the opposites of the neuter vowels beginning with *o*.
The practical application (*prayoga*) is as follows: *oṃ ādityāya namaḥ*, *eṃ ravaye namaḥ*, *uṃ bhānave namaḥ*, *iṃ bhāskarāya namaḥ*, *aṃ bhānave sūryāya namaḥ*.
By the phrase "in due order," it is stated that one should also place [the mantras] on the upper face and so forth.
Regarding the word "each":
by this, the practical application is *oṃ oṃ namo mūrdhni* (Oṃ Oṃ, salutation to the head).
By the phrase "thus deposited," the deposition of the nine planets (navagraha-nyāsa) is also indicated;
that has been described by me previously [in verses 28–35].
I praise the Lord of Day, who holds a pair of red lotuses and the gesture of granting fearlessness in his hands,
who is richly adorned with armlets, necklaces, and bracelets,
and who wears a crown of rubies.
Possessing the luster of the Bandhūka flower and adorned with three shining eyes.
Generosity is supreme.
One should meditate on the weapons upon red lotuses at the left and right shoulders; the others are below those.
Here, immediately after the meditation, the mudrās of the lotus and the orb (bimba) should be displayed.
For it is said: "The *mudrā* in the form of a lotus is declared to be this *saura-mudrā*.
And in the *Prayogasāra*: "One should display before oneself the *abja-bimba-mudrā* as previously described."
Thus it is said.
In that regard, the definition of the *alam* mudrā is as follows: having brought the two hands together facing each other with the fingers raised and joined.
One should join the thumbs at their tips; this is the *abja-mudrā* (lotus gesture). Thus it is said.

Regarding the characteristics of the *bimba-mudrā* in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Having formed the two hands in the shape of a lotus, with the two middle fingers unjoined, one should hold the [other] fingers therein; this is called the *bimba-mudrā*. Thus it is said.
It should be understood that these [mantras] are common to all Saura mantras. || 36 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and offer ten thousand oblations of fuel-sticks from milky trees, smeared with milk, while maintaining control over the senses. || 37 ||
"Vasulakṣa" means eight lakṣas.
Regarding this, there is a specific detail in the *Prayogasāra*: "Clad in red garments and adorned with red perfumes and garlands..."
At night, he should eat rice with molasses combined with ghee and milk.
"Subsisting on alms, or else free from attachment and always contented, one should constantly recite the mantra, being devoted to its propitiation. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, the general procedure for *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary observance) which will be described later should be understood here as well.
A thousand of those is eight thousand. || 37 ||

First, for the preparation of the pedestal, one should worship [the deities] in the cardinal directions and in the center; immediately thereafter, one should worship that which is abundant, stainless, essential, and worthy of propitiation. || 38 ||
Regarding the phrase "first, for the arrangement of the pedestal":

some maintain that one should first worship from Maṇḍūka up to the altar (vedikā), then worship [the principles] from Dharma up to Supreme Bliss (paramasukha), and only afterwards perform the worship of Dharma and the others.
Others, however, maintain that one should worship Prabhūta and the others in the place of Dharma and the rest, and worship Supreme Bliss in the center in the form of a fruit-slab (phalaka).
They say that there is no worship of dharma, adharma, and so forth;
this alone is the traditional teaching.
And it has been stated in the Nārāyaṇīya:
"One should fashion these feet of the pedestal in the center and in the intermediate directions with the *hṛdaya*-mantra.
This [procedure] is common to all Sūrya-mantras.

Since it is stated generally as "in the directions," only the intermediate corners beginning with the southeast (āgneya) are intended here. The reading is: "One should perform the sacrifice in the intermediate points and in the centers. As the Teachers have said:

Then one should worship Prabhūtā, Vimalā, and the one called Sārā—who is to be propitiated—within the three [triangles] beginning with Agni and in the center, prior to the arrangement of the seats for supreme bliss. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Prayogasāra*: "And one should worship these [deities] ending with Īśāna in the intermediate directions. (38)
One should visualize the supreme primordial bliss as the seat, extending to the limit of one's own form;
then again, Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, and Vimalā.
Amoghā, Vidyutā, and Sarvatomukhī are the powers (śaktis) of the seats (pīṭhas).
The wise know that their seed-syllables (bījas), which have the form of the flames of blazing lamps, are to be deposited in due order. || 40 ||
"Up to one's own reflection" means that after having worshipped the lunar and fire mandalas, the solar mandala is to be worshipped;
this refers to the visualization (dhyāna) of these [goddesses] as "blazing."
Thus it is said in the *Prayogasāra*:
"The nine Śaktis should be meditated upon as having the form of the flame of a blazing lamp. (39–40)

One should utter the three short vowels, non-neuter (masculine), conjoined with the bindu and fire (the letter *r*), as a word ending in the dative case, consisting of the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. || 41 ||

"Salutation to the solar seat of yoga (saurāya yogapīṭhāya namaḥ)," this is the mantra of the seat (pīṭhamantra) of the Sun, the Lord of the World, which should be recited immediately thereafter. || 42 ||
Regarding "a-klība":
[the vowels] *ai* and *u* constitute the triad of short vowels. Here, the two words "neuter" (*klība*) and "triad of short vowels" (*hrasva-tritaya*) are connected with the negative particle (*nañ*).
The letter *ra* is the seed-syllable for Agni.
The nine seed-syllables are *rāṃ*, *rīṃ*, *rūṃ*, *raiṃ*, and so forth.
Others, however, say that the three short vowels are *a*, *i*, and *u*, followed by *ai*.
As it is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "Having omitted the first, the penultimate, and the third [vowels], which are neuter,
one should divide [the mantra] ninefold with these vowels in their proper sequence, ending with the letter *ya*."
"The seed-syllables of the Śaktis, joined with the *bindu*, have indeed been extracted.
Elsewhere it is said that there are nine seed-syllables, excluding the letter *a*, the letter *i*, and the *visarga*.
This has been stated in both the *Prayogasāra* and the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"Having abandoned the first, the last, and the third, as well as the neuter [syllables]," thus it is said regarding the "Pīṭha-mantra."
It should be understood that this is common to all Sūrya-mantras. || 41-42 ||
Having performed the visualization of the form with the mantra "Tārādi khaṃ khakholkāya," one should invoke the Witness of all worlds into that [form] and worship it. || 43 ||
"Tārādī" means beginning with Tārā;
"khakholkāya" is the essential form [of the mantra].
This has been stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
The eighth [vowel] joined with the bindu, and likewise the second letter of the ka-series;
that very same one again alone, reversed and joined with the nasalization (anunāsika).
The fourth letter from the beginning, situated above the third,
is indeed pierced by the second vowel.
"By following the reverse order, the fourth [syllable] is obtained;
immediately after that, the sixth-syllabled Mūrti-mantra has been extracted in brief, O dear one.
It should be understood that this is the Mūrti-mantra for other Sūrya-mantras as well.
In that regard, the distinction is that the seed-syllable of space (ākāśa) and so forth are extracted.
Alternatively, it may be explained here as follows:
"Tāra" is [the syllable OM], and by the word "and so forth" (ādi), because it was produced first, it is space; its bindu [is obtained] according to the oral tradition.
Alternatively, by the method of *tantra* (abbreviated expression), two things are conveyed by the syllable *kha*: one as the seed-syllable of space (*ākāśa-bīja*) and the other as its own form.
It is also stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "In the syllable *sūryakānta*, it is said to have a dot (*bindu*) adorning its head."
And in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The letters *kha*, *kāntī*, *daṇḍinī*, *caṇḍaḥ*, *majjā*, and *daśanasaṃyutā*;
*māṃsaṃ*, *dīrghā*, and *javadvāyuḥ*—at the end of these, they know the *kṛt* suffix."
"And one should accomplish these desires through consecration, recitation, and so forth.
Thus it is said;
and the seedless [mantra] is also extracted in that very same place.
In this context, both the letter *la* and the letter *ta* are traditional options, distinguished by whether they represent the pedestal (*pīṭha*) or the altar (*vedikā*).
It should be understood that it is "seedless" (*nirbīja*) when used for the visualization of the form (*mūrti-kalpanā*), and "with seed" (*sabīja*) for recitation (*japa*) and other such rites.
This mantra is also independent (*svatantra*).
Its seer and so forth are as follows:
the seer is said to be Sūkṣmaka; Jagatī is declared to be the meter;
the deity is Sūrya; the seed-syllable and power are "kānta" (the letter *ka*) and "majjāstha" (the letter *sa*); they are remembered as being in the heart.
The wife of Agni in subtle form, ending with Svāhā, [is offered] to the subtle splendor;
the wife of Agni in subtle form, with subtle hands, [is offered] to the subtle strength, followed by the two Ṭha syllables.
Accompanied by the *sahaṃ phaṭ* syllables, these five-limbed mantras are uttered for the subtle body; or one may perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the mantra-syllables.

One should meditate upon the Sun, who has the luster of a bandhūka flower, possesses three eyes, is beautifully adorned, holds two red lotuses in his hands, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while subsisting on milk and restraining the senses;
then one should perform oblations with the finest fuel-sticks of *bilva* and *aśvattha* trees, numbering one-tenth of that amount.
The worship on the Sūryapīṭha is performed with the eight-syllable mantra,
as well as the offering of the *arghya* to be described below;
the attainment of the power of flight (*khecarīsiddhi*) is to be known as the fruit.
And it is said in the Nārāyaṇīya: "By this [means], many have attained the siddhis such as the power of moving through the air (khecaratva) and so forth.
Thus ends the section on the conceptualization of the form (mūrti).
Having recited the root mantra and subsequently having recited this [mantra], one performs the visualization of the form (mūrtikalpanā); thus say the teacher Padmapādācārya. || 43 ||
First, one should worship the limbs; on the petals of the directions are the forms of the Sun, and the four powers beginning with Āditya are to be worshipped on the petals in the corners.
The seed-syllables (bījas) of these [goddesses] are, in their respective order, the initial letters of their own names.
Uṣā, Prajñā, Prabhā, and Sandhyā are proclaimed as the Śaktis. || 45 ||
One should worship Brāhmī and the others situated on the tips of the petals; one should worship Aruṇa in front.
One should worship the limbs in the pericarp (kaṇīkā).
This is stated in the Nārāyaṇīya:

The [deities] beginning with the Heart (hṛdaya) are to be worshipped in the directions of Fire, Rakṣas, Wind, and Īśa with their respective mantras, situated within the pericarp; the Weapon (astra) is in the directions, and also in front of the direction.
By the word "first" (ādau), the worship of the eight limbs on the filaments (kesara) is indicated.
"Ādityādyāḥ" (the Sun and others) means accompanied by the seed-syllables mentioned in the Nyāsa.
Here, some, establishing grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by taking "the four forms beginning with Āditya" as the subject, do not worship Sūrya.
That is incorrect.
Because there is no reason to abandon any one among the five that have been specified;
and if it is argued that he is worshipped primarily in the pericarp (*kaṇīkā*),
there is no determining factor as to which one among the five is worshipped and which is not.
Furthermore, since renunciation has not been observed in any of the instances where the pentad was previously mentioned— both here and elsewhere—
one should worship the Sun in the center and worship Ravi and the others in the four cardinal directions, according to the method taught by the teacher Padmapāda.
The word "four" (catasraḥ) should be construed as a qualifier of the Śaktis.

Because it is stated, "one should worship Aruṇa in front," and since that eastern petal is also the front-facing petal with respect to the assigned direction, Aruṇa is to be worshipped in the place of Mahālakṣmī.
This is because of the statement by the Teacher (Ācārya): "With the Mothers ending with Aruṇā.
However, Padmapādācārya said that one should worship the Mothers and then worship Aruṇa in front of them.
For this very reason, it is stated in the Nārāyaṇīya, on the preceding leaf: "Aruṇa likewise. (44–46)
Afterwards, one should worship the eight planets, beginning with the Moon, outside of that. || 46 ||
One should worship Indra and the others, as well as their weapons, in their proper order.
Having thus worshipped Bhāskara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, according to the prescribed rite, || 47 ||
"Candrādīn" means those beginning with their own seed-syllables (*bīja*).
"Candra" refers to Soma.

In this regard, it should be understood that in the directions starting from the east, there are Candra, Budha, Guru, and Śukra; and in the directions starting from the southeast (Āgneya), there are Bhauma, Maṅgala, Rāhu, and Ketu.
The ritual application (*prayoga*), however, should be understood as previously stated.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "In the directions starting with the East, the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus are to be worshipped;
in the corners starting with the Southeast (Āgneya), Mars, Saturn, and Rāhu-Ketu."

By the phrase "according to rule" (*vidhivat*), it is stated that one should worship the external attendants (*pāriṣada*) with the mantra "Obeisance to the attendants of the Sun" (*sūryapariṣadbhyo namaḥ*), because of the statement:
"With the planets, the gods, and also the attendants of the Sun. (46–47)
One should offer the *arghya* daily, or on the day of its [the deity's] rising;
having prepared a mandala at dawn, one should worship the pedestal as before. || 48 ||
The connection is that one should worship at dawn.
"Maṇḍala" refers to a circle.
"Having made [it]" means with red sandalwood.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Having fashioned a very beautiful circular mandala with the fragrance of red sandalwood. (48)
Having placed there a beautiful copper vessel capable of holding one prastha of water, one should fill it with auspicious water while reciting the mantra. || 49 ||
Regarding the phrase "one who takes a *prastha* of water":
the measure of a *prastha* has been stated by Śrīdharācārya: "A *kuḍava* consists of four *palas*, and a *prastha* consists of four *kuḍavas*."
Thus;
the distinction is that it was recited in reverse order by Manu.
As they say:
"Reciting the mantra in the reverse order, one should complete it with very pure waters.
Thus [it is said]: "with auspicious waters."
The meaning is: by those [rays] meditated upon as being in the form of streams of nectar flowing forth from the solar disc. || 49 ||
Saffron, gorocanā, rājī, red sandalwood, bamboo, karavīra, javā, śālī rice, kuśa grass, śyāmāka grain, and rice grains; || 50 ||
Rājī is *āsurī*.
Rakta is red sandalwood.
Candana is white sandalwood.
*Vaiṇava* refers to the seeds of the bamboo;
*karavīra* refers to the flower of the red *karavīra*, according to the supreme teachers;
*javā* refers to the red *javā*.
Kuśa grass, the tips of kuśa grass, and unbroken grains of rice. || 50 ||
Having contemplated the oneness [of the image] with the sun, one should cast it into that water;
then, one should worship the Sun-god, possessing the prescribed characteristics, along with his limbs (retinue) within that [water]. || 51 ||
"One should cast [the seeds]" means that, according to availability, sesame seeds may also be used in some cases.
As it was said by the Teachers:

Gorocanā, sesame seeds, deerskin, a streak of cow's bile, the red variety of rice known as śītā, karavīra, japā, the tips of kuśa grass, and śyāmāka grains— these should be gathered according to their availability.

"Having united [the deity], one should perform the rite of the *argha* offering with a heart full of devotion. Here, the phrase "having conceived oneness" implies "oneness with one's own self," as it is said:
"Conceiving oneness with his own self, with a concentrated mind, having worshipped the Sun."
"In that vessel.
"With all its limbs" means accompanied by the six or eight limbs, because it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "One should worship thoroughly with the eight limbs."

Therein, having performed the placement of the six syllables of the mantra upon the six locations of the limbs as if they were the six limbs themselves, one should place two syllables on the belly and the back;
this is the aforementioned meditation characterized by the previously described features. || 51 ||
One who knows the ritual procedure should offer incense, flowers, and food offerings according to the rules;
having covered that [vessel], one should properly recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. || 52 ||
Having worshipped again with perfumes and other offerings, he knelt upon the ground;
then, lifting that [image] up to his head, he placed it in the sky before the sun along with its enclosures.
Fixing his gaze upon [the sun] as one with himself and mentally reciting the root mantra, he should offer the arghya water to the Lord of Day with a serene inner self. || 54 ||
Having offered a handful of flowers, one should again recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, until the Sun takes up the nectar of the arghya with his own rays. || 55 ||
By that, the sun, being satisfied, shall grant him his heart's desires;
this offering of the *arghya* increases the longevity and health of men. || 56 ||
It bestows wealth, grain, cattle, fields, sons, friends, and a wife;
it grants splendor, heroism, power, beauty, knowledge, prosperity, and good fortune. || 57 ||
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), incense and lamps are included. By the phrase "according to the rule," this is what is meant: that it should be performed with the protective enclosures (sāvaraṇam).
Having beheld the Lord, together with His enclosures, situated even within the solar orb in the sky, and having worshipped Him mentally;
as it has been said:
"Having worshipped the Sun, and likewise having beheld Him seated upon the throne and stationed in the sky, surrounded by His enclosures..."
Thus;
the connection is that "one who knows the ritual procedure should cover it. By the term "one who knows the ritual procedure," this is what is meant:
"With the left hand supported by the right, joined with the immortal seed-syllable (*amṛtabīja*) meditated upon as the nature of the moon.
"Properly" means having performed three breath-retentions (*prāṇāyāma*) and the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*).
"Again, having fully worshipped."
The word "water" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
"One should offer the *arghya*"—
the procedure for that is as follows.

Having uttered, "To the Blessed Lord Ravi, at the end of the root-mantra, I offer arghya; obeisance," one should give [the offering] with a serene inner self and with devotion; thus it is said. (52–57)
Ākāśa (ha), Agni (ra), Dīrgha-indu (ī)—these joined together form Bhuvaneśvarī;
followed by Sarga (ḥ) and Bhṛgu (bha), this three-syllabled mantra of Bhānu is proclaimed. || 58 ||
One should sequentially place the three seed-syllables from the Foundation (ādhāra) up to the tip of the feet, from the throat down to the Foundation, and from the head down to the throat. || 59 ||
He states the *tilaka-mantra* for the purpose [of the rite], beginning with "ākāśa":
*ākāśa* is *ha*; *agni* is the letter *ra*; *dīrgha* is *ā*; *indu* is the nasal dot (*bindu*). Joined with these, it becomes *hrāṃ*. *Bhuvaneśvarī* is *hrīṃ*.
"Endowed with the visarga" means joined with the visarga;
"Bhṛgu" is *saḥ*.
Thus: *hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ*.
Regarding the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth, it is said: "For this *mantra*, Brahmā is the seer, or else the sage Bhṛgu;
the meter is indeed Gāyatrī, and the deity is the one of sharp rays (the Sun).
The first [syllable] is the seed (*bīja*), and the second is the power (*śakti*).
Some say it begins with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om).
According to Padmapādācārya, in specific applications, it may begin with "Supreme Self" (*paramātman*) or "Dustless One" (*rajaḥpāda*), and so forth. (Verses 58–59)
One should fashion the limbs with the middle [syllable] joined with the six long vowels. || 60 ||
The "limbs" (aṅgāni) should be understood as the ends of the eyes;
they are not mentioned here because they will be explained later.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "In order, upon the fingers from the thumb to the little finger..."
"Having placed [the other] limbs, one should place the eye on the palm of the hand. Thus it is said.
Also in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Having assigned the five limbs to the fingers, one should place the eye on the two palms."
Likewise: "Having likewise placed the limbs [of the mantra] up to the corners of the eyes within oneself, one should remain self-restrained.
In the *Prayogasāra* and the *Nārāyaṇīya*, other limbs are also mentioned:
"The seed-syllable in reverse order, preceded by *ka-tṛtīya* (the third letter of *ka*), is called the heart."
The word *arka*, ending in the dative case (*arkāya*), is said to be *bhūrbhuvaḥ svarom*.
Jvālinī is proclaimed as the crest-mantra (śikhā), and Huṃ is declared to be the armor (varma).
This consists of the fourth letter conjoined with the second vowel and provided with a bindu.
"The Eye" (netra) ending with a vowel (i), "Mounted" (ārūḍha), and "Going" (yānta)—thus, in sequence, it is called "The Weapon" (astra).
Furthermore, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The Mantra is remembered as beginning with 'prayojana', ending with 'tilaka', and concluding with 'sākṣyaṅga'."
Thus it is said.

Regarding the specific details for the *nyāsa* in the *Kramasaṃgraha*: "Having performed the *nyāsa* of the three syllables of the mantra on the palms and backs of both hands, one should likewise place the seven planets upon the feet, the joints, and the faces."
"One should place the [mantras] beginning with *Hṛllekhā* in sequence upon the face, arms, feet, belly, and chest, and in the five locations beginning with the head.
Thus, according to Padmapādācārya, this constitutes the "fivefold form" (*mūrtipañcaka*) within the ritual placement of the nine planets (*navagrahanyāsa*). (60)
I worship the Sun, who sits upon a red lotus throne, the unique ocean of all virtues, the sovereign of all worlds,
holding in his lotus-hands a pair of lotuses, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons.
Wearing a crown of rubies, with the luster of reddish limbs, and possessing three eyes.
The meditation on weapons is as before. || 61 ||
One who has conquered the senses should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with food and clarified butter,
or with sesame seeds sprinkled with honey, using a tenth part of that amount.
A hundred thousand suns is twelve lakhs. || 62 ||
On the previously mentioned pedestal, one should worship the Sun according to this rite:
the first circuit should be with the [six] limbs (aṅgas), and the next with the planets beginning with the Moon. || 63 ||
The third [circle] should be with the world-protectors (lokapālas), and the fourth should be with their weapons.
Having thus worshipped, let the remains of the offering (nirmālya) and the radiant energy (tejas) be given to Caṇḍa.
With his senses restrained, he should offer the *arghya* as previously described to the Sun;
he too shall undoubtedly bestow upon him jewels, wealth, grain, sons, grandsons, cattle, fame, garments, ornaments, and the like. || 65 ||
Regarding "with the limbs," the meditation on the limbs is as follows:
the limbs, possessing divine forms and great power, should be meditated upon as radiant, holding lotuses in their hands, peaceful, and bestowing boons.
"The weapon, terrible with fangs, has a radiance equal to a mass of lightning.
Thus it is said; and also in the *Nārāyaṇīya* section of the *Prayogasāra*:
The [deities] of the heart and so forth are red, gentle, bestowing boons, and holding lotuses;
however, the weapon is like a mass of lightning, with fierce fangs and terrifying. Thus it is said.
"Beyond [these] by the planets beginning with the Moon":
here, one should keep in mind that they begin with the first letter of their respective names.
For it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "One should worship [the deity] accompanied by the first syllables of their own names, adorned with the moon (the vowel *i*)."
In this regard, there is this distinction:

[the planets] beginning with the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus are situated in the directions starting from the East; while Mars, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu are situated in the directions starting from the Southeast (Āgneyī). As stated by the Teacher: "The Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus shall be situated in order in the directions starting from the East."
"In the three directions beginning with Āgneyī (southeast), the planets born of the Earth—Manda (Saturn) and Ketu—are to be worshipped.

Also, in the *Prayogasāra*: "One should worship Soma in the east (Aindra), Budha in the south (Yāmya), Bṛhaspati in the west, Śukra in the north (Saumya), Aṅgāraka (Mars) in the southeast (Āgneyī), and likewise [Rāhu] in the southwest (Āsura)."
"Then Saturn, Rāhu in the northwest (Vāyavyā), and Ketu in the northeast (Īśvara).
Thus,
Tejaścaṇḍa belongs to the group of the Sun.
In the *Prayogasāra*, a specific application is stated:
"On one's own birth-day, under one's own birth-constellation (*nakṣatra*), during an eclipse, or under the constellation of one's birth;
or when there is an affliction of the planets, or when fear has arisen."
Having worshipped the god Divākara together with the planets as prescribed,
using the root-mantra of Savitṛ and the other mantras previously mentioned.
One should offer oblations to each of those planets in their respective directions in sequence;
or else, having performed the fire-rite in a single location according to the prescribed rule.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations, respectively, of fuel sticks, curd-rice, sacrificial porridge, and clarified butter,
each accompanied by the individual *vyāhṛtis* and joined with the recollection [of the deity].
The sacrificial fuel sticks (samidh) are, in order: Arka, Palāśa, Apāmārga, Aśvattha, Udumbara, Khadira, Śamī, Dūrvā, and Darbha.
Then one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for each of them individually according to the prescribed method.
By performing this sacrifice, the planetary deities (grahas), being thus propitiated, become satisfied.
All diseases perish, one obtains victory in battles, and evils such as malevolent spells and the like are pacified; of this there is no doubt.
Thus [ends the section on verses] 63–65.
Space, fire, wind, the letter *ya*, *anta* (the nasal *m*), *arghīśa* (*ha*), and *bindu*—this is declared to be the seed-syllable named Mārttaṇḍabhairava. || 66 ||
Enclosed by the seed-syllable of the Bimba, it bestows the fruit of all desires;
that which is uttered as the letter at the end of *ṭa*, joined with fire (*ra*), the eye (*i*), and the moon (*u*), is thus described. || 67 ||
He states the seed-syllable (bīja) of Mārttaṇḍabhairava as "ākāśa" and so forth:
*ākāśa* is *ha*; *agni* is *ra*; *pavana* is *ya*; *sadyānta* is *au*; *arghīśa* is *u*; and *bindu* is the nasal dot (*m*). This [syllable] is joined with these.
Here, both vowels should also be pronounced according to tradition, following the teacher’s instruction.
Brahmā is the seer; the Nivṛt is the meter.
Haṃ is the seed-syllable; Bindu is the power.
He states that the seed-syllable of the Bimba is the letter ending in ṭa (ṭha).
The letter ending in *ṭ* is *ṭha*; *dahana* is *ra*; *netra* is *i*; and *indu* is the crescent moon (*bindu*). That which is joined with these is *ṭhiram*.
This is summarized by the phrase "bestowing the fruit of all desires.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
Health, longevity, prosperity, knowledge, beauty, nourishment, wealth, fame, good fortune,
power, sovereignty, protection, intelligence, speech, and splendor—
desires of such kinds are indeed accomplished through the power of this mantra.
Thus [ends the section]. 66–67.

One should install the five forms by means of the five seed-syllables beginning with the short vowels; these [forms] are to be placed in order upon the fingers, starting from the middle finger and ending with the little finger. || 68 ||
Sūrya, Bhāskara, Bhānu, and then Ravi and Divākara;
these [names] are again [assigned] to the regions of the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet.
One should place the limbs ending with the eyes using the long-conjoined seed-syllable;
immediately thereafter, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the root seed-syllable. || 70 ||
"Five" means that which begins with the five short vowels starting from *sa* (the letter *s*). This is because it is stated in the Nārāyaṇīya [Upaniṣad]: "The forms end with *sad*."
"From the middle finger onwards" means [starting] from the middle, index, and thumb fingers up to the little finger;
this is because it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "from the middle finger up to the end of the arms."
"By the seed-syllable" means by Mārttaṇḍabhairava;
and in the preceding case as well, [it is used] joined with the long vowels, that is, joined with the six long vowels.
"The limbs ending with the eye" [is the meaning].

The masters of the tradition maintain that after performing the placement (nyāsa) of the heart, head, crest, and armor, one should then perform the placement of the weapon (astra), and only thereafter place the eye (netra). However, some say that the five limbs ending with the eye should be placed, citing the following exception: "For whichever mantra has five limbs, for that one the eye does not exist."
That is not according to the tradition— namely,
