that "the knower of mantras should perform the ancillary rites with the seed-syllable of Ramā (Śrī) enriched by the long [vowel]"—
as stated in the Śrīpaṭala.

"The best of mantra-knowers should fashion the limbs, conjoined with their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*), in sequence by means of the long [vowels] joined with the preceding *puṭa*. Thus it is stated in the *Bhuvaneśī-paṭala*.
Likewise, wherever else there is mention of "long" [vowels], one should understand the six long vowels to be intended there, as there is no reason for such a restriction.
If it is argued that there is a contraction [of the meaning] due to the statement "the limbs ending with the eyes" (*netrāntāṅgāni*), that too is not correct;

for it is consistent even according to the traditional interpretation (*sāmpradāyika-vyākhyā*). Furthermore, the statement "the limbs ending with the eyes" cannot set aside the limb of the eye (*netrāṅga*) which is directly prohibited by the rule "one should avoid its eye," since that general statement can be explained otherwise.
Furthermore, since it is stated that "the worship of the limbs [is] as before," the worship of the weapons (*astra*) in the directions has already been mentioned;
only a specific detail regarding the eye (*netra*) was stated. Later, even in the *Puruṣottama-mantra*, the limbs ending with the eye are mentioned.
And therein, the six-limbed mantras are extracted ending with the *netra* [mantra],
according to the statement: "The six-limbed mantras are taught by the knowers of the Tantra as ending with the *netra*."
This is also because of the statement in the *Prayogasāra* written in the previously mentioned mantra.
Since there are six long limbs in both this mantra and the *Nārāyaṇīya*, the traditional interpretation alone is more authoritative; enough said on this point.
Here, it should be understood that when there is an excellence in the number of eyes and limbs, there is likewise an excellence in that mantra.
Because it is established by logic. || 68–70 ||
Holding in his lotus-like hands a beautiful khaṭvāṅga and a lotus, a discus, a spear, a noose, a goad, a most radiant rosary, and a skull— his own luster resembling gold,
lotuses, and coral; he is adorned with three eyes and is made beautiful by four faces like the Vedas.
We worship Mārttaṇḍa, whose half is his beloved, who wears a jeweled crown and is radiant with necklaces. || 71 ||
The practitioner of mantra should recite the seed-syllable, encapsulated by the [two] forms, three hundred thousand times;
he should then perform a fire-oblation with ten parts of full-blown lotuses sprinkled with honey.
He speaks of the meditation [on the deity] with the words "hemā" and so forth. He is red with coral;
as it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The Lord is as crimson as vermilion, with the Sun as his beloved occupying the left half of his body."
Thus:
*sṛṇi* means a goad;
*vedavaktra* means four-faced.
This is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"The four-faced God, bearing a noose and a goad, holding a rosary and a skull-cup, and carrying a khaṭvāṅga, a lotus, a discus, and a spear."

The weapons, ending with Vāmā, are to be meditated upon on the first two [hands] above Dakṣa and the others. By the phrase "three-eyed," the state of having twelve eyes is indicated, according to the statement in the Nārāyaṇīya: "having eight arms and twelve eyes."
"Or [the mantra] 'vallabhārddha' on the left. || 71-72 ||
On the pedestal endowed with [the syllables] Dīpta and the rest,
having worshipped Uṣā and the others in the directions starting from the east within the pericarp, one should fashion the image by means of the root mantra.
Having invoked the deity, one should worship him according to the procedure to be described hereafter;
one should worship the four [deities] beginning with Sūrya in the cardinal directions and the other [deity] in the intermediate directions. || 74 ||
The limb-worship (aṅgapūjā) is as before; the eye [is worshipped] in the northeast direction. Then, outside [that], the eight planets, and after that, the world-protectors (lokapālas). || 75 ||
The practitioner of mantra should offer the *arghya* oblation to Mārttaṇḍabhairava.
Thus, the practitioner whose mantra has been perfected shall accomplish his own desired goal. || 76 ||
The meaning is that [the worship] is on a pedestal (pīṭha) endowed with [the qualities] such as "blazing" (dīpta), which refers to the solar [pedestal].
Regarding the instruction "one should fully worship Uṣā and the others," it should be understood that this occurs in the pericarp (karṇikā) situated prior to the pedestal-mantra (pīṭhamantra).
A specific detail concerning their seed-syllables (bīja) is also stated in the Nārāyaṇīya.
As they say:
"One should place Uṣā, Prabhā, Sandhyā, and Prajñā in the directions and at the pericarp of the lotus;
then one should invoke them with the letters beginning with 'da', 'ṇḍa', 'dī', 'rgha', 'sva', 'nā', 'mā', and so forth."
By the phrase "one should perform the placement," it is stated that this same sequence applies even to the placement of the seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*).
"One should worship the deity" means with the seed-syllable (*bīja*) enclosed by the *bimba* and ending in *namaḥ*.

Because of the statement, "One should worship with the image and with the heart at the conclusion of the ritual service," the phrase "the Sun and others" includes Bhāskara, Bhānu, and Arava by the word "others.
"Another in the intermediate directions" refers to the fifth sun.
"As before" means as previously described.
According to the fourth method:
"the eye.
By this, there is the worship of two limbs in the northeast (īśāna) direction.
"Regarding the planets," this refers to the sequence previously stated in the mantra;
"thereafter," by means of the vajra and so forth;
"the offering of the arghya."
The meaning is that one should also perform here the previously mentioned procedure for the *arghya* offering. (73–76)
Through a hundred thousand oblations of rice, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and bilva fruits, a treasure-trove shall arise;
through oblations of flowers produced from the rājavṛkṣa tree, there is a golden mine that is a source of Lakṣmī.
By performing a fire sacrifice with *japā* flowers, one brings kings under control without delay;
by offering *mātuliṅga* fruits in the fire, one obtains desired wealth. || 78 ||
Reciting this mantra, a mortal shall accomplish fame, sons, strength, splendor, immeasurable perfection of speech, fortune, and even good luck. (79)
Having stated that "one shall accomplish one's desired goal," he explains that very point with the words beginning with "śālī" (rice).
"Bilva" refers to bilva fruits.
As it has been said: "One who offers a hundred thousand oblations of rice, sesame, and bilva fruits along with ghee becomes a possessor of treasure."
Thus:
"from the lakṣa-homa" means twenty-five thousand for each [of the rites].
"It shall become a treasure"—
the word "of the mantra-practitioner" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
*Mātuliṅga* is the citron (*bījapūra*).
Or there is the reading "labhennidhim" (he would obtain a treasure). || 77-79 ||

The sky (viyat), joined with the half-moon (ardhendu), followed by that (tadādi) and conjoined with creation (sarga)—this two-syllabled mantra, known as Ajapā, is declared to be the celestial wish-fulfilling tree. || 80 ||
The sage is remembered as Brahmā; the goddess is declared to be Gāyatrī; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī;
and the deity is proclaimed to be the Lord of Girijā, the primordial source of the worlds. || 81 ||
He states the *ajapā* mantra as "viyat" and so forth.
Its mention here in this chapter is because it consists of the nature of Agni and Soma; for those two are mentioned at the beginning and the end.
The sky (vi), the letter *ha*, the half-moon (*ardhendu*), and the bindu—beginning with those, that is the *visarga* in creation.
By the phrase "the two-syllabled celestial tree," this is what is meant:
one should meditate in this manner at the time of recitation (*japa*).
That is explained as follows:
At the time of reciting the mantra, one should meditate upon the mantra as the twenty-seventh Brahman—the universal form, eternally blissful in nature, and filling the aperture of the *suṣumṇā*.
Having visualized oneself with all limbs permeated by its radiance, one should contemplate the twenty-sixth Lord (*Īśvara*) in the form of Ardhanārīśvara.

Having meditated upon the twenty-fifth primordial seed-syllable situated in the aperture of Piṅgalā as the form of the Puruṣa-seed in the nature of Prāṇa, one should contemplate the second seed-syllable situated in the middle of the aperture of Iḍā as the form of the twenty-fourfold Prakṛti in the nature of Apāna.

One should meditate on the left and right portions, Iḍā and Piṅgalā, as emerging from the Viśvarūpa-mantras like the light from one lamp to another, having made them marked by female and male signs within the perfectly full Suṣumṇā.
Haṃ is the seed-syllable; Saḥ is the power. || 80-81 ||
One should perform the ritual assignment of the mantra's limbs (aṅgakriyā) by joining the syllable *hasa* with the six long vowels.
*Haseti* is joined with *saṃyuktena*.
The traditionalists (*sāmpradāyikāḥ*) state the six limbs differently:
*hṛt* for the solar self (*sūryātmane*).
The head belongs to the Self that is consciousness;
the crest-lock belongs to the Self that is stainless;
the armor belongs to the Self that is without appearance.
The eye mantra is for the unmanifest self;
the weapon mantra is for the bodiless, subtle, and impelling self.
Some say it is with these [mantras] beginning with *hsā* (or *hrā*). 82.
I bow to the Lord of the Half-Mother (Ardhanārīśvara), whose form flashes like the rising sun and lightning,
who holds in his hands the noose, the gesture of fearlessness, the boon-granting mudrā, and the axe;
who is adorned with divine ornaments made of fresh jewels, and who is the root of the universe.
May the moon-crested, three-eyed Lord, whose form is both gentle and fiery, protect you. || 83 ||
The visualization of the weapons begins from the upper left and ends with the upper right.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; then, having properly offered oblations ten times that amount with milk-rice and sesame paste, the mantra becomes perfected.
A hundred thousand suns is twelve lakhs. || 84 ||

On the seat previously described as being worshipped with [the mantras] beginning with *dīpta*, one should worship the Lord; having conceptualized the form by means of the root mantra, one should worship it together with the limbs (*aṅga*) and so forth. || 85 ||

One should worship Ṛta and Vasu, the two best of men, on the petals of the directions; then, in the intermediate directions, one should worship again Ṛtajā, Gojā, the one called Abjā, and Adrijā. || 86 ||
One should worship the Lords of the World (Lokeśvaras) and their weapons daily, and one should offer the water of honor (arghya) according to the rule, by the very path previously described. || 87 ||

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having conceived the form (*mūrti*) upon the previously mentioned seat (*pīṭha*) by means of the root mantra (*mūla*), one should worship the All-pervading Lord (*vibhu*) together with the limbs (*aṅga*) and so forth.
He states the meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) with the words "truth" (*ṛta*) and so on.
There is also a reading: "one should worship with the limbs in due order."
The syntactical connection is that one should worship the [deities] beginning with Ṛta, together with the limbs, in the cardinal and intermediate directions. || 85-87 ||
Having placed that full jar upon the lotus of the Mother, which is rich with mantras, and having covered it with his left hand while reciting the assigned mantra, he remains self-controlled. || 88 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times over water that consists of nectar;
by remembering [the deity] and sprinkling [the person] with that, he shall become free from disease. || 89 ||
By this very procedure, a person obtains immeasurable longevity, health, and prosperity; one afflicted by poison shall become free from poison. || 90 ||
One should recite the mantra over the lotus of worship described by the Mother [Tantras], which is enriched with the *ajapā* and possesses a pericarp.
By the word "restrained" (*saṃyata*), this is what is meant:
having meditated on a moon-maṇḍala in the palm of the left hand and having visualized the mantra within its center, one should cover the face with that hand.

The word "remembering" (smṛtvā) is to be connected with what precedes. The gender [of the pronoun] "yam" is not intended to be significant, because it has been stated: "Whether a woman or a man, one who is consecrated according to the rule... (88–90).
Visualizing the first seed-syllable of the mantra surrounded by nectar dripping from his two ears,
and drenched by the moon moistened with the supreme nectar flowing therefrom,
the practitioner of mantra should recite this mantra to [ward off] poisons, diseases, madness, untimely death, and fever.
Having conquered [the world], possessing distinguished wealth for a hundred years, he shall live happily with his kinsmen. || 91 ||
"By the two dots" means by the two bindus that constitute the visarga, which reside within the final seed-syllable.
"From that" means from the final seed-syllable.
The method for this is as follows.

Having sat in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) in a delightful place, [one should contemplate] the *visarga* within the pericarp of the thousand-petaled lotus at the tip of the *suṣumṇā*, which is tied with knots and faces downward.

Having meditated on the two [syllables] in the form of two moon-maṇḍalas, one should contemplate the syllable *sa* located upon the pericarp of the *anāhata* lotus being sprinkled by a thick stream of nectar flowing from those two moon-maṇḍalas. One should then meditate on the drop (*bindu*) situated in the *maṇipūra*, which consists of perfect nectar and is being consecrated by the essence of nectar emerging from the syllable *sa* through the aperture of the *suṣumṇā*. Next, having contemplated the syllable *ha* residing in the *mūlādhāra* as being filled by the streaming stream of nectar, one should meditate upon oneself as being saturated by the nectar of the mantra-syllables, filled with the essence of nectar, and as if immersed in a mass of supreme bliss.
The specific details regarding this *jīva-mantra*, as taught in another tantra, are now stated:
Īśvara said: O Goddess, O sinless one, I shall describe to you the worship of the *ajapā*;
by the mere knowledge of which one attains the Supreme Brahman.
O Supreme Goddess, that man who, blinded by delusion, does not daily recite the *haṃsapada* mantra finds no liberation for himself.
O Goddess, by the grace of the glorious Guru, it is known and then recited;
through his inhalations and exhalations, the destruction of bondage occurs.
In inhalation and in exhalation, there are these two syllables, "haṃ" and "saḥ.
Therefore, the vital breath (prāṇa), known as Haṃsa, abides in the form of the Self (ātman).
The inhalations and exhalations originate from the navel and are established at the tip of the heart;
sixty breaths constitute one *prāṇa*, and six *prāṇas* are considered one *ghaṭikā*.
O Īśvarī, sixty breaths constitute a day and night; the number of recitations for the Ajapā-mantra is twenty-one thousand six hundred.
Every day, the vital breath recites the supreme mantra consisting of eternal bliss;
its arising is the commencement of the recitation, and its cessation is the offering.
O Goddess of the gods, even without recitation, the mantra-practitioner performs recitation;
therefore, this is called Ajapā, which severs the bonds of worldly existence.
O Maheśānī, having thus performed the recitation, one should offer it daily to Gaṇeśa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, O Supreme Goddess.
To the individual soul (jīvātman) and likewise to the supreme soul (paramātman),
[one should offer] six hundred, six thousand, and again six [hundred oblations], in due order.
Furthermore, one should present six thousand, then another thousand,
and again a thousand to the Guru in due order.
Upon the base, which has the luster of gold, one should contemplate the letters from *va* to *sa*;
O Supreme Goddess, the petals have the color of molten gold.
One should contemplate the letters from *ba* to *la* within the Svādhiṣṭhāna, which has the luster of coral;
and those with the brilliance of a mass of lightning within the Maṇipūraka, which is deep blue like a sapphire.
One should contemplate those ending with the letter ḍa as having the luster of great sapphires,
and one should contemplate those in the orange-colored [petals] as having the brilliance of the great fire.
O Dear One, one should contemplate the petals from *ka* to *ṭha* in the fourth center, Anāhata;
and in Viśuddhi, which is smoke-colored, one should contemplate the vowels that are red in color.
One should contemplate the two radiant syllables *ha* and *kṣa* within the command (*ājñā*), which has the brilliance of lightning,
upon a thousand-petaled lotus shining with the luster of camphor.
O Supreme Goddess, know that the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) consists of sound (nāda).
O Supreme Goddess, [these are] situated within these seven cakras.
O Dear One, one should offer this recitation performed during the day and night;
the Gāyatrī known as Ajapā is difficult to obtain in the three worlds.
For one who constantly recites the Ajapā, rebirth no longer exists;
this Gāyatrī known as Ajapā bestows liberation upon yogis.
By the mere intention of this [vidyā], a person is liberated from sins;
there is no knowledge equal to this, and no recitation equal to this.
"Merit equal to this has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again. (91)
The three *vyāhṛtis* are Agni; O Jātavedas, bring [the gods] here!
Having addressed all the ritual acts, accomplish them, O beloved of Agni! || 92 ||
This mantra beginning with "Tārā" is said to consist of twenty-five syllables;
Bhṛgu is its seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī its metre (chandas), and Agni its deity (devatā). || 93 ||
The performance of the limbs (aṅgakriyā) of the root mantra is said to be by means of its syllables divided, in sequence, into five, six, four, five, three, and two. || 94 ||
He states the mantra for Agni with the words "the vyāhṛtis.
"Agni" is its essential form;
due to the euphonic combination (saṃdhi) of the visarga, it becomes "repha."
"O beloved of Agni, Svāhā!
Some say it should be enclosed by the Praṇava and Śakti;
those desiring prosperity should recite it beginning with the Śrī-bīja.

The *praṇava* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*). By this statement—"the three *vyāhṛtis*, followed by the beloved of Agni, beginning with the *tārā* (Om)—this is the mantra"—the seven-syllabled *samṛddhi-agni-mantra* is also indicated.
As it was said by the Teacher:
"The tenth [syllable] from *viyat* (the sky) joined with the emission (*visarga*), and the sixteenth [syllable] from *bhūḥ* ending in *la*;
this Mantra of Kṛśānu (Fire), beginning with *dhruva* (the pole star), is said to bestow great prosperity.
Its seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *praṇava* (Oṃ), and its power (*śakti*) is *svāhā*.
The Vyāhṛtis and so forth are recited with this mantra;
the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is performed with the Vyāhṛtis repeated twice.
As for the meditation (*dhyāna*):

May the radiant Agni, three-faced, bearing a spear, a svastika, a noose, a goad, and granting boons and fearlessness, adorned with a crown and various ornaments, long protect you with a gracious mind.
One should recite this mantra with devotion for one hundred thousand times during the seasons, and perform the oblation with milk, honey, ghee,
and very white ṣaṣṭika rice in quantities amounting to one-tenth of that number.
Thus it is said.
The worship, however, is indeed according to the sequence that will be described hereafter.
It is also indicated that even the mantra beginning with "agni" and ending with "svāhā" is a separate mantra.
As it has been stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"The mantra is also: 'O Agni Jātavedas, bring [the deity] here; accomplish all rites from this point on, svāhā!'—thus it is declared in the sequence.
This same [mantra] is also stated in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*.
"The arrangement of the ancillary limbs (*aṅga*) is by means of two, four, five, three, two, and two syllables.
Thus, the *ṛṣi* and so forth, as well as the meditation (*dhyāna*), worship (*pūjā*), and other rites, are exactly the same. (92–94)
With a golden garland draped over his shoulders, adorned with a crimson wreath and sandalwood paste,

his head radiant with a mass of matted locks from which clusters of flames emerge; clad in a very white garment, he displays the spear, the svastika, a handful of darbha grass, a rosary for recitation, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.
I worship Agni, who bears two flames, whose three eyes are full, and whose luster is red. || 95 ||
The meditation on the weapons is performed first for the two raised hands beginning with the left, and then for the two lowered hands;
thus it continues until the end.
Immediately after the meditation, one should display the mudrā known as Saptajihvā (the Seven-Tongued).
The characteristic of *talla* is as follows:
having placed the two hands with fingers extended upon the wrists,
one should join the pair of little fingers and thumbs and extend the remaining fingers.
"This is the mudrā called Saptajihvā, which brings the Fire-god under control.
Thus it is said; it should be understood that this [mudrā] is common to all mantras dedicated to Agni. || 95 ||

Having received the mantra from the guru, the practitioner, having fasted on the fourteenth day, pure in conduct and with senses subdued, should recite it a thousand times for each sun (twelve thousand times). || 96 ||
The grammatical connection is as follows: "Having received the mantra from the guru, the practitioner, having fasted on the fourteenth day, should recite it.
Regarding "on the fourteenth day," this refers to the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra.
As it has been said: "On the fourteenth day of the beginning of the year, one who is initiated at the very start of the day..."
"One who has properly observed the fast should recite the mantra twelve thousand times. Thus [it is said]. (96)
On the day of the new moon, one should feed the Brahmins with foods consisting primarily of sweets;
according to one's ability, one should also give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). || 97 ||
Having eaten (or sacrificed), one should personally bring the materials for the fire-oblation and purify them;
then, beginning from the following day, one should perform the oblation without weariness. || 98 ||
"With substances having a predominance of sweet [ingredients]," such as sugar and other sweetening agents.
"The following day" refers to the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*).
As it has been said: "On the next day, on the first day of the lunar fortnight, one should offer oblations into the consecrated fire with these [substances]."
Thus [it is said]. And in the Nārāyaṇīya: "In the directions beginning with fire (the southeast) up to the end of the quarters, and on the lunar days, one hundred and eight [times]. (97–98)
The wise practitioner should daily offer one hundred and eight oblations each of *vaṭa* wood, rice, sesame, *rājī*, and clarified butter as the sacrificial fuel. || 99 ||
In sequence, there are six substances beginning with *vaṭa*.

However, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*, seven substances are mentioned: fuel-sticks of *nyagrodha* wood combined with rice, sesame, *rājī* grain, and ghee; these should always be accompanied by milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and ghee.
Thus it is said;
likewise: "By those seven substances, separately. (99)

Having thus completed the ten-day rite according to the prescribed rules, the knower of the ordinances, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), properly honored the best of the twice-born on the eleventh day. || 100 ||
Having worshipped [the deity], one should gratify them with wealth according to one’s means and with devotion;
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, such as a reddish-brown, milch cow. || 101 ||
Having given garments, wealth, and grain, he should satisfy [the deities] once more;
he should then worship the seat (pīṭha), together with the nine powers (navaśakti), within the limits of his own mandala. || 102 ||
Yellow, white, reddish, black, smoky, intense, emitting sparks,
radiant, and flaming— these are declared to be the nine powers of fire.

"Daśāham" (for ten days). The syntactical connection is as follows: having completed the ten-day period according to this procedure, one who knows the ritual should, on the eleventh day, offer the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) and properly honor the best of the twice-born (*dvijottama*). In that context, by the phrase "one who knows the ritual," it is meant that after performing the *mahāvyāhṛti-homa*, one should offer one oblation each for the limbs, the principal deity (*mūrti*), the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), and their weapons (*astra*).
It has been stated that this is the *pūrṇāhuti*.
By the phrase "one should properly satisfy," it is meant [that one should do so] with the ritual services (*upacāra*) such as the water of honor (*arghya*) and so forth.
"Up to the end of one's own mandala" means up to the end of the fire-mandala (*vahnimaṇḍala*). (100–103)
One should provide a seat with its own seed-syllable and fashion the image with the root-mantra;
there, one should worship the fire according to the prescribed rite and characteristics. || 104 ||
Having first performed the limb-worship (aṅgapūjā), one should worship these eight forms upon the petals:
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, and he known as Havyavāhana; || 105 ||
Another is known as Aśvodaraja, and then there is the one called Vaiśvānara;
Kaumāratejas would be the next, and Devamukha is the final one, Viśvamukha. || 106 ||
One should worship the World-Protectors (Lokeśas) on the outside, their lotus-hands resplendent with the svastika and śakti, and accompanied by their weapons such as the vajra.
"By its own seed-syllable" means by the syllable *raṃ*. "To the fire-yoga-pīṭha, *namaḥ*" is the mantra for the seat (*āsana*).
"According to the ritual rule" means with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*).

The meditation on the forms has been described according to the stated characteristics; the mention of these specific forms is for the purpose of excluding other forms. Other forms have been mentioned in the *Prayogasāra* and the *Nārāyaṇīya*.
"Agni Vaiśvānara is declared as the one behind;
the consumer of oblations (Hutāśana), the path of the oblation (Hutavartman), Jātavedas, and likewise Hutāvaha;
furthermore, Devamukha and Saptajihva—these are the forms of Agni. Thus it is said.
These [syllables] are to be understood as being absent from a mantra that lacks the three *vyāhṛtis*. || 104–107 ||
Thus one should worship daily and recite [the mantra] more than a thousand times;
within a year, one becomes possessed of an abundance of wealth and grain. || 108 ||
"One should recite more than a thousand" thus is stated as the number for the daily recitation;
this is to be understood in all cases. || 108 ||
One should offer oblations of food mixed with clarified butter; from this, one obtains prosperity within a year.
[Likewise, one may offer] flowers of the Brahmavṛkṣa tree, soaked in curd, honey, and clarified butter. || 109 ||
Or, by means of *karavīra* flowers, one may become prosperous through the mandala;
for six months one should offer oblations with the ghee of a tawny cow, and at the end of the year [the result follows].
For him, prosperity and fame honored by the three worlds arise;
one should daily offer oblations with grains of rice according to the rite, one hundred and eight times. || 111 ||
His house is filled with rice, cattle, buffaloes, food, and other provisions;
by offering oblations of sesame seeds, a person attains great prosperity. || 112 ||
With sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) produced from the Palāśa, Bilva, Khadira, Śamī, Dugdha-mahīruha, Vikaṅkata, Āragvadha, and Karavīra trees. || 113 ||
With blossoms of the kumuda, the padma, the kahlāra, and the aruṇotpala, with jasmine flowers and dūrvā grass, one should constantly offer one hundred and eight [oblations]. || 114 ||
The wise practitioner of mantras should offer oblations with one [mantra] on the first lunar days;
he shall accomplish all his desires within six months—of this there is no doubt. || 115 ||
"One should offer oblations" means for six months.
"One hundred and eight according to the rule" means that, according to the rule, it is stated that this should be done at every step.
There is an option: one may offer oblations daily, or on every first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*).

Regarding the phrase "one hundred and eight" as the constant number, it refers to a single tree from among any [trees] that produce milk. As for "with *aruṇotpala* flowers," this means with red lotuses or red water-lilies (*kuvalaya*).
As stated in the *Kośa*: "The *kokanada* is a red lotus; it refers to a red water-lily and a red *saṃdhya* flower.
Therefore, there are fifteen substances: seven sacrificial fuels (*samidh*), seven flowers, and one *dūrvā* grass.
Therein, from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) until the festival day (*parvan*), one should offer oblations every day with each of these substances according to the stated number.
In this manner, one should perform the counter-measures for up to six months.
Alternatively, according to the view that "on each day," one should offer oblations on that specific day with fifteen substances, each repeated one hundred and eight times. (109–115)
One should utter "Uttiṣṭha puruṣa," then "Haripiṅgala," followed by the supreme "Lohitākṣa," then "padaṃ dehi me dadāpaya," and finally the two syllables "Ṭha" twice. || 116 ||
The *samṛddhi* mantra is said to consist of twenty-four syllables;
its seers and other [attributes] were previously declared by means of the three groups of six elements and instruments. || 117 ||
The knower of mantras should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), joined with the [five] seed-syllables (jāti), using four pairs of syllables originating from the root mantra. || 118 ||
He states the mantra for the horse-fire: "uttiṣṭhati," followed by two *ṭha*s and *svāhā*.
By the phrase "samṛddhim anu," there is a statement of its application (*viniyoga*).
The consonants residing in the mantra are the *bījas*;
the vowels are the *śaktis*.
According to Padmapādācārya, the *praṇava* is the *bīja* and *svāhā* is the *śakti*.
Some say it begins with the *praṇava* (Oṃ);
others say it begins with the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha;
and still others say it begins with the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī.

Some also say "mṛtyuñjayādya" [is used] here; in the ritual application, "dehi me" should be known as preceding this, and the connection with the *sādhya* should also be understood. By "bhūtaiḥ" is meant the five [elements].
By means of the four methods [of extraction],
in the *Prayogasāra* and *Nārāyaṇīya*, a mantra consisting of exactly twenty syllables beginning with the *praṇava* is extracted, excluding the two words *lohitākṣa* and *meṣa*.
As it has been said:
"Having uttered 'uttiṣṭha puruṣa,' then say 'haripiṅgala dehi atha dadāpaya'; this is declared to be the mantra beginning with *tārā* (Oṃ) and ending with *svāhā*.
Thus, the limbs (*aṅga*) have been previously described as consisting of four, three, five, four, and two syllables respectively."
Thus [ends the section]. 116–118.
Emerging from a golden *aśvattha* tree, he is like fire with the luster of a mass of vermilion;
his body and the hair of his limbs are covered with flames, and he is enchanting to the world with his splendor.
He has the form of a horse, his neck is adorned with ornaments shimmering with priceless jewels.
One should visualize him covering the earth with jewels emerging from his sense organs. || 119 ||
He describes the meditation on the horse and fire with the words beginning "svarṇa" (verse 119).
One should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times with milk-rice mixed with sesame;
then, while remembering the *turagāgnimantra*, one should offer oblations into the fire ten thousand times. || 120 ||
On the pedestal previously described, one should worship [the deity] together with its limbs (aṅgas) and forms (mūrtis);
one should then worship the Fire-god (Havyavāhana) along with the guardians of the directions and their respective weapons.
The practitioner who, devoted to the morning bath, recites the mantra a thousand times, shall conquer diseases and live happily for a hundred years, endowed with prosperity. || 122 ||
Standing in water reaching up to the heart and gazing at the sun with self-restraint,
one should recite [the mantra] four thousand times daily for the duration of a year.
Having conquered the fear of untimely death, the afflictions arising from disease and poverty, the wise and radiant one shall live for a hundred years. || 124 ||

On the first lunar day (pratipad) under the asterism Kṛttikā, an oblation of rice grains brings wealth; likewise, on the first days of the lunar fortnights, wealth shall be obtained through offerings of curds or fuel-sticks of the Śamī tree. || 125 ||
Through offerings of clarified butter, one attains what is desired; through lotuses, one shall obtain a village.
With sesame seeds and jyotiṣmatī plants, a king shall conquer the kingdom of his enemy. || 126 ||
"One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Regarding that, the procedure is found in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*:
"If the eighth or fourteenth lunar day falls between the asterisms Kṛttikā and Viśākhā, then one should begin the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) here at the time of Abhijit."

Having fashioned an image of fire from any one of *śamī*, red sandalwood, or *karavīra* wood, and performing the ritual acts beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and ending with the dismissal (*visarga*) by means of the root mantra,

one who bathes at the three junctions of the day should daily recite the mantra three thousand times, or three hundred and thirty-four times; for one month, he should offer oblations of half that number using *śamī* fuel-sticks sprinkled with ghee, or likewise with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
One should also give a cow to the guru, and one becomes accomplished (*siddha*).
One should worship with *karavīra* flowers at both twilights or at midday.
"As previously stated" refers to what was mentioned immediately before.
In that place where the wish-granting tree (kalpataru) stands, a golden peepal tree (svarṇāśvattha) is to be worshipped, because it is so described in the meditation (dhyāna). 120–126.
A man should offer oblations of aśvattha wood fuel smeared with sheep's ghee;
he obtains his desired maiden, and she too shall obtain him as her husband. || 127 ||
A homa performed with pure clarified butter is traditionally known to bring about the destruction of fever.
For seven days, the practitioner of mantras should offer oblations with auspicious Bandhūka flowers.
Having subsisted for a month on cow’s milk while controlling the senses, one attains great prosperity before long, exceeding a full thousandfold. || 129 ||
The mantra-practitioner who offers a thousand oblations shall become a lord of prosperity;
by offering dūrvā grass soaked in clarified butter, a man shall live for a hundred years.

For one who daily offers one hundred and eight oblations with clarified butter while employing the *mṛgamudrā* gesture, there arises prosperity that bestows an abundance of wealth and grain. || 131 ||
If one should offer ten thousand oblations of ghee on the first day of every month,
his prosperity shall become great and remain with him for six months without departing.
He who performs oblations for half a year with blossoming red lotuses mixed with the three sweets shall become the lord of Indirā. || 133 ||
The wise man should offer oblations daily with clarified butter from a red cow mixed with the three sweets;
within half a year, he shall become a lord of the earth like Indra.
Regarding "the deer-seal" (*mṛgamudrā*): as for the characteristic of the deer-seal—
it is to join the tips of the ring fingers, the thumbs, and the middle fingers together.
One should raise the remaining fingers; this is declared to be the mṛgamudrā. Thus [ends verse 131].
While he was offering oblations for a year, Lakṣmī was coveted by Indra;
one should offer oblations with pieces of Amṛtā soaked in milk for seven days. || 135 ||
The knower of mantras who has conquered his senses, by reciting [the mantra] three thousand times every day, continuously overcomes sorcery, treachery, fever, insanity, and disease. || 136 ||
Having become radiant with splendor like that of the sun, he shall live for a hundred years [by consuming] the [seeds of] *karavīra*, *javā*, *bilva*, *palāśa*, and the *nṛpa* tree. || 137 ||

Having offered flowers—blooming white water-lilies, kuraṇṭaka blossoms, and those born of the jasmine species—smeared with the three sweets, the practitioner of mantras [should do so] at every step. || 138 ||
Having taken a prastha of pure rice that has been thoroughly cleaned, one shall obtain great fortune exceeding one's desires within a year. || 139 ||
Having prepared an oblation with cow’s milk, one should fashion a morsel from it;
taking that which is anointed with clarified butter, [one should offer it] when the carrier of oblations (the fire) has been worshipped. || 140 ||
*Amṛtā* is *guḍūcī*.
*Nṛpabhūruṭ* is *rājavṛkṣa*.
The word "having offered" (*hutvā*) applies to each [of these] individually.
"One hundred for each," according to the statement of the Teacher.
"With cow's milk" means with the milk of a red-colored cow.
This has been stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"One should offer as an oblation rice from the *śāli* variety, prepared with a *prastha* measure of red cow's milk, ground into a paste, smeared with ghee, and mixed with clarified butter. (135–140)
Having properly recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should offer oblations into the fire on the first lunar day, while meditating upon the form of the horse.
Within a year, the Fortune that fascinates the three worlds arises;
one should eat vacā consecrated with this mantra at the arrival of spring.
Sarasvatī shall dwell unwaveringly within his lotus-like mouth. || 142 ||
If a person drinks water consecrated one hundred and eight times in the morning, his digestive fire will blaze up like a sacrificial fire fed with oblations. (143)
"Having recited correctly" refers to that which begins with the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, as previously stated.
After the *kavala-homa*, one should offer oblations with clarified butter one thousand and eight times, or one hundred times; thus says the author of the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*. (141–143)
Having fashioned the mandala consisting of nine squares as previously described, one should place nine auspicious jars according to the prescribed method. || 144 ||
One should fill them in succession with decoctions produced from the bark of milk-exuding trees;
having adorned them with cloths and other ornaments, one should deposit the nine gems within. || 145 ||

In the center, one should worship the Fire, and in the pitchers, the eight forms in the sequence of the directions, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, as well as charming incense and lamps. || 146 ||
Having touched the jars, he should then recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
thereafter, he should consecrate the disciple, who is humble and has offered the ritual fee.
Having conquered fever, seizing spirits, great diseases, poverty, and other such afflictions, he, duly consecrated, shall live for a hundred years together with prosperity. || 148 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Śāradātilaka composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra. 14.
"Consisting of nine parts and having nine hubs," as previously stated in the third [chapter].
According to the stated path, in the manner described in the sixth chapter.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition. 14.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Now I shall declare the great mantras of Viṣṇu, which accomplish all aims.
By the mere remembrance of whom the virtuous have reached the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence. || 1 ||
He states the Viṣṇu-mantras that follow in sequence with the word "atha" (now).
The phrase "for all purposes" (*sarvārtha*) expresses their application for one who has desires;
he speaks to the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) with the words "of whom" (*yasya*). || 1 ||

First the syllable *tāram*, then the word *namaḥ*, followed by the two letters *na* and *ra* endowed with long vowels, and then *pavana* and *ṇāya*; this mantra, consisting of eight syllables, has been proclaimed. || 2 ||
Sādhyanārāyaṇa is declared as the sage, and the meter is said to be Gāyatrī;
the deity of the mantra is the goddess Gāyatrī, and the deity is the imperishable Viṣṇu. || 3 ||
He extracts the mantra as "tāram.
The two letters *na* and *ra* (narau), when joined with the long vowel *ā* (dīrgha ā), become "nārā.
Here, it should be understood that through the substitution of *u* for the *r* of the word *namaḥ* and the subsequent *guṇa* sandhi, it becomes the syllable *oṃ*.
"Pavana" is its name;
"ṇāya" is its essential form;
it consists of eight syllables, that is, it is an eight-syllabled mantra.
As it is said in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"The two syllables situated in the fifth and sixth [vowels] are ethereal (*nābhasa*) in sequence;
the second is conjoined with the mixed [consonant], while the third shall be the fifth [vowel]."
"Then fire and wind are proclaimed as the third and fourth [syllables], together with Ananta.
Likewise, the letter of wind at the end of the mantra is in the fourth and fifth [positions].
Here, the word "nābhasa" (ethereal) is to be supplied.

Therefore, in the fifth group of consonants (tavarga), that syllable which is of the nature of space (nābhasa) and has the form of the letter *na*—that is the third mantra, meaning the third syllable.
Here, "the third" refers to the syllable excluding the *praṇava*.
It is accompanied by *ā* and *ananta* (i.e., joined with the vowel *ā*).
The third and fourth [letters] are *na* and *ra*.
In the fourth group, the *ṭa*-varga, the fifth letter is *na*; this is the meaning.
In the fifth group, the *ta*-varga, and the sixth group, the *pa*-varga, the letters corresponding to the ether element (*nābhasa*)—namely *na* and *a*—are to be extracted in sequence.
In that regard, the second *makāra* is joined with the mixed vowel *okāra*.
*Praṇava* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *āya* is the power (*śakti*).
As it has been said in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
The imperishable Viṣṇu, possessing a blazing luster and the initial bindu of the Śruti, is the seed-syllable of the eight-syllabled mantra; by that, the state of being eight-syllabled is achieved.
"Now, following the fifteenth syllable, which consists solely of a consonant,
the remainder of the mantra is said to be the Śakti of this [mantra].
The teachers state that the one named Sādhyanārāyaṇa is the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī)."
Thus it is said in the Mantratantraprakāśa: "The inner controller (antaryāmī) is the seer (ṛṣi); the meter (chandas) is Gāyatrī."
The seers and others for each syllable are as follows:
Gautama, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra the seer,
Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Atri, and the one born from a jar (Agastya).
Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, and Virāṭ—these are the eight Vasus as their presiding deities. (2–3)
The heart-mantra is declared for Kruddholkā; the head-mantra is remembered for Maholkā. The crest-mantra is proclaimed for Vīrolkā; the armor-mantra is remembered for Dyūlkā.
This is considered the arrangement of the limbs for the *sahasrolkā* weapon-mantra.
He states the extraction of the five-limbed mantra beginning with "kruddholkāya" and so forth.
By extracting [the names] in the dative case, it was previously stated that all [mantras] end in *svāhā* and possess the [appropriate] *jāti*.
And it is said in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"With the former [syllables]—*ulkaiḥ*, *kruddha*, *mahāvīra*, *dyusahasra*—at the end of these, when joined with their case-endings, comes the beloved of Agni (*svāhā*). Thus it is said.
Elsewhere it is also stated: "Fire [is invoked] by means of words such as *kruddha* and *ulkā*, joined with the word for 'wife' (*jāyā*) and combined with the generic class-term.
By the phrase "this is considered the arrangement of the limbs," the previously mentioned *karanyāsa* (hand-assignment) is indicated.
Just as one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of creation and so forth upon the hands according to the rule with the eight mantra-syllables—
starting from the right index finger up to the left index finger— that shall be the "creation" [placement].

Here, the position begins from both index fingers and ends at the two little fingers; this sequence is for emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), while the reverse order is said to be withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) performed with the hands.
"Having performed the placement of the eight limbs, one should place the five limbs according to the sequence of their stationing.
Regarding this, there is a specific detail in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"Upon the three joints of the fingers, beginning with the little finger and ending with that [thumb]..."
One should sequentially place the eight syllables, beginning with the eldest (jyeṣṭha) and ending with tāra, as they are conjoined.
Thus [ends verses 4–5].
Furthermore, one should perform the six ancillary rites (ṣaḍaṅga) using the six syllables of Manu.
Furthermore, one should place the two remaining syllables on the belly and the back. Having secured the directions with the Cakra-mantra, one should then assign the mantra-syllables to the body.
Having described the five-limbed [mantra], he speaks again of the eight-limbed one with the words "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*).

Therein, having performed the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the six syllables just as in the six-limbed [rite], one should place [the syllables] on the belly and the back, saying: "Ṇāṃ, obeisance to the belly" (*udarāya namaḥ*) and "Yaṃ, obeisance to the back" (*pṛṣṭhāya namaḥ*).
Thus it has been said:

"The wise one should perform the eight-limbed [protection] (*aṣṭāṅgaka*) with the eight-syllable mantra used separately, [placing it] on the heart, head, crest, armor, eyes, mouth, belly, and back. Thus it was said by Īśānaśiva as well.
Its heart mantra is *tāra* (oṃ), its head is the letter *nā*, and its crest (*śikhā*) is *mo*;
the letter *nā* is the armor (*kavaca*), the letter *rā* is the weapon (*astra*), and the supreme [letter] is the eye (*nayana*).
"The belly, the back, and the two final syllables are indeed joined with *namaḥ*.
Also elsewhere: "By [the mantras] distinguished by [the parts of the body]: heart, head, the preceding [syllable], crest, armor, weapon, eyes, belly, and back."
This alone is the traditional method.
Saying "the direction is bound," he snaps his fingers.
"With the *cakra*-mantra" refers to the *aindrī-cakra* mantra and so forth, which will be explained in the subsequent chapter, beginning with the words "I bind."
In the fourth chapter, the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) was taught by means of the general weapon-mantra (*sāmānyāstramantra*).
Here, it is stated again for the purpose of explaining the specific mantra.
By the phrase "one should place the syllables of the mantra upon the body," the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is indicated.
As they say:

"In the head, the eyes, the mouth, the heart, the navel, the secret place, the knees, and the feet—this is taught as the process of emanation; likewise, the process of maintenance extends from the navel up to the heart."

"This reabsorption (saṃhāra), beginning from the feet and ending at the head, is said to be the beginning of emanation (sṛṣṭi) and so forth. However, in the *Mantratantraprakāśa* it is stated: "That which begins at the navel and is completed at the heart is to be known as the placement for stability (sthitinyāsa), which bestows both seen and unseen fruits."
This alone is the traditional method.
In that very context, there is this specific detail:
one should place each individual syllable, ending with a *bindu* and encircled by the *dhruva*.
In that regard, the placement with the fingers should be as follows: on the head, there is only the single middle finger.
The placement [of mantras] upon the two eyes is prescribed with the index and middle fingers;
the placement upon the mouth is proclaimed to be performed with the thumb and ring finger.
In the heart, the wisdom-mudrā (jñānamudrā) consists of the thumb and the little finger.
They are proclaimed at the navel; at the secret place, they are proclaimed as being without the thumbs;
and all five are proclaimed at both the knees and the feet. Thus [ends verses 5–6].
In the foundation, the heart, the mouth, the roots of the two arms, the two nostrils, the throat, the navel, the heart, the *kūrca*, and then on the sides and the back. || 7 ||
Immediately after that, [one should place them] on the head, face, eyes, ears, and nostrils;
then on the joints of the arms and feet, the fingers, the bodily constituents (dhātu), the vital breaths (prāṇa), and the region of the heart. || 8 ||
One should assign the letters one by one to the head, eyes, face, heart, belly, thighs, shanks, and the two feet, as well as to the cheeks, shoulders, and knees.
One should carefully place the discus, conch, mace, and lotus at the feet.

Having thus described the five-limbed and eight-limbed letter-assignments (*akṣaranyāsa*), he now describes the *vibhūtipañjara* assignment consisting of ten repetitions, beginning with the words "ādhāra" (the foundation).
Here, one should perform the assignment by enclosing each individual syllable within the *praṇava* (Oṃ).
For it is stated thus in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"By means of the complete reversal [of the syllables], it is all-pervasive.
And likewise, the teacher Padmapāda says: "The practitioner of mantra [should perform] the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra-syllables, enclosing each successive turn with the *praṇava* (OM)."
And it is said: "The pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) has been described.
This constitutes one repetition by means of the first half-verse.
In that regard, what is the compound?
By the second half [of the verse], the second [mudrā] is indicated;
by the third half, the third;
and by the fourth half, the five [mudrās] beginning with the fourth and ending with the eighth.
In that regard, one [finger] is among the four fingers of the right hand, excluding the thumb;
others, however, said it is among the five fingers of the three joints of the right hand.
Likewise, the second [finger] is in the left hand.
The third [digit] is on the right foot;
the fourth is on the left foot;
others, however, say it is on the joints of the two hands.
Another is at the joints of the two feet;
the third is on the fingers of the hand, excluding the two thumbs;
likewise, they say the fourth is on the toes of the feet.
The fifth [verse] is in the *hṛdaya* [section], among the skin and so forth;
the ninth is by the second half of the fifth [verse];
the tenth is by the [entire] verse.

In this regard, the experts of the tradition maintain that it is indicated by the word "carefully" (*avahita*) that one should place the four [remaining] syllables on the cheeks, shoulders, thighs, and feet, and then place the other four syllables in the positions of the discus, conch, mace, and lotus, accompanied by their respective weapon-mudrās.
As for the definition of those mudrās:
Within the left fist, the fingers of the right hand are straight;
the left thumb, joined with its surface straight, should touch the tips [of the right fingers].
Having placed the two hands facing each other with the fingers interlaced,
one should further join the two middle fingers and extend them well.
Thus, this is declared to be the mudrā of the mace, which likewise bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The characteristics of the wheel and lotus mudrās have been described previously. (7–10)
In the eight-syllabled [mantra], this [deity] should be known as consisting of the eight primal natures (aṣṭaprakṛti) for those who possess a fourfold nature.
The twelve-syllable [mantra] is declared by the wise to be distinguished by its conjunction.
In order to state the *Mūrtipañjara*, he first declares the identity of the twelve- and eight-syllable [mantras] as an introduction (*upodghāta*), saying "eight," etc.
The eight *prakṛtis* are those mentioned in the first chapter.
By the phrase "the eight prakṛtis," the nyāsa of the eight principles (tattvas) is indicated.
