Furthermore, a systematic arrangement has been stated elsewhere:
As they say:
"The placement of stability (sthitinyāsa) is prescribed for householders, bestowing all perfections;
for those in the first stage of life, the placement of origination (utpattinyāsa) is declared."
The destruction of ascetics and forest-dwellers has been proclaimed;
the destruction of even the detached householder is likewise ordained.
"The placement of the principles (tattva-nyāsa) is prescribed for those dwelling in the forest with their wives;
furthermore, for these seekers of knowledge, even the [placement] up to the end of emanation (sṛṣṭyanta) is distinguished.
Since it is stated here that "one should perform the placement in general," one should also place the twelve principles among these.
Namely: *Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme; salutation to the individual self (jīvātman) at the head,* and so forth.
As for the principles (tattvas): the individual self, the vital breath, the intellect, the mind, the heart-lotus, the solar orb, the lunar orb, and the orb of fire accompanied by its own digits.
"And Vāsudeva and the others"—thus they declared the twelve principles. (40)
Viṣṇu, who resembles ten million autumnal moons, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus;
whose abode is a white lotus; who deludes the world with his splendor;
and who wears armlets, necklaces, earrings, a great crown, and shimmering bracelets.
I bow to Him who bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the noble Kaustubha gem, and who is praised by the lords of sages. || 41 ||
As for the meditation on the weapons: there is a discus and a lotus in the upper right [hands], and likewise a mace and a conch in the two left [hands].
This is stated in the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*: "One should visualize Vāsudeva, the lord of the gods, as having four arms."
One should arrange a wheel above the right [hand] and a lotus below it.
"A mace should be depicted above the left [hand] and a very beautiful conch below it.
Thus it is said.
Here, after the visualization (dhyāna), one should display the Śrīvatsa, Kaustubha, forest garland (vanamālā), and the añjali mudrās.
Because it is said: "The añjali is the añjalimudrā, and it is also designated as vāsudeva," these [mudrās] should also be shown in the subsequent mantra. || 41 ||
One who has been initiated and has conquered his senses should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
he should then perform a thousand oblations with sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter.
On the pedestal previously described, one who knows the ritual procedure should fashion the image with the root mantra and worship Vāsudeva according to this method.
"Twelve hundred thousand" means one million two hundred thousand [recitations].
"Initiated according to the Vaiṣṇava path" is the meaning.
And that initiation is to be understood from the Vaiṣṇava tantras, such as the Nāradapañcarātra and others.
That thousand [is multiplied] by twelve, making twelve thousand.

By the phrase "one who knows the ritual procedure" (vidhānavit), it is indicated that the traditional verses (āgamaśloka) mentioned as part of the ritual service (upacāra) are necessary here. || 42-43 ||
The first enclosure should consist of the [eight] limbs, Vāsudeva and the others;
the next [enclosure] with the powers such as Śānti and so forth; and the further [enclosure] with the twelve forms. || 44 ||
The fourth [day] is considered to be with the lords of the gods and so forth, and the fifth with Vajra and so forth;
thus worshipped, Viṣṇu shall grant one's own desired object. || 45 ||

For the purification of the mind, one should offer a thousand oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with ghee while reciting the mantra; for the sake of liberation from all sins, one should likewise offer as many oblations of fuel-sticks from milky trees smeared with milk. || 46 ||
"By means of the twelve forms" refers to Keśava and the others.
The meditation on these is like that of the root deity. (44–46)

The pair of *hṛllekhā* seed-syllables, followed again by the pair of *ramā* seed-syllables, then "to Vāsudeva" at the end of *lakṣmī*, preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with "heart" (*hṛt*). || 47 ||
This fourteen-syllable mantra is declared to be the celestial wish-fulfilling tree (surapādapa).
The Heart [of the mantra] is said to consist of the two Śakti-bījas, and the Head is said to consist of the two Ramās. || 48 ||
The *śikhā* is declared for Lakṣmī, and the *varman* is proclaimed for Vāsudeva; the *astra* is shown with "namas. One should arrange everything beginning with the *tārā*. || 49 ||
He states the mantra of Lakṣmī-Vāsudeva as "hṛllekhā.
*Hṛllekhā* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Bhuvaneśī.
How the word *hṛllekhā* denotes Bhuvaneśī has already been shown previously.
*Ramā* is the seed-syllable of Śrī. "At the end of Lakṣmī" means at the end of the word *lakṣmī*. "Ending with *hṛt*" means ending with *namaḥ*.
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Lakṣmīvāsudeva.
The Praṇava is the seed-syllable (bīja), and Māyā is the power (śakti). || 47–49 ||
A body resembling lightning and the moon, attained through the union of Brahmā and Viṣṇu by the power of affection, adorned with a profusion of ornaments shimmering with jewels;
[holding] knowledge as a lotus-mirror, a jeweled pitcher, a lotus, and a mace.
May He who bears the conch and the discus grant you infinite prosperity forever. || 50 ||
"Lightning" refers to the state of oneness through the division of the body into two halves.
"Knowledge" and the others are indicated by their nominative case endings.
The grammatical connection is "wielding these afterwards.
Regarding the visualization of the weapons: the first four are in the left hands starting from the top, and the last four are in the right hands [starting from the top]. || 50 ||
One should recite this [mantra] one hundred thousand times;
then, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with a thousand blooming lotuses mixed with the three sweets (madhuratraya).
Worship should be performed upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal according to the method of the twelve-syllable mantra. || 51 ||
An oblation performed with milk-rice bestows the power to subjugate Lakṣmī;
by offering sesame seeds smeared with sweet substances, one shall accomplish all undertakings. || 52 ||
"Varṇalakṣam" means fourteen lakhs;
"tatsahasram" means fourteen thousands.
"Vikasitaiḥ" means [with blossomed].
Since even buds are permitted for use in worship, the specific mention here of "fully blossomed" [flowers] serves as an exclusion;
for the use of those that have blossomed on their own is excluded by its very prohibition. (51–52)

The Tāra (Oṃ), then "to Viṣṇu" at the heart, followed by the Lord of the Gods (Indra) ending in the dative case (sureśvarāya), then "to the one of great strength" (mahābalāya), and finally the pair of Ṭha syllables (ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ); this is the eighteen-syllable mantra. || 53 ||
The seer is Induvīrāṭ, the metre is [Anuṣṭubh], and the deity is Dadhivāmana.
With one [syllable] the heart is declared, with two the head, and with three the crest-lock (śikhā). || 54 ||
The armor (kavaca) is said to consist of five [syllables], the eye (netra) of that many syllables, and the weapon (astra) of two; such is the method for the limbs (aṅga) taught by the wise. || 55 ||
He states the mantra of Dadhivāmana as "Tāra" (Oṃ).
The word *namaḥ* is the heart-mantra (*hṛt*). Here too, as before, the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) with the visarga should be understood.
The intermediate [mantra] is: *surapatiḥ surapataye ṭhaṭhaṃ svāhā*. Some say it is encapsulated by the *praṇava* and the *śrībīja*.

The *praṇava* (oṃ) is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*). By the words "with those five," the traditionalists indicate that the wise have described another way of performing the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
That is as follows: having formed the five limbs with the five words beginning with the *praṇava*, one performs the sixth limb with the entire [mantra]. || 53–55 ||
On the crown of the head, the forehead, the pair of eyes, the ears, the nose, the lips, and the palate;
on the throat, the two arms, the back, the heart, the abdomen, and the navel. || 56 ||
One should place the eighteen syllables of the mantra upon the secret parts, the pair of thighs and knees, the two shanks, and the two feet; thereafter, one should meditate upon the deity.
In all instances such as "on the head" (mūrdhni) and so forth, there is the placement of each individual syllable.
The reading "in the pair of ears, the lips, and the palate" (karṇayugmauṣṭhatāluṣu) is a corruption;
the correct reading is "in the ears, nose, lips, and palate" (karṇanāsauṣṭhatāluṣu).
"Behind" means at the back.
However, in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*, it is said: "On the crown of the head, on the pair of eyes and ears, on the nose, and in the middle of the mouth."
In the throat, the heart, the pair of arms, the navel, the back, and the private parts;
And the syllables on the knees and the feet—
thus the locations have been stated.
By the word "afterwards," the placement of the feet (padanyāsa) is also indicated.
As they say: "One should place [the mantras] in the middle of the eyebrows, the throat, the heart, the navel, the genitals, and the foundation (ādhāra). (56-57)
Fair as a pearl, adorned with excellent ornaments of fresh gems, his lotus-face shines with clusters of locks of hair shaped like bees as he rests upon the moon;
with his two lotus-hands, he holds a golden pitcher filled with pure water.
We worship Him who holds a golden goblet filled with rice mixed with curd. || 58 ||
He speaks of meditation [dhyāna] as "liberated" (mukta), etc. || 58 ||

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice according to the prescribed rite, offering oblations of milk-rice or curd-rice soaked in clarified butter, amounting to one-tenth of that number.
One should worship him upon the previously described conceptualized seat ending with Candra; having conceived the form by means of the root mantra according to the procedure to be described. || 60 ||
Having worshipped the six limbs as before upon the filaments, and having worshipped Vāsudeva and the others, one should then worship the banner and the other [emblems]. || 61 ||
Keśava and the others [are placed] at the tips of the petals, followed by Surendra and the other [guardians];
then the thunderbolt and the other [weapons], and the eight elephants—this is declared to be the sevenfold enclosure (saptāvaraṇa) of the Lord, which is praised by the gods. || 62 ||
"Three hundred thousand" means three lakhs.
"According to the rule" is to be connected with what follows.
"Ending with Candra."
The meaning is that after having worshipped [the deity] within the solar disc (ravivahnimaṇḍala), one should finally worship the lunar disc (candramaṇḍala).
In this context, the worship extends up to the lunar disc,
because that [disc] serves as its seat.
As it has been stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "One should worship the lunar maṇḍala upon the seat consisting of dharma and jñāna."
The mantra of the lunar disc (candramaṇḍala) has also been extracted:
"To Viṣṇu together with Soma, for the nourishment of the three worlds, svāhā"—preceded by the *tāra* (oṃ) and the *hṛt* (namaḥ), one should worship that [disc] with this very mantra. Thus it is said.
This is indicated by the phrase "according to the rule.
The connection is that one should worship Him on the previously mentioned eight-syllabled seat of Nārāyaṇa, according to the procedure to be described hereafter.
"As before" means in the manner stated in the fourth [chapter].
Vāsudeva and the others, together with their Śaktis, as before;
and the eight [deities] beginning with Dhvaja, according to the well-known sequence of directions.
As it has been said:

"Dhvaja and Vainateya, Śaṅkha and Padma have gone to the cardinal directions; likewise, Vighna, Āryaka, Durgā, and Viṣvaksena have gone to the intermediate directions. Thus it is said. In that context, for the purpose of describing the worship in the east, south, north, west, and so forth, the author of the work [uses] these very [deities] for the eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa.
Vainateya and the others have been taught.
Keśava and the other eleven [deities] are on the tips of the petals; that is to say, outside of the eight-petaled lotus.
The eight elephants previously mentioned are to be placed in their respective directions. (59–62)
One should offer a thousand oblations of milk-rice and clarified butter to obtain prosperity;
by offering grain, one obtains grain, as well as those [oblations] produced from the *śatapuṣpī* flower. || 63 ||
An oblation performed with seeds numbering one thousand destroys all fear;
by offering pure curd-rice as an oblation, one is liberated from misfortune.
Recalling the form of the Three-Striding One (Viṣṇu), one should mutter the mantra with undistracted mind;
one shall be instantly liberated from bondage—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. || 65 ||
Having prepared an image on a cloth or a wall, the wise man should worship the Lord of Gods daily with fragrant flowers; thus he shall attain great prosperity. || 66 ||
*Śatapuṣpī* is well known as *sauṃpha* in the Kānyakubja dialect.
From *durgati*, meaning from poverty. (63–66)
A lotus with a pericarp radiant with the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), enriched with filaments shining with the eight syllables,
and possessing eight petals joined with pairs of mantra-syllables.
The final leaf shines with the remaining two pairs of syllables.
One should fashion the Vaiṣṇava yantra, which bestows all prosperity, encircled by the twelve syllables and surrounded on the outside by the letters of the Mātṛkā. || 68 ||
Regarding the yantra, he says "sasādhyeti" (together with the object to be accomplished).
One should write the Praṇava in the pericarp together with the person to be accomplished, the practitioner, and the ritual action.
By "with eight syllables," it is meant with the eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa.
By the phrase "with the remaining syllables," it is stated that one should write four syllables on the final petal;
the connection is that one should cause it to be surrounded outside by the letters of the Mātṛkā.
The procedure for this, as taught in another Tantra, is now set forth:
For this [mantra], the sage is Taila, the meter is Jagatī, and the deity is Hari, the giver of food;
the limbs [of the ritual] are performed with all the words beginning with the syllable Om.
The Lord, white as camphor, seated upon a lotus,
exceedingly gracious, with beautiful eyes, and enchanting with a lovely smile.
He holds a staff and a vessel of nectar, radiant like the autumnal moon,
and carries a bowl of curd-rice with side dishes and a vessel of wealth.
One should meditate upon Hari, the Lord of the Universe, who removes the suffering of the world;
having received initiation and become pure, one should recite [the mantra] twelve hundred thousand times.
At the conclusion of that, the wise practitioner should offer oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) amounting to one-tenth [of the total count];
furthermore, the worship should be performed upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal by the most excellent of practitioners.

One should draw a lotus with seventeen petals and inscribe the *praṇava* (oṃ) in its pericarp along with the name of the person to be protected; one should then encircle it in sequence with the vowels.
One should place the letters from *ka* to *kṣa*, excluding *la* and *jī*, upon the thirty-four filaments;
the mantra-syllables should be on the petals, and one should encircle the exterior with the two *tāra*s (oṃs).
Outside of those [two], the yantra formed from the two glorious seed-syllables (*śrībīja*) bestows all fruits.
Having invoked the deity into this yantra along with his limbs as before, [one should worship].
Having worshipped the Śaktis on the petals, one should worship the weapons of the world-protectors:
Pūṣā, Sumanas, Prīti, Jyoti, Saumyā, and Marīcikā.
Aṃśumālinī, Aṅgirā, Śaśinī, Candrikā, as well as Amoghā, Karuṇā, Chāyā, and Sampūrṇamaṇḍalā.
"Puṣṭi, Amṛtā, and Siddhi are declared to be the Śaktis.
Now, the yantra as described in the Brahmayāmala is stated:
Then, having made it circular in shape, one should properly inscribe the seed-syllable in the center of the moon-maṇḍala,
accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished.
Having written the syllables of Varuṇa (va) together with the fire-seed (ra), the māyā (ī),
and the bindu, one should fashion a lotus with seventeen petals and a pericarp.

O highly fortunate one, having fashioned the yantra with the mantra extending from the nāḍīs to the end of the void upon the petals of the lotus itself, and having performed the ritual anointing, one should recite the mantra.
"It is declared to be a great protection, and by its retention it brings forth prosperity.
Thus [ends the section]. Another yantra described in the Nāradakalpa is as follows:
"It is endowed with sixteen petals, possesses the *tāra* (the syllable Om), and has a radiant pericarp."
One should draw an eight-petalled lotus on the outside, with its petals aligned with the cardinal points.
Having written those eight syllables within them, one should draw a circle in front of them;
outside of that, one should draw an eighteen-petaled [lotus], and upon those petals, the eighteen syllables.
Having drawn a square at the end, provided with eight spikes,
one should inscribe the syllables in the corners, starting from the southeast, in their proper order.

"A practitioner of mantra, by means of this yantra, can effectively destroy colic, eye diseases, abdominal tumors, and the like, as well as uterine ruptures and other ailments, and even poisons. Thus it is said.
The syllable is the letter *ṭha*.
This duty to be performed by the lay practitioner (*upāsaka*), as taught in another tantra, is stated as follows:
"One should not eat *taṇḍulīśa* vegetables, nor likewise the fruit of the *udumbara* tree."
One should never eat from a vessel made of the nine types of grains used for ancestral rites;
likewise, one should not eat from a lotus leaf nor even from the leaves of the Arka plant.
One should never touch husks, cotton seeds, or ant-hills; nor should one step over cow dung or even the shadow of a Brahmin.
And one should perform the worship of the gods, the fire, and the guru, endowed with devotion.
Thus [ends verses 67–68].
Having uttered the word "udgira" by means of the sounds *praṇava* and *udgītha*, one should then speak the words "sarvavāgīśvara" at the end, followed by "īśvara. || 69 ||
One should utter "sarvam" at the end of the inconceivable state consisting of all the Vedas;
this mantra, beginning with "Tārā" (Om) and ending with "bodhaya dvitayam," is thus proclaimed. || 70 ||
The seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra] is declared to be Brahmā; the meter (chandas) is stated to be Anuṣṭubh;
the deity (devatā) is the all-pervading Hayagrīva, the bestower of the sovereignty of speech.
One should fashion the five limbs (pañcāṅga) of the mantra by means of the Tāra (Oṃ) and the individual feet of the mantra. || 71 ||
He states the Hayagrīva mantra with the words "udgirat" (emitting).
"Praṇavodgītha" refers to its essential form.
The phrase "one should utter all" in the mantra also ends in the accusative case.
The great mantra is in the form of a verse (*śloka*).
At the beginning of each verse is the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*).
The consonants within the mantra are the seed-syllables (*bīja*), and the vowels are the powers (*śakti*).
"Bestower of the sovereignty of speech"—this is the statement regarding the application (viniyoga). || 69–71 ||
The horse-faced one, possessing the luster of the autumnal moon,
adorned with ornaments made of pearls,
his pair of arms marked by the conch and the discus.
We worship him who has placed both hands upon his two knees. || 72 ||
He speaks of the meditation with the words "autumn" and so forth.
Here, immediately after the meditation, this mudrā should be displayed: the fingers of the right hand, facing downward, [should rest] upon the palm of the left hand.
Having fixed the middle one among them, one should raise it and then bend it downward.
"The mudrā dear to Hayagrīva imitates his form. Thus [it is said]. (72)

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; for the sake of attaining perfection in the mantra, one should offer oblations into the Vaiṣṇava fire ten times the number of recitations, using jasmine flowers soaked in honey. || 73 ||

One should worship Hayagrīva upon the seat (pīṭha) described as having eight syllables; having conceived the form by means of the seed-syllable (bīja), one should utter the extraction of that seed-syllable as follows: || 74 ||
"One hundred and twenty-five thousand [recitations] for the Vaiṣṇava fire, and thirty-two thousand for the Vahni [fire].
The meaning here is that one should worship the Vaiṣṇava seat (pīṭha) therein. || 73-74 ||
The seed-syllable (bīja) is said to consist of the sky (viyat), the syllable bhṛgu, the lord of the offering (arghīśa), and the bindu.
One should worship the four Vedas upon the filaments in the four directions.
He extracts the seed-syllable of Hayagrīva with the words "viyat" and so forth. "Viyat" is *haḥ*.
"Situated in Bhṛgu" means situated in the letter *sa*.
Arghīśa is the letter *ū* and the *bindu*; likewise, it is stated that in another ritual manual (*kalpa*), it is joined with the fourteenth vowel. This is said in the Śāṅkarakalpa:
"Śūnya joined with Śūnya is situated above the individual soul (jīva);
having rendered it endowed with grace, one becomes Vāgīśa, the granter of all desires. Thus [it is said].
Some read "having adorned [him] with Rudra.
This is the eight-syllable mantra beginning with this seed-syllable, ending with the word *hayagrīva* in the dative case (*ṅe*), and ending with the word *anta*. The seed-syllable is *haṃ*.
The power (śakti) is *sau*.
The meter is the *gāyatrī* of the Goddess. Everything else is to be understood as being like the previously mentioned one-syllable ritual procedure (*ekākṣaravidhāna*) that will be described later.
These two are also independent mantras.
One desiring knowledge should recite them encapsulated by Vāk, or encapsulated by Bālā and Tārtīyā; one desiring subjugation should recite them encapsulated by Kāmarāja.
*Haṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *Saṃ* is the power (*śakti*).
The seers and so forth are as follows: Brahmā, Triṣṭubh, and Hayagrīva are proclaimed as the seer and the rest.
The procedure for the six limbs is declared by means of the root mantra joined with the six long vowels.
Seated upon a white lotus, pale as milk, holding in his hands a rosary, a lotus, a book, and the gesture of granting desires;
he is beautiful with a multitude of spotless garments and ornaments.
I bow to Viṣṇu, whose face is that of a horse, the conqueror of the enemies of the gods.
Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, one should at the end perform a fire sacrifice with clarified butter ten times that number.
One should worship on the previously mentioned pedestal, having invoked the Goddess Gāyatrī, and then perform the ritual adoration.
One should utter the word "Vāgīśvara" ending in the dative case (ṅe), followed by the word "pada";
then one should say "Hayagrīvam," also ending in the dative case, and thereafter utter "dhīmahi."
One should utter "tat" at the end of the syllable *haṃsa*, and then "pravadecca pracodayāt.
The first enclosure consists of the limbs (*aṅga*), and the second consists of the eight horses (*aśva*).
Likewise, the horse of wisdom, the horse of intelligence, the horse of mindfulness,
the horse of knowledge, the horse of prosperity, and indeed the horse of the Mistress of Speech.
Vidyāvilāsasuhṛd, Hayānta, and Nādamardana;
with Medhā and the others, there should be the third [set], and they are Medhā, Sarasvatī, [Śraddhā, Dhṛti, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Tuṣṭi, and Puṣṭi].
Prajñā is the third, Vijayā the fifth, and Aparājitā;
Tuṣṭi is the seventh, Puṣṭi the eighth, and Śraddhā is considered the ninth.
In another kalpa, however, those [consorts] were Lakṣmī and the others: Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rati, Prīti, Kīrti, Kānti, Tuṣṭi, and Puṣṭi as the eighth.
The fourth [chapter] begins with Kumuda and others: Kumuda, Kumudākṣaka, Puṇḍarīka, Sarvanetra, Vāmana, and Śaṅkukarṇaka.
Sumukha and Supratiṣṭha should be [the second and third]; the fifth [should be] with the World-Guardians (Lokapālas), and the sixth should be with their weapons; thus the worship is prescribed.

The seed-syllable conjoined with the letter *ra* and situated between two *huṃ* syllables—one should recite the mantra with the name of whomever [one desires]; one will kill that person, without a doubt.
O Goddess of the Suras, by reciting for one month the king of seed-syllables situated between two *huṃ* sounds, one will cause the entire world to feel hatred; of this there is no doubt.
One should write the mantra with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) on birch bark and wear it on the arm;
this shall be a great protection that destroys all defects. Thus [it is said].
The yantra described in the Śāṅkara-kalpa is stated as follows:

One should write the name of the practitioner within two *praṇavas* (oṃ) joined together, situated between two *akāras*, using turmeric on a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*). This should be written upon the seed-syllable (*bīja*).

On the eight petals, one should write the eight-syllable mantra of Hayagrīva; on the filaments, the vowels; on the exterior, it should be encircled by the consonants from *ka* to *kṣa*; and outside of that, one should draw a square enclosure (*bhūpura*).

This is declared to be the immobilization of speech (*vākstambhana*); when enclosed within a pair of shallow bowls (*śarāva*) and wrapped with yellow thread, it produces muteness without delay. Thus [ends verse 75].

One should worship the Vedas, the limbs [of the Veda], the Smṛtis, the Nyāya, and all the Śāstras; one should honor the deities of the limbs according to the prescribed rule within the intermediate petals.
Outside, one should offer to those [deities] the weapons of Lokeśvara, beginning with the vajra.
He who worships the deity in this manner shall become Vāgīśvara himself. || 77 ||
An oblation performed with bailva fruits is proclaimed to bring prosperity;
one desiring imperishable eloquence and fortune should offer kunda flowers.
Regarding the phrase "in the intermediate directions":

the ritual application is as follows: "Obeisance to the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*) consisting of Śikṣā, Kalpa, Vyākaraṇa, Nirukta, Jyotiṣa, and Chandas; obeisance to the Smṛtis; obeisance to the treatises on Logic (*nyāyaśāstra*); obeisance to all treatises," and so forth.

"By means of the ritual procedure" (vidhānena) refers to the places of the [deities] beginning with Āgneya in the fourth row, within the petals; this is an exception to the worship of the filaments and limbs in the fourth row. (76–78)
Ghee consecrated by this mantra and cooked with the juices of *brāhmī* brings to men an unimpeded expansion of poetic talent. (79)
One should consume vacā consecrated with this mantra every morning;
one becomes a commentator on all the Vedas, Āgamas, and other scriptures before long. There is no other equal to this mantra, which bestows knowledge and sovereignty. || 80 ||
Regarding the phrase "manuneti":
because it has been stated that "even an oil that is free from impurities may be processed in a pure liquid," one should cook the ghee in four times the amount of *brāhmī* juice.
Having removed the remainder of the clarified butter, one should drink it after consecrating it with this mantra. ||79-80||
The mantra for Rāma is "Ananta agnyāsana sendur bījaṃ rāmāya hṛt. This six-syllabled mantra is declared to be a wish-fulfilling jewel that grants the desires of those who worship it. || 81 ||
Brahmā is declared the sage, the Gāyatrī the metre, and Manu the deity;
Rāma, the destroyer of the Rākṣasas, has been proclaimed by the foremost of teachers. || 82 ||
The best of mantra-knowers should perform the six limbs in sequence with his own long-syllabled seed-mantra;
he should place the six syllables of the mantra in the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), between the eyebrows, at the heart, the navel, the genitals, and the two feet. || 83 ||
He states the Rāma-mantra as "Ananta" and so forth. "Ananta" is the letter *ā*; "Agnyāsana" is the seat of the letter *r*; "sendu" means with the bindu (the nasal dot).
By the word "bīja" (seed-syllable), it is indicated that this mantra consists of a single syllable.
As it has been said:
"The bed situated in the fire, adorned with the half-moon,
is declared to be the single-syllable mantra, the king of mantras, the celestial tree."
All of this, beginning with the Ṛṣi and so forth, will indeed be explained below.
To this effect it is stated in the Nirvāṇakhaṇḍa of the Skandayāmala: "The letter *ra* is fire, and I myself am said to be that; Viṣṇu is the moon, and he is called *ma*."
But Brahmā, situated between us two, is said to have the form of the sun.
"Having swallowed the three luminaries, the all-pervading Space itself,
as Nada, designates you alone, the Supreme Lord, as Pure Being.
By the phrase "to Rāma, [the seed-syllable] Hr̥t," it is stated that this is also a five-syllabled mantra.
As they say:
"The two syllables *ra-ma* together with their bases (*sa-pratiṣṭha*), followed by *vā-yu-hṛt*, are remembered as the five-syllabled mantra.
Viśvāmitra is declared its sage (*muni*), the *paṅkti* its meter (*chanda*), and [Vāyu] its deity."
Rāmabhadra, the seed-syllable, and the power-syllable, along with the first letter [of his name],
one should sequentially place the mantra in the middle of the eyebrows, the heart, the navel, the anus, and the feet.
Alternatively, one may perform the six-limbed rite as before, or the weapon-mantra with the five-syllabled mantra;
in the center, there is a forest at the foot of a wish-fulfilling tree, crowded with flowering creepers.
Lakṣmaṇa had fixed an arrow to the corner of his eye,
while Jānakī watched the Lord as he held the two fans.
With his head radiant with a mass of matted locks, dark-complexioned, and surrounded by hosts of sages,
he sat upon the Puṣpaka chariot while Lakṣmaṇa held a parasol over him.

"One seeking victory, especially so, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, as before, [addressed] to the crusher of the ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), together with Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa. Regarding the term "mantra": it refers to the following.
Thus, when combined, the meaning is that the mantra consists of six syllables (*ṣaḍakṣara*).

By describing its application with the words "the wish-granting jewel, the *cintāmaṇi*," it is indicated that there are many varieties of six-syllabled forms and many varieties of seven-syllabled forms, even without [explicitly stating] its own seed-syllable (*svabīja*).
As it is said in the Nirvāṇakhaṇḍa of the Skandayāmala:
"O Viśvarūpa, all words that denote the universe are Your names;
nevertheless, Your root mantra is the imperishable seed of all things."

This [mantra] beginning with *praṇava* (om) leads to liberation; that beginning with *ramā* (śrīṃ) leads to enjoyment; that beginning with *vāgbhava* (aiṃ) is for the perfection of speech; and that beginning with *māyā* (hrīṃ) grants all desired objects.
"This entire [mantra] is the Great Power (Mahāśakti), the sovereign Cintāmaṇi of mantras.
Elsewhere: "The five-syllabled [mantra] beginning with Tārā, consisting of one's own desire, power, speech, and Lakṣmī..."
The six-syllabled mantra is of six kinds and bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
Preceded by each of the fifty syllables of the Mātṛkā-mantra,
[the seed-syllables] such as Lakṣmī, Vāk, and Manmatha, and others beginning with Tārā, may be employed in manifold ways.

The mantra consisting of four syllables, preceded and followed by each of the glorious seed-syllables *māyā* (hrīṃ) and *manmatha* (klīṃ), is itself the bestower of all desires; it remains so even when expanded to six syllables.
This [mantra] should end with *svāhā*, or with *huṃ phaṭ*, or with *namaḥ*.
It consists of Brahmā, Samohana, Śakti, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and likewise [the others].
Agastya and Śrī Śiva are declared here as the sages in sequence;
the meter is named Gāyatrī, and the deity is indeed Śrī Rāma.
Alternatively, from the seed-syllable *kāma* (klīm) comes the sage Viśvāmitra;
the meter is Gāyatrī, beginning with the word "devī"; and Rāmabhadra is its presiding deity.
The seed-syllables and powers are as before; thus,
the qualifying term "Destroyer of Rākṣasas" is to be prescribed.

*Rāṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *namaḥ* is the power (*śakti*). As it is stated in the *Śaunakakalpa*: "One should know that the first syllable is the seed, as well as the power and the salutation."
Thus [it is said].
Some say that *āya* is power (*śakti*). [The term] "possessing long vowels" means possessing the six long vowels.
"By its own seed-syllable" means by the seed-syllable of the mantra and so forth.
By the word "successively," it is stated that the six limbs [are performed] with six syllables.
As they say:
"Or, by means of the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels, or by the syllables of the mantra, one performs the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*).
Thus,
*andhu* refers to the secret."
By the phrase "O best of men," this is what is meant:
the placement of the five-syllable mantra is as follows;
the placement of the seven-syllable mantra is upon the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), the middle of the eyebrows, the throat, the heart, the navel, the secret place, and the feet.
With two syllables, [the breath] is at the aperture of Brahmā and the heart;
with three syllables, at the secret place and the end [of the body]; with four syllables, at the secret place and the end of the feet. || 81–83 ||

[I worship] Rāghava, whose lovely luster is like that of a dark rain-cloud, who perpetually sits in the *vīrāsana* posture, holding in one lotus-hand the *mudrā* consisting of wisdom while the other rests upon his knee; and [I worship] Sītā, standing by his side, her hand like a lotus, resembling a flash of lightning.
I worship her who gazes [at him], her limbs radiant with various ornaments such as a crown and armlets. || 84 ||
He speaks of meditation [in the section on] time.
He will describe the heroic posture (vīrāsana) later;
the characteristics of the knowledge-seal (jñānamudrā) were previously stated.
The connection is: "I worship Sītā, who is on the left side and gazing at Rāghava. In this reading, the meditation for the Sītā-mantra to be recited hereafter is also stated.
In some places, the reading is "paśyantam" (seeing).
In that case, the connection is: "I worship Rāghava, who was seeing Sītā.
And it has been said:
"With eyes meeting the lotus-face of Sītā seated upon his left lap, [he who is] cloud-like in hue.
Thus [it is said].
*Ākalpa* means ornamentation.
Here, immediately after the meditation, one should display the Garuḍa-mudrā as described in the Nārāyaṇāṣṭākṣara [mantra]. || 84 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; then, one should offer oblations into the consecrated fire with auspicious lotuses ten thousand times, and thereafter feed the Brahmins.
"Six hundred thousand [of] the color-mark" means six hundred thousand.
"In the fire of Acīta" means having invoked [the deity] into the fire of the Rāma-pīṭha. || 85 ||
One should worship [the deity] upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal and fashion the image with the root mantra.
With the mantra "Śrīṃ sītāyai" ending in the *dviṭha* (svāhā), one should worship Sītā situated at the side. || 86 ||
"Śrīṃ sītāyai svāhā.
This mantra is independent as well.
As it has been said: "The mantra of Sītā is declared to be both independent and subordinate to the [main] limbs."
Thus it is said; and also in the Nirvāṇakhaṇḍa of the Skandayāmala:
"Brahmā utters your power, the Goddess Vāc, in order to attain you."
Viṣṇu meditates upon you alone, the Suṣumṇā, the supreme power of the Lord.

"Īśvara worships Sītā within the interior of the sky in the form of a *bindu*; Sadāśiva [worships her] consisting of *nāda*; and Śiva [worships her] who has transcended the void (*khātītā*) and is beyond mind (*unmanī*).
Regarding the procedure for this and other matters, it is stated in the *Agastisaṃhitā* as follows:
Janaka is its seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī its metre (chandas), and Manu its deity (devatā).
The blessed Sītā is declared to be its seed-syllable (bīja), and the two final letters [Ṭha and Tha] are its power (śakti).
One should fashion the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) using the initial syllables joined with long vowels;
one should worship her upon the Vaiṣṇava pedestal and meditate on her as being united with Rāghava.

"Having [visualized her] with hands like golden lotuses and intent upon gazing at Rāma, one should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times; thereafter, one shall accomplish one's desired aims. Thus [ends verse 86].
In front and on both sides, [he should draw] the Śārṅga bow and arrows; outside of that, Hanumān with Sugrīva, and Bharata with Vibhīṣaṇa. || 87 ||
He was reading these names— Lakṣmaṇa, Aṅgada, Śatrughna, and Jāmbavān—
upon the petals, while Hanumān stood before him holding a book.
One should worship Bharata and Śatrughna on the two sides holding chowries;
one should worship Lakṣmaṇa in the west with two hands holding a parasol. || 89 ||
Sṛṣṭi, Jayanta, Vijaya, Surāṣṭra, Rāṣṭravardhana, Akopa, the one named Dharmapāla, and Sumantra—at the tips of the petals [he should place these]. || 90 ||
Then one should worship the Lords of the World (Lokeśas), endowed with all ornaments;
thereafter, one should worship their weapons, such as the vajra and others, on the outside. || 91 ||
Thus, when the mantra has been perfected through worship and other rites, one should accomplish the ritual actions;
one should offer oblations with jasmine flowers sprinkled with sandalwood water.

For bringing a king under one's control, [one should use] lotuses; for the abundance of wealth, grain, and so forth, [one should use] blue lotuses. By means of an oblation of blue lotuses, one shall bring the entire world under one's power. || 93 ||
A man should offer oblations with *bilva* flowers to attain wealth;
by offering *dūrvā* grass, the practitioner of mantras shall become long-lived and free from disease. 94.
The mantra practitioner, having offered red lotuses, obtains his desired wealth;
one who desires intelligence should offer fresh palāśa flowers. || 95 ||
A wise person who drinks water consecrated with that mantra becomes a poet within a year;
by eating food over which that mantra has been recited, one shall attain great health. || 96 ||
"In front" (*agre*) and "on both sides" (*pārśvadvaye*) are locative cases in apposition with different substrates (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
Therefore, the connection is as follows: "in front" means before one's face, and "on both sides" means on the left and right sides; [one should place] the Śārṅga bow and the arrows.
By this, it is stated that up to this point constitutes the primary worship (*mukhyapūjā*).
And it is said:
"On the left side of the triangle is the Śārṅga bow, and on the right are the arrows;
one should say, 'Śaṃ, obeisance to the Śārṅga bow,' and likewise, 'Śaṃ, obeisance to the arrows.'"
"Then, having obtained permission for the worship, one should worship the rays and then the limbs.
As for the worship-diagram (*pūjāyantra*), it is as described in another tantra:
"Within the eight petals of the subterranean chamber (bhūgṛha), there is an exceedingly beautiful hexagon.
Or else, it refers to the *dhāraṇayantra* which will be described in this very context.
As it is stated in the *Agastisaṃhitā*:
Then, one should draw the [mandala] starting from the hexagon and ending with the earth-element as before;
in its center, one should write the *tāra* (the syllable Om), and likewise in the six corners in sequence.
The syllables of the root mantra itself are placed at the joints, and the limb-mantra of Manmatha is placed there;
Māyā is placed on the cheeks, and the writing of the vowels is considered to be on the filaments.
On the petals, as before, the garland-mantra should indeed be written in sequence;
it should then be encircled by the ten syllables and the consonants beginning with *ka*.
One should write the seed-syllables (bījas) of Narasiṃha and Varāha in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
and here, within this yantra, one should worship [the deity] along with the limbs (aṅgas) and the retinue (āvaraṇas).
"Having written [the mantra] on gold, silver, or birch bark, one should begin the worship.
Thus,
the limbs [of the deity] are placed outside that, in the six corners beginning with the southeast (āgneya).
As it has been said: "Having worshipped the deities of the limbs in the six corners, beginning from the southeast corner.
And elsewhere also: "The first enclosure in the hexagon should consist of the limbs, starting from the southeast in due order."
Thus:
on the western side, behind the deity.
Here, having first indicated Hanumān and so forth, and subsequently [indicating him] with "the one reciting" and so forth, [it refers to] the four who are primarily [intended].
He speaks of worship along with meditation (*sādhyāna*).
By this, it is also indicated that the mantras of these four are likewise primary.
As stated in the *Agastisaṃhitā*:
I shall now proclaim the Āñjaneya-mantra, the sole means for attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
which was revealed by Śaṅkara out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Upon seeing one who is intent on the practice of mantras, ghosts, spirits, piśācas, ḍākinīs, and brahmarākṣasas flee in all directions.
This unsurpassed king of mantras is both the primary element and a subsidiary member;
having first uttered the word "namaḥ," one should then utter the word "bhagavate."
The word *āñjaneya* ending in the dative case (*ṅe*), and likewise the word *mahābala*,
followed by the feminine suffix of fire (*vahnijāyā*)— this indeed is the supreme mantra of Hanumān.
The eighteen-syllable mantra is declared to be the bestower of all accomplishments;
its seer is Īśvara himself, and Anuṣṭubh is said to be its meter.
Hanumān is declared to be the deity; "haṃ" is the seed-syllable (bīja), and the power (śakti) is that which arises at the end.
The gratification of Hanumān is indeed proclaimed as the primary fruit.
One should place [the mantra] "Namo bhagavate cāñjaneyāya" on the two thumbs; immediately thereafter, one should place [the mantra] "Rudramūrtaye" on the two index fingers.
Likewise, one should clearly place [the mantra] for Vāyusuta with the two middle fingers,
and similarly for Agnigarbha with the two ring fingers.
Furthermore, for the sake of Rāma’s messenger, the wise one uttered the mantra of the weapon for the purpose of warding off Brahmā’s weapon with his two little fingers.
Having thus performed the six-limbed yoga, O Sage, one should meditate with undistracted mind upon [the deity] who has the luster of crystal, the radiance of gold, two arms, and joined palms.
With his lotus-face repeatedly beautified by a pair of earrings,
he performed ten thousand recitations (ayuta) of the mantra before Rāma or Śiva as part of the preliminary rite (puraścaryā).
"One should indeed perform worship on a Vaiṣṇava or Śaiva pedestal,
constantly eating only at night and having conquered the senses, without the surrounding enclosures (āvṛtis).
Having extracted the letter preceded by 'ra' and joined with the mark of the bindu..."
This Nandī, together with Lakṣmaṇa and Manu, was endowed with salutation.
The sage of this [mantra] is Agastya, its meter is said to be Gāyatrī,
Lakṣmaṇa is declared to be the deity, and "laṃ" is indeed its seed-syllable and power.
Salutation indeed constitutes the application for the four aims of human life;
one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using one's own long-voweled seed-syllable.
Two-armed, with a body radiant like gold, with eyes resembling lotuses,
holding a bow and arrows in his hands, and with a mind entirely intent on the service of Rāma.
Worship should indeed be performed upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal, complete with its limbs and enclosures.
After performing the preparatory rite (*puraścaryā*) seven hundred thousand times, the practitioner, having attained perfection, may then accomplish his goals.
This same rule applies to Bharata, and this same procedure applies to Śatrughna as well;
for these are prescribed as subordinate members, yet they are also recognized as being primary.
Whether at the beginning or even at the end of the worship of Rāghava,
these [deities] must also be worshipped by those who desire the fruit of enjoyment.
In the Rāmapīṭha,
Lakṣmaṇa is always to be worshipped as a primary limb, indeed eternally with preeminence.
In such a way that there may be worship of Rāma, so too [should there be] constant worship of him as well.
If one who is firm in his vows desires the fruitfulness of the worship of Rāma, [he should act accordingly].
With that same effort, one should also perform [the rites] for Lakṣmaṇa in detail;
for indeed, O Sage, there are many varieties of the Śrī Rāma mantra.
Those seeking its accomplishment should always perform this, even for the sake of Saumitri,
either one thousand and eight times or one hundred times, with a well-composed mind.
The *lakṣmaṇa-manu* should be recited without weariness by those seeking liberation.
Those who recite the *rāma-mantra* without having first recited the *lakṣmaṇa-manu*, [attain no fruit].
Even the skillful do not attain the fruit of that which has been recited;
here, no rule regarding enemies or friends should be applied at all.
Whoever, established in solitude, should daily recite the Lakṣmaṇa-mantra,
is liberated from all sins and attains all desires.
Indeed, this mantra was taught by Śāṅgīṇā specifically for the sake of practice;
having performed the twilight worship according to the rules, the knower of mantras [should proceed] with the root mantra.
Having become disciplined at the three times of day and having personally performed the daily rites,
one who possesses initiation should proceed according to the rule, preceded by the permission of the Guru.
He who, being free from desire, worships the Lord in this manner without regard for worldly benefits, is liberated from all sins and goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Having received initiation according to the prescribed rule from a guru who is free from blemish,
devoted to right conduct and other virtues, self-controlled, a householder, and one who has conquered his senses;
In accordance with that permission, having performed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) according to the rules,
he— having burned away the entire flood of merit and demerit— is one whose mind is stainless.
One shall attain the eternal state from which there is no return;
or, if possessed of desire, having obtained one's wishes and enjoyed pleasures as desired.
Having remembered his past births for a long time, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
such is the case for the practitioner of the Śrī Rāma mantras—how could there be any possibility of sin?
Thus, for us, the mind of Lakṣmaṇa does not go to the supreme goal;
some are intended solely for liberation, while others are means for worldly ends.
"And this one alone is known as the supreme bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (Verses 87–96)

One should write the syllable *Tāraṃ* (Oṃ) in the center and the mantra in the six corners; one should then write the *Aṅga-mantra*, *Māyā* (Hrīṃ), and *Smara* (Klīṃ) at the junctions and on the flanks of the corners. Afterwards, one should place the group of vowels (*Svaragaṇa*) upon the filaments and the *Mālā-mantra* within the middle of the petals.
In the eighth [chapter], there are five syllables from the mantra, starting with the letter 'gu' (ga) and ending with the letter 'ha'. || 97 ||

Having encircled [the diagram] with the ten-syllable mantra and with the letters beginning with 'ka' (kādi) in the outer square (bhūpura), one should write the seed-syllables (bīja) of Narasiṃha and Varāha in the cardinal and intermediate directions. || 98 ||
He describes the *dhāraṇayantra* with the words "the *tāra*" and so forth.

In the center, within the pericarp (*kaṇīkā*), one should write the *praṇava* (Om) together with the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and the ritual action (*karman*).
The *manu* is the six-syllabled name of Rāma.
At the joints means at the six joints.
The limbs refers to the mantras of the six limbs.
In the corners and cheeks means in the corners and the temples.
One should draw *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) in one place and *kāma* (the syllable *klīṃ*) in another.
Then, in the location of the filaments of the eight-petaled lotus, one should write the sixteen vowels.
The *mālāmantra*, which will be described later, consists of forty-seven syllables.
"Six measured by the mouth of Guha" means six in number. "By the ten-syllable [mantra] to be described" is to be connected with "encircled by the letters beginning with Ka."
The connection is that one should write the seed-syllables in the cardinal and intermediate directions within the *bhūpura* (the outer square).
The seed-syllable of Narasiṃha will be described in the following chapter;
the seed-syllable of Varāha will be described in the mantra of Varāha. || 97–98 ||
One should utter "Namo bhagavate" followed by the dative case ending for Raghunandana;
at the end of "rakṣoghnaviṣadāya," one should pronounce "madhurādi" and so forth. || 99 ||
"To the one with a serene face," then "to the one of immeasurable splendor," then "to the child," then "to Rāma," and after that "to Viṣṇu"—
this is declared to be the Mālā-mantra, beginning with the *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*. || 100 ||
He states the *mālāmantra* with the word "namaḥ.
From "raghunandana," the fourth case ending [is applied] to form "raghunandanāya.
In the phrase "prasannavadanāya amitatejase," there is no *sandhi*.
Because forty-seven syllables are fixed within the yantra, this garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*) is also independent.
Its seer and other attributes are as follows: the sage is Pitāmaha, the metre is Sātyanuṣṭubh, and the deity is [the Lord].
And Rāma was consecrated to the kingdom; likewise, Bīja and Śakti were so in former times.
One should recite this [mantra] encapsulated by the *tāra* (om), *vāk* (aim), and *kāma* (klīm) seeds;
[placing them] on the head, around the face, between the eyebrows, and also upon the two eyes.
In the two ears, the two nostrils, the two cheeks, the two lips,
as well as the two teeth, the region of the mouth, and at the joints and tips of the arms and feet.
One should assign the syllables to the throat, the breast, the heart, the pair [of arms], the two sides, the region of the back, the abdomen, the locus of the navel, and the private parts. Then,
one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with those [syllables] numbering seven, six, seventeen, and eleven.

I bow to Murāri, whose hands hold a blue lotus, a conch, a bow, a sword, and arrows; whose eyes are like lotus petals; who wears yellow garments; and who is sweet with the nectar of his smile, possessing the pure beauty of a blooming blue lotus.
He should deliberate together with the daughter of the King of Mithilā.
Having meditated in this manner, one who has conquered the senses should mutter [the mantra] twelve lakhs of times,
using bilva fruits, flowers, and leaves combined with the three sweets (honey, ghee, and sugar).

One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) ten times the number of mantras recited, using milk-rice mixed with the three sweets and white lotuses; likewise, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) in all cases.
One should worship on the previously described pedestal, having invoked the deity into the image;
this is declared as the first enclosure of limbs (aṅgāvṛti), while the second is performed with Lakṣmaṇa and the others.
The third [wheel] consists of Nārada and others; the fourth by Lakṣmī and others;
and the fifth by the world-leaders such as Sṛṣṭi and others, situated in the four directions.
The sixth [offering] is said to be with the vajra and other implements; the seventh sacrifice is proclaimed [to be performed] by Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, Śatrughna, and Hanumān.
Sugrīva is declared the fifth; Vibhīṣaṇa is said to be the sixth;
Aṅgada is declared the seventh; and Nīla is cited as the eighth.
Nārada, Vasiṣṭha, and Vāmadeva as the third;
Jābāla, Gautama, Bharadvāja, and Kaśyapa.
Vālmīki is declared the eighth, as are Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī;
Rati, Prīti, Kīrti, Kānti, Tuṣṭi, and Puṣṭi follow in this order.
Sṛṣṭi, Jayanta, Vijaya, Siddhārtha, Kāryasādhaka,
Aśoka, Śrīvatsa, and likewise Gadā are in the eastern direction.
On the right are the Pāñcajanya conch, the gem known as Kaustubha, and the forest garland; on the left are the discus and lotus, as well as the Śārṅga bow, arrows, sword, and the Kāma-weapon.
In the west, [he should worship] the Dharma-Garuḍas and the excellent mantras of the Dharma-pālas. Thus, [99–100].
Then there is the mantra "Jānakīvallabhāya," which is dear to the Fire-god (Pāvaka). This ten-syllabled Rāma-mantra, beginning with "Hum," has thus been declared. || 101 ||
The ten-syllable mantra is also independent.
Its seer and other attributes are as follows: this ten-syllable mantra has Vasiṣṭha as its seer and Virāj as its meter.
The meter is the deity, O Rāma, and Sītā is the one who takes his hand in marriage.
The first seed-syllable is Dviṭha (KṢA), the Śakti is KĀMA (KLĪM), and the limbs are as before.
[These are placed] on the head, forehead, between the eyebrows, palate, throat, and also the heart.
One should assign the ten syllables of the mantra to the navel, the two arms, the knees, and the feet;
[one should meditate on] the city of Ayodhyā, within a variegated pavilion made entirely of gold.
Rāghava was seated upon a throne atop the Puṣpaka chariot, beneath a canopy bound with mandāra flowers and adorned with arched gateways.
He was being praised by auspicious Rākṣasas and monkeys seated upon celestial vehicles,
and attended by sages who bowed low before him.
His left lap was adorned by Sītā; he was attended by Lakṣmaṇa; he was dark-complexioned with a serene countenance, and decorated with all ornaments.
At the conclusion of the meditation, the wise practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
he should then perform a fire sacrifice with a tenth part of that number using bilva fruits mixed with sweet substances. Thus it is said.
Its worship is to be understood in the same manner as that of the six-syllable mantra. || 101 ||
A yantra consecrated through recitation and other rites, fashioned from gold leaf or similar materials, when worn upon the arm, bestows victory, prosperity, and prowess. || 102 ||
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "recitation and so forth," worship and the attainment [of results] are meant.
By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "prepared on a golden plate and so forth," silver, copper, and birch bark are meant.
Furthermore, for each specific type of writing, there is also a specific time.
As stated in the Agastisaṃhitā: "In a golden vessel it lasts for as long as one lives; in silver, twenty years;
on birch bark, twelve years; and on a copper plate, half of that."
"Thus, through a specific method of writing, the accomplishment of the yantra is established.

This ritual procedure that has been declared is to be understood as pertaining to the two-syllable mantra of Rāma, namely "Rā-ma"—this is the remainder [of the sense]. Furthermore, the fire [syllable *ra*] joined with Nārāyaṇa [the syllable *ma*], or the belly [the syllable *a*] alone.
This two-syllabled king of mantras bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The seer and other [limbs] for the single-syllable mantra are as previously stated; the six-limbed ritual is performed with the first [syllable].
There are six types [of mantras] using the Tāra, Māyā, Ramā, Anaṅga, Vāk, and one's own seed-syllables.
The two-syllable king of mantras bestows all desired fruits;
it ends with Candrabhadra, and there are likewise two types of four-syllable mantras.
The Ṛṣis and so forth for these should be understood by the wise as being the same as before. Thus [ends verse] 102.
The procedure for the Rāma-mantra, worshipped by the gods, has been declared:
one should utter "Tāram" (Om), "namo bhagavate," and then the word "Varāha. || 103 ||

For the sake of form, may there be *bhūrbhuvaḥsvaḥ* for the Lord; immediately thereafter, at the end of the word, grant me the status of lordship, and at the very end, cause it to be granted. || 104 ||
The mantra, ending with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), consists of thirty-three syllables;
Bhārgava is declared to be its sage, and Anuṣṭubh is cited as its meter. || 105 ||
The wise have declared that Devatādivārāha is the deity of this mantra;
"To the Single-Tusked One" is said to be the heart, and "To the Sky-Meteor" is remembered as the head. || 106 ||
One should assign the five limbs as follows: "To the Lord of Splendor, the Crest-lock"; "To the One of Universal Form, the Armor";
and "To the One with Great Fangs, the Weapon. Thus one should arrange the five limbs. || 107 ||
Having thus stated the fourfold mantras proclaimed in the *Mahākapila*, *Nārada*, *Hayaśīrṣa*, *Pañcarātra*, *Skanda*, *Yāmala*, and *Vaiṣṇava* Tantras,

and because the mantras of Narasiṃha and Varāha are indicated within the Rāma-mantra yantra, he first extracts the Varāha mantra— beginning with "Tāra" (the syllable Om)— since there is much to be said regarding Narasiṃha. "Vahnijāyā" is *svāhā*.
*Huṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*).
In that context, the application is stated according to the meaning of the mantra. (103–107)

I praise Him who, from the knees to the feet, resembles excellent gold; from the region of the navel downwards, possesses the luster of pearls; from the region of the throat upwards, resembles the rising sun; and from the head, has a blue radiance;
and who holds in His hands the discus, the lotus, the sword, the shield, and the one called the mace.
The primordial Boar, possessing the power of granting gifts and fearlessness, with his excellent tusk resting upon the earth as his foot. ||108||
He speaks of the meditative absorption (dhyāna), beginning with "from the foot": "rathacaraṇa" means a wheel;
"dara" means a conch shell.
"Gadākhyām" means the club named Gadā.
"Kṣitiḥ" is the earth; its "caraṇaḥ" is the foot, that is, the base. He whose fangs shine there—that is, he whose fangs are fixed in the earth—is the meaning.

The visualization of the weapons is as follows: for the two upper [hands] beginning with Dakṣa (the right), there is the first [weapon]; for the two lower ones situated beneath them, there is the other [weapon]. After this visualization, these two mudrās should be displayed.
Their characteristics are as follows:
Then, having turned the left hand upward and placed it over the deity, one should incline it;
this is declared to be the mudrā known as Vārāhī. Thus [it is said].
"The right hand facing upward and the left hand facing downward, with the tips of the fingers joined together—this is the mudrā known as Vārāhī. Thus [ends verse 108].

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with lotuses smeared with honey using one-tenth of that number; then one should worship [the deity] upon the pedestal of Viṣṇu. || 109 ||

Having conceived the image by means of the root mantra according to the procedure to be described, one should worship the limbs beginning with the heart (hṛdaya) in the four directions starting from the east. || 110 ||
In the corners and above and below [the central deity], one should place the missiles; outside of that, the discus and other weapons:
the discus, conch, sword, shield, mace, spear, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. || 111 ||

Having worshipped the world-protectors (lokeśas) externally, one should offer the weapons (astras) outside. Through meditation, the deity bestows wealth; through recitation (japa), he bestows the earth. By means of recitation, worship, and other rites, he grants riches, grain, land, and royal splendor.
On the pedestal of Viṣṇu, one should worship Varāha according to the procedure to be described; this is the implied meaning.
The phrase "starting from the east" is an exception to the previously mentioned placement beginning with the southeast (āgneya) and so forth.
"Outside of that" refers to the spaces between the petals. (109–112)
When the sun is in Leo, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight,
one should place a white stone in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), touch it, and recite [the mantra] ten thousand times.
The term "siṃha" (lion) is also an elliptical designation for Aries and Sagittarius.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, when the sun has entered Aries, Leo, or Sagittarius, one should dig."
Thus:
"a white stone" means one that abounds in fruit.
"Measuring ten palas and placed in a vessel such as one made of bilva wood," so says Padmapādācārya. || 113 ||
Facing north, one should bury that stone in the ground;
it shall destroy the afflictions caused by enemies, thieves, and malevolent spirits.
Regarding the instruction "one should bury it," it should be understood that this is done while reciting the Varāha-mantra together with the seed-syllable of the earth (Bhū-bīja).
As it has been stated by the Teachers:
The practitioner, with face turned upward, should place her beyond the human realm.
Thus [it is said]. || 114 ||
On a Tuesday at sunrise, the practitioner, reciting the mantra, should collect earth from the field of the person to be accomplished; he should then divide that earth into three parts. || 115 ||
Having placed one [portion] on the stove and likewise another in the cooking vessel, he should thoroughly stir it in cow's milk and then add the cleaned rice grains. || 116 ||
The practitioner of mantra, while reciting the mantra, should properly cook the *caru* offering in the consecrated fire;
thereafter, having removed the *caru* from the fire, he should worship the deity according to the prescribed rite. || 117 ||

Having worshipped with incense, lamps, and other offerings, one should again offer oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru) soaked in clarified butter into the kindled fire, until one hundred and eight [oblations] have been completed. || 118 ||
In this manner, one should offer oblations during seven Sundays for the sake of attaining mastery over a sacred field (kṣetra).
At dawn on a Friday, [one should take] earth from the ground where the object of the rite is to be accomplished. || 119 ||
Having taken the oblation and prepared it as before, the wise one should offer it;
thus, opposition in the field, along with calamities such as thieves and the like, shall perish. || 120 ||
One should offer three thousand oblations with this mantra using fuel-sticks produced from the rājavṛkṣa tree; for him, there shall be all prosperity. || 121 ||
The practitioner of mantra should daily offer one hundred and eight oblations of śāli rice;
his residence shall shine with abundant heaps of grain. || 122 ||
One should offer oblations with clarified butter; from the mandala, one shall obtain gold.
With parched grain smeared with honey, one obtains a maiden or whatever one desires. || 123 ||
One should offer fresh blue lotuses mixed with the three sweets;
by means of the previously mentioned number of oblations from the mandala, one attains great prosperity. || 124 ||
The teacher Padmapāda states that by the word "mantrī" (the mantra), its association with the seed-syllable *bhūḥ* is expressed;
the burying [of the vessel] occurs precisely at the time of the *abhijit* asterism, because of the statement: "In the middle of the field, at the time of *abhijit*."
"From the object of accomplishment,

which is to be seized"— the phrase "reciting" (*sañjapan*) is to be connected with every instance. By the word *samā* (in the context of *saṃjapet*), the conjunction with the seed-syllable of the earth (*bhū-bīja*) is indicated.
The connection is that one should cook the *caru* in a well-consecrated fire.
In this context, by the word "well" (*samyak*), it is meant that [the fire] has undergone the eighteen consecrations (*saṃskāra*) ending with the *homa* of the Mahāgaṇapati mantra.
By the word "mantra," the conjunction with the seed-syllable of the Earth (*bhū-bīja*) is indicated.
The application of those seeds should also be understood to apply at home.
Just as it was stated by the word "vidhi" (rite) that one should worship [the deities] from Maṇḍūka up to Puṣpa in the fire,
the word "ādi" (and so forth) includes the offering of food (*naivedya*).
Immediately thereafter:
Āro is terrestrial.
Having prepared the oblation, one should prepare the *caru* (cooked rice).

By the statement "having prepared the oblation as before, one should offer it as before," it is indicated that one hundred and eight [offerings] are to be made according to the sequence prescribed for the ritual on a Tuesday.
By the word "fresh" (*navaiḥ*), it is stated that while elsewhere stale materials may also be accepted,
here that is not the case.
By the previous calculation, it is three thousand, and so forth. (115–124)

In the center, one should write the seed-syllable accompanied by the *tāra* (oṃ); in the pair of fire-purifiers (triangles), the letters of the wheel; in the six corners, the limbs (*aṅga-mantras*); then at the joints, a lotus with petals formed by the constituent parts; and upon its filaments, the eight syllables.
One should write the eight mantra-syllables in the middle of the petals, and the fourth set of mantra-syllables, numbering eight, in the fourth [layer].
The remainder [of the letters] is on the leaf in front, within the eight-petaled lotus of the directions, enriched with the vowels situated upon the filaments. || 125 ||

One should write the mantra-syllables, numbering as many as the deities, along each petal; then, on the outside, one should write the final syllable on the filaments with the consonants from *ka* onwards on the sixteen-petaled white lotus according to the rule.
Having written the mantra-syllables in pairs, one should then write the remaining syllable located on the final petal.
Then, it is surrounded by the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished, with the seed-syllables of Tāra (Oṃ), Kṣmā (Bhūmi, Laṃ), and Kola (Vajra, Hūṃ) interspersed within them.
It is surrounded on the outside by the syllables of the mantra interspersed with the letters of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
On the corners of this earth-mandala (*bhūbimba*), one should write the seed-syllable of the Earth (*bhūbīja*) conjoined with the *sādhya*.
On the eight spikes, one should draw the Boar (*vārāha*) together with the seed-syllable of the Earth. || 127 ||
He describes the yantra with the words "in the center" (*madhye*).
In the middle of a hexagon formed by two fire-purifiers (triangles) mutually intersecting— one in the locative case (*madhye*) and the other in the locative absolute (*vyadhikaraṇe*)—

one should write the seed-syllable (*bīja*) to be described later, which is that of Varāha, together with the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*), and accompanied by the names of the practitioner and the subject, as well as the ritual action.
In this context, it should be understood that the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*) resides within the *cakra-mantra*. Regarding the "six-spoked" [figures], this refers to the hexagons (*ṣaṭkoṇa*).
The "wheel-syllables" (*cakravarṇa*) are the letters of the *cakra-mantra*, excluding the *praṇava* which will be mentioned later.
The experts of the tradition maintain that the six limbs of the *cakramantra* are located at the joints;
this is how it was explained by the teacher Padmapāda in his commentary on the verse from the *Prapañcasāra*: "the six limbs of the *cakramantra* in the apertures.
[The phrase] "with the petals of the instrument" refers to the four-petaled [lotus].
The eight-syllabled Nārāyaṇa-mantras;
on each filament, the mantra-syllables of the Vārāha-mantra, two syllables at a time,
numbering eight (vasu).
On the fourth petal there are nine syllables.
Regarding the phrase "as prescribed": here, the term "petal" and so forth is to be connected with every instance.
*Tāra* is the *praṇava* (the syllable Om).
*Kṣmā* is the seed-syllable of the Earth, extracted in the *Mahāgaṇapati-paṭala*.
The *kola*-seed is the seed-syllable of Varāha, which will be described below.
By what are these [seeds] qualified? One should encircle them with those [mantras] in whose midst are the syllables of the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
By this, it is stated that the seed-syllables (*bīja*) are to be completely enveloped by the syllables of the name of the one to be accomplished.
As it was said by the Teachers:
"One should cause [the syllables] to enter by means of the *tāra*, *mahī*, *kola*, and *arṇa* [syllables], encircled by the [syllables] of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
This means that it is surrounded by the syllables of the mantra and the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished.
The characteristic of the *dabhīta* will be explained in the twenty-third [chapter]:

"Outside of that, with the syllables of the mantra, the *dabhītas*, and the letters of the word to be accomplished (*sādhya*)," according to the statement of the Teacher; thus, the connection is that it is surrounded by the external circle of the earth.
Regarding the phrase "on the eight spikes," this refers to those formed at the tips of the eight lines of the *vaddhīta*.

In that regard, it is the traditional teaching (sampradāya) that one should write the syllable of Varāha on the right of the central line and the seed-syllable of the Earth (bhū-bīja) on the left. || 125-127 ||
The seed-syllable of Vārāha is said to be the letter *sa*, the *arghīśa* (the letter *ha*), the *bindu* (the nasal dot), and *gagana* (the letter *kha*).
[It is prepared] with yellow pigment (*rocanā*), agallochum (*aguru*), camphor (*karpūra*), lac (*lākṣā*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), and sandalwood (*candana*). || 128 ||
On an auspicious day, for the sake of accomplishing all desires, one should draw the yantra with a golden stylus upon a surface ground with cow-dung water. || 129 ||
One should inscribe the yantra on a gold plate for the attainment of royal glory;
on a silver plate for the success of obtaining a village; and on a copper plate for the acquisition of wealth. || 130 ||
One should write it on birch bark for the attainment of one's own desires, or on linen for the accomplishment of worldly goals;
having perfected the yantra through recitation, worship, and other rites, one should employ it for one's desired purpose. || 131 ||
This machine, when well-prepared, should be buried in villages, towns, or kingdoms; on an auspicious day and so forth, one should worship it together with its limbs in all directions. || 132 ||
Due to the power of the deity, that supreme region cannot be seen by those afflicted by minor deaths, thieves, and the like, nor by the great terrors of spirits and serpents. || 133 ||
He extracts the Vārāha seed-syllable with the words "sārghīśa":
*gagana* is *ha*, *arghīśa* is the vowel *ū*, and it is conjoined with the *bindu*;
this too is an independent mantra.
The seer and so forth for this [mantra] are as follows:
Hayagrīva is declared to be the seer, the metre is Triṣṭubh, and the deity is Varāha;
one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the long [vowel] joined [to the seed-syllable].
"All [rites], such as meditation and worship, for this [deity] are like those of the Vārāha-mantra.
However, in another ritual manual (*kalpa*), "bhūḥ" is extracted [as the seed-syllable].
As it has been said:
"His navel is Vāmaśravas, the progenitor; his seed is said here [to be the mantra].
By the word "etc. in the phrase "by means of recitation, worship, etc.," the *sampāta* (the ritual pouring) is intended.
As it has been said:
"One performs this consecrated mantra by pouring oblations of ghee.
It is "well-accomplished" (susādhita) through the recitation (japa), worship (pūjā), and the pouring of oblations (sampāta).
By the word "beginning with an auspicious day" (*śubhavārādau*), it should be understood that this refers to the commencement of a fixed sign (*sthirarāśi*) and so forth.
Regarding the statement "one should worship with all its limbs in the directions," the intended meaning is as follows:

having meditated upon oneself in the form of Varāha, one should invoke Varāha into that yantra, worship him, and then, according to the sequence prescribed for worship, [worship] the heart and other limbs in the four directions starting from the east.
Having worshipped the Astra-mantra, one should worship [it] in the directions, above, and below.
As it has been said:
"The practitioner of mantra, having assumed the form of a boar, should bury the yantra in the location of the target."

"Having mounted the boat called 'Sthira' (the fixed sign), one should properly cast the oars, which are the limbs, into the directions. This is the supreme [instruction]. Furthermore, even its eight-syllable mantra is revealed here in this context: oṃ namo bhagavati vajracaṇḍe hūṃ phaṭ || 10 || This is the eight-syllable mantra. It is taught by the venerable Mañjuśrī in the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*: "The eight-syllable mantra, O Goddess, is the most excellent among all mantras. It grants success in every respect; there is no doubt about it. The meaning of the mantra is as follows: "Oṃ" is the seed-syllable of the Tathāgata Vairocana. "Namaḥ" signifies salutation to the Blessed One. "Bhagavati" means "O Blessed One," denoting the state of being possessed of power (*bhaga*). "Vajracaṇḍe" means "O fierce one with a vajra," indicating the nature of the deity. "Hūṃ" is the seed-syllable of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya. "Phaṭ" signifies the destruction of all obstacles. By reciting it one hundred thousand times, one obtains the siddhi of the Pinakin. By reciting it one hundred thousand times, one obtains the siddhi of the Dhanvin. By reciting it one hundred thousand times, one obtains the siddhi of the Khadgin. By reciting it one hundred thousand times, one obtains the siddhi of the Phalakin.

"In the eight-syllabled great mantra, the first syllable is *śākhā* and so forth; the second is the *vyāhṛti*; therefore, [the mantra is] *vārāhāya hṛdam*. For this [mantra], Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Jagatī is the meter (*chanda*), and Śrī Vārāha is the deity (*devatā*).
*Bhaṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
*Oṃ* is the power (*śakti*).
The visualization (*dhyāna*)—

I worship the Lord Varāha, whose body is dark and whose lotus-face is exceedingly blue; who stands upon a lotus, holding the Earth on his lap with his noble arms, and constantly bearing the conch, mace, lotus, and discus, possessing a fierce splendor.
"He is surrounded by the splendors of the earth, Lakṣmī, and Rati, and by the radiance of his shield and sword.
The remainder is the same.
The two diagrams for this [deity] are now described:
One should write the seed-syllable in the center of the four-petalled lotus, the eight-syllabled mantra on the filaments,
and all the individual and collective *vyāhṛtis* upon the petals.
One should place the eight vowels upon the filaments, the Nārāyaṇa mantra upon the eight petals,
the consonants beginning with 'ka' upon the thirty-two petals, and the Ānuṣṭubh mantra upon the [remaining] petals.
"Surrounded on all sides by the name *Hakṣetī* and encircled by nooses and goads—one obtains every desired fruit through its recollection and retention.
Likewise: "In the center, in the seed-syllable, and likewise in the eight-spoked [wheel], one should write its eight syllables."
On the eight-petalled lotus on the outside, one should write the mantra in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
"That wheel, in the form of a pair, is renowned as the Vārāha;
whatever the practitioner of mantra desires, he shall accomplish all of it by means of this. As for the mantra: *Parajāta mahārāva varāhāṅgā'vanerdhava.*
I bow to that Lord Vālījādhava, who increases day by day.
Thus [ends the section on verses] 128–133.

The heart-mantra for the Goddess Bhagavatī should follow; immediately after that, for Dharaṇī, one should hold [the mantra] ending with "Dharaṇi" in the dual case, concluding with the two syllables of "Phaṭ," beginning with "Dhruva" (Om). || 134 ||
The Heart of the Earth (Dharāhṛdaya) is said to consist of nineteen syllables;
Varāha is declared its sage, and Nivṛt is cited as its metre. || 135 ||
The deity of all beings is considered to be the Earth (Prakṛti). The Heart is said to consist of three [syllables], and the Head is declared to consist of four. || 136 ||
The crest-lock (śikhā) is assigned three [syllables], the armor (kavaca) is considered to consist of five;
the eye (netra) is declared to be two, and the weapon (astra) likewise becomes two.
One who knows the ritual procedure should thus perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) with the syllables of the mantra. || 137 ||
In connection with the Varāha-mantra, he states the Dharaṇī-mantra, beginning with "the heart. "The heart" refers to the word *namaḥ*.
Here too, as before, the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) with the visarga should be understood.

The *praṇava* (Oṃ) is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*). By the phrase "one who knows the ritual procedure," it is indicated that [the worship] is performed with the six-limbed mudrās of Śakti. (134–137)
Dark-complexioned, adorned with variegated garments, umbrellas, and ornaments, seated upon a lotus throne, her breasts full and her body bent;
[holding] two blue lotuses and a cluster of fresh rice blossoms.
We worship the Earth who holds the parrot. || 138 ||
The practitioner of mantra should reverently recite the Heart-mantra of the Earth one hundred thousand times;
he should then perform oblations with milk-rice mixed with honey in a tenth part of that number. || 139 ||
The visualization of the weapons is as follows: the first two are at the upper right and left [hands] of Dakṣa and the others, while the other two are at their lower [hands]. (138–139)
One should worship her on the pedestal of Viṣṇu according to the procedure to be described hereafter;
first, one should worship the limbs: Earth, Fire, Water, and Air. (140)

Having worshipped [the deities] in the petals of the cardinal directions, one should worship their respective kalās in the petals of the corners; furthermore, the guardians of the quarters (āśāpālas) should be worshipped again, accompanied by their weapons such as the vajra and others. || 141 ||
In this way, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra shall accomplish his own heart's desires;
he should perform oblations with red lotuses mixed with the three sweets. || 142 ||
There would be a thousandfold prosperity on the earth through auspicious blue lotuses; likewise, by means of *priyaṅgu* flowers smeared with honey, one obtains wealth, grain, land, and royal glory.
One should offer into the consecrated fire a cluster of rice blossoms soaked in the three sweets; from the mandala, one shall become a lord of the earth. || 144 ||
Regarding "of Viṣṇu":
*glauṃ* is the seat-mantra (*pīṭhamantra*) for the yoga-seat of Vasundharā.
