It should be understood that the conceptualization of the form (*mūrtikalpana*) is performed by means of this very seed-syllable (*bīja*).
"In the petals of the directions" refers to the front, back, right, and left; "in the corner petals" refers here to those starting with the southeast (āgneya);
"their digits" refers to Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti.
By this [verse], the *svabījayoga* is indicated for the attainment of the earth according to one's own desires;
the *śrīyoga* for the acquisition of wealth and grain;
the *śaktiyoga* for fame; and elsewhere, the *varāhabījayoga* is also suggested. (140–144)
Having taken earth from the site of the person to be accomplished on a Friday at the break of day, one should cast it into water;
once that [water] has been purified, one should cook the sacrificial oblation (caru) therein. || 145 ||
One should offer that [substance] into the fire together with milk and ghee;
by thus offering it on Saturdays for six months, one shall obtain the earth. || 146 ||
The practitioner who worships the Earth in this manner becomes dear to the Earth through cattle, jewels, wealth, and so forth; of this there is no doubt. || 147 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the *Śāradātilaka* composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra. 15.
"bth" means on Friday;
"tām ambhasi" means one-third part.
Or it may be milked.
In that case, it should be understood that one portion is placed on the hearth and one portion in a vessel. (145–147)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition. 15.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Hereafter, I shall duly expound the great mantra of Nārasiṃha.
One should first utter "Ugra" and "Vīra," and immediately thereafter, "Mahāviṣṇu. || 1 ||
Having addressed the blazing state that faces all directions, one should utter "Nṛsiṃha," "Bhīṣaṇa," "Bhadra," and then "Mṛtyurmṛtyu.
"I bow" and "this" are proclaimed; this is the King of Mantras, the celestial tree. || 2 ||
The seer is Brahmā, the meter is declared to be Anuṣṭubh, and its deity is Narasiṃha, who is saluted by gods and asuras. || 3 ||

He extracts the king of mantras of Nṛsiṃha with the words "ugram" and so forth. In this mantra, all [the names] are in the accusative case. The mantra consists of thirty-two syllables and is in the form of a verse (śloka).
Because this [mantra] is Vedic, its status as beginning with the *praṇava* (OM) should be understood;
for it is stated as such in the *Tāpanīya*.
However, the traditionalists say that it should be encased by the seed-syllable of Śakti, using the term "celestial tree" (*suradruma*).
Its seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *haṃ*, and its power (*śakti*) is *īṃ*.
Thus it is stated in the Tāpanīya [Upaniṣad]:
"Om! The gods indeed said to Prajāpati: 'What is the power and the seed-syllable of the Nṛsiṃha mantra-king, which belongs to the Anuṣṭubh meter?'"
"Tell me, O Blessed One," [he said].
Prajāpati replied:
"This is indeed the Māyā of Nārasiṃha; she creates all this, she protects all this, and she destroys all this. Therefore, one should know her as this power, Māyā."
He who knows this power of illusion (māyā-śakti) crosses over evil, conquers death, attains immortality, and enjoys great prosperity.
Regarding this, the exponents of Brahman deliberate:
"Is it short, or long, or is it elided?"
If it is short, one crosses over all evil and attains immortality;
if it is long, one attains great prosperity and attains immortality;
if it is protracted, one becomes possessed of knowledge and attains immortality.
Space is the ultimate resort of all these beings.
Indeed, all these beings are born from space alone; having been born from space alone, they live;
and into space they pass away and merge.
Therefore, one should know that space is the seed. || 1-3 ||
The heart-mantra is proclaimed with four syllables; the head is likewise uttered with that same number. The crest is declared with eight, and the armor is said to consist of six.
The number of those [syllables] is said to be the "eye" (two); the weapon-mantra is formed by the syllables of the *karaṇa*.
[These are placed] on the head, forehead, and eyes; and at the joints of the mouth, arms, and feet. || 5 ||
One should then place the syllables in due order upon the tips of the fingers, the belly, the heart, the throat, both sides, the other limbs, and the crown of the head. || 6 ||
"By that many" means by four; "by those many" means by six.
"By the letters of the instruments" means by four.
The traditionalists, however, describe the six limbs differently as follows:

with the four feet beginning with *hāṃ* and accompanied by two halves, [one worships] the Self of Bliss (*ānandātman*), the Self of Love (*priyātman*), the Self of Light (*jyotirātman*), the Self of Māyā (*māyātman*), and the Self of Flame (*jvālātman*).
From "jñāna" onwards, these [mantras] constitute the six limbs in sequence.
However, in the Tāpanīya [Upaniṣad], only five limbs are mentioned: for it says, "His limbs are indeed five."
There are four feet and four limbs;
everything together with the *praṇava* constitutes the fifth. He describes the arrangement of the syllables, beginning with "the head."
In that regard, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) by pronouncing each syllable of the two *praṇavas* together with its *bindu*. As it is said in the *Tāpanīya*:
"This entire [universe] is this syllable *om*."
Therefore, there is an *oṃ* syllable on both sides of every single syllable;
the exponents of Brahman teach the placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables upon the back, which is a secondary limb [of the body].
*Kakudi aparagale*.
Now, the tenfold nyāsa, which brings about the presence of Nṛsiṃha and provides all protection as taught in another tantra, is described.
As they say:
The tenfold ritual placement (nyāsa) that brings about the presence of Nṛsiṃha is proclaimed here;
first among them, the placement on the fingers (aṅgulīnyāsa) is described.
One should place [the mantras] individually on the thumbs and other fingers at the first and last joints;
one should place the remaining [mantra] on all the fingers, and the two syllables on the palms.
In the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the forehead, the space between the eyebrows, and the eyes—and below the eyes as well;
on the cheek, at the root of the ear, and above the chin, on the lower lip.
In the throat, the right arm, the left arm, the heart, the body, the navel, the abdomen,
the palms of the right and left hands, the hips, the genitals, the thighs, the knees, and the shanks.
The wise practitioner should place the letters of the mind-mantra (mantra) in the ankles, the toes of the feet and hands, all the joints, the body hairs, and in the blood, bones, and marrow.
One should place two syllables on each part: on the feet, the ankles, the knees, the hips, the navel, the region of the heart, the arms, the throat, the chin, the lips, and the cheeks.
One should place [the syllables] on the two ears, the mouth, the nostrils, the eyes, and the head;
however, one should place the words on the face, the hair, the eyes, and the ears.
One should place [the syllables] in the mouth, the heart, the navel, and also on the hips, knees, and feet;
likewise, on the nose, eyes, ears, navel, heart, head, arms, and feet.
One should place the four syllables of Manu at the knees, hips, and navel on all sides; two halves [of the mantra] should be placed on the head, and its limbs from the heart down to the feet.
I bow here to the nine words beginning with *ugra* and ending with *namāmyaham*, [placing them] in the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, and eyelashes.
One should place [the syllables] in the heart, the navel, and from the waist down to the feet in nine locations;
one should likewise arrange those same [syllables], beginning with Vīrā (or Tārā), just as before.
"The wise one should place those very [mantras] beginning with Nṛsiṃha as before. Thus [ends verses 4–6].
Possessing a luster like a mountain of rubies, terrifying the hosts of Rākṣasas with his own radiance,
with his lotus-like hands resting upon his knees, three-eyed, and adorned with glowing red ornaments;
holding the discus and conch perpetually with his two arms, and with a face shining with prominent fangs—
I bow to the all-pervading Lord Nṛsiṃha, whose tongue is a blazing flame and whose mass of hair is uplifted. || 7 ||
He speaks of meditation with the words "māṇikyā" and so forth;
here, immediately after meditation, one should display these mudrās.
Having placed both the chin and the lips evenly between the knees,
with the hands resting on the ground, he trembled again and again.
Having opened the mouth wide and licking the tongue,
this is the Nārasiṃhī mudrā, which is proclaimed as the foremost.
Having bound the three fingers starting from the little finger with the left thumb,
one should form the *mudrā* pertaining to Nṛsiṃha like a trident, facing forward and pointing upward.
Having likewise pressed the two little fingers with the two thumbs, the remaining fingers joined together and turned downwards— this is considered the mudrā of Nṛhari.
Having turned the hands downward and extended them to the region of the navel, one should bring the shoulders together with the two index fingers; this is called the mudrā known as Antra.
Having turned the two hands upward and joined their palms,
one should place the right middle finger upon the left ring finger.
With the two index fingers joined behind and the two thumbs resting against the index fingers—
this is considered the Face Mudrā for the presence of Nṛhari.
Having likewise formed the facial mudrā, one should press the two middle fingers with the two index fingers; this is the fang mudrā, which destroys all sins. Thus it is said.
It should be understood that these [mantras] are common to all *nṛsiṃha* mantras. || 7 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations according to the rules with milk-rice soaked in ghee, once the fire has been duly consecrated. || 8 ||
When this has been done, the practitioner shall become a mantra-master endowed with majesty. One should fashion the image upon the previously described pedestal using the root mantra. || 9 ||
On that day, one should worship the enemy of the Daityas according to the prescribed rite with undivided mind;
having first propitiated the limbs [of the deity], one should then worship them again in the cardinal and intermediate directions. || 10 ||

One should again worship the Lord of Birds, Śaṅkara, Śeṣa, and the Lotus-born One in their proper order; furthermore, one should worship Śrī, Hrī, Dhṛti, and Puṣṭi within the fire-pits and other locations. || 11 ||
The world-protectors (Lokapālas) are to be worshipped, and after that, their weapons;
thus, once the mantra has been perfected through recitation and other means, one should accomplish the desired rites.
"Varṇalakṣam" means thirty-two lakhs;
"tatsahasram" means thirty-two thousand.
"According to rule" (vidhivat) means having worshipped the seat of the deity (devatā-pīṭha) therein.
"In what was previously stated" refers to the statement regarding the eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa.
"According to rule" means by the procedure that will be described hereafter.
Furthermore, by the phrase "according to rule," it is indicated that one should worship the ten enclosures (*āvaraṇas*) using the mantra taught in the *Tāpanīya* Upaniṣad.
"But 'having propitiated' is according to the manner explained above. (8-12)

I bow to Narahari, who possesses the brilliance of a rising sun at its peak, radiant with a crown and a necklace, his face formidable with fangs; who has pierced the lord of the asuras with many long arms featuring gleaming claws,
and whose three eyes are the very nature of fire, the moon, and the sun.
I worship him who vomits forth fire, terrifying with its mass of flickering crests like a cluster of lightning bolts. || 13 ||
He speaks of meditation (dhyāna) with the words "rising," etc. || 13 ||
One should contemplate a gentle rite for a gentle purpose and a fierce rite for a fierce one;
the practitioner of mantras should offer oblations with lotuses and other auspicious flowers into a fire kindled with bilva wood.
One attains a thousandfold prosperity by means of bilva leaves, or likewise by flowers or fruits; and from the oblation of dūrvā grass, one attains freedom from disease. || 15 ||
One should eat white *vacā* root, over which the mantra has been recited, every morning;
the practitioner of mantra attains perfection of speech like another Vācaspati. || 16 ||
"Saumya" refers to the subject of this meditation;
"saumyam" means the previously mentioned meditation.
The meaning is that it refers to the domain of cruel applications.
"Cruel" refers to what was just mentioned.
This has been stated by the Teachers:
And its practice is said to be twofold: clarity and, specifically, ferocity.
With clarity there should be the worship of the means (*sādhana-pūjā*); with the other, the ritual application (*prayoga-vidhi*). Thus it is said.
"Śrī" refers to the creeper of Lakṣmī.
"In that manner" means that one attains prosperity (śrī).
In the phrase "health" (arogatām), the word "attains" (āpnoti) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. || 14–16 ||
Having worshipped the deity in the water with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should daily perform oblations there with dūrvā grass, one hundred and eight times.
Calamities caused by minor spirits, fevers, and the like perish there—
in that water— therein, "calamities" (upasargāḥ) refers to misfortunes (upadravāḥ).
As it has been said by the Teachers:
"The practitioner of mantra, having worshipped with eight thousand blades of *dūrvā* grass, should then perform oblations in water;
thus the calamities surely come to peace, for there is the Vedic revelation: 'Water is indeed peace.'"
When great portents and calamities arise, this fire-oblation brings peace to men;
furthermore, whatever else is desired by one's own mind, that wish is attained, and one shall become beloved by all people.
Thus [ends the section]. 17–18.
When an evil dream occurs during the night, one should bathe and recite this mantra.
Free from drowsiness, the knower of mantras thereafter experiences auspicious dreams;
immediately following an evil dream,
he should likewise recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Regarding "good dream":
even that very same bad dream becomes one that yields the fruit of a good dream in this way. || 18-19 ||
In the great forest, which was filled with fear from tigers, thieves, wild beasts, and the like. || 19 ||
This *mantra*, when recited, protects the practitioner from other dangers;
likewise, ashes consecrated with this [mantra] [ward off] poisons, planetary afflictions, and great diseases. || 20 ||
By the power of this mantra, one shall destroy [all evils] very quickly—even in the face of terrible malevolent sorcery, insanity, great portents, and great fear. || 21 ||
A person should recite the mantra and remember the God; thus he shall be liberated from suffering.
[He should meditate on Him] in the form of a lion, most formidable, and terrifying with its claws and fangs.
Having first remembered oneself as the enemy, one should then meditate on a young deer;
having seized it by the neck, one should then swiftly hurl it away.
By this, the eradication of the enemy occurs along with his sons, friends, wife, and others. || 23 ||
"Wild animals" refers to lions and the like;
by the word "poison," the venom of snakes and so forth is meant;
and "planets" refers to the eighteen [types].
By this [mantra] "mahāmāyā-nitya," fevers and other ailments are included;
as they say:
"It shall pacify poison arising from rats, spiders, scorpions, centipedes, and the like."
This mantra should be recited one hundred and eight times over ashes and other substances.

"This mantra shall pacify ailments caused by mantras, medicinal herbs, or malevolent sorcery, as well as diseases of the head, eyes, ears, heart, throat, and belly, along with fever, erysipelas, urinary disorders, and consumption. Thus it is said.
The word "enemy" (ripum) is connected with what follows;
the syntactical construction is "one should cast that enemy.
In the reading "purā," the construction is "having first remembered oneself."
In the reading "puraḥ," the meaning is "in front of oneself. (19–23)

Having first placed the name of the one to be subdued under the word "Death" (mṛtyu), one should meditate on oneself as Hari, tearing apart the enemy with the tips of his sharp claws and fangs. || 24 ||
One should constantly recite the mantra one hundred and eight times without sloth;
before long, an enemy dear to Yama shall arise from the maṇḍala. || 25 ||
Regarding the phrase "the first word 'mṛtyu'":
in the mantra there are two words for "death," namely *mṛtyumṛtyum*.
The meaning is that one should omit the first word *mṛtyu* and, in its place, employ the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*).
"Harim himself" means having meditated upon oneself in the form of Nṛsiṃha. (24–25)
One should make an effort according to the prescribed rules to ward off the enemy army, using wood of the *bibhītaka* tree kindled in the fire for the destruction of foes. || 26 ||
Having meditated upon the god Nṛhari and worshipped him with flowers and other offerings, one should offer one thousand arrows individually, together with their roots and stalks, into the fire.
One should mutter the mantra while imagining oneself devouring the enemy, and one should cast the arrows as if striking them down. || 27 ||
The passage beginning with "one should exert effort" and ending with "it would be a calamity for the lord of the earth" constitutes a single application [of the ritual].
He describes that very effort according to the rules in the verse beginning with "he should fear.
By the term "crushing of enemies," it is indicated that one should perform the visualization (*dhyāna*) of the deity as fierce (*krūra*).
"Separately" means every day.
Regarding the phrase "one should mutter as if devouring the enemy," this is its meaning:
at the time of the fire-oblation (*homa*), one should mutter—that is, recite the mantra—while meditating upon oneself as Nṛsiṃha, thinking, "I am devouring the enemy."
Then, meditating upon himself as "I am Nṛsiṃha, piercing the enemies," one should cast those arrows into the fire.
As it has been said:
"One should recite the mantra as if devouring [the foes], and cast the fuel-sticks as if piercing the enemies."
Thus [ends the section on] verses 26–27.
Having performed oblations for seven days, the mantra-practitioner, desiring victory over the kingdom of the enemy, should dispatch the king’s desired army at an auspicious moment. || 28 ||
Having performed the sacrifice, one should dispatch the king's desired army at an auspicious moment; this is the connection [of the verse]. || 28 ||
In front of her, having visualized Nṛhari slaying the circle of his enemies, one should perform the ritual application until she returns once more. || 29 ||
Having conquered all his enemies along with the glory of heroism, the victorious king returned in comfort, [honored] with villages, fields, wealth, and other gifts. || 30 ||
With a pleased mind, he should properly gratify his minister with riches;
for if the minister is not satisfied, there will be disaster for the lord of the earth. || 31 ||
"Having remembered the ritual application (prayoga)" means that as long as [the king] does not arrive, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) and the previously mentioned meditation (*dhyāna*).
As it has been said: "As long as the enemy king has not arrived, one should recite while remembering the deity."
Thus [it is said].
The various types of meditations mentioned in other tantras are written here:
Narasiṃha, who is most terrifying, with a radiance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction,
wearing a garland of intestines, fierce, and adorned with a necklace around his neck.
He has a serpent as his sacred thread and is beautifully adorned by a lion;
he bears the moon upon his crest, has a blue throat, and possesses three eyes in each of his faces.
He was adorned with ten arms resembling iron clubs,
holding a rosary, a mace, a lotus, and a conch shell white as cow’s milk.
Holding a bow, a mace, and an excellent discus,
as well as a sword, a trident, and an arrow— Nṛhari in the form of Rudra.
Having the luster of an *indragopa* insect, blue, moon-like, and resembling gold—
from the east up to the north— it has faces directed upward and possesses all colors.
Thus one should meditate upon the formidable Hari for liberation from all diseases;
he is divine, the remover of all death, and the bestower of all perfections through mere remembrance.
When the great task was to be meditated upon, then Nṛsiṃha, the lord of all worlds, adorned with every ornament, appeared sixteen cubits in height.
Two are rich in the act of rending, and two are distinguished by the drawing out of entrails;
two bear the discus and the conch, while two carry the arrow and the bow.
Two hold swords and shields; two carry clubs and lotuses;
two bear nooses and goads; and two seize the crowns and garments of their enemies.
Thus, with one-pointed mind, one should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord Nṛhari, adorned with sixteen mighty arms, possessing the dark-blue luster of a rain cloud, and performing fierce deeds.
In matters of the highest importance, one should meditate upon Nṛhari, the primordial of all beings, the Lord who bestows all perfections, who possesses twenty-two hands.
In the right [hands], there is a discus, a lotus, an axe, a noose,
a plough, a mace, as well as the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) and a goad.
In his left hands, he holds a sharp-edged spear, a bhindipāla, a sword, a mallet, and a tomara;
and on the left side [of his body], he holds a conch, a shield, a noose, and a trident.
Then [he should offer] fire, the boon-granting [gesture], the spear, and the water-pot;
thereafter, the bow, the threatening gesture (tarjanī-mudrā), the mace, the hand-drum, and the serpent.
With two hands he presses the knees and head of his enemy;
with arms raised upward, Hari wears a garland of entrails.
With his two lower arms, he performs the rending of Hiraṇyakaśipu—
an act that brings joy to his devotees and inspires fear in the Daityas.
One should thus meditate upon Nṛsiṃha, who removes the great fear of death.
Now, another auspicious meditation is described, which cures diseases of the mouth.
Seated upon a golden-winged bird, facing forward, with a complexion like ten million full moons,

possessing manes like garlands of lightning, three eyes, and yellow garments and ornaments; holding aloft in his hands the discus, conch, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons— [he is] the death of all poisons, diseases, and so forth.
One should constantly meditate upon Śrī Nṛsiṃha, who destroys [all obstacles] with his own roars, and who is praised by the gods. Thus [ends verses 29–31].

One should draw the seed-syllable (*bīja*) conjoined with the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) in the center; then, having divided the syllables of the mantra into four parts, one should write them upon the eight petals and surround [the whole] with the alphabet (*lipi*).
On the outside, it is encircled by two houses (*geha*), namely the earth (*vasudhā*) and the enclosure (*koṇa*), bound by the seed-syllable situated in the corners.
The Yantra brings about the destruction of minor poisons, planetary afflictions, diseases, and enemies; it is the seat of glory. || 32 ||
He states the yantra: "The seed-syllable," etc. The seed-syllable is the Nārasiṃha mantra to be described hereafter. "Śrutiśaḥ" means four by four.
By the script, that is, the Mātṛkā; the seed-syllable located in the corner is the Nṛsiṃha-bīja;
the yantra is of this nature.
It was surrounded by two houses of earth that were joined and interlaced with one another.
Having fashioned the mandala consisting of nine squares and joined with the yantra, the mantra-practitioner should place nine beautiful jars within it. || 33 ||
One should worship the deity Nṛsiṃha, whose form is peaceful, in the center of vessels filled with astringent water and provided with cloth, jewels, and other offerings. || 34 ||
The practitioner of mantras should worship Tārkṣya and the others in due order, starting from the east;
then, with the waters thus consecrated, he should sprinkle his beloved person. || 35 ||
Sorcery, possession by spirits, and madness perish along with one's enemies;
then, having been consecrated, he should feed the Brahmins with the thought that they are deities. || 36 ||
Thereafter, one should worship the guru with devotion and without deception;
by this procedure, a king attains victory in battles. || 37 ||
"Joined with a yantra" means [placed] within the pericarp of the lotus in the center of the nine-spoked [diagram].
In this nine-spoked maṇḍala,
"decoction" refers specifically to the liquid obtained from the bark of milk-exuding trees.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "clothing, jewels, and so forth," gold is intended.
Regarding the phrase "peaceful form," this refers to the visualization described as being that of Māṇikya.
"Tārkṣya and the others" refers to the previously mentioned lords of birds and so forth. "In the east and so on" means in the directions beginning with the east.
The connection is that one should worship the Guru appropriately with the thought that he is a deity.
By the word "yathāvat" (as it is), the mention of the ritual services such as water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth is intended. || 33–37 ||
One should draw the five-hooded serpent marked with the seed-syllable upon the body of Śeṣa;

furthermore, one should inscribe the syllables of the mantra in sequence across the thirty-two squares. On the tail, the name—accomplished through recitation and other means—is to be written, having been consecrated by the ritual fire-offering (homa).
This yantra pacifies the suffering of spirits, epilepsy, and disease, and it destroys enemies. || 38 ||
He describes another diagram with the words "seed-syllable mark" (bījāṅka):
one should draw five lines extending from east to west,
and one should draw nine lines extending from south to north.
On the five eastern tips, the shape of a hood should be made;
on the five western tips, the shape of a tail should be made.
Therein, one should write a single seed-syllable upon each hood.
By the word "japa etc.," the installation of vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and worship are intended. The yantra found in another tantra is described as follows:
"One should diligently draw the great sixteen-spoked wheel upon birch bark."
One should write the syllables of the mantra on the petals in pairs, following the sequence of pairs.
The wise one should write the seed-syllable that deludes the three worlds within the pericarp,
encircling it with the seed-syllable of Śrī and confining it with the syllable *kroṃ*.
In disputes, quarrels, legal proceedings, and likewise in royal courts, one shall be victorious;
it bestows intelligence, brings about subjugation, and places both men and women under one's control.
One should wear it on the crest-lock, on the arm, around the neck, or as a waist-string;
everywhere one will be fortunate in the world and everywhere matchless.
The protection named Cintāmaṇi was composed by Siṃha himself;
furthermore, I shall proclaim another protection that fascinates the three worlds.
Merely by retaining this [mantra], all prosperities shall come to pass.
One should write a lotus on white birch-bark, accompanied by thirty-two lions.
In the center, one should write the seed-syllable of Siṃheśvara exactly as before,
encircling it with the seed-syllable of Śrī and provided with three concentric circles.
Having encircled it with nooses and goads, one should worship this supreme yantra named Trailokyamohana, which accomplishes all desires and purposes.
"By holding [this] Cakrarāja, the Great King, the Lord of all lords of wheels, one attains victory; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. Thus it is said.
Kṛṣṇa, Rudra, the most terrible, the formidable, the fearsome, the radiant, the formidable, the exceedingly formidable, the destroyer of Daityas, Madhusūdana.
Raktākṣa, Piṅgalākṣa, Añjana, Dīptatejas, Sughoṇa, Suhuṇu, Viśvākṣa, and Rākṣasāntaka.
Viśāla, Dhūmrakeśa, Hayagrīva, Ghanasvana,
Meghanāda, Meghavarṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, and Kṛtāntaka.
"Of intense splendor, fire-colored, most fierce, the ornament of the universe, the subduer of obstacles, Mahāsena—thus are the thirty-two lions proclaimed. (38)
The syllable *kṣa*, mounted upon fire (*ra*), joined with the human vowel (*u*), its head radiant with the *bindu* and the *nāda*, is considered the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Narahari. || 39 ||
He extracts the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha as "the letter Kṣa. Here, "Vahni" is the letter Ra, and "Manusvara" is Au.
This, too, is an independent mantra.
The seer and so forth for this [mantra] are as follows:
Atri is the seer, Gāyatrī is the meter, the Lord Śrī Nṛhari is the deity;
one should fashion the limbs [of the mantra] with the long-yoked seed-syllable.

The meditation should be as before; one should mutter the mantra with a single-pointed focus. One should properly perform the fire-oblation (homa) with ten parts of that number, using auspicious milk-rice offerings mixed with clarified butter.
One should perform all rites for this [deity], such as worship and fire-offerings (homa), as previously described;
one should also accomplish its ritual applications just like those of the King of Mantras.
"Some authorities declare that this mantra should be enclosed within the *hṛllekhā* [syllables].
Likewise: "One should draw a smooth (white) eight-petaled lotus, joined with [the seed-syllable] in the pericarp."
One should write the root mantra there, conjoined with the syllable Om;
the single-syllabled Nārasiṃha mantra, together with the practitioner, should be placed at the navel.
One should recite the mantra eight thousand times; having wound it with thread, one should then wrap it externally with gold and subsequently encircle it with silver.
Thereafter, one should carefully wrap it with copper and then with lac;
having consecrated it again with the mantra, O Dear One, one should place it in the fire.
One should wear this supreme yantra on the neck, the arm, or at the crest-lock;
then all men, women, and kings on earth shall come under one's control.
Evil beings—piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas—do not afflict him at all;
by the grace of the Cakrarāja, he shall attain victory everywhere.
The wise one should draw the great twelve-spoked wheel as before;
the learned one should inscribe upon each petal that which is conjoined with the twelve measures.
In the center, one should encircle the mantra joined with the Śakti by means of the Śrī-bīja;
this is the wheel named Kālāntaka, which brings under control both gods and demons.
One should engrave the wheel upon birch bark; it wards off all enemies, and by its mere wearing, one shall be victorious everywhere.
Then he shall become praiseworthy in the world, just like the Lord who is a man-lion. Thus [ends verse 39].
The seed-syllable is *namo bhagavate narasiṃhāya*, followed by *jvālāmāline* and then *dīptadaṃṣṭrāya*. || 40 ||
One should utter the word "agninetrāya," followed by "sarvādi" and "rakṣoghnāya.
Then one should state the word ending with "sarvabhūtavināśa," followed by the letter "na" with a long vowel, which is Marut. || 41 ||

At the end of "sarvajvaravināśānte," there are the two syllables of the Lord (Nātha), followed by the pair "daha," the pair "paca," the pair "rakṣa," then "huṃ phaṭ svāhā," preceded by the seed-syllable "dhūḥ. || 42 ||
The great mantra Jvālāmālī is said to consist of sixty-seven syllables;
the heart is said to consist of thirteen [syllables], and the head is declared to consist of ten.
The *śikhā* [mantra] is said to consist of eleven syllables, the *varma* is considered to consist of eighteen syllables,

the *netra* consists of twelve syllables, and the *astra* should consist of the *karaṇa* syllables. Having thus performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs (*aṅga*), one should meditate upon the deity of the mantra.
He states the mantra of Jvālānṛsiṃha, beginning with "the seed-syllable" (bījam). The seed-syllable is that of Nārasiṃha;
the letter *na* with a long vowel is *nā*.
The seed-syllable is *ma* and *ru*.
The seer is Brahmā; the meter is *aticchandas*; the deity is Jvālāmālin Nṛsiṃha;
the seed-syllable is *kṣauṃ*; and the power is *svāhā*.
[The mantra consists] of syllables of action, [namely] four-syllable units.
Now, it may be argued that the mantra was previously stated to have sixty-seven syllables;

however, when the limbs (*aṅga*) are mentioned by the passage beginning "the heart with thirteen," sixty-eight syllables are obtained, which constitutes a contradiction between the preceding and the following. This is true.

In that regard, regarding the assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakaraṇa*), because of the division of the words themselves, the completion of the head-limb (*śiro'ṅga*) occurs right there at "to the fang" (*daṃṣṭrāya*).
However, the crest-limb (*śikhā*) is performed with the eleven [words] beginning with "to the fire-eye" (*agninetrāya*).
In the mantra, however, since there is merely a euphonic combination (*sandhi*) between "to the fang" (*daṃṣṭrāya*) and "fire" (*agni*), there is no fault. (40–44)
With a third eye blazing like the fire of universal destruction, constantly radiant with the crests of flames,
his lotus-face possessing fierce tusks,
terrifying with its scattered mass of matted locks, he struck fear into the rākṣasas.
I worship the one who holds the conch, the discus, the sword, and the shield, and who is nourished by human flesh. || 45 ||

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with a concentrated mind; then, with a composed heart, one should offer oblations into the well-kindled fire using the clarified butter of a tawny cow, numbering one-tenth of that [recitation]. || 46 ||
One should worship the God upon the previously mentioned pedestal according to the prescribed method.
One should perform the ritual applications (prayogas) taught for the King of Mantras by means of this mantra;
indeed, this mantra is traditionally remembered as a destroyer of minor spirits and the like. || 47 ||
The statement "inspiring fear in the *rakṣasas*" should be understood as indicating the specific application (*viniyoga*). "The mass of *saṭās*" refers to the collection of hair on the shoulders;
for the lexicon states: "The word *saṭā* denotes both matted hair (*jaṭā*) and filaments (*kesara*)."
The visualization of the weapons extends from the upper left [hand] down to the lower left [hand]. (45–47)
Pāśa, Śakti, Narahari, Aṅkuśa, Varma, and Phaṭ constitute the six-syllabled mantra of Narahari, which is said to grant all desires. || 48 ||
The seer is declared to be Brahmā; the meter is said to be Paṅkti;
Narasiṃha is its deity, and the assignment of the limbs is performed with the six seed-syllables. || 49 ||
He states the Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha mantra as "pāśa. Pāśa is *āṃ*;
Śakti is the seed-syllable of Māyā (*hrīṃ*).
The seed-syllable of Narahari-Nṛsiṃha;
the goad is *kroṃ*; the armor is *huṃ*.
*Phaṭ* is the essential form (*svarūpa*). *Kṣrauṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *Māyā* is the power (*śakti*).
By the phrase "the granter of all desires," the application (*viniyoga*) is stated. || 48–49 ||
With his tongue flickering in fury and his own mouth wide open, having eyes like the moon, sun, and fire,
glowing with red light from the feet to the navel and white above, he has split the body of the lord of the Daityas;
he bears the discus, conch, noose, goad, thunderbolt, mace, and axe.
I praise Nṛsiṃha, who is terrifying with sharp and fierce fangs, and adorned with various ornaments made of jewels. || 50 ||

The *āyudha-dhyāna* (meditation on the weapons), however, is as follows: [the first two] are on the upper right and left hands; those below them are on the lower right and left hands respectively. In this sequence, with the fourth pair of right and left hands, there is the *dāraṇa-mudrā*.
Its characteristic is as follows:

"With the fingers mutually joined and facing each other, their tips straight and downward-pointing, and the thumbs straight in their natural positions—this mudrā is considered Dāraṇā. Thus [it is said].
"I praise" means I extol.
The verbal root *īḍ* means "to praise. || 50 ||
One should recite this for a period of six months (ṛtulakṣa), and then offer oblations of clarified butter;
subsequently, one should satisfy the preceptor with wealth in a well-kindled fire [with a thousand such offerings]. || 51 ||
On the pedestal previously described for the image-worship, one should fashion the form with the root mantra.
Outside the enclosure of the limbs (aṅgāvṛti), there should again be the discus, the conch, the noose, and the goad.
The wise one should worship the vajra, the kaumodakī mace, the sword, and the shield upon the petals;
Indra and the others, along with these weapons, should be worshipped on the outside. || 53 ||
A lakṣa of seasons is six lakṣas;
a thousand of those is six thousand. || 51-53 ||

Having thus performed the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) with this mantra, the knower of mantras should perform the applications (prayoga) prescribed in the ritual manuals for himself and for others. || 54 ||
"Having thus performed the *puraścaryā*. Herein is stated the general procedure for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) common to all mantras.
Regarding the meaning of the term *puraścaraṇa*, it is said in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
The practice of the root mantra is called *puraścaraṇa*,
because it must be performed prior to the ritual acts known as *viniyoga*.
"Or it is stated thus because of its application at the beginning.
Also, in the *Agastisaṃhitā*: "Now I shall declare the procedures for the rite of *puraścaraṇa*;
without which a mantra would not be perfected even in hundreds of years."
That is called *puraścaraṇa*, performed for the sake of one's own accomplishment of the mantra,
having observed the prescribed rules for the recitation as stated in one's own ritual manual.
"The ritual procedure up to the sacrifice for the twice-born has been proclaimed by the most excellent teachers. Thus [it is said].
Also, in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "The application of a perfected mantra for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, according to the path of the scriptures, has been proclaimed by the wise."

This application of the mantra is held to be preceded by *puraścaraṇa* for the sake of attaining results through the service of the mantra, just as service to a king is performed for the sake of rewards.
"Because it precedes the performance [of the rite], it is called *puraścaraṇa*. Thus [it is said].
Likewise—his own accumulated store of white, single-variety winter rice.
That which has not been killed by a Śūdra, nor that which was killed without being lifted up by the feet;
cow’s curd, milk, and ghee, as well as sugarcane products, excluding jaggery.
Sesame seeds, white mung beans, the kemuka-vajīta bulb,
coconut fruit, plantain, and likewise the lavalī.
The wise consider mango, emblic myrobalan, jackfruit, and chebulic myrobalan to be excellent as sacrificial food (haviṣya) during the intervals between vows.
Whatever is non-Vaiṣṇava, untrue, or forbidden during another vow—
all that must be abandoned here if one desires success for oneself.
Alkaline substances, salt, meat, garlic, eating from bell-metal vessels,
as well as black gram, pigeon pea, lentils, kodrava grain, and chickpeas.
"One should avoid betel-leaf, eating twice a day, living with those difficult to dwell with, negligence, that which contradicts the Śruti and Smṛti, and recitation at night. Thus it is said.

Likewise: "Withdrawal of the mind, purity, silence, reflection on the meaning of the mantra, freedom from distraction, and lack of despondency are the causes for the successful accomplishment of japa."
Likewise: sleeping on the ground, celibacy, silence, conduct free from malice, bathing three times daily at the prescribed hours, and the avoidance of trivial activities.
Daily worship, daily charity, the praise and chanting of the names of the deity,
occasional ritual offerings, and faith in the guru and the deity.
"These twelve qualities rooted in Japan shall grant the accomplishment of mantras.
Thus it is said.
Likewise—one should completely avoid speaking with women, Śūdras, outcasts, those who have fallen from their caste (vrātyas), atheists, or those who have consumed the remnants of another's meal;
one should avoid speaking untruths and speaking deviously.
One should not speak even the truth during recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and the like;
one should strictly avoid false speech and the worship of others.
Constantly free from desire toward outcasts and the like through the actions of speech, mind,
and body, one should avoid listening to singing and instrumental music and seeing dances.
One should completely avoid betel, the application of perfumes, the wearing of flowers, sexual intercourse, conversation concerning it, and social gatherings centered upon it.
One should avoid crookedness, shaving, oil massage, eating food that has not been offered, performing actions without prior intention, and activities such as rubbing the body.
One should abandon bathing with warm water, as well as fragrant substances such as *āmalaka* and the like;
one should purify the head and limbs internally and externally with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
"One should bathe with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or with pure myrobalan (amalaka) alone;
if one is able, one should bathe at the three junctions of the day, otherwise one should perform it once."
Likewise: "If one recites while having impure hands, or being naked, or even with the head covered, or while talking, it is said to be as fruitless as that [time spent]."
When a word is uttered even once, one should recite the *praṇava*;
even when a vulgar word is spoken, one should perform a single breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*).
"In the event of much idle chatter, one must certainly place [the mantras] upon the limbs and then perform the recitation;
likewise in the case of sneezing, and similarly upon touching places that should not be touched. Thus it is said. Also in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā:
One should never recite [the mantra] while wearing a turban, a bodice, or naked; with disheveled hair, surrounded by women, with impure hands, unpurified, or while prattling.
Having his hands uncovered, or even having his head covered,
or with a mind distracted by anxiety, or angry, confused, or overcome by hunger.
Neither while sitting, nor lying down, nor walking, nor standing;
one should not recite [the mantra] on a street, in an inauspicious place, or in the midst of darkness.
Nor should one recite with feet covered by sandals, nor while seated on a vehicle or a bed;
one should not recite with the feet stretched out, nor while sitting in the utkaṭāsana posture.
Upon seeing, speaking to, or hearing those who have fallen from their caste or those born of the lowest castes,
or upon sneezing, passing wind, or yawning, one should suspend the recitation of prayers.

Upon arrival, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) for these [deities], one should properly perform the six-limbed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and recite the remainder; or else, one should gaze upon the sun and other [luminaries].
Having seen a cat, a cock, a curlew, a dog, a vulture, a donkey, or a monkey, one should perform ritual sipping (ācamana) and then carry out one's duties; having touched them, bathing is prescribed.
One who performs the *puraścaraṇa* should observe these and other such restrictive rules (*niyama*). Thus it is said.
One should avoid anger, intoxication, and sneezing— these three— as well as spitting, yawning, and looking at oneself or those of low status during the practice of recitation.
"One should sip water, or if these are unavailable, one should remember me along with you;
or one should gaze at the luminaries, or perform breath control. Thus it is said.

Having spoken thus, one should perform the recitation of the stated number of times according to the prescribed method, neither too slowly nor too quickly, for the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa*.
Contemplating with the intellect the identity of the deity, the guru, and the mantra,
one should recite it with a single-minded focus from the morning until midday.
One who desires accomplishment should perform the auxiliary rites (aṅgas) with a tenth part of the recitation;
whatever number was commenced for the main recitation, that same amount should be performed day and night.
"If a person should perform [the recitation] with deficiency or excess, he becomes fallen from his vow;
in the Kali age, one must perform a recitation four times the stated number. Thus it is said.
Elsewhere also it is said: "The recitation prescribed for the *Kṛta* age is doubled in the *Tretā*;
it is declared to be tripled in the *Dvāpara*, and quadrupled in the *Kali* age."
In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*, regarding the eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa:
"The wise person, unwearied, should recite it continuously for eight hundred thousand times;
this is declared by the sages to be the attainment of the mantra in the first age."
"In the second [age] it is double that; in the third, it is triple;
and in the Kali age, it is declared by the sages such as Nārada and others to be fourfold."
Upon completing the count, one who is composed should, with his own substances, offer oblations into the fire-pit as prescribed, according to the rules, for one-tenth of the number of recitations.
Alternatively, having recited [the mantra] every day, one should perform oblations amounting to one-tenth of that number;
then, having worshipped the deity in water, one should perform [recitation] amounting to one-tenth of the oblations.
Having uttered "I satiate" at the end of the mantra, one should perform the libation with water upon the head;
likewise, one should perform one's own consecration, the Aghamarṣaṇa rite, the offering of arghya to the Sun, and the drinking of water.
One should perform prostrations with the mantra ten times for each preceding [recitation];
at its conclusion, one should perform a great worship and feed the Brahmins.
One should thus please the Guru, for by doing so the mantras of the practitioner attain success;
through such preparatory rites (puraścaraṇa), the deity becomes propitious.
The worship of the ten limbs with devotion is called *puraścaraṇa*:
recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), worship (*pūjā*), and feeding of Brahmins.
One should perform [the recitation] endowed with five limbs, each being one-tenth of the preceding;
for whichever limb is omitted, the recitation must be doubled that many times.
"And it should be performed with devotion by one who is unable [to perform the full ritual], for the sake of accomplishing the auxiliary parts.
Thus [it is said].
Also in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "But in the absence of the fire-oblation, there shall be twice as much recitation as the number of oblations."
Elsewhere also it is said: "For Brahmins who are unable to perform the rite of fire-offering (homa), the recitation (japa) is double;
for the other castes, however, it is declared to be triple and so forth."
If even one limb is lost, then one will not obtain the desired result;
whatever is deficient in its limbs cannot accomplish the intended purpose.
In every way, one should feed the Brahmins for the sake of accomplishing the integrity of the rite;
by the mere propitiation of the Brahmins, that which is deficient shall always become complete.
Actions performed with deficiency or excess do not fulfill one's desires;
however, those very same actions, when performed in their entirety, bring about fulfillment.
Therefore, one should diligently feed the learned in all rites;
for whatever rites are performed, they become fruitless if lacking the feeding of the twice-born, just like seeds sown in barren soil. Thus it is said.
Also in the Kulaprakāśatantra: "In this saṃsāra, which abounds in suffering, if one desires one's own perfection,
the reciter of mantras shall proceed to happiness solely through the worship of the five limbs."
Daily worship performed at the three times of day, as well as recitation,
libations, fire-offerings, and feeding Brahmins— this is called *puraścaraṇa*.
O Dear One, for whichever limb is deficient, the practitioner should perform twice that number of recitations,
or three, four, or five times, according to the count.
One should perform [the rite] with all its ancillaries for the sake of complete accomplishment; if one is unable to do so, one should perform it with devotion.
Even if a single ancillary is omitted, one will obtain the desired result through the mantra.
O Goddess, when the Brahmins have been well-fed with the four kinds of food and substances endowed with the six flavors, everything indeed becomes fruitful.
"O Mistress of the Kula, by means of the worship of the five limbs of a single mantra that has been correctly perfected, all mantras indeed become perfected through its power. Thus it is said.

There is a distinction in other cases: others say that for the twice-born, the king, and the Vaiśya, if they are unable to perform the fire-oblation (homa), the recitation (japa) should be performed multiplied by the number of the Vedas, the Rasas, the Nāgas, and the Indras.

If there is no fire-offering (homa) for these, then the recitation (japa) equal to it is prescribed here for those of fickle vision, as that which was previously mentioned for the [other] castes, but devoid of the fire-offering.

"Whatever caste a Śūdra may belong to, he too, being devoted and with his body bowed down by the weight of devotion, should perform the prescribed recitation (japa) according to the rules for those with curved brows. Thus it is said.
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is described in another manner:
during an eclipse of either the sun or the moon, one should first remain pure and fast.
Standing in water reaching up to the navel in a river flowing toward the ocean, one should,
with a concentrated mind, recite the mantra from the moment of its commencement until its conclusion.
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the fire oblation (homa) and other rites according to the sequence of one-tenth of that [number].
At its conclusion, for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra, one should worship and satisfy the Guru.
From that, the accomplishment of mantra will arise and the deity becomes propitious;
or else, one should satisfy the Guru—who is the very form of the deity—with devotion.
"Even if devoid of the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa), the mantra will undoubtedly be perfected;
having thus accomplished the mantra, one may then perform the rites for specific desires. Thus it is said.

Elsewhere also it is said: "Through the power of the instruction, by the grace of the venerable Guru, through the potency of the mantra, and by means of devotion, the accomplishment of the mantra arises."
"Having obtained a perfected mantra from a guru, one should cultivate the attainment of that mantra;
due to practice performed in previous births, the mantra bestows accomplishment swiftly. Thus it is said.
But elsewhere it is said: "The deity who is worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings three times a day at night becomes pleased even without the performance of the *puraścaraṇa* rite."
Likewise, in the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā: "A mantra that is perfected through preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) indeed bestows its fruit;
what is the use of fire-offerings (homa), what is the use of recitations (japa), and what is the use of elaborate mantra-depositions (nyāsa)?"
If there were no preliminary service for secret mantras,
then the preliminary service of mantras is said to be the primary seed.
Just as a person afflicted by disease is incapable of performing any actions,
so too is a mantra declared to be ineffective when it is devoid of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
For those mantras for which no specific number has been stated by the wise regarding recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa),
the number eight thousand is prescribed for both the recitation and the oblation.
And in whatever case the number of mantras is specified by the very recitation itself,
in all such instances there is an increase in the number of mantras according to the sequence of the Yugas.
The number mentioned for the Kṛta age becomes double in the Tretā;
it is said to be triple in the Dvāpara, and the number in the Kali age is fourfold.
When the substance of the oblation is not specified, sesame and clarified butter are said to be the oblation;
or alternatively, vegetables, roots, fruits, alms-food, sacrificial grains (haviṣya), or barley-meal (saktu).
Alternatively, there may be only milk for the sustenance of the body during the preliminary practice;
the practitioner of mantra should not consort with women, nor consume meat or honey.
For one who performs these [practices], nothing succeeds through mere preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*). A man performing *puraścaraṇa* should not speak with a woman or a Śūdra.
One should perform the recitation (japa), beginning in the morning and continuing until midday;
one should not speak untruth, nor should one allow the senses to be enticed by objects of desire.
The rule of uninterrupted practice has been declared; one should not let even a single day pass by.
For if a day is exceeded, the accomplishment of the mantra will certainly not come to a person.
Furthermore, a mantra that is devoid of power never succeeds;
however many times one recites it on the previous day, for exactly that many times should one recite it [on the following].
One should recite it even on another day; otherwise, it creates an obstacle to success.
However, this is not the case when one is in the presence of Śiva, the Sun, Fire, or the Guru.
The practice of recitation is praised even when a lamp is burning;
wearing clean garments, one should lie down upon a bed of kuśa grass.
One should wash that garment daily; otherwise, one will become subject to obstacles.
Bathing at the three sessions of the day is prescribed, or twice, or even once, if one lacks the capacity.
There is no fruit for one who does not bathe, nor for one who does not satisfy the ancestors,
nor for one who does not satisfy the gods, nor even for one who speaks untruths.
One should not recite the mantra while wearing a single garment, nor while covered by many garments;
nor should one ever, out of delusion, wear them in the reverse order.
A wise practitioner performing the *puraścaraṇa* should wear his garment over his left shoulder and under his right arm;
however, in the case of specific ritual applications (*viniyoga*), there may sometimes be no such restriction.
One should avoid him with great effort during the rites of *puraścaraṇa*;
having performed the mantra-recitation for the sake of consecration (*puraskāra*), the practitioner of mantra should remain self-controlled.
The wise practitioner should offer oblations into the fire in the prescribed manner, amounting to one-tenth [of the recitation],
or else one-fourth of the total recitation, while uttering the mantra ending with "svāhā."
Then, one should satisfy [the deity] with water ending in "svāhā" for a tenth part of the number of oblations;
for a tenth part of that libation, one should extract the mantra ending in "namaḥ."
One should sprinkle one's own head with water using the mudrā called *kumbha*;
having thus performed the preliminary rites of mantra according to this procedure.
"One should perform the ritual applications (viniyoga) as they begin, according to the respective rules.
Thus it is said.
Regarding the specific procedure for libation (tarpaṇa) in the Gopāla mantra, it is stated in that very same place:
"In this regard, those who know the scriptures understand that for all these Gopāla mantras, the libation (tarpaṇa) should be known as equal to the number of oblations (homa). Thus it is said.
Elsewhere also it is said: "One should satisfy the other Manus according to the number of oblations offered;
this libation is ordained as a daily rite."

Now, if an impurity such as birth or death (*sūtaka*) should occur during the course of an undertaken *puraścaraṇa*, nevertheless, the completion of that intended *puraścaraṇa* must indeed be performed.
And so says Viṣṇu:

"In the case of vows, sacrifices, marriages, *śrāddhas*, fire-oblations (*homa*), worship, and recitation (*japa*), there shall be no impurity (*sūtaka*) once they have commenced; however, if they have not commenced, there is impurity.
Regarding this, both "impurity" and "commencement" are defined in that very same [text]: [The definition of commencement follows...]
"In a sacrifice, the commencement is the selection [of priests]; in the observance of vows, it is the formal resolve;
in marriage and similar rites, it is the *nāndīmukha* ceremony; and in a *śrāddha*, it is the preparation of the cooked food. Thus it is said.

In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*, after describing all the rules for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), it says: "If one is capable, one should perform all of this; if incapable, one should recite according to one's capacity.
There is no fault in mental recitation, whether in any place or at any time."
An excellent twice-born man devoted to *japa* obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
indeed, among all sacrifices, the sacrifice of *japa* is most highly praised.
"For it is through non-violence toward living beings that this great fruit arises;
among sacrifices, I am the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña)," so said the Blessed Lord Hari.
A Brahmin shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whether he performs other rites or not, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brahmin.
"Thus say the peaceful sages, perfected in recitation, possessing nothing.
Also, in the *Padmanābhiya*: "Whatever ritual sacrifices there may be, and whatever blazing austerities,"
All those do not equal even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
"By constant recitation, the deity, being praised, becomes pleased;
being pleased, she bestows abundant enjoyments and eternal liberation. Thus it is said.

Also in the Bhṛgusaṃhitā: "The four types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), even when accompanied by the ritual sacrifices (vidhiyajña), are all not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña)."

In the *Nārāyaṇīya*, however, it is said: "For one who is unable to perform recitation [of the entire mantra] in its entirety, the recitation and so forth for the limbs (*aṅga*) and other parts should be one-tenth of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). Through such recitation, the mantra becomes empowered, and the deity of the mantra grants all desires."
The definition of *japa* is stated in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:

"Japa is the repetition of syllables; it may be loud (*ucca*), whispered (*upāṃśu*), or mental (*mānasa*). That [japa] which is performed with words that have high, low, and circumflex accents, with distinct words and syllables..."
One should recite the mantra with speech; that is the vocal sacrifice of japa.
One should utter the mantra slowly, moving the lips slightly.
That which is barely audible to the ear is known as whispered recitation (upāṃśu-japa);
that which is performed mentally, consisting of a sequence of syllables composed of phonemes, vowels, and words, is mental recitation (mānasa-japa).
Reciting while recollecting the meaning is called mental recitation (mānasa-japa). Loud recitation (uccair-japa) is superior to sacrifices and other rites by tenfold merit.
"The whispered [recitation] is a hundredfold [more effective], and the mental is remembered as a thousandfold.
Thus it is said.
Also, in the Bhṛgusaṃhitā:
"The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the sacrifice of ritual action (vidhiyajña);
the whispered (upāṃśu) is a hundredfold, and the mental (mānasa) is said to be a thousandfold.
Elsewhere, however: "One should not shake the head or the neck, nor should one move the tongue or the lips."
"One should not perform the 'tooth-strike' upon a seed that has been merely conceived in the mind. Thus it is said.
The teachers also state: "Neither too fast nor too slow.
However, there is a specific distinction in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
Moreover, I shall declare another supreme means for accomplishing mantra-siddhi:
the oneness of the mantra and the practitioner is difficult for humans on earth to attain.
This was spoken by Śiva, the knower of all things, in the Sāṅkarṣaṇa Tantra,
long ago to the wise Śukra, in the Pañcarātra known as Ānanda.
Having bestowed the consecrated and honored mantra upon the disciple,
the teacher should then effect the union of the two according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
Having interwoven the mantra with the letters of the name in their proper order,
one should write the entire name at the beginning and the end, and then inscribe the *praṇava*.
One should inscribe the vowels upon the petals and meditate on them as being of the nature of nectar,
using yellow pigment, fragrant substances, and so forth, upon a beautiful birch-bark leaf in the center of a lotus.
Having wrapped it with pure clay and then again with beeswax,
one should place it into a small earthen vessel filled with honey.
He should place that small vessel into a new jar filled with milk;
the preceptor should hold the jar near the sacrificial fire-pit.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the identity of the mantra and the practitioner,
the knower of mantras should perform oblations with the root mantra one thousand or even one hundred times.
One should pour the three auspicious sweet substances into the pitcher;
having placed them therein, one should slowly deposit that pitcher into the great waters.
The identity of the mantra and the practitioner must indeed be established for the fruit to be bestowed;
he who does not understand this is not called a preceptor.
"This secret has been told; one should not speak it to just anyone. One may, however, speak it to an excellent disciple or to a beloved son. (54)
One should offer a thousand oblations of fresh red lotuses smeared with the three sweets;
daily for a month, one's desire will be fulfilled, and after a year, one will possess wealth and grain.
One should offer a thousand oblations of red lotuses mixed with the three sweets;
thereby one shall obtain great fortune, long life, and mastery over others.
With red utpala flowers, with red kuvalaya lilies— fresh and not stale—
and with red lotuses, the kokanadas. ||55-56||

For one who offers parched grain mixed with the three sweets at the morning hours, the attainment of a maiden shall occur within a fortnight; he shall obtain an excellent bridegroom for his daughter. || 57 ||
A wise person, having anointed dūrvā grass with milk and ghee, should offer one hundred and ten oblations every day; thus, he shall properly attain a long life. || 58 ||
His diseases perish along with the effects of sorcery, malevolence, and the like;
one should offer oblations of apāmārga blossoms together with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 59 ||

One who has conquered the senses should perform this fire-oblation daily for seven days according to the measure of a thousand; it shall completely destroy all afflictions caused by malevolent spirits and diseases. || 60 ||

One should offer two thousand oblations, in due order, with sesame seeds, clarified butter, apāmārga plants, sacrificial offerings, and clarified butter; thus one shall conquer minor diseases and planetary afflictions.
For four days, one should perform three thousand oblations with pieces of *amṛtā* mixed with milk;
by this prescribed rite, the fever caused by the planets is destroyed. || 62 ||

One should write the two seed-syllables of Nṛsiṃha’s power (śakti) upon two tridents placed within the *tāra* (the syllable Om). Having seated the one afflicted by a spirit there, one should recite the six-syllabled mantra;
the spirit, having entered [the victim], shall immediately release him, crying out and overwhelmed with fear. || 63 ||
*Amṛtā* is *guḍūcī*. Regarding "when the pain has moved upward": this refers to that place which has the form of a trident (*śūla*) at the beginning of the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*).
"One should mutter the mantra" means touching the one afflicted by the planetary spirit who has been seated upon that [trident]. (57–63)
Having drawn two fire-purīṣas (triangles), one should write the Śakti together with the sādhya within them;
then, in the six corners, the six syllables of the mantra; then, the vowels situated upon the filaments;
and on the eight petals, the forty-four letters prescribed for the king of mantras in their proper sequence.
Furthermore, it is surrounded by the letters beginning with *ka* in the city of earth (*kṣitipura*), and the Cintāmaṇi jewel is placed in the corners. || 64 ||
This Nārasiṃha yantra, when inscribed on birch bark and worn upon the head, removes diseases of the head, malevolent spirits, and fevers. || 65 ||
What need is there for much speaking here? Among all mantras uttered, there is no other mantra equal to these in bestowing both curses and favors.
Regarding the yantra, he says "having written" (ālikhya):
two fire-gates (agnipuradvaya) intersecting each other;
of the mantra (manoḥ), that is, of the six-syllabled Nṛsiṃha mantra.
"Cintāmaṇi" and "Nārasiṃha" are in apposition.
Therefore, the connection is that this diagram, written on birch bark with the single-syllable mantra of Nṛsiṃha, shall take away [evil].
This has been stated in the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa*:

One should contemplate the Yantra as having a pericarp distinguished by the seed-syllable of the hexagon, joined with the syllables of Śakti and the eight parts of the fourfold root-mantra; it is surrounded by the Mother (Jananī) within the eight petals of the house of the earth (Jagatī), and contains the Cintāmaṇi jewel.

"Āṃ hrīṃ kṣrauṃ kroṃ ca huṃ phaṭ ca is the Śakti-mantra; the eight kalās are the pairs of vowels; the Cintā-mantra consists of the syllables 'a' and 'ca'; and the one-syllable mantra of Nṛsiṃha is [the syllable] 'huṃ'. Thus [ends verses 64–66].

The syllable *tāra* (OM), followed by the seed-syllable of Bhṛgu (*bha*), then the first letter (*a*) joined with the long fire-vowel (*ai*), and ending with the fire-god (*ra*), the armor (*huṃ*), and the weapon (*phaṭ*)—this is remembered as the seven-syllabled mantra. || 67 ||
The sage is declared to be Ahirbudhnya, and the meter is stated to be Anuṣṭubh;
the deity is proclaimed by the sages to be Hari himself in the form of the Cakra. || 68 ||
That which is called the heart is declared for Ācakra; the head is remembered for Vicakra;
the crest-lock (śikhā) is proclaimed for Sucakra; and the body-armor for Dhīcakra. || 69 ||
The mantra for the eye is remembered as *sañcakrāya*, and the one following that is for the flaming wheel (*jvālācakrāya*).
Each of these six limb-mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) is joined with its respective seed-syllable (*jāti*) and ends with the word *svāhā* (*dviṭha*). || 70 ||
Since the *sudarśana* mantra has been specified for the Vārāha yantra, he states it:
"The *tāra*," meaning the *praṇava*;
"Bhṛgu" is that [the letter *sa*].
The sky is *ha*; that which follows it is *sa*;
fire is *ra*.
The long vowel *ā*, joined with that [the letter *s*], makes *srā*. *Pāvaka* is the letter *r*.
And *kavaca* is *huṃ*.
The weapon is *phaṭ*.
*Saṃ* is the seed-syllable. *Hūṃ* is the power (*śakti*).
That is the supreme weapon. [The mantras] end with *dviṭha* (svāhā) and conclude with *svāhā*. 67–70.
With the mantra "I bind with the Indra-cakra; obeisance to the Cakra, Ṭha Ṭha," one should perform the binding of the directions, starting from the east. || 71 ||

By the phrase "of the eastern and other directions," it is stated that in the mantra "I bind with the *aindrī* wheel," the word *aindrī* must be modified (*ūha*) by substituting words such as *āgneyī* (southern) and so forth;
this applies likewise to all ten directions.
As it has been said:

"Having begun from the eastern direction and stated [the directions] down to the end below, having sequentially recited for the ten [directions], and having likewise said 'I bind with the wheel, obeisance,' and 'to the wheel, the head'—this is the binding of the directions. (71)
"Trailokyānte rakṣa yugam huṃ phaṭ svāhā," beginning with "dhruva"—this is the mantra for the fire-enclosure (agniprākāra), for the protection of oneself once again. || 72 ||

In this mantra, "trailokyānte," the word *trailokya* should be understood as ending in the accusative case (*trailokyam*), because of the hearing of the verb "protect" (*rakṣa*). As it has been said: "Commanded [to act] with 'Protect, protect the three worlds! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā!'"
"This mantra, beginning with 'Tāra', is known as the 'Fire Enclosure' (Agniprākāra). || 72 ||
The best of men should construct the enclosure with that mantra;
he should place the bright [syllable], resembling white, red, and collyrium, upon his head. || 73 ||
One should sequentially place other colors resembling fire in the middle of the eyebrows, the mouth, the heart, and at the joints of the private parts, the knees, and the pair of feet.
"One should perform it.
The supreme teachers maintain that one should mentally contemplate a rampart of fire while circumambulating oneself clockwise and pour out water.
And it has been said:
And immediately thereafter, for the sake of protection against ghosts, spirits, and demons, one should establish a wall of fire all around oneself.

"The practitioner of mantra should scatter water and flowers along with unbroken rice grains (akṣata), consecrated by the fire-seed syllable and the weapon-mantra, all around for the sake of removing fear and obstacles. Thus [it is said]. "White," etc.
The meditation on the syllables A, U, and M in their proper sequence;
the placement of the final letter at the junctions of the two pairs of words. || 73-74 ||
[He is] one whose brilliance at the end of the eon illuminates the entire three worlds with his splendor;
red-eyed, with tawny hair, causing fear to the host of enemies, and possessing a terrifying roar with fierce fangs;
[holding] in his own hands the discus, conch, mace, lotus, a very broad pestle, bow, noose, and goad.
I meditate upon her who, with her arms, bears within her heart the primordial enemy of Mura known as the Discus.
"At the end of the eon" (kalpānte):
the bow together with the arrow is to be understood [in this way].
As it has been said:
"With two [hands] he holds the discus and the sword, and with [the others] the mace, the lotus, the thunderbolt, the missile, the noose, and the goad.
For this very reason, he will state later in the context of worship that there is "a bow together with an arrow.
Regarding the visualization of the weapons: the first [set] is held by the right and other upper hands, while the other is held by those below them.
Here, immediately following the meditation, one should display the wheel mudrā. || 75 ||

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice (homa) of one thousand oblations, using sesame seeds, mustard seeds, lotuses, wood-apple fruits, and milk-rice, respectively. || 76 ||
One should worship the image of Viṣṇu upon the pedestal, fashioning it with the root mantra;
having first worshipped the limbs, one should then worship the weapons, such as the discus and others, outside of that.
Then one should worship the discus, conch, mace, lotus, pestle, bow with arrow, noose, and goad upon the tips of the petals, followed by Lakṣmī and the others. || 78 ||
Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī, followed by Rati and Prīti; thereafter Kīrti and Kānti, and Tuṣṭi and Puṣṭi—all these are traditionally remembered as pairs.
Yellow, red, white, and dark-blue; the weapons of Indra and the others outside of that—once the mantra has been thus perfected, one should perform the prescribed applications. || 80 ||
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, one who desires long life should perform the *dūrvā* oblation, which bestows both visible and invisible fruits. || 81 ||
"Arka-lakṣa" means twelve lakhs;
this refers to the total thousand-fold [repetition] in sequence, not for each [individual] one.
"With sesame seeds" means twenty-four hundred for each.
Regarding the statement "on the seat of Viṣṇu" as described in the *Nārāyaṇāṣṭākṣara*:
"having worshipped"—the word "in the filaments" (*kesareṣu*) is to be understood as the ellipsis; "outside of that" means in the middle of the petals.
"A bow with an arrow" refers to one [deity].
"On the tips of the petals" is connected with what follows.
"Lakṣmī and the others" refers to those whose seed-syllables (bīja) and so forth are mentioned in the subsequent chapter.
"In pairs" means: the first two are yellow; Rati and Prīti are red.
In the penultimate [syllable] it is white;
in the final, it is dark blue.
By the statement "it is fit to perform the applications," this is what is meant.
Oṃ, may we know the Sudarśana; may we meditate upon the King of Wheels (Cakrarāja); may that Wheel impel us.
In its ritual applications, there is a recitation of the root mantra ten times the number of its syllables (*daśāṃśa*).
Some read "may we meditate upon the Mahācakra" instead.
In the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*, however, the following Gāyatrī is recited: "We know the Discus; we meditate upon the Thousand-flamed One; may He who wards off [obstacles] inspire us.
All three of these positions are indeed traditional.
And the determination [of the practice] is according to the teacher’s instruction;
"long life" refers to the state of being a conqueror of death (*mṛtyuñjaya*) and so forth. (76–81)
One who desires prosperity should offer oblations with full-blown lotuses drenched in clarified butter;
one desiring intelligence should offer oblations with flowers produced from the Brahma-tree (Butea monosperma).
He who offers three days of oblations with eight thousand one hundred and eight consecrated pills shall conquer all calamities.
For the attainment of cattle, one should offer oblations with cow-ghee for three days;
an oblation of Udumbara fuel-sticks shall bestow sons upon men.
One should visualize a wheel resembling the fire of universal dissolution upon his head;
within seven days, he who is afflicted by fever and fainting will meet his death from that [magical] circle.

"Desirous of prosperity" (*śrīkāma*) indicates that it begins with the seed-syllable *Śrī*. "By one desirous of intelligence" (*medhākāmena*) should be understood as beginning with the *Vāgbhava* syllable.
[The text] says "he offers oblations" (*juhoti*).
"Three days" means either three or four days,
according to the statement: "The most excellent of mantra-reciters should offer a thousand or eight pellets of guggulu for three days or four days."
"Purū" is guggulu.
"Nikhilāpada" refers to its being the seed-mantra (bīja) of Nṛsiṃha and so forth.
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "fainting shall occur. (82–85)

One should contemplate the letter *sa* at the head of the enemy, devoid of vowels such as *a* and so forth, and surrounded by the words "go away, go away" (*yāhi yāhi*); this brings about the expulsion [of the enemy]. || 86 ||
Regarding "akārādi" (beginning with the letter *a*):
it should be understood that the seed-syllable of wind (*vāyu-bīja*) is joined to the letters beginning with *a*.
By means of that, [the sequence] beginning with *yaṃ yāṃ* brings about eradication (*uccāṭana*); this is to be understood as occurring over ten days.
As it has been said by the Teachers: "This enemy is repelled after ten days. (86)
By this method, the enemy shall meet his death from the circle [of practitioners].
[One should visualize] the syllable *sā*, resembling the autumn moon, raining down streams of nectar. || 87 ||
He upon whose head one meditates on this [mantra] shall live free from all disease.
Having visualized oneself as situated at the hub of the wheel, one should recite this mantra. || 88 ||
"Even a single person standing on the field of battle may conquer many adversaries by this method"— by this statement, another similar application is also indicated. As the Teachers have said:
Or, one should meditate for seven days upon the head of the enemy as being peaceful and the color of a crow;
through the sharpness of one’s intellect, this quickly causes [the enemy] to be driven away or even killed. Thus it is said.
By the phrase "resembling the autumn moon," it should be understood that [the syllable] is white, such as *vaṃ* or *vām*.
One should recite the syllable *sa*, the letter *s*.
It should be understood that the mantra of the Gītā begins with *oṃ* at the end of the fourth quarter, while the three preceding quarters end with *namaḥ*, *srāra*, *nārā*, *huṃ phaṭ paṇe*. (87–89)
One should offer fuel-sticks of Apāmārga until ten thousand have been completed. || 89 ||
For him, no affliction from Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Piśācas, or enemies shall arise, [by means of the substances] produced from Nirguṇḍī, Sarja, Kanaka, and white Kiṃśuka. || 90 ||
An oblation performed with fuel-sticks of *samidvara* removes minor diseases and malevolent spirits;
likewise, a sacrificial porridge (*caru*) cooked in clarified butter with fuel-sticks of *apāmārga*. || 91 ||
One should offer these [substances] with clarified butter separately one hundred and eight times;
furthermore, one should give the sacrificial porridge (caru), consecrated by the residual drops (sampāta), to the practitioner. || 92 ||
All acts of malice committed through black magic perish in every way for him;
[this occurs when] fuel-sticks of Apāmārga are soaked with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 93 ||

The practitioner of mantra should perform ten thousand oblations and offer bali-offerings in the various directions with curd-rice, using the mantra, for the pacification of minor diseases and other ailments. || 94 ||
Regarding "of the *apāmārga*":
it should be understood that the *vaṣaṭ* call takes the place of *phaṭ*.
*Sarja* is *śāla*.
*Kanaka* is *dhattūra*.
The minor ailments (*kṣudraroga*) are the six well-known diseases beginning with *stambha*.
The planetary spirits (*graha*) are the eighteen great planets (*mahāgraha*) and the seven intermediate spirits (*vyantara*).

"Separately" means individually. "One should give the *caru*" refers to the remainder of the *caru* used for the fire-oblation (*homa*) that has been consecrated with mantras. "Accomplished by the *sampāta*" means accomplished by the *sampāta* (the residue) from each respective substance.

"Having offered [the oblation], one should consume the remainder of the *caru* that has been poured together and consecrated with mantras," as stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*. By the word "in every way" (*sarvathā*), the smearing of that ash [is indicated].
"Anointing with its ashes destroys minor planetary afflictions and diseases," as stated in that very same [text].
[This is done] with the *bali* mantra to be recited by Manu. (89–94)
