One should offer four thousand oblations individually with fuel-sticks from milk-trees, milk, clarified butter, and ghee; thus there shall be peace in every direction.
"With milk" means with the seven substances;
"separately" means individually. || 95 ||
The practitioner of mantra should draw two pairs of wheels extending from south to north;
he should write the syllables of the mantra beginning with the Vedas in the center and on the six corners.
The center is yellow, the six corners are red, and the interior is dark blue;
the rim is white, adorned with shimmering flames of fire. || 97 ||
From "moving southward and northward" up to "there is no doubt," there is one application.
Regarding "the pair of wheels":
it has six spokes and is provided with a rim and a felly.
"Mantravarṇān" refers to the syllables of the Sudarśana mantra.
"Antaram" refers to the joints of the six spokes.
"Nemim" refers to the rim-line of the wheel.
Regarding the phrase "with flames of fire":
the meaning is that curved lines in the shape of fire-tongues should be drawn. As it has been said: "crowded with arranged lines of fire."
Thus [ends the section on verses] 96–97.
One should likewise construct a circular mandala for the Earth outside according to the prescribed rule;
one should then place a jar filled with red water in the north.
Having invoked Janārdana, whose self is the wheel, one should worship him therein;
then, the knower of the ritual rules should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the southern mandala.
"Regarding 'pāthīva': it is black in color. This has been stated in the Nārāyaṇīya:"
"And the outer black-colored line is the earthly (pārthivī).
By the phrase "one should do thus according to the rule," it is indicated that this [rite] is to be performed on the lunar days beginning with the fifth and ending with the full moon.
As it has been said: "During the *pūrṇā* [lunar days], auspicious rites such as marriage, processions, nourishing ceremonies (*puṣṭika*), and pacifying rituals (*śāntika*) should be performed.
Likewise: "The five asterisms beginning with Hasta, Revatī, Aśvinī, and the three Uttaras..."
Śraviṣṭhā, Rohiṇī, and Puṣyā are honored for rites of pacification (śāntika). Thus it is said.
"By red water" means having made the water red with the juice of lac and so forth;
"in the Saumya" means in the wheel situated in the northern direction;
"in that" refers to the jar.
"In the southern mandala" means in the wheel situated in the southern direction.

By the phrase "knowing the procedure," it is indicated that one should establish a small hearth (*hasantikā*) with its feet [properly aligned], install the fire therein, and perform the rite of *homa*. (98–99)
In sequence, with ghee, apāmārga, rice, mustard seeds, sesame, milk-porridge, and the two products of the cow (milk and curd), one hundred and twenty-six [oblations] are offered. || 100 ||
One who knows the ritual procedure should offer oblations into the kindled fire for each respective substance;
he should then pour the remnants of the offerings into the water of the consecrated jar situated within the auspicious mandala. || 101 ||
Having formed a ball from half a *prastha* of cooked rice (*caru*), one should place it therein;
one should set aside half of that for the purpose of offering the external oblation (*bali*). || 102 ||
Having brought that initiate back who has bathed and is adorned with pure garments, the mantra-practitioner should place him to the south, immediately after the water-pot and the fire. || 103 ||

With *apāmārga* plants and *apāmārga* fuel-sticks; and it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The *apāmārga* fuel-sticks with clarified butter. *Gavya* refers to the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).

Because it is stated, "with all products of the cow," [the recitation] amounts to one thousand and eight for each substance combined. This is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "by the count of eight thousand."
The mention of ghee twice is for the sake of indicating the sequence.
By the phrase "one who knows the ritual procedure should pour [the remainder]," it is indicated that there is a pouring of the remainder (*saṃpāta*) even in the *aṣṭadravyahoma*.
The term "for each substance" (*pratidravyam*) is connected to both [parts of the sentence] according to the maxim of the eye of a crow (*kākākṣigolakanyāya*).
As it has been said: "Having offered [the oblation] and having duly cast the remnants of that offering here for each substance.
Also in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "One who knows the ritual procedure should cast the remnant of the offering into the jar for each substance."
Thus [it is said].

By the phrase "one who knows the ritual procedure" (*vidhānavit*), it is indicated that in the oblation of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and so forth, the *saṃpāta* (remnants of the offering) consists merely of touching the water-jar (*kalaśa*) with the hand at the conclusion of each oblation (*āhuti*).
In the expression "when the gentle mandala has been worshipped," the two locative case endings (*saptamī*) are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
"In that" means at the mouth of the vessel.
"One should cast [it]" refers to the previously mentioned [mudrā], which is to be employed together with the *Sudarśana-gāyatrī* ending in *vaṣaṭ*.
"Half of that remaining" refers to half of the milk-rice (*pāyasa*) prepared for the purpose of the fire-oblation (*homa*).
"South" refers to the [fourth] wheel;
the meaning is that one should place the laughing goddess (*hasantī*) who resides there elsewhere.
With the mantra of the *Gītā*—namely, "Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, Hūṃ Phaṭ" ending with the three feet, and "Oṃ" at the end of the fourth foot—the practitioner (*mantrī*) [should perform the rite].
The specific complete integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) of the object to be accomplished has been indicated. || 100–103 ||
Having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for those two, one should lead them outside the village when the moon is in the eighth zodiac sign;
there, one should place them as before, along with the ritual grass coverings, in their proper order.
Regarding the term *nīrājya*:
the *nīrājana* rite is performed with the Gītā-mantra.
It should be understood that the *nīrājana* performed simultaneously from both the water-pot (*kumbha*) and the fire (*agni*) requires the assistance of another person.
The phrase "those two" refers to the water-pot and the fire; one should place them in the eighth zodiac sign.
The positions of the signs are stated in the *Kādima-tantra*:
"Aries and Taurus are in the east, Gemini in the southeast, and likewise Cancer in the south."
Cancer and Leo are there, and Virgo is situated in the southwest.
Libra and Scorpio are situated in the west; Sagittarius is situated in the northwest;
Capricorn and Aquarius are in the north; and Pisces is situated in the northeast. Thus it is said.
The meaning is that, having identified the location of this zodiacal sign, one should place [the fire] in the eighth sign from that of the person to be accomplished (sādhya).
"As before" means that one should establish the fire on its southern side.
As it has been said:
"Then one should cast all [the substances], beginning with fire, into the western part of the jar. || 104 ||

Having offered oblations into the fire as before, one should present the bali offering with the remaining food in the ten directions according to the rule, using the mantra that will be stated hereafter. || 105 ||
"According to the previous [method]" means with eight substances and in the stated measure.
"With the remaining food" means with the food left over from the oblation (*huta*).
This is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "One should offer the bali-oblation with the remnants of the oblation using this mantra."
Thus [it is said].
The Teachers also [state]: "The bali offering [is made] with the food remaining from the oblation."
"According to the rule" (yathāvidhi) also indicates the offering to the world-protectors (lokapāla-bali). || 105 ||

Then, for the sake of peace, [one should offer] the heart-mantra: "May they, together with their hearts, Viṣṇu, and their hosts—those who bring peace to all—at the end, accept this bali offering for the sake of tranquility. (106)
One should properly feed the Brahmins with food that is predominantly sweet, doing so with great respect;
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, accompanied by garments and ornaments. || 107 ||

This ritual shall swiftly destroy for men the afflictions of malevolent spirits, diseases, planetary influences, and fevers, as well as the torments caused by Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Mārīs, and the like; of this there is no doubt. (108)
He states the mantra for the bali offering with the words "sahṛt":
the word *hṛt* means the word *namaḥ*; the heart is the word *namaḥ*. The mantra ends with this.
Its nature as the source of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) and so forth should be understood.
*Mārī* is a specific type of *kṛtyā* (sorcery).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [powers such as] *ityā* and other such words are included. (106–108)
Having constructed a cage with planks from milky trees, and having filled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the practitioner of mantra should place the object of the rite within it.
Having touched one who wears clean garments and whose limbs are purified, one should properly recite the mantra;
meanwhile, the fire should be established in the directions beginning with the east by the most excellent of Brahmins. || 110 ||
One who knows the ritual procedure should have the golden [image] fashioned from the materials previously specified;
the patron, according to his own capacity, should satisfy those [artisans] with sacrificial fees. || 111 ||
Then, having bowed to the Guru, one should gratify him with wealth, grain, and other offerings.
This rite is declared to be the remover of all diseases and the destroyer of sorcery, malice, and the like. || 112 ||
This rite is proclaimed as the remover of untimely death for men;
it is performed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or with decoctions derived from milk-bearing trees. || 113 ||

One should sprinkle with consecrated jars that are filled, over which mantras have been recited, and into which the *sampāta* offering has been poured; [one should thus sprinkle] the man afflicted by planetary influences or suffering from malevolent magic.
By this swift rite, a man becomes healthy through the well-performed procedure of ablution on a Sunday. || 115 ||
One desiring an easy delivery should bathe the woman with these waters;
by sprinkling her seven times, all complications shall perish.
The phrase "of milk-bearing trees" (*kṣīraśākhinām*) is also an elliptical designation for the *palāśa* tree.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"In vessels fashioned from the leaves of *palāśa* and milk-bearing trees..."
Thus [it is said].
And the Teachers [state]: "A cage should be constructed with planks made of *pālāśa* wood or from trees growing on mountain breasts."
By this, one should understand that the same applies to the milk-trees as well.

"One should recite [the mantra] correctly" means until the completion of the fire-offerings being performed in the four directions. [This is done] with the eight substances, such as clarified butter and so forth, as previously specified.
By the phrase "one who knows the ritual procedure" (vidhānavit), it is stated that for each substance there is one hundred and twenty-six oblations.
In the expression "filled with the five products of the cow" (pañcagavyaiḥ pūritaiḥ), the instrumental case is used in a non-co-referential sense;
"with jars" (kalaśaiḥ) refers to nine jars.
The oblation is implied by the term "sampāta. The oblation itself consists of the eight previously mentioned substances and is performed the previously mentioned number of times.
The connection is that by this procedure, a person quickly becomes healthy.
The method for its performance is as follows:

having constructed the previously described nine-naveled mandala, having established the nine jars as before and filled them with the prescribed substances, having worshipped the deity mentioned in the mantra in the center, and having worshipped the eight weapons in the eight surrounding jars, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the requirements of the rite.
"One should perform the consecration with jars joined by the pouring together of those [substances].
In the case of five jars, having drawn a mandala of five lotuses, the discus, mace, club, and noose are to be worshipped in the cardinal directions;
the rest is as before.

"By means of the procedure for consecration" (abhiṣekasya vidhānena) means by the method of establishing a single flask (ekakalaśa-sthāpana-prakāra) in the manner previously described. By the phrase "well-prepared" (susādhitaiḥ), it is implied that the fire-oblation (homa) and the sprinkling of the remains (sampāta) are performed as before.
By means of the consecration performed on seven Sundays.

Ghee boiled in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and consecrated with this mantra, when consumed by pregnant women or those afflicted by planetary influences, brings about auspiciousness. (117)
Regarding the term *pañcagavya*:

according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*), "An unctuous substance (*sneha*) may be prepared even without a paste (*akalka*) when it is to be processed with a liquid alone," that ghee should be prepared without a paste.
In that case:
"Wherever there are five or more substances in a preparation involving fats,
they say that [the fat] should be equal in measure to the milk"—
so it is said.
Having added the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) equal in measure to the ghee, one should cook the ghee.
Although water is obtained by the [general] statement [of the recipe], it should not be added;
this is because the cow's urine already possesses the essence [of water]. || 117 ||
When Venus is situated in its exaltation, a ring made of three metals, properly prepared by a wise man, shall destroy minor spirits, malevolent planets, and fevers. || 118 ||
When Venus is situated in its exaltation sign, Pisces, it is "well-accomplished" (sādhusādhitā), according to the method stated in the sixth [chapter]. || 118 ||

Having made knots on the thread according to the number of its syllables, one should prepare it—consecrated by means of recitation and other rites—to be worn on the hand or around the neck for the pacification of suffering. || 119 ||
"By the number of its syllables" means by the number of syllables in the mantra;
this applies to both cases.
Therefore, having made seven threads, seven knots should be tied therein.
The specific details of this ritual practice are found in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"One should offer oblations of *apāmārga* wood-fuel smeared with cow-products, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and ghee;
and jars placed upon a junction of white and copper threads that have been strewn around."
At the time of the fire-oblation (homa), one should consecrate vessels filled with the decoction of milk-trees;
then, one should bathe [the image] with as many pours of that liquid as were offered, preceded by the remnants of the products of the cow.
"One should fashion that thread, knotted, upon his hand and so forth through recitation.
By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "through recitation and so forth," [it is meant] worship and the [ritual] accomplishment on the hand and the ear.
It should be known that the male is on the right and the female on the left. || 119 ||
Having touched the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should recite the mantra up to a thousand times;
that [substance] should be placed upon a lotus leaf or on a leaf from the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree. || 120 ||
Or the practitioner of mantras should bury the fruit of a bilva tree in his own house or that of another; there shall be protection from all dangers, and all prosperity will increase. || 121 ||
The bark of *palāśa* and milk-exuding trees, abundant *malayaja* (sandalwood), saffron, *yāminī*, *kuṣṭha*, *bilva*, *apāmārga*, and mustard seeds. || 122 ||
Sesame, dūrvā grass, barley, the goddess, a pair of tulasī leaves, kuśa grass, lakṣmī, gorocana, a lotus, and vacā mixed with cow dung. || 123 ||

While reciting the mantra, one should cast [the substance] combined with *viṣṇukrāntā* and *arka* into a vessel filled with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), over a consecrated fire. || 124 ||
Having placed it [in the vessel], one should boil it properly until it becomes ashes.
Then, taking that [ashes], one should again recite [the mantra] a million times while perceiving the deity. || 125 ||
One should smear all the limbs with this [substance] and place a small amount on the head;
it wards off the suffering caused by malevolent spirits, hostility, planetary influences, insanity, and disease. || 126 ||
It is the supreme pacifier of all enemies, the remover of all sins, the bestower of auspiciousness and subjugation for men, and the warder-off of all calamities. || 127 ||
It is especially praised for pregnant women, children, and the sick;
it is proclaimed that there is no protection superior to this in the world. || 128 ||
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "on a lotus leaf, etc.," one should understand vessels such as those made of *brahmapatra* and so forth.
The connection is that the practitioner, a man, should bury [the substance] in his own house or in the house of another.
*Puru* refers to *guggulu*.
Yāminī is turmeric (haridrā). Kuṣṭha is kūḍa.
"Bilva" refers to the five parts of the bilva fruit.
The goddess is Sahadevī.
"Padma" refers to the five-limbed lotus.
In the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*, which is a commentary on the passage beginning with "the lotus petals and so forth," it is stated that there are five parts of the *vilva* and five parts of the lotus.
"Arka" refers to the bark of the *arka* tree;
"that" refers to the vessel.
"One should boil it correctly" means while reciting the mantra, as previously stated.
"Ten million" (prayuta) refers to one hundred thousand times ten.
In some places, the reading is "ayutam" [instead of "ayuta"]. (120–128)
Mustā, śuṇṭhī, niśā, vahnī, elā, yaṣṭī, vacā, vṛṣā, pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, mañjiṣṭhā, drākṣā, dārvī, and rohiṇī. || 129 ||

And one should cook one *prastha* of the three fruits along with those pastes in the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) together with clarified butter, prepared according to rule with this mantra. || 130 ||

The wise know pure *pañcagavya-ghṛta* (ghee prepared with the five products of the cow) to bestow beauty and grant sons to women, to remove the fear of ghosts and spirits, and to protect the fetus. || 131 ||
Mustā is *moccha* (muthā).
Niśā is turmeric (*haridrā*).
Vahni is *citraka*;
yaṣṭi is *yaṣṭimadhu*;
vṛṣā is *āḍharūṣa*.
"Vāsaka" means *yāvat*.
"Dārvī" is *dāruharidrā*.
"Rohiṇī" is *kaṭakī*.

The three fruits are *haritakī*, *bibhītaka*, and *āmalaka*. "According to rule" means in the manner prescribed by the medical treatises (*vaidyaka-śāstra*). Regarding that, the measure for the milk has already been stated.
Since it is stated that "the paste (kalka) is one-fourth the quantity of the oil," one *kuḍava* measure of paste should be taken.
Because of the rule stating "five and so forth," each of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) should be equal in quantity to the oil.
Having removed the remainder of the clarified butter (*ājya*), and having cooled it, it is consecrated by this mantra and empowered with recitation (*saṃjapta*). (129–131)
One should write the seven letters ending in *ṭ* in the center, and then write the syllables of the mantra in the six corners; this wheel wards off calamities.

Regarding the yantra, he says "the letters ending in ṭ" (ṭāntān): having written seven instances of the letter ṭha in the six triangles beginning with the center, one should write the syllables of the mantra in sequence upon those ṭhas;
it should be understood that the names of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), the practitioner (sādhaka), and the rite (karman) are also to be written in the center.
"Āpad" refers to asthma and fever, according to the statement in the Nārāyaṇīya: "The Cakra [discus] removes asthma and fever. || 132 ||

One should write the *tāra* (the syllable Om) together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the center of the hexagon; the remaining syllables [of the mantra] should be placed on the six points.
The auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) are to be placed at the junctions of those [points]; this is the yantra.
It provides protection when properly consecrated with recitation. || 133 ||
He states another *yantra* with the word "six" (*ṣaḍ*).
"In the six corners" refers to those beginning with fire (the southeast).
By the term "according to rule" (*vidhivat*), it is stated that there is a recitation (*japa*) of one thousand and eight [times].
It provides protection; the remainder [of the sentence] is that it is established there.
As it has been said:
"In the center, the *tāra* (om), and thereafter the mantra letter by letter in the six corners."

And on the outside, one should draw the limb [of the deity] upon gold, copper, silver, or stone, according to the prescribed rite; then, having consecrated it with mantras, that installed wheel destroys the fear of thieves, malevolent planets, and enemies, and provides protection. Thus [ends verse 133].

One should write the syllable *tāra* (OM), containing the name of the practitioner (*sādhya*), at the end of each [line] in the corners; the remaining six mantra-syllables are placed in the [remaining] corners.
Then, the limbs (*aṅga*) are placed at the joints of the sixteen-spoked [wheel].
It consists of sixteen syllables and is preceded by the word "vasudhā. || 134 ||

Having recited [the mantra] until the prescribed number of repetitions is completed, this yantra—which is beneficial for pregnant women—shall destroy malevolent magic, planetary afflictions, and insanity. || 135 ||
He states another yantra with the words "the Tāra," etc. "Situated at the end of Ṭha" is an adjective qualifying Tāra.
"Sixteen-spoked" [refers to the wheel].
In a circle divided into sixteen equal parts, one should draw lines at every fifth mark;
beginning from the first mark, this is considered a sixteen-spoked [wheel].
Thus is the method for drawing the sixteen-spoked [cakra].
The "sixteen-syllabled" refers to the sixteen-syllable wheel-mantra to be described hereafter.
According to others, by the term "sixteen-syllabled," one means a sixteen-petaled lotus, above which is a circle, and above that, the earth-maṇḍala.
And the mantra is: Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā.
This has been stated in the Nārāyaṇīya: "One should write the syllables of the mantra in the six outer corners starting from Sāṃkhya (the northeast) and proceeding counterclockwise."

"One should draw the mantra upon sixteen petals outside the circular junctions of the limbs, and again draw a circle within the square of the earth; this should be done according to the prescribed rule.
In some versions, the reading is "the sixteen-syllable [mantra] on that many petals."
After "having recited," the word "having offered" (hutveti) is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 134-135 ||

In the center, one should write the *tāra* (the syllable Om) together with the name of the practitioner (*sādhya*) and the mantra; then, in the six corners and at the junctions, the limbs of the mantra (*aṅga*).
At the end, there is a lotus with eight petals, shining with twice-four [thirty-two] filaments, whose pericarp consists of the letters beginning with *ka*.
With its own name, one should draw a sixteen-petaled lotus shining with the sixteen vowels.
One should draw it surrounded by three lines with the *hakṣa* syllables, and encircled by three nooses and two goads.

He states another yantra with the words "in the middle" (*madhye*). "The mantra" (*manum*) refers to the wheel-mantra excluding the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*). "At the end" (*ante*) means outside the hexagon.
Of the arts and of the musical notes.
"Eight-syllabled" refers to the eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa.
"Two Vasu petals" means sixteen petals.

The meaning is that the name of the practitioner (*sādhya-nāman*) is surrounded three times by its own name together with *ha* and *kṣa*; that is, the name of the practitioner is placed between *ha* and *kṣa*. That [sequence] is repeated three times with the [syllables] *tri-pāśāṅkuśābhyām*.

As for the phrase "surrounded three times" (*triḥ-pravītam*), when there is an expectation as to how it is repeated three times, [the answer is: one repetition consists of the practitioner's own name together with *ha* and *kṣa*, and the second...
The third [syllable] is with the noose, and the second is with the goad.
This is because the second three-footed [mantra] is explained as the meditation on recurrence (āvṛtti-dhyāna) by virtue of its nature as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
That very one is indeed to be saluted.

Some read the text as "with the *tāra*, the noose, and the goad" (*tārapāśāṅkuśābhyām*) and apply it as follows: among those [three repetitions], one is with *ha* and *kṣa* along with its own name; another is with the *tāra*; and the third is with the noose and the goad. This alone is the traditional position (*sāmpradāyika*).
Some explain that the meaning of the second "tri" is indeed the *praṇava* itself, because it consists of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*;
the dual number is used with reference to its repetition.
As it has been said:

"The *cakrayantra* consists of three enclosures (*trivīta*), with the sky (*vyoma*) as the final syllable, and the noose (*pāśa*) and goad (*aṅkuśa*) formed by one's own name. Regarding the commentary on this, the teacher Padmapāda states:
The *guṇa* is the *praṇava*. There are three repetitions consisting solely of *ha* and *kṣa*.

In the second repetition, having uttered the *tāra*, one should utter two syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then again utter the *pāśa*, and then again utter two syllables of the name of the *sādhya*.

Furthermore, having uttered the seed-syllable of the goad (Aṅkuśa), one should again utter two syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Thus they say that one should encircle [the name] with these letters.
In the commentary on the phrase "encircled by the noose and the goad" (*pāśāṅkuśaveṣṭita*), the *Apekṣitārthadyotikā* states: "three times by the noose and also three times by the goad. || 136 ||
*Tāraṃ namo bhagavate mahāsudarśanāya ca*—this sixteen-syllable mantra of the Discus (Cakra), ending with *varma* and *astra*, has been proclaimed. || 137 ||
He extracts the sixteen-syllable mantra beginning with "tāra.
This too is an independent mantra;
its seer and all other details are as previously stated for the former mantra.
Now, the yantra found in another tantra is described:
having drawn a six-spoked wheel, one should place the Sudarśana [mantra] on its spokes;
outside of that, an eight-spoked lotus, and on its petals, the supreme eight-syllabled [mantra].
Outside of that, there should be a twelve-spoked [wheel]; one should write the twelve-syllable [mantra].
Then, a sixteen-spoked lotus; one should write the root mantra.
The most excellent preceptor should surround the supreme yantra with the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) and draw the Mahāsudarśana [mantra] on the outside.
Tāraṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, Mahāsudarśana, and to the Great Wheel, possessing great radiance and a blazing form!

O Sage, having written a pair of protective syllables on all sides and the word *dviṭha* (*svāhā*) within the *mahābala* [mantra], one should inscribe the object of the rite (*sādhya*) in the center, within the belly of the *praṇava*.
"The Yantra bestows all accomplishments," thus the Lord himself declared. || 137 ||
This wheel-mantra has been proclaimed as the dispeller of all fears, the pacifier of minor ailments and untimely death, and the increaser of victory for kings. || 138 ||
Having drawn eight lines and bound them externally in sequence according to the Vedas,
one should divide the mantra of Hṛṣīkeśa according to its respective positions.
One should draw the feet situated within four squares. || 139 ||
One should correctly write the mantra of the wheel, consisting of eight syllables, within two compartments; then,
one should write it together with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in the central compartment.
This may be the yantra known as the Seven-Compartmented.
It is fitting, O Hṛṣīkeśa, that by your glorification the world rejoices and is filled with devotion;
the demons, struck with fear, flee in all directions.
And all the hosts of perfected ones pay him homage. || 141 ||

Regarding the seven-compartment yantra, he says "lines" (*rekhā*). One should draw lines extending from east to west; the connection is that their ends (*śirāṃsi*) are to be bound externally in sequence by the quarters (*śrutiśaḥ*).
One should join the tip of the first line with the tip of the fourth;

by this, some say it becomes like a *harītakī* (yellow myrobalan) fruit. However, masters such as Padmapādācārya have explained it as being "like a triple-edged arrow" (*triśa*) as praised in the Vedas.
In their view, the meaning is that one should join the tip of the first line with the tip of its own third line.
Others, however, the venerable Pūjyapāda himself, explain it thus:
having fixed the tip of the first line with the tip of its own fourth line, and then again having fixed the tip of the third line with the tip of the sixth line, and then...
One should connect the tip of the fifth line to the tip of the eighth line;
likewise on the second side as well.
Then, only the second and seventh lines remain in the middle.
Then, starting from the eastern end of the second line, one should lead it toward the north and join it with its western end.
Likewise, starting from the eastern end of the seventh line, one should lead it toward the south and join it with its western end.
In this way, the statement "on the outside" becomes meaningful.
Thus, the three central compartments become connected by a single line.
This is the summary: the drawing of this yantra should be understood according to the tradition of one's own guru.

One should write the four-footed lines of the *aṣṭākṣara* mantra, which are free from the *pratiṣṭhā*, located within the four compartments, specifically in the first, second, sixth, and seventh positions.
The characteristics of Vidarbha will be described in the twenty-third [chapter].
In the two *koṣṭhas* consisting of the third and fifth [syllables],
"properly" means together with the *sādhya*.
"In the middle square" means in the fourth square.
"Together with the object of accomplishment" (*sasādhya*) is understood as being connected to the word "diagram" (*cakra*).
This has been stated by the Teachers: "The Sudarśana [diagram], with the object of accomplishment written in three squares."
Thus [ends the section]. 139–141.
That which consists of seven compartments, when worn, protects one from great fear;
it is proclaimed by the wise as a pacifier of bad dreams, evil omens, and the like. || 142 ||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Śāradātilaka composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra. 16.
"It has been maintained" (bth).
The manner of maintaining it was stated by the Teachers:
Having properly inscribed this yantra upon birch bark, a linen cloth, or a very smooth rag, the practitioner should again roll it into a pill, coating it with lac. Then,
having empowered it by the falling of oblations of clarified butter offered into the fire of ashes and other materials, [he should apply it].
When properly recited, all disturbances indeed come to complete pacification. Thus it is said.
The meaning is "that mantra," for the word *mantra* is used in the neuter gender in many places.
Therefore, this is the sense:
The *Gītā-mantra* together with the *Abhīta*, as well as the eight-syllabled (*aṣṭākṣara*) and the discus (*cakra*) mantra, when recited, bestow this fruit.

As it was said by the Teachers: "In the proper place, this well-prepared diagram, consecrated with the three mantras—the *Hṛṣīkeśa-vidabhīta* and the eight-syllabled—constantly provides protection against malevolent planets and other such dangers."
Having performed the five-limbed ritual (*pañcāṅga*) with the four quarters of the mantra "O Hṛṣīkeśa" and with the entire [mantra], [one should meditate]:
"Agni is his head, the moon and sun are his eyes, the quarters are his ears, and speech is his knowledge as well as the Vedas;
Vāyu is his breath, the universe is his heart, and from his two feet the earth [arises]; for he is the inner self (*antarātman*) of all beings."
Having meditated thus, one should worship the deity in the pericarp, the limbs (aṅgas) on the petals, and the world-protectors (lokapālas) outside of that.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of one million recitations;
the fire-oblation (homa) consists of one-tenth of that number performed with clarified butter.
The fruit is the destruction of all evils, the pacification of all [misfortunes], the warding off of all malevolent planets, and the slaying of all demons. || 142 ||
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition. 16.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Now I shall proclaim the mantra of the glorious Puruṣottama, the root of the world.
It is indeed concealed in the Vaiṣṇava Tantra, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Because they are concealed within the Vaiṣṇava Tantras and because they are established as objects of remembrance at the end [of the ritual], he begins to state the mantras beginning with Puruṣottama, starting with the word "atha.
And it is said in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"The fourfold division of Viṣṇu known by the name Puruṣottama..."
Among them, Trailokyamohana is considered the first, regarded as the primordial nature (prakṛti).
"Śrīkara, Hṛṣīkeśa, and Kṛṣṇa as the fourth;
or Śrīdhara may be the fourth, or some say Pradyumna. Thus it is said.
The expression "Puruṣottama" is used because there is no distinction between the mantra and the deity.
Because it is an extreme secret, it has been concealed;
for this very reason, the teachers have performed its extraction in the Guptapaṭala.
By the phrase "enjoyment and liberation," the ritual application (viniyoga) has been stated. || 1 ||
The seed-syllables *tāra*, *māra*, *rama*, and *rāmā* [are placed] at the end of the word *namas* for Puruṣottama;
then again, after *apratirūpa*, the word *lakṣmīnivāsa*. || 2 ||
At the end of "sakala," [place] "jagatpūrvam" (preceded by the world), then again the word "kṣobhaṇe" (O agitator);
then [the mantra] joined with "sarvastrīhṛdaya" (the heart of all women), and again the word "vidāraṇa" (tearing asunder). || 3 ||
After that, [there arose] a sound from the women of beautiful human form at the end of the gods and demons, which caused intoxication with pride throughout the three worlds. || 4 ||
The pair [of opposites] torments the minds; again, the pair inflames them; further, the pair withers them; and again, the pair kills them. (5)
Next, two [mantras] for paralyzing; then again, two for deluding;
next, two for causing flight; and thereafter, a pair for attracting. || 6 ||
And joined with "samastaparamopetasubhagena," followed by the word "sarvasaubhāgya," and ending with the words "kareti" joined [to it]. || 7 ||
The word "sarvakāmaprada" (bestower of all desires), followed by [the name] "amuka," then the pair of syllables "hana," and after that, with the discus, the mace, and subsequently the sword. || 8 ||
One should pierce the pair [of wheels] with all the arrows, then move to the next position with the noose;
then, at the end of each pair of spokes, one should strike the pair again with the goad. || 9 ||

Then there are two instances of the word "kuru," followed by "atha," "u," "kim," "tiṣṭhasi," and again the word "padam"—all this until the end of the line, where the desired [result] immediately follows. || 10 ||
Then, having addressed me as "Siddha," followed by "Bhavati," "Ante," "Sa-varma," and "Phaṭ"—this mantra, ending with "Namaḥ," is said to consist of two hundred syllables. || 11 ||
The sage Jaimini is declared to be its seer, and its meter is said to be immeasurable;
Puruṣottama is the deity, the origin of all the worlds. || 12 ||
He extracts the mantra: *tāra*. *Tāra* is the *praṇava* of the Goddess.
Since the *oṃkāra* is generally stated to be the beginning of all mantras, it likewise stands at the beginning here, either by that [general rule] or according to the tradition (*sampradāya*).

Alternatively, by applying the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a pair of identical terms) to "tāraśca tāraśca," the form "tārau" is obtained; subsequently, this is compounded with the words beginning with "rama.
In that case, the first word "tāra" refers to the *praṇava* (OM), and the second word "tāra" refers to the *devī-praṇava*.
This interpretation is the view of the teacher Padmapādācārya.
Māra is the seed-syllable of desire (kāma). Ramā is the seed-syllable of Śrī. Nati is the word "namas."
"Sarvastrīhṛdaya" is the essential nature [of the mantra].
Here, there is no sandhi (euphonic combination) anywhere.
All [the words] ending in the accusative case are the objects of the verb "ābhāṣya" (addressing), whereas in the mantra they appear in the vocative case.
In the mantra as well, the word "samīhitam" (the desired object) ending in the accusative case signifies "is accomplished.
Regarding the statement "consisting of two hundred syllables," some hold that the phrase "amuka" refers to the name of the person for whom the rite is performed (*sādhya*).
Others, however, maintain that because the words "durita" (evil) and so forth are inserted in place of the word "amuka," it is said to be "endowed with two hundred syllables."
They stated that even the presence of extra syllables does not constitute a fault.
Some say as follows: "Encased by Śakti and Śrīmārī, it brings about the delusion of the world through mere remembrance."
The Praṇava is the seed-syllable (bīja), and Huṃ is the power (śakti). || 2-12 ||
One should say "Tribhuvana" after the word "Puruṣottama";
then "Madonmādakara," followed by "Huṃ" and the entire "Hṛdaya. || 13 ||
At the end of the word "jagatkṣobhaṇa" (shaker of the world), [place] "lakṣmīdayita" (beloved of Lakṣmī) and "huṃ" on the head;
joined with the supreme "manmatha" (the god of love), it bestows desires upon the progenitor. || 14 ||
Huṃ is the crest-mantra, supremely endowed and joined with auspicious syllables; "huṃ" is proclaimed as the armor that brings about all prosperity. || 15 ||
Then, [one should describe] the beautiful women accompanied by gods, asuras, and men;
thereafter, one should speak of that which causes the heart to rend. || 16 ||
"Holding all weapons, O fulfiller of all desires, [that is the supreme].
Then 'slay' twice, the heart, and the bindings thereafter. || 17 ||
[The mantra consists of: "ākarṣaya" (attract), followed by the two words "mahābala" and "humasraka";
then the word "tribhuvaneśvara", and finally "sarvajanān". (18)

"Manāṃsi, hana-yugmānte, dāraya-dvitayaṃ ca me, vaśamānaya, huṃ-netraṃ, tārādyāḥ phaṭ, ending with namaḥ— these are the six limb-mantras (ṣaḍaṅgamantraḥ) taught by those who know the tantras, ending with the eye-mantra (netrāntāḥ). || 19 ||
He extracts the six-limbed mantras beginning with *puruṣottama*.
In the *śikhā* mantra, there is a euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) between the word *aṅgaje* and the preceding [syllable].
As it has been said: "Having uttered the syllables of Manmatha, one should thereafter utter the syllables of the Supreme Lord born from the limbs."
Thus, in the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), both [the terms] "heart" (*hṛdaya*) and so forth constitute its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Regarding the phrase "beginning with *tārā*":

The six-limbed mantras ending with the eyes have been stated; they are taught as beginning with *tāra* (the syllable Om), beginning with *praṇava* (the syllable Om), and ending with *phaṭ* and *namaḥ*. This is the connection [of the words]. By the phrase "by those who know the Tantras," this is what is meant: The six limbs are: the heart, the head, the crown-lock, the armor, the two eyes, and the weapon. Their mantras are taught as follows: *oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *oṃ śirase svāhā*, *oṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *oṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *oṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ*, *oṃ astrāya phaṭ*. These are the six-limbed mantras. They are taught as beginning with *tāra* (the syllable Om) and beginning with *praṇava* (the syllable Om), and ending with *phaṭ* and *namaḥ*. This is what is stated by those who know the Tantras.
As they say:

"Having placed the pervasive mantra upon the hands, and having placed the [five] limbs upon the fingers and the palms, one should place the arrows together with Anaṅga; thereafter, one should place the pervasive mantra upon the body."
One should perform the placement syllable by syllable using the Mātṛkā, encapsulated by the seed-syllables of Māra;
and one should place the syllables of the Māra-mālā mantra as the limbs [of the deity], just like the Mātṛkā.
One should count forty letters in the belly, heart, throat, mouth, and nose,
and three letters throughout the entire body, once each.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the forms preceded by *klīm* and the syllables of the Mother-mantra (*mātṛkā*), as well as those preceded by Kāma and Rati.
Prior to the seat-mantra (*pīṭhamaṃtra*), one should place the Garuḍa-mantra upon the heart using the Garuḍa-mudrā.
As they say:

"Having performed the rites up to the placement of the seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*) in the body according to the stated method, one should place that mantra in the heart with the *Garuḍa-mudrā*, and then place the seat-mantra (*pīṭhamanu*). (13–19)
At the end of the syllables of Trailokyamohana, one should again utter the word Hṛṣīkeśa;
thereafter, one should speak Apratirūpa and so forth, following after Manmatha. || 20 ||
First the word for "all" (sarva), then the feminine noun, followed by "drawing the heart" (hṛdayākarṣaṇam);
then the mantra "Come! Come! (āgacchāgaccha), preceded by the syllable Om and joined with "namas. || 21 ||
Having performed the pervasive placement with this mantra and having assigned [the mantras] to the arms, one should contemplate the eight weapons together with their mudrās and mantras. || 22 ||
In the pervasive mantra (*vyāpakamantra*), the connection of the word *apratirūpa* is only with what precedes it, and not with anything else.
Having placed the eight weapons on the arms together with their respective mudrās and mantras, one should meditate upon the deity; this is the remainder of the sense.
The eight weapons are those described in the meditation (*dhyāna*).
The sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa) will also be explained in that very same place.
As for the characteristics of the mudrās:
the noose-mudrā (pāśamudrā) should be understood as previously described.
Alternatively, this is the *pāśa-mudrā*,
as they say:
"Having joined the tips of the index fingers and thumbs, the other [fingers] are bent."
Thus, the pāśamudrā is fully described.
One should join the tip of the middle finger of the left hand with the tip of the index finger.
One should press the ring finger and the little finger with its thumb.
"One should display the bow on the right shoulder; this is declared to be the Madra-dhanuṣ.
Alternatively, this is to be known as the Dhanurmadrā, as they say:
The practitioner should touch the base of the arm with that very tip of the arm; this is the bow mudrā (dhanurmudrā), which increases fame, renown, strength, and valor. Thus it is said.
"Having bound the little finger and the ring finger with one's own thumb on the left side, while the remaining fingers are extended and closely joined, this is the sword mudrā. Thus it is said.
The mudrās of the conch, mace, discus, club, and goad have been described by me previously.
Immediately following this, one should place the Śrīvatsa, Kaustubha, and forest garland upon the body in their respective locations using their own mantras and mudrās.
As it has been said:
Then the wise one should place the ornaments upon his own body according to their proper positions.
The mudrās for these have been described previously.
The mantras, however, will be stated [in the following verses]. 20–22.
Situated in the midst of the ocean of milk, with celestial trees standing in close proximity,
it has dispelled the weight of darkness by the rays of the rising sun and moon.
It was filled with swarms of bees, dancing like dark clouds at the sight of it, and thronged by bees delighted by the fragrance of blossoming flowers. || 24 ||
The quarters of the sky were made resonant by flocks of warbling cuckoos, and it was filled with breezes carrying the fragrance of various flowers. || 25 ||
In groves of wish-fulfilling creepers, it was adorned by throngs of Siddhas sporting there, and graced by the songs of celestial Gandharva maidens. || 26 ||
There was a vast and wonderful garden filled with many lotus ponds;
in its center stood a pavilion made of jewels, adorned with arched gateways. || 27 ||
Seated upon a magnificent and auspicious great lion-throne at the foot of the celestial tree, which is constantly attended by the six seasons, [he shone] with supreme majesty. || 28 ||
One should meditate upon the Lord of the World, who consists of the universe, seated together with his beloved upon Garuḍa, who is stationed in the center of a red lotus. || 29 ||

By the word "milk" (*kṣīra*), it is stated that immediately after [the element] earth, one should employ the milk-ocean, the jewel-island, the marvelous garden, the jeweled pavilion, the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*), the great lion-throne, and Garuḍa in the ritual placement of the seats (*pīṭhanyāsa*) and so forth.
[23–29] One should worship the Lord Śrī Puruṣottama together with Kamalā, who rests upon his own lap, and the lotus.

One should meditate in the mind upon Him who is reddish-hued, whose face is a smiling lotus, who holds in His hands the conch, noose, mace, bow, arrow, sword, club, and goad, and who has fixed His gaze upon her who embraces Him with arms as radiant as a lotus. || 30 ||
Regarding meditation, he says "the deity," meaning [one should meditate on her] as having the luster of a lotus— that is, as being yellow in color.
In that regard, Kamalā has two arms.
In her left hand she holds a lotus, while with her right she embraces [her consort].
As it has been said:
"She is yellow, holding a lotus in her left hand, and embracing her lord with her [right] hand."
Elsewhere it is said: "With a most beautiful lotus held in her left hand, shining like molten gold.

As for the visualization of the weapons: in the left hands, starting from the top, are the conch, the bow, and the mace; in the right hands, starting from the top, are the goad, the mallet, the sword, and the discus.
As it is said in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"One should visualize a wheel, radiant as the sun, in the lower right hand;
likewise, a sword in the one above that, and a mallet in the one to its left."
One should visualize a beautiful goad in the upper right hand;
in the upper left hand one should visualize a noose, and below that, a conch shell.
One should meditate on a bow with an arrow in the [other] left hand, and a mace in the lower hand. Thus it is said.
The placement of the previously mentioned weapons upon the body should be understood according to this sequence.
Here, following meditation, these mudrās are to be displayed.
As they say: "The Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha, and that called the Vanamālā, [are formed] with the Māra-bīja."
The two fists are joined with the thumbs pointing upward, placed at the head and mutually touching.
"Then, one should apply that mudrā called Trailokyamohana to the head.
Thus [ends verse 30].
Having meditated thus upon the beloved of Śrī, the self-controlled practitioner should then perform the fire-pit shaped like a half-moon and recite the mantra four hundred thousand times.

One should indeed offer oblations into the Vaiṣṇava fire with lotuses born from jasmine, and subsequently with flowers and barley grains in due order; thereafter, one should also feed the Brāhmaṇas. || 32 ||
The term "the master" (vaśī) has already been indicated by the Teacher previously;
as they say:
"Having meditated, one who has received the initiation of the mantra should recite this mantra fifty thousand times."
And by offering oblations with these substances, one becomes entitled to the ritual acts of Manu’s descendant.

One should offer a hundred oblations each of curd, ghee, and milk; then ten thousand oblations of cooked milk with ghee and sacrificial grain (havis); likewise, a measure of a drona with unbroken sesame seeds; and similarly, ten times ten oblations with the three sweets (trimadhu) and excellent seasonal fruits.
"One should fully satisfy one's excellent guru with a hundred fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood. Thus it is said.
"One should offer oblations"—the remainder is "one-tenth" (daśāṃśam).
Thus it has been said: "One-tenth [of the total] in the Vaiṣṇava fire."
By the phrase "subsequently in order," the offering of libations (tarpaṇa) and so forth is indicated. || 31-32 ||
Desiring to worship the Lord of the World, the preceptor should purify himself, the sacrificial materials, and the sacrificial ground by means of the Gāyatrī mantra. || 33 ||
By the word "guide" (deśika), it is stated that [the Lord] is the cause of desire and so forth. || 33 ||
"Trailokyamohanāya vidmahe," one should utter this word; then "smarāya dhīmahi," and finally "tanno Viṣṇuḥ pracodayāt. || 34 ||
This is declared to be the Gāyatrī, belonging to Viṣṇu, which bestows all perfections.
Then, one should prepare a seat upon the previously mentioned Vaiṣṇava pedestal. || 35 ||
The mantra of this King of Birds is proclaimed as *Ṭha* twice (Ṭha-Ṭha). One should recite it according to the Svatantra system, for it bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).
Its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details are as follows:
Saṃkarṣaṇa is the sage, Gāyatrī the metre, and Puruṣottama the deity; [these are to be placed] on the head, the forehead, the eyes, the arms, the feet, and the tips of the joints.
Having properly assigned the syllables, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with five,
three, five, and again three [syllables].
"One should form the limbs with four [syllables] each using colored powders;
her worship and other rites are declared to be like those of the two-hundred-syllable [mantra]. Thus it is said.
"In the previously mentioned seat spoken of as the fifteenth" means that one should worship the powers (śaktis) beginning with Vimalā by means of this [seat].
As for the worship-diagram (pūjāyantra), it is that which is described in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*.
For example:
"One should draw an eight-petalled lotus with fragrant sandalwood paste; it should have two doors and be richly adorned. One should write the word 'Kāma' in its center. Thus it is said.
"Of this" refers to the seat. || 34–36 ||
With a one-pointed mind, he should [visualize] the deity within the form mentally conceived by means of the root mantra. || 36 ||
Having invoked [the deity] with the mantra, the wise one should worship with the pervasive [mantra].
The seed-syllable of the Goddess is proclaimed to be the letter *Bhṛgu* (B) joined with the final letter (*L*) and the moon (*I*). || 37 ||
The expression "with undivided mind" indicates that it is impossible to perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) without focused attention.
Regarding the word "having invoked":
the connection is that one should invoke the deity with the pervasive mantra and worship him within the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
"By the pervasive [mantra]" means by that very pervasive mantra mentioned previously.
"The wise one" refers to the fact that it has been stated that the sixteen types of offerings are performed with the pervasive mantra alone.

As it has been said: "This [procedure] was taught by the ancient masters at the end of the invocation (āvāhana) and the dismissal (visarga). He extracts the seed-syllable (bīja) of the Goddess as follows: "Bhṛgu... and so forth.
That [syllable] is Bhṛgu;
it is joined with La and Va,
and is accompanied by the Moon (the nasal bindu).
This is the seed-syllable (bīja) of the Goddess.
By means of this, one should first perform the worship of the Goddess seated upon the lap; this is the implied meaning for the worship of the limbs (aṅgapūjā).
Thus it has been said:
"Having worshipped Kamalā on the left thigh, one should then worship the enclosures (āvaraṇas) again.
Also elsewhere: "Having worshipped Śrī seated upon the left thigh, one should worship the limbs (aṅgas)."
Thus it is said.
Having worshipped the ornaments here, one should worship the limbs.
This has been stated in the Nārāyaṇīya:
The learned one should worship the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha upon the chest above the breast, the forest garland around the neck, and other items such as the yellow garment. Thus [ends verses 36–37].
First, one should worship the deities of the limbs according to the prescribed rite within the pericarp;
thereafter, one should worship Lakṣmī and the others, who hold chowries, upon the petals.
Bowed down by the weight of their beautiful breasts, which shone with strings of pearls;
resembling the hibiscus flower, they moved slowly with the intoxication of amorous play. || 39 ||

The wise say that the seed-syllable of the Goddess, adorned with vowels devoid of the three short [vowels], the letter *la*, and the *kaubasarga* (the visarga of Kubera), is their mantra in due order. || 40 ||
Regarding the phrase "by means of the ritual procedure" (*vidhānena*):

having worshipped the mantras ending with *varma* (the armor-mantra) in the four cardinal directions starting from the tip of the filaments, one worships *astra* (the weapon-mantra) in the intermediate directions and *netra* (the eye-mantra) in front; this is the meaning.
This has been stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:

One should worship the four limbs beginning with the heart in the directions starting from the east; then, once the [other] limbs have been worshipped, one should worship the weapon (astra), and thereafter worship the eye (netra) in front. Thus it is said.

Elsewhere it is also said: "The limbs [are assigned] to the directions and intermediate directions, with the armor (*varma*) as the limit; the weapon (*astra*) is in front, and the eye (*netra*) is likewise.
This refers to the petals and the bases of the petals.
"Lakṣmī and the others" refers to those mentioned in the previous mantra.
"In creation" means emission (*visarga*).
The vowels are devoid of these eight [consonants].
The connection is as follows: they say that the seed-syllable (bīja) of these goddesses is the mantra consisting of these [vowels]: ā, ī, ū, e, e, o, au, and aṃ. || 38-40 ||
On the tips of the petals, one should worship the conch, the Śārṅga bow, the discus, the sword,
the mace, the goad, the pestle, and the noose— these are the weapons of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
The mantras are declared in sequence by means of their respective mudrās and their respective seed-syllables (manus).
The first mantra for Jalacarā is said to be the two syllables "ṭha" at the end. || 42 ||
To Śārṅga with the arrow, ending with *svāhā*, is the immediately following mantra;
at the end of "Sudarśana Mahācakrarāja" there should be the pair *dahadaha*.
Drive away all fear of the wicked; sever the two [arms] separately!
Tear asunder the two feet! Devour, devour the mantras of others! 44 ||
Consuming and terrifying the pairs, with the armor syllable *vaṃ* and two *phaṭ*s for each, followed by "Obeisance to the Wheel" (*cakrāya namaḥ*)—this is declared to be the third mantra. || 45 ||
"Along with their own mudrās" means that one should worship these weapons at the tips of the petals together with their respective mantras and their own mudrās; this is the connection.
The characteristics of those mudrās have been stated by me previously.
The first is the conch mantra;
it should be understood as "to the aquatic one" (jalacarāya) and "to the great aquatic one" (mahājalacarāya).
Furthermore, the mention of "the two Ṭhas at the end" indicates that the recitation of the armor (kavaca) and weapon (astra) mantras should precede it.
By the phrase "proclaimed by Manu," the application [of the mantra] at the end of "Obeisance to Pāñcajanya" is indicated.
The Teachers first extracted the mantra for the Discus (Cakra), ending with "To Mahāsudarśana, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," and then extracted "Obeisance to Sudarśana.
Following that, the mantras for the Conch and the other [emblems] were extracted.
Regarding this, the teacher Padmapāda has explained that even in the mantras for the conch and other items, the word "mahā-" should be used at the beginning and "pāñcajanyāya namaḥ" etc. at the end.
The same mantras have been extracted in this very manner in the *Mantratantraprakāśa* and the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*.
The author himself has also stated this quite clearly by saying "namas cakrāya" in the mantra for the discus, and "kaumodakīpara" in the mantra for the Kaumodakī mace.
Therefore, this mantra is: *oṃ mahājalacarāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā pāñcajanyāya namaḥ* (1).
At the end of "mahāśabdānte" and at the end of "śārṅgāya saśarāya," the phrase "svāhāntaḥ" indicates that "huṃ phaṭ svāhā" should be recited;
otherwise, one would simply say "svāhā."
As it has been said: "The mantra for the bow Śārṅga, together with the arrow, is *huṃ phaṭ* [repeated] twice.
The Teachers also, having extracted "Huṃ Phaṭ Svāhā for the mace," stated: "[Huṃ Phaṭ Svāhā] for the Śārṅga bow and for the arrow."
In that context, by the use of the word "ca" (and), there is an inclusion of "huṃ phaṭ svāhā.
This has been explained by the commentators on that [text] regarding the subsequent two [weapons], the sword and the goad as well.
By the word "manu," it is stated: "Obeisance to the Śārṅga bow."
Next is the mantra of the Śārṅga bow: "Obeisance to the Great Śārṅga, together with his arrow, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā; obeisance to the Śārṅga. [2] Then, "Sudarśana... [3]
"Separately" means: "Kuru kuru, chinda chinda.
"Individually" means: [the same].

"Eat, eat! Terrify, terrify!"—between these two, it should also be understood that "O beings" (*bhūtāni*) is to be inserted. As stated by the Teachers: "Eat, eat, O beings; terrify, terrify, *varma*, *phaṭ*."
In another place as well: "the two [syllables] that terrify the elements," "huṃ phaṭ" is the pair;
"the two ṭha-s" means "svāhā."
"Cakrāya" should be understood as "to the Sudarśana [discus].
As it has been said:
"Svāhā to the Sudarśana, and then 'obeisance'—thus the mantra of the discus is taught."
Thus.
"The third" refers to the wheel-mantra (cakramantra). The mantra is as follows:

Sudarśana, Great Wheel-King! Burn, burn! Cause fear to all the wicked! Act, act! Cut, cut! Tear asunder, tear asunder! Destroy the mantras of others! Devour, devour! Eat, eat! Terrify, terrify the spirits! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! Homage to Sudarśana! (3) || 45 ||
At the end of the word *khaḍgatīkṣṇa*, there should be the pair *chinda* followed by *hum* and so forth;
this mantra is proclaimed for the fourth [mudrā], O Kaumodakī of great power! || 46 ||
The mantra ending in *svāhā* and dedicated to the goddess Kaumodakī is proclaimed by the wise as: *sarvāsurāntakipadaṃ prasīdayugavarmaphaṭ*. || 47 ||
Regarding "khaḍga": it should be understood as "mahākhaḍga. The reading "chindikaṭṭayugaṃ pṛthak" is a corruption.

Because it contradicts many texts and because it fails to extract the required words. As it was said by the Teachers: "At the end of the sharp blade [of the sword], one should cut with the sword-mantra."
Thus,

because such [a mantra] has been extracted in the *Mantra-tantra-prakāśa* within the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*, it is stated: "The mantra beginning with *huṃ phaṭ* consists of the pair 'sword' (*khaḍga*) and 'sharp-cutter' (*tīkṣṇacchinda*)."

Therefore, this reading is: "the pair of *chinda*, *hum*, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), *phaṭ* and *svāhā* are also included. [The mantra is: "Obeisance to the sword" (*khaḍgāya namaḥ*).
The fourth is the Sword Mantra. The mantra is as follows:
*mahākhaḍga tīkṣṇa chinda chinda hūṃ phaṭ svāhā khaḍgāya namaḥ* (4).
*Kaumodakī* refers to one who is devoted to the great *Kaumodakī*.
It ends with *namaḥ kaumodakye*.
The mantra, however, is as follows:
O Mahākaumodakī of great power, destroyer of all asuras, be gracious, be gracious! Huṃ phaṭ svāhā! Homage to Kaumodakī. (5) || 47 ||
At the end of the goad is a pair of plows; this is declared to be the sixth mantra.
At the end of the *saṃvartaka* [wind] is a pestle, followed again by a pair of *pothaya* [blows]. || 48 ||
"Huṃ phaṭ" ending with "dviṭha"—this is proclaimed as the seventh mantra.
Then, [utter] "bind with nooses," twice; then "attract," two words. (49)
The mantra is said to end with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā) and consist of six syllables with the eighth [syllable] being 'Sa'.
Afterwards, one should worship the Lords of the Quarters together with their weapons, such as the vajra and others. || 50 ||
"Aṅkuśā," "Mahāṅkuśā," and "This one"—the collective mantra is *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. As it has been said: "Above the pair of goads and the letter *ka*, [place] *huṃ* and so forth."
"Salutation to Manu as the goad"—
this is the sixth [mantra] for the goad.
The mantra, however, is:
"Mahāṅkuśa kaṭṭa kaṭṭa huṃ phaṭ svāhā, homage to Aṅkuśa. (6) "Muśala" refers to the Great Muśala; "mantra" refers to "homage to Muśala."
"Seventh" refers to the mace (*muśala*).
The mantra is: *saṃvarttaka mahāmuśala pothaya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā, namo muśalāya* (7).
"Noose" (*pāśa*) refers to the great noose (*mahāpāśa*).
The phrase "ending with the wife of Vahni" means ending with *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
As it has been said: "Above the word *mahāpāśa*, there are two *bandha*s and likewise two *karṣa*s, followed by *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*."
Regarding "the mantra of the noose":
it is "namaḥ pāśāya" (salutation to the noose).
This is the eighth [mantra] of the noose.
The mantra, however, is: *mahāpāśa bandha bandha ākarṣaya ākarṣaya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā pāśāya namaḥ* (8).
Elsewhere, it is stated that these [mantras] begin with the *praṇava* and the word *kāma*.
The weapon-mantras will be explained in sequence: "beginning with Tāra, Māra, and the seed-syllables.
There is a specific distinction regarding their worship.
As the teachers have said:
"In the directions starting from the east, there are the discus, mace, club, and pestle;
and then in the corners, starting from the southeast, there are the bow, sword, goad, and noose."
Thus.
The colors of the weapons are also described in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: "The discus is like the sun; the sword resembles the sky;
the mace is to be known as dark-blue; and the goad is black in color."
"One should know the noose to be yellow; one should remember the conch as having the luster of the moon;
the bow should have the color of molten gold; and the mace is like fire. Thus it is said.
By the word "afterwards" (paścāt), it is stated that the Śrīvatsa, Kaustubha, and Vanamālā should also be worshipped in their respective places with their own mudrās and mantras;
for this is stated in works such as the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā* and the *Mantratantraprakāśa*.
Some, however, worship them only during the primary worship (*pradhānapūjā*).
Thus it was said by me previously;
therein, the characteristics of the mudrās were stated by me previously.
The mantras are as follows:
Oṃ mahāśrīvatsāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā, obeisance to Śrīvatsa. Oṃ mahāmṛtasambhavāya huṃ phaṭ svāhā, obeisance to Kaustubha.
Oṃ mahāvanamāle huṃ phaṭ svāhā | Homage to Vanamālā. || 48-50 ||
Thus constantly worshipping Puruṣottama in the prescribed manner, one attains great fortune, incomparable good luck, and fame;
one obtains longevity, health, sovereignty, and whatever the mind desires. || 51 ||
"Yathāvat" means in the manner previously described. || 51 ||
Having worshipped the God according to the prescribed rite with *hayāri* flowers,
one should offer oblations with *śaśiprasūna* flowers one thousand and eight times.
Within a single month, all kings shall come under his control;
by offering oblations of ripe bilva fruits, one shall obtain irreproachable prosperity.
By offering a thousand oblations of *jyotiṣmatī* oil, numbering eight (the Vasus), he obtains that very same [result] once again with full-blown red lotuses. || 54 ||
He is born truly fortunate among all; there is no doubt in this matter.
By means of this ritual procedure, the practitioner is liberated from great disease. || 55 ||
An oblation of *aśvattha* fuel-sticks bestows wealth acquired from others;
by an oblation of *dūrvā* grass smeared with clarified butter, one is released from great danger. || 56 ||
He who recites the mantra of one's name ten thousand times shall become like that person's servant; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. || 57 ||
What is the use of saying more here? By means of this [mantra], the supreme practitioner shall accomplish all desires, like another Viṣṇu manifest before his eyes. || 58 ||
"Hayāri" refers to the *karavīra* flower.
"According to the prescribed rite" means preceded by the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭhapūjā*) in the fire. "With moon-blossoms" means with white water-lilies (*kumuda*).
"Vasusaṃkhyaka-sahasra" means eight thousand. "Yasya nāmayutam" means [the name] of such-and-such, in place of the word "amuka. (52–58)
Having uttered the word "uttiṣṭha" (arise), [the mantra consists of] Śrī, Krodhīśa, and Hutāśana, ending with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), and is endowed with eight syllables. || 59 ||
He states the mantra that bestows prosperity (*śrīkaramantra*) with the words "uttiṣṭha" and so forth.
*Śrī* is its essential form (*svarūpa*).
*Krodhīśa* is *ka*.
Hutāśa is *repha* (the letter *ra*).
It consists of eight syllables (*vasvakṣara*). Some say it begins with the seed-syllable of Śrī (*śrīṃ*), while others say it begins with the *tāra* (*oṃ*).
As it has been said:
"Some desire this [mantra] to begin with the seed-syllable of Śrī, while others desire it to begin with Tārā."
The teachers beginning with Padmapādācārya maintain that [the mantra] is encapsulated by the Praṇava, Māra, and Śrī-bījas;
for this very reason, there is the expression "endowed with" (samanvita). || 59 ||
Vāma shall be its seer (ṛṣi), and Paṅkti is declared to be its meter;
the wise have stated that its deity is Hari, known as Śrīkara. || 60 ||
The Heart-mantra is the pair that terrifies; the Head-mantra is the pair that causes fear;
the Topknot-mantra is the pair that crushes; and the Armor-mantra is the pair that destroys. || 61 ||
The weapon, the pair of protective syllables, and all the *hum* mantras are uttered;
[they are placed] on the head, in the two eyes, at the throat, and again in the heart and belly. || 62 ||
One should duly assign the mantra-syllables to the pair of thighs, shanks, and feet; one should assign this mantra, "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth," to the face. || 63 ||
"The arms have been made into the Rājanya; they should be placed upon the pair of arms.
That which is the Vaiśya is his thighs; one should place this upon the two thighs. (64)
One should place the mantra on the two feet; from the two feet, the Śūdra was born.
Then, one should place the discus, the conch, the mace, and the lotus upon the tips of the hands.

Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body, [one should meditate on] the God seated upon Garuḍa, who stands upon a red lotus throne within the previously mentioned pavilion. || 66 ||
"Vāma" means Vāmadeva; as it has been said: "The seer of this [mantra] is Vāmadeva. "Oṃ" is the seed-syllable (bīja), and "svāhā" is the power (śakti).
As it has been said:
"Viṣṇu with the bindu is declared to be the seed-syllable (bīja); Śakti is to be known as its head (śiras)."
The connection is that these have been proclaimed by the wise as things to be contemplated.
By the phrase "by the wise," it is stated that one should perform the eight-limbed [yoga] instead of the five-limbed.
As they say:

And one should perform the eight-limbed ritual (aṣṭāṅga) with the syllables of the mantra according to the prescribed path in due order, [applying them] to the heart, head, face, topknot, armor, weapon, eyes, belly, and back. Thus it is said.
"At the crown" (mūrdhni):
this is the ritual placement according to the order of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa).
As they say:
"This emanation is taught as extending from the navel to the heart; likewise, its persistence extends from the feet to the head. This is described as the sequence beginning with emanation."
"One should place [them]" means with their respective mantras and their respective mudrās. (60–66)
He whose radiance is like the mountain of gold, whose face is like a lotus, whose eyes are like lotuses,
who holds the discus, conch, mace, and lotus, whose appearance is captivating,
whose chest is marked by the Kaustubha gem, and who is adorned with a crown, armlets, and other ornaments.
I meditate upon Acyuta, the Lord of the Universe, whose vehicle is Tārkṣya, within my heart.
The locations for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) are to be known through the meditation on the weapons (*āyudhadhyāna*).
Regarding the meditation on the weapons: the first [pair] is on the two upper hands starting from the right, and the others are on the two hands situated below them.
Here, immediately after the meditation, one should display the mudrās of the Śrīvatsa, the Kaustubha gem, and the forest garland (*vanamālā*). || 67 ||

The practitioner of mantra should recite this mantra eight hundred thousand times, and then perform the fire sacrifice with one-tenth that number [of oblations] using fuel-sticks from the *bilva* tree or milk-exuding trees, as well as red lotuses. || 68 ||
Having offered oblations of milk, rice, and ghee, one should satisfy the Guru with wealth;
once the image has been fashioned with the root mantra, one should worship the Deity daily. || 69 ||
First, one should worship the limbs upon the filaments; then Śrī, Rati, Dhṛti, and Kānti—each holding a playful lotus—upon the petals in the cardinal directions. (70)

One should worship the forms beginning with Vāsudeva, colored yellow, reddish, dark-brown, and blue, on the petals at the intermediate directions; and one should worship the pair of treasures on the two sides.
"Kṣīradruma" refers to the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa trees.
By means of those eight substances, the accomplishment of the ten-part (daśāṃśa) portion is achieved for each one according to the prescribed method.
"In that which is prepared with the root-mantra" [is the meaning].
The phrase "on the previously mentioned Vaiṣṇava seat" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
"Having worshipped the limbs" is the ellipsis.
"Having worshipped" [refers to] "in the filaments" is the ellipsis.
Others worship in the pericarp;
"on the sides" means on the outside of the eight petals. (68–71)
One should worship Viṣvaksena in the northeast, followed immediately by the world-protectors (lokapālas).
Having thus worshipped the God, one shall accomplish one's own desired aim. || 72 ||
The wise practitioner should offer ten thousand oblations of dūrvā grass and sacrificial porridge (caru) mixed with clarified butter.
Afterwards, the person for whom the rite is performed (sādhya) should eat the consecrated porridge from which the remainder has been poured out.
On the day of the Sun, one should properly feed the Brahmins with sweet foods;
one should satisfy the Guru with wealth, garments, grain, and ornaments. || 74 ||
Having conquered untimely death, diseases, and other afflictions, he attains a long life;
one should offer thirty thousand oblations of lotuses sprinkled with clarified butter.
Lakṣmī shall dwell in him and shall not abandon even his sons;
by performing oblations with fuel-sticks of the Bilva tree, one becomes the Lord of Wealth himself.
One should offer oblations with rice grains mixed with betel nut flowers and sprinkled with honey; before long, a treasury of prosperity will arise.
"One should worship Viṣvaksena.
Here, the Viṣvaksena-mudrā should be displayed.
As they say:
Having placed the left index finger near the tip of the nose,
one should hold the right index finger like a staff.
"This is the mudrā of Viṣvaksena; one should display it during his worship.
Thus [it is said]. "Īśa" refers to the position outside the lotus.
Others worship him in front.
This concludes the second enclosure.
"Immediately thereafter" refers to the vajra and so forth.
"Caru" refers to the remains of the oblation.
"Well-prepared" means by means of recitation (*japa*) and other such practices. (72–77)
One who offers a hundred thousand oblations with clarified butter conquers enemies on earth;
a lotus-thread, consecrated by this mantra, when bound upon the arm [achieves the same]. || 78 ||
One shall destroy diseases, premature death, and sufferings; there is no doubt about this.
Day by day, one should sprinkle oneself with handfuls of water. || 79 ||
At the times of bathing, he shall become endowed with the prosperity of good fortune and beauty.
Having brought lotus-threads equal in number to the syllables of the mantra, eight knots should be tied with the mantra;
this bestows the fruits mentioned therein. (78–80)
With both arms raised, the practitioner should gaze at the solar disc.
One of sharp intellect should daily recite this mantra one thousand times;
all his heart's desires shall be fulfilled—of this there is no doubt. (81)
By the phrase "one of sharpened intellect," it is meant that one should meditate upon the deity therein.

The yantra as described in the *Gautama-kalpa* is stated as follows: the syllable *Tāra* (Om) together with the name of the target (*sādhya*) is placed in the eight spokes, while the syllables of the root mantra are placed in the corners.
Each of the powers [is placed] at the three clusters of points of the triangle; this is the six-limbed [rite].
One should write the eight-syllable mantra on an external eight-petalled lotus;
one should encircle it on the outside with the five limbs, conjoined with the twelve-syllable mantra.
A twelve-petalled lotus, and outside the circle, a hexagon;
in the corners, the seed-syllable of Anaṅga, and outside, an eight-petalled lotus.
One should place the *kalās* (sixteen vowels) upon the filaments (*kesara*) and the *śrīkara* mantra in pairs upon the petals;
[the mantra begins with] *tāraḥ* (oṃ), followed by *śrīkara-kṛṣṇau* in the locative case (*ṅe*), ending with *gopīkucāntataḥ*.
This mantra, "bhūṣaṇāya," is encircled by its noose and goad, and surrounded by the staff and the void; this is the most excellent yantra.
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas—
all these likewise go to their dissolution merely by wearing the yantra.
This great yantra, when fully accomplished, is the supreme remover of epilepsy;
by wearing this yantra inscribed with the name of the person to be influenced, it brings them under one's control.
"Whatever one desires, O child, that one attains when composed in meditation. (80–81)
Having first uttered "Kṛṣṇāya," then "Govindāya," followed by the word "Gopījana," and at the end of that the word "Vallabhāya," ending with the two syllables "Svāhā" (dviṭha). || 82 ||
The eighteen-syllable mantra beginning with the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) has been declared;
Nārada is said to be its sage, and the Gāyatrī is stated to be its meter. || 83 ||

Kṛṣṇa, who bestows the fruits of all desires, has been described as the deity. One who knows the mantra should perform the five limbs of the mantra in sequence using syllables numbering four, six, four, four, and two, combined with the seed-syllable (jāti) of the mantra. || 84 ||
He states the mantra of Gopāla as "kṛṣṇāya.
"dviṭha" is svāhā.
*Klīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*).
As it has been said:

"I shall declare the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of this mantra along with its power (*śakti*): the syllable *Śakra* (H) is illumined by the left eye (Ī), and together with *Pradyumna* (Ū), this is declared to be the seed-syllable. This *Prādyumna* mantra is the deluder of the world."

The *haṃsa* (the letter *ha*) is fat (*medas*), joined with the circle of the mouth (*vaktra-vṛtta*); it is endowed with the eyes of the boar (*potrī-netra*) and so forth, and consists of four syllables (*yugārṇa*).
This is declared to be the *śakti*, the beloved of Agni, who is to be worshipped by all the hosts of gods; she bestows the fulfillment of desires. Thus [it is said].
Regarding the instruments, there are four [verses], 82–84.
One should remember Govinda, the lotus-eyed one, who is enchanting and delightful, in beautiful Vṛndāvana, surrounded by thousands of cowherd girls. || 85 ||
With their bee-like eyes sent toward the lotus-face of their beloveds,
they were tormented by the arrows of love and longed for an embrace.

Bowed under the weight of their high breasts, which were radiant with strings of pearls and yellow garments; with their braided hair and lower cloths slipping loose, their speech faltering with intoxication. || 87 ||
Illumined by the radiance of their rows of teeth, with their lower lips quivering and curved, they seemed to entice [him] with various amorous gestures profound with emotion. || 88 ||
The connection is that [Kṛṣṇa] was deluding the cowherd girls. "Of himself" means of the Self who is the soul of the universe;
the meaning is: of Kṛṣṇa, whose very form is their own self.
Those lower [teeth] which are throbbing, vibrating, adorned, and blossomed—[with these they are endowed]. || 85–88 ||
With the splendor of a full-blown blue lotus, a moon-like face, and a fondness for peacock-feather ornaments;
bearing the Śrīvatsa mark and the magnificent Kaustubha gem, clad in beautiful yellow garments;
his body darkened by the pollen from the lotus-eyes of the cowherd women, and surrounded by throngs of cowherds and cattle—[I bow to Him].
I worship Govinda, who is intent on playing the flute with its sweet notes, and whose limbs are adorned with divine ornaments. || 89 ||
*Phulleti* means it blooms. *Indīvaram* is the blue water-lily (*nīlotpala*). *Barhāvataṃsam* is an ear-ornament made of peacock feathers.
He is intent on playing the flute. By this, the meditation on the two-armed form is described.
Here, one should display another visualization, showing the flute, the śrīvatsa, the kaustubha jewel, the forest garland, and the bilva mudrā.
In that regard, the definition of the Veṇubilva mudrā is as follows: the thumb of the left hand is joined to the lip;
its little finger is touched by the right thumb, while that [right] little finger is extended.
The index, middle, and ring fingers are slightly contracted and moved;
this is declared here as the flute-mudrā, a well-guarded favorite of Hari.
It is said that among the acyuta-mudrās, the bhadra is shaped like a bilva fruit.
Having raised the left thumb and bound its tip with the thumb of the other hand,
and having firmly pressed those [fingers] with the fingers of the left hand,
one of pure intellect, reciting the seed-syllable of Māra, should place [the mudrā] firmly upon the heart.
