This seal, known as Bilva, has been clearly described here; it must be kept secret by those who know the ritual procedure.
Whatever collection of evil deeds you have committed here or in the past through mind, speech, or body— whether consciously or unconsciously—
a man who understands this mudrā destroys it all; thus do the hosts of gods declare.
"All people constantly bow down to him; they become subject to his will. (89)
One should recite this mantra twenty thousand times according to the rule;
with a concentrated mind, one should offer oblations with reddish lotuses consisting of a tenth part of that number.
By the phrase "according to rule," this is what is meant:
as they have said— "On a mountain peak, on a riverbank, at the root of a *bilva* tree, in water reaching the heart, in a cow-pen, or in the temple of Viṣṇu..."
Seated at each of these places individually—namely, beneath an Aśvattha tree and also on the shore of the ocean—[one should perform the rite].
One should recite the excellent ten-syllable mantra four times ten thousand times, separately and in sequence;
if it is the eighteen-syllable mantra, the prescribed number is said to be two times ten thousand.
Taking vegetables, roots, fruits, curds produced from cow's milk, alms-food, grain-meal,
and milk-rice, he should stay in succession in different locations such as on mountain peaks and other places.
And I have here described one preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) for those who are incapable;
once this is completed, the master of practitioners (*sādhakeśa*) should again recite [the mantra] according to the rule for the sake of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Having recited ten hundred-thousand times the ten-syllable mantra which bestows inexhaustible fruit, one of trained intellect [should do so];
if it is a mantra with two hollow syllables, then five hundred-thousand times.
Thus.
"One-tenth of that" means one-tenth of five hundred thousand [recitations].
By the word "concentrated" (*samāhita*), this is what is intended:
as they have said— "When pure-minded, one should begin the rite of oblation with lotus flowers mixed with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and well-sprinkled with sugar and ghee."
Thus [ends verse] 90.
One should worship the Son of Devakī according to the rules upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal;
having propitiated the limbs and the enclosures, one should worship His beloved consorts on the petals. || 91 ||
Kālindī, known as Nāgnajitī, then Mitravindā;
after her, Cāruhāsinī, and another, Rohiṇī, and then Jāmbavatī. || 92 ||
Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā were described as having beautiful ornaments, wearing yellow garments, being gentle, and holding lotuses in their lotus-like hands. || 93 ||

The practitioner of mantras should worship the eight elephants, beginning with Erāvata, outside of that; then he should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas), and outside of those, the weapons such as the thunderbolt (vajra). || 94 ||
Thus one should worship the god Govinda, the Lord of the worlds, and perform the ritual applications (prayoga) desired by oneself as prescribed in the Kalpas. || 95 ||
One who desires blameless prosperity should offer oblations with *lakṣmī* flowers;
one should offer oblations with ghee and food for the sake of the abundance of ghee and food. || 96 ||
The term "Vaiṣṇava" refers to what is stated regarding the eight-syllable mantra of Nārāyaṇa. By the word "properly," this is what is meant:
one should worship the Lord with the seven enclosures beginning with Dāma and ending with the Vajra weapon.

Either the fivefold enclosure (pañcāvaraṇa) beginning with the limbs (aṅga) mentioned in the text and ending with the vajra-weapons; or the threefold enclosure consisting of the limbs, the world-protectors (lokapāla), and their weapons;
or the single enclosure consisting of the eight black [deities].
As it has been said:
"The seven-fold enclosure (āvṛti) described as bringing all happiness in the rite of worshiping Acyuta [Viṣṇu]—
or else, one should perform this three-fold enclosure with the deities beginning with Aṅga, Purandara, and Aśani."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Vāsudeva, he who is called Nārāyaṇa,
the son of Devakī, the best of the Yadus, and also Vārṣṇeya.
At the end of the word *asurākrānta*, the seventh is *bhārahārī*;
and these eight, ending in the dative case, are in order the establishers of the Dharma.
"Or rather, the worship of the enemy of Kaṃsa should be performed with these very [mantras].
Thus, all four of these positions are indeed primary;
the difference arises from the distinction between ritual manuals (kalpa).
"Having propitiated... on the filaments... refers to the eight [elephants] beginning with Airāvata that have been mentioned. (91–96)
One should honor Brahmins with wild flowers, kings with *jāti* blossoms, Vaiśyas with dark-colored flowers, and Śūdras with fresh blue lotuses. || 97 ||
One should bring all people under control with salt, and women with lotuses;
a homa performed in cow-pens with milk-rice and sesame flour [achieves the same]. || 98 ||
Govinda, the beloved of Gokula, quickly effects the pacification of the cows;
he is the Lord who assumes the form of a child and is adorned with a garland of tinkling bells. || 99 ||
Having remembered [the deity], the practitioner of mantras should offer libations with auspicious waters, perceiving them as milk;
being pleased, he bestows upon that person wealth, grain, garments, and other such things. (100)
One should draw the *piṇḍa* [mantra] surrounded by the root [mantra], with the letters of the essence (*rasārṇa*) at the corners of a pair of burning cities (triangles).
One should fashion a lotus with ten petals shining with ten syllables, surrounded by the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*).
The lotus, situated upon the filaments, has petals formed by the modifications of the vowels and shines with sixteen syllables.
The filaments are rich with consonants, and the syllables of the Anuṣṭubh meter are yellow on the petals of the two pairs of transformations. ||101||

This Yantra, presided over by Govinda, is encircled by the noose (pāśa) and the goad (aṅkuśa), and is adorned with the eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣara) upon the three junctions of the pair of earth-fortresses (kṣauṇīpura). It is remembered as bestowing the fruits of virtue, wealth, and desire, and as providing protection from all [evils]. || 102 ||
He describes the yantra with the words "the piṇḍa":
the piṇḍa-bīja which is about to be described,
within a hexagon consisting of a pair of fire-triangles (dahanapura) intersecting one another.
*Rasārṇa* consists of six syllables.
He will describe the six-syllable, ten-syllable, sixteen-syllable, *anuṣṭubh*, and eight-syllable [mantras].
*Vikṛtidala* means the sixteen-petaled [lotus].
The *vikṛti* [mandala] has thirty-two petals, half the number of petals in the *yuga*.
In both of these cases, there is the inscription of a single syllable in each of the locations for the filaments (*kesara*).
With the noose (*pāśa*) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*), there is one enclosure (*āvṛti*). || 101–102 ||

The letter *pa*, the end of the five [vowels], situated on the letter *ra* and adorned with the *mānava-bindu* (the nasal dot), is declared to be this "seed of the aggregate" (*piṇḍabīja*), which is supreme and brings about all accomplishments. || 103 ||
He states the seed-syllable of the *piṇḍa*: "The end of the five" (*pañcāntaka*).
The end of the five is *ga*; *dharā* is *la*; *ira* is *ya*. That which is situated therein is *glya*.
*Manu* is *au*, and there is also the *bindu*; joined with these, it becomes *glyauṃ*.
By the phrase "the supreme bringer of all accomplishments," its independence is indicated; it consists of three syllables because it ends with *namaḥ*.
Alternatively, its state of having three syllables is stated by virtue of beginning with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and the *māyā* (Hrīṃ).
Its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details are now stated: the sage is declared to be Nārada, and the meter is said to be Gāyatrī.
The deity is Bālakṛṣṇa, whose limbs arise from the seed-syllable pervaded by the six long vowels.
May Mukunda protect you— he who has the luster of a blooming blue lotus, whose eyes are like red lotuses, who rests upon a lotus, whose calves and hips are adorned with tinkling bells,
who holds with his two arms the most pure fresh butter and milk-rice, and who is worshipped by the entire universe.
May He, who is surrounded by cows, cowherds, and cowherdesses, and whose neck is adorned with the shimmering Ruru-deer skin, long protect you all.
"One should recite the excellent mantra one hundred thousand times and perform ten thousand oblations with milk-rice (pāyasa).
The worship, moreover, is performed upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal with the limbs [of the deity], the guardians of the directions, and the vajras. Thus it is said.
The sage is declared to be Nārada; the meter is said to be Jagatī;
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the deity; and *glauṃ* is proclaimed as the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and *ya* as the power (*śakti*).
One should perform the six-limbed ritual with the root mantra and meditate upon the God of gods,
Janārdana, standing at the foot of a Kadamba tree.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with a face like the full moon,
he is served by hosts of gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, kinnaras, and uragas.
The enchanting son of Devakī, beloved of the cowherds and cowherdesses,
adorned with a peacock feather and graced by a forest garland.
Resembling the full moon, lovely, dwelling in Vṛndāvana,
playing the flute, stainless, and enchanting to all living beings.
It was being licked by calves, deer, lions, and likewise by birds;
it was endowed with all ornaments and beautified by every kind of decoration.
With his chest illuminated by the Kaustubha gem and covered with a peacock-feather garment,
he is the immeasurable and inconceivable Gopāla in the form of a child.
One should meditate upon that Lord of the gods, the sole leader of all worlds,
together with his limbs (the vyuha-forms) such as Vāsudeva and others, and thirdly with [his consorts] such as Ukmiṇī and others.
The sixfold enclosure is also said to consist of the moon and the rainbow;
the recitation should be forty thousand times, and thereafter one should perform the fire-oblation with a tenth part of that number.
"One should satisfy [the deity] with milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with sugar for that long;
this world will immediately become subject to the control of one who has attained mastery over the mantra. || 103 ||
The mantra consisting of six syllables is proclaimed as "Smaraḥ kṛṣṇāya ṭhaṭha. || 104 ||
He states the six-syllable [mantra] as "Smara. "Smara" refers to the seed-syllable of Kāma.
By the phrase "Manu is proclaimed," it is stated that this too is an independent mantra.
The recitation (*japa*) of this [mantra] consists of six hundred thousand repetitions of eighteen syllables, beginning with the sages (*muni*) and ending with the subjects (*prajā*).
It should be understood that the fire-oblation (*homa*) is one-tenth of that amount, performed with the substances prescribed for the eighteen-syllable mantra.
As for the five ancillaries (*pañcāṅga*):

"One should perform the five-limbed ritual (*pañcāṅga*) with the words of the wheel ending in *svāhā*, which are established in their proper places, joined with the protection of the three worlds, and accompanied by the [mantra] ending in *asurāntaka*.
Thus [it is said]. (104)
One should utter "gopījanavallabhāya" followed by "agnisundarī";
this ten-syllable mantra bestows both seen and unseen fruits. || 105 ||
He speaks of Daśārṇa as "Gopī";
Agnisundarī is Svāhā.
By the phrase "bestowing both seen and unseen fruits," its independence is stated.
Everything regarding this should be understood as being like that of the six-syllable mantra. || 105 ||

Having first uttered the syllable Om (praṇava), then the heart-mantra "Kṛṣṇa" ending in the dative case (kṛṣṇāya), and thereafter that same mantra for the Son of Devakī accompanied by "huṃ phaṭ svāhā," [one should worship]. || 106 ||
This sixteen-syllable mantra of Govinda has been proclaimed;
it states that the sixteen syllables consist of the *praṇava* (Om),
the heart (*hṛdaya*), and the word *namaḥ*.
The word ending in the genitive case *kṛṣṇa* is [joined] with *kṛṣṇāya*;
and that same word ending in the genitive case is [joined] with *tena devakīputrāya*.
By the phrase "of Govinda," it is stated that this too is an independent mantra.
All of this should be understood as being like that of the ten-syllable [mantra]. || 106-107 ||
The *piṇḍa* [mantra] is the seed-syllable of the Lord of Pleasure (*ratipati*), followed by "namo bhagavate. || 107 ||

To the son of Nanda, who possesses a body like that of a child, who is dark-complexioned, and who is the beloved of the community of cowherd women; [the mantra] ends with two *ṭha* syllables (svāhā). || 108 ||
The mantra of Gopāla, the Lord of the Universe, is declared to be in the Anuṣṭubh meter. "Anaṅga," "Kṛṣṇa," and "Govinda" ending in the dative case constitute the eight-syllable mantra. || 109 ||
He states that the "piṇḍa" consists of thirty-two syllables;
this refers to the previously mentioned piṇḍa-bīja.
The "seed of the Lord of Rati" is the Kāma-bīja.
By the phrase "of Gopāla, the Lord of the World," it is stated that this mantra is also independent.
Its seer and other details are as follows:
for this [mantra], Nārada is the seer (ṛṣi), and Anuṣṭubh is declared to be the meter (chandas).
The deity is declared to be named Hari, and the limbs [of the mantra] consist of the syllables beginning with *ā* and *cakrā*.
One should meditate upon Hari holding a jeweled cup in his right hand and a golden staff in his left, embraced by the two goddesses.
One should recite the excellent mantra one hundred thousand times and offer ten thousand oblations of milk-rice;
the worship, however, is performed upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal with the limbs [of the deity], the guardians of the directions, and the vajras.
"Thus, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra shall become a possessor of sovereignty over the three worlds. Thus it is said. He states the eight-syllable [mantra] as "anaṅga," etc.;
"anaṅga" refers to the seed-syllable of Kāma (Klīm).
The two names Kṛṣṇa and Govinda [are used] in the dative case: *kṛṣṇāya* and *govindāya*.
This too is an independent mantra.
Its sage, meter, and all other details are to be understood as being the same as those previously stated for the six-syllable mantra. (107–109)
One should duly draw four clear lines— east, west, south, and north—
forming a square with spikes rising at the corners, joined by two concentric circles, starting from the center and ending at the periphery.
Having written the letters of the verse beyond that, one should inscribe eight syllables in the eight spaces between the squares.
Outside of that, the Yantra of the Son of Devakī is subsequently surrounded by twelve syllables. 110.
Regarding the statement "first," he describes the *kāmaliṅga* yantra:
one should draw two lines from east to west and two lines from south to north.
Thus, when both are combined, there are four lines.
This very point has been stated by the word "according to rule" (vidhivat).
It should be joined with spikes (*śūla*) protruding from the corners.
One should draw four diagonal lines (*karṇasūtra*) outward from the corners of the central square; by this, the shape of a spike indeed comes into being.
It is joined with a pair of circles;
therein, one circle touches the ends of the lines, while the second is in the central square within the space between those circles.
This is the "eastern middle" [circle].
The beginning of the writing starts from the central square;
"ending there" means that the completion occurs in that very central square.
Therein is the sequence for writing the syllables:

having written the first three letters in the three central squares arranged from east to west, one should write the syllable *deva* in the two squares on both sides of the diagonal line within the space between the two circles in the southeast corner.
Then, in the two upper squares to the right, one should write the two syllables "de ve.
However, the letter *ta* is to be pronounced as it stands in the central square.
Then, having pronounced those same two syllables situated to the right of the central square, [one writes them] in the two squares on both sides of the middle line in the southwest corner.
One should write the two syllables *va-re*.
In the western [section], however, it is exactly as in the southern one.
Then, in the northwest corner, in the two squares on both sides of the middle line, one should write the two syllables *ru-ṭe*.
Then, in the northern direction, it is exactly as in the southern.
In the northeast corner, one should write the two syllables "de-va" in the two squares on both sides of the central line.
Then, one should read the syllables written in the eastern direction from top to bottom.

Such is the sequence for writing the syllables of the verse-mantra. "Beyond" means outside the central square; within the first circle, two squares remain on each side of the diagonal lines in every corner. Therein, one should write the eight previously mentioned syllables starting from Īśāna (the northeast) and proceeding clockwise.
Thereafter, immediately following that;
on the outside of that, on the exterior of the second circle;
it is surrounded by twelve syllables, namely the fifteen syllables of the Vāsudeva mantra as previously stated.

By writing the twelve syllables within the twelve compartments produced by the "spear" (śūla) grid, a circle (*vṛtta*) is formed by implication; thus it is called a "circle. Such a yantra bestows the aforementioned results.
This is the traditional position.
One should draw four lines extending from east to west and four lines extending from north to south;
thus, nine compartments are formed.
They say that among these, the central compartment should be provided with two concentric circles.
They must be questioned regarding the explanation of the phrase "the middle, the beginning, and its end.
By the word "etcetera" in the expression "on birch bark and so forth," copper, silver, gold, and other such materials are included.
Furthermore, the specific time associated with each particular type of writing should also be understood according to what was previously stated.
"According to the rule" (*yathāvidhi*): the rule has been shown thus in the context of writing [the mantra]. (110–113)
To that one who is well-praised among the gods of gods, to that god who is the chosen delight;
to him who is celebrated as the source of joy, to that celebrated son of Devakī. || 111 ||
This yantra, written according to the prescribed rules upon birch bark or other suitable material and constantly worn upon the arm, bestows the fruit of all desires. (112)
This, which has been well-proven and effectively accomplished, should be inscribed on a plank of *palāśa* wood;
one should bury it in a cow-pen, and there will always be an increase in the cattle. || 113 ||
One should write a verse in sixty-four squares on birch bark, beginning with the words "śivādi" and "daityādi" in sequence;
that is well known as the *sarvatobhadra* (all-auspicious) diagram.
This yantra bestows fame, fortune, and victory. || 114 ||
Fashioned from a plank of Khadira wood and placed in the cow-pen of cattle, it provides protection, destroys thieves and demons, and is beneficial for cows along with their calves. || 115 ||
O protector of cows who possesses milk, O you who are patient toward the earth and whose syllables are patience;
O lord of cows, O sky-like one, O protector of the earth, O you who traverse the sky, O destroyer of the wicked and the destroyer of the night. || 116 ||
He states another yantra with the words "the verse" (śloka).
This refers to the verse that is about to be spoken.
Regarding the phrase "in the sixty-four squares":
It should be understood that [this applies] to all those [diagrams] possessing spikes (*śūla*).
As it has been stated in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*:
"Endowed with sixty-four squares and adorned with garlands of spikes."
Thus: Śiva and so forth refers to Īśāna and so forth;
Daitya and so forth refers to Nairṛta and so forth.
The methods for inducing emesis (*lekhanaprakāra*), such as those to be accomplished by producing the *koṣṭha*, should be understood as explained by me in the tenth [chapter].
These two [mantras] are also perfected mantras (*siddhamantra*); with these, one should respectively provide protection for the afflicted and for children. (114–116)
Brahmā is seated upon the earth and endowed with the *śāntibindu*;
he is declared to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the mind-born god (Kāmadeva), who deludes the three worlds. || 117 ||
He states that the single-syllable mantra of desire is "brahma.
What is Brahmā?
It is *la*, which signifies the earth (*bhūmi*).
Seated thus, it is *śāntirī*; with the *bindu*, it becomes *klīṃ*.
The letter *ka* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the letter *ī* is the power (*śakti*).
This has been stated in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*: "In the fourth [letter], there are the seed-syllable and the power.
By the phrase "deluding the three worlds," the fact that it begins with the letters *ha* and *sa* is indicated. The state of beginning solely with the letter *ha* bestows great subjugation (*vaśya*).
The state of beginning with the letter *sa* alone bestows long life.
As it has been said:
"Madana, mounted upon the *haṃsa*, quickly becomes the agitator of the three worlds."
Joined with Hayu [the Sun], it causes passion; likewise, joined with Jīva [Jupiter], it is praised for longevity. Thus [ends verse 117].
The seer is declared to be Sammohana; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī.
The deity is the manifest Sarvasammohana (the Deluder of All), whose banner is the sea-monster. || 118 ||
Because of the statement, "Sarvasammohanakṛṣṇa shall be the deity of these two," by the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*), even Kṛṣṇa alone [is intended].
In that regard, according to the view where Sarvasammohanakṛṣṇa is the deity, there is meditation on the eight-armed form.
As they say:
Seated upon the lofty shoulder of the Suparṇa— the universal life-force, possessing the splendor of a rising sun— was the coral-formed [Viṣṇu], whose every limb was churned by Aṅgaja (Kāma).
Holding a discus, a sword, a goad, and a noose, as well as a flower-arrow, a sugarcane-bow, a mace, and a club in his arms,
he possesses a pair of large, long, reddish, and rolling lotus-eyes.

Having thus meditated upon [the deity] as non-different from one's own self, one should then mutter either the single-syllable or the eight-syllable mantra for one hundred thousand times during the day, while offering blossoms of the *kiṃśuka* tree sprinkled with the three sweets (*trimadhura*).
"One should offer oblations with a thousand suns [of fuel] and satisfy [the deity] with pure waters for that long.
Thus, he may also be meditated upon as having eight arms.
As it is said in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*:
"One should constantly meditate upon Puruṣottama as having eight arms and a reddish hue,
embraced by Ramā on his left, and enchanting the three worlds."
He holds a discus, a sword, and a mace in his right hands,
while in his left hands he carries a goad, a noose, a conch, and likewise a bow with an arrow.
"And bearing the Kaumodakī mace, adorned with all ornaments—by ten hundred thousand recitations, his mantra becomes perfected. Thus it is said.
For these two mantras, all rites such as worship and so forth are exactly like those for the Puruṣottama mantra.
As they say:
"Generally, the procedure for Puruṣottama is thus; anything other than that should be understood from that [source]."
Thus [it is said].
However, in the case where Kṛṣṇa alone is the deity, all matters such as meditation and worship are to be understood according to the method described for the eighteen-syllable mantra.
And there is another distinction: this very [mantra], when encased by the seed-syllable of Ramā (Śrī), bestows all desired objects.
One should meditate upon the auspicious Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa in a golden pavilion.
That very same [mantra], when enveloped by Māyā and brought under the power of Vidyā, certainly grants subjugation;
by its very nature, however, this [mantra] bestows wealth as well as enjoyments.
O best of the twice-born, if one who knows the true essence of the mantras should desire knowledge,
he should meditate there upon Viṣṇu, who is as radiant as the moon, accompanied by Bhāratī.
"Then, O capable one, the well-adorned speech of Viṣṇu should be meditated upon as filling the three worlds with prose, verse, and sacred scriptures."
One should mutter the desired mantra encircled by the *tāra* for the sake of dharma and liberation;
for its accomplishment, one should meditate upon Śrī Hari as white, surrounded by hosts of sages. Thus it is said.
But elsewhere it says: "Seated upon a lotus throne, Nakulī, possessing a left eye and a crescent moon.
By this, it is stated that the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśī follows the seed-syllable of Kāma.
And as for meditation:
[one should meditate on her] arisen from the center of the navel and emerged at the center of the eyebrows,
seated within the lotus of the *praṇava*, adorned with ornaments of pearls.
"One should practice [the visualization] of her holding a pen and a book in her hand.
Regarding that very point, there is this specific detail: "If the Mantra is recited with the syllables in a different order, it will cause agitation among the people."

Elsewhere it is also said: "Having meditated upon the Eternal One, who holds a boon-granting noose and goad, and carries a skull-bowl filled with wine, one should recite the seed-syllable of desire for the attainment of desired goals.
And elsewhere: "By reciting the seed-syllable even once, one destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin."
Likewise, by one recited by a twice-born, or even by four others who are celibate students.
Moreover, the fruit of all sacrifices is obtained by reciting it three times;
likewise, by reciting it four times, all the hosts of gods are satisfied.
By reciting it five times, the practitioner pleases the Lord of Devas; by six times, likewise the ancestors;
and by seven times, all the lords of yogis.
Recited eight times, the Grandfather himself is pleased;
recited nine times, Viṣṇu is pleased; and recited ten times, Śaṅkara is pleased.
O Sage, the causal principle known as Pradhāna, which is the qualified Prakṛti,
gratifies the supreme practitioner by means of the eleven names.
Likewise, when recited twelve times, it bestows the all-pervading, beneficial Person and grants liberation to the foremost of practitioners who recite it constantly.
O Sage, when received according to the prescribed rite, it bestows liberation upon you;
otherwise, O dear one, O Sage, it grants worldly enjoyment and the power to attract women.
"For in whatever measure the practitioner recites [the mantra], having attained pervasion, in that same measure the women of the Siddhas and Vidyādharas are accomplished. Thus [ends verse 118].
The procedure for the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) is declared by means of the seed-syllable conjoined with the long vowels. || 119 ||
"With the long [vowel] and with the six longs.
Immediately after this, one should place the five arrows in the forehead, face, throat, heart, and mūlādhāra,
as they are mentioned as constituting the enclosure (*āvṛti*) in the subsequent worship.
As it has been said by the Teachers: "His body is one in which the seed-syllables of the arrows have been deposited. (119)
I worship him who is as red as the Javā flower, richly adorned with jewel ornaments, bearing the fish-banner, with beautiful unguents applied to his limbs;
he holds in his lotus-like hands the goad, the sugarcane bow, the flower-arrow, and the noose. ||120||
The visualization of the weapons extends from the upper left hand to the upper right hand.
Here, immediately after the visualization, these mudrās are to be displayed:
having joined the two hands together with the fingers extended.
The two index fingers rest on the backs of the middle fingers, and the two thumbs are joined with the middle fingers.
"This is declared to be the Kāmamudrā, which brings joy to all sentient beings; with the two fists placed at the crown of the head, this is the Trailokyamohinī mudrā. Thus [ends verse 120].

One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times, and perform a fire sacrifice with one-tenth of that number [of oblations] using blossoming *kiṃśuka* flowers mixed with the "three sweets. || 121 ||
One should worship Makaradhvaja on the seat according to the prescribed rite that will be described hereafter.
Furthermore, [the powers are] Mohinī, Kṣobhiṇī, Trāsā, Stambhinī, and Ākarṣiṇī. || 122 ||

Having offered the seat beginning with the seed-syllable (bīja) to the pīṭha-śaktis—Drāviṇī, Unmādinī, Klinnā, and Kledinī—one should fashion the form [of the deity] by means of the root-mantra (mūla). || 123 ||

"One should worship according to the procedure to be described in the seat that is about to be mentioned" means that after worshipping [the principles] from Maṇḍūka up to the Supreme Reality (paratattva), one should worship the powers of the seat (pīṭhaśaktis) which are about to be described. "Beginning with the seed-syllable" (bījādyaṃ).
The meaning is that one should worship the seat with the mantra: *klīṃ kāmayogapīṭhāya namaḥ*. || 121-123 ||
In this [mandala], one should worship the God correctly according to the method that will be described.
Having first worshipped the limbs and the enclosure, one should worship the arrows in the center and in the cardinal directions. || 124 ||
First, that which begins with *drām* is drying; then that which begins with *drīm* is deluding.
That called "kindling," beginning with *klīm*, follows; then that which begins with *blūm* is burning. || 125 ||
Then, at the end of the creation, [he was] again Mādana, the fifth;
those deities of the arrows should be meditated upon with their lotus-hands holding the arrows of salutation. || 126 ||
Having stated "by what will be described," he declares the path with the words "having sacrificed. The word "in the pericarp" (*kaṇīkāyām*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
As it has been said: "Having sacrificed in the pericarp, [one should sacrifice] the limbs."
The fifth [syllable] is *madhya*.
This is because of the statement: "In the directions [place] the arrows (*śara*), and again the fifth in the middle.
It should be understood that in cases such as *drām*, the teachers employ the convention of the letter *ṅa* for the *anusvāra*.
Thus ends the chapter with the verse beginning "Bhṛgu. Regarding the phrase "prostration":
the prostration is performed with one hand, while an arrow is held in the other hand. (124–126)
There, in the middle [of the eight directions], the eight Śaktis are to be worshipped in due order:
Anaṅgarūpā and the others, namely Anaṅgamadanā, Anaṅgamanmathā, [Anaṅgamekhalā, Anaṅgavegā, Anaṅgāṅkuśā, and Anaṅgamālinī]. || 127 ||
Anaṅgakusumā, then Anaṅgamadanāturā, Anaṅgaśiśirā, Anaṅgamekhalā, and Anaṅgadīpikā. || 128 ||
Holding play-lotuses, with smiling faces and beautifully adorned—these sixteen Śaktis are to be worshipped on the sixteen petals outside. || 129 ||
Another is Yuvativīpralambhā, Jyotsnā, Subhrū, Madadravā, Suratā, Vāruṇī, Lolā, and again Kānti Saudāminī. || 130 ||
Kāmacchatrā, Candrarekhā, Śuklī, and Madanā—these are Jyotirmāyāvatī and the others, their hands radiant with white lotuses. || 131 ||
Young women with smiling faces, slow-moving due to the intoxication of passion, are to be worshipped again on the tips of the petals as the attendants of Smara. || 132 ||
Sorrow and delusion, another [state of] dalliance, the confusion of one afflicted by passion;
the bashful youth, the lover, the mango-blossomed one, and he who is fond of sexual pleasure. || 133 ||
Summer, the end of the heat, autumn, another [season], winter, the cool season, and intoxication;
bearing sugarcane, bows, flowers, and arrows, they are red and well-adorned. || 134 ||

One of refined intellect should worship the eight [goddesses] who are richly adorned with side-arms and quivers, whose minds are attached to their consorts, who delight in sexual pleasure, and who pervade the eight directions. || 135 ||

The *parabhṛt* and *sārasa*, followed by those called *śuka* and *medha*, and further the two—the play of the outer corners of the eyes and the play of the eyebrows—are proclaimed as *hāva* and *bhāva*. || 136 ||

By the phrase "in due order," it should be understood that all [mantras] beginning with young women have *māyā* as their seed-syllable (*bīja*), whereas those beginning with [the goddesses of] desire have *kāma* as their seed-syllable. As they say:

"The worship of the Śaktis and others with the *hṛllekhā* mantra and their own names"—this very point is indicated by the phrase "one of distinguished intellect," which is connected to every [preceding] case. The word *yuvatayaḥ* means "young women. (127–136)
In its four corners, his four attendant goddesses are to be worshipped:
Mādhavī, Mālatī, Hariṇākṣī, and Madotkaṭā. || 137 ||
Those holding white chowries, adorned with all ornaments;
thereafter, one should worship the Lords of the World (Lokeśvaras) on the outside, and subsequently their weapons in due order. || 138 ||
Thus, he who worships the God with fragrant flowers and other offerings shall attain good fortune and, through his prosperity, surpass even the Lord of Wealth. || 139 ||
One who should offer oblations for three days with ashoka flowers mixed with curd, one thousand and eight times, shall become beloved by all the worlds. || 140 ||

The preeminent practitioner of accomplishment should offer oblations with cow-ghee, reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times, while the sacrificial fire is ablaze with the dripping of the clarified butter. || 141 ||
With the *sampāta* clarified butter, the woman should feed her husband;
whatever she commands by this means, he always carries out. || 142 ||
One who desires a daughter should offer oblations of parched grains mixed with curd within a mandala;
he shall obtain his desired daughter, and she too shall obtain a virtuous husband. || 143 ||
The connection is that one should offer [the oblation] into the fire, the carrier of offerings, while it is unattended.
"With the *sampāta*" means while causing the residue to fall into another vessel.
By the phrase "O best of practitioners," the recitation of the *sampāta* mantra one hundred and eight times is indicated. || 141 ||
He states the application of the residual drops (*sampāta*) with the words "of the residual drops" (*sampātasya*).
The connection is that one obtains a maiden within the circle (*maṇḍala*).
By this, the oblation (*homa*) for forty-nine days is taught. (142–143)
In the center, illuminated by desire, shines a hexagon; outside this,

an eight-petaled lotus possessing the qualities and syllables of the Gāyatrī, accompanied by the six syllables of the Mālā-mantra, together with another eight-petaled lotus, all surrounded by the enclosure of the earth (Kṣauṇīpura).
This world-enchanting yantra was described by the one whose mind-born passion (Manobhava) resides in the corners. || 144 ||

Regarding the yantra, he says "kāma" and so forth: within the center of the hexagon, one should write the name of the rite together with the names of the practitioner and the person to be acted upon, inside the seed-syllable of Kāma (klīm).
One should write the six limbs of Kāma in the six corners starting from the southeast (āgneya) and proceeding clockwise.
As it has been said:
"One should write the six limbs in the corners starting from the southeast (agni-kona) in their proper sequence."

Having written the syllables of the *gāyatrī* to be described hereafter three by three within this outer eight-petaled [lotus], one should write the six syllables of the *mālāmantra* to be described on the tips of the petals.
One should understand that the terms "root" (*mūla*) and "eight-petaled" (*vasudala*) refer to the middle of a petal in one instance and the tip of a petal in the other.
The connection is that it is surrounded by a city on earth (kṣauṇīpura) with the Mind-born (Manobhava, i.e., Kāmadeva) placed in its corners.

As stated by the Teachers: "Having drawn the seed-syllable of Māra together with the object of attainment (sādhya) in the pair of fire-cities (analapura) within the pericarp (karṇikā), one should place the six limbs (aṅga) in its cavities, and outside, the syllables of the Māra-gāyatrī in groups of three."
The *mālāmantra* is also [placed] on the tips of the petals, and the god of love (*anaṅga*) on the corners of the earth [petals], starting from the mouth of Guha. Thus [ends verse 144].

At the end of the word "Kāmadevāya," one should utter the dative case ending "-ṅe"; then "vidmahe" [should follow], then "puṣpabāṇaṃ dhīmahi" should be, and finally "tanno'naṅgaḥ pracodayāt. || 145 ||
He extracts the *kāmagāyatrī*: "To Kāmadeva," ending in the dative case (*ṅe*); [and] "to Puṣpabāṇa," [ending in the dative case as] "to Puṣpabāṇa. || 145 ||
At the end of "namas," one should say "to Kāmadeva," and then "to the Beloved of all people," followed by "to the Deluder of All People" at the end of "sarvavarṇa. || 146 ||

One should utter "jvaladvayaṃ prajvalārṇān" for all people; then the heart-mantra "mama" followed by the word "vaśaṃ" repeated twice constitutes the head-mantra. This is the garland-mantra (mālāmanu), consisting of forty-eight syllables. || 147 ||
Regarding the *mālā-mantra*, he says "at the end of 'namas'. "Sarva" refers to the two syllables [sa-ra] at the end;
"hṛdaya" refers to its essential form.
"Śiraḥ svāhā.
This is an independent mantra.
Its seer and other details are as follows:
Nārada, Jagatī, Kāma, and the [other] sages and so forth have been fully proclaimed;
the six-limbed [mantra] consists of seven, seven, nine, seven, ten, eight, and six syllables respectively.
Or rather, there is the one born from nectar, the supreme god whose banner is the makara;
and another who is born of mental resolve, both of whom possess unbroken forms and wield small bows.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*) with the Flower-Arrow [mantra] and the others, ending with *svāhā*;
one should then place the arrows upon the forehead, mouth, throat, heart, and navel.
The remainder is otherwise described as being like the seed-syllable for worship and so forth;
beginning with the seed-syllable *māra* at the start of recitation and such, it brings the three worlds under control.
Having smeared [the ground] with fragrant mud, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus;
in its pericarp, one should draw two mandalas encircled by the fire-syllable (ra).
In its center, one should write the Kāma-mantra joined with the name of the target and the ritual action;
the wise practitioner should then encircle that Kāma-mantra with Kāma-mantras interspersed with the name of the target.
One should likewise draw Śrī in the six corners— namely, those of Indra, Nirṛti, and Vāyu— and likewise Māyā in the corners of Agni, Varuṇa, and Śūlin (Īśāna).
The wise knower of mantras should surround the filaments with the syllables of the *kāma-gāyatrī*,
and place the letters of the *māra-mālā-mantra* upon the eight petals.

One should draw [the mandala] with a number of mouths equal to the caves; one should inscribe the Mātṛkā, and outside, one should draw the orb of the earth, as well as the Śrī-māyā in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Having thus drawn the yantra on a cloth made of gold,
or on a silver plate, a copper plate, or even on birch bark or linen.
Or else, having established the breath within a vessel made of fine threads,
one should offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter preceded by the discharge of the mantra upon the yantra.
Having worshipped and recited it ten thousand times, one should wear that unsurpassed [mantra];
one attains sovereignty over the three worlds, highly honored even by the gods.
It is the summoning of celestial women, those dwelling in the world of the nāgas,
as well as piśācas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, apsarases, and kinnaras.
And those wicked beings who were once prowling from afar,
upon seeing this king of machines, flee away, utterly bewildered.
What is the use of saying more here? It brings happiness to all the world, instantly attracts women, and subdues kings upon this earth.

"It brings about the perfection of yoga for men, enables them to cross the ocean of worldly existence, and bestows both enjoyment and liberation upon men; thus it was proclaimed by the Self-born One. (146-147)

One should draw Kāma in the center, surrounded by the word "Smara" enclosed on both sides by the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Afterwards, one should properly write within the interior of the betel leaves the syllables *tāra* (OM), *vikāra* (KĀ), *pakṣaka* (KHA), *para* (PHA), *nāsā* (M), *dhī* (I), *jhiṇṭīśa* (SA), and *ghān* (NA) upon the eight petals adorned with tridents.
On whichever night one should consume the yantra after performing the recitation, she shall become subject to his will. || 148 ||

Thus has been described the complete worship of the Flower-Arrowed One (Kāmadeva), along with its primary and secondary limbs, which bestows good fortune, splendor, wealth, a wife, sons, and prosperity. || 149 ||
He describes another yantra with the words "sādhyeti" (beginning with 'sādhya').

In the center—that is, within the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus—one should write the Kāma (the god of love), surrounded by *smara* (love-seeds) or *kāmabīja*s (seeds of desire) encased by the names of the object (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and the ritual action (*karman*).
This Kāma should be written together with the names of the object, the practitioner, and the ritual action.
Regarding what is to be written on the eight petals, he says "tāra" (the Savior).
By "tāra," which is counted as three, the letter *i* is meant;
others say it refers to the *praṇava* (Oṃ), but that is incorrect.
This is because it contradicts many texts by Padmapādācārya and others, which state:
"The final vowel is the modification (vikāra);
the second vowel is the alternative (pakṣa)."
Some traditionalists, however, maintain that there are fifteen vowels;
this is according to the view of Padmapādācārya.
"Ko" refers to Vāyu (the letter *ka*); "tena" means "by him"; "yaḥ sa paraḥ" means "that which is beyond him"; by that [phrase], the letter *ma* is formed.

This has been stated by Gautama in the *Mantravyākaraṇa*: "What could be the designator of Brahman? The word *ka* is the designator of the head. What could be the designator of the Sun? The word *ka* is the designator of the Wind."
Regarding the statement that "the letter *kha* is the substitute for the nasal (*andha*)," that is incorrect,
because it contradicts the works of the teacher Padmapāda. By the word "nasal" (*nāsā*), that which is to be articulated as a nasalized sound (*anunāsika*) is meant.
Even among those, since there is no reason to skip the first one, it is the letter *ṅa*.
Some have said that the nose is the letter *a*, but that is incorrect,
precisely because it contradicts that very text and others.
Aghīrarghīśaḥ is Ū; Jhiṃṭīśa is E;
Gha is its own form (svarūpa).
In some places, the reading "jhiṇṭīśakān" is found; that is an error.

As it has been stated by the Teachers: "Rich with the syllables at the end of the seasons, the joints of the seasons, and the ends of the eighteen sacrificial fuel-sticks belonging to the lunar fortnights..."
Thus it is said.
In the commentary on this, the teacher Padmapāda explained:
"Tāra" is "i".
The *ṛtvij* is *aḥ*; the *pakṣa* is *aṃ*;
the eighteenth is *maḥ*.
The *samit* is *ṅa*, the *ṛtu* is *ū*,
the *gaṇḍānta* is *e*,
and the *gānta* is *gha*.
Regarding the phrase "rich with tridents," one should fashion tridents at the tips of the petals. || 148-149 ||

Worship that primordial Viṣṇu in his form as the Fish, by whom all the Vedas were recovered from the oceans after he had slain the exceedingly fierce Śaṅkha-asura, and who formerly bestowed them upon the Grandfather (Brahmā). ||150||

Having thus described the mantras of Viṣṇu along with their elaborations, [the author] praises Viṣṇu through the sequence of his ten incarnations—beginning with the verse "ādāya" and so forth—in order to generate firm devotion in the mind of the disciple.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: by him who, having slain the demon Śaṅkha, took [the Vedas] from the ocean, all the Vedas were given to the Grandfather, Brahmā.
In the reading "vedān," the meaning is "those" (te). || 150 ||
When the great ocean was churned by the gods and asuras for the sake of divine nectar, using Vāsuki and Mount Mandara [as the churning rod and rope],
the earth was violently shaken by the great force.
I remember that tortoise situated upon its support. || 151 ||
The connection is that [it] belongs to the earth as its support. || 151 ||
I take refuge in that Primordial Boar, by whom the earth—girdled by the oceans, clothed in the rivers, bearing Mount Meru as a crown—was lifted up from the tip of his tusk. ||152||

I do not forget that Nṛsiṃha who, arising from within the pillar with an intellect patient of breaking the pride of his devotees, was tearing apart the enemy of the gods with the tips of his sharpened claws. ||153||
The connection is that by the very tip of his fang, the earth, having become such as this, was uplifted from the tip of his fang. || 152-153 ||
The earth, adorned by the four oceans,
is not sufficient as a mere deposit for the foot of one [Buddha],
let alone for another among the gods.
I remember Trivikrama, who has gone everywhere. || 154 ||
The connection is that the abode of the gods is not sufficient for the placement of another, a second foot. ||154||
Having slain kings twenty-one times,
he who, by the strength of his staff-like arms, duly performed a blood-offering for his ancestors.
I bow with devotion to that foremost of heroes. || 155 ||
Having taken birth in the lineage of the Raghus and having constructed a bridge across the waters of the ocean,
he who subdued the Lord of Laṅkā.
I bow with devotion to that Lord of Sītā. || 156 ||
Having dragged all the asuras with his plow,
he reduced them to powder with blows from his club—
he who, having encountered Kṛṣṇa, became even more powerful.
With devotion, I worship that Balabhadra Rāma. || 157 ||
The grammatical connection is that he reduced them to powder, having obtained Kṛṣṇa as his ally and strength. (155–157)
In ancient times, intending to conquer the primordial asuras,
he assumed the guise of one clad in rags and composed a treatise whose efficacy is unfailing.
I bow down to that Buddha, who is the fundamental source. || 158 ||
At the end of the eon, he struck [the earth] with all his hooves in a mere twinkling of an eye—
he who is called Bhīma because he consumes everything with his splendor.
We worship that horse, who is the soul of the universe. || 159 ||
Holding a conch, a beautiful discus, a mace, and a lotus in his hands, mounted upon Garuḍa,
marked with the Śrīvatsa, he is the primordial source of the universe.
I praise Viṣṇu, dark as the tamāla tree, within my heart. || 160 ||
The syntactical connection is that he should wear [the robes] while honoring the appearance marked by the robe-signs. || 158–160 ||

I repeatedly remember the primordial one, who resembles a lotus, whose face is beautified by an inner smile, whose lotus-eyes are fully blossomed, and who reclines upon the special couch of Śeṣa in the ocean of milk—the source of the Vedas. (161)

One should propitiate the Lord of the World, who is identical with the universe, the Supreme Person, by means of this hymn of praise, for the attainment of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. || 162 ||
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Śāradātilaka composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra. 17.
A particular is indeed a particular because it is unique. 161–162.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, based on the authentic tradition. 17.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Next, I shall declare the mantras of Maheśa, which bestow all prosperity.
By means of which the sages of old swiftly attained union with Śiva. || 1 ||

He states the Śaiva mantras that follow in sequence with the word "atha" (now), and by the phrase "those which bestow all prosperity," etc., he explains their application for each respective qualified practitioner. || 1 ||
The heart-mantra (hṛdaya) is *va*, the witness (*sākṣin*) is *la*, and it is joined with *na* and *ta*;
this five-syllabled mantra, preceded by *tāra* (om), is declared to be six syllables. || 2 ||
The sage is Vāmadeva, the meter is Paṅkti, and Īśa is its deity;
the preceptor should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) of the mantra using six syllables. || 3 ||
One should assign the five forms, beginning with the mantra-syllables, in their proper order:
[to] the index finger, the middle finger, the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb; and again [to the same]. || 4 ||
He extracts the mantra as "the heart" (*hṛdayam*).
The heart is the word *namaḥ*.
Following that is *śa*, which is accompanied by the witness *i* (the vowel *i*), thus forming *śi*.
The letter *la* ending in *vaḥ*, the infinite (*ananta*) [letter *ha*] ending with that, or by that [letter *ya*] which is Marut;
by the phrase "consisting of six syllables," it is stated that [the mantra] begins with the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable].
The first seed-syllable is *u*, and the power (*śakti*) is *m*.
Some say that by adding the seed-syllable of the *prāsāda* mantra after the *praṇava*, it becomes a seven-syllabled mantra.
In another tantra:
Having encapsulated the mantra of Haṃsavāgīśvara at the beginning and the end, the wise one should recite the Śiva-mantra; he will immediately attain conviction.
"One who, solitary, with mind and self restrained, recites the *sampuṭa* of the Śiva-mantra diligently for one month, attains his desired object under his control. Thus it is said.

Regarding this, the supreme gurus maintain that by the word *vāgīśvara* [in the mantra], one should take the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable alone, devoid of the letter *ra*, as well as the third [seed-syllable].
By the phrase "with six," only the extraction of the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅga-mantra*) is stated.
Since the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) will be explained later, there is no tautology.
"According to the sequence, the Guide":
it has been stated that the *praṇava* (oṃ) comes first for each syllable;
the last [finger] is the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*). (2–4)
These [faces] are known as Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta, and Vāmadeva;
they are located respectively in the mouth, heart, feet, and private parts, and again upon one's own head. || 5 ||
Then, one should place the six limbs of the mantra, conjoined with their respective seed-syllables (jāti), in sequence upon the five faces— the eastern, southern, western, northern, and the central.
Those are the forms:
Sadyas is Sadyojāta;
Vāma is Vāmadeva.
Īśa is Īśāna.
"One should place them in the locations ending with the head and the top of the head"—this is the connection with what follows.
And those forms (mūrtis) should end in the dative case with the word "namaḥ," according to the masters of tradition.
The term "on the head" (*mūrdhani*) is connected to both [the preceding and following phrases] by way of the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣigolakanyāya*).
Furthermore, their subsequent connection is as follows: "one should place them on the head and on the five faces of the *Narasiṃha*.
This has been stated by the Teachers:
"Also by the names of the mouth, heart, feet, secret place, and head;
and in the eastern, southern, western, and northern faces, as well as in the head. Thus it is said.
Regarding "the limbs of the mantra":
the application therein is as follows—*oṃ hṛt*, *naṃ śiraḥ*, and so forth.
However, those who know the tradition [state]:
Oṃ oṃ, to the abode of omniscience, the heart;
oṃ naṃ, to the abode of satisfaction, the head;
oṃ maḥ, to the abode of primordial awakening, the crest-lock.
Oṃ śiṃ, to the abode of unimpaired power, armor; Oṃ vāṃ, to the abode of independent power, the eye;
Oṃ yaṃ, to the abode of infinite power, the weapon.
Thus they maintain that there are six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga).
This is stated in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā:
"In the same manner, one should further establish its six ancillaries."
Likewise, omniscience, contentment, and awakening, which are devoid of beginning and end.
"Unimpeded power, sovereignty, and infinite energy.
In some places, however, there is an exchange between the path (*varman*) and the eye (*netra*).
As it has been said:

"Omniscience, contentment, beginningless awakening, sovereignty, eternal unimpaired power, and infinite power—those who know the Veda declare these to be the six limbs of the Great Lord. Thus [it is said].
This should be inferred according to the tradition of one's own teacher. 5-6.
Immediately thereafter, for the sake of protection, one should perform the *golaka-nyāsa* (the deposition of the spheres) upon the heart,
the mouth, the two shoulders, the two elbows, the throat, the navel, and the two sides.

Thereafter, one should place [the mantras] on the back, the heart, then the head, the mouth, the two eyes, the two nostrils, and subsequently at the joints of the arms and legs, including their tips. || 8 ||
Again, [one should place them] on the head, face, heart, belly, thighs, and the two feet;
then in the heart, the lotus-face, the axe, and the deer, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons. || 9 ||
The most excellent of teachers should duly place the six syllables of the root mantra in sequence upon the mouth, shoulders, heart, feet, thighs, and belly. || 10 ||
One should then place them on the crown of the head, the forehead, the belly, the shoulders, and the heart;
thereafter, the wise person should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with this mantra. || 11 ||

"Salutation be to the one in the form of Sthāṇu, whose essence is the nectar of the light-liṅga, whose limbs are illuminated by the fourfold manifestation, to Śambhu. Having thus offered his body [in dedication], he should meditate upon the Lord of Pārvatī. || 12 ||
He says "one should perform" regarding the placement of the spheres (*golaka-nyāsa*) consisting of ten repetitions.
This means immediately after that, namely after the placement of the principles (*tattva-nyāsa*). The placement of the principles is as follows:
Furthermore, the placement of the Śiva-principles (śaivatattvanyāsa) will hereafter be explained by grace:
"Obeisance to the Supreme Five-Syllabled One, whose self is the name of the principles."
By way of repetition, it is joined with the letters of the five-syllabled Śiva mantra, both separately and together:
the second [syllable] and those following with the letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *na*, and the first [syllable] with those beginning with the fixed [syllable *oṃ*].
Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara,
as well as Śuddhavidyā, Māyā, Kāla, Niyati, and Kalā.
One should place the Puruṣa, characterized by the coloring of memory, as well as Prakṛti, intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkṛti),
and mind (manas) within the heart; likewise, the sense organs such as hearing and so forth in their respective locations,
and speech and so forth, along with the objects of sound and so forth, in the head, mouth, navel, anus, and feet.
One should assign Ākāśa and the others to these [sites], as well as the pentad to be described hereafter;
[these are] Sadāśiva and the rest, ending with Ākāśādyādhipati, in their respective order.

One should place the kalās beginning with Śāntyatītā and ending with Kalā, starting from Nivṛtti and so forth, according to their respective seed-syllables, from the feet to the head and from the head to the feet.
Śāntyātman is Īśāna with the head [ending] in *mūrdhan* joined by *ṅe*; Sadāśiva is joined by *ṅe*.
Satyātman is Tatpuruṣa with the face [ending] in *vaktra* joined by *ṅe*; Īśvara is joined by *ṅe*.
The essence of Nāda is Aghora-hṛdaya, joined with the suffix -ṅe; Maheśvara is the essence of Bindu, and Vāmadeva-guhya is Viṣṇu, joined with the suffix -ṅe.
The seed-syllable is *sadyojāta*, and Brahmā is the foot (*pāda*) joined with the vowel *ṅe*;
likewise are those beginning with Īśāna, starting from the upper face, preceded by Sadāśiva.
"In the five faces beginning with the upper one, [place those] preceded by the syllables ending in Ṅ.
Regarding "from their own seed-syllables": *hlāṃ hlīṃ hrūṃ hyaiṃ hauṃ*.
[One should worship] Īśāna and the others—namely Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta;
[and] those beginning with the upper face—namely the upper, eastern, southern, northern, and western [faces].
The ritual application (prayoga) is as follows: *Oṃ hoṃ namaḥ śivāya parāya śivātmane namaḥ*.
*Naṃ kṣaṃ hauṃ namaḥ śivāya parāya śaktyātmane namaḥ | Maṃ laṃ hauṃ namaḥ śivāya parāya sadāśivātmane namaḥ,* and so forth.
One round [of recitation] is performed with the first quarter-verse.
The second [enclosure] extends from the throat to the heart;
the third extends from the head to the nose.
Then, with half of that [measure], there are four enclosures.
Elsewhere, in all cases, only the four joints of the forearm and the feet are taken;
here, however, including even the middle joint of the fingers, there are five joints,
with the sixth being the tip.
In each [finger], there is one covering for each.
Regarding the term "the tip" (*sāgram*), it should be understood that the fingers possess "tip-ness" (*agratva*) due to their connection with the final joint.
In this regard, some authorities everywhere maintain that this is the placement of five syllables (*pañcākṣaranyāsa*).

In that system, there would be a contradiction with the statement "the six syllables of the root mantra" and also with the statement from another source: "One should place the six syllables in sequence upon the heart, the face, and the pair of shoulders and thighs.
To avoid this contradiction, they say that the *praṇava* (oṃ) should precede each individual syllable.

Even so, the separate instruction of six locations for the eighth, ninth, and tenth [recitations] would be redundant. Furthermore, because it contradicts the statement in another tenth recitation—“three in the face, shoulders, and heart; the others in the feet, thighs, and belly”—that [positioning] is inconsistent. However, some say there are only eight placements: two at the joints of the arms, one at the tips [of the fingers], and likewise one each for the pair of arms and the pair of feet.
This is indeed mistaken;
for in all instances where the placement of the spheres (*golaka*) is discussed, as well as in other texts, it is stated that there are only ten coverings (*āvṛti*).
Furthermore, there is no reason to restrict the meaning of the word *sandhi*.
Then the eighth [digit] is with half of that;
again, the ninth is with half of that.
Regarding this, the traditionalists maintain that the placement (nyāsa) should be performed upon the ṭaṅka and other [parts] with their respective mudrās.
A *ṭaṅka* is an axe.
As for the characteristics of the *mudrās*: having joined one hand across the fingers of the other two hands...
If they are joined together and then extended, this mudrā is considered to be that of the axe (paraśu).
Having joined the tips of the ring finger, the thumb, and the middle finger together, one should extend the remaining fingers; this is declared to be the *mṛgamudrā*. Thus it is said.
"The left hand is raised and extended, forming the *abhaya-mudrā*;
the right hand is turned downward and extended, forming the *vara-mudrā*. Thus it is said.
"The tenth [is formed] with half [of that].
Regarding "in due order":
the connection is that the supreme teacher should again install those forms in due order.
By the word "yathāvat" (accordingly), it is stated that these are the syllables of the mantras beginning with the *praṇava*.
By the word "deśikottama" (supreme teacher), it should be understood as "with those respective fingers.
This is to be inferred for the two previous types of placement (*nyāsa*) as well.
"Shoulder" refers to the two shoulders. || 7-12 ||
One should constantly meditate upon Maheśa, who resembles a mountain of silver, who is adorned with the beautiful crescent moon,
whose limbs are radiant with jewel ornaments, who holds an axe, a deer, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in his hands,
who is gracious, seated upon a lotus, praised on all sides by hosts of immortals, and clothed in a tiger skin.
The primordial source of the universe, possessing universal forms, the remover of all fears, five-faced, and three-eyed. || 13 ||
"One should meditate" means that a white lotus is to be visualized as his seat.
Regarding the meditation on the weapons: in the first case, they are in the two upper hands starting from the right; in the latter case, they are in the two hands below those.

In this very sequence, the previously mentioned ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed upon one's own body. Here, following the meditation, the *padma*, *liṅga*, and *mudrās* should be displayed, as well as the *āyudha-mudrās*.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Because, having displayed the lotus and the liṅga mudrās before him...
The definition of the lotus mudrā (*padmamudrā*) has been stated previously.
As for the characteristics of the *liṅgamudrā*:
one should raise the right thumb and bind it with the left thumb;
one should then encircle the fingers of the left hand with the fingers of the right hand.
"This is declared to be the Liṅgamudrā, which brings about the presence of Śiva. Thus [it is said].
It should be understood that this [mantra] is common to all Śaiva mantras. || 13 ||
One initiated according to the Śaiva path should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
he should offer oblations of auspicious milk-rice for that many thousands of times.
Thereupon, the mantra becomes perfected, bestowing the fulfillment of the practitioner’s desires. || 14 ||
"Initiated by the Śaiva path" means one who has received initiation;
and that [initiation] is to be understood from the Śaiva Tantras, such as the Kāmika.
The grammatical connection is: "one should mutter the mantra consisting of twenty-four hundred thousand *tattvas*."
And it is said: "One should recite four hundred thousand syllables.
This refers to twenty-four thousand repetitions of that number.
In this context, it should be understood that for the sprinkling of substances, the root mantra ends with *hūṃ phaṭ*.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya* and the *Prayogasāra*:
"Having thus performed the sprinkling with the root mantra ending in the armor (*varma*) and weapon (*astra*) mantras, [the substance] is prepared."
Thus [ends the section]. 14.
One should worship the God upon a pedestal endowed with the nine Śaktis, beginning with Vāmā:
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, then Raudrī, Kālī, Kalapadā, and so forth. || 15 ||
The one called Vikāriṇī is proclaimed first, then Vikariṇī;
next is Balapramathanī, and then Sarvabhūtadamanī. || 16 ||
These are declared to be the powers (śaktis) of the Śaiva-pīṭha, ending with Manonmanī.
After [the invocation], one should say "Salutation to the Blessed One" (namo bhagavate), followed again by "sakalādi" (and so forth). || 17 ||

Then, [the mantra] beginning with "Tāra" (Oṃ) is: "Salutation again to the one endowed with the power of the self of qualities, then to the Infinite, the Supreme, the essence of the seat of yoga. || 18 ||
Regarding the phrase "the deity":
the connection is that one should worship the deity on the seat (*pīṭha*) consisting of the nine powers, beginning with Vāmā.
In this context, the meaning is that after having fully worshipped the seat from Maṇḍūka up to the Supreme Reality (*paratattva*), one should worship the nine powers.
The phrase "beginning with Kalā" is an adjective for the following [deities].
Their meditation is described in the *Prayogasāra* and the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
White, red, black, yellow, dark-blue, crimson, white, and black.
"And one should remember those red Śaktis, in the form of seats, in their proper sequence. (15–18)
With this mantra, one should offer a seat to the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain;
having conceptualized the form with the root mantra, one should invoke Śiva there and worship him. || 19 ||
By the phrase "of the Lord of Girijā," this is stated:

having worshipped the seat in the self-sacrifice (ātmayāga) and having offered [substances] beginning with welcome (svāgata) and ending with fragrance (gandha), one should offer five handfuls of flowers with the mantra: "Salutation to You who have become the Immovable One (sthāṇu)."
As it has been said by the Teachers: "The practitioner, composed in mind, should properly offer handfuls of flowers upon his own body three or five times with this mantra. (19)
One should worship the forms in the pericarp; Īśa is situated in the direction of Īśāna (the northeast), resembling pure crystal, while Tatpuruṣa and the others are in the [other] directions.
Yellow, black, white, and red, bearing weapons similar to those of the Principal [Deity], and endowed with four faces—one should worship them duly. || 21 ||
The syntactical connection is that one should duly worship the four forms, beginning with Tatpuruṣa, in the directions starting from the pericarp.
By the word "duly" (*yathāvat*), it is stated that [the worship] consists of the syllables of the mantra beginning with the *praṇava* (OM).
The syntactical connection is that one should worship the fifth, Īśa, located in the northeast direction, resembling pure crystal. (20–21)
In the corners, one should worship the kalās, Nivṛtti and the others, in sequence, which consist of the form of light;
one should worship the limbs situated on the filaments and the Vidyeśas located on the petals.
In the corners, beginning with the southeast (āgneya),
are the four [powers] beginning with Nivṛtti, as mentioned in the second [chapter].
"Consisting of fire" is the visualization (dhyāna).
It should be understood that the seed-syllables of the fivefold elements (*pañcīkṛtabhūta*) and so forth are those mentioned in the first chapter.
Others maintain that the statement "one should also worship Śāntyatītā in Īśa" is indicated by the word "in sequence" (*kramāt*). || 22 ||
Ananta, named Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Anantara, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, and thereafter Trinetra. || 23 ||
Afterwards, [he should worship] the one named Śrīkaṇṭha and immediately thereafter Śikhaṇḍin;
[and the colors] red, yellow, white, reddish, black, red, collyrium-colored, and dark.

Wearing crowns with the young moon upon them, seated upon lotuses, adorned with ornaments, three-eyed, holding tridents, vajras, bows, and other weapons in their hands, they were captivating to the mind. || 25 ||
One should worship Umā to the north and so forth, and then Caṇḍeśvara again;
thereafter Nandin and Mahākāla, and then Gaṇeśa and Vṛṣabha once more. || 26 ||
Then [he visualizes] Bhṛṅgarīṭi and Skanda, these [deities] seated upon lotus-thrones,
[colored] respectively golden, water-like (white), ruddy, dark, pearl-white, moon-white, and pale-red.
Then Indra and the others, joined with their weapons such as the thunderbolt (vajra), are to be worshipped.
In this manner one should worship the God and recite [the mantra] a thousand times daily. || 28 ||
Completely liberated from all sins, one shall attain desired prosperity;
by reciting it two thousand times, one is freed from diseases—of this there is no doubt. || 29 ||
One should recite the mantra three thousand times and shall obtain a long life;
by reciting it ten thousand times, one shall obtain all desires. || 30 ||
One should reverently offer one hundred thousand oblations with pure sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter;
this will destroy the afflictions born of portents—of this there is no doubt.
By reciting it ten million times, a human being becomes Śiva himself. || 31 ||
He states the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) as "Ananta" and so forth. "Astra" means the arrow.
The connection is that one should subsequently worship these [deities] starting from the north.
"Śatalakṣam" means ten million.
This yantra is drawn according to another tantra: "One should lay down six lines upwards and likewise six lines across."
It has the form of a conjoined tip-to-tip, with a straight tip and a visible line.

Having divided the square diagram into two parts, one should place the lotus with the sounds of the Vasu-patra and endowed with the letters of the Mātṛkā; this is the yantra known as the five-syllabled one.
One should place the five-syllabled mantra in the center; after that, the twelve-syllabled mantra;
likewise, having placed the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), one should thereafter place the twelve Suns.
Then, having assigned the Bṛhatsaura [mantra], thereafter the Kalā-śaktis,
then Gāyatrī and the eight Mothers, and thereafter the vowels.
"The Mātṛkās, the world-protectors, and the yantra known as the five-syllabled one. Thus:
the heart [mantra] is "Oṃ ṅeṇa bhagavan āditya," and "Saṃge saha."
The first ray is *sadyojāta*, and there are two *ṭha*s in *māneṅe*. This is the great solar [mantra]; the digits (*kalā*) are the powers beginning with Amṛtā.
"To Tatpuruṣa" is the Gāyatrī.
The *mātṛkā* consists of the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *sa*.
Another *yantra* described in the *Śaiva Āgamas* is stated as follows:
"Within a hexagon, one should place the *prāsāda* mantra joined with the *sādhya*, and the root-mantra (*mūla*) upon the corners."
The limbs are at the joints; outside of that, there is a five-petalled lotus here.
Then, one should write the five forms beginning with Īśāna, ending with the heart (hṛdaya).
Outside of that, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus endowed with the eight groups of the Mātṛkā letters.

Having encircled the yantra—which has been perfected through recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), and other rites—with the Anuṣṭubh [verse], it bestows the fruits of the four aims of life (caturvarga): health, long life, progeny, and sovereignty. Thus [ends verses 23–31].
The six-syllabled mantra, conjoined with Śakti, is declared to be the eight-syllabled mantra;
its seer and metre were proclaimed of old, and its deity is Umāpati.
He states another mantra with the word "six" (ṣaḍ).
"Enclosed" (ruddha) means encapsulated (sampuṭita).
The Praṇava is the seed-syllable (bīja), and Māyā is the power (śakti).
"Previously spoken":
Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is the meter (chandas). || 32 ||
The limbs have been described previously; one should contemplate Soma as the Lord.
Regarding the "limbs":
therein, the experts of the tradition maintain that the ritual of the six limbs is performed with the six syllables beginning with the seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels.
The practical application, however, is: *hrāṃ oṃ* for the heart.
Hroṃ is the head;
Hrūṃ Maḥ is the crest-lock;
Hraiṃ Śiṃ is the armor.
Hrauṃ is for the eye;
Hraḥ Yaṃ is for the weapon;
Soma refers to [the deity] accompanied by Umā. || 33 ||

I bow to the one who has the luster of the bandhūka flower, who possesses three eyes, who wears the crescent moon, whose face is smiling, who holds a trident, a skull-cup, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with his hands, and who possesses a beautiful laugh;
[I bow] to her who rests upon the pillar-like left thigh of the one whose hand shines with a beautiful red lotus.
[He saw] the body of his beloved, adorned with shimmering ornaments made of jewels, closely embraced by his hand. ||34||

The meditation on the weapons [is performed] in the two upper hands of Dakṣa and others in the first case, and in the two lower hands in the last case; or it is in the left hand, as it is said: "In the palm.
Thus it has been stated:
Her body is embraced by her who rests upon her left thigh, holding a red lotus in her own left hand;
"with the hand" refers to the right one. || 34 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rule;
then, one should perform the fire oblation with the best twigs of the *āragvadha* tree, smeared with the three sweets, one thousand times.
One should worship Umāpati on the seat previously described with perfumes and flowers;
outside, the enclosures of the limbs (aṅgāvṛti) beginning with Hṛllekhā should be worshipped as before. || 36 ||
"One hundred thousand times ten million" means fourteen million;
"one thousand times that" means fourteen thousand.
"According to the rule" means by means of the ritual procedure for the mouth of the Tantric fire.
"Just as before" refers to what was stated in the ninth chapter regarding [the deities] beginning with their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*).
The connection is that they are to be worshipped "according to the prescribed ritual. (35–36)

In the center, the east, the south, the north, and the west, according to the prescribed rule, are Hṛllekhā, Gaganā, Raktā, the fourth is Karālikā, and Mahocchuṣmā; these [five goddesses] possess a radiance equal to the five elements respectively. || 37 ||

Holding a noose, a goad, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, and adorned with immeasurable ornaments, one should worship Vṛṣabha and the others in order on the petals starting from the east. || 38 ||
He states the procedure itself with the words "in the center" (*madhye*).
"The center" refers to the middle of the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
The phrase "in the western directions" is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*).
"Consisting of the five elements" refers to earth and so forth. (37–38)
Resembling the Himalayas, possessing sharp horns and three eyes, blazing with all ornaments, he was the very embodiment of the Vedic meters in person. || 39 ||
Then one should worship Kṣetrapāla, who has three eyes, is naked, possesses the luster of a dark rain-cloud, and whose hands sport with a skull and a trident. || 40 ||
Then one should worship Caṇḍeśa, who has the form of red [color], possesses three eyes, and whose hands shine with a trident, an axe, a rosary, a bracelet, and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). || 41 ||

One should worship Durgā, who holds a discus, a conch, and grants fearlessness and desired boons; she possesses the luster of emerald, is gentle, three-eyed, and adorned with beautiful ornaments. || 42 ||
Then one should worship the lovely six-faced child, who has twelve eyes, shines like the rising sun, and holds a wish-fulfilling branch and a jeweled bell. || 43 ||

One should worship Nandin, who is gentle, adorned with red ornaments, possessing a dark-complexioned body, and holding an axe, an excellent sword, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. || 44 ||

One should worship Vighnanāyaka, who holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, who has the luster of saffron, and whose crest is adorned with a crescent moon. || 45 ||

Then one should worship the General, who is dark-complexioned, holding a red lotus in his hand, with that same hand placed upon his left lap, possessing three eyes, and adorned with red garments. || 46 ||
He describes the very sequence preceded by meditation in the verse beginning with "Himalaya.
The completion of each individual meditation occurs at every verse.
"Eṇa" means a deer.
The sequence for the meditation on the weapons, however, should be sought in their respective sections.
"From there" means upon the tips of the petals. (39–46)
Then the eight Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī and possessing the characteristics previously described, should be worshipped;
one should also worship the world-protectors, Indra and the others, in their respective directions. || 47 ||
One should worship those weapons, beginning with the vajra, outside of that in their proper sequence.
The mantra-practitioner who thus worships the Lord of Gods, the consort of Umā, shall become beloved by all the worlds and possessed of the wealth of good fortune. || 48 ||
Those possessing the characteristics previously described, having the nature as stated [above]. (47–48)

The mantra known as Prāsāda, which begins with the letter *sa* (sāntaḥ), is joined with the letter *ya* (sadyānta), has its head adorned with the *bindu*, and bestows all perfections upon those who worship it. || 49 ||
The sage is Vāmadeva, the metre is Paṅkti, and the deity is Sadāśiva;
the ritual of the six limbs is proclaimed by means of the seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels. || 50 ||

The preceptor should assign the forms beginning with Īśāna to the thumb and the other fingers. One should know that their seed-syllables (bījas) are, in order: the one called Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta. || 51 ||
He states the mantra for the temple (*prāsāda*) with the words "ending in *sa*" (*sānta*).
"Ending in *sa*" means *ha*; "ending in *dyā*" means *au*; thus, it is *hau*.
The etymology of this name has been stated by the teachers: "Because it pacifies (*prasādana*) the mind, this mantra is designated as 'the temple' (*prāsāda') according to its true nature."
Thus [it is said].
Some say it is "encased by Hṛllekhā.
The letter *ha* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *oṃ* is the power (*śakti*).
As it has been said:

"The mantra known as Prāsāda is said to be ending with the nasal (m), joined with grace (anugraha), with its head adorned by the Bindu; 'haṃ' is remembered as the seed-syllable (bīja) and 'auṃ' as the power (śakti)."
By the phrase "bestower of all accomplishments" (sarvasiddhida), the application (viniyoga) is stated.
"With the seed-syllable" (bījena) means with the root mantra.
Having recited the half-verse beginning with "Vāmadeva," one should then recite the half-verse beginning with "six long [vowels]."
The transposition [of the order] is due to the error of the scribe. || 49-51 ||

The element of space (viyat), conjoined in reverse order with the five short vowels beginning with *o*, should again be placed upon those respective fingers, preceded by their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*). || 52 ||
Likewise, they [are placed] respectively in the locations of the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet;
and in the openings directed upward, eastward, southward, northward, and westward. || 53 ||
"By means of those beginning with *o*" refers to *o*, *e*, *u*, *i*, and *a*.
"Each respective" [refers to those].
Whichever [finger] was placed upon whichever [limb],
with that very finger— closed together with the thumb— at the head;
with the thumb and forefinger together, at the mouth.
With the thumb and middle finger at the heart;
with the thumb and ring finger at the secret place;
and with the thumb and little finger at the two feet.
"In this way, it is so even for the five faces," say the traditionalists (*sāmpradāyikāḥ*).
"In that manner" (*tathā*) means the conjunction of the upward-facing face and the others.
"Tāḥ" refers to the forms (mūrtis).
The connection is that one should place those [forms], beginning with their respective seed-syllables (bījas), by means of the corresponding fingers. || 52-53 ||
Then the wise one should properly assign the thirty-eight kalās upon his body;
he should correctly place the Ṛgvedic mantras beginning with Īśāna on his fingers in due order.
The best of teachers should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger;
