he should then place those [fingers] again upon the head, the face, the lotus of the heart, the private parts, and the feet.
He begins to explain the deposition of the thirty-eight *kalās* with the word "tataḥ" (then).

Although this deposition was stated by the author as an ancillary part of the *Prāsāda-mantra*, it should nevertheless be understood that this *Pañcarcavidhāna* is independent and common to all Śaiva mantras.
The teachers have stated this quite independently;
by saying "one should fashion the limbs," he himself has indicated that independence.
Those six limbs belong to the five *ṛc*s alone, and not to the *Prāsāda* mantra.
As it has been said:
"I shall duly explain the procedure for the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the thirty-eight kalās, which is the essence of the Śaiva Āgamas,
together with the five Brahmans beginning with Īśa, preceded by the Ṛṣis and others, along with their specific ancillaries."
Therefore, the Ṛṣis and other details mentioned in another Tantra are written here:
"Īśa, Anuṣṭubh, Bhūri, and Śeṣa for the one named Tatpuruṣa; Gāyatrī, Āpaḥ.
Again, Agni, Anuṣṭubh, Āpaḥ for Vāmadeva; Bhaga, Ahaḥ, Hasta, and Anuṣṭubh for Aghora; and Bhaga. Thus it is said.
He states the sequence of the ritual placement (nyāsa) itself with the words "Īśāna and the others. Those verses are as follows: 1. Īśāna, the Lord of all sciences...
The overlord of all beings, the overlord of Brahmā, may Brahmā Śiva be auspicious to me; Sadāśiva! Om.
2. We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva; may that Rudra inspire us.
3. To the non-terrible ones, and to the terrible ones, and to those more terrible than the terrible, to all the Śarvas everywhere—to you who possess the forms of Rudra, let there be homage.

4. Salutation to Vāmadeva; salutation to the Eldest; salutation to the Most Excellent; salutation to Rudra; salutation to Time; salutation to the Maker of Time; salutation to the Maker of Strength; salutation to Strength; salutation to the Destroyer of Strength; salutation to the Tamer of All Beings; salutation to Him who transcends the mind.
I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta! In existence, in non-existence, and beyond existence, favor me;
salutations to Bhavodbhava.
By the word "correctly" (samyak), this is what is meant:
these [mantras] are to be understood according to the Drāviḍa recension in the Nārāyaṇīyopaniṣad of the Taittirīya branch;
however, the Āndhra recite them otherwise.
The recitation of that [mantra] is not intended here.
By the phrase "to the best of teachers" (deśikāmattama), the application beginning with "salutation to the two thumbs" (aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ) and so forth is stated. || 54–55 ||
One should place [the mantras] on the faces starting from the top and then further arrange the limbs (aṅgas).
Having uttered the five *tāras*, the heart-mantra "to the Omniscient One" (*sarvajñāya*) is proclaimed. || 56 ||
The word "to him who is satisfied by the garland of nectar and splendor" follows;
then, at the end of that, the limb of the head is "Brahma-śiras," which is blazing. || 57 ||
To Śikhiśikha, who is beyond [all] and possesses primordial awakening, belongs that crest;
to Vajrin, whose hand holds the thunderbolt, who is independent, belongs the body-armor. || 58 ||

Having addressed [the disciple] with "Sauṃ Vauṃ Hauṃ," the best of preceptors should perform the following for one whose power has been eclipsed: he should utter the eye-mantra "Ślīṃ" before him; then, ending with "Huṃ Phaṭ," he should utter the weapon-mantra for the sake of the infinite power over the bound soul (paśu). He should then perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using the weapon-mantra. || 59 ||
It was stated that one should fashion the limbs; he states those very limbs with the words "tāra" and so forth.
"The five *tāras*" is as stated in the twelfth [chapter], regarding the conceptualization of the forms (*mūrti*).
*Śiroṅga* means the head;
it is connected with the following word *jvalita* (blazing). *Tanucchada* means armor.
The connection is that the best of instructors should perform these six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga) as they have been described.
By the term "the best of instructors" (deśikasattama) here, this is what is intended:
the word *nitya* (constant/perpetual) should be employed before the phrase *tṛptāya* in the section concerning the head-ancillary (*śiro'ṅga*).
Immediately after the mantra "Ślīṃ" in the Astra [mantra], there is the application of the Śakti-bīja. || 56–59 ||
One should sequentially assign the five kalās of Īśāna to the five faces located in the east, south, west, north, and the center. || 60 ||
Īśāna, the Lord of all sciences, is the first digit, Śaśinī;
Īśvara, the Lord of all beings, is Aṅgadā immediately following that. || 61 ||
At the end of the word *brahmādhipati*, [one says] "the lord of Brahmā. Then, the third [line] should be "granting the desires of Brahmā," and after that, "may Śiva be mine. (62)
Marīcī is declared in the Tantra as the fourth, and Sadāśivā;
then Aṃśumālinī, the supreme one, preceded by the Praṇava and followed by "namaḥ. || 63 ||

He states the sequence for the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the portions of the mantra of Īśa with the words "beginning with" (pūrva). The term "of the portions" (kalānām) refers to the [mantra] beginning with "iṣṭade".
The phrase "sadāśivoṃ" is to be connected with what follows.
The fifth [mantra] is *parā*. Regarding the phrase "beginning with *praṇava*," the meaning is that they begin with *praṇava*, *śakti*, *prāsāda*, and so forth.
The teacher Padmapāda also taught the yoga of the five-syllable mantra,
saying "accompanied by *namaḥ*";
thus, all five [syllables] are in the dative case.
Since it will be stated later that "all the digits (kalās) end in the dative case," the application is as follows:
*oṃ hrīṃ hauṃ namaḥ śivāya*, *īśānaḥ sarvavidyānāṃ śaśinyai namaḥ*, and so forth. (60–63)
Immediately after that, the practitioner of mantra should place the four digits (kalās) of Puruṣa in sequence upon the faces facing east, west, south, and north.
"Ādyā tatpuruṣāya" is said to be "vidmahe," which expresses peace; then "mahādevāya" followed by the word "śabda" (i.e., "śabde") is "dhīmahi. || 65 ||

The second [syllable] is said to be *vidyā*, then *rudraḥ* is the *pada*; thereafter, *pratiṣṭhā* is said to be the third, [ending with] *pracodayāt*. Beyond that is *nivṛtti*, all of which begin with the *praṇava* and are accompanied by *namaḥ*. || 66 ||
"Of the Person" (puruṣasya) means "of that Person" (tatpuruṣasya).
It is connected with the following word, "may he impel" (pracodayāt).
That [word] is in the dative case, being directed toward him.
The word "all" (sarvāḥ) is also [to be understood] as having the dative case ending. || 64–66 ||
The practitioner of mantra should duly assign the eight parts of the Aghora mantra to the heart, the two shoulders, the neck, the navel, the belly, the tail, and the chest. || 67 ||
First, the first digit (kalā) was uttered as "aghorebhyaḥ";
then, immediately following that, "moha" occurs at the end of "atha ghorebhyaḥ. || 68 ||
After Ghorānta, Kṣamā is proclaimed as the third;
after Ghorataras, Nidrā follows, who is omnipresent and devoted to all things.
Disease is declared to be the fifth, following after all [the others];
death is said to be the sixth; thereafter, salutations to you. || 70 ||
Hunger is said to be the seventh [form] from those forms of Rudra, and thirst is said to be the eighth; these, beginning with Dhruva, are accompanied by the word "namas. || 71 ||
"According to the rule" indicates the placement (*nyāsa*) by means of the fingers which is about to be described.
Now, "from the terrible ones" (*ghorebhyaḥ*); this much is the portion of the *ṛc*.
"These" (etāḥ) means those ending in the dative case (caturthyanta). || 67–71 ||
One should place thirteen left digits upon the secret parts, the pair of thighs, the pair of knees and shanks, the two buttocks, the waist, and both sides. (72)
The first [kalā] is for Vāmadeva; at its end is the thunderbolt (vajra), and it is the first kalā. "Salutation to Jyeṣṭha" is proclaimed as the second, which is protection (rakṣā). || 73 ||
"Syādrudrāya namaḥ" at the end is declared as the third, Rati;
"Kālāya namaḥ" at the end is proclaimed as Pālinī. || 74 ||
The fifth [syllable] should be *kalakāmā*, and then for the sake of the modification (*vikaraṇa*);
thereafter, the sixth is said to be *namaḥ saṃyamanī*. || 75 ||
The power of action (balakriyā) is prescribed for the transformation of strength; salutations! Vṛddhi shall be the eighth, and at the end of strength is the stable digit (sthirā). || 76 ||
After that, at the end of *pramathanā*, "namo rātri" is uttered;
at the end of "namo sarvabhūtadamanāya," the *kalā* is *bhrāmaṇī*. || 77 ||
The twelfth digit (kalā) is declared by those who know the mantra to be Mohinī, ending with "namas.
After that, Jarā is declared as the thirteenth, beginning with "unmanāya," followed by "namaḥ.
These [syllables] are proclaimed to begin with the Praṇava (Oṃ), end in the dative case, and conclude with "namas. || 78 ||
*Mushka* refers to the scrotum.
*Vāmakalā* refers to the aspects of Vāmadeva.
Regarding the term *kalakāmā*, *kalā* here refers to the aspect of desire (*kāma*) belonging to the portion of the *Ṛgveda*.
"Salutation to Vikaraṇā"—this is a portion of the Ṛgveda;
"Bala"—this is a portion of the Ṛgveda;
"Kriyā" is a Kalā.
In this case as well, the portion of the *ṛc* verse is "Obeisance to Vikaraṇa. (72–78)
The practitioner of mantras should correctly place the eight kalās arising from Sadyojāta in due order upon the soles of the feet, the two palms, the nose, the head, and the pair of arms. || 79 ||
"I take refuge in Sadyojāta; may there be the first kalā, Siddhi.
Again, let there be obeisance to Sadyojāta; this is declared to be Vṛddhi. (80)
In the state of *bhava*, the third is *dyuti*; immediately after that, in the state of *abhava*, is the fourth, which is called *lakṣmī*. Following that is the stage of *nātibhava*. || 81 ||
Medhā is declared as the fifth; worship me further with devotion.
Prajñā is proclaimed as the sixth; at the end of existence, Prabhā shall be the [seventh] digit.
After that, Udbhavā—homage to her—and Svadhā shall be the eighth digit. || 82 ||
All the thirty-eight kalās are said to begin with the syllable Om (praṇava), end in the dative case, and be followed by "namaḥ," concluding with the five Brahma-mantras. || 83 ||
Thus, having thus disposed his body, he himself becomes Gaṅgādhara;
then, becoming composed, he should meditate upon the god Sadāśiva. || 84 ||
*Bhūyaḥ* is for the purpose of completing the meter;
*bhava* is a portion of a *ṛc*;
and "the five *brahma*-words" refers to the words of the five *ṛcs*.
Here, having sequentially uttered the words of the five verses together with their *kalās*, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) using the fingers beginning with the thumb.

Thus, the *kalās* of the first verse are placed with the fist including the thumb; the *kalās* of the second verse with the index finger and thumb; the *kalās* of the third verse with the middle finger and thumb; the *kalās* of the fourth verse with the ring finger and thumb; and the *kalās* of the fifth verse with the little finger and thumb.
As it has been said: "Thus, one of clear intellect should arrange [the fingers]," and so forth.
Also elsewhere:
One should assign Sadyojāta and the others in sequence with the fingers beginning with the little finger;
likewise, Īśāna with the thumbs, and [Aniṣṭha] with the fist and the thumb. Thus it is said.
Because this [deity] is independent, the meditations, the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-pūjā*), and so forth must be explained.
Among these, the meditation is to be understood as stated by the author of the treatise on the occasion of the worship of the palace enclosure (*prāsādāvaraṇa*).
As for the worship of the enclosures, it is as stated by the Ācārya:

Having thus [performed] the preliminary worship with these five Brahmans, one should then propitiate Śiva with these *ṛc* verses in the middle, east, south, north, and west directions; furthermore, with the limbs (*aṅga*) beginning with Ananta, with Umā and the others starting from Īśāna, and again with the weapons (*kuliśa*) and so forth— one should worship the Lord as it has been taught.
The ritual procedure for the Five Brahmans bestows all happiness, fame, worldly enjoyment, and liberation. Thus [ends the section from verses 79–84].

I bow to the Lord who is adorned with five faces—the colors of a pearl, yellow, white, coral, and red—each possessing three eyes; who wears a crown of the moon and possesses the luster of ten million full moons;
and who holds a trident, an axe, a sword, a thunderbolt, fire, a serpent-king, a bell, and a goad.
One should meditate upon him holding a noose that removes fear, resplendent with immeasurable ornaments. || 85 ||
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra five hundred thousand times;
one should then perform a fire oblation (homa) with karavīra flowers soaked in honey, consisting of one-tenth of that number.

Regarding "muktā": the upper face is pearl-colored (white), the eastern face is yellow, the southern face is blue, the western face is pearl-colored (white), and the northern face is the color of coral.
By the etymological derivation "it gives milk" (*payo dadāti*), it is specifically the blue cloud that is intended.
As it is stated in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*:
"Its eastern face is gentle, with a luster like that of the rising sun."
Rich with the lotuses of his three eyes, he has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
The right [face] is like a dark blue cloud, adorned with the moon;
it is terrible, with crooked, knitted brows, and three red, round eyes.
The upper [face] resembles coral, adorned with dark locks of hair;
it is playful, possesses three eyes, and has the moon as its crest-ornament.
The western face has the luster of the full moon, radiant with three eyes,
bearing the crescent moon, gentle, and enchanting with a subtle smile.
The fifth [face] resembles crystal, radiant with the crescent moon;
it is exceedingly gentle and brilliant with three wide-open eyes. Thus.
The term "Indumukuṭa" (Moon-crested) is to be understood as applying to each face.
A *ṭaṅka* is an axe.
*Nāgeśa* is the Lord of Serpents.
It is the remover of fear and bestows fearlessness.
As for the meditation on the weapons: starting from the top, the first [weapons] such as the trident (śūla) and so forth are on the right, while the last ones are on the left.
This has been stated in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
In the right [hands], he holds a trident, an axe, a vajra, a sword, and a blazing fire;
and in the left, he holds a serpent-king, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a bell, a noose, and a goad, all radiant. Thus it is said.

Elsewhere, it is stated according to the sequence that the first [hand] is on the upper right and the last is on the left: "Holding with his arms a trident, a serpent, a hatchet, a bell, a sword, a spear, a vajra, a noose, fire, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Elsewhere, even a reversal is mentioned.

As they say: "Holding in his right hands a serpent, a bell, a goad that inspires fear, and a noose, and likewise in his other hands a trident, an axe, a sword, a thunderbolt, and fire, in due order. Elsewhere, a meditation on him as having one face and four arms is described.
Alternatively, one should worship him as having one face, endowed with four arms, bearing the moon on his crest, holding a rosary and a trident in succession,
and possessing a *khaṭvāṅga* and a skull-bowl in his hands.
Thus [it is said].
But elsewhere: "I bow my head to the God whose severed arm-stumps are adorned with an axe, a trident, a staff of knowledge, and a skull-bowl. (85-86)
On the previously mentioned pedestal, one should fashion the image with the root mantra;
having invoked it, one should worship it along with that image and the surrounding enclosures (āvaraṇas). || 87 ||
One should worship Īśāna, who is three-eyed and white, holding a spear, a hand-drum, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting gesture with his hands, in the northeastern direction. || 88 ||
One should worship Tatpuruṣa in the east, who has four faces and three eyes, holds a battle-axe, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, and is radiant like lightning. || 89 ||
Holding in his hands a rosary of beads, a noose for deer, a goad, a hand-drum, a skull-topped staff, a sharpened trident, and a skull-cup. || 90 ||
The best of mantra-knowers should worship Aghora in the southern direction—he who has the luster of collyrium, four faces, fearsome fangs, and is terrifying, possessing three eyes. || 91 ||
Vāmadeva has the luster of saffron, four faces, and three eyes;
he holds in his hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a rosary, and an axe.
One should properly worship the graceful Sadyojāta, who has a smiling face, is gentle, resembles camphor and the moon, and possesses three eyes. || 93 ||
One should worship the four-faced Lord in the western direction, whose hands hold the deer-eyed goddess Guṇābhīti, and whose crown shines with the crescent moon as its crest-jewel.
Regarding the term "mūrti":
by the word "ādi" (and so forth), the enclosure of the limbs (*aṅgāvṛti*) is indicated.

The compound *mūrttyādyāvaraṇaiḥ* should be understood as a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member) compound, consisting of the enclosure of the form (*mūrttyāvaraṇa*), the enclosure of the limbs (*aṅgāvaraṇa*), the enclosures [such as] Ananta, Indra, Vajra, and so forth, and those [enclosures]. Thus, it should be analyzed as "by the enclosures beginning with the form."

Having worshipped the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*) with that pentad beginning with the withdrawal of the five forms (*mūrti-pañcaka-nivṛtti*), [one worships] the second with the limbs (*aṅga*) and the third with the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) and so forth; this is the meaning.
This is stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Endowed with the enclosures of the forms and the limbs.
It is also stated elsewhere, after describing the worship of the forms:

Then, on the petals in the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest, one should worship the other [limbs]; the limbs have been described, and one should also worship the weapon (astra) in the cardinal directions.
"By means of mantras bearing their own names, [one should worship] Ananta and Sūkṣma," and so forth.
Also, in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā: "One should worship the Supreme Lord."
"And with the Brahmās and the six ancillaries.
Thus it has been stated by Padmapādācārya as well: "The external enclosure should be understood as being outside the enclosure of the forms (mūrti)."
Therefore, the claim made by some that there is a covering of the limbs (*aṅgāvaraṇa*) prior to the covering of the forms (*mūrttyāvaraṇa*) is incorrect;
for it is stated even in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "One should worship the limbs of the forms according to the rule."
Regarding the mention of the directions in the passage beginning with "pūrvataḥ" (from the east), it should be understood that this is done by subsuming the well-known directions themselves.

By the phrase "the best of mantra-knowers should worship correctly," it is meant that one should worship Īśa and the others using the seed-syllables and so forth as prescribed in the section on ritual placement (*nyāsa*). (Verses 87–94)

Then, the wise practitioner should worship the kalās, such as Nivṛtti and the rest, which consist of the form of fire, in the corners in due order; and on the filaments, he should worship the six limbs as before. || 95 ||
One should worship the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), beginning with Ananta, upon the petals all around;
then, on the exterior, Umā and the others, as well as Indra and the other guardians together with their weapons. || 96 ||

Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, endowed with supreme devotion, the practitioner of mantra should please Him with dances, songs, and other offerings, as well as with captivating hymns. || 97 ||
Regarding the phrase "consisting of light" (*tejorūpā*):
the teachers have stated the reason why these [beings] lack the form of a body and so forth:
"Because they are the power (*śakti*) of the elements, because they are all-pervasive, or because of their cessation within the world, [they lack bodies]."
"Those which consist of light and are devoid of hands, feet, and color have been declared by the wise. Thus [it is said].
In another tantra, her form is also described:
"Nivṛtti has a golden complexion and beautiful limbs; she wears white ornaments and holds in her hands a vajra, a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness, and a lotus."
White in complexion, holding a rosary of white beads, a lotus, and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands, she is radiant with all ornaments; Pratiṣṭhā is exceedingly beautiful.

One should meditate upon the Vidyā-kalā, who holds a spear, a rosary, a lotus, and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands; she is radiant with the red glow of *guñjā* seeds, possesses matted hair and the crescent moon, has three faces, and three eyes.

The digit of Peace (śāntikalā) has four faces and four arms; she is dark-complexioned, wears blue garments, and carries a skull-bowl. She holds a banner, a rosary, a lotus, and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands, and possesses three eyes.

"Resembling crystal, with five faces, holding the Vedas, a rosary, a garland, and the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness; possessing matted hair and the moon, she is Śāntyatītā, adorned with transparent ornaments.
By the word "kalās," it is meant that [the goddesses] such as the unquintuplicated seed-syllables of the elements mentioned in the first chapter are intended.
By the word "successively" (kramāt), this is stated:
having worshipped the fourfold [kalās] beginning with Nivṛtti in the [directions] starting from Āgneya, one should worship Śāntyatītā first in the place of Īśa.
Others, however, say that one should worship Īśāna and Śāntyatītā in the center.
This is in agreement with the *Prapañcasāra*,
since it first mentions "east, upward, and east" and subsequently states that the forms (*mūrti*) are to be placed in the directions previously mentioned.
Others, however, describe the worship of these two as follows.
One should worship Umā and the others as before, beginning from the north.
Regarding this, two yantras found in another tantra are described:
a six-cornered mandala on the outside, smeared with *rocanā* and sandalwood paste.
The practitioner of mantra should scratch out the Prāsāda mantra, conjoined with the name, using dūrvā grass.
Outside, in the six corners, one should write the six-syllable mantra preceded by the *praṇava*;
on the outer [circle], one should inscribe thirty-three petals with the thirty-three syllables.
The six syllables of Īśāna, the seven of Tatpuruṣa,
the six syllables of Aghora, and the seven of Vāmadeva.
"One should write the syllables of *sadyojāta* and likewise the seven [syllables] ending with *namaḥ*;
having encircled it with the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra, one should wear this supreme yantra.
Within the hexagon, one should place the *prāsāda* mantra joined with the *sādhya*, and the root mantra (*mūla*) on the corners.
The limbs are at the joints; outside of that, there is a five-petaled lotus here.
Then, one should write the five forms beginning with Īśāna ending with ṅa;
outside of that, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus joined with the eight groups of the Mātṛkā letters.

Having encircled the yantra with the Anuṣṭubh [verse], it—when accomplished through recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites—bestows the fruits of the four aims of life: health, long life, progeny, and sovereignty. Thus [ends verses 95–97].
The syllable *tāra* (oṃ), *māyā* (hrīṃ), *viyat* (ha), and the *bindu* (ṃ) accompanied by the nasal vowel (*anusvāra*);
joined with these five syllables, the mantra is considered to consist of eight letters (*vasuvarṇa*). || 98 ||
He states the eight-syllable Prāsāda mantra as "Tāra" and so forth.
*Tāra* is the *praṇava* (Om).
*Māyā* is the seed-syllable of Śakti.
The letter *vi* (the sky), *ha*, the nasal drop (*bindu*), and the anusvāra; with *oṃ* joined to that, it becomes *hauṃ*.
This is the five-syllabled mantra, namely the Śaiva Pañcākṣara.
In the eight-syllabled [mantra], there are eight syllables; its seer (*ṛṣi*) and meter (*chandas*) are as previously stated.
The deity is Umāpati. || 98 ||
The wise practitioner should perform the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and other rites as described for the five-syllable mantra. || 99 ||
"According to what was stated regarding the five syllables":
those who know the tradition maintain that the six limbs [are consecrated] with the six syllables beginning with *māyā* (the seed-syllable *hrīm*) and the six long vowels.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the placement (*nyāsa*) of the five forms is included. || 99 ||
I bow to the Lord, the color of vermilion, whose beautiful crescent moon shines as an ornament upon his jeweled crown,
who has an eye blazing on his forehead, whose lotus-face is graced with a smile, and whose limbs are adorned with divine ornaments and unguents;
he who gazes at his beloved, who rests her hand upon his left thigh and holds a crimson water-lily.
With the palms of her hands placed upon the tips of her rounded, lofty breasts, she holds a water-pot with her left hand.
The best among those who know mantras should recite this mantra eight hundred thousand times;
he should then perform a thousand oblations with milk-rice soaked in ghee. || 101 ||
On the eastern pedestal, having conceptualized the form with the root mantra, one should worship it;
first with the limbs [of the deity], and subsequently with the enclosures beginning with Ananta.
The third [mudrā] was clearly demonstrated by Umā and the other leaders of the world;
the fourth and fifth are proclaimed as being formed with their weapons. || 103 ||
Thus, the best of practitioners should worship the deity every day;
having obtained prosperity along with sons, friends, and others, he rejoices. || 104 ||
"I bow" (vande).
"Veda" refers to a book, while "ṭaṅka" means an axe.
The phrase "with the hand placed upon the left thigh" refers to the right hand.
"An orange water-lily" refers to the left hand;
"with the palm placed [there]" refers to the left hand.
The lower left [hand].
As it has been said:
"Of her who has placed her right lotus-hand upon her left lap, likewise [her] left arm..."
"With his left arm, which holds her breast, resting upon the red lotus placed [there] by his beloved"—
the meaning is that the desired boon is held in the raised left hand.
In Vedaṭaṅka, situated on the right; "with Umā and the others" refers to those mentioned previously. (100–104)
*Tāraṃ* (Oṃ), *sthirā* (Svā), together with the moon (*karṇendu*) [H], *bhṛguḥ* (Bha), adorned with *sarga* (Ḥ):
this three-syllabled essence is declared as the mantra for conquering death and other purposes. || 105 ||
The seer is Kahola; the meter is said to be the Devyādigāyatrī;
and Mahādeva Mṛtyuñjaya is declared to be its deity. || 106 ||
Having thus stated the mantras of the five-faced Śiva, he now states the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, which has the upper face as its primary aspect, beginning with "tāram":
*tāram* refers to the Praṇava (Oṃ);
*sthirā* refers to *jaḥ*.
*Karṇe* means the left ear, which is *ū*.
Alternatively, by the word *karṇa*, the number six is indicated; with that, *ū* is joined with the moon-bindu (*indubindu*), resulting in *jūṃ*.
*Bhṛgu* is the letter *sa*, and *sarga* is the visarga; it is joined with that.
"Upon the meeting of the constituent parts of a *dvandva* compound, the first [part] is grasped at the beginning"—
although this is a general rule (*sāmānyaparibhāṣā*), nevertheless, in the previous commentary, it is set aside by a specific statement (*viśeṣavacana*).
As it has been stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
The first [letter] of the Vedas (Ka), the eighth (Tha), joined with the sixth vowel (Ū), the half-moon (Anusvāra), and the fourth vowel (I);
then two *jala* letters (Ja and Sa) ending in a bindu (Jasau), followed by the moon (Sa) joined with a bindu.
The seed-syllables of the five-syllable mantra have been declared with care;
from its beginning, it is said to consist of three syllables by means of those three seeds in sequence.
"With the final seed-syllable of that very [mantra], it is declared to be the single-syllabled [form].
These are the Mṛtyuñjaya mantras, proclaimed in sequence with ever-increasing results.
Also, in the Nārāyaṇīya: "The syllable *sa* together with *śiva* (i.e., *sa-śiva*) in the middle of the left arm, along with the *bindu*, is *sakala-bhṛgu* (i.e., *sah*)."
Thus [it is stated].
In its commentary, it is said: "With Śiva, joined with the sixth vowel";
by the word "Śiva," the sixth vowel is intended here.
The Praṇava is the seed-syllable (bīja) and "sa" is the power (śakti);
"jūṃ" is the seed-syllable—so say the teachers beginning with Padmapādācārya. (105–106)
One should perform the six-limbed practice with the long-conjoined Bhṛgu-mantra. || 107 ||
"With Bhṛgu" means with the letter *sa*. "Endowed with the long [vowel]" means endowed with all six long vowels;
the meaning is that one should perform this after the placement of the syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*) at the navel, the heart, and between the eyebrows. || 107 ||
One whose eyes are the moon, sun, and fire; whose face is smiling; who dwells within two lotuses;
whose hands shine with the gestures of mudrā, a noose, a deer, and a rosary; who has the luster of the moon;
whose body is bathed in the nectar flowing from ten million moons; and who is radiant with ornaments such as necklaces.
One should meditate upon Paśupati, the conqueror of death, who deludes the entire universe with his splendor. || 108 ||
"Situated within two lotuses" means that one [lotus] faces upward and the second, upon which he sits, faces downward at the head. "Mudrā" refers to the *jñānamudrā*.
The meditation on the weapons extends from the upper right [hand] down to the lower right [hand]. || 108 ||

One of vast intelligence should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with ten parts of that number, using pieces of *amṛtā* soaked in pure milk and clarified butter. || 109 ||
In the Śaiva [tradition], one should worship on the pedestal and fashion the image with the root mantra;
having propitiated the limbs and the surrounding deities, one should subsequently sacrifice to the lords of the world.
Then the best of practitioners should worship the weapons outside of that;
once this mantra has been perfected through recitation, worship, and other rites, he should proceed with the mantra in due order.
The mantra-practitioner should perform the applications prescribed in the ritual manual for the sake of attaining the desired fruit:
for one month, he should recite the mantra a thousand times while using pieces of *sudhā* mixed with milk. (112)

When the fire has been propitiated, one who has conquered his senses, being fully contented, should offer oblations according to the rules; by that, Śaṅkara becomes satisfied, his body drenched in nectar. || 113 ||
It increases longevity, health, prosperity, fame, and sons.
[The oblation consists of] nectar, banyan wood, sesame seeds, dūrvā grass, milk, clarified butter, and milk-offering. || 114 ||

Having spoken thus, one should offer oblations with these seven substances for seven days, diligently performing the rite daily, eight times more than the required number, in sequence according to the ten-fold portion. || 115 ||
The minister should daily feed seven Brahmins with sweet foods;
he should increase the days of fire-offerings (homa) in accordance with the specific transformations [of the situation]. || 116 ||
"Three hundred thousand" means three lakhs.
By the phrase "one of vast intellect," it is stated that one should worship the Śaiva seat (pīṭha).
*Amṛtā* is *guḍūcī*.
"Pure" means filtered through cloth and so forth.
"Sudhā" is *guḍūcī*.
"Mantrī" refers to [the practitioner].
The state of having a single-syllable seed-mantra and so forth has been stated.
The connection is that one should offer oblations for a month;
"a thousand" refers to each [day].
"Propitiated according to rule" means that one has fully worshipped the Śaiva seat in the fire. "Milk and oblation" refers to milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
"Transformation" refers to [the resulting state].
According to the sequence of diseases, there is an increase of days by fourteen, twenty-one, and so forth. (109–116)
One should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Hotṛ priests consisting of reddish-brown, milch cows;
thereafter, one should gratify the Guru with wealth and other gifts, regarding him as a deity.
By this method, one should be cured of afflictions such as malevolent spells, sorcery, and fever;
freed from these, he shall easily live for a full hundred autumns.
In cases of malevolent sorcery, acute fever, terrible insanity, diseases of the head, incurable illnesses, poisonings, and the like, as well as in great burning sensations and extreme fear; || 119 ||
This *homa* is declared to bestow peace and grant all forms of prosperity;
one should perform the oblation with these materials according to the prescribed rule throughout three lifetimes. || 120 ||
One should feed Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas with sweet foods;
thus one attains long life and obtains desired prosperity. || 121 ||
"By these substances" refers to the seven previously mentioned items.
"In three births" refers to the asterisms numbered first, tenth, and nineteenth.
"According to the rule" means in the manner previously described. (119–121)
A wise person should daily offer eleven oblations with *dūrvā* grass;
this shall conquer untimely death and increase longevity and health.

A fire sacrifice performed with the finest sacrificial fuel (samidh) produced from the nectar-creeper (sudhāvallī), the kāśmarī tree, and the bakula tree over three lifetimes removes all death and disease. || 123 ||
An oblation offered with cooked rice prepared by a perfected one (siddha) destroys even great fevers;
an oblation with fuel-sticks of Apāmārga is the cleanser of all diseases.
A pair of lotuses, their stalks fashioned from the Praṇava (Oṃ), with syllables as petals in their centers, and the middle of each adorned by the letter *Bhṛgu* (Bha);
within them dwells Umā’s Lord (Śiva), moistened by the nectar flowing from his own letters.
May he be meditated upon in the heart constantly for the pacification of all suffering. || 125 ||
Regarding "praṇava":
the syllable *jūṃ* is placed within the mantra, and it is repeated eight times upon the eight petals.
Regarding "bhṛguvilasita": [it refers to the syllable *ha*, the play of Bhṛgu].
With the letter *sa* accompanied by the *visarga*, one should visualize a pair of lotuses; within them, one should visualize Umā and Īśa taking up residence—this is the connection.
Thus, one should meditate upon Umā and Īśa in the midst of the enclosure formed by the two lotuses.
The letter *sa* resides in the pericarp (*kaṇīkā*); it is moistened by the nectar that flows forth from it. || 125 ||
In the gentle lotus abounding with yantras, one should place a pitcher according to the prescribed method,
endowed with the nine gems and adorned with two fine silk cloths.

Having filled it with pure waters, one who knows the ritual procedure should worship the deity therein with the sixteen services according to the rules. One should then consecrate the beloved disciple—who is disciplined and has offered the sacrificial fee. || 127 ||
This consecration is proclaimed as the warder-off of mental anguish, physical ailments, great diseases, sorcery, and malevolent incantations; it bestows fame, prosperity, and victory. || 128 ||
He speaks of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with the word "yantra": "rich in yantras" means joined with the yantras to be described;
"in the lotus" refers to the location of the auspicious water-pot (*bhadra-kamaṇḍalu*).
"Saumya" means charming.
"By the stated path" means according to the method described in the sixth chapter.
By the phrase "the knower of the ritual through the ritual," this is what is meant:
that in the secondary offerings (*upacāra*), specific substances are used with their respective mudrās, as stated in the verses of the *Turyektagama*. (126–128)

One should inscribe the *dhruva* (the syllable *oṃ*) enriched with the letters of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the center; the final letter of the mantra situated in the middle of the petals at the cardinal directions;

and the earth-element (*kṣi*) in the corners. Then, one should place the moon-syllables (*ca*) in the cardinal directions and the letter *ṭa* in the intermediate directions. This is said to be the *yantra* that removes all fears, as well as poison, spirits, and untimely death.
It is gladdening, pacifying the suffering of disease and delusion, bestowing prosperity, and granting fame. || 129 ||
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Śāradātilaka composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra. 18.
Regarding the statement "in the center" (*madhye*) in the *Bṛhat-tantra-mālā*:
it means in the center, within the pericarp (*kaṇīkā*).
The middle one is the syllable *jūṃ*;
the last is *saḥ*;
and the moon is the syllable *ṭha*.
As it has been said:
"Having established an outer city-gate (bhūpura) marked on the cardinal and intermediate directions by Khaḍgīśa and Lāṅgalin, one should place within it a well-adorned pitcher. || 129 ||
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition. 18.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter.
Now I shall proclaim the jewel of a mantra, which bestows all human goals;
by reciting which, the lords of sages attained divine knowledge. (1)
Thus, immediately after the description of the primary mantra of the upper face, he states the gentle (Śaiva) mantra of the primary southern face, beginning with "Now" (*atha*).
By the phrase "bestowing all human goals," the ritual application (*viniyoga*) is stated. || 1 ||

First to you, Dakṣiṇāmūrti; then the word "to you" (tubhyam); then the word "immediately following" (anantaram); then at the end of the word "at the root of the banyan tree" (vaṭamūla), the word "dwelling in the west" (paścānnivāsine). || 2 ||
Afterwards, one should utter the word "namaḥ" to the one whose limbs are solely devoted to meditation;
this is declared to be Rudra, the source of bliss, conjoined with the power of Tārā. || 3 ||
The thirty-six-syllable mantra bestows the fruits of all desires; Śuka is declared to be its sage, and the Anuṣṭubh is said to be its meter. || 4 ||

The deity of the Dakṣiṇāmūrti mantras is declared to be Śambhu. That which is called the heart (hṛdaya) is said to consist of six syllables, and the head (śiras) is declared to consist of two. || 5 ||
The *śikhā* (crown) is declared to consist of eight [syllables], the *kavaca* (armor) is considered to consist of eight gold [syllables],
the *netra* (eye) is said to consist of five, and the *astra* (weapon) is illustrated as consisting of three.
These six limb-mantras, beginning with Tāraśakti and ending with Hrīṃ,
along with their respective seed-syllables, have been correctly proclaimed by the most excellent of teachers.
He extracts the mantra with the words "dakṣiṇā" (the right).
This mantra is in the form of a verse.
It is "bound by Tāra and Śakti," meaning it is enclosed or encapsulated by both; therefore, there is a reversal at the end.
The seed-syllable is *praṇava* (Oṃ) and the power is *māyā* (Hrīṃ). In the sequence beginning with *hrāṃ*, the letter *ṅa* is added to the letter *ma*.
The practical application is as follows: Oṃ Hrīṃ Dakṣiṇāmūrttaye Hrāṃ Hṛdayāya Namaḥ; Oṃ Hrīṃ Śirase Svāhā, and so forth.
By the phrase "by the supreme teachers who teach according to the tradition," it is stated that [the rite] should be performed together with the six-limbed mudrās of Śiva. (2-7)

On the crown of the head, the forehead, the two eyes, the two ears, the pair of cheeks, then the nose, the mouth, the joints of the arms, the throat, the breasts, the heart, and the region of the navel. || 8 ||
One should then place the syllables in sequence upon the hips, the secret place, and the joints of the feet;
thereafter, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) over the body with the Praṇava (Tāra) and the Śakti-mantra.

The meaning of "on the head" and so forth is that, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-four syllables upon the thirty-four locations, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the two remaining [syllables].
As it has been said: "Thus, having performed the placement of the syllable preceded by *praṇava* and *hṛllekhā*, and so on."
The teachers also state: "Furthermore, the knower of mantras should place the pervasive [mantra] by means of two [syllables].
However, some say that one syllable each should be placed on the two breasts and the two nipples, thus asserting a placement of twenty-two syllables.
This alone is the traditional position.
As it was stated by the Teachers: "Ten [fingers] on the two cheeks, the eyes, the two nostrils, and the mouth," and so forth.

In his commentary on the verse of the Teacher (Ācārya) written previously, Padmapādācārya explained that by the phrase "one who knows the mantra" (*mantravit*), the meaning is "one who knows the identity of the initial and final *praṇavas* and the *śaktis*.
This was also indicated by the Root Author himself when he stated, "pervasive through the *tāra* and the *śakti*."

Therefore, the application is *oṃ hrīṃ daṃ namaḥ* and so forth. Master Padmapāda states that by the phrase "the mantra-practitioner who has received initiation," the conjunction of the *praṇava* (oṃ) and the *śakti* (hrīṃ) at the beginning of the placement-mantras (*nyāsa*) and other such rites is indicated. (8–9)
On the delightful slope of the Golden Mountain (Hemācala), frequented by Siddhas and Kinnaras, where the heat was warded off on all sides by the branches of various trees. || 10 ||
It was embraced by flowering trees entwined with networks of vines in full bloom, and it was served by breezes from waterfalls issuing forth from crevices in the rocks. || 11 ||
Where swarms of female bees were singing, flocks of peacocks were dancing, and the quarters of the sky were made resonant by the warbling of throngs of cuckoos; || 12 ||
It was frequented by deer free from mutual envy, and constantly visited by the foremost sages, such as Śuka and others. || 13 ||
Beheld by the gods led by Purandara who had come for service, there stood a banyan tree of great height, radiant with fruits like rubies. || 14 ||
It was adorned with dense leaves made of emeralds and embellished by hanging ornaments fashioned from the nine precious gems. || 15 ||
It was adorned with fragrant flowers born of both water and land,
and attended by flocks of parrots who were reciting the Vedas and Shastras.
Having contemplated that wonderful, auspicious shade of skill which prevents the continuity of cyclic existence, [he sat] upon the beautiful jeweled lion-throne situated at its base. || 17 ||

One should meditate upon the primordial source of the worlds, the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who is seated, possessed of immeasurable splendor, whose face resembles the autumnal moon, and who is being praised by hosts of sages desiring divine knowledge. || 18 ||
Regarding meditation, he says "hemā" and so forth; the connection is that one should contemplate a banyan tree on the slope of the Golden Mountain (Hemācala).
The word "lambamānaiḥ" refers to the hanging roots of the banyan tree.
*Lībaṇī* is the Gauḍa dialect term. By this, the following is meant:
[the] jeweled pavilion—

Immediately thereafter, on the slope of the Golden Mountain (Hemācala), there is a banyan tree, and beneath it, a jeweled lion-throne; this is the specific detail for the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa), while the rest is the same. || 10-18 ||
Resembling Mount Kailāsa, adorned with a mass of matted hair flashing like a crescent moon,

intent on gazing at his nose, possessing three eyes, seated in the vīrāsana posture, his hands graced by the mudrā, the ṭaṅka, the deer, and the knee, and having a serene countenance— [He is] thus meditated upon.
I bow to the supreme Maheśa, who has serpents bound upon his shoulders and is surrounded by sages. || 19 ||
He speaks of meditation with the words "on Kailāsa.
He will describe the *vīrāsana* posture in the final chapter.
The *mudrā* is the *jñānamudrā*.
As it was said by the Teachers: "The mudrā that bestows the goal of auspiciousness. Here, *ṭaṅka* means an axe.
The first two weapons are in the right hands, and the other two are in the left hands.
One should recite the mantra two million times—specifically twenty-one lakhs—and then perform a fire offering with one-tenth of that number of pure sesame seeds mixed with milk. || 20 ||

One should worship the Supreme Lord according to the prescribed rite upon the seat proclaimed by the five syllables, using the spontaneously arisen services beginning with water for the feet. || 21 ||
Having thus performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*), the wise practitioner becomes one whose mantra is perfected;
subsisting on alms and with senses subdued, he should recite this mantra for one month. (22)
By constantly reciting this mantra four thousand times, one attains the supreme essence of speech;
having chanted it three times, one should drink water with it. || 23 ||
The best of practitioners, constantly meditating upon Dakṣiṇāmūrti, attains the capacity for expounding the scriptures within the span of a year. || 24 ||
"Three hundred thousand" means three lakhs.
"With those that have arisen" means with those that have been gathered together or produced.
By this, it is stated that one should perform the ritual services (*upacāra*) in the manner described, and not with water and so forth. || 20–24 ||

Ghee boiled with the paste of *brāhmī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), white mustard (*siddhārtha*), *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, long pepper (*kaṇā*), and blue lotus (*utpala*), combined with fragrant substances, [prepared] in the juice of *brāhmī*. || 25 ||
Siddhārtha is white mustard;
kaṇā is long pepper;
utpala is nut-grass (mustā).
By the word *sugandhi* (fragrant), cinnamon-bark (*tvak*), cardamom (*patra*), eaglewood (*elā*), and saffron (*kesara*) are meant.
This is stated in the *Vaidyaka-nighaṇṭu*:
"Cinnamon-bark, cardamom, eaglewood, and saffron constitute the *cāturjāta*, which is fragrant."
From the paste of these [drugs] cooked in *brāhmī* juice, ghee is prepared.
Regarding that:
"The fat is perfected in pure water, or sequentially with decoctions and fresh juices."
One should add a fourth, sixth, or eighth part of the paste.

Thus, according to this statement regarding specific technical definitions, one should cook six *pala* of clarified butter with a paste (*kalka*) measuring one *pala*. Wherever there are five or more substances in the preparation of an unctuous substance (*sneha*), they say that those [other] substances should be equal in measure to the unctuous substance; and for fewer than that, the unctuous substance should be four times the quantity.
Because it has been stated thus, there are twenty-four palas of *brāhmī* juice;
when boiled down until only the ghee remains, it is removed from the heat and bestows the fruit of liberation.
"Śṛtam" means cooked or prepared by boiling. || 25 ||
Ten thousand verses have been well-composed by this Manu;
when drunk, they bestow poetic splendor, protection, longevity, prosperity, and fortitude. || 26 ||
"Well done, it is accomplished.
This is the meaning:

having worshipped the pedestal of the deity in the ghee according to the stated method, and having worshipped the deity there along with his retinue, one should then establish the external fire and [worship] there as well.
Having worshipped the Devapīṭha with the juice of *brāhmī* and offered oblations, one should sprinkle it with the clarified butter resulting from that residue (*sampāta*).
Regarding the word "drunk" (*nipītam*),
the remainder of the sense is "in the morning by one who is pure."

The yantra mentioned in another tantra is now described: "Now I shall explain the Dakṣiṇāmūrti-yantra, which bestows intelligence, the perfection of knowledge and speech, and poetic inspiration, and which accomplishes all aims."
One should draw a lotus flower complete with ivory leaf-patterns upon a birch bark,
using the tips of *dūrvā* grass mixed with animal bile, within the pericarp.
Then, having written the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), one should write the Anuṣṭubh verse on the petals;
outside of that, a square enclosure for the earth, and in its corners, Nakulīśvara.
Having invoked the deity into that [liṅga], worshipped it, and gratified it with libations, one should wear it;
immediately, the knowledge of Brahman and other such attainments shall come into his hands. Thus [it is said]. 26.

First the syllable *praṇava*, then the word *hṛdayam*, followed by the word *bhagavate* joined with the suffix *-ṅe*; one should then utter the word *dakṣiṇāmūrtaye* for me, [ending] with *medhām*. || 27 ||
Bestow [this mantra]; this twenty-two-syllable mantra ends with two *ṭha*s. The sage is Caturmukha, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity of the mantra is [Caturmukha]. || 28 ||
The one known as Dakṣiṇāmūrti is described as being intent upon the exposition of the Vedas;
one should fashion the six limbs [of the mantra] with the six long vowels conjoined with the syllable *tāra* (Om). || 29 ||
He states another mantra: "The Praṇava," etc. The heart is the word *namaḥ*.
Here too, as before, the euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) is made with the visarga.
In this [mantra], "dakṣiṇāmūrttīḥ" means "to Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Regarding the phrase "mahyaṃ medhām," some say it is "hasamedhām," while others say it is "prajñāmedhām."
Some say that the word *prajñā* occurs in place of *medhā*;
however, this should be understood according to the respective traditions of one's own teachers.
The *nāda* ending with the *praṇava* is the seed (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*).
In the *Śaktirahasya* of the *Nāradīya*, however, it is stated that "vāgbhava" is used here;
"enclosed by the *tāra*" means encapsulated by the *praṇava*;
and "by the six long vowels."
The meaning is "by these," namely: ā, ī, ū, e, au, and aḥ. || 27–29 ||
Alternatively, one may arrange [the mantra] sequentially with words derived from human speech;
one should then contemplate the Lord of Mantras situated at the foot of the banyan tree as previously described. || 30 ||
Alternatively:
here, the supreme gurus maintain that the six-limbed [nyāsa] consists of the six words beginning with *praṇava* (om) and ending with *namaḥ*.
As for the placement of the syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*), however, it is described in the *Nāradīya*:
"In the head, forehead, heart, nose, cheeks, the two rows of teeth, the tongue-tip, the throat, the two arms, the heart, the navel, the two testicles, the anus, the thighs,
the knees, the shanks, the heels, the feet, and in all the joints, [one should place] the final [syllable]. Thus it is said.
Regarding the phrase "situated at the root of the banyan tree," there is this specific detail:
"seated upon the throne of exposition, treading upon Apasmṛti with his feet.
Having the color of crystal and silver, holding in the tips of his hands a rosary of pearls, a jar of nectar, and the mudrās of vidyā and jñāna;
with a serpent as a sash, moon-crested, and three-eyed.
I praise Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who wears various ornaments. || 31 ||
The "snake-girdle" (*uragakakṣa*) refers to a snake tied as a sash hanging down.
The visualization of the weapons extends from the upper right hand down to the lower right hand.
As it has been said: "In the right [hands], there is a rosary (*akṣamālā*) and the purifying gesture of knowledge (*jñānamudrā*)."
In the left [hands], a book and a jar full of nectar; thus [it is said]. || 31 ||
Remaining established in the vow of celibacy, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
one should then offer oblations into the consecrated fire with lotuses mixed with ghee, numbering one-tenth of that amount.
On the previously mentioned pedestal, one should worship according to the method to be described;
one should worship the limbs externally and perform worship upon the eight petals. || 33 ||
[Sarasvatī], causing [Brahmā] to recite, holding a book, with a smiling face;
behind her is Brahmā, then Sanaka, and after him Sanandana. || 34 ||
Outside, he saw Sanatkumāra, Śuka, Vyāsa, Gaṇeśvara, and hosts of Siddhas, Gandharvas, lords of Yogins, and Vidyādharas. || 35 ||
Outside, one should worship Lokeśvara and others, equipped with vajras and other weapons; when this mantra has been perfected through such offerings and rites, the supreme practitioner— || 36 ||
By consecrating pure waters with this mantra, the wise man becomes beloved in speech, like another Vācaspati. (37)

One should sprinkle [water] upon one's own head; one shall obtain prosperity and health. Standing in water reaching only the neck, one should recite the mantra a thousand times every day for up to a month; one will become the foremost among poets. || 38 ||
"Outside" means at the ends of the four corners. || 35 ||
Desiring prosperity, one who meditates on the Lord together with Gaurī standing at His side should recite the mantra ten thousand times; he shall obtain abundant fortune. || 39 ||
Regarding the word "Gaurī":
her meditation is as follows—
The wise seeker of power and desire should worship the Lord of Gods together with the Goddess.
Resplendent like the rising sun, with a radiance resembling the bandhūka flower.
Adorned with a pair of full, lofty, and firm breasts,
having two eyes and two arms, holding a lotus in her hand, and enchanting all people.
A person should worship her while visualizing her stationed on the left side of the God;
at that time, there is a specific modification in the mantra: one should place Śrī in the position of Medhā.
Thus it is said.
In the term "śrīkāmī," it should be understood that [the name] is encased by the syllable "śrī. || 39 ||

Eating rice boiled in cow’s urine, or food obtained as alms, while remaining pure and reciting the mantra twenty thousand times, the practitioner explains the Vedas, Shastras, and other scriptures that he has never heard before; of this there is no doubt. (40)
Regarding the application of the term "while eating," the specific visualization for meditation is as follows:
"His two hands are resplendent with a book of the Jātavedas [Fire-God] emitting light from the left hand,
and with the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyāmudrā*) and a rosary."

The connection is with the phrase "eating alms-food" (*bhikṣānnam athavā*). In the expression "not heard" (*aśrutān*), it should be understood as being "unrefined by the ignorant" (*bālāpuṭitatvam*). || 40 ||
These two leaders of mantras, served by Siddhas, Gandharvas, Munis, and the lords of Yogins, have been proclaimed for the delight of those who possess knowledge, speech, and wealth. || 41 ||
By the word "accomplished" (*siddha*), applications such as subjugation (*vaśya*) and others are also indicated.
As it has been said:
"One who desires subjugation should visualize Mahādeva as being red in color."
"One should contemplate the Goddess seated upon his left thigh, overwhelmed with passion;
and one should remember the two Śivas, contemplating each other for the purpose of creating progeny. Thus it is said.
The yantra described in the Kalpa is written as follows: On birch bark, one should draw a lotus with ten petals using yellow pigment (rocanā).
In the center of the pericarp, within the syllable *tāra* (Om), one should write the mantra together with the name of the practitioner, arranged in pairs.
One should encircle even the outermost petal of the leaves with the letters of the mantra;
then, having performed worship, one attains omniscience through the fruit of its recitation by the ear.

By means of this, one goes [to success] and accomplishes daily feats such as paralyzing [an enemy], subjugating others, and whatever else is desired here; O wise ones, it grants all desires both in this world and the next.
First is the red one, the seat of fire (Ra), immediately followed by the Bindu;
then the second [syllable] is situated in the seed-syllable of fire (Ra) with a long vowel, adorned by the Moon of Peace (Sa). || 42 ||
The third [mantra] is Lāṅgalī-sargī, endowed with three seed-syllables;
it is declared to be the essence of Nīlakaṇṭha, the supreme remover of the two kinds of poison. || 43 ||
The two syllables "ha-ra" followed by the fire-born wife (svāhā) are proclaimed as the Heart mantra.
In Kapardin, the pair of syllables "ṭha-ya" is declared to be the Head mantra. || 44 ||
"To Nīlakaṇṭha" followed by the pair "ṭha-ṭha" is declared to be the crest-mantra (śikhāmantra).
At the end of the word "Kālakūṭa," the term "viṣabhakṣaṇam" is joined. || 45 ||
"Huṃ Phaṭ" is the armor (kavaca) prescribed for Nīlakaṇṭha by the wise; "Svāhā" at the end is the weapon (astra). Those who know the mind recognize these as the five limbs (pañcāṅga). || 46 ||
One should place the three seed-syllables in sequence upon the crown of the head, the throat, and the heart-lotus;
then, becoming composed, one should meditate upon Nīlakaṇṭha.
He states the mantra of Nīlakaṇṭha: "Lohita" means *pa*; "Agnī" means *ra*, which is its seat, hence *pra*; "Sadya" means *o* together with the nasal drop (*bindu*), hence *proṃ*.
The long vowel *ā* is the seed-syllable of Fire (*vahni-bīja*), which is the letter *ra*; that which stands upon it is *nra*.
*Śānti* is *ī*, which is the crescent moon (*indu-bindu*); joined with that, it becomes *nrīṃ*.
*Lāṅgalī* is the letter *ṭha*.
In the *sarga* [mantra], the *visarga* is conjoined with it. Aruṇa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chanda*).
The first [syllable] is the seed (*bīja*), and the last is the power (*śakti*).
Poison is of two kinds: stationary (sthāvara) and mobile (jaṅgama).
"This [mantra] removes that" is the stated application (viniyoga).
"Ṅeyuta" is the form ending in the singular dative case. || 42-47 ||
Possessing the brilliance of ten thousand rising suns, radiant with the crescent moon upon his mass of matted locks,
adorned by the lords of serpents, holding in his hands a rosary, a trident, a skull-cup,
and a khaṭvāṅga staff; three-eyed, with five faces shining beautifully, he is most handsome.
I worship the illustrious Nīlakaṇṭha, who is clothed in a tiger skin, whose abode is the lotus, and who possesses a beautiful blue throat. || 48 ||

One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times and then properly offer oblations into the consecrated fire with clarified butter mixed with sesamum seeds, ten parts of which [the recitation] correspond to. || 49 ||

One should worship him in a Śaiva seat according to the ritual procedure for Mṛtyuñjaya. When the mantra has been mastered through such worship and other means, the practitioner [overcomes] the two kinds of poison. || 50 ||
Like another Nīlakaṇṭha, he shall destroy [the affliction] very quickly with the auspicious waters contained in the pitcher, consecrated by this mantra. || 51 ||
One should sprinkle [the mantra] upon one overcome by poison; he will certainly be freed from the poison.
Having touched the one overcome by poison, one should recite the mantra; at that very moment, he shall become free of poison. || 52 ||
One should extract the uneven [syllables] from the two sides by means of the two seed-syllables ending in the nominative case;
one should withdraw everything situated in the middle by means of this mantra ending in the middle [case]. || 53 ||
What is the use of saying more here? For one who knows the mantra, this very mantra turns the poison Kālakūṭa itself into the supreme nectar when consumed. || 54 ||
Regarding meditation, he says "bāla" (infant).
The meditation on the weapon is as before. (48–54)
The seed-syllable consisting of fire (Ra), the sun (Repha), the wind (Ya), and the sixth vowel (Ū) with a bindu (Ṃ)—known as Cintāmaṇi—it bestows all prosperity. || 55 ||
The sage is declared to be Kāśyapa; the meter is stated to be Anuṣṭubh;
the deity is proclaimed to be Ardhanārīśvara, the Lord of the worlds. || 56 ||
One should perform the six limbs in sequence by means of the six consonants beginning with the letter *ra*.
Immediately after the principal mantra of the southern face, he states the Cintāmaṇi mantra, the principal mantra of the northern face, beginning with "Agni.

"Agni" is the letter *ra*; "Saṃvarta" is *kṣa*; "Āditya" is *ma*; *ra* is its own form. "Anila" is *ya*; *au* is its own form; the sixth vowel is *ū*, which is the nasal dot (*bindu*). This is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) joined with these elements.
In this context, even the pronunciation of the two vowels should be understood through the teacher’s instruction:
the letter *ra* is the seed (*bīja*),
and the vowel *ū* is the power (*śakti*).
By the phrase "bestowing all prosperity," [it is meant that] in rites of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), [the mantra] begins with the letter *sa* and is white;
in attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) and subjugation (*vaśya*), it is as extracted and visualized accordingly.
In agitation (*kṣobha*), it begins with the letter *ha* and is red; in driving away (*uccāṭana*), it begins with the letter *ya*, is smoky-colored, and the *haṃsa* etc. is also as previously stated.
For the purpose of immobilization, it begins with the letter *la* and is yellow; for the purpose of liberation, it begins with *ha*, is devoid of the letter *ra*, and is perfumed.
By thus indicating [the mantra], its application (viniyoga) has been stated.
Their conjunction is established by the statement: "Prior to the single [syllable] situated above the fire.
By the phrase "Lord of the worlds," it is further stated that Umāpati is also the deity.
As the teachers have said: "The meter is Anuṣṭubh and the deity is Umāśa.
With the six syllables ending in 'yā', the limb is either the deity Ardhanārīśa."
Thus [it is said].
Regarding "beginning with *r*":
in the conjunction of *k* and *ṣ*, there is *kṣ*; thus, the letter *kṣ* consists of two consonants.
Thus, those who know the tradition maintain that the six limbs are formed by the six syllables beginning with *ra* and ending with *ya*, accompanied by the bindu.
Resplendent with blue coral, possessing three shining eyes,
holding in his hands a noose, a red lotus, a skull, and a trident,
his head adorned by the Lord of Ambikā, and his ornaments eternally distributed [between them].
I bow to that form whose crown is bound with the crescent moon. || 58 ||

Regarding the Ardhanārīśvara aspect, he describes the visualization as "nīla" (blue) and so forth: the half belonging to Ambikā’s Lord is Maheśa, which is blue, while the half belonging to Pārvatī has the luster of coral; in the tips of the hands of the Goddess's half, there is a noose and a lotus.
"Others [say it is] produced from half a hand of Maheśa;

it is 'adorned with distinct ornaments' in the sense that the portion belonging to Maheśa is adorned with serpents and the like, while the portion belonging to Pārvatī is adorned with jeweled earrings and the like."
Regarding the view of Umāpati, the meditation described by the Teacher is as follows:
He whose lofty crown is bound with a serpent, the moon, and the Gaṅgā; whose feet are bowed to by hosts of gods; who possesses the eyes of a woman; and who embodies the grace of a woman.
May the Lord, bearing a serpent, an axe, a trident, a sword, fire, a skull, an arrow, and a bow, protect you for a long time.
This meditation pertains to the sphere of preliminary practice (*prayoga*).

However, for the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), daily recitation (*nityajapa*), and so forth, one should meditate specifically on Ardhanārīśvara, as the teachers have said: "Either the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*) who is half-female, charming with gestures (*hāva*) and expressions (*bhāva*), or else the terrifying half-male."
For the sake of prosperity, one should meditate upon [the deity] holding a noose, a blue lotus, a skull-cup, and a trident during the rite of recitation. Thus [ends verse 58].
The mantra-practitioner should thus recite the seed-syllable one hundred thousand times and should contemplate in this manner;
he should offer oblations of ten thousand sesame seeds and rice grains sprinkled with honey. || 59 ||
On the seat proclaimed by Śiva, one should worship first with the six limbs as they have been described;
then with Vṛṣa and the others, followed by the Mothers, and finally by the world-protectors and their weapons. || 60 ||
Thus one should worship the supreme deity Ardhanārīśvara;
he becomes beloved of splendor, beauty, fame, fortune, and eloquence.
One should recite this mantra ten thousand times, beginning with the palace (prāsāda), for the pacification of disease;
this seed-syllable is surrounded by vowels and drips with the supreme nectar. || 62 ||
Meditated upon as situated on the lunar disc at the crown of the head, it removes poison and disease;
this seed-syllable, enveloped by the vowels in reverse order, resides within the abode of fire.

Shining with the consonants beginning with *ra* and surrounded on the outside by a hexagon—when remembered at the crown of the head of one afflicted by spirits, it quickly destroys those spirits. || 64 ||
One should worship on the pedestal;
that is to say, Umesham (the Lord of Uma).
The syntactical connection is: "In this manner, one should worship the Supreme Ardhanārīśvara."
The meaning is "in this manner, by way of instruction.

Therein, having worshipped the Śaiva seat (pīṭha), one should invoke and worship Ardhanārīśvara; the first enclosure (āvaraṇa) is with the limbs (aṅgas); the second with the eight syllables beginning with *ra*;
the third with the Mothers (mātṛs); and thereafter with the world-protectors (lokapālas) and the [weapons] beginning with the thunderbolt (*vajra*).

As it has been stated by the Teachers: "Then, beginning from the initial ignition, one should worship with the eight syllables of the mantra situated in the directions along with the Mothers; this is declared to be another method of ritual application."

The letter *ṭha* situated within the lunar orb is to be meditated upon above the head of one afflicted by poison; this is the implied meaning. "In the fire-house" means in a triangle with its apex pointing upward.
"Beginning with the letter *ra*" refers to *ra*, *kṣa*, *ma*, and *ra*. (59–64)

The seed-syllable situated upon the moon, sequentially accompanied by the sixteen vowels, should be visualized as emitting a stream of supreme nectar into the eyes; when thus meditated upon, it removes disease. || 65 ||
In the same way, the seed-syllable *smṛ* (ṬHA) remembered within the womb removes diseases such as colic; it is situated in the moon and resides in the letter *ṬHA*.
"In the same way" means that the letter *ṬHA*, surrounded by vowels, has the form of a flowing stream of nectar. (65–66)
In cases of *sphoṭa*, poison, fever, burning sensations, delusion, headache, and vertigo; || 66 ||
This seed-syllable, when meditated upon in that manner, destroys each respective affliction;
this seed-syllable, brilliant and resembling saffron, is situated within a triangle. (67)
Upon whose head the practitioner of mantra meditates, that person becomes submissive without delay.
The seed-syllable bearing the name of the target, situated within the abode of fire (the triangle), has the letter *ra* positioned above it. || 68 ||
It is enclosed by two fire-houses with corners joined by fire, surrounded by the vowels in reverse order, and placed in the position of the hearth. || 69 ||
One brings [the person] under control like a servant, even before long until death, by means of an image made of rice-flour mixed with the three sweets. (70)
Having established the vital breaths and having divided [the mantra], the self-controlled practitioner should offer oblations;
by this very method for three days, the object of his practice shall come under his control. || 71 ||
"So be it.
One should meditate upon the syllable *ṭha*, surrounded by vowels and dripping with a flood of nectar;
thus meditated upon, it shall bring about destruction.
In those respective places:
the letter *ra* (repha) is for Agni.
Having fashioned the yantra on birch bark or similar material, one should bury it in the hearth; this is the meaning. || 67–70 ||
"An image (puttalī)" means one measuring twelve finger-breadths.
"One whose vital breath has been established" means...
In the twenty-third [chapter], according to the manner that will be explained. || 70–71 ||
The name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) is placed within the letter *ma*, while the name of the fire-god (*anala*) is situated in the *gadā* [the letter *ga*].
This is located in the moon [the letter *ca*] within a square, encircled by the corner ending in *ṭa*. || 72 ||
The seed [mantra] placed upon a betel leaf and consecrated with this mantra, when consumed, will completely destroy diseases of the head; of this there is no doubt. (73)
The letter *ma* refers to that which resides within the mantra.
Regarding the phrase "possessing the fire-breath" (*analastha*), it means being joined with the disease of the upward-moving *repha*.
In the commentary on the verse "risen from the poison-fire," the teacher Padmapāda explained this as the *repha* associated with poison.
The syllable *ca* (the moon) is situated upon the letter *ṭha*;
the connection is that the seed-syllable is encircled by a square formed by the corner of the letter *ṭha*. || 72–73 ||
Having drawn a triangle with Bandhujīva flowers, containing the seed-syllable within,
and having properly established the fire therein and worshipped the deity, || 74 ||

One should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the sacrificial residue mixed with flour-meal. A ring made of the three metals, sprinkled with this residual ghee and worn, destroys malevolent spirits, vetālas, magical spells, and diseases. || 75 ||
With the juice of the *bandhujīva* flower.
Elsewhere, the word *bandhujīva* is read as the *javā* flower;
and it has been said: "The *japā* [flower] is in the triangle, in the fire [element]."
The author of the *Vijñānacandrikā*, the commentator on the *Prapañcasāra*, has explained this as: "Bandhujīva means *bandhūka* or *japā*.
Regarding the phrase "made of the three metals," it is according to the method stated in the sixth [chapter].
The teacher Padmapāda stated that three metals should be taken in a quantity equal to the number of syllables in the mantra. (74–75)
Having inscribed this mantra, devoid of the upward fire (ūrdhvavahni), within a pair of fire-houses (vahni-geha),
and surrounded by the city of earth (mahīpura) with fire in its three corners— this is declared to be the Yantra that is the enemy of the planets.
Agni (the southeast) is Raṃ; [this is] in the six corners, namely the intermediate directions. || 76 ||
Upon a stable earthen bowl marked with the seed-syllable of fire (raṃ) and a six-cornered and a triangle, one should duly place a lamp with ghee from a tawny cow, a lotus, and a thread. || 77 ||
Having covered him with this jar, one should draw this diagram on its back;
having placed the person afflicted by a spirit within it, one should mutter the Cintāmaṇi mantra.
Entering him, even a cruel planet will release him in an instant by all means. || 78 ||
Regarding the phrase "likhite" (written):
it should be understood as "with red powder.
And it is said in the Nārāyaṇīya:
"O Tārā, [the syllable] marked with the seed-syllable is situated in the fire-house at the corners, colored with red powder.

This is explained in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā* as follows: "Having joined the fire-house with red powder, one should write the fire-seed-syllable in its corners and write the *praṇava* (OM) in its center."
"This bowl"; "of this jar";
"this" is what has been said.
"One should write" means by means of recitation (*japa*).
"Here" means on the surface of the written yantra.
"One should recite" (japet):
the ellipsis is "having touched that which is swallowed.
"One should release" (muñcet).
By means of the mantra-consecration (mantrābhiṣeka).
As it is stated in the Nārāyaṇīya:
"Having covered that [vessel] with another jar, when the self-yantra has been performed through recitation (japa)..."
Having placed the *cintāmaṇi* upon the back of a jar and swallowed it, one should recite the mantra.
"For the purpose of destroying the possession by a planet, one should perform an ablution for the one seized by it.
Regarding the word "sva" (one's own), [it refers to] the Cintāmaṇi diagram;
regarding the word "tena" (by that), [it means] by the Cintāmaṇi mantra—so says the *Laghuṭīkā*.
This has been explained. || 77-78 ||
Having written this mantra within two fire-pits (kṛśānu),
one should then write the consonants upon its spokes and pairs of vowels at the joints;
it is encircled by the *dhruva* [syllable] and situated in the center of a house of earth (*dharaṇīgṛha*).
This yantra bestows the fruit of one's desires upon human beings.
"Upon its spokes and in its corners:
the consonants *ra*, *kṣa*, *ma*, *ra*, and *ya* are situated as seeds;
the pair of vowels *au* and *ū* are situated as seeds."
One repetition is performed with the *dhruva* (the *praṇava*).
It should be known that the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha is written within the corners of the house on the earth. || 79 ||
One should write this mantra, enriched with the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), within a triangle inside a hexagon;
the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) in the [other] six corners; the syllables of the mantra in the openings of the eight petals;
surrounded on the outside by the *kalās*, and subsequently encircled by the consonants beginning with *ka* and *ya*.
This yantra, joined with the orb of the earth and conjoined with Nṛhari and Anu, destroys calamities and malefic planets.
Regarding "the eight mantra-syllables":
there are six consonants (*hal*) and two vowels (*svara*), according to the principle of one syllable per letter.
By means of the sixteen digits (*kalā*), which are the vowels.
By the phrase "with the letters beginning with *ka* and those beginning with *ya*," the threefold repetition by means of the *mātṛkā* is indicated.
Regarding "nṛhariman":
the seed-syllable of Nṛhari (Nṛsiṃha) is to be placed in the corners of the earth-pavilion (*bhūgṛha*).
As it has been said: "In the corner of the evil house, [one should worship] Nārasiṃha. (80)

Having established the jar upon this yantra according to the prescribed method, the consecration performed shall bring peace from the harm caused by magical spells (kṛtyā), elemental spirits (bhūta), and enmity. || 81 ||
"By the path previously described" means according to the manner stated in the sixth [chapter]. || 81 ||

One should write this mantra, surrounded by vowels, with the letter *ṭa* in its center; then, in the six corners, one should place the fire-god (*hutāśana*) surrounded by the letters beginning with *ka*,
followed by a pair of earth-fortresses (*dharāpura*) joined with the three-cornered seed-syllable of Nṛhari.
This is declared to be the "Encircled" [mantra], which destroys evil deeds, diseases, and malevolent spells. || 82 ||
In the middle of the letter *ṭa*, that is, between the two *ṭha*s;
in the six corners, that is, in the hexagon;
the fire, which is the letter *ra*. || 82 ||
The letter *kṣa* possesses fire (*ra*), wind (*ya*), the left ear (*u*), and the half-moon (*bindu*).
This is declared to be the seed-syllable of Tumburu, by which practitioners attain success. || 83 ||
He states the seed-syllable of Tumburu as "the letter Kṣa.
The letter Kṣa is its essential form.
Fire is the letter Ra; wind is Ya; the left ear is the letter U; and the half-moon is the Bindu. It is joined with these.
The seed-syllables and their powers are as before. || 83 ||

One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the seed-syllable possessing the six long vowels; that seed-syllable, excluding the letter *kṣa*, is sequentially endowed with *ja*, *bha*, *sa*, and *ha*. || 84 ||
These four seed-syllables of the goddesses are to be known as the goddesses in sequence:
Jayā, Vijayā, then Ajitā, and Aparājitā. || 85 ||
"Six long [vowels]" refers to the extraction of the six-limbed mantra;
the ritual placement (nyāsa), however, he will explain later.
"Jabhasaha" is its essential form.
These four seed-syllables of the goddesses, joined in sequence in the place of the letter *kṣa*,
have been stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"The seed-syllable, endowed with *ja*, *bha*, *sa*, and *ha*, [is placed] in the place of the field (*kṣetra*) according to the sequence."
Also in the Nārāyaṇīya: "The root [mantra] is endowed with ja, bha, sa, and ha; it is the abode of the seed-syllables of the goddesses."
The seeds have been extracted precisely from the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*; however, the word "jvala" appears in some places due to a scribe's error. (84–85)
Having placed the seed-syllables on the fingers, one should then perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) upon the two hands;
thereafter, one should assign the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), beginning with the little fingers and ending with the palms.

"Bīja" refers to the root seed-syllable (*mūlabīja*). "Pervading the two hands" means that the root seed-syllable [is to be placed] here on the palms of the hands and above them; this is the understood remainder of the sentence.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Having placed that root-mantra upon the fingers, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) upon the two hands."

Since the placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) is already established by the rule "one should place the seed-syllables on the fingers beginning with the thumb," the repetition [in the phrase] "on the little finger and so forth" is for the purpose of a specific injunction. || 86 ||
One should place the deities and goddesses, beginning with their respective seed-syllables, on the little finger and the other fingers;
then, one should place them from the feet up to the head upon the limbs using the closed fist.
One should perform the pervasive placement with the two palms from the head down to the feet;
then, the person of vast intelligence should assign the six limbs to their respective locations. || 88 ||
One should sequentially place the deity and the goddesses as before upon the head, the heart-lotus, the navel, and the secret organ; thereafter, one should meditate upon the deity.
"From its own seed-syllable," etc.:
the root-mantra of the God, however, consists of the four [syllables] accompanied by *ja*, *bha*, *sa*, and *ha*.
[He should grasp it] with the right fist.
Regarding the limbs— namely the feet, knees, private parts, navel, heart, throat, mouth, and head—
it is as stated by the author of the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā* concerning the base and the root.
And it is said in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
Having placed [the mudrās] on the limbs starting from the feet with the fist, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) on the head and so forth with both hands;
thus it is said,
"one should make the pervasive placement."
The word "with the root [mantra]" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
