By the phrase "one of vast intellect," it is stated that this is accompanied by the Śaiva mudrās.
"As before" means:
From their respective seeds, and so forth. (87–89)
Reddish in hue, adorned with the crescent moon, possessing three eyes,
and holding in his hands a khaṭvāṅga staff, a noose, a goad, and a white skull-cup;
four-faced, with a flat nose, and wearing priceless ornaments.
I praise the Lord, whose limbs are anointed with red unguent and who wears garments of flowers. || 90 ||
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations accompanied by honey and ghee.
One should worship the deity, together with the surrounding retinues, upon the pedestal to be described hereafter. || 91 ||
He describes the meditation: "having a red luster.
The *sṛṇi* is a goad.
This is the visualization of the weapons, beginning from the lower right hand and ending with the lower left hand. (90–91)
One should assign the neuter vowels *e* and *o*, together with the two pairs at the beginning and end of the vowels, to the limbs starting with Dharma and ending with Adharma. || 92 ||
Regarding the visualization of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) within one's own body, he says "napuṃsaka" and so forth. The reading "anulomavilomagaiḥ" is an accidental error caused by the scribe;
the correct reading is "svarādyantadvayena ca."
As it is stated in the Nārāyaṇīya:
"The wise one [should worship] with the four beginning with 'na' and ending with the vowels, in their respective order."
In the *Prayogasāra* it is also said: "By these two [consonants] and those two [vowels], one performs the worship of Dharma and the others in sequence.
Thus, all sixteen vowels become utilized.
The application has been written in this very manner by the author of the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*.
By that [application], one [denotes] non-masculine [entities] such as *dharma* and so forth;
and by *a*, *ā*, *aṃ*, *aḥ*, and so forth, one [denotes] non-*dharma* (*adharma*) and so forth.
"One should place" means in the four locations previously mentioned. || 92 ||

Thereafter, one should place the qualities corresponding to the body with the letter *i*, and then, by means of the subsequent syllable of Peace (*śānti*), [place] those consisting of Māyā and Vidyā in due order.
Then, having placed the lotus with the syllable *arghīśa* upon the lower and upper coverings,
the practitioner of mantra should worship the powers, beginning with Vāmā, in sequence using the diphthongs.
"Qualities" refers to the three colors, such as *sattva* and the others;
"by peace" means by the vowel *ī*.
By the letter *u*, which is the subsequent vowel to that;
by the letter *ū*, which is [the vowel] of Arghīśa;
thus, by the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*).
E, E, O, AU, and EBHIḤ. How these arise through phonetic combination has been explained in the second chapter. || 93-94 ||
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Icchā, whose forms are like flames—
having thus prepared the seat (pīṭha), one should fashion the image with the root mantra.

Having invoked the deity, one should worship Him upon that [lotus] together with His enclosures (āvaraṇas). Outside the enclosure of the limbs (aṅgāvṛti), one should worship the Goddess on the petals of the northeast direction. || 96 ||
Jayā and the others [should be visualized] with their respective seed-syllables, red in color and anointed with red unguents;
they are enriched with crimson garments and flowers, and their mouths are filled with betel-leaf.
"Intent on playing the lute, afflicted by intoxication and passion,
and having the nature of flames"— this is the meditation on the *pīṭha-śaktis*.
As it is said in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"The radiant powers (śaktis) shall possess the luster of blazing flames.
Thus,
by uttering the root seed-syllable (mūlabīja), the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra)— "Obeisance to the yogic seat of Tumburu"— is also indicated.

Regarding the phrase "when the seat has been thus conceived": the word "thus" (evam) means that by whatever manner the seat was conceived within the body, by that very same sequence it is also conceived as the seat in the mandala.
"In that" (tasyām) [refers to the aforementioned seat].
In the case of a physical form: || 95-98 ||
One should worship the female messengers (dūtīs), beginning with their seed-syllables (bījas), in sequence within the corners starting from the northeast (īśa). || 98 ||
These women—unfortunate, fortunate, Karālī, and Mohinī—with palms joined in reverence and their lotus-like faces slightly bowed, [stood there]. || 99 ||
One should know the four mantras of the female messengers (dūtī), beginning with Śā, which are richly adorned like the goddess herself; these syllables are topped by a crescent moon. || 100 ||
"In the corners beginning with Īśa" means starting from the northeast corner and proceeding counter-clockwise until reaching the southeast.
"Beginning with the seed-syllables" means beginning with the seed-syllables that are about to be described.
The goddesses, Jayā and the others, possess ornaments similar to those [of the principal deities].
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"And the female messengers (dūtīs), possessing such forms, with their palms joined in reverence and their faces slightly bowed..."
"Those situated from Śarva to Agni.
Thus [are] "the Śādikas."
[The letters] śa, ṣa, sa, and ha;
[and] the half-moon and the bindu.
As it is said in the *Prayogasāra*:
"The sibilants (ūṣman) topped with a bindu are the seed-syllables (bīja) of the female messengers (dūtī).
Thus it is said.
Also in the Nārāyaṇīya: "The seed-syllables of the messengers are the sibilants topped with a bindu."
Thus [ends the section] 98–101.
One should worship the World-Protectors outside, accompanied by their weapons such as the vajra and so forth.
For one who thus worships with devotion by means of the path taught by the God, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that is difficult to attain. || 101 ||
The wise person, having meditated upon the seed-syllable situated within the cities of wind and fire, should recite it;
by that, fevers, spirits, and great diseases perish at that very moment. || 102 ||
Regarding "vāyu":
the meaning is that there is the wind-maṇḍala mentioned in the first chapter, within that is the city of fire, and inside that is the seed-syllable.
"Having remembered [it] on the head" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 102 ||
Meditating upon the heart of the angry person, one should recite the seed-syllable with undistracted mind;
by the power of this mantra, that person quickly becomes submissive. || 103 ||
For heart disease, jaundice, constipation, asthma, and cough, one should drink this water, consecrated with recitation, in the morning for the pacification of those ailments. || 104 ||
In the phrase "he becomes submissive," there is the use of the seed-syllable of Kāma;
in the phrase "for the pacification of disease," there is the use of the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha. || 103-104 ||
Having fashioned the mandala consisting of nine sections, the mantra-practitioner should place therein nine beautiful vases possessing the characteristics previously described. || 105 ||
One should properly worship the God in the center, and the Goddesses residing in the previously mentioned jars;
having worshipped them, one should consecrate the devoted wife who stands at the corners as the messenger (dūtī). || 106 ||

That woman obtains a son, even if she is barren; how much more so, then, another? He brings peace to those who have committed acts against spirits, rites of sorcery, or treachery, and he bestows prosperity. || 107 ||
This consecration has been described as that which increases the victory of kings. || 108 ||
"Endowed with nine parts" and "having nine centers" are stated in the third [chapter].
"As previously mentioned" refers to what was stated in the sixth [chapter].
In the phrase "situated in the corners, beginning with Īśa,

one obtains a son," there is the state of beginning with the *māyābīja* (the seed-syllable of Māyā). In "Vijayavardhana," there is the state of beginning with the *durgābīja* (the seed-syllable of Durgā).
This is to be known. || 105–108 ||

Within [is] the seed-syllable, its filaments shining with the groups of vowels; outside of that, the petals are joined by the goddesses and their messengers in due order in the cardinal and intermediate directions,
surrounded by the letters beginning with 'ka', and further encircled by the enclosure of the earth.
This yantra is declared to bestow all happiness and destroy diseases, malevolent rites, and planetary afflictions. || 109 ||
He describes the yantra: "In the interior," etc.

Having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus, one should write the root-mantra (mūla) in its pericarp (karṇikā). Then, one should write the seed-syllables (bīja) of the goddesses in the petals facing the cardinal directions and the seed-syllables of the female messengers (dūtī) in the intermediate directions, in sequence, as previously described. || 109 ||

First the Praṇava, then the heart-mantra, followed by Paśupati ending in the dative suffix -ṅe; then the Tāra (Om), "namo," the word for "beings" (bhūta), and then "adhipataye" with the syllable Dhruva (Om). || 110 ||
Homage to Rudra; from the word Khaḍgarāvaṇa, there is a pair, followed by a pair of sporting [forms], and then separately a pair of dancing [forms]. (111)
Then, for the body, [one should add] "at the edge of a heap of cremation-ground ashes," and again the word "to the one who bears a bell, a skull, a garland, and so forth. || 112 ||
At the end of *vyāghracarmapada*, [recite] *paridhānāya*;
after that, at the end of *śaśāṅkakṛtaśabda*, [recite] *śekharāya*. || 113 ||

Then, the word *kṛṣṇasarpa* (black serpent) follows, then *yajñopavītine* (to the one wearing the sacred thread), then *calayugmaṃ* (the pair of moving ones), then *valguyugam* (the pair of leaping ones), and finally *anivartakapāline* (to the protector who does not turn back). || 114 ||
Then there is a pair of *hana*s, followed by a pair of *bhūta*s that cause terror;
again, in the center of the mandala, there should be a pair of *kaṭa*s thereafter. || 115 ||
Pacify with the Rudrāṅkuśa mantra; then cause entry with the pair [of mantras];
after that, cause possession, and then utter the Caṇḍāsipada.
Then Agnisundarī commanded Rudra, the lord of the earth:
"This is the mantra of Khaḍgarāvaṇa, consisting of one hundred and seventy syllables. || 117 ||

"Bhūtādhipataye svāhā"—this is declared to be the mantra for worship. One should place the seed-syllables beginning with the letter *ka* (the first letter of the alphabet), preceded by the five short vowels starting with *sa* (i.e., *sa*, *si*, *su*, *se*, *so*). || 118 ||
He states the mantra of Khaḍgarāvaṇa:
"Praṇava" means [the syllable Om]; "ending in the dative case" refers to Paśupati, that is, "to Paśupati."
*Tāra* is the *praṇava*.
Then [comes] *adhipataye*;
here there is a euphonic combination (*sandhi*) with the preceding word.
"Dhruvam" refers to the *praṇava*.
"Pṛthak" means moving about while dancing repeatedly.
"Rudraḥ" refers to his essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Immediately thereafter is Agnisundarī Svāhā;
there is no conjunction with anything else. Oṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), and Svāhā is the power (śakti).
The beloved is space (kha). || 110–118 ||
One should place the five forms beginning with Īśāna on the body and the faces in sequence;
the ritual of limb-protection (aṅgakriyā) is considered to be performed with the [seed-syllable] joined with the six long vowels and the bindu. || 119 ||
"Īśāna and the others" refers to those mentioned in the previous chapter.
"In the body" means in the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet.
"In the faces" refers to [the following].
In the five [vowels] beginning with *ū*,
by means of the letter *kha*. || 119 ||
Holding a bell, a skull-cup, a goad, a severed head, a sword, a shield, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a trident, a ḍamaru drum, and the gesture of fearlessness;
red-limbed, adorned with a crescent moon, and possessing three eyes.
I praise the Lord, who has five faces, whose lotus-like mouth is ruddy like a parrot.
Having recited the mantra twenty thousand times, one should offer oblations with milk-rice mixed with ghee, amounting to a tenth part of that number, for the sake of its accomplishment. || 121 ||
The meditation on the weapons is performed in the two upper [hands] of Dakṣa and others in the first [case], and in the two lower ones in the last; thus it ends. 120–121.

One should worship Khaḍgarāvaṇa on the seat described by the five syllables; the formation of the form [of the deity] occurs through the seed-syllable, which is beautiful and possesses the mantra-point (bindu). 122.
One should offer the limbs at the bases of the petals and the female messengers (dūtīs) upon the petals;
[the first is] Culukuṇḍā, the second Praskhalinī, and the third Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā. || 123 ||
Phalgunī, Ṭiriṭillī, the fifth, Mantramālikā, the seventh, Śaṅkhinī, and then this Candrāṅkitajaṭā—these [are the goddesses]. || 124 ||
On the eastern leaf and the others, with the left [hand], [one worships] Khaḍgarāvaṇavallabhā, then Aindrī, Kaumārikī, Brāhmī, Vārāhī, and Vaiṣṇavī. || 125 ||
One should worship Vaināyakī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Māheśī in the cardinal directions;
the preceptor should worship two door-keepers at each gate, starting from the east.
One should again worship the two named Raudra and Piṅgala, who are terrifying in the cremation ground, as well as Dṛḍhakarṇa and Bhṛṅgirīṭi in the northern direction. || 127 ||
One should again worship Āmardaka and Mahākāla as the guardians of the corners, as well as Kumbhakarṇa, the one named Aśoka, Bhallāṭa, and Jātahāraka. || 128 ||
Then one should worship the world-protectors, beginning with Indra, together with their weapons;
having gratified the god Maheśvara with incense, lamps, and other offerings. || 129 ||
The worship is performed on the five-syllable seat of Śiva as described in the *Pañcākṣara*.
"By the seed-syllable" means by that which will be explained immediately hereafter.
*Tat* is the seed-syllable. *Manuḥ* is *auḥ*. *Dūtīriti*.
These will be described below.
"The one with a moon-marked matted lock" refers to the eighth [mudrā].
"With the left hand" means in a counter-clockwise direction.
"In the north" is connected with what follows. "Guardians of the corners" refers to those beginning with Agni (the southeast).
The worship of the limbs is performed upon the filaments. || 122–129 ||
Then, outside, one should offer the *bhūtabali* with the fivefold cruel oblation (*pañcakrūrāndhasa*).
Thus, when the mantra has been mastered through worship and other means, [the practitioner] becomes the best among those who know mantras. || 130 ||
He shall destroy all beings, including the great terrors of malevolent spirits and planetary seizures;
the frightened beings carry out the command of that Great-Souled One.
What is the use of saying more here? On this earth, there is no other mantra equal to this one for the purpose of subduing living beings. || 132 ||
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Śāradātilaka composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra. 19.
The *Bṛhatī* states: "He offers the five cruel oblations in the form of cooked rice,
curd, barley flour, turmeric, parched grain, and sesame seeds."
As it has been stated by the Teachers: "Parched grain, sesame, *nakta*, dust, ocean, flour, and rice—these are known as *bhūtakrūra*.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition. 19.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
Hereafter, I shall duly describe the unsurpassed Aghora-weapon mantra.
By the mere remembrance of whom all calamities are destroyed. || 1 ||
Then "māyā," then "sphuradvayam," then again "prasphuradvitayam," followed by "ghoraghoratarā" at the end, and then again the word "tanurūpa. || 2 ||
At the end of that, there should be a pair of *caṭa*, followed by a pair of *pracaṭa*;
then a pair of *kaha*, a pair of *vama*, and again a pair of *bandha*. || 3 ||
The two [syllables] "ghātaya" followed by "varma" (huṃ) ending with "phaṭ" are proclaimed;
this great mantra of the Aghora-weapon consists of fifty-one syllables. || 4 ||
Aghora is declared to be its sage (ṛṣi), and Triṣṭubh is stated to be its meter; Aghoraruḍra is designated as the deity by those most skilled in mantras. || 5 ||
The heart is said to consist of five [syllables], the head is declared to consist of six;
the crest is described as having ten, and the armor is considered to have that same number.
The eye is said to consist of the Vasus (8) and the Varṇas (36), and the weapon is declared to consist of the Mātras (12) and the Arṇas (50).
These are to be placed in order upon the head, eyes, face, throat, heart, navel, anus, and thighs. || 7 ||
One should place [the mantras] upon the pair of knees, shanks, and feet with the Rudra-bhinnākṣara syllables—namely, with five, then six, two, and eight syllables. || 8 ||
By means of the four syllables and the six syllables, and again by means of the instruments—through the four, the six, and the two eyes—this division of syllables has been declared. || 9 ||
He extracts the mantra as "māyā. Māyā is the seed-syllable of Śakti.
"Tanurūpā" means its own essential form.
The armor [mantra] is *hūṃ*.
By this, it is stated that for specific desires, there is the addition of the respective seed-syllable at the end.
As they say:
A mantra ending in *hum* is for immobilization; one ending in *krom* is for attraction and completion;
one ending in *vaṣaṭ* is for subjugation; and one ending in *namaḥ* is for the destruction of poison.
For the destruction of planets, thieves, and enemies, it is prescribed that [the mantra] ends with *huṃ* and *kroṃ*;
for the attainment of all desired things, it should end with *śakti* (phaṭ); and for killing, it should end with *kṣauṃ*.
"This mantra, ending with *phaṭ*, is a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpapādapa*) for the destruction of spirits (*bhūtasaṃhāra*).
However, in the *Īśvarakalpa*, a forty-one-syllable mantra is extracted, beginning with *prasphurad-vaya-bandha-dvaya-vajrītaḥ*.
The consonants within the mantra are the seed-syllables (*bīja*).
The vowels are the powers (*śakti*).
"Huṃ" is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and "Hrūṃ" is the power; thus say the teacher Padmapādācārya.
This is connected later with the phrase "by those who know the mantra."
Therefore, even within the eleven divisions of the *aṅga-mantras*, the conjunction with the *praṇava* and the *māyā-bīja* is indicated for each one,
according to the consensus of the teacher Padmapāda. By those [divisions], there are ten.
With the eight syllables beginning with *vasu* (the Vasus); with the twelve syllables beginning with *māsa* (the months).
In some places, there is a reading: "with the final syllables."
The meaning is: "by the remaining syllables.
"Divided by Rudra" means divided elevenfold.
He states that very division:
"By five" means by four instruments. 1-9.
Resembling a water-laden cloud, with formidable fangs, three eyes, and wearing serpents, he is Aghora; clad in red garments and smeared with red unguents,
he holds an axe, a *ḍamaru* drum, a sword, a shield, an arrow, and a bow.
I meditate upon him holding the skull-bowl of the hell-beings of Triśikhin. || 10 ||
Regarding the meditation, he says: "With the right arms [he holds] the axe, sword, arrow, and trident; with the left arms, the other [weapons]. Thus is the meditation on the weapons. 10.
In the rite of malevolent magic (abhicāra) and the destruction of planetary influences, the omnipresent Lord is black in color;
in the rite of subjugation (vaśya), he resembles safflower; and in liberation (mukti), his radiance is like that of the moon. || 11 ||
Regarding the destruction of planets and planetary abnormalities, as they say: "Kṛṣṇa [is the remedy] for malevolent magic (abhicāra) and planetary abnormalities.
The mention of "malevolent magic" and so forth is illustrative.
By this, one should understand that specific meditations correspond to specific desires;
as they say:
"A bow [measured] by five hundred cubits is equal to a thousand years."
Aiming and drawing his arrows, he discharged them incessantly until the very end.
He was rushing through the enemy army like a cloud vomiting lightning,
with blazing tawny hair standing erect and his body draped in an elephant hide.
For the destruction of the armies of his enemies, he should meditate upon the one of great roar,
who has three feet, two hands, and one eye, and who resembles a mass of blue collyrium.
One should visualize [the deity] with a trident, sword, and needle in hand, possessing terrible fangs and a loud, boisterous laugh,
for the destruction of terrible epilepsy and for the pacification of planetary afflictions.
For the purpose of exorcising an enemy, one should meditate upon that fierce adversary running behind with bow and arrow; then he shall depart for another land.
He holds a sword, a shield, a bell, a vetāla, and a trident, as well as a skull-cup; he is terrifying with his tawny hair standing erect.
For the destruction of ghosts, spirits, and the like, one should meditate upon the Terrific One who laughs with a loud roar,
who holds the Sītā-lotus and the moon within his lap, and whose splendor is like that of the moonstone and the moon.
Clad in space alone, his limbs adorned with ornaments for children such as tiger-claw pendants,
he has two arms and the form of a three-and-a-half-year-old child.
He who thus remembers Aghora— whose limbs are beautiful, whose face is pleasant and gentle, and whose hair is dark and curled— shall become a conqueror of death.

"By meditating upon him who resembles molten gold, who holds a trident, a sword, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and whose abode is a red lotus, one shall attain supreme prosperity. Thus [it is said]. (11)

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and, for the sake of the mantra’s accomplishment, the practitioner of mantra should offer oblations with auspicious sesame seeds sprinkled with ghee, numbering one-tenth of that amount. || 12 ||
By the word "with pure [substances]," it is stated that one should remove the refuse, wash [the area], and dry it. || 12 ||
In the Śaiva [tradition], one should worship on the pedestal (pīṭha) within a lotus situated inside a hexagon;
having performed the worship of the limbs (aṅgapūjā) upon the filaments, one should thereafter perform it upon the petals. || 13 ||
The preceptor should worship his eight weapons: the axe, the hand-drum, the sword, the shield, the arrow, the bow, the trident, and the skull-cup. || 14 ||
Then, on the tips of the petals, one should worship Brāhmī and the others, who possess the characteristics previously described;
afterwards, one should worship the World-Protectors (Lokeśas) together with their respective weapons. || 15 ||
"One should worship the deity"—this is the ellipsis.
Regarding "the hexagon":
having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus and having constructed a hexagon upon it, one should make a square with four doors.
Those possessing the characteristics previously described, whose essential nature is as stated in the sixth chapter. || 13–15 ||
Thus, when the mantra has been perfected through worship and other rites, the practitioner should perform his desired applications; they will succeed—of this there is no doubt. || 16 ||
In due order, the wise one should offer a thousand oblations each night of ghee mixed with *sarpis*, *apāmārga*, sesame, mustard seeds, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*). || 17 ||
This person shall instantly destroy the afflictions caused by spirits, magical rites, and other such calamities, using [a paste] derived from white kiṃśuka, nirguṇḍī, hemā, and apāmārga. || 18 ||
The oblation performed with the choice fuel-sticks, as previously described, grants peace from malevolent spirits.
[The twigs] of Apāmārga and Āragvadha, sprinkled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), || 19 ||
One who is self-restrained should offer fuel-sticks at night on the fifth day of the dark fortnight;
by offering one thousand oblations separately for each, the subjugation of spirits shall occur. || 20 ||

Having offered one thousand oblations each, in sequence, with ghee, apāmārga, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), sacrificial grain, and clarified butter, the wise practitioner should pour the remnants into a vessel.
With the ghee containing these remnants, he should feed the person to be treated for the pacification of malevolent spirits. || 21 ||
"Apāmārga" refers to *apāmārga* fuel-sticks.
Regarding "with clarified butter":
the meaning is that clarified butter is the sixth substance.
Hemadhattūra is [the plant].
"As before" means one thousand [recitations] each during the night.
"An oblation of the five products of the cow" means milk-rice prepared with the five products of the cow.
This is stated in the *Kriyākālaguṇottara Tantra*:
"Pure *caru* produced from the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and likewise fresh ghee.
Having offered these, it should be understood that [the rite] is performed at night. (16–21)
In the center, one should write the Śakti together with the object of accomplishment (sādhya) and accompanied by the group of vowels; on the filaments, the eight groups of consonants;
and within the petals, the letters of the mantra numbering three times their qualities (thirty).

Likewise, at the tips [of the petals], one should place the armor (kavaca) and the weapon (astra), which illuminate the corners, situated within a pair of fire-purified [triangles] located in the outer square.
In this yantra, by performing the rite for the water-pot according to the previously mentioned procedure, all suffering is removed. ||22||
He states the yantra: "In the center," etc.;
"the one to be accomplished" (sādhya), etc., which is an elliptical expression for the practitioner (sādhaka) and others.

Alternatively, that which is to be accomplished is the *sādhya*; [the mantra] is accompanied by that. Thus, "bring such-and-such of so-and-so under control, bring it under control!"—this meaning is encompassed by the word *sādhya*.

Having drawn an eight-petalled lotus, one should write the seed-syllable of Śakti within its pericarp (*karṇikā*), surrounded by the vowels, together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the ritual action (*karma*). As it has been said: "The pericarp shines with the syllables of the *sādhya* situated within the *Hṛllekhā*, and it is encircled by the [vowels] *kala*."
"The eight groups" refers to *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, *śa*, and *la*.
They are measured by their qualities [the vowels] in groups of three.
The syllables of the mantra, beginning with *sphura* and ending with *caṭacaṭa*, [are placed] at the foremost points, that is,
on the tips of the petals;
likewise, three times each.
One should write the syllables of the mantra beginning with *pracaṭa* and ending with *ghātaya*.

Outside of that, having formed two triangles intersecting one another, one should write the *varma* (armor) and *astra* (weapon) mantras in their corners. "According to the previous procedure" means by the method stated in the sixth [chapter].
As it has been said:

"That [lotus] has its petals arising from the three syllables of the mantra, with the tips of the petals facing outward; and on its exterior, it is provided with the armor (*kavaca*) and weapon (*astra*) mantras resting upon the fire-enclosed triangle."

However, some, through a remote connection, claim that there is a hexagon in the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus, [placing] the armor in the triangle, fire in the pair of cities, and the Śakti in the center;
but that is irrelevant.
Because it contradicts the words of the recorded teachers. || 22 ||

In the hexagon, the Śakti is surrounded by a pair of *sphura* syllables; in the corners of the [outer] pair of circles, it is surrounded by the remaining letters of the mantra— six, six, six, four, four, and four— forming an eight-petaled lotus, which is encircled by two fire-cities (triangles) and the armor (*varma*) and *phaṭ* mantras.
This is the terrible machine consisting of two wheels with four spokes, encircled by a silver rim. || 23 ||
This yantra is declared to be the destroyer of petty thieves, seizing spirits, serpents, ghosts, and epilepsy, and it bestows all forms of prosperity. || 24 ||
He describes another yantra with the word "six" (ṣaṭ).

Within a hexagon—which vibrates with the sequence of single syllables and possesses corners in pairs—one should draw the Śakti in the center, properly surrounded by a pair of [circles], together with the object of attainment (sādhya), the practitioner (sādhaka), and the ritual action (karman).
Regarding the phrase "by the remaining [parts]":
"By those beginning with Ghorā and ending with Ghātayā," and "enclosed by the pair of burning and filling" refers to the exterior.
By the phrase "bestowing all accomplishments," this is what is meant:

as they have said— "Now, desiring victory over an enemy, one should fashion an effigy of the foe using *ghātaya* (the 'kill' mantra) and [his] name; having placed it upon the cremation ground, one should recite the mantra one million times."
A wise person should offer ten thousand oblations of *kāraskara* fruits sprinkled with salt, pungent substances, smoke, fire, *sūraṇa*, *unmatta*, and water.
For *uccāṭana* (eradication), the *prasphura* syllable is joined with *puṭa*; for *mohana* (bewildering), it is joined with *kaha*;
for *stambhana* (paralyzing), it is joined with *caṭa* and *puṭa*; and for *viyoga* (separation), it is joined with *pracaṭa*.
"Vam" is for intoxication; furthermore, "bandha" repeated twice is for binding. Thus it is said.
Now, the yantra of the thirty-four-syllable Aghora is described:

first, a lotus joined with seven rows of petals; then, in the center of the pericarp, in the middle of the Tāra [syllable Om]... [the name of the person to be accomplished], conjoined with the essence of the Three Vedas (Trayīsāra), should be placed there.
Having bound this king of yantras— encircled by the script of the letters of *manu* arranged in pairs within the petals— with threads,
she who carries it on her hand, neck, head, or waist shall become a vessel for complete prosperity.
Likewise, there is no need for further elaboration regarding the powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth.
Thus,
it is endowed with seven rows and possesses seventeen petals.
The mantra should be understood as that which was previously stated by me in the first chapter.
The limb-protection (*aṅga*) consists of six-syllable mantras for the armor (*varma*) and weapon (*astra*), ending with *ṭhaṃ* and *phaṭ*.
Everything else regarding this [mantra] should be known to be like the previous mantras.

Regarding the forty-one syllable [mantra]: "The six-limbed [protection] should be performed with the six syllables preceded by Śakti, followed by Veda, Ṣaḍveda, Diṅnāga, and Ṣaḍ, ending with *huṃ* and *phaṭ*; the rest is declared as before. (23–24)
The syllable *tāra* (om), followed by *vānta* (ha), situated on *dharā* (la), adorned with the left eye (*i*) and the moon (*bindu*);
then *pārśva* (va) joined with *baka* (ka) and *karṇa* (ra)—this is the six-syllabled mantra ending with *varma* (huṃ) and *astra* (phaṭ). || 25 ||
The mantra known as the Pāśupata weapon wards off evil planets and minor obstacles;
its six limbs consist of the six syllables ending in *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, accompanied by their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*). || 26 ||
He states the Pāśupata weapon: "Tāra" and so forth.
*Tāra* is the Praṇava (Om).
*Vānta* is *śa*; *dharā* is *la*; [the weapon] is situated upon that.
By that [the letter *śa*], with the left eye (*vāmanetra*) which is the crescent moon (*indu*), i.e., the bindu, it becomes *ślīṃ*.
*Pārśva* is *pa*; *vaka* is *śa*; joined with the ear (*karṇa*) and the vowel *u*, it becomes *śu*.
Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ); Śrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Huṃ is the power (śakti);
"Graha" and so forth constitute the statement of the application (viniyoga).
By means of the six syllables residing in the mantra,
ending with *huṃ* and *phaṭ*,
[one should strike] each [of them] individually.
"Hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth, together with the [seed] syllables. || 25-26 ||
[He who is] radiant like the midday sun, bearing the moon, blazing with a terrifying loud laugh, three-eyed, adorned with serpents, with a crest of peacock feathers and a beard of shimmering hair;
the All-pervading Lord, holding in his lotus-like hands a trident, a mallet, a sword, and a spear.
One should meditate upon Paśupati, who has four faces formidable with fangs and whose form consists of divine weapons. || 27 ||
The meditation on the weapons, however, is performed with the right hand and the one above in the first case, and with those below it in the last case.
The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with cow's clarified butter in a consecrated fire, using a tenth part of that number. || 28 ||

In the Śaiva seat, one should worship the God first with the limbs (aṅgas), then with the eight Mothers, then with the world-protectors beginning with Indra, and thereafter with the weapons beginning with the thunderbolt. || 29 ||
One should pour water consecrated with this mantra into the mouth of the one who has been seized;
by the power of the mantra, the seizing spirit will immediately release him while crying out. || 30 ||
A king should discharge arrows consecrated with this mantra in battle;
he shall conquer all enemies in an instant, like a second Pārtha. || 31 ||
The "one hundred thousand with color" (varṇalakṣa) means six hundred thousand.

It should be understood that in the phrase "releasing," the mantra begins with the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha; in the phrase "one should recite," it begins with the seed-syllable of Durgā, and so forth. (28–31)
The heart-mantra for Kṣetrapāla consists of the final letter of the [Brahmin] class (kṣa), joined with *au* and the nasal drop (*bindu*).
This mantra for Kṣetrapāla, preceded by the *Tāra* (Oṃ), is proclaimed to consist of eight syllables. || 32 ||
He states the mantra of the Kṣetrapāla with the words "the final letter" (varṇa), etc. The final letter is *kṣa*;
*au* is its own form (*svarūpa*).
The word "hṛn" is the term "namaḥ.
Regarding the phrase "vasuvarṇe 'yam," it should be understood that, having referred to the quality of being "vasuvarṇa," the state of being preceded by "tārā" (the syllable Om) is prescribed.
Brahmā is the seer, Gāyatrī is the meter;
*kṣauṃ* is the seed-syllable, and *āya* is the power.
In some instances, it is extracted as a single syllable alone.
As it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
"The seed-syllable consisting of the final letter [of the alphabet] conjoined with the vowel 'au' and the bindu bestows all accomplishments."
Regarding this, there is a specific detail in the *Prayogasāra*:
"Forty-nine varieties of Kṣetrapāla have been proclaimed;
they are differentiated by the various seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the Mātṛkās and by their distinct names."
Ajara, Apakumbha, and Indrasū; after him, Īḍācāra, Ulkasaṃjña, Ūṣmāda, and Ṛṣisūdana.
Ṛmukta, Lṛptakeśa, Lṛpaka, Ekadaṃṣṭraka,
Erāvata, Oghabandhu, and likewise Auṣadhighna (or Auṣadhīśa).
Añjana, Astrabāhu (or Astrarā), Kavala, Kharukhānala,
Gomukha, Ghaṇṭāda, Ṅaṇāra, and Caṇḍacāraṇa.
Chaṭāṭopa, Jaṭālākhyo, Bhaṅgāra,
then Ñaṅga, Cara, Ṭaṅkapāṇi, as well as another, Aṣṭhāṇabandhu, and Ḍāmara.
Ḍhakkārava, Nakarṇa, Taḍiddehasthira,
Dantura, Dhanada, Natikrānta, and Pracaṇḍaka.
Phaṭkāra, Bīrasandha, the one called Bhṛṅga, Meghabhāsura,
Yugānta, Raurava, Lamboṣṭha, and likewise Vasu.
Śukananda, the one named Ṣaḍāla, Sunāman, and likewise Haṃdhruka—
these are declared to be the divisions born from the womb of the letters of the Mātṛkā.
Whichever letter of its name is seen first among the letters in another *mātṛkā*, there he is the protector of that field (*kṣetrapālaka*).
In each respective case, he is established through these specific distinctions;
therefore, the Kṣetrapāla, who is superior in every respect, must be worshipped.
"Whoever performs any ritual action anywhere without first worshipping the Kṣetrapāla, the Kṣetrapāla destroys the fruit of that person's action; of this there is no doubt. (32)
One should apply the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) to this [mantra] by means of the seed-syllable (bīja) possessing the six long vowels. Brahmā is its seer (ṛṣi); the Gāyatrī meter is declared for it;
Kṣetrapāla is the deity, and "pālaya" (protect) is declared as the power (śakti). || 33 ||
Resembling a mountain of blue collyrium, with tawny hair standing erect,
possessing round and fierce eyes, holding a mace and a skull-cup,
clad in space as his garment, adorned with serpents, and having formidable fangs.
I bow down to the Lord, the master of the field, whose form is wondrous. || 34 ||
"By the seed-syllable" means by the second part of the mantra. || 33 ||
"Blue" means dark blue; for that very reason, he resembles a mountain of collyrium.
"Taken up" means grasped with both hands—this is the ellipsis.
Regarding the mace and skull-cup: the visualization of the weapons is that there is a mace in the right hand and a skull-cup in the left.
"Clad in space" means naked.
"He who holds a skull-bowl and a mace in his hand," according to the *Nārāyaṇīya*;
"holding a fierce mace and a skull-bowl in his hands," according to the *Prayogasāra*.
In some places, the reading is "a mass of matted hair" (*jaṭākalāpam*). (34–35)

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with caru mixed with ghee in a tenth part of that number; thereafter, one should worship the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapāla). || 35 ||
On the seat imagined as Dharma and so forth, one should first worship the limbs;
thereafter, [one should worship] the one named Anala, Agnikeśa, and Karāla. || 36 ||
One should worship Ghaṇṭārava, Mahākopa, and the one known as Piśitāśaya—
those with tawny eyes and hair standing erect— on the petals all around.
One should worship the World-Guardians (Lokapālas) and their weapons as before, along with the images of the principal deities, which are adorned with various ornaments. || 38 ||
"Dharmādikalpita" refers to the fourth mode previously mentioned; it does not, however, refer to the worship of the Śaktipīṭha.
"Mahākopam" should be understood as "mahākrodham" (great wrath).
This is because it is stated thus in the *Prayogasāra* and the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"The visualization of Anala and the others [is performed] in their primary forms. (35–38)
One should offer this bali-oblation to him together with his retinue:
first two *ehi* [mantras], and afterwards two *purus* for the wise one. || 39 ||
Again, he should cause the pair [of feet] to break, and again cause the pair to dance;
then, O Mahābhairava, the pair of feet of the obstacle-maker follows after that.
"O Kṣetrapāla, accept the offering; O Pāvakasundarī, accept the offering. This is declared to be the mantra for the offering (bali), which bestows the fruits of all desires. || 41 ||
"Accompanied by his retinue" means together with his limbs (*aṅga*) and so forth.

"Bestower of the fruit of all desires" refers to him when he has become perfected (*siddha*). And the author of the *Āpekṣitārthadyotanikā* states that perfection is attained through a thousand recitations. (39–41)

Having prepared a large morsel of food with side-dishes, the practitioner, during the nights, should offer the oblation into the hand of the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapāla), while recollecting him as described. || 42 ||
Satisfied by this offering of strength, the Guardian of the Field bestows beauty, intelligence, strength, health, splendor, nourishment, fame, and prosperity. || 43 ||
An *upadaṃśa* is a side dish;
[this applies] during the nights,
after one watch has passed.
As previously stated regarding the aforementioned meditation:
[she is] mounted upon a blue elephant;
"in the hand" means in the skull-cup held in the left hand.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"With this perfected mantra, one should offer the bali-oblation upon that skull-cup;
for the others situated in the eight directions starting from the left arm, [one offers] with [the mantras] beginning with 'Anala'."

Also in the *Prayogasāra*: "Alternatively, having meditated upon Kṣetreśa, who possesses the previously described characteristics and is mounted upon a black dog, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) upon its skull."

The ritual procedure for that is as follows: after midnight on the night [of the practice], having smeared an area the size of a cow-hide in the courtyard, having placed there red perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth,

having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs, having recited the root mantra ten times, having worshipped the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and having invoked the Guardian of the Field (*kṣetrapāla*) therein and performed the ritual services (*upacāra*).

Having worshipped [the deity] along with the enclosures and having become secluded from people, one should offer bali and water three times into that skull-cup with the left hand using the bali-mantra.

Then, having offered it once to the deities of the limbs beginning with "To Agni, Svāhā" and so forth, and to the [principal] forms, and having washed one's hands, one should oneself, being the deity, repeat the root mantra one hundred and eight times. || 42-43 ||
One should extract "Vaṭuka" ending in the dative case (vaṭukāya), and likewise "Āpaduddhāraṇa.
Then, one should again extract "Vaṭuka" ending in the dative case, preceded by two instances of "Kuru. || 44 ||
This great mantra, consisting of twenty-one syllables and constrained by Śakti, is proclaimed as the celestial wish-fulfilling tree for the attainment of one's desired fruits. (45)
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka is declared by the wise to be the seer; the Anuṣṭubh is the meter;
and Lord Bhairava, the deliverer from calamity, is the deity. || 46 ||
He states the mantra for rescuing from calamity: "uddharet" (one should rescue).
"Vaṭukaṃ" is in the dative case (ending in -ṅe), meaning "to Vaṭuka. Likewise, [the word] "tathā" is also in the dative case.
By that [mantra], for the sake of rescuing one from calamity;
"obstructed by power" (śaktiruddha) means enclosed within the seed-syllable of Śakti.
"The celestial tree" (surapādapa) means the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru), because it grants the desires of practitioners.
Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ);
"vaṃ" is the seed-syllable (bīja), Māyā is the power (śakti). The portion situated within the enclosure is in some cases additional. || 44-46 ||

One should install the forms on the fingers, body, and face as previously described, preceded by the seed-syllables of the Śaktis enriched with the five short vowels beginning with *sa* (sadya). || 47 ||
One should join the letter *va*, enriched with the five short vowels, to the [faces] beginning with Īśāna;
likewise, by means of the power (*śakti*) conjoined with the six long vowels and the letter *va* possessing those [vowels]. || 48 ||
One should conceive of the limbs as being endowed with their respective origins and beginning with the syllable Om;
its meditation is declared to be threefold, according to the distinction of Sāttvika and the other qualities.
"Aṅgulī" means among the fingers,
beginning with the thumb.
"Deha" means [the body].
In the head, face, heart, secret place, and feet.
Regarding "in the faces":
in the upward, eastern, southern, northern, and western [faces].
Regarding the phrase "as before":
it has been stated that for the installation (*nyāsa*) of Īśāna and the others upon the body and the faces, the installation is performed with their respective fingers.
Sadyojāta and the others are associated with the vowels beginning with *o*, excluding the neuter vowels.
Regarding the phrase "in Īśāna and the others":
by the word "others" (ādi), Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Sadyojāta are included.
The practical application is as follows: *hroṃ voṃ īśānāya namaḥ* on the thumb, and so forth.
"By one possessing that" means by one endowed with the six long vowels.
The practical application is as follows: "Oṃ hrāṃ vāṃ, salutation to the heart," and so forth. (47–49)
I bow to the Child, who resembles crystal, whose face is radiant with locks of hair,
and who is adorned with divine ornaments made of fresh jewels, such as tinkling bells and anklets;
he is of brilliant form, clad in pure white garments, exceedingly gracious, and possesses three eyes.
With his two lotus-like hands, Śūladaṇḍa constantly holds Vaṭuka.
This is declared to be sattvic meditation, which wards off untimely death, generates longevity and health, and bestows fruits not obtained through other means. || 51 ||
In the *sāttvika* meditation, the trident and staff are held in the left and right hands respectively.
As it is stated in the *Viśvasāroddhāra*:
"The trident is in the left hand, and the subtle staff is in the right."
Thus [ends the section on] verses 50–51.
Resembling the rising sun, three-eyed, with red unguents and garlands, smiling-faced, bestowing boons, holding a skull, the gesture of fearlessness,
and a trident in his hands; blue-necked, adorned with hundreds of noble ornaments, and radiant with the crescent moon upon his crest.
I always meditate upon the God who wears garments as crimson as the bandhūka flower and who removes all fear. || 52 ||
In the meditation on the King (Rājasadhyāna), the first two [attributes] are on the left hands and the last two are on the right hands.
As it is stated in the Viśvasāroddhāra:
"On the right [hands] are the trident and the gesture of fearlessness; on the left, the skull-cup and likewise the gesture of granting boons."
Thus [ends the verse]. 52.
One should meditate upon Maheśa, who is as beautiful as a blue mountain, who wears the crescent moon and a garland of severed heads,

who is clothed in the directions (naked), whose hair is tawny, and who holds in his lotus-like hands a hand-drum, a goad, a sword, a noose, a serpent, a bell, and a skull-cup, possessing terrifying fangs.
He has the appearance of a serpent, possesses three eyes, and is adorned with shimmering jeweled girdles and anklets.

The rājasa meditation has been described as bestowing the accomplishment of dharma, kāma, and artha; the tāmasa meditation subdues enemies and dispels the effects of magical spells, spirits, and planetary influences. || 54 ||

In the *tāmasa* meditation, however, [the deities] are in the first [position] for the two above Dakṣa, in the second for the two below him, in the penultimate [position] for the two below that, and in the final [position] for the two below those.
Here, immediately after the meditation, one should display the *ḍamaruka-mudrā*.
Its definition is as follows:
"Having formed a very loose fist with the middle finger slightly raised, one should lift it upward from the right side and move it toward the region of the ear.
This is the Ḍamaruka mudrā, which destroys all obstacles. (53–54)
One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
he should then perform oblations with sesame seeds mixed with honey in a quantity equal to one-tenth of that [recitation]. || 55 ||
The number of syllables is twenty-one hundred thousand. || 55 ||
Upon a seat fashioned from dharma, adharma, and so forth, and adorned with lotuses, which is joined with a sky-lotus situated within a triangle inside a hexagon; || 56 ||
One should worship the god Vaṭuka and fashion his form with the root mantra;
then, one should invoke the god with the Sadyojāta mantra, beginning with the root mantra. || 57 ||
One should establish the Supreme Lord with the Vāmadeva mantra;
immediately thereafter, the presence [of the deity] should be effected with the root mantra (mūlamantra). || 58 ||
Immediately thereafter, the wise one should perform the complete restraint with the Aghora mantra;
then, with the mantra called Puruṣa, he should display the Yoni-mudrā. || 59 ||
One should perform the salutation to the deity with a concentrated mind by means of Īśāna;
all of this should be performed with devotion, accompanied by their respective mudrās. || 60 ||
"On the prepared seat" means in the manner described in the fourth [chapter];
however, the powers of the seat (pīṭhaśakti) are not present here.
On what kind of pedestal?
On one joined with a lotus in the void situated within a triangle inside a hexagon.
Again, of what kind?
Adorned with lotuses:

having fashioned a *mātṛkā*-lotus by that [means], a triangle above it, a hexagon above that, an eight-petalled lotus above that, and a square with four gates above that— this is the worship diagram (*pūjāyantra*).
As it is stated in the Viśvasāroddhāra:
"Upon a square seat, a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp is fashioned;
and in its center, a hexagonal mandala is prescribed."
And in the center of that is a triangle, and in the center of that is a sky-lotus;
having invoked Vaṭuka in the center—
thus [it is said].

The "sky-lotus" is the lotus of the colors mentioned in the *Mātṛpaṭala*. It is connected to the five [faces] starting from the root with the mantra *sadyojāta*, and so forth. Thus it is applied to the five.
"With their respective mudrās" means that the mudrās will be described in the twenty-third [chapter]. The añjali joined at the forehead is the vandanā-mudrā. (56–60)
The preceptor should worship the deities beginning with Īśāna according to the path of ritual placement (nyāsa);
having performed the rite of sakalīkaraṇa, he should worship the forms as previously described. || 61 ||
One should worship the Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga, upon the petals of the lotus in the sky:
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and Unmattabhairava.
The wise practitioner should worship these—the Kapālin, the one named Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra—in sequence within the six corners, as well as the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in their proper order. || 63 ||
Regarding the phrase "by way of ritual placement" (*nyāsamārgeṇa*):
[the placement] is performed upon the body of the deity at the head and other locations using the various fingers, even across the five faces, but not upon the fingers themselves.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Just as [it is done] for oneself, so should the ritual placement be performed for the deity, excluding the hands."
Thus:
one should worship with "Hrīṃ Voṃ, obeisance to Īśāna," and so forth.
It should be understood that in this case, one first performs the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the body of the deity, and only afterwards the worship.
Having performed the *sakalīkaraṇa* (the rite of infusion), one should worship the Deity; this is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*).
The phrase "one should worship the forms (*mūrtīḥ*) as before" is to be supplied.
By the expression "as before," it is stated that in the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*), the worship of the forms takes place in the east, south, north, west, and in the northeast (*īśa*).
However, there is a specific distinction in the *Viśvasāroddhāra*: "One should worship the five [faces] of Brahmā—Indra, Agni, Yama, Soma, and the Waters.
It is stated that these should be preceded by their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*): *aṃ, iṃ, uṃ, ṛṃ, lṛṃ, eṃ, oṃ, aṃ*.
As for the ritual application: "Aṃ, obeisance to Asitāṅga Bhairava," and so forth.
The term *bhairava-pada* is to be applied to all [the deities].
Furthermore, the mention of Bhairava is for the purpose of excluding the Mothers (*mātṛ*).
By the word "wise one" (*sudhīḥ*) in sequence, it is stated that there is worship beginning with the southeast (*āgneya*) and so forth. (61–63)
Outside of that, one should worship these sons of Ḍākinīs starting from the east and ending with the northeast; first the sons of Rākiṇīs, and then [the others]. 64.
Then the sons of Lākinī, after that the sons of Kākinī, then again the sons of Śākinī, and once more the sons of Hākinī. || 65 ||
Afterwards, one should worship the sons of Mālinī, and after that, the sons of the Goddesses;
then, one should worship the sons of Umā, Rudra, and the Mothers on the right side. || 66 ||
"The practitioner of mantras should worship the thirteen groups of sons: those with upward faces [granting] sons above, and those with downward faces [granting] sons below. || 67 ||
Outside of that, one should worship the world-protectors (lokeśas) and the vaṭukas upon the lotus petals:
the son of Brahmāṇī in the east, and the son of Māheśī in the northeast.
One should worship Vaiṣṇavī’s son in the north, Kaumārī’s son in the northwest, and then again worship Indrāṇī’s son in the west. || 69 ||
One should then worship the son of Mahālakṣmī in the western direction,
Vārāhī’s son in the south, and Cāmuṇḍā’s son in the southeast.
"Outside of that" means outside the hexagon.
The connection is that one should worship these [deities] to be described hereafter, from the east up to the northeast, within the eight petals. (64–70)
One should worship the Vaṭukas in the ten directions, as well as Dhenuka, Tripurāntaka, Vetāla, the one named Vahnijihva, the one named Kālānta, and Karālaka.
One should worship Ekapāda, Bhīmadaṃṣṭra, Acala, and Hāṭakeśvara;
then, one should again worship Śrīkaṇṭha and the others in the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and the spaces between them. || 72 ||
In the same manner, one should worship [the deities] beginning with Krodhīśvara and ending with Bhṛgu on the outside;
then, the wise practitioner should worship the three beginning with Nakulīśa on the right.
Regarding the phrase "in the cardinal and intermediate directions":
there are four cardinal directions and four intermediate directions; the spaces between them are eight, thus making sixteen.
"Again, in the same manner" means likewise.
In the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and the spaces between them.
Therein, the eight cardinal directions, the eight intermediate directions, and the sixteen spaces between them—these thirty-two locations are to be known. || 71-73 ||
One should worship the lords of yoga, accompanied by their Śaktis, who reside in the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms,
together with the Yoginīs, situated in the directions of Īśa, Agni, and Nirṛti.
Thus, one should worship the god Vaṭuka according to the prescribed method;
that person becomes the master of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. || 75 ||
The phrase "endowed with their powers" (*śaktisaṃyutān*) is merely a general qualification. When the question arises as to what those powers are, there is the expression "together with the Yoginīs.
This has been stated in the *Viśvasāroddhāra*:

Then one should worship the lords of yoga (yogīśas) who reside in the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms, together with the yoginīs, in the northeast, southeast, and southwest. Thus [ends verses 74–75].

Having propitiated Vighna and Durgā and having offered the bali according to the prescribed rite, the practitioner of mantra should accomplish his desired objects and obtain the success as described. || 76 ||
Regarding the mere act of desiring, he states the technical definition: "an obstacle" (vighna). || 76 ||
Rice of the *śāli* variety, minced meat with ghee, parched grain flour, sugar, molasses, sugarcane juice, and cakes, all mixed together and anointed with honey. || 77 ||

Having formed a morsel of food and propitiated the deity according to the previously mentioned method, one should offer a bali-oblation to him at night with red sandalwood, flowers, and other offerings. || 78 ||
Then, by means of this powerful [mantra], the affairs of the practitioner are accomplished;
the mantra-master should offer oblations with flour-mash (sapiṣā), and he shall attain the success as described. || 79 ||
One should offer oblations with *dakṣa* wood-shavings for subjugation (*vaśya*) to bring people under one's control;
for the attainment of a son, the wise man should offer oblations with full-blown white water-lilies (*kairava*). || 80 ||
One should offer oblations of sesame seeds and rice for the attainment of wealth, grain, and other riches;
by offering oblations of bilva flowers, one obtains great prosperity.
One may bring women under one's control by using salt mixed with sweet substances.
One who desires rain should offer oblations with the best fuel-sticks of cane (vetasa).
One should offer oblations daily with food for the attainment of wealth, grain, and other riches;
for the purpose of subjugation, the practitioner of mantra should offer honey for three days. || 83 ||
He describes that very performance of the bali offering with the words "śālyanna" and so forth.
*Palala* means meat.
*Ekīkṛta* means a morsel or mouthful in the form of a lump.
The connection is as follows: having propitiated the deity at night with red sandalwood, flowers, and so forth, according to the previously mentioned method, one should offer the *bali* at night.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), incense, lamps, and food offerings are included.

By the phrase "previously mentioned," it is stated that in the *bali-mantra* for the *Kṣetrapāla*—where the word "Kṣetrapāla" occurs—one should substitute the word "Vaṭuka," and [the offering should be made] in the hand of the deity.
"As previously stated" means that which resides within one's own mind. (77–83)
By means of the medicinal oblation (homa) prescribed for disease, diseases perish instantly;
likewise in cases of malevolent spells (kṛtyā), hostility from planets (graha), and the occurrence of possession by spirits (bhūta) or epilepsy (apasmāra). || 84 ||
Seated upon a tiger skin, one should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds;
the spirits and other such beings flee and, out of fear, do not look toward that direction.

Regarding the phrase "as stated for the disease": it means that for whichever disease a specific medicine is prescribed in the medical treatises (vaidyaka-śāstra), one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with that [medicine]. ||84-85||
Beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day,
[one should offer oblations] with sesame seeds mixed with rice and soaked in the three sweets.
Having worshipped Vaṭukeśvara with offerings of various kinds of food and fruits, one should offer oblations three thousand times daily into the consecrated fire.
Having constantly offered the food offering (naivedya), one should present the bali-oblation at midnight;
thus, being self-restrained, one should recite [the mantra] twenty-one thousand times. || 88 ||
On the day of completion, having slain a goat at night, one should offer the bali-oblation;
thereafter, the king who has commissioned the rite should satisfy the practitioner with wealth. || 89 ||
Satisfied by this rite, Vaṭukeśa bestows splendor,
strength, fame, sons, beauty, fortune, and freedom from disease.
All enemies perish, kinsmen and relatives flourish, and no drought shall arise in the realm of that king. || 91 ||
One should offer ten thousand oblations with *leṇa* seeds alone when desiring a paralyzing spell;
this is the ritual procedure taught for the purpose of liberation from shackles and the like. || 92 ||
The passage beginning with "Kṛṣṇa" and ending with "of the king" constitutes a single syntactical construction. *Avagraha* means the absence of rain. Regarding the *viṣaya*:
In the region. || 86-92 ||
A widow desiring sons should recite [the mantra] over one *pala* of *vacā* powder, stir it with cow’s clarified butter, divide it, and consume it from the mandala. || 93 ||
One obtains a disciplined son endowed with intelligence, health, and strength;
at the beginning and end of the ritual application, one should offer an oblation to the Vaṭuka.
"Having divided" means [the area] measuring slightly less than forty-nine *guñjās*. The mandala [is completed] in forty-nine days.
However, there is a specific distinction in the *Viśvasāroddhāra*:
O Goddess, having placed one pala of vacā powder together with a kuḍava and a pala of [other] substances upon a lotus leaf, one should set it down in the presence of the God.
Having worshipped the perfected ones (siddhas) according to the rules, the wise one should touch that medicinal herb and recite the mantra a thousand times while honoring the perfected ones.
Having meditated upon the goddess who has bathed after her menses, he should cause her to consume that great medicine. Thus [ends verses 93–94].
The wise have declared that the bali offering is of two kinds: rājasa and sāttvika.
The rājasa is rich in meat and blood, and consists of three palas. || 95 ||
Combined with mung-bean milk-porridge and stirred with the three sweets, this sattvic offering is devoid of meat; the remainder is as previously stated. || 96 ||
A Brāhmaṇa who is self-controlled and pure should offer a sattvic oblation;
with this mantra, he should prepare the ash that grants the accomplishment of all goals. || 97 ||
"Rājasa [is characterized by] an abundance of flesh and blood.
In this regard, when there is the inquiry as to what constitutes "flesh," it is specified as being "endowed with three *pala*s.
Therein, the three *pala*s consist of those produced from land-dwellers, sky-dwellers, and water-dwellers.
As it is stated in the Viśvasāroddhāra: "The meat of a ram and a cock,
rice cooked with ghee, parched grain flour, cakes, molasses, and sugarcane juice."
"Honey, fish, wood-apple, and so forth are declared to be the materials for the bali offering.
Thus it is said. [The offering] should consist of black pepper and cumin, as well as jaggery and sugar-candy, combined with cow's milk mixed with shali rice grains.
Saindhava salt, burnt by means of a fish, combined with three palas [of other ingredients]. Thus it is said.
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere: "The wise man, having mixed three *pala* of powdered *māṣa* beans with curd, milk, ghee, and jaggery-rice, [should offer it]."
Some read the text as "three fruits" (phalatrayam); that is to be considered. || 95-97 ||
Uśīra, sandalwood, kuṣṭha, camphor, saffron, the root of white arka, vārāhī, lakṣmī, and [the milky sap] of milk-trees. || 98 ||
Having dried the bark and root of the bilva tree, one should grind them into a fine powder;
this powder, mixed with cow dung collected from under the sky (in the open air), [is used]. || 99 ||
Having formed the funeral cakes and dried them,
one should burn them in the consecrated fire with the root mantra and cast the ashes into a pure vessel.
One should perfume the ashes purified by fire with *ketakī* and *mālatī* flowers;
then, having well-worshipped the ashes, one should touch them and recite the mantra ten thousand times. || 101 ||
Whoever takes this and applies it as a sectarian mark (puṇḍra) every day at dawn, their diseases, sorcery, malevolent acts, and great planetary afflictions shall perish. || 102 ||
No fear arises for him from enemies, thieves, wild beasts, or the like;
all his prosperities increase, and he is honored by all people. || 103 ||
The king, along with his ministers and retinue, shall become subject to him.
One should perform the consecration for the king who desires victory. || 104 ||
He explains the *bhasmasādhana* itself, beginning with "uśīram" and so forth.
*Ghanasāra* is camphor.
*Vārāhī* is *śūkarī*, *kācī*, *māgadhī*, *gṛṣṭi*, and *kārikā*.
Thus, in Kaiyaṭadeva’s Nighaṇṭu, the medicinal herb known as Vārāhī is well-known;
it is called Śamī, Lakṣmī, Śivā, Śītā, Māṅgalyā, and Keśahṛtphalā.

Thus, in Kaiyaṭadeva’s *Nighaṇṭu*, the word *lakṣmī* is said to denote the *śamī* tree. "Seized in the sky" means not touching the surface of the earth. A *puṇḍra* is a triple-mark (*tripuṇḍra*), that is, a horizontal tilaka.
"The deer is the tiger";
"one should perform the consecration" means within seven or five days.

Because of the statement, "or even for seven days or five days," one should perform the initial commencement after first selecting an auspicious day as the seventh or fifth [from that point]. (98–104)
In the previously described pavilion, which has been prepared and adorned with canopies and banners, one should draw a *sarvatobhadra* diagram and fill its pericarp. || 105 ||
Having placed eight *droṇas* of purified, auspicious *śāli* rice,
and half that amount of husked rice along with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken grains (*akṣata*) therein, || 106 ||
Having placed a pitcher fashioned from gold or other materials and endowed with the nine gems, and having filled it with pure water, one should cast [the following] into it. || 107 ||
Sprouts from milk-exuding trees, Lakṣmī, Dūrvā grass, and Sahā;
camphor, sandalwood, Bilva, Uśīra, and again Kuṅkuma. || 108 ||
One should wrap kaṅkola, aguru, jasmine, mallikā, campaka, and utpala,
along with gomedaka and pomegranate, with a pair of silk cloths.
He states the method of consecration (abhiṣeka) with the words "as previously stated.
This means "stated in the third [chapter]. Regarding "eight droṇas": [the meaning follows].
Half a khārī;
"half of that" means a fourth part of a khārī.
The nine gems are mentioned in the sixth [chapter].
*Pravāla* means sprouts.
*Sahā* is *sahadevī*.
"Gomeda is produced from leaves"—according to the Viśvakośa: "Gomedaka refers to a yellow gem, to the kakkola plant, and also to that which is produced from leaves. (105–109)
Having invoked Vaṭuka into that [vessel], one should worship him with the rājasa offering;
outside, in the eight jars, one should worship the eight Bhairavas. || 110 ||
One should worship the thirteen Gaṇas in the thirteen jars;
the wise practitioner should worship the Lokapālas in the ten outer jars. || 111 ||
Outside of that, in the eight jars, one should worship the lords of the gods beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha;
and in the thirty-five jars, one should worship in sequence the lords of the letters beginning with Ka.
Thus, one should properly worship the fivefold enclosure with perfumes and other offerings;
the supreme preceptor, having touched those jars, should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
*Rājasam* refers to the forms described in the *Rājasadhyāna*.
*Lokeśān* refers to the *lokeśa-vaṭukas*.
By the word "in sequence" (*kramāt*), it is indicated that there are thirty-two [deities] surrounding [the central one], and three to the south.
"Having touched" applies to both cases; [this is done] with a tuft of grass (*kūrca*) and so forth. (110–113)
One should offer a thousand oblations separately with milk-rice, clarified butter, and pure sesame seeds;
having touched those jars, one should present the bali offering every day.
In the manner prescribed by the king, the best of preceptors, having had the [text] recited by the twice-born on an auspicious day at a favorable moment during the night, || 115 ||

While auspicious and benedictory words were being recited by those pure [brahmins] who had mastered the Vedas, and while the five musical instruments resounded, he bowed down to Vaṭukeśvara. || 116 ||
One of clear intellect should consecrate as king that man who has conquered his senses, whose body is pure, who is dear to the brahmins, who is a believer, and whose speech is truthful. || 117 ||
The consecrated king, having prostrated before his supreme preceptor, should offer abundant sacrificial fees; thus the preceptor becomes pleased. || 118 ||
The consecrated king is truly the Indra of the earth;
he conquers rival monarchs and is praised by all people. (119)
"Separately" means individually. By that, there is a homa of three thousand [offerings] every day for seven days or five days.
Having performed his consecration, the lord of the earth rules over the entire earth, encircled by the four oceans, for six months each month. || 120 ||
By repeating this very [practice], he states the specific result with the words "kṛta" etc.
There are six repetitions, meaning one repetition every month for six months. || 120 ||

For the purpose of pacifying calamities concerning elephants and horses, the practitioner, having constructed a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in their stables according to the rules, should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rite. || 121 ||
One should daily feed three times ten thousand Brahmins with milk-rice, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and various kinds of foods, edibles, fruits, and so forth. || 122 ||
Regarding the word "gaja":

having established the pitchers (kumbhas) according to the previously mentioned procedure, having worshipped them with fragrant ointments, flowers, and so forth, and having prepared the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the rules, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rite; such is the connection [of the words].
In that context, "by the rite" means [drawing] a triangle.
"According to the rule" means having worshipped Vaṭuka in the fire and having honored Vaṭuka there. (121–122)
Having established the water-pots here according to the procedure previously described, the preceptor,
having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, should sprinkle the elephants with their waters.
By this very means, their stables increase day by day, and in battles, great power arises, even greater than before. || 124 ||
All diseases perish, as do the malevolent spells and acts of hostility committed by others;
there is no protection greater than this for them upon the surface of the earth. || 125 ||
Having consecrated the protector of the earth who is intent on victory over his enemies, the minister should offer the bali-oblation at night according to the prescribed rite. || 126 ||
According to the method previously described;
according to the fourth method.
"The jars" refers to five.
Here,
[the word] "in five jars" means "having worshipped."
In the center is Vaṭuka and Īśāna; the remaining four are the other forms—this is the sense.
And it has been said:
"Having established the fivefold state upon a pure ground smeared with cow-dung..."
One should place five beautiful jars in the enclosures according to the sequence of creation.
One should again fill each [vessel] separately with water scented with incense and other fragrances;
[and place therein] ruby, pearl, diamond, sapphire, and likewise emerald.
Having cast the five jewels that have been prescribed into those five [vessels], one should worship the deity and the [five] forms there according to the ritual injunctions. Thus it is said.
But elsewhere it is said: "Gold, silver, pearl, rājāvarta, and coral—
these are declared to be the five jewels."
The connection is that one should sprinkle the elephants, the horses, and the stables—that is, the elephant-stables and horse-stables.
Those are the elephants and horses.
[It is said: "Power is born."
The word "of them" (teṣām) is understood to carry over [from the previous verse].

It also applies to the phrase "the diseases perish. The section ending with "having consecrated" (abhiṣicya) and "he should take away" (haret) is a restatement of the previously mentioned consecration and bali-offering. (123–126)

Having slain the goat, which is free from deficient limbs and was previously described as being of the *rājasa* nature, [one should offer it] at the time of presenting the oblation, together with the entire army of one's enemies. 127 //
One of refined intellect should offer [the oblation] as a *bali* to Vaṭuka;
likewise, the wise one should interpose the name of the enemy within the *bali-mantra*. || 128 ||
Day after day, together with your own retinue and accompanied by dogs, devour the blood and flesh of the enemy faction. || 129 ||
This is declared to be the bali-mantra, which bestows victory upon all.
Delighted by this offering, Vaṭuka shall [destroy] the enemy army. || 130 ||
One should distribute all food among the troops with an angry mind;
when this is done, the enemy force is destroyed—of this there is no doubt. By this means, a king attains the glory of victory without effort. || 131 ||
He states the specific distinction regarding that very point with the words beginning "not deficient," etc. (vv. 127–131).
One should write the glorious *māyā* (hrīṃ), *smara* (klīṃ), and *kūṭa* (sauḥ) here in the center;

on the eight petals, the word *vaṭukāya* repeated twice; and the other letters of the mantra on the outside. Then, on the sixteen petals (eight pairs) outside of that, and subsequently on petals of that same number (thirty-two).
One should draw the yantra within the outer enclosure (bhūpura), beginning with the thirty-two petals and including all the letters from 'ka' to 'sa'.
This yantra is a deliverer from calamities, a remover of the fear of untimely death, a constant bestower of all prosperity, and a granter of all good fortune. || 133 ||
It is a protector for those afflicted by malevolent planets, and it increases the victory of kings;
because it delivers one from calamity, it is capable of rescuing one from distress. || 134 ||
Those who know mantras say that there is no other mantra in the tantras.
He speaks of the yantra as "śrīmāya": *śrī* is the seed-syllable *śrī*.
Māyā is the seed-syllable of power (śakti-bīja). Smara is the seed-syllable of desire (kāma-bīja), namely *klīṃ*.
Kūṭa is *kṣrīṃ*.
In the center of the pericarp.
As it is stated in the *Viśvasāroddhāra*:
"First, the wise one should place the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī there in the middle of the pericarp."
Then, having placed the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should place the seed-syllable of Kāma thereafter.

Then, one should extract the mantra of the pericarp (kaṇīkā), which consists of the peak syllable (kūṭākṣara) followed by the fire-syllable (ra) conjoined with the māyā-syllable (ī), and combined with four seed-syllables. Thus it is said.
By this, the interpretation of certain [authorities] that one should draw a diagram (kūṭa) in the form of the god of love (Smara) is refuted.
On the eight petals, one should write according to the sequence of single syllables beginning with "Baṭukāya.
This refers to the syllables of the mantra.
[The letters] beginning with Ā and ending with Māyā [are placed] on the first sixteen petals;
"outside of that" means outside of the first sixteen petals.
On sixteen petals corresponding to that number;
above that, on the second set of sixteen petals, one should write the sixteen vowels. || 132-134 ||
Arghīśa is the peak of fire; that which stands at the end of *la* is declared to be the end of *da*. || 135 ||
This Caṇḍa mantra, ending with *phaṭ* and consisting of three syllables, has been proclaimed;
its sage is said to be Trika, and its meter is declared to be Anuṣṭubh. || 136 ||
Caṇḍeśa is declared to be the presiding deity; one should again perform the ritual of the limbs (aṅgavidhi).
"Dīpta Phaṭ" is declared as the heart, and "Jvala Phaṭ" is said to be the head. || 137 ||
Śikhā is known as *jvālāmālinī* phaṭ; phaṭ is considered the armor (*kavaca*).
"Hana phaṭ" is declared to be the eye (*netra*), and "sarvajvālini phaṭ" is supreme.
Having thus performed the assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should then meditate upon the deity. || 138 ||
He states the fierce mantra: "Argīśa," etc.
Argīśa is *ū*. The letter ending in *d* is *dh*. That which resides at the end of *l* is the fire-peak (*vahniśikhara*), by which [is meant] *rdhva*.
The syllable *ū* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *phaṭ* is the power (*śakti*). "Trika" is the name of the seer (*ṛṣi*). 135–138.
I meditate upon Caṇḍeśvara in my heart— red-bodied, three-eyed, adorned with red garments,
holding a ṭaṅka-axe, a trident, and a crystal rosary.
Bearing a water-pot and having the moon as his crest-ornament. || 139 ||
He describes the meditation: "Caṇḍeśvara," etc.
*Ṭaṅka* means an axe.
This has been stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"Bearing a trident, an axe, a discus, and a rosary, he has three eyes.
Thus is the visualization of the weapons, starting from the upper left and ending with the lower left. 139.

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice (homa) consisting of one-tenth that number, using pure sesame seeds and rice grains mixed with the three sweets. || 140 ||
One should properly worship Caṇḍeśa on the seat (pīṭha) proclaimed by the five syllables;
when the form has been fashioned with the seed-syllable, that [syllable] is joined with the bindu upon the tortoise. || 141 ||
The worship mantra for Caṇḍeśvara is considered to be preceded by the seed-syllable *hṛt* (namas).
One should worship him with the limbs (*aṅga*), the Mothers, all the weapons beginning with the vajra, and so forth. || 142 ||
*Tad* is the seed-syllable;
*kūrma* is the letter *ca*. (140–141)
He states the mantra for worship: "Caṇḍa... and so forth.
*Caṇḍeśvarāya* is the essential form;
*hṛt* is *namaḥ*.
"Preceded by its own seed-syllable" means preceded by its own *bīja*.
And the Teachers have stated that one should recite the *gāyatrī*;
as they say:
Having uttered "Caṇḍa Caṇḍāya," one should say the word "vidmahe" as before;
then, having said "Caṇḍeśvarāya," one should utter the word "dhīmahi."
Having said "Tannaścaṇḍa," one should further recite "Pracodayāt.
This Caṇḍagāyatrī brings about the presence [of the deity] through its recitation. Thus [it is said]. (142)
The fourfold enclosure has been declared for the worship of Caṇḍeśa; when the mantra is thus perfected, the practitioner of the mantra becomes wealthy without delay. || 143 ||
One should daily satisfy [the deity] one hundred and eight times with this mantra;
thus, endowed with sons and friends, one attains great prosperity.
"One attains glory" means that it begins with the seed-syllable *śrī*. || 144 ||
If the practitioner of mantras offers ten thousand oblations into a fire kindled with the wood of that [tree] using full-blown priyaṅgu flowers, agitation arises before him. || 145 ||
By the word "mantrī," it is indicated that [the mantra] begins with the seed-syllable of Durgā. || 145 ||
Having ground the bark of the *sādhya* tree together with salt and flour, one should fashion a beautiful effigy and consecrate it with the wind-mantra (*samīraṇa*). || 146 ||
Having repeatedly cut [the effigy], one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times at night;
by doing this for seven days, the person to be subdued will become a slave of his own accord. || 147 ||
Regarding the phrase "the tree of the person to be accomplished" (sādhyavṛkṣa): the bark of the tree belonging to the asterism of that person to be accomplished is what is meant;
he will describe those [trees] in the twenty-second [chapter].
*Piṣṭa* means rice-flour.
As it has been stated by the Teachers:
"With the well-ground and finely polished powders of the *sādhya*-constellation, the foot [of the *sādhya*], *rapa*, and *carman*, together with salt..."
"Having fashioned a doll, whether stationary or moving, and having recited [the mantra] at night, one should perform the fire offering (*homa*). Thus [it is said regarding] the doll:
it should be ninety-six finger-breadths in length.
"Having established the breath (prāṇa) in the wind" means by way of twenty-three modes.
"Cutting again and again" refers to the manner that will be explained in the twenty-second [chapter].
Regarding the term "the one to be accomplished":
the gender is not intended to be restrictive;
one may bring under control both a man and a woman.
As it has been said:

"If a man [practices this] for seven days, or if a woman [practices] for a long time, he will certainly become submissive; there is no room for objection here that in this very birth, for in another body there may be doubt. Thus it is stated.
