And yet, when it is stated in general terms that "it is to be accomplished," this refers to [substances] such as seeds and the like.
Regarding the specific details therein, the *Nārāyaṇīya* states: "Having kindled a fire with *apāmārga* plants, a twice-born man shall thus bring [another] under his control.
When the fire is blazing, he should likewise offer oblations using funeral pyre wood and an image [of the target]."
"In this way, the king shall be brought under control; indeed, he shall be submissive to the Vaiśya and the Śūdra. Thus it is said.
In this context, one should understand that [the practitioner] becomes a servant through desire and so forth. (146–147)
One who is proficient in the Śaiva mantras should worship the Caṇḍeśvara mantra;
such a person attains all desires and rejoices both in this world and in the hereafter. || 148 ||
By the phrase "in the Śaiva mantras," this is what is meant:
as many recitations of the Caṇḍeśvara mantra as there are, so many should be the recitations of the six-syllabled Śaiva mantra.
As they say: "As many times as the three-syllabled [mantra] is recited, so many times should the six-syllabled one be recited."
For in this way, a person attains success pertaining to both this world and the next. Thus it is said.
"Regarding the phrase 'all desires':
one should offer oblations of rice grains mixed with sesame seeds into a fire of gold-wood for the sake of Arka;
for Unmāda, there is an oblation of milk, and its pacification occurs in a fire of Khadira wood. Thus it is said.

Whatever flowers correspond to the [desired] colors, if the practitioner performs the fire-oblation with them for seven days, he shall obtain a dwelling in that very form; this mantra destroys debt and grants all desires.
Such [passages] are to be understood as beginning with this. || 148 ||
Salutations again and again to Śaṅkara, who consists of the forms of earth, water, fire, wind, ether, Yama, Indra, the Moon, and the Sun, and who dwells within all beings. || 149 ||
The praise of Śiva follows at the end of the Śaiva mantras beginning with "dhara. By the verse beginning with "dhara," his nature as the eightfold form (aṣṭamūrti) is declared.
"Makheśa" refers to the sacrificer (yajamāna). || 149 ||
Salutations again and again to the one who has made his abode in the end of the Vedas, to the Veda itself, to the source of the Vedas, to the Great Splendor beyond the senses, the eternal. || 150 ||
Regarding the phrase "śrutyante":

because it is the subject matter expounded by the Upaniṣads, the term is used figuratively to mean "having made its dwelling there. "Śrutaye" means "for the sake of Śruti," that is, for the sake of that which is of the nature of Śruti.
To him from whom the birth of the Śrutis [the Vedas] proceeds;
thus, to the proclaimer of the beginningless Veda.
"To the one beyond the senses" (atīndriyāya).
For it is said in the Śruti: "From which words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach it. (150)
Salutations be to you, Śambhu, who cannot be defined through the divisions of gross and subtle;
salutations to Bhava, the destroyer of the suffering born of worldly existence. || 151 ||
"To Bhava," that is, to the one named Bhava;
"Bhava" means birth, [and it refers to] the destroyer of the suffering of that [birth]. || 151 ||
Homage again and again to the All-Knowing One, who is far beyond the path of logic, who bestows the fruits of austerities, and who is generous in granting the four aims of human life. || 152 ||
Reasoning is fallacious reasoning;
[salutation] to the bestower of the fourfold aims of life. 152.

Salutations again and again to the Great One, who is empty of beginning, middle, and end; to Him who has cast off all fear; to the object of meditation for yogis; to the one devoid of qualities. || 153 ||
Salutations again and again to the Soul of the Universe, the inconceivable one, whose crest is the shimmering moon; to the one who destroys the pride of Kandarpa, the slayer of Time. || 154 ||
The beginning is creation, the middle is preservation, and the end is dissolution; therein [the Lord is] for the sake of the void,
because no fruit is attained,
and for the sake of the inconceivable.
Because of the absence of limitation;
[salutation] to Kāla and Antaka. 153–154.
Salutations again and again to him who dwells as a consumer of poison, who has attained the shoulders of a bull, and whose matted locks are bound together like a garland of rivers. || 155 ||
Salutations again and again to the pure one, whose nature is purity, the inner self of the pure; to the destroyer of the city [of the body], the full, whose name is auspicious. || 156 ||

Salutations again and again to the Lord of the Universe, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon his own devotees, who is himself free from desire, and who dwells in the void. || 157 ||
To him by whom that very river Gaṅgā was bound as a wreath upon his *kaparda*—that is, his mass of matted hair (*jaṭājūṭa*).
The lexicon states: "His *kaparda* is his mass of matted hair. (155–157)
Salutations again and again to the one who is the root of the three forms, to the three-eyed one;
salutations again and again to the one whose form is the abode of the three luminaries, to the destroyer of rebirth. || 158 ||
Salutations again and again to the Beloved, whose feet are reddened by the rays from the crest-jewels of the gods and asuras, who has given half of his own body to his beloved.
With this hymn of praise during worship, one should devoutly propitiate the Supreme Lord, the omniscient Master of the universe, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 160 ||
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the *Śāradātilaka* composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra. 20.
"Bth" refers to the three forms of the Trimūrti, namely the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
"Of the three abodes" refers to the sun, fire, and moon. (158–160)
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition. 20.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter;
now begins the section on the Gāyatrī.
Now, therefore, I shall expound the Gāyatrī in its true nature as consisting of the three Vedas, by which Brahman—characterized as Being, Consciousness, and Bliss—is revealed. (1)
Having thus stated the five Tantric mantras of the deities, he begins to state some Vedic mantras, such as the Gāyatrī and others, with the words "Now then" (*atho*).
She is "of the nature of reality" (*tattvarūpām*) because the twenty-four syllables consist of the essence of the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*);
these syllables will be explained in the section on the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
By this, the assignment of the principles (*tattvanyāsa*) along with the syllables of the *gāyatrī* is also indicated.

By the phrase "consisting of the three Vedas" (*trayīmayīm*), it is stated that by reciting this [mantra] properly according to the rules, one attains the fruit of reciting the three Vedas— that *gāyatrī* by which Brahman, characterized as Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), is revealed.
Thereafter, he will explain at the end that the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) is the means for realizing That.
The Teachers have stated that the *vyāhṛtis* and so forth are the means for realizing That:
"The *vyāhṛtis* begin with the word *bhūḥ*; the word *bhūḥ* exists in That."
That state is declared to be "Being" (sat), because it consists solely of that and because it is the ground of all beings.
Because it is real and because it is the cause, the word *bhuvaḥ* is connected [to the previous];
and because it takes all as its own through its own nature, it is called *svariti*.
Because of its greatness (*mahattva*) and its majesty (*mahaḥ*), it is connected with the word *mahaḥ*;
that indeed is the entire multitude of people, and therefore the personified utterance (*vyāhṛti*) is *janaḥ*.
It is remembered as austerity through the nature of knowledge, and likewise as suffering;
it is remembered as truth because of its supremacy, its being the Self, and its infinite knowledge.
Next, the relationship between the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis* is stated:
the syllable *a* is *bhūr*, the syllable *u* is *bhuvaḥ*, and the syllable *m* is said to be *svar*.
Bindu is Mahas, likewise Nada is Jana, Śakti is known as Tapas,
and Śānti is declared to be Satya— that which is the supreme state.
Here too, that subject previously mentioned is now described in detail;
next, the identity of the Praṇava, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Gāyatrī is declared.
By this [mantra], the singular dual form refers to that which is the cause of the creation and so forth of all things, existing in the solar orb as light.
That which is to be meditated upon, the supreme bliss, is designated as the Supreme Brahman;
it is that which is expressed by the word "Savitṛ" in the nominative singular case.
In this context, [the term] is derived from a verbal root denoting the procreation of living beings;
thus, it refers eternally to the progenitor of all classes of living beings.
It is remembered as *vareṇya* because it is worthy of being chosen (*varaṇīyatva*),
that is, because it is to be served, worshipped by all, and prayed to.
Thus, for the first eight-syllable [mantra], the *vyāhṛti* is declared to be "Bhūḥ";
it is called "Bharga" because of its burning (*bharjana*) of evil, and likewise because of its being affectionate toward its devotees (*bhaktasnigdha*).
Of the god who is eternally endowed with qualities such as the bestowing of rain,
and who likewise shines with abundant splendor.
The word *dhīmahi* is derived from the verbal root *dhyai*, meaning "to contemplate";
[we contemplate] with that divine eye which consists of knowledge and is foremost among the Vedas (*nigama*).
The visible golden deity is the Sun, eternally established;
he whose splendor is devoid of inferiority is "golden" (hiraṇmaya).
We always contemplate thus: "I am that which is subtle.
In this way, the second eight-syllable mantra's utterance is declared to be *Bhuvaḥ*.

The word *dhiyaḥ* refers to the intellects (*buddhi*) and the mind (*manas*); the form *yaḥ* is used because of Vedic usage (*chāndasa*), and there is a change of gender (*liṅgavyatyāsa*) based on the rule regarding suffixes, inflections, and voices (*suptiṅupagraha*).
That incomparable splendor of yours, which consists of all the Vedas and deities,
is said here to be the cause for the destruction of the sins of those who worship it.
The grammatical substitute *naḥ* is prescribed for the genitive plural of the word *asmad*; therefore, the meaning is "of us. The word *pracodayāt* is used in the sense of a prayer or entreaty.
The third [foot] of the eight-syllable [pāda] is also declared to have the *svarita* accent.
Thus, it is remembered that this [verse] consists of ten pādas, three of which are eight-syllabled.
There are four [verses] consisting of six syllables each and [one] consisting of twenty-four syllables;
such is this [hymn] of the great god Savitṛ.
May that supreme Bharga, the most excellent one who effects the destruction of the sins of those who worship him,
whom we have meditated upon— may he impel our intellects.
Thus has the Gāyatrī been described here; now its head is stated:
"Water, light, and essence"—by this, the splendor of Soma and Agni is expressed.
The entire world is composed of that; it is known as the two-fold essence of nectar and fire.
Because it is imperishable and because of its abundance, it is called Brahman.
When Brahman, whose nature is bliss and which is characterized by existence, knowledge, and so forth,
is expressed as "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," it is proclaimed as "so 'ham" (I am that).
"But this [work] is called the 'Head' because it is the head of the essence of the Vedas. || 1 ||
In the *Prapañcasāra Tantra*, chapter 30, verses 7–31:
The seven *vyāhṛtis* beginning with *praṇava* (OM) should follow the word "tat" (*tat-pada*) and so forth.
The *gāyatrī* consisting of twenty-four syllables is joined with the *śiras*. (2)
This mantra is proclaimed as the essence extracted from all the Vedas;
Brahmā, the Goddess, the Gāyatrī, and the Supreme Self are thus declared [to be its forms]. || 3 ||
These sages and others are proclaimed by the seers as the Ṛṣis of the Praṇava:
Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Bhṛgu, Gautama, and Kaśyapa.
They know Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha to be the sages (ṛṣis) of the vyāhṛtis;
furthermore, [the meters] are Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Paṅkti. || 5 ||
The Triṣṭubh and Jagatī meters have been declared by the wise.
[The lords of the quarters are] Anila (the Wind) in the seven rivers, Sūrya (the Sun), Vākpati (the Lord of Speech), Varuṇa, and Vṛṣa (the Bull). || 6 ||
The Viśvedevas are proclaimed as their respective deities in order;
for the Gāyatrī, the sage is said to be the highly effulgent Viśvāmitra. || 7 ||
It is said that the meter (chandas) is Gāyatrī, and the deity (devatā) is remembered as Savitṛ.
With its head (śiras), the sage (muni) is Brahmā, and the meter is remembered as Devyādika. || 8 ||
The wise have declared that the Supreme Self (Paramātman) is the deity of this Gāyatrī.
The phrase "beginning with the Praṇava" is to be connected with each individual Vyāhṛti;
the phrase "beginning with the word 'tat'" is to be connected with what follows.
Regarding the phrase "from the head":
"Oṃ āpo jyotī raso'mṛtaṃ brahma bhūrbhuvaḥ svarom. The connection is that the sages have proclaimed that the seer (ṛṣi) and other [components] of the Praṇava have been thus described.
The ritual procedure for this has been stated, beginning with the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and so forth: "The syllable *re* shall be the seed-syllable; the letter *ya* is called the power (*śakti*);
and *ṇi* is declared to be the bolt (*kīlaka*) of the three-footed Gāyatrī. Thus [it is said].
In another ritual manual: "That which is the seed-syllable (bīja) is the power (śakti), and the nasal (ṇa) is the pin (kīlaka).
The seven vyāhṛtis, beginning with Bhūḥ, [are placed] on the heart, the two faces, the two shoulders, and the pair of thighs.
Having placed [the syllables] in the belly, the knower of mantras should place the syllables of the Gāyatrī on the body:
in the joints of the feet, in the penis, in the navel, and in the heart, throat, and joints of the arms. || 10 ||

Furthermore, the practitioner [should visualize] on the face, nose, cheeks, eyes, ears, eyebrows, and head, as well as on the western, northern, southern, eastern, and upward-facing [directions]. || 11 ||
By the statement "one who knows the mantra should perform the nyāsa," it is implied that after having performed the placement of the *praṇava*, the seven *vyāhṛtis* are likewise to be placed.
As they say: "Aṃ, salutation to Brahmā at the navel; uṃ, and to Viṣṇu at the heart;
maṃ, salutation to Śiva on the head—one should perform the placement while recollecting each respective form."
Regarding the phrase "at the joints of the feet": there are four syllables at the four joints of the two feet.
As it has been said: "at the four joints of the two feet."
This ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is to be performed beginning from the fingers.
Although the word "joint" (*sandhi*) is mentioned here, it should nevertheless be understood that the placement is to be prescribed specifically upon the limbs themselves.
Thus, there are four syllables for the four joints of the two arms.
In the Nyāsa and other rites, each individual syllable [is used].
By treating the word *ṇiya* as distinct, it consists of twenty-four syllables.
By the term "practitioner" (*sādhaka*), it is indicated that the Praṇava (Oṃ) is placed at the beginning of each syllable and the word *namaḥ* at the end.
But in another Kalpa, however:
"Now I shall declare the assignment of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa), as well as the seer, the meter, and the deity;
having remembered the principles (tattva), the powers (śakti), the phonemes, and the mudrās, one should assign the phonemes in their proper order."
The yellow [mudrā] called Mitroktāgnicālāhlādinī consists of hands with fingers curved;
it destroys delusion and sin when directed forward, and it is performed with the two big toes.
The *madhucchandas* [mudrā] is the sounding of water; the *prabhā* is dark like the interior of a lotus bud;
the *samukha* and *sampuṭa* destroy minor sins; and the *saṃ* [mudrā] is at the two ankles.
Born from the splendor of the sun at midday in the Garga region, Kapila has outstretched hands with extended and upturned fingers;
his *viṃ* [mark] on the shanks destroys all sins.
Upamanyu, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyut, Vāyu, and Viśvabhṛt;
[this is] the Vistīrṇa hand-gesture, formed by joining the palms with the index fingers extended and released.
The knee [should be] like a sapphire, destroying diseases and planetary afflictions;
[the presiding deities are] Kaśyapa, Supratiṣṭhā, Yama, Kha, and Vilāsinī.
Resembling fire, with the two hands joined face-to-face and the little fingers interlocked,
while the other fingers are spread apart and the two thumbs are joined together.
The wise practitioner should place the two-faced [mantra] which destroys the sin of foeticide upon the thighs;
Bhṛgu, the Goddess, water, and fragrance are the radiant forms of the two preceding [limbs].
The three-faced [mantra], through the application of the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), removes the sin of approaching those who should not be approached in the secret place; it is *reṃ*.
The four-faced [mantra] consists of the *atyaṣṭi* and *uṣṇih* meters, with the essence at the beginning, and its play is like lightning.
From the middle yoga, the syllable *ṇiṃ* removes the sin of eating forbidden food;
it belongs to Viṣṇu, is in the Anuṣṭubh meter, has the name Virūpākṣa, and consists of five faces.
From the union with the ring finger comes Hatyāhara; likewise, from the union with the hip come Hārīta, Bṛhatīndra, Tvak, Kīrti, and Nīla. Thus it is for those two.

When the little fingers of two hands joined horizontally are released, it is the *Ṣaṇmukha* mudrā; it destroys the sin of killing a human and is known as the *Bhaṃ* mudrā of Yājñavalkya, to be placed at the navel.
The syllable *paṃ* is the bearer of the lineage of knowledge; the word *durgā* is red and faces downward;
with the hand formed by the tips of the curved fingers, the syllable *rgoṃ* in the belly brings benefit to cattle.

The poet’s [mudrā] consists of the *triṣṭubh* and *anuṣṭubh* meters; for the two hands, with palms facing upward as before, one should form a cupped *añjali* gesture pervaded by red luster, and place them upon the breasts to remove female afflictions.

One should know that the Aṅgiras mudrā is the *jagatī* [hand position]; for Śarva, the hands are joined with the thumbs at the tips released; the *śakaṭa* mudrā consists of two fists, and for the Guru, it is placed at the heart.
Yama is seated upon the earth in the lap of Tvaṣṭṛ, possessing a golden complexion;
with his two hands closed in fists, his left index finger is extended upward.
The Vakrāgra, when joined with Nyubjā, removes the mental sins of the throat;
Āpastamba, Śakvarī, Pāyu, Āpyāyinī, and Vasu [are likewise].
The two bright hands, facing each other with fingers interlaced and thumbs extended,
joined at the mouth in the *grathitaka* mudrā with the syllable *dhīṃ*, removes the sins of the ancestors (or the king).
In the *saṃvarta* [mudrā], the two index fingers (*marutpādau*) are pure and have the luster of rubies;
the left [index finger] has its tip pointing upward, while the other is likewise but with its tip pointing downward.
Facing well toward the front, the syllable *maṃ* in the middle of the palate destroys former sins;
Kātyāyana, Trivṛt, Soma, and the ear—may I be free from poison.
Two [types] have their tips turned upward and elevated; "lamba" has a hanging nose, while "hin" has a sunken one.
"Asita" has excessively long limbs, "atyaṅgirā" has skin [the color of] gold, and "pāṇḍu" is so called because of its pale complexion.
With the hands joined together and palms facing upward, one should place them before the eyes;
Vyāsa, Dhṛti, the gods, Cakṣus, Sūkṣma, and Rakta are positioned face-to-face.

The two *akaniṣṭha* [fingers] joined together, with the tips of the remaining [fingers] bent and joined—this is the seal that destroys the sin of killing fish and other living beings; the twice-born should place it between the eyebrows.
Parāśara, Dhṛti, Dasra, Jihvā, Yoni, and Rukmaruk;
the tortoise is stepped upon on the back, facing downward with his right side [pressed down].
This [deity] on the forehead is the destroyer of all sins; Śaṅku, Kṛti, and Prajāpati are located there.
Jayā is the vital breath (prāṇa), shining like a crane (valākā); from the two armpits, the hands along with their supports [emerge].
The boar-faced deity (Vārāha) is in the middle of the upper left; he bestows happiness and wealth upon the eastern face.
The deities whose nature is the conch reside in the heart, the lotus, and the two ears, which are blue.
With fingers extended, the lion [mudrā] at the right face bestows prosperity; with the right hand in the form of Śiva, I am Śivā; "Mā hara" (Do not take) refers to the two hands previously mentioned.
With the tips slightly curved, it is the "Great Stride" (mahākrānta) when held upward; it bestows the state of Hari.
When concealed in the form of Gautama, it is the mallet (mudgara) with the two hands slightly raised.
With the right fist grasping the index finger of the left hand, [this mudrā] bestows the bliss of Brahman; O Western Face, grant this!
Śātātapa, Kṛtivīṣṇu, Guṇa, and Bhadreśa, assuming various forms—
some facing south, some with faces turned downward, and others with sprouts upon their heads— what indeed is the song of the barley?
Thus [ends the section] 9–11.
The knower of mantras should place ten steps in these locations:

on the head, between the eyebrows, the heart, and the mouth; on the throat, the heart, the navel, and the private parts; on the two knees and the pair of feet; and he should place that head upon his own head. || 12 ||
He states the placement of the words with the phrase "the words," meaning in these [sections] that are about to be described. The words, however, are as follows:
by means of one, three, two, fire (three), two, fire (three), two, one, and one syllable respectively.

In another ritual manual (*kalpa*), even the placement of the head-word is mentioned: "Oṃ! Water in the two breasts, splendor in the nose, taste in the eyes, nectar in the mouth, Brahman in the head, and *bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ* in the tuft of hair. Thus [ends verse 12].
The heart is declared for Brahmā; the head is said to be for Viṣṇu;
the tuft (śikhā) is for Rudra; and the armor (kavaca) is said to be for Īśvara. || 13 ||
The eye is said to belong to Sadāśiva, and the weapon is remembered as belonging to the Soul of All;
thus the six limbs have been described, and one should assign them to their respective places. || 14 ||
He states the six limbs [of the mantra] with the words "of Brahmā.
The author's intended meaning throughout is that the extraction of the Ātmanepada form is implied by the phrase "the weapon is remembered as being for the Universal Self" (astraṃ sarvātmane smṛtam).
Thus, the practical application is: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Heart, which is the Self of Brahmā," and so forth.
The traditionalists, however, [prescribe]: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ; that [splendor] of Savitṛ, to the Self of Brahmā—[this is] the heart. To the most excellent, to the Self of Viṣṇu—[this is] the head.
To the splendor of the God, to the Self of Rudra—[this is] the crest-lock."

They prescribe the arrangement of the six limbs as follows: "We meditate upon" is for the armor (*kavaca*) to the Self who is the Lord; "who [awakens] our thoughts" is for the eye (*netra*) to the Self who is Sadāśiva; and "may he impel" is for the weapon (*astra*) to the Universal Self (*sarvātman*).
But in another Kalpa:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva are, in order, the six limbs—beginning with the Vyāhṛtis—of that [deity] who is the essence of the splendor of all souls. Thus it is said.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the three *vyāhṛtis* and the three words are included;
the application is as follows: *oṃ bhūr brahmatejase*, and so forth. (13–14)
I bow to Sāvitrī, who possesses three eyes with faces having the lusters of pearl, coral, gold, sapphire, and white;
who is adorned with a jeweled crown set with the moon; whose essence consists of the principles and the letters;
and who holds in her hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a goad, a whip, a bright skull-cup, and a cord.
I worship her who carries a conch, a discus, and a pair of lotuses in her hands. || 15 ||
He speaks of meditation with the words "liberated" and so forth.
*Kaśā* is the whip, a cord for striking horses and the like.
*Śubhram* (bright/white) is an adjective qualifying the skull-cup (*kapāla*).
The cord is a quality (guṇa).
As for the meditation on the weapons:
in the two upper right hands are the discus and conch, and in the two lower ones are the discus and conch.
Below those two are a noose and a skull-bowl;
below those two are a whip and a goad;
and below those two are the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting.
In this context, immediately after meditation, one should display the mudrās such as the Varada and others;
as they say:
"One should display the Varada, Abhaya, Lotus, King of Birds, and Śakti mudrās."
Meditation at the three junctions of the day,
as follows:
[one should meditate on her] mounted upon a swan, seated upon a white lotus, adorned with ornaments of red gems, and possessing an eye in her forehead.

One should meditate upon Gāyatrī, the mother of the three worlds, who is worthy of worship at the morning twilight; she holds a rosary called the Veda, a sacrificial ladle, a lotus, and a staff in her four arms; she is the Ṛg-savitrī, of youthful age, and resides within the orb of the fierce-rayed sun.
O Mother of the Universe, worshipped by the gods, auspicious Gāyatrī, daughter of Brahmā;
I invoke you for the sake of worship—come, O destroyer of sin, and purify me!
The Goddess, whose vehicle is the lord of bulls, bears a blazing trident;
she wears white garments and is adorned with ornaments of white serpents.
Adorned with white garlands and a rosary, she is red in color and the consort of Śaṅkara;
she bears matted locks, she is the earth, the supporter, the source of the earth, and she is born from the body of the Lord of Existence (Bhava).
O Mother Bhavānī, Sovereign of the Universe, come and purify me;
you are the evening twilight, Kṛṣṇā, Viṣṇu’s deity, and Sarasvatī.
Moving through the sky, she has a black face; another [form] holds a conch and a discus.
She is adorned with black garlands and ornaments, the supreme one who consists of all knowledge.
"O Mother Vāgdevatā, whose beautiful hands hold a lute and a rosary, whose excellent face is graced with a smile—you who are worthy of praise—come when called and purify me! (15)
Having first performed breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should recite the Gāyatrī at the two twilights, joined with the seven vyāhṛtis and accompanied by the Śiras. || 16 ||
Reciting [the mantra] three times with the intellect, one should restrain the vital breaths with a concentrated mind;
this is declared to be *prāṇāyāma*, which removes all sins. || 17 ||

The plural number in the word *prāṇāyāmān* (breath-restraints) is restricted to the number three according to the principle of the *kapiñjala-adhikaraṇa*. He states their very nature [as follows]: "Seven," etc.
The connection is that one should recite it three times with the intellect. || 16-17 ||
The initiated one, subsisting on alms and with senses subdued, should recite the Gāyatrī joined with the three Vyāhṛtis one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rule.
Regarding the *vyāhṛtis*:
the first consists of the triad of *vyāhṛtis*.
However, it should be understood that one who seeks liberation (*mokṣārthin*) should recite [the Gāyatrī] together with the fourth quarter: "parorajase sāvadom."
Its seer (ṛṣi) is Vimala, its meter (chandas) is Gāyatrī, and its deity (devatā) is the Supreme Self (paramātman). "A hundred thousand according to the principles" means twenty-four hundred thousand.
"By the rite" means by that which was prescribed for the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary preparatory practice). || 18 ||

For the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra, one should offer three thousand oblations each of milk-rice, sesame seeds, dūrvā grass, and the excellent fuel-sticks of the milk-tree, individually. || 19 ||
Regarding "milk-rice" (kṣīraudana):
milk, cooked rice, sesame seeds, and dūrvā grass constitute the fourfold set of substances.
The milk-yielding trees are the aśvattha, udumbara, plakṣa, and vaṭa. || 19 ||
Having fashioned a mandala with a brilliant triangular pericarp, the wise one should worship the solar pedestal there with the nine powers beginning with Dīptā.
One should worship the Goddess in the form fashioned with the root mantra.
Regarding the "maṇḍala," it is the *sarvatobhadra*.
The meaning is that one should draw a tripled (*triguṇita*) yantra within its pericarp, which is radiant with three triangles;
for the word "triangle" (*trikoṇa*) serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) for the tripled [yantra].
As it was said by the Teachers: "Now, when the most excellent and variegated mandala, tripled,
has been described," as previously stated therein.
"Blazing and so forth" refers to those described in the fourteenth chapter. (20–21)
In the three corners, Brahmā and the others should be worshipped, and outside, the Śaktis. || 21 ||
Then the Ādityas and others, together with Ūṣā and the rest, should be worshipped in sequence.
Thereafter, one should worship the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) according to the rule upon the filaments.
"In the corners" means in the southeast, west, and northeast. "Brahmā and the others" refers to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa.
The powers (śaktis) are those named Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī. "In the three corners" means specifically in the eastern, southwestern, and northwestern sectors.
With these, the first enclosure is completed.

Although it is stated here that [the deities] beginning with Brahmā [are to be worshipped], nevertheless, the worship of the Śaktis should be known as preceding it, according to the statement of the Ācārya: "Having first worshipped the forms of the three Śaktis."

Elsewhere it is also said: "One should likewise conquer Gāyatrī in the [direction] born of the hundred-sacrificed one (Agni), Sāvitrī in that arisen from the night-walker (Rākṣasa/NW), Sarasvatī in the one gone by wind (Vāyu/NE),
Brahmā in the fire-eater (Agni/SE), Viṣṇu in the one belonging to Varuṇa (NW), and Īśa in the sixth spoke (SW)."

Elsewhere as well: "Gāyatrī, red in color, dressed in red, four-faced, and holding a water-pot, a rosary, and a lotus, stands in the eastern corner; Brahmā, who resides in the southeast, is like her."
Sāvitrī, holding a lotus, a discus, an arrow, and a mace in her hands, adorned with a crown and armlets, arose from the corner of the night-walker; likewise Varuṇa and Viṣṇu.

"Holding a *ṭaṅka*, an eye, and the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting, with three eyes and her matted hair adorned by the moon, Vāṇī is situated in the northwest, radiant and dressed in white; likewise, Īśvara is in the northeast. However, in another ritual manual (*kalpa*), it says: "In the six corners: in the east for Sāvitrī, and in the southwest for Gāyatrī."
Salutation to Sarasvatī in the northwest, to Brahmā in the southeast, to Viṣṇu in the west, and to Rudra in the northeast; this is the first enclosure. Thus it is said.
In this regard, the deities beginning with Āditya are those mentioned in the fourteenth chapter;
Uṣā and the others are also to be worshipped here according to the very method stated in that same chapter.
By this, the second enclosure (āvāraṇa) is completed.
"Tataḥ" refers to the third enclosure.
"Yathāvidhi" refers to the fourth—
According to the method stated in the preceding chapter. || 21–22 ||
Next, one should worship Prabhā, then the eternal Viśvaṃbharā; furthermore, one should worship Vilāsinī, Prabhāvatī, Jayā, and Śānti. || 23 ||
Then one should worship Kānti, Durgā, Sarasvatī, and thereafter Viśvarūpā; then one should worship the goddess named Viśālā, Vyāpinī, and Vimalā. || 24 ||

Then one should worship her who dispels darkness, the subtle one, the source of the universe, the bringer of victory, whose abode is the lotus, the supreme beauty, and whose form is the lotus. || 25 ||
Regarding the term *prahlādinī*: their visualization is described elsewhere as follows: "They have forms white as jasmine and the moon, adorned with jewels, pearls, and so forth."
"Those whose hands are like lotuses with the two goads of their virtues, and whose faces are [like] those of Pralhādinī," and so forth.
The three obstructions [are each overcome] by eight [qualities]. For this very reason, he will later state that there are ten obstructions. (23–25)
One should worship Brahmā and the others, along with Aruṇa, on the exterior according to the prescribed characteristics;
thereafter, one should worship the planets on the outside, together with Indra and the other deities and their weapons. || 26 ||
In this manner, one should worship the Goddess with these ten protective deities;
thus, O best of the twice-born, he shall become an enjoyer of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
A knower of mantras should offer oblations of sesame seeds for thousands of recitations of the essential truth;
liberated from all sins, he attains a long life. || 28 ||
The phrase "the Brāhmī and others, along with Aruṇa" means that they end with Aruṇa.
The meaning is that Aruṇa is to be worshipped in the place of Mahālakṣmī.
However, the teacher Padmapāda states that the worship of Aruṇa is superior.
"Having the characteristics previously described" means those whose meditations are as stated in the sixth chapter; by means of these, the seventh [chapter].
"The planets" refers to those mentioned in the mantra of the Sun;
with these [mantras], the eighth [offering] is performed.
But in another Kalpa: "The eighth [day] is with the planets, ending with those belonging to the retinue of Āditya.
The ninth [day] is with Indra and the others.
The tenth [chapter] is by means of their weapons. || 26-28 ||

Then, for the sake of longevity, the practitioner of mantras should offer three thousand oblations of clarified butter alone, or with honey, or with *dūrvā* grass, the three [medicinal herbs], and sesame seeds. || 29 ||
Then, one should offer ten thousand oblations with red lotuses smeared with the three sweets;
thereafter, Great Fortune (Mahālakṣmī) shall belong to him within six months—of this there is no doubt. || 30 ||
One should offer oblations for the sake of Brahmanic glory with flowers born of the Brahma-tree (Banyan).
What is the use of saying more here? This knowledge, when properly and well-accomplished by the twice-born, is considered a perfected cow of plenty that grants all desires. || 31 ||
Regarding "of life":
[the phrase] "with an oblation of clarified butter" is one [alternative];
"with [it] alone" is another.
"With milk-rice"; and it is connected with "with ghee.
"Three thousand," thus [it is said].
The number for all five is also [five].
As it has been said:
"One desiring long life should offer oblations of milk-rice, sacrificial food, and clarified butter, as well as clarified butter alone."
The mantra-practitioner [should perform the rite] three thousand times with all [the ingredients], including dūrvā grass and sesame seeds. Thus [it is said].

The *dhāraṇa*-yantra situated in another tantra is described as follows: it has a pericarp consisting of the six syllables beginning with *bhūḥ*, shining at the corners of the external fire of *Śakti*; it possesses eight lotus petals with filaments formed by pairs of vowels; and its leaves are marked by the three-syllable groups of the mantra.

"The yantra of the Gāyatrī has been described as marked with the directions by [the syllables] beginning with *mahaḥ*, encircled by the fourth part of the Cūḍā-mantra, and marked with the *tāra* (om) at the corners of the earth. Thus it is said.
But in the *Rāmavallabha*, the tantra is stated to be twelvefold by way of being the *gāyatrīyantra*. (29–31)
I shall now declare the Āgneya mantra, which accomplishes all purposes;
its sage is said to be the high-minded Mārīca Kāśyapa. || 32 ||
The metre here is Triṣṭubh, and the deity is proclaimed to be Agni Jātavedas;
[the verses consist] of nine, seven, six, seven, and again eight [syllables]. || 33 ||
The ritual for the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) has been declared by means of the seven syllables of the root mantra.
He states the *triṣṭubh* mantra as being "of Agni. That mantra is as follows:
"Oṃ! Let us press the Soma for Jātavedas; may he burn away the wealth of the one who acts as an enemy.
May Agni carry us across all difficulties and beyond all misfortunes, as if by a boat across the ocean.
This mantra is well known in the Ṛgveda, and therefore it has not been stated here.
It should be recited enclosed by the *hṛllekhā* mantra.
The qualification "Mārīca Kāśyapa" must be applied.
The consonant portion is the seed (bīja), and the vowel portion is the power (śakti). || 32–34 ||
In the thumbs, ankles, and shanks; in the two knees and the pair of thighs; || 34 ||
In the hips, the navel, the heart, the two breasts, the two sides, the back, between the shoulders, and in the upper arms and forearms; || 35 ||
In the elbows, the forearms, and the surfaces of the wrists;
in the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears; and in the skull, the brain, and the head. || 36 ||
The mantra-practitioner should gradually place the syllables arising from the mantra upon the crest-lock, the forehead, the eyes, the ears, the lips, and the tongue. (37)
The wise practitioner should place the syllables of this mantra upon the throat, arms, heart, belly, hips, private parts, thighs, knees, shanks, and feet. || 38 ||
He states the placement of the steps with the word "śikhā": *śikhā* means the head;
*guhya* means the private organ.
In this placement of the steps, there are two steps for the eyes, two steps for the two ears, and one step elsewhere.
As it was stated by Īśānaśiva:
"In this context, the locations of the steps are remembered as the head, the forehead, the eyes, and the ears."
"The lower lip, tongue, and throat; the arms, heart, and region of the navel;
the waist, as well as the thighs, knees, shanks, and feet—these are the locations for the ears and eyes, while each of the others has but one. Thus it is said.
There are eighteen steps.
They are as follows:
by means of [the numbers] five, four, two, one, three, two, one, one, two, and two fires (three).
"Indeed, there are eighteen words consisting of two fires, two fires, two eyes, and two colors. (37–38)
She possesses a radiance equal to a garland of lightning, stands upon the shoulders of the Lord of Beasts, and is terrifying;
she is attended by maidens whose hands gleam with swords and shields,
and who hold in their hands a discus, a spear, a sword, a shield, an arrow, a bow, a bowstring, and a threatening forefinger.
One should meditate upon Durgā, who possesses the nature of fire, who bears the moon, and who has three eyes. || 39 ||
"Lightning" refers to the conch;
"quality" refers to the trident.
"the tridents called 'arrows' and 'bows,'" according to the statement of the Ācārya.
As for the meditation on the weapons:
[they are placed] on the first two of the right and left upper hands.

In the two below that, [place] the sword and the arrow; in the two below those, the trident and the threatening gesture (tarjanī); in the two below those, [place] the spear and the threatening gesture.
As it has been said:
"One should contemplate a vast divine garden on the delightful slope of the Golden Mountain, adorned with wish-fulfilling trees and possessing a ground of gold. (1)
One should contemplate a divine pavilion of variegated jewels situated in the midst of that [space], which is surrounded by a formidable mass of fire.
Upon that lion-throne, in the pericarp of the lotus, one should contemplate [the deity], who is black in color, terrifying, and possessing a loud laugh with fangs bared. (3)
One should meditate upon that goddess, who is golden-hued, situated above a lion with an extremely fierce face, blazing with crests of fire vomiting forth flames.
The goddess resembles the tip of a lightning bolt and is like ten million rising suns;
she holds in her right hands what are known as a discus, a sword, an arrow, and a trident.
With her left arms she holds a conch, a discus, a bow, an arrow, and a raised index finger;
she is endowed with a crescent moon and possesses three most terrifying eyes.

With her mass of hair blazing upward, intent on the removal of all [sins], endowed with the protective armor of her limbs, and surrounded by missiles and weapons— Vindhyavāsinī, who is served by Indra and the other guardians of the world. Thus [ends verse 39].
"Thumb" refers to the two big toes of the feet. "Of the shoulders" is a separate [phrase].
"In the middle" means in the neck. "In the upper arms" means—
The region between the root of the arm and the elbow;
the *masta* is the junction of the forehead and the hair;
the *mastiṣka* is the area above that.
The head is the *brahmarandhra*.
"The syllables" refers to forty-four.
Because of the separate recitation of the word *pariṣat* [in the mantra], here there is the placement (*nyāsa*) of two syllables upon each of the two locations beginning with the thumb. (34–37)
One of vast intellect should recite the mantra a thousand times;
at its conclusion, [one should perform the fire sacrifice] with sesame seeds, white mustard, various roots, and excellent sacrificial fuel-sticks. || 40 ||
With clarified butter from milk-trees, with sacrificial oblations, and with foods mixed with ghee—one hundred and forty-four [offerings] should be presented. || 41 ||
One should offer four thousand oblations into the fire that carries the sacrificial offerings.
By the phrase "of vast intellect," it is stated that this mantra is to be grasped through this method of initiation.
This has been said by the Teachers:
"First, initiation (dīkṣā) is performed duly by the most excellent teachers;

then the arrangement of the weapons (astra-klpti) is proclaimed, and after that, the ritual procedure (prayoga-vidhi). Also elsewhere: "One should explain the weapons only to one who has been initiated, and he [the initiate] should practice them."
Thus:
with *citramūla* means with the roots of the *citraka* plant;
with *havis* means with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
With sesame, clarified butter,
reeds, milk-tree wood, fuel, oblation, and clarified butter—
all mixed with ghee and sprinkled with ghee— one should perform the fire-oblation in sequence; when combined, these will accomplish the goal.
Thus says the Teacher; by this, there are nine substances.
With each individual substance, there are four hundred and ninety-four oblations. (40–42)
In the Sarvatobhadra mandala, the pericarp is marked with six angles. || 42 ||
One should worship the pedestal of the Goddess according to the procedure that will be described hereafter;
immediately thereafter, one should worship Jayā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, and Bhadrakālī.
One should worship the nine Śaktis: Sumukhī, the one known as Durmukhī, then Vyāghramukhī, and then Siṃhamukhī Durgā. || 44 ||
Regarding "maṇḍala":
it is stated in the third [chapter]. It is marked with six corners.
The meaning is that one should draw the sixfold yantra within the pericarp of that lotus;
for it is indicated by the term "six-cornered" (ṣaṭkoṇa).
This has been stated by the Teachers:
First, having encircled the letters known as the *dīkṣaka* with the Power (*śakti*),
one should then construct outside of that a sixfold yantra, radiant with the blood of the evil-colored one.
An eight-petaled lotus on the outside;
and so forth.
"One should worship the Śaktis. Their visualization is described elsewhere: "Resembling blazing fire, they are adorned with ornaments of serpents."
The nine Śaktis, beginning with Jayā, should be meditated upon as holding a trident, an axe, and a ḍamaru in their lotus-like hands. Thus [ends the section on verses 42–44].

The preceptor should offer the seat with the aforementioned lion-mantra; having visualized the form [of the deity] by means of the root-mantra, he should invoke it into that [seat] and worship it. || 45 ||
The wise one should worship the six limbs as before upon the filaments;
furthermore, the eight forms arising from the eight feet beginning with Agni should be worshipped outside.
Regarding the phrase "it has been stated":

by the expression "beginning with Agni" in the eleventh [chapter], it was stated that the forms (mūrtis) have Agni and the others as their starting point, both in the context of worship and in ritual placement (nyāsa).
He will explain that group of eight feet beginning with Agni later on. (45–46)
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, he who is named Havyavāhana, another known as Aśvodaraja, and furthermore the one called Vaiśvānara—[these are the names]. || 47 ||
Kaumāratejas, Viśvamukha, and Devamukha are recorded [as names].
It has been stated that "the forms (mūrtis) are to be worshipped. In response to the inquiry as to which those are, he says: "Jātavedas," and so forth.
The repetition of the forms is for the purpose of excluding other forms.
The meditation upon these has been described elsewhere:
"Resplendent like ten million flashes of lightning, adorned with all ornaments..."
With his own great arms, [he holds] a trident, an arrow, a bow, and a skull-bowl.
Wearing red garments, terrifying with their cruel glances, and having mouths like blazing fire, they are the embodiments of Jātavedas and the other [deities]. Thus [ends verses 47–48].
Then, [he meditated on] earth, water, fire, air, and space, together with the self and ending with the syllable *namaḥ*.
One should worship [the deities] in the four directions, and again the *kalās* (subtle powers) in the corners, ending with "to the Self" (*ātmane'ntān*),
such as "Obeisance to the Self of the Elemental Principle" (*bhūtatattvātmane namaḥ*) and so forth.
The meditation for these [elements] should be understood as described in their respective places.
For water, the meditation on Varuṇa, which will be described later, is to be known.
These are the kalās consisting of Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti.
The meditation on these should be understood as described in the mantra of the palace (prāsāda). || 48-49 ||
In the directions beginning with the east, the energy-phonemes (varṇa-śaktis) beginning with the letter JA should be worshipped. || 49 ||
Awake, scorching, containing the Vedas within her womb, having the form of fire, accompanied by the crescent moon, the slayer of Śumbha, moving through the sky immediately thereafter. || 50 ||
Vāgīśvarī, Madavahā, Somarūpā, Manojavā, Marudvegā, Rātrisaṃjñā, Tīvrakopā, and Yaśovatī. || 51 ||
She whose essence is water, who is ever-pure, compassionate, and captivating;
she who transcends all, the mother of the Vedas, devoted to that [Supreme], and fond of self-restraint. || 52 ||
Samārādhyā, Nandinī, Parā, Ripuvimadīnī, Ṣaṣṭhī, Daṇḍinī, Tigmā, Durgā, and Gāyatrī follow thereafter. || 53 ||
Niravadyā, Viśālākṣī, Śvāsodvāhā, and Nādinī;
Vedanā, Vahnigarbhā, and likewise the one called Siṃhavāhā. || 54 ||
The forty-four [qualities] are: the leader, the invincible, the one who desires to sport behind, the remover of heat, the one who has abandoned faults, and the one without rivals. || 55 ||
Regarding the phrase "in the directions beginning with the east":
one should worship eleven Śaktis in each individual direction.
As it has been said: "And the knower of the ritual of mantras should [worship] eleven in each direction."
"Jārṇādyāḥ" means those beginning with the letters of the mantras starting from the waking state (*jāgrat*).
"Tatparā" means devoted to that.
*Damanapriyā* is a specific epithet; *parā* is a name for a *kalā*; and *ṣaṣṭhī* is also a name. (49–57)
Then one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) together with their weapons, such as the vajra and others.
When this mantra has been perfected through such means as recitation (japa), the most excellent practitioner— || 56 ||
One shall be the master of the Āgneya weapon; its ritual procedure is now proclaimed.
That which is called the Āgneya weapon is the mantra recited in reverse order. || 57 ||
The seers and other [components] of this mantra have been declared as those previously mentioned;
one should assign its six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in reverse order. || 58 ||
"Pratiloma" means the reverse order of numbers;
it means the reverse order of social classes (*varṇa*).
Because the inverse order of the castes has already been mentioned.
Regarding the phrase "one should fashion":

by means of the previously stated number of syllables, according to tradition, [the mantra is formed] with *tāra* (om), *māyā* (hrīṃ), *durgā*, and so forth, ending with *jātavedase māṃ rakṣa rakṣāgnaye astrāya phaṭ*.
As it has been said:
"By means of the stones numbering the limbs of the world (36), and the minerals numbering the joy of Nanda (9),
which are reversed and placed upon the heads of the three seed-syllables beginning with Tāra..."

One should fashion the six limbs of the fire-weapon (dahanāstra) with the first word [“agnaye”], followed by “māṃ rakṣa,” and ending with “phaṭ,” each joined with its respective seed-syllable (jāti). Thus [ends verses 57–58].

One should perform the placement of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa) and the placement of the words (padanyāsa) in reverse order; one should understand the various types of meditation only through the instructions of the guru, and not otherwise. || 59 ||
Regarding the distinctions of meditation (*dhyānabheda*):
therein, the meditation on the deity of the fire-weapon (*āgneyāstra*) is as follows—
In the center of the palm-forest, upon the ground of fire abounding in ramparts, there is the Fire-god.
Near the base of a great palmyra tree, which was beautifully adorned.
Or, she may be stationed in the southeast corner, which has the shoulders of a lion, with her feet moving,
possessing a brilliance equal to ten million flashes of lightning, and blazing like the fire at the end of an aeon.
Her face possesses natural, fierce fangs; her waist is radiant with a garland of bells;
and she holds a trident, the lord of serpents, a *ḍamaru* drum, lightning, and fire—all blazing with light.
She was adorned with her own jeweled bracelets and anklets,
which were crowded with small bells, and further embellished with formidable ornaments fashioned by the lord of serpents.
One should contemplate the Goddess, who consists of the colors of fire and so forth, as being the very nature of consciousness. Thus [ends verse 59].
The arrangement of the recitation should be as before;
for his success, he should offer oblations with the same number [of mantras] using sacrificial porridge well-cooked with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 60 ||
"As before" means according to the previously stated number.
The distinction [is found] in another tantra:
Silent, devoted to his vow, a master of mantra, pure in conduct, and having conquered his senses, the wise practitioner—
seated upon the previously mentioned seat in the svastika posture, facing east—
should recite the Āgneya-weapon mantra the previously stated number of times for the sake of attaining success. Thus it is said.
Regarding the phrase "its proofs":
because it is unestablished for both parties, it is unfit for formal application.
As it has been said:
For those who desire to perform these rites for the sake of what is truly incurable,
the fierce deities of the divine weapons will surely destroy them.

Therefore, with every effort, having purified the body through vows such as eating only at the sixth mealtime and so forth, and having mastered the weapons, one should perform the ritual actions. Thus it is said.
Elsewhere also it is said: "Having accomplished the vidyā up to its reverse and direct orders, the preceptor should commence the ritual application of these weapons according to the stated path. (60)
One should perform the worship of Śakti as before, but in reverse order;
in all cases, the preceptor should perform a recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra twice the usual number.
Regarding "worship":
therein, the specific detail is stated in another tantra— having invoked the Goddess upon the previously mentioned seat, according to the path already described.
One should worship [the deity] along with its limbs using excellent fragrant flowers, employing the root mantra.
The limbs [of the deity] are in the corners beginning with the southeast (Agni), and likewise in the northeast (Īśāna) are the forms of Vahni;
furthermore, Durgā, Nārāyaṇī, Durmanā, and the beloved of Śamana (Yama).

One should worship these eight powers of the [eight] syllables—Nityānandotkarā, Suveśā, and Jāgarapriyā—in the third enclosure; outside of that, one should worship the powers of the mantra-syllables and the world-protectors (lokapālas). Thus it is said.

"In all cases" means that in the ritual applications (*prayoga*), one should perform a recitation (*japa*) twice the length of what is prescribed for the application; that is, one should perform a recitation double the amount of the recitation stated in the specific rite. || 61 ||
One should perform cruel rites according to the reverse order;
rites for pacification and nourishment should be performed according to the natural order. || 62 ||
By means of the reverse procedure with the *āgneya* weapon; by the "forward" procedure, that is, with the mantra beginning *jātavedase*. ||62||
At the time of practice, one should recite the eight quarters in reverse order;
by this procedure, the mantra subsequently becomes purified. || 63 ||
"One should recite" means individually.
"Purified" is as it has been stated:
For the pacification of all defects such as *sthirā* and others, as well as those caused by malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), one should recite the eight-syllable mantra of Manu. Thus [it is said]. (63)
The first five-syllabled quarter, beginning with *agni*, should be known as consisting of the organs of cognition;
the other five-colored quarter, beginning with *dhūma*, is traditionally taught as consisting of the organs of action. || 64 ||
"Consisting of the organs of cognition" means that the nose,
tongue, eyes, ears, and skin are the organs of cognition;
their nature as such [is established] according to the sequence of the letters.
The same applies to what follows.
"Action" refers to speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals. 64.
The third quarter, beginning with *śva*, consists of five syllables and is known to be composed of the five elements;
the fourth quarter, beginning with *tya*, consists of seven syllables and has the form of the [four] constituent elements (*dhātu*). || 65 ||
The five elements: earth, water, fire, air, and space. "Element" (dhātu) means—
Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen. || 65 ||
The fifth quarter, preceded by *daḥ*, consists of six syllables and has the form of a wave (*ūrmi*).
Another six-syllable [quarter] begins with the letter *ta*; it is considered to be composed of the six sheaths (*ṣāṭkauśika*). || 66 ||
The other [mantra] with the preceding [syllable] consists of five letters and is said to be composed of sound and the other [sensory objects];
the eighth, beginning with the letter *sa*, should be known as consisting of speech and the other [faculties] in the five-lettered [mantra]. || 67 ||
"Wave" (ūrmī) refers to those consisting of hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death.
"Consisting of the six sheaths" (ṣāṭkauśika) refers to...
Tendons, bones, marrow, skin, flesh, and intestines.
Regarding "sound and so forth": sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
Regarding "speech" (vacana):
[the functions] of speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and bliss. || 66–67 ||
Thus, through the union with reality (tattva), the arrangement of the feet has been declared;
from each respective word and syllable, that many fire-deities arise.
By the phrase "thus, through union with reality," the placement of the principles (*tattvanyāsa*) by means of these syllables is indicated. || 68 ||
They were like images of the primary forms, possessing splendors described according to their respective colors;
with blazing hair and faces, they were terrifying with fearsome fangs.
The deities born from the sense organs are said to have their gaze directed upwards;
the deities arising from the feet of the Bhūtas are proclaimed to have faces turned sideways. || 70 ||

Arising from the syllables of the elements and forms, they are adorned with two faces; those born from the *ūmī* have upward-turned faces, while those arising from the *kośa* have faces turned sideways. || 71 ||
All these women are traditionally considered impotent, being born from the objects of the senses;
they are described as having faces turned downwards or sideways, and are the deities of the [social] classes.
O gentle one, those facing forward are remembered as being for this purpose, while those with faces turned away are for other rites;
from these have arisen innumerable deities with blazing countenances.
"Arising from the sense organs" means originating from the first two words. The connection is that women arise from the sense objects and are endowed with downward and horizontal faces.
"Arising from sense objects and faculties" refers to those arising from the final two quarters;
this is the summary of all [the verses].
Thus it is said that the deities of the syllables have been described. (69–73)
By means of these mantras, the wise practitioner may burn the kingdom along with its mountains and forests;
he should employ this weapon during the constellations presided over by humans.

One should employ [the rites] during the Āsura constellations and withdraw them during the Devatārā ones. The three following Pūrva[-phalgunī], Uttarā[-phalgunī], Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, and Rohiṇī—these, the wise declare, are the human constellations. || 75 ||
Jyeṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Mūla, Dhaniṣṭhā, Āśleṣā, Kṛttikā, Citrā, Maghā, and Viśākhā are the stars whose presiding deities are Rākṣasas. || 76 ||
Aśvinī, Revatī, Puṣya, Svātī, Hastā, Punarvasu, Anurādhā, Mṛgaśiras, and Śravaṇā are the asterisms presided over by deities. || 77 ||
One should commence an undertaking on the Nandās; one should discharge weapons on the Riktās;
one should perform the gathering [of troops] on the Bhadrās; and on the Jayās, it is exceedingly excellent. || 78 ||
The commencement [of the ritual] should take place on Tuesday or Saturday;
the dismissal or the withdrawal [of the deity] should occur on Thursday or Friday. || 79 ||
Regarding "on the Nandas":
on the first, sixth, and eleventh lunar days.
Regarding "on the Riktās": [on the fourth, ninth, and fourteenth].
On the fourth, ninth, and fourteenth [lunar days]. Regarding "on the Bhadrās":
on the second, seventh, and twelfth [lunar days].
"May there be victory!
[This is said] on the third, eighth, and thirteenth [lunar days].
"The extraction is exceedingly excellent"—this is to be supplied [to complete the sense].
"One should perform the gathering during the Bhadrā muhūrtas, but especially during the Jayā muhūrtas," according to this statement. (74–79)
An undertaking should be made in fixed signs, and a dismissal in movable signs;
a wise person should perform the withdrawal of weapons in both types of signs.
"In the fixed signs" means in Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius.
"In the movable signs" means...
In Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn;
"in both" means in those of dual nature.
In Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces. || 80 ||
During the dark fortnight (kṛṣ� with fire (anala),
and during the bright fortnight (śukla), one should again withdraw the weapon into oneself in due order.
By "fire," however, is meant the wind moving through the right nostril;
the traditionalists, moreover,
hold this view that by the word "fire" here, the fire-maṇḍala is intended.
The syllable *raṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
It also denotes the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) beginning with Kṛttikā.
Likewise, by the word "moon" (*śaśin*), the lunar disc, the lunar seed-syllable, and the gentle lunar days (*tithis*) are expressed.

Therefore, this is the meaning: having meditated upon the circle of fire conjoined with its own seed-syllable, one should perform the rite of dismissal (visarjana) specifically by means of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra). || 81 ||
The wise one should perform the emission and withdrawal with the *bhānu* [mantra] during both fortnights;
facing westward, he should accomplish all rites everywhere. || 82 ||
"By means of Bhānu" means by means of meditating upon one's own self in the form of the sun.

Thus, having contemplated one's own self in the form of the sun, the wise person should perform liberation (*mokṣa*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) in both fortnights according to the previously mentioned method; this is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
The only distinction is the meditation on one's own self as having the form of the Sun.
As it has been stated by the Teachers:
"Fire is said to have the nature of the stars; the Moon is declared to have the nature of the lunar days (tithis)."
"By means of those two, the Maker of Day performs the acts of emission and withdrawal. Thus [it is said].
"Everywhere" means at the beginning, during the performance, and at the conclusion.
"Beginning" refers to the resolution to perform the ritual action preceded by the preparation of the necessary materials.
The performance of the fire-oblation (*hutakriyā*) is the discharge of the weapon-mantra (*astravimocana*).
Immediately after the visible result has been attained, the dismissal (*udvāsana*) is the withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*).
Elsewhere, it is stated that the commencement may also take place without a fixed time restriction.
"In times of fear from enemy armies and the like, or when there is great danger of an intense nature, no restriction regarding time should ever be observed for these practices. (82)

The mantra-practitioner [should prepare] pieces of wood from the *nakṣatra* tree, inscribed with the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) together with the ritual action (*karman*), combined with the syllables of the respective mantra according to the number of its syllables. || 83 ||
One should offer oblations into a kindled fire to slay one's enemy, beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight. || 84 ||
The "constellation-trees" (nakṣatravṛkṣa) are those which will be described in the twenty-second [chapter].
Regarding the phrase "shavings" (śakalān):
they are measured at one span (prādeśa).

Those [syllables] joined with the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and combined with the respective mantra-syllables—according to this sequence: "At the end of the name, the mantra becomes the 'sprout' (*pallava*); this is considered [the method] for killing"—thus the *pallava* is described. (83–84)
One should take excellent sacrificial fuel-sticks produced from the Dhattūra, Viṣa, Vṛkṣa, and Akṣa trees, each smeared separately with Rājī oil, seven thousand times for each. || 85 ||
Becoming self-restrained, one should offer oblations; the enemy shall go to the city of Yama.
One should perform the homa for seven nights with white mustard seeds soaked in oil. || 86 ||
The *kāraskara* is a poisonous tree; the *akṣa* is the *bibhītaka*; and *siddhārthasneha* is mustard oil. ||85-86||
With wet clothes and at the time of the *viṣṭi* yoga, by means of this mantra and black pepper, that enemy is seized by a fever equal to the fire of universal destruction. || 87 ||

Having written the name of the enemy according to the prescribed rite upon a palm leaf, and having encircled it with the Fire-weapon mantra (āgneyāstra), one should place it in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). || 88 ||
If one who is afflicted by fever performs oblations with black pepper while enraged, he becomes possessed by that fever;
by taking it and casting it into cold water, he shall become submissive. || 89 ||
"Viṣṭikāle" means during the *viṣṭi* lunar phase (*karaṇa*),
because it is said that therein the destruction of poison and enemies, and so forth, will be accomplished.
"Yathāvidhi" means accompanied by the ritual action.
"Enveloping" refers to drawing [the lines] all around;
"with the juice of *dhattūra*"—thus say the supreme gurus. (87–89)
Having ground the seeds of Apāmārga together with black pepper and honey,
one should then throw them into very hot salt water and boil the mixture.
One should pour a little water at a time with a ladle made of *kāraskara* wood into the heart, the mouth, and the nose of the image of the bear. || 91 ||
The practitioner of mantras, reciting the Āgneya mantra, shall soon become afflicted with fever;
by casting that [substance] into boiling water, he shall effortlessly destroy his enemy. || 92 ||
*Kāraskara* means *kucilā*. 90–92.
Having smeared an image of the enemy with sharp oil, one should heat it at night in a kindled fire while reciting the mantra in reverse order. || 93 ||
One is afflicted by fever immediately; from the *homa* of this [mantra], death occurs.
With pungent oil, namely mustard oil (*sarṣapataila*), one performs it in reverse order; this is the fiery weapon (*āgneyamastra*).
"Homa" means, by implication, [the offering] into the effigy;
"of this" refers to the enemy. || 93-94 ||
In the ocean waters, indeed, stirred by asafoetida, poison, and cumin seeds; || 94 ||

When [the liquid] has boiled, one should cast the effigy—fashioned from the wood of the tree belonging to the victim's birth-star—with its face turned downwards, using a staff made from a poisonous tree. || 95 ||
Striking that head while reciting the Astra-mantra in reverse order, the enemy shall die from fever-induced delusion within seven days. || 96 ||
In the ocean water;
in the salt water.
"In reverse order" means:
The distinction arises from the intended meaning;
therefore, the sense is "the Agneya weapon. (94–96)
With his feet seized by the lordly serpents of the sun’s chariot, struck by their venom, naked, his limbs smeared with oil, and scorched by the rays of the sun. || 97 ||
Having visualized one's own enemy with his face turned downward, one should offer libations with boiling water while gazing at the sun; thus the enemy shall become dear to death. || 98 ||
"Nāgendra" means a serpent. "One should satisfy" refers to Durgā. || 97-98 ||

Meditating upon her who bears a pestle and a trident, and possesses the luster of a dark cloud at the end of time, one should [offer oblations] with cotton seeds and nimba leaves soaked in the fat of a ewe. || 99 ||

Having performed the oblation with this weapon-mantra, the preceptor should cause his enemies to hate one another, while meditating upon the terrifying Durgā, who holds a raised index finger and a trident. || 100 ||
By offering oblations of sprouts from a Viṣavṛkṣa tree sprinkled with buffalo ghee, the knower of mantras causes the enemy's army to be driven away in an instant. || 101 ||
"Tarjanīm" means the *tarjanī* mudrā.
Its definition is stated in the *Durgāpaṭala* (verses 99–101).
Having meditated upon the Goddess as previously described, one should offer oblations for three days with four [grains] combined with black pepper and sprinkled with goat's blood. || 102 ||
One should effect the eradication of the enemy's army; of this there is no doubt.
[One should meditate on] Durgā, blazing like the fire of universal destruction, with a trident in her hand and emitting flames.

Having meditated, and having offered oblations with seeds produced from the thorn-apple (dhattūra) smeared with mustard oil—or with black pepper together with mustard—one shall utterly delude one's enemies. || 104 ||
The phrase "smeared with mustard oil" (sarṣapatailāktaiḥ) also applies to what follows [in verses 102–104].
Meditating upon Durgā, who resembles black collyrium and holds a trident and a sword, [one should apply] wounds produced from the Nakṣatra-tree combined with oil. || 105 ||
One should offer oblations with the *samidvaris* for one month to slay an enemy;
[visualizing] her mounted upon a lion, running toward the fleeing foe. || 106 ||
Recalling Durgā as she discharges arrows released from her bow, their tips ablaze with tongues of fire, one should offer libations of warm water;
by beholding the solar orb, the enemy shall be driven away. || 107 ||
The bhallāta nut causes wounds. || 105-107 ||

One should meditate upon her who holds a fist and a mace in her hands against the most difficult diseases, whose luster is equal to a flash of lightning, [and who is worshipped] with offerings soaked in buffalo ghee. || 108 ||

One should offer oblations with the dregs of grain and the finest fuel-sticks of *nimba* and *bibhītaka*; furthermore, by using *kodrava* grains, the immobilization of the enemy's army shall occur. || 109 ||
One should meditate upon Gāṇidurgā, who is red in color and holds a noose and a goad;
[one should perform this] in a fire kindled with the wood of the tree belonging to the person to be accomplished (sādhya), using salt and sweet substances. || 110 ||
One who knows the mantra should perform oblations at night for seven days to bring kings under control;
one should visualize Viśvadurgā as red in color, holding a noose and a goad. || 111 ||
The practitioner of mantra who offers oblations at night with blossoming *phalinī* flowers sprinkled with sandalwood water shall bring the entire universe under his control. || 112 ||

Meditating upon Goddess Sindhudurgā—who resembles the autumnal moon, from whom supreme nectar flows, and who holds a noose and a goad—one should worship her with the best of sacrificial fuel. || 113 ||
One should offer oblations of reeds sprinkled with honey for the attainment of rain, [visualizing the goddess] holding a skull, a trident, a noose, and a goad in her hands. || 114 ||
Meditating upon Agnidurgā, who resembles the flower of the hibiscus, one should offer oblations using a salt effigy combined with the three sweets. || 115 ||
The knower of mantras shall attract the desired objects to be accomplished; there is no doubt in this matter.
This Triṣṭubh meter, beginning with "atidurgā" and ending with "ṣaḍanta," has been proclaimed. || 116 ||
Then, that which begins with Gāṇī and ends with Durvarṇā is proclaimed as Gāṇidurgā; that which begins with Viśvā and ends with the letter Aṇ is proclaimed as Viśvadurgā. || 117 ||
That [mantra] beginning with "Sindhu" and ending with "va" is called Sindhudurgā;
the wise know that this one beginning with "Agni" and ending with "tya" is Agnidurgā. || 118 ||
The five [mantras] beginning with *atidurgā* are indeed specific varieties of the *jātavedas* mantras that will be described below. *Pulākaiḥ* means with worthless grains. Regarding the word *ati*:
Beginning with "atidurgāṇi viśvā," all verses up to the end of the *pariṣad* [are to be recited]. The same applies to what follows. However, the author of the *Gūḍhārthadīpikā* [states as follows]:
Saying "He sits upon," he wandered about indeed while reciting the three-syllable mantra. ||108-118||

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the courtyard, one should daily worship the Goddess with fragrant flowers and other offerings, following the very same procedure previously described. || 119 ||
One should offer the bali-oblation with caru during the nights; this bestows all accomplishments. There is no doubt that it wards off sorcery, disease, fear, injury, spirits, and the like. || 120 ||
Having duly propitiated the fire with pleasing perfumes and flowers, the practitioner of mantra, standing before it with one-pointed mind, should recite the mantra. || 121 ||
This recitation leads to all accomplishments; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
One should offer oblations facing west with salt sprinkled with sweet substances. || 122 ||
"Of that" refers to the fire. || 121 ||
By means of the number of syllables in the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should bring his enemy under his own control.
Having washed the śāli rice and dried it, he should make the grains pure. (123)

Having recited the mantra over the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the wise one should cook the sacrificial oblation (caru) in the consecrated fire, having first poured it out while continuing the recitation of the mantra. || 124 ||
Having worshipped the Goddess as before, one of clear intellect should offer eight thousand oblations of this sacrificial porridge mixed with clarified butter into the fire. || 125 ||
The wise practitioner, while pouring the remnants into a vessel, should have the person to be treated (sādhya) consume it;
he should then bury the remainder in the water that has fallen within the courtyard. || 126 ||
Malevolent spells (*kṛtyā*), diseases, along with the afflictions caused by spirits and seizing demons, are destroyed;
furthermore, a spell produced by enemies shall devour those very same enemies. || 127 ||

With rice grains, with oblation-materials, with milks, with the best fuel-sticks of milk-exuding trees, and with clarified butter combined with the three sweets—one should perform these [offerings] separately, one thousand times each. || 128 ||
One should perform the oblation; that is the ground for success, and the practitioner will certainly achieve it.
When the Sun is situated in the sign of Aries, on an auspicious day, the knower of mantras [should act]. || 129 ||
In a river flowing toward the ocean, which always possesses abundant water, one should take up sand, dry it, and purify it thoroughly. || 130 ||

Having placed them in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and in the consecrated sacrificial fire, one should fry them with a ladle made from the wood of the Brahmaruha tree, using the mantra, for the sake of success. || 131 ||
Bhāskara states the application for sand as follows:
"In that which flows to the ocean" refers directly [to the river];
"in the five products of the cow" refers to the *pañcagavya*.
In those [vessels] sufficient for stirring. || 129–131 ||

When the sun is situated in Leo, Aries, or Sagittarius, during the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) of the dark fortnight, and under the asterisms of Viśākhā, Kṛttikā, Mūla, Hasta, the three Uttaras, or Maghā; || 132 ||
A wise person should perform the laying of the sand on the Rohiṇī or Śravaṇa nakṣatras, or on days presided over by Saturn or Jupiter; avoiding other times, he should carry out the rite. || 133 ||
For the protection of houses, villages, and kingdoms, one should [use] auspicious sands.
By the phrase "houses, villages, and so forth," cities and the like are included. (132–134)
These measures—the *prastha*, *āḍhaka*, and *ghaṭa*—are used for pits of medium size and so forth. || 134 ||

The preceptor should cast those [mantras] recited into the nine [vessels] and worship them in sequence; beginning from the center, he should worship the goddesses and the weapons ending with the skull. || 135 ||
Having worshipped the discus, conch, sword, shield, arrow, bow, trident, and skull-bowl with their respective mantras, one should finally offer the bali-oblation. || 136 ||
"Prastha" means measured by a *prastha* in the house; measured by an *āḍhaka* in the village or town;
and measured by a *ghaṭa* in the kingdom.
Eighty guñjās make one karṣa;
four times that is a pala;
four palas make one kuḍava.
Four *kuḍavas* make one *prastha*;
four *prasthas* make one *āḍhaka*;
and four *āḍhakas* make one *droṇa*.
Four *droṇas* constitute a *ghaṭa*.
Some say it is twenty-four finger-breadths plus ten finger-breadths [in circumference]. (134–135)
"By their respective mantras" refers to those stated in the seventeenth [chapter]; "at the end, the bali offering" refers to that for the Goddess, the wheels, and the weapons. (135–136)
One should offer oblations to the lunar mansions, the planets, the zodiac signs, and the lords of the world;
wherever this protection is established, there prosperity increases. || 137 ||
Minor planets, great diseases, Saturn, spirits, and reptiles—all these go to destruction by this rite; of this there is no doubt. (138)
The word "nakṣatra" (constellation) is also indicative of the presiding deities (*adhipati*).
These are the offering mantras (*balimantra*) for them:
*Namaḥ* to all beings (*bhūta*), including the deities of the constellations (*aśvinīdevatā*), who roam by day and by night.

In this manner, [the offerings] for the deities of the Bharaṇī and the first quarter of Kṛttikā, and for the deities of the remaining three quarters of Kṛttikā, and so forth, should be inferred. Then, [the offerings] for their respective lords: for the Aśvin deities, the lords of Aśvinī;
likewise, [the offerings] for Yama and the others should be inferred.
Then follows the *rāśibali* (sacrifice to the zodiac signs):
to the deities of Aries and their respective lords, [offered] at the first quarter of Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and Kṛttikā. In this manner, it should be extended to Taurus and the subsequent signs.
Then follows the offering to the planets (*grahabali*).
To the deities of Mars, who is the presiding deity of the zodiac sign Aries and the lord of the asterisms Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and the first quarter of Kṛttikā;
in this same manner, it should be inferred for the others as well.
The offering to Lokeśa in the Vāstu [ritual] should be understood as described by me;
one should present the bali offering all around. (137–138)
The wise one [should prepare] a *kuḍava* measure of purified sand in a vessel made from the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree and mixed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). || 139 ||
Having deposited [the wealth] according to the prescribed rite, wherever one establishes it, there prosperity increases day by day along with the passage of time and other factors. || 140 ||
Great portents, sorcery, malice, and powerful planetary influences are destroyed for those who are purified,
according to the manner described starting with "in the river" and so forth.
The modification is sixteen *kuḍavas*, namely one *prastha* of cow urine and the other ingredients. (139–141)
One should perform the installation of the charu, the cow, and the stone according to this procedure. || 141 ||
There should be one *prastha* of cow urine and half that amount of cow-dung water;
the milk should be seven times the clarified butter, and the curd three times the cow urine. || 142 ||
It is said that all [the substances] should be equal to cow urine, or all [of them] together should be equal [to the urine].

The cows should be tawny, white, snow-white, smoky-colored, or reddish-brown in luster; in their absence, it is stated that all [colors] may be used, or in every case, [the milk] should originate from a tawny cow. || 143 ||
"According to the rule" means by the previously mentioned method of installation.
"Of the two stones for chewing."

Regarding the products of the cow, there is a specific instruction in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "Having placed rice, barley, mung beans, black gram, wheat, wood-apple seeds, sesame, lotus seeds, and lotus leaves in a vessel made from cow-products, one should bury it in the earth during the *nāga-yoga*."
Regarding the greatness of the Nāgayoga:
