"In the Sarpa-muhūrta, during a Sarpa asterism and Sarpa-karaṇa, this conjunction is called Nāgayoga; or else, it is the conjunction of the [Sarpa] karaṇa and the [Sarpa] asterism. Thus it is said.
One should bury a headless trunk, with five lotus petals and a single, unbroken, firmly bound stalk,
into a vessel filled with cow’s milk.
"Then, by means of mindfulness, [the danger] is destroyed within the house. Thus it is said.
The asterisms and other factors for its installation are also mentioned in that very same place:
Pūṣan, Puṣya, Punarvasu, Vasu, Hari, Citrā, Śaśin (the Moon), as well as Rohiṇī; those lunar days are the Aṃśumat, Phaṇin, Yama, and the first fifteen [days] of the fortnight, and Hari.

The days [of the week] are those of Mercury, Moon, Venus, and Jupiter; the signs are Gemini, Cancer, Sagittarius, Aquarius, and the final two (Pisces and Aries)—these are declared to be the zodiacal signs for the application of cow's products. Thus it is said.
"Or everything. By the word "or," two other modes are suggested.
It should also be understood that there is the mode of joining [the elements] with their respective mantras.
As it has been said:

"One *prastha* of urine, half a *pala* of cow dung, one *prastha* of milk, half of that [milk] for curd, and half of the curd for clarified butter—this is the measure; one should offer the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) with their respective mantras."

Two parts of urine, one part of feces, eight parts of milk, and an equal amount of curd; or half as much milk, or a fourth part of clarified butter. Thus it is said. The mantras have been stated by the teachers.
That is to say:
one should gradually join the products of the cow with the syllables *tā-ra-bha-vā-bhi-ra-tha-g-bhīḥ*;
or alternatively, the five [products] should be joined with the five eight-syllable mantras of the Self. (141–143)
On a board consisting of forty-nine squares belonging to the Brahma-tree, having omitted the corner squares, one should place the fire-god Jātavedas, beginning with Śakti. || 144 ||
Having written [the mantra] starting from the central square, one should worship the deity there;
having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) with the ritual residue (sasampāta), one should bury it as previously described.
One should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) as before; its fruit has been stated previously. || 145 ||
"Forty-nine" refers to the sequence of eight lines each extending east-west and north-south.
Having written the seed-syllable of Śakti in the central square, one should write the Jātavedas mantra in three successive rounds starting from the east.
In that regard, regarding the third enclosure: there is the abandonment of the four outer corners. (144–145)
In the center, having placed eight feet within eight squares of the *māyā*, it is encircled by the letters of the *mātṛkā*;
situated upon the orb of the earth, it destroys the diseases of all beings.
This is the yantra for protection, longevity, prosperity, and fame. || 146 ||
He describes the yantra: "In the center," etc.
One should draw four lines, two extending from east to west and two extending from south to north; thus, there will be nine compartments.
"In the middle" means in the central square. || 146 ||

The knowledge of the fire-weapon (āgneyāstra), as well as the acts of its discharge and withdrawal—whatever person has been instructed by a guru in these, the three worlds are dependent upon him. || 147 ||
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the *Śāradātilaka* composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra. 21.
Regarding the phrase "the actions of emission and withdrawal": emission (*visarga*) is withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
Appropriation (*ādāna*) is the subsequent mental form of the mantra following the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
As they say:
"Having performed the killing according to the ritual rules by means of a perfected mantra, the knower of mantras..."
At the conclusion of the ritual activities, one should perform the worship of the deity with special care.
Having satisfied the Brahmins according to his ability and having bid farewell to the mantra-forms,
he stands in water reaching up to his neck in a river flowing to the ocean.
One should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times throughout a day and night; thus one should take possession of that pure mantra. || 147 ||
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition. 21.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter:
Next, I shall describe the weapon of Time (dināstra) and the weapon of Sorcery (kṛtyāstra), which crushes the enemy.
Those most proficient in mantras declare that the Atidurgā mantra is a weapon for the distressed. || 1 ||
Thus it is said:
"Atidurgam" is the mantra previously mentioned. || 1 ||
This mantra is declared to be the *kṛtyāstra* when recited in reverse order;
likewise, those who know the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and so forth of the *dināstra* understand them as being proclaimed in reverse order.
This [path] is exceedingly difficult to traverse.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the six limbs, etc.," it is meant that the placement of syllables and words occurs in both cases.
Those [mantras] recited in direct order (*anuloma*) are those stated in the verse beginning with *jātavedase*.

According to the tradition, [the mantra] for Jātavedas begins and ends with *hrāṃ* and so forth. As it has been said: "The six words of the Atidurgā mantra should be formed as before using the first word of the Mantra, preceded by *hrāṃ* and ending with *hrāṃ*."
The teachers also state: "In the *anuloma* recitation, the recitation of the limbs (*aṅga*) is also in the *anuloma* order.
This was explained by the teacher Padmapāda as meaning that, because of the word "also" (*api*), this applies to the words (*pada*) and syllables (*akṣara*) as well.

The six limbs of the mantra in reverse order have been stated as being fiery (āgneya). As it has been said: "One should likewise fashion the six limbs of the reverse-order mantra by means of syllables numbering, respectively, seven, eight, three, ten, seven, and six."
And the Teachers [state]: "In the case of a rite performed in reverse order, those [mantras] should likewise be in reverse order.
Here too, the word "likewise" (*tathā*) has been explained by Padmapādācārya as being "as before."
The meditation on these two is as follows:
[one should meditate on her] standing upon the shoulders of the aforementioned lion in the midst of a garden,
resembling a dark cloud, fierce, and adorned with ornaments of serpents.

"One should contemplate the form of Atidurgā, who runs hither and thither with her own staff-like right arms holding a trident, a sword, an axe, a shield, a club, and a threatening forefinger. Thus it is said.

"One should meditate upon her as seated on a lion, composed, and adorned with lotus-hands displaying the gestures of granting boons (*varada*), poverty-alleviation (*daridra*), and fearlessness (*abhīti*); she is known by the name Antapratilomā.
As for the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), it should be understood as being performed precisely through the preparatory rite of the *jātavedas* mantra. (2)
The wise practitioner should visualize the enemy, situated within the solar orb, with his face turned downward and struck by poison,
as being seized from the root by the Kuṇḍalinī rising up.
"Struck by poison" means struck by the poisons of the serpents situated upon the chariot of the Sun. || 3 ||
One should immediately cast [the seed-syllable] into the Mūlādhāra, which blazes like the fire of Time; within three days, the enemy, overcome by fever, shall give up his life-breaths. || 4 ||
In the *mūlādhāra*, at the region between the anus and the genitals, one should perform meditation on the flickering fire of Time (*kālapāvaka*). || 4 ||
With his limbs struck by the weapon of Time (Dināstra), the enemy has come under one's own mastery;
his body is consumed by the fire kindled by the five vital winds (pañcavāyu). || 5 ||
Meditating [on this], one should mutter the mantra; immediately he shall become beloved by Yama.
Svādhiṣṭhāna is the region above the genitals. || 5-6 ||
The enemy located in Maṇipūra, with a body blazing with fire.
Meditating on the weapon of Time (Dināstra), he should perform the recitation; he shall fall under the power of Death.
Maṇipūraka is the location at the navel. 6–7.
The enemy, who had been established by the Unstruck Sound (anāhata), was utterly consumed by the fire of the mantra. || 7 ||
Bound with a swift noose, one is led away by the servants of Yama.
This is the unstruck heart (anāhata-hṛdaya). 7–8.
The enemy has gone to a pure place, yet he is afflicted by the five arrows of the weak. || 8 ||
If [the breath] is remembered as facing downward, one would quickly become lifeless after three finger-breadths.
The throat is the purification. || 8-9 ||
One should burn the enemy situated within one's own command with the fire of knowledge through the intellect. || 9 ||
Having abandoned son, friends, wife, and others, one should approach death; standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should meditate upon the orb of the Sun. || 10 ||
"With the arrow of the day" means with the weapon of the day.
"The command" refers to the space between the eyebrows.
"The mantra" [is as follows]. (9–10)
One should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times over an enemy whose entire body has been burnt; within seven days, that person goes to the world of Yama.
This is connected with the word "should recite" (japet). || 11 ||
One should recite the mantra for seven days, beginning on a Tuesday, starting from sunrise until sunset. || 12 ||
One who is afflicted by a fever of the combined humors (sannipāta), or an enemy seized by Yama—
[if] Āra, that is Bhauma [is so affected],
one should recite [the mantra]. || 12–13 ||
Having stayed for three nights in the abode of Durgā, the practitioner of mantra should subsist on a diet of barley.
One should contemplate the enemy as having his body pierced by the five arrows of the day;
by reciting this mantra, the enemy, afflicted with fever, shall go to his death. || 14 ||
Meditating on the enemy as before. || 13-14 ||

Having touched (or remembered) Durgā and reciting the mantra while fasting for three days, one should visualize one's own enemy impaled on a trident and set ablaze by the weapon of the Day-maker (the Sun). || 15 ||
Overcome by a great fever, he becomes a guest of Yama;
his enemy, who has entered the solar orb, is bitten by the serpents on his chariot. || 16 ||

Meditating on one whose entire body is consumed by the fire of poison, one should satiate him with warm water using the "cloud-arrow" (dhanabāṇa) mudrā; thus he shall become a favorite of Yama. || 17 ||
Having visualized the enemy’s body seized by flames issuing from the orb of the sun, one should recite the mantra; thus, he sports in the presence of Yama. || 18 ||
"Poison and fire": the poison is that which has arisen from the serpents on his chariot. (15–18)
Stationed upon the solar disc joined with the planets, pierced by arrows consisting of mantras,
and having restrained his own enemy, the knower of weapons should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
Bound by meditation— meaning having visualized him— he swiftly leads the enemy, like a messenger of Yama joined with the planets and seized by Rāhu, to the abode of Yama. (19–20)
Resembling the fire of universal dissolution, she was like another Kālarātri.
Holding a trident and a noose, she is terrible, seated upon the shoulders of a lion, and stationed within the orb of the sun; from her three red eyes, [rays] emerge. || 21 ||
Scorching her enemies with sparks of fire, she has a body in disarray;
her fangs are clearly visible against her lower lip, and her face is terrifying with dancing frowns. || 22 ||
Threatening her own enemy with a terrifying forefinger, she illuminated the expanse of the quarters with the network of rays from her fangs. (23)
The practitioner of mantra should recite three times the terrifying [mantra] that rends the chest of the enemy with a trident; thus he shall slay his own foe. || 24 ||

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the weapon-mantras, [one should meditate on her] whose radiance is like the fire of universal destruction, who wears red garments, who is wrathful, and who is endowed with three red eyes. || 25 ||
Mounted upon a lion, she rushed toward the fleeing enemy;
having severed his head with her sword, she departed for the expanse of the sky in an instant.
Having meditated upon Durgā, one should recite the mantra for three days while abstaining from grain-based food;
by this very procedure, the enemy shall become as dear to death as life itself. || 27 ||
Regarding the passage beginning with "pralayānala" and ending with "bhayaṅkarīm," the word "having meditated upon" (dhyātvā) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 20-27 ||
One should perform these rites during the day, but not at night.
Before a liṅga facing westward, there should be a living buffalo.
Having buried [the object] and constructed a triangular pit over its head, the most excellent of preceptors, in that kindled fire, according to the rule... || 29 ||

The excellent sacrificial fuel-sticks of *kāraskara*, smeared with goat's blood, should be provided with the syllables of the mantra combined with the name of the person to be accomplished, arranged in the form of triangles. || 30 ||

Having meditated upon the Goddess as being like the fire of universal dissolution, terrible, and adorned with thirty-two arms, one should offer a thousand oblations while she resides within the orb of the sun.
With her weapons raised and blazing, she dances upon the head of a lion;
she has great fangs, is most terrifying, with flaming hair and a roaring mouth. || 32 ||
With her face of raw entrails and flesh, and three fierce eyes like fireflies,
by this rite the enemy shall be tormented by a great fever.
He abandons his own body along with his sons, friends, and others.
Regarding the phrase "facing west":
this refers to the western orientation of the door of the temple of Śiva.
Some say that the stationary linga faces west;
this alone is the traditional position.
[Regarding] "the three triangles":
Having drawn the triangles,
[one should place] the syllables of the mantra according to the *pallava* method. (28–33)
The practitioner, having suspended the serpent above hot water, [should proceed]. || 34 ||
Durgā, seated within the orb of the sun, resembling a thousand suns, possessing a thousand hands and feet, and a thousand eyes, heads, and faces. || 35 ||
Meditating upon her whose limbs are bound by a thousand serpents and who terrifies the three worlds, one should offer warm water into the serpent-mouth with this [mantra]. || 36 ||
Bound by the noose of Time, the enemy shall release his own life, [facing] her who roars like Narasiṃha and resembles the midday sun. || 37 ||
Meditating with one-pointed mind upon her who is seated upon a fierce lion, whose appearance is most terrifying, and who has pinned her enemies upon her trident, he recited the mantra. || 38 ||
One should offer warm water for three days at the mouth of the serpent;
the enemy shall go to the abode of Yama—of this there is no doubt. || 39 ||
"A serpent" means a living black snake,
with its head turned downward.
With this weapon-mantra,
one should perform the libation using a ladle made of *kāraskara* wood.
By the phrase "with undistracted mind," it is stated that satisfaction is achieved by that [devotion] alone. || 34–39 ||
Then, according to the prescribed ritual, one should cast an image of a bear or a tree—upon which wind has been established—into hot water enriched with poison. || 40 ||
Resembling the sun, the moon, and fire, she held a sword and a shield,
and was filled with hundreds of sparks issuing from her three eyes.

Meditating upon her as seated upon a lion, richly adorned with serpents, bestowing fear upon the three worlds, and holding a sword and a severed head, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times. || 42 ||
By this rite, the enemy becomes seized by death.
One should construct an excellent triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the temple of Durgā. || 43 ||
There, into the kindled fire, he cast an effigy made of buffalo dung,
smeared with the blood of a goat, and into which breath had been infused.
Having repeatedly cut [the victim], one should offer oblations at night with [flesh] mixed with goat's blood, while meditating upon Durgā dancing upon the chest of Mahiṣa. || 45 ||
She was of terrible appearance, piercing the body of Mahiṣa with her trident,
terrifying the armies of the Asuras with incessant bursts of loud laughter.
Resembling the fire of universal dissolution, endowed with three wandering eyes, her lips were bitten together, and her lotus-face was terrifying with its fangs. || 47 ||
Surrounded by maidens bearing swords and shields,
the enemy goes to the presence of Yama by this rite.
Thus has the weapon of Time (Dināstra), which effects the subjugation of enemies, been described.
The most excellent knower of mantras should perform the ritual applications as instructed for the Kṛtyā weapon.
The grammatical construction is: "One should mutter the mantra according to the prescribed rule.
The "rule" (vidhi) consists of the application of the name [of the deity] by means of the "sprout" (pallava).
"Severed" (kṛtta) means cut by the "sword" (khaḍga); thus, the enemy is struck down. || 40-49 ||
The goddess Kuṇḍalī, who has the form of a serpent (or all things), having risen from the foundation, then proceeds through the path of the aperture of Brahmā to the region of the sky. || 50 ||
Having seized the enemy with her mouth and turned back toward her own home, one should meditate upon her as blazing like the fire of cosmic destruction and recite the mantra. || 51 ||
Within seven days, the deluded enemy meets his death when [the victim's body] is offered on a Tuesday into the funeral fire,
having been anointed with mustard oil.
Having consecrated one kuḍava of siddhārtha seeds with mantras, one should offer them as oblations for only half a month;
the enemy, consumed by the blazing fire of the kṛtyā weapon, shall go to the city of Yama. || 53 ||
On the fourteenth day, at midnight, the practitioner of the weapon-mantra should take the bones from a funeral pyre,
smear them with wound-oil, and then offer them as oblations into the fire of the pyre.

By this rite, the cowardly enemy shall meet his death. "In the funeral fire" means in the fire established in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), which has been consecrated with the prescribed purificatory rites (saṃskāra).
Wound oil; Bhallātaka oil. || 50–55 ||
[The image] fashioned from the bones of parched grain, drenched with oil from the wounds of an enemy. || 55 ||
The practitioner should offer oblations at night to an image into which life has been infused;
by cutting it up again and again with the blood of an old goat for seven days, the enemy shall perish.
Tuṣa is the husk of grain.
"Bone" refers to human bones. Having combined these two together, one should fashion an image. || 55-56 ||
Having touched the sand from a cremation ground, one should recite [the mantra] one million times along with unbroken grains of rice;
one should then scatter that sand into a pond or similar body of water, as well as water boiled with the weapons of sorcery (kṛtyāstra). || 57 ||
That [poison], when drunk, will soon destroy all people, by means of the ashes of a *preta* consecrated with mantras on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kṛṣṇāṅgāra. || 58 ||

Having fashioned these pills from buffalo ghee, churned [together] a number of times equal to the syllables of that mantra, and having properly consecrated them with breath-intonation (japa), || 59 ||
With a firm mind, one should offer oblations into the fire kindled with funeral pyre wood;
before three fourteenth days have passed, the enemy shall fall under the power of death. || 60 ||
"Boiled with the weapon-mantra of Kṛtyā" means by throwing sand into a pond or similar body of water. (57–60)
One should cast the ashes of a cremation ground and white mustard seeds into the five products of the cow;
then, one should meditate upon the Goddess within buffalo [milk], possessing a radiance like the fire of cosmic destruction.
One who knows the Astra-mantra should roast [the seeds] while reciting the mantra over a fire kindled with poison-trees;
then, in the temple of Durgā, he should offer ten thousand oblations with this [mantra].
Taking that ash again, one should throw it into the enemy's army;
that army will be split in many ways, deluded by the disease of fever. || 63 ||
If one casts away weapons and flees at the time of battle, or if [the enemy] is thrown into houses, villages, and the like, it shall effect eradication in an instant. || 64 ||
The application [of the mantra] is performed with the five products of the buffalo (pañcagavya) through ritual service (upacāra). || 61–64 ||

On the seven days of the week, during the periods of the Kulika, one should take seven pebbles from the dwellings of Durgā, excluding the northeast direction, and recite the mantra over them. || 65 ||
One should roast them with the five products of a buffalo as before;
having recited the mantra further, one should scatter these [grains] throughout the houses, villages, and cities. || 66 ||
That region is quickly destroyed, consumed by the fire born of the mantra.
Regarding "in seven cycles":
the Kulikas of the seven cycles have also been described by me in the eleventh [chapter].

Therein, excluding the eastern direction, one should take one pebble each day from the seven pebbles located in the seven places starting from the southeast (āgneya) of the temple of Durgā, in the order of the days beginning with Sunday,
during the *kulika* period; then, on the seventh day, having combined them all together and touched them, one should recite the mantra as previously described.
One should fry [the substance] in a fire of poisonous wood using a ladle made of poisonous wood. || 65-67 ||
The three are Brahmadaṇḍī, Markaṭikā, and Karakrośanikā.
On a Tuesday during the *kulika* period, one should take [the substance] and recite the mantra;
on the fourteenth day, while reciting the mantra, one should bury it in the house of an enemy. || 68 ||
The enemy’s destruction occurs together with his sons, wife, and so forth;
or the practitioner of mantra may dig up each one individually from the mandala, and that same result shall follow. || 69 ||
*Markaṭī* is *kapikacchū*.
*Karakrośanikā* is *vajradaṇḍa*. *Utsāda* is the eradication [of an enemy] such that there is no returning again. (67–69)
One should bury six sets of six dots, accompanied by cooked rice, within a doll;
having touched it, one should mutter the Astra-mantra starting from midnight on the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
One should bury this [image], inscribed with the name of the enemy, in a cremation ground;
that enemy will quickly perish along with his family and kinsmen. || 71 ||
Regarding the term "the sixfold six-dot":
the *ṣaḍbindu* is a specific kind of insect,
and it is produced at the first fall of rain.
It has another name, *pañcakuṣṭha*.
It has five white spots;
one spot is of a different color.
This has been stated in the *Nītinirṇīta* and the *Aupanishada*:
"In the five-spotted insect, there should be five white spots;
likewise, there is one of a different color, and it is very glossy in its hue."
"At the commencement of the clouds, he would be celebrated as 'the six drops'.
Regarding "in a puppet" (puttalyām): it means in one produced from the tree [corresponding to] the birth-star (janmarkṣa) of that person.
The syntactical connection is that one should mutter the weapon-mantra (astramantra) conjoined with the name of the enemy. In this regard, the application is according to the *pallava* method.
In some places, the reading is "samāyuktām" (conjoined).
Then, [it serves as] an adjective for the doll. || 70-71 ||

The mantra-practitioner, having touched fragments of skull-pots equal in number to the syllables of the *kṛtyā* weapon-mantra, should recite that weapon-mantra while first performing the rite of establishing the vital breath (*prāṇasthāpana*). || 72 ||
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, in a cremation ground consisting of poisonous trees, one should then offer oblations with the flame of a *kṛtyā* weapon, smeared with the blood of a goat.
"The enemy, utterly deluded by a great fever, shall go to the city of Yama.
The connection [of the ritual] is as follows: "one should offer oblations in the cremation ground of skull-fragments smeared with human blood.
Regarding the word "having touched" (saṃspṛśya):
Those very [fires]. "Born from a poison-tree" means in a fire kindled by poisonous wood; this is the ellipsis. (72–74)
One should place a snake into a jar that is completely filled with water. || 74 ||
Having covered him with a skull-bowl, one should conceal him with a red cloth;
one should worship him with red flowers and other offerings, and having touched him, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times. || 75 ||
On a Saturday, in the middle of the night, one should offer oblations into a cremation fire kindled with *kāraskara* wood; then the enemy shall go to the city of Yama.
"Ahimiti" refers to Kṛṣṇa while alive; "enaṃ" refers to this jar.
That jar is in the form of an enemy. || 74-76 ||

Having prepared a water-pot with the wood of the tree belonging to the lunar mansion of the person for whom the rite is intended, one should fill it with the five products of the buffalo and cast that cat into it. || 77 ||
One should perform all rites, such as recitation and worship, exactly as before, in a fire produced from *kāraskara* wood and kindled with the *Kṛtyāstra* mantra. || 78 ||
Having offered ten thousand oblations with wound-healing oil (vraṇataila), one should then lift that jar up to the head and recite the mantra with undistracted mind.
By performing the sacrifice according to this rite for three days, the enemy is driven away. || 79 ||
Having fasted for one night, he should cause the beautiful [child]—who resembles the calf of a buffalo—to drink a *prastha* of buffalo milk consecrated by the mantra. || 80 ||

With all his limbs bound with kuśa grass and having quickly fixed his vital breaths, the knower of mantras [should place him] in a fire kindled with kāraskara wood and [anoint him] with wound-oil. || 81 ||
Having performed the fire sacrifice, O child, one should offer ten thousand oblations with a restrained mind;
by this alone, the enemy shall go toward the city of Yama. || 82 ||
A black cat.
Regarding "recitation, worship, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes covering [the vessel] with a skull and wrapping it in red cloth.
"Born from *kāraskara*" means fueled by wood from the *kāraskara* tree.
"In the fire" means in the cremation-ground fire.
"With wound-oil" means with *bhallātaka* oil.
By the phrase "with undistracted mind," it is indicated that this same [mental state] applies even to the previously mentioned jar-homa. (77–82)

When the fire has been placed in a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and kindled with the mantra, and has been honored with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should perform ten thousand oblations (juhuyāt) in sequence. || 83 ||
Then, for seven days, she should be treated with oils of *rājī*, *bhallātaka*, and sesame;
subsequently, when the time for delivery has arrived, the buffalo-cow should be kept where the wind is present.

Having worshipped her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, he should touch her with the *kūrca* grass while reciting the mantra, mentally contemplating the calf from the head down to the vulva. || 85 ||
Having drawn it forth, one should offer into the kindled fire that which has fallen into the hand. When this is done, a Kṛtyā arises, blazing from the sacrificial fire. || 86 ||
She devours the enemy before long, even if he is protected by the Lord;
then, seeking her creator, she enters back into the fire. || 87 ||
The best among those who know mantras, who would perform such rites, should recite mantras such as Mṛtyuñjaya and others for the sake of self-protection. || 88 ||
"Successively" means that there is ten thousand oblations for each [deity].
The word "oil" (taila) is connected with each [item]. "With the breath established" means with the vital breath firmly fixed.
"Falling into the hand" means not having touched the ground. "One should offer" means one should perform the oblation.
Because it is said that [the mantra] seeks even the performer with the thought of him being an enemy, he states its protection [as follows]: "He should recite... (verses 83–88).
Now, the ritual procedure for the mantra of salt is being declared.
It was previously stated that the *Ṛk* and other mantras are to be recited over salt-water. (89)
In the salt waters you are sharp; you are fierce, O Heart.
Earth is the mother of the salt, and Varuṇa is the father of the mantra. || 90 ||
While salt is being offered as an oblation, whence can there be sleep, and whence delight?
Salt burns; salt cooks and causes to cook; salt cuts and breaks. (91)
Burn the limbs of such-and-such a person; burn the flesh, burn the skin!
Burn the skin, bones, and marrow; from the bones, burn the marrow!
Even if he dwells a hundred yojanas away, or across a distance of a hundred rivers, or within a city surrounded by iron walls and secured by a hundred bolts of black serpents; || 93 ||
"Having burnt him, lead him quickly before me by the power of Lavaṇa;
there he shall come under my control through the prowess of the mantra of Lavaṇa. || 94 ||
That night which was yours when you were pierced by arrows and impaled upon the tip of a stake—that night for you was a great night, that night for you was a most profound night. || 95 ||
The second is proclaimed as Lavaṇā and others; the third is Dahā and others.
Having burned that, the fourth would be Anyā; then the fifth is Yātā, which was mentioned previously. || 96 ||
The sage is declared to be Aṅgiras; the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh;
and the deities are Agni, Rātri, Durgā, and Bhadrakālī. || 97 ||
He states the ritual procedure for the *lavaṇa* mantra with the words "atho" (now then).
Regarding the form "lavaṇādidvitīyā," the sandhi is formed because it is Vedic: first, the rule *eco'yavāyāvaḥ* changes the *ai* to *āy*, and then the letter *y* is elided;
alternatively, the term refers to the nominal stem *lavaṇa* alone.
Therefore, the second [case-ending] occurs in *lavaṇe* and so forth;
as stated by the Teacher: "The second [case-ending is used] in *lavaṇe*.
The other is the third [case-ending].

Thus, this group of five Ṛks together with the *ciṭi* mantra constitutes one *vidyā*. Its nature as beginning with the *praṇava*, the *pāśa*, and so forth, and its nature as beginning with the three syllables and the seed-syllables of Vāyu, Indra, and Amṛta, are to be understood from the oral tradition (*sampradāya*).
The extraction of the mantra as taught by the teacher Padmapāda is as follows:
Having uttered "earth" (pṛthivī) and "water" (udakam), followed by "salt-water" (lavaṇāmbhasi);
then "you are sharp" (tīkṣṇo'si) and "you are fierce" (ugro'si)—this is the speech regarding the salt-heart (lavaṇasya hṛdayam).
"Earth is the mother of Lavaṇa, and Varuṇa is his father;
this is the first [line], and 'in Lavaṇa' is the beginning of the second."
When [the fire] is being offered oblations, how can there be sleep, and how can there be pleasure?
It is just as when one says, "He cooks salt," and likewise, "He causes it to be cooked."
Having said, "Cut the salt," let it also be spoken: "Break it! Burn the limbs of so-and-so! Burn the flesh! Burn the skin!"
And for the third [case], there is the beginning with *ṭac*:
"skin, bone, marrow"—from "bones" (*asthibhyaḥ*), apply the suffix *aś* and burn the marrow (*majjikā*).
(In some manuscripts, however, the reading is *tvagasṛṅmāṃsamedo'sthibhyaḥ śabdam iti*. Then, having introduced it with "If" (*yadi*), one should utter the word "dwells" (*vasati*).
[The distance is] a *yojana*, or a hundred *varṇas*, or at the end of a hundred rivers.)
"Having burnt that," from "lead me quickly" at the beginning of the fourth [chapter],
until the end of "in front," there should be the words "of salt" and "by fire."
In the city, they are red-colored; on the rampart, they are black-colored.
At the end of "Sarpa," in the syllables of "Kṛtārghatila," right here are the syllables of subjugation.
The syllables of the *lavaṇa-mantra* preceded by the word *māyā* should be employed:
"That night of yours when you were pierced by arrows and placed upon the tip of a stake."
Having recited "yā te rātriḥ," one should utter "mahārātriḥ";
having said "sā te rātrirmahā," the fifth [verse] is indeed "niśā. Thus it is said.
In another commentary as well: "Varuṇa shall be the mother of this salt, and likewise Varuṇa shall be the father;
the second [syllable] is declared to be in salt.
Thus it is said.
Likewise—one should recite: "At the end of [the name of] so-and-so, burn the five limbs;
having said 'burn the flesh,' and having said 'burn the skin,' one should conclude."
Then, having uttered "burn" (daha) for the third time, one should say "skin" (tvak);
from that, "bones and marrow" (asthi-majjāni); and from the bones, "marrow" (majjikā), followed by "burn" (daha). Thus it is said.
Likewise: "O you, that night at the end of your own stake, for one pierced"—these are three syllables;
and at the end of "for one impaled on the tip of the stake," one should utter "O you."

"May there be night, and may there be the Great Night, that night which is without [the presence of] such-and-such"—thus shall be the fifth verse; this mantra begins with the *praṇava* (Oṃ). Thus [it is said].
Likewise, it was stated by the teachers here, on the occasion of describing the meters: "Aṅgiras shall be the seer; the meters are Anuṣṭubh and Triṣṭubh."
This very view is accepted by the authors of the *Mantramuktāvalī* and the *Mantradevaprakāśikā*, among others.
The teacher Padmapādācārya stated the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the power (*śakti*) as follows: "Hrīṃ is declared to be the seed-syllable, and Krom is likewise said to be the power.
By those same authorities, another mantra yielding an equal fruit has been stated:
Having repeated the sound "ciṭi," one should utter the word "citkāli";
at the end of the great word "citkāli" comes "hrīṃ," followed by "svāhā" (sauṣaṭ), ending with the two "ṭha" syllables.
"It should be known that another mantra is likewise taught by Śiva as having equal fruit. (89–97)
With a concentrated mind, one should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) using the syllables of the *ciṭi* mantra.
The heart is said to consist of five [syllables], and the head is traditionally taught to consist of three letters.
The crest (śikhā) is said to consist of five colors; the armor (kavaca) consists of the letters of the [five] organs;
the eye (netra) is declared to consist of five; and the weapon (astra) is proclaimed to consist of a pair.
He states the six-limbed [practice]—beginning with "ciṭī"—and by the word "samāhita," it is indicated that one should perform either five limbs or five parts.
As the teachers have said: "By these *ṛg* verses, the five-limbed [rite] is proclaimed, or else by means of five [limbs]."
"Or, the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) are recited with the syllables of the Vidyā, preceded by the Praṇava. Thus [ends verses 98–99].
One should utter *tāra* (oṃ), followed by two *ciṭi*s, and after that, *caṇḍāli*;
then one should speak the word *mahat*, beginning with [the name], and after that, "of mine" (*amukaṃ me*). || 100 ||
"Vaśamānaya ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ"—this is declared to be the *ciṭi* mantra;
consisting of twenty-four syllables, it bestows the fruits of all desires. || 101 ||

He extracts the *ciṭi*-mantra as follows: "Tāra" means the syllable *tām*, which begins with the word "mahat," thus [referring to] Mahācaṇḍālī. Here, the substitution of *ā* for *mahat* is according to the rule *ānmahataḥ*.
In some places, however, the reading is *mahāpadādyām*. As it has been said:
"Having uttered 'Mahācāṇḍālī,' one should consecrate [the object] with the mantra 'Cāṇḍālī.'"
Thus [ends the section on] verses 100–101.

I worship the Three-eyed Fire, who is infused with fresh saffron, adorned with hundreds of beautiful ornaments, seated upon a red lotus, and holding in his hands the sacrificial ladle (sruva), the spear (śakti), the boon-granting gesture (vara), and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya). ||102||
She has the splendor of a dark rain-cloud, a moon-like face, and breasts adorned with a beautiful string of pearls;
she holds in her hands a skull, a noose, a goad, and a trident.
I bow to Yāmavatī, who is clad in blue garments. || 103 ||
She has the luster of a dark rain cloud, her hands are enriched with a sword, a conch, a trident, and a scimitar; she bears the crescent moon upon her crest,
is formidable, possesses three eyes, and has conquered the host of enemies.
One should remember the Goddess, who holds in her hand the means to shatter all miserable states of existence. || 104 ||
Holding a ṭaṅka, a skull-bowl, a hand-drum, and a trident, adorned with a crescent moon,
with tawny hair standing erect and white, fearsome fangs.
May Bhadrakālī be for my prosperity. || 105 ||

Regarding the visualization of the weapons in the meditation on Agni: in the first [meditation], they are at the top of the right hand and others; in the last, they are at the bottom of those same hands.
However, in the subsequent [meditation], they extend from the bottom of the left hand to the bottom of the right hand.
In the meditation on Durgā, the visualization of the weapons extends from the top of the right hand to the bottom of the right hand.
A chisel; an axe—from the lower right hand up to the upper right hand. (102–105)

One should properly recite the five *ṛks* ten thousand times, and then offer oblations into the consecrated fire with clarified butter sprinkled over the sacrificial grain (*havis*) in quantities amounting to one-tenth of that recitation. || 106 ||
"Properly joined" means that one should recite the five *ṛks* together with the *ciṭi*-mantra ten thousand times (*ayuta*).
As it has been stated by the Teachers: "The practitioner of mantra, being self-restrained, should recite the mantra accompanied by the five *ṛks* ten thousand times."
Or, being properly concentrated, one should recite this three thousand times. Thus it is said.

However, there is a distinction in another tantra: "The self-controlled one [should practice] in a fortress-like abode of Durgā that has arisen spontaneously, situated on the banks of principal rivers such as the Gaṅgā."
"One should recite this three thousand times, or else ten thousand times;
however, one should recite the previously mentioned *ciṭi* mantra four times that number. (106)
Thus, having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*), one becomes skilled in the practical application (*prayoga*).
For the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), Agni and Yāmavatī are to be meditated upon. || 107 ||
The practitioner of mantras should meditate upon Durgā Bhadrakālī during the rite of killing;
standing in water reaching up to the knees, he should recite the mantra at night. (108)
By this, the desired object to be accomplished becomes a servant in an instant.
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, the wise one should mutter this mantra. || 109 ||
For one who recites [this] one thousand and eight times, that which is to be accomplished shall come under his control.
Standing in water reaching only to the neck, one should properly mutter the five *ṛc* verses. || 110 ||
By this method, one shall bring kings under control with seven islands;
having written that [mantra] on a palm leaf, it should be bound together with the name of the person to be accomplished. || 111 ||
Having cast it into water mixed with milk, one should boil it during the night;
the person to be acted upon will become submissive to him—there is no need for hesitation in this matter. || 112 ||
Having written this on a palm leaf, one should bury it in the house of Bhadrakālī;
this is declared to be the practice for bringing all living beings under one's control. || 113 ||

By the phrase "having thus performed the preliminary practice" (*evaṃ kṛtapuraścarya*), the daily worship (*nityapūjā*) is also indicated; for without that, the [preliminary practice] cannot be accomplished.
This has been stated by Rāmakaṇṭha:
She is terrifying and multiformed, with sharp fangs and intoxicated with passion;
she is the slayer, the deluder, the beloved, and also the bearer of the water-pot.
And she who performs the rite of subjugation—these are the powers of the mantra of salt. The power enclosed by the noose and the goad is the power that makes all things possible.
The seat-mantra (pīṭhamaṃtra) should begin with the syllable *dhruva* (om) and end with *namaḥ*.
Having invoked the deities into the form (mūrti), one should worship them thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings.
First, there is the enclosure by the limbs (aṅgas), and second, by the forms of fire;
outside of that, it is declared to be [enclosed] by the Śaktis, such as the one with a trident in hand, and so forth.
The fourth [consecration] is performed with Utkaṭa and others; this fifth enclosure of the mantra of the Refuge is proclaimed as the ritual procedure for the Lords of the World (Lokeśas).
Śūlahastā, Vikeśī, Dāruṇā, Lavaṇapriyā,
Varā, Karālī, and Attyugrā are the eight Śaktis of Tāmasa.
Utkaṭa, Vikaṭākṣa, Śūlahasta, Mahābala, Agnijihva, Khaḍgadhara, Kapālī, and Tāraṇapriya—thus [are they]. (107–113)

Having written the mantra together with the name of the person to be accomplished upon a copper plate, one should heat it in a fire of khadira wood for one month; thus, the man shall become submissive. || 114 ||

Having properly prepared a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the characteristics prescribed in the scriptures, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) therein upon the consecrated bearer of oblations (havyavāhana). || 115 ||
Having washed it with cow's milk and dried it, the wise man should offer well-ground salt as an oblation; within seven days, he shall bring people under his control. || 116 ||
Likewise, one should offer oblations with rock salt sprinkled with curd, honey, and clarified butter;
by this, one shall subjugate all the gods in no time, let alone earthly kings. || 117 ||
"Thus" means that it has been designated by the name of the object to be proven (sādhya). || 114-117 ||
One should take one *prastha* of pure salt, divide it into five separate portions, and with devotion, offer each portion individually with one verse for five days. || 118 ||
By this rite, he over whom one recites the name shall soon come under one's control.
Taking pure salt, one should offer it into the fire together with honey. || 119 ||
By forty-nine oblations, one brings the desired object under control;
by constantly offering pure salt as an oblation, one shall bring enemies under control. || 120 ||
One should offer oblations with well-ground salts mixed with the three sweets; by doing so, one shall subjugate women, men, and even kings. || 121 ||
"Pure" means washed as before.
"Salt" refers to *saindhava* (rock salt).
The same applies to what follows as well. (118–121)
One should recite the mantra beginning from the third day of the dark fortnight until the eighth day.
One should fashion five effigies, complete with their primary and secondary limbs, equal in size, and auspicious.
One [image] should be made from a tree suitable for the ritual; another is considered to be made of flour;
another may be made of clay from the site of a wheel-maker's workshop; and another is recorded as being made of beeswax. || 123 ||
One *kuḍava* of salt produced from a ship, ground into powder and purified, should be sprinkled with milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey, respectively. || 124 ||
Then, with this [mixture] properly blended with jaggery, clarified butter, and honey, one should fashion a gentle effigy, beautiful in all its limbs. || 125 ||
He states another practice with the words beginning "the mantra" and so forth.
"Until the eighth" refers to the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa).
"One should perform" means on the eighth day.
"With their limbs and sub-limbs" means:
the limbs, however, are the skin, chest, heart, sides, waist, feet, shoulders, neck, and arms.
The back, the belly, the thighs, and the shanks—this is the summary of the limbs.
The secondary limbs are the two eyebrows, the two cheeks, the pupils, the nose, the two lips,
the teeth, the tongue, the chin, the mouth, and the navel.
"The hips, the private parts, the knees, the wrists, the heels, the ankles, as well as the fingers of the hands and the soles of the feet.
Thus [it is said]. "With the tree of the person to be accomplished" (sādhyadrumeṇa).
"With the tree of the victim's lunar mansion.
He will describe the trees of the victim's lunar mansions in this very [section].
"[An image] made of flour."
Made of rice flour;
*cakrī* means a potter;
*siktha* means beeswax.
"Produced from a pot" means sea-salt;
"with this salt";
"Saumyā" means beautiful.
The five [fingers] are also twelve finger-breadths each. || 122–125 ||
One should project the mantra-consecrated yantra into their hearts;
having established the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) within them, one should worship them with flowers and other offerings. (126)

Thereafter, when only one watch (yāma) of the night of the eighth day of the dark fortnight has passed, having performed the placement of the Mother-deities (mātṛkā-nyāsa), he should immediately follow it with the placement of the mantra (mantra-nyāsa). || 127 ||
With a concentrated mind, one should place the twenty-four syllables beginning with *Tārā*, which have arisen from the *ciṭi* mantra, in these respective locations. || 128 ||
"Yantra" refers to that which will be described in the subsequent chapter. "The vital breaths" (prāṇān) refers to the manner that will be described in the subsequent chapter.
The Teachers, however, state: "In that [image], one should establish the vital breaths according to the injunctions of the Guru's instruction."
Regarding this, the traditionalists state the following distinctions:

touching the heart of the image, one says, "The vital breaths (prāṇas) are here; the individual soul (jīva) is stationed here"; touching the sense organs, one says, "All the senses—speech, mind, sight, hearing, and smell [are here]"; and touching all the limbs, one says at the head, "May the vital breaths come here and remain happily for a long time."
While touching [the limbs], one should mutter "svāhā.
"Mantra-installation" (mantranyāsa) means [installing] the five limbs with the five [seed] syllables. || 126-128 ||
Then, on the crown of the head, the forehead, the two eyes, the two ears, the nose, the mouth, and the chin;
then on the throat, the heart, the pair of breasts, the belly, the navel, and the two hips. || 129 ||
Having placed the remaining four syllables on the penis, the hands, the two thighs, the two knees, the two shanks, and the two feet; || 130 ||
Thus, with all his limbs arranged [in the mudrās], wearing red garlands and unguents, clad in red garments and purified, he [should fashion] a wooden effigy (puttalī) made of hard wood. || 131 ||
One should dig a pit facing downwards in the sacrificial fire-pit (kuṇḍa) beneath the seat made of flour;
likewise, one should place an earthen image at the position of one's own feet. || 132 ||
One should suspend an image made of beeswax from the sky above the sacrificial pit;
thereafter, while touching a doll fashioned from salt, one should recite the mantra.
Having withdrawn the five Ṛg-verses and the one thousand and eight syllables according to the rule, one should again place the syllables of the *ciṭi*-mantra upon her body.
Alternatively, he says another [method]: "ciṭo" and so forth. Regarding "dāruṇā":

it means one should dig and bury [the image] made from the wood of the tree belonging to the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) of the person for whom the rite is intended (sādhya), into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
In that case, it should be understood that the burial is two finger-breadths deep.
"With the face downward" refers to the sphere of the rite of killing;
for the rite of subjugation, it should be understood that [the image] is with the face upward.
As they say: "One should bury the image made of wood, with its face turned upward, two finger-breadths below the interior of the pit.
And the teachers say: "One should bury a wooden image, consecrated with mantras, in the pit with its face turned upward. (129–131)
"One should place it likewise" means that one should place it face-down. The determination regarding the specific objects [of the practice] is to be understood as previously stated.
For these two as well, they should be buried at a depth of two finger-breadths.
The term "one should suspend" means [she should be suspended] face-downward.
As they say: "One should suspend the woman born of passion above, with her feet upward, so that she is touched by the smoke."
Thus [it is said].
And the Teachers [state]: "One should suspend in the sky a figure made of beeswax, standing upright with its face turned downwards.

"According to the rule" means that having performed the six-limbed nyāsa (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) upon one's own body and upon the effigy (*puttalī*), one should mutter the five *ṛc*s together with the *ciṭi*-mantra.
Thus it has been said:
"One should place the limbs upon one's own body as well as upon the image. Regarding the word "having withdrawn," it means [placing them] in reverse order upon one's own body and also upon the image.
As it has been said:
"Having assigned the limbs and the *anu* (the subtle body) to the effigy, one should then assign them using the method of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-yukti*).
By the word "again immediately thereafter," this is stated:
having performed the assignment upon one's own body and completed everything up to the *ātmayāga*, one subsequently performs the assignment upon the doll (*puttalī*).
Therefore, afterwards, the worship of the deity is performed upon that image (puttalikā) on the seat. || 134 ||
In the joint of the big toe, the forepart of the foot, the knees, the shanks, the thighs, the anus, the region of the genitals, then the navel, the abdomen, and the lotus of the heart; || 135 ||
One should place [the mantras] on the two breasts, the neck, the chin, and again on the face; then on the two nostrils, the two ears, the two eyes, the forehead, and the head. || 136 ||
Regarding the word "aṅguṣṭha":
in the six [locations] ending with the thighs, there is the placement of one syllable each;
elsewhere, in the two locations, there are two syllables everywhere.
As it has been stated by the Teachers:
"Below the secret [center] there should be non-duality; above, when the pair exists, there should be duality. (135-136)

Having taken fire and kindled it with wood corresponding to the asterism of the person to be accomplished, one should worship the deity mentioned in the mantra within that fire using a silver vessel. || 137 ||

Having offered arghya with kuśa grass, incense, and rājapuṣpa flowers, the wise one, with a restrained mind, should prostrate at the beginning and end of the ritual application while reciting these mantras. || 138 ||
O slayer of enemies, O carrier of oblations, you are the mouth of the night;
together with her, be satisfied by this sacrificial offering consecrated with mantras. || 139 ||
O Jātavedas, Great God, with the luster of molten gold;
O Lord of Svāhā, consumer of all, destroyer of enemies, burn up the salt! || 140 ||
Oṃ! O Sovereign, O Śarvarī, O Śarvāṇī, the entire world is swallowed and released by you.
O Great Goddess, salutations to you; O Giver of Boons, be the fulfiller of desires. || 141 ||
O Great Goddess, composed of darkness, O you of excellent vows, wife of Mahādeva:
having offered a man as an oblation during the three watches of the night, bring him under my control, O Goddess.
Oṃ! O Durgā, who are free from all difficulties, the bolt that bars the way to misfortune;
O Goddess who bears the discus and the conch, you who strike terror into wicked enemies and beings. || 143 ||
Salutations to you! O Caṇḍikā, burn my enemies and bring them under my control.
O Śākambharī, Great Goddess, O sinless one, be my refuge. || 144 ||
Oṃ! O Bhadrakālī, you who are desired by the world, bestower of auspicious success!
Slay, slay my rivals; burn them, wither them, and torment them! || 145 ||
Having cut and hacked [them] with spears, swords, javelins, thunderbolts, and other weapons, slay them!
O Mahādevī, O Mahākālī, protect us, O you whose nature is invulnerable! || 146 ||
"In that" means on the seat described in another tantra. The worship of the deity in the fire has already been explained in the fourth chapter itself.
Since there is no purpose for mentioning that here, he will also describe the offering of the *arghya* later on.
As they say:
"In the eastern part of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [one should prepare] a square and elevated [altar]."
One cubit in length, with feet and other parts dyed red with lac, it is new.
It should have variegated limbs and a beautiful form, elevated to the height of a *kuṇḍa*,
measuring either four finger-breadths or eight finger-breadths.
The seat should be twelve finger-breadths higher than the sacrificial pit;
having first spread upon it a very pure and beautiful cloth.
Having multiplied the fine [cotton] fourfold, one should spread it over that [ground], measuring seven cubits in length and nine in width,
and then further spread two red cloths upon it.
"Extensive and exceedingly subtle, multiplied as before, it is the ninth. Thus [it is said].

Having prepared a seat according to the method taught in another tantra, and having fully worshipped the previously mentioned pedestal (*pīṭha*) therein, one should invoke the deity and worship them together with their retinue as before.
Then, having filled a silver cup with pure water mixed with red sandalwood and other substances to be described hereafter, one should offer the *arghya* with that.
Thereafter, one should attend upon the deity with the mantras to be described hereafter.
*Kuśīta* is red sandalwood. *Rāji* is black mustard.
"At the beginning of the application," etc.
This [is used] at the beginning and at the end of the application of this mantra.

Although these two deities alone are intended here for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśīkṛti*), nevertheless, because of the context of the section on salutation (*natiprakaraṇa*), the mantras of the other two are also stated.
Their purpose will become clear later in the rite of killing (*māraṇakarma*). (137–146)
Having clearly visualized the target and split the effigy into seven parts, one should then recite the five verses and offer oblations into the kindled fire. || 147 ||
The first is the right foot, followed by that hand;
the head is declared to be the third, and after that, the left hand. || 148 ||
From the middle, the fifth part shall be above, and the sixth part is said to be below;
the seventh is the left foot—thus is the sequence of parts remembered.
"Puttalīm" means made of salt;
it is stated that she was "nibhīdya" (having been broken open).
He states that very division with the word "first":
the teachers have also mentioned another method— "the right foot first, and the right half as the second."
The third [should be] the right hand, and the fourth above the throat.
"The fifth [hand] shall be the left hand, and the sixth the left half [of the body];
the seventh shall be the left foot, and the others shall be engaged in the act of offering oblations. (147–149)
Or, having performed the oblation according to the rule by dividing each of these aforementioned items sevenfold,
one should worship the fire and then prostrate like a staff.
The sacrificer should gratify his own guru with wealth and grain;
by this ritual procedure, the practitioner of mantras may bring under his control both asuras and gods. || 151 ||
Furthermore, O best of kings, regarding the killing of men, rulers, ministers, and royal women, the four types of effigies previously described [should be used]. (152)
The supreme adept, knowing the ritual procedure, should establish [the deities] as before;
he should then fashion the other [deity] according to the procedure that will be described. || 153 ||
Regarding the phrase "in those mentioned":
in each of the seven portions to be cut off (*avadāna*), there are seven divisions each; thus, there are forty-nine oblations (*āhuti*).
This same sequence for cutting off the portions is to be understood everywhere in the case of the aforementioned effigies (*puttalī*).
There is a distinction elsewhere:
"Or, one may perform the oblation with the seven limbs divided into groups of seven according to their sequence;
or one may offer with those seven limbs divided into eleven parts. Thus it is said.
Elsewhere also it is said: "Having made each one of the seven limbs a seventh part, or having made them portions of Rudra, the best of counselors should offer the oblation. Thus [it is stated].
In the subjugation of women (*strī-vaśīkaraṇa*), the sequence beginning with the left foot is to be understood, because it is stated:
"For women, starting from the left. Likewise, in the killing of women (*strī-māraṇa*), the sequence of dismemberment beginning with the right foot is to be understood.
"One should prostrate" means with the mantras mentioned previously.
By the phrase "the lord of practitioners, knowing the ritual procedure," the digging of two finger-breadths below the dolls is indicated. (150–153)

With the excrement of a boar and a pigeon, sesame, the three pungents (trikaṭu), rāmaṅga, nimba, white mustard, siddhārtha, sādhya, and dust from the left foot of a woman who has recently given birth; || 154 ||

Having properly fashioned a doll from [substances] ground with buffalo urine and mixed with the previously mentioned salts, one should perform the rite of infusing life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā). || 155 ||
One should perform all [rites] such as recitation (japa) and worship according to the previously mentioned method.
Then, at night, when the fire has been kindled in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that was prepared earlier; || 156 ||
Having propitiated either Durgā or Bhadrakālī according to the prescribed rite, the practitioner, holding a sharpened weapon in his left hand, [should proceed]. || 157 ||
Beginning with the left foot and ending with the right limb, one who has conquered the senses and abstains from food should offer oblations after repeatedly cutting [the limbs]. || 158 ||
Starting from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
the wise practitioner should perform the fire oblation according to this very procedure.
By practicing this for three weeks, one may destroy one's own enemy.
Tryūṣaṇa consists of ginger (śuṇṭhī), long pepper (pippalī), and black pepper (marīca). Rāmaṅga is asafoetida (hiṅgu).
*Bhallāta* causes wounds;
*nimba* refers to the seed of the *nimba* tree. Here, the oil extracted from sesame, *bhallāta*, *nimba* seeds, and white mustard is to be taken.
As it has been stated by the Teachers: "With neem, sesame, white mustard, and oil prepared from wound-causing [plants]," etc. The previously mentioned salt is sea salt (*sāmudra*).
By the phrase "having properly fashioned the doll," a specific detail mentioned in another tantra is indicated: "The distance from her feet to her waist is four finger-breadths;
the abdomen is one and three-quarter finger-breadths, and the belly is likewise [one and three-quarter finger-breadths]."
The measurement of the region of the throat from the opening of the mouth is two finger-breadths.
"The measurement of the face from the head should be two and a half finger-breadths here;
all effigies of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) are recorded as being twelve finger-breadths. Thus it is said.
However, there is a specific detail in another tantra:
"Having fashioned the face with five parts, and the neck with half of that [again],
one should fashion all the other limbs of the dolls with the remainder."
For the rite of killing, one should fashion that [effigy] in the form of wood, measuring twelve finger-breadths or ninety-six finger-breadths,
according to the sequence of the mother-finger-breadths.
"This is the procedure prescribed for that [line] prepared for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa).
For the rites of subjugation (vaśya) and attraction (ākarṣaṇa), one should perform it with that [line] as described, measuring twelve finger-breadths."
"According to the rule" means in the manner previously described.
"One should perform the homa" refers to doing so every day.
"Three weeks" means by these very seven [days]. By that, the accomplishment of the preliminary practice (*prayoga*) occurs within three months.
Regarding the specific sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the rite of killing (*māraṇa-karman*), it is stated in another tantra:
"In the rite of killing, one should give a red cow accompanied by her calf, along with gold and pearls; furthermore, one should give seven *karṣas* as the sacrificial fee. Thus it is said.

Another distinction: one should perform rites for malevolent magic (*ābhicārika*) in a cremation ground or a deserted place, wherever on earth the practitioner performs the oblation for malevolent magic.
There, for the sake of his own success, he should have protection provided on all sides by soldiers;
otherwise, another king, having learned of him through spies, will slay him.
"One should perform the ritual for peace within one's own kingdom, but not within one's own territory [if it involves hostile rites].
If, through negligence, a practitioner of mantras should perform it while deluded by ignorance, then enemy kings will surely afflict that kingdom gradually. Thus it is said.
There is also another distinction mentioned in another tantra: "Then, having fasted during that night,
on the following day the practitioner [should proceed] by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth, as well as by the recitation of the Gāyatrī and fire-offerings (homa)."
Having become free from sin, that self-controlled one may practice once again. (154–160)
Then *kāraskara* is *dhātrī*, and furthermore, *udumbara* is a tree. || 160 ||
Jambu, Khadira, and Kṛṣṇa; those known as Vaṃśa and Pippala; those named Nāga and Rohiṇa; and those designated as Palāśa and Plakṣa. || 161 ||
The trees known as ambaṣṭha, bilva, and arjuna; the vikaṅkata tree; the vakula, sarala, sarja, vañjula, panasa, and arka. || 162 ||
The *śamī*, *kadamba*, *nimba*, *āmra*, and *madhūka* are the trees of the constellations (*nakṣatrarukṣa*). Kāraskara says that the *kāraskara* is the *kucilā*.
Dhātrī is the āmalakī;
for Mṛgaśiras, however, it is the white-sap khadira;
for Ārdrā, it is the black-sap khadira.
Nāga is nāgakesara;
rohiṇa is the vaṭa tree;
plakṣa is the parkaṭī.
The *ambaṣṭha* is the *āmrāta*;
the *arjuna* is the *kakubha*;
the *vikaṅkata* is the tree for the sacrificial ladles (*sruk*).
The *sarja* is the *śāla*;
the *vañjula* is the *aśoka*.
Regarding these, the fruit has been stated in general: one desiring long life should never cut down a tree belonging to one's own natal asterism (*nakṣatra*).
Thus [ends the section on verses] 160–163.
The mantra-practitioner should perform all [procedures], beginning with self-protection, just as previously described. || 163 ||
There is no other mantra equal to this mantra for the perfect accomplishment of desired fruits; this is the truth, and not otherwise. || 164 ||
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the Śāradātilaka composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra. 22.
As before,
according to the path taught for the Āgneya weapon.
And this protection of oneself should be understood as pertaining specifically to the rite of slaying. || 163–164 ||
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition. 22.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
Next, I shall declare the Traiyambaka mantra, which is composed in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
Time itself is unable to look upon the man who devotes himself to him. || 1 ||
Vasiṣṭha is declared to be its sage (ṛṣi), and the Anuṣṭubh is cited as its meter;
Tryambaka, the Lord of Pārvatī, is clearly seen as its deity. || 2 ||
Now, the mantra is as follows:
"We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity."
"May I be released from death as a cucumber from its stalk; may I not [be released] from immortality. Some say it is "encased by the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra."
The traditionalists, however, desire the mantra to be encapsulated by the *praṇava*, *prāsāda*, *mṛtyuñjaya*, and *vyāhṛti* mantras.
The syllable *Śrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and *Māyā* is the power (*śakti*).
As it has been said:
"The two Śrī-devīs, the Praṇavas, the Bījas and Śaktis, and Yoga [are employed] in the worship of Śiva.
Thus [ends the first section]. (1–2)
The assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) should be performed using the distinct portions of the mantras:
the heart is declared to consist of three [syllables], and the head is said to consist of four. || 3 ||
The *śikhā* (crown) is declared to consist of eight [syllables], the *kavaca* (armor) is considered to consist of nine;
the *netra* (eye) is said to consist of five, and the *astra* (weapon) is illustrated as consisting of three.
He states the division itself with the words "the heart" (*hṛdayam*).

According to the view of those for whom there is an encapsulation (*sampuṭa*) beginning with the *praṇava* and so forth, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are formed by these syllables beginning with that [the *praṇava*].
As it has been said:
"The Prāsāda, Mṛtyuñjaya, Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, together with their respective limb-mantras (aṅga-mantras) in sequence.
However, the traditionalists [state]:
having uttered the Praṇava, the Prāsāda, the Mṛtyuñjaya, the syllables of the Vyāhṛtis, and "namo bhagavate rudrāya," one says "to the Trident-bearer, svāhā" for the heart.
To the embodiment of nectar, protect me—*māṃ jīvaya*—this is for the head (*śiraḥ*).
To the one with the moon on his head, the matted-haired one, *svāhā*—this is for the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
To the destroyer of Tripura, *hāṃ hīṃ*—this is for the armor (*kavacam*).
"To Trilocana, the mantra of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, [assign] the eye;
to Agnitraya, 'jvala jvala māṃ rakṣa'; to Aghorāstra, the weapon"—thus they call this the six-limbed [rite]. (3–4)
Immediately thereafter, [the syllables] are placed in the eastern, western, southern, and northern faces;
then in the chest, throat, and mouth; and again in the navel, heart, back, and belly. || 5 ||
Then, [one should place them] on the penis, anus, root of the thighs, the two knees, and thereafter on the two elbows, the two breasts, the two sides, and again on the two feet. || 6 ||
One should place the syllables of the mantra in sequence upon the two hands, the two nostrils, and the head;
one should then place the eleven words upon the head, the pair of eyebrows, and the eyes.

One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in this manner: again on the face, on the two cheeks, then on the heart, on the belly, and further on the private parts, the thighs, the knees, and the feet. || 8 ||
He states the assignment of the phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*) itself, beginning with "pūrva" (the first).
By the word "chest" (*uraḥ*), the broad upper portion of the heart is understood here.
There are two [phonemes] at the roots of the thighs.
Two [syllables] are on the two thighs;
two more are on the two circles situated above the knees in that pair of circles;
thus, there is the placement of two syllables in each of all the locations.

The traditionalists teach the placement of the phonemes (*varṇanyāsa*) encased within the *praṇava* (Oṃ). In another Tantra, other locations are mentioned: "Furthermore, [they are placed] on the tips of the feet, the joints, the private parts, the foundation, the belly, the heart, and the neck."
In the two arms, the joints, the tips of the fingers, the mouth, the lips, the nose, the palate, the eyes, the ears, the eyebrows, and the head. Thus [it is said].
Regarding the words:
"By means of [the mantras] consisting of six, four, three, two, four, two, three, two, three, and one syllables. (5.8)
I bow to Śiva, the beloved of Kailāsa, who bathes his head with the nectar-essence from two jars held in his hands,
who holds those two [jars] with two [other] hands, who bears a deer and a rosary with two [more],
and whose two hands rest upon a jar of nectar placed on his lap.
I worship the three-eyed God, who wears a crown of the new moon and resides within a pure lotus. || 9 ||
One who has conquered the senses should thus recite this mantra one hundred thousand times while meditating;
one should offer ten thousand oblations with the ten substances, saturated with clarified butter. || 10 ||
"Those two" refers to the two jars.
Here, immediately after meditation, one should display these mudrās.
As they say:
"One should display the five gestures (mudrās) of the Liṅga, the Fist, the Lotus, and Śakti. (9–10)
The wise know that the materials ending with dūrvā grass consist of bilva, palāśa, khadira, and vaṭa; sesame and mustard seeds; milk boiled with milk; and curd. || 11 ||
The bilva fruit;
then, three fuel sticks from each of these; and [the milk] produced from a cow.
Milk-rice. || 11 ||

One should worship the Bull-bannered Lord on the seat described by the five syllables, having conceived the form [of the deity] through the root mantra according to the method that will be explained. || 12 ||
The syntactical connection is that one should worship the Bull-bannered Lord on the pedestal according to the method to be described hereafter. || 12 ||
Having first worshipped the limbs (aṅgas), one should afterwards worship the forms (mūrtis) of the Sun, Moon, Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, Ether, and the Self. || 13 ||
Now, the eight forms to be worshipped in the second enclosure (āvaraṇa) in sequence; having thus worshipped them,
[one worships] in the pericarp (kaṇīkā).
The syntactical connection is that one should worship the forms subsequently in the second enclosure (*dvitīyāvaraṇa*).
He states those very [forms] with the words beginning "arketi.
*Īra* means wind.
The self is the sacrificer.
And thus says the Śruti: "The self, indeed, is the sacrificer of the sacrifice; the officiating priests are the limbs. || 13 ||
She is Rāmā, Rākā, Prabhā, Jyotsnā, Pūrṇā, Eṣā, Pūraṇī, and Sudhā. || 14 ||
Then, these eight should be worshipped in sequence in the third enclosure:
Viśvā, Vidyā, Sitā, Prahvā, Sārā, Sandhyā, Śivā, and Niśā. (15)
In the fourth enclosure, these eight Śaktis are to be worshipped in sequence:
Āryā, Prajñā, Prabhā, Medhā, Śānti, Kānti, Dhṛti, and Mati. || 16 ||
In the fifth enclosure, these [deities] are to be worshipped in sequence thereafter:
Dharā, Māyā, Avanī, Padmā, Śāntā, Amoghā, Jayā, and Amalā. || 17 ||
Thereafter, the world-protectors (lokapālas) residing in the sixth enclosure are to be worshipped.
When this has been performed, this great mantra becomes fit for practical application. || 18 ||
The five enclosures, beginning with the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti), are to be worshipped on the petals at the base of each petal, one after another.
There is also a reading "pāvanī" for "dhārāmā. After that [is the instruction].
The worship with the vajra and so forth has been described.
As they say: "The Ānuṣṭubha [mantra] is declared to be the eightfold enclosure; such is the most excellent procedure."

However, in another ritual manual (*kalpa*), it is stated: "The seventh [offering] should be for the World-Guardians (*lokapāla*s), and the eighth for the planets beginning with the Sun. To indicate this very point, the author of the text has described the worship ending with the World-Guardians. (14–18)
A wise person should offer ten thousand oblations with *bilva* fuel-sticks for the sake of prosperity;
one should offer oblations with fuel-sticks of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree for the sake of spiritual luster.
Having offered ten thousand oblations with fuel-sticks of khadira wood, one shall obtain beauty and nourishment;
one should offer fuel-sticks of the vaṭa tree until ten thousand have been reached.
The practitioner shall become prosperous with wealth and grain in no time at all;
by offering sesame seeds that same number of times, he is liberated from all sins. || 21 ||
"Made of khadira wood": the remainder of the phrase is "with seven types of fuel-sticks. (20–21)
Having offered ten thousand oblations of *siddhārtha* seeds, the king conquers his enemies;
by this very procedure, untimely death shall perish. || 22 ||
An oblation performed with milk-rice bestows protection, prosperity, fame, and beauty;
by offering pure food mixed with the milk of a goat, one may destroy the effects of a malevolent spell (kṛtyā). || 23 ||
With the milk of a beast, that is, with cow’s milk. || 23 ||
This very oblation is considered to bring about peace, glory, and prosperity;
by means of an oblation of curd, one should cause mutual discord among enemies. || 24 ||
Every day, the practitioner of mantra should offer one hundred and eight blades of dūrvā grass;
having conquered all diseases, he shall attain a long life. || 25 ||
On one's birth day, desiring blameless fortune, incomparable health, and glory, one should offer oblations of milk-rice mixed with clarified butter. || 26 ||
On his own birth-day, the wise man, seeking mastery, should properly offer one hundred and twenty oblations of dūrvā grass smeared with cow’s milk and ghee. || 27 ||
Freed from all diseases, the wise man shall live for a hundred years;
[he should offer] three sticks of *kāśmarī* wood, milk, and food, each three hundred times. || 28 ||
At the end, one should offer oblations and feed the Brahmins with sweet foods;
one should respectfully gratify one's own guru with wealth, grain, and other such gifts. || 29 ||
One attains freedom from disease, long life, and prosperity by offering oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee on every lunar festival (parvan). || 30 ||
One obtains the glory of sovereignty within six months; there is no doubt about this.
"Pṛthak" means individually. || 28 ||
"Anāmaya" means health. According to Amarasimha: "Anāmaya shall be health. (29–30)
One should offer oblations of parched grain purified with mantras for the sake of obtaining a maiden and for the attainment of a bridegroom. || 31 ||
By performing oblations with fuel-sticks from milk-trees, one brings Brahmins and others under one's control.
Having bathed, one should mutter the mantra a thousand times while facing the sun.
Freed from mental and physical ailments, one shall attain long life;
by means of this mantra, one may accomplish all that is desired for oneself. || 33 ||
The syntactical connection is that "that maiden should offer oblations for the sake of obtaining a husband.
The milk-trees are the aśvattha, udumbara, plakṣa, and vaṭa.
These [substances] act as the *vaśa* (subjugation) agents for the Brāhmaṇas and others respectively.

It should also be understood that the three sweets (*madhuratraya*) are to be applied to the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes respectively, according to the statement of the Teacher: "But the breast-milk, sweetened with honey, is for the *homa* rite."
The yantra from another tantra is stated as follows:
In the pair of *vimbas*, let the fire-god (*kṛśānu*) engrave this mantra of Maheśvara together with the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*).
Then, in its [six] corners, one should place the consonants known as Agni and the others, which remove death; and in the six joints, the *satarā* (the syllable *oṃ*).

An eight-spoked [wheel], surrounded by the two *tāra* mantras and the *vyāhṛtis*, followed by the *nārasiṃha* mantra, then the thirty-two-petaled [lotus] with the *tryambaka* mantra, and further encircled by the *jagajjanmabhūmi* [mantra]. Thus [ends the section]. (31–33)
It is declared to consist of one hundred syllables through the letters of the Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, and Anuṣṭubh meters;
its sages and other attributes are exactly as previously stated, and its presiding deity is Supreme Radiance.
He states the hundred-syllable mantra: "The Gāyatrī," etc. Regarding the term "hundred-syllable": the Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables, while the Triṣṭubh consists of forty-four syllables.
This was stated with the intention that the *anuṣṭubh* consists of thirty-two syllables.
However, some have claimed that because this mantra is Vedic, it possesses one hundred syllables due to the addition of the *praṇava* at the beginning and the end;
that is irrelevant.

For, in the description of the six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*), two ancillaries are mentioned: "The crest-lock (*śikhā*) is said to consist of twenty-two [syllables], and the armor (*kavaca*) is considered to have that same number. This would be inconsistent [if the previous count were applied].
Thus, it applies to all three previously mentioned mantras as well.
As it has been said: "The ṛṣis and so forth, previously mentioned, are of three kinds. (34)
The heart is said to consist of thirteen Rudra-syllables; the head is declared to consist of [twenty-two];
the tuft (śikhā) is said to consist of twenty-two, and the armor (kavaca) is considered to consist of that same number. || 35 ||
The eye-mantra consists of fifteen syllables, and the weapon-mantra consists of seventeen syllables;
one should perform all the procedures, such as the placement of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa), according to the path previously described. || 36 ||
"By the Rudra-syllables" means by eleven syllables.
"By that many" means by twenty-two syllables. (35–36)

I take refuge in that Truth which is free from the conceit of "mine," the primordial source of the words of the Vedas, the cause of the universe, pervading all that is moving and unmoving, meditated upon by the best of sages whose senses are restrained,
consisting of the sun, fire, and moon, possessing a body of a hundred syllables, and eternally the essence of the stars.
We bow to that Great Splendor, the abode of the qualities of eternal bliss, which transcends all attributes. || 37 ||
He speaks of meditation (dhyāna) as "the Truth.
This meditation consists of the contemplation of the formless Brahman;
it is the Truth.
It has the nature of the exclusion of the unreal, according to the Vedic revelation: "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite.
It is devoid of measurement.
It is not made an object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), according to the Vedic revelation: "From which words turn back. It is the primordial [source] of the voices of the Vedas.
The expounder of the Vedas,
as established by the aphorism of Bādarāyaṇa, "Because He is the source of the Śāstra";
and the cause of the world.
Because of the aphorism, "The origin and so forth of this," [He is] pervading all that is stationary and moving;
for there is the Śruti beginning with, "Thousand-headed."
By the best of sages, such as Nārada and others,
it is said to consist of the sun, fire, and moon, according to the sequence of deities beginning with Gāyatrī;
