or else, it consists of those [deities] wherein Viṣṇu is in the sun, Rudra in fire, and Brahmā in the moon.
Because it has arisen from that;
or rather, he will later state its nature as being the syllable *oṃ*.
By this, through its consisting of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*, it possesses the nature of fire (*agni*), the moon (*indu*), and the sun (*arka*).
Regarding the phrase "having a body of a hundred syllables":
the supreme majesty is expressed by means of a hundred syllables.

This expression is used because of the non-difference between the signified and the signifier, or because of the non-difference between cause and effect due to the fact that [the Lord] has the scripture as His source, or because He is of the nature of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman).

Alternatively, since he possesses the nature of the Sun, Fire, and Moon, the connection is made through the relationship of cause and effect by stating that his body consists of a hundred syllables (*śatākṣaravapuḥ*).
The author himself will explain his nature as the syllable *Oṃ* in the final chapter.
His state of being the eternal bliss of consciousness is his very essential nature.
And that state of being the *ālaya* (receptacle) belongs to the Blessed One only figuratively.
It is beyond the qualities (*guṇas*)—namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—and is devoid of them;
this is well-known in the *Vedaśiras*.
"Great" (mahaḥ): because it is eternally luminous, it is as if great.
And all these words are merely indicative (lakṣaka) of that reality, not denotative (vācaka).
Although these words have the same referent and are not synonyms, there is no tautology because they function to exclude what is other than that [referent].
Alternatively, "maha" refers to Kuṇḍalinī, whose nature is light;
she is called "satya" (the Real) because of her eternity.
For it is said: "The eternal power is the supreme goddess. Its measure—that is, its limitation—is transcended; for it is said: "She is all-pervading, subtler than the subtlest" (1.55).
She pervades all that is stationary and moving;
for it is said: "She is omnipresent, possessing universal forms, and unconditioned by space, time, and so forth" (1.51–52).
She is meditated upon by the best of sages whose senses are restrained.
For it is said: "She is always the object of meditation for yogis," and also:
"She dances perpetually and effortlessly within the lotus-heart of yogis" (1.53).
She has the form of the sun, fire, and moon.
As it is said: "The Goddess who gives birth to the three abodes" (1.56), and also: "She whose form consists of the Moon, Sun, and Fire. Her body is composed of one hundred syllables.
As it is said: "Awakened by the Universal Self (Viśvātman), she gives birth to the world consisting of mantra" (1.57).
It is of the nature of the *tārā* [syllable].
In its center, one should contemplate the Goddess, straight in form and radiant as lightning.
"Oṃkāra-rūpiṇī, Jyotsnā, Ātma-rūpā, Śubhodayā"—
so it is said.
She is the abode of the qualities of eternal bliss.
Because of the statement, "The source of the qualities of eternal bliss" (1.51),
she is *guṇaparā*— both supreme in her qualities and supreme in her very form as the qualities.
For it is said: "Śakti is Kuṇḍalinī, whose body consists of the three guṇas and who resembles a flash of lightning" (25.66);
and also because it is said: "By way of the division into the supreme and the non-supreme, she is considered this Supreme Śakti. (37)
One who knows the mantra and has conquered the senses should recite this one hundred thousand times; he should offer oblations with milk-rice mixed with ghee, ten thousand times. || 38 ||
With thickened milk-rice, with milk-rice. || 38 ||
One should worship properly on the Saura-pīṭha according to the procedure to be described;
the best of teachers should first worship the primary enclosure with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). || 39 ||
One should worship the three enclosures (āvṛtis) in sequence with the powers (śaktis) of the Gāyatrī;
the fifth enclosure is said to consist of the powers arising from the Triṣṭubh.
The fourfold enclosure is said to consist of the powers of the *anuṣṭubh* meter;
the tenth is said to be composed of Indra and the other [deities], and that which follows it is considered to consist of the thunderbolt and the other [weapons]. || 41 ||
When the mantra has been thus perfected, the practitioner shall become like the sun;
he should worship [it] in the pericarp.
By the phrase "the supreme guide in sequence," it is stated that [this applies] to the base, middle, and tip of the petals.
Regarding the word "three":
they consist of the deities of the eight groups of eight.
Regarding "triṣṭubh":
with [verses] beginning with the jagatī, there are eleven in each direction.
Regarding "the fourfold": [it refers to this].
By virtue of having the form of eight times eight powers;
it should be understood that this occurs again in the eight directions. || 38-42 ||
One should offer oblations of pieces produced from plastered lime, combined with milk. || 42 ||
One obtains a long life, free from anxiety and devoid of disease;
one would obtain that very same fruit by [offering] dūrvā grass sprinkled with ghee. || 43 ||
One who knows the ritual injunctions should offer red lotuses sprinkled with the three sweets;
within six months, he shall attain Mahālakṣmī.
One should offer oblations with red lotuses smeared with the three sweets for the sake of all prosperity; by offering oblations with *śrī* flowers, one shall become the abode of *Ramā*.
One should daily offer a thousand oblations for one month with auspicious sesame seeds;
one should daily feed twice the number of Brahmins with foods mixed with sweets. || 46 ||
Completely liberated from all sins and entirely freed from all diseases, having conquered the effects of malevolent spells, treachery, and planetary afflictions, he lives a long life. || 47 ||
The practitioner of mantra, devoted to the morning bath, should daily recite [the mantra] one hundred times while gazing properly at the sun;
he shall live for a hundred autumns.
Sudhālatā is *guḍūcī*.
"Numbered by the sun" means twelve. (42–48)
One should daily recite the hundred-syllable mantra, conjoined with the Tāra and the Vyāhṛtis, one hundred and eight times for the attainment of the fruit of supreme liberation. || 49 ||
"Enclosed" (*saṃruddha*) means encapsulated (*sampuṭita*).
As it has been stated by the Teachers:
"The excellent mantras, beginning with the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*, and ending with the *vyāhṛtis* and the *tāra* (the *praṇava*)."
Some, however, say that by the word *saṃruddha* (obstructed) they mean *saṃrodhana* (obstruction).

And according to the principle stated in the passage, "The mantra is known as an obstruction when it occurs at the beginning, end, and middle," they desire the *tāra* (oṃ) and the *vyāhṛtis* at the beginning of each mantra.
That is not traditional, because it contradicts the written statement.
One should recite this mantra beginning with the Gāyatrī for liberation from all sins;
one should recite this mantra beginning with the Triṣṭubh for the destruction of all enemies. || 50 ||
One should recite the mantra beginning with the Anuṣṭubh for the attainment of longevity and health;
this hundred-syllable mantra is declared to bestow all human goals. || 51 ||
"Beginning with the Gāyatrī," as it has been stated;
"beginning with the Triṣṭubh."
The *triṣṭubh*, *anuṣṭubh*, and *gāyatrī* [metres].
"The *anuṣṭubh* comes first," etc.;
[the sequence is] *anuṣṭubh*, *gāyatrī*, *triṣṭubh*. || 50–51 ||
The ritual application of the verse dedicated to Varuṇa is now correctly described;
it is seen in the Ṛgveda as the first among the fixed verses (dhruvā) by the wise. || 52 ||
Vasiṣṭha is declared to be the sage, the Triṣṭubh is cited as the meter, and Varuṇa is proclaimed as the deity; the arrangement of the limbs is performed with the [corresponding] syllables. || 53 ||

The heart is said to consist of eight syllables; the head is declared to have seven. The crest (śikhā) is described as having six syllables, while the armor (kavaca) is considered to have eight. The eye is said to have seven syllables, and the weapon (astra) is proclaimed to have six. || 54 ||
"May it be tasted as firm," as the mantra says:
"O Varuṇa, dwelling in these firm dwellings, may you release us from that bond."
Seeking favor from the lap of Aditi—do you ever protect us with your blessings.
Thus [ends the section on verses] 52–54.
In the joints of the fingers and toes, in the feet, the anus, the perineum, and the navel;
in the belly, the back, the heart, the breasts, the throat, and the joints of the forearms. || 55 ||

One should place the syllables of the mantra according to the prescribed rule upon the mouth, the cheeks, the nose, the eyes, the ears, the space between the eyebrows, the head, the crown of the head, and all the limbs. || 56 ||
He explains the placement of the letters (varṇanyāsa) with the words "at the tips" and so forth:
at the joints of the feet, including the tips, there are ten letters;
at the ends of the throat, there are nine letters.
There are ten syllables at the joints of the upper arms;
thirteen in the remaining [joints];
and the head is the joint of the hair and the forehead.
The head is the *brahmarandhra*. || 55-56 ||

For the sake of prosperity, one should meditate upon Varuṇa, who is as radiant as the moon, seated upon a lotus, holding a noose, a goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting mudrā, his entire body adorned with ornaments of pearls, and appearing serene.
Regarding meditation, he says "candre" (in the moon):
the meditation on the weapons is [performed] in the first [case] for the two upper [hands] starting from the right, and in the last [case] for the two lower ones.

The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with clarified butter, using a tenth part of that amount, for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra. || 58 ||
One should properly worship Varuṇa upon the seat (pīṭha) imagined as Dharma and the other [qualities];
having performed the worship of the limbs (aṅga-pūjana), one should again worship Śeṣa, Vāsuki, and Takṣaka. || 59 ||
Then one should properly worship Karkeṭaka, Padma, Mahāpadma, and the two belonging to the Kulika family named Śaṅkhapāla upon the petals. || 60 ||
Immediately after that, one should worship Indra and the others, as well as their weapons.
Regarding the phrase "Dharma and so forth":
this refers to the worship being performed without the preliminary worship of the pedestal-shaktis (pīṭhaśakti).
By the word "correctly" (*samyak*), it is stated that the *pīṭha-śaktis* mentioned in other tantras are to be worshipped. They are as follows:
Sudhā, Kumudinī, Pūrṇā, Vāruṇī, and Viśvatomukhī.
And [the rivers] Taraṅgiṇī, Surasā, Suśītā, and Āpyāyanī likewise. Thus [it is said].
"Having performed the worship of the limbs" means [worship] on the filaments;
"one should worship properly on the petals."
By the word "correctly" (*samyak*), it is stated that the meditation on Śeṣa and the others must be performed; this should be understood as I have explained it in the *Tvaritā-paṭala*. (58–61)
For the sake of liberation from debt, one should recite the mantra every day one hundred and eight times.
By this recitation, one obtains great and imperishable prosperity;
the practitioner of mantras should offer oblations of pieces of white sugarcane soaked in clarified butter. || 62 ||
For four days, for the sake of liberation from a debt of one thousand and ten, and for great prosperity,
[one should offer] fuel-sticks made of Vetasa wood smeared with milk for three days.

One who knows the mantras and has conquered the senses should perform oblations for the successful attainment of rain, according to this procedure, when the Sun has entered the asterism Śatabhiṣaj. || 64 ||
One who seeks mastery should offer four hundred oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee for the destruction of debt, the attainment of prosperity, and the increase of power and health. || 65 ||
A fire sacrifice performed on a Friday with milk-rice mixed with sesame flour shall produce great prosperity and destroy all calamities.
A wise person, having crossed a river, should offer four hundred oblations for three days with rice grains sprinkled with ghee; thus, he shall paralyze the enemy army. || 67 ||
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of liberation from debt" (*ṛṇamuktyai*):
the meaning here is that one should recite the mantra while additionally pronouncing the word "debt" (*ṛṇa*) before the word "fetter" (*pāśa*).
"White sugar-cane pieces" refers to those commonly known as *pavaṇḍās*.
Separated by a river, situated on an island. || 61–67 ||
Having worshipped the fire facing west in the evening, the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra four hundred times; thus he shall be liberated from all calamities.
The minister, having turned his face toward the west, should perform the libation with pure waters for the destruction of all calamities and the attainment of all prosperity. (69)
What is the use of saying more here? By means of this mantra, the practitioner, intent upon recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites, shall accomplish all desires.
The ritual procedure for the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra is now being declared; by means of this, those mantras previously mentioned become endowed with life. || 71 ||
Regarding the word "by which":

although there is no ritual installation of breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) for mantras because they possess efficacy by their very nature, nevertheless, an installation is performed for those [mantras] written on diagrams (*yantra*) and so forth; thus, it is said that they possess breath by means of that [installation].

By means of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the rite of installing life-force), everything—including the previously mentioned application of mantras and yantras, as well as puppets (*puttalī*) and so forth—is rendered possessed of installed life-force.
This mantra, being the very essence of all, must necessarily be known; such is its praise.
As it has been said:
Therefore, without that [wisdom], these aforementioned applications would be useless, like those whose life has departed.
Thus [it is said]. (71)
The Śakti is formed by the noose (pāśa) and goad (aṅkuśa) joined together, adorned with the Bindu;
the seven letters beginning with Ya and ending with Sa are conjoined with Vyoma (Ha), Sadya (Sa), and Indu (the Bindu). || 72 ||
At the end of that, there should be the Haṃsa-mantra; then one should utter the word "amuṣya" (of such-and-such);
afterwards, one should say "prāṇāḥ" (vital breaths), and after that, "iha prāṇāḥ" (vital breaths here). || 73 ||

One should say: "The life-force (jīva) of so-and-so is here established; [the name] of so-and-so. At the end of "so-and-so," one should utter: "all the sense-faculties (sarvendriyāṇi), speech, mind, and sight. || 74 ||
"O ear, nose, feet, and vital breaths, having come here, may you remain happily for a long time; at the end, [you shall go] to the wife of Agni"—this is declared to be the *prāṇa-mantra*. || 75 ||
He states the extraction of the mantra: "pāśa," etc.
First the seed-syllable of the noose (pāśa), then the seed-syllable of power (śakti), then the seed-syllable of the goad (aṅkuśa).
"Vālī" is the letter *ya* adorned with a bindu, i.e., *yaṃ*.
The term *yādyāḥ* refers to the recitation of the letter *ya* as extracted [from the alphabet].
Alternatively, by means of a *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* compound, there are seven [seeds], but the seed *tadyam* is not distinct [from them].

The previous separate extraction of all seven was for the purpose of indicating that they possess the nasal bindu; however, the author did not mention the placement (*nyāsa*) of this seed during the subsequent occasion of ritual deposition (*nyāsa*).
Therefore, it is extracted separately from this.
As it was said by the Teachers:
"After the mantra of Śakti and Manas, which are separated by the noose (pāśa) and the goad (aṅkuśa)..."
"Having uttered the group of syllables *yā*, *di*, *va*, *su*, *varṇa*, together with *sa* and *haṃsa*.
Also elsewhere: "The seed-syllables of Aṅkuśa, Vāyu, Anala, Avani, and Varuṇa."
*Vyoma* is *ha*, *sadya* is *o*, *indu* is the *bindu*; thus, by that [combination], *hīṃ*.
This is also explained by the teacher Padmapāda in the *Prapañcasāra-paddhati*: "The *gaṇa* is *o*, therefore [the mantra is] simply *hom*.
The reading "the *haṃsa-mantra* in the *samanta*" is a corruption.
Regarding "and here" (iha ca):
the particle *ca* is not situated in the middle of the mantra.
In some places, the reading is "here from that" (ihata).
Then, the meaning is "from this word. Regarding the phrase "sthito'muṣya," the sandhi [conjunction] occurs in accordance with the requirements of the meter.
In the mantra, however, there is no euphonic combination (*sandhi*).
It is the same in the case of "sarvendriyāṇi amuṣvā.
The mantra consists of sixty-six syllables.
The meaning of this word was stated in the fourth [chapter].
Here, in the mantra "having come here" (*ihāgatya*), it should be understood that the word "eva" is present as "having come right here" (*ihaiva āgatya*).
And so say the teachers: "That very [deity], joined with the word 'āgama' and the word 'iha', joined with the word 'sukham' and the pair of words ending in 'ṭha', [should be invoked]."
Thus it is said.
The teacher Padmapāda has also recited it in this very same way:
"Āṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), and Krīṃ is the power (śakti). (72–75)
One should first employ the *pāśa* and other [fetters] for each respective word;
this is declared by the wise to be the *prāṇamantra* in these applications. || 76 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are proclaimed by those learned in the Tantras as the Munis;
and the meters of the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman Vedas are declared by those expert in prosody.

She is said to be the deity whose nature is consciousness, whose essence is the vital breath (prāṇa), and who is Śakti. Regarding the specific [procedure] at the time of ritual application, he says: "Perception," etc.
As for Padmapādācārya, however:
This being so, it is stated that there is a threefold repetition of the syllables beginning with *ya* as the preparatory mantra (*prayogamantra*),
for the purpose of attracting the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the individual soul (*jīva*), and all the sense organs. Some, however, describe a fourfold repetition of the syllables beginning with *ya*.
For the purpose of drawing in the generalities and particulars of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the individual soul (*jīva*), and the sense organs (*indriya*).
Some [teach] fivefold repetition for the purpose of drawing in the generalities and particulars of the vital breath, the individual soul, the sense organs, and the specific sense organs.
Some say that there is no repetition [of the mantra],
for the purpose of attracting each and every one of those mentioned in the mantra.

By the term "by the wise" (*manīṣibhiḥ*), it is indicated that at the beginning of the *haṃsa*-mantra, namely *oṃ kṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ hrīṃ oṃ*, and at the end of *svāhā*, namely *oṃ kṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ hrīṃ oṃ*—
It has been indicated that this is what should be recited.

In Padmapādācārya’s commentary on the verse, "This mantra is thus proclaimed by the very number of planets," he explains that "planets" (graha) refers to seven, and thus [the mantra] is endowed with that same number of syllables.

Therefore, it should be understood that at the time of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) for a self, a mechanical device, a doll, or the like, one should employ the word "of such-and-such" (*amuṣya*) in each instance; in place of the word "such-and-such," one should employ the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) in the genitive case and then recite the mantra. (76–78)
The heart is said to consist of the guttural class of consonants (kavarga) together with the elements beginning with space (viyat).
Immediately after that, the head is proclaimed by the words beginning with the *ca*-group;
thereafter, the tuft (*śikhā*) is celebrated by the words beginning with the *ṭa*-group associated with the organs of knowledge. || 79 ||
The armor is proclaimed by means of the organs of action, beginning with the *ta*-group;
vision is declared by means of the organs of speech and so forth, beginning with the *pa*-group.
If his weapon is proclaimed as being joined with *buddhi* and the others, then the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*s), together with their respective origins, are declared to end in *ātman*. 81.
One should place the seed-syllable of the noose (pāśa) from the navel down to the feet;
thereafter, one should place the seed-syllable of power (śakti) from the heart down to the navel. || 82 ||
Then one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the goad from the crown of the head down to the heart;
thereafter, one should place the seven [syllables] beginning with *ya* in order upon the elements within the heart.
He states the six limbs with the words "by the *ka*-group," etc.
Here, because of the mention of "the elements beginning with space" (*viyatpūrvabhūtaiḥ*), the order of creation described in the first chapter is intended.
Therefore, it should be understood that there is a corresponding transposition of the syllables.
As it has been said: "Each [letter] is accompanied by the groups beginning with *ka* and so forth, followed by their respective letters joined with the *bindu*.
Since it was stated previously that "the final letters of each class are of the same genus as those preceding them," the application is as follows.
Ṅaṃ kaṃ khaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ, to the self of space, air, fire, water, and earth—*hṛt*.
Ñaṃ caṃ chaṃ jhaṃ jaṃ, to the self of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—*śiras*.
Ṇaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ, to the self of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—*śikhā*.
Naṃ taṃ thaṃ dhaṃ daṃ, for the self of speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—*varma*.
Maṃ paṃ phaṃ bhaṃ baṃ, for the self of speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and procreating—*netra*.
Śaṃ yaṃ raṃ vaṃ laṃ haṃ ṣaṃ kṣaṃ saṃ laṃ, for the self of intellect, mind, ego, consciousness, and knowledge—*astra*.
The teacher Padmapāda has also stated that the phonemes are to be enclosed by vowels and may even be reversed;
this is according to the sequence.
It is said that the placement of *oṃ* occurs within the *ojas*. (78–83)

Then, the knower of the ritual should separately assign the two letters of the same color to the *prāṇa* and the *jīva*; with this entire [mantra], he should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*). Then, he should meditate upon the Goddess as the life-force of all beings and as consisting of the universe.
Regarding the term "prāṇa":
the word "in the heart" (hṛdaye) is understood to follow [from the previous context].
By this, the placement (nyāsa) of both prāṇa and jīva is also to be performed in the heart alone.
"Individually" means each one separately.
"By this [phrase] taken as a whole" means by the entire expression.
The meaning is "by means of the root [mantra].
By the phrase "one who knows the ritual procedure" (*vidhānavit*), it is stated that [the placement extends] from the crown of the head down to the feet.
As it has been said: "One should place the root [mantra] pervasively, beginning from the head. (84)
Seated in the center of a red ocean and a reddish boat,
she holds in her lotus-like hands a noose, a goad, a bow of sugarcane, arrows, a trident, and a skull-cup.
I bow to the Goddess, who is red in color and has three eyes. || 85 ||
Regarding "raktābdhi" (red ocean): "rakta" (red) is a qualifier for "pīta" (yellow).
As for the visualization of the weapons, however, they are first [placed] in the upper left and right hands.
Between those two which are below;
[it is] between the skull and the trident of those two which are below. || 85 ||
Having meditated thus upon the Mother of the World, one should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times;
one should then perform oblations with sacrificial porridge mixed with ghee, numbering one-tenth of that amount. || 86 ||
The meaning of "with a tenth part thereof" (*taddaśāṃśena*) is as follows:

*oṃ āṃ svāhā*, *oṃ hrīṃ svāhā*, *oṃ krīṃ svāhā*, *oṃ yaṃ mṛtāyai svāhā*. Having thus offered oblations once each with these mantras joined by the vowels beginning with *ā* and the names beginning with Vaivasvata, one should likewise offer with the syllables *oṃ kṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ hrīṃ oṃ*.
"Having performed the oblation with the root mantra, one should offer it the stated number of times"—this is the meaning accepted by the teacher Padmapāda. || 86 ||
One should worship according to this rite upon the Śakti-pīṭha, which is enriched with six corners;
one should honor Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara within the six corners.
One should then worship Vāṇī, Lakṣmī, and Umā, followed by the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
On the petals, the Mothers (mātaraḥ) are to be worshipped, and outside of that, the world-protectors (lokapālakāḥ). || 88 ||
Thus one should worship the Goddess with fragrant flowers and other offerings;
when the mantra has been mastered in this way, it shall grant the fruits of the six rites. || 89 ||
By the phrase "at the Śaktipīṭha," it is stated that the nine Pīṭha-Śaktis mentioned here are to be worshipped.
Regarding the word "pūjayet" (one should worship),
it is connected with the subsequent term "Jagaddhātrīm" (the Sustainer of the World).
By this which is about to be stated;
he states that very procedure with the words "one should worship.
In that regard, the method is as follows:

The supreme gurus maintain that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa are situated in the east, the northwest, and the northeast respectively, while Vāṇī and the others are in the southeast, the west, and the north.
One should keep in mind the previously mentioned seed-syllables (bīja) of Brahmā and the other deities, as well as their Śaktis.
"One should worship" refers to worshipping them upon the filaments (kesara). || 87–89 ||
The preceptor should establish the vital breaths everywhere by means of this mantra;
he should employ the female messengers (dūtīs) at the end of the seed-syllable (bīja) and at the beginning of the words "amuṣya. || 90 ||
Then there is Mṛtā, Vaivasvatā, Bhūyaḥ, Jīvahā, Prāṇahā, Ākṛṣyā, Grathanī, and thereafter Pramādā and Visphuliṅginī. || 91 ||
These nine vital breaths (prāṇas) are known as the messengers (dūtīs) of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
"Everywhere" refers to the self, the mechanical doll, and so forth. He extracts the mantras of the messengers with the words "the seed," etc.
"At the end of the seed-syllable" means at the end of the *haṃsa*-mantra preceded by the nooses (*pāśa*) and so forth.
Some say "at the end of the seed-syllable" means at the end of the three seed-syllables;
that is irrelevant.
Because it would contradict the words of the Teacher;
furthermore, the phrase "at the beginning of those words" would be incoherent.
That is to say, "at the beginning of those words."

At the beginning of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya). As it has been said: "Then, having uttered the female messengers (dūtīs) beginning with 'ya', the practitioner of mantra [should utter] the name of the person to be accomplished."

*Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hrīṃ oṃ kṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ hrīṃ oṃ yaṃ.* Having recited from *yaṃ mṛte amuṣya* up to *mṛtātmakān prāṇānihāhara*, or *prāṇā iha prāṇā*, or *ihaiva* and so forth, ending with *oṃ*; then again having recited from *āṃ* up to *oṃ*; and then having recited from *yaṃ mṛte amuṣya* up to *mṛtātmakaṃ jīvamihāhara*, or *jīva iha sthita*, or *ihaiva* and so forth, ending with *oṃ*; then again having recited from *āṃ* up to *oṃ*; [then] *yaṃ mṛte amuṣya*.

Having uttered "Bring all the senses, which consist of the deceased, here; or again, all the senses here, here," and so forth, ending with *oṃ*, one should say: "O *yaṃ*, bring the speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and breath of the deceased [Name], which consist of the deceased, here; or: 'Speech, mind, eyes, ears, nose, and breath, here!
Here indeed! and so forth, ending with *oṃ*."
In this manner, the mantras beginning with "Vaivasvata" and so forth are to be adapted accordingly. || 90-92 ||
Of one whose movements are bound by the noose and whose mind is seized by power.

Having fashioned an effigy of the person to be subdued (sādhya) measuring twelve finger-breadths, one should draw forth the life-breaths of that person who has been brought under control by means of these [mantras] using the goad. || 93 ||
At the time of midnight, while the person to be acted upon is asleep, one should place that life-force yantra, together with the insect, within the lotus of his heart.

He describes the method for the simultaneous installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) with the passage beginning with "by the noose" (*pāśena*) and ending with "in all rites" (*sarveṣu karmasu*).
By means of these female messengers (*dūtībhiḥ*),
the *yantra* consisting of the vital breath— which will be described later— is [to be installed] together with the insects.

In this context, the meaning is that one should begin the ritual application (*prayoga*) after having placed a living insect along with the *yantra* inside the heart of the effigy of the target (*sādhya*) prior to the commencement of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*, and then covering it.
Regarding what must be done during the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*, he says "at midnight" (*niśītha*), etc.
The teacher Padmapāda, however, says that awakening occurs by striking with the staff of Time (kāladaṇḍa),
for otherwise the installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) would be impossible.
And he [the disciple] is bound and suddenly struck violently on the head with the staff of Time.
The practitioner should then meditate upon the object of attainment, whose entire collection of sense-faculties has been struck and agitated.
Because of this statement. || 92-94 ||
Then, on the petals [are the deities] of Vāyu, Vahni, Indra, and Varuṇa;
thereafter, within the pericarp, [are those] of Īśa, Rakṣasa, Śītāṃśu, and Yama.
One should visualize [the letters] beginning with *ya*, joined with swans, having the form of bees, their bodies connected by threads produced from the bindu at the head. 96.
In this manner, one should mentally visualize [the bees] in the form of Bhr̥ṅgis within the lotus of one's own heart;
having dispatched the Bhr̥ṅgis residing in the lotus of one's heart through the path of the breath. || 97 ||

From each of the lotuses at the heart of the objects to be accomplished, the practitioner who knows the ritual procedure should bring forth a single bee and place it either in the effigy or within his own heart. 98.
Restrained, one should perform the severing of the thread with the fire-seed (raṃ);
then, having drawn forth the bees from the heart of the target, one should paralyze them with the earth-seed (laṃ). || 99 ||
In this manner, one should perform eleven repetitions in all ritual acts;
for the rites of subjugation and attraction, the wise practitioner should visualize [the deities] as red in color. || 100 ||
One should meditate on smoke-colored [deities] for delusion and hatred, on black ones for the rite of killing, on yellow ones for paralyzing, and on those for drawing in the vital breaths. || 101 ||
One should establish the vital breaths drawn from the heart of the target within one's own heart;
for cruel rites, their establishment is said to be within a doll (puttalī). || 102 ||
In those cruel rites, the skillful practitioner should always visualize the life-breaths of the victim as frogs and his own as serpents.

Regarding the phrase "on the petals," he states the location of the messengers (dūtīs) such as Mṛtā and the others in one's own heart, in the heart of the target (sādhya), and in the heart of the effigy (puttalī).

"One should contemplate them in the form of bees" means that one should meditate on Mṛtā and the others— who are in the form of the letters beginning with *ya*— as bees upon the filaments of the lotus-petal of the target's heart, and as female bees (*bhṛṅgī*) within the lotus of one's own heart.
Regarding the word *śiras* (head):
it refers to those threads produced from the drops (*bindu*) located at the heads of the seed-syllables beginning with *ya*; [the deities] have their forms bound together by those threads.
As it was said by the Teachers: "bound by their own drops."
"In the effigy" refers to rites of forceful action (*krūrakarman*);
"in one's own mind" refers to rites such as subjugation (*vaśyādi*).
Regarding the phrase "one who knows the ritual procedure" (*vidhānavit*):
it has been stated that [the practitioner] is the hook for the entry and exit [of the breath] through one's own *vahni-nāḍī* (fire-channel),
by means of the fire-seed syllable *raṃ*.

"Restrained" (saṃyataḥ) means being attentive to the thought that "in each and every petal is the location of the dead and so forth," by means of the seed-syllable *glauṃ* associated with the earth (*bhū*).

In this regard, the method is as follows: having extracted the power (*śakti*) of the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) in five ways—namely, in the form of the power of the fetters (*pāśa*), fire (*tejas*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), the great bee (*mahābhramara*), and the staff of time (*kāladaṇḍa*)—and while uttering the seed-syllable of the fetters (*pāśabīja*), one binds the object by the neck with the fetter; having brought it under one's own control by means of the fiery energy of the seed-syllable of power (*śaktibīja*), one draws it forward with the goad and establishes it before oneself; then, while uttering the eight [seed-syllables] beginning with *yā*, one pervades and seizes the skin and other constituents of the object, and finally devours the object with the great bee.

Having awakened that sleeping [deity] by striking with the *kāladaṇḍa*, saying "Kṣam," one uproots [the obstruction] along with its retinue; having united it with the great bee that is one's own vital power (*prāṇaśakti*) by saying "Sam," and having contemplated identity with oneself by saying "Haṃsa"; then, for the sake of enlivening in rites such as subjugation (*vaśya*), having performed the immersion by saying "Hrīm īm"; and having addressed one's own deceased [state] by saying "Yaṃ mṛte" and so forth; then, having joined the vital breaths of one's own deceased [state] with the vital breaths of others by saying "Amuṣya mṛtātmakā iha prāṇā" and so forth; [one concludes] with "Ram."

Having performed the severing of the thread of the victim’s life, and having established the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) of the victim within the doll whose heart contains the insect, or within oneself, one should stabilize them with the syllable *glaum* and likewise bring back the life-force (*jīva*) and other elements of that deceased person.
Or else, one may simultaneously establish the vital breaths and other factors of the deceased.

Then, if [the ritual is performed] upon one's own heart, one should recite: "Cet-ām hrīm," and so forth, in the form: "In me are the vital breaths (prāṇas); here are the vital breaths; in me is the life-force (jīva); here it is situated.

If [it is performed] upon a doll (puttalī), one should mutter: "In the doll are the vital breaths; here are the vital breaths; in the doll is the life-force; here it is situated. Such is the procedure for the consecration of the deceased.

In this manner, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) of Vaivasvata and the others should also be established. Then, having recited the syllables beginning with *ya* up to the end of the *homa*, one should again swallow the elements and the life-force (*jīva*) of the target (*sādhya*), together with their attendants, as they are contracted within one's own mandala. Having addressed the messengers (*dūtīs*) beginning with *ya* in the vocative case, and having said for the target: "Bring the vital breaths of such-and-such here! The vital breaths of such-and-such are here, the vital breaths are here!"— [End of sentence fragment]
Furthermore, one should say, "Bring the elements of that person here," and so forth;
the same applies to a living being as well.
This very same method applies to a mechanical doll (puttalī) as well.
As it has been said:
"This same method would apply even to the absorption of the vital breaths drawn from the location of the target into a doll (*puttalī*) or similar object.
Thus [it is said].
One should perform the previously mentioned rite eleven times; this is the minimum limit. Beyond this, one may perform it at will.
As it has been said: "Having performed this rite of the installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), [one should offer] eleven [oblations] at minimum. (95–103)
Then, with the letters beginning with *ya* written on the petals of the wind, fire, Śakra, Varuṇa, Īśvara, Rākṣasa, Indu, and Preteśa,
accompanied by the *bindu* and joined with the *kṣa* situated as the *haṃsa*, [one should place] the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Then, the machine of the vital breath, encircled by the phonemes, is situated upon the earth.

Thus, one who is skilled in the application of this mantra and knows its meaning, as taught by Manu, can bring all the gods under his control; how much more so, then, ordinary human beings on earth? (105)
He describes the yantra with the words "vāyu" and so forth.
"By the letters beginning with ya" means by those ending in *hom*.
"Situated on earth" means—
The meaning is that it is surrounded by an underground chamber (*bhūgṛha*) on the outside.
However, the teacher Padmapāda explains the *yantra* differently as follows:

having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth within the power (*śakti*) situated in the center of an eight-petaled lotus, one encircles her with the noose (*pāśa*) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*), and then places the eight vowels beginning with *ya* upon the eight petals.
Having written [the mantra] and having wrapped the remainder around the outside, one should draw a noose and a goad within two *bhūpura*s; such is the procedure for the *yantra*. || 104-105 ||
I shall now describe in due order the mudrās, such as the āvāhanī and others, by which all the deities rejoice when they are properly performed. (106)
The añjali gesture, formed with both hands and fully filled with flowers, is declared by the best of teachers to be the āvāhanī mudrā. || 107 ||
That very same [mudrā], when turned face downwards, is said to be used for the rite of installation (sthāpana).
It consists of two fists joined together, with the pair of thumbs raised up. || 108 ||
This mudrā is taught by those who know the tantras as being for the purpose of summoning;
that same mudrā, when the thumb is held deep within, is proclaimed for the purpose of restraint. || 109 ||
The two fists made with palms facing upward are known as the *sammukhīkaraṇa* (making face-to-face).
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs upon the limbs of the deity constitutes *sakalīkṛti* (the act of making complete). || 110 ||
The mudrā says, "She is the invoker. [The root] *rā* means "giving. The etymological derivation of *mudrā* is: she bestows (*rāti*) joy (*mudaṃ*), therefore she is called *mudrā*.
This very point is indicated by the statement, "All the deities rejoice in this.
For this reason, the arising of joy in the deities occurs through that vision.
Indeed, one's own fingers—the thumb and the others—consist of the five elements, being of the nature of ether, air, fire, water, and earth.
Through the mutual union and the symbolic form of these [energies], a certain joy arises— preceded by the manifestation of the deity— which brings about their presence.
As it has been said:
The elements, beginning with earth, are considered to correspond respectively to the fingers starting from the little finger;
their manifold expansion arises through various modes of mutual interpenetration.
"However, during the time of secret recitation, in meditation, and in rites for specific desires, the respective mudrās that cause the presence of the deity should be employed. Thus it is said.
Elsewhere also it is said: "It bestows joy (mudaṃ rāti), therefore it is called mudrā; indeed, it is but a single fist.
Because of slight variations, it generates anger or joy in living beings."
"For that very reason, these mudrās are considered to bestow joy upon all the gods;
O Śivā, those mudrās should always be displayed at the time of worship. Thus [it is said].

Likewise: "By the sequence of the path of the elements starting from the void (khādi), and by the sequence of the fingers starting from the big toe (aṅguṣṭha), a certain [power] arises through the mutual union of the risen [elements]; she brings about proximity and prostration. Thus it is said.
Thinking, "May he be summoned by this [mantra]," the invocation (āvāhanī) should be performed preceded by a prayer.
However, there is a specific distinction in another tantra:
having formed a *añjali* with both hands, [one should place it] upon the root-joints of the two ring fingers (*anāmikā*).
"One should place the two thumbs [within]; this is known as the *āvāhanī* (invocation) mudrā.
This indeed is the traditional position. (106–110)

The fist formed with the left hand, with the index finger extended and pointing downward—this is the *avaguṇṭhana* (veiling) mudrā; when it is rotated all around, it becomes [the *parāvṛtti* mudrā]. || 111 ||
"Whirled" means by way of a counter-clockwise rotation.
Those following the tradition say that this mudrā is formed with both hands. As it has been said: "Having completely veiled [it] with the armor [mudrā] using the pair of arms..."
Thus [ends the section]. 111.
Furthermore, with the little fingers and ring fingers joined facing each other,
and likewise the index and middle fingers, this is proclaimed as the Dhenu-mudrā.
The best of teachers should perform the *amṛtīkaraṇa* (the rite of making [the offering] nectar) with that [mudrā].
He describes the *dhenumudrā* as "mutually," meaning that the little fingers and ring fingers are joined facing each other, and likewise the index and middle fingers are joined facing each other.

The fingers of both hands should be joined at their previous middle sections with the spaces between them interlaced, such that the right little finger is entwined [with the left]. Therein, the right little finger, having passed over the back of the right ring finger, reaches its left side and is joined with the left ring finger;
the left little finger, however, remains as it was, joined with the right ring finger.
In this manner, the left index finger, having crossed over the back of the left middle finger, should be joined with the right middle finger which has come to its right side;
the right index finger, remaining as it was, should be joined with the left middle finger.
As it has been said: "The fingers of the left hand [should be joined] at the joints of the fingers of the right hand."
Having inserted the two index fingers between the two middle fingers, one should join the two little fingers with the two ring fingers; that is the *dhenumudrā*.
Thus [ends the section on] verses 112–113.
With the thumbs interlocked and the fingers of the hands extended. || 113 ||
This Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) is joy; the wise should employ this seal for the purpose of bringing [the deity] to the state of supremacy in the ritual of the deity-sacrifice. || 114 ||
He speaks of the Mahāmudrā: "Mutually," etc.
By interlacing the two thumbs of the hands, they take the form of a knot; the remaining fingers are straight.
These mudrās, as well as the specific mudrās mentioned by me for their respective mantras, one should not show to anyone.
As it is said in the Mahāsaṃhitā:
"One should never display the mudrā in a gathering of many people;
this is a secret, O best of sages, therefore one should employ it in private."
One should not reveal the characteristics of the mudrās to one who has not been initiated;
the deities become agitated with him, and it shall be fruitless.
Elsewhere also it is said: "One should not show the rosary or the mudrā even to one's guru."
Furthermore, one should perform all of these in secret;
for those seeking liberation, they should be shown by means of the mind alone.
Regarding this, they say: "The wise know that for those seeking liberation, mudrās are mental constructs of form."
But for all others, the wise recommend [offering] with both hands.
Thus [ends the section on] verses 113–114.
Because it is joined with the letters from 'A' to 'Kṣa', it is celebrated as the "Akṣamālā" (rosary of syllables).
One should fashion a rosary for recitation using beads equal in number to those letters. || 115 ||
He speaks of the *akṣamālā* (rosary): "Ādi" and so forth.
The meaning is that the *akṣamālā* is a garland (*mālā*) of phonemes (*varṇa*) beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the letter *kṣa*.
Here, the single additional *kṣa* is itself the *meru* (the central bead).

By this, it is also indicated that a rosary should be made with fifty beads. As it has been said: "Having visualized the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa' situated within the *brahmanāḍī*, and having joined each letter with the nasal bindu, one should then recite the excellent mantra."
Having joined [the letters] beginning with 'a' and likewise those beginning with 'ka' in their proper sequence,
one should then conceive of the letter 'kṣa' as Meru there, O Goddess of the Universe.
Then the script shall consist of one hundred and fifty beads;
by means of this, the recitation of all mantras accomplishes all goals. Thus it is said.
In this context, it should be understood that the use of the term "akṣamālā" (rosary) is figurative.
By this, it is also stated that such a rosary is intended for the *puraścaraṇa* rite;
furthermore, it is thereby implied that a rosary should be made of one hundred and eight beads even for daily recitation (*nityajapa*).

Having recited [the alphabet] from *a* to *la*, and having recited it again in reverse order from *la* to *a*, one should recite it eight times with each of the eight groups of consonants (*aṣṭavarga*), making the letter *kṣa* the central peak (*meru*).
As they say: "The fifty beads of the rosary-string, beginning with *a* and ending with *la*..."
The letter *kṣa* is situated on Mount Meru, and from the letter *la* onwards, they follow in reverse order.
"By means of the division into eight groups, there shall be one hundred and eight [mantras].
Reciting each mantra with an interval of one [between them] bestows fruit in this manner. Thus it is said.
But in another tantra, there is this distinction: liberation [is attained] by twenty-five [recitations], the accomplishment of wealth by thirty;
all purposes by twenty-seven, and the rite of sorcery by fifteen.

"Success in rites for desired objects (*kāmyakarman*) shall come with fifty [beads]; with one hundred and four, all success; and with a rosary of one hundred and eight [beads], protection. Thus, with twenty-seven, five hundred and four, and one hundred and eight [beads], it serves for the sake of accomplishing all tasks for everyone and for the purpose of daily recitation (*nityajapa*).
It has been stated that one should fashion a rosary;
as they say:
"A rosary consists of one hundred and eight beads, or fifty, or forty-four."
And with twenty-seven syllables, the recitation is common to all. Thus [ends verse 115].
A rosary of rudrākṣa beads produces one's heart's desires through recitation;
a garland fashioned from lotus seeds is considered a destroyer of enemies. || 116 ||
A garland made of knots of *kuśa* grass destroys all sins;
one fashioned from *putrajīva* fruits brings about the attainment of sons. || 117 ||
A rosary fashioned from silver and gems grants one's desired objects when recited;
likewise, a rosary constructed of gold bestows all wishes. || 118 ||
A garland fashioned from coral bestows abundant wealth;
a crystal garland grants good fortune; and one fashioned from pearls confers prosperity. (119)
Fashioned with conch shells and gems, it produces imperishable fame;
when composed of all these together, this garland leads men to liberation. || 120 ||
He describes the specific fruit resulting from specific types of gems with the words "rudrākṣa" and so forth. "By all these" means five gems for each [deity].
However, there is a distinction in the Piṅgalāmata:
The practitioner of mantra should fashion a rosary for recitation from one hundred and eight beads made of crystal, coral, pearl, gold, or putrajīva fruit.
One should employ [the fingers] in sequence for liberation (mokṣa), sorcery (abhicāra), pacification (śāntika), subjugation (vaśya), and attraction (ākarṣa);
the jewels of the fingers, beginning with the thumb, are moved by the thumb. Thus it is said.
The method for fashioning the rosary, as stated in another tantra, is as follows:
"The procedure for the rosary is now described in brief.
Having diligently procured beads according to availability and according to one's understanding,"
They should be uniform in shape, neither too thick nor too thin,
not damaged by insects, not decayed, and fresh.
Having washed each of those separately with the five products of the cow,
one should then [use] that which is woven by a virtuous woman of the foremost twice-born and provided with a knot.
Having tripled the thread that was previously washed three times,
one should arrange nine *aśvattha* leaves in the shape of a lotus.
One should place there the thread and the gems, having washed them with scented water;
then, one should project the *tāra*, the *śakti*, and the *mātṛkā* onto both the thread and the gems.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa), one should worship with clarified butter and offer oblations according to one's capacity;
then, taking each individual gem, one should join it there to the thread.
Having joined face to face and back to back,
one should place the bead counted according to the prescribed number in front as the Meru.
One should fashion a knot-tying within each individual garland;
having properly established the vital breaths therein, one should worship them with ritual offerings.
"Having thus prepared the rosary, one should then perform the recitation (*japa*) with the *mātṛkā* [alphabet].

Having worshipped the Guru, one should receive [the mantra] from his hand for the sake of attaining all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). Thus it is said. Furthermore, elsewhere: 'One should obtain a thread woven by a woman of the same caste.'"
One should immerse the scripture and the gems in the five products of the cow for three days.
Then, on the fourth day, he should wash it with the Astra-mantra;
subsequently, the practitioner should tie it with the Hṛdaya-mantra in the shape of a cow's tail.
One should then place a nāgapāśa and a brahmagranthi in the middle of the jewel;
then, with the mantra *huṃ*, one should bind Mount Meru with the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) itself.
Having prepared the previously described mandala and worshipped one's chosen deity therein,
the wise practitioner, remaining self-controlled, should recite the mantra eight thousand times.

"One should offer oblations with clarified butter in ten parts of that [number], using the mantras as previously prescribed. Regarding this, however, in the Śaiva Āgama: "A cord resembling a cow's tail, single-pointed (or snake-shaped) and joined at its ends, should be threaded with white and other colored threads for the successful accomplishment of their respective rites."
Having thus prepared the rosary, one should then begin the consecration;
one should wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and pure water while reciting the Sadyojāta mantra.
One should rub it with sandalwood, agallochum, perfumes, and so forth, while reciting the Vāmadeva mantra;
one should fumigate it with the Aghora mantra, and smear it with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
"One should consecrate each [bead] one hundred times with the fifth mantra alone;
and one should consecrate the *meru* (the central bead) with the fifth mantra in the same manner. Thus it is said.
The method of recitation (*japa*) regarding the rosary is also stated in that very same place:
One should place the rosary on the middle finger and rotate it in sequence with the thumb;
this method of counting the Mātṛkā-gaṇa bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One should perform the highest rite with the thumb and the ring finger;
however, for the rite of attraction, one should recite with the thumb and the middle finger.
Indeed, for the rites of inciting hatred and eradication, the recitation is performed with the joining of the index finger and the thumb;
for the rite of killing, one should perform the recitation with the little finger and the thumb.
At times other than the time of recitation, one should worship that rosary and keep it concealed.
When the thread has worn out, one should knot a new thread and recite the mantra one hundred times.
If one has touched something forbidden, one should recite [the mantra] after washing as is appropriate.
In cases of coughing, sneezing, or yawning, one should discard a single turn [of the rosary].
If, through negligence, the ring finger is touched, an *āvartaka* occurs;
one should discard [the rosary] and, having tied it again, use it as before.
"When that [consecration] has been performed, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind;
once it has been thus consecrated, one must never recite another mantra."
Elsewhere also it is said: "One should recite that very mantra upon which the rosary is fixed;
the wise should never perform the recitation of any other mantra."
One should not touch the thread with the index finger, nor shake it, nor wave it about;
one should not touch it with the left hand, nor allow it to fall from the hand.
When moving the beads with the thumb, one should not touch another bead;
during the time of recitation, the wise practitioner should never cross over the *meru* bead.
And at the time of changing [the beads], one should not cause them to clash.
Having thus understood everything regarding the rosary, one should begin the recitation. Thus it is said.
The teachers also say: "One should recite with the mind fixed on that [deity], using the index finger, the fist, or the fingers as a rosary.
And elsewhere: "That which is recited with the tips of the fingers, and that which is recited when the *meru* is bypassed..."
"That which is recited without [proper] counting becomes fruitless. Thus it is said.

There is a specific distinction elsewhere: one who desires the highest accomplishment should conceal the rosary obtained from the guru, or, in his absence, one fashioned by oneself, until the completion of all rites.
One should not show one's own mantra or rosary even to the guru;
O Six-faced One, the rosary must be kept secret at the time of recitation.
A scripture belonging to the views of others would be entirely fruitless; therefore, it should always be concealed with effort in all circumstances by the wise. Thus [it is said].
In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*, recitation (*japa*) is also described by means of fingers and finger-joints. As it is said:
"The fruit obtained through the count of finger-recitation is declared to be single-fold."
One should know that [the merit] is eightfold for those on the lines, and a hundredfold for those with skill.
In that regard, while performing the counting of beads with the fingers, one should count using all the fingers including the thumb;
an action performed without the thumb shall be fruitless.
One should daily perform the recitation of mantras using the finger-joints,
specifically employing the two middle joints of the middle and ring fingers.
Circumambulating Mount Meru,
one should count in sequence starting from the base joint of the ring finger up to the base joint of the middle finger.
Having conceived Mount Meru from the middle of the ring finger up to the base of the index finger by means of a pair of middle joints, one should count this according to its [respective] type.
One should not separate the fingers when the palms are slightly contracted;
for if there is a separation of the fingers, the recitation flows away through the gaps.
Since the Rākṣasas seize that recitation which one performs by transgressing the rules of counting, a wise person should count it in every respect.
Thus [ends the section], verses 116–120.

Now, in accordance with all tantras, I shall correctly explain in this tantra the characteristics of the six rites (ṣatkarma), which grant the accomplishment of the fruits of their application. || 121 ||
The wise proclaim the six rites (ṣatkarma) which end with killing: pacification, subjugation, immobilization, then inciting enmity and expulsion. || 122 ||
The removal of diseases, malevolent rites, planetary seizures, and the like is declared to be *śānti* (pacification).
Bringing all people under one's influence and making them obedient is declared to be *vaśya* (subjugation). || 123 ||
The obstruction of the activity of all [enemies] is declared to be "stambhana" (paralysis).
Causing mutual hatred among those who are affectionate toward one another is considered "vidveṣaṇa" (inciting enmity). || 124 ||
Uccāṭana is proclaimed as the expulsion from one's own country and so forth;
māraṇa is declared to be the taking away of the life-force of living beings. || 125 ||
He states the six rites with the word "atha" (now). "Obedience" means acting according to one's word. "The subduing of all" [is explained as follows].
[This refers to] the people, water, semen, the edge of a sword, the army, the words of an opponent, the wind, and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), one's own country and others—such as the house, village, city, and so on—are included. (121–125)
Having understood one's own deity, time, and other factors, one should accomplish the ritual acts;
[the deities are] Rati, Vāṇī, Ramā, Jyeṣṭhā, Durgā, and Kālī, in their respective order. || 126 ||
The deities of the six rites have been declared; one should worship them at the beginning of the ritual.
The directions are considered to belong to Īśa, Candra, Indra, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Agni. || 127 ||
Regarding the term "one's own deity" (*svadevatā*):

here, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one includes the seat, mudrās, the rising of the breath (*bhūtodaya*), the maṇḍala, the arrangement of syllables, the methods of describing colors, the writing materials, the pen, the sacrificial fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the fuel-sticks (*samidh*), recitation (*japa*), the rosary (*mālā*), and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "one should worship" (*prapūjayet*): [it refers to these aforementioned items].
In that regard, the specific flowers are described in the *Piṅgalāmata*:

"For the rites of immobilization (*stambha*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), subjugation (*vaśya*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), pacification (*śānti*), and malevolent magic (*māra*), the flowers are respectively yellow, blue, red, smoky-grey, white, and black."
He says that the directions are presided over by the Lords (Īśas).
There is a specific distinction elsewhere:
"In the east-facing [direction] there shall be subjugation (vaśya), while in the south there is that which pertains to malevolent rites (ābhicārika)."
One should know that binding is in the west, and pacification is remembered as being in the north.
Furthermore, attraction is in the southeast, and likewise, killing is in the southwest;
expulsion is in the northwest, and in the northeast is that which bestows liberation.
Thus [ends the section on] verses 126–127.
Starting from sunrise, ten successive *ghaṭikās* constitute the seasons beginning with spring, occurring day after day throughout the day and night. || 128 ||
Spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, winter, and the cool season—
winter is prescribed for rites of pacification, while spring is for the rite of subjugation.
The winter season is to be known for immobilization (stambhana), summer is said to be for inciting enmity (vidveṣa);
the rainy season is to be known for eradication (uccāṭana), and autumn for the rite of killing (māraṇa). || 130 ||
Regarding the word "sūrya":
"day by day" means every single day;
within the course of a day and night (ahorātra), starting from sunrise, the seasons beginning with spring occur sequentially during each ten-ghaṭikā period—this is the syntactical connection.
In this context, the primary season consists of exactly two months;
however, it should be understood that this [shorter duration] is intended for urgent matters.
With this intention in mind, it has been stated elsewhere as well:
The second, third, and likewise the fifth day of the bright fortnight,
when joined with Mercury, Jupiter, or [Venus], or else the seventh day for rites of pacification (śāntika).
The sixth, the thirteenth, the fourth, and likewise the ninth— when joined with Monday,
Thursday, or Jupiter— are praised by the wise for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika).
The eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh lunar days,
when conjoined with Venus or Saturn, are recommended for the rite of inciting enmity.
Furthermore, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, as well as on a Saturday or the eighth day,
the recitation (japa) prescribed here by Śaṅkara is recommended for the purpose of eradication (uccāṭana).
The new moon (amāvasyā), the eighth day (aṣṭamī) of the dark fortnight, and likewise the fourteenth day (caturdaśī)—
when these are joined with the Sun, its son [Mercury], or also with the Son of the Earth [Mars]—
are praised for the rites of killing (māraṇa), paralyzing (stambhana), deluding (moha), and causing enmity (droha). Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā it is also stated:
"The well-known seasons should be adopted for the performance of the six rites and so forth; however, the practice of mantras may be performed in whichever season one chooses."
"In the forenoon for the sake of subjugation and nourishment," and so forth;
thus it is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*.

"Nourishment, attraction, auspiciousness, eradication, pacification, immobilization, and obstruction [are achieved] respectively when Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, the Moon, Saturn, and Mercury [are the lords of the week]. Thus it is said.
There is another distinction in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"Winter is white and old; spring is red and young;
the infant season is described as pale-red and white."
"Summer has a smoky body, the arrival of the rains has a dark-blue body, and the autumn season is black in color; these are the seasonal entities beginning with the period of peace."

Another distinction is stated in the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*: "In rites for pacification (*śāntika*), recitation (*jāpa*) is mental; in rites for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), it is said to be whispered (*upāṃśu*);
in rites of sorcery (*ābhicāra*), it should be audible. [The practitioner] should face east, north, or south."

However, it should be understood that the mention of midnight (*ardharātra*) in the context of employing the weapons of the days (*dināstra*) and so forth for the purpose of killing is a specific injunction made for that particular case;
but here, because of the employment of the word "season" (*ṛtu*), it is not so. (128–130)
The wise declare that the postures known as Padma (Lotus), Svastika, Vikaṭa, Kukkuṭa, Vajra, and Bhadra are the [six] āsanas. || 131 ||
Regarding "padma" and so forth:
among those, he will state the definitions of the first and the last at the end.
As for the definitions of *vikaṭa* and *kukkuṭāsana*, they are as follows:
One should display the pair of arms between the knees and the shanks;
this is the vikaṭāsana, performed while seated in the utkaṭāsana.
Having first assumed the utkaṭāsana posture, and then placing both feet evenly together with the two hands between the knees—this is declared to be the kukkuṭāsana. Thus it is said.

Elsewhere, specific seats have been described: for immobilization (stambhana), there should be an elephant hide; likewise, for killing (māraṇa), a buffalo hide; for expulsion (uccāṭana), a sheepskin; and for the rite of subjugation (vaśya), a tiger skin.
"In cases of inciting enmity, the skin of a jackal is prescribed, and likewise for pacification;
the seat of tiger skin is declared to be that which brings about all supernatural accomplishments. Thus [ends verse 131].
The six mudrās should be known in sequence as those called the lotus, the noose, and the mace;
and those named the club, the thunderbolt, and the sword, for the rites of pacification and the others. || 132 ||
Regarding the "six mudrās": "The mudrā formed by the pair of the little finger and the thumb is considered the triangular *aśani* [thunderbolt] mudrā"—this is the definition of the *aśani* mudrā.
The definitions of the other mudrās were stated by me on the occasion of the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *puruṣottama* mantra. || 132 ||
Water is praised for rites of pacification; fire is declared for subjugation;
earth is praised for paralyzing; space is proclaimed for causing enmity;
wind is remembered for eradication; and fire is considered for killing. || 133 ||
During the respective emergence of each element, the practitioner with a sharpened mind should properly perform the corresponding rite, conjoined with its specific maṇḍala. || 134 ||
Regarding the phrase "the rising of the respective elements" (*tattadbhūtodaya*):
the rising of the elements will be explained in the final chapter.
However, the specific details have been stated by Īśānaśiva:
In the case of both earths (*ubhayadharaṇi*), one should accomplish the desired goal over a long period;
in the case of both winds (*ubhayamaruti*), it may succeed after a short time of ripening.
In the case of both skies and fires (*ubhayagaganavahni*), there is neither success nor loss.
Then, situated in both waters, it shall quickly grant one's desires.
When the moon is situated in earth, one should perform rites for pacification (śāntika) or nourishment (pauṣṭika);
with the moon and wind, subjugation (vaśya) and attraction (ākarṣaṇa); on the ground of the sun, one should perform immobilization (stambhana); and in the water of the sun, likewise.
[It is used] for subjugation, causing the Maruts to roam, and for eradication.
"In the sky of the Sun it is enchanting; in the fire of the Sun, it would most swiftly subdue the host of enemies and even slay them.
Thus, it is joined with the respective maṇḍalas as described in the first chapter.

By the phrase "by the minister with a sharpened mind," it is stated that one should perform the respective actions after understanding day and night through their division into upward and downward [movements].
This was said by Gautama: "The upward movement of the pervasive wind of the body is *prāṇa* during the day."
The downward-moving apāna is night, as it abides within the body.
"In times of fear from enemy armies and the like, the knower of mantras should perform at that very moment the rites taught therein;
he should properly carry out, according to the divisions, such acts as eradication (uccāṭana) and so forth. (133–134)
The seed-syllables of the mantras for the six rites, corresponding respectively to the moon, water, earth, space, wind, and fire, are as follows. || 135 ||
Regarding the phrase "the cool-rayed one" (śītāṃśu): the sixteen vowels are the two *saṅgas* (conjunctions) with the color of the moon.
Those colors other than these are to be understood as the elemental colors mentioned in the second chapter.
As it has been said:
"One should perform rites of protection and immobilization with [mantras] consisting of the earth-element (yellow) syllables;
rites of pacification, nourishment, and attraction with those consisting of the water-element (white) syllables."
Burning, delusion, and the breaking of limbs, as well as attraction, are produced by mantras consisting of fire;
while the breaking of armies, confusion, expulsion, and acts of hatred are produced by those born of wind.
Various powders such as black ashes and the like are for the purpose of killing;
for minor rites, they are established with colors numbering according to the rows, using those originating from the sky (ākāśa). Thus it is said.
The teachers also state: "The rites of immobilization (*stambhana*) and so forth should be performed with groups of ten syllables.
However, some say that *sava*, *la*, *ha*, and *ra* [should be used].
As it is stated in the Mahākapilapañcarātra: "Laṃ is to be known as yellow earth; vaṃ is declared to be white water; raṃ is red fire; marut is black; and yaṃ haṃ is the exceedingly white ether."
However, there is a distinction in another text: "A vessel made of gold, silver, stone, or fine clay is prescribed for rites such as pacification (śānti) and so forth;
one fashioned from bilva, akṣa, or śigru wood is for rites such as killing (māraṇa) and expulsion (uccāṭana). Thus it is said.
Elsewhere also: "In rites such as *śāntika* (pacification) and others here, vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay are highly recommended.
Those made from *śelu*, *akṣadruma*, and *śigru* trees are used for the rite of *vidveṣaṇa* (enmity)."
"Vessels are also highly recommended for acts such as driving away, eradication, and killing.

However, in the *Kulaprakāśatantra* it is said: "Three mudrās are prescribed for the fire-oblation (*homa*): the deer-mudrā (*mṛgī*), the goose-mudrā (*haṃsī*), and the sow-mudrā (*śūkarī*). The sow-mudrā involves the contraction of the hands; the goose-mudrā is formed by releasing the little fingers."

The *mṛgī* (deer) mudrā consists of the little finger and the index finger extended; these three are considered the mudrās. In sacrifices and rites for pacification (*śāntika*), the *haṃsī* (goose) is proclaimed [as the appropriate mudrā].
"In rites of sorcery, however, she is proclaimed as Śūkarī. Thus [it is said].
In the Piṅgalāmata, however, other mudrās are also mentioned:
"Then, in the homa of substances, by the joining of the index finger and the thumb,
there are respectively the destruction of fever, the affliction of enemies, eradication, and delusion."
Furthermore, a distinction regarding the classes [of mantras] has been stated;
as they say:
"The classes [of mantras] end with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *vauṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ*."
In pacification, subjugation, as well as in immobilization, causing enmity, expulsion, and killing—thus [it is said].
Elsewhere also: "In worship, for the pacification of anger and so forth, one should employ the word *namaḥ*;
and in fire-rituals, for subjugation and so forth, one should employ the word *svāhā*."
"The syllable *phaṭ* is used for killing and similar acts; the word *haṃ* for inciting enmity and the like;
*vauṣaṭ* should be used for nourishing and so forth; and *vaṣaṭ* is prescribed for hatred and destruction. Thus it is said.
Likewise, elsewhere it is said: "One should employ *svāhā* in rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), burning (*saṃtāpa*), and fire-offerings (*homa*);
one should utter *namaḥ* for the pacification of anger, for propitiation (*śānti*), and for worship (*pūjana*)."
Vauṣaṭ is used for the rites of enchantment (sammohana), illumination (uddīpana), nourishment (puṣṭi), and the conquest of death (mṛtyuñjaya);
likewise, the syllable Huṃ is used for the destruction of affection (prītināśa), as well as for cutting (chedana) and killing (māraṇa).
In rites of eradication, inciting hatred, and likewise in the transformation of the intellect, one should employ *phaṭ*;
and for the destruction of obstacles and malevolent planets, one should employ the utterance *huṃ phaṭ*.
"And for the purpose of illuminating the mantra, whether in gain or loss, *vaṣaṭ* is prescribed.
However, in the *Piṅgalāmata*: "That recitation (*japa*) [is performed] with [mantras] ending in *laṃ* for paralyzing (*stambhana*); for causing hatred (*vidveṣa*), they are endowed with *huṃ*;
for driving away (*uccāṭana*), they reside in the seed-syllable of air (*yaṃ*) and are accompanied by the visarga for success."
For killing, [the mantra is recited] with blazing *phaṭ* sounds joined with the letter *repha* (r) above and below;
for cutting, it is endowed with the word *chindhi*; for nourishing and replenishing, it is with the word *gava*.
By the best of teachers, who have brought about the cessation of death through the utterance of immortal syllables,
or by those characterized by the epithets arising from the perfection of their own ritual manuals;
Thus, whatever action is performed is a means for achieving a desired result.

Regarding specific substances as well, in the *Mohaśūrottara*: "O Goddess, in rites for pacification (*śāntika*), sacrificial fuel-sticks of *dūrvā* grass and *bhavya* wood, combined with cow's ghee, should be offered so that pacification may clearly occur."
In the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*), fuel-sticks (*samidh*) produced from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree should be offered;
when combined with the fat of a ewe, the accomplishment of immobilization will certainly occur.

Sticks of Khadira wood, combined with pungent oil, are prescribed for the rite of killing; they should be offered as oblations by the master practitioner, by which means the act of killing is accomplished.
For the purpose of eradication, those born from the mango tree, combined with pungent oil,
can uproot the entire earth along with its mountains, forests, and groves.

For the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), one should always perform *homa* with pomegranate flowers mixed with goat’s ghee, O Goddess of gods; thus one may bring under control all things, both moving and unmoving.

And for the purpose of creating enmity, the *unmatta* fuel-sticks are prescribed to be offered; when combined with linseed oil (*atasī-taila*), they are considered the supreme means for inciting hostility. Thus it is said.
In the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā, a specific rule regarding the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles is also stated:
"The *sruk* and *sruva* should be made of iron for rites such as those of killing (*māraṇa*);
however, in all other cases, such as rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and the like, they should be made of gold."
Elsewhere, the tongues for those respective rites have also been described by the wise:
"The tongue named Hiraṇyā is for rites of pacification (*śāntika*); likewise, the one named Gaganā (or Kanakā) is used;
the red one for rites of attraction (*karṣaṇa*); and the black one for minor rites (*kṣudrakriyā*)."
"That which is called Suprabhā, the seers declare to be the tongue that effects piercing;
the exceedingly red tongue, which is multiform and bestows all accomplishments, is for attracting.
Likewise, elsewhere: "The one named Kanaka is intended for paralyzing and similar rites; the red one is indeed intended for inciting hatred and similar rites."
Indeed, the color black is prescribed here by the best of wise men for killing, while the color bright red is for pacification.
"She who is intensely red in the Bahurūpottara [direction] bestows success in exorcism (uccāṭana);
she extends prosperity from the south; and she always spreads auspiciousness in the center. Thus it is said.
Elsewhere, a distinction regarding the fires is also stated:
"In the common (laukika) fire, there should be rites for pacification (śāntika) and prosperity (pauṣṭika), as well as auspicious ones;
in a fire produced from a banyan tree, there is immobilization (stambhana) and delusion (moha); and in a fire situated in a cremation ground, there is killing (māraṇa)."
"Enmity [is performed] in the fire of *bibhītaka*; these are considered the fires for the six rites. Thus it is said.

But elsewhere it is said: "Desiring to perform a gentle rite, the practitioner should offer oblations into a fire kindled with wood from the *bilva*, *arka*, trees struck by lightning, or those scorched by the sun;
however, for a fierce rite, the mantra-master should do so in a fire piled with wood from poisonous trees, trees of discord, *śelu*, *nimba*, and *dhattūra*.
In the *Somaśambhu-paddhati*, a rule is also stated regarding the specific fires (*agnimukhas*) for these rites:
Having meditated upon the sacrificial pit as having the face of the sun, one should accomplish the desired goal with heart-mantras and oblations;
thereafter, one should perform the consecration of the disciple and the daily fire-sacrifice in the western direction.
For subjugation, attraction, good fortune, nourishment, and the bestowal of luck,
as well as for pacification and the purification of evil, the fire sacrifice in the left [direction] is recommended.
One should worship at the eastern face for the sake of desiring to conquer by means of pills, collyrium, swords, and foot-ointments, and for the purpose of producing withering.
"For the purpose of killing, expulsion, creating enmity, and paralyzing, [the practice] is in the south;

however, the rite of atonement is in that same [direction], while for liberation it is in the west. Thus it is said. Attracting and so forth should also be performed at the times previously specified.
As it has been said:
"Attraction should take place in the spring.
However, in the *Kāmika*, there is a specific number for the oblations and so forth:
In rites for pacification, nourishment, or subjugation, the feeding of Brahmins should be ten times the number of oblations offered; this is considered the best practice.

The number of Brahmins to be fed for the purpose of subduing (stambhana) is considered to be equal to the number of *tattvas*, or half of that as the middling, or one hundredth part as the lowest; or it may be twice the measure stated [for other rites].
Three times the number [of oblations] is prescribed for subduing and driving away, while twice that is proclaimed for causing enmity;
even in the rite of killing, it should be equal to the number of oblations offered.

At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, one should feed the foremost of Brahmins— who are born of extremely pure lineages and are learned in the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches— with delicious sacrificial foods.

Having paid homage to them according to the prescribed ritual with the understanding that they are deities, it shall become extended [in its efficacy] through the recitation of the *yathāśī* mantras and bestow the desired fruit. Thus [it is said].
He states the sacrificial fee for the ritual application:
"In the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*), the wise practitioner should give twenty-five gold pieces;
in the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*), the measure should be thirty; and in the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), sixty gold pieces."
"In cases of enmity, fifty-five [should be given], but for killing, more than a hundred;
one should give eight to the best of the twice-born, especially for fields and the like. Thus it is said.
"Especially" means that one should act in such a way that contentment arises. || 135 ||
Grathana, vidarbha, sampuṭa, rodhana, yoga, and pallava—these are the [six] arrangements for the six types of ritual actions. || 136 ||
One should interpose the letters of the name with the syllables of the mantra according to the prescribed rule;
one should know that this is "stringing" (grathana), which is highly recommended for rites of pacification (śāntika). || 137 ||

One should write the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished situated between two pairs of mantra-syllables; this is to be known as *vidarbha* by practitioners for the rite of subjugation. || 138 ||
