The mantra should be at the beginning and at the end of the name; this is considered a "casket" (saṃpuṭa).
This is declared by those who know the mantras to be excellent for the purpose of paralyzing. || 139 ||

The mantra should be placed at the beginning, end, and middle of the name; this is considered the method for immobilization (*rodhana*). This is declared to be highly recommended in the rites for causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*). || 140 ||
He recites the mantra.
"Separated" means interrupted.
As it has been said: "First one syllable of the mantra, then again one syllable of the name."
The phrase "mantrākṣaram" refers to the text;
thus [it says] "mantrārṇa."

The compound means that the syllable of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is situated between pairs of mantra-syllables. As it has been said: "Where two mantra-syllables [surround] each single syllable of the one to be accomplished, that is declared to be *vidarbha*."
Thus it is said:
"This arrangement is considered to be the *sampuṭa*.
Regarding this, some authorities state that the mantra should be recited in reverse order at the end of the name.
This indeed is the traditional position.
As it has been said:
"One should first utter the mantra, and immediately thereafter the name of the object to be accomplished (sādhya)."
Furthermore, when the mantra is reversed at the end, that is known as *sampuṭa* (the encapsulated). Thus it is said.
The author of the treatise has also stated: "The person who worships the mantra by encasing it with the *bhūtalipi* [earth-script] one hundred times, both in direct and reverse order..."
In this context, regarding single-syllable mantras and the like, that very [procedure] is to be repeated.
Others say otherwise:
that a portion of the single syllable must be performed.

That is incorrect; for by that same logic, the same consequence would apply even to a word consisting of multiple syllables. However, the teacher Padmapāda maintains that in the case of a word with an uneven number of syllables, it must be repeated. (136–140)
The addition of the name at the end of the mantra is considered the *yoga* for eradication (*uccāṭana*).
The addition of the mantra at the end of the name is considered the *pallava* for killing (*māraṇa*). || 141 ||
White, red, yellow, mixed, black, and smoke-colored—these are proclaimed as the colors of the deities mentioned in the mantras for the six types of ritual actions. || 142 ||
The transposition of the quarters in this verse, "mantrasyā'nte," is an error:
"At the end of the name, the mantra should be placed; this is considered the 'union' (yoga) for the purpose of eradication (uccāṭana).
At the end of the mantra, the name should be placed; this is considered the 'sprout' (pallava) for the purpose of killing (māraṇa)."
Thus, however, is the reading that should be recited;
and so too the teacher Padmapāda [states]:
"Yoga is the joining of the mantra at the end of the name."

In the rites of paralyzing (*stambhana*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), the "Sprout" (*pallava*) consists of joining the name of the target at the end of the entire mantra.
Its application is for the rite of killing (*māraṇa*).
It is also stated elsewhere: "In the 'Sprout,' the sequence of mantra-words should follow the name of the target at the beginning."
"Rituals of recitation (*japa*) are at the end of the mantra"—thus it has also been stated by Gautama regarding the act of killing (*māraṇa*).
Regarding the hymn to Bhairava as well: "When the mantra is half-finished, the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is placed in front; the 'sprout' (*pallava*) is its reverse.
The application of the "yoga-sprout" (*yogapallava*) and others is also mentioned elsewhere.
As they say: "In rites for pacification, nourishment, divine invocation, and the purification of expiation; in subjugation and illumination—the wise employ the yoga."
"For killing, for destroying poison, for subduing planets and spirits, and for expulsion and inciting enmity—the sprout is prescribed. Thus it is said.
There is a distinction elsewhere: the wise practitioner should place the mantra at the beginning of each successive half-measure and at the end;
its designation in the middle is said to be "seized" (grasta).
In all rites such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) and those for killing (*māraṇa*),
one should first write the name, or else in the middle, O Great-Minded One.
Having thus divided the mantra into two parts, it is declared in its entirety;
one should employ it without hesitation in rites of hatred and eradication.
The wise practitioner should place the mantra at the beginning and at the end with half and half [of its syllables] respectively;
when the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) is inserted by the reciter, it is placed both in the middle and at the end.
That mantra, which always grants the accomplishment of all aims, is pervaded by that [seed-syllable].
Regarding the reduction of half-and-half [syllables] here, the traditionalists maintain that when there are an uneven number of syllables, the former [portion] is greater and the latter is less.
[This applies] in the rites of paralyzing, stunning, possession, subjugation, and eradication.
One should first write the mantra once, and again three times at the end;
the designation "beginning and end" refers to that which is in the middle. Thus do the experts know it.
One should draw the mantra in three ways: first, that which generates supreme hatred between those joined in mutual affection; second, the beginning and end; and likewise, the middle portion.
They know that [mantra] which has the name of the person to be accomplished once in the middle as "facing in all directions";
it pacifies all calamities and destroys even great death.
"It generates all good fortune and bestows immortality upon the deceased. Thus it is said. Furthermore, other [weapons] are mentioned in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
"Then there are the chain, the needle, the iron arrow, the saw, and the thunderbolt."
The *bhuśuṇḍī*, mallet, discus, scissors, pestle, and lotus.
One should assign the Ṭaṅka, Śūla, Asi, and Śakti [weapons] to the mantra-ritual;
six syllables of the mantra are at the beginning, six again at the end, and the remaining [syllables] are in between.
The name of the subject is thus declared; this is the sequence for the other chains:

[the syllables] are formed by the numbers six, three, fourteen, seven, thirteen, fifteen, four, twelve, two, five, sixteen, eleven, eight, nine, ten, and twenty-one, respectively, starting from the chain.
In breaking bonds, destroying enemies, severing and splitting alliances,
routing armies, creating enmity, and interrupting or shaking incantations;
In all rites of killing, as well as in slaying, paralyzing, and attracting,
chains and other such instruments are to be employed in conjunction with the syllables of the mantra of the one to be accomplished.
Thus [ends the section on] verses 141–142.
The substances for writing mantras are sandalwood, gorocanā, turmeric, soot from a house, charcoal from a funeral pyre, and the eight poisons; these are used for rites of killing. || 143 ||
Hawk, fire, and lumps of salt; the juice of *dhattūra*; then house-soot and the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*); these are declared to be the eight poisons (*viṣāṣṭaka*). || 144 ||
In the sequence beginning with "sandalwood" (*candana*) and so forth, this is the specific rule for rites such as pacification (*śānti*);
however, the general rule to be described later should also be understood,
with the exception of the rite of killing (*māraṇa*).
"Śyena": Śyena is the abode of the hawk;
Agni is the variegated one.
A lump of salt is "impure salt.
The three pungents (*trikaṭuka*) are dry ginger, long pepper, and black pepper.
In the *Piṅgalāmata*, a specific type of scraping instrument (*lekhanī*) is also mentioned.
[The threads] are made from dūrvā grass, peacock feathers, fire, bibhītaka seeds,
human bone, poison, charcoal, the three metals, gold, silver, and the arka plant.
"The pen is born for subjugation, attraction, torment, paralysis, and killing;
for the destruction of all calamities, as well as for pacification and nourishment. Thus it is said.
Elsewhere it is also said: "One should draw the yantra with a pen made from dūrvā grass shoots for subjugation (vaśya);
for attraction (ākarṣaṇa), with one made from a peacock's quill; and for contraction (saṅkoca), with one produced from a sage (muni)."
O beloved, that which is made of gold or silver, or even any other [metal], is a protection for all;
or else, one made of the Karañja wood is used, while for the purpose of killing, one made of human bone is employed.
The [mudrā] originating from the rājavṛkṣa tree is to be known for the rite of paralyzing,
as well as for rites of pacification (śāntika), enrichment (pauṣṭika), and likewise for the ritual procedures concerning longevity.
For the pacification of all calamities, one should employ [a mantra] born of the Jāti class;
alternatively, one born of the Apāmārga plant grants success in auspicious rites.
"And among all the Asuras, one made of sharp iron is praised;
if it is forged on a terrible day of the Viṣṭi-karaṇa or on a Tuesday, it should be known as equal to a flaming sword, a cutter of all beings. Thus it is said.
Regarding the specific substrates as well: that which is written on a human skin or on a tiger skin brings about paralysis;
on donkey skin, it causes enmity, and likewise on a banner, it effects eradication.
"For the sake of achieving the subjugation and attraction [of beings], one should employ it on birch bark. Thus [it is said].
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the rosary for recitation (japamālā) should be understood as previously described. (143–144)
Having correctly understood the deities, the times, the mudrās, and so forth, the wise one should employ the six rites for the sake of attaining the results as described. || 145 ||
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the *Śāradātilaka* composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra. 23.
The word *bth* [is used] because the deity brings [it] together; the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) has already been explained previously.
Having performed this renunciation of optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) and so forth, and having established self-protection (*ātmarakṣā*), one should perform everything else;
for there is the possibility of being overcome by gods and others in one who is intent upon optional rites.
As they say:
"For one who is attached to rites performed for specific desires, the mantra becomes an enemy even if it is auspicious; through the opposite of that, it attains the state of perfection. (145)
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
Now I shall explain the varieties of yantras, which are concealed within the tantras.
By means of which practitioners constantly accomplish their own desired aims. || 1 ||
Now, regarding the word *yantra*: its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is stated in the *Saṃhitā*—
“O one whose wealth is austerity, here the syllables of one’s desires are restrained (*niyantryante*).”
Because of being constrained by long-lasting suffering arising from defects such as desire, anger, and the like.
They say it is a "yantra.
Just as a mantra is the form of the deity, so too is a yantra the form of the deity.
Therefore, it has been stated by those who establish [this] that [the Veda] is capable of accomplishing what is desired. || 1 ||
One should write one's own name to be accomplished, joined with the vowels,
upon a lotus that has petals enriched by the consonant groups and filaments consisting of the vowels; it should be encircled on the outside by the letter *ha* (gagana) together with the long vowels.
This is the highly praised protective yantra. || 2 ||
He states the protective yantra: "In the lotus" (*abje*), etc. The two locative cases in *mārṇe* and *abje* are used with different referents (*vyadhikaraṇe*).

The syntactical connection is as follows: one should write one's own object of accomplishment (*svasādhya*)—accompanied by the letter *sa* (the letter *sa* together with the bindu)—in the middle of the letter *a* situated within the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
It should be understood that in all cases [the mantra] is accompanied by the object to be accomplished (sādhya), the means of accomplishment (sādhaka), and the ritual action (karman).
In that regard, the word for one's own name is in the genitive case for the object to be accomplished and in the accusative case [for the means];
thereafter, the word expressing the fruit is in the accusative case.
Regarding this, the traditionalists maintain that one should repeat "Do so" twice.

[The mantra is placed] upon that [lotus] whose petals (patrāṇi) are enriched with groups (varga), meaning its leaves (dalāni) are joined with the groups beginning with ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa, and la;
and upon that [lotus] whose filaments (kesareṣu) consist of the vowels arranged in pairs.
With the seed-syllables *hāṃ* and so forth, together with the long vowels and the [six] spaces (*gagana*),
the Mātṛkā is the deity here.
Having worshipped her and performed the rite of enlivening (*prāṇapratiṣṭhāpana*), one should wear it.
In all these yantras, the general procedure is stated here:

for rites such as *uccāṭana* (driving away), when the yantra is to be drawn, there are five mantras consisting of pairs of wind-syllables (*vāyvakṣara*) in the following order: *aṃ āṃ namaḥ*, *eṃ kaṃ namaḥ*, and so forth.

Having visualized a triangle therein, one should place the first mantra in its center and the second, third, and fourth mantras in the corners starting from the southeast (*agni*), while the fifth [mantra] is placed in the remaining corner.
One should worship after having meditated upon [the deity] in the center.
The application (viniyoga) described in this manner should be understood as applying to the previously mentioned locations for protection and so forth.
With these ten [syllables] repeated ten times each, ending in "namaḥ" and joined with the nasal bindu, they should be used in pairs.
The practitioner of mantra should perform worship in the center of the yoni and in its three corners.
Thus says the Teacher (Ācārya).
Furthermore, elsewhere the Teachers state:
"The previously mentioned ten elemental syllables, repeated ten times for each [element], joined with the *bindu* and ending with *namaḥ*."
"Furthermore, having again established the colors of the elements and their non-existence within the middle, end, and middle of the *yoni*, [one should proceed].

*Hlāṃ hvīṃ hrūṃ hyaiṃ hauṃ*—these are the unevolved (*apañcīkṛta*) seed-syllables (*bīja*). Having written one seed-syllable from among these for the respective purpose, and having written the applications of the goal (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and the ritual action (*karman*) upon the upper and lower portions of its bindus, [one writes] *lhvauṃ*."

Having written "hsauḥ" as the life-force (*jīva*) of the yantra in the lower portion of the central seed-syllable (*madhyabīja*), one should write the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of the yantra—namely "haṃsaḥ so'ham"—facing the center, in the four directions of the central seed-syllable starting from the northeast (*aiśānī*) in sequence. Then, having written "iṃ īṃ" on both sides of the central seed-syllable, and also having written "uṃ ūṃ," and having written whatever specific [mantras] are prescribed for that particular yantra, one should write the *yantragāyatrī* on the eight petals according to the sequence of its three syllables. Outside of that, in the ten directions, [one writes] "laṃ raṃ..."
Having written the heart-mantra of the yantra—*maṃ kṣaṃ vaṃ yaṃ saṃ haṃ hrīṃ āṃ*—one should also write the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra outside of it. One should encircle that with its respective mandala.
This should be understood to apply to the previously mentioned yantras as well.
As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"The life-force (*jīva*) of the yantra is *lhvauṃ* (or *hsauḥ*); one should place it below the central seed-syllable.
One should write the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as 'haṃsaḥ so'ham' in the sequence beginning from the northeast."
One should place *iṃ* and *īṃ* on the eyes, and likewise *uṃ* and *ūṃ* on the ears;
however, in the case of the eight-petalled lotus and other such diagrams, the writing of the Gāyatrī is prescribed as the specific distinction.

"One should write the syllables of the Yantra-Gāyatrī three times on each leaf; at the beginning, in the spaces between the lines, one should write the *Pratiṣṭhā* and the *Prāṇadā* [mantras]. Thus it is said.
Also, in another Tantra: "La-ra-ma-kṣa-anvaya-saha-hrīṃ-āṃ."
The heart of the yantra, joined with a bindu, should be written all around.
"The *Haṃsa* and *Sohaṃ*, representing *Prāṇa* and *Jīva*, should be carefully inscribed upon the yantra.
A wise person should write *Haṃsāvau* joined with the *sarga* (visarga) at the edge of the yantra. Thus [ends the section on] the Yantra-Gāyatrī. As for the Gāyatrī of the yantra:
"Let us know the King of Yantras; let us meditate upon the Bestower of Boons;
may that Yantra inspire us. Thus [ends the verse].
There is also another specific detail stated by the author of the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*.

Where no specific support (adhāra) is mentioned, one should write [the mantra] on birch bark, a cloth for the eyes, or palm leaf—using the supports prescribed for rites such as pacification (śānti)—and having bound it into a pellet, covered it with thread and lac, and wrapped it in silver, copper, gold, vermilion, or any other suitable material;

then, having meditated upon the presiding deity by means of the seed-syllable (bīja), the mantra, or the alphabet (mātṛkā), worshipped it, recited it, and offered oblations, one should apply it to the throat and other parts of the body. || 2 ||
When the pair of earth-fortresses (bhūmipura) have been joined together, one should write the Māyā-bīja (hrīṃ) in the center, conjoined with the name of the person to be influenced (sādhya).
Encircled by the earth-fortress at the corner of the letter Va, that [diagram] is highly effective for subjugation (vaśya).
Vaśyakṛt says "enclosed" (*puṭīkṛta*).
The connection is that [the deity] is enclosed together with the earth-city (*mahīpura*) within the pair of earth-cities.
"Enclosed" means situated within that which has been enclosed, like something placed inside a container.
Regarding the instruction "one should write":

first, having drawn a square, one should draw a second [square] inside it with its corners touching the cardinal points of the first's lines, and a third inside that with its corners touching the intermediate points of the second's lines; then, in the center of that, one should write the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīm*) together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
In that regard, the method for writing the object of the rite (*sādhyakarman*) should be understood as it was described in the section on the "Threefold" (*triguṇita*) and so forth.
Then, the connection is that [the diagram] encircled by the corner of the letter *va* brings about subjugation (*vaśya*) in a superior manner.
And it has been said in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"Of the external [diagram], there is a triangle situated in the middle of the lines; within such a triple Indra-abode, surrounded by a jar, there shall be the subjugation of Śakti.
This has been explained in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*.
Having drawn a terrestrial mandala, one should draw a triangular figure in its eastern, southern, western, and northern directions such that it forms a corner; then,
having drawn another terrestrial mandala within that, and again drawing one within that as well, one should write the Śakti together with the sādhya in the center and encircle it with a fourth jar.

Alternatively, because the letters *na* and *ta* are identical in the Nāgarī script, one should read "in the corner of the *va* [letter], the earth-fortress (*mahi-pura*) has come here. Then, having constructed two inner earth-fortresses as previously described and having inscribed the *Śakti* there, the explanation should be understood as follows: the earth-fortress that has come here—meaning it is connected—is surrounded by those two [inner fortresses] in the corner of the *va*.
In this context, Śakti is the deity. || 3 ||
In the center, one should write the three-syllabled Mṛtyuñjaya mantra with the letter *sa* (sā) at its beginning and end,
enclosing the name of the practitioner (*sādhya*) within it; then, one should write the vowels located upon the filaments,
and on the eight petals, the name enclosed by the mantra, followed by the consonant groups (*varga*s) at their tips.
The supreme yantra called Mṛtyuñjaya is said to be formed by folding two lotus petals together. || 4 ||
It destroys poison, fever, and diseases of the head; it bestows the victory of prosperity, grants beauty and nourishment, brings subjugation, and accomplishes all desires and goals. || 5 ||

He describes the Mṛtyuñjaya Yantra: "In the center," etc. In the center, within the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus, one should write the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*), distinguished by two qualifiers, in the middle of the letter *kṣa*.
The meaning is that one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), enclosed within the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra, upon the eight petals;
"groups" refers to the consonants beginning with *ka*,
and "at their tips" means at the tips of those petals.
"Formed into a lotus-cup" means with a lotus facing downward below and facing upward above. The deity here is Mṛtyuñjaya. (4–5)

Having drawn the Cintāmaṇi diagram enriched with the name of the person to be healed within the house of earth (the center), surrounded on the outside by the house of fire (the triangle), one should enclose it externally with the eight-syllable mantra; this yantra shall bring about the pacification of fever.
The mantra consisting of eight syllables, beginning with "saṃplavas" and "plāvayas," has been proclaimed;
this very one is effective in destroying the fever caused by the planets. || 7 ||
Regarding the fever-destroying [mantra], he says "sādhya" and so forth.
"Cintāmaṇi" refers to the Śaiva [mantra].
"By the second [syllable] analagehena."
In this case, the deity is Cintāmaṇi;
it is he alone. Even the mantra by itself, when propitiated, destroys fever.

And it is said in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "One should revive one who has been bitten by sprinkling water over them while reciting [the mantra] oneself, and also by hearing the sound of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments played while that [mantra] is being recited. (6–7)
One should write the mantra "Kurukulle" enclosed within two *tāra* (oṃ) syllables inside a pair of fire-chambers in the central corners and openings; this yantra quickly destroys serpents. || 8 ||
Regarding the mantra for destroying snakes, he says "Tāra": the phrase "enclosed by two Ṭhas" is an adjective qualifying the mantra.
By this, the form is as follows: first *tāra* (OM), at the end *svāhā*, and in the middle the essential nature *kurukulle*.
Thus, this mantra consists of seven syllables. One should write [it] with *rocanā* (yellow pigment) in the pair of fire-chambers that are mutually intersecting.
And it is said in that very same place: "Drawn with yellow pigment on birch bark within a hexagon.

The meaning is that it destroys [the enemy] from his house and causes him to be driven out from his hole. Likewise, in the Nārāyaṇīya: "It causes a serpent to emerge from its holes; likewise, when placed [in the house], it drives one out from the dwelling."
Herein is the deity Kurukullā. ||8||

Having inscribed the syllable Oṃ, Māyā (Hrīṃ), and so forth, along with the mantra of Agnivadhū (Svāhā) in the pairs of corners starting from the center within a girdle of fire, one should fashion this Yantra on birch bark; it destroys enemies and serpents. 9.
He states another serpent-destroying yantra with the word "Oṃ":
"Mekhale" is its essential form.
The seven-syllable mantra begins with the syllable Oṃ and the Māyā-bīja (Hrīṃ).
"Having written" means with *gorocanā*, as it is stated in the Tantra. "Enemies" refers to the *nāgas*; "their bearer" refers to one who possesses them.
In the *Nārāyaṇīya*, because it is stated: "having an action equal to that previously mentioned," the deity here is Mekhalā. || 9 ||
In the pair of fire-houses marked with tridents, one should write the mantra of Dhūmāvatī in sequence;
in the intermediate corners starting from the center, the yantra situated in the wind-house is encircled by the letters of fire and wind.
The performer of the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*) says:
"marked with tridents" refers to the tips of the outer corners; "from the center, etc. refers to the interior.
There are two seed-syllables in the center, and the remaining syllables are in the corners. "The abode of Marut" refers to what was stated in the first chapter (1.23).
"Hutāśa" is the letter *ra*, and "Anila" is the letter *ya*; by these, there are two enclosures.
Therefore, it should be understood that first there are two enclosures, and afterwards the enclosure of the wind-houses;
here the deity is Dhūmāvatī. 10.

The two letters *da* and *ta*, followed by *sā*, *rghīśa* (the letter *ha*), and *bindu* (the nasal *m*), and ending with *dviṭha* (the letter *kṣa*)—this is declared to be the mantra of Dhūmāvatī, which effects the subjugation of enemies. || 11 ||
One should bury this—prepared with poison and golden water in a piece of cloth from a corpse—in a cremation ground; this will swiftly cause the destruction of one's enemies. || 12 ||
He states the *dhūmāvatī* mantra with the words "dāntau" and so forth.
"Dāntau" refers to two *dhakāra*s. "Argīśa" is the letter *ū*, and "bindu" is the nasal dot (*anusvāra*); each of these is at the end of them. Thus, it becomes *dhūṃ dhūṃ*.
The mantra consists of eight syllables.
By the phrase "the subduer of enemies," its separate worship is also indicated.

Its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details are as follows: the seer is named Pippalāda; the meter (*chandas*) is *nivṛt*; the deity (*devatā*) is Jyeṣṭhā; and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the subjugation of enemies.
The six limbs [are formed] with the six syllables devoid of the two seed-syllables.

The visualization is as follows: she causes distress to all people, her mind is extremely dejected, she is tall, wears soiled garments, has disheveled hair, is coarse, is a widow, has sparse teeth, bears the banner of a crow, makes the sound of a crow, holds a winnowing basket, has three coarse eyes, and is addicted to quarreling.

Having fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, meditating, naked, and with his hair loosened, he should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while eating only at night in a cremation ground, an empty house, on a mountain, or in a forest. Thus, he becomes one who has completed the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
And it is said in the *Dhūmāvatī-kalpa*: "Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme Vidyā, Dhūmāvatī.

Her six-syllable Vidyā, ending in *svāhā*, is to be known as *dhūmāvati svāhā*. Here, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are to be applied with the six syllables of the Vidyā [along with the nasal bindu]. One should first perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), reciting [the mantra] naked in the temple of Jyeṣṭhā on the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, with hair loosened."

Then, in an empty house, on a mountain, in a cremation ground, or even in a forest, the night-eater (the practitioner), meditating upon Dhūmāvatī before him, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
She is mounted upon a crow, exceedingly black, with sparse teeth, loose hair, detached, smoke-colored eyes, afflicted by hunger and thirst, terrified of adversaries, fickle, and lustful for passion.

May Dhūmāvatī bestow upon you abundant prosperity— she who is joyful yet weary-limbed, soiled with the sweat of exertion, manifestly proud yet deformed, and who holds the tip of a winnowing fan in her hand.
"This is the eldest goddess named Dhūmāvatī, the bestower of boons.
The reading "dānta" is a scribal error.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The mantra of Dhūmāvatī consists of the syllables 'dhṛ', 'guṇa', 'mā', 'va', 'ti', and 'śira' as its name."
Thus [it is said].
He will state later that [the vessel] is "smoky" (dhūmāvatī) and "leaf-going" (patragāminī).
Regarding the phrase "with golden waters" (kanakāmbhobhiḥ):
The meaning is that one should write with *kāraskara* wood specially rubbed with the juice of *dhattūra* leaves; "on a *preta*-rag" means on a garment for the deceased. || 11-12 ||

Having drawn two houses for the fire (the letter Ra) and written the mantra of the two syllables "Dhiṭha" for Vaivasvata (Yama), with the moon-disk fashioned between the middle and the end—this is the yantra that is the enemy of great spirits and piśācas. || 13 ||
Regarding the destroyer of spirits (bhūtaghna), he says "Hutāśa" and so forth: "Dviṭhaḥ Svāhā.
This is a seven-syllable mantra.
"Madhyāntam" is an adverbial modifier;
it means "from the middle to the end.
By this, the meaning is that one should inscribe the seven syllables within the six corners in the middle.
"Madhyādyam" is an alternative reading found in some versions.
"Indubimbe" refers to the [meter] Vṛtta.
Here, Yama is the presiding deity. || 13 ||

Having written the name [of the practitioner] within the pair of *ma*-cells, the knower of mantras should write the syllables *ṅa*, *ña*, *ṇa*, and *na*— together with the letter *na*— in the corners of the *dhūmāvatī* yantra.
This supreme [yantra] is encircled by a *ghurmuṭikā* and the like, and is surrounded by three houses of air (*vāyu*).
A yantra placed upon the ground between the living and the dead causes enmity among enemies. || 14 ||
First, the pair of *ghurmuṭikās*, then the pair of *markaṭikās*:
"O Terrible One! O Causer of Enmity! O Causer of Enmity and Agitation! (15)
Then, from the two [syllables] Ghorā and Aghorā, [the syllables] amuka-amuka, followed by the pair vidveṣaya, huṃ, and phaṭ, constitute the vidyā called Ghurmuṭikā. || 16 ||
The author of the *Vidveṣaṇakṛt* says: "The name.
The name consists of the form of the action involving both the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the agent who accomplishes it (*sādhaka*).
Regarding the phrase "in a pair of square enclosures marked by the letter *ma*": within one [square] is the name of the object to be accomplished, and in the other is the name of the agent.
In the corners of that square marked with the letter *ma*, one should write [the syllables] starting from the northeast (īśāna).
By the phrase "one who knows the mantra," the presence of the bindu (*m*) for the letters *ṅa*, *ña*, and *ṇa* is indicated.

Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should place the letter *ma* in its pericarp (*karṇikā*), the syllables of Dhūmāvatī on its petals, and above those, the encirclement by Ghurmuṭikā and the others.
Outside are three wind-palaces;
here, Dhūmāvatī and Ghurmuṭikā are the presiding deities. In the phrase "of such-and-such and such-and-such," the names of those to be accomplished (sādhya) are to be inserted.
In the *Nārāyaṇīya*, this is the specific detail:
"One should strike the wheel with a cotton-stick for the purpose of causing enmity between two. (14–16)

One should duly draw four clear lines facing east, west, south, and north, forming a square with spikes rising at the corners, provided with two concentric circles, and containing the center and the preceding [sections]. Having written the syllables of the mantra beyond that, one should write eight syllables in the eight spaces of the eight squares.
This is the twelve-syllable mantra of the King of the Departed (Yama), arising from the trident, as prescribed according to the ritual rules. || 17 ||
O you who are like the abode of Yama, O you whose rising is red as the dawn;
O you who are without wings yet possess a womb, O you who are like a Yakṣa, free from disease, and the source of the earth. || 18 ||
"The eight-syllable mantra 'ukto dhūmāndhakārāya svāhā' has been declared. || 19 ||
He states the yantra for killing: "In front," etc.
This has been explained in the seventeenth [chapter].
Here, regarding the spikes, one writes twelve syllables within the twelve compartments produced by the spikes.
As it has been said: "Yamāntaka [is to be placed] on the tips of the petals and on those situated outside the rim.
By this, it is stated that twelve tridents (śūla) are to be drawn at the ends of the twelve lines, because it is so stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*.
The distinction lies in its being a different mantra.
Regarding the phrase "stated according to the rule":
the rule is as follows—one should first draw the heads of a buffalo and a horse on both sides, and then construct the yantra in the space between them.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "With charcoal from a funeral pyre, the eyes of a monkey, and the juice of *nimba*, [mixed] with the blood from the head of a buffalo or a dog.
Yama is the presiding deity (*devatā*).
As it has been said: "In killing, bewildering, paralyzing, creating enmity, causing expulsion, and subjugating—thus the *yamārgala* verse is established in many ways."
"One should draw a twelve-spoked wheel provided with three concentric circles.

Also, in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "On a cloth that has four threads [in the warp], three folds, and four thicknesses, and which is eightfold on the outside, one should write that mantra according to the prescribed rule."
This has been explained in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanī*:

having drawn a triple circle and, in its center, having drawn two lines in the form of north and south and two lines in the form of east and west, and having drawn four lines in the corners starting from the southeast, [one places] eight tridents at the tips of the lines extending toward the cardinal directions and four tridents at the tips of the lines in the corners. This is it.
Having written [the diagram], one should inscribe the syllables of the mantra therein according to the method prescribed in the treatise. (Regarding the phrase "up to that end":
starting from the center, one should write the verse of Yamarāja in such a way that it forms two concentric circles.)

In the remaining squares, one should surround [the central deity] from the front in a clockwise direction with the "enveloping of smoke and darkness" (dhūmāndhakārāveṣṭhana) to be described; at the locations of the stakes (śūlasthāna), one should surround [it] with the twelve-syllable mantra to be described. He states the mantra for the smoke and darkness as "ukteti.
Thus [ends the section] in the *Gūḍhārthadīpikā*. (17–19)
The Praṇava, then *ṣṭhrīṃ*, then *daṃṣṭrā*, and after that *vikṛtānta*;
[followed by] *ānanāya* and *vadhūḥ*—this twelve-syllable mantra belongs to Vahni (Fire). || 20 ||
He states the mantra of Yamāntaka: "The Praṇava," etc.
After reciting "Then Māyā," some say that the Praṇava, Māyā, and Aṣṭrīṃ should precede "Vikṛtānana huṃ phaṭ svāhā.
The six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) for these two mantras is as follows: *Oṃ hrāṃ* to the black-colored one, [assigned to] the heart.
The head with the remainder of the mantra.
*Oṃ*, to the one wearing a crown of nine-faced tawny matted locks, for the crest (*śikhā*).
*Oṃ hūṃ*, to the one possessing the splendor of the rising of a thousand suns, for the armor (*varma*).
Oṃ hrīṃ, to the three-eyed one, [the seed-syllable] trinetram.
Oṃ śrīṃ, to the one whose face is distorted by the eyebrows, huṃ astram.
Meditation [on this] is to be learned from the mouth of the Guru. || 20 ||
Having drawn this [diagram] upon a board made from a poison-tree, or on human skin, or else on a cloth, using the eight poisons, one should bury it in a cremation ground at night. || 21 ||
Overcome by a great fever, his mind agitated by fainting, the enemy goes to the realm of Yama within a fortnight; of this there is no doubt. || 22 ||
Of the poison-tree *kāraskara*.
On the cloth, that is, on a *preta*-cloth.
"With the eight poisons" means:
"By means of those [materials] mentioned at the end of the previous chapter.
"Having drawn" means with a pen made from a crow's wing.
"One should bury it in a cremation ground" means having placed it within a pair of earthenware bowls (*śarāva*), one should lead it between two smooth [surfaces]; this is the implied meaning.
Rice, powdered *rājanī* (turmeric), ghee, curd, milk, and honey—
Palala, mung beans, black gram, parched grain flour, fried rice grains, and sweetmeats;

With these substances, an offering (bali) should be presented to the eight deities of the southern direction of the maṇḍala— namely Yamarāja, Kāladharma, Anuvaivasvata, Śāntapretarāja, Mṛtyu, and Kṛtānta— using their names ending in the dative case and followed by "namaḥ," beginning with the eight-syllable mantra. Then, having offered an offering to the Mothers and the World-Protectors (Lokapālas) in their respective directions using their own names, one should offer to the Yakṣas in the north and to the Nairṛtas in the southwest.
One should offer the *bali* to the Rākṣasas and to all beings in every direction.
Having first performed the *bali* at the mouth of Yama in the northeast (Īśāna) with either the twelve-syllable or the eight-syllable mantra, this [following] is the *bali*.
As it is stated in the Nārāyaṇīya:

"Placed within a pair of earthen bowls, brought between two [persons] who are affectionate toward one another—this is the Wheel of King Yama; one who creates hatred should bury it in a cremation ground.
As for Bali, he is mentioned here in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā* as being understood in these three rites within this yantra.

In that regard, for causing enmity (*vidveṣa*), one should write [the mantra] on a garment of a deceased person according to the method taught in the *Nārāyaṇīya*, and bury it in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*).
For killing (*māraṇa*), one should write it on a board from a poisonous tree or on human skin according to the procedure stated by the author of the manual, and bury it in a cremation ground.

For paralyzing (*stambhana*), however, there is a specific variation of this very same diagram in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The paralyzing diagram situated upon Mount Meru—one should place that beneath a grinding stone."
Regarding its commentary, it is stated in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanī*:

"Having drawn a wheel with a yellow substance using a copper needle upon a board of *bibhītaka* wood, a stone, or a brick; having placed [the figure] upon Mount Meru, worshipped it, recited the mantra, and offered the sacrificial oblation (*bali*), one should bury it in places such as the path of an enemy, the house of an enemy, a cremation ground, beneath a discarded offering (*nirmālya*), or under a grinding stone, during a fixed lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) or zodiac sign."
As it has been said: "One should bury [the mantra] written with a copper stylus in yellow ink for the purpose of paralyzing;
even in a battle as vast as the Mahābhārata, it will [subdue] the enemy's elephants. (21–22)
In the eighty-one squares, one should write *hrūṃ* in the center;
then, in the rows situated in the cardinal directions, one should write the seed-syllables *kṣraṃ*, *śrūṃ*, and *vlūṃ*.
In the remaining squares, beginning from the northeast (Īśāna) and the southwest (Niśācara), one should write the mantra of Kālī row by row.
Outside of that, one should draw the Yantra encircled by Yama and encircled by Agni and Pavana.
Kālīmāraramālīkā, līnamokṣakṣamonalī;
māmodetatademomā, rakṣatattvatvatakṣara. This is declared to be the mantra of Kālī, the Night of Time for her own enemies. (24)
Yama, Apāṭaṭa, Pāmāya; Māṭa, Moṭaṭa, Moṭamā;
Vāma, Bhūri, Ribhūmova; Ṭaṭarī, Svastva, Rīṭaṭa. || 25 ||
This verse, which is declared to be destructive of enemies, is of such a nature.
He states another yantra for killing with the words "eka" and so forth;
this has been explained in the Paṭala on Tvaritā.
"In the middle of the fire, there is the letter *ra* in the middle cell," so say the teachers beginning with Padmapāda.
The distinction lies in its being a different mantra.
By the phrase "outside of that," it is stated that one should encircle [the diagram] with the *Tvaritā* mantra ending in *vaṣaṭ*.
Regarding the phrase "encircled by Yama":
having first inscribed [the mantra] once starting from Īśāna and ending with Nirṛti, one should then inscribe it again starting from Nirṛti and ending with Īśāna.
The Teachers have stated: "One should write the Kālī-mantra starting from Śiva and then from Nirṛti," and subsequently said, "thus, it is encircled by Yama in due order."
Some say that there are four feet in each of the four directions.
The letter *ra* is Fire (*agni*) and the letter *ya* is Wind (*pavana*); from these two, the two enclosures (*āvṛti*) arise.
This is the traditional position (*sāmpradāyika-pakṣa*).
However, some have said that by the term "fire and wind" (āgnipavana), their house is meant; that is contrary to tradition,
as it contradicts many texts such as the Mantramuktāvalī.
As it has been said: "One should write the Tvaritā-vidyā ending with *vaṣaṭ* on the outside as before;
then, the syllables contained within the Yama-mantra and the fire-seed (*vahnibīja*) all around."
The seed-syllable consisting of wind is on the outside of that, all around.
"One should write the seed-syllable consisting of *prabhañjana* (the wind) all around on the outside of that,
on a cloth made of silk, on a garment of *śāva*, or even on birch bark. The author himself will explain this in the subsequent yantra.
Regarding the phrase "encircled by the seeds of fire and wind":
it should be understood that one should offer one thousand and eight oblations of buffalo ghee with the Tvaritā-vidyā, pour the residue (sampāta) onto the yantra, and subsequently bury the yantra.
As it has been said: "With buffalo ghee, accompanied by one thousand and eight [oblations]..."
"By means of the oblation, one should join the *sampāta* with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
This method of inscribing the mantra is intended for a male;
however, for a female, one should write the verse of Yama in place of the verse of Bhadrakālī, and surround the verse of Yama with the verse of Bhadrakālī.
"The rest is the same," say those who know the tradition.
Here, by the phrase "Kālarātri [is] the destroyer of the enemies of her own foes," the independence of these two is also stated. (23–26)
One should write [the mantra] with the eight poisons, charcoal, the resin of the nimba tree, and lampblack. || 26 ||
This machine, known as "Subjugation," [is drawn] with a crow's wing on a piece of cloth;
[it should be placed] at a banyan tree, an anthill, a cremation ground, or a crossroads. || 27 ||
When the wind is situated in the south, the practitioner should bury [the object] at midnight;
by this means, the enemy will in every way meet his death within seven days. || 28 ||
He is seized by great diseases or he may even fall;
this wheel has been fashioned upon a stone or a brick. || 29 ||
If one digs at night where the ground has been smeared with the juice of the *markaṭī* and *viṣadaṇḍī* plants while turned face-down, there will be repeated misfortune.
"Aṅgāra" refers to funeral-pyre charcoal.
[The compound means] "by means of the soot of these.
In that regard, the method for preparing the soot is as follows:

In a human skull, one should prepare [the wick] from the fat of humans and so forth, using a wick made of the cloth from the shroud of a corpse impaled on a stake, and consisting of the eight poisons and other such substances.
"On the cloth" means on the cloth from the shroud of a corpse impaled on a stake.
As it has been said:
"On a silk cloth, on a garment, or on a corpse," it is said.
[It refers to] a *vibhītaka* tree;
[or] in the hollow of a tree.
As it has been said: "One should place [it] in an anthill, at a crossroads, or in the hollow of an uncut tree.
This means when the wind is situated in the south, that is, when the sun's rays are blowing from the south.
"Death" refers to the tree of fear;
"by great diseases" refers to the crossroads;
"fallen" refers to the cremation ground.
The word "vā" (or) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
By this, Padmapādācārya explains that there is a deficiency of parts in an anthill (*valmīka*);
[the same applies] to a stone.
On a washerman’s stone;
on a brick— that is,
one located in a temple of Śiva.
The staff-bearer is the Brahmadaṇḍin. As it is said: "The minister should station him in villages, cities, and so forth, wherever [it is appropriate]."
In this context, at the place where the name of the person to be converted (sādhya) is located, the names of the village and the city should be written. || 26–30 ||

One should write [the syllables] in sixty-four squares, starting from the northeast (Īśāna) and proceeding counter-clockwise (starting from the north), encircling them with the verse beginning with "Kālī," and thus one should fashion this yantra surrounded by the seed-syllables of fire and wind. ||31||

One should bury it face down wherever there is uneven ground smeared with ink and covered by *markaṭī* plants; this will always cause the expulsion of men, as well as the destruction of crops, drought, and the loss of cattle. || 32 ||
The one who performs the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*) says "one should write":
this [diagram] is also like the sixty-four squares of Tvaritā.
"Kālīm" refers to the Kālī mantra consisting of the verse mentioned immediately prior.
The phrase "by which nature" is connected with what follows later.
The encircling (*veṣṭana*) is as described in the previous *yantra*.
Here, prior to the encircling by Yama, there is also the encircling by Tvaritā ending in *vaṣaṭ*.

In this matter, according to the tradition, regarding the encircling with the letter *ra*, one should encircle [the diagram] with a *ra* joined to the object of the rite (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and the ritual action (*karman*). However, when aiming at a woman, the previously mentioned method should be applied.
But in another Tantra: "In a sixty-four-square grid, [one should place] Kālī, the syllables beginning with the faults of the Lord (*īśadoṣa*), and so forth."
Having placed the syllables beginning with *huṃ* in the center and in the four [directions].
In the interval between those [mantras] and the name and action of the sādhya,
one should perform the rites with the *śikhā-vidyā*, the *yāmya-mantra*, and the *dahana* [mantra].
"Having enveloped it with air and prepared this well-composed [mixture],
one shall quickly accomplish rites such as killing and eradication. Thus,
"ink" refers to the previously mentioned soot.
Daṇḍī is Brahmadaṇḍī;
Markaṭī is Kapikacchu. The deity of both, however, is Taritā. || 31–32 ||
Having written the name of Jambha and the others, situated in the midst of Tumburu, within the circle of passion;

then one should write the goddesses on the petals located in the directions, and Kāmadeva in the corners along with their names; and from the outside, it should be encircled by the noose and the goad.
This yantra brings subjugation, removes fear from planets and other such sources, and dispels minor malevolent spells.
Jambhe jambhini, two *ṭha*s; mohe mohini, two *ṭha*s;
andhe andhini, two *ṭha*s; rundhe rundhini, two *ṭha*s. (34)
The author of the *Vaśyakṛt* says: "The name.
This refers to the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*) together with the means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*).
"In the center of the *tumburu*" means within the *tumburu* situated in the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
Then, one should write the four seed-syllables of the goddesses as taught in the Tumburu-mantra, together with their names, upon the petals in the intermediate directions while reciting them.
By this, the following meaning is established:
the Kāma-bīja (Klīm) is placed within each goddess-seed syllable, and the name is placed within that; thus it is for the four petals in the corners.
The deity is Tumbaru. || 33–34 ||
Having abandoned desire, one should draw the mantra for peace within this human skull yantra;
by heating it during the twilights, one shall bring even a powerful person under control.
"Having abandoned desire" means:
having abandoned and cast off the fivefold seed of desire, one should write the syllable of peace, the long *ī* with the bindu;
the rest is as before.
"Uccaiḥ" means "excessively. || 35 ||
Having abandoned [the previous] peace, one should draw the armor on a cloth or on human skin;
surrounded by fire and wind and situated in a cremation ground, it shall destroy enemies. || 36 ||
"One should write" means in a place of peace. "Varma hūṃ" refers to the cloth, that is, a *preta*-cloth.
The remainder is that it is enclosed by fire and wind;
the rest is as before. || 36 ||
Having removed the armor, one should inscribe the weapon-mantra upon a wooden board produced from an unscarred tree;
that [mantra], joined with fire and wind, should be written with blood enriched by poison. || 37 ||
The *akṣatṛ* tree is the *bībhītaka*. "In the quadrangle" means in the courtyard.
Here too, it should be understood that [the site] is surrounded by houses on the south and west sides. || 37 ||
One should bury the recited [mantra] at a crossroads; it creates mutual enmity.
Having omitted the two letters *ra* and *ya*, one should write the letter *la* in the middle. || 38 ||
Encircled by Dharāpura and placed within bricks, it shall effect the immobilization of all; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. || 39 ||
"Recited" means with the seed-syllable of Tumburu.
"Having abandoned" means having written the seed-syllable of Tumburu, one should write the letter *la* there.
"With the city of the earth" [means as follows].
The cessation of fire and wind;
the remainder is as before.
"At the end of the bricks" means at the end of two bricks.
In the three subsequent divisions, the city of the Earth alone should be constructed. || 38-39 ||
Having omitted the letter *la*, one should write the seed-syllable of Vāyu in its place upon the banner-cloth with poison, blood, ink, and crow-dung. (40)
One should place [the mantra] in a cremation ground to bring about the destruction of one's own enemies;
there, having omitted the wind-seed (ya), one should write the syllable *phaṭ*. || 41 ||
If one buries [the substance] in the desired location according to the prescribed rite, using the blood of a crow on a garment from a corpse, it creates enmity among men. || 42 ||
In the center of that, or in the center of the *tumburu*, one should write the wind-seed-syllable *yaṃ*.
The rest is the same.
[The offering is] the blood of a red cat.
*Masī* is the aforementioned soot;
*dhvajavāsasi* means on the cloth of a funeral banner (*pretapatākā*). || 40 ||
"According to the rule" means as stated [in the previous verse]: "with a line drawn by a crow's wing-feather.
"Desired" means...
The meaning is that "place" (deśa) refers to that location where the act of causing enmity is performed and where it is transgressed. || 41-42 ||
Having removed the seed-syllable of the weapon from this [mantra], one should write the letter *ḷ* joined with the *uṣman* (*ṝ*) therein;
this shall be the yantra, encased within the three metals.
One should write there the syllable *laṃ* and the syllable *glauṃ*, which pacify all diseases and bring peace to [the effects of] sorcery, malice, and the like, omitting the seed-syllable. || 44 ||
Enclosed on the outside by the letter KṢA, further encircled by nooses and goads, and again surrounded by the letter ṬA, it is situated in the center of the earth-maṇḍala. || 45 ||
It is surrounded on the outside, in sequence, by the letters of the alphabet (mātṛkā) ending with the visarga (sarga), each joined with the nasal bindu and enclosed within a circle. || 46 ||
One should bury this machine, fashioned upon a silken cloth and placed between two bricks, at the front of an army; it will certainly effect immobilization. || 47 ||
"Externally" means outside the lotus;
"by the letter *ṭha* following *ṭa*" [means by the letter *ṭha*].
"Ending with the emission" (sargānta) means ending with the visarga. || 43-47 ||

In the center, one should write the seed-syllable of Śrī Narasiṃha; then, outside of that, on the filaments (kesara), one should write the vowels in the directions of Varuṇa, Candra, Yama, and Indra. In the center, one should write the Gāruḍa mantra.
Having written the semi-vowels (antasthā) in the directions of Vāyu, Agni, Nirṛti, and Śiva, it is surrounded by the letters.
The Gāruḍa-yantro is surrounded by eight companions known as the Saṃvartakas. || 48 ||
He describes the Gāruḍa yantra, beginning with the word "in the center":

in the middle, that is, in the pericarp (kaṇīkā), is the seed-syllable of Narasiṃha conjoined with Śrī, as stated in the sixteenth chapter. By the word "Śrī," the letter *ra* is understood as a single constituent part.
It should be known as "that which is above.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The fire possessing a bindu [is located] in the pericarp at the end of the upward [path]."
Vārīḍ is the western direction;
Candra is the northern direction;
Yama is the southern direction.
"Indra" refers to the eastern direction.
"One should draw in the center" means that one should write the final syllable of the Gāruḍa mantra within the pericarp (kaṇīkā).
The semi-vowels *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* together with the bindu (*m*) are the "intermediate" (*antasthā*).
The reading "vargāvṛtam" is an error;
the traditional reading is "varṇāvṛtam," which belongs to the *pāṅkta* [meter].
It is surrounded on all eight sides by the syllables *sa* joined with the visarga, and by the *kṣa* syllables associated with the *saṃvartaka* fires.
Thus it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "This yantra, surrounded by the *lipi* [alphabet] and encircled by the eight syllables of the *sagī*, protects from the serpents.
This is explained in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*.
The meaning is that one should encircle it with written syllables like a garland and write the final letter along with the *visarga* in the eight directions;
Garuḍa is the presiding deity. || 48 ||
The *saṃvartaka* mantra, joined with two eyes (*netra*), with *tāra* on the side and *agnisundarī*, is declared to be the *gāruḍa* mantra, which destroys the two kinds of poison. || 49 ||
Remembering himself as Garuḍa, a person should mutter this mantra;
by the mere sight of him, he shall destroy whatever arises from the race of serpents. || 50 ||

He states the Gāruḍa mantra as follows: "Saṃvarttaka" refers to *kṣa*; "netra" is the vowel *i*, joined with which it becomes *kṣi*. "Pārśva" is the letter *pa*; "Tāra" is the *praṇava* (*oṃ*); and "Agnisundarī" is *svāhā*. Thus, the mantra is *oṃ kṣi pa svāhā*.
By the phrase "destroyer of the two types of poison," the independence of the mantra alone is expressed;
this indeed is the fruit of the yantra.
The two types of poison are the stationary (sthāvara) and the mobile (jaṅgama).
The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [limbs] of the mantra are as stated in another tantra:
"The seer and others are proclaimed to be Rudra, Paṅkti, and Garuḍa.
'Hṛdayam' at the end of the pair of 'Jvala's is the Heart; the word 'Mahāmati' is the Head."
Garuḍa should be "craḍānanaṃ," and at the end of Garuḍa is the crest-mantra "śikhi.
Having uttered the armor-mantra, one should then say "Garuḍān" followed by the pair "prabhañjana."
O you who possess the pair of divisions, endowed with terror, O pair, subdue!
O mantra of the eye, assuming a fierce form, remove all poison.
The two words "bhīṣaya" and "sarvam" [form one part], while the two words "daha" and "bhasmīkuru" form the other; the weapon-mantra (astramantra) is "apratihatabala apratihata."
At the end of the *śāsana* mantra, ending with *huṃ phaṭ* or *svāhā*, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of these limbs—
ending with the eyes— upon the feet, waist, heart, face, and head,
as well as upon the fingers starting from the thumb; having done so, one should meditate upon the deity.

[One should meditate upon] the syllable *kṣa*, situated within the lotus formed by the two fire-syllables at the end of the consonant groups (*varga*), consisting of the first letter of the five elements, adorned with ornaments,
granting the boons of fearlessness by means of the lords of serpents, possessing lotus-eyes and a beautiful face, having a snout for severing wicked snakes,
destroying all the poison of the god of love, and being the very life-force [of the practitioner].
"I worship the King of Birds, whose body is the triple Veda, who is the essence of immortality, and who is the foremost among living beings.
Following this, the Garuḍa-mudrā should be displayed;
its characteristics are to be understood as I have described them in the fourth chapter.

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to its syllables (varṇalakṣa) and perform oblations with black flowers smeared with ghee amounting to one-tenth of that number. One should worship this [deity] upon the lotus of the Mātṛkās, and one should also worship the limbs (aṅgas), the eight serpents, the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), and their weapons.
This same procedure applies to the seed-syllable (bīja) as well.
In the Nārāyaṇīya, however, it is said: "Thus the six limbs of Viyati [Viṣṇu] have been described, ending with the corners of his eyes;
from the knees to the navel he has the luster of gold, and from the navel upwards he has the brilliance of snow."
Red as saffron from the neck up to the tips of the hair, with eyes other than white,
pervading the entire universe, Tārkṣya has red eyes and is adorned with serpents.
The wise practitioner should visualize himself as having a blue-tipped nose and golden wings;
he should appear black when dealing with poison in battle, and red-hued in the rite of paralyzing (stobha).
One should contemplate the yellow [Tārkṣya-mantra] for paralyzing, and the moon-like [Vairocana-mantra] for destruction. Thus [ends verses 49–50].
One should duly inscribe the syllable *ma*, situated upon the syllable *bhṛ* (i.e., *bha*), together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the center;
the vowels should be placed on the filaments, and one should write the central seed-syllable in the openings between the eight petals.
One should assign the consonants beginning with *ka* to the filaments, and the central seed-syllable to the sixteen petals.
The Yantra known as Sañjīvana, situated within the city of water, removes minor ailments. || 51 ||
He describes the *sañjīvana* (reviving) machine with the words "in the center":
"in the center" means in the pericarp (*kaṇīkā*);
"situated in Bhṛgu" means situated in the letter *sa*; "the phoneme" refers to the letter *va*.
"Therefore, one should write the seed-syllable 'svam' in accordance with the rule, conjoined with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya)";
this means it should be enveloped by the letter *va*.
And it is said in the Nārāyaṇīya:
One should write the seed-syllable named Jīva, free from fear, situated within a jar in the center;
thus,
the central seed-syllable is one's own.
The letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *sa*;
on the sixteen-petaled [lotus] which has twice the number of petals of the earth (eight);
the central seed-syllable is one's own.
Salilapura is as described in the first chapter;
here, the deity is Mṛtyuñjaya. || 51 ||

In the center, one should write the *piṇḍa-mantra*; on the petals and so forth, one should write the letters of the lords of the directions—starting from the direction of Varuṇa, then the lord of the stars (the Moon), the lord of the pretas (Yama), and Indra—and also the letters of space in the center.
One should encircle the outside with the letters beginning with *ya* in the directions of Vāyu, Agni, Rākṣasa, Śiva, and Īśvara.
The supreme machine known as the Piṇḍa is fashioned with the letters beginning with *ka* and the left eye [the letter *i*]. 52.
He describes the *piṇḍayantra* with the words "in the center" (*madhye*).

In the center, that is, within the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus, one should write the *piṇḍa* (syllabic aggregate) which is about to be described; in the middle of that, one should write the name, adorned with the respective seed-syllables and enclosed by a triangle (*vidabhīta*).

According to the statement in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The seed-syllable of the noose (*pāśa*) for subjugation (*vaśya*), the seed-syllable of Varuṇa for pacification (*śānti*), and the seed-syllable of the fire of wrath (*krodhāgni*) for eradication (*uccāṭana*).
[These are placed] on the petals and so forth, and on the filaments (*kesara*). The vowels (*acaḥ*) are the vowel-phonemes.
By a sequence of two each:
"Vārīśā" refers to the western direction;
"Tārādhipā" refers to the northern direction.
"Pretādhīśvara" refers to the southern direction; "Śakra" refers to the eastern direction;
and in the center of the Viyati-garuḍa mantra is the final syllable within the pericarp (kaṇīkā).

The [vowels] beginning with *yā* and the consonants *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*; by means of the long *ī* (dīrghaikāra) in the left eye; and together with the bindu—it should be known that this occurs three times.
"Three times one should encircle the lotus with the Māyā [syllable], joined with the Bindu," according to the statement in the Nārāyaṇīya; here, the deity is the Piṇḍātman. || 52 ||

The four-faced one (the syllable *ca*) conjoined with the lord of men (*ma*), the sound of the twice-born (*u*), and fire (*ra*) is declared to be this seed-syllable of the *piṇḍa*, which accomplishes all the goals of men. || 53 ||
A yantra consecrated with this seed-mantra is a supreme protector;
it generates longevity and health, and bestows fortune, good luck, and subjugation. || 54 ||
This [mantra], when worn upon the head, cuts through thieves, serpents, wild beasts, predators, spirits, and diseases;
it provides protection for the fetus of women, grants sons, destroys misfortunes, and brings about unsurpassed subjugation of the world. (55)

He extracts the seed-syllable of the *piṇḍa* as "manu. Here, "manu" refers to the vowel *u*, "indubindu" refers to the nasal drop (*bindu*), "ajeśa" is the letter *jha*, and "agnī" is the letter *ra*. Joined with these, "caturānana" is the letter *ja*.
It is called "the accomplisher of all aims."
In that regard, the method is also stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:

"A yellow, radiant, thunderbolt-shaped *piṇḍa* situated within the houses of the Moon and Indra (the North and East), when visualized before a horse and so forth, shall cause the immobilization of the army. Likewise, [a *piṇḍa*] of that same form, situated within the cities of the Moon, Indra, and Fire (the North, East, and South) at the crown of the head, [should be meditated upon]."

One should visualize that very [mantra], which wards off all hostile elephants, buffaloes, and the like, as having a brilliance equal to fire within the enemy army; thus the host of enemies shall retreat with their ranks scorched by the massed flames. When visualized in conjunction with wind and fire, it certainly effects paralysis (*stambha*) in an enemy's magical pillar through meditation. Possessed by such [meditation], the malevolent spirits (*graha*) and others depart, abandoning their victim and crying out in distress.
When this [mantra] is written with *rocanā* on a cloth or other surface and worshipped there, thieves, petty spirits, malevolent beings, serpents, and the like abandon that house.

The weapon-mantra (*astra*) situated in the *aindra* [square] paralyzes even rising snakes. That mass of energy (*piṇḍa*), which is within the *vāruṇa* [square] and possesses the power of grace and increase, when applied to the bitten head, effects the destruction of the poison. Thus it is said.
The deer, the tiger,
the wild beast (vyāla), the wicked elephant,
and the seven small [creatures].
"Subject to the world. In this regard, the specific detail is as follows:
one should draw [the design] within a lotus, upon a moon, joined with the seed-syllable of the name inside the *piṇḍa*.

The *Tārkṣya* (Garuḍa) machine is described as being separated [by the vowels]; likewise, the letters *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* should be written. One should encircle the lotus three times with the *Mahāmāyā* mantra joined with the moon (*i*).
This machine should be drawn with *rocanā* (yellow pigment) mixed with cow-dung water. On birch bark, one should write it with a golden stylus and encircle it with lacquer or silver.
One should accomplish the rite through recitation, worship, and fire-oblation using gold. It bestows long life, purification, nourishment, fortune, good luck, and subjugation.

This yantra removes the fear of thieves, wild beasts, houses, forests, water, and so forth; it bestows sons, protects the fetus, and dispels the afflictions of planets, serpents, spirits, and diseases. One should know this yantra to be the accomplisher of all aims. When placed upon the head, it is unsurpassed for bringing the world under one's control.

For the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), one should always recite the *piṇḍa* mantra enclosed by the *pāśa* up to the end of the *śikhā*. It may be fashioned from a leaf blown by the wind or from a crow’s wing.

A yantra devoid of the moon (the nasal bindu) at its end effects the eradication of an enemy. The practitioner of mantra should recite the *piṇḍa* mantra encased within the fire of wrath (*krodhāgni*) for the purpose of eradication.
Space (*ākāśa*), fire (*agni*), the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) with the ear (*karṇa*), and the fire of wrath (*krodhāgni*)—this is what is called [the *krodhāgni*]. Thus [ends verses 53–55].
In the center, within a water-house (toyagṛha) and in the hollow of the letter *la*, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) enriched with the syllable *sa*;
on the eight petals, one should write the *haṃsa*-mantra all around, encircled by the syllables of *haṃsa*.
This yantra, encircled by an earth-house (*bhūmigṛha*), should always be worn upon the head.
It shall destroy the enemies of minor and major fevers and diseases, and bestow fame and prosperity. || 56 ||
He states another yantra with the words "in the middle" (madhye).
The two locative endings in "madhye toyagṛhe" are in different grammatical cases;
[the meaning is] "in the middle," that is, in the pericarp.
And the water-house is as described in the first chapter.

In the cavity of the letter *la*, one should write the name of the goal (*sādhya*) ending in *la* and enriched with the letter *sa*, together with the letter *sa*, along with the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the ritual action (*karman*).
The deity is Haṃsa. || 56 ||
One should write one's own name to be accomplished in the middle of the letter *ī*, and having written it again upon the eight petals, one should encircle it;
this becomes a yantra situated within a city of earth that brings people under control. || 57 ||
Having inscribed this yantra upon a copper plate, one should worship it;
it will bring all mortals under one's control—of this there is no doubt. || 58 ||
The author of the *Vaśyakṛt* says "the vowel *ī*. That is the vowel *ī*;
by means of that vowel *ī*.
Māyā is the deity. ||57-58||
In the center, one should write the letter ending in *m* (ma), placed by Bhṛgu (*b*) and surrounded by the letters of the name;
then, on the eight petals, one should again write the letter ending in *ṭ* (ṭa) accompanied by the letter ending in *l* (la).
This is declared to be the excellent diagram called Sañjīvana, situated within the orb of the earth.
Worn upon the arm, it shall dispel the fear arising from weapons (or enemies). || 59 ||
Regarding the phrase "in the center, removing the fear of weapons":
"in the center" means within the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus.

The meaning is that one should write the letter *bha*, which is placed upon the letter *sa* (the letter of Bhṛgu), surrounded by the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and the ritual action (*karman*).
The syllable ending in *ṭ* (ṭha) conjoined with that ending in *l* (la);
its presiding deity is Mṛtyuñjaya.
One should write the syllable *sa*—surrounded by its own vowels and joined with the *sādhya* (the name of the person)—along with the *haṃsa* mantra at the end of each of the eight petals.
This diagram, surrounded on the outside by the "house of water" (*va*) and encircled by the letter *la*, is a destroyer of fever.
He states [the mantra] that destroys the poison: "vārṇāvṛtam" means surrounded by the letter *va*;
"ṭānte" means at the end of the letter *ṭha*.
The connection is that one should surround the Lāntāvṛta on the outside with the "water-house" (ambugṛha), which is described in the first chapter. Haṃsa...
The deity. || 60 ||

One should write the name ending in *ṭā* within the space of the letter *kṣa*, constricted by the three syllables of the *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra; outside of that, in the spaces of the eight petals, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) as before. Likewise, on the lotus with eight petals joined with filaments, one should write the name in the same manner.
And likewise, upon a thirty-two-petaled lotus, the filaments are joined with the consonants beginning with 'ka'.
The Yantra called Mṛtyuñjaya, which is encircled by the letter *ī*, destroys all diseases and malevolent spells, and bestows the attainment of all auspiciousness. || 62 ||
Regarding the statement "it ends in Ṭa," which destroys disease and malevolent spells:
the two locative cases in "Ṭānte" and "kṣakāravivare" are in different grammatical relations (vyadhikaraṇa).
The syntactical connection is: "one should write the name enclosed by the three-syllabled Mṛtyuñjaya mantra."
The meaning is that, as before, the name is enclosed by the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra.
On the sixteen-petaled lotus, which possesses eight filaments and two groups of eight petals;
"in the same manner" means:
The meaning is that the name [of the deity] is as before.
Likewise, in the thirty-two-petaled lotus whose filaments are joined with the consonants beginning with *ka*, the meaning is that the name is as before.
Mṛtyuñjaya is the presiding deity. (61–62)
One should draw two *praṇavas* (oṃs) conjoined with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), surrounded by the syllable *glauṃ*.
Having again drawn an eight-spoked wheel of vajras with the *tāra* (oṃ) shining at its center,
one should then draw the syllable *laṃ* in the corners and the directions, along with the noose, goad, and the three-syllabled mantra.
The *vīta* is the pillar-yantra, surrounded by the eight divine sciences beginning with Jambha. || 63 ||
In *jambhe*, the wife of Vahni (the syllable *ra*) comes first, followed by *jambhini* and two *ṭha*s;
in *mohe*, the wife of Pāvaka (*sa*) occurs, and then *mohini* followed by two *ṭha*s. || 64 ||
Andhe, Hutabhuj, Jāyā, and then Andhinī—this is the pair of Ṭha syllables (Ṭha-Ṭhā). Rundhe, Kṛśānupatnī, and Rundhinī joined with two Ṭha syllables (Ṭha-Ṭhā). || 65 ||
The performer of the rite of immobilization (stambhana) says "glauṃ. Regarding the phrase "one should inscribe," the meaning is "within the circle."
The grammatical connection is: "having drawn the eight vajras and the eight syllables, [one draws] the outer *bhūpura* (earth-fortress).
This was stated by the Teachers:
"The pair of *praṇavas* situated between the pair of earth-syllables (*la*), and that which has gone to *ṭha*; in the midst of those, the *dhruva* (oṃ) and the earth-syllable (*la*) between them."
"In the northeast corner, one should write *glauṃ* surrounded by the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) placed between a noose and a goad;
then, one should draw the eight [deities] beginning with Jambha; thus one achieves victory.
The term "in the corners" refers to the corners of the *bhūpura* (the outer square).
"Pāśāṅkuśatryakṣarī" means the three-syllable mantra consisting of the noose (pāśa), Māyā, and the goad (aṅkuśa). The deity is Bhūmi. (63–65)
Having written the name [of the target] at the end, one should again write that same [name] eight times in the directions;
then, one should draw a circle of the earth with a king and a serpent joined to one another, and write the name on the two faces of the bībhīta fruit; thus the yantra is completed.
When placed upon the remains of offerings, it always effects the paralysis of the speech of enemies.
Regarding the statement that it "causes the paralysis of speech," he says "ending in *la*":
one should write the name ending in the letter *kṣa*, which is the final letter of the *la*-group; according to the oral tradition, this should be understood as being surrounded by the letter *la*.
"Tam" refers to the letter *la*.
Alternatively, since it ends in *la*, one should read "bhūstam," with the letter *la* inserted on both sides of the name.
Regarding the word "abhitaḥ":
it means that the eight syllables are to be written specifically within the pericarp (*kaṇīkā*).
This is also the meaning of the term "in the directions" (*dikṣu*) in the root text.
In the eight [directions], one should draw Śaṅkhapāla and [the others] together with their own emblems,
using red ochre.
Regarding the term *nirmālya*:
it refers to the *nirmālya* of Śiva,
according to the statement in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*.
It should be known that the paralyzing of the speech of enemies is accomplished by [the mantra] "śilākrānta.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"At the end of the eight-fold enclosure of flesh, the name [is placed], free from fear of the knower of flesh."
One should draw the vajra of Indra with eight spokes, surrounded by terrestrial and celestial beings.
One should write the name of the two serpents on the mouth and also on the board of *bibhītaka* fruit using red chalk (*gairika*).
One should carve the stone upon the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) and place it within a pillar. Thus [it is said]. (66)

One should write the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) enriched with the name of the person to be protected on the outside; then, in the middle of the petals in the cardinal directions, one should write *tat* and *glaum*, and in the other [intermediate] petals, one should write *gaṃ* accompanied by *lāṃ* in the corners of the earth-fortress (*mahīpura*).
Within the eight thunderbolts, one should place the armor-mantra situated inside a water-fortress, which itself rests within a circle of the earth.
One should place the yantra, situated within the Night-Vināyaka, into two shallow bowls (śarāva).
Placed in a secret location and worshipped every day, it effects the paralysis of speech and of enemy armies and the like. (68)
And another [author] who effects the paralysis of speech says "sādhya" and so forth;
one should write [this] in the pericarp of an eight-petaled [lotus].
"Tat" refers to *hūṃ*.
On the other intermediate petals,
one should write "gaṃ" accompanied by "laṃ"— that is, *glaṃ*— in the corners of the enclosure of the earth (*mahīpura*).
It should be understood that this is done on the cloth using substances derived from the night (such as saffron).
Those who know the tradition maintain that one should fashion an image of Gaṇapati made of turmeric within a *vināyaka* [statue] of the night, and the yantra should be placed in its belly.
However, some say it should be wrapped with the mantra of Haridrā-Gaṇapati;
that is contrary to the tradition.
Because the mantra has not been extracted here,
it is said to be "worshipped" with yellow flowers.
Vināyaka is the deity.
The two genitive cases in "of the enemies' words" (*vairiṇāṃ vācām*) are in apposition with different referents;
they may also mean "of the enemies' armies and so forth."
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [the author refers to] the movement of the dispute and so forth.
This has been stated in the Nārāyaṇīya: "One should write upon cloth with the juices of the night."
Having placed that [image] made of powdered charcoal within the belly of the obstacle-maker (Vighna).
Having placed [the substance] in a pair of earthen bowls, one should worship it with yellow flowers;
there shall be immobilization (stambha) in matters such as rain, armies, speech, disputes, and arrivals. Thus [ends verses 67–68].
Having drawn eight straight lines, and having again drawn six lines across them, one should duly write the syllable *kṣa* accompanied by a dot (*bindu*) in the outer enclosure; then,
one should write the letter *dh* (for *dharaṇī*) in the inner row, within the remaining three squares.
Having prepared this celebrated and joyful machine, which destroys fever. 69.
Having worshipped this yantra and offered a bali-oblation to the spirits,
one should then bind it upon the head of the patient for liberation from all fevers.
Regarding the statement "having made" (*kṛtvā*) in the context of the fever-destroying [yantra]:
it means by means of an external enclosure within twenty squares.
"According to rule" means by way of circumambulation (*prādakṣiṇyena*).
Within the row, in the twelve squares, "Earth" (*dharā*)— that is, *laṃ* joined with the nasal bindu— is to be connected [to each].
Having unified the three inner compartments within the [outer] three compartments, one should write the name there.
"Having given an offering to the spirits" means it should be understood as being with rice of five colors.
As it is said in the Nārāyaṇīya:
"Having drawn eight straight lines and six horizontal lines in two enclosures,
one should write 'Nāri', 'Bāhya', and 'Puṭa' [in the outer enclosure], and 'Kṣa' and 'Indra' in three places for the name."

"Having offered an oblation (*bali*) of five-colored [grains], one should perform the sequence as prescribed for the daily [rite] and for the pacification of the appearance of fever, such as the deity of fever (*jvaradeva*) and so forth. Thus it is said.
In the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*, this is explained as "having offered an oblation of rice (*odana*) of five colors."
The deity is Bhūḥ. || 69–70 ||
One should write the syllable *tāraṃ* (oṃ) in the pair of fire-fortresses (*vahni-pura*), and on their two sides, the syllable *la* and the fire-seed-syllable (*agnibīja*).
The yantra [is completed] with these in the corners and in the east and west.
This [mantra], entwined with the noose and the goad, destroys fever. || 71 ||

Having worshipped the yantra with the mantra consisting of the Tāra (Om), the noose (Pāśa), and the goad (Aṅkuśa), one should bind it to the hand or other limbs of the person afflicted by fever for the sake of pacifying the fever. || 72 ||
Regarding the other [mantra] that destroys fever, he says "tāra" (the syllable Om).

When the two "cities of fire" (vahni-pura) are written in the form of right and left [squares], the letter *la* is placed at their sides—that is, at the sides of the *tāra*. Then, the seed-syllable of fire (*agni-bīja*) is placed in all the corners; this means in every corner.
"And of the two directions, east and west, situated on the outer part: 'pāśāṅkuśa' etc.
Others, however, read the text as "guṇāṅkuśāvītam."
The word "guṇa" (quality) refers to the number three; therefore, the meaning is that one should draw three goads (aṅkuśas) in each of the eastern and western sections.
This has been stated in the Nārāyaṇīya:
