"One should write the *tāra* (the syllable Om) in the two fire-houses facing north and south."
"On both sides of Tāra, [one should place] Indra; in the corner squares, Fire;
and outside the wheel in the east and west, it is adorned with three goads.
In this context, the deity consists of the Praṇava, the noose, and the goad. (71–72)
One should write the name within a circle, surrounded by the letters ending in *ṭa* (the *ṭavarga*), enriched with the vowels as its filaments;
this eight-petaled lotus, situated upon the city of the earth (*vasudhāpura*) and ending with the *ṭa*-letters, is a yantra that bestows luster and destroys fever.
Regarding the other fever-destroying [remedy], he says "piṇḍa":
in the previously mentioned *piṇḍa*,
[the word] ends with the letter *ṭha* accompanied by the visarga (*ṭhaḥ*).
The grammatical connection is that "this is named Tadvidabhīta.
Here, the deity is the one whose essence is the *piṇḍa*. || 73 ||
The syllable *māyā* (hrīṃ), encircled by the two *lū* syllables, *ja*, *la*, *dvi*, *ṭha*, and *va*, and written between the letters ending in *ṭa* according to the prescribed rule,
is surrounded externally by the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) at the bottom with half-moons for faces.
The mechanical device instantly suppresses the infant's desire to cry.
*Tāra* (Om) is the heart that removes the crying of children;
*ludvayaṃ* is *lulu*;
*jalaṃ* is *vaṃ*.
*dviṭhaḥ svāhā*. She is called *sādhyā* because she is to be accomplished (*sādhyā*) by means of ritual procedure (*vidhi*) alone; that is, she has accomplishment as her inherent nature.
The suffix *ac* is applied here according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*.

Having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) within the middle circle, joined with this mantra and surrounded by the *māyā* syllable (*hrīṃ*), one should draw two outer circles and bind [the design] by encircling it with downward-facing half-moons.
It is implied that it is encircled twice by downward-facing, downward-opening half-moons.
Or rather, it should be read as: "The instrument that destroys the child's desire to cry in two ways.
And it is said in the *Nārāyaṇīya*: "The *tāra* (OM), the pair of *lu*s, *udaka*, and *śiras*—by these syllables..."
The Śakti is surrounded by the vowels (a-vatī) and the consonants (śaśāṅkau);
it is encircled on the outside by downward-facing half-moons.
That yantra quickly removes the crying of infants. Thus [it is said].
And this has been explained in the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*:
"Having drawn the Goddess and having written the child's name in its center, one should encircle it like a garland with the mantra *oṃ lulu vaṃ svāhā*.
Then, having drawn two moon-maṇḍalas outside of that and having adorned each one with downward-facing half-moons, one should bind [the diagram]."
The deity is Śakti. || 74 ||
Having written the syllable of the sky (Ha) with a bindu (Ṃ), conjoined with the name [of the person] and placed within a triangle joined by three *lu* sounds (the letter *la*),
and bound within a pair of squares of the earth (La), this yantra shall be the destroyer of all fevers.
Regarding the fever-destroyer, he says "vyoma" and so forth.
"Vyomārṇa" means the letter *ha*. Of what kind?

*Bindu* is *ma*, and *bindumā* refers to those two; that which is accompanied by them is *sabinduma*. Having written that which is called *ākhyāvidabhīta* together with the *bindu*—that is, having written it in the middle (this is the ellipsis)—the meaning is that one should write *laṃ* in the center, surrounded by the letters of the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the object of practice (*sādhya*).
One should write three *lu*s in each corner.
It is fixed upon the hand and so forth—this is the ellipsis.
As it is stated in the *Nārāyaṇīya*:
"Three *lu*s in its corners, and in the center, the *vi* with poison (*saviṣa*)."
This machine, known as the *Abhīta*, removes all fevers;
its presiding deity is Vyoman. 75.
One should draw a lotus named Sārṇa with eight petals on the outside;

then, on the exterior, there should be a thirty-petaled lotus containing the letters from Ka to Śa. This diagram, surrounded by a circle of water, is prescribed to be fashioned upon the inner bark of a birch tree.
It pacifies elemental spirits, diseases, and great fevers; it destroys malevolent spells and bestows prosperity. || 76 ||
He describes another yantra with the words "sārṇam" (containing the letters).
Regarding the phrase "parilikhed" (one should draw), it refers to the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus.
Although one might expect the word "aṣṭapatreṣu" (on the eight petals) to be used, he instead says "bāhye" (on the exterior).
Therefore, there are two locative cases in different grammatical relations.
Thus, one should write the syllable *sa* (Sakāra) along with Bhṛgu on the outer parts of the eight petals.
The intention is that the vowels should be written in pairs at the base of each petal, in the place of the filaments.
Regarding this, some read "eight petals of letters" (*varṇāṣṭapatra*), while others read "sixteen petals" (*dvyaṣṭapatra*).
Here, the deity is Mātṛkā. || 76 ||
Having inscribed in sequence the semi-vowels along with the nasal bindus within sixty-four squares, he then [prepared] the yantra,
which was joined with tridents fashioned at the heads of the lines, for the purpose of pacifying yellow fever.
Cakra spoke regarding the destroyer of fever (*jvaraghna*):
having written the semi-vowels (*antasthavarṇa*), namely *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*,
[one should proceed] "in sequence"— by this it is stated.

In the first enclosure, one should write the syllable *yaṃ* with a bindu in twenty-eight squares; in the second enclosure, the syllable *raṃ* with a bindu in twenty squares; in the third enclosure, the syllable *laṃ* with a bindu in twelve squares; and in the four inner squares, the syllable *vaṃ*.
It should be understood that this writing is to be done on the ground using substances corresponding to the colors of those respective elements.
As it is stated in the Nārāyaṇīya:
"In the field of sixty-four squares, illuminated by thirty-six spikes,
within the compartments and lines of the three Jvara-nāśas and the Sun, [the arrangement proceeds] in due order."
"One should write the semi-vowels (antasthā) together with their bindus; one should worship that wheel situated upon the ground.

All fevers of this person who lies down perish according to the ritual procedure. Thus it is said. In the *Apekṣitārthadyotanikā*, it is explained that one should write [the mantra] on the ground using the appropriate colored substances and then place it upon the bed.
The deities are wind, fire, earth, and water. || 77 ||
Within the space between the two cities of the earth-layered enclosure, one should draw the consort of the Lord of the Mountain-Daughter;
one should write the Praṇava for her, situated within an eight-cornered figure—this is declared to be the supreme remover of fever.
He says something else as well: "Puṭitā" refers to Māyā, the consort of the Lord of Girijā;
Śakti is the deity. || 78 ||
One should write the name within the moon in the center of the letters; outside that, in front, is the city of the earth (the square grid).
This yantra, surrounded by circles, is declared for the subjugation of men and for the pacification of all afflictions.
The author of the *Vaśyakṛt* says "vārṇe" (in the vowel).

The two locative cases in "śaśāṅkamadhye" (in the middle of the moon) and "vārṇe" (in the vowel) are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). "Outside" refers to that which ends in the letter *ṭ*.
One should encircle it with the letter ṭha;
the moon is the deity. || 79 ||

One should write the *māyā* (the syllable Hrīṃ) together with the object to be accomplished within the interior of a beautiful *nāgalatā* leaf, situated between two houses of fire marked with svastikas;
whoever, surrounded by nooses and goads, heats this at night—
While he is reciting the mantra, she who is to be accomplished approaches him of her own accord. || 80 ||
Regarding the statement "She [says] that which effects the subjugation of women," the phrase "encircled by noose and goad" refers to the interior of the hexagon.
"Lalitā" refers to [the goddess].
In an unbroken betel leaf;
"the mantra" refers to the Śakti enclosed by the noose and the goad.
This is the traditional position.
"One should heat" means [in] the flame of a lamp. Thus it was said by the Teachers:

One should draw the diagram of the *nāgavallī* leaf upon a petal, featuring the name of the target (*sādhya*) situated within the fire-triangle (*hṛllekhāgni*), surrounded externally by the syllable *āṃ*, adorned with two fire-houses (*vahnigehe*), weapons (*astra*), and three *svastikas*.
Having recited the *Śakti* mantra accompanied by the *pāśa* and *aṅkuśa* seed-syllables, one should heat it over the flame of a lamp.
"At night, with her body bowed in devotion, overcome by the arrows of Love and trembling with passion, she approaches.
Thus [is described] Śakti, the deity. 80.

One should write the *māyā* (hrīṃ) together with one's own name and that of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the center of a hexagon; in its corners, one should inscribe the *śakti* (hūṃ) along with the name of the person to be accomplished. On the outside, a square enclosure (*bhūmipura*) with corner-houses should be drawn on a betel leaf.
If one causes her to eat what has been consecrated by recitation at night, she will remain under his control for a long time. || 81 ||
He says something else as well, beginning with "six.
Here too, the deity is Śakti.
[The phrase] "prepared on a betel leaf" is used.
The phrase "with *kokilākṣa* thorns" is an ellipsis;
the phrase "recited with the *māyā* [syllable]" is an ellipsis.
However, there is a distinction elsewhere.

The writing of the Kāma-mantra within the six corners and its external encirclement by the power of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) is prescribed. Alternatively, the traditional reading in the root text is "one should write Smara" (the god of love).
This has been stated by the Teachers:

One's own name, situated within the power (Śakti), placed inside a pair of fire-palaces (triangles), surrounded by the Mānmatha seed-syllable (Klīm) interlaced with the name of the target, and further encircled externally by the Śakti and the element of water (Pāthīva);
then, with thorns arising from the eyes of the Smara located in its corners and of the Anyapuṣṭa:

"Written and consecrated upon betel-leaf, it deludes the mind of a woman. The phrase "let her eat" is not to be made known; if it is eaten while known by the woman, it does not bring her under control at all.
Thus, even in other applications, the secret is that it should be given without having informed the person of what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
In another Tantra:
"The eighth [letter] of Vāyu, joined with the fire-bindu (*agni-bindu*), is the letter of the fully developed *māyā*."

In the center, it is surrounded by two circles containing the name of the person to be accomplished; outside of that, it is joined with the sixteen vowels on the petals; thereafter, there is the circle of the earth, and in its corner is placed the seed-syllable of Kāma—this is the yantra that brings the world under control. Thus [it is said].

But elsewhere: one should draw an eight-petaled lotus in the yantra, joined with two circles containing the *sādhya* (the name of the person to be acted upon) in the center of the *hṛllekhā*; that [lotus] should contain its seed-syllable, and the lotus should also be enriched outside with sixteen petals.
Having written upon the petals of the lotus the earth-mandala (*pārthivamaṇḍala*), measured by the number of vowels.
"In the corner [of the hexagon], one should write the syllable *kṣiṃ*, which captivates the minds of all people; this is the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* yantra.

Elsewhere, however: "The wise man should write his own name situated within the *Śakti* (the triangle) in the abode of fire (the hexagon), surrounded by the syllable *hrīṃ*; having interlaced it with the name of the target (*sādhya*), he should write the *Aṅkuśa* (the hook)."
One should draw this, indicated by the thorns, upon the very broad back of a serpent, surrounded on the rear by the abode of the wind (the letter Ya), which is enchanting to the minds of women.
Having thus formed the center of a hexagon, joined with the sky (Ha) and fire (Ra), and variegated with the Bindu and Māyā (the letter I).

"In its corners, one should draw a goad-weapon, then again an eight-petaled lotus containing power (*śakti*), followed by a pair of petals adorned with the digits of the moon situated at the gateway; this, drawn on birch bark with yellow pigment (*gorocanā*) and the rut of a noble elephant, the lords of sages declare to be the diagram for subjugation (*vaśya*). Thus it is said.

And in another tantra, the teachers [state]: "This [mantra] of the Lord consists of the letter *sa* (sānta) joined with the crest (*śikhī*) and the letter *la* (*lava*), with the portion of fire (*dahana*) as the goal (*sādhya*) and the portion of *māyā* as the practitioner (*sādhaka*), surrounded by the *kalās*;
it has a double-faced trident shining in its center."
That which is called Yantra is the subduer of the limbs of men who have bowed down.
Having taken earth from a potter’s finger-ring, mixed with the fat from within a lizard,

and combined with the dust from the foot of the person to be overcome, one should fashion an image of that person out of very soft clay; then, having inscribed the mantra upon the heart of that form, one should place the person to be overcome within its cavity and [direct it] toward his enemies.
Having recited [the mantra] over it and buried it there, one should urinate upon it every day for a long time; this brings about subjugation. Thus [ends verse 81].

One should write the name within the Śakti [triangle] and surround it on all four sides with the seed-syllables; this enclosure should be encircled by the seed-mantras of Śakti, Manobhava, Aṅkuśa, and Praṇava. Having recited [the mantra] over an image of the person to be influenced made of flour, one should roast it while blowing upon it with the three sweets (trisvādu).
One should eat it; the person to be accomplished will certainly and always come under his control like a servant. || 82 ||

The author of the *Vaśyakṛt* says "in the *śakti*. This means: in the heart of the effigy made of flour representing the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Having drawn the *śakti*, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished together with the ritual action therein, and then encircle that *śakti* with the four seed-syllables (*bīja*).
In this regard, some say that the mantras are the *nṛsiṃha*, *cintāmaṇi*, *śakti*, and *durgā* seed-syllables (*bījas*).
Others, however, state that one should encircle [the deity] with four seed-syllables;
he clarifies that very point with the words beginning "encircled by Śakti" (*vītaṃ śakti-*), and so forth.
Furthermore, one should construct the enclosure (*vīta*) using the four seed-syllables mentioned in the verse.
Regarding this, some read "marut-proṃ-bījakaiḥ" and assert that *yam* is the fifth; however, that is incorrect.
Because it contradicts other tantras.
As the teachers have said:
"One should surround the name of the object to be accomplished, situated within the *śakti*, with four seed-syllables."
"Bound by the syllables of the *śakti*, *manobhava*, *aṅkuśa*, and *lipi*, it is completely encircled.
Regarding this, the teacher Padmapāda has explained that "completely encircled" (*samāveṣṭita*) is a gloss for "bound together" (*samābaddha*).
Some, however, say it is [bound] by four *śakti*-syllables.
Purified by recitation, with the vital breath firmly established;
Śakti is the deity. 82.
One should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) within a lotus whose filaments and petals shine with the vowels;
this is declared to be the "Manmatha Yantra," which bestows good fortune, prosperity, and victory. (83)
He states another yantra with the words "Kāma" and so forth.
Here, Kāma is the deity. Certain yantras for attaining supernatural powers (siddhi) are [derived] from the Siddhayogeśvarīmata.
For the benefit of the entire world, they are clearly written here by me.
One should write the name, encircled by the Māyā syllable, within the pericarp;
having placed it upon the eight petals, it should be surrounded by the Aghoreśvarī mantra.
The mantra "Aghoreśvari Huṃ Phaṭ" is declared; now follows the Vedic one. The thirty-two-syllable Aghora mantra is placed on the outer eight petals.
Having encircled it three (or two) times with the *māyā* syllable (*hrīṃ*), one should place the syllable *kroṃ* at the end of the lines.

This protection, when performed according to the rite, destroys the affliction caused by ghosts, spirits, *piśācas*, *śākinīs*, planetary spirits, and *rakṣasas*, and remains stationed in the arm. || 1 ||
One should write the name in the pericarp, and beneath it the three-syllable mantra;
on the eight petals, one should write the Māyā-bīja, in a very clean vessel of bell-metal.
When the yantra is drawn with yellow pigment (rocanā) and placed in the midst of milk, he becomes subject to one's control; the mantra is *māyā* enclosed by the *tāra*.
One should write the name encased within the seed-syllable *kṣamā* on four leaves;
when these are cast into clarified butter or suspended inside a house, [the desired result follows].
Peace, prosperity, fame, and nourishment are constantly produced for him;
through the application of the power of the yantra, there is neither disease nor fear from enemies. (3)
The fire-mandala, surrounded by flames and joined with the syllable *haṃ* within the three triangles,
has the name encased by the letter *ra* in its center and is externally encompassed by the Śakti.
Whether written on a cloth from a cremation ground or on a skull, once quickly heated,
it will undoubtedly cause a fierce fever for the enemy.

Having written the name in the center of an eight-petaled lotus, with "huṃ" in the cardinal directions and below, and [the syllables] situated in the intermediate directions, this protection in milk brings victory in gambling.
Situated in the center of the circle of the sky is the [seed-syllable] named; then, on the outside, are the sixteen vowels, and outside of that is the circle of fire, dense with flames.
This yantra, which destroys good fortune, should be drawn on a cloth from a cemetery using the juice of *dhattūra* and buried in ground belonging to a *preta*.
One should write the name in the pericarp, and "hrīṃ" on the four petals within the lotus, using yellow pigment (rocanā), elephant-ichor (hastidāna), and saffron (kuṅkuma) on an auspicious day.
Then, having wrapped it with a grain of rice and placed it in a vessel containing ghee,
incomparable good fortune arises for women for as long as they live.
In the center of an eight-petaled lotus, the name should be surrounded by the *visarga*;
on the outer petals, it should be accompanied by the letter *pa* and the *visarga*.
Having drawn this yantra with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma), one should cause it to be given;
for whoever has entered a prison, their liberation is thereby brought about.
Having written the syllable *hrīṃ* in the center of an eight-petaled lotus and the syllable *krom* on the petals of the directions,
this yantra,
when worn upon the body, liberates a living being from disease; even one who is weak shall regain his strength.

In a square, one should place the name within the interior of the syllable *Haṃ* (or *Ha*) minus its head; outside of that, a city of earth (*bhūpura*) should be drawn, with its corner-energies (*śakti*) reaching out.
Having written this on a shallow dish with a pen made from a crow's feather,
one should fill it and place it face-down upon the ground, and then one faints over it.
In a dispute with those of evil intent who speak contrary truths,
there shall be a paralysis of the mouth for such men, or they will certainly achieve victory in the assembly.
It is called "encased by the letter *la*," with two *la*s above and below it;
on the outside are two squares, surrounded everywhere by powers (*śakti*).
When this is written with yellow pigment on birch bark and worn in a secret place,
there shall be no fear for one traveling a distance of a hundred yojanas.

One should write the name in the center of an eight-petaled lotus, with the syllable *hrīṃ* on the collection of petals; outside, one should draw two circles on birch bark using saffron and cow-dung earth.
This knowledge named Ajitā provides protection when one is in battle, on a difficult path, or in fear of kings and others; it remains present upon the arm. (12)
The name is situated between two *praṇavas* in the center of the four-petaled [lotus];
there are three *praṇavas* on the petal in the western direction and three from the east.
One should write each [syllable] individually on birch bark with yellow pigment (rocana), one on the left and one on the right;
this is declared to be the protection of life when an extremely unbearable disease has arisen. (13)
One should write the name situated in the center of the four *ṭhaṃ* (or *vaṃ*) syllables, and outside of that,
on the eight petals, one should write *raṃ* using yellow pigment (*rocanā*), camphor, and saffron.
This Vaiśvānarī protection, when placed around the necks of children, [guards them]. || 14 ||
The name should be situated within a circle, and outside of that, a square;
outside of that, all the vowels should be placed, and one should draw a circle outside of that.
Therein, one should fashion twelve petals within this space; [this is] the protection "vañcī-vañcī," which obstructs the five divine [powers]. (15)

Within a triangle surrounded by flames, the name is enclosed by *j*, *r*, and *jhūṃ*; this is encircled on the outside by the *va* letters together with the *visarga*, and beyond that is the circle of fire (*vahni-maṇḍala*).
Having written this [mantra], which is filled with flames, upon birch bark with cow-dung and saffron, and having bound it to one's own hand, it shall remove fever and quartan fever.
The account is established with the syllables *roṃ hrīṃ namaḥ* surrounding [the name] on the outside;
then, on the outside of that, in the corner of the fire-mandala, is the syllable *laṃ*.
Outside of that is the city of the Earth, surrounded by Śaktis at the four corners;
this protection, situated on the arms, destroys fever when applied with a single interval.
One should write the name in the center and the seed-syllables *rūṃ* (or *valaṃ*) on the eight petals;
this, prepared with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and sandalwood, is a destroyer of double-day fevers (*dvyāhikajvara*).
One should draw the name "Rūṃ" in the center of a hexagon and [the syllables] in its corners;
seen drawn on a wall with chalk, this brings about the constant destruction of fever. (19)

The word *vasameti*, with the syllable *vāyu* (va), the long final vowel (*ī*), the letter *anila* (la), and the head (*śa*)—this mantra, yellow like a petal of Indra’s lotus, effects immobilization. (20)
One should write the name of the enemy within a moon [diagram] on a cloth using *tāla* [powder];
one should dig this into the path of the army—it is the supreme method for paralyzing an army. Thus [ends verse 83].
The preceptor should draw these diagrams with a golden stylus, using saffron, yellow pigment, lac, musk, elephant-ichor, and sandalwood.
He states the substances for writing the Nārāyaṇīya yantra with the word "kāśmīra" and so forth:
*kāśmīram* is saffron;
*rocanā* is *gorocanā* (cow bezoar).
Lākṣā is lac.
With this alone, all [substances] are to be rubbed.
Mṛgamada is musk.
Ibhamada is elephant-ichor.
The drawing is done with these very [pigments] mixed together.
As they say:

"One who desires the fulfillment of all undertakings should draw the yantras with musk, deer musk, and saffron, consecrated [with mantras], fragrant, mixed with yellow pigment (rocanā), and blended with the juice of lac. Thus it is said.
In another place, specific substances are also mentioned:
Indeed, *rocanā* combined with the ichor of a lordly elephant is likewise used for subjugation (*vaśya*);
[it is also used] with embers from a funeral pyre mixed with poison and *dhattūra*.
"One should accomplish minor rites such as striking and driving away;
the killing [of an enemy] is taught to occur through the combination of poison, *arka* milk, and *guñjā*. Thus it is said.
"With a golden stylus" refers to the beginning of auspicious rites.
In other rites, however, the six types of pens mentioned for the sixfold rites are to be understood as applicable.
Furthermore, writing—aside from the specific substrates explicitly prescribed—is to be known as occurring on other materials such as gold, silver, copper, birch bark, and so forth.
In this regard, the specific times previously mentioned should also be observed.
Elsewhere, specific bases have also been mentioned—
for pacifying rites (*śāntika*) and for nourishing rites (*pauṣṭika*), as well as in the procedure for desiring long life,
for the subduing of serpents, and likewise for the immobilization of speech.
For the production of delusion, [practice] upon a stone is praised;
for inciting enmity, upon a donkey skin; and for a great expulsion, upon a banner.
"Having written [the mantra], one shall accomplish everything—fever, burning heat, sorrow, and likewise the slaying of enemies—on a yellow cloth, and not otherwise. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, the specific details regarding the auspicious moments (*muhūrta*) and so forth, as stated in another tantra, are also written here: [The specific details regarding the auspicious moments and so forth are written here.]
On an auspicious day, under a favorable constellation, in a good location free from thorns and debris.
There, the teacher together with his disciples, or in the absence of those, the disciple himself,
having sat down facing either north or east and having prostrated, [should proceed].
"Then one should draw the yantra after [worshipping] the Guru, the Lord Viśveśvara.
Regarding specific desires, the specific lunar mansions (nakṣatras) for those purposes are also stated in that same source:
"One should draw it under Puṣya for subjugation and attraction; under Āśleṣā, it is taught for causing enmity."
"Killing is prescribed under Ārdrā, and under Maghā there shall be eradication. Thus [it is said].
"In the serpent asterism" means in Aśleṣā.
In that very context, regarding the retention [of breath], there is also a specific location:
"In the hand, on the neck, and on the topknot, so that it may be present [there].
Thus,
these aforementioned yantras must not be given to just anyone, nor in any manner whatsoever.

Thus it is stated in the Hiraṇyagarbha-saṃhitā: "O son, this highly efficacious yantra must not be given by you to one who is not a disciple, nor to a sinner, nor to one who is not tranquil, nor to one who is unfriendly."
"It should be given to a disciple who is established in the mantra, endowed with pure devotion, and a bestower of wealth; otherwise, one shall go to hell. (84)

A practitioner of mantra should never wear a yantra that has touched the ground, been touched by a corpse, been burnt, come into contact with discarded offerings (nirmālya), become shattered, or been stepped over. || 85 ||
"Touching the ground" means directly. || 85 ||
Now, for the sake of all prosperity, I praise Ambikā, the cause of the universe, the Goddess consisting of bliss, whose very nature is the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman). || 86 ||
I praise; I extol. || 86 ||
The primordial mother of all, who bestows her own form upon the lotus-born Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
and who effects the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the three worlds.
Having offered praise with these words, O Mother, I purify myself before you. || 87 ||
"Bestowing a body"— this is the reason for their having a physical form. For this very reason, there is a further qualification [in the following verse].
The connection [of the verse] is: "By praising you, I shall purify my speech. || 87 ||
The possession of power by the Lord, the enemy of Manmatha, who assumes the forms of earth, water, fire, wind, ether, the sacrificial priest, the moon, and the sun— [is truly wondrous].
You alone, O daughter of the King of Mountains, are indeed the cause. || 88 ||
O Mother, I understand that very reason for the excellence of the triple-streamed Gaṅgā, who is honored by all the worlds:
it is because her waters are variegated by the pollen of the lotuses of Your feet.
That which is the constant revolving within the matted locks of Śambhu. || 89 ||
The presentation of the eightfold form (aṣṭamūrti) is [expressed] by the words "pṛthivī" and so forth;
[it is called] "possessing power" (śaktimattā), otherwise [the Lord would be] inactive due to being unattached. ||88||
The moon, the lord of the digits, delights the night-lily,
yet no other [sun] delights the day-lily, nor any other;
for in the act of gladdening one, only one is desired as supreme.
But you, by your own view, take delight in the phenomenal world. || 90 ||
Not another lotus; not any other night-blooming lily.
Even now you are in the bloom of fresh youth for all the worlds;
though you are the daughter of the King of Mountains, you are exceedingly tender; even the Mother of the Three has not beheld such beauty as yours.
O Gaurī, you are the object of meditation; you do not stand on the path of the mind.
The phrase beginning with "ādyā" (first) refers to the four apparent contradictions (*virodhābhāsa*).
The resolution is that she was not "observed" because she was not known by way of her limited extent;
thus, she does not stand within the path of the mind.
"The answer is: 'of inconceivable form. || 91 ||
Having attained after a long time a birth among humans— which is so difficult to obtain— and having further acquired the full capacity of their own senses,
those who do not worship you, O Mother of the worlds;
Having climbed to the top of a ladder, they fall once again. || 92 ||
"Among human beings," because the scripture has human beings as its intended audience. || 92 ||
O Bhavānī, those who, full of longing, worship you with sandalwood paste mixed with camphor powder and cool water, and with flowers of exquisite fragrance;
Indeed, they are renowned as sovereigns over all the worlds without exception. || 93 ||
The leaders are the *ādhibhuvaḥ*.
According to the lexicon (*kośa*): "The *ādhibhū* is the leader (*nāyaka*), the guide (*netṛ*). (93)
Having entered the central path of the first lotus and fashioned the universe like a sleeping serpent-king,
she bears the graceful play of a circle of lightning-vines.
Tearing asunder five lotuses, she was enduring [the ordeal]. || 94 ||
Her body sprinkled by the nectar-essence flowing from that [moon],
she returned once more to her abode by that same path;
those in whose hearts you never manifest shall not exist [in this world].
O Mother, O wife of Maheśvara, [be gracious] to those who bear the embryo. || 95 ||
"Having entered"—this is a couplet [of verses]. "The middle path" refers to the central channel (*suṣumnā*).
"Lightning-creeper" refers to her form as *Kuṇḍalinī*.
"In the first lotus" means in the *ādhāra*.
Here, having restated the sequence from "the first" up to "bearing," the syntactical connection is: "having entered the middle path, split open the five lotuses.
These are the five lotuses.
[The centers] called Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūraka, Anāhata, Viśuddha, and Ājñā;
Kha is the Brahma-randhra. 94–95.
With a face made beautiful by a mass of hanging curls, with full and sloping breasts and a slender, rounded waist,
her hands were adorned with a painting of a jar, a rosary, and a lotus— emblems of contemplation.
I mentally revolve your form, O Gaurī. || 96 ||
The gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) is [formed by] the hand of reflection;
it is a written book.
This is the meditation on the form of Sarasvatī. || 96 ||
Having resorted to yoga and conquered the six enemies, and having bound the group of senses within a tranquil mind—
[one beholds her] who is deep red, with hands endowed with the noose, goad, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.
O Sovereign Lady of the World, the yogis gaze upon you. || 97 ||
Resembling refined gold, she is being consecrated by four elephants with jars of swirling nectar,
while she herself carries two beautiful lotuses in her two hands.
Padmā as well—you alone are she who bestows both fearlessness and boons. || 98 ||
Having mounted the king of beasts upon eight female elephants, who carried various formidable weapons and whose temples were dripping with ichor, he—
possessing the luster of a blade of *dūrvā* grass— [overwhelmed] the wings of the enemies of the immortals.
O Goddess Bhavānī Durgā, you are she who humbles all. || 99 ||
The characteristics of the yogas and so forth, as well as the group of six enemies (ariṣaḍvarga), he will explain immediately hereafter. || 97–99 ||
Her face was beautified by the spray of water from the summer heat,
she wore a necklace fashioned from a string of *guñjā* berries, and her garment was made of leaves; she was the dark-hued embodiment of the science of the God of Love.
I repeatedly remember the intoxicated young Pulinda woman. || 100 ||
One whose conduct is governed by the bodiless god [Kāma], that is, one for whom desire is predominant. || 100 ||
Followed by swans whose flight drew them far away by the tinkling of their anklets— as if they were embodied, wealthy voices—
and resembling two lotuses with well-formed stalks rising upward with faces turned above.
O Consort of Śrīkaṇṭha, I bear your two feet upon my very head.
As he was gazing with eyes untroubled by dense passion, the bull-bannered god, as if unsatisfied by looking with his two eyes, produced a third eye on his forehead to behold him.
O Bhavānī, I bow even to both your shanks. || 102 ||
With the words beginning with "by swans" (haṃsaiḥ), there is a description from the feet up to the head;
"speech" (vacana) means sound (śabda). || 101 ||

I remember her thighs, which surpassed the pride of an elephant’s trunk in their girth and outshone the plantain tree in their paleness; they were fashioned as if by the Creator himself, having been deemed capable of supporting the weight of her hips.
O Mother, by your middle age, you are like a pillar. || 103 ||
Her hips and breasts were simultaneously expanding;
drawn toward the age beyond childhood, her physical essence was being transformed,
her form becoming manifest through the play of the line of hair.
May the praise of the Wondrous One flash forth within the center of my heart. || 104 ||
*Avalepa* means arrogance;
*madhyamena vayasā* means by youth. || 103-104 ||
Filled with the waters of loveliness by her fresh youth, it was like an invincible pond bestowed upon her friend Smara, who fears the fire from Shiva’s eye.
O Goddess, I shall never forget your navel.
A *palvala* is a small pond. || 105 ||
Upon your two lotus-like breasts, which bear ashes suggestive of the embrace of the Lord (Śiva) following the application of saffron paste,
the foam is momentarily regained by you as you emerge from your bath like an elephant.
Anointed with vermilion, they remind one of the two frontal globes of an elephant in rut.
*Piśuna* means a slanderer or informer;
*bhasita* means ashes. || 106 ||
His two arms, beautiful with streams of radiant luster flowing from his neck,
were indeed fashioned like long nooses by the god of love— the enemy of his own heart— to seize him by the throat.
O Mother, do not transgress the path of my memory.
Regarding the phrase "exceeding the throat":
it means exceeding or surpassing the throat of Hara (Śiva).
Binding with a noose that is greater than what is required for binding is indeed appropriate.

Alternatively, they possess a splendor like that of two streams of luster which flow from Pārvatī’s throat—streams that are superior to, or exceeding, [the luster of] her throat, and are therefore bright. || 107 ||
O Daughter of the Mountain King, your neck is not too long, it steals the grace of beautiful conch shells, shines with various heavy ornaments, and possesses enchanting qualities.
Having reflected, I never attain satisfaction at any time. || 108 ||
Kambu means a conch shell. || 108 ||
A face with exceedingly long eyes, a noble forehead-plate, the lines of the cheeks slightly blossoming with a gentle smile,
lips like the bimba fruit, and a prominent, long nose.
He who remembers you even once is indeed born [again]. || 109 ||
*Abhijātam* means beautiful. *Daram* means slightly.
"He alone is truly born" means that his birth alone is meaningful. || 109 ||

He who, with his mind, contemplates your mass of hair— which possesses the brilliance of the crescent moon, is laden with abundant fragrance, and is distinguished by swarms of bees hovering over its flowers— [attains liberation].
O Goddess, his ancient bond falls away of its own accord.
The ancient noose is of the nature of ignorance. || 110 ||
The wise person who, with a heart ever moist with devotion, recites here this hymn— the ripened fruit of sacred learning and virtuous conduct—
becomes a high station for prosperity, bowing at the feet of the Victorious One.
For a long time, [he was] marked by the glory of the crowns of the lords of the earth. || 111 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the *Śāradātilaka* composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra. 24.
[It is] the ripening of good conduct for the ears—the two auditory organs—of the wise. || 111 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, according to the tradition of the true lineage. 24.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
Now I shall explain the yoga, together with its limbs, which bestows supreme consciousness.
Those proficient in yoga declare that the union of the individual soul (jīva) and the Self (ātman) is oneness. || 1 ||
There are five initiations known as Laiṅgī, Kriyā, Mantravatī, Svavedha, and Jñāna;
these are fourfold, being designated as Samaya, Sāmānya, Nirvāṇa, and Viśeṣa.
Thus, in all initiations, the Guru should awaken the disciple;
whether he is awakened or remains unawakened, otherwise he does not become initiated.
Because of this statement, since initiation cannot be accomplished without yoga, many methods of yoga have been taught regarding the practical application of the Sūrya-mantra and others.
With the word "atha" (now), he promises to explain yoga for the sake of understanding those [methods].
It is "with its limbs," meaning it is endowed with the ancillaries such as *yama* (restraint) and *niyama* (observance).
The meaning is that it bestows consciousness and grants liberation in the form of the experience of eternal bliss.
By this, the view held by some— that liberation is the destruction of the specific qualities of the self— is refuted,
because the absence of happiness cannot constitute a human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
Relying on the Vedānta position, he says: "Unity.
And that [unity] is established by such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). As stated in the *Prayogasāra*: "Of the partless, immeasurable God, the Supreme Self..."
"They say that *sandhāna* is yoga, the means for the eradication of *saṃsāra*. (1)
The supreme knowers understand the realization [of reality] through the non-difference of Śiva and the self;
those who know the Āgamas have declared that knowledge consists of the essence of Śiva and Śakti. || 2 ||
He states the doctrine of the *Pratyabhijñā* and other texts that proceed from the system of the Sūtras proclaimed by Śiva—beginning with the word "Śiva.
"Understanding" (*pratipatti*) means knowledge.
"The others" refers to the Śaivas.
As it is stated in the *Śivasūtravṛtti*:
"The intellect, belonging to the *sāttvika* nature, arises through reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) for one whose self is restrained;
wandering about, it reaches Śiva and dissolves along with the senses."
Even amidst the division of the three [qualities]— whether abiding in *sattva* or abiding in *tamas*, distinguishing between the qualities—
the embodied soul thus wanders, going from one state to another state.

Constrained by the eightfold group [of elements], which takes the form of the emergence of the subtle elements (tanmātra) through the path of mind, ego, and intellect, one experiences the suffering born from their corresponding perceptions.

"He experiences enjoyment while under the control of another; there, Śiva may withdraw that [enjoyment]. Also, in the *Svacchandabhairava*: "The vibration of the bliss of Śiva, even if as small as an atom, removes all defects;
and through the destruction of the three impurities (*mala*), Māyā goes forth along with its root."

In the *Ānandabhairava* as well: "Having abandoned the contemplation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, as well as the riches of its objects, one should gradually enter the state of Śiva with a mind characterized by the nature of one's own Self.
He states the doctrine of the *Uttarāmnāya*: "Śiva," etc.
Knowledge consisting of Śiva and Śakti means the knowledge of the non-difference between Śiva and Śakti.

As they say: "This power, composed of consciousness and having the nature of supreme bliss, is bound by the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest; she is the all-pervasive one situated within her own *māyā*."
Immediately after the creation of all classes of beings here,
even by mortals dwelling in all their respective bodies, there was mutual [interaction].
"Bound by beginningless superimposition and consisting of the forgotten nature of the Self, this Goddess Śivā (Viśvā) becomes one with the Self of all in Śiva. Thus [ends the verse]. 2.
The learned authorities declare that knowledge belongs to others than the Ancient Person (Purāṇapuruṣa).
Having first conquered the enemies of the self, such as desire and the rest, one should practice yoga. || 3 ||
He states the view of the Vaiṣṇavas and others who maintain the doctrine of difference with the words "purāṇa" and so forth.
Puruṣottama [is the Supreme Person]; "puruṣa" [refers to] the person in the Sāṃkhya system.
In the Nyāya system, it is Īśvara;
in the Vaiṣṇava system, it is Nārāyaṇa.
The means of acquaintance with that [reality] is Yoga.
In this regard, it is understood that because it is worthy of veneration and because it was presented first, the first view is the one favored by the author of the treatise. || 3 ||
They say that desire and anger, greed and delusion, as well as pride and envy—these are the six internal enemies of the self that bestow suffering. || 4 ||
"Kāma" refers to desire for the enjoyment of women and so forth;
"krodha" refers to the wish to harm living beings and the like.
Greed is thirst for wealth and the like;
delusion is ignorance of reality;
and pride is the arrogance of thinking, "I am happy, wealthy, and learned."
The connection [of the verse] is as follows: "Envy is hatred toward the welfare of others;

these are called one's own sixfold group of enemies because they bestow suffering. Their status as enemies arises from their obstruction of the activity of contemplating the true nature of the self. || 4 ||
Having conquered these through the eight limbs of yoga, practitioners of yoga attain the state of yoga:
first restraint (yama) and observance (niyama), then posture (āsana) and breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 5 ||
Pratyāhāra, that which is called dhāraṇā, dhyāna, together with samādhi—these they say are the eight limbs for the yogi in the practice of yoga. (6)
He states the means for this victory with the words "yoga," and he specifies those [limbs] with the words "yama" and so forth. || 5-6 ||
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, straightforwardness, forgiveness, fortitude, moderation in food, and purity—these are the ten *yamas*. || 7 ||
He states their essential nature in sequence, beginning with "non-violence" (ahiṃsā):
non-violance is the inclination toward the practice of thinking, "I shall not kill anyone";
truthfulness is the state of mind inclined toward the practice of thinking, "I shall not speak untruth."
Abstention from theft is non-stealing. Abstention from the desire for sexual enjoyment is celibacy. Abstention from cruelty toward living beings is compassion.
Rectitude (*ārjava*) is the cessation of mental crookedness.

Forbearance (*kṣamā*) is a state of mind inclined toward the absence of anger when confronted by one who seeks to overcome. Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the absence of anxiety resulting from the non-attainment of desired objects and the like.
"Moderate diet" (*mitāhāra*) refers to eating only as much food as is necessary for the maintenance of the body, achieved by gradually reducing one's intake.

"Purity" (*śauca*) is the practice of the aforementioned cleanliness and ethical conduct (*śīla*) for the sake of mental clarity. These are the "restraints" (*yama*); the term *yamu* signifies "to cease," meaning they consist of the cessation of desire and other such impulses.
In this context, steadfastness (*dhṛti*) is present throughout all of them.
Through non-violence and celibacy, desire is conquered; through compassion and patience, anger;
and through non-stealing, truthfulness, and straightforwardness, greed.
Of delusion, by moderation in food and purity; of pride, by forbearance and straightforwardness;
of envy, by non-violence, compassion, straightforwardness, and forbearance.
Thus, other matters should also be inferred accordingly.
As it is said in the *Saṃhitā*:
"O Sage, [this practice] produces no distress for any living beings whatsoever."
Non-violence is said to consist in the absence of [harmful] actions of speech, mind, and body.
"Furthermore, the description of things exactly as they have been seen or heard is called truth.
O ascetic, one should not take even a blade of grass that belongs to another.
Non-stealing. Thus:
"In all circumstances, through action, mind, and speech, the total renunciation of association with women is declared to be celibacy (brahmacarya)."
"Compassion (dayā) is the pursuit of the eradication of suffering, having perceived the suffering of others as one perceives one's own. Thus,
in all worldly dealings, by means of the actions of mind, speech, and body—
"May there be straightforwardness (*ārjava*) characterized by the absence of crookedness toward all.
May there be forbearance (*kṣamā*), such that his conduct toward those who do him harm, as well as toward his kinsmen, is always and everywhere the same in every respect."
"Fortitude is the absence of desire and effort even toward objects that have arisen and are full of allure;
it is eating only a fourth part of what is fit to be eaten by one whose mind is pure."
They declare that moderate eating is beneficial, purifying, and very sharp [in its effects].
They say that the impurity which has emerged from the pores of the skin and from the nine apertures is the dirt of the openings; its washing with water is called purification (*śauca*).

"The wise declare that purity consists of being thoroughly cleansed with earth and water externally, or else internally, up to the previously mentioned purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). Thus [ends verse] 7.
Austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the deity, listening to the established doctrines, modesty, intelligence, recitation of mantras, and burnt offerings; || 8 ||
These ten observances (niyamas) have been proclaimed by those expert in the Yoga scriptures.
Regarding "austerity" (tapas):
the practice of vows such as the Kṛcchra and others is austerity.
Contentment is the state of having very few desires.
One who possesses the conviction that there is a future world is an *āstika*;
the state of being such is *āstikya*.
This means the practice of dharma and so forth with the understanding of the next world.
Giving (*dāna*) is the distribution of wealth according to one's means for the sake of the gods, ancestors, and humans.
The worship of the gods serves to remove obstacles for one who is engaged in the means to liberation through the very performance [of rituals] in the manner described.
The study of the Siddhānta, the Upaniṣads, the *Mokṣopāya*, the *Upadeśa*, the *Parimala*, and other such scriptures; and *hrī* (shame), which is a natural aversion toward ignoble conduct,
because if that were lacking, knowledge would not arise due to the impurity of the mind.
*Manas* is reflection (*manana*).
And thus says the *Smṛti*: "One should hear from the statements of the *Śruti*, and one should reflect by means of logical arguments."
"Japa" refers to the method already described.
This is because of the statement, "For one who performs japa, there is no sin," and because it serves as a means for the purification of the mind.
*Huta* refers to the *agnihotra* and other fire-sacrifices,
because by their non-performance there arises a transgression (*pratyavāya*) through mental impurity, which in turn prevents the arising of knowledge;
or alternatively, *huta* refers to the fire-oblation consisting of one-tenth of the recitation of mantras (*mantra-japa*).
And as it has been said:
"A mantra is not perfected through non-recitation, nor does it grant fruit without oblations;
if unworshipped, it takes away one's desires; therefore, one should practice these three."
Regarding the term "niyamas":
they possess the status of a *niyama* (observance) because they must necessarily be performed.
Therefore, one should never abandon them due to laziness or similar causes.
As it is stated in the Saṃhitā:
"Austerity is intended to be fasting according to the prescribed rules;
and the practice of begging for alms is for the sake of satisfaction through effortless fasting."
This is contentment.
Thus, they declare that orthodoxy (*āstikya*) is faith in what is taught in the Vedas and other authoritative sources.
Having meditated upon one's chosen deity, [one should perform this] daily with the thought of offering it to that deity.
Food and other offerings given to a worthy recipient are called *dāna*;
likewise, the proper daily worship of one's chosen deity according to the prescribed rites.
That worship indeed occurs either at the three junctions of the day or at one time;
likewise, there is the hearing and reciting (or remembering) of the established doctrines of the Vaiṣṇava Āgamas.
"Shame is the non-engagement in that which is utterly censured by the Vedas and other [authorities], as well as by worldly people.
Thus it is said.

"That investigation which is carried out through reasonings, even while remaining firmly established in the words [of scripture]—this is the understanding taught in the treatises. Thus it is said. "Japa is the constant repetition of the mantra received from the Guru."
Gold is offered as an oblation with substances prescribed in the ritual manual. Thus [ends verses 8–9].
The lotus posture, the one called the swastika, the thunderbolt, and likewise the auspicious posture. || 9 ||
The fivefold sequence of postures is thus declared; among them, the *vīrāsana* is described as follows:
having properly placed both soles of the feet upon the thighs. (10)
Then, one should bind the two thumbs with the hands in reverse order;
this is called the lotus posture (padmāsana), which is heart-pleasing to yogins. || 11 ||
Regarding the "fivefold posture":

standing leads to fatigue, while lying down on a bed or similar surface is overcome by sleep; therefore, only one who is seated possesses the qualification for the practice of knowledge (*jñānābhyāsa*).
In that regard, if one sits in just any manner whatsoever, there will be disease and a lack of favorable conditions for the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī.
Therefore, there is the prescription of the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) and others.
As it is said in the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*:
"By means of the posture one destroys physical ailments; by means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one destroys sin."
The yogi should always suppress mental modification through pratyāhāra (withdrawal of the senses).
"Through the *dhāraṇās* one attains steadiness of mind; through knowledge, supreme sovereignty;
and in *samādhi*, having abandoned both auspicious and inauspicious karma, one attains liberation. Thus [it is said].
Regarding the word "from the thighs" (*ūrveḥ*):
"Upon the thighs" means upon each other's thighs;
this is because the term "out of sequence" (*vyutkramāt*) applies here as well.
Regarding the instruction "one should bind," the phrase "out of sequence" implies that on the back portion there is a displacement of one cubit (*hasta*).
Regarding the binding of the thumbs, however, each respective thumb is bound by that very same hand. (9–11)
Having placed both soles of the feet properly between the knees and the thighs, the yogi should enter with an upright body; that they call the Svastika posture. || 12 ||
Regarding "between the knees": on the right [side] one places the left foot, and on the left, the right.
In the previous posture, a straight body is achieved simply by binding the big toes.
But because it is not so in this case, it is said to be "with an upright body. || 12 ||
One should place the two ankles very firmly on either side of the perineal seam;
with the heels positioned below the scrotum, one should bind the feet with both hands. || 13 ||
The Bhadrasana is declared to be the supreme posture honored by yogis:
one should place the feet successively upon the thighs, with the toes pointing backward. (14)
One should place the hands as described; this is the unsurpassed Vajrāsana posture.
Having placed one foot below, one should likewise rest the other upon the thigh. || 15 ||
The yogi should sit with the body straight; this is called the *vīrāsana*.
Regarding the term "sīvanyā": the *sīvanyā* is the upward line between the anus and the genitals.
On its two sides:
on the left side, the ankle of the right foot;
on the other, the other [ankle].
The testicles (*vṛṣaṇa*) and the scrotum (*aṇḍakoṣa*) [should be positioned] below; the implication is that the heels (*pādapārṣṇī*) are reversed.
The lexicon states: "The two knots there are the *ghuṭikā*; the *gulpha* (ankles) are masculine; the *pāṣṇī* (heels) are below them.
One should bind with the two hands as before—the implication being the two thumbs.
By means of the binding of the big toes, the straightness of the body is accomplished.
As it is said in the *Yogasāra*:
"Having placed the two ankles on either side of the seam of the spine at the base of the torso..."
The right ankle on the left [thigh] and the other right [ankle] on the right [thigh].
"Placing the left hand upon the right and the other hand upon the left, one should bind the two thumbs together with the hands in reverse order. Thus [it is said].
"Upon the thighs," etc.
One should place the two feet in succession at the base of one's own thighs. "Facing inward" means the fingers are directed toward oneself;
the construction is that one should place the hands with fingers facing inward upon the knees.
In this context, the straightness of the body is established simply by the placing of the hands upon the knees. "One" refers to the lower buttock. (13–16)
One should draw in the external air through the *iḍā* for sixteen measures. || 16 ||
The yogi should retain [the breath] when full for sixty-four measures;
it should be properly directed into the center of the suṣumṇā slowly for thirty-two measures. || 17 ||
The best among those who know yoga should exhale this [air] through the piṅgalā channel;
those expert in the science of yoga call this prāṇāyāma. || 18 ||

One should practice this for him again and again in succession, alternating [the order], according to the sequence of increasing the measures, correctly [reaching] twelve and sixteen [breaths]. || 19 ||
Prāṇāyāma is indeed of two kinds: with seed (sagarbha) and without seed (agarbha). The wise know that which is joined with recitation, meditation, and so forth, as "with seed. || 20 ||
The wise know that breath control (prāṇāyāma) devoid of that [meditation] and lacking its core essence to be inferior.
For a person practicing it in sequence, the emergence of sweat in the body is the lowest stage. || 21 ||
The intermediate [type] is considered the supreme abandonment of the ground when accompanied by trembling;
for the superior [type], the attainment of qualities is desired as long as the practice continues. || 22 ||
Regarding "by sixteen measures" (*ṣoḍaśamātrayā*): the definition of a measure (*mātrā*) is stated in another tantra:
"In as much time as one's own hand [takes to move] around one's own knee-circle..."
"It is equal to one's own single breath; thus it goes.
Others, however, state the definition of *mātrā* differently:
"First, having rubbed one's own knee-circle three times with the hand..."
"Having performed one snap of the fingers, that shall be the shortest *mātrā*.
Elsewhere, however: "It is equal to the snapping of a finger, and it is remembered as being composed of eight of those [snap-sounds].
But in the *Vāyavīya Saṃhitā*: "Having circumambulated the knee, neither too fast nor too slow..."
"One should snap the fingers; that is proclaimed as 'mātrā'.
Thus, "one should draw [the breath] in" refers to *pūraka* (inhalation);
"one should retain what has been filled" refers to *kumbhaka* (retention).
The phrase "properly situated in the middle of the *suṣumṇā*" is connected with what precedes it.
"One should exhale" refers to the exhalation (*recaka*).
Some authorities maintain that the sequence begins with exhalation and ends with the retention (*kumbhaka*).

Thus, by this sequence—repeatedly, again and again, in succession, increasing by one at a time, or by two or three, and so on, or by reversing that order—that is, in the opposite manner from what was previously stated—one should practice twelve or sixteen *prāṇāyāmas*. This is the syntactical connection.
As it has been said: "The self-controlled person, being pure, should perform sixteen *prāṇāyāmas* together with the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*)."

"Whoever is a twice-born man that performs this every day at dawn and at dusk— even if he is burdened by the sin of killing an embryo— these [mantras] purify him within a month, burning away the mass of his misdeeds like cotton. Thus it is said.
He states the opinion of others in the verse beginning with "japa.
The grammatical connection is: "The wise [others] know [it thus].
And it should be understood that this breath control (prāṇāyāma) pertains to the subject of worship.
As it has been said:
"This breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is declared to be 'without seed' (vigarbha), which destroys all evils; when combined with the 'seed' (garbha), its fruit is said to be a hundredfold."

"He who is endowed with recitation and meditation is said to be 'without the embryo' (agarbha); he who is joined with that [breath-control] along with those aged sages devoted to sacrifice is 'with the embryo' (sagarbha). Thus [it is said]. The ellipsis is "the practice of breath-control" (prāṇāyāma). (16–22)
The forceful withdrawal of the senses as they roam unimpeded among their objects is called *pratyāhāra*. || 23 ||
In the thumb, the ankle, the knee, the thigh, the suture, the genitals, and the navel;
then in the heart, the neck, the throat region, the uvula, and finally in the nose.

The retention of the vital breath (prāṇamarut) at the center of the eyebrows, on the forehead, at the crown of the head, or at the "twelve-finger limit" (dvādaśānta), according to the prescribed rule, is called dhāraṇā. || 25 ||
By the words beginning with "of the senses" (indriyāṇām), it is stated that the mind alone must be made to abide in one place;

for these [senses] possess the power to grasp their respective objects only when accompanied by the mind, and therefore they are restrained precisely through the restraint of that [mind]. This is the intended meaning.
*Lambikā* refers to the root of the palate.
The head (*mastaka*) is the junction of the forehead and the hair;
the crown of the head (*mūrdhan*) is the portion above that;
and the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*) is the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
"According to rule" means by the sequence taught by the Guru.
In the *Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā*, five types of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) are described: "The concentration on the elements, that on the mind, and the concentrations on each [of the others] individually."
When the mind has attained immobility, however, concentration (dhāraṇā) is prescribed.
That Earth element, radiant like yellow orpiment and gold, endowed with the essence of aesthetic beauty,
joined with the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā), square in shape, and residing in the heart—
having dissolved my vital breaths there for five *ghaṭikās*, I shall maintain concentration upon it together with the mind.
This is always known as the earth-based concentration (kṣitiparā), which causes stability and is the support of forbearance. || 1 ||

One should meditate upon that [moon] resembling a half-moon, white as a kunda flower, located at the throat, endowed with the principles (tattvas), accompanied by the nectar and the seed-syllable "Va," and eternally joined with Viṣṇu;
having dissolved the vital breaths there for five ghaṭikās, one should maintain it with a focused mind.
This retention of the Varuṇī [wind] becomes the digestion of the unbearable Kālakūṭa poison. || 2 ||
One should meditate upon Śiva established in reality, resembling an *indragopa* insect, as the fire within that triangle—
a manifold brilliance, beautiful as coral— and united with Rudra;
having dissolved the vital breaths there for five *ghaṭikās*, one should maintain concentration accompanied by the mind.
This Vaiśvānara-dhāraṇā bestows a body that possesses a form like fire. || 3 ||
The lotus-root together with its stalk that was seen between the eyebrows is likewise composed of *sattva* and accompanied by the letter *ya*; there, the Lord (*Īśvara*) is the presiding deity.
Having dissolved the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) there for five *ghaṭikās*, one should maintain concentration joined with the mind.
By constantly maintaining the retention of the vital breath (vāyu), one certainly attains movement through the sky.
The space situated at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), which resembles perfectly pure water,
is joined with its Lord Sadāśiva and associated with the syllables of the letter *ha*.
Having dissolved the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) there for five *ghaṭikās*, one should maintain [the mind] together with the consciousness (*citta*).
This is declared to be the concentration on space (nabhodhāraṇā), which is skillful in shattering the door-panel of liberation.
All the five dhāraṇās that accomplish karmas are difficult to obtain;
through the realization of them, one is liberated from all sins. (21–25)
Meditation here is said to be the contemplation of one's chosen deities within the self by means of a concentrated mind that possesses inner consciousness. || 26 ||

The sages declare that the constant cultivation of the equality between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) is samādhi, which is described as having eight characteristics. || 27 ||
Thus, meditation with an internal object (*sagarbha-dhyāna*) has been described regarding one's chosen deities (*abhīṣṭadeva*).
Meditation without an internal object (*vigarbha-dhyāna*) is also described in another tantra,
as they say:
That mind which is unwavering in reality is considered the supreme meditation;
that meditation becomes both with attributes (saguṇa) and likewise without attributes (nirguṇa).
With qualities, through the distinction of colors, and likewise without qualities as the absolute;
[it surpasses] thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices.
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of a single practice of meditation.
Seated comfortably, one should fix the mind within and the eyes directed downward.
"Equanimity toward all bodies and meditation are said to bestow perfection;
by fixing one's gaze on the tip of the nose and meditating, one is released from bondage," and so forth.
One should contemplate the Supreme Lord in the anus, the penis, the navel, the heart, the region of the throat, the place of the uvula and the lambikā, and between the eyebrows.
Having meditated upon that which is devoid of qualities, shaped like the sky, resembling water in a mirage,
and consisting of all things within the void, the yogi shall attain yoga.
Thus ends [the section] with verse 27.
The body, which possesses a dual nature, is ninety-six finger-breadths in length;
they know that the *kanda* (the root-center) is located between the anus and the genitals, measuring two finger-breadths in height. || 28 ||
Therefore, it is twice as wide and beautified by its circular form;
three principal channels have arisen there, which are proclaimed [as such]. || 29 ||
The channel *iḍā* is situated on the left, while *piṅgalā* is considered to be on the right;
the channel *suṣumṇā* is located between them, resting upon the spinal column. || 30 ||
Having entered through the two big toes, then through the two heels, and again through the head, she reached the station of Brahmā, manifesting in the form of the Moon, Sun, and Fire. || 31 ||
Situated in the center of that [channel] is the channel called Citrā, beloved by yogins;
they know the supreme Brahmarandhra within it, resembling the fiber of a lotus stalk. || 32 ||

In order to explain the movement of the vital air (*vāyu*) within the various locations of the channels (*nāḍī*) starting from the *mūlādhāra* inside the body for the sake of attaining yoga-siddhi, he states the measurement of the body with the word "six" (*ṣaḍ*).
It is "of a dual nature," meaning it consists of both Śiva and Śakti.

"Consisting of Agni and Soma," or "consisting of semen and blood," is a restatement of what was said in the first chapter. "From that" means from the height. "Resorting to the backbone" means situated within it.
As they say: "That which has entered the cavity between the base of the head and the end of the staff... [This refers to] the two *śiphās*, that is, the two roots. (28–32)
They know the supports therein to be manifold due to differences of opinion;
they call this the divine path, the cause of the bliss of immortality. || 33 ||
The moon moves in the iḍā and the sun in the piṅgalā;
those who know the principles of yoga recognize both of them as being within the suṣumṇā.
Some say there are twelve supports (ādhāras), others say sixteen,
and still others say there are many; as they have said:
Then, during the dissolution of Brahmā, the wise one should meditate upon the sequence of the cakras:
first the Ādhāra-cakra, and immediately after that the Kuladīpa.
Then the Vajra (sacrifice) wheel is proclaimed, which is supreme and consists of the Svādhiṣṭhāna;
as well as the Raudra and Karāla wheels, which consist of the Gahvara.
And [he saw] the bestower of knowledge, three-faced and three-legged, holding a staff of death;
then the wheel of the syllable *ū*, and thereafter the noble Kāla with a skull-bond.
The Lamp, which produces agitation, consists of the essence of the turbid bliss;
it is known as Maṇipūraka, the plowshare that pierces the knot.
The supreme passion and enthusiasm is called the state of intoxication (*māda*).
Thereafter, the net of conceptual constructions (*kalpajāla*) should be contemplated, and then the surging wave of sound (*ghoṣakallolana*).
The station called Nādāvarta is proclaimed, and following that is Tripuṭa;
Kaṅkāla is the wheel of the mind (manas-cakra), renowned as Puṭabheda.
The unfolding of the great knot, known as the blazing of the bonds,
is likewise the unstruck (*anāhata*) lotus-cavity and the space-wheel (*vyomacakra*).
Awakening, that which is named Dhruva, Kālakandalaka, then Krauñca,
the manifestation of Bheruṇḍa, Ḍāmara, and Kulapīṭhaka.
The throat is the supreme purification, known as Kulakolāhala, Hālāhalāvarta, Mahāratha, and Ghorabhairava.

"One should meditate upon the wheel consisting of the Great Void (mahāvyoma), which is of the nature of Śakti; it is known as Ghūrṇaka, Kampada, Ājñā, Kākapuṭa, Śṛṅgāṭa, that which is called Kāmarūpa, and the supreme Pūrṇagiri. (33-34)
Those who know the scriptures say that there is a most beautiful triangle situated in the center of the *ādhāra-kanda*, a divine abode of lights. || 35 ||
There, the Supreme Deity Kuṇḍalinī, whose form is like a flash of lightning, throbs as the soul of all, having a shape resembling a sleeping serpent. || 36 ||
The Kundalinī energy, having taken refuge in the Haṃsa, sustains herself;
the Haṃsa is eternally dependent on the vital breath (prāṇa), and the vital breath is dependent upon the channels (nāḍīs). || 37 ||
He states the location of Kuṇḍalī as "the Ādhāra.
The meaning is that the power Kuṇḍalī sustains both the individual self (ātman) and the supreme self (paramātman), and thus becomes a participant in their union.
Of what nature? It means that she has taken refuge in the *haṃsa*, which is the individual soul (*jīvātman*), being the substratum of the living soul.
The *haṃsa* is the support of the vital breaths; that is to say, it is the support of the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*).
The vital breath (prāṇa) has the channels (nāḍī) as its substratum. || 35-37 ||
Just as the wind rises from the *ādhāra* (the foundational center) of all embodied beings, it pervades the body through its own channels and proceeds outward. || 38 ||
It is said to be twelve finger-breadths in measure; therefore, it is called "prāṇa. To the question of how it has its locus in the channels (nāḍīs), he says: "from its support" (ādhārāt).
Because it performs the act of going forth (prayāṇa), the etymological derivation of the word "prāṇa" as "that which goes forth" is thus demonstrated.
"By the measure of twelve finger-breadths" should be understood as referring to the left and right [sides].
The fruit of this is stated in another tantra:
"Eating, sexual union, combat, and likewise the gathering of fruits and flowers."
One should perform cruel deeds when Vāyu is situated in the south.
One should perform all journeys, marriage rites, and whatever other auspicious ceremonies there may be when the wind is situated in the left [nostril].

Likewise: "Physical exertion, sleeping, cruel acts, and the performance of the six rites and so forth—these are accomplished by means of the Sun; there is no need for deliberation on this point. Elsewhere: "Furthermore, when a man afflicted by disease is situated on the right side of the deity..."
Standing there, the inquirer asks: "Does that man live long and free from disease?

If the left [hand] is afflicted with pain, or if the Lord (the right hand) has its body leaning toward the left, and the inquirer asks while standing on the left, then the left [hand], being free from ailment, indicates that she will live for a long time. Thus it is said.
"When the deity has departed, if a man stands on the right side and asks [about his condition] while [the deity] remains on the left,
the wise declare that even from such a reversal, the collection of diseases is indeed difficult to cure.

Alternatively, by the statement "having emerged from the support, he proceeds outside," everything is stated regarding the creation and dissolution, the two junctions, the day and night, and so forth.
As they say:

"The wise man should know the rising [of the breath] at the root of his own big toe, the persistence of the gods in the bulbous root (kanda), and indeed the dissolution of men in the nostril, the thumb, and the forefinger, during the morning and evening twilights."
[One perceives] the arising and the dissolution, the continuous downward movement, night and day,
the upward movement and likewise the downward, as well as the moon moving upward and the sun moving [downward].
Thus [ends the section on] verses 38–39.
On a pleasant, pure, and soft seat, covered with cloth, an antelope skin, and kusha grass. || 39 ||

Having mastered a single posture and having correctly understood the arising of the vital breaths within the body by means of the life-force (prāṇavāyu), the yogi should become devoted to the path of yoga. || 40 ||
The wise one should mutter the mantra of each respective element for the sake of attaining firmness of the body;
the movement of the earth is staff-like, located below both nostrils. || 41 ||
The upward movement of water, the horizontal movement of fire, and the movement of the wind through the sky— among these elements,
the arising of space (ākāśa) is traditionally held to be in their midst.
He describes the method of yoga: "in a delightful [place].
This means in a secluded place;
otherwise, there would be distraction of the mind.
It has been stated that the seat should be soft because, if it were hard, the mind would go toward the pain of the body right there.
He says "staff" (*daṇḍa*) and so forth for the purpose of service to living beings. (39–42)
The knower of the self should perform the rites of immobilization (stambhana) and subjugation (vaśya) at the rising of the earth-element;
and the rites of pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika) during the period of water and fire. || 43 ||

The killing [of enemies] and other rites, the expulsion of opposing forces (marutaḥ), and the destruction of minor poisons (kṣveḍa) and the like are prescribed when the planet Mars (vihāyas) is in its rising. 44.
In this context, he describes the arising of the respective elements, beginning with "of the earth" (dharaṇeḥ);
[then follows] "of water" (vasoḥ) and "of fire" (agneḥ). || 43–44 ||
Having firmly bound the sensory organs with his fingers, being fully composed, he should cover both ears with his two thumbs and both eyes with his two index fingers. || 45 ||
Firmly binding the mouth with the other fingers and the two middle fingers at the nostrils, one should contemplate the oneness of the self, the vital breath, and the mind. || 46 ||
One should properly retain the *maruta* (vital air); this is the yoga beloved by yogis.
As one practices it gradually and slowly, the *nāda* (inner sound) arises for him. || 47 ||
The first sound is like the song of a female bee in rut;
the other is similar to the sound of a flute filled with air.
Resembling the sound of a bell, and subsequently like the roar of thick clouds—for a man who practices in this manner, there occurs the destruction of the darkness of saṃsāra. || 49 ||
First, the imperishable knowledge characterized by the *haṃsa* arises.
Regarding the term "bound":
otherwise, if the vital air (*vāyu*) were to exit forcibly through the path of the senses, there would be injury to it.
The instruments are the sense organs.
The word "both" (ubhe) applies to all three [cases].
"Ghana" refers to one whose sound is dense like the roar of a cloud; this is a *madhyapadalopa* compound.
It connects with this [word] "evam" (thus).
They describe the ten sounds as follows: the first sound is *ciṇī*, the second is *ciñciṇī*, the third is *cicicākī*, and the fourth is the *gharghara* tone.
The fifth is slightly higher; the sixth has a sweet, intoxicated sound;
the seventh is a subtle resonance; and the eighth is the "flute-increasing" (veṇuvardhana).
"The ninth is the sweet sound, and the tenth is the sound of a drum. Also, in the *Haṃsopaniṣad*: "Then, within the ten sheaths, one experiences the *nāda*.
By virtue of the *haṃsa*, the *nāda* arises in ten ways."
The first is *ciṇi*;
the second is *ciṇiciṇi*;
the third is the sound of a bell.
The fourth is the sound of the conch;
the fifth is the sound of the lute strings;
the sixth is the sound of the cymbals.
The seventh is the sound of the flute;
the eighth is the sound of the kettle-drum;
the ninth is the sound of the drum.
The tenth is Meghanāda.
Having abandoned the ninth, one should practice the tenth;
by this, the mind dissolves.
When the mind has dissolved, when conceptualization and doubt have departed, and when merit and demerit have been burnt away, [one realizes]: "Sadāśiva, Om.
Sadāśiva, whose essence is Śakti, who is established everywhere, is himself self-luminous, pure, awakened, eternal, stainless, and peaceful; thus he shines forth.
This is the characteristic of the *haṃsa*, consisting of both Śiva and Śakti, or the individual soul (*jīvātman*).

But in the *Prayogasāra*: "Trembling, the bristling of the body hair, bliss, purity, stability, lightness, the clarity of luminous knowledge, and the state of being a collection of the non-dual self."
Ten states arise in the yogi as indicators of accomplishment:
thereafter come knowledge of the three times, great wisdom, and mental agreeableness.
The voluntary restraint of the vital breaths, the mastery over the channels (nāḍīs),
perfection of speech, longevity, and the practice of sorcery (indrajāla).
"The transition from one body to another, the manifestation of the light of the Self, and the ten cognitive states are seen in the yogi who has attained yoga. (45–50)
The wise have declared that the *bindu* and the *sarga* consist of the nature of Puruṣa and Prakṛti, respectively. || 50 ||

From those two, there sequentially arise the Haṃsa-sounds, which conclude with the Bindu and the Sarga (visarga) respectively; they are called Puruṣa and Prakṛti, where 'haṃ' is the Puruṣa and 'saḥ' is the Prakṛti.
The *ajapā* has been described by those two; this individual soul (*jīva*) abides therein.
Considering the Person (*puruṣa*) to be its own support, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) remains eternally established [in him]. (52)

When it attains that state, then "so'ham" becomes "aham. Thereafter, having elided the letter *sa* and the letter *ha*, one should perform the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) according to the preceding form; then that becomes the *praṇava*. || 53 ||
He states the origin of the *praṇava*: "puṃ" [and so on].
"In sequence" means that from the *bindu* comes *haṃ*, and from the *visarga* comes *saḥ*.
The names "puṃ" and "prakṛti" are merely conceptual designations.
In reality, they are nothing other than the *bindu* and the *visarga*.
"Haṃ" signifies the male (*pumān*).
For this very reason, when the particle *a-* is joined at the beginning here, it results in "ahaṃ," which is the world-renowned representation of the Self.
It attends upon and propitiates [the Puruṣa].
The connection is that Nature (prakṛti), considering the Puruṣa to be its own support, remains eternally fixed upon him alone.
However, when the reading is "nityam ātmanaḥ" instead of "nityam ātmani," then the two genitive cases in "ātmanaḥ prakṛteḥ" are in apposition.

Nature (*prakṛti*) is ignorance (*avidyā*); because it fashions the individual soul (*jīva*) by way of its difference from Brahman, it is as if non-different from Him. Having gone to its own locus—which is the locus of Being—it attains that state; such is the connection [of the words]. Regarding the phrase "that state":
Due to the non-difference between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, there is the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, expressed as "I am indeed the Supreme Self.
This is its meaning;
it has been made manifest that such identity arises from the practice of the *ajapā*.

Regarding the word "lopayitvā" (having elided): the elision occurs precisely because the two consonants are considered [merely] imagined (*kalpita*). The single-substitute form (*pūrvarūpa*) is established by the rule "eṅaḥ padāntādati" (Pāṇini 6.1.109). || 50–53 ||
