The yogi should always contemplate the Praṇava, which consists of supreme bliss, is eternal, whose nature is characterized solely by the quality of consciousness, and which abides as non-different from the Self. || 54 ||
"Consisting of supreme bliss" is because of the Vedic revelation: "Bliss is the nature of Brahman, and that is established in liberation.
It is eternal, as will be shown by the very scripture cited below.
Consciousness is knowledge, and that is its single quality;
it consists of that, according to the Vedic revelation: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite.
Alternatively, consciousness is of the nature of knowledge and is one.

According to the Vedic scripture, "Brahman is one only, without a second," it [the Self] appears in the form of the imagined qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas due to its agency in the production of the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra).
It abides as non-different from the Self, because the word "I" (so'ham) arises from that [Self], and that word has the Self as its referent. || 54 ||

The virtuous, established in the Self, behold within themselves the primordial Self—the object of knowledge that lies far beyond the reach of the words of scripture—by means of the quality of self-realization; they perceive it as the singular ocean of the essence of bliss, whose nature is like a star.
Regarding the term "tradition" (āmnāya):
it refers to the first [category], based on the Vedic revelation (śruti) which states, "From whence words turn back."
"Because it has the scripture as its source.
The meaning is that it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), being knowable through the quality of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedya*).
"Bliss" (*ānanda*).
"Bliss is the form of Brahman," according to the Śruti.
It consists of the Tāraka [Om], in the manner previously described.
Yogins, established in the Self, are devoted to its contemplation through practice characterized by earnestness, continuity, and long duration. (55)
Truth, free from causes, the primordial source of the words of the Vedas, the cause of the universe, pervading all that is stationary and moving, incomparable, the consciousness residing within;
the Self whose form is the sun, fire, and moon, and who is the essence of the stars— ever-present.
The virtuous, whose senses are restrained, behold that abode of eternal bliss and auspicious qualities. ||56||
True;
for it is so according to the Vedic revelation, "Truth is knowledge.
It is free from causes.
Because it is eternal, it is not something to be produced;
or rather, it is free from those causes that are based on fallacious reasoning;
it is the primordial source of the words of the Vedas.
Because it is stated in the sūtra "śāstrayonitvāt" that [Brahman] is the author of the Veda,
or because it consists of the Praṇava,
[Brahman] is the cause of the universe.
For the Śruti says: "Indeed, from bliss alone these beings are born.
It is said to be "pervasive" because the world is of the nature of its illusory transformation (*vivarta*).
"Without compare" means by virtue of being non-dual;
consciousness is internalized.
"Direct consciousness" (pratyak-caitanya) means consciousness whose nature is the Self (ātman). "Whose body is like that of the sun, moon, and fire" means whose form is light (prakāśa-rūpa).

However, this example does not apply to the case of grasping an objective form (*ākāra*), because that [consciousness] is either formless or consists of the nature of the *praṇava*; thus, the statement "like that" [is made]. || 56 ||
That which is being measured by the sevenfold manifestations of Tāra,
which is inaccessible to the [ordinary] measures of mind, which is sought after by the crest-jewels of the Vedas,
which is the cessation of all movement through consciousness, and which is the Imperishable (Acyuta).
Devote yourselves to that supreme splendor, which is a dense ocean of nectar.
Regarding the phrase "of Tāra":
it is that which is defined by the [six] names beginning with A, U, M, Bindu, Nāda, Śakti, and Śānta; this is what is being described.
He states this very point as "inaccessible to the means of valid cognition" (mānair agamyam).
The crest-jewel of the Vedas is the Upaniṣad; that is what is to be sought, because it appears as "existence" (sattā) whose essence is being.
Consciousness (saṃvit) is illumination.
"By faith all this is real, real"—and from the Śruti: "By consciousness all this shines.
It is all-pervading, omnipresent;
it is imperishable, never-failing.
It is "unfailing" because it is of a single nature.
Due to the instruction in different sentences, there is no tautology among the words situated in the three verses. || 57 ||
They worship the Person, the size of a thumb, who is golden-hued, radiant, many-colored, the root of the three forms, and the seed of the Vedas and other scriptures.
Pure consciousness alone, situated within the solar orb.
Since it is stated in the scriptures that even the meditation on the Saguna Brahman is a cause for liberation through the gradual attainment of the world of the Saguna Brahman (Hiraṇyagarbha),
he prescribes the meditation on the Saguna Brahman for those who are incapable of meditating on the Nirguna Brahman— beginning with the words "the golden one" (hiraṇmayam).
By the phrase "the root of the three forms," his names to be practiced in meditation are indicated.
As they say: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Oṃkāra, as well as Pralaya;
Sarvavyāpin, Ananta, Tāra, Sūkṣma, and Śuklaka; Vaidyuta, Paraṃbrahma, Eka, and also Ekarudraka;
Īśāna, Bhagavān, and then Maheśvara; Mahādeva, Sadāpūrva, and Śiva—these three are the primordial ones.

The "Protected" (*rakṣita*) and the "Understood" (*avagata*) are likewise considered the "Dearest" (*priyatama*). The "Eternally Satisfied" (*nityatṛpta*), the "First" (*ādya*), and those ending with the sixteenth are proclaimed [as the remaining states].

The "First" (*ādya*) and the "Understanding" (*avagama*) are designated as the "Beloved" (*kānta*); the "Listener" (*śrotṛ*) and the "Master" (*svāmin*). Furthermore, the "Capable" (*samartha*), the "Barley-gruel" (*yāvaka*), the "Desire for Action" (*kriyecchā*), and the "Blazing" (*dīpta*).

Also, the "Attained" (*avāpta*), the "Embraced" (*āliṅgita*), the "Violent" (*hiṃsaka*), and the "Burning" (*dāhaka*). In the increase of emotion (*bhāvavṛddhi*), there is the "Quality" (*guṇa*), the "Seed" (*bīja*), the "Firm" (*dhruva*), and that which is joined with the beginning of the Vedas (*vedādirādiyuk*).
"Umādhya, mapara, trimātra, yoni, dehāśraya, saṃvāda, ātman, and sarvādika—these are the three [groups]. Thus [ends verse 58].
They meditate upon the Primordial One, who reclines upon the coils of the serpent of the Milk Ocean, accompanied by Kamalā,
his lotus-eyes blossoming like collyrium.
With his four faces, he touched the lotus at his navel. || 59 ||
The one who resides in the sacred tradition, possessing two arms, dark as a rain cloud,
with the Śrīvatsa, Kaustubha, mace, lotus, conch, and discus rising forth;
he whose abode is the lotus of the heart, the sole root of the universe— [I bow to him].
The wise do not behold the Ancient Person.
He describes another form of worship with form for the sake of gradual liberation in two verses beginning with "dhyāyanti" (they meditate).
[The Lord] whose speech is well-composed and woven by the *āmnāyas*, that is, the Vedas. (59–60)

From the Bindu arises the Nāda; when the Nāda has fully emerged, the Tāra—the cause of the universe—is the lotus-face of Reality (Tattva), surrounded by the phonemes born of the elements. It is the fourfold feet (or faces) of the Veda, the body of the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva), whose root is bliss.
May he protect you—he who is bathed by the flood of divine nectar trickling from the crescent moon upon his crown. || 61 ||
He describes the yoga of meditating on another form for the sake of gradual liberation, beginning with the word "bindoḥ" (of the point):
"The *bindu* is the self of Śiva, the form of the head of the syllable *oṃ*.
The lotus-face of reality is the lotus-face consisting of the twenty-four principles. (61)
The *piṇḍa* is Kuṇḍalinī, whose nature is Śiva;
the *pada*, however, is Haṃsa, the inner self of all.
The *rūpa* is Bandhu, possessing infinite (or gentle) luster.
The nature of bliss is the state of identity with Śiva. || 62 ||
He speaks of yoga with seed (*sabījayoga*)—beginning with the word "the body" (*piṇḍa*).
Because it consists of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*, the "body" is the *praṇava* (OM).
Kuṇḍalinī is of that same nature; she alone is the auspicious Self (*śivātman*), the inner self of all, the *haṃsa*.
Her "pada" is her station.
The infinite splendor of these two takes the form of the *bindu*.
However, in the ultimate sense, the state of aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*) of Śiva and Śivā is beyond form and is indeed formless.
Alternatively, *atīta* is the second person plural imperative of the root *i* preceded by the prefix *ati*.
O worlds, having transcended the entire universe through such meditation, *atīta* means "go" (*ātiyāta*)—that is, proceed toward the state of identity with Śiva. || 62 ||
The wise declare that the yoga of the *piṇḍa* and so forth, through its identity with Śiva, is "yoga with seed" (*sabījayoga*),
[and] absorption into Śiva, who is endowed with eternal qualities.
seedless yoga, which is independent of fruit. || 63 ||
He states that through this, liberation as union (sāyujya-mukti) occurs—[referring to] "the body" (piṇḍa), etc.
He describes liberation as similarity of form (sārūpya-mukti)—[referring to] "Śiva. ||63||
Having pierced the interior of the Suṣumṇā, the consort of the king of serpents who is the root and remains ever-awake,
she— resembling a shimmering flash of lightning— quickly reaches the assembly of the Ādhāra;
[she thus bathes] the Lord with floods of divine nectar flowing from the orb of the moon situated within the lotus of the sky.
Having honored her, one should again contemplate this Kuṇḍalinī as she has returned to her own abode.

Now, he describes the method of Rājayoga and other practices, which consists of meditating upon the Kuṇḍalinī that is accessible solely through one's own direct experience, beginning with the word "mūlāt":
from the root, that is, from the Mūlādhāra;
"unnidrā" means awakened or manifest.
Because Kuṇḍalī has the form of a serpent, she is designated as the queen of the kings of serpents.
She moves swiftly through the interior of the Suṣumnā,
passing through the collection of supports (ādhāra) consisting of Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūraka, Anāhata, Viśuddha, and Ājñā.
"Upon the lotus of the sky" means upon Śiva, the lord of the thousand-petaled [lotus].
"One's own home" means the *mūlādhāra*. || 64 ||
Having grasped by the hand that Swan— who is eternal, infinite, and possessed of imperishable qualities— the Śakti Kuṇḍalinī, who has emerged from her own support and is the mother of all beings,
she went to the abode of Śambhu; and having herself experienced the supreme bliss with him, [she remained there].
Resplendent with the brilliance of ten million suns, she returns to her own abode; thus should she, the enchantress of the world, be meditated upon. || 65 ||
The connection is that one should grasp that *jīva*, which is being recited as the *haṃsa*, in the hand.
And how the *jīva* recites has already been explained in the introduction to the *haṃsa* mantra itself.
Its own support is the *mūlādhāra*.
Taking "haṃsa" from the preceding verse, the specific instruction is "go. || 65 ||
Having led the unmanifest *parabindu* of accumulated luster to the abode of Śiva,
the Kuṇḍalinī-śakti— whose body consists of the three *guṇas* and who resembles a flash of lightning—
[reaches] this city situated in the midst of the nectar of bliss, possessing the splendor of ten million moons and suns.
Having gazed [upon him], the Blessed Lady returned to her own city; she is to be meditated upon, not perceived through qualities.
"Having led the unmanifest supreme bindu"—this is the distinction from what precedes. One's own city is the *mūlādhāra*. || 66 ||
In the midst of the two winds colliding and agitating one another,

transcending the mass of sounds, we worship Her who arises within the light resplendent with the brilliance of ten million flashes of lightning— She who is as crimson as fresh aloe-wood and the twilight.
The supreme deity, consisting of the nectar of intense bliss, who has attained the state of Paraśiva.

Regarding the phrase "by the two winds": the meaning is that through the restraint of the *apāna* wind and the restraint of the *prāṇa* wind, there occurs a mutual friction between those two as they move upward and downward respectively.
Herein, the specific distinction consists precisely in the transcending of sound produced by the friction of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, as well as the meditation on the slightly red [light].

As it has been said: "In meditation on the white [form], there is the play of speech; in the reddish [form], subjugation occurs. Also elsewhere: "One should meditate on her as having the luster of a hibiscus flower for subjugation and attraction, as white for pacification, and as yellow for immobilization."
One should visualize her as dark-complexioned for liberation, black-colored for killing, and with a smoky luster for causing hatred and expulsion.
Thus, these and other incidental fruits should also be understood. || 67 ||
In going and coming,
that Kundalī, who is like a swift-footed courser, brings about the fruits of yoga; this Muditā is the wish-fulfilling cow of the Kula.
She is the wish-fulfilling creeper for those who worship her. || 68 ||
Regarding "going":
here, the distinction is that in matters of going and coming, it is "pertaining to the legs" (*jāṅghikī*). || 68 ||

Having duly sprinkled the six lotuses with showers of falling supreme nectar that bestow awakening— [the power] which resides in the *bindu* situated in the *ādhāra*, resembling the awn of wild rice, and consisting of eternal bliss— [one should worship her] arisen in the middle of the bow.
One should meditate upon the deity, who is composed of pure consciousness and possesses the radiant luster of the Bandhujīva flower. ||69||
"Support" (ādhāra): the support is the *mūlādhāra*-cakra.
The power (*śakti*) situated there is the triangle; its central location is the point (*bindu*), and she resides therein.

Alternatively, the power (śakti) that resides in the support, namely the triangle, and the seed-syllable of desire (kāmabīja) situated therein, is also indeed a seed-syllable of power. The meaning is "dwelling in its head," which is the bindu.
As they say: "Resembling ten million flashes of lightning, with a luster that surpasses the brilliance of the fire of time by its own radiance..."

One should meditate upon Kāma, who is endowed with a radiance resembling a mass of rays from a thousand suns; who throbs within the womb; who possesses the brilliant luster of a blossoming, deep-red bandhūka flower; and whose head is adorned with ten million beautiful moons.
"Above that is the flame of fire, radiant with the luster of a mass of creepers of long-lasting light;
it is subtle, situated in the space within the path of Brahman, and is the digit consisting of pure consciousness. Thus [it is said].
"The middle of the bow" refers to the middle of the eyebrows, the *ājñācakra*.
Regarding that which has arisen:
here, this alone is the distinction. || 69 ||
The sun of the heart-lotus, residing in the orb [of the heart], she who rivals the flash of lightning,
with her splendor as red as the rising sun, she who outshines the darkness known as Nāda—
the eternal state consisting of pure consciousness, curved like a half-moon.
One of pure intellect should meditate upon that all-pervading Lord, the embodiment of splendors, who moves in the form of the imperishable syllable.
The word *matsara* has a similar meaning [to *matsya*].
The syntactical connection is: "scorning the darkness with a splendor as red as the rising sun.
Herein, the specific distinction is that the departure toward the Lord from the very heart constitutes the visualization (*varṇamayadhyāna*).
And this is because, according to their view, there are distinct *kuṇḍalīs* for each wheel (*cakra*), since they accept a hexad of *kuṇḍalīs*. (70)
On her forehead, she who resembles the full moon, sprinkling this god with nectar through the brilliance of her frost-like pearl-strings, and delighting him with her immeasurable body;
she who, having attained the form of his own body, stands pervading the universe as the mother of all letters.
One should meditate with a perfectly composed and undisturbed mind upon Ambikā, who consists of pure consciousness.
Regarding the term *bhāla*:
here, the distinction is that it denotes both command (*ājñā*) and the state of being the originator of the phonemes (*varṇotpādakatva*), as stated by Śiva.
Thus it has been said:

"The wise say that the Svayambhū-liṅga is within the central cavity of one's own source (the vulva), while the one called Bāṇa is within the heart-lotus; another is in the intermediate space, and yet another is in the lotus of the sky. Thus [it is said]. (71)
At the root, on the forehead, and in the heart, the Great Goddess Savitri shines with a radiant form; her waist is bent by the weight of her full and lofty breasts,
and her limbs are thoroughly drenched in the flowing nectar from every wheel [of her body].
May the primordial goddess of speech grant you complete and perfect prosperity.

He describes the union with Śiva at the three locations, beginning with "in the root": having gone from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *ājñā*, there is a specific cessation [of movement] from that point. || 72 ||
Emerging from her own abode with graceful charms, casting beautiful smiles upon the lotuses at every step along the path,
that goddess, adorned with earrings, possesses the splendor of the most youthful sun.
One should illuminate one's own splendor with the nectars of the abode of Śiva.
Arisen through practices such as the binding of the base (*ādhārabandha*),
the *kuṇḍalinī* honors the auspicious seed-syllable of the three abodes with nectars.
May the consort of Śiva bestow auspiciousness upon you. || 74 ||
Her face is adorned with a crescent moon and resembles a mass of vermilion,
beautified by three eyes full of bliss; her body,
the very essence of the god of love, is bent low by her full and lofty breasts.
May the wife of Śambhu bestow immeasurable prosperity.
Henceforth, speaking of specific meditations on Kuṇḍalinī for the sake of strengthening latent impressions (vāsanā), he utters a hymn beginning with "nijabhavana" (in her own abode).
Due to the contraction of the apāna wind, there is the ādhāra-bandha;
likewise, even in the restraint of the prāṇa wind, that which is denoted by the word "pramukha" occurs.
The *Anaṅgatantra* is that in which the bodiless one (Kāmadeva) is preeminent. || 73–75 ||
Her lotus-eyes are long, adorning the quarters of the sky; her lotus-feet are rubbed by the tips of the crowns of millions of prostrate gods;
she bears the crescent of the young moon and a circle of pot-like breasts.
May the consort of the Lord of Umā, possessing the luster of a bandhūka flower, flash forth within my heart. || 76 ||
Regarding "long and not long":
the length is due to the side-glance, while the lack of length is due to its contraction.
"Vinatamarutām" refers to the Vinata gods.
By the tips of the crests, that is, by the upper parts of the crowns. || 76 ||

These six wheels, situated within the body, are composed of the letters starting with 'A' and ending with 'KṢa', divided by the number of eyes (two), multiplied by the six directions (six), and further increased by the oceans (four). They are surrounded respectively by the vowels beginning with 'Ā' and the consonants beginning with 'Sa'.
They are inhabited by Ḍākinī and the other goddesses, and are well-known as being presided over by Brahmā and the other deities.
May the Supreme Deity, shattering [all obstacles], bestow joy upon the minds of the three worlds. || 77 ||
He describes the meditation on Kuṇḍalinī according to the sequence of the internal alphabet (antarmātṛkā) with the words "by the letters" (*varṇaiḥ*).
The oceans are four; the directions are ten; the suns are twelve; the digits are sixteen; and the eyes are two.
By the phrase "beginning with *sa*" (*sādibhiḥ*), the reverse order is indicated.

Regarding the term "by the first" (*ādyaiḥ*): its status as "first" is due to its abiding in the *mūlādhāra*. Alternatively, it may mean "together with the first," namely with the letters beginning with *sa* and ending with *ka*. The construction is: "with the sixteen vowels joined by *ha* and *kṣa*."

Regarding this, some maintain that the term "by the first" (*ādyaiḥ*) is used for the sake of distinction, because [the vowels] beginning with *a* are situated in the Viśuddha-cakra in their regular order. Alternatively, while *a* is the first in other contexts, here, due to the reverse order, *sa* is the first; thus it is said "by the first."
In the two petals, the term *kṣaha* is used for the sake of the reverse order;
they are those inhabited by the *ḍākinīs* and so forth—
namely, by *Ḍākinī*, *Rākinī*, *Lākinī*, *Kākinī*, *Śākinī*, and *Hākinī*.

[The Lord] pierces those situated within the six cakras, who are surrounded by deities beginning with Brahmā; the stability [of the hierarchy] starting from Brahmā has been explained in the Fourth Chapter (the Dīkṣāpaṭala). Such is the connection.
As it has been said:

"The Ādhāra [cakra] has four petals, possesses a reddish luster, and is the locus of the final letter of the vowels; Svādhiṣṭhāna resembles a great flash of lightning and has six petals ending with the letter 'ba'."
The Maṇipūraka is reddish in appearance and has ten petals, beginning with the letter Ḍa and ending with Pha; the Anāhata city is golden with twelve petals, endowed with the letters ending in Ka.
The city of the Ājñā [cakra] is a pure lotus with sixteen petals, endowed with a brilliant luster, possessing the two syllables *ha* and *kṣa* on its two pairs of petals, and shining like a jewel.
Above that is a thousand-petaled lotus, blossoming and facing downward.
"I worship the state of Śiva, which consists of eternal bliss, the source of power, pure and rosy-red.

Elsewhere, however: "This Mūlādhāra is the abode of Brahman, shining like gold; Ḍākinī is the presiding deity here. Svādhiṣṭhāna is declared to be the dwelling of Viṣṇu, shining like the rising sun; Rākiṇī is the presiding deity here."
Maṇipūraka is blue, the abode of Rudra, where the deity is Lākinī; Anāhata is red, the house of Īśvara, and Śākinī is said to be here as well.

"This is the pure abode of Sadāśiva; here also is Kākinī, who is smoke-colored. Ājñāpura is as lovely as the autumnal moon; here Hākinī is said to dwell; this is the house of Śiva. Thus it is said. In the *Adhyātmaviveka*, the fruit resulting from the movement of the individual soul (*jīva*) through each of these petals is stated:
Between the anus and the genitals is the four-petalled wheel, the *ādhāra*.
Therein reside the [four joys]: the supreme (*parama*), the innate (*sahaja*), the bliss (*ānanda*) preceded by the hero (*vīra*), and so forth.
And Yogānanda shall be his fruit in the petals starting from Īśāna;
Svādhiṣṭhāna, however, is at the base of the *liṅga* and has six petals according to the sequence.
They say that in the petals starting from the east, these fruits occur in sequence:
humility, cruelty, pride, destruction, and after that, fainting.
Contempt and lack of trust certainly arise for the wandering *jīva* [at this stage].
In the navel is the ten-petaled wheel known as *maṇipūraka*.
In this context, deep sleep is thirst; likewise, envy, backbiting, shame, fear, disgust, delusion, passion, and despondency [are the afflictions].
In the heart is the Anāhata-cakra, endowed with twelve petals;
[the qualities associated with it are] fickleness, destruction of desire, deceit, deliberation, and remorse.
Hope, illumination, anxiety, exertion, and possessiveness arise; then, in sequence, hypocrisy, agitation, discernment, and likewise egoism.
These fruits are said to belong to the Self situated in the petals starting from the east;
at the throat is the location of Bhāratī, the Viśuddhi [cakra] with sixteen petals.
In that regard, the Praṇava, Udgītha, Huṃ, Phaṭ, Vaṣaṭ, Svadhā, as well as Svāhā, Namaḥ, and Amṛta—these are the seven; and the six notes beginning with Ṣaḍja are the poison.
Thus, the sixteen fruits situated on the petals starting from the east [are assigned] to the self. Thus [ends verse 77].
She whose body is adorned by the qualities of the support (*ādhāra*), who swiftly pierces the three *liṅgas*,
who is preeminent through the awakening of the dense bliss of pure consciousness, and who [is nourished] by the nectar flowing from the moon of the agitated *dhruvamaṇḍala*— the lotuses...
One should meditate upon the auspicious Śivā, who resembles a stream of blossoming lotuses and possesses the form of intense lightning.

Regarding the phrase "from the support" (ādhārāt): the nature of the support is a circular orb with a triangular pericarp; from that [arises] the circle of qualities (guṇavṛtta), which consists of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
(Regarding the term *liṅgatrayam*, variant readings such as *nirgacchantīm* and *nirgatvarīm* are seen in some places. || 78 ||

The crest-jewel of bliss, eternally sought by the crowns of the Vedas, adorned with the crescent moon, presiding over all worlds, and intent on shattering the distress of his devotees— this is the supreme state of the Lord.
One will certainly bestow auspicious forms upon Ambikā. || 79 ||
I take refuge in the left half of the Great Lord, whose anklets tinkle sweetly like the song of Mañjuśrī, who is the root of the world and the very root of all speech. (80)
Resplendent with the hue of a massive sapphire, bowed by the weight of her breasts,
her beauty enhanced by a multitude of shining, exquisite ornaments—
she who is the sole root of the universe and is constantly sought after by the crest-jewels of the Vedas.
We take refuge in the unbroken head of Maheśvara. || 81 ||
Having dissolved the five causal elements into the void—which is devoid of space, time, and the like; which is the supreme Śiva consisting of pure consciousness;
and which is without support—one should settle the self within it with an unwavering mind, having withdrawn all the senses.
The yogi attains the fruit of yoga, which is easily accessible, eternally manifest, and actionless.
"Digiti" means from the perspective of space and time;
by the word "ādi" (and so forth), it is meant that [the object] is also unlimited in terms of its own nature.
"Kāraṇapañcakasya" refers to the pentad of causes: the material cause, the inherent cause, the instrumental cause, the efficient cause, and the auxiliary cause.
Although the logicians maintain that there are only three causes— since the instigating cause (*prayojaka*) and the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri*) are included within the efficient cause (*nimitta*)—
nevertheless, this presentation of five causes is made by relying on slight distinctions.
Alternatively, the five causes are the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) which serve as the material causes for the five gross elements (*bhūta*).
As it is said in the Mahākapilapañcarātra:
"Having abandoned the five measures (mātrās) and then the five causes,
and having made the divine the cause, one should unite [the self] with the supreme state."
Therefore, in that which is empty, formless, without support, and devoid of a basis, one [should perceive] oneself— the individual soul (jīvātman).
Having established the fruit of yoga with an unwavering mind, he proceeds. || 82 ||
I bow to that Mahābala,
who is cooled by the embrace of the creeper of consciousness (saṃvit),
and by whom the ripe fruit of liberation has been swallowed.
[This was said] to those who had taken refuge in the branches of the traditional scriptures (māmnāya).
Therefore, there arose the preeminent elephant among all teachers,
whose nature was to delight in sporting within the ocean of the six duties;
he whose name, "Victory," spread throughout the three worlds—
The virtuous proclaim him as "the learned teacher. || 84 ||
His son was Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose power was fully manifested and who became a teacher of teachers;
through the sprinkling of the nectar of compassion from whose feet—
Having achieved their purpose, they attain supreme prosperity.
To that master Ācārya Vidyāvibhava was born the lord Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra,
who [excelled] in all branches of learning and in every art.
He who attained great renown even while sleeping. || 86 ||
The author describes his own lineage [beginning] with Mahābala.
Mahābala was the ancestor of the author;
his son was Ācāryapaṇḍita; his son was Śrīkṛṣṇa. (83–86)
Having extracted the entire essence from all the scriptures,
that wise one composed this tantra named the *Śrīśāradātilaka* in chapters equal in number to the principles (*tattva*).
For the sake of bestowing joy upon the learned for a long time. || 87 ||
By "the number of principles" (tattvasaṃkhyaiḥ), it means by the number twenty-five.

Herein, the first chapter is devoted to the exposition of the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) by way of establishing the process of emanation (sṛṣṭi). The twenty-three intermediate chapters, however, are devoted to the exposition of both nature (prakṛti) and its transformations (vikṛti).

The final chapter, however, is devoted to establishing the Puruṣa as distinct from both Prakṛti and Vikṛti. Thus, it is stated that this treatise consists of twenty-five principles (tattvas). || 87 ||

I bow to the body of Śambhu, which is without beginning or end; with half of his own form, he eternally creates the world-form. Even the most exalted speech is meaningful when it concerns her, the wife of Śaṅkara, who is bowed by the weight of her breasts—the very essence of word and meaning.
May she be for prosperity; may she be the pacifier of the flood of sufferings born of worldly existence. || 88 ||
Bestower of happiness, giver of fortune, she who forms half the body of Śaṅkara—may Pārvatī be forever pleased with us by this offering of flowers from the book. 89.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the Śāradātilaka composed by the illustrious Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra. 25.

Concluding the meaning of the entire Tantra by stating that the Supreme Deity alone is to be meditated upon, he performs an auspicious benediction with the words beginning with *anādi*: "May [the Goddess] who is without beginning...
It is said: "Treatises that begin with an auspicious word, have an auspicious word in the middle, and end with an auspicious word, flourish."
"They are the manly efforts of heroes and the manly efforts that prolong life," according to the statement of the Blessed Patañjali. May there be auspiciousness. 88–89.
This Padārthādarśa is completed.

In the southern region of Mahārāṣṭra, there was a city known as Janasthāna, situated on the shimmering banks of the Godāvarī and teeming with people. There, accompanied by the daughter of Janaka and Lakṣmaṇa, [the Lord dwelt].
In ancient times, Rāma dwelt in this place with a deeply contented mind.
In that city, in a great, pure, and renowned family of the most excellent Brahmins,
there was the noble Śrī Bhaṭṭarāmeśvara.
By his virtues, he became a lion to the great elephants of disputants.
From him was born the one named Śrī Bhaṭṭa Pṛthvīdhara, whose intellect was as sharp as the point of a blade of kuśa grass;
this follower of the Bhaṭṭa school taught [the scriptures] in many ways.
The Vedānta scripture, such as that spoken by the Serpent [Patañjali], etc. || 3 ||
I suspect that it was out of fear of him alone that the preeminent teacher of the gods took up residence in heaven, and that Śeṣa immediately entered the depths of the netherworld for fear of defeat;
as for others, what news can there be of them, those whose armor is merely feigned and who are fickle? Enough with them!
Indeed, it is not possible to describe his complete power even with a hundred mouths.
After some days, this man of exceedingly pure conduct arrived at Vārāṇasī, the royal capital of Śiva;
there he took up residence, following in the footsteps of that [sage].
The wise man, having reflected upon the body's end as his limit... || 5 ||
Therefore, this Rāghavabhaṭṭa arose, renowned as a master of Vedānta and Sāṃkhya, a preeminent authority in the system of Bhaṭṭa, a treasury of all mathematics, a jewel-mine of literature,
a storehouse of Āyurveda, skilled in the arts, and a teacher in the treatises on love and worldly prosperity.
He was always skilled in music and had reached the further shore of the treasure of the True Path. || 6 ||
O Śrī Durgā, O Gaṇanāyaka, O Guru of the planets, O Govinda, O Lord of Gaurī— this person,
with head bowed and palms joined in reverence, entreats you all.
Should there be any lapse here in the discernment of mantras, worship, and so forth, due to delusion, [may it be forgiven].
May that which has occurred occasionally from me, whose heart is permeated by devotion, be forgiven as I am but a servant. || 7 ||

For the benefit of the world, Rāghava, with his exceedingly hot and sharp intellect, revealed this treatise on mantras— a treasure of hidden meaning— just as one might reveal a supreme hoard by means of the ointment of traditional lineage.
O virtuous ones, quickly grant your satisfaction in this work, having tasted the fulfillment of each of your own desires.
Abandon your own wickedness through the thought of what is beneficial; otherwise, you will find no attainment of your goals.
A slanderous person is inwardly impure, with a mind averse to rejoicing in the virtues of others;
yet my mind does not despair regarding him, for he has desisted from doing harm.
Some expounders are like scribes; others, the listeners, are for the most part like the mute; still others are like parrots, uttering only the chatter of the virtuous;
while those who are truly learned are solely experts in unraveling the knots of the text.
Only two or three are wise enough to understand what has been said there; yet even among them, only five or six truly comprehend it. || 10 ||
In the year named Raudra, measured by the sky (0), arrows (5), and earth (1)— that is, 1500—
during the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, on the solar lunar day (the seventh) joined with the asterism Siddha,
this beautiful and lucid [commentary] was composed for this Tantra by the wise Śrī Rāghava.
This *Ṭīkā*, titled *Sadgurusampradāyavimalā*, was composed in Viśveśapurī. || 11 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the *Padārthādarśa*, a commentary on the *Śāradātilaka* composed by Śrī Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which follows the authentic tradition. 25.
